Clinically, it may mimic gynecological malignancies, necessitating careful diagnostic evaluation.

Genitourinary tuberculosis, unspecified, refers to tuberculosis affecting the urinary or genital tract without a specific site identified. It is caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. Common synonyms include urogenital tuberculosis and tuberculosis of the genitourinary system. The condition typically involves the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and genital organs. Symptoms may include flank pain, hematuria, and genital ulcers. It often presents with extrapulmonary tuberculosis and can lead to complications such as infertility or renal failure if untreated. Diagnosis usually requires imaging, culture, or nucleic acid amplification testing.

code_desc: tuberculosis of skin and subcutaneous cellular tissue
summary: Tuberculosis of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, also known as cutaneous tuberculosis, is a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It presents as painless, slowly progressive nodules or ulcers, often on the face, neck, or extremities. Common synonyms include lupus vulgaris and scrofuloderma. The infection spreads via hematogenous dissemination from a primary tuberculosis focus. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with untreated pulmonary tuberculosis. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, biopsy, and acid-fast staining. Treatment typically requires long-term antitubercular therapy.

code_desc: erythema nodosum with hypersensitivity reaction in tuberculosis
summary: Erythema nodosum with hypersensitivity reaction in tuberculosis is a cutaneous manifestation of tuberculosis, typically presenting as tender, red, painful nodules on the shins. It results from a Type III hypersensitivity reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens. Common synonyms include tuberculous erythema nodosum and reactive erythema nodosum. The condition is often associated with pulmonary tuberculosis and may occur in the presence of active or latent infection. Other causative agents are rare but may include other mycobacteria or infections. The lower extremities, particularly the shins, are most commonly affected, though involvement can occur elsewhere.

Tuberculosis of peripheral lymph nodes, also known as scrofula or lymph node tuberculosis, is a form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects cervical lymph nodes but can involve other peripheral groups. The infection leads to granulomatous inflammation, caseous necrosis, and formation of cold abscesses. Common synonyms include scrofula and tuberculous lymphadenitis. Clinically, it presents with painless, firm, and mobile lymphadenopathy, often accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever and weight loss. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis.

Tuberculosis of the eye, also known as ocular tuberculosis or uveitis tuberculosis, is a rare form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the uveal tract, leading to anterior or posterior uveitis. Other involved structures may include the retina, choroid, and optic nerve. Symptoms often include redness, pain, blurred vision, and photophobia. The condition may present as a chronic, slowly progressive disease, sometimes mimicking other inflammatory eye disorders. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, imaging, and microbiological testing. Treatment usually requires long-term antitubercular therapy.

Tuberculosis of the ear, also known as otitic tuberculosis or tuberculous otitis, is a rare form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the middle ear and mastoid process, leading to chronic suppurative otitis media. The disease may spread to adjacent structures such as the temporal bone, cranial nerves, or intracranial regions. Common symptoms include ear discharge, hearing loss, and facial nerve palsy. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. Early diagnosis and multidrug therapy are essential to prevent complications.

Tuberculosis of the thyroid gland, also known as tuberculous thyroiditis or scrofula of the thyroid, is a rare form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the thyroid in individuals with underlying immunosuppression or active pulmonary tuberculosis. The disease presents as a painless, slowly growing mass in the anterior neck, often accompanied by lymphadenopathy. Histopathologically, caseating granulomas are characteristic. It is more common in endemic regions and may mimic thyroid cancer, necessitating careful diagnostic evaluation.

Tuberculosis of the adrenal glands, also known as adrenal tuberculosis or tuberculous adrenalitis, is a rare extrapulmonary form of tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the adrenal cortex, leading to granulomatous inflammation and possible adrenal insufficiency. The condition often presents as a solitary or bilateral lesion, and may be associated with systemic tuberculosis. Common synonyms include adrenal tubercle and tuberculous adrenal disease. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and may occur as part of disseminated tuberculosis.

Tuberculosis of the spleen is a rare extrapulmonary form of tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically presents as a solitary or multiple nodular lesion within the spleen, often asymptomatic but may cause splenomegaly or constitutional symptoms. Common synonyms include splenic tuberculosis and splenic TB. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated TB. While the spleen is the primary site, involvement of other organs such as the liver, lymph nodes, and bones may occur. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and histopathological examination.

Tuberculosis of the esophagus is a rare extrapulmonary form of tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically presents with chronic symptoms such as dysphagia, odynophagia, and weight loss. The infection leads to granulomatous inflammation and stricturing of the esophageal wall. Common synonyms include esophageal tuberculosis or tuberculous esophagitis. The condition most commonly affects the middle and lower thirds of the esophagus, though any segment may be involved. Complications may include perforation, stricture, and fistula formation. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic biopsy and acid-fast bacilli staining or culture.

Tuberculosis of other specified organs refers to tuberculosis affecting body parts not typically included in pulmonary or extrapulmonary classifications, such as the central nervous system, bones, or joints. It is caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and less commonly by other mycobacteria. Common synonyms include tuberculous meningitis, tuberculous osteomyelitis, and tuberculous spondylitis. The condition often presents with systemic symptoms and localized signs depending on the affected organ. Diagnosis typically involves imaging, microbiological testing, and clinical evaluation. Treatment follows standard anti-tuberculosis therapy.

Acute miliary tuberculosis is a severe form of tuberculosis characterized by widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis throughout the body. It presents as numerous small, millet seed-like granulomas in various organs, most commonly the lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Caused by hematogenous spread from a primary infection, it often results from immune suppression. Synonyms include miliary TB and disseminated tuberculosis. The condition is associated with fever, weight loss, and respiratory symptoms, and may progress rapidly without prompt treatment.

code_desc: tuberculosis of Other specified miliary tuberculosis
summary: Tuberculosis of other specified miliary tuberculosis refers to a disseminated form of tuberculosis characterized by the presence of numerous small, millet seed-like granulomas in multiple organs. It is caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and less commonly by other mycobacterial species. The condition typically affects the lungs, lymph nodes, and other organs such as the liver, spleen, and brain. Common synonyms include miliary TB and disseminated tuberculosis. It often occurs in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to severe systemic illness.

Miliary tuberculosis is a severe form of tuberculosis characterized by widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis through the bloodstream, leading to the formation of small, millet-seed-like nodules in various organs. Common synonyms include disseminated tuberculosis and hematogenous tuberculosis. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It typically affects the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lymph nodes, often presenting with systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and night sweats. The condition is more common in immunocompromised individuals.

Bubonic plague is an acute infectious disease caused by *Yersinia pestis*, transmitted primarily through the bite of infected fleas. It is characterized by the formation of painful, swollen lymph nodes, known as buboes, typically in the groin, axilla, or neck. Common synonyms include black death and pneumonic plague (when involving the lungs). The disease can progress to septicemia or pneumonia if untreated. It is endemic in certain regions and poses a significant public health risk due to its high mortality rate without prompt antibiotic treatment.

Cellulocutaneous plague, also known as cutaneous plague or localized plague, is a severe skin infection caused by *Yersinia pestis*. It typically presents as a rapidly expanding, painful, necrotic lesion at the site of bacterial entry, often following a flea bite. Common synonyms include bubonic plague and primary plague. The infection primarily affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues, with the lymph nodes draining the affected area often becoming swollen and tender. It is most commonly seen in regions where *Yersinia pestis* is endemic. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are crucial to prevent progression to more severe forms of plague.

Septicemic plague is a severe and often fatal form of plague caused by *Yersinia pestis*. It occurs when the bacteria enter the bloodstream, leading to systemic infection and widespread tissue damage. Common synonyms include bloodstream plague and malignant plague. The condition primarily affects the circulatory system and can involve multiple organs. Symptoms include high fever, extreme weakness, shock, and bleeding. It is typically transmitted through flea bites or direct contact with infected animals. Without prompt treatment, septicemic plague can progress rapidly and result in death.

Primary pneumonic plague is a severe and rapidly progressive form of plague caused by *Yersinia pestis*. It affects the lungs and is transmitted through inhalation of infectious aerosolized droplets. Common synonyms include inhalational plague and pulmonary plague. The disease presents with high fever, cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis, often leading to respiratory failure and death if untreated. It is the most lethal form of plague, with a high mortality rate without prompt antibiotic therapy. The lungs are the primary affected organ, and the infection can progress to systemic involvement.

Secondary pneumonic plague is a severe form of plague characterized by the inhalation of *Yersinia pestis* bacteria from the respiratory secretions of an infected person. It typically develops as a complication of primary pneumonic plague or from exposure to infected animals. Common synonyms include inhalational plague and pneumonic plague. The causative agent is *Yersinia pestis*, and the disease primarily affects the lungs and respiratory tract, leading to rapid progression, severe pneumonia, and high mortality if untreated.

Pneumonic plague is a severe and often fatal form of plague caused by *Yersinia pestis*. It affects the lungs and is characterized by rapid onset of fever, cough, chest pain, and respiratory distress. Unlike other plague forms, it is transmitted directly from person to person via airborne droplets. Common synonyms include pulmonary plague and inhalational plague. The disease primarily targets the respiratory system, leading to pneumonia and acute respiratory failure if untreated. Early antibiotic intervention is critical for survival.

"Other specified types of plague" refers to clinical presentations of plague that do not fit the classic categories of bubonic, septicemic, or pneumonic plague. It encompasses atypical or rare forms, often with overlapping features. Caused by *Yersinia pestis*, these cases may present with localized lymphadenopathy, systemic symptoms, or mixed manifestations. Common synonyms include "atypical plague" or "unclassified plague." Typically affects lymph nodes, lungs, and bloodstream, depending on the variant. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and epidemiological context.

Plague, unspecified, is a severe infectious disease caused by *Yersinia pestis*. It is characterized by sudden onset of fever, chills, headache, and lymphadenopathy, often leading to systemic infection. Common synonyms include bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic plague. The disease primarily affects the lymphatic system, lungs, and bloodstream. It is transmitted through flea bites, direct contact with infected animals, or inhalation of respiratory droplets. Without prompt treatment, it can be fatal. The unspecified category includes cases where the specific form of plague is not clearly identified.

Ulceroglandular tularemia is a severe bacterial infection caused by *Francisella tularensis*. It presents with a characteristic ulcer at the site of infection, often on the skin, and regional lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include glanders and rabbit fever. The disease typically affects the skin, lymph nodes, and occasionally the eyes or respiratory tract. It is transmitted through bite wounds, inhalation, or contact with infected animals. Symptoms include fever, chills, malaise, and localized pain. Prompt antibiotic treatment is essential to prevent complications.

Enteric tularemia is a systemic infection caused by *Francisella tularensis*, primarily affecting the gastrointestinal tract. It is a rare variant of tularemia, often resulting from ingestion of contaminated food or water. Common synonyms include gastrointestinal tularemia or typhoidal tularemia. The causative agent is *F. tularensis* subspecies *tularensis* or *holarctica*. The infection typically affects the intestines, liver, and spleen, and may present with fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Systemic involvement can lead to sepsis if untreated.

Pulmonary tularemia is a severe respiratory infection caused by *Francisella tularensis*, a gram-negative coccobacillus. It typically results from inhalation of aerosolized bacteria, often following exposure to infected animals. Common synonyms include ulceroglandular tularemia and pneumonic tularemia. The infection primarily affects the lungs, leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. It may also involve the lymph nodes, causing regional lymphadenopathy. Without prompt treatment, it can progress to severe pneumonia or systemic complications. The disease is highly contagious and requires immediate antibiotic intervention.

Oculoglandular tularemia is a form of tularemia characterized by conjunctival inflammation and preauricular lymphadenopathy. It is caused by *Francisella tularensis*, the same bacterium responsible for systemic tularemia. The infection typically presents with redness, swelling, and discharge in the eye, often following contact with infected animals or contaminated materials. Common synonyms include oculoglandular infection and preauricular tularemia. The primary affected areas are the conjunctiva and regional lymph nodes, particularly those near the ear. It is a rare but potentially severe condition requiring prompt antibiotic treatment.

"Other specified tularemia" refers to cases of tularemia that do not meet the criteria for the more common forms, such as ulceroglandular or glandular tularemia. It is caused by *Francisella tularensis*, the same pathogen responsible for typical tularemia. This variant may present with atypical clinical features. Common synonyms include unspecified or other forms of tularemia. It typically affects the respiratory system, skin, or lymph nodes, though manifestations can vary. The condition is rare and often diagnosed in immunocompromised individuals or those exposed to infected animals.

Unspecified tularemia refers to a systemic infection caused by *Francisella tularensis*, a gram-negative coccobacillus. It is a zoonotic disease with various clinical presentations, including ulceroglandular, glandular, oculoglandular, and pneumonic forms. Common synonyms include rabbit fever and tularexia. The infection typically affects the lymph nodes, skin, eyes, and lungs, depending on the route of exposure. It is often associated with contact with infected animals or arthropod bites. Diagnosis is confirmed through microbiological testing or serology. The condition is rare but can be severe, with potential for systemic spread if untreated.

Cutaneous anthrax is a severe bacterial infection caused by *Bacillus anthracis*, primarily affecting the skin. It typically presents as a painless, black eschar at the site of entry following exposure to infected animals or contaminated materials. Common synonyms include malignant edema and woolsorter's disease. The infection usually occurs on the face, neck, and hands, and can progress to systemic involvement if untreated. It is characterized by an initial papule that evolves into a vesicle, then a necrotic ulcer with a central eschar. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical to prevent complications.

Pulmonary anthrax is a severe, often fatal form of anthrax caused by *Bacillus anthracis*. It results from inhalation of spores, leading to acute respiratory distress and systemic infection. Common synonyms include inhalational anthrax and pulmonary infection with *B. anthracis*. The disease primarily affects the lungs, progressing to hemorrhagic pneumonia and septicemia. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and cyanosis. Rapid progression and high mortality rate necessitate early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics.

Gastrointestinal anthrax is a severe, often fatal infection caused by *Bacillus anthracis*, primarily affecting the gastrointestinal tract. It typically occurs in individuals exposed to infected animal products, such as meat or hides. Common synonyms include intestinal anthrax and edematous plague. The disease presents with symptoms like abdominal pain, vomiting, and hematemesis, often progressing to sepsis. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the esophagus, stomach, and large intestine may also be involved. Without prompt treatment with antibiotics, the mortality rate is high.

Anthrax septicemia is a severe, often fatal systemic infection caused by *Bacillus anthracis*. It typically affects individuals exposed to infected animal products, such as through cuts or inhalation. The disease progresses rapidly, leading to septic shock and multi-organ failure. Common synonyms include malignant pustule and woolsorter's disease. The bacteria produce toxins that cause widespread tissue damage and coagulopathy. Inhalation is the most lethal route, primarily affecting the lungs, while cutaneous and gastrointestinal forms may occur. Early diagnosis and aggressive antibiotic therapy are critical for survival.

Other specified manifestations of anthrax refer to less common or atypical forms of the disease caused by *Bacillus anthracis*. These presentations may involve unusual sites or clinical features not fitting the classic cutaneous, inhalational, or gastrointestinal forms. Synonyms include rare or variant anthrax. The bacterium produces toxins and exotoxins that lead to systemic inflammation and tissue necrosis. While the skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are typically affected, other specified manifestations may involve the eyes, central nervous system, or other organs, often presenting with severe systemic illness and high mortality if untreated.

Anthrax, unspecified, is an acute infectious disease caused by *Bacillus anthracis*. It is characterized by systemic infection following exposure to the bacterium, often through inhalation, ingestion, or skin contact. Common synonyms include glanders and charbon, though these refer to related but distinct conditions. The disease typically affects the skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract, with varying clinical presentations. Without prompt treatment, it can lead to severe systemic illness and high mortality. The causative agent, *Bacillus anthracis*, forms spores that can persist in the environment for long periods.

*Brucella melitensis* is the most virulent species of the *Brucella* genus, causing brucellosis, a zoonotic bacterial infection. Common synonyms include undulant fever and Malta fever. It is primarily transmitted through ingestion of contaminated dairy products or direct contact with infected animals. The causative agent is *Brucella melitensis*, which typically affects the reticuloendothelial system. Commonly involved organs include the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Symptoms include fever, sweating, joint pain, and fatigue. The infection can lead to chronic complications such as arthritis and endocarditis.

*Brucella abortus* is a gram-negative coccobacillus causing brucellosis, a zoonotic infection primarily transmitted through contact with infected animals or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. Common synonyms include undulant fever and Malta fever. The causative agent, *Brucella abortus*, primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and joint pain. It commonly involves the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes, and may disseminate to the bones, joints, and central nervous system. The infection is more prevalent in agricultural settings and among those handling livestock.

Brucella suis is a Gram-negative coccobacillus causing brucellosis, a zoonotic infection primarily transmitted through ingestion of contaminated animal products. Common synonyms include brucellosis and undulant fever. The causative agent is Brucella suis, a species within the genus Brucella. It typically affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to symptoms such as fever, malaise, and joint pain. Commonly involved organs include the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It may also cause chronic infection with granulomatous lesions. The condition is more prevalent in individuals exposed to infected animals, such as veterinarians and farmers.

Brucella canis is a bacterial infection primarily affecting dogs, caused by the bacterium Brucella canis. It is also known as canine brucellosis or contagious abortion. The infection leads to reproductive issues such as infertility, miscarriage, and stillbirth. It can also cause systemic symptoms including fever, weight loss, and joint pain. Commonly affected body parts include the reproductive organs, joints, and lymph nodes. Transmission occurs through contact with infected bodily fluids, particularly semen and vaginal secretions. The disease can be zoonotic, posing a risk to humans, especially those with compromised immune systems.

Other brucellosis refers to brucellosis caused by species of *Brucella* other than *B. abortus*, *B. melitensis*, *B. suis*, and *B. canis*, which are the most commonly implicated in human disease. Common synonyms include undulant fever and Mediterranean fever. The causative agents include *B. caprae*, *B. suis biovar 3*, and *B. neotomae*. This condition typically affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to fever, malaise, and joint pain. It may also involve the central nervous system, liver, and spleen. The clinical presentation is often non-specific and may mimic other infectious or inflammatory diseases.

Brucellosis, unspecified, is a zoonotic infectious disease caused by bacteria of the genus *Brucella*. Common synonyms include undifferentiated brucellosis and undetermined brucellosis. The causative agents include *Brucella abortus*, *B. melitensis*, *B. suis*, and *B. canis*. The infection typically affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to symptoms such as fever, malaise, and joint pain. It may involve the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. The disease can present acutely or chronically, with potential complications including arthritis and endocarditis. Transmission occurs primarily through contact with infected animals or consumption of unpasteurized dairy products.

Glanders is a severe, often fatal infectious disease primarily affecting horses, donkeys, and mules. It is caused by *Burkholderia mallei*, a gram-negative bacterium. Less commonly, it can occur in humans, particularly those with close contact with infected animals. The disease is characterized by suppurative granulomas, abscesses, and necrosis, typically involving the respiratory tract, skin, and lymph nodes. Common synonyms include "equine glanders" and "malleformia." The infection can lead to systemic spread and is classified as a Category B bioterrorism agent due to its potential for aerosol transmission and high mortality rate.

Melioidosis is a bacterial infection caused primarily by *Burkholderia pseudomallei*. It is also known as Whitmore's disease. The infection can present as acute or chronic, with systemic involvement. Commonly affected organs include the lungs, liver, spleen, and skin. It is endemic in tropical regions, particularly Southeast Asia and northern Australia. Symptoms range from localized abscesses to fulminant sepsis. The disease is often acquired through contact with contaminated soil or water, and can be challenging to diagnose due to its varied clinical manifestations.

Spirillary fever, also known as Mediterranean fever or Brill-Zinsser disease, is a recurrent febrile illness caused by the bacterium *Rickettsia conorii*. It typically affects individuals previously infected with Mediterranean spotted fever. The disease is characterized by fever, headache, and a rash, often beginning at the site of a tick bite. Commonly affected areas include the skin, lymph nodes, and occasionally the lungs. The condition is more prevalent in warm climates and is transmitted through tick bites, particularly from *Rhipicephalus sanguineus*.

Streptobacillary fever, also known as Carrion's disease or bartonellosis, is a bacterial infection caused by *Bartonella bacilliformis*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. The disease primarily affects the bloodstream and skin, leading to symptoms such as fever, malaise, and characteristic skin lesions called "carrion's nodules." It is endemic to the Andean regions of South America. The infection can progress to a chronic phase with persistent fever and anemia. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent complications.

Unspecified rat-bite fever is a systemic bacterial infection typically following a rodent bite, though transmission can occur through contact with infected excreta. Common synonyms include streptobacillary and spirillary fever. The condition is primarily caused by *Streptobacillus moniliformis* or *Spirillum minus*. It commonly affects the skin, joints, and internal organs, with symptoms including fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. The infection can progress to sepsis if untreated. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and exposure history, as culture techniques may be challenging. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent complications.

Listeriosis is a severe bacterial infection caused primarily by *Listeria monocytogenes*. It is a foodborne illness that can affect immunocompromised individuals, pregnant women, and the elderly. Common synonyms include listerial infection or listeriosis. The bacteria can invade multiple organs, but the central nervous system is frequently affected, leading to meningitis or encephalitis. Other common sites include the placenta, fetus, and gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms range from fever and muscle pain to severe neurological complications. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are crucial for favorable outcomes.

Erysipelothrix infection is a rare bacterial infection caused primarily by *Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae*. It commonly affects the skin, particularly in individuals with occupational exposure to animals or fish. The infection presents as a painful, erythematous, raised rash, often with a well-defined border. Systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise may occur, especially in immunocompromised patients. Other affected areas include the joints, heart, and central nervous system. Synonyms include erysipeloid and erysipelothrix infection. The bacterium is a gram-positive coccus often found in the environment and gastrointestinal tracts of animals.

Pasteurellosis is an acute bacterial infection caused by *Pasteurella multocida*, commonly affecting the respiratory tract, skin, and soft tissues. It often results from animal bites or scratches, particularly from cats and dogs. Symptoms include localized inflammation, pain, swelling, and sometimes systemic signs like fever. The infection can progress to abscess formation or septicemia if untreated. Synonyms include cat-scratch disease and animal bite infection. It primarily affects the skin, respiratory system, and occasionally the central nervous system.

"Other specified zoonotic bacterial diseases" refers to bacterial infections transmitted from animals to humans that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include zoonotic bacterial infections or animal-borne bacterial diseases. Causative agents vary but may include *Rickettsia*, *Leptospira*, and *Bartonella*. These diseases typically affect the skin, respiratory system, and mucous membranes, with symptoms ranging from fever and rash to systemic illness. Transmission often occurs through bites, contact with infected animals, or contaminated environments.

Unspecified zoonotic bacterial disease refers to a bacterial infection transmitted from animals to humans, where the specific causative agent or affected site is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include undetermined zoonotic infection or unspecified animal-borne bacterial illness. Causative agents may include various bacteria such as *Salmonella*, *Leptospira*, or *Campylobacter*, depending on the source animal. Typically, these infections affect the gastrointestinal tract, respiratory system, or skin, though the exact manifestation can vary. Diagnosis often relies on clinical presentation and epidemiological history rather than definitive pathogen identification.

Lepromatous leprosy, also known as type 1 leprosy, is a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*. It is characterized by widespread bacterial proliferation and poor immune response, leading to granulomatous inflammation and nerve damage. Common synonyms include lepromatous leprosy and type 1 leprosy. The infection primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, mucosa of the upper respiratory tract, and eyes. Lesions are usually hypopigmented, thickened, and accompanied by loss of sensation. The disease progresses slowly and is more severe than tuberculoid leprosy.

Tuberculoid leprosy, also known as type 1 leprosy, is a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*. It is characterized by immune-mediated granulomatous inflammation, leading to well-defined, hypopigmented skin lesions with loss of sensation. The disease primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucosa of the upper respiratory tract. Common synonyms include paucibacillary leprosy and borderline tuberculoid leprosy. Lesions are typically found on the face, hands, and feet, and may result in nerve damage and deformities if untreated.

Indeterminate leprosy, also known as group I leprosy, is an early, non-specific stage of leprosy characterized by hypoesthetic skin lesions and minimal nerve involvement. It is caused by *Mycobacterium leprae* and may progress to other forms of leprosy if untreated. Common synonyms include early leprosy and pre-morbid leprosy. Typically affecting the skin and peripheral nerves, this form is more prevalent in individuals with partial immunity. Lesions are usually small, erythematous, and poorly defined, often occurring on the face, arms, and legs. The condition is less contagious compared to other leprosy types.

Borderline leprosy, also known as borderline tuberculoid or mid-borderline leprosy, is a form of leprosy characterized by a mix of tuberculoid and lepromatous features. It is caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*. Common synonyms include borderline tuberculoid and mid-borderline leprosy. This condition typically affects the skin, nerves, and mucous membranes, particularly the face, hands, and feet. Patients exhibit few to several hypopigmented or reddish skin lesions with minimal nerve involvement. The immune response is intermediate, leading to partial containment of the bacteria.

Other specified leprosy refers to leprosy cases that do not meet the criteria for the main categories of lepromatous, tuberculoid, or borderline leprosy. It encompasses a range of clinical presentations with variable symptoms and skin lesions. Common synonyms include atypical leprosy and leprosy not otherwise specified. The causative agent is *Mycobacterium leprae*. This form typically affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes, particularly the upper respiratory tract. It may present with hypopigmented or erythematous patches, nerve thickening, and loss of sensation. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and skin smear or biopsy.

Leprosy, unspecified, refers to a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium leprae* and, less commonly, *Mycobacterium lepromatosis*. It primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucosa of the upper respiratory tract. The disease is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and nerve damage, leading to loss of sensation and potential deformities. Common synonyms include Hansen's disease. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. The clinical presentation can vary widely, ranging from paucibacillary to multibacillary forms, depending on the immune response. Early diagnosis and treatment with multidrug therapy are essential to prevent long-term complications.

code_desc: pulmonary diseases due to other mycobacteria
summary: Pulmonary diseases due to other mycobacteria refer to infections of the lungs caused by mycobacterial species other than *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* or *Mycobacterium leprae*. Common synonyms include nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) lung disease. Causative agents include *Mycobacterium avium complex*, *Mycobacterium kansasii*, and *Mycobacterium abscessus*. These infections typically affect the lungs, causing symptoms such as chronic cough, fever, and weight loss. They are more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with preexisting lung conditions.

code_desc: cutaneous diseases due to other mycobacteria
summary: Cutaneous diseases due to other mycobacteria refer to infections caused by non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) that primarily affect the skin. Common synonyms include mycobacterial skin infections and NTM dermatitis. Causative agents include *Mycobacterium avium* complex, *M. marinum*, and *M. kansasii*. These infections typically manifest as chronic, indolent lesions, often on the hands, feet, or extremities. Lesions may present as nodules, ulcers, or erythematous plaques. The condition is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with chronic skin conditions. Diagnosis involves microbiological culture and histopathological examination.

Disseminated disease due to other mycobacteria refers to systemic infection caused by non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), which spread beyond the initial site of infection. Common synonyms include disseminated mycobacterial infection or extrapulmonary mycobacterial disease. Causative agents include *Mycobacterium avium complex*, *Mycobacterium kansasii*, and *Mycobacterium marinum*. Typically affecting immunocompromised individuals, the infection can involve the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, bones, and disseminate to multiple organs. It is often associated with underlying conditions like HIV or chronic lung disease.

Other specified mycobacterial diseases refer to infections caused by mycobacteria that do not fit into the more commonly recognized categories such as tuberculosis or leprosy. These infections are often caused by non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), including species like *Mycobacterium avium* and *Mycobacterium kansasii*. They typically affect the lungs, lymph nodes, and skin, and may present with chronic or granulomatous inflammation. Common synonyms include NTM infections and atypical mycobacterial diseases. These conditions are often seen in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying lung disease.

Unspecified diseases due to mycobacteria refer to infections caused by mycobacterial species that are not classified under more specific categories such as tuberculosis or leprosy. Common synonyms include atypical mycobacterial infections or nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) diseases. Causative agents often include *Mycobacterium avium* complex, *M. kansasii*, and *M. tuberculosis* variants. These infections typically affect the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, and disseminated systems, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Clinical presentation varies widely depending on the organism and host immunity.

Faucial diphtheria is an acute bacterial infection characterized by the formation of a thick, grayish-white pseudomembrane on the tonsils and soft palate. Caused primarily by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*, it may also involve *Corynebacterium ulcerans* or *Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis*. Common synonyms include pharyngeal diphtheria and tonsillar diphtheria. The infection typically affects the upper respiratory tract, particularly the pharynx, tonsils, and soft palate, and can lead to systemic complications due to the exotoxin produced by the bacteria.

Nasopharyngeal diphtheria is an acute bacterial infection characterized by the formation of a pseudomembranous exudate in the nasopharynx. Caused primarily by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*, it may also involve *Corynebacterium ulcerans* or *Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis*. The infection typically affects the nasopharyngeal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as sore throat, fever, and respiratory distress. Synonyms include diphtheritic angina and pharyngeal diphtheria. Complications may include airway obstruction and systemic toxicity due to diphtheria toxin.

Anterior nasal diphtheria is a rare form of diphtheria characterized by the presence of a grayish pseudomembrane in the anterior nasal cavity. It is caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* and occasionally *Corynebacterium ulcerans*. The infection typically affects the nasal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, discharge, and occasional systemic involvement. It is often associated with poor hygiene and close contact with infected individuals. Synonyms include nasal diphtheria and corynebacterial nasopharyngitis. The condition is more common in children and can progress to systemic complications if left untreated.

Laryngeal diphtheria is an acute bacterial infection characterized by the formation of a pseudomembrane on the mucous membranes of the larynx. Caused primarily by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*, it may also involve *C. ulcerans* or *C. pseudotuberculosis*. The infection leads to inflammation, hoarseness, stridor, and potential airway obstruction. Common synonyms include diphtheritic laryngitis or laryngeal diphtheria. It typically affects the pharynx, larynx, and adjacent structures, with systemic complications possible if left untreated.

Conjunctival diphtheria is a rare, severe ocular infection characterized by a grayish-white pseudomembrane on the conjunctiva. It is caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* or *Corynebacterium ulcerans*. Common synonyms include diphtheritic conjunctivitis and membranous conjunctivitis. The infection typically affects the bulbar conjunctiva and can spread to the cornea, leading to potential vision loss. It is more common in children and individuals with compromised immune systems. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with antitoxins and antibiotics are essential to prevent complications.

Diphtheritic myocarditis is an inflammatory condition of the heart muscle caused by toxins from *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*. It occurs as a complication of diphtheria, primarily affecting the myocardium. Common synonyms include diphtherial myocarditis or diphtheritic carditis. The toxin leads to necrosis and fibrosis of cardiac muscle, potentially resulting in arrhythmias and heart failure. The condition typically affects the myocardium, with possible involvement of the endocardium and pericardium. It is most commonly seen in children and individuals with inadequate immunity to diphtheria.

Diphtheritic peritonitis is a rare, severe form of peritonitis characterized by a pseudomembranous exudate on the peritoneal surfaces, resembling diphtheria. It is typically caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* or other gram-positive bacilli. Common synonyms include pseudomembranous peritonitis and diphtheroid peritonitis. The condition primarily affects the abdominal cavity, involving the peritoneum, and may extend to the intestinal walls. It is often associated with systemic toxicity and can lead to sepsis if not promptly treated with antitoxins and antibiotics.

Diphtheritic cystitis is a rare inflammatory condition of the bladder characterized by the formation of pseudomembranous exudates resembling diphtheria. It is typically caused by bacterial infections, most commonly by *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Streptococcus pyogenes*. The condition presents with symptoms such as dysuria, hematuria, and bladder discomfort. It predominantly affects the bladder mucosa, occasionally involving the urethra. Synonyms include diphtheroid cystitis and pseudodiphtheric cystitis. The disease is more common in males and often occurs in association with other systemic infections or immunocompromised states.

Cutaneous diphtheria is a localized form of diphtheria characterized by the formation of a grayish pseudomembrane on the skin. It is caused primarily by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* and occasionally by *Corynebacterium ulcerans*. Common synonyms include epidermic diphtheria and cutaneous diphtheroidal infection. The condition typically affects exposed areas such as the face, neck, and extremities. It is more prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and low immunization rates. The infection is usually less severe than respiratory diphtheria but can lead to complications if left untreated.

"Other specified diphtheria" refers to cases of diphtheria that do not meet the criteria for classical diphtheria but are still classified under the broader category of diphtheria. It is typically caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* and occasionally by *Corynebacterium ulcerans*. The condition is characterized by the presence of a pseudomembrane in the upper respiratory tract, often accompanied by systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include atypical diphtheria or non-classical diphtheria. It primarily affects the pharynx, larynx, and nasal passages.

Diphtheria, unspecified, is an acute bacterial infection caused primarily by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*. It typically affects the upper respiratory tract, leading to a pseudomembrane formation in the throat. Common synonyms include diphtheritic infection and corynebacterial infection. The disease can also involve the skin, causing cutaneous diphtheria. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, and difficulty breathing. Complications may arise from toxin production, affecting the heart and nervous system. Prompt antibiotic treatment and antitoxin administration are critical for recovery.

code_desc: whooping cough due to bordetella pertussis [b. pertussis]
summary: Whooping cough, caused by *Bordetella pertussis*, is a highly contagious respiratory infection characterized by severe coughing fits followed by a high-pitched "whoop" sound upon inhalation. Common synonyms include pertussis and the 100-day cough. The bacterium colonizes the respiratory tract, primarily affecting the bronchi and bronchioles. It is most severe in infants and young children, though can occur in adults. Symptoms include paroxysmal coughing, post-tussive vomiting, and cyanosis. Complications may include pneumonia, seizures, and apnea. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets.

code_desc: whooping cough due to bordetella parapertussis [b. parapertussis]
summary: Whooping cough due to *Bordetella parapertussis* is an acute respiratory infection characterized by severe coughing fits followed by a high-pitched "whoop" sound during inhalation. It is less severe than pertussis caused by *Bordetella pertussis* but can lead to complications such as pneumonia. Common synonyms include parapertussis and pertussis-like illness. The infection primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, with symptoms often beginning with mild cold-like signs before progressing to persistent coughing. It is more common in younger children and can be transmitted via respiratory droplets.

code_desc: whooping cough due to other specified organism
summary: Whooping cough due to other specified organism refers to a severe respiratory infection characterized by prolonged coughing fits followed by a high-pitched "whoop" sound during inhalation. It is caused by pathogens other than *Bordetella pertussis*, the primary agent of pertussis. Common synonyms include pertussis-like illness or atypical whooping cough. Causative agents may include *Bordetella parapertussis*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, or other bacteria. The infection primarily affects the upper and lower respiratory tract, leading to symptoms such as coughing, difficulty breathing, and fatigue. It predominantly occurs in infants and young children but can affect individuals of all ages.

Whooping cough, unspecified organism, is an acute respiratory infection characterized by paroxysmal coughing followed by a high-pitched inspiratory whoop. It is caused by Bordetella pertussis, though other Bordetella species may occasionally be involved. The disease primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, leading to inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles. Common synonyms include pertussis and the 10-day cough. It predominantly affects infants and young children but can occur in adults. Complications may include pneumonia, apnea, and bronchopneumonia. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets.

Scarlet fever is an acute bacterial infection caused by group A Streptococcus, most commonly Streptococcus pyogenes. It typically presents with a sore throat, fever, and a characteristic diffuse, sandpaper-like rash that begins on the neck and spreads to the trunk and extremities. The rash fades in areas where skin folds meet, leaving a 'palmar' or 'pastoral' pattern. Common synonyms include scarlatina and erythrophlegmon. The infection primarily affects the pharynx, skin, and mucous membranes, with complications such as rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis possible if untreated.

Erysipelas is an acute, superficial bacterial skin infection characterized by a bright red, raised, and sharply demarcated rash, often accompanied by fever and malaise. Common synonyms include St. Anthony's fire and exanthema. It is primarily caused by *Streptococcus pyogenes* (group A streptococcus). The infection typically affects the lower extremities, particularly the legs, but can occur on the face or other areas. It spreads rapidly through the lymphatic system and is more common in individuals with compromised skin integrity or lymphatic obstruction.

Meningococcal meningitis is a severe bacterial infection caused by *Neisseria meningitidis*, leading to inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Common synonyms include bacterial meningitis and meningococcal infection. The disease typically affects the central nervous system, causing symptoms such as fever, headache, and neck stiffness. It can progress rapidly, leading to complications like septicemia, seizures, and brain damage. Prompt antibiotic treatment is critical to prevent severe outcomes.

Meningococcal encephalitis is a severe central nervous system infection caused by *Neisseria meningitidis*. It presents with inflammation of the brain tissue, often following meningococcal meningitis. Common synonyms include meningococcal brain infection or meningococcal meningoencephalitis. The condition primarily affects the brain and spinal cord, leading to symptoms such as fever, seizures, altered mental status, and potentially life-threatening complications. It is more common in children and young adults, with rapid progression and high morbidity if not promptly treated with antibiotics.

Meningococcemia is a severe bloodstream infection caused by *Neisseria meningitidis*. It often presents with fever, rash, and systemic inflammation. Common synonyms include meningococcal septicemia and meningococcemia. The bacteria primarily affect the bloodstream and can lead to meningitis or septic shock. It predominantly affects children, adolescents, and young adults. Complications include disseminated intravascular coagulation and multiorgan failure. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are critical for survival.

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is a severe complication of meningococcal sepsis characterized by bilateral adrenal hemorrhage and necrosis. Caused by *Neisseria meningitidis*, it leads to adrenal insufficiency and shock. Common synonyms include adrenal hemorrhage syndrome and fulminant meningococcemia. The condition primarily affects the adrenal glands, often in conjunction with systemic infection. It is more common in children and young adults, and presents with symptoms such as fever, rash, hypotension, and altered mental status. Early recognition and aggressive treatment are critical to improve outcomes.

Meningococcal carditis, unspecified, is a rare but severe infection caused by *Neisseria meningitidis* affecting the heart muscle. It typically presents with symptoms such as chest pain, arrhythmias, and cardiovascular instability. The condition is part of the broader spectrum of meningococcal disease, which can also involve the meninges, bloodstream, and other organs. Common synonyms include meningococcal myocarditis and meningococcal endocarditis. The heart is the primary affected organ, though systemic involvement is possible. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are critical to prevent complications and mortality.

Meningococcal pericarditis is a rare but severe infection characterized by inflammation of the pericardium caused by Neisseria meningitidis. It is a complication of meningococcal disease, often occurring in conjunction with meningitis or septicemia. The infection leads to pericardial effusion and potentially cardiac tamponade. Common synonyms include bacterial pericarditis due to meningococcus. The primary affected body part is the pericardium, with systemic involvement possible. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical to prevent mortality.

Meningococcal endocarditis is a rare and severe infection involving the inner lining of the heart chambers, caused by *Neisseria meningitidis*. It is uncommon compared to other forms of endocarditis, which are more frequently caused by streptococci or staphylococci. The infection can lead to systemic complications, including sepsis and purpura fulminans. It typically affects the heart valves, particularly the mitral and tricuspid valves, and is often associated with underlying heart disease or immunocompromised states. Synonyms include meningococcal infective endocarditis or meningococcal endocardial infection.

Meningococcal myocarditis is a rare but severe cardiac complication caused by Neisseria meningitidis infection. It involves inflammation of the myocardium, often as a part of disseminated intravascular coagulation during meningococcal sepsis. Common synonyms include meningococcal cardiac involvement or septic myocarditis. The condition primarily affects the heart muscle, leading to arrhythmias, heart failure, and potentially sudden cardiac death. It typically occurs in conjunction with meningococcal disease, predominantly in children and young adults. Early recognition and aggressive antimicrobial therapy are critical for improved outcomes.

Meningococcal optic neuritis is an inflammatory condition affecting the optic nerve, typically occurring as a complication of Neisseria meningitidis infection. It is characterized by inflammation and potential damage to the optic nerve, leading to visual disturbances. Common synonyms include optic neuritis associated with meningococcal disease. The causative agent is Neisseria meningitidis, and the condition primarily affects the optic nerve, often resulting in vision loss. It is more commonly seen in children and young adults.

Meningococcal arthropathy is a rare complication of meningococcal infection, characterized by joint inflammation. It typically occurs in conjunction with meningococcal disease, often following bacteremia. The condition is caused by *Neisseria meningitidis* and may present with joint pain, swelling, and effusion. Commonly affected joints include the knees, ankles, and wrists. Synonyms include septic arthritis due to meningococcus and meningococcal septic arthritis. The condition is more prevalent in children and adolescents. Early diagnosis and antimicrobial therapy are crucial to prevent joint damage.

"Other specified meningococcal infections" refers to meningococcal disease cases that do not meet the criteria for meningococcal meningitis or septicemia but involve *Neisseria meningitidis*. Common synonyms include meningococcal septicemia and meningococcemia. The bacteria primarily affect the bloodstream and can lead to systemic complications such as purpura fulminans. Affected body parts include the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the central nervous system. The condition is characterized by rapid progression and can be life-threatening without prompt treatment.

Meningococcal infection, unspecified, refers to a bacterial infection caused by *Neisseria meningitidis* that affects the meninges or bloodstream. Common synonyms include meningococcemia and meningitis due to *N. meningitidis*. The infection typically involves the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid, and can lead to systemic complications. It primarily affects the central nervous system but may also involve other organs. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and rash. Rapid progression can lead to septic shock and death if untreated.

Tetanus is a severe, potentially fatal infectious disease caused by the bacterium *Clostridium tetani*. The toxin produced, tetanospasmin, leads to generalized muscle stiffness and spasticity, often beginning in the jaw (lockjaw) and spreading to the neck, trunk, and limbs. Common synonyms include lockjaw and tetanus toxoid. The infection typically enters through contaminated wounds, especially deep, anaerobic injuries. It primarily affects the neuromuscular junction, causing painful spasms and rigidity. Prompt treatment with antitoxin, antibiotics, and supportive care is essential. Vaccination is the most effective prevention method.

Streptococcal septicemia is a severe bloodstream infection caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS) or other streptococcal species. It often develops from local infections such as pharyngitis or skin lesions. Common synonyms include streptococcal sepsis and invasive group A streptococcal disease. The infection can lead to systemic inflammation, multiorgan failure, and toxic shock syndrome. Typically affected body parts include the skin, throat, and lungs, with potential spread to the bloodstream and vital organs. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical to prevent mortality.

Staphylococcal septicemia, unspecified, is a systemic infection caused by Staphylococcus species, most commonly S. aureus. It results from the entry of bacteria into the bloodstream, leading to widespread inflammation and potential multi-organ dysfunction. Common synonyms include staphylococcal bacteremia and septicemia due to staphylococcus. The infection can affect various organs, including the lungs, kidneys, liver, and skin, often following trauma, surgery, or immunocompromised states. Clinical features may include fever, chills, hypotension, and organ failure. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent progression to septic shock.

Methicillin susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) septicemia is a bloodstream infection caused by S. aureus that remains susceptible to methicillin. It typically arises from local infections such as skin abscesses, pneumonia, or urinary tract infections. Common synonyms include MSSA bacteremia and Staphylococcus aureus septicemia. The infection can affect multiple organs, leading to systemic symptoms like fever, hypotension, and organ dysfunction. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent progression to septic shock.

Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA) septicemia is a severe bloodstream infection caused by MRSA, a strain of *S. aureus* resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics. It often arises from localized infections such as skin abscesses, pneumonia, or surgical sites. Common synonyms include MRSA bacteremia and septicemia due to MRSA. The infection can lead to systemic inflammation, sepsis, and multi-organ failure. Typically affected body parts include the skin, lungs, and soft tissues, with potential spread to the bloodstream. Prompt antibiotic therapy and source control are critical for management.

Other staphylococcal septicemia refers to a systemic bacterial infection caused by species of *Staphylococcus* other than *Staphylococcus aureus*. Common synonyms include non-*aureus* staphylococcal septicemia. Causative agents often include *Staphylococcus epidermidis*, *Staphylococcus haemolyticus*, and *Staphylococcus lugdunensis*. This condition typically affects the bloodstream, leading to fever, chills, and potentially septic shock. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with indwelling medical devices. Infection may originate from skin, urinary tract, or surgical sites. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent complications.

Pneumococcal septicemia, caused primarily by *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, is a severe bloodstream infection characterized by systemic inflammation and potential multi-organ failure. Common synonyms include streptococcal septicemia and pneumococcal bacteremia. The bacteria typically affect the lungs, leading to pneumonia, which may progress to septicemia. Other affected sites include the meninges, joints, and bloodstream. Symptoms include fever, chills, hypotension, and organ dysfunction. Prompt antibiotic therapy is critical to prevent mortality.

Septicemia due to anaerobes is a systemic infection caused by anaerobic bacteria that have entered the bloodstream, leading to widespread inflammation and potential organ failure. Common synonyms include anaerobic septicemia and gas gangrene in certain contexts. Causative agents often include *Bacteroides*, *Clostridium*, and *Fusobacterium* species. It typically arises from infections in the abdomen, pelvis, or soft tissues, such as abscesses or surgical sites. Symptoms include fever, hypotension, and multiorgan dysfunction. Prompt antibiotic therapy and source control are critical for management.

code_desc: septicemia due to gram-negative organism, unspecified
summary: Septicemia due to gram-negative organism, unspecified refers to a systemic infection caused by gram-negative bacteria entering the bloodstream. Common synonyms include gram-negative sepsis or bacteremia. Causative agents often include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species. The infection typically affects the bloodstream, lungs, urinary tract, and abdominal cavity. It is associated with fever, hypotension, organ dysfunction, and can progress to septic shock if untreated. Prompt identification and antibiotic therapy are critical for improved outcomes.

code_desc: septicemia due to hemophilus influenzae [h. influenzae]
summary: Septicemia due to *Haemophilus influenzae* is a systemic infection caused by the bacterium *H. influenzae*, typically affecting individuals with compromised immune systems or underlying respiratory conditions. Common synonyms include sepsis caused by *H. influenzae* or bacterial septicemia. The infection often originates from the respiratory tract and can lead to dissemination to the bloodstream, causing multi-organ involvement. It is a serious condition that may present with fever, chills, hypotension, and organ dysfunction. The most common serotype associated with invasive disease is type b, though non-typeable strains are also implicated.

code_desc: septicemia due to escherichia coli [e. coli]
summary: Septicemia due to *Escherichia coli* (E. coli) is a systemic infection caused by the bacterium *E. coli*, which enters the bloodstream and leads to widespread inflammation and potential organ failure. Common synonyms include bloodstream infection or septicemia. *E. coli* is a common causative agent, often originating from urinary tract infections, abdominal infections, or post-surgical sites. It typically affects the circulatory system, lungs, kidneys, and liver, and can progress to septic shock if untreated. Prompt antibiotic therapy is critical to prevent mortality.

Septicemia due to Pseudomonas is a systemic infection caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a gram-negative bacillus. It often arises from hospital-acquired infections, particularly in immunocompromised or critically ill patients. Common synonyms include Pseudomonas sepsis or Pseudomonas bloodstream infection. The bacteria can affect multiple organs, leading to pneumonia, urinary tract infections, wound infections, and meningitis. Clinical features include fever, chills, hypotension, and organ dysfunction. Prompt antimicrobial therapy is essential due to the organism's intrinsic resistance and ability to form biofilms.

Septicemia due to *Serratia* is a systemic infection caused by *Serratia* species, commonly *Serratia marcescens*. It often arises from hospital-acquired infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Symptoms include fever, chills, hypotension, and multi-organ dysfunction. Commonly affected sites include the urinary tract, lungs, and bloodstream. Synonyms include *Serratia sepsis* or *Serratia bloodstream infection*. The bacteria are Gram-negative rods, often found in water, soil, and hospital environments. Prompt antimicrobial therapy is critical to prevent progression to septic shock.

code_desc: other septicemia due to gram-negative organisms
summary: Other septicemia due to gram-negative organisms refers to a systemic infection caused by bacteria that are gram-negative in appearance, excluding those classified under specific categories like E. coli or Klebsiella. Common synonyms include gram-negative septicemia and systemic gram-negative infection. Causative agents often include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus species, and Enterobacter. This condition typically affects the bloodstream and can lead to sepsis, with common involvement of the lungs, urinary tract, and skin. It is associated with fever, hypotension, and multi-organ dysfunction.

"Other specified septicemias" refers to systemic infections caused by the presence of pathogenic microorganisms in the bloodstream, not classified under more specific categories like septicemia due to a particular organism or type. Common synonyms include bloodstream infection or bacteremia. Causative agents may include bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Streptococcus species. These infections typically affect the circulatory system and can lead to complications in the lungs, kidneys, and other organs. The condition is often associated with underlying illnesses or immunocompromised states.

Unspecified septicemia refers to a systemic infection resulting from the presence of pathogenic microorganisms in the bloodstream, with the specific organism not identified. It is a severe condition characterized by fever, chills, tachycardia, and potential organ dysfunction. Common synonyms include sepsis and blood poisoning. Causative agents may include bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Streptococcus species. Typically, the infection originates from the respiratory, urinary, or gastrointestinal tracts, and can affect multiple organs, including the lungs, kidneys, and liver.

Pulmonary actinomycotic infection is a rare, chronic bacterial infection caused by *Actinomyces* species, most commonly *Actinomyces israelii*. It typically presents as a granulomatous inflammation of the lungs, often following aspiration or trauma. The infection may spread to adjacent structures, leading to abscess formation. Common synonyms include pulmonary actinomycosis. Clinically, it may mimic tuberculosis or fungal infections. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, but can also involve the pleura, bronchi, and mediastinum. Diagnosis is often confirmed through microbiological culture or histopathological examination. Treatment involves prolonged antibiotic therapy, typically with penicillin or clindamycin.

Abdominal actinomycotic infection is a rare, chronic bacterial infection caused by *Actinomyces* species, most commonly *Actinomyces israelii*. It typically presents as a suppurative, granulomatous process involving the abdominal cavity, often following trauma or surgery. The infection may mimic abscesses or malignancies and is characterized by sulfur granules in affected tissues. Common synonyms include abdominal actinomycosis or actinomycotic peritonitis. The infection primarily affects the abdominal wall, peritoneum, and adjacent organs such as the liver or spleen. It is more prevalent in males and often occurs in the context of prior abdominal procedures.

Cervicofacial actinomycotic infection is a chronic, suppurative bacterial infection caused primarily by *Actinomyces israelii*. It often presents as a slowly progressing, granulomatous lesion with sulfur granules. Common synonyms include cervicofacial actinomycosis and lupus vulgaris-like infection. The infection typically affects the jaw, neck, and soft tissues of the face, often following trauma or dental procedures. It may spread to adjacent structures, leading to abscess formation and fibrosis. Diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of sulfur granules and culture. Treatment involves long-term antibiotic therapy, usually with penicillin.

Madura foot, also known as mycetoma or madurella, is a chronic subcutaneous infection characterized by granulomatous inflammation and the formation of sinus tracts with purulent discharge. It is primarily caused by filamentous fungi (e.g., *Madurella mycetomatis*) or actinomycetes. The infection typically affects the feet, especially in tropical and subtropical regions, and may spread to the lower limbs. Common synonyms include mycetoma and madurella. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with poor hygiene.

code_desc: actinomycotic infection of other specified sites
summary: Actinomycotic infection of other specified sites refers to infections caused by *Actinomyces* species, typically *A. israelii*, in locations not primarily classified as the jaw, face, or neck. These infections are chronic, suppurative, and often present with abscesses, granulation tissue, and sulfur granules. Common synonyms include actinomycosis of unspecified sites or extraglandular actinomycosis. The infection may affect the thorax, abdomen, or soft tissues, often following trauma or dental procedures. It is more common in adults and may mimic malignancy due to its indolent nature.

Actinomycotic infection of unspecified site is a chronic, suppurative infection caused by *Actinomyces* species, most commonly *A. israelii*. It typically presents as a slowly progressing, granulomatous process with sulfur granules. Common synonyms include actinomycosis and chronic actinomycosis. The infection often affects the cervicofacial region, thoracic cavity, or abdominal area, though it may occur elsewhere. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with trauma or foreign bodies. Diagnosis is confirmed by microbiological culture and histopathological examination. Treatment involves long-term antibiotic therapy, usually with penicillin or clindamycin.

Gas gangrene is a severe, rapidly progressive necrotizing infection caused by anaerobic bacteria, most commonly *Clostridium perfringens*. It often follows trauma, surgery, or ischemia, leading to tissue necrosis and gas production. Synonyms include clostridial myonecrosis and erysipelas-like infection. The infection typically affects muscle-rich areas such as the limbs, abdomen, and perineum. Symptoms include severe pain, swelling, crepitus, and systemic toxicity. Prompt surgical debridement and antibiotic therapy are critical for survival.

Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous infection primarily affecting the upper respiratory tract. Caused by *Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis*, it leads to progressive destruction of nasal and pharyngeal tissues. The disease is characterized by formation of hard, nodular lesions and thickened mucosa. Common synonyms include rhinoscleroma and rhinoscleromatis. It typically affects the nasal septum, turbinates, and nasopharynx. The infection is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions and is associated with malnutrition and immunocompromise.

Necrobacillosis is a bacterial infection characterized by the formation of necrotic lesions, typically caused by *Fusobacterium necrophorum*. Common synonyms include actinobacillosis and actinobacillary infection. The disease primarily affects the oral cavity, respiratory tract, and genital areas. It is often associated with trauma or pre-existing conditions such as periodontal disease. The infection can lead to abscesses and systemic spread in immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical signs, culture, and histopathology. Treatment involves antibiotics targeting anaerobic bacteria.

Infant botulism is a paralytic illness caused by neurotoxins produced by *Clostridium botulinum* in the gastrointestinal tract of infants. It is distinct from foodborne botulism and is often associated with ingestion of spores, commonly found in honey or environmental sources. The toxin affects the neuromuscular junction, leading to descending flaccid paralysis, respiratory compromise, and potentially life-threatening respiratory failure. Common synonyms include infant botulism, infantile botulism, and toxemia of the newborn. The condition primarily affects the neuromuscular system, with symptoms typically beginning in the neonatal or early infancy period.

Wound botulism is a rare but severe form of botulism caused by *Clostridium botulinum* neurotoxin produced in contaminated wounds. It occurs when the bacterium enters an open wound, particularly in individuals with compromised immune systems or those using injectable drugs. Common synonyms include traumatic botulism and wound-associated botulism. The toxin leads to descending flaccid paralysis, starting with cranial nerve involvement and progressing to respiratory failure. Typically affected body parts include the wound site, facial muscles, and respiratory muscles. Early diagnosis and antitoxin administration are critical for recovery.

Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a life-threatening systemic infection characterized by high fever, hypotension, and multi-organ dysfunction. Common synonyms include staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. It is primarily caused by toxin-producing strains of *Staphylococcus aureus* or, less commonly, *Streptococcus pyogenes*. The condition typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs, with involvement of the circulatory system and kidneys. It is often associated with tampon use, surgical wounds, or nasal packing. Prompt recognition and treatment with antibiotics and supportive care are critical.

"Other specified bacterial diseases" refers to bacterial infections that do not fit into more specific categories but are recognized as distinct clinical entities. Common synonyms include unspecified bacterial infections or miscellaneous bacterial diseases. Causative agents vary widely, including *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. These infections can affect multiple body systems, with common sites including the respiratory tract, skin, urinary tract, and bloodstream.
