It is more common in children and often presents with mild to moderate illness, resolving spontaneously without specific antiviral treatment. Complications are rare but may include seizures or neurological deficits.

Meningitis due to echo virus, also known as enterovirus meningitis, is an inflammation of the meninges caused by enteroviruses, particularly echoviruses. It typically presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Common synonyms include viral meningitis and enteroviral meningitis. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, with the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid being the main sites of involvement. It is more common in children and often resolves spontaneously without specific antiviral treatment.

Other specified viral meningitis refers to meningitis caused by viruses not classified under more specific categories such as enteroviruses or herpesviruses. Common synonyms include non-enteroviral viral meningitis. Causative agents may include arboviruses, mumps virus, or varicella-zoster virus. The condition typically affects the meninges, the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms often include fever, headache, and neck stiffness. It is generally less severe than bacterial meningitis but may require supportive care and monitoring for complications.

Unspecified viral meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by a virus, where the specific pathogen is not identified. Common synonyms include aseptic meningitis or viral meningitis, unspecified. Causative agents often include enteroviruses, herpesviruses, and influenza viruses. The condition typically affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. It is generally less severe than bacterial meningitis and often resolves spontaneously with supportive care.

code_desc: other enterovirus diseases of central nervous system
summary: Other enterovirus diseases of the central nervous system refer to infections caused by enteroviruses that primarily affect the brain and spinal cord. Common synonyms include aseptic meningitis and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Causative agents include polioviruses, coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and enterovirus 71. These viruses typically target the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the meninges, brain, or spinal cord. Symptoms may include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and neurological deficits. The disease is more common in children and can range from mild to severe, with potential for long-term neurological complications.

Lymphocytic choriomeningitis is a viral infection caused by the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), a member of the Arenaviridae family. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to meningitis or meningoencephalitis. Common synonyms include aseptic meningitis and lymphocytic meningitis. The infection typically begins with flu-like symptoms, followed by neurological manifestations such as headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. It is most commonly seen in immunocompetent individuals, often acquired through contact with infected rodents. The disease can be mild or severe, with potential for long-term neurological complications.

Meningitis due to adenovirus is an inflammatory condition affecting the meninges, typically caused by adenovirus serotypes 3, 4, and 7. It is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. The infection primarily targets the central nervous system, with the meninges being the main affected site. It is often associated with viral respiratory infections. Synonyms include viral meningitis and adenoviral meningitis. Complications are rare but may include seizures or neurological deficits.

code_desc: other specified non-arthropod-borne viral diseases of central nervous system
summary: "Other specified non-arthropod-borne viral diseases of the central nervous system" refers to viral infections of the CNS caused by agents not transmitted by arthropods. Common synonyms include "non-arthropod-borne viral encephalitis" and "viral meningitis of unspecified etiology." Causative agents may include enteroviruses, herpesviruses, and adenoviruses. These conditions typically affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and neurological deficits. The exact etiology is often identified through laboratory testing.

code_desc: unspecified non-arthropod-borne viral diseases of central nervous system
summary: Unspecified non-arthropod-borne viral diseases of the central nervous system refer to viral infections of the brain and spinal cord caused by viruses not transmitted by arthropods. Common synonyms include "viral encephalitis of unspecified etiology" or "non-vectorborne CNS viral disease." Causative agents may include herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, or enteroviruses. These infections typically affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, altered mental status, and seizures. The condition is often diagnosed when specific viral agents cannot be definitively identified.

Variola major is a severe, often fatal viral infection caused by the variola virus, a member of the Orthopoxvirus genus. It is characterized by a high fever, malaise, and a distinctive rash that progresses through macules, papules, vesicles, and pustules. The rash typically appears on the face, arms, legs, and trunk. Common synonyms include smallpox and variola. The disease primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, with systemic involvement leading to complications such as pneumonia and sepsis. It is highly contagious and has a case fatality rate of 30% in unvaccinated individuals.

Alastrim, also known as alastrim disease or alastrim syndrome, is a rare, chronic inflammatory condition primarily affecting the skin and joints. It is characterized by the formation of painful, erythematous nodules and plaques, often accompanied by joint involvement. The exact etiology is unknown, though it is believed to have an autoimmune component. Commonly affected areas include the scalp, face, and extremities. The condition is more prevalent in middle-aged adults and may be associated with other autoimmune disorders. Treatment typically involves corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents.

Modified smallpox is a rare, attenuated form of smallpox caused by the variola virus, typically resulting from exposure to a less virulent strain. It presents with milder symptoms, including a less severe fever and a less extensive rash. Common synonyms include attenuated smallpox or mild smallpox. The condition primarily affects the skin, with characteristic lesions appearing on the face, arms, and legs. Although rare, it can occur in individuals exposed to vaccine-derived or naturally occurring variants of the virus. The disease is now largely eradicated due to global vaccination efforts.

Smallpox, unspecified, is a severe, highly contagious viral disease caused by the variola virus. It is characterized by a fever, malaise, and a progressive rash that develops into fluid-filled blisters. The rash typically begins on the face and spreads to the limbs and trunk. Common synonyms include variola and smallpox. The disease primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, with systemic involvement. While smallpox was eradicated globally in 1980, it remains a potential bioterrorism agent. The condition is rare but can lead to serious complications, including scarring, blindness, and death.

Pseudocowpox is a rare, self-limiting viral infection characterized by the appearance of papules, vesicles, and pustules, often with central umbilication. It is commonly mistaken for true cowpox. The condition is caused by orthopoxviruses, most frequently the cowpox virus. Common synonyms include "vaccinia-like disease" and "cowpox-like eruption." Typically affecting the hands, feet, and face, it may also involve mucous membranes. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected animals, particularly rodents. The disease is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with close contact with animals.

Contagious pustular dermatitis, also known as acneiform dermatitis or pustular eczema, is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by the development of sterile pustules and scaling. It is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and other bacterial agents. The condition typically affects the face, neck, and upper chest, often in individuals with atopic diathesis. It is contagious through direct contact and may present with pruritus and erythema. The exact pathogenesis involves a combination of immune response and bacterial colonization. Treatment usually includes topical or systemic antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents.

Paravaccinia, unspecified, is a rare viral infection characterized by a vesicular rash, typically occurring at the site of vaccination. It is considered a variant of the vaccinia virus, though the exact causative agent may not be identified. Common synonyms include "vaccinia-like" or "vaccinal" rash. The condition primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, with lesions often appearing at the vaccination site or nearby. It is most commonly observed in individuals who have received smallpox vaccine, particularly those with compromised immune systems. The infection is generally self-limiting but may require supportive care in severe cases.

Postvaricella encephalitis, also known as varicella encephalitis or herpes zoster encephalitis, is a rare but severe central nervous system infection occurring after varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection. It typically affects the temporal and frontal lobes, leading to inflammation and potential neurological complications. The condition is caused by reactivation of VZV in immunocompromised individuals or during the acute phase of varicella. Symptoms include fever, seizures, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. Early diagnosis and antiviral therapy are critical to improving outcomes.

Varicella (hemorrhagic) pneumonitis is a severe pulmonary complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection, characterized by hemorrhagic infiltration of the lung parenchyma. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. Common synonyms include varicella pneumonia and VZV pneumonia. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to respiratory distress, hemoptysis, and hypoxia. Causative agents are primarily VZV, though co-infections with other pathogens may occur. It is a rare but life-threatening condition requiring prompt antiviral therapy.

Postvaricella myelitis, also known as postherpetic myelitis or varicella-zoster virus myelitis, is an inflammatory condition of the spinal cord that occurs following varicella infection. It is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). The condition typically affects the thoracic and cervical spinal cord regions, leading to symptoms such as weakness, sensory loss, and sometimes bladder or bowel dysfunction. It is a rare but serious complication, often presenting weeks to months after the initial varicella outbreak. The inflammation is thought to result from viral reactivation and immune-mediated mechanisms.

Chickenpox with other specified complications refers to varicella infection complicated by additional clinical manifestations beyond the typical rash. Caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), it commonly affects children but can occur in adults. Synonyms include varicella with complications or VZV-related complications. Common complications include pneumonia, encephalitis, and secondary bacterial infections. The rash typically involves the face, scalp, and trunk, but complications may affect multiple organ systems. Prompt recognition and management are essential to prevent severe outcomes.

Chickenpox with unspecified complication refers to a varicella infection complicated by an unspecified secondary condition. Caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), it typically affects children but can occur in adults. The disease presents with a characteristic rash, fever, and malaise. Common synonyms include varicella complications or VZV-related complications. The rash primarily involves the skin and mucous membranes, but complications may affect the lungs, central nervous system, or other organs. The exact nature of the complication is not specified in this classification.

Varicella, also known as chickenpox, is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It presents as an acute illness characterized by a pruritic rash that progresses through macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts. The rash typically involves the face, scalp, and trunk, with lesions appearing in crops. Fever and malaise may accompany the rash. The condition is common in children but can occur in adults. It is generally self-limiting, with full recovery in most cases.

Herpes zoster with meningitis is a neurological complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation, characterized by a painful dermatomal rash and inflammation of the meninges. Common synonyms include shingles with meningitis or VZV meningitis. The virus, VZV, typically affects the trigeminal nerve, leading to rash on the face or scalp, and may spread to involve the central nervous system. It commonly affects older adults or immunocompromised individuals, with symptoms including fever, headache, and altered mental status. The condition requires antiviral therapy and supportive care.

code_desc: herpes zoster with unspecified nervous system complication
summary: Herpes zoster with unspecified nervous system complication refers to a shingles infection involving the nervous system without a specified type of complication. Caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), it typically affects dermatomes along sensory nerves. Common synonyms include postherpetic neuralgia and zoster-related neurological involvement. The condition often involves the trigeminal nerve, thoracic, or lumbar regions, leading to pain, sensory loss, or motor deficits. It may present with neurological symptoms such as facial paralysis, motor weakness, or encephalitis, depending on the affected nerves.

Geniculate herpes zoster, also known as Ramsay Hunt syndrome, is a rare form of shingles caused by the reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) affecting the geniculate ganglion. It typically presents with a vesicular rash on the auricle and surrounding areas, accompanied by facial paralysis, often involving the seventh cranial nerve. Common synonyms include Ramsay Hunt syndrome and herpes zoster oticus. The condition primarily affects the ear, face, and oral cavity, with symptoms including ear pain, hearing loss, and vertigo. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals.

Postherpetic trigeminal neuralgia is a chronic neuropathic pain condition characterized by severe, lancinating facial pain following herpes zoster infection of the trigeminal nerve. It results from damage to the sensory nerve fibers of the trigeminal nerve, often due to varicella-zoster virus reactivation. Common synonyms include postherpetic neuralgia of the trigeminal nerve and post-shingles trigeminal neuralgia. The condition typically affects the second and third divisions of the trigeminal nerve, causing pain in the cheek, upper lip, and jaw areas.

Postherpetic polyneuropathy is a chronic neuropathy that develops after a herpes zoster infection, most commonly caused by varicella-zoster virus. It is characterized by persistent sensory abnormalities, including pain, paresthesias, and hypoesthesia, often in the distribution of the affected dermatome. Synonyms include postherpetic neuropathy and herpes zoster neuropathy. The condition typically affects the trunk, face, and extremities, with sensory involvement predominating. It is more common in older adults and those with impaired immune function.

Herpes zoster myelitis is a rare, severe inflammation of the spinal cord caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with prior shingles. The condition presents with spinal cord inflammation, leading to neurological deficits such as weakness, sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction. Common synonyms include postherpetic myelitis and zoster myelitis. The infection often affects the thoracic or lumbar spinal segments, resulting in transverse myelitis. Prompt antiviral therapy is critical to prevent long-term disability.

code_desc: herpes zoster with other nervous system complications
summary: Herpes zoster with other nervous system complications, also known as shingles with neurological involvement, is caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It typically presents as a painful rash along a single dermatome, often accompanied by neurological symptoms such as meningitis, encephalitis, or cranial nerve palsies. Commonly affected areas include the thoracic and trigeminal nerve distributions. Complications may involve sensory, motor, or autonomic dysfunction. Synonyms include zoster neuritis and postherpetic neuralgia with neurological sequelae. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and older adults.

Herpes zoster dermatitis of the eyelid, also known as ophthalmic herpes zoster or shingles of the eyelid, is a viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It presents as a painful, unilateral rash with vesicles along the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, commonly affecting the eyelid, forehead, and orbital regions. The condition may lead to complications such as conjunctivitis, keratitis, or uveitis. It typically occurs in individuals with compromised immunity or those who have had prior varicella infection. Synonyms include herpes zoster ophthalmicus and zoster sine herpete.

Herpes zoster keratoconjunctivitis is a viral infection caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV) affecting the eye. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with prior chickenpox. The infection involves the trigeminal nerve and manifests as a painful rash on the face, often accompanied by conjunctivitis and corneal involvement. Common synonyms include herpes zoster ophthalmicus and ocular herpes zoster. The condition primarily affects the conjunctiva, cornea, and sometimes the eyelids, potentially leading to severe complications such as corneal ulceration and vision loss.

Herpes zoster iridocyclitis is an inflammatory eye condition caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), typically affecting the trigeminal nerve. It presents with anterior uveitis, often accompanied by herpes zoster ophthalmicus rash on the forehead and scalp. Common synonyms include herpes zoster uveitis and VZV-associated iridocyclitis. The condition primarily affects the cornea, iris, and ciliary body, leading to symptoms such as pain, redness, photophobia, and blurred vision. Prompt treatment with antiviral and corticosteroid therapy is essential to prevent complications like glaucoma and corneal scarring.

code_desc: herpes zoster with other ophthalmic complications
summary: Herpes zoster with other ophthalmic complications refers to ocular involvement caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), leading to conditions such as keratitis, uveitis, and optic neuritis. Common synonyms include herpes zoster ophthalmicus and Ramsay Hunt syndrome when facial nerve involvement occurs. The virus reactivates in sensory ganglia, typically affecting the trigeminal nerve distribution. Commonly affected areas include the eyelids, cornea, conjunctiva, and retina. Complications may result in vision loss if not promptly treated with antiviral therapy and supportive care.

code_desc: otitis externa due to herpes zoster
summary: Otitis externa due to herpes zoster is a secondary infection of the external auditory canal caused by varicella-zoster virus. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with prior herpes zoster infection. The condition presents with ear pain, itching, and discharge, often accompanied by vesicular rash. Common synonyms include herpes zoster otitis externa. The causative agent is herpes zoster virus, and the primary affected area is the external ear canal, sometimes extending to the tympanic membrane.

code_desc: herpes zoster with other specified complications
summary: Herpes zoster with other specified complications refers to shingles complicated by additional clinical manifestations beyond the typical rash and neuralgia. Caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV), it commonly affects the trigeminal, thoracic, or lumbar dermatomes. Synonyms include zoster with complications or postherpetic neuralgia with secondary issues. Complications may involve ocular, neurological, or visceral involvement. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or older adults. Early treatment with antivirals can reduce severity and prevent long-term sequelae.

Herpes zoster with unspecified complication refers to a reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) leading to shingles, accompanied by an unspecified secondary complication. Common synonyms include postherpetic neuralgia or zoster-related complications. The virus, VZV, typically affects the trigeminal nerve, thoracic dermatomes, or other sensory ganglia. Commonly affected areas include the face, chest, and limbs. Complications may involve neurological, ocular, or visceral involvement, though the specific nature is not specified in this classification.

code_desc: herpes zoster without mention of complication
summary: Herpes zoster, also known as shingles, is a viral infection caused by the reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in previously infected individuals. It presents as a painful, unilateral dermatomal rash with vesicles, typically affecting the trunk, face, or extremities. Common synonyms include shingles and zona. The condition is characterized by neuralgia and may follow a previous varicella infection. It is more prevalent in older adults and immunocompromised individuals. The rash usually resolves within 2–4 weeks, though postherpetic neuralgia can occur. No complications are mentioned in this description.

Eczema herpeticum is a severe viral infection characterized by a widespread, painful rash with fluid-filled blisters, typically occurring in patients with pre-existing atopic dermatitis. Caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1, it presents as confluent, crusted lesions on previously inflamed skin. Common synonyms include herpes gestationis and eczema herpeticum. The face, scalp, and flexural areas are typically affected. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt antiviral therapy to prevent complications such as keratitis or encephalitis.

Genital herpes, unspecified, is a viral infection characterized by recurrent painful blisters or sores on the genital or anal regions. It is caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), primarily HSV-1 and HSV-2. Common synonyms include herpes genitalis and genital herpes infection. The condition typically affects the vulva, penis, scrotum, anus, and surrounding areas. It is highly contagious and often presents with prodromal symptoms such as itching or tingling before lesion formation. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity.

Herpetic vulvovaginitis is a viral infection affecting the vulva and vagina, primarily caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 may also be involved. It presents with painful, clustered vesicles and ulcers, often accompanied by itching and burning. Common synonyms include genital herpes and recurrent genital herpes. The infection typically affects the vulva, vagina, and perianal area, with a predilection for females. It is transmitted through sexual contact and can lead to recurrent outbreaks. Complications may include neonatal herpes if transmitted during childbirth.

Herpetic ulceration of the vulva is a painful, acute genital infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-2. It presents as clusters of small, shallow ulcers or vesicles on the vulvar skin and mucosa. Synonyms include genital herpes and primary herpes infection. The condition typically affects the vulva, perineum, and sometimes the rectum. It is characterized by fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy during the initial episode. Recurrent episodes may occur with less severe symptoms. Transmission occurs through direct contact with active lesions. Diagnosis is often clinical, confirmed by viral culture or PCR. Treatment includes antiviral therapy to reduce severity and frequency.

Herpetic infection of the penis, also known as genital herpes or penile herpes, is a viral infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 can also be a cause. It presents with painful vesicular lesions, often accompanied by itching, burning, and flu-like symptoms. The infection typically affects the glans, shaft, and surrounding areas of the penis. It is highly contagious and recurrent episodes are common. Transmission occurs through direct sexual contact. Complications may include urethritis, lymphadenopathy, and increased risk of HIV transmission.

Other genital herpes refers to herpes infections affecting the genital area caused by herpes simplex viruses other than HSV-1 or HSV-2. Common synonyms include recurrent genital herpes or genital herpes infection. The primary causative agents are HSV-1 and HSV-2, though HSV-1 is increasingly associated with genital infections. The condition typically affects the vulva, penis, anus, and surrounding perineal areas. It presents with painful blisters, ulcers, and flu-like symptoms, often recurring due to latent viral activity. Transmission occurs through direct contact during outbreaks or asymptomatic shedding.

Herpetic gingivostomatitis is a highly contagious viral infection primarily affecting young children. Caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), it presents with painful oral ulcers, gingival inflammation, and vesicles. Common synonyms include acute herpetic stomatitis and gingivitis herpetica. The infection typically involves the oral mucosa, gums, and lips, with systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Transmission occurs via direct contact with lesions or saliva. Complications are rare but may include secondary bacterial infections. The condition is self-limiting, resolving within 7–14 days without specific treatment.

Herpetic meningoencephalitis is a severe central nervous system infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1. It involves inflammation of the meninges and brain parenchyma. Symptoms include fever, headache, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. The condition typically affects the temporal and frontal lobes. Synonyms include HSV encephalitis and viral meningoencephalitis. It predominantly occurs in immunocompromised individuals or neonates, with HSV-1 being the primary causative agent. Prompt antiviral therapy is critical to prevent mortality and neurological sequelae.

code_desc: herpes simplex with unspecified ophthalmic complication
summary: Herpes simplex with unspecified ophthalmic complication refers to ocular involvement caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1, leading to inflammation of the eye structures. Common synonyms include herpes keratitis or herpetic eye infection. The condition primarily affects the cornea, conjunctiva, and sometimes the uvea. It can result in pain, redness, photophobia, and visual impairment. Complications may include scarring, ulceration, or glaucoma. The infection often follows a prodromal phase with systemic symptoms before ocular manifestations. Prompt antiviral treatment is essential to prevent severe sequelae.

Herpes simplex dermatitis of the eyelid is an inflammatory skin condition caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1. It presents as a red, swollen, and sometimes painful rash on the eyelid, often with vesicles. Synonyms include herpes keratoconjunctivitis and herpetic blepharitis. The infection typically affects the periorbital area, including the eyelid and surrounding skin. It may spread to the eye, causing conjunctivitis. Immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk. The condition is contagious and often resolves with antiviral therapy.

Dendritic keratitis is a corneal infection characterized by branching, tree-like epithelial infiltrates, typically caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). It is a form of herpetic keratitis, often presenting with epithelial ulceration, photophobia, and tearing. Common synonyms include herpetic dendritic ulcer and HSV keratitis. The condition primarily affects the cornea, with involvement of the epithelium and, in severe cases, the stroma. It commonly occurs in immunocompetent individuals, often following a prodromal episode of herpes labialis. Prompt antiviral treatment is essential to prevent corneal scarring and vision loss.

Herpes simplex disciform keratitis is a chronic, recurrent corneal inflammation caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). It presents as a well-demarcated, elevated, infiltrative lesion on the cornea, often with a disc-like appearance. The condition typically affects the central or paracentral cornea and may lead to scarring and visual impairment. Common synonyms include discoid keratitis and HSV disciform keratitis. It is a hallmark of recurrent herpetic eye disease, often associated with prior herpes simplex infection. The anterior stroma is primarily involved, with possible involvement of the endothelium in severe cases.

Herpes simplex iridocyclitis is an inflammatory eye condition caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1. It affects the anterior uvea, including the iris and ciliary body, leading to symptoms such as pain, redness, photophobia, and blurred vision. Common synonyms include acute herpes keratoconjunctivitis and HSV uveitis. The infection often results from reactivation of latent virus in the trigeminal nerve. It predominantly affects the eye, with potential complications like glaucoma, cataracts, and corneal scarring. Prompt antiviral treatment is essential to prevent vision loss.

code_desc: herpes simplex with other ophthalmic complications
summary: Herpes simplex with other ophthalmic complications refers to ocular infections caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1, leading to conditions such as herpetic keratitis, uveitis, and retinitis. Common synonyms include herpes keratitis and ocular herpes. The infection primarily affects the cornea, conjunctiva, and uvea, potentially causing severe vision loss if untreated. Complications may involve epithelial defects, stromal scarring, and secondary glaucoma. The virus is transmitted through direct contact with infected secretions. Prompt antiviral treatment is essential to prevent progression and preserve visual function.

Herpetic septicemia is a severe systemic infection caused by herpesviruses, most commonly herpes simplex virus (HSV) or varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It is characterized by widespread inflammation, necrosis, and septic shock. Common synonyms include herpes septicemia and viral septicemia. The condition typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs, with a high mortality rate if untreated. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to multi-organ failure. Clinical presentation includes fever, rash, and systemic toxicity. Prompt antiviral therapy is essential for survival.

Herpetic whitlow is a painful, vesicular skin infection of the fingers or toes caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1. It presents as clusters of small, fluid-filled blisters, often accompanied by redness, swelling, and tenderness. The infection typically results from autoinoculation of oral HSV-1 or direct contact with an infected sore. Common synonyms include digital herpes and herpetic whitlow. It predominantly affects the fingers, particularly the thumb and index finger, and may occur in individuals with compromised immune systems or those who frequently handle contaminated objects.

Visceral herpes simplex refers to infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) affecting internal organs. Common synonyms include herpes hepatitis and visceral HSV infection. The primary causative agents are HSV-1 and HSV-2, though HSV-1 is more frequently associated with visceral involvement. This condition typically affects the liver, lungs, and central nervous system, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Clinical manifestations may include fever, hepatitis, pneumonia, and encephalitis. Diagnosis is often confirmed through viral culture, PCR, or serology. Treatment involves antiviral therapy with acyclovir or related agents.

Herpes simplex meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1. It typically presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. The infection often spreads from a localized herpes lesion, frequently in the orofacial region. It can lead to complications such as encephalitis or hydrocephalus. Common synonyms include HSV meningitis or primary herpes meningitis. The central nervous system, particularly the brain and meninges, is the primary affected area. Prompt antiviral therapy is essential to prevent severe outcomes.

Herpes simplex otitis externa is a rare, severe form of external ear canal infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1. It presents with intense pain, erythema, swelling, and purulent discharge in the ear canal. Common synonyms include herpes-related otitis externa or HSV otitis externa. The condition predominantly affects the external auditory canal, often in immunocompromised individuals. It may lead to complications such as tympanic membrane perforation or hearing loss if untreated.

Herpes simplex myelitis is an inflammatory condition of the spinal cord caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1 or HSV-2. It is a rare but serious complication of herpes infection, often occurring in immunocompromised individuals. The disease presents with spinal cord inflammation, leading to motor and sensory deficits, often affecting the thoracic or lumbar regions. Common synonyms include HSV myelitis or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) when associated with viral infections. Clinical features include fever, back pain, and progressive neurological dysfunction. Early diagnosis and antiviral therapy are critical to prevent severe disability.

code_desc: herpes simplex with other specified complications
summary: Herpes simplex with other specified complications refers to infections caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1 or HSV-2, that present with additional clinical manifestations beyond the typical skin or mucosal lesions. Common synonyms include herpes simplex virus infection with systemic involvement or generalized herpes. The condition may affect the skin, mucous membranes, eyes, and occasionally the central nervous system, leading to complications such as encephalitis, keratitis, or disseminated infection in immunocompromised individuals.

Herpes simplex with unspecified complication refers to an infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1 or HSV-2, leading to lesions that have developed into an unspecified secondary complication. Common synonyms include herpes simplex infection with complication or HSV-related complications. The condition commonly affects the oral or genital mucosa, but may involve other sites. Complications may include secondary bacterial infections, scarring, or systemic spread, though the specific nature is not detailed. It is often associated with immunocompromised individuals or recurrent episodes.

code_desc: herpes simplex without mention of complication
summary: Herpes simplex is a viral infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), primarily HSV-1 and HSV-2. It presents as recurrent, painful, fluid-filled blisters on mucocutaneous surfaces. Common synonyms include cold sores and fever blisters. The infection typically affects the lips, mouth, and genital areas. HSV-1 is more commonly associated with oral infections, while HSV-2 is predominantly linked to genital herpes. The condition is characterized by prodromal symptoms followed by vesicle formation, ulceration, and healing. Transmission occurs through direct contact with lesions or bodily fluids.

Postmeasles encephalitis is a rare but severe neurological complication that occurs following measles infection, typically within 3 to 21 days after recovery. It is characterized by inflammation of the brain, leading to symptoms such as fever, seizures, altered mental status, and coma. The causative agent is the measles virus, which may directly invade the central nervous system. Common synonyms include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), though SSPE is a chronic progressive form. The condition primarily affects the brain, particularly the temporal and frontal lobes, and can lead to irreversible neurological damage.

Postmeasles pneumonia is a respiratory complication that occurs following recovery from measles. It typically develops 1–2 weeks after the initial infection and is characterized by inflammation of the lung parenchyma. Common synonyms include measles pneumonia and post-rubella pneumonia. The primary causative agent is the measles virus, though secondary bacterial infections such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae may contribute. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to symptoms like cough, fever, and dyspnea. It is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals.

Postmeasles otitis media is a secondary middle ear infection that occurs following measles virus infection. It is characterized by inflammation and fluid accumulation in the middle ear, often leading to hearing loss and tympanic membrane changes. Common synonyms include post-measles serous otitis media and measles-associated otitis media. The causative agent is the measles virus, which predisposes the middle ear to bacterial superinfections, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. It typically affects the middle ear and tympanic membrane, with symptoms emerging weeks after the resolution of the acute measles illness.

Measles keratoconjunctivitis is an ocular complication of measles infection, characterized by conjunctival injection and corneal involvement. It occurs due to the measles virus, which affects the conjunctiva and cornea, leading to inflammation. Common synonyms include acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, though the latter is more commonly associated with adenovirus. The condition typically affects the eyes, with the cornea and conjunctiva being the primary sites of involvement. It is more prevalent in children and can occur during the prodromal phase of measles.

Measles with other specified complications refers to measles infection complicated by additional clinical manifestations beyond the typical rash and systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include measles with secondary infections or measles with sequelae. The causative agent is the measles virus, a paramyxovirus. Typically affected body parts include the respiratory tract, eyes, and skin. Complications may involve pneumonia, encephalitis, otitis media, and diarrhea. The condition is more severe in malnourished or immunocompromised individuals, and can lead to long-term health issues or mortality if not managed appropriately.

Measles with unspecified complication refers to a severe manifestation of measles characterized by complications beyond the typical rash, fever, and cough. Common synonyms include measles with complications or complicated measles. Caused by the measles virus (rubeola virus), it typically affects the respiratory system, skin, and immune system. Complications may include pneumonia, encephalitis, or secondary bacterial infections. The condition primarily affects children but can occur in unvaccinated individuals of any age. It is a reportable disease and can lead to significant morbidity and mortality if not managed promptly.

Measles is an acute viral infection caused by the measles virus (Morbillivirus), primarily affecting the respiratory tract and skin. It presents with fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis, and a characteristic maculopapular rash that begins at the hairline and spreads downward. Koplik spots may appear on the oral mucosa. The disease is highly contagious and typically affects children, though susceptible adults can also be infected. Common synonyms include rubeola. The rash usually resolves within a week, and recovery is generally complete in healthy individuals.

Rubella with unspecified neurological complication refers to a rare manifestation of rubella infection involving the nervous system. Caused by the rubella virus, it typically occurs in children and can lead to various neurological symptoms such as encephalitis, meningitis, or cerebellar ataxia. Common synonyms include congenital rubella syndrome with neurological involvement and rubella-associated encephalopathy. The central nervous system is predominantly affected, with potential involvement of the brain and spinal cord. The condition is more severe in immunocompromised individuals and can result in long-term neurological deficits.

Encephalomyelitis due to rubella is a rare but severe neurological complication of rubella virus infection, primarily affecting the central nervous system. It involves inflammation of both the brain (encephalitis) and the spinal cord (myelitis). Common synonyms include rubella encephalitis and rubella myelitis. The causative agent is the rubella virus, which is transmitted via respiratory droplets. The condition typically affects the cerebrum, cerebellum, and spinal cord, leading to symptoms such as fever, seizures, and motor dysfunction. It is more commonly seen in young children and immunocompromised individuals.

Rubella with other neurological complications refers to neurological manifestations occurring in conjunction with rubella infection, typically in congenital cases. Caused by the rubella virus, it can lead to encephalitis, meningitis, or microencephaly. Common synonyms include congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) and German measles with neurological involvement. The central nervous system is predominantly affected, with potential involvement of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Other complications may include hearing loss, cataracts, and cardiac anomalies. The condition is most severe when infection occurs during the first trimester of pregnancy.

Arthritis due to rubella, also known as post-rubella arthritis or rubella-associated arthritis, is a rare complication following rubella infection. It is caused by the rubella virus, which can trigger an immune-mediated inflammatory response in joints. The condition typically affects small joints of the hands and feet, presenting as symmetric, non-erosive polyarthritis. Symptoms include joint pain, swelling, and stiffness, often occurring weeks after the initial viral infection. It is more common in women and usually resolves spontaneously without long-term joint damage. Synonyms include post-rubella arthritis and rubella-induced arthritis.

Rubella with other specified complications refers to the viral infection caused by the rubella virus, typically presenting with a maculopapular rash, low-grade fever, and lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include German measles and three-day measles. Complications may involve the eyes, ears, and central nervous system. Congenital rubella syndrome can occur if infected during pregnancy, affecting the fetus. The virus is transmitted via respiratory droplets. While most cases are mild, complications can lead to arthritis, encephalitis, or hearing loss. Vaccination with MMR is highly effective in prevention.

Rubella with unspecified complications refers to a viral infection caused by the rubella virus, typically presenting with a mild rash, fever, and lymphadenopathy. While generally mild in children, it can lead to various complications, particularly in pregnant women. Common synonyms include German measles or three-day measles. The virus primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and mucous membranes. Complications may involve the eyes, joints, and, in fetal cases, congenital rubella syndrome. The disease is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets. Vaccination is the most effective preventive measure.

Rubella, also known as German measles or three-day measles, is a viral infection caused by the rubella virus. It typically presents with a mild fever, conjunctivitis, and a fine, pink rash that begins on the face and spreads downward. The rash usually lasts for three days, hence the common name. The infection is most commonly seen in children and is characterized by swollen lymph nodes. It primarily affects the skin, eyes, and lymphatic system. The virus is transmitted via respiratory droplets. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine provides effective prevention.

Erythema infectiosum, also known as fifth disease, is a viral illness caused by human parvovirus B19. It primarily affects children and is characterized by a distinctive bright red rash on the cheeks, often described as a "slapped cheek" appearance, followed by a lacy rash on the trunk and limbs. The infection is contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets. Common symptoms include low-grade fever, headache, and mild cold-like symptoms. The rash may persist for weeks and can be exacerbated by sunlight or heat. It typically affects the skin and is more common in preschool and school-aged children.

"Other specified viral exanthemata" refers to acute, self-limiting skin rashes caused by viruses not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified viral exanthems or non-specific viral rashes. Causative agents may include enteroviruses, parvovirus B19, and other less commonly identified viruses. These eruptions typically affect the trunk, face, and extremities, presenting as maculopapular or morbilliform lesions. They are often accompanied by mild systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. The condition is commonly seen in children and resolves without specific treatment.

Viral exanthem, unspecified, refers to a rash caused by a viral infection without a specific etiology identified. Common synonyms include viral rash or exanthema. It is typically characterized by a maculopapular rash that may involve the trunk, face, and extremities. Common causative agents include enteroviruses, parvovirus B19, and adenoviruses. The rash is often accompanied by fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy. It is more common in children and usually resolves spontaneously without specific treatment.

Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease, is a viral illness primarily affecting young children. Caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) and occasionally HHV-7, it presents with a high fever followed by a rash. The rash typically appears after the fever subsides, consisting of pink or red maculopapular lesions on the trunk and neck. Common symptoms include mild respiratory signs and lymphadenopathy. The condition is generally self-limiting and affects infants and toddlers, with no specific treatment required.

code_desc: roseola infantum due to human herpesvirus 6
summary: Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease, is a viral illness caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) and occasionally HHV-7. It primarily affects young children, typically between 6 months and 2 years of age. The condition is characterized by a sudden high fever followed by a pinkish-red rash that appears after the fever subsides. The rash typically involves the trunk and may spread to the limbs. Other symptoms may include mild cough, runny nose, and irritability. The illness is generally self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment.

code_desc: roseola infantum due to human herpesvirus 7
summary: Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease, is a viral illness caused primarily by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) and less commonly by human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7). It predominantly affects young children, typically between 6 months and 2 years of age. The illness is characterized by a sudden high fever followed by a pinkish-red rash that appears after the fever subsides. The rash typically involves the trunk and spreads to the limbs, face, and neck. Other symptoms may include mild cough, runny nose, and irritability. The condition is generally self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment.

Orthopoxvirus infection, unspecified, refers to a group of viral infections caused by orthopoxviruses, including variola (smallpox), cowpox, and vaccinia. Common synonyms include smallpox, cowpox, and vaccinia infection. The virus typically affects the skin, causing characteristic vesicular or pustular rashes, and may involve the mucous membranes. Systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy are also common. While smallpox is eradicated, other orthopoxviruses remain endemic in certain regions. The infection is primarily transmitted through direct contact with infected lesions or respiratory droplets.

Monkeypox is a viral zoonotic disease caused by the monkeypox virus, a member of the Orthopoxvirus genus. It is also known as pox virus, monkeypox virus, or variola-like virus. The illness typically presents with fever, headache, lymphadenopathy, and a characteristic vesicular rash that progresses through various stages. The rash commonly affects the face, mouth, and genital areas, and may spread to other parts of the body. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected animals or humans, or via contaminated materials. The disease is generally self-limiting, with symptoms resolving within 2–4 weeks.

Other orthopoxvirus infections refer to illnesses caused by orthopoxviruses other than variola (smallpox) and monkeypox. Common synonyms include camelpox, cowpox, and vaccinia. These infections are typically caused by viruses such as cowpox virus, monkeypox virus, and variola virus. The primary affected body parts include the skin, with characteristic vesicular or pustular lesions, often on the hands, face, and mucous membranes. Systemic symptoms like fever and lymphadenopathy may also occur. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected animals or humans, and some viruses are zoonotic in nature.

Parapoxvirus infection, unspecified, is a viral disease caused by members of the Parapoxvirus genus, including orf virus and pseudocowpox virus. It typically presents as cutaneous lesions, often on the face or hands, characterized by papules, vesicles, and pustules. The infection is usually self-limiting and more common in animals, though human cases can occur through direct contact. Common synonyms include orf, contagious pustular dermatitis, and pseudocowpox. It predominantly affects the skin and mucous membranes, with lesions often resolving without scarring.

Bovine stomatitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the oral mucosa of cattle, characterized by ulcerative lesions and discomfort. Common synonyms include oral ulceration and mouth rot. The primary causative agents are infectious pathogens such as *Pasteurella multocida*, *Streptococcus spp.*, and *Actinobacillus spp.*, often associated with trauma or stress. The condition typically affects the tongue, lips, and hard palate, leading to reduced feed intake and weight loss. It is commonly seen in calves and young cattle, particularly in crowded or unsanitary conditions.

Sealpox is a rare, non-contagious skin condition characterized by the formation of painless, firm nodules or cysts, typically on the face, neck, and upper trunk. It is also known as epidermal inclusion cyst or pilar cyst. The condition is caused by the accumulation of keratin within a closed sac, often due to blocked hair follicles. It is not associated with any known infectious agent and is generally benign. Common synonyms include epidermal cyst and pilar cyst. The lesions are typically slow-growing and may persist for years without treatment.

Other parapoxvirus infections are a group of viral diseases caused by various parapoxviruses, including orf, pseudorabies, and bovine papular stomatitis virus. These infections typically present as cutaneous lesions characterized by papules, vesicles, or pustules. Common synonyms include orf virus infection and pseudorabies. The lesions most commonly affect the face, lips, and hands, often resulting from direct contact with infected animals. These infections are generally self-limiting but can cause significant discomfort and secondary bacterial infections if left untreated.

Yatapoxvirus infection, unspecified, refers to a viral illness caused by members of the Yatapoxvirus genus, which is part of the Poxviridae family. Common synonyms include yateapox and yateapox-like virus infection. The causative agents are typically Yatapoxvirus species, though specific strains may not be identified. The infection primarily affects the skin, causing characteristic rashes and lesions. It may also involve the mucous membranes. The disease is generally self-limiting, though symptoms can vary in severity. It is more commonly reported in tropical regions and is often associated with animal exposure.

Tanapox is a rare, self-limiting viral infection caused by the Tanapoxvirus, a member of the Poxviridae family. It is characterized by a brief, localized skin eruption, typically presenting as a single or multiple discrete papules or vesicles. The condition is often mistaken for chickenpox or molluscum contagiosum. Common synonyms include "tanapox virus infection" and "tanapox disease." It primarily affects the skin, with lesions commonly appearing on the face, trunk, and extremities. The disease is more prevalent in tropical regions and is transmitted through direct contact with infected skin or bodily fluids.

Yaba monkey tumor virus, also known as simian type D retrovirus or SDRV, is a retrovirus that primarily affects non-human primates. It is associated with the development of tumors, particularly in the oral cavity and lymphoid tissues. The virus is transmitted through bodily fluids and can cause malignancies such as fibrosarcomas. While it is not known to infect humans, it serves as a model for studying retrovirus-induced cancers. The condition is rare and typically observed in captive primates.

Other poxvirus infections refer to a group of viral diseases caused by poxviruses other than variola (smallpox) or molluscum contagiosum. Common synonyms include orthopoxvirus infections. Causative agents include cowpox, monkeypox, and vaccinia viruses. These infections typically present with characteristic skin lesions, often starting as papules or vesicles, and may involve the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the lymph nodes. They are commonly transmitted through direct contact with infected animals or humans, and symptoms range from mild to severe depending on the virus and host immunity.

Poxvirus infections, unspecified, refer to illnesses caused by various poxviruses without specific identification of the virus type. Common synonyms include variola, molluscum, or cowpox infections. These infections are typically caused by members of the Poxviridae family, such as Variola virus, Molluscum contagiosum virus, or Orthopoxvirus. The primary affected body parts include the skin, where characteristic vesicular or pustular lesions develop. Systemic involvement may occur in severe cases, particularly with variola. Clinical manifestations vary depending on the specific virus but often include fever, malaise, and cutaneous eruptions.

Sylvatic yellow fever is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes species mosquitoes in forested areas. It is also known as jungle yellow fever. The virus affects the liver, leading to jaundice, liver failure, and hemorrhagic symptoms. Common synonyms include forest yellow fever and viral hemorrhagic fever. The disease typically affects the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, with severe cases resulting in multi-organ failure and high mortality. It is endemic in parts of Africa and South America.

Urban yellow fever is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. It is characterized by fever, headache, muscle pain, and fatigue, progressing to jaundice and multi-organ failure in severe cases. Common synonyms include yellow fever and African yellow fever. The disease typically affects the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, leading to hemorrhagic manifestations. It is endemic in tropical regions of Africa and South America. Vaccination is the most effective preventive measure.

Yellow fever, unspecified, is an acute viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The disease typically affects the liver, causing jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and potentially severe hepatic necrosis. Common synonyms include yellow fever, jaundice, and hepatic hemorrhagic fever. Symptoms include fever, chills, headache, muscle pain, and in severe cases, bleeding and multi-organ failure. The condition predominantly affects the liver and can lead to systemic complications.

Japanese encephalitis is a viral central nervous system infection caused by the Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected Culex mosquitoes. The disease primarily affects the brain, leading to inflammation and potential severe neurological complications. Common synonyms include Japanese B encephalitis and St. Louis encephalitis-like disease. It predominantly affects children and is endemic in Asia, with the brain being the main target organ.

Western equine encephalitis is a viral disease caused by the western equine encephalitis virus, a member of the Togaviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis. Common synonyms include equine encephalitis virus and western horse encephalitis. Symptoms include fever, headache, and neurological manifestations. It typically affects the brain and spinal cord, with potential complications such as seizures and coma. The disease is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals.

Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) is a severe viral encephalitis caused by the eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV), transmitted primarily through mosquito bites. It belongs to the Togaviridae family and is endemic in the eastern United States and parts of Canada. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain. Common synonyms include EEE and eastern equine encephalitis virus infection. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological manifestations, including seizures, coma, and death. The virus is most commonly found in birds, which serve as amplifying hosts.

St. Louis encephalitis (SLE) is a viral infection caused by the St. Louis encephalitis virus, a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected Culex mosquitoes. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis or meningitis. Common synonyms include St. Louis encephalitis virus infection and flavivirus encephalitis. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological manifestations, including confusion, seizures, and coma. The disease typically affects the brain, particularly the cerebral cortex and cerebellum. It is more common in older adults and can result in long-term neurological disability or death.

Australian encephalitis, also known as Murray Valley encephalitis, is a viral infection caused by the Murray Valley encephalitis virus, a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, primarily from the Culex annulirostris species. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain (encephalitis). Common symptoms include fever, headache, confusion, and seizures. It predominantly affects the brain and spinal cord, with severe cases potentially resulting in coma or death. The condition is endemic to northern Australia and is more common during the wet season.

California virus encephalitis is a rare viral infection affecting the central nervous system, primarily caused by the California encephalitis virus, a member of the Togaviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, particularly those of the Culex species. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, and neurological symptoms such as confusion and seizures. It predominantly affects the brain, leading to encephalitis, and occasionally the spinal cord. Common synonyms include California encephalitis and Western equine encephalitis, though the latter refers to a related but distinct virus. The condition is more prevalent in rural areas of the western United States.

Other specified mosquito-borne viral encephalitis refers to encephalitic illnesses caused by viruses transmitted primarily by mosquitoes, excluding more commonly recognized types like Japanese encephalitis or West Nile virus. Common synonyms include mosquito-borne encephalitis and arboviral encephalitis. Causative agents vary by region and include viruses such as Dengue, Chikungunya, and Zika. These infections typically affect the central nervous system, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, and in severe cases, seizures or coma. The disease primarily targets the brain and spinal cord, with systemic involvement possible in severe instances.

Mosquito-borne viral encephalitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the brain caused by viruses transmitted through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis and arboviral encephalitis. Causative agents may include members of the Flaviviridae and Bunyaviridae families, such as West Nile virus, dengue virus, and Japanese encephalitis virus. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, and in severe cases, seizures or coma. It typically targets the brain and spinal cord.

Russian spring-summer encephalitis, also known as taiga encephalitis, is a viral infection caused by flaviviruses, primarily the western equine encephalitis virus. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, particularly in forested areas. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain. Common symptoms include fever, headache, and neurological deficits. It predominantly affects children and young adults, with a higher incidence during spring and summer. The condition can progress to severe encephalitis, potentially resulting in long-term neurological complications or death.

Louping ill is a severe, often fatal, viral disease primarily affecting sheep, though it can also infect other animals and humans. Caused by the louping ill virus, a member of the Flaviviridae family, it is transmitted by ticks. The disease is characterized by fever, neurological symptoms, and high mortality. In humans, it is also known as sheep plague or tick fever. Commonly affected body parts include the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis, and the respiratory system. The condition is typically seen in regions where the tick vector is prevalent.

Central European encephalitis (CEE), also known as tsutsugamushi disease or scrub typhus, is a viral infection caused by the genus Orientia, primarily O. tsutsugamushi. It is transmitted to humans via the bite of infected chiggers, which are larval mites. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to fever, headache, confusion, and potentially severe encephalitis. Commonly affected body parts include the brain and meninges. It is endemic in rural areas of Central and Eastern Europe, as well as parts of Asia. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent complications.

Other specified tick-borne viral encephalitis refers to viral infections of the central nervous system transmitted by ticks, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) variants. Causative agents include flaviviruses such as tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV) and others. The condition primarily affects the brain and spinal cord, leading to inflammation. It is typically seen in endemic regions with tick exposure, often presenting with fever, headache, and neurological symptoms.

Tick-borne viral encephalitis, unspecified, is a central nervous system infection caused by flaviviruses transmitted primarily through tick bites. Common synonyms include tick-borne encephalitis and TBE. The causative agents include tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV), which belongs to the Flaviviridae family. The infection typically affects the brain and spinal cord, leading to inflammation. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological complications. It is more common in endemic regions of Europe and Asia. The disease can progress to meningitis, encephalitis, or myelitis.

code_desc: viral encephalitis transmitted by other and unspecified arthropods
summary: Viral encephalitis transmitted by other and unspecified arthropods refers to inflammation of the brain caused by viruses spread through arthropod vectors not classified as mosquitoes or ticks. Common synonyms include arthropod-borne viral encephalitis. Causative agents may include viruses such as West Nile virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and others depending on the vector. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, and seizures. It typically targets the brain and spinal cord, with severity varying based on the virus and immune status of the host.

Crimean hemorrhagic fever (CHF), also known as Congo virus disease, is a severe viral illness caused by the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV), a member of the Bunyaviridae family. It primarily affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhagic symptoms, organ failure, and high mortality. The virus is transmitted through tick bites or contact with infected animal blood. Commonly affected body parts include the liver, spleen, and kidneys, with systemic involvement leading to coagulopathy and multi-organ dysfunction. Symptoms include fever, hemorrhage, and shock.

Omsk hemorrhagic fever is an acute viral illness caused by the Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It is characterized by fever, hemorrhagic manifestations, and systemic involvement. Common synonyms include Omsk virus hemorrhagic fever and Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus infection. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to capillary leakage and bleeding. It commonly involves the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes, with potential complications such as shock and multi-organ failure. Transmission occurs via infected rodents, primarily the bank vole. The illness is endemic in parts of Russia and Siberia.

Kyasanur forest disease (KFD), also known as monkey fever or chikungunya-like fever, is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Kyasanur forest disease virus (KFDV), a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected ticks, particularly *Haemaphysalis spinigera*. The disease typically affects the lymph nodes, liver, and spleen, causing fever, headache, muscle pain, and in severe cases, hemorrhage and multi-organ failure. It is endemic to parts of India, particularly the Western Ghats.

Other tick-borne hemorrhagic fever refers to a group of viral infections transmitted through tick bites, characterized by fever, hemorrhagic manifestations, and multi-system involvement. Common synonyms include tick-borne viral hemorrhagic fevers. Causative agents include species such as *Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus*, *Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus*, and *Siberian tick typhus virus*. These infections primarily affect the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy, organ dysfunction, and potentially severe hemorrhage. The disease typically involves the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, with symptoms ranging from mild flu-like illness to life-threatening systemic failure.

Mosquito-borne hemorrhagic fever is a severe viral infection characterized by fever, bleeding, and organ failure. Common synonyms include dengue fever and yellow fever. Caused by viruses such as Dengue virus, Yellow fever virus, and Zika virus, it is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, liver, and hematopoietic tissues, leading to coagulopathy and multi-organ dysfunction. It predominantly impacts tropical and subtropical regions, with high morbidity and mortality in severe cases.

"Other specified arthropod-borne hemorrhagic fever" refers to hemorrhagic fever syndromes caused by arthropod-transmitted viruses not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include "other arboviral hemorrhagic fever." Causative agents may include viruses such as Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus, Kyasanur forest disease virus, and others. The condition typically affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhage, fever, and systemic inflammation. It primarily impacts the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, with symptoms ranging from mild flu-like illness to severe multi-organ failure. Transmission occurs via arthropod vectors like ticks and mosquitoes.

Arthropod-borne hemorrhagic fever, unspecified, refers to a group of viral infections transmitted by arthropod vectors, characterized by fever, hemorrhagic symptoms, and multi-organ involvement. Common synonyms include viral hemorrhagic fever and arthropod-transmitted hemorrhagic fever. Causative agents may include viruses such as dengue, yellow fever, and others, though the specific agent is unspecified. The condition typically affects the vascular system, liver, and kidneys, leading to coagulopathy and organ failure. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Phlebotomus fever, also known as sandfly fever or visceral leishmaniasis, is a vector-borne illness caused by *Leishmania* parasites transmitted through the bite of infected *Phlebotomus* sandflies. It primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. The disease can manifest as cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral leishmaniasis, with visceral form being the most severe. Common synonyms include kala-azar and black fever. It predominantly affects tropical and subtropical regions, with the liver, spleen, and bone marrow being the main involved organs.

Tick-borne fever, also known as bovine anaplasmosis or tropical tick fever, is an infectious disease primarily affecting cattle. It is caused by the bacterium *Anaplasma marginale*, transmitted through tick bites. The disease leads to fever, anemia, jaundice, and sometimes death. It primarily affects red blood cells, causing hemolytic anemia. Commonly affected body parts include the liver and spleen, which may show enlargement. The condition is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions where ticks are endemic.

Venezuelan equine fever (VEF), also known as Venezuelan horse sickness or equine encephalosis, is an acute viral disease caused by the Venezuelan equine encephalomyelitis virus (VEEV), a member of the alphavirus genus. It primarily affects horses, causing high fever, neurological signs, and often death. Humans may develop flu-like symptoms, though severe cases are rare. The virus is transmitted by mosquitoes, particularly those of the *Culex* and *Aedes* genera. The central nervous system is typically affected, leading to encephalitis in both animals and humans.

Other mosquito-borne fever refers to a group of infectious diseases transmitted by mosquitoes, characterized by fever as a primary symptom. Common synonyms include arboviral fever and vector-borne fever. Causative agents vary and may include viruses such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and West Nile virus. These illnesses typically affect the systemic circulation, lymphatic system, and central nervous system. Symptoms often include fever, headache, myalgia, and rash. The condition primarily impacts tropical and subtropical regions, with varying severity and potential for complications.

West Nile fever, unspecified, is a viral illness caused by the West Nile virus (WNV), primarily transmitted through mosquito bites. It typically presents with flu-like symptoms such as fever, headache, and body aches. Common synonyms include West Nile virus infection and West Nile fever. The virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family and is mainly spread by Culex species mosquitoes. The disease primarily affects the bloodstream and central nervous system, though most infections are mild and self-limiting. Rarely, it can progress to severe neurological complications like encephalitis or meningitis, predominantly affecting older adults.

West Nile fever with encephalitis is a viral illness caused by the West Nile virus (WNV), primarily transmitted through mosquito bites. It ranges from mild flu-like symptoms to severe neurological complications. Common synonyms include West Nile virus infection and West Nile encephalitis. The virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family. Typically, it affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain (encephalitis) and spinal cord (myelitis). Symptoms may include fever, headache, fatigue, and in severe cases, seizures, coma, or death. The disease predominantly affects older adults and immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: west nile fever with other neurologic manifestation
summary: West Nile fever with other neurologic manifestations is a viral infection caused primarily by the West Nile virus (WNV), transmitted through mosquito bites. It can progress to severe neurological illness, including encephalitis or meningitis. Common synonyms include West Nile virus infection and West Nile neuroinvasive disease. The virus affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and in severe cases, paralysis or coma. Typically affected body parts include the brain, spinal cord, and meninges. Complications may involve muscle weakness, vision loss, and long-term neurological deficits.

code_desc: west nile fever with other complications
summary: West Nile fever is a viral illness caused by the West Nile virus (WNV), primarily transmitted through mosquito bites. It can lead to a range of complications, including encephalitis, meningitis, and paralysis. Common synonyms include West Nile virus infection and West Nile encephalitis. The virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family and is typically associated with fever, headache, and muscle pain.
