Rabies is a viral infection caused by the rabies virus, primarily transmitted through the bite of an infected animal. It affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and ultimately fatal outcomes if untreated. Common synonyms include hydrophobia and furious rabies. The virus is neurotropic, targeting the brain and spinal cord. It is most commonly found in mammals such as dogs, bats, raccoons, and foxes. Symptoms include fever, anxiety, hallucinations, and paralysis. Once clinical signs appear, the disease is almost always fatal. Prompt post-exposure prophylaxis is critical for prevention.

Mumps orchitis is an inflammation of the testicle caused by the mumps virus, typically occurring in post-pubertal males following a mumps infection. It is a complication of viral mumps and usually presents with unilateral swelling, pain, and tenderness in the affected testis. Common synonyms include epididymo-orchitis due to mumps. The causative agent is the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus. The condition primarily affects the testes, with potential complications such as infertility. It is more common in adolescents and young adults who have not been vaccinated.

Mumps meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by the mumps virus, typically occurring as a complication of mumps infection. It presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. Common synonyms include viral meningitis due to mumps or mumps-associated meningitis. The causative agent is the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus. The central nervous system, particularly the meninges, is primarily affected. It usually affects children and adolescents, with a mild course and a favorable prognosis. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine significantly reduces its incidence.

Mumps encephalitis is a rare but serious complication of mumps virus infection, characterized by inflammation of the brain. It typically occurs in adolescents and adults. The causative agent is the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus. Common synonyms include acute mumps meningitis and mumps-induced encephalitis. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain, and may involve the meninges. Symptoms include fever, headache, confusion, and seizures. It is more common in post-pubertal individuals and can lead to long-term neurological sequelae if not promptly treated.

Mumps pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas that occurs as a complication of mumps virus infection. It typically presents with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The mumps virus, primarily transmitted via respiratory droplets, is the known causative agent. While rare, it can occur in both children and adults. The pancreas is the most commonly affected organ, though involvement of other organs may occur. Synonyms include post-mumps pancreatitis and mumps-associated pancreatitis. The condition is more common in males and often follows a febrile illness. Early diagnosis and supportive care are essential for management.

Mumps hepatitis is a rare complication of mumps infection, characterized by inflammation of the liver. It typically occurs in the post-acute phase of mumps and is more common in adults. The condition is caused by the mumps virus, which belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family. Common synonyms include mumps-induced hepatitis and viral hepatitis associated with mumps. The liver is the primary affected organ, though the condition may also involve the pancreas and other organs. Symptoms include jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and fatigue. It is generally self-limiting but requires monitoring for severe liver dysfunction.

Mumps polyneuropathy is a rare neurological complication following mumps infection, characterized by acute, often symmetric, peripheral neuropathy. It typically presents with weakness, sensory loss, and reflex changes, predominantly affecting the distal limbs. Common synonyms include post-mumps polyneuropathy and mumps-induced neuropathy. The causative agent is the mumps virus, though the exact pathogenic mechanism remains unclear. It primarily affects the motor and sensory nerves, with the lower extremities most commonly involved. The condition is usually self-limiting but may lead to prolonged disability in some cases.

Mumps with unspecified complication refers to mumps infection involving an organ or system other than the parotid glands, with the specific complication not identified. Common synonyms include mumps with extraparotid involvement or mumps with unspecified sequelae. The condition primarily affects the salivary glands, central nervous system, and male reproductive organs in adolescents and adults.

Mumps is a viral infection caused by the mumps virus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. It primarily affects the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands, leading to swelling and tenderness. Common synonyms include epidemic parotitis and parotiditis. The disease is typically transmitted through respiratory droplets. Symptoms include fever, headache, and muscle aches, with the characteristic swelling of the parotid glands on one or both sides. It predominantly affects children but can occur in adults. The infection is usually self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment.

Ornithosis with pneumonia, also known as psittacosis or parrot fever, is a zoonotic infection caused by *Chlamydia psittaci*. It primarily affects the respiratory system, leading to pneumonia characterized by fever, cough, and respiratory distress. The disease is transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized particles from infected birds. Commonly affected body parts include the lungs and occasionally the liver and spleen. Symptoms may range from mild flu-like illness to severe pneumonia. Diagnosis is often confirmed through serological testing or PCR. Treatment typically involves antibiotics such as doxycycline or tetracycline.

Ornithosis with other specified complications refers to a zoonotic respiratory infection caused by *Chlamydia psittaci*, primarily transmitted through inhalation of infected bird droplets. Common synonyms include psittacosis and avian chlamydiosis. The disease typically affects the respiratory system, causing pneumonia, and may lead to systemic complications such as myocarditis, hepatitis, or encephalitis. Symptoms include fever, cough, and malaise. Complications may arise from untreated infection or immune response. Diagnosis involves serological testing and PCR. Treatment typically involves antibiotics like doxycycline.

Ornithosis with unspecified complication refers to a respiratory infection caused by *Chlamydophila psittaci*, typically acquired from contact with infected birds. Ornithosis, unspecified, is a zoonotic respiratory infection caused by *Chlamydia psittaci*. Common synonyms include psittacosis and parrot fever. The respiratory tract is the primary affected area, though systemic involvement can occur. Diagnosis is often confirmed through serology or PCR. Treatment typically involves antibiotics such as doxycycline or tetracyclines. The condition can range from mild to severe, with complications including pneumonia and systemic spread.

Herpangina is a viral infection characterized by fever and painful ulcers in the mouth. Common synonyms include acute necrotizing ulcerative pharyngitis. It is most commonly caused by enteroviruses, particularly coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71. The condition typically affects children, with lesions appearing on the soft palate, uvula, and tonsillar areas. Symptoms include sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and malaise. It is highly contagious, spreading through respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces. The illness is usually self-limiting, resolving within 7–10 days without specific treatment.

Epidemic pleurodynia, also known as pleurisy or epidemic myalgia, is an acute viral infection characterized by severe, sharp chest pain due to inflammation of the pleura. Caused primarily by Coxsackievirus B, it may also involve other enteroviruses. The condition typically affects the chest wall and surrounding muscles, causing episodic, stabbing pain that may radiate to the abdomen. Symptoms include fever, muscle aches, and respiratory discomfort. It is more common in adolescents and young adults, with outbreaks often occurring in community settings. The illness is self-limiting, resolving within days to weeks without specific treatment.

Coxsackie carditis, unspecified, is a viral myocarditis caused by coxsackievirus, typically serotypes A or B. It presents with inflammation of the heart muscle, leading to symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis, coxsackie virus myocarditis, and enteroviral myocarditis. The condition primarily affects the myocardium, and may involve the pericardium or endocardium. It is more common in children and young adults, often following a viral infection. The exact pathogenesis involves immune-mediated damage following viral infection.

Coxsackie pericarditis is an inflammatory condition of the pericardium caused by coxsackievirus, a member of the enterovirus family. It typically presents with chest pain, fever, and pericardial effusion. Common synonyms include viral pericarditis and enteroviral pericarditis. The infection is usually self-limiting and affects the heart's outer lining. It is more common in children and young adults, often following a viral upper respiratory infection. Complications such as constrictive pericarditis may occur if left untreated.

Coxsackie endocarditis is a rare, acute inflammatory condition affecting the inner lining of the heart chambers, primarily caused by coxsackievirus B, a member of the enterovirus family. The condition is often associated with fever, heart murmurs, and systemic symptoms. Though uncommon, it may occur in immunocompromised individuals or following viral infections. Synonyms include viral endocarditis and enteroviral endocarditis. The myocardium and valves are most commonly affected.

Coxsackie myocarditis is an inflammatory condition of the myocardium caused by coxsackievirus, a member of the enterovirus family. It typically affects the heart muscle and is often associated with viral infections, particularly in children. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis and enteroviral myocarditis. The condition may present with symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It is more commonly seen in males and can lead to complications like heart failure or cardiomyopathy if left untreated. The virus primarily targets the myocardial cells, leading to inflammation and impaired cardiac function.

Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a viral infection characterized by fever, oral ulcers, and vesicular rashes on the hands, feet, and mouth. Common synonyms include herpangina and oral-vesicular disease. Caused primarily by enteroviruses, most commonly coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71. Typically affects children under 10 years old. The infection is highly contagious, spreading through respiratory droplets, fecal-oral route, and contact with contaminated surfaces. Symptoms usually resolve within 7–10 days without specific treatment.

code_desc: other specified diseases due to coxsackie virus

Infectious mononucleosis, also known as mono or glandular fever, is a viral infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). It commonly affects adolescents and young adults. The condition is typically self-limiting, though recovery can take several weeks. It is transmitted through saliva, hence the nickname "kissing disease." Rarely, complications such as airway obstruction or splenic rupture may occur.

Trachoma, initial stage, is a chronic bacterial infection of the conjunctiva caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It begins with mild conjunctival inflammation, follicular conjunctivitis, and episodic tearing. Common synonyms include inclusion conjunctivitis or trachomatous conjunctivitis. The infection primarily affects the upper eyelid margins and conjunctiva, leading to scarring and potential corneal complications if untreated. It is prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and limited access to clean water.

Trachoma, active stage, is a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It affects the conjunctiva and cornea of the eye, leading to inflammation, scarring, and potential blindness. Common synonyms include granuloma inguinale and lymphogranuloma venereum, though these refer to different stages or forms of the infection. The condition typically affects the eyelids, conjunctiva, and cornea, with symptoms including redness, itching, and discharge. It is prevalent in areas with poor hygiene and limited access to clean water.

Trachoma, unspecified, is a chronic infectious eye disease caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It leads to inflammation of the conjunctiva and eyelids, resulting in scarring and potential corneal opacity. Common synonyms include blinding trachoma and granulomatous conjunctivitis. The infection typically affects the conjunctiva, eyelids, and cornea, with recurrent episodes leading to trichiasis and visual impairment. It is prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and limited access to healthcare.

Inclusion conjunctivitis is an acute bacterial infection of the conjunctiva, commonly caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It presents with redness, discharge, and subepithelial inclusion bodies in affected cells. Common synonyms include neonatal conjunctivitis and chlamydial conjunctivitis. The infection primarily affects the conjunctiva and can involve the cornea, leading to potential scarring. It is most commonly seen in newborns due to perinatal transmission, but can also occur in adults through sexual contact. Prompt treatment with antibiotics is essential to prevent complications.

Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is a highly contagious viral conjunctivitis characterized by inflammation of the conjunctiva and cornea. Common synonyms include acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis and pharyngoconjunctival fever. Caused primarily by adenovirus types 8, 19, 37, and 55, it often presents with redness, watery discharge, photophobia, and subepithelial corneal infiltrates. The infection typically affects the eyes, with involvement of the conjunctiva and cornea, and may spread to the pharynx. It is prevalent in community settings and spreads through direct contact or contaminated surfaces.

Pharyngoconjunctival fever is a viral illness characterized by fever, sore throat, and conjunctivitis. Common synonyms include epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and pool fever. Caused primarily by adenovirus types 3, 4, and 7, it is highly contagious. The infection typically affects the pharynx, conjunctiva, and occasionally the respiratory tract. Symptoms often develop 2–10 days after exposure and may include malaise and lymphadenopathy. The illness is self-limiting, with resolution usually occurring within 7–14 days. It is common in children and outbreaks often occur in communal settings like schools or swimming pools.

Other adenoviral conjunctivitis refers to a form of conjunctivitis caused by adenoviruses other than those typically associated with epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC). Common synonyms include non-EKC adenoviral conjunctivitis and atypical adenoviral conjunctivitis. The causative agents are adenovirus serotypes 3, 4, 7, and 14, among others. This condition primarily affects the conjunctiva and may involve the cornea, leading to symptoms such as redness, itching, and watery discharge. It is usually self-limiting but can cause significant discomfort and is highly contagious through direct contact.

Epidemic hemorrhagic conjunctivitis is an acute, highly contagious viral conjunctivitis characterized by inflammation and bleeding of the conjunctiva. Common synonyms include hemorrhagic conjunctivitis and epidemic conjunctivitis. Caused primarily by enterovirus 70 and coxsackievirus A24, it is also associated with other adenoviruses. The condition typically affects the eyes, causing redness, swelling, and subconjunctival hemorrhages. It often spreads rapidly in communities, particularly in warm, humid climates, and is more common in children. Systemic symptoms are usually mild, and the infection resolves spontaneously within 7–14 days.

Other viral conjunctivitis refers to inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by viruses other than adenovirus. Common synonyms include acute infectious conjunctivitis and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. Causative agents may include enteroviruses, herpes simplex virus, and varicella-zoster virus. The condition typically affects the eyes, causing redness, itching, and watery discharge. It is highly contagious and often presents with bilateral involvement. The cornea may be affected in some cases, leading to epithelial keratitis. The infection is usually self-limiting but may require supportive care and isolation to prevent spread.
