It is more prevalent in young children and can progress to trachoma if untreated. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected secretions. The condition is a leading cause of preventable blindness in developing regions.

code_desc: unspecified diseases of conjunctiva due to viruses
summary: Unspecified diseases of conjunctiva due to viruses refer to inflammatory conditions of the conjunctiva caused by viral agents, where the specific virus is not identified. Common synonyms include viral conjunctivitis, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, and acute viral conjunctivitis. Causative agents may include adenoviruses, herpes simplex virus, and enteroviruses. The condition typically affects the conjunctiva, sometimes involving the cornea. It is characterized by redness, irritation, and watery discharge, often with a prodromal phase of systemic symptoms. Transmission occurs via direct contact or airborne routes.

Molluscum contagiosum is a viral skin infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of the poxvirus family. It presents as small, raised, pearly papules with a central dimple, often containing a cheesy core. Common synonyms include molluscum virus and poxvirus infection. The condition is highly contagious, spread through direct contact. It typically affects the face, neck, arms, and trunk, especially in children and immunocompromised individuals. Lesions may resolve spontaneously over months to years without scarring.

Viral warts, unspecified, are benign skin growths caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). Common synonyms include common warts, plantar warts, and flat warts. The condition typically affects the hands, feet, and face, with plantar warts often found on the soles. Transmission occurs through direct contact with the virus. While generally asymptomatic, warts may cause discomfort or itching. Treatment options include topical agents, cryotherapy, and surgical removal. The exact HPV type varies by lesion type, but HPV subtypes 1, 2, 4, and 7 are frequently implicated.

Condyloma acuminatum, also known as genital warts, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 and 11. It presents as soft, flesh-colored papules or cauliflower-like growths, typically appearing on the genitalia, perianal region, and sometimes the mouth. The condition is highly contagious, spreading through direct skin-to-skin contact. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to complications such as dysplasia or malignancy in persistent infections.

Plantar wart is a viral infection caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 1, 2, and 4. It typically appears on the soles of the feet, especially between the toes, and presents as a hard, rough lesion with a central black dot resembling a seed. Common synonyms include verruca plantaris and plantar verruca. The condition is contagious and spreads through direct skin contact or via contaminated surfaces. It is more prevalent in individuals with compromised immune systems or those who walk barefoot in public areas.

"Other specified viral warts" refers to warts caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that do not fit into the more commonly recognized categories such as common warts, plantar warts, or genital warts. Synonyms include flat warts and filiform warts. These warts are typically caused by HPV types 3, 10, 28, and 4. They commonly affect the face, neck, and hands, and are more prevalent in children and adolescents. The lesions are small, flat, and flesh-colored, often appearing in clusters. Transmission occurs through direct skin contact. Treatment options include cryotherapy, topical agents, and laser therapy.

Sweating fever, also known as fever with excessive sweating or hyperhidrosis with fever, is a condition characterized by elevated body temperature accompanied by profuse sweating. It may occur as a symptom of various underlying infections or systemic illnesses. Common causative agents include viral infections such as influenza, bacterial infections like typhoid fever, and parasitic diseases. The condition typically affects the entire body, with sweating most prominent on the face, neck, and trunk. It is often associated with chills, fatigue, and malaise, and may indicate a more severe systemic process requiring medical evaluation.

Cat-scratch disease, also known as lymphadenopathy due to *Bartonella henselae*, is a bacterial infection transmitted through cat scratches or bites. Common synonyms include lymphadenopathy caused by *Bartonella henselae* and cat scratch fever. The causative agent is *Bartonella henselae*, a gram-negative bacillus. The infection typically affects the lymph nodes, most commonly in the axilla, neck, and groin. Symptoms include fever, malaise, and localized lymphadenopathy. It primarily affects children and immunocompetent adults, with a benign course in most cases. Complications are rare but may include ocular or central nervous system involvement.

Foot and mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious viral infection affecting cloven-hoofed animals. Caused by the foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV), it leads to severe oral and hoof lesions. Common synonyms include mouth and foot disease and vesicular disease. The virus belongs to the *Picornaviridae* family and has multiple serotypes. Clinical signs include fever, blisters, and lameness. The disease primarily affects cattle, pigs, sheep, and goats, with lesions commonly found in the mouth, feet, and udders. It is a major concern for livestock industries due to its rapid spread and economic impact.

Cytomegaloviral disease is a viral infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It typically presents as a mild, self-limiting illness in immunocompetent individuals but can lead to severe complications in immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients. Common synonyms include congenital CMV infection and CMV mononucleosis. The virus primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, with common involvement of the liver, spleen, lungs, and central nervous system. In congenital cases, it may cause hearing loss, visual impairment, and microcephaly.

Hemorrhagic nephrosonephritis is a rare, severe kidney disorder characterized by inflammation and bleeding in the renal parenchyma. It often presents with hematuria, proteinuria, and renal dysfunction. Common synonyms include hemorrhagic urethritis and hemorrhagic glomerulonephritis. The condition is typically caused by infections such as streptococcal or staphylococcal organisms, or by systemic diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus. It primarily affects the kidneys, particularly the glomeruli and tubules, leading to acute renal failure if left untreated.

Arenaviral hemorrhagic fever is a severe viral illness characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. Caused by arenaviruses, it includes diseases such as Lassa fever and Argentine hemorrhagic fever. Common synonyms include Lassa fever and Machupo fever. The virus primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy and bleeding. It also impacts the liver, kidneys, and immune system. Transmission occurs via rodent vectors, with human-to-human spread possible in certain cases. The disease progresses rapidly, often resulting in high mortality if untreated.

Epidemic vertigo is a term used to describe outbreaks of vertigo affecting multiple individuals within a community, often linked to viral infections. Common synonyms include epidemic vestibular neuritis and viral-induced vertigo. It is typically caused by viruses such as herpes simplex virus, influenza, and enteroviruses. The condition primarily affects the inner ear and vestibular system, leading to symptoms like dizziness, imbalance, and nausea. It commonly impacts the posterior semicircular canal and can involve the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem. The disease is more prevalent in adults and can spread through respiratory or close contact routes.

code_desc: other specified diseases due to chlamydiae
summary: "Other specified diseases due to chlamydiae" refers to infections caused by chlamydial organisms that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include chlamydial infections or chlamydial disease. Causative agents include *Chlamydia trachomatis*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, and *Chlamydia psittaci*. These infections typically affect the respiratory tract, eyes, and genital tract. They may present with symptoms such as pneumonia, conjunctivitis, or urethritis. The condition is often asymptomatic or presents with non-specific symptoms, requiring diagnostic testing for confirmation.

code_desc: other specified diseases due to viruses
summary: "Other specified diseases due to viruses" refers to viral infections that do not fit into more specific categories and are classified based on clinical presentation. Common synonyms include unspecified viral infections or viral diseases not otherwise specified. Causative agents vary widely and may include herpesviruses, flaviviruses, or picornaviruses. These conditions typically affect the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or neurological systems, depending on the virus involved. Symptoms range from mild fever and rash to severe systemic illness. Diagnosis is often based on clinical features and laboratory testing.

code_desc: adenovirus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
summary: Adenovirus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site refers to adenovirus-related illness not specifically categorized under other systemic or localized conditions. Common synonyms include acute respiratory disease and pharyngitis. Caused by adenoviruses, which are non-enveloped DNA viruses, this infection typically affects the respiratory tract, eyes, and gastrointestinal system. It may present with fever, cough, sore throat, conjunctivitis, and diarrhea. While often mild, it can lead to more severe complications in immunocompromised individuals or young children. The infection is highly contagious and spreads via respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces.

code_desc: echo virus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
summary: Echo virus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site refers to infections caused by enteroviruses, specifically the echovirus group, when the specific clinical condition or affected site is not specified. Common synonyms include enterovirus infection and echovirus infection. Causative agents are echoviruses, which are part of the Picornaviridae family. These viruses typically affect the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, but can also involve the central nervous system, leading to a range of symptoms from mild to severe. The infection is often asymptomatic or presents with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, rash, and respiratory issues.

code_desc: coxsackie virus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
summary: Coxsackie virus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site refers to cases where the infection is attributed to coxsackieviruses but is classified under other diagnostic categories or the site of infection is not specified. Caused by enteroviruses, particularly coxsackievirus A and B, it typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the heart or nervous system. Common synonyms include hand, foot, and mouth disease and herpangina. The infection is often mild but can lead to complications in vulnerable populations.

code_desc: rhinovirus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
summary: Rhinovirus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site refers to rhinovirus-induced illness occurring in patients with pre-existing conditions or when the site of infection is not clearly specified. Common synonyms include common cold or viral upper respiratory infection. Caused by rhinoviruses, this infection primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, including the nose, throat, and bronchi. It is typically mild, self-limiting, and more common in children. Complications may arise in individuals with underlying respiratory conditions.

code_desc: human papillomavirus in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
summary: Human papillomavirus (HPV) in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site refers to HPV-related conditions not otherwise specified or categorized. Common synonyms include HPV infection of unspecified site. Causative agents are HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, and others. Typically affects skin and mucosal surfaces, including genital, oral, and anogenital regions. May present as warts or precancerous lesions. Often asymptomatic but can lead to benign or malignant transformations. Diagnosis is usually via histopathology or molecular testing. Management depends on site and severity, ranging from observation to surgical or ablative therapies.

Retrovirus, unspecified, refers to a group of viruses that use RNA as their genetic material and replicate via reverse transcription. These viruses can cause a range of diseases, though the specific type is not identified. Common synonyms include retroviral infection or RNA virus. Causative agents may include human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV), and others. Typically, these viruses affect the immune system, particularly CD4+ T cells, and can lead to conditions such as acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) or leukemia. The infection can also impact the central nervous system and other organs.

code_desc: human t-cell lymphotrophic virus, type i [htlv-i]
summary: Human T-cell lymphotrophic virus, type I (HTLV-I) is a retrovirus that primarily infects CD4+ T-cells. It is also known as human T-lymphotropic virus type I. The virus is associated with adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and tropical spastic paraparesis/HTLV-I-associated myelopathy. HTLV-I is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and from mother to child. Common synonyms include HTLV-1 and human T-lymphotropic virus type I. The infection typically affects the immune system, central nervous system, and hematopoietic tissues.

code_desc: human t-cell lymphotrophic virus, type ii [htlv-ii]
summary: Human T-cell lymphotrophic virus type II (HTLV-II) is a retrovirus belonging to the HTLV family. It is primarily associated with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy and can cause adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL) in some cases. HTLV-II is also known as human T-lymphotropic virus type II. The virus infects CD4+ T-cells and is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and from mother to child. It predominantly affects the lymphatic system and is more commonly found in certain geographic regions. While less oncogenic than HTLV-I, HTLV-II can contribute to immunosuppression and opportunistic infections.

Human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) is a lentivirus that primarily infects CD4+ T cells, leading to progressive immune system deterioration. It is less transmissible and causes a slower progression to AIDS compared to HIV-1. Common synonyms include HIV-2 and human immunodeficiency virus type 2. The causative agent is the HIV-2 virus. Typically, the infection affects the immune system, particularly CD4+ T cells, and can lead to opportunistic infections and malignancies in advanced stages.

"Other specified retrovirus" refers to retroviral infections not classified under more specific categories such as HIV or HTLV. It encompasses a variety of retroviruses that may cause immunodeficiency, malignancies, or other systemic conditions. Common synonyms include unspecified retroviral infection. Causative agents vary but may include lentiviruses or other retroviruses. These infections typically affect the immune system, leading to opportunistic infections and malignancies, and may involve the central nervous system, lymphatic system, and other organs. Diagnosis often requires molecular testing and clinical evaluation.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a common viral infection causing acute respiratory illness, particularly in infants and young children. It is also known as bronchiolitis or viral croup. Caused by the RSV virus, it primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, including the bronchioles, leading to inflammation and mucus production. Symptoms range from mild cold-like symptoms to severe bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Complications may include wheezing, apnea, and respiratory distress. The virus is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces.

Hantavirus infection is a viral disease caused by hantaviruses, primarily transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents. Common synonyms include hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), depending on the region and virus type. The disease typically affects the lungs and kidneys, leading to pulmonary edema and renal failure. Symptoms include fever, muscle pain, and in severe cases, respiratory distress. It is most commonly associated with Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Asia and Europe.

SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV) is a zoonotic RNA virus that causes severe acute respiratory syndrome. It primarily affects the respiratory system, leading to pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome. The virus is transmitted via respiratory droplets and has a high mortality rate. Common synonyms include SARS virus and SARS-CoV. The causative agent is SARS-CoV, which belongs to the Coronaviridae family. It was first identified in 2003 during an outbreak in China. The disease typically affects the lungs and can lead to systemic complications.

Parvovirus B19 is a single-stranded DNA virus causing fifth disease, erythema infectiosum, or slapped cheek syndrome. It primarily affects children, presenting with a characteristic rash on the face and truncal erythema. The virus infects erythroid progenitor cells, leading to transient aplastic crisis in individuals with hemolytic anemias. Common synonyms include human parvovirus B19 and parvovirus B19. It is transmitted via respiratory droplets. Typically affects the skin, bone marrow, and hematopoietic system.

"Other specified chlamydial infection" refers to chlamydial infections that do not meet the criteria for more specific categories, such as chlamydia trachomatis infections. It encompasses infections caused by Chlamydia species affecting various body systems. Common synonyms include unspecified chlamydial infection. The causative agent is typically Chlamydia trachomatis, though other species may be involved. These infections commonly affect the genital tract, respiratory system, and eyes, leading to conditions like conjunctivitis, pneumonia, and urethritis. The clinical presentation varies depending on the affected site.

"Other specified viral infection" refers to viral infections that do not meet the criteria for more specific diagnoses but are clinically significant. Common synonyms include unspecified viral infection or other viral infections. Causative agents vary widely and may include herpesviruses, adenoviruses, or enteroviruses. These infections typically affect the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or neurological systems. Symptoms may include fever, fatigue, and localized inflammation. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and laboratory testing when necessary.

Unspecified chlamydial infection refers to a clinical diagnosis where the infection is known to be caused by Chlamydia species but the specific site or type is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include chlamydial infection, unspecified. The causative agents are primarily *Chlamydia trachomatis* and *Chlamydia pneumoniae*. This condition can affect various body systems, including the respiratory tract, urogenital tract, and eyes. It is often asymptomatic or presents with nonspecific symptoms, making diagnosis challenging without targeted testing.

Unspecified viral infection refers to a clinical diagnosis given when the specific virus causing the illness is not identified. Common synonyms include viral syndrome or undetermined viral infection. Causative agents may include a wide range of viruses such as influenza, enteroviruses, or herpesviruses. Typically affecting the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or neurological systems, symptoms often include fever, fatigue, and systemic malaise. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and laboratory findings when specific testing is inconclusive or unavailable.

Louse-borne (epidemic) typhus is a severe acute febrile illness caused by *Rickettsia prowleai* transmitted via body lice. It is characterized by high fever, headache, rash, and systemic toxicity. Common synonyms include epidemic typhus and murine typhus. The disease primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and systemic organs. It predominantly occurs in impoverished populations with poor hygiene and overcrowding. Complications include pneumonia, meningitis, and multi-organ failure, with high mortality if untreated.

Murine (endemic) typhus is an acute febrile illness caused by *Rickettsia typhi* transmitted via infected fleas. Common synonyms include endemic typhus and murine typhus. The disease typically affects the systemic circulation and skin, with fever, headache, and a maculopapular rash being common symptoms. Lesions often appear on the trunk and extremities. It primarily occurs in areas with poor sanitation and rodent infestations. The infection is self-limiting in most cases but can lead to complications such as pneumonia or meningitis in severe instances.

Brill's disease, also known as acute interstitial nephritis, is a rapidly progressive kidney disorder characterized by inflammation of the renal interstitium. It is commonly caused by drug allergies, infections, or autoimmune reactions. The condition primarily affects the kidneys, leading to impaired renal function, hematuria, and proteinuria. Common synonyms include acute tubulointerstitial nephritis and drug-induced interstitial nephritis. It typically involves the renal tubules and interstitial cells, with potential complications such as acute renal failure. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent irreversible kidney damage.

Scrub typhus is an acute febrile illness caused by *Orientia tsutsugamushi*, transmitted via chiggers. Common synonyms include tsutsugamushi disease and scrub fever. It predominantly affects the skin, lymph nodes, and liver, with systemic involvement. Clinical features include fever, headache, rash, and eschar at the site of chigger bite. Complications may involve pneumonia, renal failure, and meningitis. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and serological testing. It is endemic in Asia, the Pacific Islands, and parts of Africa, with a higher prevalence in rural and agricultural areas.

Typhus, unspecified, is an acute febrile illness characterized by high fever, headache, and rash. It is caused by rickettsial bacteria transmitted primarily through lice or fleas. Common synonyms include epidemic typhus and scrub typhus, though the latter is caused by *Orientia tsutsugamushi*. The disease typically affects the skin, liver, and circulatory system, with systemic involvement. It is more common in areas with poor sanitation and overcrowding. Complications may include pneumonia, renal failure, and shock. Diagnosis is often clinical, supported by serology or PCR. Treatment involves antibiotics such as doxycycline.

Spotted fevers, also known as rickettsial infections, are a group of tick-borne diseases caused by bacteria of the genus Rickettsia. Common causative agents include Rickettsia rickettsii (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), Rickettsia conorii (Mediterranean spotted fever), and Rickettsia typhi (typhus). These infections typically present with fever, headache, and a characteristic rash, often with a macular or maculopapular appearance. The rash may include a central eschar at the site of the tick bite. Commonly affected body parts include the trunk, limbs, and face. The disease can progress to severe complications if untreated, affecting the cardiovascular and neurological systems.

Boutonneuse fever, also known as Mediterranean spotted fever or Rickettsia conorii fever, is an acute infectious disease caused by Rickettsia conorii. It is transmitted through the bite of infected ticks, primarily the brown dog tick. The disease typically affects the skin, causing characteristic eschars at the site of the tick bite, along with fever, headache, and malaise. Other common symptoms include rash, lymphadenopathy, and sometimes involvement of the liver and lungs. It predominantly affects individuals in Mediterranean regions and is more common in males. The infection can lead to complications if not treated promptly with appropriate antibiotics.

North Asian tick fever, also known as Siberian tick typhus or tsutsugamushi disease, is an acute infectious illness caused by *Orientia tsutsugamushi*. Transmitted through the bite of infected chigger mites, it primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and liver. Common symptoms include fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. The disease is endemic in forested regions of East Asia, particularly affecting individuals exposed to tick-infested environments. Complications may involve respiratory and neurological systems if left untreated.

Queensland tick typhus, also known as Queensland tick fever or Australian tick typhus, is a tick-borne infectious disease caused by *Rickettsia australis*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected *Ixodes holocyclus* ticks. The disease primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and liver, with characteristic symptoms including fever, headache, malaise, and a maculopapular rash. The rash typically begins on the trunk and spreads peripherally. The condition is endemic to eastern Australia and is more common in children and outdoor workers. Early diagnosis and treatment with doxycycline are essential to prevent complications.

Ehrlichiosis, unspecified, is a tick-borne infectious disease caused by bacteria of the genus *Ehrlichia*, most commonly *Ehrlichia chaffeensis* and *Ehrlichia ewingii*. It primarily affects white blood cells, leading to fever, headache, and malaise. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected ticks, particularly the lone star tick and American dog tick. Common synonyms include human monocytic ehrlichiosis and granulocytic ehrlichiosis, depending on the specific organism. It predominantly affects the bloodstream and immune system, with systemic involvement in severe cases.

Ehrlichiosis chafeensis is a tick-borne rickettsial infection caused by *Ehrlichia chaffeensis*. Commonly known as human monocytic ehrlichiosis, it primarily affects monocytes and is transmitted through the bite of infected lone star ticks. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, muscle pain, and leukopenia. It predominantly affects the monocytic lineage of white blood cells. Common synonyms include human monocytic ehrlichiosis and ehrlichiosis caused by *E. chaffeensis*. The infection is more prevalent in the southeastern United States.

Other ehrlichiosis refers to a group of tick-borne infectious diseases caused by various species of the Ehrlichia genus. Common synonyms include human monocytic ehrlichiosis and human granulocytic anaplasmosis. The causative agents include Ehrlichia chaffeensis and Ehrlichia phagocytophila. These infections primarily affect white blood cells, particularly monocytes and granulocytes. Symptoms typically include fever, headache, muscle pain, and leukopenia. The disease can involve multiple body systems, with systemic involvement common. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected ticks, most commonly the lone star tick and the black-legged tick.

Other specified tick-borne rickettsioses refer to rickettsial infections caused by species not classified under the primary categories such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever or scrub typhus. Common synonyms include atypical rickettsioses. Causative agents include Rickettsia conorii, Rickettsia aeschlimannii, and Rickettsia sibirica. These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, and systemic organs. Symptoms often include fever, rash, and systemic inflammation. The disease is transmitted through tick bites and is more prevalent in endemic regions.

Tick-borne rickettsiosis, unspecified, refers to infections caused by Rickettsia species transmitted through tick bites. Common synonyms include spotted fever and typhus-like illnesses. The causative agents may include Rickettsia rickettsii, Rickettsia conorii, and Rickettsia typhi. These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, and systemic organs. Symptoms often include fever, rash, headache, and muscle pain. The disease can lead to complications such as meningitis, pneumonia, and organ failure if untreated. It primarily affects the skin and systemic tissues, with the rash commonly appearing on the trunk and extremities.

Q fever is an acute or chronic zoonotic infection caused by *Coxiella burnetii*, a gram-negative bacterium. It is transmitted primarily through inhalation of contaminated aerosols, often from infected animals. Common synonyms include query fever and Queensland fever. The infection typically affects the lungs, causing pneumonia, and may involve the liver, leading to hepatitis. In chronic cases, endocarditis can develop. Symptoms include fever, headache, and muscle pain. It is more prevalent in agricultural settings and among individuals exposed to livestock.

Trench fever is a bacterial infection caused by *Bartonella quintana*, transmitted primarily through body lice. It is characterized by intermittent fever, severe headache, muscle pain, and a distinctive erythematous rash. Common synonyms include "trench mouth" or "war fever." The disease typically affects the reticuloendothelial system, with symptoms often resembling those of a severe flu. It predominantly occurs in individuals with poor hygiene or living in crowded conditions, such as soldiers or the homeless. The infection usually resolves spontaneously but may lead to complications like endocarditis if untreated.

Rickettsialpox is a mild, self-limiting infectious disease caused by the bacterium Rickettsia akari. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mites, primarily found in rodent-infested environments. Common synonyms include molluscum contagiosum-like disease and oriental spotted fever. The illness typically presents with a characteristic eschar at the site of the bite, followed by fever, headache, and lymphadenopathy. Skin lesions, often resembling molluscum, are commonly observed on the face, trunk, and extremities. The disease primarily affects the skin and lymphatic system, with rare involvement of other organs.

Other specified rickettsioses refer to rickettsial infections not classified under more specific categories such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever or typhus. Common synonyms include atypical rickettsioses. Causative agents include Rickettsia conorii, Rickettsia aeschlimannii, and Rickettsia sibirica. These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, and vascular system, presenting with fever, rash, and systemic inflammation. They are often transmitted via tick bites and can involve multiple organ systems. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and serological testing.

Rickettsiosis, unspecified, refers to infections caused by rickettsial organisms, a group of bacteria transmitted primarily by arthropods such as ticks and mites. Common synonyms include spotted fever and typhus group diseases. The causative agents include Rickettsia species, such as R. conorii and R. prowasekii. These infections typically affect the skin, vascular system, and internal organs, with symptoms ranging from fever and rash to more severe systemic involvement. The condition is often diagnosed based on clinical presentation and epidemiological factors when specific rickettsial species cannot be identified.

Falciparum malaria, also known as malignant tertian malaria, is a severe and potentially life-threatening infection caused by *Plasmodium falciparum*. It is characterized by high fever, chills, headache, and anemia, with complications such as cerebral malaria, renal failure, and hypoglycemia. The parasite primarily infects red blood cells, leading to sequestration in vital organs. Common synonyms include tertian malaria and falciparum infection. It predominantly affects the liver, red blood cells, and brain, with systemic involvement in severe cases.

Vivax malaria, also known as benign tertian malaria, is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium vivax*. It is characterized by periodic fever, chills, and sweating every 48 hours. The infection typically affects the liver and red blood cells. Common synonyms include tertian fever and benign malaria. *P. vivax* is the most common causative agent, though *P. ovale* may also be involved. The disease is generally less severe than other malaria types but can lead to relapses due to hypnozoites in the liver. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Quartan malaria is a form of malaria characterized by fever every fourth day, caused primarily by *Plasmodium vivax* and, less commonly, *P. malariae*. It is also known as tertian malaria, though this term is more commonly associated with *P. falciparum* and *P. ovale*. The disease primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to cyclical fever, chills, and sweating. While generally less severe than falciparum malaria, it can cause prolonged illness and complications such as anemia and splenomegaly.

Ovale malaria is a form of malaria caused by *Plasmodium ovale*, a less common parasitic protozoan. It is characterized by intermittent fever, chills, and headache, with symptoms typically recurring every other day. The parasite primarily infects red blood cells, leading to mild to moderate illness. It is often mistaken for *P. vivax* due to similar clinical features. Common synonyms include tertian malaria, though this term is more commonly associated with *P. vivax* and *P. malariae*. The disease predominantly affects the liver and red blood cells, with occasional involvement of the spleen. It is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

"Other malaria" refers to malaria caused by species of *Plasmodium* other than *P. falciparum*, *P. vivax*, *P. ovale*, or *P. malariae*. Common synonyms include non-falciparum malaria or tertian malaria. Causative agents include *P. knowlesi*, *P. malariae*, *P. ovale*, and *P. vivax*. The disease primarily affects the red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and anemia. It is typically transmitted through the bite of infected *Anopheles* mosquitoes. While generally less severe than falciparum malaria, it can still cause significant morbidity and is commonly found in Southeast Asia and parts of Africa.

Mixed malaria refers to an infection caused by the simultaneous presence of more than one species of Plasmodium in a host. Common synonyms include co-infection or compound malaria. The causative agents typically include Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae. This condition is most commonly observed in regions with high malaria transmission. The infection primarily affects the red blood cells, leading to symptoms such as fever, chills, and anemia. It can also involve the liver and other organs, depending on the species involved. Mixed malaria can complicate treatment and increase the risk of severe disease.

Malaria, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium species transmitted through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes. It primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and flu-like symptoms. Common synonyms include falciparum malaria, tertian malaria, and quartan malaria, though these refer to specific species. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. Without proper treatment, it can progress to severe complications such as cerebral malaria, anemia, and organ failure.

Induced malaria refers to the deliberate or accidental introduction of Plasmodium parasites into a host, typically for research or therapeutic purposes. Common synonyms include experimental malaria or artificial malaria. The causative agents are species of Plasmodium, most commonly P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae. The infection primarily affects the erythrocytes, leading to fever, chills, and anemia. It may also involve the liver and spleen. While generally used in controlled settings, it can mimic natural malaria and requires careful monitoring to prevent complications.

Blackwater fever is a severe complication of malaria, primarily caused by *Plasmodium falciparum*. It is characterized by the hemolysis of red blood cells, leading to the presence of free hemoglobin in the urine, giving it a dark, "blackwater" appearance. Common synonyms include hemoglobinuria and acute renal failure due to hemolysis. The condition typically affects the kidneys and red blood cells, and can result in acute kidney injury. It is often associated with the use of antimalarial drugs like primaquine in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)-deficient individuals.

Other pernicious complications of malaria refer to severe, life-threatening manifestations beyond typical fever and anemia. Common synonyms include severe malaria and complicated malaria. Causative agents are primarily *Plasmodium falciparum*, though other species may contribute. These complications often affect the brain (cerebral malaria), kidneys (acute renal failure), lungs (acute respiratory distress syndrome), and circulatory system (shock). They can also lead to multi-organ failure and are more common in young children, pregnant women, and immunocompromised individuals. Early recognition and prompt treatment are critical to prevent mortality.

Visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar, is a severe parasitic infection caused by *Leishmania donovani*, *L. infantum*, or *L. chagasi*. It primarily affects the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, leading to systemic inflammation and organ enlargement. Common symptoms include fever, weight loss, anemia, and lymphadenopathy. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies and is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. If left untreated, it can be fatal. Synonyms include visceral leishmaniasis and kala-azar.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis, urban, is a parasitic skin infection caused by *Leishmania* species transmitted through the bite of infected sand flies. Common synonyms include mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis. The disease primarily affects the skin, causing ulcerative lesions, often on the face, ears, and extremities. It is more prevalent in urban and peri-urban areas due to increased human-sand fly contact. The causative agents include *Leishmania braziliensis*, *L. mexicana*, and *L. viannae*. Lesions may progress to extensive tissue destruction and secondary bacterial infections if left untreated.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis, Asian desert, is a parasitic skin infection caused by *Leishmania* species, primarily *L. tropica* and *L. major*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. The disease presents as one or more ulcerative skin lesions, typically on exposed areas such as the face, arms, and legs. Common synonyms include oriental sore and tularaemia-like ulcer. Lesions are often painless, with a raised border and central necrosis. The infection is endemic in arid regions of Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa. Without treatment, lesions may heal spontaneously but can leave permanent scarring.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis, Ethiopian, is a parasitic skin infection caused primarily by *Leishmania aethiopica*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. The disease is endemic in parts of Ethiopia and other African regions. Clinically, it presents as one or more ulcerative skin lesions, often with a raised border and a necrotic center. Common synonyms include Ethiopian leishmaniasis and African cutaneous leishmaniasis. Lesions typically occur on exposed areas such as the face, arms, and legs. The infection may resolve spontaneously but can lead to scarring and disfigurement.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis, American, also known as diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis or mucosal leishmaniasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Leishmania mexicana* and *Leishmania braziliensis*. It primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and sometimes internal organs. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. Commonly affected areas include the face, ears, and mucosal surfaces. Lesions often present as nodules or ulcers, and the infection can lead to disfiguring skin damage. It is endemic in parts of Central and South America.

Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, also known as American leishmaniasis, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by *Leishmania braziliensis* and other *Leishmania* species. It primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, leading to ulcerative lesions on the nose, mouth, and face. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected sand flies. Clinically, it presents with non-healing sores and mucosal destruction, often resulting in disfiguring complications. It is endemic in tropical regions of the Americas.

Leishmaniasis, unspecified, is a parasitic disease caused by species of the genus *Leishmania*, transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. It encompasses various clinical forms, including cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral leishmaniasis, but the unspecified category may include cases where the specific type is not determined. Common synonyms include kala-azar and东方脓肿. The disease primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs, particularly the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Symptoms vary widely depending on the form and severity of the infection.

Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It primarily affects the heart, leading to cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and potentially heart failure. The disease is transmitted through the feces of infected triatomine bugs, blood transfusions, or from mother to child. Common synonyms include Chagas' disease and American trypanosomiasis. The heart is the most commonly affected organ, though the parasite can also involve the digestive tract, nervous system, and eyes. Chronic infection often results in progressive cardiac damage.

code_desc: chagas' disease with other organ involvement
summary: Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It primarily affects the heart, digestive system, and nervous system. The disease progresses through acute and chronic phases. In the chronic stage, it can lead to cardiomyopathy, megacolon, and megaesophagus. Other organ involvement may include liver and neurological complications. Common synonyms include Chagas' disease and Trypanosoma cruzi infection. Transmission occurs via triatomine bugs, blood transfusions, or vertical transmission. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent severe complications.

code_desc: chagas' disease without mention of organ involvement
summary: Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It is primarily transmitted through the feces of triatomine bugs, though other routes include blood transfusion and congenital transmission. The disease typically affects the heart, digestive system, and nervous system, but the clinical description here focuses on the acute phase. Common synonyms include Chagas' disease and American trypanosomiasis. The infection often begins with a localized lesion at the site of entry, followed by systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy.

Gambian trypanosomiasis, also known as human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) or sleeping sickness, is a parasitic disease caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense* and *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense*. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms such as sleep disturbances, confusion, and eventually coma. The disease progresses in two stages: an initial hemolymphatic phase and a later neurological phase. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, predominantly affecting rural populations.

Rhodesian trypanosomiasis, also known as African animal trypanosomiasis or nagana, is a parasitic disease caused by *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense*. It primarily affects domestic and wild animals, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. The infection is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The parasite invades the bloodstream and lymphatic system, leading to fever, anemia, and eventual organ failure. While rare in humans, it can occur and is more severe than human African trypanosomiasis. The disease is characterized by periodic fever and progressive neurological symptoms as the parasite crosses the blood-brain barrier.

African trypanosomiasis, unspecified, is a parasitic disease caused by species of *Trypanosoma*, primarily *T. brucei gambiense* and *T. brucei rhodesiense*. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The infection affects the bloodstream and central nervous system, leading to fever, headache, and eventually neurological symptoms. Common synonyms include sleeping sickness and trypanosomiasis. The disease predominantly affects sub-Saharan Africa, targeting the blood and nervous system.

Trypanosomiasis, unspecified, refers to infections caused by species of the protozoan genus *Trypanosoma*, typically transmitted by blood-sucking insects. Common synonyms include African sleeping sickness and Chagas disease, though the latter is caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms. It can also involve the lymphatic system and bloodstream. The causative agents include *T. brucei* and *T. cruzi*, among others. The disease is endemic in certain regions of Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East.

Relapsing fever, louse-borne, is a tick-borne spirochetal infection caused by *Borrelia recurrentis*. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of fever, headache, and muscle pain, often following louse infestation. Common synonyms include relapsing fever and louse fever. The disease primarily affects the bloodstream and lymphatic system, with systemic involvement leading to splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. Transmission occurs via the bite of infected body lice, and it is more prevalent in areas with poor hygiene and overcrowding. Complications may include anemia, meningitis, and circulatory collapse if untreated.

Relapsing fever, tick-borne, is an acute bacterial infection characterized by recurring fever episodes. Caused by *Borrelia* species, particularly *B. recurrentis*, it is transmitted via the bite of infected soft ticks. Common synonyms include tickborne relapsing fever and African relapsing fever. The infection primarily affects the bloodstream and lymphatic system, leading to systemic symptoms such as headache, myalgia, and arthralgia. It commonly involves the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes, and can progress to hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. The disease is prevalent in rural areas of Africa, the Middle East, and parts of South America.

Relapsing fever, unspecified, is a systemic infection characterized by recurring episodes of fever, typically caused by spirochetes of the genus *Borrelia*. Common synonyms include recurrent fever and relapsing spirochetal fever. The causative agents are primarily *Borrelia recurrentis* and *Borrelia persica*, though other species may be involved. The infection primarily affects the bloodstream and lymphatic system, leading to symptoms such as chills, headache, and muscle pain. It is transmitted through lice or ticks and commonly affects the lymph nodes, spleen, and liver. The disease course is marked by periods of fever followed by remission, hence the term "relapsing."

Bartonellosis is a group of bacterial infections caused by species of the genus Bartonella. Common synonyms include Carrion's disease and Mal de Ojo. The most well-known causative agents are Bartonella bacilliformis and Bartonella henselae. Bartonella bacilliformis primarily affects the blood and heart, leading to Oroya fever and verruga peruana, while Bartonella henselae causes cat-scratch disease, mainly affecting the lymph nodes. The infection is typically transmitted through insect vectors or direct contact with infected animals.

Lyme disease is an infectious illness caused by the bacterium *Borrelia burgdorferi*, transmitted through the bite of infected ticks. It is also known as Lyme borreliosis. Common synonyms include tick-borne relapsing fever and early Lyme disease. The disease typically affects the skin, joints, nervous system, and heart. Early symptoms include a characteristic erythema migrans rash, fever, fatigue, and joint pain. If untreated, it can lead to chronic complications such as arthritis, neurological issues, and cardiac abnormalities. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and serological testing. Treatment involves antibiotics, usually doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime.

Babesiosis is a parasitic infection caused by species of *Babesia*, primarily transmitted through tick bites. It primarily affects red blood cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. Common synonyms include babesial infection or babesial disease. The causative agents include *Babesia microti* and *Babesia divergens*, among others. It typically affects the liver, spleen, and bone marrow, and can cause fever, fatigue, and jaundice. Immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk for severe complications, including organ failure.

"Other specified arthropod-borne diseases, other" refers to infectious diseases transmitted by arthropods that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include vector-borne illnesses or arthropod-transmitted infections. Causative agents may include viruses, bacteria, or parasites such as those causing dengue, Lyme disease, or leishmaniasis. These diseases typically affect the skin, joints, nervous system, and internal organs, depending on the pathogen. Clinical presentations vary but often include fever, rash, joint pain, and systemic symptoms. Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation, serology, and sometimes molecular testing.

Arthropod-borne disease, unspecified, refers to illnesses transmitted by arthropods such as mosquitoes, ticks, or fleas, but without a specific identification of the pathogen or vector. Common synonyms include vector-borne disease or insect-borne illness. Causative agents may include viruses, bacteria, or parasites, though the exact agent is not specified. These diseases typically affect the skin, nervous system, and internal organs, with symptoms ranging from fever and rash to severe systemic involvement. The condition is often diagnosed based on clinical presentation and epidemiological context.

Early congenital syphilis, symptomatic, is a severe infection transmitted from an untreated syphilis-infected mother to her fetus. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically manifests within the first two years of life. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis and neonatal syphilis. The infection commonly affects the skin, mucous membranes, bones, and teeth, leading to characteristic lesions such as rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities. It may also involve the central nervous system, causing neurosyphilis. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent long-term complications.

Early congenital syphilis, latent refers to a stage of syphilis infection in infants where the disease is present but without active clinical manifestations. It occurs when a mother with syphilis transmits the infection to her fetus during pregnancy. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. This stage typically affects the bones, liver, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis, latent syphilis, and asymptomatic congenital syphilis. The condition may progress to active disease if untreated.

Early congenital syphilis, unspecified, refers to syphilis acquired by a fetus during pregnancy, typically presenting within the first two years of life. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it can affect multiple organ systems. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis and neonatal syphilis. The infection often involves the skin, mucous membranes, bones, and central nervous system. Symptoms may include rash, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, and skeletal abnormalities. It is a serious condition requiring prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent long-term complications.

Syphilitic interstitial keratitis is a late-stage ocular manifestation of syphilis, typically occurring in the tertiary phase. It is characterized by diffuse infiltration of the corneal stroma, leading to opacification and potential vision loss. The condition is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. Common synonyms include interstitial keratitis of syphilis and syphilitic keratitis. It primarily affects the cornea, often bilaterally, and may be associated with other systemic syphilitic lesions. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent irreversible corneal damage.

Juvenile neurosyphilis, unspecified, is a rare neurological complication of syphilis occurring in children. It results from Treponema pallidum infection that has progressed to the central nervous system. Common synonyms include congenital neurosyphilis and neurosyphilis in childhood. The condition typically affects the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as meningitis, seizures, and developmental delays. It is often associated with congenital syphilis but can also occur in children exposed postnatally. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and serological testing. Treatment typically involves penicillin-based antibiotics.

Congenital syphilitic encephalitis is a rare neurological complication of congenital syphilis, occurring when Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta and infects the fetal central nervous system. It typically presents in the neonatal period with symptoms such as seizures, irritability, and developmental delay. Common synonyms include congenital neurosyphilis and neonatal syphilitic encephalitis. The infection primarily affects the brain, leading to inflammation and potential long-term neurological deficits. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent severe morbidity.

Congenital syphilitic meningitis is a severe neurologic complication of congenital syphilis, occurring when *Treponema pallidum* infects the central nervous system of a fetus. It typically presents in the neonatal period with signs of meningeal inflammation. Common synonyms include neonatal syphilitic meningitis and congenital neurosyphilis. The infection can affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to complications such as hydrocephalus, cranial nerve palsies, and developmental delays. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent long-term neurological damage.

Other juvenile neurosyphilis refers to neurosyphilis occurring in children, typically secondary to congenital syphilis. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and presents with neurological manifestations such as meningitis, ataxia, and cranial nerve palsies. Common synonyms include congenital neurosyphilis and early neurosyphilis in children. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, with involvement of the brain, meninges, and spinal cord. Clinical features may include seizures, developmental delay, and cranial nerve abnormalities. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent long-term neurological damage.

Other late congenital syphilis, symptomatic refers to manifestations of syphilis that occur after the first year of life and are not classified as early or late congenital syphilis. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and typically presents with a variety of symptoms affecting multiple organ systems. Common synonyms include late congenital syphilis and symptomatic congenital syphilis. Affected body parts may include bones, teeth, skin, and internal organs such as the liver and spleen. The condition can lead to significant morbidity if left untreated.

Late congenital syphilis, latent, refers to a non-active stage of syphilis that occurs in infants born to mothers with untreated syphilis. It is characterized by the absence of active clinical manifestations but the presence of serological evidence of infection. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis in remission or latent congenital syphilis. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. This condition typically affects bones, teeth, and the central nervous system, with potential long-term complications if left untreated.

Late congenital syphilis, unspecified, is a manifestation of syphilis that develops years after birth in individuals infected during pregnancy. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it can present with a variety of systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis with late manifestations or late-stage congenital syphilis. Typically affects bones, teeth, skin, and internal organs. Characterized by gummas, skeletal abnormalities, and dental issues. May also involve neurological and ophthalmological complications. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and serological testing. Treatment involves penicillin therapy to prevent long-term disability.

Congenital syphilis, unspecified, refers to syphilis transmitted from an infected mother to her fetus during pregnancy. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it can lead to severe multisystem involvement. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis and neonatal syphilis. Typically affects the skin, bones, liver, and central nervous system. Symptoms may include rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities. Untreated, it can result in long-term complications or mortality. The condition is diagnosed through clinical findings and laboratory tests. Early treatment with penicillin is crucial to prevent severe sequelae.

Genital syphilis (primary) is an infectious disease caused by *Treponema pallidum*, a spirochete. It is characterized by the appearance of a painless, firm chancre at the site of infection, typically on the genitals, anus, or mouth. The lesion is usually solitary, round, and ulcerated, with indurated borders. Common synonyms include primary syphilis and hard chancre. The infection is transmitted through direct contact with a syphilitic sore. If left untreated, it can progress to secondary and tertiary stages, but primary syphilis is often asymptomatic or easily overlooked.

Primary anal syphilis is the initial stage of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically presents as a painless, ulcerative lesion at the site of infection, commonly affecting the anus, perianal area, or genitalia. Known synonyms include anal chancre or primary syphilis. The lesion is often solitary, firm, and indurated, with a clean base and no surrounding erythema. It is highly contagious and may resolve spontaneously, but without treatment, the infection progresses to secondary and tertiary stages. Transmission occurs primarily through sexual contact.

Other primary syphilis refers to the initial stage of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*, characterized by the appearance of a painless chancre at the site of infection. Common synonyms include primary syphilis and initial syphilis. The chancre typically develops 10–90 days post-exposure and is often found on the genitals, anus, or mouth. It is usually solitary, firm, and indurated. The condition is highly contagious and can progress to secondary syphilis if untreated. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent complications.

code_desc: secondary syphilis of skin or mucous membranes
summary: Secondary syphilis of skin or mucous membranes is a stage of syphilis characterized by a transient, widespread rash and mucosal lesions. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically occurs 2–12 weeks after initial infection. Common synonyms include eruptive syphilis and generalized syphilic eruption. The rash consists of non-pruritic, erythematous papules or plaques, often on the palms and soles. Mucous membrane involvement may present as painless ulcers in the mouth or genital areas. Lymphadenopathy is frequently present. This stage is highly contagious and may resolve spontaneously, but untreated cases can progress to tertiary syphilis.

Adenopathy due to secondary syphilis refers to the enlargement of lymph nodes as a manifestation of the systemic spread of *Treponema pallidum*. Common synonyms include lymphadenopathy in secondary syphilis. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. This condition typically affects lymph nodes in the head, neck, and axillae, often presenting as painless, firm, and non-tender swellings. It is part of the systemic dissemination phase of syphilis, occurring weeks after the primary chancre. The lymphadenopathy is often generalized and may be accompanied by other secondary symptoms such as rash and mucous membrane lesions.

Syphilitic uveitis, unspecified, is a form of uveitis caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. It occurs in the late stages of the disease, typically secondary or tertiary syphilis, and is characterized by inflammation of the uveal tract, including the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. Common synonyms include uveitis due to syphilis or ocular syphilis. The condition may also involve other ocular structures such as the retina and optic nerve, leading to vision loss if untreated. It is often associated with systemic manifestations of syphilis and requires prompt diagnosis and treatment with penicillin-based therapy.

Syphilitic chorioretinitis (secondary) is an ocular manifestation of secondary syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically presents as bilateral, diffuse chorioretinal inflammation with serpiginous or geographic lesions. Common synonyms include syphilitic retinochoroiditis and secondary syphilitic retinochoroiditis. The condition primarily affects the retina and choroid, often involving the posterior pole. It is associated with systemic syphilis and may occur 6–12 weeks after primary infection. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent progression and visual loss.

Syphilitic iridocyclitis (secondary) is an inflammatory condition of the anterior uvea, occurring during the secondary stage of syphilis. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. Common synonyms include secondary syphilitic uveitis and iridocyclitis. The condition typically affects the iris and ciliary body, leading to symptoms such as pain, photophobia, and blurred vision. It often presents with a hypopyon and posterior synechiae. The disease may involve multiple organs, but ocular manifestations are a hallmark of secondary syphilis. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent progression and complications.

Secondary syphilitic periostitis is a bone inflammation associated with secondary syphilis, characterized by periosteal new bone formation and sometimes bone destruction. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically affects the long bones, particularly the tibia and fibula, and may involve the skull and jaw. Synonyms include syphilitic osteitis and periostitis secondary to syphilis. Clinically, it presents with pain, swelling, and sometimes sinus tracts. Diagnosis is confirmed through serologic testing and imaging, with treatment involving penicillin-based antibiotics.

Secondary syphilitic hepatitis is a rare manifestation of syphilis occurring during the secondary stage of the infection. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and presents with liver involvement characterized by elevated transaminases and sometimes jaundice. Common synonyms include syphilitic hepatitis and hepatic involvement in secondary syphilis. The condition typically affects the liver, but may also involve the skin, mucous membranes, and lymph nodes. It is often associated with other secondary syphilitic symptoms such as rash and mucous patches. Diagnosis requires serological testing for syphilis and clinical evaluation. Treatment with penicillin is effective.

Secondary syphilis of other viscera refers to the dissemination of *Treponema pallidum* beyond the skin and mucous membranes to internal organs. Common synonyms include systemic syphilis and generalized secondary syphilis. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. Typically, it affects the liver, spleen, bones, and central nervous system. Symptoms may include fever, malaise, and organ-specific manifestations. It occurs weeks to months after primary infection and is often accompanied by a rash and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis involves serological tests and clinical evaluation.

Secondary syphilis relapse refers to the recurrence of symptoms following a previous episode of secondary syphilis, typically after treatment with penicillin. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. Common synonyms include recurrent secondary syphilis or syphilis relapse. Symptoms often include skin rashes, mucocutaneous lesions, and systemic manifestations such as fever and lymphadenopathy. The rash commonly affects the palms, soles, and trunk, while mucous membranes in the mouth and genital areas are frequently involved. Relapse may occur if treatment is incomplete or if the patient is re-exposed to the organism.

Acute syphilitic meningitis (secondary) is a neurological complication of secondary syphilis, typically occurring 2-10 weeks after primary infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it presents with fever, headache, and meningeal signs. Common synonyms include secondary syphilitic meningitis and neurosyphilis. It primarily affects the meninges and central nervous system, with possible involvement of the brain and spinal cord. The condition is often associated with other secondary syphilis manifestations, such as skin lesions and mucous membrane involvement. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent progression to tertiary syphilis.

Syphilitic alopecia is a late-stage manifestation of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It presents as patchy, non-scarring hair loss, typically on the scalp, face, and neck. Common synonyms include syphilitic baldness and alopecia syphilitica. The condition results from immune-mediated damage to hair follicles following untreated or inadequately treated syphilis. It is more prevalent in men and often occurs in the tertiary stage of the disease. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are crucial to prevent progression and systemic complications.

Other forms of secondary syphilis refer to generalized manifestations occurring 2–10 weeks after primary infection, following the resolution of the chancre. Common synonyms include generalized secondary syphilis and mucocutaneous syphilis. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, this stage is characterized by widespread skin rashes, mucous membrane lesions, and systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Typically affected areas include the palms, soles, mucous membranes, and genital regions. It may also involve the lymph nodes, liver, and central nervous system. Without treatment, the infection can progress to tertiary syphilis.

Unspecified secondary syphilis refers to the symptomatic stage of syphilis occurring 2-12 weeks after primary infection, characterized by non-specific systemic manifestations without a defined lesion. Common synonyms include generalized secondary syphilis. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically presents with rash, mucous membrane lesions, and systemic symptoms. The rash is often maculopapular, generalized, and non-pruritic, affecting the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the nails and hair. Constitutional symptoms such as fever and malaise are also common.

code_desc: early syphilis, latent, serological relapse after treatment
summary: Early syphilis, latent, serological relapse after treatment refers to a recurrence of syphilitic antibodies following successful treatment, indicating possible reinfection or incomplete eradication of *Treponema pallidum*. This stage occurs after the initial infection has been treated, often with penicillin, but serologic tests show a resurgence of positive results. It is distinct from active disease and typically affects the bloodstream and central nervous system. Synonyms include latent syphilis with serologic relapse and late latent syphilis. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*, and affected areas may include the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs.

Early syphilis, latent, unspecified refers to a stage of syphilis where the infection is present but without active symptoms. It occurs within the first year after infection and may progress to late syphilis if untreated. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. Common synonyms include asymptomatic syphilis or latent syphilis. It typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and systemic organs. The condition may be detected through serological tests due to the absence of visible signs.

code_desc: aneurysm of aorta, specified as syphilitic
summary: Aneurysm of the aorta, specified as syphilitic, is a complication of tertiary syphilis characterized by localized dilation of the aortic wall due to chronic inflammation and degeneration. Common synonyms include syphilitic aortic aneurysm and syphilitic aortitis. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis, this condition typically affects the descending thoracic aorta. It is associated with late-stage syphilis and may present with chest pain, hypertension, or rupture. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent severe morbidity and mortality.

Syphilitic aortitis is a complication of tertiary syphilis characterized by inflammation of the aorta, leading to aortic dilation and potential aneurysm formation. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically affects the ascending aorta and aortic arch. Common synonyms include aortitis due to syphilis and syphilitic aortic aneurysm. The condition often presents with chest pain, hypertension, and signs of aortic insufficiency. It is more prevalent in males and may occur years after untreated syphilis infection. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent severe cardiovascular complications.

Syphilitic endocarditis of valve, unspecified, is a rare complication of secondary syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It involves inflammation and destruction of heart valves, typically the aortic or mitral valve, leading to valvular dysfunction. The infection results from hematogenous spread of the spirochete. Common synonyms include syphilitic myocarditis or valvular syphilis. Clinically, it may present with fever, heart murmur, and signs of heart failure. Diagnosis often requires serological testing and echocardiography. Treatment involves long-term penicillin therapy.

Syphilitic endocarditis of the mitral valve is a rare, late-stage complication of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It involves inflammation and destruction of the mitral valve leaflets, leading to valvular dysfunction. The infection typically affects the left side of the heart, particularly the mitral valve, and may result in regurgitation or stenosis. Common synonyms include syphilitic myocarditis and syphilitic valvular disease. The condition is more prevalent in untreated or inadequately treated syphilis, often presenting with systemic symptoms and cardiac complications.

Syphilitic endocarditis of the aortic valve is a late-stage complication of syphilis, typically occurring in tertiary syphilis. It results from the invasion of Treponema pallidum into the aortic valve, leading to valvular destruction and vegetative growth. Common synonyms include aortic valvular syphilis and syphilitic aortitis. The condition primarily affects the aortic valve, often causing aortic regurgitation and aortic aneurysm. It is associated with systemic involvement, including gummas and neurosyphilis. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological tests and histopathological findings. Treatment involves long-term penicillin therapy.

Syphilitic endocarditis of the tricuspid valve is a rare, late-stage complication of syphilis, typically occurring in patients with a history of untreated or inadequately treated syphilis. It involves inflammation and destruction of the tricuspid valve, leading to valvular dysfunction. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. This condition often affects the right side of the heart, particularly the tricuspid valve, and may present with signs of heart failure, embolism, or valvular regurgitation. Synonyms include syphilitic valvulopathy and syphilitic myocarditis. It is more commonly seen in individuals with a long-standing infection.

Syphilitic endocarditis of the pulmonary valve is a rare, late-stage complication of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It involves inflammation and destruction of the pulmonary valve, leading to valvular dysfunction. This condition typically presents in individuals with a history of untreated syphilis, often decades after initial infection. Syphilitic pericarditis is a rare complication of tertiary syphilis, characterized by inflammation of the pericardium. Cardiovascular syphilis, unspecified, refers to syphilis-related cardiovascular involvement without specific localization. Tabes dorsalis is a late-stage complication of neurosyphilis, characterized by degeneration of the dorsal columns and posterior root ganglia of the spinal cord. General paresis, also known as general paresis of the insane or paralytic dementia, is a late-stage neurosyphilis complication. Syphilitic meningitis is a late-stage complication of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It occurs in tertiary syphilis and involves inflammation of the meninges. Asymptomatic neurosyphilis is a late-stage manifestation of syphilis characterized by the presence of neurologic abnormalities without overt clinical symptoms. Syphilitic encephalitis is a rare neurological complication of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It occurs in the tertiary stage of the disease and involves inflammation of the brain. The condition typically affects the cerebrum, cerebellum, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as headache, seizures, and cognitive decline. Syphilitic parkinsonism is a rare neurological complication of neurosyphilis, occurring in the tertiary stage of syphilis. The condition is often associated with other neurosyphilis manifestations, such as tabes dorsalis and general paresis. Syphilitic disseminated retinochoroiditis is a late-stage ocular manifestation of syphilis, typically occurring in the tertiary phase. Syphilitic optic atrophy is a late-stage complication of syphilis, typically occurring in the tertiary phase. It results from damage to the optic nerve due to syphilitic inflammation and granuloma formation. Common synonyms include optic atrophy due to syphilis or neurosyphilitic optic atrophy. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. The condition primarily affects the optic nerve, leading to progressive visual loss. Syphilitic retrobulbar neuritis is a neurological complication of syphilis characterized by inflammation of the optic nerve behind the eyeball, leading to visual disturbances. Syphilitic acoustic neuritis is a late-stage complication of syphilis, characterized by inflammation and degeneration of the auditory nerve, leading to sensorineural hearing loss. Syphilitic ruptured cerebral aneurysm is a severe complication of neurosyphilis, occurring when Treponema pallidum infection leads to weakening of cerebral blood vessels, resulting in aneurysm formation and subsequent rupture. Other specified neurosyphilis refers to neurosyphilis cases that do not meet the criteria for definite, probable, or possible neurosyphilis but are associated with central nervous system involvement. This condition typically affects the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as headache, cognitive decline, and motor dysfunction. Neurosyphilis, unspecified, is a late-stage manifestation of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It refers to central nervous system involvement without specifying the exact subtype. Syphilitic episcleritis is an inflammatory condition affecting the episcleral layer of the eye, typically associated with syphilis. Syphilis of the lung is a rare manifestation of tertiary syphilis, occurring when the Treponema pallidum bacterium invades the pulmonary tissue. Syphilitic peritonitis is a rare, late-stage complication of syphilis caused by the Treponema pallidum bacterium. It occurs when the infection disseminates to the peritoneal cavity, leading to inflammation and potential perforation of the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include tertiary syphilitic peritonitis or peritoneal syphilis. The condition typically affects the abdomen, with involvement of the peritoneum and adjacent organs. It is associated with systemic manifestations of tertiary syphilis and may present with abdominal pain, fever, and ascites. Diagnosis often requires serological testing and histopathological examination.

Syphilis of the liver is a rare manifestation of systemic syphilis, occurring in the late stages of the disease. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochetal agent of syphilis. The condition typically affects the liver, leading to parenchymal inflammation and sometimes cirrhosis. It may present with symptoms such as jaundice, hepatomegaly, and elevated liver enzymes. Synonyms include hepatic syphilis or syphilitic hepatitis. While the liver is the primary site, the infection can also involve other organs, including the heart, brain, and skin, as part of the multisystemic nature of syphilis.

Syphilis of the kidney is a rare manifestation of secondary or tertiary syphilis, caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically occurs in the context of disseminated disease and involves renal parenchyma, leading to interstitial nephritis and glomerular changes. Common synonyms include renal syphilis or syphilitic nephritis. The condition primarily affects the kidneys, with potential involvement of the urinary tract and systemic organs. Clinical features may include proteinuria, hematuria, and renal dysfunction. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent progression and complications.

Syphilis of bone, also known as osteosyphilis or syphilitic osteomyelitis, is a rare manifestation of tertiary syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically affects the long bones, particularly the tibia and femur, and may involve the vertebrae.
