It is more common in males and often occurs in the setting of untreated or inadequately treated syphilis. Clinical features may include pain, swelling, and limited mobility in the affected area. Radiographic findings show lytic lesions and bone deformity. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are essential to prevent complications.

Syphilis of muscle, also known as myositis syphilitica or syphilitic myositis, is a rare manifestation of tertiary syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It presents as chronic inflammation and fibrosis of skeletal muscle, often affecting the proximal muscles of the lower limbs. The condition is associated with systemic syphilis and may occur in the context of late-stage infection. Clinically, it may present with muscle pain, weakness, and atrophy. It is less commonly seen than other forms of syphilitic involvement, such as gummas or neurosyphilis. Diagnosis typically requires serological testing and histopathological confirmation.

code_desc: syphilis of synovium, tendon, and bursa
summary: Syphilis of synovium, tendon, and bursa is a late-stage manifestation of syphilis, typically occurring in individuals with a history of untreated syphilis. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it involves inflammation and destruction of synovial membranes, tendons, and bursae. Common synonyms include syphilitic arthropathy and tertiary syphilis affecting joints. The condition primarily affects the joints, especially the knees, wrists, and ankles, and may lead to chronic pain, swelling, and joint deformity. It is often associated with other systemic manifestations of tertiary syphilis.

code_desc: other specified forms of late symptomatic syphilis
summary: Other specified forms of late symptomatic syphilis refer to manifestations occurring more than 2 years after primary infection, not fitting into classic late stages. Common synonyms include late syphilis and tertiary syphilis. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, this condition typically affects the skin, bones, cardiovascular system, and central nervous system. Symptoms may include gummas, aortic aneurysms, neurosyphilis, and skin lesions. It is less common than early syphilis but can lead to severe complications if untreated. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and serological tests.

Late symptomatic syphilis, unspecified, refers to manifestations occurring more than one year after initial infection, typically involving multiple organ systems. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it may present with skin lesions, neurological symptoms, cardiovascular abnormalities, and mucocutaneous involvement. Common synonyms include tertiary syphilis and late-stage syphilis. Affected areas include the skin, mucous membranes, central nervous system, and cardiovascular system. Symptoms may include gummas, neurosyphilis, aortitis, and joint pain. Diagnosis relies on clinical findings and serological tests. Treatment involves prolonged penicillin therapy.

Late syphilis, latent refers to a non-active phase of syphilis that occurs years after initial infection, characterized by the absence of clinical symptoms but presence of detectable antibodies. It may progress to tertiary syphilis if untreated. Common synonyms include asymptomatic syphilis or latent syphilis. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. Typically affects the cardiovascular system, central nervous system, and skin, with potential for organ damage and neurosyphilis. It is diagnosed through serologic testing.

Late syphilis, unspecified, refers to the tertiary stage of syphilis that develops years after the initial infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it can affect multiple organ systems. Common synonyms include tertiary syphilis and late-stage syphilis. The condition may manifest as gummas, cardiovascular syphilis, or neurosyphilis. Typically affected areas include the skin, bones, cardiovascular system, and central nervous system. Symptoms vary widely and may include skin lesions, neurological deficits, and systemic complications. Diagnosis often involves serological tests and clinical evaluation. Treatment with penicillin remains the gold standard.

Latent syphilis, unspecified, refers to a stage of syphilis where the infection is present but without active symptoms. It occurs after the primary and secondary stages and is characterized by the absence of clinical manifestations. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. It typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include asymptomatic syphilis and latent syphilis. Syphilis, unspecified, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It progresses through distinct stages, including primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary phases. code_desc: gonococcal infection (acute) of lower genitourinary tract

code_desc: gonococcal infection (acute) of upper genitourinary tract, site unspecified
summary: Gonococcal infection (acute) of the upper genitourinary tract, site unspecified, refers to a bacterial infection caused primarily by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. Gonococcal cystitis (acute) is a bacterial infection of the urinary bladder caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It typically presents with symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic pain. Gonococcal prostatitis (acute) is a bacterial infection of the prostate gland caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It is a complication of gonococcal urethritis and typically affects men. Symptoms include fever, chills, pelvic pain, dysuria, and purulent discharge. Common synonyms include acute gonococcal prostatitis and gonococcal pelvic infection. The infection primarily involves the prostate, seminal vesicles, and sometimes the epididymis. It is transmitted through sexual contact and requires prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent complications such as infertility.

Gonococcal epididymo-orchitis (acute) is a bacterial infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* affecting the epididymis and testis. Clinical features include fever, malaise, and sometimes purulent discharge from the urethra. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent complications.

Gonococcal seminal vesiculitis (acute) is an inflammatory condition of the seminal vesicles caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It typically presents with acute pelvic pain, fever, and urinary symptoms. Common synonyms include acute gonococcal prostatitis and acute seminal vesiculitis. The infection spreads from the urethra to the seminal vesicles, often in men with concurrent urethritis. It is a complication of gonococcal infection and can lead to infertility if untreated. The primary causative agent is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and the seminal vesicles are the main affected body part.

Gonococcal cervicitis (acute) is an inflammatory condition of the cervix caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Gonococcal endometritis (acute) is a bacterial infection of the endometrium caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It typically occurs in women following pelvic inflammatory disease or childbirth. It is a complication of untreated gonorrhea and can result in infertility if not promptly treated. Gonococcal salpingitis, specified as acute, is an inflammatory condition of the fallopian tubes caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It typically presents with lower abdominal pain, fever, and malaise. Common synonyms include acute tubo-ovarian infection and pelvic inflammatory disease. The infection often spreads from the cervix to the upper genital tract. It primarily affects women of reproductive age and can lead to complications such as infertility or ectopic pregnancy if untreated. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent long-term sequelae.

code_desc: other gonococcal infection (acute) of upper genitourinary tract

Gonococcal cystitis, chronic, is a persistent inflammation of the bladder caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It often presents with symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic pain. Gonococcal prostatitis, chronic, is a long-standing inflammation of the prostate gland caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Gonococcal epididymo-orchitis, chronic, is a long-standing inflammation of the epididymis and testicle caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. Gonococcal seminal vesiculitis, chronic, is a persistent inflammatory condition of the seminal vesicles caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It often follows untreated or inadequately treated acute gonococcal infection. Common synonyms include chronic gonococcal seminal vesiculitis and chronic gonococcal prostatic involvement. The condition typically affects the seminal vesicles and may involve the prostate, leading to symptoms such as pelvic pain, dysuria, and infertility. Gonococcal cervicitis, chronic is a persistent inflammation of the cervix caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It often follows an untreated or inadequately treated acute infection. Gonococcal endometritis, chronic, is a long-standing inflammation of the endometrium caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. The condition primarily affects the female genital tract, specifically the uterus. It may present with chronic pelvic pain, irregular bleeding, and infertility. Complications can include tubo-ovarian abscesses and pelvic inflammatory disease. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endometrial biopsy and culture.

Gonococcal conjunctivitis neonatorum is a severe ophthalmic infection occurring in newborns, typically within the first week of life. Common synonyms include gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum and neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis. Prompt treatment with topical antibiotics is essential to prevent long-term ocular damage.

Gonococcal iridocyclitis is an acute uveitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, primarily affecting the anterior segment of the eye. Gonococcal endophthalmia is a severe ocular complication caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, typically resulting from disseminated gonococcal infection. The condition primarily affects the eye, often leading to vision loss if untreated. It is more common in women but can occur in men as well. Prompt diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical to prevent irreversible damage.

Gonococcal keratitis is a severe, sight-threatening corneal infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. "Other gonococcal infection of eye" refers to a gonococcal infection affecting the ocular structures outside the conjunctiva and cornea, such as the eyelids, lacrimal system, or orbit. Prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics is essential to prevent complications.

Gonococcal arthritis is a reactive arthritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, typically affecting young adults. It is a complication of untreated or inadequately treated gonorrhea.

Gonococcal synovitis and tenosynovitis is a complication of gonorrhea caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. Common synonyms include disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) and gonococcal arthritis. The condition presents with joint pain, swelling, and fever, often following untreated or inadequately treated genital infections. It is more common in women but can occur in men as well. Gonococcal bursitis is a form of infectious arthritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, primarily affecting the anserine bursa in the knee. It presents with acute inflammation, pain, swelling, and warmth over the affected bursa. Common synonyms include gonococcal septic bursitis or gonococcal synovitis. The condition is more prevalent in sexually active individuals and can occur in both men and women. It is part of disseminated gonococcal infection and may be associated with joint involvement. Diagnosis is confirmed through culture or nucleic acid amplification testing of synovial fluid. Prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics is essential to prevent complications.

Gonococcal spondylitis is a rare, severe form of arthritis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, typically affecting the spine. It often presents with acute back pain, fever, and neurological deficits. Common synonyms include gonococcal vertebral osteomyelitis and gonococcal spondylodiscitis. The infection primarily targets the lumbar spine but can involve other spinal regions. It is more common in men who have sex with men and is associated with disseminated gonococcal infection. Early diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antibiotics are critical to prevent complications such as spinal instability or paralysis.

"Other gonococcal infection of joint" refers to a disseminated form of gonococcal infection affecting joints, typically occurring in individuals with compromised immune systems. It is caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* and often presents with arthritis, tenosynovitis, and dermatitis. Common synonyms include disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) and gonococcal arthritis. The infection commonly affects large joints such as the knees, wrists, and ankles, and may involve the skin and tendon sheaths. It is associated with systemic symptoms like fever and malaise.

Gonococcal infection of the pharynx, also known as pharyngeal gonorrhea or pharyngeal gonorrhea, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It typically affects the posterior pharynx and is often asymptomatic or presents with mild sore throat. Common synonyms include pharyngeal gonorrhea and pharyngeal infection due to *N. gonorrhoeae*. The infection is more prevalent in men who have sex with men but can occur in other populations. Transmission occurs through oral-genital contact. Complications may include dissemination to other sites, such as the joints or skin.

code_desc: gonococcal infection of anus and rectum
summary: Gonococcal infection of the anus and rectum is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It typically affects individuals engaging in anal intercourse. Common synonyms include rectal gonorrhea and anorectal gonorrhea. Symptoms may include rectal pain, discharge, and bleeding. The infection can lead to complications such as proctitis or systemic spread. It is often asymptomatic in men who have sex with men. Diagnosis involves nucleic acid amplification tests or cultures. Treatment typically requires antibiotics effective against drug-resistant strains.

Gonococcal keratosis, also known as blennorrhagia, is a mucocutaneous manifestation of gonorrhea caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It presents as small, flat, reddish papules or plaques, often with a serous or purulent discharge. The lesions typically appear on the genitalia, particularly the penis, vulva, and perianal regions. The condition is characterized by a burning sensation and may be accompanied by urethritis or cervicitis. It is more commonly observed in men but can occur in women. Diagnosis is confirmed through microscopic examination or culture of the lesion. Treatment involves appropriate antibiotic therapy.

Gonococcal meningitis is a severe bacterial infection of the meninges caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It is a rare but serious complication of gonococcal infection, typically affecting individuals with untreated or inadequately treated genital gonorrhea. The infection spreads through the bloodstream to the central nervous system. Common synonyms include meningitis due to *N. gonorrhoeae* or gonococcal meningitis. Symptoms include fever, headache, stiff neck, and altered mental status. It predominantly affects the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, with potential involvement of the brain and spinal cord. Prompt antibiotic therapy is critical to prevent severe neurological complications.

Gonococcal pericarditis is a rare but serious infection of the pericardium caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It typically occurs in the context of disseminated gonococcal infection, often affecting young adults. The condition presents with fever, chest pain, and pericardial effusion. Common synonyms include gonococcal pericardial infection or gonococcal cardiac involvement. It primarily affects the pericardium but may involve other organs, such as the joints and skin, in a triad of symptoms. Early diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antibiotics are crucial to prevent complications.

Gonococcal endocarditis is a rare but severe infection of the inner lining of the heart, typically caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It often affects individuals with pre-existing valvular heart disease or those who have had intravenous drug use. The infection can lead to endocardial destruction, valvular damage, and systemic complications. Common synonyms include gonococcal infective endocarditis. It primarily involves the heart valves, particularly the mitral and aortic valves, and may present with fever, heart murmurs, and embolic events. Early diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antibiotics are critical to prevent mortality.

"Other gonococcal heart disease" refers to cardiac complications arising from Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection beyond typical endocarditis. Common synonyms include gonococcal endocarditis and gonococcal myocarditis. The causative agent is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, primarily affecting the endocardium, myocardium, and pericardium. It often occurs in individuals with pre-existing valvular abnormalities or immunocompromised states. Clinical features may include fever, heart murmurs, and signs of cardiac dysfunction. Complications can lead to valvular damage and systemic spread. Diagnosis involves microbiological confirmation and echocardiography. Treatment requires prolonged antibiotic therapy.

Gonococcal peritonitis is a rare but severe inflammation of the peritoneum caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It typically occurs in individuals with a history of gonorrhea, often following ascending infection from the genital tract. The condition can present with acute abdominal pain, fever, and signs of peritoneal irritation. Common synonyms include gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease and gonococcal pelvic abscess. It predominantly affects the female reproductive organs, though it may spread to the abdominal cavity. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antibiotics are essential to prevent complications.

code_desc: gonococcal infection of other specified sites
summary: Gonococcal infection of other specified sites refers to Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection affecting areas not typically classified as genital, urinary, or rectal. Common synonyms include disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) or systemic gonococcal disease. The bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the causative agent. This condition typically affects joints, skin, and soft tissues, often presenting with migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, and dermatitis. It may occur in individuals with compromised immune systems or those who engage in high-risk sexual behaviors. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications.

Chancroid is a bacterial infection characterized by painful genital ulcers, typically caused by *Haemophilus ducreyi*. It is also known as soft chancre or venereal ulcer. The infection primarily affects the genital area, including the penis, scrotum, and vulva. It is more common in individuals with compromised immune systems or those engaging in high-risk sexual behaviors. Transmission occurs through direct sexual contact. The ulcers are usually solitary, suppurative, and may be accompanied by inguinal lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and confirmed by culture or nucleic acid amplification testing.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by specific serovars of *Chlamydia trachomatis* (L1, L2, L3). It presents as a painless genital ulcer followed by regional lymphadenopathy, often leading to painful, suppurative inguinal lymph node swelling. Common synonyms include granuloma venereum and lymphogranuloma. LGV primarily affects the genital tract, rectum, and perianal region, with a higher prevalence in tropical and developing regions. It is more common in men who have sex with men and can cause complications such as strictures and abscesses if untreated.

Granuloma inguinale, also known as donovanosis, is a chronic bacterial infection characterized by painless, ulcerative lesions primarily affecting the genital area. Caused by *Klebsiella granulomatis* (formerly *Calymmatobacterium granulomatis*), the infection leads to granulomatous inflammation and tissue destruction. Commonly seen in tropical regions, it predominantly involves the perineum, penis, and vulva. Lesions are often indurated, erythematous, and may ulcerate, with a tendency to spread if untreated. The condition is associated with immunocompromised individuals and can lead to severe complications if left unmanaged.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, unspecified site
summary: Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis*, unspecified site, refers to infections caused by *C. trachomatis* affecting genitourinary sites not specifically identified. Common synonyms include chlamydial infection, non-specific urethritis, and cervicitis. The causative agent is *Chlamydia trachomatis*, which typically affects the cervix, urethra, vagina, and rectum. It often presents with nonspecific symptoms such as discharge, itching, or burning. Transmission occurs primarily through sexual contact. If untreated, it can lead to complications like infertility or pelvic inflammatory disease.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, pharynx
summary: Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting the pharynx refer to infections caused by the bacterium *Chlamydia trachomatis* that primarily involve the pharyngeal region. Commonly known as pharyngeal chlamydial infection or pharyngitis due to *C. trachomatis*, this condition is typically transmitted through oral-genital contact. It may present with symptoms such as sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and mild fever. The pharynx is the most commonly affected site, though it may also involve the conjunctiva or genital tract in some cases. Diagnosis often involves nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) from throat swabs.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, anus and rectum
summary: Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting the anus and rectum refer to infections caused by chlamydial organisms in the anorectal region. Commonly known as anorectal chlamydial infection or chlamydial proctitis, this condition is primarily caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* serovars D through K. It typically affects individuals engaging in anal sexual activity and may present with symptoms such as rectal discharge, pain, and bleeding. The infection can lead to complications like reactive arthritis or rectal strictures if left untreated.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, lower genitourinary sites
summary: Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting lower genitourinary sites refer to infections caused by *C. trachomatis* in the urethra, cervix, vagina, or bladder. Common synonyms include chlamydial urethritis, cervicitis, and vaginitis. The causative agent is *Chlamydia trachomatis*, which primarily affects the mucosal surfaces of the genital and urinary tracts. These infections are often asymptomatic but can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy if left untreated. Transmission occurs through sexual contact.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, other genitourinary sites
summary: Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting genitourinary sites refer to infections caused by *C. trachomatis* in the urethra, cervix, vagina, or bladder. Common synonyms include chlamydial urethritis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. The bacterium primarily infects mucosal surfaces, leading to inflammation and potential complications such as infertility. Symptoms may include discharge, dysuria, and lower abdominal pain. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves antibiotic therapy, with azithromycin or doxycycline being commonly prescribed.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, unspecified genitourinary site
summary: Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting unspecified genitourinary sites refer to infections caused by *C. trachomatis* in the genital or urinary tract, not classified under specific serovars or sites. Common synonyms include chlamydial infection, non-specific urethritis, or cervicitis. The causative agent is *Chlamydia trachomatis*, which primarily affects the genital tract, including the urethra, cervix, and sometimes the rectum. It can lead to symptoms such as discharge, itching, and discomfort, and is transmitted through sexual contact.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, peritoneum
summary: "Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis*, peritoneum" refers to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting the peritoneum. Common synonyms include chlamydial peritonitis and pelvic inflammatory disease. The causative agent is *Chlamydia trachomatis*, primarily transmitted through sexual contact. It typically affects the female reproductive system, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries, and may involve the peritoneum. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Complications can lead to infertility or ectopic pregnancy if untreated.

code_desc: other venereal diseases due to chlamydia trachomatis, other specified site
summary: Other venereal diseases due to *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting sites other than the genital tract include infections such as trachoma and conjunctivitis. Caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*, these conditions primarily affect the eyes, leading to inflammation and potential scarring. Common synonyms include trachoma and inclusion conjunctivitis. The infection typically involves the conjunctiva and can spread to the cornea, causing vision impairment if untreated. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected ocular secretions. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are essential to prevent complications.

"Other specified venereal diseases" refers to sexually transmitted infections (STIs) that do not meet the criteria for more specific STI classifications. Common synonyms include unspecified or other STIs. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, or parasites, such as *Treponema pallidum* (syphilis), *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* (gonorrhea), or *Human papillomavirus* (HPV). These infections typically affect the genital tract, mouth, or rectum, and may present with symptoms like ulcers, discharge, or warts. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and laboratory testing.

Venereal disease, unspecified refers to a sexually transmitted infection (STI) where the specific diagnosis is not identified. Common synonyms include sexually transmitted infection (STI) or venereal infection. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, or parasites such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, or HIV. Typically affects the genital tract, urinary system, and may involve the eyes, throat, or skin. Symptoms may include discharge, pain, ulcers, or systemic manifestations. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and laboratory testing.

Leptospirosis icterohemorrhagica is a severe form of leptospirosis characterized by jaundice and bleeding manifestations. It is caused by *Leptospira* species, particularly *L. interrogans*. Common synonyms include Weil's disease and hemorrhagic leptospirosis. The condition typically affects the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, leading to hemolytic anemia, renal failure, and coagulopathy. It is more prevalent in individuals exposed to contaminated water or soil, such as farmers or sewage workers. Clinical features include fever, rash, jaundice, and bleeding tendencies. Early diagnosis and supportive care are critical for improved outcomes.

Leptospiral meningitis, also known as aseptic meningitis, is a bacterial infection caused by *Leptospira* species. It typically presents with fever, headache, and meningeal irritation. The infection often follows exposure to contaminated water or soil, commonly affecting individuals with occupational or recreational risk. The causative agents include *Leptospira interrogans* and other serovars. The central nervous system, particularly the meninges, is primarily affected. It may progress to more severe systemic illness if untreated. Common synonyms include leptospirosis meningitis or aseptic meningitis of leptospiral origin.

Other specified leptospiral infections refer to clinical presentations caused by *Leptospira* species that do not fit the criteria for classic leptospirosis, icteric leptospirosis, or severe leptospirosis. Common synonyms include atypical leptospirosis or non-icteric leptospirosis. Causative agents include *Leptospira interrogans* and other serovars. These infections typically affect the kidneys, liver, and cardiovascular system, presenting with fever, headache, myalgia, and renal dysfunction. They may occur in individuals with occupational or environmental exposure to contaminated water or soil.

Leptospirosis, unspecified, is a bacterial infection caused by *Leptospira* species, primarily *Leptospira interrogans*. It is transmitted through contact with water or soil contaminated by the urine of infected animals. Common synonyms include Weil's disease and leptospirosis. The infection typically affects the kidneys, liver, and lungs, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, muscle pain, and jaundice. In severe cases, it can progress to multi-organ failure. The disease is more common in tropical and subtropical regions, often affecting individuals exposed to contaminated environments.

Vincent's angina, also known as trench mouth or Vincent's infection, is a severe form of acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis. It is caused by a mixed bacterial infection, most commonly involving *Fusobacterium nucleatum* and *Treponema pallidum*. The condition primarily affects the gingival tissues, leading to painful, necrotic ulcers and pseudomembranes. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor oral hygiene. Symptoms include severe gingival pain, halitosis, and swollen, bleeding gums. The infection can progress to involve the periodontal tissues and adjacent mucosa.

Initial lesions of yaws are the first clinical manifestations of a chronic infectious disease caused by *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. These lesions typically appear as painless, firm papules or nodules, often on the limbs, especially the lower extremities. Common synonyms include "filariasis" and "lues morbus." The infection is endemic in tropical regions and primarily affects children. The lesions may ulcerate and progress to more severe stages if untreated. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent long-term complications.

code_desc: multiple papillomata due to yaws and wet crab yaws
summary: Multiple papillomata due to yaws and wet crab yaws is a skin condition characterized by the development of multiple, soft, moist, and verrucous growths, typically appearing on the face, neck, and extremities. It is caused by *Treponema pertenue*, the spirochete responsible for yaws, a tropical infectious disease. Synonyms include "lupus pernio" and "verrucous yaws." The condition is more prevalent in children and is associated with poor hygiene and tropical climates. Wet crab yaws refers to the more severe, ulcerative form of the disease, often involving the genital and perianal regions.

code_desc: other early skin lesions of yaws
summary: "Other early skin lesions of yaws" refers to non-gumma-forming skin manifestations of the treponemal infection yaws. Common synonyms include "macular syphilides" or "non-gumma skin lesions." Caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*, these lesions typically appear as painless, flat, reddish macules or papules, often on the limbs. They are more common in children and adolescents. The lesions may be asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously, but they can progress to more severe forms if left untreated. The disease is endemic in tropical regions with poor sanitation.

Hyperkeratosis due to yaws is a chronic skin condition caused by the bacterium *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. It manifests as thickened, rough, and sometimes fissured skin lesions, commonly on the hands, feet, and lower limbs. Synonyms include yaws-induced hyperkeratosis and tropical ulcer. The disease primarily affects children in endemic regions, leading to disfiguring skin changes and potential secondary infections. The hyperkeratotic lesions are a result of prolonged inflammatory response and tissue repair mechanisms. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent long-term complications.

code_desc: gummata and ulcers due to yaws
summary: Gummata and ulcers due to yaws is a chronic infectious dermatosis caused by *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. It presents as painless, soft, non-healing nodules (gummata) and ulcerative lesions, typically on the lower extremities, genitalia, and perianal regions. Common synonyms include yaws, frambesia, and syphilis-like disease. The infection is endemic in tropical regions and primarily affects children. Lesions may progress to fibrosis and deformity if untreated. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact.

Gangosa, also known as gangrene or gangrenous infection, is a severe condition characterized by the death of tissue due to lack of blood supply or infection. Common causative agents include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *Clostridium* species. It typically affects extremities, particularly the feet and hands, but can occur in any body part. The condition often presents with discoloration, necrosis, and foul odor. Prompt treatment with antibiotics and surgical debridement is essential to prevent systemic spread and complications.

code_desc: bone and joint lesions due to yaws
summary: Bone and joint lesions due to yaws are chronic inflammatory conditions caused by the spirochete *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. Common synonyms include yaws, framboesia, and laï. The disease primarily affects the skin, bones, and joints, with characteristic swelling and destruction of long bones, especially in the lower extremities. Lesions may lead to deformities and functional impairment. The infection is endemic in tropical regions and is transmitted through direct contact. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent severe complications.

Other manifestations of yaws refer to the late-stage complications of the tropical bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. These include destructive lesions on the bones, skin, and mucous membranes, often leading to deformities. Synonyms include "lateral yaws" and "mucous membrane yaws." Commonly affected areas include the hands, feet, nose, and oral cavity. The condition is prevalent in tropical regions with poor sanitation and is transmitted through direct skin contact.

Latent yaws is a chronic, asymptomatic stage of yaws, a bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. It typically follows the initial active phase and may persist for years without symptoms. The infection primarily affects the skin, bones, and joints, leading to destructive lesions and deformities. Common synonyms include "late yaws" or "inapparent yaws." It is prevalent in tropical regions with poor sanitation and is often transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent long-term complications.

Yaws, unspecified, is a chronic bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. It primarily affects children in tropical regions and is characterized by skin lesions, mucosal damage, and bone involvement. Common synonyms include "fray," "lues morbus," and "boutonniere." The disease typically presents with painless papules that progress to ulcers and nodules, often on the limbs. It may lead to disfiguring deformities and is transmitted through direct skin contact. The infection can affect the skin, bones, and mucous membranes, with the lower extremities being most commonly involved.

Primary lesions of pinta are chronic skin infections caused by *Treponema carateum*, a spirochete related to syphilis. These lesions typically appear as painless, irregularly shaped macules or papules, often with a rough, scaly surface. They most commonly affect the extremities, particularly the legs, and may be accompanied by depigmentation. Synonyms include "pinta" and "carate." The disease is endemic in tropical regions and is transmitted through direct contact with infected skin. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are essential to prevent progression and complications.

Intermediate lesions of pinta are a stage in the progression of pinta, a chronic skin infection caused by *Treponema carateum*. These lesions appear as irregular, flat, or slightly raised patches with a rough, scaly surface, often on the limbs. They may exhibit color changes, such as pink or red hues, and are typically asymptomatic. Synonyms include "pinta stage II" or "erythematous lesions of pinta." The disease primarily affects the skin, particularly in endemic regions of Central and South America. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected skin or contaminated objects.

Late lesions of pinta are chronic, disfiguring skin manifestations that develop years after the initial infection. Caused by *Treponema carateum*, this condition primarily affects the skin, particularly the scalp, face, and extremities. Synonyms include "pinta chronic" and "late-stage pinta." Lesions typically present as hypopigmented, scaly patches that may progress to atrophy or ulceration. The disease is endemic to certain regions of Mexico and Central America. Unlike syphilis, pinta does not involve the mucous membranes or internal organs. Treatment with antibiotics such as penicillin can lead to resolution of lesions, though scarring may persist.

Mixed lesions of pinta refer to a form of syphilis characterized by a combination of papular, macular, and nodular skin lesions. Caused by *Treponema carateum*, this condition is endemic to certain regions of Central and South America. The lesions typically appear on the extremities, face, and trunk. Synonyms include "pinta" and "pintas." The disease is transmitted through direct contact with lesions and is often associated with poor hygiene. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are essential to prevent progression and complications.

Pinta, unspecified, is a chronic infectious skin disease caused by *Treponema carateum*. It primarily affects the skin, particularly in tropical regions. The infection typically begins with a painless papule that may progress to a hypopigmented, scaly lesion. Common synonyms include "carate" and "pinta." The disease is transmitted through direct contact with infected skin lesions. While not life-threatening, it can lead to cosmetic disfigurement. It predominantly affects the extremities and is more common in children. Treatment with antibiotics such as penicillin is effective if initiated early.

Nonvenereal endemic syphilis, also known as endemic syphilis or yaws, is a chronic bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. It primarily affects children in tropical regions and is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact. The disease typically presents with painless, firm papules that progress to ulcers and疣状 lesions, most commonly on the lower extremities. Other manifestations include gummas, bone lesions, and joint damage. Unlike venereal syphilis, it lacks a latent stage and is less likely to involve the central nervous system. The condition is treatable with penicillin.

"Other specified spirochetal infections" refers to spirochete-related conditions not classified under syphilis, Lyme disease, or relapsing fever. Common synonyms include unspecified spirochetal infections. Causative agents may include *Treponema* species, *Borrelia* species, or *Francisella* species. These infections typically affect the skin, joints, nervous system, and mucous membranes. They often present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis relies on clinical context, serology, and molecular testing. Treatment usually involves antibiotics like penicillin or doxycycline, depending on the suspected pathogen.

Spirochetal infection, unspecified, refers to a bacterial infection caused by spirochetes, a spiral-shaped bacterium. Common synonyms include syphilis, Lyme disease, and relapsing fever. The causative agents vary, including *Treponema pallidum* (syphilis), *Borrelia burgdorferi* (Lyme disease), and *Borrelia recurrentis* (relapsing fever). These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, central nervous system, and cardiovascular system. Symptoms may include rash, fever, joint pain, and neurological manifestations. Diagnosis often involves serological tests and clinical evaluation. Treatment typically involves antibiotics, with penicillin being a common choice.

Dermatophytosis of the scalp and beard, also known as tinea capitis or ringworm of the scalp, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes. Common causative agents include *Trichophyton tonsurans*, *Trichophyton violaceum*, and *Microsporum canis*. It typically affects the scalp, beard area, and occasionally the eyebrows. The infection presents as circular, scaly patches with broken hairs, leading to alopecia. It is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected animals or contaminated objects.

Dermatophytosis of the nail, also known as tinea unguium or onychomycosis, is a fungal infection affecting the nail plate. It is caused by dermatophytes, most commonly *Trichophyton rubrum*, *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*, and *Candida* species. The infection leads to nail thickening, discoloration, brittleness, and deformation. It typically affects the toenails, especially in older adults, and may spread to fingernails. Risk factors include poor circulation, diabetes, and a history of athlete's foot. Diagnosis is often confirmed through microscopic examination or culture. Treatment involves antifungal medications, either topical or systemic, depending on severity.

Dermatophytosis of the hand, also known as tinea manuum, is a fungal infection affecting the skin of the hands. It is caused by dermatophytes, most commonly *Trichophyton rubrum* and *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*. The infection typically presents as red, scaly, itchy patches on the palms and fingers, sometimes extending to the nails. It is often acquired through direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects. The condition is more prevalent in individuals with frequent hand washing or those living in warm, moist environments. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical appearance and confirmed with potassium hydroxide preparation or fungal culture.

code_desc: dermatophytosis of groin and perianal area
summary: Dermatophytosis of the groin and perianal area, commonly known as tinea cruris or "jock itch," is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton rubrum* and *T. mentagrophytes*. It typically affects the groin, inner thighs, and perianal region, presenting as erythematous, scaly, and pruritic lesions. The infection is more prevalent in males and often occurs in warm, moist environments. It may spread to adjacent areas and is contagious through direct contact or fomites. Secondary bacterial infections can occur if the skin barrier is compromised.

Dermatophytosis of the foot, commonly known as athlete's foot, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton rubrum*, *T. mentagrophytes*, and *Epidermophyton floccosum*. It typically affects the interdigital spaces, soles, and heels, presenting with itching, scaling, and maceration. The infection is contagious and often spreads in moist environments. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with poor foot hygiene. Diagnosis is usually clinical, though mycological confirmation may be required for treatment guidance.

Dermatophytosis of the body, also known as tinea corporis, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton rubrum*, *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*, and *Microsporum canis*. It typically presents as a circular, erythematous, scaly rash with a raised border, often accompanied by itching. The infection commonly affects the trunk, arms, and legs, and may spread to other areas if left untreated. It is contagious and can be transmitted through direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical appearance and confirmed by fungal microscopy or culture. Treatment involves antifungal medications, either topical or systemic, depending on the severity.

Deep seated dermatophytosis refers to a chronic fungal infection caused by dermatophytes that invade deeper layers of the skin, hair, or nails. Common synonyms include endophytic dermatophytosis and kerion. The causative agents most frequently involved are *Trichophyton rubrum*, *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*, and *Microsporum canis*. This condition typically affects the scalp, feet, nails, and occasionally the groin. It often presents with erythematous, scaly plaques, hair loss, and nail dystrophy. Diagnosis is confirmed through fungal culture or histopathology. Treatment usually involves prolonged antifungal therapy.

Dermatophytosis of other specified sites refers to fungal infections caused by dermatophytes affecting areas not typically classified as scalp, nails, or groin. Common synonyms include tinea versicolor and pityriasis versicolor. The causative agents include Malassezia species, particularly Malassezia furfur and Malassezia sympodialis. This condition primarily affects the trunk, neck, and upper extremities, presenting as hypopigmented, scaly patches. It is more common in warm, humid climates and can be recurrent. Transmission occurs through direct contact or environmental exposure.

Dermatophytosis of unspecified site refers to a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes, which are fungi that thrive on keratin. Common synonyms include ringworm, tinea, or fungal infection. The causative agents vary by region but commonly include *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Epidermophyton* species. This condition typically affects the scalp, feet, groin, and nails, but the site is unspecified in this context. It presents as circular, erythematous, scaly patches with possible hair loss or nail dystrophy. Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical examination and fungal culture.

Pityriasis versicolor, also known as tinea versicolor, is a common fungal infection caused by Malassezia species, particularly Malassezia furfur and Malassezia sympodialis. It presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the skin, often with a fine scale. The rash typically affects the trunk, neck, and upper arms, and is more prevalent in warm, humid climates. The condition is not contagious but can recur due to factors like excessive sweating and oily skin. It is generally benign and responds well to antifungal treatments.

Tinea nigra is a superficial fungal infection characterized by brown or black, hyperpigmented, scaly patches on the skin. Common synonyms include chromoblastomycosis and tinea nigra nigra. The condition is typically caused by the dermatophyte *Fonsecaea pedrosoi*, though *Cladophialophora bantiana* and *Ajellomyces spp.* may also be involved. It most commonly affects the palms and soles, though other areas may be involved. The lesions are asymptomatic and often mistaken for melanotic macules or other pigmented lesions. Diagnosis is confirmed by potassium hydroxide preparation or fungal culture.

Tinea blanca is a superficial fungal infection of the skin characterized by hypopigmented, circular, scaly patches. Commonly known as tinea versicolor or pityriasis versicolor, it is caused primarily by *Malassezia* species, particularly *Malassezia furfur* and *Malassezia sympodialis*. The infection typically affects the trunk, neck, and upper arms, and is more prevalent in warm, humid climates. It is not contagious but may recur due to fungal overgrowth on sebum-rich skin. The condition is often asymptomatic but can cause mild pruritus.

Black piedra is a chronic fungal infection of the hair shafts, characterized by the formation of hard, black, calcified nodules. It is caused by the dermatophyte *Trichophyton funicola*. Common synonyms include "black fungus of the hair" and "piedra nigra." The infection typically affects the scalp, eyebrows, and beards, predominantly in tropical and subtropical regions. It is more common in children and individuals with poor hygiene. The nodules are usually asymptomatic but may cause cosmetic concern. Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic examination of the affected hair.

Other specified dermatomycoses refers to fungal infections of the skin caused by dermatophytes, excluding more common conditions like tinea corporis or tinea pedis. Common synonyms include tinea versicolor and tinea manuum. Causative agents include Malassezia species, Trichophyton, and Microsporum. These infections typically affect the scalp, trunk, hands, and nails. They present as scaly, itchy patches with variable coloration. Diagnosis is confirmed via potassium hydroxide preparation or fungal culture. Treatment involves antifungal agents such as terbinafine or ketoconazole.

Dermatomycosis, unspecified, refers to a fungal infection of the skin caused by dermatophytes, a type of fungi that thrive on keratin. Common synonyms include tinea and ringworm. The infection typically affects areas such as the scalp, feet, groin, and nails. Causative agents include Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton species. The condition presents as circular, erythematous, scaly patches with well-defined borders, often accompanied by itching. It is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact or contaminated objects. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through clinical examination and fungal microscopy. Treatment involves topical or oral antifungal agents depending on the severity and location of the infection.

Candidiasis of the mouth, also known as oral thrush, is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It presents as white, creamy plaques on the mucous membranes of the oral cavity, often with red, inflamed bases. Common synonyms include oral candidosis and thrush. The infection typically affects the tongue, inner cheeks, and roof of the mouth. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals, infants, and those using antibiotics or corticosteroids. Symptoms may include soreness, difficulty swallowing, and a burning sensation.

Candidiasis of the vulva and vagina, also known as vaginal yeast infection or moniliasis, is a common fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It affects the mucosal surfaces of the vulva and vagina, leading to symptoms such as itching, burning, and a thick, white discharge. Other species like *Candida glabrata* and *Candida tropicalis* may also be involved. The infection is more prevalent in women with hormonal imbalances, diabetes, or a weakened immune system. It is characterized by erythema, swelling, and a cottage cheese-like discharge.

Candidiasis of other urogenital sites refers to yeast infections caused by *Candida* species, primarily *Candida albicans*, in areas beyond the vulva, vagina, and penis. It commonly affects the urethra, perineum, and surrounding skin. Synonyms include intertrigo and candidal balanitis. This condition is more prevalent in individuals with diabetes, immunosuppression, or those using antibiotics. Symptoms include erythema, scaling, itching, and sometimes discharge. It is treated with topical antifungals such as clotrimazole or miconazole.

Candidiasis of skin and nails is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida* species, most commonly *Candida albicans*. It manifests as a superficial infection characterized by erythema, scaling, and sometimes pustules on the skin, often in moist areas like the groin, axillae, or under the breasts. Nails may become thickened, discolored, and brittle. Synonyms include cutaneous candidiasis and tinea cruris (though the latter is typically caused by dermatophytes). The infection is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with diabetes.

Candidiasis of the lung, also known as pulmonary candidiasis or invasive candidiasis affecting the respiratory tract, is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It occurs when the immune system is compromised, such as in patients with HIV, diabetes, or those undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like cough, fever, and hemoptysis. Other *Candida* species, including *C. tropicalis* and *C. krusei*, may also be involved. It is a rare but serious condition requiring antifungal treatment.

Disseminated candidiasis is a severe systemic fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida albicans*, though other species like *C. glabrata* and *C. krusei* may also be involved. It occurs when opportunistic Candida species invade multiple organs, typically in immunocompromised individuals. Commonly affected sites include the bloodstream, kidneys, liver, brain, and heart. Synonyms include systemic candidiasis and invasive candidiasis. Symptoms vary but often include fever, organ dysfunction, and sepsis. Early diagnosis and antifungal therapy are critical for management.

Candidal endocarditis is a rare but serious infection of the inner lining of the heart, typically affecting the heart valves. It is caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans, though other species like Candida glabrata or Candida krusei may also be involved. This condition often occurs in patients with pre-existing valvular heart disease, prosthetic valves, or those with compromised immune systems. Symptoms may include fever, fatigue, and signs of heart failure. It is sometimes referred to as fungal endocarditis or mycotic endocarditis. The infection can lead to valve destruction and systemic embolization if left untreated.

Candidal otitis externa is a fungal infection of the external ear canal caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It often occurs in individuals with predisposing factors such as immunosuppression, diabetes, or prolonged use of topical corticosteroids. The condition presents with pruritus, erythema, and a moist, malodorous discharge. Common synonyms include fungal otitis externa or candidal swimmer's ear. It typically affects the ear canal but may extend to the tympanic membrane in severe cases.

Candidal meningitis is a rare fungal infection of the meninges caused primarily by *Candida* species, most commonly *Candida albicans*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, neonates, or patients on broad-spectrum antibiotics. The infection can spread from contiguous sources like sinusitis or otitis media. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. Diagnosis involves lumbar puncture and fungal cultures. Treatment requires antifungal therapy, often with amphotericin B. Synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis, though this is more commonly associated with *Cryptococcus* species.

Candidal esophagitis is a fungal infection of the esophagus caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It occurs when the fungus overgrows, often in immunocompromised individuals or those on prolonged antibiotic therapy. Common symptoms include dysphagia, odynophagia, and retrosternal pain. The condition may also present with white plaques or pseudomembranes on the esophageal mucosa. Other synonyms include esophageal candidiasis or moniliasis. It typically affects the esophagus but can extend to the pharynx and stomach in severe cases.

Candidal enteritis is a fungal infection of the gastrointestinal tract caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or on prolonged antibiotic therapy. The condition presents with symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. It commonly affects the small intestine, particularly the duodenum and jejunum. Other species of *Candida*, including *C. glabrata* and *C. tropicalis*, may also be involved. Synonyms include candidiasis of the intestine and fungal enteritis.

code_desc: other candidiasis of other specified sites
summary: "Other candidiasis of other specified sites" refers to fungal infections caused by *Candida* species affecting sites not typically classified under mucocutaneous or systemic candidiasis. Common synonyms include superficial candidiasis or localized candidal infections. The causative agent is primarily *Candida albicans*, though other species like *C. glabrata* or *C. tropicalis* may be involved. These infections typically affect skin folds, nails, or other less common areas such as the perineum or ear canals, often in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor hygiene.

Candidiasis of unspecified site refers to an infection caused by Candida species, most commonly *Candida albicans*, affecting any body part not specifically identified. It is a fungal infection characterized by inflammation, erythema, and sometimes purulent discharge. Common synonyms include yeast infection or moniliasis. While it can occur in various locations, it frequently affects the oral cavity, vulva, and skin folds. The infection is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals, those with diabetes, or those using antibiotics. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation and microscopic examination. Treatment involves antifungal agents such as topical clotrimazole or systemic fluconazole, depending on severity.

Primary coccidioidomycosis, also known as Valley fever, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, where inhaled spores germinate and form spherules. Common symptoms include cough, fever, chest pain, and fatigue. The infection typically presents as a self-limiting pulmonary illness, though it can progress to disseminated disease in immunocompromised individuals. It is endemic in arid regions of the southwestern United States, Central America, and parts of Mexico. The disease is also referred to as San Joaquin fever or desert fever.

Primary extrapulmonary coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It occurs when the immune system fails to contain the fungus after initial inhalation, leading to dissemination beyond the lungs. Commonly affected sites include the skin, bones, central nervous system, and joints. Synonyms include coccidioidal osteomyelitis, meningitis, and cutaneous coccidioidomycosis. Symptoms vary by location but often include fever, pain, and localized swelling. Diagnosis is confirmed through serology, culture, or histopathology. The infection is more prevalent in arid regions and can be severe in immunocompromised individuals.

Coccidioidal meningitis is a severe central nervous system infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It typically occurs in individuals with compromised immune systems or following disseminated coccidioidomycosis. The infection leads to inflammation of the meninges, often accompanied by fever, headache, and neurological symptoms. Common synonyms include fungal meningitis and coccidioidal meningitis. It primarily affects the brain and spinal cord, and may spread to other organs in immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis involves cerebrospinal fluid analysis and fungal cultures. Treatment usually requires prolonged antifungal therapy.

Other forms of progressive coccidioidomycosis refer to disseminated or chronic infections caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *C. posadae*. These forms occur when the initial pulmonary infection spreads beyond the lungs, commonly affecting the skin, bones, central nervous system, and joints. Synonyms include disseminated coccidioidomycosis and chronic coccidioidomycosis. Symptoms vary by affected site but often include skin lesions, osteomyelitis, meningitis, and arthritis. The disease is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those living in endemic regions.

Chronic pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, often developing after a primary infection that progresses from an acute to a chronic form. Common synonyms include coccidioidal pneumonia and valley fever. The infection typically presents with chronic cough, chest pain, and fibrosis. It is endemic in arid regions of the southwestern United States, Central, and South America. Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for dissemination beyond the lungs.

Pulmonary coccidioidomycosis, unspecified, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs following inhalation of arthroconidia. Common synonyms include valley fever and San Joaquin fever. The infection typically presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. While often self-limiting, it can progress to chronic or disseminated disease in immunocompromised individuals. The lungs are the main affected body part, though dissemination to other organs may occur.

Coccidioidomycosis, unspecified, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to acute or chronic pulmonary disease. Common synonyms include Valley fever and San Joaquin fever. The infection can disseminate to other organs, such as the skin, bones, and central nervous system, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include fever, cough, and chest pain, with systemic involvement possible in severe cases. The disease is endemic to arid regions of the southwestern United States and parts of Central and South America.

Retinitis occurs when the infection spreads via the bloodstream to the retina, leading to inflammation and potential vision loss. Common synonyms include histoplasmosis with ocular involvement. The condition is more common in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The eyes, particularly the retina, are the main affected body parts.

Infection by *Histoplasma capsulatum* causing pericarditis is a fungal infection that affects the pericardium. *H. capsulatum* is a dimorphic fungus commonly found in soil enriched with bird or bat droppings. It is more prevalent in endemic regions and often presents with fever, chest pain, and signs of pericardial effusion. The infection is acquired through inhalation of spores and is more common in immunocompetent individuals, though severe cases can occur in immunocompromised hosts.

Infection by *Histoplasma capsulatum* leading to endocarditis is a rare but severe fungal infection affecting the heart valves. Synonyms include histoplasmosis endocarditis and fungal endocarditis due to *H. capsulatum*. The infection primarily affects the heart valves, particularly the mitral and aortic valves.

Infection by *Histoplasma capsulatum* causing pneumonia is a fungal infection that primarily affects the lungs. The infection is often acquired through inhalation of spores from contaminated soil or bird droppings. Clinically, it may present with symptoms similar to other respiratory infections, including fever, cough, and chest pain. Pneumonia is a common manifestation, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or those with heavy exposure.

Infection by *Histoplasma capsulatum*, other refers to systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungus *Histoplasma capsulatum*. Commonly known as histoplasmosis, this condition primarily affects the lungs, with dissemination possible in immunocompromised individuals. The infection typically begins as a respiratory illness, often asymptomatic or resembling pneumonia. It is endemic in regions with high bird or bat activity. Infection by *Histoplasma duboisii* causing meningitis is a rare fungal infection primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. Infection by *Histoplasma duboisii* causing retinitis is a rare fungal infection primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. Infection by *Histoplasma duboisii* leading to endocarditis is a rare but severe fungal infection primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. Infection by *Histoplasma duboisii* causing pneumonia is a fungal disease primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. It is also known as African histoplasmosis or disseminated histoplasmosis. Infection by *Histoplasma duboisii*, also known as African histoplasmosis or dimorphic fungal infection, is caused by the dimorphic fungus *Histoplasma duboisii*. Histoplasmosis, unspecified, meningitis is a fungal infection of the central nervous system caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*. It presents with symptoms such as fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Histoplasmosis, unspecified, retinitis refers to an inflammatory condition affecting the retina caused by the fungus *Histoplasma capsulatum*. Histoplasmosis, unspecified, pericarditis refers to an infection of the pericardium caused by the fungus *Histoplasma capsulatum*. This fungal infection typically affects the lungs but can disseminate to other organs, including the heart. Common synonyms include fungal pericarditis and histoplasma pericarditis. The condition is more common in individuals with weakened immune systems or those exposed to bird or bat droppings. Symptoms may include fever, chest pain, and pericardial effusion. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological tests and imaging. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy.

Histoplasmosis, unspecified, endocarditis refers to a fungal infection involving the heart valves, caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*. This condition arises when the fungus, commonly found in soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings, enters the bloodstream and colonizes the endocardium. Histoplasmosis, unspecified, pneumonia is a fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*, primarily affecting the lungs. It occurs in individuals exposed to bird or bat droppings, often in endemic areas. The infection typically presents with flu-like symptoms, including fever, cough, and chest pain. The lungs are most commonly affected, though the infection may spread to other organs in immunocompromised individuals.

Histoplasmosis, unspecified, other refers to an infection caused by the fungus *Histoplasma capsulatum*, primarily affecting the lungs. It is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and can present acutely or chronically. Common synonyms include pulmonary histoplasmosis and endemic mycosis. The infection typically involves the respiratory tract, with possible dissemination to other organs in immunocompromised individuals. It is endemic in certain regions, particularly the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. The disease is often asymptomatic or presents with flu-like symptoms, and diagnosis is confirmed through serology, culture, or imaging.

Blastomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis* and related species. It primarily affects the lungs but can disseminate to other organs. Common synonyms include North American blastomycosis and Gilchrist's disease. The infection often presents with flu-like symptoms initially, progressing to chronic pulmonary disease. Dissemination may involve skin, bones, and genitourinary tract. Diagnosis is confirmed through culture, serology, or biopsy. Treatment typically involves antifungal medications such as itraconazole or amphotericin B. The disease is endemic in certain regions of the United States, Canada, and Africa.

Paracoccidioidomycosis, also known as South American blastomycosis or Filariasis, is a systemic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* and *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects the lungs, skin, and mucous membranes, with a predilection for the upper respiratory tract. The infection is endemic in Latin America and typically presents with chronic respiratory symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and systemic involvement. It is more common in males and those exposed to environmental sources of the fungus, such as soil and organic matter. The disease can progress to severe pulmonary and extrapulmonary manifestations if left untreated.

Lobomycosis, also known as chromoblastomycosis, is a chronic fungal infection caused by species of the genus *Lobomycetes*, particularly *L. loboi*. It primarily affects the skin, especially in tropical and subtropical regions. The infection typically presents as a slowly progressive, verrucous lesion with a granular surface. It commonly involves the limbs, particularly the feet and hands, and may spread to deeper tissues. The disease is characterized by the formation of sclerotic bodies within the epidermis. It is more prevalent in individuals with compromised immune systems or those exposed to traumatic injuries.

Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous infection primarily affecting the nasal mucosa. Caused by *Rhinosporidium seeberi*, a protozoan parasite, it is characterized by the formation of polypoid, friable, and often hemorrhagic lesions. Common synonyms include rhinosporidial sinusitis and rhinosporidial rhinitis. The disease typically involves the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and occasionally the conjunctiva or larynx. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, with a predilection for males and those with immunocompromised status. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical findings and histopathological examination.

Sporotrichosis is a subcutaneous fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species. It typically presents as a chronic, progressive infection following traumatic inoculation of the fungus, often through thorn pricks or insect bites. The disease commonly affects the upper extremities, with characteristic nodules and ulcerative lesions along lymphatic channels. Synonyms include rhino-pharyngeal sporotrichosis and lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. It may disseminate to the lungs, bones, or central nervous system in immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis is confirmed by culture or histopathology. Treatment involves antifungal agents such as itraconazole or potassium iodide.

Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, characterized by verrucous or granulomatous lesions. Common synonyms include mycotic granuloma and chromophilic mycosis. It is caused by dematiaceous fungi, most commonly *Cladophialophora bantiana*, *Phialophora verrucosa*, and *Fonsecaea pedrosoi*. The infection typically affects the lower extremities, especially in individuals with frequent exposure to soil or plant material. Lesions are often slow-growing, hyperpigmented, and may ulcerate. Diagnosis is confirmed by histopathology and fungal culture. Treatment may involve antifungal medications, surgical debridement, or a combination.

Aspergillosis is a fungal infection caused by species of the genus *Aspergillus*, most commonly *A. fumigatus*. It primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying lung disease. The infection can manifest as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis, or invasive aspergillosis. Symptoms include cough, fever, and hemoptysis. Invasive forms can spread to other organs, such as the brain, heart, or kidneys. Synonyms include aspergillosis, fungal lung infection, and mold infection. The condition is more prevalent in patients with cystic fibrosis, HIV, or those on immunosuppressive therapy.

Mycotic mycetomas are chronic, suppurative infections characterized by the formation of granulomas with fungal elements. Common synonyms include eumycetoma and chromoblastomycosis. They are primarily caused by dematiaceous fungi such as *Madurella mycetomatis*, *Pseudallescheria boydii*, and *Exophiala* species. These infections typically affect the skin and subcutaneous tissues, often involving the feet, legs, and hands. They are more common in tropical and subtropical regions, with a predilection for males and agricultural workers. The infection may progress to systemic involvement if left untreated.

Cryptococcosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection typically involves the lungs and central nervous system, leading to pneumonia and meningitis. Common synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and pulmonary cryptococcosis. The disease may present with symptoms like fever, cough, headache, and altered mental status. Diagnosis is confirmed through fungal cultures, antigen detection, or microscopy. Treatment involves antifungal medications such as amphotericin B and flucytosine.

Allescheriosis, also known as petriellidosis, is a rare parasitic infection caused by the protozoan *Petriella petriellii*. It primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the stomach and intestines, leading to chronic inflammation and ulceration. The infection is typically acquired through ingestion of contaminated food or water. Clinically, it may present with symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. The condition is more commonly reported in tropical and subtropical regions. Diagnosis is often confirmed through endoscopic biopsy and microscopic examination of tissue samples.

Zygomycosis, also known as phycomycosis or mucormycosis, is a severe fungal infection caused by fungi in the order Mucorales. Common causative agents include *Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, and *Absidia* species. This condition typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with diabetes or on immunosuppressive therapy. It commonly involves the sinuses, lungs, skin, and brain, often presenting with rapid tissue necrosis and angioinvasion. Clinical manifestations include fever, nasal congestion, and black eschars. Early diagnosis and treatment with antifungal agents like amphotericin B are critical for improving outcomes.

Phaeohyphomycosis is a fungal infection caused by dematiaceous (dark-pigmented) fungi, commonly known asphaeohyphomycosis, dematiaceous mycosis, or melanin-producing fungal infection. It is caused by various species of dematiaceous fungi, including *Exophiala*, *Cladophialophora*, *Lophophora*, and *Hortaea*. These infections typically affect the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and sometimes the lungs or central nervous system. Clinical presentations vary from localized cutaneous lesions to disseminated disease, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. The infection is characterized by the presence of brown or black pigmented hyphae in tissue.

"Other and unspecified mycoses" refers to fungal infections not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include "miscellaneous mycoses" or "unspecified fungal infections." Causative agents vary widely and may include dermatophytes, yeasts, and molds. These infections typically affect the skin, nails, mucous membranes, or lungs. They may present as superficial or systemic infections, often with nonspecific symptoms. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, microscopy, culture, or molecular methods. Treatment depends on the causative agent and infection site, often involving antifungal medications.

Opportunistic mycoses are fungal infections that occur in immunocompromised individuals, typically caused by organisms that are usually non-pathogenic in healthy hosts. Common synonyms include endemic, subcutaneous, and superficial mycoses. Key causative agents include *Candida* species, *Aspergillus*, *Histoplasma*, *Cryptococcus*, and *Penicillium*. These infections commonly affect the respiratory tract, skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs such as the lungs, liver, and brain. They often present with chronic or progressive symptoms and require antifungal therapy for effective management.

Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma haematobium* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the blood fluke *S. haematobium*, transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater. The cercariae penetrate the skin and migrate to the urinary tract, where adult worms reside in the bladder and ureters. Eggs laid by the worms cause inflammation and fibrosis, leading to hematuria, dysuria, and potentially urogenital complications such as bladder cancer. Common synonyms include urinary schistosomiasis and bilharzia. The disease primarily affects the urinary system, with significant morbidity in endemic regions of Africa, the Middle East, and parts of the Americas.

Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma mansoni* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the trematode *Schistosoma mansoni*. The cercariae penetrate the skin upon contact with contaminated water, migrating to the portal venous system where adult worms reside. Eggs laid by the worms cause inflammation and fibrosis in the liver and intestines. Common synonyms include bilharzia and snail fever. The disease primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract and liver, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly. Chronic infection can result in portal hypertension and other systemic complications.

Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma japonicum* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the trematode *S. japonicum*, transmitted through contact with contaminated water. The larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through the bloodstream, and mature into adult worms in the mesenteric veins. The disease primarily affects the intestines and liver, leading to granulomatous inflammation, fibrosis, and portal hypertension. Common synonyms include Japanese schistosomiasis and oriental schistosomiasis. It is endemic in parts of Asia, particularly China, and is associated with poverty and poor sanitation.

Cutaneous schistosomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by Schistosoma species, primarily S. haematobium and S. mansoni. It occurs when cercariae penetrate the skin, leading to an acute inflammatory response. Common synonyms include swimmer's itch and cercarial dermatitis. The condition typically affects the legs, arms, and trunk, with lesions characterized by redness, itching, and blisters. Symptoms usually resolve within weeks, but chronic infection may lead to systemic complications. Transmission occurs through contact with contaminated freshwater.

Other specified schistosomiasis refers to infections caused by species of *Schistosoma* not classified under the more commonly recognized forms such as *S. mansoni*, *S. haematobium*, or *S. japonicum*. It encompasses cases where the causative agent is less frequently identified or where the clinical presentation does not fit the typical patterns of the more common species.
