The infection primarily affects the intestines, bladder, or liver, depending on the species involved. Common synonyms include unspecified schistosomiasis and other schistosomiasis.

Schistosomiasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by trematode flukes of the genus *Schistosoma*. Common synonyms include bilharzia and snail fever. The disease results from penetration of cercariae into the skin upon contact with contaminated water. The parasites migrate to the mesenteric veins, leading to inflammation and fibrosis of the liver and intestines. It primarily affects the genitourinary and gastrointestinal systems, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and hematuria. The infection is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Opisthorchiasis is a parasitic infection caused by liver flukes of the genus *Opisthorchis*, most commonly *Opisthorchis viverrini* and *Opisthorchis felineus*. It results from ingestion of undercooked fish containing metacercariae. The flukes primarily infect the bile ducts and liver, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potentially cholangiocarcinoma. Common synonyms include clonorchiasis and liver fluke infection. The disease is endemic in parts of Asia and Eastern Europe, with chronic infection being the most common clinical manifestation.

Clonorchiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the liver fluke *Clonorchis sinensis*. Common synonyms include Chinese liver fluke infection and opisthorchiasis. The parasite primarily affects the bile ducts, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. Transmission occurs through consumption of undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae. Chronic infection can result in cholangitis, cholecystitis, and an increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and fatigue. The disease is endemic in parts of Asia, particularly Korea, China, and Vietnam.

Paragonimiasis is a parasitic infection caused by lung flukes of the genus *Paragonimus*, most commonly *Paragonimus westermani*. It is also known as lung fluke disease or pulmonary paragonimiasis. The parasite is acquired by ingesting undercooked crustaceans, leading to migration of larvae through the intestinal wall into the lungs, where they mature and lay eggs. Symptoms include cough, hemoptysis, and chest pain. In advanced stages, the infection may spread to the brain, liver, or abdominal cavity, causing extrapulmonary paragonimiasis. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by identifying eggs in sputum or stool.

Fascioliasis is a parasitic infection caused by the liver flukes *Fasciola hepatica* and *Fasciola gigantica*. It primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. The disease is acquired through ingestion of metacercariae found in contaminated water or vegetation. Common synonyms include liver fluke infection and fasciolosis. Symptoms include abdominal pain, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. The infection is endemic in agricultural regions with favorable conditions for intermediate snail hosts. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by stool examination or serology.

Fasciolopsiasis is a helminthic infection caused by the fluke *Fasciolopsis buski*, commonly found in humans in Asia. It primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the ileum and cecum. The infection is acquired through the ingestion of contaminated water or food containing metacercariae. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia. Common synonyms include intestinal fluke disease and giant intestinal fluke infection. The condition is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions with poor sanitation.

Metagonimiasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Metagonimus yokogawai*, a trematode that infects the small intestine. It is acquired by consuming undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae. The larvae migrate to the bile ducts, where they mature and cause inflammation. Common synonyms include fish trematodosis or intestinal fluke infection. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and eosinophilia. The condition primarily affects the biliary system and small intestine, with a higher prevalence in regions where raw or undercooked fish is consumed.

Heterophyiasis is a helminthic infection caused by heterophyid flukes, commonly *Heterophyes heterophyes* and *Fasciolopsis buski*. It is prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and contaminated water. The parasites infect the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malnutrition. Common synonyms include heterophyid infection and heterophyosis. Transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated food or water containing metacercariae. The condition is typically found in Asia, Africa, and parts of South America, affecting primarily children and individuals with poor hygiene practices.

Other specified trematode infections refer to parasitic infestations caused by trematodes (flukes) that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous fluke infections. Causative agents may include species such as *Fasciola hepatica*, *Clonorchis sinensis*, and *Schistosoma* spp., depending on the region. These infections typically affect the liver, bile ducts, intestines, or vascular system, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, jaundice, and gastrointestinal distress. Diagnosis often involves stool or blood tests, and treatment usually involves antiparasitic medications.

Trematode infection, unspecified, refers to parasitic infestation caused by flatworms of the class Trematoda. Common synonyms include fluke infection or helminthic trematode infection. Causative agents include species such as Schistosoma, Fasciola, and Clonorchis. These parasites typically affect the liver, intestines, lungs, and blood vessels. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and systemic inflammation. The infection is acquired through ingestion of contaminated food or water. Diagnosis often involves stool examination or serological testing. Treatment typically involves antiparasitic drugs such as praziquantel.

Echinococcus granulosus infection of the liver, also known as hepatic hydatid disease, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The liver is the most commonly affected organ, followed by the lungs. The infection results from ingestion of eggs, leading to formation of fluid-filled cysts that may grow slowly over years. Symptoms are often absent in early stages but can include abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and complications such as cyst rupture or secondary infections. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by imaging and serology.

Echinococcus granulosus infection of the lung, also known as pulmonary hydatid disease, is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*. The infection typically results from ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments or food. The larvae form cysts in the lungs, which can grow slowly over years. Common symptoms include cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. The liver is the most commonly affected organ, but pulmonary involvement is also frequent. Diagnosis is often made via imaging and serology. Treatment may involve surgical removal or antiparasitic drugs.

Echinococcus granulosus infection of the thyroid is a rare parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the dog tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*. It typically presents as a slow-growing, painless mass in the thyroid gland. The infection is part of cystic echinococcosis, a zoonotic disease commonly affecting the liver and lungs, though the thyroid is an uncommon site. Synonyms include cysticercosis or hydatid disease. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments. The condition is more prevalent in endemic regions with close human-canine contact.

Echinococcus granulosus infection, also known as hydatid disease, is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The infection primarily affects the liver and lungs, though other organs may be involved. It is transmitted through ingestion of eggs shed in the feces of infected dogs. The larvae form hydatid cysts, which can grow slowly over years, leading to complications such as cyst rupture, anaphylaxis, or secondary infections. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by imaging and serological tests. Treatment involves surgical removal and/or anthelmintic therapy.

Echinococcus granulosus infection, unspecified, is a parasitic disease caused by the tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*. It leads to the formation of cysts, primarily in the liver and lungs, though other organs may be affected. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and cystic echinococcosis. The infection occurs through ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments or food. Cysts grow slowly, causing symptoms such as pain, swelling, and potentially life-threatening complications if left untreated. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via imaging and serological tests. Treatment involves surgical removal and/or antiparasitic drugs.

Echinococcus multilocularis infection of the liver, also known as alveolar echinococcosis, is a chronic parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis. This infection primarily affects the liver, leading to the formation of multinodular, destructive lesions. It is commonly found in endemic areas of Europe, Asia, and North America. The disease can also involve the lungs and other organs, but the liver is the most frequently affected site. Transmission occurs through ingestion of eggs from contaminated soil or feces of definitive hosts.

Echinococcus multilocularis infection, also known as alveolar echinococcosis, is a chronic parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis. The infection primarily affects the liver, where it forms multicystic, invasive lesions. It can also involve the lungs, brain, and other organs. Common synonyms include alveolar echinococcosis and multilocular echinococcosis. The disease is more prevalent in endemic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America, often transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food or water.

Echinococcus multilocularis infection, unspecified, is a chronic parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus multilocularis*. Commonly known as alveolar echinococcosis, it primarily affects the liver but can involve other organs. The infection results from ingestion of eggs, typically through contaminated food or water. It is characterized by slow-growing, invasive lesions that mimic malignancy. The disease is more prevalent in endemic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America. Clinical manifestations depend on the extent of organ involvement, often leading to progressive organ dysfunction.

Echinococcosis, unspecified, of the liver is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Echinococcus* species, most commonly *E. granulosus* and *E. multilocularis*. It results from ingestion of eggs from infected animals, leading to formation of hydatid cysts in the liver, which is the most commonly affected organ. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and cyst rupture. The condition is also known as hydatid disease or alveolar echinococcosis, depending on the species involved. It is endemic in certain regions with close human-animal contact.

Echinococcosis, other and unspecified, refers to infections caused by tapeworms of the genus *Echinococcus*. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and cystic echinococcosis. The primary causative agents are *Echinococcus granulosus* and *Echinococcus multilocularis*. This condition typically affects the liver and lungs, but can also involve the brain, spleen, and other organs. It is characterized by the formation of hydatid cysts, which may grow slowly and cause complications such as rupture or secondary infections. Transmission occurs through ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments or direct contact with infected animals.

Taenia solium infection, intestinal form, is caused by the ingestion of T. solium eggs, leading to larval migration and cyst formation in tissues. The adult tapeworm resides in the small intestine, while larvae can affect various organs, most commonly the central nervous system, causing neurocysticercosis. Common synonyms include cysticercosis and pork tapeworm infection. The causative agent is the pork tapeworm, *Taenia solium*, and the infection primarily affects the intestines and central nervous system.

Cysticercosis is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*, the pork tapeworm. It occurs when ingested eggs hatch into larvae, which form cysts in various tissues. Common synonyms include neurocysticercosis when affecting the central nervous system. The infection typically involves the skin, muscles, and organs, but the brain and spinal cord are frequently affected. Symptoms depend on cyst location and may include seizures, headaches, or localized pain. Diagnosis often involves imaging and serological tests. Treatment depends on the affected site and may involve antiparasitic drugs or surgical removal.

Taenia saginata infection, also known as beef tapeworm infection, is caused by the adult stage of Taenia saginata, a cestode parasite. Infection occurs through ingestion of undercooked beef containing viable cysticerci. The adult worm resides in the small intestine, where it attaches to the intestinal wall. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss, though many infections are asymptomatic. The condition primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, with the small intestine being the main site of parasitic activity. Common synonyms include beef tapeworm disease and taeniasis saginata.

Taeniasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by tapeworms of the genus *Taenia*. Common synonyms include beef tapeworm infection and pork tapeworm infection, though the specific species may not be identified. The causative agents are typically *Taenia saginata* (beef tapeworm) and *Taenia solium* (pork tapeworm). The infection primarily affects the small intestine, where the adult worms attach to the intestinal wall. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss. Transmission occurs through ingestion of undercooked meat containing tapeworm larvae.

Diphyllobothriasis, intestinal, is a parasitic infection caused by the tapeworm *Diphyllobothrium latum*, also known as the broad tapeworm. It is acquired by consuming undercooked freshwater fish containing the larval stage of the parasite. The adult worm resides in the small intestine, where it attaches to the intestinal wall and absorbs nutrients. Common symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. The infection may also lead to vitamin B12 deficiency due to the worm's interference with absorption. It is most commonly found in regions with a high consumption of raw or undercooked fish.

Sparganosis, also known as larval diphyllobothriasis, is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Diphyllobothrium latum*. The larvae migrate through the body, typically entering via the skin or orally, and can cause inflammation and granulomatous reactions in affected tissues. Commonly involved sites include the subcutaneous tissues, eyes, lungs, and brain. Symptoms vary depending on the location of the larvae, ranging from localized swelling to severe complications if the central nervous system is involved. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with treatment involving antiparasitic medications.

Hymenolepiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the tapeworm *Hymenolepis nana* or *Hymenolepis diminuta*. It primarily affects the small intestine and is commonly seen in children. The infection is transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food or water containing infective eggs. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Common synonyms include intestinal hymenolepiasis and dwarf tapeworm infection. The disease is more prevalent in crowded living conditions and among immunocompromised individuals.

"Other specified cestode infection" refers to infestations caused by tapeworms that do not fit the criteria for more specific cestode infections. Common synonyms include unspecified tapeworm infection. Causative agents may include species such as *Dipylidium caninum*, *Taenia* spp., or *Echinococcus* spp. These infections typically affect the intestines but can also involve other organs, such as the liver or brain, depending on the species. Clinical presentation varies but may include abdominal pain, weight loss, and the passage of proglottids. Diagnosis often involves stool examination or imaging.

Cestode infection, unspecified, refers to parasitic infestation caused by tapeworms belonging to the class Cestoda. Common synonyms include tapeworm infection or trematode infection, though the latter is more specific to flukes. Causative agents vary but may include species such as *Taenia* spp., *Diphyllobothrium* spp., and *Echinococcus* spp. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, but can also involve the liver, lungs, and brain, depending on the species. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, weight loss, and malabsorption. Diagnosis often involves stool examination or imaging.

Trichinosis is a parasitic infection caused by the roundworm *Trichinella spiralis*. It is acquired by consuming undercooked meat containing encysted larvae. The infection primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract and skeletal muscles, with larvae migrating through the bloodstream to muscle tissue. Common synonyms include trichiniasis and spiracosis. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and muscle inflammation. Complications may arise in severe cases, affecting the heart and lungs. The disease is more common in regions where wild game consumption is prevalent.

Bancroftian filariasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Wuchereria bancrofti*, the most common filarial worm worldwide. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, primarily *Culex*, *Anopheles*, and *Aedes* species. The infection primarily affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and elephantiasis, particularly in the lower limbs and genitalia. It is also known as tropical filariasis or filarial lymphedema. Symptoms include swelling, skin thickening, and recurrent infections. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Malayan filariasis, also known as bancroftian filariasis, is a parasitic disease caused by *Wuchereria bancrofti*. The infection primarily affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and hydrocele. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, particularly *Culex* and *Anopheles* species. Commonly affected areas include the lower limbs, genitalia, and breasts. The disease is endemic in Southeast Asia and is characterized by chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the lymphatic vessels. Symptoms often develop years after infection and may include swelling, skin changes, and recurrent infections.

Loiasis, also known as African eye worm infection, is a filarial disease caused by the parasitic nematode *Loa loa*. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected cyclops, small water fleas found in freshwater. The adult worms migrate through subcutaneous tissues, often causing visible movement of the worm under the skin, particularly around the eyelids. Common symptoms include itching, swelling, and a characteristic "eye worm" appearance. The disease primarily affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues, with occasional involvement of the lymphatic system. It is endemic in Central and West Africa.

Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is a neglected tropical disease caused by the parasitic worm *Onchocerca volvulus*. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies (*Simulium* species). The adult worms reside in subcutaneous tissues, producing microfilariae that migrate to the skin and eyes, leading to severe itching, skin lesions, and potential blindness. Commonly affected areas include the skin, eyes, and lymphatic system. The disease is endemic in rural areas of Africa, the Americas, and the Middle East.

Dipetalonemiasis is a filarial disease caused by nematodes of the genus *Dipetalonema*, primarily *Dipetalonema lutzi* and *Dipetalonema perstans*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected blood-feeding flies, particularly *Hippelotes* species. The infection primarily affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues, causing chronic inflammation, nodules, and sometimes lymphatic involvement. Common synonyms include *Lutzomyia fever* and *Cutaneous filariasis*. The disease is endemic in tropical regions of Africa and South America.

Mansonella ozzardi infection is a filariasis caused by the nematode Mansonella ozzardi. It is also known as Ozzard's filariasis. The infection is transmitted through blood-feeding flies, primarily Simulium species. The parasites primarily infect the subcutaneous tissues and lymphatic system, leading to symptoms such as skin nodules, lymphadenopathy, and intermittent fever. The disease is commonly found in tropical regions of South America. It is generally asymptomatic or causes mild symptoms, and diagnosis is typically achieved through microfilariae detection in blood samples. No specific treatment is routinely required, as the infection often resolves spontaneously.

Other specified filariasis refers to filarial infections caused by species not classified under the major categories of lymphatic (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, Brugia timori) or subcutaneous (Onchocerca volvulus) filariasis. Common synonyms include non-Wuchereria/Brugeia filariasis. Causative agents may include Mansonella perstans, Loa loa, and others. These infections typically affect the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and lymphatic system, leading to symptoms such as skin thickening, nodules, and lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis often relies on microfilariae detection or serological tests.

Dracontiasis is a rare parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Dracunculus medinensis*, also known as the Guinea worm. The infection is acquired through drinking water contaminated with copepods containing infective larvae. The worm matures in the subcutaneous tissues, typically in the lower extremities, and causes painful, serous, and sometimes hemorrhagic lesions. The condition is also referred to as Guinea worm disease. It is primarily found in tropical regions with limited access to clean water. The disease is not transmitted directly between humans.

Unspecified filariasis refers to a group of parasitic infections caused by filarial nematodes, typically transmitted by vector insects. Common synonyms include lymphatic filariasis and tropical filariasis. The causative agents may include *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*, and *Brugia timori*. These infections primarily affect the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and hydrocele. They may also involve the genital and urinary systems. The condition is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, often presenting with chronic symptoms due to immune responses and parasite persistence. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical findings and serological tests when specific species are not identified.

Ancylostomiasis due to *Ancylostoma duodenale* is a parasitic infection caused by the human hookworm *Ancylostoma duodenale*. Common synonyms include hookworm infection and duodenal hookworm disease. The larvae penetrate the skin, typically through contaminated soil, and migrate to the lungs before reaching the intestines. Adult worms attach to the intestinal mucosa, causing chronic blood loss and anemia. The infection primarily affects the small intestine, particularly the duodenum, and is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and iron-deficiency anemia.

Necatoriasis, caused by *Necator americanus*, is a soil-transmitted helminth infection acquired through penetration of hookworm larvae into the skin, typically from contaminated soil. The larvae migrate to the lungs, then to the intestines, where they mature into adult worms and attach to the intestinal mucosa. Common synonyms include hookworm infection and American hookworm disease. *Necator americanus* is the primary causative agent, with *Ancylostoma duodenale* as a less common alternative. The infection primarily affects the small intestine, causing anemia, malnutrition, and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Ancylostomiasis due to *Ancylostoma braziliense* is a parasitic infection caused by the hookworm *A. braziliense*, which primarily affects the intestines. Common synonyms include Brazilian hookworm infection and visceral larva migrans. The larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through the body, and cause tissue damage, particularly in the lungs and intestines. Symptoms include cutaneous reactions, coughing, and gastrointestinal issues. The infection is common in tropical and subtropical regions, affecting both humans and animals, especially those with barefoot exposure.

Ancylostomiasis due to *Ancylostoma ceylanicum* is a parasitic infection caused by the hookworm *Ancylostoma ceylanicum*, which primarily affects the small intestine. Common synonyms include tropical pulmonary eosinophilia and visceral larva migrans. The larvae migrate through the lungs, causing respiratory symptoms, before establishing adult worms in the intestine. Infection leads to anemia, protein loss, and malnutrition. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas with poor sanitation. The condition predominantly affects the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, with systemic involvement in severe cases.

"Other specified ancylostoma" refers to infections caused by species of *Ancylostoma* not classified under *Ancylostoma duodenale* or *Ancylostoma ceylanicum*. Common synonyms include hookworm infections caused by other *Ancylostoma* species. Causative agents include *Ancylostoma braziliense* and *Ancylostoma caninum*, though the latter primarily affects animals. Human infections are rare but can occur through skin penetration. Typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, causing anemia, malnutrition, and intestinal inflammation. Transmission occurs via contaminated soil, leading to cutaneous larva migrans or intestinal infestation.

Ancylostomiasis and necatoriasis are helminthic infections caused by hookworms, primarily *Ancylostoma duodenale* and *Necator americanus*. These parasites infect the small intestine, leading to anemia, protein loss, and malnutrition. Common synonyms include hookworm infection and soil-transmitted helminthiasis. Transmission occurs via penetration of skin by infective larvae, often from contaminated soil. The larvae migrate through the lungs before establishing residence in the intestinal mucosa. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fatigue. These infections are prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions with poor sanitation.

Ascariasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Ascaris lumbricoides*, a nematode roundworm. Common synonyms include intestinal roundworm infection and giant intestinal roundworm disease. The larvae migrate through the lungs before maturing in the small intestine, where adult worms reside. Symptoms include abdominal pain, malnutrition, and intestinal blockage. Children are most commonly affected, with infection occurring via ingestion of contaminated soil. Complications may involve visceral larva migrans or pneumonitis. Diagnosis is often clinical, with stool examination for eggs confirming the infection.

Anisakiasis is a parasitic infection caused by ingestion of larvae of the nematode *Anisakis* species. Common synonyms include fish tapeworm infection and anisakidosis. The larvae typically attach to the mucosa of the stomach or small intestine, causing acute inflammation, pain, and sometimes obstruction. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and allergic reactions. The condition is most commonly acquired through consumption of raw or undercooked marine fish or squid. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with endoscopy used for confirmation and removal of larvae.

Strongyloidiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Strongyloides stercoralis*. It primarily affects the small intestine, where the larvae migrate through the intestinal wall. The infection can be asymptomatic or present with gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. In immunocompromised individuals, it may lead to disseminated strongyloidiasis, involving the lungs, liver, and other organs. Synonyms include filariasis and strongyloidiasis. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, often acquired through skin contact with contaminated soil.

Trichuriasis is a helminthic infection caused by the whipworm *Trichuris trichiura*, commonly affecting the large intestine. It is also known as whipworm infection or threadworm disease. The parasite attaches to the intestinal wall, leading to inflammation, mucosal damage, and symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rectal prolapse. Children and individuals in areas with poor sanitation are most commonly affected. Heavy infestations may result in anemia and growth impairment. Transmission occurs via ingestion of infective eggs present in contaminated soil or food.

Enterobiasis, also known as pinworm infection, is a common intestinal parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Enterobius vermicularis*. The infection primarily affects the colon and perianal region, with adult female worms migrating to the perineum to lay eggs, causing intense itching. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs, often through contaminated fingers, surfaces, or inhalation. It is most common in children and spreads easily in crowded conditions. Symptoms include perianal pruritus, restlessness, and occasionally abdominal discomfort. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by the tape test.

Capillariasis is a parasitic infection caused by the trematode *Capillaria philippinensis*, primarily affecting the lungs. It is also known as philippinensis capillariasis or pulmonary capillariasis. The larvae migrate through the bloodstream to the lungs, where they mature and cause inflammation. Symptoms include cough, hemoptysis, and respiratory distress. The condition is endemic in Southeast Asia, particularly among individuals exposed to contaminated water. Diagnosis is often challenging due to the non-specific symptoms and the difficulty in detecting the parasites. Treatment typically involves antiparasitic medications such as albendazole or ivermectin.

Trichostrongyliasis is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the family Trichostrongylidae. Common synonyms include gastrointestinal strongyloidiasis and small intestinal nematodiasis. The primary causative agents are *Strongyloides stercoralis*, *Trichuris trichiura*, and *Ancylostoma duodenale*. This condition primarily affects the small intestine and rectum, with *T. trichiura* causing whipworm infection. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often transmitted through contaminated soil.

Other specified intestinal helminthiasis refers to infections caused by parasitic worms that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified intestinal helminthiasis. Causative agents may include species such as *Strongyloides stercoralis*, *Trichuris trichiura*, and *Enterobius vermicularis*. These parasites primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the small intestine, large intestine, and rectum. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and intestinal obstruction. Transmission typically occurs through ingestion of infective eggs or larvae.

Mixed intestinal helminthiasis refers to the concurrent infection of the intestines by multiple species of helminths. Common synonyms include polyparasitism or mixed worm infestation. Causative agents may include nematodes such as *Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Trichuris trichiura*, and *Strongyloides stercoralis*, as well as cestodes like *Hymenolepis nana* and *Taenia* species. The primary affected body parts are the small and large intestines, with potential for systemic complications. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, malnutrition, and anemia. Diagnosis typically involves stool examination for ova and parasites.

Intestinal helminthiasis, unspecified, refers to infection of the gastrointestinal tract by parasitic worms. Common synonyms include intestinal worm infestation or helminthic infection. Causative agents may include roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, and tapeworms. The condition primarily affects the small and large intestines, sometimes extending to the stomach or colon. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and malnutrition. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through stool examination for ova or larvae. Treatment involves anthelmintic medications.

Toxocariasis is a parasitic infection caused by the larvae of *Toxocara canis* and *Toxocara cati*, common intestinal roundworms of dogs and cats. Infection occurs through ingestion of eggs from contaminated soil or via accidental ingestion of infected animals. The larvae migrate through tissues, primarily affecting the liver, lungs, and eyes, leading to visceral or ocular disease. Symptoms vary from asymptomatic to fever, cough, and eosinophilia. Ocular involvement may result in blindness. Synonyms include visceral larva migrans and ocular larva migrans.

Gnathostomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genus *Gnathostoma*, typically *Gnathostoma spinigerum*. It is acquired through ingestion of undercooked meat containing larvae or via skin penetration. The infection leads to migratory cutaneous lesions and can affect multiple organs, including the lungs, brain, and subcutaneous tissues. Common synonyms include visceral gnathostomiasis and cutaneous gnathostomiasis. Symptoms include itching, swelling, and sometimes severe systemic reactions. The condition is endemic in parts of Asia, Latin America, and Africa.

Other specified helminthiasis refers to parasitic worm infections caused by helminths not classified under more specific categories such as ascariasis or schistosomiasis. Common synonyms include unspecified helminth infection. Causative agents may include various nematodes, trematodes, or cestodes, depending on the region and exposure. Typically, these infections affect the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, liver, or skin, depending on the parasite. Symptoms vary but often include abdominal pain, malnutrition, and allergic reactions. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through stool examination or imaging. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs tailored to the specific parasite identified.

Helminth infection, unspecified, refers to parasitic worm infestations caused by various species of roundworms, flatworms, or flukes. Common synonyms include helminthiasis and parasitic worm infection. Causative agents may include nematodes like Ascaris lumbricoides, trematodes such as Schistosoma species, and cestodes like Taenia. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, liver, lungs, and blood, depending on the parasite. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, weight loss, and malnutrition. Diagnosis often involves stool examination or imaging. Treatment depends on the specific helminth involved.

Intestinal parasitism, unspecified refers to the presence of parasitic organisms in the gastrointestinal tract without a specific identification of the parasite. Common synonyms include intestinal infestation and helminthic infection. Causative agents may include protozoa such as Giardia lamblia and Entamoeba histolytica, or helminths like Ascaris lumbricoides and Trichuris trichiura. The primary affected body parts are the small intestine, large intestine, and sometimes the stomach. Symptoms may include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through stool examination.

Meningoencephalitis due to toxoplasmosis is a central nervous system infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection leads to inflammation of the brain and meninges, resulting in symptoms like fever, headache, seizures, and altered mental status. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic encephalitis and cerebral toxoplasmosis. The causative agent is *Toxoplasma gondii*, a protozoan parasite. The brain, particularly the basal ganglia and thalamus, is typically affected.

Conjunctivitis due to toxoplasmosis is an inflammatory eye condition caused by the protozoan parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically presents as a unilateral, acute conjunctival infection with redness, swelling, and sometimes a watery discharge. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic conjunctivitis or ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection often affects the conjunctiva and may involve the cornea or uvea. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, and can be associated with systemic toxoplasmosis. Transmission occurs via contaminated material, often from cat feces or undercooked meat.

Chorioretinitis due to toxoplasmosis is an inflammatory eye infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It primarily affects the choroid and retina, leading to focal necrotizing lesions. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic chorioretinitis and ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection is typically acquired through ingestion of oocysts from contaminated food or water. It commonly affects the posterior segment of the eye, especially in immunocompromised individuals or those with reactivated latent infections. Symptoms may include decreased vision, floaters, and photophobia.

Myocarditis due to toxoplasmosis is an inflammatory condition of the heart muscle caused by the protozoan parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*. It is a rare but serious complication, often occurring in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include toxoplasma myocarditis. The infection typically affects the myocardium, leading to symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It may also involve the lungs and central nervous system. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing, PCR, or biopsy. Treatment involves antiparasitic medications like pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine, along with supportive care.

Pneumonitis due to toxoplasmosis is an inflammatory lung condition caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection leads to interstitial pneumonia characterized by non-caseating granulomas. Common synonyms include pulmonary toxoplasmosis and opportunistic pneumonitis. The primary causative agent is *Toxoplasma gondii*, which is transmitted via ingestion of oocysts or tissue cysts. The lungs are the main affected body part, though systemic involvement can occur.

Hepatitis due to toxoplasmosis is a rare form of liver inflammation caused by the protozoan parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection can lead to fever, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic hepatitis and parasitic hepatitis. The parasite is transmitted via ingestion of oocysts from contaminated food or water, or through congenital transmission. The liver is the primary affected organ, though the infection can disseminate to other organs, including the brain, leading to severe complications.

Toxoplasmosis of other specified sites refers to infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii* affecting organs or tissues not typically associated with the central nervous system or ocular involvement. Common synonyms include extraneural toxoplasmosis and non-CNS toxoplasmosis. The parasite primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, with common sites including the lungs, liver, and lymph nodes. It may also involve the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and muscles. Clinical presentation varies but often includes fever, lymphadenopathy, and organ-specific symptoms. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing and imaging, with treatment typically involving antiparasitic medications.

Multisystemic disseminated toxoplasmosis is a severe opportunistic infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. It presents with systemic involvement of multiple organs, most commonly the brain, lungs, liver, and lymph nodes. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic encephalitis and disseminated toxoplasmosis. The infection typically manifests as focal or diffuse lesions in the central nervous system, accompanied by fever, headache, and neurological deficits. It is a life-threatening condition requiring prompt antiparasitic therapy.

Toxoplasmosis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It can present systemically or as an ocular infection, often in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic encephalitis and ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection typically affects the brain, eyes, and other organs. Symptoms may include fever, headache, seizures, and vision loss. It is transmitted via ingestion of oocysts from contaminated food or water, or congenitally. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing or PCR. Treatment involves antiparasitic medications such as pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine.

Urogenital trichomoniasis, unspecified, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the genital tract, including the vagina, urethra, and sometimes the penis. Common synonyms include trichomoniasis vaginitis and trichomonas infection. The condition is characterized by symptoms such as itching, burning, and abnormal discharge. It is more commonly diagnosed in females but can occur in males as well. Transmission occurs through sexual contact, and diagnosis is typically confirmed via microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves antiprotozoal medications such as metronidazole or tinidazole.

Trichomonal vulvovaginitis is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the lower genital tract, including the vagina and vulva in women, and the urethra and prostate in men. Common synonyms include trichomoniasis or trichomonal infection. The condition is characterized by inflammation, itching, burning, and a frothy, malodorous vaginal discharge. It is transmitted through sexual contact and is more prevalent in women, though men can also be asymptomatic carriers. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests.

Trichomonal urethritis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the urogenital tract, causing inflammation of the urethra, vagina, and sometimes the cervix. Common synonyms include trichomoniasis and trichomonal infection. Symptoms may include itching, burning, and abnormal discharge. The infection is more common in women but can also occur in men, though often asymptomatic. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves antiprotozoal medications such as metronidazole or tinidazole.

Trichomonal prostatitis is a rare form of prostatitis caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis*, a protozoan parasite. It is less common than bacterial prostatitis and often presents with symptoms similar to other inflammatory conditions of the prostate. The infection primarily affects the prostate gland, leading to inflammation and possible urethral involvement. Common synonyms include trichomonal urethritis and trichomonal infection of the prostate. Transmission typically occurs through sexual contact, and diagnosis may require nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment usually involves antiprotozoal medications such as metronidazole or tinidazole.

Other urogenital trichomoniasis refers to a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis*, primarily affecting the urogenital tract. It commonly involves the vagina, urethra, and prostate in men. The infection is characterized by inflammation, discharge, and discomfort. Synonyms include trichomonal urethritis and trichomoniasis. While *T. vaginalis* is the sole known causative agent, the term "other" may sometimes be used to distinguish it from non-specific urethritis. It is more prevalent in women but can also affect men, often asymptomatic in males. Diagnosis typically involves microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests.

Trichomoniasis of other specified sites refers to infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis* in locations other than the genital tract, such as the urethra, bladder, or rectum. Though less common, it can occur in individuals with compromised immune systems or through sexual contact. Symptoms may include irritation, discharge, or discomfort in the affected area. Diagnosis typically involves microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests. This condition is often asymptomatic but can lead to complications if untreated. It is important to note that *T. vaginalis* is a flagellate protozoan parasite primarily associated with genital infections.

Trichomoniasis, unspecified, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the urogenital tract, commonly involving the vagina, urethra, and prostate in males. Common synonyms include trichomonad infection or trichomonal vaginitis. Symptoms may include itching, burning, and abnormal discharge. The infection is more prevalent in women but can also occur in men. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves antiprotozoal medications such as metronidazole or tinidazole.

Pediculus capitis, commonly known as head lice, is a parasitic infestation caused by the human head louse, Pediculus humanus capitis. These tiny, wingless insects feed on human blood and lay eggs (nits) on hair shafts. The condition is highly contagious and typically affects the scalp, particularly behind the ears and at the nape of the neck. Common synonyms include "lice" or "head lice." Transmission occurs through direct head-to-head contact or sharing of personal items. Symptoms include intense itching and a sensation of movement on the scalp.

Pediculus corporis, commonly known as the body louse, is a parasitic insect that infests the clothing and bedding of humans, particularly in poor hygiene or overcrowded conditions. It feeds on human blood and causes intense itching and skin irritation. The louse is a member of the Pediculidae family and is transmitted through direct contact or shared personal items. It primarily affects the torso, neck, and arms, and is more prevalent in warm, humid environments. Synonyms include human body louse and clothing louse. The primary causative agent is Pediculus humanus corporis.

Phthirus pubis, or pubic louse, is a contagious ectoparasitic infestation affecting the pubic hair region. Common synonyms include crabs and pubic lice. The causative agent is *Pthirus pubis*, a species of louse that feeds on human blood. Infestation typically occurs in the pubic area, groin, and adjacent regions. Symptoms include intense pruritus, erythema, and visible lice or nits. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact or sharing of infested items. It is commonly seen in sexually active individuals but can affect anyone. Treatment involves topical insecticides and thorough cleaning of affected areas.

Mixed pediculosis infestation refers to the presence of more than one species of lice on a single host. Common synonyms include coinfection or polymicrobial pediculosis. The causative agents typically include *Pediculus humanus capitis* (head lice), *Pediculus humanus corporis* (body lice), and *Pediculus humanus pubis* (pubic lice). This condition most commonly affects the scalp, body, and pubic areas, often seen in crowded or unsanitary conditions. Symptoms include intense itching, rash, and visible lice or nits. Treatment usually involves combing, topical insecticides, and environmental control.

Pediculosis, unspecified, refers to infestation by lice, typically head, body, or pubic lice. Common synonyms include lice infestation or pediculosis capitis/body/pubis. The causative agents are Pediculus humanus capitis, Pediculus humanus corporis, and Phthirus pubis. The condition is characterized by itching, rash, and visible nits or lice on the affected areas. It commonly affects the scalp, body, and pubic regions, particularly in children and individuals in close contact. Transmission occurs through direct contact or shared personal items. Treatment involves topical insecticides and thorough cleaning of belongings.

Scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by the mite *Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*. It is characterized by intense pruritus and a rash consisting of small red bumps or burrows. Common synonyms include itch mite and scabetic disease. The mites burrow into the epidermis, triggering an allergic reaction. The condition primarily affects the hands, wrists, feet, and genitalia, with common sites including the fingers, elbows, and buttocks. Transmission occurs through prolonged skin-to-skin contact. The infection is prevalent in crowded living conditions and among immunocompromised individuals.

Other acariasis refers to infestations caused by mites other than scabies or demodicosis. Common synonyms include mange and acarosis. Causative agents include species such as *Sarcoptes scabiei* (varieties affecting animals), *Demodex folliculorum*, and *Psoroptes* species. These mites typically affect the skin, hair follicles, and mucous membranes. Infestations can occur in both humans and animals, with symptoms including pruritus, erythema, and crusts. The condition is often diagnosed through clinical examination and skin scrapings.

Acariasis, unspecified, refers to infestation with mites, typically causing dermatological symptoms. Common synonyms include scabies or demodicosis, though these terms may denote specific mite species. The causative agents are various mites, most commonly *Sarcoptes scabiei* for scabies. The condition primarily affects the skin, particularly areas such as the hands, wrists, elbows, and genital regions. It may also involve the scalp, face, and nails. Symptoms include intense itching, rash, and skin lesions. Diagnosis is often clinical, based on symptoms and physical examination. Treatment involves topical or systemic acaricides.

Myiasis is an infestation of living tissue by fly larvae. Common synonyms include myiases and larval infestation. It is caused by various dipteran flies, with *Dermatobia hominis*, *Lucilia* species, and *Fannia canicularis* being notable pathogens. Typically affecting skin and mucous membranes, it commonly occurs in tropical and subtropical regions. The condition may involve wounds, nasal passages, ears, and gastrointestinal tract, depending on the species. Clinical manifestations include localized inflammation, necrosis, and sometimes systemic symptoms. Prompt identification and removal of larvae are essential for effective treatment.

"Other arthropod infestation" refers to infestations caused by arthropods not classified as lice, mites, or ticks. Common synonyms include insect bites or arthropod bites. Causative agents may include flies, mosquitoes, bed bugs, and fleas. These infestations typically affect exposed body parts such as the skin, scalp, and ears. Symptoms often include itching, redness, and localized inflammation. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and patient history. Treatment involves removing the arthropod, managing symptoms, and preventing reinfestation.

Hirudiniasis is a condition caused by the bite of leeches, typically *Hirudo medicinalis*, which secrete anticoagulants like hirudin. It results in localized bleeding, swelling, and sometimes secondary infections. Common synonyms include leech infestation or leech bite. The condition most commonly affects the lower extremities, particularly in individuals who have been in aquatic environments or have used leeches for therapeutic purposes. Symptoms may include pain, erythema, and prolonged bleeding. Complications can arise from excessive blood loss or infection if left untreated.

"Other specified infestations" refers to parasitic infestations not classified under more specific categories, often involving ectoparasites. Common synonyms include unspecified parasitic infestations. Causative agents may include lice, mites, ticks, and fleas. These infestations typically affect the scalp, skin, ears, and hair. Symptoms include itching, irritation, and visible parasites. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and physical examination. Treatment involves targeted topical or systemic agents depending on the parasite involved.

Infestation, unspecified, refers to the presence of parasitic organisms in a host without specifying the type of parasite or affected site. Common synonyms include parasitism or infestation. Causative agents may include ectoparasites such as lice, mites, or fleas, and endoparasites like worms. Typically affects skin, hair, or gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms may include itching, irritation, or systemic manifestations depending on the parasite. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and sometimes laboratory testing. Treatment varies based on the identified parasite and affected area.

Acanthamoeba infection is a rare but serious parasitic disease caused by free-living amoebae of the genus *Acanthamoeba*. Common synonyms include granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE) and naegleria fowleri infection, though the latter is caused by a different species. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis, but can also involve the eyes, causing keratitis. The causative agents include *Acanthamoeba polyphaga*, *Acanthamoeba castellani*, and *Acanthamoeba tripartita*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals or those with ocular trauma, presenting with fever, seizures, and neurological deficits.

code_desc: other specific infections by free-living amebae
summary: "Other specific infections by free-living amebae" refers to infections caused by amebae that are not typically pathogenic but can cause disease under certain conditions. Common synonyms include granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE) and naegleria meningitis. The primary causative agents are Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia mandrillaris. These infections typically affect the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis or meningitis. Acanthamoeba may also cause keratitis, particularly in contact lens users. The infections are rare but can be severe and often fatal if not promptly diagnosed and treated.

Psorospermiasis is a rare, chronic granulomatous infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii*, a dimorphic fungus. It typically presents as a slowly progressing, painless nodule or ulcer, often on the skin, especially in areas of minor trauma or puncture wounds. Common synonyms include sporotrichosis and roseogranuloma. The infection can disseminate to lymph nodes, bones, and viscera in immunocompromised individuals. It is often acquired through contact with contaminated soil, plants, or animal secretions. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Sarcosporidiosis is a parasitic infection caused by species of the genus *Sarcocystis*, primarily affecting the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include sarcocystosis and sarcocyst infection. The causative agents are various *Sarcocystis* species, with *S. suihominis* and *S. neurona* being notable. The disease typically affects the intestines, leading to inflammation and ulceration. In severe cases, it may disseminate to other organs, including the central nervous system. It is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and those exposed to infected animals.

code_desc: other specified infectious and parasitic diseases
summary: "Other specified infectious and parasitic diseases" refers to infections caused by various pathogens that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified infectious diseases and parasitic infections. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites such as *Plasmodium*, *Toxoplasma*, or *Leishmania*. These diseases typically affect the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or central nervous systems, and may present with fever, rash, or organ dysfunction. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and laboratory testing.

Unspecified infectious and parasitic diseases refer to infections caused by microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites that have not been specifically identified or classified. Common synonyms include undiagnosed infectious diseases and unspecified parasitic infections. Causative agents may vary widely, including organisms like *Plasmodium*, *Toxoplasma*, or *Mycobacterium* species. These conditions can affect multiple body systems, but are most commonly seen in the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and hematological systems. Clinical presentation is often nonspecific, including fever, fatigue, and systemic inflammation.

code_desc: late effects of respiratory or unspecified tuberculosis
summary: Late effects of respiratory or unspecified tuberculosis refer to long-term complications arising after active tuberculosis has been resolved. These can include pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, pleural thickening, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Common synonyms include post-tuberculosis sequelae or residual tuberculosis damage. Causative agents are typically Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Affected body parts primarily involve the lungs, but may extend to the pleura and occasionally other organs. These effects can lead to progressive respiratory impairment and increased susceptibility to infections.

code_desc: late effects of central nervous system tuberculosis
summary: Late effects of central nervous system tuberculosis refer to long-term complications following primary tuberculosis infection involving the brain or spinal cord. Common synonyms include post-tubercular neurological sequelae and tuberculous encephalomyelitis sequelae. Causative agents are Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These effects typically involve the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to conditions such as hydrocephalus, stroke-like symptoms, seizures, cognitive deficits, and motor impairments. Late onset may occur months to years after initial infection or treatment.

Late effects of genitourinary tuberculosis refer to long-term complications arising from prior tuberculosis infection of the urinary tract. Common synonyms include post-tubercular urological complications or tuberculous bladder disease. Caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, these effects often involve the bladder, ureters, and kidneys. Common manifestations include bladder contracture, ureteral strictures, hydronephrosis, and chronic kidney disease. Patients may present with urinary retention, recurrent infections, or renal failure. Diagnosis typically requires imaging and urodynamic studies, with management focusing on surgical correction and renal protection.

code_desc: late effects of tuberculosis of bones and joints
summary: Late effects of tuberculosis of bones and joints refer to long-term complications following healed tuberculosis infection in the musculoskeletal system. Common synonyms include post-tubercular osteoarticular sequelae and tuberculous arthritis sequelae. Caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, these effects often involve joint contractures, deformities, and chronic pain. Commonly affected areas include the spine (tuberculous spondylitis), hips, knees, and shoulders. Patients may experience limited mobility and functional disability. These sequelae can develop years after initial infection and treatment. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent irreversible damage.

code_desc: late effects of tuberculosis of other specified organs
summary: Late effects of tuberculosis of other specified organs refer to chronic complications arising from prior tuberculosis infection in non-respiratory sites. These effects may include fibrosis, organ dysfunction, or structural damage. Common synonyms include post-tubercular sequelae or residual tuberculosis damage. Causative agents are Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Typically affected body parts include the lymphatic system, genitourinary tract, bones, and joints. Symptoms may vary but often involve pain, swelling, or organ failure, depending on the affected area. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, imaging, and sometimes biopsy.

Late effects of acute poliomyelitis refer to long-term or delayed complications arising from a past poliovirus infection. These can include post-polio syndrome, characterized by progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and joint pain. Common synonyms include post-polio sequelae or residual effects of polio. The causative agent is the poliovirus, which primarily affects the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, leading to muscle atrophy and paralysis. Typically affected body parts include the limbs, particularly the lower extremities, and the respiratory muscles in severe cases.

Late effects of viral encephalitis refer to long-term neurological and psychological complications that may develop months to years after an acute infection. Common synonyms include post-encephalitic syndromes or sequelae. Causative agents include herpes simplex virus, West Nile virus, and Japanese encephalitis virus. These effects often involve the central nervous system, leading to cognitive impairment, seizures, motor deficits, behavioral changes, and psychiatric symptoms. Affected body parts primarily include the brain, particularly the temporal and frontal lobes, and may extend to the spinal cord or peripheral nerves in some cases.

Late effects of trachoma refer to long-term complications arising from repeated ocular infections caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. These effects include scarring of the eyelids, misalignment of the eyelashes (trichiasis), and eventual corneal opacity, leading to vision loss or blindness. Synonyms include trachomatous scarring and trachomatous trichiasis. The primary causative agent is *C. trachomatis*, with the disease predominantly affecting the conjunctiva and cornea, especially in children and women in endemic regions.

code_desc: late effects of other and unspecified infectious and parasitic diseases
summary: Late effects of other and unspecified infectious and parasitic diseases refer to long-term complications arising from past infections caused by various pathogens such as tuberculosis, HIV, leishmaniasis, or schistosomiasis. These effects may manifest years after the initial infection has resolved. Commonly affected systems include the respiratory, neurological, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal systems. Symptoms may vary widely and can include chronic fatigue, organ dysfunction, or autoimmune-like conditions. Synonyms include post-infectious complications or sequelae of infectious diseases.

Acute nasopharyngitis, commonly known as the common cold, is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract. It primarily affects the nasal passages and pharynx, causing symptoms such as sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and sore throat. Common synonyms include viral upper respiratory infection and acute coryza. The most frequent causative agents are rhinoviruses, followed by coronaviruses, adenoviruses, and respiratory syncytial virus. It predominantly affects the nose, throat, and adjacent mucosal surfaces, with symptoms typically resolving within 7–10 days without specific treatment.

Acute sinusitis is an inflammatory condition of the paranasal sinuses, typically lasting less than four weeks. It is commonly caused by viral infections, though bacterial pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis* may also be involved. Common symptoms include nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, purulent nasal discharge, and sometimes fever. It often follows upper respiratory tract infections and primarily affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses. Synonyms include acute rhinosinusitis and acute sinus infection.

Acute maxillary sinusitis is an inflammation of the maxillary sinuses, typically lasting less than four weeks. It is often caused by viral infections, though bacterial pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis* may contribute. Common symptoms include facial pain or pressure, nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, and fever. It commonly affects the maxillary sinuses, which are located in the cheekbones. Synonyms include acute bacterial rhinosinusitis and acute sinus infection. The condition may spread to adjacent structures if untreated.

Acute frontal sinusitis is an inflammation of the frontal sinuses, typically lasting less than four weeks. It often follows upper respiratory infections and is characterized by symptoms such as frontal headache, nasal congestion, and purulent nasal discharge. Common causative agents include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. It may present with fever and facial tenderness. Synonyms include acute frontal sinus infection or frontal sinus inflammation. The condition primarily affects the frontal sinuses, located above the eyebrows.

Acute ethmoidal sinusitis is an inflammation of the ethmoid sinuses, typically caused by viral infections, though bacterial agents like *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Haemophilus influenzae* may also be involved. It often presents with symptoms such as facial pain, nasal congestion, and purulent nasal discharge. Common synonyms include acute ethmoid sinus infection or ethmoid sinus inflammation. The condition primarily affects the ethmoid sinuses, which are located between the eyes and nose, and may spread to adjacent structures if untreated. It is more common in individuals with nasal allergies or structural abnormalities.

Acute sphenoidal sinusitis is an inflammation of the sphenoidal sinuses, typically caused by viral or bacterial infection. It often follows upper respiratory tract infections and can lead to severe headaches, orbital pain, and fever. Common causative agents include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. The condition primarily affects the sphenoid sinuses, located behind the ethmoid sinuses, and may spread to adjacent structures such as the cranial cavity or eye socket. Synonyms include acute sphenoid sinus infection or sphenoidal sinus inflammation.

Other acute sinusitis refers to inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting less than four weeks, typically caused by viral infections, though bacterial or fungal pathogens may also be involved. Common synonyms include acute rhinosinusitis and acute sinus infection. It predominantly affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses. Symptoms include nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, purulent nasal discharge, and sometimes fever. It often follows upper respiratory tract infections and is more common in adults than in children. Treatment may involve decongestants, nasal irrigation, and antibiotics if bacterial involvement is suspected.

Acute sinusitis, unspecified, is an inflammatory condition of the paranasal sinuses lasting less than four weeks. It is characterized by nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, and thick nasal discharge. Common synonyms include acute rhinosinusitis and acute sinus infection. Causative agents often include viral pathogens such as rhinovirus, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus, though bacterial causes like *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae* may also occur. The condition primarily affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses. It typically follows upper respiratory tract infections and is more common in adults.

Acute pharyngitis is an inflammation of the pharynx, commonly presenting with sore throat, pain, and difficulty swallowing. It is often caused by viral infections, though bacterial pathogens such as *Streptococcus pyogenes* can also be responsible. Common synonyms include acute sore throat and pharyngitis. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, with symptoms often involving the tonsils and larynx. It is more prevalent in children and young adults, typically resolving within a week without specific treatment in viral cases.

Acute tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils, typically characterized by sore throat, fever, and swollen, red tonsils often with white or yellow exudate. Common synonyms include acute pharyngitis and tonsillar infection. The condition is most commonly caused by viral agents such as adenovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and influenza virus, though bacterial causes like Group A Streptococcus are also frequent. It primarily affects the pharyngeal tonsils, with symptoms often localized to the throat and surrounding areas.

Acute laryngitis and tracheitis refer to inflammation of the larynx and trachea, commonly caused by viral infections such as influenza or rhinovirus. Bacterial agents like Streptococcus pyogenes may also contribute. Symptoms include hoarseness, sore throat, cough, and stridor. The condition typically affects the upper respiratory tract, involving the vocal cords and tracheal mucosa. It is more prevalent in children and individuals with compromised immune systems. Common synonyms include acute laryngotracheitis and viral croup. The inflammation often results from viral upper respiratory infections, leading to airway obstruction in severe cases.

Acute laryngitis is an inflammation of the larynx, typically causing hoarseness, sore throat, and voice changes. It is commonly caused by viral infections, though bacterial or fungal causes may occur. Common synonyms include acute pharyngolaryngitis or laryngeal inflammation. The condition primarily affects the vocal cords and surrounding mucosa, often leading to cough and difficulty speaking. It is most prevalent in adults and children, with risk factors including vocal strain, smoking, and upper respiratory infections. Symptoms usually resolve within 1-2 weeks without specific treatment.

code_desc: Acute laryngitis without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute laryngitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the larynx, typically characterized by hoarseness, sore throat, and cough. Common synonyms include acute laryngeal inflammation or laryngotracheitis. It is most commonly caused by viral infections, such as rhinovirus or influenza, though bacterial agents like Streptococcus pyogenes may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the vocal cords and surrounding mucosa, often resulting from overuse, irritation, or infection. It is more prevalent in adults and children, with symptoms usually resolving within 1–2 weeks without specific treatment.

Acute laryngitis with obstruction is an inflammatory condition of the larynx characterized by swelling and narrowing of the airway, leading to breathing difficulties. Common synonyms include acute laryngeal edema and acute laryngeal obstruction. It is often caused by viral infections, such as influenza or common cold viruses, though bacterial agents like Streptococcus pyogenes may also be involved. Allergies, vocal strain, and irritants can contribute. The primary affected area is the larynx, with potential involvement of the upper airway, including the pharynx and trachea. Symptoms include hoarseness, stridor, and respiratory distress.

Acute tracheitis is an inflammation of the trachea, typically presenting with a harsh, barking cough and stridor. It often follows a viral upper respiratory infection. Common synonyms include tracheal croup and acute laryngotracheitis. Causative agents include viruses such as parainfluenza, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus. Bacterial causes like Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus may occur secondary to viral infection. The condition primarily affects the tracheal mucosa and submucosal glands, with symptoms often peaking within 2–3 days. It is most common in young children but can occur in adults.

code_desc: Acute tracheitis without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute tracheitis is an inflammatory condition of the trachea, typically presenting with a sudden onset of cough, stridor, and respiratory discomfort. It often occurs following viral upper respiratory infections. Common synonyms include acute tracheobronchitis and viral tracheitis. Causative agents are predominantly viral, such as influenza, parainfluenza, and respiratory syncytial virus. Bacterial causes like Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae may also contribute. The condition primarily affects the trachea and proximal bronchi, with symptoms usually resolving within days to weeks without specific treatment.

Acute tracheitis with obstruction is an acute inflammation of the trachea characterized by swelling and mucus production, leading to partial or complete airway blockage. Common synonyms include acute laryngotracheitis and tracheal inflammation. It is often caused by viral infections, particularly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza, and parainfluenza, though bacterial agents like Streptococcus pneumoniae may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the trachea, with symptoms including stridor, cough, and difficulty breathing. It is most commonly seen in children but can occur in adults with underlying respiratory conditions.

Acute laryngotracheitis is an acute inflammation of the larynx and trachea, commonly presenting with a barking cough, stridor, and hoarseness. It predominantly affects children, particularly those under 5 years old. Common synonyms include croup and acute spasmodic laryngitis. The condition is typically caused by viral infections, most commonly parainfluenza viruses, though respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and adenoviruses may also be implicated. The larynx and trachea are the primary affected areas, with swelling and edema leading to airway narrowing.

code_desc: Acute laryngotracheitis without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute laryngotracheitis is an inflammation of the larynx and trachea, typically presenting with a sore throat, hoarseness, and a barking cough. Common synonyms include croup and acute laryngotracheobronchitis. The condition is most commonly caused by viral infections, particularly parainfluenza viruses, although bacterial causes such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae may occur. It predominantly affects children, especially those under five years of age, due to the anatomical narrowness of their airways. The inflammation primarily involves the larynx and upper trachea, leading to variable degrees of respiratory distress.

Acute laryngotracheitis with obstruction is an acute inflammation of the larynx and trachea, often causing respiratory distress due to swelling and mucus buildup. Common synonyms include croup and acute laryngotracheobronchitis. It is most commonly caused by viral infections, particularly parainfluenza viruses, though bacterial causes may also occur. The condition primarily affects the upper airway, including the larynx, trachea, and sometimes the bronchi. It predominantly occurs in young children, with symptoms such as stridor, hoarseness, and a barking cough. Obstruction can lead to severe breathing difficulties, requiring prompt medical evaluation.

Acute epiglottitis is a severe, rapidly progressive inflammation of the epiglottis, often leading to airway obstruction. Common synonyms include acute laryngitis and epiglottic edema. It is most commonly caused by *Haemophilus influenzae* type b, though other bacteria such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Staphylococcus aureus* may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the epiglottis and surrounding structures in the upper airway, particularly in children under 5 years old. Symptoms include high fever, dysphagia, drooling, and stridor. Prompt recognition and management are critical to prevent respiratory compromise.

code_desc: Acute epiglottitis without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute epiglottitis is a severe, rapidly progressing inflammation of the epiglottis, typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Haemophilus influenzae* type b. It presents with sudden onset of sore throat, dysphagia, drooling, and stridor, often without significant airway obstruction initially. Synonyms include acute laryngitis or epiglottic inflammation. The condition primarily affects the epiglottis and surrounding structures in the upper airway, predominantly in children, though it can occur in adults. Prompt diagnosis and management are critical to prevent airway compromise.

Acute epiglottitis with obstruction is a severe, life-threatening inflammation of the epiglottis causing airway blockage. Common synonyms include acute laryngitis and epiglottic edema. It is most commonly caused by *Haemophilus influenzae* type b, though other pathogens like streptococci and staphylococci may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the epiglottis, arytenoids, and surrounding laryngeal structures. It predominantly occurs in children under 5 years old but can also affect adults. Symptoms include sore throat, drooling, stridor, and respiratory distress. Rapid airway management is critical due to the risk of complete airway obstruction.

Croup is an acute inflammatory condition affecting the upper airway, primarily the larynx and trachea. It is characterized by a distinctive barking cough and stridor, often worsening at night. Common synonyms include acute laryngotracheobronchitis and croup syndrome. The most common causative agent is the parainfluenza virus, though respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus, and influenza can also cause it. Typically affecting young children, especially those between 6 months and 3 years of age, croup is more prevalent in males. The inflammation leads to airway narrowing, causing respiratory distress.

Supraglottitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the supraglottic structures, including the epiglottis, arytenoids, and aryepiglottic folds, without a specific etiology identified. Common synonyms include acute supraglottitis and epiglottitis. It is often caused by viral infections, most commonly Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pyogenes, and influenza viruses. The condition primarily affects the upper airway, leading to swelling, stridor, and potential airway obstruction. It is more common in children but can occur in adults. Prompt diagnosis and management are critical to prevent respiratory compromise.

Supraglottitis unspecified, without obstruction refers to inflammation of the supraglottic structures, such as the epiglottis, arytenoids, and laryngeal ventricles, without airway compromise.
