Common synonyms include acute supraglottitis and epiglottitis. It is typically caused by viral infections, most commonly Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pyogenes, and respiratory syncytial virus. The condition predominantly affects children, though adults can also be involved. Symptoms include sore throat, fever, and dysphonia, with potential progression to respiratory distress if left untreated.

Supraglottitis unspecified, with obstruction refers to inflammation of the supraglottic structures, such as the epiglottis, arytenoids, and vocal folds, leading to airway compromise. Common synonyms include acute supraglottitis and epiglottitis. It is most commonly caused by viral infections, particularly Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pyogenes, and influenza viruses. Typically affecting children and immunocompromised individuals, the condition can cause severe respiratory distress, stridor, and difficulty swallowing. Prompt diagnosis and management are essential to prevent airway obstruction and respiratory failure.

code_desc: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple or unspecified sites
summary: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple or unspecified sites refer to inflammatory conditions affecting various upper respiratory tract areas, often with overlapping symptoms. Common synonyms include common cold, viral coryza, and acute rhinosinusitis. Causative agents are primarily viruses such as rhinovirus, coronavirus, and adenovirus. Typically affecting the nose, throat, pharynx, and sinuses, these infections may also involve the larynx and trachea. Symptoms include rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, and fever. They are usually self-limiting but can lead to secondary bacterial complications.

Acute laryngopharyngitis is an inflammation of the larynx and pharynx, often presenting with sore throat, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Common synonyms include acute pharyngolaryngitis and acute laryngitis with pharyngeal involvement. It is typically caused by viral infections, most commonly adenovirus, influenza, and rhinovirus. Bacterial causes such as Streptococcus pyogenes may also occur. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal and laryngeal mucosa, with symptoms often worsening during sleep due to postnasal drip. It is more common in children and adults with compromised immune function.

code_desc: Acute upper respiratory infections of other multiple sites
summary: Acute upper respiratory infections of other multiple sites refer to infections involving multiple upper respiratory tract areas beyond the common sites like the nose, pharynx, and larynx. Common synonyms include multifocal upper respiratory infections or polyphonic upper respiratory infections. These infections are typically caused by viral agents such as rhinovirus, influenza virus, and respiratory syncytial virus. They commonly affect the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and sometimes the ears and sinuses, leading to symptoms like congestion, sore throat, cough, and fever. Bacterial complications may occur in predisposed individuals.

code_desc: Acute upper respiratory infections of unspecified site
summary: Acute upper respiratory infections of unspecified site refer to inflammatory conditions affecting the upper respiratory tract without a specific localization. Common synonyms include common cold and viral rhinitis. These infections are primarily caused by viruses, most notably rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, and influenza viruses. Typically affecting the nasal passages, pharynx, and larynx, symptoms include rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, and fever. They are highly contagious and often self-limiting, with resolution within a week. Bacterial causes are less common but may occur in complications such as sinusitis or otitis media.

Acute bronchitis and bronchiolitis are inflammatory conditions affecting the lower respiratory tract. Acute bronchitis involves inflammation of the bronchi, often following a viral upper respiratory infection, while bronchiolitis affects the smaller airways, primarily the bronchioles. Common causative agents include respiratory viruses such as rhinovirus, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Both conditions typically present with cough, wheezing, and dyspnea. Acute bronchitis is more common in adults, whereas bronchiolitis predominantly affects infants and young children. Synonyms for bronchitis include acute tracheobronchitis, and for bronchiolitis, obstructive bronchiolitis or viral bronchiolitis.

Acute bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial tubes, typically caused by viral infections, though bacterial or fungal causes may occur. It presents with cough, often productive of mucus, along with symptoms such as chest discomfort, fever, and fatigue. Common synonyms include acute tracheobronchitis. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, with involvement of the trachea in some cases. It is most commonly seen in adults and is often a complication of upper respiratory infections. Risk factors include smoking and exposure to irritants. The illness is usually self-limiting, resolving within a few weeks.

Acute bronchiolitis is an acute inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles), primarily affecting infants and young children. Common synonyms include viral bronchiolitis and bronchiolar infection. It is most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), though other viruses like influenza and parainfluenza may also be responsible. The condition typically presents with cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. It primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, including the bronchioles and alveoli, leading to airflow obstruction and increased mucus production. Complications may include pneumonia or respiratory failure in severe cases.

code_desc: Acute bronchiolitis due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
summary: Acute bronchiolitis due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a viral infection affecting the lower respiratory tract, primarily in infants and young children. It causes inflammation and obstruction of the bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include RSV bronchiolitis and viral bronchiolitis. RSV is the primary causative agent, though other viruses like parainfluenza and adenovirus may also contribute. The condition typically affects the lungs, particularly the small airways, and can progress to pneumonia in severe cases.

code_desc: Acute bronchiolitis due to other infectious organisms
summary: Acute bronchiolitis due to other infectious organisms is an acute inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles) caused by pathogens other than respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Common synonyms include viral bronchiolitis or infectious bronchiolitis. Causative agents may include influenza virus, parainfluenza, adenovirus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. The condition primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly the bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. It is most commonly seen in young children but can occur in adults with underlying lung disease.

A deviated nasal septum is a condition where the thin wall of cartilage and bone separating the two nostrils is displaced to one side, leading to impaired airflow and potential breathing difficulties. Common synonyms include septal deviation and nasal septum deviation. It is often caused by congenital factors, trauma, or prior nasal surgery. The condition primarily affects the nasal cavity, potentially leading to chronic sinusitis, nasal obstruction, and sleep disturbances. It may also contribute to recurrent nosebleeds and facial pain. The septum is typically affected in the midline of the nose.

Nasal polyps are noncancerous, inflammatory growths that develop in the nasal passages or paranasal sinuses. They are characterized by edematous, polypoid masses composed of mucosal tissue. Common synonyms include nasal polyps, ethmoidal polyps, and antrochoanal polyps. Causative agents often include chronic inflammation, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. These lesions typically affect the nasal cavity and maxillary, ethmoidal, and frontal sinuses, leading to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and hyposmia.

A polyp of the nasal cavity is a non-cancerous, inflammatory growth arising from the mucous membranes of the nasal passages or paranasal sinuses. Common synonyms include nasal polyp, ethmoidal polyp, and sinonasal polyp. It is typically caused by chronic inflammation, often associated with conditions such as allergic rhinitis, asthma, or aspirin sensitivity. The most commonly affected areas are the nasal passages and ethmoid sinuses. These polyps can cause nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and impaired sense of smell. They are more prevalent in adults and may be associated with chronic sinusitis.

Polypoid sinus degeneration refers to the chronic inflammation and structural changes in the paranasal sinuses, leading to the formation of polypoid lesions. It is characterized by mucosal thickening, edema, and impaired sinus drainage. Common synonyms include chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and eosinophilic sinusitis. Known causative agents include allergic rhinitis, asthma, and infections such as fungal or bacterial sinusitis. The condition predominantly affects the maxillary, ethmoid, and frontal sinuses, often involving the nasal cavity. It is more common in adults and is associated with persistent nasal obstruction, postnasal drip, and reduced sense of smell.

"Other polyp of sinus" refers to benign, inflammatory growths arising in the paranasal sinuses, distinct from fungal or inflammatory polyps. Common synonyms include nasal polyp, sinonasal polyp, or ethmoid polyp. Causative agents often involve chronic inflammation, allergies, infections, or environmental irritants. These polyps typically affect the ethmoid, maxillary, or sphenoid sinuses, leading to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and facial pain. They are more common in adults and may be associated with conditions like asthma or cystic fibrosis. Surgical removal or medical management with corticosteroids is often required.

Unspecified nasal polyp refers to a non-specific enlargement of the nasal mucosa, typically presenting as a polypoid lesion in the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses. It is often associated with chronic inflammation and may be a component of allergic fungal sinusitis or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Common synonyms include nasal polypoid changes and mucosal hypertrophy. Causative agents may include allergens, chronic infection, or environmental irritants. The condition primarily affects the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses, leading to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and altered sense of smell.

Chronic pharyngitis and nasopharyngitis refer to long-standing inflammation of the pharynx and nasopharynx, often causing persistent sore throat, postnasal drip, and throat clearing. Common synonyms include chronic sore throat and persistent pharyngitis. Causative agents include viral infections, bacterial pathogens such as *Streptococcus* species, allergens, and irritants like cigarette smoke. These conditions typically affect the pharyngeal and nasopharyngeal mucosa, with possible extension to the larynx. Symptoms may be exacerbated by environmental factors and underlying conditions such as rhinitis or gastroesophageal reflux.

Chronic rhinitis is a persistent inflammation of the nasal mucosa lasting more than 12 weeks, characterized by symptoms such as nasal congestion, postnasal drip, and rhinorrhea. Common synonyms include chronic nasal inflammation and persistent rhinitis. It may result from allergic or non-allergic causes, including environmental irritants, viral infections, and structural abnormalities. Causative agents include allergens like pollen and dust mites, as well as irritants such as cigarette smoke and chemical fumes. The condition primarily affects the nasal passages and may involve the paranasal sinuses.

Chronic pharyngitis is a persistent inflammation of the pharynx, often lasting more than three months. Common synonyms include chronic sore throat and laryngopharyngitis. It is typically caused by recurrent infections, postnasal drip, allergens, or irritants. Known causative agents include bacteria such as *Streptococcus* species, viruses, and environmental factors like cigarette smoke. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as dryness, irritation, and a sensation of a foreign body. It may also involve the larynx and tonsillar regions.

Chronic nasopharyngitis is a persistent inflammation of the nasopharynx, often lasting more than 12 weeks. Common synonyms include chronic pharyngitis and chronic rhinopharyngitis. It is typically caused by recurrent viral infections, allergens, irritants, or bacterial agents such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae*. The condition primarily affects the nasal cavity, pharynx, and eustachian tubes, leading to symptoms like nasal congestion, postnasal drip, sore throat, and ear pressure. It is more common in adults and can be associated with conditions like sinusitis or allergies.

Chronic sinusitis is a prolonged inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting more than 12 weeks. It is characterized by symptoms such as nasal obstruction, facial pain, and nasal discharge. Common synonyms include chronic rhinosinusitis. Causative agents may include bacterial, viral, or fungal infections, as well as allergens and structural abnormalities. The condition typically affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses. It is often associated with nasal polyps, mucosal edema, and impaired mucociliary clearance.

Chronic maxillary sinusitis is a persistent inflammation of the maxillary sinuses lasting more than 12 weeks. It often results from prolonged obstruction of the sinus ostia, leading to mucus retention and bacterial overgrowth. Common causative agents include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. Symptoms include nasal congestion, facial pain, and purulent nasal discharge. It may affect adjacent structures such as the orbit or cranial cavity if untreated. Synonyms include chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and chronic maxillary sinus infection.

Chronic frontal sinusitis is a prolonged inflammation of the frontal sinuses, typically lasting more than 12 weeks. It is characterized by symptoms such as persistent nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, and thick nasal discharge. Common synonyms include chronic frontal sinus infection or frontal sinus mucosal inflammation. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Haemophilus influenzae*, though viral or fungal causes may also play a role. The condition primarily affects the frontal sinuses, located above the eyebrows, and may lead to complications if untreated.

Chronic ethmoidal sinusitis is a persistent inflammation of the ethmoid sinuses, typically lasting more than 12 weeks. It is characterized by nasal congestion, facial pain, and thick nasal discharge. Common synonyms include chronic ethmoid sinus inflammation or ethmoid sinus disease. Causative agents often include bacterial infections, such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Haemophilus influenzae*, as well as fungal pathogens. The condition primarily affects the ethmoid sinuses, which are located between the eyes and nasal cavity, and may spread to adjacent structures like the orbit or cranial cavity if untreated.

Chronic sphenoidal sinusitis is a persistent inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, typically lasting more than 12 weeks. It often presents with symptoms such as headache, nasal obstruction, and facial pain. Common synonyms include chronic sphenoid sinus infection or sphenoidal sinus disease. Causative agents may include bacterial pathogens like *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, though viral or fungal causes are less common. The condition primarily affects the sphenoid sinus, which is located behind the ethmoid sinus and adjacent to the skull base. It may also involve surrounding structures such as the cranial nerves and orbit.

Other chronic sinusitis refers to persistent inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting more than 12 weeks, excluding cases caused by specific pathogens like *Fungus* or *Aspergillus*. It is often associated with structural abnormalities, allergies, or immune dysfunction. Common synonyms include chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps. The condition primarily affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses. Symptoms include nasal obstruction, facial pain, and nasal discharge. Treatment typically involves medical management with nasal corticosteroids, saline irrigation, and sometimes surgery.

Unspecified sinusitis (chronic) refers to persistent inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting more than 12 weeks, with no specific cause identified. Common synonyms include chronic sinusitis of unspecified type. Causative agents may include bacterial, viral, or fungal pathogens, though often no single agent is definitively identified. The condition typically affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses. Symptoms include nasal congestion, facial pain, and postnasal drainage. It may be associated with allergic rhinitis or structural abnormalities. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and imaging if necessary.

code_desc: Chronic disease of tonsils and adenoids
summary: Chronic disease of tonsils and adenoids refers to long-standing inflammation or infection of the palatine tonsils and adenoids, often leading to structural changes and functional impairment. Common synonyms include chronic tonsillitis and chronic adenoiditis. The condition is typically caused by recurrent bacterial or viral infections, with Streptococcus pyogenes being a common causative agent. It predominantly affects the pharyngeal region, including the tonsillar crypts and adenoidal tissue in the nasopharynx. Symptoms may include persistent sore throat, nasal obstruction, and sleep disturbances. It is most commonly seen in children.

Chronic tonsillitis and adenoiditis refers to long-standing inflammation of the tonsils and adenoids, often leading to recurrent infections. Common synonyms include chronic pharyngitis and recurrent tonsillitis. The condition is typically caused by bacterial agents such as Streptococcus pyogenes, although viral causes are also possible. It predominantly affects the pharyngeal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and adenoids, commonly seen in children. Symptoms include persistent sore throat, difficulty breathing, and sleep disturbances due to airway obstruction. Complications may involve hearing loss or obstructive sleep apnea.

Chronic tonsillitis is a persistent inflammation of the palatine tonsils, often resulting from recurrent acute episodes or unresolved infections. Common synonyms include chronic tonsillar disease or recurrent tonsillitis. The condition is primarily caused by bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pyogenes, though viral agents may also contribute. It typically affects the palatine tonsils, leading to symptoms like sore throat, halitosis, and lymphadenopathy. The disease may progress to form tonsillar stones or cause obstructive sleep apnea. It predominantly affects the oropharyngeal region.

Chronic adenoiditis is a persistent inflammation of the adenoids, typically resulting from recurrent or unresolved upper respiratory infections. Common synonyms include chronic hypertrophic adenoiditis and chronic nasopharyngitis. The condition is often caused by bacterial agents such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. It primarily affects the nasopharyngeal region, leading to symptoms like nasal obstruction, snoring, and sleep apnea. It is most commonly seen in children, though can occur in adults with underlying immune or anatomical abnormalities.

Chronic tonsillitis and adenoiditis refers to long-standing inflammation of the tonsils and adenoids, often leading to recurrent infections. Common synonyms include chronic pharyngitis and recurrent tonsillitis. The condition is typically caused by bacterial agents such as *Streptococcus pyogenes* and viral pathogens. It predominantly affects the pharyngeal region, including the palatine tonsils and the lymphoid tissue of the nasopharynx. Symptoms may include sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and breathing issues, especially in children. Complications may involve obstructive sleep apnea or middle ear infections.

Hypertrophy of tonsils and adenoids refers to the abnormal enlargement of the palatine tonsils and pharyngeal adenoids. Common synonyms include tonsillar hypertrophy and adenoid hypertrophy. This condition is often caused by chronic inflammation, recurrent infections, or allergic reactions. It typically affects the throat and upper airway, leading to symptoms such as obstructive sleep apnea, snoring, and breathing difficulties. The enlarged tissues can also contribute to nasal congestion and speech changes. It is most commonly seen in children but can occur in adults. The condition may require medical evaluation and treatment such as medication or surgical intervention.

Hypertrophy of tonsil with adenoids refers to the abnormal enlargement of both the palatine tonsils and the adenoids, commonly seen in children. This condition is often caused by recurrent infections, allergies, or chronic inflammation. Synonyms include tonsillar and adenoidal hypertrophy. The enlarged tissues can obstruct the airway, leading to breathing difficulties, sleep apnea, and speech issues. It primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, including the nasopharynx and oropharynx. The condition may also contribute to hearing problems due to Eustachian tube blockage. Treatment may involve observation, medications, or surgical removal.

Hypertrophy of tonsils alone refers to the non-inflammatory enlargement of one or both tonsils without accompanying adenoid hypertrophy. Common synonyms include unilateral or bilateral tonsillar hypertrophy. This condition is often caused by chronic inflammation, recurrent infections, or anatomical factors. It typically affects the oropharyngeal region, leading to symptoms such as obstructive sleep apnea, breathing difficulties, and speech changes. The tonsils, located in the lateral walls of the pharynx, are the primary affected structures. It is more common in children but can occur in adults.

Hypertrophy of adenoids alone refers to the non-inflammatory enlargement of the adenoids without involvement of other lymphoid tissues. Common synonyms include adenoid hypertrophy or enlarged adenoids. This condition is primarily caused by chronic inflammation, recurrent infections, or allergic reactions. It predominantly affects the nasopharynx, leading to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, and sleep disturbances. It is most commonly seen in children, with the tonsils and lymph nodes often remaining unaffected.

Adenoid vegetations refer to hyperplastic growths of lymphoid tissue in the nasopharynx, commonly seen in children. They are also known as nasopharyngeal lymphoid hyperplasia or lymphoid polyps. The condition is typically caused by recurrent upper respiratory infections, leading to chronic inflammation. It primarily affects the adenoids, which are located in the nasopharyngeal region. Symptoms may include nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, snoring, and recurrent ear infections. The condition is more prevalent in children but can occasionally occur in adults. Treatment may involve observation, corticosteroids, or surgical removal if symptoms are severe.

code_desc: Other chronic disease of tonsils and adenoids
summary: "Other chronic disease of tonsils and adenoids" refers to long-standing inflammatory or structural conditions affecting the tonsils and adenoids, excluding specific infections. Common synonyms include chronic tonsillitis and chronic adenoid hypertrophy. Causative agents may include recurrent bacterial or viral infections, allergies, or immune responses. These conditions typically affect the oropharyngeal region, leading to symptoms such as persistent sore throat, difficulty breathing, and sleep disturbances. The tonsils and adenoids are the primary affected body parts.

code_desc: Unspecified chronic disease of tonsils and adenoids
summary: Unspecified chronic disease of tonsils and adenoids refers to long-standing inflammatory or structural abnormalities affecting the tonsils and/or adenoids without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include chronic tonsillitis or chronic adenoiditis. While specific pathogens like Streptococcus pyogenes may contribute, the exact causative agent is often unknown. This condition typically affects the pharyngeal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and adenoids, leading to symptoms such as chronic sore throat, nasal obstruction, and sleep disturbances. It is more common in children but can occur in adults.

Peritonsillar abscess, also known as quinsy or retropharyngeal abscess, is a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and the surrounding pharyngeal wall. It typically arises from complications of acute tonsillitis, often due to Streptococcus pyogenes. The condition primarily affects the peritonsillar region, causing severe sore throat, trismus, and dysphagia. It is more common in adolescents and young adults. Other causative agents may include Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobic bacteria. The abscess can extend into adjacent structures, leading to airway compromise if left untreated.

Chronic laryngitis and laryngotracheitis refer to long-standing inflammation of the larynx and upper trachea, often resulting from persistent irritation or infection. Common synonyms include chronic laryngeal inflammation and tracheal inflammation. Causative agents may include viral infections, such as influenza or respiratory syncytial virus, bacterial pathogens like Streptococcus, or chronic irritants such as smoking, allergens, or acid reflux. The condition primarily affects the larynx and trachea, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, chronic cough, and throat discomfort. It is more common in adults and can be associated with underlying respiratory conditions.

Chronic laryngitis is a prolonged inflammation of the larynx, typically lasting more than three weeks. It is characterized by persistent hoarseness, sore throat, and a sensation of a lump in the throat. Common synonyms include persistent hoarseness and laryngeal inflammation. Causative agents include vocal strain, smoking, acid reflux, infections, and environmental irritants. The condition primarily affects the vocal cords and surrounding mucosal tissues of the larynx. It is more common in individuals with chronic throat irritation or underlying respiratory conditions.

Chronic laryngotracheitis is a long-standing inflammation of the larynx and trachea, often presenting with persistent hoarseness, cough, and throat irritation. Common synonyms include chronic laryngotracheal inflammation and chronic upper airway inflammation. It is frequently caused by recurrent infections, allergens, or irritants. Known causative agents include viral infections, such as Epstein-Barr virus, and environmental factors like smoking or air pollution. The condition primarily affects the larynx and trachea, with potential extension to the bronchi in severe cases. It is more common in adults and may be associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by an immune response to airborne allergens. Common synonyms include hay fever and allergic rhinitis. It is caused by allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold spores, and pet dander. The condition typically affects the nasal mucosa, leading to symptoms like sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and itching. It may also involve the eyes, causing conjunctival irritation. The disease is often seasonal or perennial, depending on the allergen. It is a common condition affecting the upper respiratory tract and can significantly impact quality of life.

Allergic rhinitis due to pollen, also known as hay fever or pollinosis, is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by an immune response to airborne pollen. Common causative agents include grass, tree, and weed pollens. Symptoms involve sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and itching. The condition typically affects the upper respiratory tract, including the nose, eyes, and throat. It is often seasonal, peaking during pollen release periods. Patients may experience fatigue and sleep disturbances due to symptoms. Diagnosis is based on clinical history and allergen-specific IgE testing. Treatment includes avoidance, antihistamines, nasal corticosteroids, and immunotherapy.

Allergic rhinitis due to food, also known as food-induced rhinitis or allergic rhinitis from dietary allergens, is an immune-mediated condition characterized by nasal inflammation triggered by ingestion of specific foods. Common causative agents include shellfish, dairy, eggs, and nuts. Symptoms such as sneezing, nasal congestion, and itching typically affect the nasal passages. It may also cause systemic reactions in severe cases. The condition is often misdiagnosed as non-allergic rhinitis, necessitating thorough allergy testing for accurate diagnosis.

code_desc: Allergic rhinitis due to animal (cat) (dog) hair and dander
summary: Allergic rhinitis due to animal hair and dander is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction triggered by exposure to allergens from cats or dogs. Common synonyms include pet allergy or animal dander allergy. Causative agents include proteins found in saliva, skin secretions, and shed hair. The condition primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as sneezing, nasal congestion, itching, and watery eyes. It may also lead to postnasal drip and sleep disturbances. Individuals with a personal or family history of allergies or asthma are at higher risk.

code_desc: Allergic rhinitis due to other allergen
summary: Allergic rhinitis due to other allergen refers to nasal inflammation caused by allergens not classified as pollen, dust mites, or animal dander. Common synonyms include non-IgE-mediated rhinitis and allergic rhinitis of unknown origin. Causative agents may include mold spores, cockroach allergens, or certain foods. The condition typically affects the nasal passages, leading to symptoms such as sneezing, nasal congestion, and itching. It may also involve the eyes and throat, causing conjunctivitis and postnasal drip. Diagnosis often requires allergy testing to identify specific triggers.

Allergic rhinitis, cause unspecified, is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by an allergic reaction to an unidentified allergen. Common synonyms include hay fever or allergic rhinitis. While specific causative agents are not identified, common triggers may include pollen, dust mites, mold spores, or animal dander. The condition primarily affects the nasal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and itching. It may also involve the eyes, causing conjunctival irritation. The disease typically presents in childhood or early adulthood and can be seasonal or perennial in nature.

code_desc: Other diseases of upper respiratory tract
summary: "Other diseases of upper respiratory tract" encompass a variety of inflammatory and infectious conditions affecting structures such as the nose, pharynx, larynx, and sinuses. Common synonyms include rhinosinusitis, pharyngitis, and laryngitis. These conditions are often caused by viral agents like rhinovirus, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus, though bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus pyogenes and Haemophilus influenzae may also be involved. Symptoms typically include nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, and difficulty breathing. These disorders are more prevalent in children and individuals with compromised immune systems.

Hypertrophy of nasal turbinates refers to the abnormal enlargement of the turbinates, which are bony structures covered with mucosa within the nasal cavity. This condition leads to nasal obstruction, congestion, and difficulty breathing. Common synonyms include nasal turbinate hypertrophy and inferior turbinate hypertrophy. It is often caused by chronic inflammation, allergies, infections, or anatomical abnormalities. The inferior turbinates are most commonly affected, though the middle and superior turbinates may also become enlarged. Symptoms include nasal congestion, postnasal drip, and snoring. Treatment may involve medical management or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Other diseases of nasal cavity and sinuses
summary: "Other diseases of nasal cavity and sinuses" encompasses a range of non-specific inflammatory and structural conditions affecting the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses. Common synonyms include rhinosinusitis, sinusitis, and nasal inflammation. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or fungal pathogens, as well as allergens and irritants. These conditions typically affect the nasal mucosa, maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses, often leading to symptoms such as nasal congestion, discharge, facial pain, and reduced sense of smell. Chronic forms may involve structural abnormalities like nasal polyps or deviated septum.

Nasal mucositis (ulcerative) is an inflammatory condition characterized by ulceration and erosion of the nasal mucosa. Common synonyms include nasal ulceration and nasal mucosal erosion. It is often caused by viral infections such as herpes simplex virus, bacterial infections like *Staphylococcus aureus*, or prolonged use of nasal decongestants. The condition primarily affects the nasal passages, including the septum and vestibule. Symptoms include pain, crusting, and nasal discharge. It may also occur as a complication of radiation therapy or chemotherapy.

code_desc: Other disease of nasal cavity and sinuses
summary: "Other disease of nasal cavity and sinuses" refers to inflammatory or structural conditions not classified as rhinitis, sinusitis, or nasal polyps. Common synonyms include chronic rhinosinusitis without polyps and non-allergic rhinitis. Causative agents may include environmental irritants, allergens, or chronic infections. Typically affects the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses, leading to symptoms such as nasal congestion, postnasal drip, and facial pressure. It may result from prolonged exposure to irritants or underlying immune disorders.

code_desc: Other diseases of pharynx not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of pharynx not elsewhere classified" refers to pharyngeal conditions that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified pharyngeal disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viruses, bacteria), trauma, or idiopathic factors. Typically affects the pharyngeal mucosa, including the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx. Symptoms may involve pain, swelling, or difficulty swallowing. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and may include antibiotics, antivirals, or supportive care.

Unspecified disease of pharynx refers to pharyngeal disorders not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include pharyngitis of unspecified type or pharyngeal inflammation of undetermined origin. Causative agents may include viral or bacterial pathogens, though exact etiology is often unclear. This condition typically affects the pharyngeal mucosa, potentially involving the nasopharynx, oropharynx, or hypopharynx. Symptoms may include sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and hoarseness. It is often diagnosed when specific pathogens or conditions cannot be definitively identified.

Cellulitis of the pharynx or nasopharynx is a bacterial infection characterized by inflammation and swelling of the soft tissues in the throat or upper airway. Common synonyms include pharyngeal cellulitis and nasopharyngeal cellulitis. It is typically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, and sometimes Haemophilus influenzae. The infection often spreads from adjacent structures such as the nasal cavity or sinuses. It commonly affects the posterior pharyngeal wall, tonsillar regions, and nasopharyngeal mucosa, leading to symptoms like pain, fever, and difficulty swallowing.

Parapharyngeal abscess is a deep neck space infection characterized by a collection of pus in the parapharyngeal space, often resulting from spread of infection from adjacent structures. Common synonyms include lateral pharyngeal abscess and retropharyngeal abscess. Causative agents typically include bacteria such as Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and anaerobes. The condition most commonly affects the pharynx, soft tissues of the neck, and may involve the carotid sheath. It is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. Clinical features include fever, sore throat, trismus, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Retropharyngeal abscess is a collection of pus in the retropharyngeal space, typically affecting children. It often results from bacterial spread from the upper respiratory tract or following trauma. Common causative agents include Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae. The condition may present with dysphagia, odynophagia, and respiratory distress. It commonly involves the pharyngeal and cervical regions, potentially extending to the mediastinum. Synonyms include retropharyngeal cellulitis and retropharyngeal infection.

Edema of the pharynx or nasopharynx refers to swelling of the tissues in the throat or upper airway, leading to potential airway obstruction. Common synonyms include pharyngeal edema and nasopharyngeal swelling. Causative agents include infections (viral, bacterial), allergic reactions, trauma, or systemic conditions like anaphylaxis or angioedema. Typically affects the pharyngeal walls, soft palate, uvula, and nasopharyngeal mucosa. It may present with dysphonia, dysphagia, or respiratory distress. Prompt evaluation is essential to prevent airway compromise.

A cyst of the pharynx or nasopharynx is a benign, fluid-filled sac that develops in the upper respiratory tract. Common synonyms include nasopharyngeal cyst and pharyngeal cyst. These cysts are typically congenital, arising from embryonic remnants of the pharyngeal pouches. They are most commonly found in the nasopharynx, particularly near the area of the tonsillar fossa. Causative agents are usually developmental rather than infectious. Symptoms may include nasal obstruction, recurrent sinusitis, or hearing loss, depending on the cyst's location. They are typically diagnosed via imaging studies such as CT or MRI.

code_desc: Other diseases of pharynx, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of pharynx, not elsewhere classified" refers to pharyngeal conditions that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous pharyngeal disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viruses, bacteria), trauma, or inflammatory processes. Typically affects the pharyngeal mucosa, including the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx. Symptoms often include sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and voice changes. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical evaluation and imaging. Treatment varies depending on underlying cause.

code_desc: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx
summary: Paralysis of the vocal cords or larynx refers to the loss of voluntary control over the muscles of the larynx, leading to impaired speech, breathing, and swallowing. Common synonyms include laryngeal paresis or vocal cord palsy. Causes include neurological disorders such as stroke, Parkinson’s disease, or vocal cord dysfunction, as well as trauma, tumors, or infections. The condition primarily affects the larynx, vocal cords, and adjacent structures, potentially impacting the pharynx and respiratory system. Symptoms may include hoarseness, stridor, and dysphagia.

code_desc: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, unspecified
summary: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, unspecified, refers to the loss of function in the muscles controlling the vocal cords, leading to impaired voice production and potential breathing difficulties. Common synonyms include laryngeal paresis or vocal cord palsy. Causative agents may include neurological disorders, trauma, infections, or iatrogenic injury. Typically affects the larynx, vocal cords, and surrounding structures, with symptoms such as hoarseness, aphonia, and respiratory distress.

code_desc: Unilateral paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, partial
summary: Unilateral partial paralysis of the vocal cords or larynx involves weakened or impaired movement of one side of the larynx, often resulting in hoarseness, breathy voice, or aspiration. Common synonyms include unilateral vocal cord palsy or recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. Causative agents may include viral infections, trauma, surgery, tumors, or neurological conditions such as stroke or multiple sclerosis. The condition primarily affects the vocal cords, arytenoids, and surrounding laryngeal structures, with potential impact on phonation and airway protection.

code_desc: Unilateral paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, complete
summary: Unilateral paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, complete, refers to the loss of function in one side of the larynx, resulting in impaired vocal cord movement. This condition may manifest as hoarseness, breathy voice, or aspiration. Common synonyms include unilateral vocal cord paralysis and laryngeal palsy. Causative agents include vocal cord nerve injury, stroke, tumors, infections, or trauma. Typically affects the recurrent laryngeal nerve, leading to dysfunction of the affected vocal cord. The condition primarily impacts the larynx and vocal cords, with potential effects on phonation and airway protection.

code_desc: Bilateral paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, partial
summary: Bilateral partial paralysis of the vocal cords or larynx involves weakened or impaired function of both sides of the laryngeal muscles, leading to dysphonia, breathing difficulties, and potential aspiration. Common synonyms include bilateral laryngeal paresis and bilateral vocal cord paresis. Causative agents may include neurological disorders such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, or motor neuron disease, as well as trauma, infections, or iatrogenic injury. The condition primarily affects the larynx, vocal folds, and adjacent respiratory structures.

code_desc: Bilateral paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, complete
summary: Bilateral paralysis of vocal cords or larynx, complete, refers to the total loss of function in both vocal cords, resulting in an inability to produce sound and protect the airway. Common synonyms include complete laryngeal palsy and bilateral vocal cord palsy. Causative agents may include neurological disorders such as stroke, trauma, or tumors affecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Typically, the vocal cords and laryngeal muscles are affected, leading to respiratory distress and aspiration risk.

code_desc: Polyp of vocal cord or larynx
summary: A polyp of the vocal cord or larynx is a benign, gelatinous growth arising from the vocal fold mucosa. Common synonyms include vocal cord polyp, laryngeal polyp, or true polyp. It is typically caused by chronic vocal abuse, trauma, or inflammation. The condition predominantly affects the true vocal cords, leading to hoarseness, vocal fatigue, and breathiness. It is more common in adults, especially those with occupational voice use. The lesion is usually solitary and may vary in size, often responding to voice therapy or surgical removal.

"Other diseases of vocal cords" encompasses a range of conditions affecting the laryngeal structures beyond common disorders like laryngitis or vocal nodules. Synonyms include laryngeal pathology and vocal fold disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viral, bacterial), trauma, chronic irritation, or neoplasms. These conditions typically affect the vocal cords, arytenoids, and surrounding laryngeal tissues, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, dysphonia, and breathing difficulties. They may result from inflammation, structural abnormalities, or neoplastic growths.

Edema of the larynx refers to swelling of the laryngeal tissues, often leading to airway obstruction. Common synonyms include laryngeal edema and acute laryngeal swelling. It is commonly caused by allergic reactions, infections, trauma, or irritation. Causative agents may include allergens, viral infections like epiglottitis, or anaphylaxis. The condition typically affects the vocal cords, epiglottis, and surrounding subglottic regions, potentially compromising respiration. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt intervention to prevent airway compromise.

code_desc: Other diseases of larynx not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of larynx not elsewhere classified" refers to laryngeal conditions that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include idiopathic laryngeal disorders and unspecified laryngeal diseases. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, or unknown factors. Typically affects the laryngeal mucosa, vocal cords, and subglottic region. Symptoms often include hoarseness, dysphonia, and respiratory distress. Diagnosis is usually made through laryngoscopy and clinical evaluation. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and may involve medical or surgical intervention.

Unspecified disease of larynx refers to a broad category of laryngeal disorders where the specific diagnosis cannot be determined. Common synonyms include undifferentiated laryngeal disease or unspecified laryngeal pathology. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viral, bacterial), trauma, chronic irritation, or neoplastic processes. Typically affects the laryngeal mucosa, vocal cords, and surrounding structures. Symptoms may include hoarseness, dysphonia, and breathing difficulties. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment depends on underlying cause and severity.

Cellulitis and perichondritis of the larynx is an acute bacterial infection involving the laryngeal soft tissues and cartilage. It often presents with fever, sore throat, dysphonia, and respiratory distress. Common causative agents include Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae. Synonyms include laryngeal cellulitis and laryngeal perichondritis. The condition typically affects the supraglottic region, including the epiglottis and arytenoids, and can lead to airway compromise if left untreated. It is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals.

Stenosis of the larynx refers to the narrowing of the laryngeal airway, leading to breathing difficulties. Common synonyms include laryngeal stricture and laryngeal stenosis. It can result from trauma, infection, prolonged intubation, or inflammatory conditions. Causative agents include burns, granulomatous diseases, and chronic irritation. The condition primarily affects the larynx, potentially involving the trachea. Symptoms include stridor, dyspnea, and hoarseness. It may lead to respiratory distress if left untreated. Diagnosis is typically made through endoscopy and imaging. Treatment options range from corticosteroids to surgical intervention, depending on severity.

Laryngeal spasm is an abrupt, involuntary contraction of the laryngeal muscles, leading to transient airway obstruction. Common synonyms include laryngospasm and spasmodic laryngitis. It is often triggered by irritation, acid reflux, or allergens, and may occur during intubation or in response to vocal strain. The condition primarily affects the larynx, particularly the vocal cords and surrounding musculature. It is more common in children but can occur in adults. Symptoms include stridor, coughing, and difficulty breathing, typically resolving spontaneously within minutes.

code_desc: Other diseases of larynx, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of larynx, not elsewhere classified" refers to laryngeal conditions that do not fit specific categories such as cancer or inflammatory disorders. Common synonyms include idiopathic laryngeal diseases and unspecified laryngeal disorders. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, or environmental irritants. Typically affecting the vocal cords, glottis, and surrounding structures, these conditions may present with symptoms like hoarseness, dysphonia, and respiratory distress. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and may involve medication, voice therapy, or surgery.

code_desc: Upper respiratory tract hypersensitivity reaction, site unspecified
summary: Upper respiratory tract hypersensitivity reaction, site unspecified, refers to an allergic response affecting the upper airway without a specific location identified. Common synonyms include allergic rhinitis, rhinoconjunctivitis, and upper airway allergy. Causative agents often include pollen, dust mites, animal dander, mold spores, and irritants like smoke or chemicals. The condition typically affects the nasal passages, throat, and conjunctiva, causing symptoms such as sneezing, itching, nasal congestion, and watery eyes. It is mediated by IgE antibodies and often occurs seasonally or in response to environmental triggers.

code_desc: Other and unspecified diseases of upper respiratory tract
summary: "Other and unspecified diseases of upper respiratory tract" refers to conditions affecting the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pharynx, or larynx that are not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include unspecified upper respiratory tract infections or chronic rhinosinusitis. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or fungal pathogens, as well as allergens or irritants. These conditions often present with symptoms such as nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, and difficulty breathing. They can be acute or chronic, with varying severity and underlying causes.

Viral pneumonia is an inflammatory lung infection caused by viral pathogens, leading to fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonia and viral lung infection. It typically affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly the alveoli and interstitial tissue. Common causative agents include influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza, adenovirus, and coronavirus. Symptoms often include fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is more prevalent in children, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised patients. Complications may include secondary bacterial infection or acute respiratory distress syndrome.

Pneumonia due to adenovirus is a respiratory infection caused by adenoviruses, which can affect the lungs and airways. Common synonyms include viral pneumonia and adenoviral pneumonia. The condition typically presents with fever, cough, and respiratory distress. Adenoviruses, particularly serotypes 3, 7, and 14, are common causative agents. It primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, including the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation and impaired gas exchange. While more common in children, it can occur in immunocompromised individuals. The infection is usually self-limiting but may require supportive care in severe cases.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to respiratory syncytial virus
summary: Pneumonia due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a lower respiratory tract infection caused by the RSV, a common paramyxovirus. It primarily affects the bronchi and alveoli, leading to inflammation, mucus production, and airway narrowing. Common synonyms include RSV pneumonia and viral bronchiolitis. The infection is more severe in infants, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include cough, fever, tachypnea, and in severe cases, respiratory distress. Complications may involve bronchopneumonia or respiratory failure. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets and close contact.

Pneumonia due to parainfluenza virus is a lower respiratory tract infection caused by members of the Paramyxoviridae family, most commonly parainfluenza virus types 1, 2, 3, and 4. It often presents with symptoms such as fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. The infection primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include viral pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome in severe cases. It predominantly affects children and immunocompromised individuals, with type 3 being the most prevalent cause in hospitalized patients.

Pneumonia due to SARS-associated coronavirus, also known as SARS-CoV pneumonia, is an acute respiratory infection caused by the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (SARS-CoV). It primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include SARS-related pneumonia and coronavirus-induced pneumonia. The condition typically presents with fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. It is more severe in older adults and those with underlying health conditions. The virus spreads through respiratory droplets and can lead to complications such as acute respiratory distress syndrome.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other virus not elsewhere classified
summary: Pneumonia due to other virus not elsewhere classified refers to viral pneumonia caused by viruses not specifically identified or classified under other pneumonia categories. Common synonyms include viral pneumonia of unspecified etiology. Causative agents may include influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza, and adenovirus. The infection primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation of the alveoli. It commonly presents with symptoms such as fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. The condition can affect individuals of all ages but is more severe in young children, elderly, and immunocompromised patients.

Viral pneumonia, unspecified, is an inflammatory lung condition caused by a viral infection. It affects the alveoli, leading to fluid accumulation and impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonia and viral lung infection. Causative agents may include influenza viruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus, and parainfluenza virus. Typically affecting the lungs, it can also involve the respiratory tract. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is more common in young children, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with treatment focused on supportive care.

Pneumococcal pneumonia, caused primarily by *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, is a bacterial infection affecting the lungs. It commonly presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and difficulty breathing. The infection leads to inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli, resulting in consolidation. It typically affects the lower lobes of the lungs. Synonyms include streptococcal pneumonia or pneumococcal infection. Complications may include sepsis, pleural effusion, or meningitis. Risk factors include smoking, alcohol use, and immunocompromised states.

Other bacterial pneumonia refers to inflammation of the lungs caused by bacterial infection, excluding the most common pathogens like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. It may involve various bacterial species such as *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, or *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. The infection typically affects the alveoli and interstitial tissues, leading to symptoms like fever, cough, and dyspnea. It commonly occurs in the lower lung lobes and can progress to complications such as pleural effusion or sepsis. Clinically, it may present similarly to other forms of pneumonia but is distinguished by specific microbiological findings.

Pneumonia due to *Klebsiella pneumoniae* is a bacterial infection characterized by lobar consolidation, often with cavitation, and systemic symptoms such as fever and leukocytosis. It is commonly associated with alcoholism, diabetes, or immunocompromised states. *K. pneumoniae* is a gram-negative bacillus that typically affects the lungs, particularly the lower lobes. Known synonyms include Klebsiella pneumonia, bacterial pneumonia, and hospital-acquired pneumonia. The infection can lead to complications like sepsis or abscess formation.

Pneumonia due to *Pseudomonas* is a bacterial lung infection caused primarily by *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. It is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and often affects immunocompromised patients. The infection typically involves the lungs, leading to inflammation, purulent secretions, and potential respiratory failure. Common synonyms include *Pseudomonas pneumonia* or *Pseudomonal pneumonia*. It is associated with conditions like cystic fibrosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and ventilator-associated pneumonia. The bacteria produce greenish pus and are resistant to many antibiotics, necessitating targeted therapy.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to Hemophilus influenzae [H. influenzae]
summary: Pneumonia due to *Hemophilus influenzae* is a bacterial infection of the lungs caused by *Haemophilus influenzae*, a gram-negative coccobacillus. It commonly affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly in individuals with underlying respiratory conditions or compromised immunity. The infection may present with symptoms such as cough, fever, and purulent sputum. While *H. influenzae* is a known cause of respiratory infections, it is less frequently associated with pneumonia compared to other pathogens like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. It may also be a causative agent in conditions such as epiglottitis and meningitis. The infection is often treated with antibiotics effective against gram-negative organisms.

Pneumonia due to streptococcus, also known as streptococcal pneumonia, is an infectious lung condition caused by various species of Streptococcus bacteria, most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae. It typically affects the alveoli in the lungs, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation. Common symptoms include fever, cough, chest pain, and difficulty breathing. The infection can spread to other parts of the body in severe cases. It is more prevalent in individuals with weakened immune systems or underlying respiratory conditions. Prompt antibiotic treatment is essential to prevent complications such as sepsis or respiratory failure.

Pneumonia due to Streptococcus, unspecified, is an acute respiratory infection caused by various Streptococcus species, most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae. It affects the alveoli of the lungs, leading to inflammation, fluid accumulation, and impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include bacterial pneumonia and streptococcal pneumonia. The condition typically presents with fever, cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. It predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the lower lobes, and can progress to complications such as sepsis or respiratory failure if untreated.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus, group A
summary: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus group A, also known as streptococcal pneumonia, is an acute lung infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. It typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation. Common synonyms include pyogenic pneumonia and streptococcal pneumonitis. The infection often presents with fever, cough, and chest pain. While less common than bacterial pneumonias caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, S. pyogenes can cause severe illness, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Complications may include sepsis and pleural effusion.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus, group B
summary: Pneumonia due to Streptococcus group B, also known as beta-hemolytic streptococcal pneumonia, is a bacterial infection caused primarily by *Streptococcus agalactiae*. It typically affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include streptococcal pneumonia and group B strep pneumonia. The infection is more prevalent in neonates and immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include fever, cough, and respiratory distress. It can progress to severe complications such as sepsis if untreated. The infection primarily targets the respiratory system, particularly the alveoli and bronchioles.

Pneumonia due to other Streptococcus refers to lung infection caused by streptococcal species other than *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. Common synonyms include streptococcal pneumonia. Causative agents may include *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Group A) and *Streptococcus agalactiae* (Group B). This condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying respiratory conditions. Symptoms include fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. Diagnosis is confirmed through sputum culture or blood tests. Treatment involves antibiotics targeting streptococcal organisms.

Pneumonia due to *Staphylococcus* is an infectious lung condition caused by *Staphylococcus aureus*, a common bacterial pathogen. It often presents with acute symptoms such as fever, cough, and purulent sputum. Common synonyms include staphylococcal pneumonia or *S. aureus* pneumonia. The infection primarily affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation. It can occur as a primary infection or as a complication of other illnesses, such as aspiration or immunosuppression. The condition may progress to severe respiratory distress or sepsis if untreated.

Pneumonia due to Staphylococcus, unspecified, is an infection of the lungs caused by *Staphylococcus* species, most commonly *S. aureus*. It typically affects the alveoli, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation. Common synonyms include staphylococcal pneumonia and staph pneumonia. The infection can range from mild to severe, often presenting with fever, cough, and purulent sputum. It is more prevalent in individuals with underlying conditions such as diabetes, immunosuppression, or recent respiratory infections. Complications may include abscess formation or sepsis.

code_desc: Methicillin susceptible pneumonia due to Staphylococcus aureus
summary: Methicillin susceptible pneumonia due to *Staphylococcus aureus* is a bacterial lung infection caused by a strain of *S. aureus* that remains sensitive to methicillin. It typically affects the lower respiratory tract, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, and purulent sputum. Common synonyms include MSSA pneumonia and *S. aureus* pneumonia. The infection may occur in hospitalized patients or those with underlying conditions, often complicating other illnesses. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent progression and complications.

code_desc: Methicillin resistant pneumonia due to Staphylococcus aureus
summary: Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus* (MRSA) pneumonia is a severe lung infection caused by a strain of *S. aureus* resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics. Common synonyms include healthcare-associated pneumonia and community-acquired MRSA pneumonia. It typically affects the lungs, leading to inflammation, consolidation, and potential respiratory failure. Risk factors include recent hospitalization, antibiotic use, and immunocompromise. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and purulent sputum. Complications may involve sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Prompt identification and targeted antibiotic therapy are critical for management.

Other Staphylococcus pneumonia refers to pneumonia caused by staphylococcal species other than *Staphylococcus aureus*, such as *Staphylococcus epidermidis* or *Staphylococcus haemolyticus*. It is less common than aureus-induced pneumonia and often occurs in immunocompromised individuals or following trauma. The infection typically affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and consolidation. Symptoms include fever, cough, and respiratory distress. It may present as community-acquired or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Diagnosis is confirmed through sputum culture or bronchoscopy. Treatment involves antibiotics effective against coagulase-negative staphylococci.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other specified bacteria
summary: Pneumonia due to other specified bacteria refers to lung infection caused by bacterial pathogens not classified under common categories like streptococci, staphylococci, or gram-negative rods. Common synonyms include bacterial pneumonia with unspecified organism. Causative agents may include *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*, and *Streptococcus pneumoniae* in certain contexts. The infection primarily affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation, fluid accumulation, and impaired gas exchange. It commonly occurs in individuals with weakened immunity or underlying respiratory conditions.

Pneumonia due to anaerobes is an infection of the lungs caused by anaerobic bacteria, which thrive in low-oxygen environments. Common synonyms include anaerobic pneumonia or mixed anaerobic infection. Causative agents often include *Bacteroides*, *Clostridium*, and *Peptostreptococcus* species. This condition typically affects the lower lobes of the lungs and is often associated with aspiration or underlying respiratory compromise. It may present with symptoms such as fever, cough, and purulent sputum. Diagnosis is confirmed through sputum culture, imaging, and sometimes bronchoscopy. Treatment involves antibiotics effective against anaerobes, such as clindamycin or metronidazole.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to escherichia coli [E. coli]
summary: Pneumonia due to *Escherichia coli* is a bacterial infection of the lungs caused by *E. coli*, typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals or following aspiration. It is a less common but serious form of pneumonia, often associated with healthcare-associated infections. Common synonyms include *E. coli pneumonia* or *bacterial pneumonia caused by *E. coli*. The infection primarily affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation, consolidation, and impaired gas exchange. Complications such as sepsis or respiratory failure may occur if untreated.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other gram-negative bacteria
summary: Pneumonia due to other gram-negative bacteria refers to lung infection caused by gram-negative organisms not classified as *Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*, or *Enterobacter*. Common causative agents include *Acinetobacter*, *Serratia*, *Proteus*, and *Morganella*. This condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation, fluid accumulation, and impaired gas exchange. It is often seen in hospitalized patients or those with underlying respiratory conditions. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and purulent sputum. Diagnosis is confirmed through sputum cultures, blood tests, and imaging. Treatment involves targeted antibiotic therapy based on susceptibility results.

Pneumonia due to Legionnaires' disease is a severe form of atypical pneumonia caused by *Legionella pneumophila*. It is characterized by fever, cough, respiratory distress, and systemic symptoms such as confusion and gastrointestinal upset. Common synonyms include legionellosis and Legionnaires' disease. The infection primarily affects the lungs, leading to alveolar inflammation and pulmonary edema. It is acquired through inhalation of contaminated aerosols, commonly in water systems. The condition can progress rapidly and is more severe in immunocompromised individuals. Early diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antibiotics are critical for recovery.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other specified bacteria
summary: Pneumonia due to other specified bacteria refers to lung infection caused by bacterial pathogens not classified under common categories like streptococci, staphylococci, or Haemophilus. Common synonyms include bacterial pneumonia with unspecified etiology. Causative agents may include *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*, or rare organisms such as *Legionella* or *Pseudomonas*. Typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation, fluid accumulation, and impaired gas exchange. It can occur in both community-acquired and hospital-acquired settings, with symptoms such as fever, cough, and dyspnea.

Bacterial pneumonia, unspecified, is an acute infection of the lungs caused by bacterial pathogens. It leads to inflammation of the alveoli, resulting in consolidation and impaired gas exchange. Common causative agents include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition typically affects the lungs, particularly the lower lobes, and may present with symptoms such as fever, cough, and purulent sputum. It is often diagnosed based on clinical features and imaging, with treatment involving antibiotics. Synonyms include community-acquired pneumonia and hospital-acquired pneumonia, depending on the setting.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other specified organism
summary: Pneumonia due to other specified organism refers to lung infection caused by pathogens not classified under typical categories like bacteria, virus, or fungus. Common synonyms include atypical pneumonia or interstitial pneumonia. Causative agents may include *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*, *Legionella pneumophila*, and *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*. This condition primarily affects the alveoli and interstitial tissues of the lungs, leading to inflammation, impaired gas exchange, and potential respiratory failure if untreated. It is often seen in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying respiratory conditions.

Pneumonia due to *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is a respiratory infection characterized by interstitial pneumonia, often presenting with a subacute onset of cough, fever, and malaise. It is a common cause of atypical pneumonia, particularly in children and young adults. The infection primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, involving the alveoli and interstitial spaces. *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is a bacterium lacking a cell wall, making it resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics. Common synonyms include walking pneumonia and atypical pneumonia. The condition is typically mild but can lead to complications such as pleural effusion or respiratory failure in severe cases.

Pneumonia due to *Chlamydia* is an infectious lung condition caused by *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*, a gram-negative intracellular bacterium. Common synonyms include community-acquired pneumonia and atypical pneumonia. The infection primarily affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms often include cough, fever, and malaise. It is more prevalent in adults and can predispose individuals to other respiratory infections. The disease is typically treated with antibiotics such as macrolides or fluoroquinolones.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other specified organism
summary: Pneumonia due to other specified organism refers to lung infection caused by pathogens not classified under typical categories like bacteria, virus, or fungus. Common synonyms include atypical pneumonia or interstitial pneumonia. Causative agents may include mycoplasma, chlamydophila, or rickettsia. This condition primarily affects the alveoli and interstitial spaces of the lungs, leading to inflammation, impaired gas exchange, and potential respiratory distress. It is often seen in immunocompromised individuals or those exposed to specific environmental factors.

code_desc: Pneumonia in infectious diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Pneumonia in infectious diseases classified elsewhere refers to pneumonia caused by pathogens not specifically categorized under other major infectious disease classifications. Common synonyms include atypical pneumonia or non-typical pneumonia. Causative agents may include Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila. This condition typically affects the lungs, causing inflammation of the alveoli. It is often associated with mild to moderate symptoms, though severe cases can lead to respiratory failure. The infection is more common in children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals.

Pneumonia in cytomegalic inclusion disease (CMID) is a severe respiratory infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It commonly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients. The infection leads to interstitial and alveolar pneumonia characterized by CMV inclusion bodies in lung tissue. Other affected organs may include the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract. Synonyms include CMV pneumonia and congenital CMV infection in neonates. Clinical features include fever, cough, dyspnea, and respiratory failure.

Pneumonia in whooping cough, also known as pertussis-associated pneumonia, is a severe complication of pertussis caused by *Bordetella pertussis*. It typically affects infants and young children, presenting with persistent cough, fever, and respiratory distress. The infection leads to inflammation and consolidation of lung tissue, often involving the lower respiratory tract. Common synonyms include pertussis pneumonia and whooping cough pneumonia. It is characterized by coughing fits followed by a high-pitched inspiratory whoop. Complications may include hypoxia and respiratory failure.

Pneumonia in anthrax, also known as pulmonary anthrax, is a severe respiratory infection caused by *Bacillus anthracis*. It typically affects the lungs and is characterized by acute inflammation, hemorrhage, and necrosis of lung tissue. Common synonyms include inhalational anthrax and anthrax pneumonia. The infection occurs following inhalation of spores, leading to rapid progression and high mortality if untreated. It is rare but highly lethal, often presenting with non-specific symptoms initially, followed by respiratory distress and systemic complications. The lungs are the primary affected organ, with potential spread to other tissues in advanced cases.

Pneumonia in aspergillosis refers to lung infection caused by *Aspergillus* species, commonly *A. fumigatus*. It occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying lung disease. The infection can present as acute invasive aspergillosis, chronic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Common synonyms include aspergillosis pneumonia and invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. The condition primarily affects the lungs, often leading to inflammation, necrosis, and hemorrhage. It may also disseminate to other organs in severe cases. Symptoms include fever, cough, hemoptysis, and respiratory distress. Diagnosis involves imaging, culture, and serological tests. Treatment typically involves antifungal therapy.

Pneumonia in other systemic mycoses refers to fungal infections of the lungs caused by opportunistic pathogens that primarily affect immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include pulmonary mycoses and fungal pneumonia. Causative agents include *Histoplasma capsulatum*, *Coccidioides immitis*, *Blastomyces dermatitidis*, and *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis*. These infections typically affect the lungs, leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and dyspnea. They may disseminate to other organs in severe cases. Diagnosis often involves imaging, culture, and serology. Treatment depends on the specific fungus and patient immune status.

code_desc: Pneumonia in other infectious diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Pneumonia in other infectious diseases classified elsewhere refers to pneumonia that occurs as a complication of another infectious disease not specifically categorized elsewhere. It may present with symptoms such as fever, cough, and respiratory distress. Common causative agents include bacteria like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, viruses such as influenza, and opportunistic pathogens in immunocompromised individuals. The lungs are typically affected, with inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Synonyms include secondary pneumonia or pneumonia associated with systemic infection.

Bronchopneumonia, organism unspecified, is an acute inflammation of the bronchioles and alveoli, typically involving the lower lung lobes. It is characterized by patchy consolidation and infiltrates on imaging. Common synonyms include lobar pneumonia and bronchopneumonia. Causative agents are often bacteria such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the bronchial tree and alveolar sacs, and may present with fever, cough, and dyspnea.

Pneumonia, organism unspecified, refers to an infection of the lungs characterized by inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. It is a clinical diagnosis made when the causative agent is not identified. Common synonyms include acute bronchopneumonia and lobar pneumonia. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites, with *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and respiratory viruses being frequent causes. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the alveoli and bronchioles. Symptoms typically include fever, cough, dyspnea, and chest pain.

Influenza is a viral respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses, primarily types A, B, and C. Common synonyms include flu and grippe. It typically affects the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, muscle aches, and fatigue. The virus spreads through respiratory droplets. Complications may include pneumonia, especially in high-risk groups like the elderly, young children, and immunocompromised individuals. Seasonal outbreaks are common, with peak activity during winter months. Vaccination is a key preventive measure.

Influenza with pneumonia is a severe respiratory infection characterized by influenza virus-induced pneumonia. Common synonyms include viral pneumonia and influenza-associated pneumonia. The primary causative agents are Influenza A and B viruses, though other pathogens may coexist. It typically affects the lungs, causing inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Complications may involve respiratory failure, sepsis, and multi-organ dysfunction. It predominantly affects the lower respiratory tract but can progress to systemic involvement. High-risk groups include the elderly, young children, and immunocompromised individuals.

Influenza with other respiratory manifestations refers to influenza infection accompanied by additional respiratory symptoms beyond typical upper respiratory involvement. Common synonyms include influenza with pneumonia or influenza complicated by bronchitis. Caused primarily by influenza viruses A and B, it often affects the lungs, leading to pneumonia, and may involve the bronchi and trachea. Clinical features include fever, cough, shortness of breath, and in severe cases, respiratory failure. It predominantly affects the lower respiratory tract but can extend to the upper airways.
