Complications such as acute respiratory distress syndrome may occur in vulnerable populations.

Influenza with other manifestations refers to influenza infection accompanied by systemic symptoms beyond typical respiratory involvement. Common synonyms include influenza with complications or extrapulmonary influenza. Caused primarily by influenza A and B viruses, it often affects the respiratory tract but can involve the cardiovascular, neurological, and gastrointestinal systems. Common symptoms include fever, cough, fatigue, and muscle aches, with potential for secondary bacterial infections or severe systemic illness. It predominantly affects the lungs but may extend to other organs, particularly in high-risk populations.

code_desc: Influenza due to certain identified influenza viruses
summary: Influenza due to certain identified influenza viruses is an acute respiratory infection caused by influenza A, B, or C viruses. Common synonyms include seasonal flu, flu, and influenza. The virus primarily affects the upper and lower respiratory tract, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, and body aches. Complications may involve pneumonia, bronchitis, or exacerbation of chronic conditions. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets. It predominantly affects the respiratory system but can also impact systemic organs in severe cases.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus
summary: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus is a respiratory infection caused by avian influenza viruses, such as H5N1 or H7N9. Common synonyms include avian flu or bird flu. These viruses primarily affect the respiratory tract, causing symptoms like fever, cough, sore throat, and pneumonia. Though typically found in birds, some strains can infect humans, leading to severe illness. The virus is transmitted through contact with infected birds or contaminated surfaces. While most affected body parts are the respiratory system, systemic complications may occur. It is a zoonotic disease with potential for pandemics.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus with pneumonia
summary: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus with pneumonia is a severe respiratory infection caused by avian influenza viruses, such as H5N1 or H7N9. It typically affects the lungs, leading to pneumonia characterized by inflammation and fluid accumulation. Common synonyms include avian flu pneumonia or highly pathogenic avian influenza pneumonia. The condition primarily targets the respiratory system, often presenting with fever, cough, and respiratory distress. It is more severe in humans compared to seasonal influenza and can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome. Transmission usually occurs through direct contact with infected birds or contaminated environments.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus with other respiratory manifestations
summary: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus with other respiratory manifestations is a severe respiratory infection caused by avian influenza viruses, such as H5N1 or H7N9. Common synonyms include avian flu or bird flu. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract, causing symptoms like fever, cough, sore throat, and difficulty breathing. It may also lead to systemic complications such as pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and multi-organ failure. The disease typically affects the lungs and can spread to other organs. It is most commonly seen in individuals exposed to infected birds or contaminated environments.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus with other manifestations
summary: Influenza due to identified avian influenza virus with other manifestations is a severe respiratory infection caused by avian influenza viruses, such as H5N1 or H7N9. It presents with systemic symptoms beyond typical flu, including high fever, cough, and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include avian flu with extrapulmonary involvement. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract but can lead to complications in other organs. It typically targets the lungs, but may also involve the nervous system, gastrointestinal tract, and cardiovascular system. Transmission occurs mainly from birds to humans, often through close contact with infected poultry.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified 2009 h1n1 influenza virus
summary: Influenza due to the 2009 H1N1 influenza virus is an acute respiratory infection caused by the pandemic H1N1 virus, first identified in 2009. Common synonyms include swine flu and novel H1N1 influenza. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, and body aches. It can lead to severe complications like pneumonia, particularly in high-risk groups. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets. The condition is highly contagious and can cause widespread outbreaks. Vaccination and antiviral therapy are key preventive and treatment measures.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified 2009 H1N1 influenza virus with pneumonia
summary: Influenza due to the 2009 H1N1 influenza virus with pneumonia is a respiratory infection caused by the pandemic H1N1 virus. It presents with fever, cough, sore throat, and muscle aches, often progressing to pneumonia. Common synonyms include swine flu and H1N1 influenza. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation in the lungs. Complications may involve the cardiovascular and nervous systems. It is transmitted via respiratory droplets and can affect individuals of all ages, though severe cases are more common in children, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified 2009 H1N1 influenza virus with other respiratory manifestations
summary: Influenza due to the 2009 H1N1 influenza virus, also known as swine flu, is a viral respiratory infection caused by the H1N1 strain of the influenza A virus. It presents with typical flu-like symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, and body aches, often accompanied by other respiratory manifestations like pneumonia. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract, including the lungs and airways. Common synonyms include swine influenza and pandemic H1N1. It can lead to severe complications, particularly in high-risk populations such as the elderly, young children, and those with chronic illnesses.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified 2009 H1N1 influenza virus with other manifestations
summary: Influenza due to the 2009 H1N1 influenza virus with other manifestations is a respiratory infection caused by the pandemic H1N1 influenza A virus. Common synonyms include swine flu and novel H1N1 influenza. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, and body aches. It may also lead to complications like pneumonia, bronchitis, or exacerbation of chronic conditions. The disease can affect individuals of all ages but is more severe in children, elderly, and those with underlying health issues. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets.

code_desc: Influenza due to novel influenza a
summary: Influenza due to novel influenza A is a viral respiratory infection caused by newly emerged strains of the Influenza A virus, such as H1N1, H5N1, or H7N9. It presents with acute symptoms including fever, cough, sore throat, and muscle aches. Common synonyms include novel influenza A virus infection or pandemic influenza. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract, with potential complications like pneumonia. It spreads through respiratory droplets and can lead to severe illness, particularly in high-risk populations. Vaccination and antiviral therapy may reduce severity and transmission.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified novel influenza A virus with pneumonia
summary: Influenza due to identified novel influenza A virus with pneumonia is a severe respiratory infection caused by a newly identified strain of Influenza A virus. It presents with fever, cough, and respiratory distress, often progressing to pneumonia. Common synonyms include novel influenza A virus pneumonia and avian influenza pneumonia. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract, with pneumonia typically involving the lungs. Known causative agents include subtypes such as H5N1, H7N9, and others. It predominantly affects the lower respiratory system and can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified novel influenza A virus with other respiratory manifestations
summary: Influenza due to identified novel influenza A virus with other respiratory manifestations is a viral infection caused by a newly identified strain of influenza A virus, leading to respiratory symptoms beyond typical influenza. Common synonyms include novel influenza A virus infection or new influenza A strain. The causative agent is a novel influenza A virus, which may belong to subtypes such as H1N1, H3N2, or novel variants. The infection primarily affects the respiratory tract, including the upper and lower respiratory systems, and may present with fever, cough, sore throat, and in severe cases, pneumonia. Complications can involve the lungs, heart, and other organs.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified novel influenza A virus with other manifestations
summary: Influenza due to identified novel influenza A virus with other manifestations is a respiratory infection caused by a newly identified influenza A virus strain. It presents with typical influenza symptoms such as fever, cough, and sore throat, but may also involve systemic complications. Common synonyms include novel influenza A virus infection or new influenza A strain illness. The virus primarily affects the respiratory tract but can lead to multi-system involvement. Known causative agents include various subtypes of influenza A virus, such as H1N1, H3N2, and others. The condition predominantly impacts the lungs and can spread to other organs in severe cases.

code_desc: Bronchitis, not specified as acute or chronic
summary: Bronchitis, not specified as acute or chronic, refers to inflammation of the bronchial tubes, leading to coughing, mucus production, and possible wheezing. Common synonyms include acute bronchitis and chronic bronchitis, though the latter is more accurately classified as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Causative agents include viral infections (e.g., influenza, RSV), bacterial pathogens (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae), and environmental irritants like smoke or pollution. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, and is commonly seen in smokers and individuals with compromised immune systems.

Chronic bronchitis is a long-term inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes characterized by persistent cough and mucus production. It is a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Common synonyms include chronic productive cough and chronic bronchial inflammation. The primary causative agent is long-term exposure to irritants, most commonly cigarette smoke. Other causes include air pollution, occupational dusts, and chemical fumes. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to narrowing and increased mucus secretion. It predominantly impacts the lungs, particularly the lower respiratory tract.

Simple chronic bronchitis is a long-term inflammation of the bronchial tubes characterized by persistent cough and mucus production. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and chronic productive cough. It is primarily caused by long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational dusts. The condition predominantly affects the large airways, leading to bronchial hyperresponsiveness and impaired mucociliary clearance. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and commonly involves the trachea and bronchi.

Mucopurulent chronic bronchitis is a persistent inflammatory condition characterized by chronic cough and production of mucopurulent sputum. It involves long-term irritation and infection of the bronchial airways. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and obstructive bronchitis. Causative agents include cigarette smoke, air pollution, and respiratory infections. The condition primarily affects the large airways, including the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to mucous hypersecretion and impaired mucociliary clearance. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Obstructive chronic bronchitis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by persistent bronchial inflammation and mucus hypersecretion, leading to airflow obstruction. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and mucous bronchitis. The primary causative agent is long-term exposure to irritants, most commonly cigarette smoke. It typically affects the large airways, including the bronchi, and is associated with symptoms such as chronic cough and sputum production. The condition predominantly impacts the lungs, particularly the bronchial tree.

Obstructive chronic bronchitis without exacerbation is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by persistent bronchial inflammation and airflow limitation, primarily affecting the large airways. It is defined by chronic cough and sputum production lasting at least three months in two consecutive years. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and chronic obstructive airway disease. Causative agents include long-term exposure to cigarette smoke, air pollutants, and occupational irritants. The condition typically affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to mucus hypersecretion and airway narrowing. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Obstructive chronic bronchitis with acute exacerbation is characterized by chronic airway inflammation and mucus hypersecretion, leading to airflow obstruction. Acute exacerbations involve worsening symptoms such as increased cough, sputum production, and dyspnea, often triggered by infections or environmental irritants. Common causative agents include respiratory viruses, bacteria, and pollutants. The condition primarily affects the large airways, with involvement of the bronchi and bronchioles. Synonyms include chronic bronchitis flare-up and acute bronchial exacerbation. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

code_desc: Obstructive chronic bronchitis with acute bronchitis
summary: Obstructive chronic bronchitis with acute bronchitis refers to a combination of chronic airway inflammation and a recent exacerbation of bronchial obstruction. It is characterized by persistent cough, sputum production, and airflow limitation. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis with acute exacerbation and acute bronchitis superimposed on chronic bronchitis. Causative agents include cigarette smoke, air pollution, and respiratory infections. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to mucus hypersecretion and airway narrowing. It commonly involves the lungs and is associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Other chronic bronchitis refers to a long-term inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes characterized by persistent cough and mucus production. It is often associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and may result from prolonged exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, or occupational dust. Common synonyms include chronic bronchial inflammation and chronic productive cough. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airway narrowing and impaired airflow. Infectious agents like respiratory viruses or bacteria may contribute to acute exacerbations.

Unspecified chronic bronchitis refers to persistent inflammation of the bronchial tubes without a specific identified cause. It is characterized by chronic cough and mucus production lasting at least three months in two consecutive years. Common synonyms include chronic cough with mucus and unspecified bronchitis. Causative agents may include long-term exposure to irritants such as tobacco smoke, air pollution, or occupational dust. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airway obstruction and impaired respiratory function.

Emphysema is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to reduced gas exchange and air trapping. Common synonyms include pulmonary emphysema and hyperinflation. The primary causative agent is long-term exposure to irritants, most notably cigarette smoke. Other causes include air pollution, occupational dusts, and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli in the upper lobes, causing progressive dyspnea and impaired respiratory function.

Emphysematous bleb is a rare, life-threatening condition characterized by the presence of gas-forming organisms within a subcutaneous or intramuscular abscess, leading to the formation of gas-filled cavities. Common synonyms include gas gangrene or gas-forming infection. Causative agents typically include *Clostridium perfringens*, *Clostridium novyi*, and *Clostridium septicum*. The condition most commonly affects the lower extremities, particularly in patients with diabetes or trauma, but can occur in other areas such as the abdomen or chest. It is associated with severe pain, crepitus, and systemic toxicity. Early diagnosis and aggressive treatment are critical to prevent rapid progression and mortality.

Other emphysema refers to a group of chronic lung conditions characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to reduced gas exchange and hyperinflation of the lungs. Common synonyms include centriacinar, panacinar, and mixed emphysema. It is primarily caused by long-term exposure to cigarette smoke, but can also result from genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli in the distal airways, leading to progressive dyspnea and impaired respiratory function.

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by variable and recurring symptoms, including wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It involves hyperresponsiveness of the airways to various stimuli, leading to bronchoconstriction and airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include reactive airway disease and bronchial asthma. Known causative agents include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and animal dander, as well as irritants such as smoke and air pollution. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles in the respiratory system.

Extrinsic asthma, also known as allergic asthma, is an inflammatory airway disorder triggered by exposure to external allergens. It is characterized by reversible airway obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and eosinophilic inflammation. Common causative agents include house dust mites, pollen, mold spores, and animal dander. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It often presents in childhood or early adulthood and is associated with atopy.

Extrinsic asthma, unspecified, is an allergic form of asthma characterized by airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness triggered by external allergens. Common synonyms include allergic asthma and atopic asthma. Causative agents often include environmental allergens such as pollen, dust mites, animal dander, and mold spores. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. It is typically diagnosed in individuals with a personal or family history of atopy.

Extrinsic asthma with status asthmaticus is a severe, acute exacerbation of allergic asthma characterized by persistent bronchoconstriction unresponsive to standard bronchodilators. It is typically triggered by allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold, or animal dander. Common synonyms include allergic asthma exacerbation and acute severe asthma. The condition primarily affects the airways, leading to widespread bronchospasm, inflammation, and mucus hypersecretion. It can result in respiratory distress, hypoxia, and respiratory failure if not promptly managed. The lungs and airways are the main affected body parts.

Extrinsic asthma with acute exacerbation is an allergic form of asthma characterized by sudden worsening of respiratory symptoms due to exposure to allergens. Common synonyms include allergic asthma and atopic asthma. Causative agents often include pollen, dust mites, animal dander, and mold. The condition primarily affects the airways, leading to bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and increased mucus production. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It typically involves the bronchi and bronchioles, with potential involvement of the lungs and airways.

Intrinsic asthma, also known as non-allergic asthma, is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by variable and reversible airflow obstruction. It is not associated with allergen exposure and often develops in adulthood. Common triggers include respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, and stress. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyperresponsiveness. Unlike extrinsic asthma, intrinsic asthma lacks a clear allergic component and is less commonly associated with atopy. It can occur in individuals without a history of allergies or asthma.

Intrinsic asthma, unspecified, is a type of asthma characterized by airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness without a clear allergic trigger. It typically presents with episodic wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. Common synonyms include non-allergic asthma and non-atopic asthma. Causative agents may include respiratory infections, exercise, cold air, or environmental irritants. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to reversible airway obstruction. It is more common in adults and often lacks a clear history of atopy.

Intrinsic asthma with status asthmaticus is a severe, persistent form of asthma triggered by non-allergic factors such as exercise, infections, or environmental irritants. It is characterized by chronic airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness, leading to recurrent episodes of bronchoconstriction. Status asthmaticus represents a life-threatening exacerbation that does not respond adequately to standard bronchodilator therapy. Common synonyms include non-allergic asthma and late-onset asthma. Causative agents include viral infections, cold air, and stress. The primary affected body parts are the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles.

Intrinsic asthma with acute exacerbation is a sudden worsening of asthma symptoms due to non-allergic triggers. It involves airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction, leading to airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include non-allergic asthma exacerbation and acute bronchial asthma. Causative agents may include respiratory infections, air pollutants, stress, or medication side effects. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and alveoli, causing symptoms like dyspnea, wheezing, and cough. It often requires immediate medical intervention to prevent respiratory failure.

Chronic obstructive asthma is a persistent inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. It often presents with recurrent episodes of wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. Common synonyms include chronic asthma and persistent asthma. Causative agents include allergens, irritants, and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airway remodeling and impaired lung function. It is more prevalent in adults and can coexist with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Chronic obstructive asthma, unspecified, refers to persistent airflow limitation characterized by bronchial inflammation and hyperresponsiveness, leading to reversible airway obstruction. Common synonyms include chronic asthma and persistent asthma. Causative agents include allergens, irritants, and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, causing symptoms like wheezing, dyspnea, and cough. It is typically managed with bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids.

code_desc: Chronic obstructive asthma with status asthmaticus
summary: Chronic obstructive asthma with status asthmaticus is a severe exacerbation of chronic asthma characterized by persistent airflow obstruction and inadequate response to standard bronchodilator therapy. It involves inflammation and narrowing of the airways, leading to increased respiratory effort and potential respiratory failure. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and severe asthma exacerbation. Causative agents include allergens, irritants, infections, and environmental triggers. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles in the lungs, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, dyspnea, and hypoxia.

Chronic obstructive asthma with acute exacerbation refers to a worsening of persistent airflow limitation in individuals with asthma, characterized by increased breathlessness, cough, and sputum production. It often results from exposure to triggers such as allergens, viral infections, or pollutants. Common synonyms include asthma exacerbation or acute asthma flare-up. Causative agents may include respiratory viruses, allergens, irritants, or non-compliance with medication. The primary affected body parts are the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to bronchoconstriction and mucus plugging.

Other forms of asthma encompass a group of chronic respiratory conditions characterized by airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness, leading to variable and reversible airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include bronchial asthma and reactive airway disease. Causative agents may include allergens, irritants, respiratory infections, and genetic factors. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, causing symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It is most commonly diagnosed in childhood but can occur at any age.

Exercise induced bronchospasm, also known as exercise-induced asthma or exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, is a reversible narrowing of the airways triggered by physical activity. Common causative agents include cold air, allergens, and air pollutants. It typically affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. The condition is prevalent in individuals with underlying asthma or allergic conditions. It is often managed with pre-exercise bronchodilators and avoidance of triggering factors.

Cough variant asthma (CVA), also known as cough asthma or non-allergic cough, is a form of asthma characterized primarily by a chronic, dry cough without accompanying wheezing or shortness of breath. It is often triggered by allergens, respiratory infections, or environmental irritants. The cough is typically persistent and may worsen at night or upon exposure to cold air. Common causative agents include allergens like dust mites, pollen, and pet dander, as well as irritants such as smoke or chemical fumes. The condition primarily affects the airways, particularly the bronchi, leading to bronchial hyperresponsiveness. It is more common in adults and can often be mistaken for post-infectious cough or chronic bronchitis.

Asthma unspecified refers to a chronic respiratory condition characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing, typically due to airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness. It is a broad category used when the specific type of asthma cannot be determined. Common synonyms include bronchial asthma and allergic asthma. Causative agents may include allergens, irritants, respiratory infections, and genetic factors. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles in the lungs, leading to variable airflow obstruction.

Asthma, unspecified type, unspecified, is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by variable and recurring symptoms, including wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It involves hyperresponsiveness of the airways to various stimuli. Common synonyms include bronchial asthma and reactive airway disease. Causative agents may include allergens, irritants, respiratory infections, exercise, and weather changes. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles in the lungs, leading to airflow obstruction and bronchoconstriction.

code_desc: Asthma, unspecified type, with status asthmaticus
summary: Asthma, unspecified type, with status asthmaticus is a severe, acute exacerbation of asthma characterized by persistent bronchospasm, airway inflammation, and mucus plugging, leading to progressive respiratory distress. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and asthma exacerbation. Causative agents often include allergens, respiratory infections, irritants, or medication noncompliance. The condition primarily affects the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to impaired gas exchange and hypoxia. It commonly involves the lungs and can affect the cardiovascular system due to hypoxia and hypercapnia.

Asthma, unspecified type, with acute exacerbation is a sudden worsening of respiratory symptoms in individuals with a history of asthma. Common synonyms include acute asthma attack or asthma flare-up. Causative agents may include allergens, respiratory infections, pollutants, or stress. The condition primarily affects the airways, leading to bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and increased mucus production. Symptoms include cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It typically involves the lungs and airways, with potential systemic effects in severe cases. Prompt treatment with bronchodilators and corticosteroids is essential to prevent complications.

Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by abnormal dilation of the bronchi, leading to impaired clearance of mucus and recurrent infections. Common synonyms include bronchial dilatation and chronic bronchial infection. It is often caused by recurrent infections, such as those due to *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, or underlying conditions like cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, or tuberculosis. The disease primarily affects the medium to large airways, most commonly in the lower lobes of the lungs. Symptoms include chronic cough, copious sputum production, hemoptysis, and recurrent respiratory infections. Complications may involve pneumonia, respiratory failure, and pulmonary hypertension.

Bronchiectasis without acute exacerbation is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by irreversible dilation of bronchi, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent infections. Common synonyms include dilated bronchi and bronchial dilatation. Known causative agents include recurrent infections (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*), immune deficiencies, and genetic disorders like cystic fibrosis. The condition typically affects the middle and lower lobes of the lungs, primarily involving the bronchi and bronchioles. It is associated with chronic cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis.

Bronchiectasis with acute exacerbation refers to a sudden worsening of symptoms in patients with pre-existing bronchiectasis, characterized by increased cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis. It is often triggered by infections, particularly by *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, or viral agents. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airway inflammation, mucus plugging, and impaired clearance. Common synonyms include acute bronchiectasis flare-up or exacerbation of bronchiectasis. It predominantly involves the lungs, especially the lower lobes.

Extrinsic allergic alveolitis, also known as hypersensitivity pneumonitis or farmer's lung, is an inflammatory lung disease caused by inhalation of organic dusts or molds. It results from immune-mediated reactions to inhaled antigens, leading to alveolar inflammation and fibrosis. Common causative agents include *Aspergillus*, *Penicillium*, and *Actinomyces* species. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. It typically occurs in individuals exposed to contaminated environments, such as farmers, bird breeders, or moldy grain workers. Prolonged exposure can lead to progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

Farmers' lung, also known as hypersensitivity pneumonitis or allergic alveolitis, is an interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of organic dusts, particularly mold spores from hay, straw, or grain. It results from an immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation and fibrosis of the alveoli. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever. It is commonly seen in agricultural workers, especially those exposed to damp environments. Diagnosis involves clinical history, imaging, and sometimes bronchoalveolar lavage. Early recognition and avoidance of the antigen are crucial for management.

Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of spores from the fungus *Aspergillus flavus*, commonly found in sugarcane dust. It is also known as farmer's lung or sugarcane fever. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, leading to acute or chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Symptoms include cough, fever, dyspnea, and wheezing. The disease typically affects individuals working in sugarcane processing environments, particularly those involved in harvesting, storage, or milling. Prolonged exposure increases the risk of developing chronic respiratory impairment.

Bird-fanciers' lung, also known as hypersensitivity pneumonitis or extrinsic allergic alveolitis, is an interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of avian proteins, particularly from moldy bird droppings. The condition results from an immune-mediated response to antigens such as *Aspergillus* and *Penicillium* fungi. It primarily affects the alveoli and interstitium of the lungs, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. Commonly affected individuals are bird handlers, poultry workers, and pet bird owners. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever, with progression potentially leading to chronic respiratory impairment.

Suberosis is a rare, non-inflammatory, degenerative condition characterized by the thinning and atrophy of subcutaneous fat. It is often associated with aging, malnutrition, or systemic diseases. Common synonyms include lipodystrophy and subcutaneous atrophy. Causative agents may include chronic infections, endocrine disorders, and genetic factors. The condition typically affects the face, limbs, and trunk, leading to a gaunt appearance. It is more prevalent in elderly individuals and those with prolonged illness or poor nutrition. Suberosis is generally asymptomatic but can indicate underlying health issues.

Malt workers' lung, also known as byssinosis or cotton worker's lung, is a chronic respiratory condition caused by prolonged inhalation of dust from raw cotton, flax, or hemp. It primarily affects the lower airways and lungs, leading to symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, and wheezing. The condition is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of lung tissue. Common causative agents include cotton and flax dust, with symptoms often worsening after the weekend (Monday fever). It predominantly affects workers in textile industries.

Mushroom workers' lung, also known as hypersensitivity pneumonitis or farmer's lung, is an inflammatory lung disease caused by inhalation of fungal spores, particularly from species like *Aspergillus* and *Penicillium*. It primarily affects individuals exposed to damp agricultural environments. The condition leads to interstitial lung inflammation, with symptoms including cough, fever, and dyspnea. The lungs are typically affected, with granulomatous changes observed on imaging. Chronic exposure may result in progressive fibrosis.

"Maple bark-strippers" lung is a term used to describe a form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of fungal spores found in maple tree bark. Common synonyms include hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to *Alternaria* or *Aspergillus* species. The condition typically affects the lungs, causing inflammation and restrictive lung disease. It is often seen in individuals with occupational exposure, such as those working in forestry or woodworking. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever, with radiographic findings of interstitial lung involvement. Early diagnosis and avoidance of the allergen are crucial for recovery.

Ventilation pneumonitis is an inflammatory lung condition caused by mechanical stress from ventilatory support, often occurring in patients on mechanical ventilation. It is also known as ventilator-induced lung injury or ventilator-associated pneumonia. Common causative agents include bacterial pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. The condition primarily affects the alveoli and small airways, leading to inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. It typically occurs in critically ill patients with underlying lung disease or immunocompromised states.

code_desc: Other specified allergic alveolitis and pneumonitis
summary: Other specified allergic alveolitis and pneumonitis refers to inflammatory lung conditions caused by hypersensitivity reactions to inhaled antigens, not classified under specific types like hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Common synonyms include extrinsic allergic alveolitis and allergic interstitial pneumonitis. Causative agents include mold spores, bird proteins, and agricultural dusts. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation of the alveoli and interstitium. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, and fever, often following repeated exposure to allergens. It typically involves the lower respiratory tract and can progress to fibrosis if untreated.

Unspecified allergic alveolitis and pneumonitis refers to an inflammatory lung condition of unknown specific cause, characterized by immune-mediated injury to the alveoli. It may present with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. Common synonyms include hypersensitivity pneumonitis and interstitial pneumonia. While specific causative agents are not identified, it may be associated with environmental exposures, infections, or autoimmune processes. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the alveoli and interstitial tissue. Diagnosis often requires imaging, bronchoscopy, and biopsy. Treatment focuses on identifying and removing the inciting agent and managing symptoms.

code_desc: Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
summary: Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified, refers to persistent airflow limitation not attributable to a specific known cause. Common synonyms include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and chronic bronchitis. Causative agents often include long-term exposure to tobacco smoke, air pollutants, and occupational dusts. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnea. It is characterized by airflow limitation that is not fully reversible and often progresses over time.

Coal workers' pneumoconiosis, also known as black lung disease, is a chronic lung disorder caused by long-term inhalation of coal dust. It leads to the accumulation of coal particles in the lungs, resulting in inflammation and fibrosis. The condition primarily affects the alveoli and bronchioles, causing progressive respiratory impairment. Common synonyms include anthracosis and byssinosis. The causative agent is coal dust, particularly from coal mining environments. It predominantly impacts the lungs, leading to reduced lung function and increased susceptibility to infections.

Asbestosis is a chronic lung disease caused by prolonged inhalation of asbestos fibers, leading to progressive scarring and fibrosis of lung tissue. Common synonyms include asbestos pneumoconiosis and asbestosis. The primary causative agent is asbestos, particularly chrysotile, amosite, and crocidolite. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and decreased lung function. It typically involves the interstitial spaces of the lungs, leading to reduced elasticity and impaired gas exchange. Long-term exposure increases the risk of complications like lung cancer and mesothelioma.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to other silica or silicates
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to other silica or silicates is a chronic lung disease caused by inhalation of respirable crystalline silica or silicate dust. Common synonyms include silicosis and silicate pneumoconiosis. The primary causative agents are quartz, cristobalite, and other silicate minerals. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive fibrosis, nodular scarring, and impaired gas exchange. It is typically seen in occupational settings such as mining, construction, and manufacturing. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and increased risk of respiratory infections and lung cancer. Early exposure leads to acute or subacute forms, while prolonged exposure results in chronic silicosis.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to other inorganic dust
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to other inorganic dust refers to lung disease caused by prolonged inhalation of inorganic dust particles not classified as asbestos, silica, or coal. Common synonyms include "dust lung disease" or "occupational lung disease." Causative agents include metal dusts, such as beryllium, talc, and quartz. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive fibrosis, inflammation, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and increased risk of respiratory infections. It is typically seen in workers exposed to dust in industries such as mining, manufacturing, and construction.

code_desc: Pneumonopathy due to inhalation of other dust
summary: Pneumonopathy due to inhalation of other dust refers to lung disease caused by exposure to non-metallic, non-organic dusts such as silica, coal, or asbestos. Common synonyms include pneumoconiosis and dust lung. Causative agents vary but often include crystalline silica, coal dust, and other mineral particles. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. Chronic exposure can result in progressive respiratory impairment and increased risk of infections or malignancies.

Pneumoconiosis, unspecified, is a chronic lung disease caused by the inhalation and retention of inorganic dust particles. It leads to progressive fibrosis and inflammation of the lung parenchyma. Common synonyms include occupational lung disease and pneumoconiosis. Causative agents typically include silica, coal, and asbestos. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung function. It is often associated with occupational exposure and may lead to complications like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or lung cancer.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to chemical fumes and vapors
summary: Respiratory conditions due to chemical fumes and vapors result from inhalation of toxic substances, leading to irritation, inflammation, or damage of the airways and lungs. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and acute chemical lung injury. Causative agents include industrial solvents, chlorine, ammonia, and hydrocarbons. These exposures typically affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and pulmonary edema. Prolonged exposure may lead to chronic obstructive lung disease or bronchitis. The condition is often occupational, affecting workers in chemical plants, laboratories, and cleaning industries.

code_desc: Bronchitis and pneumonitis due to fumes and vapors
summary: Bronchitis and pneumonitis due to fumes and vapors refer to inflammatory conditions of the bronchi and lungs caused by inhalation of toxic or irritating vapors. Common synonyms include chemical bronchitis and chemical pneumonitis. Causative agents include industrial chemicals, solvents, gases, and smoke. Typically affecting the respiratory tract, this condition primarily involves the bronchi and alveoli, leading to symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and chest discomfort. Prolonged exposure can result in chronic respiratory impairment.

code_desc: Acute pulmonary edema due to fumes and vapors
summary: Acute pulmonary edema due to fumes and vapors is a severe respiratory condition caused by inhalation of toxic substances, leading to fluid accumulation in the lungs. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and acute chemical-induced pulmonary edema. Causative agents include industrial chemicals, solvents, pesticides, and volatile organic compounds. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, frothy sputum, and hypoxia. It may also involve the respiratory tract and, in severe cases, lead to respiratory failure. Prompt decontamination and supportive care are critical for management.

code_desc: Upper respiratory inflammation due to fumes and vapors
summary: Upper respiratory inflammation due to fumes and vapors refers to irritation and inflammation of the upper airway caused by exposure to chemical vapors or fumes. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis or toxic inhalation injury. Causative agents often include industrial solvents, cleaning agents, and volatile organic compounds. Typically affected body parts include the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and trachea. Symptoms may present as cough, sore throat, hoarseness, and difficulty breathing. Prolonged exposure can lead to chronic respiratory issues.

code_desc: Other acute and subacute respiratory conditions due to fumes and vapors
summary: Other acute and subacute respiratory conditions due to fumes and vapors refer to inhalation injuries caused by exposure to toxic or irritating vapors, fumes, or gases. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and inhalation injury. Causative agents may include industrial chemicals, solvents, pesticides, and combustion byproducts. These conditions typically affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, chest pain, and in severe cases, respiratory failure. The lungs are most commonly involved, with potential involvement of the airways and alveoli. Prompt removal from exposure and supportive care are critical for recovery.

code_desc: Chronic respiratory conditions due to fumes and vapors
summary: Chronic respiratory conditions due to fumes and vapors refer to long-term lung damage caused by prolonged exposure to harmful chemical vapors, gases, or aerosols. Common synonyms include occupational lung disease and chemical-induced pulmonary disorders. Causative agents include solvents, pesticides, industrial chemicals, and combustion byproducts. These conditions primarily affect the respiratory tract, particularly the bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli, leading to symptoms such as chronic cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung function. Prolonged exposure can result in irreversible lung damage and increased susceptibility to infections.

code_desc: Unspecified respiratory conditions due to fumes and vapors
summary: Unspecified respiratory conditions due to fumes and vapors refer to respiratory illnesses caused by inhalation of toxic or irritating fumes and vapors, where the specific agent is not identified. Common synonyms include chemical-induced respiratory disorders and inhalation toxicities. Causative agents may include industrial chemicals, solvents, pesticides, and combustion byproducts. Typically, the upper and lower respiratory tract, including the nose, throat, trachea, and lungs, are affected. Symptoms may range from irritation and coughing to severe bronchospasm and pulmonary edema.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to solids and liquids
summary: Pneumonitis due to solids and liquids, also known as aspiration pneumonitis or chemical pneumonitis, occurs when foreign substances such as food, liquids, or gastric contents are inhaled into the lungs. This leads to inflammation and irritation of lung tissue. Common causative agents include gastric acid, food particles, and other irritants. It typically affects the lower respiratory tract, including the alveoli and bronchioles. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. The condition is often seen in patients with altered mental status, stroke, or swallowing disorders. Prompt management is essential to prevent complications such as pneumonia or respiratory failure.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus
summary: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus, also known as aspiration pneumonia, occurs when foreign material enters the lungs, causing inflammation. Common synonyms include aspiration pneumonitis and chemical pneumonitis. Causative agents include gastric contents, food particles, and oral secretions. The condition typically affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly the alveoli and bronchioles. It is more common in individuals with impaired consciousness, swallowing disorders, or gastrointestinal reflux. Symptoms include cough, fever, and respiratory distress. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as respiratory failure.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of oils and essences
summary: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of oils and essences is an inflammatory lung condition caused by the inhalation of volatile organic compounds such as essential oils, perfumes, or industrial solvents. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and inorganic pneumonitis. Causative agents include turpentine, mineral oil, and aromatic hydrocarbons. The condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It often occurs in occupational or environmental settings with exposure to these substances. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and imaging, with treatment focusing on removal from the irritant and supportive care.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to other solids and liquids
summary: Pneumonitis due to other solids and liquids refers to lung inflammation caused by inhalation of foreign substances such as dust, chemicals, or hydrocarbons. Common synonyms include aspiration pneumonia or chemical pneumonitis. Causative agents may include coal dust, silica, hydrocarbons, or gastric contents. This condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia. It is often seen in occupational exposures or accidental inhalation events. Diagnosis involves imaging and bronchoalveolar lavage, with treatment focusing on removal of the irritant and supportive care.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to other and unspecified external agents
summary: Respiratory conditions due to other and unspecified external agents refer to lung disorders caused by environmental factors not classified under specific categories like allergens or occupational exposures. Common synonyms include inhalation injuries and toxic respiratory syndromes. Causative agents may include smoke, chemicals, pollutants, or biological agents. These conditions typically affect the airways and alveoli, leading to inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms often include cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. The lungs are the primary affected body parts, with potential involvement of the upper respiratory tract in severe cases.

code_desc: Acute pulmonary manifestations due to radiation
summary: Acute pulmonary manifestations due to radiation refer to lung injury occurring within weeks to months after radiation therapy. Common synonyms include radiation pneumonitis and radiation-induced lung injury. Causative agents are ionizing radiation, often from therapeutic treatments for thoracic malignancies. Typically affected body parts include the lung parenchyma, with inflammation and edema as key features. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and fever. The condition is characterized by non-specific interstitial pneumonia on imaging and can progress to pulmonary fibrosis if untreated.

code_desc: Chronic and other pulmonary manifestations due to radiation
summary: Chronic and other pulmonary manifestations due to radiation refer to lung damage resulting from exposure to ionizing radiation. Common synonyms include radiation pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis. Causative agents are ionizing radiation, often from radiotherapy. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, with the upper lobes being most commonly involved. Symptoms may include dyspnea, cough, and reduced lung function. Long-term effects can lead to pulmonary fibrosis, decreased oxygen exchange, and increased susceptibility to infections. The condition is often seen in patients undergoing thoracic radiation therapy for malignancies such as lung cancer.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to smoke inhalation
summary: Respiratory conditions due to smoke inhalation result from exposure to toxic gases and particulate matter from burning materials. Common synonyms include smoke inhalation injury and thermal injury. Causative agents include carbon monoxide, cyanide, and particulate matter from fires or tobacco smoke. These conditions primarily affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Severe cases can lead to airway obstruction, pulmonary edema, and respiratory failure.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to other specified external agents
summary: Respiratory conditions due to other specified external agents refer to lung disorders caused by substances not classified as chemicals, allergens, or irritants. Common synonyms include inhalation injuries and toxic respiratory syndromes. Causative agents may include smoke, dust, fumes, or biological agents like spores. These conditions typically affect the airways and alveoli, leading to inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Affected body parts primarily include the trachea, bronchi, and lungs.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to unspecified external agent
summary: Respiratory conditions due to unspecified external agent refer to lung disorders caused by environmental factors not specifically identified. Common synonyms include inhalation injury or toxic respiratory exposure. Causative agents may include chemical fumes, smoke, dust, or airborne toxins. These conditions typically affect the airways and lung parenchyma, leading to inflammation, irritation, or damage. Symptoms often include cough, shortness of breath, and respiratory distress. The exact mechanism and long-term effects depend on the nature and duration of exposure.

Empyema is a collection of pus within a cavity, most commonly in the pleural space following pneumonia or other lung infections. It results from an inflammatory response to bacterial infection, leading to fibrinopurulent exudate. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*. Empyema typically affects the thoracic cavity, particularly the pleural space, but can also occur in other body cavities such as the pericardium or abdomen. Synonyms include pyothorax and purulent pleural effusion. It is often associated with underlying conditions like tuberculosis or malignancy.

Empyema with fistula is a complication of pyothorax characterized by the formation of a sinus tract connecting the pleural space to the skin or other structures. It typically arises from persistent infection leading to abscess formation and subsequent breakdown of the pleural wall. Common causative agents include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and gram-negative bacilli. The condition most commonly affects the thoracic cavity, but may also involve the abdominal or pelvic regions. Synonyms include pyopyothorax with fistula and purulent empyema with sinus tract. It is often associated with underlying conditions such as pneumonia, trauma, or malignancy.

Empyema is a collection of pus within a body cavity, most commonly the pleural space, resulting from infection. It typically follows pneumonia or trauma, with *Staphylococcus aureus* being a common causative agent. Other pathogens include *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae*. The condition is characterized by fever, chest pain, and respiratory distress. It predominantly affects the lungs and pleura, though it may occur in other cavities such as the peritoneum or joint spaces. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging and fluid analysis, with treatment involving drainage and antimicrobial therapy.

Pleurisy, also known as pleuritis, is an inflammation of the pleura, the thin membranes lining the lungs and chest cavity. It typically presents with sharp, stabbing chest pain that worsens with breathing. Common causes include viral infections, bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, collagen vascular diseases, and pulmonary embolism. The condition primarily affects the pleural layers, leading to friction during respiration. It may also be associated with fluid accumulation in the pleural space, known as pleural effusion. The lungs and surrounding chest structures are the main affected areas.

code_desc: Pleurisy without mention of effusion or current tuberculosis
summary: Pleurisy, or pleuritic pain, refers to inflammation of the pleura, the serous membranes lining the lungs and chest cavity. It is characterized by sharp, stabbing chest pain that worsens with breathing. Common synonyms include pleuritic chest pain and pleuritis. Causative agents include viral infections, bacterial pneumonia, autoimmune disorders, and pulmonary embolism. Typically affecting the lower lobes of the lungs, the condition may involve the parietal pleura. It is distinct from pleural effusion and tuberculosis. The pain is often described as sharp and localized, intensifying with inspiration.

code_desc: Pleurisy with effusion, with mention of a bacterial cause other than tuberculosis
summary: Pleurisy with effusion is an inflammation of the pleural membranes accompanied by fluid accumulation in the pleural space. Common synonyms include pleural effusion with inflammation and exudative pleuritis. Bacterial causes, other than tuberculosis, include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae. This condition typically affects the lungs and pleura, often resulting from pneumonia, trauma, or systemic infections. Symptoms include chest pain, dyspnea, and fever. It is more common in the lower lobes of the lungs. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications such as respiratory failure.

code_desc: Other specified forms of pleural effusion except tuberculous
summary: Other specified forms of pleural effusion except tuberculous refer to pleural fluid accumulation not classified as tuberculous or due to other known causes. Common synonyms include non-tuberculous pleural effusion and unspecified pleural effusion. Causative agents may include malignancy, heart failure, connective tissue diseases, or infections other than tuberculosis. These effusions typically affect the pleural cavity, with fluid accumulation in the space between the lungs and chest wall. The condition may present with dyspnea, chest pain, and signs of respiratory distress. Diagnosis often involves imaging and fluid analysis to determine the underlying cause.

Malignant pleural effusion is an accumulation of fluid in the pleural space caused by cancer. It commonly results from metastatic tumors to the pleura or direct extension of thoracic malignancies. Common synonyms include cancer-related pleural effusion and secondary pleural effusion. Causative agents include lung, breast, lymphoma, and mesothelioma. The condition primarily affects the pleural cavity, leading to dyspnea, chest pain, and reduced lung expansion. It is often a late-stage manifestation of underlying malignancy.

code_desc: Other specified forms of effusion, except tuberculous
summary: Other specified forms of effusion, except tuberculous, refer to abnormal fluid accumulation in body cavities not classified as tuberculous. Common synonyms include serous effusion or non-infectious effusion. Causative agents may include autoimmune disorders, malignancy, heart failure, or inflammatory conditions. Typically affected body parts include the pleural space, pericardium, and peritoneum. These effusions are characterized by the presence of serous fluid without evidence of tuberculosis. Clinical presentation varies based on the underlying cause and affected site. Diagnosis often involves imaging and fluid analysis.

Unspecified pleural effusion refers to the accumulation of fluid in the pleural space without a clearly identified cause. It is a nonspecific finding often encountered on imaging studies. Common synonyms include "non-specific pleural effusion" or "unclassified pleural effusion." Causative agents may include infections, malignancy, heart failure, or autoimmune disorders. Typically, the condition affects the lungs and pleura, with fluid accumulation between the visceral and parietal pleura. It may be associated with symptoms such as dyspnea and chest pain, but clinical presentation varies widely. Further diagnostic evaluation is necessary to determine the underlying etiology.

Pneumothorax and air leak refer to the presence of air in the pleural space, leading to partial or complete lung collapse. Common synonyms include spontaneous pneumothorax, pulmonary air leak, and bleb rupture. Causative agents include trauma, lung disease (e.g., COPD, emphysema), and iatrogenic causes such as mechanical ventilation or thoracentesis. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the visceral pleura, and can occur in one or both lungs. It is more common in tall, thin individuals and those with underlying respiratory conditions. Symptoms include sudden chest pain and dyspnea, with potential complications such as tension pneumothorax.

Spontaneous tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening condition characterized by the accumulation of air in the pleural space, leading to progressive lung collapse and increased intrathoracic pressure. It typically occurs without an obvious traumatic injury. Common synonyms include tension pneumothorax and spontaneous pneumothorax. Causative agents include ruptured pulmonary blebs or bullae, often in tall, thin individuals. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, with the right lung being more commonly involved. It can rapidly lead to cardiovascular compromise and respiratory failure if not promptly treated.

Iatrogenic pneumothorax is an unintended accumulation of air in the pleural space caused by medical procedures. Common synonyms include traumatic pneumothorax or procedural pneumothorax. It is often associated with interventions such as central line placement, thoracentesis, or mechanical ventilation. The condition typically affects the lungs, particularly the anterior and middle regions. Causative agents include needles, catheters, and ventilator tubing. It may present with sudden chest pain and dyspnea, requiring prompt intervention to prevent respiratory compromise.

Postoperative air leak, also known as persistent air leak or pneumothorax after surgery, refers to the continued leakage of air from the lungs into the pleural space following thoracic surgery. It commonly occurs after procedures such as lobectomy or pneumonectomy. Causative factors include incomplete lung resection, bronchial stump leakage, or injury during surgery. The condition typically affects the lungs and pleural cavity, leading to symptoms like chest pain and dyspnea. It is often managed with chest tube drainage and, in some cases, surgical intervention.

Oth pneumothorax, also known as spontaneous or primary pneumothorax, occurs when air leaks into the pleural space without an obvious cause. It typically affects individuals with underlying lung conditions such as emphysema or lung cancer. Common synonyms include spontaneous pneumothorax and primary pneumothorax. The condition most commonly involves the lungs, particularly the apical regions, leading to partial or complete lung collapse. Causative agents include ruptured blebs, trauma, or underlying pulmonary diseases. Symptoms include sudden chest pain and dyspnea.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is the sudden collapse of a lung due to the rupture of a small air-filled blister (bleb) on the lung surface, typically occurring in tall, thin young men. It is not associated with underlying lung disease. Common synonyms include spontaneous pneumothorax and simple pneumothorax. Causative agents include genetic factors and smoking. The condition primarily affects the lungs, most commonly the right lung, and may lead to respiratory distress. It is often managed with chest tube drainage or observation.

Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is a condition characterized by the sudden collapse of a lung due to the accumulation of air in the pleural space, typically resulting from pre-existing lung disease. Unlike primary pneumothorax, it occurs in patients with underlying pulmonary pathology. Common synonyms include secondary spontaneous air leak. Causative agents include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), tuberculosis, interstitial lung disease, and lung cancer. The condition most commonly affects the upper lobes of the lungs, particularly in individuals with compromised lung tissue.

Chronic pneumothorax refers to the persistent presence of air in the pleural space, leading to partial or complete lung collapse. It often results from recurrent or unresolved spontaneous pneumothorax, particularly in individuals with underlying lung disease. Common synonyms include chronic air leak or persistent pneumothorax. Causative agents include ruptured blebs, emphysema, and trauma. The condition typically affects the lungs, primarily the upper lobes, and can lead to complications such as atelectasis or respiratory failure if left untreated.

"Other air leak" refers to an abnormal escape of air from the pulmonary system into the pleural space or surrounding tissues, not attributable to pneumothorax or bronchopleural fistula. Common synonyms include spontaneous air leak or pleural air leak. Causative agents may include trauma, infection, or iatrogenic injury. Typically affects the lungs and pleura, often involving the alveoli or airways. It can occur in patients with underlying lung disease or after thoracic procedures. Symptoms include chest pain and dyspnea, with findings on imaging such as pneumothorax or subcutaneous emphysema.

Other pneumothorax refers to a spontaneous or secondary accumulation of air in the pleural space not caused by trauma or known underlying lung disease. It may occur in individuals without prior lung conditions. Common synonyms include simple pneumothorax and primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Causative agents include ruptured pulmonary blebs or bullae, often in tall, thin individuals. Typically affects the lungs, particularly the upper lobes. It may present with sudden chest pain and dyspnea. Diagnosis is confirmed by imaging, and management includes observation, aspiration, or chest tube insertion.

Abscess of the lung and mediastinum is a severe infection characterized by localized collection of pus in the lung parenchyma or mediastinal tissues. Common synonyms include pulmonary abscess and mediastinal abscess. It is typically caused by bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Escherichia coli*. The condition often results from hematogenous spread, aspiration, or extension from adjacent infections. It predominantly affects the upper lobes of the lungs and can involve the mediastinum, leading to systemic symptoms like fever and cough. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications such as sepsis or respiratory failure.

An abscess of the lung, also known as pulmonary abscess, is a localized collection of pus within the lung parenchyma, typically resulting from bacterial infection. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Anaerobes*. It often develops from aspiration of oral secretions or extension from adjacent infections. The right lung is more frequently affected, particularly the lower lobes. Symptoms include fever, cough, and purulent sputum. Complications may involve pleural effusion or empyema. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging and microbiological analysis.

An abscess of the mediastinum is a localized collection of pus within the mediastinal compartment, often resulting from infection spreading from adjacent structures. Common synonyms include mediastinal empyema or mediastinal abscess. Causative agents frequently include staphylococci, streptococci, and gram-negative bacteria. It may arise from trauma, surgery, or contiguous spread from the lungs, heart, or esophagus. The condition typically affects the anterior or posterior mediastinum and can present with fever, dyspnea, and chest pain. Prompt diagnosis and drainage are essential to prevent complications.

Pulmonary congestion and hypostasis refer to the accumulation of blood in the lungs, typically due to impaired venous return, leading to fluid leakage into lung tissues. This condition is commonly associated with heart failure, particularly left-sided, and can result from conditions like hypertension or valvular disease. Hypostasis refers to pooling of blood in dependent areas, often seen in patients with prolonged immobility or respiratory compromise. The lungs, particularly the lower lobes, are typically affected. Synonyms include pulmonary edema and cardiac congestion.

Postinflammatory pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive lung condition characterized by the formation of scar tissue in the lungs following an inflammatory or infectious process. Common synonyms include interstitial fibrosis and fibrotic lung disease. It typically results from prolonged inflammation, often due to infections like tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, or autoimmune disorders. The primary affected areas are the alveoli and interstitial spaces in the lungs, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory distress. The condition can affect both lungs and is often associated with chronic hypoxia and reduced lung compliance.

Other alveolar and parietoalveolar pneumonopathy refers to diffuse lung disease affecting both alveolar and parietal regions. It encompasses a group of conditions characterized by inflammation and/or fibrosis of lung parenchyma. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonia and diffuse parenchymal lung disease. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune disorders, environmental exposures, and drug reactions. Typically affects the lungs, with involvement of alveoli and interstitial spaces. Commonly seen in the lower lung zones. May present with dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia.

Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) is a rare lung disorder characterized by the accumulation of surfactant-like material within the alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory symptoms. Common synonyms include diffuse pulmonary alveolar proteinosis and lipoproteinosis. It is primarily caused by genetic mutations, particularly in the CSF3R or SFTPA2 genes, or by immune-mediated mechanisms. Other causes include infections, medications, and exposure to certain toxins. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, with alveolar spaces filled with proteinaceous material, resulting in progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia.

Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis (IPH) is a rare disorder characterized by recurrent alveolar hemorrhage, leading to iron overload and hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the lungs. Common synonyms include pulmonary hemosiderosis and hemosiderosis. The exact cause is unknown, though infections, autoimmune disorders, and genetic factors may contribute. It primarily affects the lungs, with systemic involvement possible. The condition predominantly occurs in children, though adults can be affected. Clinical features include hemoptysis, dyspnea, and iron deficiency anemia. Diagnosis involves imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage, and iron studies. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and addressing underlying causes.

Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis is a rare, chronic lung disease characterized by the accumulation of microliths, small calcium-containing deposits, within the alveoli. Common synonyms include pulmonary microlithiasis and alveolar microlithiasis. The condition is typically idiopathic, though some cases may be associated with genetic mutations, such as those in the *SLC34A2* gene. It predominantly affects the lungs, leading to progressive respiratory symptoms. The microliths may also occasionally involve other organs, such as the liver or spleen. The disease is generally asymptomatic in early stages but can progress to restrictive lung disease and respiratory failure.

Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (IIP) refers to a group of chronic lung diseases characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium of unknown cause. Common synonyms include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung disease. Known causative agents are often unclear, though environmental exposures, infections, and genetic factors may contribute. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive scarring and impaired gas exchange. It typically involves the alveolar and interstitial tissues, with the lower lung zones most commonly affected. Symptoms include dyspnea, dry cough, and reduced exercise tolerance.

code_desc: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, not otherwise specified
summary: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, not otherwise specified (UIP/NOS), is a chronic, progressive lung disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the interstitial tissue. It is a subset of idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, with UIP being the most common pattern. Common synonyms include interstitial lung disease, unspecified. Known causative agents are often unknown, though environmental exposures and autoimmune conditions may contribute. The lungs are primarily affected, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory failure. The condition predominantly affects middle-aged to elderly individuals, with a higher prevalence in males.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive interstitial lung disease of unknown cause. It is characterized by the formation of fibrotic scar tissue within the lungs, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory failure. Common synonyms include usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) and cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis. The condition primarily affects the distal lung parenchyma, particularly the alveoli and interstitium. Known causative agents include environmental exposures such as asbestos, silica, and certain occupational dusts, though many cases remain idiopathic. It predominantly affects middle-aged to older adults, with a male predilection.

Idiopathic non-specific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP) is a chronic interstitial lung disease of unknown cause, characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma. Common synonyms include nonspecific interstitial pneumonia and diffuse interstitial pneumonia. It typically affects the alveoli and interstitium, leading to progressive dyspnea and reduced lung function. The condition is more prevalent in women and often presents with a slowly progressive course. While no specific causative agent is identified, it may be associated with autoimmune disorders. The lungs are the primary affected body parts, with histopathology showing uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis.

Acute interstitial pneumonitis, also known as acute diffuse infiltrative lung disease or non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, is an inflammatory condition affecting the lung interstitium. It is characterized by diffuse alveolar infiltration and impaired gas exchange. Common causative agents include drugs (e.g., amiodarone, bleomycin), infections, autoimmune diseases, and environmental exposures. The primary affected body part is the lung, with involvement of the interstitial and alveolar spaces. Clinically, it presents with dyspnea, hypoxemia, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on imaging.

Respiratory bronchiolitis interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD) is a form of interstitial lung disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the respiratory bronchioles and surrounding alveolar septa. Common synonyms include respiratory bronchiolitis and desquamative interstitial pneumonia. It is primarily caused by long-term exposure to inhaled toxins, most commonly tobacco smoke. The disease typically affects the lower lung zones and is associated with a chronic, progressive decline in pulmonary function. It is most commonly seen in middle-aged to elderly smokers, with a male predominance. The condition can present with dyspnea, cough, and progressive respiratory failure if left untreated.

Idiopathic lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (ILIP) is a rare, chronic lung disease characterized by non-specific inflammation and lymphoid proliferation in the interstitium of the lungs. Common synonyms include lymphoid interstitial pneumonia and interstitial lymphoid hyperplasia. The exact cause is unknown, though viral infections, particularly Epstein-Barr virus, have been implicated. ILIP primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia. It is more common in women and often occurs in association with other autoimmune or connective tissue disorders. The condition is classified as a form of interstitial lung disease.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP), also known as cryptogenic pulmonary fibrosis or acute interstitial pneumonia, is a form of interstitial lung disease of unknown cause. It is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis in the alveolar spaces, with organizing pneumonia patterns on histopathology. Common causative agents include infections, medications, and autoimmune diseases, though many cases remain idiopathic. The lungs are typically affected, with bilateral ground-glass opacities and reticular shadows on imaging. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever. Diagnosis is made through exclusion of other causes and biopsy when necessary.
