Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP) is a rare, often idiopathic interstitial lung disease characterized by the accumulation of alveolar macrophages and desquamated pneumocytes in the alveolar spaces. Common synonyms include respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD) and desquamative interstitial pneumonia. It is typically caused by environmental exposures such as cigarette smoke, though a subset may be linked to drug toxicity or infections. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing progressive dyspnea and a restrictive ventilatory defect. It predominantly involves the lower lung zones and is more common in middle-aged smokers.

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare, progressive lung disease characterized by the proliferation of abnormal smooth muscle-like cells, leading to cystic lung lesions and obstructive symptoms. Common synonyms include pulmonary LAM and tuberous sclerosis complex-related LAM. The condition is primarily associated with mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes, often linked to tuberous sclerosis complex. It predominantly affects women of childbearing age and involves the lungs, lymphatic system, and occasionally the kidneys. Symptoms include dyspnea, chylous effusions, and spontaneous pneumothorax.

Adult pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH) is a rare granulomatous disorder characterized by the proliferation of Langerhans cells in the lungs. It is also known as eosinophilic granuloma of the lung or Hamman-Rich syndrome. The exact cause is unknown, though smoking is a significant risk factor. The disease primarily affects the upper lobes of the lungs, leading to nodules, cavities, and interstitial inflammation. It may also involve other organs, such as bones and the skin, but the lungs are most commonly affected. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. Diagnosis is typically made via imaging and biopsy.

Interstitial lung diseases of childhood are a group of disorders characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include diffuse parenchymal lung disease and interstitial pneumonia. These conditions can be idiopathic or secondary to infections, autoimmune diseases, or environmental exposures. Causative agents may include viral infections, inhalation of irritants, or genetic factors. Typically affecting the alveolar walls and surrounding tissues, they primarily involve the lungs, though systemic manifestations may occur. The disease can present with progressive dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia.

Neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia of infancy (NEHI), also known as congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS), is a rare disorder characterized by abnormal development of neuroendocrine cells, primarily affecting the autonomic nervous system. It is caused by mutations in the PHOX2B gene. The condition typically presents with impaired respiratory control, leading to hypoventilation, especially during sleep. It may also involve abnormalities in gastrointestinal and cardiovascular functions. Commonly affected body parts include the respiratory system, gastrointestinal tract, and autonomic nervous system. The condition is typically diagnosed in the neonatal period.

Pulmonary interstitial glycogenosis (PIG) is a rare, idiopathic interstitial lung disease primarily affecting newborns and young children. It is characterized by the abnormal accumulation of glycogen in the alveolar epithelium and interstitium. Common synonyms include congenital interstitial glycogenosis and infantile interstitial glycogenosis. The exact cause is unknown, though some cases may be associated with genetic factors or metabolic disorders. The lungs are the primary affected body part, with diffuse interstitial involvement leading to respiratory distress and hypoxia. The condition is often diagnosed postmortem, though some cases may present with chronic respiratory symptoms.

Surfactant mutations of the lung refer to genetic alterations affecting surfactant proteins, leading to impaired lung function. Common synonyms include neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and surfactant deficiency. These mutations are often caused by inherited defects in genes such as SFTPA1, SFTPB, SFTPC, and SFTPD. The condition primarily affects the alveoli, leading to respiratory distress, particularly in newborns. Affected individuals experience reduced surfactant production, resulting in alveolar collapse and increased respiratory effort. The lungs are the main body part involved, with systemic complications possible in severe cases.

code_desc: Alveolar capillary dysplasia with vein misalignment
summary: Alveolar capillary dysplasia with vein misalignment (ACDVM) is a rare congenital lung disorder characterized by abnormal development of pulmonary capillaries and misaligned pulmonary veins. It results in impaired gas exchange and severe respiratory distress in newborns. Common synonyms include congenital pulmonary venous malformation and alveolar capillary dysplasia. The condition is typically caused by genetic mutations, though the exact causative agents are not fully understood. It predominantly affects the lungs, leading to respiratory failure and often results in early mortality.

code_desc: Other interstitial lung diseases of childhood
summary: Other interstitial lung diseases of childhood refer to a group of rare, heterogeneous disorders characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology. Causative agents may include infections, environmental exposures, or autoimmune conditions. These diseases primarily affect the lungs, leading to progressive respiratory impairment. They are most commonly seen in children with underlying immunodeficiencies or genetic disorders. Clinical features include dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia, with imaging showing ground-glass opacities and reticular patterns. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent irreversible lung damage.

code_desc: Other specified alveolar and parietoalveolar pneumonopathies
summary: Other specified alveolar and parietoalveolar pneumonopathies refer to lung inflammation affecting the alveoli and parietal layers, not classified under other major categories. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonitis and diffuse alveolar damage. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viral, bacterial), autoimmune diseases, or environmental exposures. Typically affects the lungs, with symptoms such as dyspnea and cough. Often seen in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying lung disease. Diagnosis involves imaging and biopsy. Treatment depends on underlying cause.

Unspecified alveolar and parietoalveolar pneumonopathy refers to diffuse lung disease involving both alveolar and parietal regions without a specific etiology. It is a nonspecific term used when the exact cause or type of pneumonia is not determined. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonia and diffuse infiltrative lung disease. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or fungal infections, as well as environmental exposures or autoimmune conditions. The lungs are typically affected, with involvement of both alveoli and interstitial tissue. This condition may present with symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia.

code_desc: Lung involvement in conditions classified elsewhere
summary: Lung involvement in conditions classified elsewhere refers to pulmonary manifestations of systemic diseases not primarily categorized as respiratory disorders. Common synonyms include secondary pulmonary involvement or extrapulmonary lung disease. Causative agents may include autoimmune diseases, infections, or malignancies. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and infiltrates. Conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, and systemic lupus erythematosus can present with lung involvement. Diagnosis often requires imaging and biopsy. Treatment targets the underlying condition.

Rheumatic pneumonia is a rare complication of acute rheumatic fever, characterized by inflammation of the lungs secondary to immune-mediated injury. It is not directly caused by a bacterial infection but rather by the body's immune response to streptococcal infection. Common synonyms include post-streptococcal pneumonia and rheumatic lung involvement. The condition typically affects the alveoli and interstitial tissue, leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and dyspnea. It is most commonly seen in children and adolescents following untreated streptococcal pharyngitis.

Lung involvement in systemic sclerosis, also known as interstitial lung disease or pulmonary hypertension, is a common and serious complication. It results from fibrosis of lung parenchyma and vascular abnormalities. Common synonyms include diffuse interstitial pneumonia and pulmonary fibrosis. The primary causative agent is the autoimmune process associated with systemic sclerosis, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, with potential involvement of the heart and vasculature. Symptoms may include dyspnea, dry cough, and reduced exercise tolerance. Early diagnosis and management are critical to improve outcomes.

Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is a clinical syndrome characterized by new pulmonary infiltrates accompanied by symptoms of respiratory insufficiency. It is a serious complication in sickle cell disease and other hemoglobinopathies. Common synonyms include sickle cell acute chest syndrome and pulmonary infiltrates with or without fever. Causative agents include infection, vaso-occlusion, and fat embolism. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, with involvement of the pulmonary parenchyma and vasculature. It can lead to hypoxia, respiratory failure, and increased mortality if not promptly managed.

code_desc: Lung involvement in other diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Lung involvement in other diseases classified elsewhere refers to pulmonary manifestations secondary to systemic conditions not primarily classified as respiratory diseases. Common synonyms include secondary pulmonary involvement or extrapulmonary disease affecting the lungs. Causative agents vary widely, including infections (e.g., tuberculosis, HIV), autoimmune disorders (e.g., lupus, scleroderma), and malignancies (e.g., lymphoma, metastatic cancer). Typically affected body parts include the alveoli, bronchioles, interstitium, and vasculature, leading to symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia.

"Other diseases of lung" encompasses a variety of non-specific or less commonly classified pulmonary conditions not categorized as pneumonia, neoplasm, or tuberculosis. Common synonyms include interstitial lung disease and diffuse lung disease. Causative agents may include environmental toxins, occupational exposures, autoimmune disorders, or idiopathic factors. These conditions typically affect the lung parenchyma, alveoli, and interstitial tissue, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, or impaired gas exchange. They may present with dyspnea, cough, and reduced oxygenation.

Pulmonary collapse, also known as atelectasis or lung collapse, refers to the partial or complete collapse of a lung or portion of a lung due to airway obstruction, loss of air, or compression. Common causes include mucus plugging, tumors, pneumothorax, or post-operative complications. It most commonly affects the alveoli and bronchi, leading to reduced gas exchange. Symptoms may include dyspnea, cough, and decreased breath sounds. The condition can occur in any lung but is frequently seen in the lower lobes. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to prevent hypoxemia and respiratory failure.

Interstitial emphysema is a condition characterized by the presence of air within the connective tissue surrounding the alveoli, typically occurring in the lungs. It is commonly seen in newborns, particularly premature infants, and is often associated with respiratory distress syndrome. Common synonyms include pulmonary interstitial emphysema and air in the interstitial spaces. Causative agents include barotrauma from mechanical ventilation, surfactant deficiency, and alveolar rupture. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, especially the perihilar regions, and may lead to complications such as pneumothorax or pulmonary hypertension.

Compensatory emphysema is a condition characterized by the enlargement of air spaces in the lungs, typically occurring in response to localized obstructive lung disease. It results from the redistribution of airflow to unaffected areas, leading to overinflation. Common synonyms include secondary emphysema and compensatory pulmonary hyperinflation. Causative agents often include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), tuberculosis, and bronchial obstruction. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the upper lobes, and is associated with reduced lung elasticity and impaired gas exchange.

Pulmonary eosinophilia is a clinical syndrome characterized by an increased number of eosinophils in the lungs, often associated with inflammation. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic lung disease. It is typically caused by parasitic infections, allergic reactions, or drug-induced hypersensitivity. Common causative agents include *Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Strongyloides stercoralis*, and certain medications like sulfa drugs. The condition primarily affects the lungs, but may also involve the skin, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs in systemic forms. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever.

Acute edema of lung, unspecified refers to sudden fluid accumulation in the lung parenchyma, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Causative agents often include heart failure, hypertension, acute myocardial infarction, and systemic hypertension. It may also result from non-cardiogenic causes such as sepsis or pulmonary embolism. The primary affected body part is the lung, with symptoms including dyspnea, cough, and crackles on auscultation. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt intervention.

code_desc: Pulmonary insufficiency following trauma and surgery
summary: Pulmonary insufficiency following trauma and surgery refers to impaired lung function resulting from injury or operative intervention. Common synonyms include post-traumatic pulmonary insufficiency and postoperative respiratory insufficiency. Causative agents include chest trauma, thoracic surgery, and prolonged intubation. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, diaphragm, and airways. This condition may manifest as reduced oxygenation, hypoxemia, and respiratory distress. It is often managed with oxygen therapy, mechanical ventilation, and supportive care.

code_desc: Acute respiratory failure following trauma and surgery
summary: Acute respiratory failure following trauma and surgery is a life-threatening condition characterized by inadequate gas exchange due to pulmonary injury or dysfunction. Common synonyms include post-traumatic respiratory failure and postoperative respiratory failure. Causative agents include pulmonary contusions, pneumonia, atelectasis, and pulmonary edema. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, airways, and sometimes the diaphragm. It often results from chest trauma, major surgery, or complications from anesthesia. Clinical features include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and respiratory distress. Prompt intervention is critical to prevent progression to respiratory arrest.

code_desc: Other pulmonary insufficiency, not elsewhere classified, following trauma and surgery
summary: Other pulmonary insufficiency, not elsewhere classified, following trauma and surgery refers to impaired lung function that occurs after traumatic injury or surgical intervention, without a specific underlying diagnosis. Common synonyms include post-traumatic pulmonary insufficiency and postoperative pulmonary dysfunction. Causative agents may include direct lung injury, atelectasis, pneumonia, or pulmonary edema. Typically affected body parts include the lungs and airways. This condition is often seen in patients with chest trauma, thoracic surgery, or prolonged intubation.

code_desc: Acute and chronic respiratory failure following trauma and surgery
summary: Acute and chronic respiratory failure following trauma and surgery refers to impaired gas exchange leading to hypoxemia and hypercapnia, often resulting from lung injury, pneumonia, or atelectasis. Common synonyms include post-traumatic respiratory failure and postoperative respiratory insufficiency. Causative agents include pulmonary contusions, aspiration, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and surgical complications. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, airways, and diaphragm. It may develop after chest trauma, abdominal surgery, or head injury with secondary pulmonary involvement. Chronic cases may arise from prolonged ventilation or unresolved pulmonary damage.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity reaction to *Aspergillus* species, most commonly *A. fumigatus*. It primarily affects individuals with preexisting lung conditions such as cystic fibrosis or asthma. The disease is characterized by airway inflammation, mucus plugging, and immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity. Clinically, it presents with fever, cough, wheezing, and progressive respiratory decline. Radiographic findings often show central bronchiectasis and fleeting infiltrates. ABPA can lead to bronchial destruction and fibrosis if untreated. Synonyms include allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and aspergillus hypersensitivity syndrome.

Transfusion related acute lung injury (TRALI) is a rare but serious pulmonary complication occurring within 6 hours of blood transfusion. It is characterized by non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, hypoxemia, and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include transfusion-induced lung injury and transfusion-associated acute lung injury. Causative agents often include antibodies against HLA or neutrophil proteins, as well as lipids from stored blood products. TRALI primarily affects the lungs, leading to impaired gas exchange and potential respiratory failure.

"Other diseases of lung" encompasses a variety of non-infectious and non-malignant pulmonary conditions. Common synonyms include interstitial lung disease and diffuse pulmonary disorders. These conditions may result from environmental exposures, autoimmune processes, or idiopathic causes. Causative agents include occupational toxins, allergens, and autoimmune antibodies. Typically affecting the interstitium and alveoli, these diseases can lead to inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired gas exchange. Commonly impacted body parts include the lungs, with potential involvement of the pleura and bronchi. Symptoms often include dyspnea, cough, and reduced exercise tolerance.

Acute respiratory failure is a life-threatening condition characterized by inadequate gas exchange, leading to hypoxemia and/or hypercapnia. It results from impaired oxygenation or ventilation. Common synonyms include acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. Causative agents include pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pulmonary edema, and neuromuscular disorders. The primary affected body parts are the lungs and airways, with potential involvement of the heart and central nervous system. Prompt intervention is critical to prevent complications and mortality.

code_desc: Other pulmonary insufficiency, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other pulmonary insufficiency, not elsewhere classified" refers to impaired lung function not attributable to specific known diseases. It encompasses a broad range of conditions affecting gas exchange or ventilation. Common synonyms include unspecified pulmonary insufficiency or unclassified pulmonary dysfunction. Causative agents may include environmental toxins, chronic inflammation, or systemic illnesses. Typically affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli and airways, leading to reduced oxygenation and increased work of breathing. Often seen in patients with complex or undiagnosed respiratory issues.

Chronic respiratory failure is a progressive condition characterized by persistent impairment of gas exchange, leading to inadequate oxygenation and/or carbon dioxide elimination. It commonly results from long-standing lung diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), interstitial lung disease, or neuromuscular disorders. Synonyms include chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure and chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure. The primary affected body parts are the lungs and respiratory muscles, with systemic complications affecting multiple organ systems over time.

Acute and chronic respiratory failure refer to impaired gas exchange leading to inadequate oxygenation and/or carbon dioxide elimination. Acute forms develop rapidly, often due to pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or trauma, while chronic cases progress over time, commonly associated with COPD, interstitial lung disease, or neuromuscular disorders. Both affect the lungs and can impact the cardiovascular system. Synonyms include respiratory insufficiency and hypoxemic or hypercapnic failure. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, with systemic consequences affecting multiple organs.

code_desc: Other diseases of lung, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of lung, not elsewhere classified" refers to lung conditions that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous pulmonary disorders. Causative agents may include environmental toxins, infections, or autoimmune factors. Typically affects the lung parenchyma, airways, or pleura. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. Diagnosis often requires imaging and biopsy. This category encompasses a wide range of conditions with varied etiologies and presentations.

"Other diseases of respiratory system" refers to a broad category of conditions affecting the respiratory tract not classified as pneumonia, tuberculosis, or influenza. Common synonyms include chronic respiratory diseases and miscellaneous pulmonary disorders. Causative agents vary, including environmental toxins, allergens, and occupational exposures. These conditions typically affect the lungs, airways, and pleura, causing symptoms such as chronic cough, shortness of breath, and wheezing. Examples include interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Tracheostomy complications refer to adverse events following tracheostomy placement, a surgical procedure creating an opening in the trachea for airway access. Common complications include infection, granulation tissue formation, tube blockage, and accidental decannulation. Synonyms include tracheostomy-related adverse events or tracheal stenosis. Causative agents may include bacterial pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Typically affected body parts include the trachea, surrounding soft tissues, and airway structures. Complications can lead to respiratory distress, pneumonia, or airway obstruction.

Tracheostomy complication, unspecified, refers to any adverse event occurring following tracheostomy placement that cannot be classified under specific categories. Common synonyms include tracheostomy-related adverse event or tracheostomy-associated complication. Causative agents may include infection, bleeding, granulation tissue, or tube displacement. Typically affecting the trachea, upper airway, or surrounding structures, these complications can lead to airway obstruction, respiratory distress, or infection. They may arise from improper technique, infection, or patient-related factors. Prompt recognition and management are critical to prevent severe outcomes.

Infection of tracheostomy refers to a bacterial or fungal infection involving the tracheostomy site, tube, or surrounding tissues. Common synonyms include tracheostomy site infection or tracheostomy-related infection. It is typically caused by gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Streptococcus* species. The infection primarily affects the tracheostomy stoma, tube, and adjacent airway structures. It can lead to symptoms like purulent secretions, redness, swelling, and fever. Prompt management is essential to prevent complications such as tracheal stenosis or respiratory failure.

Mechanical complication of tracheostomy refers to physical damage or dysfunction resulting from the tracheostomy tube or surgical site. Common synonyms include tracheostomy-related injury and tracheal trauma. Causative agents often involve improper tube placement, excessive pressure, or prolonged use. Typically affected areas include the trachea, cricoid cartilage, and surrounding soft tissues. Complications may manifest as tracheal stenosis, granulation tissue, or tube displacement. This condition can lead to airway obstruction, respiratory distress, or infection if not promptly addressed.

Other tracheostomy complications encompass a range of issues arising from tracheostomy placement or management. Common synonyms include tracheostomy-related complications and tracheostomy-associated problems. Causative agents may include infection, prolonged intubation, improper tube placement, or trauma. Typically affected body parts include the trachea, surrounding soft tissues, and airway structures. Complications may manifest as granulation tissue, stenosis, subcutaneous emphysema, or pneumothorax. These conditions can lead to respiratory distress, airway obstruction, or infection, requiring prompt clinical evaluation and intervention.

code_desc: Other diseases of trachea and bronchus not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of trachea and bronchus not elsewhere classified" refers to inflammatory or structural disorders of the trachea and bronchus that do not fit specific categories such as infections or tumors. Common synonyms include idiopathic tracheobronchitis and chronic tracheobronchial inflammation. Causative agents may include environmental irritants, allergens, or unknown factors. These conditions typically affect the trachea and bronchi, leading to symptoms like coughing, wheezing, and airflow obstruction. They are often diagnosed when other specific causes have been ruled out.

Acute bronchospasm is a sudden, temporary narrowing of the airways characterized by bronchial smooth muscle contraction, leading to airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include acute bronchial spasm and bronchial asthma exacerbation. It is often caused by allergens, viral infections, irritants, or exercise. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, causing symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It is commonly seen in individuals with underlying asthma or reactive airway disease.

code_desc: Other diseases of trachea and bronchus
summary: "Other diseases of trachea and bronchus" encompasses a range of non-neoplastic, non-infectious conditions affecting the airways. Common synonyms include tracheobronchial disorders and chronic airway diseases. Causative agents may include environmental irritants, allergens, and occupational exposures. These conditions typically affect the trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as chronic cough, wheezing, and airflow obstruction. Examples include chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma, and tracheal stenosis. The primary sites of involvement are the upper and lower respiratory tract.

Mediastinitis is an inflammation of the mediastinum, the central compartment of the thoracic cavity containing vital structures such as the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus. It is commonly caused by bacterial infections, often following procedures like median sternotomy or esophagectomy. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus species*, and *Escherichia coli*. It may also result from fungal infections in immunocompromised patients. Symptoms include chest pain, fever, and respiratory distress. The condition can lead to severe complications such as sepsis and cardiac involvement if left untreated. Synonyms include mediastinal inflammation and postoperative mediastinitis.

code_desc: Other diseases of mediastinum, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of mediastinum, not elsewhere classified" refers to rare or unspecified conditions affecting the mediastinum that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include idiopathic mediastinal diseases or miscellaneous mediastinal disorders. Causative agents may include infections, tumors, or inflammatory processes, though specific etiologies are often unknown. These conditions typically involve the mediastinal structures, including lymph nodes, blood vessels, and surrounding tissues, and may present with symptoms such as dyspnea, chest pain, or cough. Diagnosis often requires imaging and biopsy.

Disorders of the diaphragm encompass conditions affecting the primary muscle of respiration, leading to impaired breathing. Common synonyms include diaphragmatic dysfunction and diaphragm paralysis. Causative agents may include neuromuscular diseases, chest trauma, infections, or pleural effusion. These disorders typically affect the diaphragm itself, with secondary involvement of the lungs and respiratory system. Symptoms often include dyspnea, reduced tidal volume, and paradoxical abdominal movement during inspiration. Diagnosis involves imaging, electromyography, and pulmonary function tests. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve mechanical ventilation, muscle stimulation, or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Other diseases of respiratory system, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other diseases of respiratory system, not elsewhere classified" refers to respiratory conditions that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous or unspecified respiratory disorders. Causative agents may include environmental irritants, pathogens like bacteria or viruses, or unknown factors. These conditions typically affect the airways, lungs, or pleura, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. They may include interstitial lung disease, chronic bronchitis, or unspecified pulmonary infiltrates. Diagnosis often requires imaging, biopsy, or laboratory tests when specific etiologies are not identified.

Unspecified disease of the respiratory system refers to a broad category of conditions affecting the lungs, airways, or other respiratory structures when the specific diagnosis is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include undiagnosed respiratory disorder or unspecified pulmonary condition. Causative agents may vary and can include infections, environmental exposures, or unknown factors. Typically, the disease affects the trachea, bronchi, lungs, or pleura, leading to symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. This classification is often used when diagnostic tests fail to pinpoint a specific etiology.

code_desc: Disorders of tooth development and eruption
summary: Disorders of tooth development and eruption encompass abnormalities in the formation, eruption, or positioning of teeth. Common synonyms include dental dysplasia, hypodontia, and odontogenic anomalies. These conditions may result from genetic factors, environmental influences, or systemic diseases. Causative agents include genetic mutations, infections, nutritional deficiencies, and syndromes such as cleidocranial dysplasia or Down syndrome. Typically affected body parts include the maxilla and mandible, with impacted, missing, or supernumerary teeth being common manifestations. These disorders can affect both primary and permanent dentition.

Anodontia is a rare developmental disorder characterized by the complete absence of all permanent teeth. It is often congenital and may occur in conjunction with other systemic conditions. Common synonyms include hypodontia and odontogenic anaplasia. The condition is typically associated with genetic syndromes such as ectodermal dysplasia, Down syndrome, and cleidocranial dysplasia. It primarily affects the maxilla and mandible, leading to significant dental and functional impairments. Causative agents include genetic mutations and environmental factors during embryonic development.

Supernumerary teeth are additional teeth beyond the normal number, commonly found in the maxillary anterior region. They may occur as isolated findings or in association with genetic syndromes such as cleidocranial dysplasia. Common synonyms include hyperdontia and extra teeth. These teeth can be conical, tuberculate, or supplemental in shape. Causative factors include genetic mutations, trauma, or developmental anomalies. They often affect the upper jaw, particularly between the central incisors, and may lead to malocclusion or delayed eruption of adjacent teeth.

code_desc: Abnormalities of size and form of teeth
summary: Abnormalities of size and form of teeth, also known as dental dysplasia or odontodysplasia, refer to developmental defects affecting tooth morphology and dimensions. These may include enamel hypoplasia, hypocalcification, or structural anomalies. Common causes include genetic factors, infections (e.g., rubella, syphilis), trauma, or systemic illnesses during tooth development. Typically affecting primary and permanent teeth, these conditions may involve incisors, molars, or premolars, leading to malocclusion, functional impairment, or aesthetic concerns.

Mottled teeth, also known as fluorosis or mottled enamel, is a developmental dental condition characterized by irregular discoloration and opacity of tooth enamel. It results from excessive fluoride exposure during tooth formation, typically in childhood. The condition may present as white streaks, brown spots, or pitting on the teeth. Common synonyms include dental fluorosis and mottled enamel. Affected teeth are usually the permanent ones, and the condition primarily impacts the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth. Causative agents include high fluoride intake from water, supplements, or topical applications.

Disturbances of tooth formation, also known as dental dysplasia or amelogenesis imperfecta, refer to abnormalities in the development of teeth. These conditions may affect enamel, dentin, or both, leading to structural or functional impairments. Common causative agents include genetic mutations, systemic diseases, and environmental factors such as radiation or nutritional deficiencies. The primary affected body parts are the enamel and dentin of both primary and permanent teeth, often resulting in hypoplasia, hypomineralization, or structural defects. These disorders can significantly impact dental function and aesthetics.

code_desc: Hereditary disturbances in tooth structure, not elsewhere classified
summary: Hereditary disturbances in tooth structure, not elsewhere classified, refer to genetic conditions affecting the development and morphology of teeth. Common synonyms include hereditary enamel defects and inherited dental anomalies. These conditions are caused by mutations in genes involved in tooth formation, such as those encoding enamel proteins. Typically affecting enamel and dentin, they may result in hypoplasia, hypomineralization, or structural abnormalities. Affected individuals often exhibit malformed or discolored teeth, primarily in the primary and permanent dentition. The condition may be inherited in an autosomal dominant or recessive pattern.

Disturbances in tooth eruption refer to abnormal timing, sequence, or pattern of tooth emergence. Common synonyms include delayed eruption, premature eruption, and ectopic eruption. These disturbances may result from genetic factors, systemic diseases, or local conditions such as hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, or infection. They commonly affect the primary and permanent dentition, with the maxillary and mandibular incisors and first molars being the most frequently involved. Clinical manifestations may include missing teeth, impacted teeth, or malpositioned eruption.

Teething syndrome refers to a collection of symptoms experienced by infants and young children during the eruption of their primary teeth. Common symptoms include irritability, drooling, chewing behavior, and mild fever. It is often mistaken for an infection. Synonyms include teething, tooth eruption, and dental eruption. The condition is caused by the mechanical pressure of emerging teeth through the gums. Typically affected body parts include the gums, jaw, and surrounding oral tissues. No specific causative agents are known, as it is a physiological process.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of tooth development and eruption
summary: "Other specified disorders of tooth development and eruption" refers to rare, non-specific conditions affecting tooth formation and eruption, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include "unspecified dental developmental anomalies." Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental exposures, or systemic diseases. These disorders typically affect the primary and permanent dentition, leading to delayed eruption, hypoplasia, or enamel defects. They may involve multiple teeth and are often diagnosed through clinical and radiographic evaluation.

code_desc: Unspecified disorder of tooth development and eruption
summary: Unspecified disorder of tooth development and eruption refers to a general category of conditions affecting the formation and eruption of teeth without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include developmental dental anomalies or generalized hypodontia. Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental influences, or systemic diseases. Typically, the condition affects the dental structures, including enamel, dentin, and the alveolar bone, leading to delayed, absent, or malformed teeth. It may involve both primary and permanent dentition, often impacting multiple teeth in the oral cavity.

code_desc: Diseases of hard tissues of teeth
summary: Diseases of hard tissues of teeth encompass conditions affecting enamel, dentin, and cementum. Common synonyms include dental caries, dental decay, and tooth decay. These conditions are primarily caused by bacterial infection, particularly *Streptococcus mutans*, leading to demineralization and cavitation. They typically affect the crown and root surfaces of teeth, with a predilection for primary and permanent molars. Poor oral hygiene, diet high in fermentable carbohydrates, and reduced salivary flow are significant risk factors. Early detection and treatment are crucial to prevent progression and maintain dental function.

Dental caries, also known as tooth decay or cavities, is a chronic bacterial infection caused primarily by Streptococcus mutans and other acidogenic bacteria. These microorganisms metabolize dietary sugars to produce acids, which demineralize tooth enamel and dentin. The condition typically affects the occlusal surfaces, pits, and fissures of posterior teeth, as well as smooth surfaces of anterior teeth. If left untreated, caries can progress to pulp involvement, leading to pain, infection, and potential tooth loss. Prevention involves good oral hygiene, fluoride use, and regular dental check-ups.

Dental caries, unspecified, refers to the decay of tooth structure caused by bacterial activity leading to demineralization. Common synonyms include tooth decay, cavities, and caries. The primary causative agents are bacteria such as *Streptococcus mutans* and *Lactobacillus*, which metabolize sugars to produce acid. This condition typically affects the enamel and dentin of the teeth, most commonly in the pits and fissures of molars and on the smooth surfaces of anterior teeth. It is a prevalent chronic disease affecting the oral cavity.

Dental caries limited to enamel, also known as incipient caries or enamel caries, refers to early-stage tooth decay confined to the enamel layer. It is primarily caused by acid produced from bacterial metabolism of dietary sugars, with *Streptococcus mutans* being a common causative agent. This condition typically affects the occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth and smooth surfaces of anterior teeth. Early detection is crucial for non-invasive treatment, such as fluoride application or remineralization, to prevent progression into dentin.

Dental caries extending into dentine refers to the progression of tooth decay beyond the enamel into the underlying dentine. This condition is caused primarily by bacterial acid production, leading to demineralization and structural damage. Common synonyms include dentin caries and pulp exposure. The causative agents are mainly *Streptococcus mutans* and other cariogenic bacteria. It typically affects the coronal dentine of posterior teeth, particularly molars, and can lead to pulp involvement if left untreated. Early detection and intervention are crucial to prevent further complications.

Dental caries extending into the pulp, also known as pulpitis or irreversible pulpitis, is a severe form of tooth decay that progresses beyond the dentin to invade the pulp chamber. This condition is primarily caused by Streptococcus mutans and other cariogenic bacteria. It typically affects the posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their complex anatomy and difficulty in cleaning. Symptoms include severe pain, sensitivity to hot or cold, and swelling. If left untreated, it can lead to pulp necrosis and abscess formation.

Arrested dental caries refers to a non-progressive stage of tooth decay where the lesion stops advancing due to the body's immune response or remineralization. Common synonyms include static caries and non-progressive caries. It is typically caused by bacterial plaque, particularly *Streptococcus mutans*, and is often associated with early enamel demineralization. Arrested caries most commonly affects the occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth and the root surfaces in adults. It may appear as white or brown spots on the enamel and is often asymptomatic. Early detection through dental examination or radiographic imaging is crucial for appropriate management.

Odontoclasia refers to the pathological fracture of a tooth, typically resulting from trauma or excessive occlusal forces. It is also known as tooth fracture or dental fracture. Common causative agents include physical trauma, bruxism, and dental caries leading to weakened tooth structure. This condition most frequently affects the anterior teeth, particularly the incisors and canines, due to their exposure and role in biting. The fracture may involve enamel, dentin, or pulp, leading to pain, sensitivity, and potential pulp necrosis if left untreated. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent complications and restore function.

Dental caries pit and fissure refers to early-stage tooth decay occurring in the deep grooves and pits of molars and premolars. Common synonyms include pit and fissure caries and occlusal caries. Caused primarily by Streptococcus mutans and other cariogenic bacteria, this condition results from acid production due to fermentable carbohydrates. It typically affects the occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth, particularly in children and adolescents. Early detection through visual examination or radiographic imaging is crucial for effective management.

Dental caries of smooth surfaces refer to decay occurring on the non-occlusal, flat areas of teeth, commonly on the cervical regions or between teeth. It is primarily caused by Streptococcus mutans and other cariogenic bacteria that produce acid from fermentable carbohydrates. This condition is prevalent in children and adolescents, particularly in the pits and fissures of molars, as well as on the lingual surfaces of anterior teeth. It is also known as smooth surface caries or cervical caries. Poor oral hygiene and dietary habits contribute to its development.

Dental caries of root surface, also known as root caries or cervical caries, refers to the demineralization of the root surface due to bacterial acid production. It commonly occurs in areas where the root is exposed, such as in elderly patients with gingival recession. The primary causative agent is *Streptococcus mutans*, though other bacteria may contribute. This condition typically affects the cervical region of the tooth, particularly in the presence of poor oral hygiene, dry mouth, or periodontal disease. It is a progressive lesion that can lead to pulp involvement if left untreated.

Other dental caries refers to the decay of tooth structure caused by bacterial acid production, primarily from *Streptococcus mutans* and *Lactobacillus* species. It results from the interaction of bacteria, dietary sugars, and host factors, leading to demineralization of enamel and dentin. Common synonyms include dental decay, tooth decay, and caries. The condition typically affects the crown of teeth, especially in pits, fissures, and interproximal surfaces. It is most prevalent in primary and permanent teeth, with a higher incidence in children and adolescents. Early detection and preventive measures are crucial to minimize complications such as pulp involvement and tooth loss.

Excessive dental attrition refers to the progressive loss of tooth structure due to mechanical wear from occlusal forces, often involving the approximal and occlusal surfaces. Common synonyms include occlusal wear, tooth surface wear, and attrition. Causative agents include bruxism, parafunctional habits, malocclusion, and abrasive substances. Typically affects the incisal edges of anterior teeth and occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth, leading to enamel and dentin loss, sensitivity, and potential pulp exposure.

Excessive attrition, unspecified, refers to abnormal, accelerated tooth wear due to mechanical forces beyond normal occlusal contact. Common synonyms include attrition without bruxism and excessive tooth wear. Causative agents may include bruxism, parafunctional habits, malocclusion, or abrasive substances. This condition typically affects the occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth, leading to enamel loss, dentin exposure, and potential pulp involvement. It can result in tooth sensitivity, fractures, and compromised dental function. Diagnosis relies on clinical examination and patient history to identify contributing factors.

Excessive attrition limited to enamel refers to the progressive loss of tooth enamel due to mechanical wear from tooth-to-tooth contact. Common synonyms include enamel wear and dental attrition. Causative agents often include bruxism, parafunctional habits, and malocclusion. This condition typically affects the occlusal surfaces of the anterior and posterior teeth, with the incisal edges of anterior teeth and cuspal areas of posterior teeth being most commonly involved. It may lead to increased tooth sensitivity and structural compromise without significant dentin exposure.

Excessive attrition extending into dentine refers to the progressive loss of tooth structure due to mechanical wear, often involving enamel and underlying dentine. Common synonyms include pathological attrition and excessive tooth wear. This condition is typically caused by bruxism, parafunctional habits, or abnormal occlusal forces. It predominantly affects the occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth, leading to sensitivity, tooth fracture, and potential pulp exposure. The anterior teeth may also be involved in severe cases. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent further damage and complications.

Excessive attrition extending into the pulp is a severe form of tooth wear characterized by the loss of hard dental tissues, progressing to expose the pulp. Common synonyms include advanced attrition and pulpal exposure due to attrition. Causative agents include bruxism, parafunctional habits, and malocclusion. This condition typically affects posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their role in chewing. Pulp exposure can lead to pain, sensitivity, and infection, necessitating endodontic treatment or extraction. It is often associated with long-term abrasive behaviors and improper occlusal forces.

Excessive attrition, localized, refers to accelerated wear of dental hard tissues, primarily enamel and dentin, in specific areas. Common synonyms include localized dental wear and focal attrition. It is often caused by bruxism, acid erosion, or abrasive habits. The maxillary and mandibular incisors, as well as the posterior teeth, are typically affected. This condition may lead to sensitivity, tooth structure loss, and functional or aesthetic concerns. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent further damage.

Excessive attrition, generalized, refers to widespread, accelerated tooth wear due to mechanical forces exceeding normal physiological limits. Common synonyms include generalized tooth wear and attrition. Causative agents include bruxism, parafunctional habits, acidic dietary intake, and improper occlusal relationships. This condition typically affects the occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth, leading to enamel loss, dentin exposure, and potential pulp involvement. It may also impact anterior teeth if present. Clinical features include flattened occlusal surfaces, increased dentin translucency, and tooth sensitivity. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent further damage.

Abrasion of teeth refers to the gradual loss of tooth structure due to mechanical wear from friction or grinding. Common synonyms include attrition and abrasion. It is typically caused by bruxism, improper brushing techniques, or the use of abrasive dental products. The condition most commonly affects the occlusal surfaces of the anterior and posterior teeth, particularly in individuals with malocclusion or those who clench their teeth. Prolonged abrasion can lead to sensitivity, enamel thinning, and increased risk of dental caries. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent further damage.

Abrasion, unspecified, refers to a superficial wound caused by friction or scraping of the skin against a rough surface. Common synonyms include scrape, scratch, or rub wound. It typically results from trauma, such as falls, sports injuries, or accidental contact with abrasive materials. The causative agents are usually mechanical forces rather than infectious organisms. Abrasions most commonly affect the limbs, face, and hands, particularly areas exposed to external surfaces. They often present with erythema, minor bleeding, and sometimes pain or crusting. Healing is generally rapid with proper care.

Abrasion limited to enamel refers to superficial loss of dental enamel caused by mechanical friction without penetration into the dentin. Common synonyms include enamel wear and abrasive tooth damage. Causative agents include toothbrush abrasion, abrasive toothpaste, and bruxism. This condition typically affects the labial or buccal surfaces of the anterior teeth, particularly in areas with heavy brushing or malocclusion. It may lead to increased tooth sensitivity and aesthetic concerns. Early diagnosis and modification of abrasive habits are essential for prevention and management.

Abrasion extending into dentine refers to a superficial tooth surface injury that penetrates through the enamel into the underlying dentine. Common synonyms include dental abrasion with dentinal exposure. This condition is typically caused by mechanical wear from brushing, abrasive toothpaste, or occlusal forces. It most commonly affects the cervical regions of the anterior teeth. Symptoms may include sensitivity to temperature, sweet foods, and tactile stimuli. Early diagnosis and preventive measures are essential to avoid further damage and complications.

Abrasion extending into the pulp is a type of traumatic injury where the surface layer of the skin is scraped away, exposing the underlying tissue and potentially damaging the pulp, which is the innermost part of the nail bed. Common synonyms include laceration with pulp involvement or superficial pulp injury. This condition is typically caused by mechanical trauma, such as friction or blunt force. It commonly affects the fingers and toes, particularly the distal phalanges, and is often seen in sports injuries or accidental trauma. Prompt cleaning and protection are essential to prevent infection and promote healing.

Abrasion, localized, refers to a superficial injury caused by friction or scraping of the skin against a rough surface. It results in the removal of the epidermis, often leading to minor bleeding and a reddish or pinkish wound bed. Common synonyms include scrape, scratch, or graze. Causative agents typically include blunt objects, rough surfaces, or environmental elements like gravel or pavement. This condition most commonly affects areas of the body with exposed skin, such as the elbows, knees, hands, and forearms. It is generally a minor injury with a low risk of infection if properly cleaned and cared for.

Abrasion, generalized, refers to widespread superficial skin damage caused by friction or mechanical trauma. Common synonyms include generalized skin abrasion and widespread friction injury. It is typically caused by contact with rough surfaces, such as gravel, sand, or fabric. The condition commonly affects exposed body parts like the arms, legs, and face. Clinically, it presents as redness, erythema, and superficial epidermal loss without deep tissue involvement. Healing is usually rapid with minimal scarring. Secondary infections may occur if not properly managed.

Erosion of teeth refers to the loss of tooth structure due to chemical exposure rather than bacterial action. Common synonyms include dental wear and non-carious tooth wear. It is typically caused by acidic substances such as citrus fruits, carbonated drinks, and gastric reflux. The condition primarily affects the enamel, leading to a smooth, shiny surface and increased susceptibility to decay. It commonly involves the anterior teeth and lingual surfaces of posterior teeth. Prolonged exposure can result in sensitivity, discoloration, and structural weakening.

Erosion, unspecified, refers to the loss of superficial tissue without full-thickness destruction. It is a non-specific term often used when the exact type or location of erosion is not clearly defined. Common synonyms include superficial ulceration or mucosal erosion. Causative agents may include mechanical trauma, chemical exposure, infection (e.g., herpes simplex virus), or inflammatory conditions. Typically affects mucous membranes, such as the gastrointestinal tract, oral cavity, or genital areas. It is often associated with inflammation or irritation. Diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and sometimes histopathological confirmation.

Erosion limited to enamel refers to the loss of the outermost layer of tooth structure due to chemical or mechanical factors, without involving the dentin. Common synonyms include enamel dissolution and non-carious enamel loss. Causative agents often include acidic dietary intake, gastric reflux, or excessive brushing. This condition typically affects the labial or buccal surfaces of anterior teeth, particularly in individuals with habits like frequent consumption of acidic foods or beverages. It may present as smooth, shiny areas or pits on the enamel surface. Early detection is crucial to prevent progression to dentin involvement.

Erosion extending into dentine refers to the loss of tooth structure due to chemical exposure, progressing beyond the enamel to the underlying dentine. Common synonyms include dental erosion and non-carious tooth wear. Causative agents often include acidic foods, beverages, gastric reflux, and certain medications. This condition typically affects the labial surfaces of anterior teeth and the lingual surfaces of posterior teeth, with a predilection for areas with thin enamel. It may lead to sensitivity, discoloration, and structural compromise if left untreated.

Erosion extending into the pulp is a severe form of tooth decay where the enamel and dentin are lost, exposing the pulp chamber. This condition is often caused by dental caries, trauma, or acid exposure. Common synonyms include pulp exposure, carious pulp involvement, and pulpal erosion. It typically affects posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their complex anatomy and difficulty in cleaning. The pulp becomes inflamed or infected, leading to pain, sensitivity, and potential necrosis. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent further complications such as abscess formation.

Erosion, localized, refers to a shallow loss of surface tissue without full-thickness involvement. It commonly occurs in mucous membranes or skin. Synonyms include superficial ulceration or mucosal erosion. Causative agents may include mechanical trauma, chemical exposure, inflammatory conditions, or irritants. It typically affects areas subject to friction or irritation, such as the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, or genital regions. Clinical presentation includes erythema, pain, and sometimes bleeding. Diagnosis is often based on clinical appearance and history.

Erosion, generalized, refers to the loss of surface tissue without full-thickness destruction, commonly observed in mucous membranes. It may result from chronic irritation, autoimmune conditions, or inflammatory processes. Common synonyms include mucosal erosion and superficial erosion. Known causative agents include Helicobacter pylori, autoimmune disorders like pemphigus, and chronic acid reflux. Typically affects the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and genital mucosa. It presents as red, raw areas with minimal exudate and may be asymptomatic or associated with burning or discomfort.

Pathological tooth resorption is an abnormal process involving the loss of tooth structure due to excessive resorption by odontoclasts. Common synonyms include internal root resorption and external root resorption. It is often associated with trauma, inflammation, or infection, with *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans* as potential causative agents. The condition typically affects the root dentin, with the apical region being most commonly involved. It may occur unilaterally or bilaterally and is more prevalent in permanent teeth, particularly molars and premolars.

Pathological resorption, unspecified, refers to the abnormal breakdown and reabsorption of tissue or bone without a specific identifiable cause. It may occur in various contexts, such as osteoporosis or inflammatory conditions. Common synonyms include idiopathic resorption and diffuse resorption. Causative agents may include hormonal imbalances, chronic inflammation, or metabolic disorders. Typically affects bones, teeth, and soft tissues, leading to structural weakening and potential functional impairment. The condition is often diagnosed when specific etiologies are ruled out.

Pathological resorption, internal, refers to the abnormal breakdown and reabsorption of tissue by the body's own cells, often leading to structural damage. Common synonyms include self-digestion and autolysis. This process is typically caused by enzymatic activity from damaged or dying cells, often associated with inflammation, infection, or neoplastic processes. It commonly affects tissues such as bone, cartilage, and connective tissue, and may occur in conditions like osteomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, or certain cancers. The affected areas may show signs of tissue loss, ulceration, and reduced function.

Pathological resorption, external, refers to the abnormal loss of tissue or bone due to excessive breakdown by inflammatory or immune processes. It commonly occurs in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, periodontal disease, and certain infections. Synonyms include external resorption and secondary resorption. The process typically affects teeth, bones, and connective tissues, leading to structural compromise. Causative agents may include bacteria, autoimmune factors, or chronic inflammation. It is often associated with periodontitis, periapical lesions, and joint inflammation. The condition results in progressive tissue destruction and may require surgical or pharmacological intervention.

Other pathological resorption refers to the abnormal breakdown and absorption of normal tissue, often due to inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic processes. Common synonyms include osteomyelitis, granulomatous disease, or reactive resorption. Causative agents may include bacteria, fungi, or autoimmune factors. This condition typically affects bones, joints, and surrounding soft tissues, leading to pain, swelling, and structural damage. It is often associated with chronic inflammation or infection, and may present with systemic symptoms such as fever and weight loss. Diagnosis usually involves imaging and biopsy.

Hypercementosis is a condition characterized by excessive deposition of cementum on the root surfaces of teeth. It is often seen in conjunction with periodontal disease or trauma. Common synonyms include cemental hyperplasia and excessive cementum formation. The primary causative agents are chronic inflammation and mechanical irritation. It typically affects the furcation areas and apical regions of molars and premolars. Clinically, it presents as a hard, calcified tissue covering the root, which may lead to root resorption or difficulty in endodontic treatment. The condition is more prevalent in adults and is often associated with periodontitis or trauma.

Ankylosis of teeth refers to the fusion of a tooth root to the surrounding alveolar bone, resulting in the loss of the periodontal ligament space. This condition can lead to reduced tooth mobility and may affect the eruption of adjacent teeth. Common synonyms include dental ankylosis and cementoblastoma. Causative agents may include trauma, infection, or genetic factors. It typically affects the anterior maxillary teeth, particularly the incisors and canines, and is more common in children and adolescents.

Intrinsic posteruptive color changes refer to persistent discoloration of skin or mucosa following an inflammatory or infectious eruption. These changes result from altered pigmentation due to melanocyte dysfunction or deposition. Common synonyms include post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation. Causative agents include infections (e.g., syphilis, leprosy), autoimmune disorders, and inflammatory conditions. Typically affecting the face, neck, and extremities, these changes may be asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously or require treatment.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of hard tissues of teeth
summary: "Other specified diseases of hard tissues of teeth" refers to dental conditions affecting enamel, dentin, or cementum that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified dental hard tissue disorders. These conditions may arise from trauma, developmental anomalies, or secondary to systemic diseases. Causative agents can include bacteria, physical injury, or metabolic factors. Typically affecting the crown or root structures, these disorders may present with discoloration, structural defects, or pathological changes in the tooth's hard tissues.

Cracked tooth is a dental condition characterized by a fracture in the enamel or dentin of a tooth, often extending into the pulp. Common synonyms include fractured tooth and tooth fracture. It is typically caused by trauma, bruxism, or excessive occlusal forces. The condition most commonly affects the posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their structural vulnerability and occlusal stress. Symptoms may include pain, sensitivity, and difficulty in chewing. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications such as pulp necrosis or tooth loss.

code_desc: Other specific diseases of hard tissues of teeth
summary: "Other specific diseases of hard tissues of teeth" refers to non-caries, non-periodontal disorders affecting enamel, dentin, or cementum. Common synonyms include enamel hypoplasia, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and amelogenesis imperfecta. These conditions are often genetic, with causative agents including inherited mutations in enamel or dentin proteins. They typically affect the entire dentition, causing structural abnormalities, discoloration, and increased susceptibility to wear. Affected body parts include primary and permanent teeth, leading to functional and aesthetic concerns.

code_desc: Unspecified disease of hard tissues of teeth
summary: Unspecified disease of hard tissues of teeth refers to pathological conditions affecting enamel, dentin, or cementum when the specific diagnosis is not determined. Common synonyms include undifferentiated dental hard tissue disorder or unspecified dental hard tissue pathology. Causative agents may include trauma, caries, bruxism, or systemic factors. Typically affects enamel, dentin, and cementum of primary or permanent teeth, often leading to structural damage, discoloration, or loss. Diagnosis is made when specific etiologies are ruled out.

code_desc: Diseases of pulp and periapical tissues
summary: Diseases of pulp and periapical tissues encompass infections and inflammation affecting the dental pulp and surrounding bone. Common synonyms include pulpitis and periapical disease. Causative agents often include *Streptococcus* species, *Actinomyces*, and *Prevotella*. These conditions typically affect the pulp and periapical region of teeth, leading to pain, swelling, and potential tooth loss. They are commonly associated with dental caries, trauma, or poor restorations. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent progression and systemic complications.

Pulpitis is an inflammation of the dental pulp, typically caused by bacterial infection, trauma, or irritants. It results in pain, often described as sharp or throbbing, and may be sensitive to temperature changes. Common synonyms include reversible pulpitis and irreversible pulpitis, depending on the severity and duration. Causative agents include *Streptococcus mutans* and other oral bacteria, as well as physical trauma from dental procedures or fractures. The condition primarily affects the teeth, particularly the pulp chamber and root canals, and is most commonly seen in posterior teeth due to their complex anatomy.

Necrosis of the pulp is the death of the soft tissue within a tooth, typically due to loss of blood supply. Common synonyms include pulp gangrene and pulpal necrosis. It is most commonly caused by dental caries, trauma, or infection leading to irreversible pulpitis. The condition primarily affects the dental pulp of posterior teeth, particularly molars, and may progress to periapical abscess if untreated. Clinical signs include discoloration, pain, and swelling. Early diagnosis and root canal treatment are essential to prevent further complications.

Pulp degeneration refers to the progressive loss of vitality and function in the dental pulp, often resulting in necrosis. Common synonyms include pulp necrosis and pulp gangrene. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, trauma, or irreversible pulpitis. The condition primarily affects the tooth's pulp chamber and root canals. It is most commonly seen in posterior teeth due to their complex anatomy and higher susceptibility to caries and trauma. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent complications such as periapical disease and abscess formation.

code_desc: Abnormal hard tissue formation in pulp
summary: Abnormal hard tissue formation in the pulp, also known as pulpal calcification or dentin dysplasia, refers to the deposition of mineralized tissue within the dental pulp. This condition may result from chronic inflammation, trauma, or developmental anomalies. Common causative agents include pulp necrosis, infection, and prolonged irritation. It typically affects the pulp chamber and root canals, leading to radiopaque lesions. Synonyms include pulp stone formation and odontoblastic pearl formation. The condition is most commonly observed in posterior teeth, particularly molars.

code_desc: Acute apical periodontitis of pulpal origin
summary: Acute apical periodontitis of pulpal origin is an inflammatory condition affecting the periapical tissues, typically resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial infection. It is characterized by severe, localized pain, often radiating to the jaw or ear. Common synonyms include acute periapical abscess and apical abscess. The primary causative agents are anaerobic bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, and *Treponema denticola*. This condition most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular anterior and posterior teeth, particularly those with untreated caries or dental trauma.

A periapical abscess without sinus is a localized infection at the root tip of a tooth, resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial invasion. It typically presents as a painful, swollen lesion without an associated draining sinus tract. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus species*, and *Prevotella*. This condition most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, particularly molars. Synonyms include apical abscess and radicular abscess. It often arises from untreated dental caries, trauma, or periodontal disease.

Chronic apical periodontitis is a long-standing inflammatory condition affecting the periapical tissues surrounding the root of a tooth. It typically results from persistent infection originating from a non-vital pulp, often due to dental caries, trauma, or faulty restorations. The most common causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, though other bacteria may also contribute. This condition primarily affects the apical region of the tooth, leading to the formation of a granuloma or cyst. Synonyms include periapical granuloma, periapical cyst, and apical periodontal lesion. It is most commonly seen in the anterior and posterior regions of the maxilla and mandible.

A periapical abscess with sinus is a localized infection at the root tip of a tooth, extending to form a draining sinus tract. Common synonyms include apical abscess with fistula and periapical granuloma with sinus. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Streptococcus* species, *Actinomyces*, and *Prevotella*. The condition predominantly affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, often resulting from untreated dental caries or pulp necrosis. The sinus tract allows pus to drain, providing temporary relief but requiring endodontic treatment for resolution.

A radicular cyst, also known as a periapical cyst or granuloma, is a slow-growing, fluid-filled lesion that develops at the apex of a non-vital tooth root. It arises from the persistence of the dental follicle or inflammatory changes following pulp necrosis. Common causative agents include dental caries, trauma, and pulp infection. The cyst typically affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior regions, particularly around molars and premolars. It is often associated with a history of dental trauma or untreated dental caries. Radiographically, it appears as a well-defined radiolucency at the root apex.

code_desc: Other and unspecified diseases of pulp and periapical tissues
summary: "Other and unspecified diseases of pulp and periapical tissues" refers to inflammatory or degenerative conditions affecting the dental pulp and surrounding periapical tissues when the specific diagnosis is not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include pulp necrosis, periapical abscess, and apical periodontitis. Causative agents often include bacterial infections, such as *Streptococcus* species, and physical trauma. These conditions typically affect the root apices of posterior teeth, particularly molars, and may present with pain, swelling, or radiolucency on imaging.

Gingival and periodontal diseases are inflammatory conditions affecting the supporting structures of the teeth. Common synonyms include periodontitis and gingivitis. These diseases are primarily caused by bacterial plaque, with *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans* and *Porphyromonas gingivalis* being notable pathogens. They typically affect the gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, leading to gingival inflammation, recession, and potential tooth loss if untreated. The condition is more prevalent in adults but can occur at any age. Poor oral hygiene, systemic factors, and genetic predisposition contribute to disease progression.

Acute gingivitis is an inflammatory condition of the gums characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding upon probing. It is commonly caused by bacterial plaque accumulation, leading to an immune response. Synonyms include gingival inflammation and early periodontal disease. The most prevalent causative agents are gram-negative anaerobic bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. The condition primarily affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, often involving multiple teeth. It is typically reversible with proper oral hygiene and professional dental care.

Acute gingivitis, plaque induced, is an inflammatory condition of the gums caused by the accumulation of dental plaque. It is characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding of the gingival tissues. Common synonyms include gingival inflammation and plaque-induced gingivitis. The primary causative agent is bacterial plaque, particularly *Streptococcus* species and *Porphyromonas gingivalis*. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, often involving the anterior teeth. Poor oral hygiene is a major contributing factor.

Acute gingivitis, non-plaque induced, is a sudden inflammatory condition of the gingiva not caused by dental plaque. It is characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding of the gums. Common synonyms include acute gingival inflammation and non-plaque-related gingivitis. Causative agents may include hormonal changes, systemic illnesses, medications, or irritants. Typically affecting the marginal and interdental papillae, this condition is often transient and may resolve with appropriate management. It is distinct from plaque-induced gingivitis, as it lacks the presence of microbial biofilm.

Chronic gingivitis is a mild, persistent inflammatory condition affecting the gums, primarily caused by bacterial plaque accumulation. It is characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding upon brushing. Common synonyms include marginal gingivitis and plaque-induced gingivitis. The primary causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, along with other periodontal pathogens. It typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, often involving multiple teeth. Poor oral hygiene is a major risk factor, and early intervention can prevent progression to periodontitis.

Chronic gingivitis, plaque induced, is a common inflammatory condition affecting the gums, primarily caused by the accumulation of dental plaque. It is characterized by red, swollen, and bleeding gums. Common synonyms include chronic marginal gingivitis and plaque-induced gingivitis. The primary causative agent is bacterial plaque, particularly species such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, with symptoms often worsening if left untreated. It is prevalent in adults but can occur in children and adolescents.

Chronic gingivitis, non-plaque induced, is a persistent inflammatory condition of the gingiva not caused by dental plaque. It is characterized by red, swollen, and bleeding gums. Common synonyms include chronic marginal gingivitis and inflammatory gingivitis. Causative agents may include hormonal changes, systemic diseases, medications, or irritants. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, often involving multiple sites in the mouth. It is more prevalent in adolescents and young adults, and may be associated with conditions like diabetes or pregnancy. Treatment focuses on addressing underlying causes and maintaining good oral hygiene.

Gingival recession refers to the apical displacement of the gingival margin, exposing the root surface. Common synonyms include gingival recession and root exposure. It is often associated with periodontal disease, aggressive brushing, trauma, or systemic conditions such as vitamin C deficiency. The condition typically affects the maxillary anterior teeth, though it can occur in other areas. It is a common clinical finding in periodontal assessment and may contribute to increased susceptibility to caries and root surface pathology.

Gingival recession, unspecified, refers to the apical migration of the gingival margin, exposing the root surface without a specific underlying cause identified. Common synonyms include gingival recession and gingival root exposure. Causative agents may include periodontal disease, aggressive tooth brushing, trauma, orthodontic movement, or systemic factors such as smoking and hormonal changes. This condition typically affects the maxillary and mandibular anterior and posterior regions, often involving multiple teeth. It is associated with increased risk of root caries and periodontal complications.

Gingival recession, minimal, refers to a slight exposure of the root surface due to apical migration of the gingival margin. It is often asymptomatic and may be detected during routine dental examinations. Common synonyms include mild gingival recession and slight root exposure. Causative agents may include periodontal disease, aggressive tooth brushing, orthodontic movement, or trauma. The condition typically affects the interdental papilla and is commonly observed in the anterior maxillary region. It may progress if underlying factors are not addressed.

Gingival recession, moderate, refers to the apical displacement of the gingival margin, exposing root surfaces, typically involving 3–5 mm of recession. Common synonyms include gingival recession of moderate severity and root exposure. Causative agents often include periodontal disease, aggressive tooth brushing, orthodontic movement, and trauma. It commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth, particularly in areas with heavy plaque accumulation. The condition may lead to increased susceptibility to caries and root sensitivity. Clinical assessment involves probing depth and recession measurement.

Gingival recession, severe, refers to the significant apical migration of the gingival margin, exposing root surfaces. Common synonyms include advanced gingival recession and root exposure. It is often caused by periodontal disease, aggressive tooth brushing, trauma, or genetic factors. The condition primarily affects the interdental and marginal gingiva, commonly involving the maxillary and mandibular anterior and posterior regions. Severe cases may lead to increased susceptibility to caries, hypersensitivity, and aesthetic concerns. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent further tissue loss and maintain periodontal health.

Gingival recession, localized, refers to the apical migration of the gingival margin on one or more teeth, exposing root surfaces.
