Common synonyms include unspecified dental anomalies or generalized periodontal disease. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, trauma, systemic diseases, or genetic factors. These disorders typically affect the teeth, gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, leading to symptoms such as pain, swelling, mobility, or tooth loss. They are often diagnosed when specific etiologies or clinical features are not clearly defined.

code_desc: Unspecified disorder of the teeth and supporting structures
summary: Unspecified disorder of the teeth and supporting structures refers to a broad category of dental conditions that do not fit specific diagnostic classifications. Common synonyms include generalized dental disease or unspecified dental anomaly. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, systemic diseases, or genetic factors. Typically affects teeth, gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone. This diagnosis is used when the exact nature of the disorder is not clearly defined or documented. It may encompass issues such as enamel hypoplasia, developmental defects, or inflammatory conditions.

Diseases of the jaws encompass a range of conditions affecting the maxilla and mandible, including infections, tumors, and developmental anomalies. Common synonyms include mandibular and maxillary disorders. Causative agents vary, with bacterial infections like osteomyelitis, viral causes such as herpes zoster, and fungal infections being prevalent. Other causes include trauma, congenital defects, and systemic diseases like Paget's disease. These conditions typically affect the bones, teeth, and surrounding soft tissues of the oral cavity, leading to pain, swelling, deformity, and functional impairment.

Developmental odontogenic cysts are benign, fluid-filled lesions originating from odontogenic tissues during tooth development. Common synonyms include dentigerous cyst and follicular cyst. These cysts are typically associated with unerupted teeth and result from developmental abnormalities in the enamel epithelium. The most common causative agents are genetic factors and developmental disturbances. They predominantly affect the maxilla and mandible, often involving the posterior regions. These cysts may expand the jaw and cause displacement of adjacent teeth. Early diagnosis and management are essential to prevent complications.

Fissural cysts of the jaw, also known as nasopalatine duct cysts or incisive canal cysts, are developmental fluid-filled lesions arising from remnants of the nasopalatine duct. They are typically benign and result from epithelialization of the duct during tooth development. These cysts most commonly occur in the maxillary incisor region, affecting the palatal aspect of the anterior maxilla. They are usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on radiographic imaging. No specific causative agent is identified, but they are associated with developmental anomalies of the maxillary process.

"Other cysts of jaws" refers to non-odontogenic cysts that develop in the jaw bones, distinct from developmental or odontogenic cysts. Common synonyms include odontogenic keratocysts and follicular cysts. These cysts are typically caused by epithelial remnants, trauma, or inflammatory processes. They most commonly occur in the maxilla and mandible, often in the posterior regions. They may present as painless swellings and can lead to bone expansion, tooth displacement, or pathologic fractures if left untreated. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and histopathological examination.

Central giant cell (reparative) granuloma is a benign, inflammatory lesion characterized by the presence of multinucleated giant cells and mononuclear inflammatory cells. It is often associated with reactive changes to foreign bodies or trauma. Common synonyms include reparative granuloma and inflammatory granuloma. The condition is typically caused by retained foreign material, such as glass or metal, or following trauma. It most commonly affects the jaw bones, particularly the maxilla and mandible, but can occur in other skeletal sites. The lesion is usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on radiographic imaging.

Inflammatory conditions of the jaw encompass a range of disorders characterized by inflammation of the jaw bones, teeth, or surrounding soft tissues. Common synonyms include osteomyelitis, periodontitis, and periapical abscess. These conditions are often caused by bacterial infections, such as *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, and may result from dental trauma, poor oral hygiene, or systemic diseases. Typically affected areas include the maxilla and mandible, with symptoms such as pain, swelling, and dental mobility. In severe cases, the infection can spread to adjacent structures, leading to complications like cellulitis or sepsis.

Alveolitis of the jaw, also known as dry socket or alveolar osteitis, is an inflammatory condition characterized by pain and delayed healing following tooth extraction. It occurs when the blood clot at the extraction site is dislodged or dissolves prematurely, exposing the underlying bone and nerves. Common causative agents include bacterial infection, trauma during extraction, or poor oral hygiene. The condition typically affects the maxilla or mandible, most commonly in the lower jaw. Symptoms include severe, radiating pain, halitosis, and an empty socket appearance. It is a complication of tooth extraction, particularly in the mandibular molar region.

code_desc: Periradicular pathology associated with previous endodontic treatment
summary: Periradicular pathology associated with previous endodontic treatment refers to inflammatory or infectious lesions surrounding the root of a tooth that have developed after prior endodontic intervention. Common synonyms include apical periodontitis, periapical abscess, or residual infection. Causative agents often include *Enterococcus faecalis*, *Streptococcus species*, and *Prevotella* spp. This condition typically affects the apical region of teeth, most commonly in molars and premolars, and may result from incomplete root canal treatment, treatment failure, or reinfection.

Perforation of the root canal space refers to an unintended breach in the dentinal walls of a root canal, allowing extrusion of pulp tissue or intrusion of oral contents. Common synonyms include root canal perforation and apical root canal breach. Causative agents include instrumentation errors, overpreparation, or accidental removal of tooth structure. This condition typically affects the apical region of posterior teeth, particularly molars, and may lead to inflammation, infection, or failure of endodontic treatment. Early detection and repair are crucial to prevent complications such as periapical lesions or abscess formation.

Endodontic overfill occurs when gutta-percha or other filling material extends beyond the apical foramen during root canal treatment. This condition can lead to postoperative pain, periapical inflammation, and delayed healing. Common synonyms include apical overfilling and excessive obturation. Causative factors may include improper length determination, inadequate condensation of filling material, or technical errors during the procedure. The condition typically affects the root canal system of posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their complex anatomy and greater root curvature.

Endodontic underfill refers to incomplete filling of the root canal system during endodontic treatment, leaving voids or unsealed areas. This can lead to persistent infection and reinfection. Common synonyms include incomplete obturation and canal underfilling. Causative agents are typically bacteria such as *Enterococcus* species, *Streptococcus* species, and *Prevotella*. The condition most commonly affects posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their complex anatomy and narrow canals. Proper technique and radiographic evaluation are essential to prevent underfilling.

code_desc: Other periradicular pathology associated with previous endodontic treatment
summary: Other periradicular pathology associated with previous endodontic treatment refers to inflammatory or infectious conditions occurring around the root of a tooth that has undergone prior endodontic therapy. Common synonyms include apical periodontitis, residual periapical lesion, or persistent infection. Causative agents may include *Enterococcus faecalis*, *Streptococcus* species, or *Prevotella* species. This condition typically affects the apical region of the root, often in teeth with a history of failed or incomplete root canal treatment. It may present with radiolucency, pain, or swelling and is often managed with retreatment, surgery, or antibiotic therapy.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of the jaws
summary: "Other specified diseases of the jaws" refers to jaw conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as osteomyelitis or tumors. Common synonyms include unspecified jaw disorders. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, trauma, or systemic conditions. These diseases typically affect the maxilla and mandible, causing pain, swelling, and functional impairment. They may arise from complications of dental procedures, chronic inflammation, or metastatic spread. Diagnosis often requires imaging and clinical evaluation to determine the underlying cause and guide treatment.

Exostosis of the jaw, also known as osteochondroma or jaw exostosis, is a benign bony growth that develops on the surface of the jawbone. It is typically composed of compact bone covered by a layer of cartilage. Common synonyms include osteochondroma and jaw bone tumor. The condition is often caused by genetic factors, such as mutations in the EXT1 or EXT2 genes, or may result from trauma or chronic irritation. It most commonly affects the mandible and maxilla, particularly in the region of the ramus and condyle. The growth is usually slow-growing and asymptomatic, though it may cause cosmetic concerns or functional issues if it becomes large.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of the jaws
summary: "Other specified diseases of the jaws" refers to jaw conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as osteomyelitis or tumors. Common synonyms include unspecified jaw disorders or miscellaneous jaw diseases. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, or systemic conditions. These diseases typically affect the maxilla and mandible, leading to pain, swelling, or functional impairment. They are often diagnosed when the exact cause or classification is unclear, requiring further investigation.

Unspecified disease of the jaws refers to a broad category of conditions affecting the maxilla and mandible when the specific diagnosis is not determined. Common synonyms include undiagnosed or unspecified jaw pathology. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, developmental anomalies, or neoplasms. Typically, the condition affects the bones and tissues of the upper and lower jaws, potentially involving teeth, periodontal structures, and adjacent soft tissues. It is often diagnosed when clinical findings do not clearly point to a specific known disorder.

Diseases of the salivary glands encompass conditions affecting the major and minor salivary glands, primarily the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands. Common synonyms include sialadenitis, sialolithiasis, and sialoadenosis. These conditions are often caused by bacterial infections, viral agents like mumps, or obstruction due to stones (sialoliths). Inflammation, swelling, and pain are typical symptoms. Sialadenitis is the most common, often secondary to blockage or infection. Autoimmune disorders such as Sjögren's syndrome may also affect salivary function. The parotid gland is most frequently involved, followed by the submandibular gland.

Atrophy of the salivary gland refers to the shrinkage and loss of function in salivary gland tissue, leading to reduced saliva production. Common synonyms include salivary gland hypoplasia and glandular atrophy. This condition may result from chronic inflammation, autoimmune disorders, infections, or prolonged use of medications such as anticholinergics. It most commonly affects the parotid and submandibular glands. Symptoms include dry mouth, difficulty in chewing, and increased risk of dental caries. The condition is often asymptomatic in early stages but can significantly impact oral health and quality of life.

Hypertrophy of the salivary gland refers to the abnormal enlargement of one or more salivary glands, most commonly the parotid or submandibular glands. It may result from chronic inflammation, infection, or obstruction of the gland ducts. Common synonyms include salivary gland hyperplasia or sialoadenomegaly. Causative agents may include viral infections such as mumps, bacterial infections, or autoimmune conditions. The condition typically affects the parotid glands, though the submandibular and sublingual glands can also be involved. Symptoms often include swelling, pain, and difficulty in swallowing.

Sialoadenitis is an inflammatory condition of the salivary glands, most commonly affecting the parotid and submandibular glands. It can be acute or chronic, often presenting with swelling, pain, and tenderness. Common synonyms include salivary gland inflammation and sialadenopathy. Causative agents include bacterial infections such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, viral agents like mumps, and obstructive factors like sialolithiasis. The condition typically affects the major salivary glands, particularly those located in the head and neck region.

An abscess of the salivary gland is a localized collection of pus resulting from a bacterial infection within the glandular tissue. Common synonyms include sialadenitis with suppuration and salivary gland abscess. The condition is typically caused by bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *E. coli*. It most commonly affects the submandibular and parotid glands, often due to obstruction of the salivary ducts, leading to stasis and secondary infection. Clinical features include pain, swelling, redness, and tenderness in the affected area, with possible fever and systemic symptoms in severe cases.

Fistula of salivary gland is an abnormal passage connecting a salivary gland to the skin or another anatomical structure, often resulting from chronic infection, obstruction, or trauma. Common synonyms include sialocele and salivary gland fistula. The most frequent causative agents are bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Streptococcus species*. This condition typically affects the parotid and submandibular glands, with the parotid duct being the most commonly involved site. It presents as a draining sinus or swelling near the gland, often accompanied by recurrent infection or inflammation.

Sialolithiasis is the formation of salivary gland stones, most commonly in the submandibular gland. It results from the deposition of calcium salts within the salivary ducts, leading to obstruction and subsequent gland dysfunction. Common synonyms include salivary calculi or sialoliths. The condition is often caused by decreased saliva flow, dehydration, or anatomical factors. It typically affects the submandibular, parotid, and minor salivary glands, with the submandibular gland being the most frequently involved. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and infection of the affected gland.

A mucocele of the salivary gland is a benign, cystic lesion resulting from the obstruction of a salivary gland duct, leading to accumulation of mucus. Common synonyms include ranula and mucocele. It is most commonly caused by trauma or ductal injury, often affecting the minor salivary glands. The lesion typically presents as a painless, bluish swelling, most frequently located on the lower lip or floor of the mouth. It is more prevalent in children and young adults. Treatment often involves surgical excision to prevent recurrence.

Disturbance of salivary secretion refers to abnormal production or flow of saliva, leading to dryness or excessive moisture in the mouth. Common synonyms include xerostomia (dry mouth) and sialorrhea (excessive salivation). Causative agents may include medications (e.g., anticholinergics, antidepressants), autoimmune disorders (e.g., Sjögren’s syndrome), radiation therapy, infections, or neurological conditions. The primary affected body parts are the salivary glands and oral cavity. This condition can impact dental health, swallowing, and overall comfort.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of the salivary glands
summary: "Other specified diseases of the salivary glands" refers to salivary gland disorders not classified under more specific categories such as sialadenitis or sialolithiasis. Common synonyms include idiopathic sialadenopathy and nonspecific salivary gland inflammation. Causative agents may include viral infections (e.g., mumps), autoimmune conditions, or environmental irritants. These conditions typically affect the major salivary glands, particularly the parotid and submandibular glands, leading to symptoms such as swelling, pain, and reduced saliva production. The exact cause is often unclear, and diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and imaging.

code_desc: Unspecified disease of the salivary glands
summary: Unspecified disease of the salivary glands refers to conditions affecting the salivary glands when the specific diagnosis cannot be determined. Common synonyms include nonspecific salivary gland disorder or undifferentiated salivary gland disease. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune processes, or idiopathic factors. Typically, the parotid and submandibular glands are most commonly affected. Symptoms often include swelling, pain, and dry mouth. Diagnosis is usually made by exclusion after ruling out more specific conditions. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve supportive care, antibiotics, or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Diseases of the oral soft tissues excluding lesions specific for gingiva and tongue
summary: Diseases of the oral soft tissues, excluding those specific to the gingiva and tongue, encompass a range of conditions affecting the lips, palate, floor of the mouth, and buccal mucosa. Common synonyms include oral mucosal disorders and non-gingival oral lesions. These conditions may arise from infections, autoimmune processes, or malignancies. Causative agents include viruses (e.g., herpes simplex, human papillomavirus), bacteria, fungi, and chemical irritants. Autoimmune conditions such as pemphigus and lichen planus are also prevalent. Typical affected areas include the buccal mucosa, lips, and soft palate, often presenting with ulcers, erosions, or white patches.

Stomatitis and mucositis (ulcerative) refer to inflammatory conditions characterized by painful ulcers and erosions in the mucous membranes, most commonly affecting the oral cavity. Common synonyms include oral ulceration, aphthous stomatitis, and mucosal inflammation. Causative agents include viral infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus), bacterial infections, fungal pathogens like Candida, autoimmune disorders, and irritants such as spicy foods or ill-fitting dentures. The primary affected areas are the lips, tongue, cheeks, and palate, with symptoms including pain, burning, and difficulty in eating or speaking.

Stomatitis and mucositis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the mucous membranes in the oral cavity and/or gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include oral inflammation and mucosal ulceration. Causative agents may include viral infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus), bacterial infections, fungal infections (e.g., candida), chemical irritants, or autoimmune conditions. The condition typically affects the mouth, lips, tongue, and gastrointestinal tract, presenting with pain, erythema, ulceration, and difficulty in eating or swallowing. It is often associated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or systemic diseases.

Mucositis (ulcerative) due to antineoplastic therapy is an inflammatory and ulcerative condition affecting mucous membranes, primarily in the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and genital areas. Caused by chemotherapy and radiation therapy, it results from damage to rapidly dividing mucosal cells. Common synonyms include chemotherapy-induced mucositis and radiation-induced mucositis. Symptoms include pain, erythema, and ulcers, leading to difficulty in eating and swallowing. Causative agents include alkylating agents, antimetabolites, and ionizing radiation. The condition is often dose-dependent and can significantly impact patient quality of life.

Mucositis (ulcerative) due to other drugs refers to inflammation and ulceration of mucous membranes caused by medications not classified as chemotherapy or radiation. Common synonyms include drug-induced mucositis and medication-related oral ulcers. Causative agents may include anticonvulsants, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and certain antibiotics. Typically affecting the oral cavity, this condition may also involve the gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms include pain, erythema, and ulceration, often leading to difficulty in eating or swallowing. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and medication history.

Other stomatitis and mucositis (ulcerative) refers to inflammatory ulcerative lesions affecting the mucous membranes, primarily in the oral cavity. Common synonyms include aphthous stomatitis and recurrent aphthous ulcers. Causative agents may include viral infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus), immune-mediated factors, nutritional deficiencies, or mechanical trauma. The condition typically affects the oral mucosa, including the lips, tongue, and cheeks, causing painful ulcers and discomfort. It is often self-limiting but can recur.

Cancrum oris, also known as necrotizing stomatitis or mulberry mouth, is a severe, rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the oral cavity. It is most commonly caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Streptococcus pyogenes*. The condition typically affects the gingiva, buccal mucosa, and palate, leading to extensive ulceration, tissue necrosis, and foul-smelling purulent discharge. It is often associated with poor oral hygiene, malnutrition, and immunocompromised states. The infection can spread rapidly, causing systemic complications if left untreated.

Oral aphthae, also known as canker sores or aphthous ulcers, are recurrent, painful, shallow ulcers that occur in the oral mucosa. They typically present as round or oval, yellowish lesions with a red halo. Common synonyms include aphthous stomatitis and recurrent aphthous ulcers. The exact cause is multifactorial, involving immune dysregulation, genetic predisposition, and potential triggers such as stress, trauma, or nutritional deficiencies. They most commonly affect the cheeks, lips, tongue, and soft palate. The condition is not contagious and usually resolves spontaneously within 7–14 days.

code_desc: Cellulitis and abscess of oral soft tissues
summary: Cellulitis and abscess of oral soft tissues refer to bacterial infections affecting the mucosal and submucosal layers of the mouth. Common synonyms include odontogenic cellulitis and pericervical cellulitis. Causative agents often include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus species*, and anaerobic bacteria. These infections typically affect the lips, cheeks, floor of the mouth, and submandibular regions. Cellulitis presents with erythema, swelling, pain, and fever, while abscesses are localized collections of pus. Prompt antibiotic therapy and drainage are essential for management.

Cysts of oral soft tissues are fluid-filled sacs that develop in the non-keratinized mucosa of the mouth. Common synonyms include mucous cysts and ranulas. They are typically caused by trauma, mucus retention, or obstruction of salivary glands. These cysts most commonly occur on the lips, cheeks, and floor of the mouth. They are usually benign, well-circumscribed, and may fluctuate in size. While they often resolve spontaneously, larger cysts may require intervention. Infection or rupture can lead to complications, necessitating clinical evaluation and management.

Diseases of the lips encompass a variety of conditions affecting the vermilion border and surrounding skin. Common synonyms include cheilitis and lip lesions. These conditions may result from infections, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV-1), or non-infectious causes like eczema, psoriasis, or nutritional deficiencies. Causative agents include viruses, bacteria, fungi, and environmental irritants. Typically affected areas include the vermillion border, lips, and adjacent skin. Symptoms often involve dryness, cracking, erythema, and ulceration. Diagnosis is usually clinical, with biopsy or culture used when necessary.

code_desc: Leukoplakia of oral mucosa, including tongue
summary: Leukoplakia of the oral mucosa, including the tongue, is a chronic, precancerous condition characterized by white, adherent patches on the mucous membranes. Common synonyms include oral leukoplakia and epithelial dysplasia. It is often caused by chronic irritation from tobacco use, alcohol consumption, or ill-fitting dental prostheses. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and floor of the mouth. Clinically, it presents as non-removable white plaques that cannot be attributed to any other diagnosable disease. Early diagnosis and removal of irritants are crucial to prevent progression to malignancy.

code_desc: Other disturbances of oral epithelium including tongue
summary: Other disturbances of oral epithelium including tongue refer to non-specific inflammatory or degenerative changes affecting the oral mucosa, particularly the tongue. Common synonyms include oral mucositis and mucosal dystrophy. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus), irritants, nutritional deficiencies, or autoimmune conditions. Typically, the dorsal and lateral surfaces of the tongue are affected, along with the buccal mucosa. These conditions often present with erythema, ulceration, or leukoplakia, and may be associated with systemic disease or local trauma.

Minimal keratinized residual ridge mucosa refers to a thin, non-keratinized mucosal layer that persists over the residual ridge after tooth loss. It is commonly seen in the maxillary and mandibular posterior regions. Synonyms include atrophic mucosa and hypokeratotic ridge mucosa. This condition is often associated with long-term edentulism, poor oral hygiene, and reduced saliva production. Causative agents include chronic inflammation, mechanical trauma, and systemic factors such as diabetes or nutritional deficiencies. The affected areas typically include the alveolar ridges, especially where multiple teeth have been lost.

Excessive keratinized residual ridge mucosa refers to an abnormal thickening and hyperkeratosis of the mucosa over the residual ridge following tooth loss. This condition is commonly seen in the maxillary and mandibular ridges. Synonyms include hyperkeratotic residual ridge and keratinized mucosa of the edentulous ridge. It is often caused by chronic irritation from ill-fitting dentures, mechanical trauma, or poor oral hygiene. The affected areas typically include the hard palate, alveolar ridges, and surrounding soft tissues. Clinically, it presents as a firm, rough, yellowish lesion that may lead to discomfort and difficulty in denture retention.

code_desc: Other disturbances of oral epithelium, including tongue
summary: Other disturbances of oral epithelium, including the tongue, refer to non-specific inflammatory or proliferative changes affecting the oral mucosa. Common synonyms include oral mucosal disorders and oral epithelial abnormalities. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus, candida), irritants, trauma, or systemic conditions. These disturbances typically affect the tongue, buccal mucosa, and palate. Symptoms may include erythema, ulceration, or leukoplakia. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and biopsy. Treatment depends on underlying cause and may involve antifungals, antivirals, or topical corticosteroids.

code_desc: Oral submucosal fibrosis, including of tongue
summary: Oral submucosal fibrosis (OSF), also known as submucous fibrosis of the mouth or leukoplakia with fibrosis, is a chronic, progressive fibrotic condition affecting the oral mucosa. It is characterized by thickening and scarring of the submucosal connective tissue, leading to restricted mouth opening and tissue stiffness. Common causative agents include areca nut chewing, tobacco use, and certain industrial chemicals. The condition predominantly affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and palate, with the tongue being a frequently involved site. It is more prevalent in males and is associated with an increased risk of oral cancer.

code_desc: Other and unspecified diseases of the oral soft tissues
summary: "Other and unspecified diseases of the oral soft tissues" refers to inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic conditions affecting the mucous membranes and tissues within the mouth that are not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include unspecified oral mucosal disorders or non-specific oral soft tissue diseases. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or autoimmune factors. Typically affected areas include the lips, tongue, cheeks, palate, and gums. These conditions may present with symptoms such as pain, swelling, ulcers, or discoloration. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and biopsy.

code_desc: Diseases and other conditions of the tongue
summary: Diseases and other conditions of the tongue encompass a range of disorders affecting the oral mucosa. Common synonyms include oral tongue disorders and lingual conditions. Causative agents vary, including infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus, candida), trauma, nutritional deficiencies, and autoimmune diseases. Typically affected body parts include the dorsal, ventral, and lateral surfaces of the tongue. Conditions such as geographic tongue, glossitis, and oral thrush are frequently encountered. Symptoms may involve pain, swelling, altered taste, and changes in tongue appearance. Diagnosis often relies on clinical examination and, in some cases, biopsy or laboratory testing.

Glossitis is an inflammation of the tongue, characterized by swelling, redness, and sometimes pain. It can lead to atrophy of the papillae, giving the tongue a smooth, shiny appearance. Common synonyms include tongue inflammation or glossal inflammation. Causative agents include infections (e.g., fungal, bacterial, viral), nutritional deficiencies (e.g., B12, iron), allergic reactions, and irritants. The condition typically affects the entire tongue but may be localized. It is more common in individuals with oral infections, anemia, or autoimmune disorders.

Geographic tongue, also known as benign migratory stomatitis or erythema migrans, is a benign, non-scarring condition characterized by irregular, red, smooth patches on the dorsal surface of the tongue, surrounded by a white or yellowish border. The affected areas may shift over time, giving the appearance of a map. The exact cause is unknown, though it may be associated with stress, irritants, or allergic reactions. It commonly affects the tongue but can also involve the cheeks and lips. No specific causative agents are identified, and the condition is generally asymptomatic or causes mild burning sensations.

Median rhomboid glossitis is a chronic, non-epithelialized, smooth red patch located in the midline of the dorsal tongue. It is most commonly seen in adults and is often asymptomatic. The condition is associated with a deficiency of vitamin B12 or iron, though it may also occur in individuals with normal nutrient levels. Common synonyms include median rhomboid glossitis, median glossitis, and rhomboid glossitis. The lesion typically affects the central part of the tongue and is not associated with candidiasis. The exact etiology is multifactorial, involving nutritional factors and possibly local irritation.

Hypertrophy of tongue papillae refers to the abnormal enlargement of the lingual papillae, leading to a coarse, thickened appearance of the tongue. Common synonyms include lingual papillitis and geographic tongue when associated with atrophy. It is often caused by chronic irritation, smoking, ill-fitting dentures, or nutritional deficiencies. The condition primarily affects the dorsal surface of the tongue, with the circumvallate papillae being most commonly involved. It is generally benign but may cause discomfort or altered taste perception.

Atrophy of tongue papillae refers to the wasting or shrinkage of the lingual papillae, leading to a smooth, glossy appearance of the tongue. Common synonyms include fungiform papilla atrophy and tongue papilla atrophy. This condition is often associated with nutritional deficiencies, particularly iron or B vitamins, as well as anemia, aging, and chronic illness. It may also result from smoking or systemic diseases such as syphilis or diabetes. The dorsum of the tongue is most commonly affected, with reduced taste sensation and potential difficulty in food texture perception.

Plicated tongue, also known as circumvallate tongue or lingual papillitis, is a rare congenital condition characterized by the abnormal folding or segmentation of the tongue's surface. It results from the incomplete fusion of the median and lateral lingual swellings during embryonic development. The condition typically affects the dorsal surface of the tongue, where the circumvallate papillae are located. Common synonyms include lingual plication and congenital tongue plication. Causative agents are primarily developmental, with no known infectious or inflammatory etiology. The affected body parts include the tongue, particularly the posterior region.

Glossodynia, also known as burning mouth syndrome, is a chronic condition characterized by a burning sensation in the mouth without an identifiable cause. It commonly affects the tongue, lips, and palate. Common synonyms include burning mouth syndrome and oral dysesthesia. Causative agents may include hormonal changes, nutritional deficiencies, infections, or psychosomatic factors. The condition is more prevalent in postmenopausal women and can significantly impact quality of life. Diagnosis is often based on clinical evaluation and exclusion of other oral disorders.

code_desc: Other specified conditions of the tongue
summary: "Other specified conditions of the tongue" refers to tongue disorders not classified under more specific categories, such as infections or tumors. Common synonyms include nonspecific tongue lesions or unspecified tongue disorders. Causative agents may include trauma, irritants, allergic reactions, or systemic diseases. Typically affected body parts include the dorsal surface, lateral borders, and underside of the tongue. These conditions often present with symptoms like pain, swelling, or altered taste, and require further diagnostic evaluation to determine the underlying cause.

Unspecified condition of the tongue refers to a broad category of tongue disorders where the specific diagnosis cannot be determined or is not documented. It may encompass various symptoms such as swelling, pain, or discoloration without a clear etiology. Common synonyms include "undetermined tongue disorder" or "non-specific tongue condition." Causative agents may include infections, trauma, allergic reactions, or systemic diseases. Typically, the tongue is the primary affected body part, though associated oral structures may also be involved. This diagnosis is often used when clinical findings are inconclusive or incomplete.

Diseases of the esophagus encompass a range of conditions affecting the muscular tube that transports food from the throat to the stomach. Common synonyms include esophageal disorders and gastroesophageal diseases. Causative agents vary, including acid reflux, infections (e.g., *Candida*, *Herpes simplex*), and autoimmune factors. Typical conditions include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), esophageal cancer, and eosinophilic esophagitis. These primarily affect the esophagus, with potential complications involving the stomach and adjacent structures. Symptoms often include dysphagia, heartburn, and chest pain.

Achalasia and cardiospasm are disorders characterized by the failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax properly, leading to difficulty in swallowing and food retention in the esophagus. The condition results from impaired neuromuscular function of the esophageal muscles and the absence of peristalsis. Common synonyms include esophageal achalasia and cardiospasm. Known causes include neuronal degeneration, autoimmune factors, and infections, though often idiopathic. The primary affected body parts are the esophagus and the lower esophageal sphincter.

Esophagitis is an inflammatory condition of the esophagus, typically characterized by irritation or damage to the mucosal lining. Common synonyms include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) when caused by acid reflux. Causative agents include gastric acid, infections (e.g., *Candida*, *Herpes simplex*, *H. pylori*), medications (e.g., NSAIDs), and caustic substances. The condition primarily affects the esophageal mucosa, with symptoms such as dysphagia, heartburn, and chest pain. It may also involve the lower esophageal sphincter and adjacent gastric regions.

Esophagitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the esophageal mucosa without a specified cause. Common synonyms include non-specific esophagitis or idiopathic esophagitis. It may result from various causative agents such as reflux, infections, medications, or autoimmune factors. The condition primarily affects the esophagus, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, heartburn, and chest pain. It is often associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) but can occur independently. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopy and biopsy to rule out other specific types of esophagitis.

Reflux esophagitis is an inflammatory condition of the esophagus caused by the backflow of gastric contents into the distal esophagus. Common synonyms include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and acid reflux. The primary causative agent is the chronic exposure of the esophageal mucosa to gastric acid and pepsin. It typically affects the lower esophagus, with possible extension to the upper portion. Symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia. Risk factors include obesity, hiatal hernia, and delayed gastric emptying. Complications may involve strictures or Barrett's esophagus.

Acute esophagitis is an inflammatory condition of the esophagus characterized by irritation and damage to the mucosal lining. Common synonyms include reflux esophagitis and erosive esophagitis. It is most commonly caused by gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), but may also result from infections, medications, or chemical exposure. The condition typically affects the lower esophagus, with symptoms such as dysphagia, chest pain, and heartburn. In severe cases, ulcers or strictures may develop. Diagnosis is often confirmed through endoscopy.

Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the esophagus, leading to structural changes and dysfunction. Common synonyms include eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) and allergic esophagitis. It is often associated with food allergies, environmental allergens, and genetic predispositions. The esophagus is the primary affected site, with symptoms such as dysphagia, food impaction, and reflux. It is more prevalent in children and adults with atopic conditions.

Other esophagitis refers to inflammation of the esophagus caused by factors other than the common types such as reflux or infections. It may result from chemical irritation, medications, or autoimmune processes. Common synonyms include non-ulcerative esophagitis and eosinophilic esophagitis. Causative agents may include NSAIDs, alcohol, or allergens. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, leading to symptoms like dysphagia and chest pain. It is often diagnosed through endoscopy and biopsy.

Esophageal ulcer is a condition characterized by erosion of the esophageal mucosa, leading to pain and potential bleeding. Common synonyms include esophageal ulceration and gastroesophageal ulcer. It is often caused by gastric acid reflux, infection with *Helicobacter pylori*, or prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The condition primarily affects the distal esophagus, though it can occur anywhere along the esophageal tract. Symptoms include dysphagia, chest pain, and hematemesis. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy. Complications may include stricture formation or perforation.

Ulcer of esophagus without bleeding refers to a localized erosion or ulceration of the esophageal mucosa that does not involve active hemorrhage. Common synonyms include esophageal ulcer and non-bleeding esophageal ulcer. Causative agents often include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or infection with *Helicobacter pylori*. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, particularly in individuals with chronic acid reflux. Symptoms may include dysphagia, chest pain, or a sensation of food retention. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy.

Ulcer of the esophagus with bleeding refers to an open sore in the esophageal lining that results in gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Common synonyms include esophageal ulcer and Mallory-Weiss tear. Causative agents include prolonged vomiting, alcohol abuse, corrosive ingestion, and severe coughing. It typically affects the lower esophagus, often near the gastroesophageal junction. Symptoms include hematemesis, melena, and dysphagia. The condition is associated with increased risk of complications such as perforation and stricture formation. Prompt endoscopic evaluation and management are essential to control bleeding and prevent recurrence.

Stricture and stenosis of the esophagus refer to narrowing of the esophageal lumen, leading to difficulty in swallowing. Common synonyms include esophageal narrowing and esophageal obstruction. Causes include chronic inflammation, strictures from peptic reflux, infections like tuberculosis, or malignancies. Long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a frequent cause. The condition typically affects the mid- to lower esophagus, though it can occur anywhere along the tract. Symptoms include dysphagia, regurgitation, and weight loss. Diagnosis is often confirmed via endoscopy and manometry. Treatment involves dilation, surgery, or addressing underlying causes.

Perforation of the esophagus is a serious condition characterized by a tear or hole in the esophageal wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the mediastinum or pleural cavity. Common synonyms include esophageal rupture and esophageal perforation. Causative agents include trauma, iatrogenic injury, corrosive ingestion, and spontaneous rupture in elderly patients. The condition typically affects the mid- to lower esophagus. It can result in severe complications such as mediastinitis, sepsis, and pneumothorax if not promptly treated.

Dyskinesia of the esophagus refers to abnormal motility of the esophageal muscles, leading to impaired swallowing and food passage. Common synonyms include esophageal dysmotility and achalasia. It may result from neurological disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents include neurodegenerative conditions, myopathies, and prolonged gastroesophageal reflux disease. The condition primarily affects the esophagus, with symptoms such as dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain. It can also involve the lower esophageal sphincter, leading to delayed gastric emptying.

Diverticulum of the esophagus, acquired, refers to the protrusion of the esophageal wall through a weak area, forming a pouch. Common synonyms include esophageal diverticulum and traction diverticulum. It is typically caused by increased intraluminal pressure, often due to chronic coughing, vomiting, or straining. The most commonly affected regions are the mid-esophagus and the lower esophageal sphincter area. This condition is more prevalent in older adults and may present with symptoms such as dysphagia, regurgitation, or chest pain. Complications may include infection, bleeding, or perforation.

Gastroesophageal laceration-hemorrhage syndrome refers to traumatic injuries to the lower esophagus and upper stomach, often resulting in bleeding. Common synonyms include Boerhaave syndrome and Mallory-Weiss tear syndrome. Causative agents typically involve forceful vomiting, retching, or physical trauma. The condition primarily affects the distal esophagus and gastric cardia. Symptoms include hematemesis, dysphagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy, and management involves hemostasis, fluid resuscitation, and sometimes surgical intervention.

"Other specified disorders of esophagus" refers to esophageal conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as motility disorders or strictures. Common synonyms include miscellaneous esophageal disorders. Causative agents may include chronic irritation, infections, or iatrogenic factors. These disorders typically affect the esophageal mucosa, muscular layer, or both, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, pain, or reflux. They may occur in any age group but are more common in adults, often associated with lifestyle factors or underlying systemic diseases.

Esophageal reflux, also known as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or acid reflux, is a chronic condition characterized by the backward flow of stomach contents into the esophagus. This occurs due to transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, allowing gastric acid and bile to ascend. Common causative agents include obesity, hiatal hernia, dietary factors, and delayed gastric emptying. The primary affected body parts are the esophagus, where irritation and inflammation occur, and may extend to the larynx and lungs, causing complications such as aspiration or chronic cough.

Esophageal hemorrhage refers to bleeding from the esophagus, often presenting as hematemesis or melena. Common synonyms include upper gastrointestinal bleeding and esophageal variceal hemorrhage. Causative agents include esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss tears, gastritis, and tumors. It typically affects the distal esophagus, with varices most commonly occurring in patients with portal hypertension. Clinical features may include hematemesis, hypotension, and melena. Prompt evaluation is essential to identify the source and initiate appropriate management.

Esophageal leukoplakia is a precancerous condition characterized by white, thickened patches on the esophageal mucosa. Common synonyms include esophageal candidiasis and lichen planus of the esophagus. It is often caused by chronic irritation, infection with *Candida albicans*, or autoimmune conditions. The condition primarily affects the mid to lower esophagus. Risk factors include smoking, alcohol use, and immunosuppression. Clinical presentation may include dysphagia, odynophagia, and a sensation of food sticking. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy. Early detection and management are crucial to prevent progression to esophageal cancer.

Tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal connection between the trachea and esophagus, typically occurring in the neonatal period. It results from failure of the foregut to septate properly during fetal development. Common synonyms include esophageal-tracheal fistula and tracheo-esophageal fistula. Causative agents are primarily congenital, though rare cases may arise from trauma, infection, or iatrogenic causes. The condition predominantly affects the upper thoracic region, involving the distal trachea and proximal esophagus. It can lead to life-threatening complications such as aspiration and respiratory distress if untreated.

Barrett's esophagus is a chronic condition characterized by the metaplastic replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus with columnar epithelium, typically containing intestinal metaplasia. It is most commonly associated with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). The primary causative agent is chronic acid reflux, leading to mucosal injury and subsequent metaplasia. The condition predominantly affects the lower esophagus, with the fundic gland metaplasia being a hallmark feature. It is a known precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Synonyms include columnar-lined esophagus and reflux-related metaplasia.

Infection of the esophagostomy is a complication arising from bacterial colonization or invasion of the surgical opening created for enteral access. Common synonyms include esophagostomy site infection or esophagostomy tract infection. Causative agents often include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Escherichia coli*. The infection typically affects the esophagostomy tract and surrounding tissues, potentially leading to erythema, purulent discharge, pain, and systemic symptoms. It is most commonly seen in patients with chronic illness or those requiring long-term enteral feeding.

Mechanical complication of esophagostomy refers to structural damage or obstruction occurring at the site of an esophagostomy, a surgical opening in the esophagus. Common synonyms include esophagostomy stricture, esophagostomy fistula, or esophagostomy leakage. This condition is often caused by improper placement, infection, or granulation tissue formation. It typically affects the esophagus and surrounding tissues, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, pain, and secretion leakage. The condition may result from both surgical and traumatic causes, with bacterial infections being a common causative agent. Early recognition and intervention are crucial to prevent severe complications.

Other specified disorders of esophagus refer to esophageal conditions that do not meet the full criteria for more specific diagnoses such as gastroesophageal reflux disease or achalasia. Common synonyms include esophageal motility disorders and miscellaneous esophageal abnormalities. Causative agents may include chronic irritation, infections, or structural abnormalities. These disorders typically affect the esophageal musculature and lining, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain. They are often diagnosed through endoscopy and manometry.

Unspecified disorder of esophagus refers to a broad category of esophageal conditions that do not fit specific diagnostic criteria. Common synonyms include esophageal dysfunction or esophageal disease of unspecified type. Causative agents may include chronic irritation, reflux, infections, or structural abnormalities. Typically affects the esophageal mucosa, muscular layers, and may involve the gastroesophageal junction. Symptoms often include dysphagia, heartburn, and chest pain. Diagnosis is made when specific etiologies are excluded. It is a nonspecific term used when the exact cause or type of disorder remains undetermined.

Gastric ulcer is a chronic condition characterized by the erosion of the stomach lining, leading to the formation of a crater-like lesion. Common synonyms include peptic ulcer disease (PUD) when involving the stomach or duodenum. The primary causative agents are *Helicobacter pylori* infection and the prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It typically affects the stomach, particularly the antrum and body, and may also occur in the duodenum. Symptoms often include epigastric pain, nausea, and bleeding. Complications such as perforation or obstruction can arise if left untreated.

Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage is a sudden, severe erosion of the gastric mucosa leading to bleeding. Common synonyms include acute gastric ulcer hemorrhage and bleeding gastritis. Causative agents include NSAIDs, alcohol, H. pylori infection, and stress. Typically affects the antrum or body of the stomach. Symptoms include epigastric pain, hematemesis, melena, and hypovolemic shock. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy. Treatment involves acid suppression, eradication of H. pylori, and management of bleeding. Complications include perforation and recurrent bleeding.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage, without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage is a sudden, severe ulceration of the stomach lining accompanied by bleeding. Common synonyms include acute gastric erosive lesion and acute gastric ulceration. Causative agents include NSAIDs, alcohol, Helicobacter pylori infection, and stress. Typically affecting the antrum or body of the stomach, this condition presents with epigastric pain, hematemesis, and melena. It can lead to hypovolemic shock if bleeding is significant. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy, and management involves acid suppression, eradication of H. pylori, and cessation of causative agents.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage, with obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and obstruction is a severe condition characterized by a sudden rupture of a gastric ulcer, leading to bleeding and partial or complete blockage of the stomach outlet. Common synonyms include acute gastric ulcer hemorrhage and gastric outlet obstruction. Causative agents often include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and alcohol. The stomach is the primary affected area, with complications such as hematemesis, melena, and vomiting. It typically presents with epigastric pain, hemodynamic instability, and signs of bowel obstruction. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent mortality.

Acute gastric ulcer with perforation is a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease, characterized by a full-thickness break in the gastric wall, leading to peritonitis. Common synonyms include gastric perforation and acute gastric rupture. Causative agents include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol consumption. The stomach is typically affected, often in the antrum or body. Symptoms include sudden severe abdominal pain, guarding, and systemic signs of infection. Prompt surgical intervention is often required to prevent sepsis and mortality.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with perforation, without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with perforation is a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease, characterized by a sudden rupture of the gastric wall, leading to peritonitis. Common synonyms include gastric perforation and acute gastric rupture. Causative agents often include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol consumption. The condition primarily affects the stomach, most commonly the antrum or body. Symptoms include severe epigastric pain, guarding, and systemic signs of infection. Prompt surgical intervention is typically required to prevent mortality.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with perforation, with obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with perforation and obstruction is a severe gastrointestinal emergency characterized by a break in the gastric wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the peritoneal cavity. This often results in bowel obstruction due to inflammation and adhesions. Common synonyms include perforated gastric ulcer and gastric perforation with obstruction. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, alcohol, and stress. The stomach is the primarily affected body part, with complications involving the peritoneum and adjacent bowel.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation is a severe gastrointestinal emergency characterized by the rapid development of a gastric ulcer complicated by bleeding and a full-thickness perforation of the stomach wall. Common synonyms include acute gastric perforation with hemorrhage and ulcerative gastritis. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), alcohol, and stress. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum and body, and can lead to peritonitis if perforation occurs. It is often associated with peptic ulcer disease and requires immediate medical intervention.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation, without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation is a severe gastrointestinal condition characterized by sudden erosion of the gastric mucosa, leading to bleeding and a full-thickness rupture of the stomach wall. Common synonyms include acute gastric ulcer with perforation and bleeding. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol consumption. The condition typically affects the lesser curvature of the stomach, with complications such as hematemesis and peritonitis. It requires urgent medical intervention to prevent life-threatening complications.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation, with obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation, with obstruction is a severe gastrointestinal emergency characterized by a rapidly developing ulcer in the stomach, leading to bleeding, perforation, and bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include acute gastric ulcer with complications. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, alcohol, and stress. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum and body, and can lead to life-threatening complications if not promptly treated.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer without mention of hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Acute gastric ulcer is a sudden inflammation and erosion of the gastric mucosa, typically occurring in the antrum or body of the stomach. Common synonyms include acute gastritis with ulceration and erosive gastritis. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), excessive alcohol consumption, and stress. The condition primarily affects the stomach lining, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is distinct from hemorrhage or perforation, as it lacks these complications.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer refers to an erosive lesion in the stomach lining, typically occurring in the antrum or body. Common synonyms include acute peptic ulcer and acute gastritis with ulceration. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), excessive alcohol use, and stress. The condition primarily affects the gastric mucosa, with symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is distinct from hemorrhagic or perforated ulcers and does not involve obstruction. Diagnosis is often confirmed via endoscopy.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, with obstruction
summary: Acute gastric ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation, with obstruction refers to an ulceration of the gastric mucosa causing partial or complete blockage of gastric outflow. Common synonyms include acute gastric outlet obstruction due to ulcer. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol consumption. Typically affecting the antrum or pylorus, this condition may present with epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is often associated with peptic ulcer disease and may require endoscopic evaluation and management.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage refers to a long-standing ulcer in the stomach lining that has ruptured, leading to bleeding. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer with bleeding and chronic gastric ulcer hemorrhage. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and other factors may also contribute. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum or body. Symptoms may include hematemesis, melena, and abdominal pain. Complications can include anemia and perforation. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via endoscopy.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage, without mention of obstruction
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage refers to a long-standing ulcer in the stomach lining that has caused bleeding, without evidence of intestinal obstruction. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer with bleeding or chronic peptic ulcer with hemorrhage. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and other factors may contribute. The stomach, particularly the antrum or body, is typically affected. Symptoms may include hematemesis, melena, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopy and imaging. Complications can lead to anemia and further gastrointestinal bleeding.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage, with obstruction
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and obstruction refers to a long-standing ulcer in the stomach that has caused bleeding and/or blockage of the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer with complications. Causative agents often include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and alcohol. The stomach is the primary affected area, with complications involving the duodenum or proximal small intestine. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, vomiting, and hematemesis.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation refers to a complication of a long-standing gastric ulcer that has eroded through the stomach wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include perforated gastric ulcer or gastric ulcer perforation. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and other factors may contribute. The condition typically affects the stomach, particularly the antrum or body, and can lead to severe peritonitis if not promptly treated.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation, without mention of obstruction
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation, without mention of obstruction, refers to a complication of a long-standing gastric ulcer where the ulcer has eroded through the gastric wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include gastric perforation or ulcer perforation. Causative agents often include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive acid secretion. The primary affected body part is the stomach, with perforation typically occurring in the lesser curvature. This condition is associated with severe abdominal pain, peritonitis, and requires urgent medical intervention.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation, with obstruction
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation and obstruction is a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease, typically affecting the stomach. It involves the rupture of a long-standing ulcer, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the abdominal cavity, often causing peritonitis. Obstruction may result from scarring or edema around the ulcer site. Common causative agents include *Helicobacter pylori* infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and distension. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum or body. Synonyms include perforated gastric ulcer with obstruction and gastric ulcer perforation with bowel obstruction.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation refers to a long-standing ulcer in the stomach lining that may bleed or rupture, leading to severe complications. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer with complications. Causative agents often include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol use. The primary affected body part is the stomach, particularly the antrum or body. Hemorrhage may present with hematemesis or melena, while perforation can cause acute abdomen and peritonitis.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation, without mention of obstruction
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation refers to a long-standing ulcer in the stomach lining that has progressed to cause bleeding and a full-thickness tear, potentially leading to peritonitis. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer complications and perforated ulcer. Causative agents often include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive acid secretion.
