Eosinophilic gastritis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of eosinophils into the gastric mucosa. It is often associated with allergic or hypersensitivity reactions. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and eosinophilic infiltration of the stomach. Known causative agents include food allergens, parasites, and medications. The condition typically affects the stomach, though it may involve other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopic biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration. Treatment involves identifying and eliminating allergens, along with corticosteroids or other immunomodulatory therapies.

code_desc: Eosinophilic gastritis, without mention of hemorrhage
summary: Eosinophilic gastritis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of eosinophils into the gastric mucosa. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and eosinophilic infiltration of the stomach. The condition is often associated with allergic reactions, parasitic infections, or immune-mediated processes. Known causative agents include food allergens, helminths, and environmental allergens. It typically affects the stomach, though it may involve other gastrointestinal segments. Symptoms may include dyspepsia, nausea, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopic biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration without evidence of hemorrhage.

Eosinophilic gastritis with hemorrhage is an inflammatory condition characterized by infiltration of eosinophils in the gastric mucosa, often leading to ulceration and bleeding. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and eosinophilic gastritis with ulceration. It is associated with parasitic infections, allergic reactions, and hypersensitivity to food or medications. The stomach is primarily affected, but involvement of the intestines may occur. Clinical presentation includes abdominal pain, vomiting, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopic biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration and evidence of hemorrhage.

Disorders of stomach function encompass a range of conditions affecting gastric motility, secretion, or emptying. Common synonyms include gastroparesis, dyspepsia, and gastric hypomotility. These disorders may result from neurological damage, diabetes mellitus, infections, or medications. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori, medications like opioids and anticholinergics, and systemic diseases. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, esophagus, and duodenum. Symptoms often involve nausea, vomiting, bloating, and early satiety. Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation, imaging, and gastric emptying studies. Management focuses on symptom relief and underlying cause treatment.

Achlorhydria is a condition characterized by the absence or significant reduction of hydrochloric acid in gastric juice. It results from impaired function of the parietal cells in the stomach. Common synonyms include hypochlorhydria and achlorhydria. Causative agents may include chronic atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, long-term use of proton pump inhibitors, and autoimmune disorders. It primarily affects the stomach, leading to impaired digestion and increased risk of infections and nutrient deficiencies, particularly vitamin B12.

Acute dilatation of the stomach, also known as gastric distension or gastric atony, is a condition characterized by rapid and excessive expansion of the stomach due to gas or fluid accumulation. Common causes include obstruction, pyloric stenosis, or dysfunction of the vagus nerve. It may result from ingestion of air, delayed gastric emptying, or mechanical blockage. The condition typically affects the stomach, with symptoms such as epigastric pain, distension, and nausea. In severe cases, it can lead to gastric rupture or perforation. Synonyms include gastric distension, gastric atony, and pyloric obstruction.

Persistent vomiting is a prolonged and recurrent forceful expulsion of gastric contents through the mouth. Common synonyms include continuous emesis and chronic vomiting. It may result from gastrointestinal infections, food poisoning, gastroenteritis, or motility disorders. Causative agents include viral pathogens like norovirus, bacterial toxins, medications, or metabolic disturbances. The primary affected body parts are the stomach and gastrointestinal tract, with potential systemic involvement in severe cases. Prolonged vomiting can lead to dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and malnutrition.

Gastroparesis is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction. Common synonyms include delayed gastric emptying and gastric dysmotility. It is often associated with diabetes mellitus, postvagotomy, or idiopathic causes. The primary affected body part is the stomach, where impaired motility leads to symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, bloating, and early satiety. Other complications may involve the small intestine and may contribute to malnutrition and weight loss. Diagnosis typically involves gastric emptying studies or gastric manometry. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and underlying causes.

Gastrostomy complications refer to adverse effects arising from the placement of a gastrostomy tube, commonly used for enteral nutrition or decompression. Common synonyms include gastric tube complications or percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) complications. Causative agents may include infection, mechanical irritation, or improper placement. Typical complications involve peritonitis, gastric leakage, tube blockage, and granulation tissue formation. These often affect the stomach, surrounding abdominal tissues, and the gastrostomy site. Infections may be caused by bacteria such as *Escherichia coli* or *Staphylococcus aureus*. Proper care and monitoring are essential to minimize risks.

Gastrostomy complication, unspecified, refers to any adverse event occurring after the placement of a gastrostomy tube, without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include gastrostomy site infection, tube displacement, or leakage. Causative agents may include bacterial pathogens, improper tube placement, or mechanical trauma. Typically affected body parts include the abdominal wall, gastric mucosa, and surrounding tissues. Symptoms may involve pain, infection, bleeding, or obstruction. Management depends on the underlying cause and may require medical or surgical intervention.

Infection of gastrostomy refers to a bacterial infection involving the gastrostomy site, often leading to localized inflammation, erythema, and purulent discharge. Common synonyms include gastrostomy site infection or perigastrostomy infection. Causative agents typically include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Escherichia coli*. The condition primarily affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues around the gastrostomy tube insertion site, occasionally extending to deeper structures if left untreated. It is commonly seen in patients with long-term enteral feeding.

Mechanical complication of gastrostomy refers to structural issues arising from the gastrostomy tube or site, often leading to obstruction, perforation, or leakage. Common synonyms include gastrostomy-related complications or tube-related mechanical issues. Causative agents may include improper tube placement, tube migration, or occlusion by food or secretions. Typically affecting the stomach and surrounding tissues, this condition can also involve the esophagus or abdominal wall. It is most commonly seen in patients with long-term enteral feeding. Clinical manifestations include pain, vomiting, and signs of peritonitis. Prompt evaluation and intervention are essential to prevent severe complications.

Other gastrostomy complications encompass a range of issues arising from the placement or maintenance of a gastrostomy tube. Common synonyms include gastrostomy site infections, tube dislodgement, and gastric perforation. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Typically affected body parts include the abdominal wall, stomach, and surrounding tissues. Complications may present as infection, leakage, obstruction, or granulation tissue formation. Proper tube care and monitoring are essential to prevent and manage these issues.

code_desc: Dyspepsia and other specified disorders of function of stomach
summary: Dyspepsia refers to a group of symptoms involving upper gastrointestinal discomfort, including epigastric pain, bloating, early satiety, and nausea. It encompasses functional disorders of the stomach and may involve the proximal small intestine. Common synonyms include indigestion and epigastric distress. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, or motility disorders. Typically affects the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract. Often associated with stress, dietary factors, or medications like NSAIDs. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with exclusion of organic disease.

Unspecified functional disorder of the stomach refers to persistent gastrointestinal symptoms without an identifiable organic cause. Common symptoms include epigastric pain, bloating, and altered digestion. Synonyms include functional dyspepsia and non-ulcer dyspepsia. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving stress, dietary habits, and altered gastric motility. The stomach is the primary affected organ, with possible involvement of the duodenum. Diagnosis is typically made after ruling out structural or inflammatory diseases through endoscopy and imaging. Treatment focuses on symptom management and lifestyle modifications.

code_desc: Other disorders of stomach and duodenum
summary: "Other disorders of stomach and duodenum" encompasses a range of non-specific or less commonly classified conditions affecting the upper gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include gastritis, duodenitis, and peptic ulcer disease. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, alcohol, and stress. These disorders typically affect the stomach lining and duodenum, causing symptoms like pain, nausea, and bleeding. They are often associated with inflammation, erosion, or ulceration of the mucosal layer. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment involves addressing underlying causes and managing symptoms with medications.

Acquired hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a condition characterized by thickening of the pyloric muscle, leading to narrowing of the pyloric canal and obstruction of gastric emptying. Common synonyms include hypertrophic pyloric stenosis and pyloric stenosis. It is most commonly seen in infants, typically between 2 to 8 weeks of age. The exact cause is unknown, though it may have a genetic component. The primary affected body part is the pylorus, the distal portion of the stomach. Symptoms include projectile vomiting, weight loss, and dehydration. It is not caused by infection or inflammation, but rather by abnormal muscle hypertrophy.

Gastric diverticulum refers to a small pouch-like protrusion of the gastric wall through a weak point in the muscular layer. It is also known as a gastric hernia or diverticulosis of the stomach. The condition is often asymptomatic but may present with symptoms such as epigastric pain, bleeding, or obstruction. Common causes include increased intraluminal pressure, chronic vomiting, or congenital weakness. It typically affects the distal stomach, particularly the greater curvature, and is more prevalent in the elderly. While rare, it can be associated with conditions like achalasia or chronic gastritis.

Chronic duodenal ileus refers to a prolonged functional obstruction of the duodenum, leading to impaired passage of intestinal contents. It is often associated with neuromuscular dysfunction rather than mechanical blockage. Common synonyms include chronic duodenal obstruction and chronic duodenal dysmotility. Causative agents may include diabetes mellitus, scleroderma, and post-surgical scarring. The primary affected body part is the duodenum, with potential secondary involvement of the stomach and proximal small intestine. Symptoms typically include nausea, vomiting, and epigastric discomfort. Diagnosis is often made through imaging and motility studies.

Other obstruction of the duodenum refers to a blockage in the duodenum not caused by a known specific lesion such as a tumor or stricture. Common synonyms include idiopathic duodenal obstruction and non-specific duodenal obstruction. Causative agents may include inflammatory processes, congenital anomalies, or post-surgical adhesions. The condition typically affects the second and third parts of the duodenum, leading to symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. It is often diagnosed when other causes of duodenal obstruction have been ruled out.

Fistula of the stomach or duodenum is an abnormal connection between these organs and another structure, such as the skin, intestine, or bile duct. Common synonyms include gastric or duodenal fistula. Causative agents include peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, trauma, or post-surgical complications. This condition typically affects the stomach and duodenum, with drainage of gastric contents leading to complications like infection or malnutrition. It is often associated with chronic inflammation or structural damage in the gastrointestinal tract.

Gastroptosis is a condition characterized by the abnormal downward displacement of the stomach from its normal anatomical position. It is also known as ptosis of the stomach. Common synonyms include gastric ptosis and stomach prolapse. The condition is often associated with weakened abdominal muscles, obesity, or prior abdominal surgery. Causative factors may include chronic coughing, pregnancy, or diaphragmatic dysfunction. Typically, the stomach descends into the pelvic cavity, leading to symptoms such as epigastric discomfort, bloating, and early satiety. It predominantly affects the stomach, with potential involvement of surrounding structures. Diagnosis is usually made through imaging studies such as X-ray or CT scan.

code_desc: Hourglass stricture or stenosis of stomach
summary: Hourglass stricture or stenosis of the stomach refers to a severe, circumferential narrowing of the gastric lumen, typically occurring in the distal stomach, resembling an hourglass shape. Common synonyms include gastric stenosis and gastric outlet obstruction. It is most frequently caused by peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, or postsurgical scarring. The condition primarily affects the antrum or pylorus, leading to impaired gastric emptying and symptoms such as epigastric pain, vomiting, and weight loss. Diagnosis is often confirmed via endoscopy and imaging studies.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of stomach and duodenum
summary: "Other specified disorders of stomach and duodenum" refers to gastrointestinal conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as gastritis or peptic ulcer disease. Common synonyms include unspecified gastric or duodenal disorders. These conditions may arise from various causes, including infections (e.g., *Helicobacter pylori*), medications (e.g., NSAIDs), or autoimmune factors. They typically affect the stomach and duodenum, presenting with symptoms like dyspepsia, nausea, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy. Management depends on underlying etiology and may involve dietary changes, medication, or surgical intervention.

Pylorospasm is a condition characterized by abnormal, involuntary contractions of the pyloric sphincter, the muscular valve between the stomach and the small intestine. This leads to intermittent obstruction of gastric emptying, causing symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. Common synonyms include pyloric spasm and gastric outlet obstruction. It may be idiopathic or secondary to peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, or neuromuscular disorders. The primary affected area is the pylorus, with secondary involvement of the stomach and duodenum.

code_desc: Angiodysplasia of stomach and duodenum without mention of hemorrhage
summary: Angiodysplasia of the stomach and duodenum refers to abnormal development or malformation of blood vessels in these regions, typically characterized by dilated, fragile vessels prone to bleeding. Common synonyms include vascular malformations or telangiectasias. While the exact cause is often unknown, factors such as chronic inflammation, aging, or genetic predisposition may contribute. This condition predominantly affects the stomach and duodenum, with the fundus of the stomach being a common site. It is more prevalent in older adults and may be associated with other systemic conditions like collagen vascular diseases.

code_desc: Angiodysplasia of stomach and duodenum with hemorrhage
summary: Angiodysplasia of the stomach and duodenum with hemorrhage refers to abnormal vascular malformations in the gastric and duodenal mucosa leading to recurrent, often painless gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include vascular ectasia and telangiectasia. The condition is frequently associated with aging, chronic hypertension, and conditions like cirrhosis or collagen vascular diseases. It typically affects the distal stomach and proximal duodenum. Hemorrhage is usually mild to moderate, presenting as melena or hematochezia, and may require endoscopic intervention for diagnosis and management.

code_desc: Dieulafoy lesion (hemorrhagic) of stomach and duodenum
summary: Dieulafoy lesion is a rare, acquired condition characterized by a submucosal arterial anomaly that protrudes through the mucosa, leading to sudden, severe upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include arteriovenous malformation and vascular ectasia. The exact etiology is unknown, though trauma, chronic inflammation, or prior endoscopic procedures may contribute. It most commonly affects the stomach and duodenum, particularly the prepyloric region. The lesion appears as a small, red, raised mucosal lesion with a central ulceration. Diagnosis is often made endoscopically, and treatment typically involves endoscopic therapy or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of stomach and duodenum
summary: "Other specified disorders of stomach and duodenum" refers to gastrointestinal conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as gastritis or peptic ulcer disease. Common synonyms include unspecified gastric or duodenal disorders. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, or stress. These conditions typically affect the stomach and duodenum, presenting with symptoms like pain, nausea, and bleeding. They are often diagnosed when symptoms are atypical or when no specific etiology can be identified.

code_desc: Unspecified disorder of stomach and duodenum
summary: Unspecified disorder of the stomach and duodenum refers to a broad category of gastrointestinal conditions affecting the upper digestive tract without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include nonspecific gastritis or duodenitis. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, alcohol, or autoimmune factors. Typically affects the stomach lining and duodenum, presenting with symptoms like dyspepsia, abdominal pain, and nausea. Diagnosis is often made when specific conditions are ruled out through endoscopy and biopsy.

Gastrointestinal mucositis (ulcerative) is an inflammatory condition characterized by ulceration and erosion of the mucosal lining of the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include ulcerative gastroenteritis and inflammatory bowel disease. It is often caused by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, infections, or autoimmune disorders. The condition typically affects the stomach, small intestine, and large intestine, leading to symptoms such as pain, bleeding, and malabsorption. In severe cases, it can result in perforation or significant systemic complications.

Complications of bariatric procedures encompass a range of issues arising from weight loss surgeries such as gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, and adjustable gastric banding. Common synonyms include post-bariatric complications and surgical weight loss sequelae. Causative agents may include infection, nutritional deficiencies, and mechanical issues like staple line leaks. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and skin. Symptoms may involve nausea, vomiting, malnutrition, and metabolic imbalances. These complications can occur in the short or long term and vary in severity.

Complications of gastric band procedure may include band erosion, slippage, or migration, often leading to gastric outlet obstruction. Common synonyms are gastric band complications or laparoscopic adjustable gastric band (LAGB) issues. Causative factors include improper placement, overinflation, or infection. Typically affected areas include the stomach, esophagus, and surrounding abdominal structures. Other complications may involve port malfunction, pouch dilation, or ulceration. These issues can result in symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, pain, and difficulty swallowing. Early recognition and intervention are crucial for effective management.

code_desc: Infection due to gastric band procedure
summary: Infection due to gastric band procedure, also known as plication or band-related infection, is a complication following laparoscopic gastric banding. It typically involves the abdominal wall or the gastric pouch. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. The infection may present with pain, erythema, swelling, or discharge at the site of the band or port. It can lead to abscess formation and requires antibiotic therapy and sometimes surgical intervention. The condition predominantly affects the abdominal region and the gastric pouch.

code_desc: Other complications of gastric band procedure
summary: Other complications of gastric band procedure encompass a range of issues arising from the placement or malfunction of a gastric band. Common synonyms include gastric band complications or post-gastric banding problems. Causative agents may include improper band placement, over-tightening, infection, or erosion. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, esophagus, and surrounding tissues. Symptoms may involve pain, nausea, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. These complications can lead to gastric outlet obstruction, band erosion, or port site infections. Early recognition and intervention are critical to prevent severe morbidity.

Complications of other bariatric procedures encompass a range of adverse effects following weight-loss surgeries such as gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, or adjustable gastric banding. Common synonyms include post-bariatric complications or bariatric surgery complications. Causative agents may include surgical errors, infections, or nutritional deficiencies. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and metabolic organs. Symptoms may involve leakage, strictures, malabsorption, or hormonal imbalances. These complications can lead to severe morbidity if not promptly managed.

code_desc: Infection due to other bariatric procedure
summary: Infection due to other bariatric procedure refers to postoperative infections following bariatric surgeries such as gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, or adjustable gastric banding. Common synonyms include post-bariatric surgical infection or bariatric procedure-related infection. Causative agents often include bacteria like *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. These infections typically affect the surgical site, abdomen, or adjacent organs such as the liver or intestines. They may present with fever, wound erythema, purulent drainage, or systemic signs of sepsis. Prompt diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are crucial to prevent complications.

code_desc: Other complications of other bariatric procedure
summary: "Other complications of other bariatric procedures" refers to secondary issues arising from procedures like gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy. Common synonyms include post-bariatric complications or secondary bariatric adverse events. Causative agents may include nutritional deficiencies, infections, or mechanical issues. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and metabolic systems. Symptoms may involve malabsorption, anemia, osteoporosis, or surgical site infections. These complications often require multidisciplinary management to address both physical and metabolic consequences.

Acute appendicitis is an inflammatory condition of the appendix, typically caused by obstruction leading to bacterial infection. Common synonyms include acute appendicitis and appendicitis. The causative agents are often *Escherichia coli* and other gastrointestinal pathogens. The appendix, a small tube-like structure attached to the cecum, is the primary affected organ. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and vomiting. It is most common in individuals aged 10 to 30 years. Prompt diagnosis and surgical removal (appendectomy) are critical to prevent complications such as perforation.

Acute appendicitis with generalized peritonitis is a severe complication of appendicitis where the inflamed appendix ruptures, leading to infection of the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include perforated appendicitis and diffuse peritonitis. The causative agent is typically *Escherichia coli*, though other bacteria may be involved. The condition primarily affects the appendix and spreads to the peritoneum, causing generalized inflammation. It commonly occurs in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and guarding. Prompt surgical intervention is essential to prevent sepsis and mortality.

Acute appendicitis with peritoneal abscess is a severe complication of appendicitis characterized by infection and pus formation in the peritoneal cavity. It typically develops from untreated or inadequately treated appendicitis. Common synonyms include perforated appendicitis with abscess formation. The causative agent is usually *Escherichia coli*, though other bacteria may be involved. The condition primarily affects the appendix and surrounding abdominal organs, leading to localized or generalized peritonitis. It is most common in young adults and presents with abdominal pain, fever, and systemic signs of infection.

code_desc: Acute appendicitis without mention of peritonitis
summary: Acute appendicitis is an inflammatory condition of the appendix, typically presenting with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and fever. It results from obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, often due to fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign bodies. Common synonyms include acute appendicitis and appendicitis. The condition primarily affects the appendix, located in the right lower abdomen. While peritonitis is a potential complication, it is not mentioned here. Causative agents include bacterial infections, with *Escherichia coli* and *Bacteroides* species being common pathogens.

Appendicitis is the acute inflammation of the appendix, a small tube attached to the cecum. It typically presents with periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, accompanied by fever, nausea, and vomiting. Common causative agents include fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, and intestinal obstruction. Synonyms include acute appendicitis and appendicitis. The condition primarily affects the appendix and surrounding structures in the right lower abdomen. If untreated, it can lead to perforation and peritonitis.

Other appendicitis refers to inflammation of the appendix not classified as acute or chronic appendicitis. It encompasses atypical presentations or complications of appendicitis. Common synonyms include appendicular inflammation or appendiceal disease. Causative agents are primarily bacterial, with *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae* being frequently implicated. The appendix is the primary affected body part, though complications may involve the peritoneum,阑尾周围组织, or adjacent organs. Clinical features may vary, including atypical pain locations and delayed presentation.

"Other diseases of the appendix" refers to non-inflammatory conditions affecting the appendix, such as appendiceal tumors or congenital anomalies. Common synonyms include appendiceal neoplasms and appendicular malformations. Causative agents may include genetic factors or unknown etiologies. These conditions typically affect the appendix itself, with potential involvement of surrounding structures like the cecum. They are rare compared to appendicitis and may present with nonspecific symptoms such as abdominal pain or mass. Diagnosis often requires imaging or histopathological examination.

Hyperplasia of the appendix, also known as lymphoid hyperplasia or lymphoid hyperplasia of the appendix, is a benign proliferation of lymphoid tissue within the appendix. It is commonly seen in children and young adults. The condition is typically asymptomatic but may present with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, similar to appendicitis. The exact cause is unknown, though it is thought to be related to chronic inflammation or immune stimulation. It most commonly affects the appendix and is not associated with malignancy.

code_desc: Other and unspecified diseases of appendix
summary: "Other and unspecified diseases of appendix" refers to appendiceal conditions not classified as acute or chronic appendicitis. Common synonyms include appendicular disorders and unspecified appendiceal pathology. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, although specific pathogens are often not identified. These conditions typically affect the appendix, with possible involvement of surrounding tissues. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, and gastrointestinal disturbances. Diagnosis is usually made through imaging or histopathological examination when specific causes are not evident.

Inguinal hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakness or defect in the inguinal canal, commonly occurring in the groin area. It is classified as direct or indirect based on the location of the defect. Common synonyms include groin hernia and femoral hernia, though the latter occurs in the femoral canal. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, congenital weakness, and aging. Typically affects the inguinal region, with indirect hernias more common in males and direct hernias in adults. It may present as a reducible swelling, often accompanied by discomfort or pain.

Inguinal hernia with gangrene is a severe complication where a portion of the intestine protrudes through a weakened abdominal wall and becomes ischemic, leading to tissue death. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia with necrosis and strangulated hernia. Causative agents are primarily mechanical factors such as increased intra-abdominal pressure. The condition typically affects the groin area, involving the inguinal canal. It is more common in males and often presents with severe pain, erythema, and signs of systemic toxicity. Prompt surgical intervention is critical to prevent mortality.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with gangrene, unilateral or unspecified (not specified as recurrent)
summary: Inguinal hernia with gangrene is a severe condition characterized by the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakened inguinal canal, leading to compromised blood supply and tissue death. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia with necrosis and strangulated hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure and congenital or acquired weakness of the inguinal ring. Typically affects the groin area, often unilateral. Complications may include sepsis and bowel perforation if not promptly treated.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with gangrene, unilateral or unspecified, recurrent
summary: Inguinal hernia with gangrene refers to a condition where a portion of the intestine protrudes through a weak spot in the abdominal wall, leading to compromised blood supply and subsequent tissue death. It can be unilateral or unspecified and may recur following previous repair. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia with gangrene or strangulated hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure and congenital weakness. Typically affects the groin area, with potential involvement of the femoral canal. Prompt surgical intervention is critical to prevent complications such as sepsis.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with gangrene, bilateral (not specified as recurrent)
summary: Inguinal hernia with gangrene, bilateral, refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakened inguinal canal, resulting in compromised blood supply and tissue necrosis in both sides. Common synonyms include bilateral strangulated hernia and bilateral incarcerated hernia with gangrene. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, congenital weakness, and chronic coughing. Typically affects the groin area, with potential involvement of the scrotum or labia. Complications include sepsis and bowel perforation if not promptly treated.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with gangrene, bilateral, recurrent
summary: Inguinal hernia with gangrene, bilateral, recurrent, is a severe condition characterized by the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakened inguinal canal, leading to compromised blood supply and subsequent tissue death in both sides. Common synonyms include bilateral incarcerated hernia with gangrene and recurrent inguinal hernia with necrosis. Causative factors include chronic straining, increased intra-abdominal pressure, and congenital weakness. Typically affects the groin area, with potential involvement of the scrotum or labia. Recurrence indicates prior hernia repair failure. Prompt surgical intervention is critical to prevent complications such as sepsis.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia with obstruction without mention of gangrene
summary: Inguinal hernia with obstruction refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect in the inguinal canal, leading to bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia and strangulated hernia. The condition is typically caused by increased intra-abdominal pressure, often due to chronic cough, obesity, or heavy lifting. It most commonly affects the inguinal region, particularly in males. The herniated bowel becomes trapped, leading to pain, nausea, and vomiting. Prompt surgical intervention is necessary to prevent complications.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with obstruction, without mention of gangrene, unilateral or unspecified (not specified as recurrent)
summary: Inguinal hernia with obstruction refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weak spot in the groin area, leading to bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia and strangulated hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure and congenital or acquired weakness of the abdominal wall. Typically affects the inguinal canal, more common in males. Symptoms include pain, swelling, nausea, and vomiting. The condition may occur unilaterally or bilaterally, without mention of gangrene or recurrence. Prompt surgical intervention is often required to prevent complications.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with obstruction, without mention of gangrene, unilateral or unspecified,recurrent
summary: Inguinal hernia with obstruction refers to a condition where a portion of the intestine becomes trapped in the inguinal canal, leading to bowel obstruction. It may result from a previous hernia repair or congenital weakness in the abdominal wall. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia and strangulated hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure and anatomical defects. Typically affects the groin area, more common in males. Recurrence may occur after surgical repair. Symptoms include pain, nausea, vomiting, and a non-reducible mass. Gangrene is not mentioned, so the condition is not considered strangulated.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with obstruction, without mention of gangrene, bilateral (not specified as recurrent)
summary: Inguinal hernia with obstruction refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakened inguinal canal, leading to bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia and obstructed hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure and congenital weakness. Typically affects the groin area, with bilateral involvement possible. The condition may present with pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is more common in males and often occurs in infants, elderly individuals, or those with chronic cough or straining. Surgical intervention is usually required to prevent complications.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, with obstruction, without mention of gangrene, bilateral, recurrent
summary: Inguinal hernia with obstruction is a condition characterized by the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakened inguinal canal, leading to bowel obstruction. It commonly occurs in both inguinal sides, particularly in males, and may recur after previous repair. Common synonyms include incarcerated hernia and obstructed hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, congenital weakness, and prior surgery. Typically affects the groin area, with potential involvement of the spermatic cord or bowel. Recurrence is associated with incomplete hernia repair or persistent weakness.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene
summary: Inguinal hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through a weak spot in the abdominal wall in the groin area. It occurs when part of the intestine or fatty tissue pushes through a defect in the inguinal canal. Common synonyms include indirect and direct hernias. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, congenital weakness, or age-related muscle atrophy. The condition typically affects the inguinal region, with indirect hernias more common in males and direct hernias more prevalent in older adults. It is often asymptomatic but may present as a reducible swelling.

code_desc: Inguinal hernia, without mention of obstruction or gangrene, unilateral or unspecified (not specified as recurrent)
summary: Inguinal hernia refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weak spot in the abdominal wall into the groin area. It is commonly seen in males and often presents as a reducible swelling in the inguinal canal. Common synonyms include groin hernia and indirect hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, congenital defects, and aging. The condition typically affects the inguinal region, with unilateral involvement being most common. The condition typically presents with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. It is distinct from Crohn's disease in that it affects only the colon and does not involve skip lesions.

Vascular insufficiency of the intestine refers to inadequate blood supply to the gastrointestinal tract, leading to ischemia and potential necrosis. Common synonyms include intestinal ischemia and mesenteric ischemia. Causative agents include atherosclerosis, embolism, thrombosis, and hypotension. This condition primarily affects the small intestine, though the colon may also be involved. It is often associated with reduced perfusion due to occlusion of mesenteric arteries or veins. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and bowel infarction if untreated. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent severe complications.

Acute vascular insufficiency of the intestine, also known as acute mesenteric ischemia or acute intestinal infarction, is a life-threatening condition characterized by reduced blood flow to the intestines, leading to tissue necrosis. Common causes include embolism, thrombosis, or hypoperfusion. It typically affects the small intestine, though the colon may also be involved. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and bowel obstruction. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent irreversible damage and mortality.

Chronic vascular insufficiency of the intestine refers to prolonged inadequate blood supply to the intestinal tissues, leading to ischemia and potential necrosis. Common synonyms include chronic intestinal ischemia and chronic mesenteric insufficiency. Causative agents often include atherosclerosis, thromboembolism, and vasculitis. This condition primarily affects the small intestine, though the colon may also be involved. It is more common in elderly individuals and those with cardiovascular risk factors. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and malabsorption. Diagnosis typically involves imaging and vascular studies.

Unspecified vascular insufficiency of the intestine refers to impaired blood flow to the gastrointestinal tract without a specific identified cause. It may result from thrombosis, embolism, or vasospasm. Common synonyms include ischemic bowel disease and mesenteric ischemia. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, hypotension, or clot formation. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the colon can also be involved. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, and bowel dysfunction. Diagnosis typically involves imaging and vascular studies. Treatment focuses on restoring blood flow and managing underlying conditions.

code_desc: Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis
summary: Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis refers to inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract not caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include idiopathic colitis and noninfectious inflammatory bowel disease. Causative agents may include medications, food intolerances, autoimmune disorders, or ischemia. Typically affects the colon and small intestine, causing symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and inflammation. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and biopsy. It is a broad category encompassing various conditions with overlapping clinical features.

code_desc: Gastroenteritis and colitis due to radiation
summary: Gastroenteritis and colitis due to radiation, also known as radiation enterocolitis, is an inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract caused by exposure to ionizing radiation. It typically affects the small intestine and colon, with symptoms including diarrhea, abdominal pain, and bleeding. Common causative agents are ionizing radiation from cancer treatments, particularly pelvic or abdominal radiotherapy. Synonyms include radiation-induced colitis and radiation enteropathy. The condition often presents with mucosal damage, ulceration, and fibrosis, leading to complications such as strictures or fistulas.

Toxic gastroenteritis and colitis refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract caused by toxic substances, often resulting from ingestion of contaminated food or water. Common synonyms include food poisoning and acute gastroenteritis. Causative agents include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Salmonella*, and *Escherichia coli*, as well as toxins from *Clostridium perfringens*. The condition typically affects the stomach, small intestine, and colon, leading to symptoms like nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. It is characterized by rapid onset and systemic toxicity in severe cases.

Allergic gastroenteritis and colitis refer to inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract triggered by immune-mediated responses to dietary or environmental allergens. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome and allergic colitis. Causative agents often include cow's milk protein, soy, and other food allergens. The condition typically affects the small intestine and colon, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. It is most commonly seen in infants and young children, though it can occur in adults with underlying hypersensitivity. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, dietary history, and exclusion of other causes.

Eosinophilic gastroenteritis and colitis is a rare inflammatory condition characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the gastrointestinal tract, leading to mucosal inflammation and ulceration. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteropathy and eosinophilic colitis. The condition is often idiopathic, though allergic reactions, parasitic infections, and autoimmune processes may contribute. It typically affects the stomach, small intestine, and colon, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. The disease can present with variable severity and may be associated with other eosinophilic disorders.

Eosinophilic gastroenteritis is a rare inflammatory condition characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the gastrointestinal tract. It may present with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and malabsorption. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastritis and eosinophilic enteritis. The condition can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly the stomach and small intestine. Causative agents are often unknown, though allergies, parasitic infections, and immune-mediated mechanisms are implicated. It is associated with conditions like asthma and eczema. Diagnosis involves endoscopy and biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration. Treatment typically includes corticosteroids and dietary modifications.

Eosinophilic colitis is an inflammatory bowel condition characterized by the infiltration of eosinophils into the colonic mucosa, leading to inflammation and potential ulceration. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and eosinophilic colonic inflammation. The condition is often associated with parasitic infections, allergic reactions, or immune-mediated processes. It may also occur in conjunction with other eosinophilic disorders such as eosinophilic esophagitis. The large intestine, particularly the colon, is the primary affected area, though involvement of the stomach or small intestine may occur. Clinical presentation includes abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss.

code_desc: Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis
summary: Other and unspecified noninfectious gastroenteritis and colitis refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract not caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include idiopathic or unspecified gastroenteritis and colitis. Causative agents may include medications, autoimmune disorders, ischemia, or dietary factors. Typically affects the stomach, small intestine, and colon, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and inflammation. Diagnosis is often made after excluding infectious and known inflammatory causes.

code_desc: Intestinal obstruction without mention of hernia
summary: Intestinal obstruction is a blockage preventing the passage of intestinal contents, leading to distension, pain, and potential bowel ischemia. Common synonyms include bowel obstruction and ileus. Causative agents include adhesions, tumors, strictures, and foreign bodies. It typically affects the small intestine, though the large intestine can also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and distension. Diagnosis often involves imaging and clinical assessment. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as perforation or sepsis.

Intussusception is a condition in which a segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment, leading to bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include ileocolic intussusception and intestinal invagination. It is most commonly caused by viral infections, particularly rotavirus, or lymphoid hyperplasia in children. Other causes may include tumors or Meckel's diverticulum. The condition predominantly affects the small intestine, especially the ileum and cecum, and is most prevalent in infants and young children. Symptoms include abdominal pain, vomiting, and the passage of currant jelly stool. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications such as bowel necrosis.

Paralytic ileus is a condition characterized by the temporary absence of peristalsis in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to bowel obstruction without mechanical blockage. Common synonyms include adynamic ileus and ileus. It is typically caused by factors such as abdominal surgery, electrolyte imbalances, infections, or medications like opioids. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the large intestine may also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal distension, pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by imaging studies. Treatment focuses on correcting underlying causes and managing symptoms.

Volvulus is a condition characterized by the twisting of a loop of intestine around its mesenteric axis, leading to intestinal obstruction and potential ischemia. Common synonyms include intestinal volvulus and mesenteric torsion. It is often caused by anatomical abnormalities, congenital malformations, or adhesions. The most commonly affected areas are the sigmoid colon, cecum, and small intestine. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and bowel obstruction. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as necrosis and perforation.

Impaction of the intestine refers to the mechanical obstruction of the bowel lumen, typically due to the accumulation of hardened fecal matter or foreign bodies. Common synonyms include bowel obstruction and fecal impaction. Causative agents may include chronic constipation, dietary insufficiency, medications, or structural abnormalities. The condition most commonly affects the colon, particularly the sigmoid and rectal regions. Symptoms include abdominal distension, pain, nausea, and inability to pass stool or gas. It is more prevalent in elderly individuals and those with neurogenic bowel dysfunction. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as bowel perforation or ischemia.

Impaction of intestine, unspecified, refers to the mechanical obstruction of the intestinal lumen, typically due to accumulation of fecal matter, foreign bodies, or masses. Common synonyms include bowel obstruction, fecal impaction, and intestinal blockage. Causative agents may include chronic constipation, tumors, strictures, or ingestion of foreign objects. The condition most commonly affects the colon, particularly the sigmoid and rectal regions, but can occur in any segment of the gastrointestinal tract. It may lead to distension, pain, vomiting, and bowel dysfunction if left untreated.

Gallstone ileus is a rare complication of cholelithiasis, characterized by the passage of a gallstone into the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly causing an obstructing ileus in the distal small intestine. It typically occurs in elderly patients with a history of biliary disease. The stone may traverse the biliary tract and enter the duodenum, often through a fistula between the gallbladder and duodenum. Common synonyms include choledocholithiasis with intestinal obstruction or biliary stone ileus. The primary causative agent is a gallstone, and the condition predominantly affects the small intestine, particularly the terminal ileum.

Fecal impaction is a severe constipation condition characterized by the accumulation of hardened stool in the rectum or colon, leading to bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include rectal fecaloma and impacted stool. It is often caused by chronic constipation, medication side effects, neurological disorders, or pelvic floor dysfunction. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the rectum, and can lead to complications such as bowel incontinence, fecal incontinence, or perforation if untreated. Prompt medical intervention is necessary to relieve the obstruction and prevent further complications.

Other impaction of the intestine refers to the mechanical obstruction of the gastrointestinal tract not caused by tumors, strictures, or adhesions. It commonly results from retained foreign bodies, fecal matter, or impacted masses. Synonyms include foreign body impaction and intestinal obstruction due to non-mechanical causes. Common causative agents include ingested objects, dietary indigestion, and gastrointestinal motility disorders. The condition typically affects the small or large intestine, with the ileum and cecum being the most commonly involved segments. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Prompt diagnosis and removal of the obstructing material are essential to prevent complications such as bowel perforation or necrosis.

Other specified intestinal obstruction refers to mechanical blockage of the gastrointestinal tract not classified under more specific categories. It may result from adhesions, tumors, or external compression. Common synonyms include unspecified intestinal obstruction or non-specific intestinal blockage. Causative agents can include post-surgical adhesions, hernias, or foreign bodies. Typically affects the small intestine, though large bowel involvement is possible. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Diagnosis often requires imaging studies such as X-ray or CT scan. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve surgical intervention or bowel rest.

code_desc: Intestinal or peritoneal adhesions with obstruction (postoperative) (postinfection)
summary: Intestinal or peritoneal adhesions with obstruction refer to the formation of fibrous bands between abdominal organs or the peritoneum, leading to bowel blockage, often following surgery or infection. Common synonyms include postoperative adhesion syndrome and post-inflammatory adhesions. Causative agents include surgical procedures, infections such as appendicitis or diverticulitis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Typically affecting the small intestine, colon, and mesentery, this condition can cause symptoms like abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation.

Other specified intestinal obstruction refers to mechanical or functional blockage of the gastrointestinal tract not classified under other specific categories. Common synonyms include partial bowel obstruction and ileus. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, strictures, or foreign bodies. This condition typically affects the small intestine, though the colon may also be involved. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies such as abdominal X-rays or CT scans. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve bowel rest, hydration, and surgical intervention if necessary.

Unspecified intestinal obstruction refers to a blockage in the gastrointestinal tract where the specific cause or location is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include nonspecific intestinal obstruction or undetermined intestinal obstruction. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, hernias, or inflammatory processes. It typically affects the small intestine, though the large intestine may also be involved. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Diagnosis is usually made through imaging studies such as X-ray or CT scan when a definitive cause cannot be determined.

Diverticula of the intestine refer to small, abnormal pouches that protrude from the walls of the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly in the colon. These outpouchings are often associated with increased intraluminal pressure and weakened muscular layers. Common synonyms include diverticulosis and diverticular disease. The primary causative agent is chronic constipation and a low-fiber diet, which contribute to elevated colonic pressure. The sigmoid colon is most frequently affected, though diverticula can occur in other segments of the gastrointestinal tract. Complications such as diverticulitis, perforation, and bleeding may arise.

Diverticula of the small intestine refer to the protrusion of the intestinal wall through weak points, typically in the muscular layer. Common synonyms include intestinal diverticula and Meckel's diverticula, though the latter is a congenital remnant. Causative factors include chronic inflammation, increased intraluminal pressure, and weakened musculature. These diverticula most commonly occur in the ileum, particularly near the ileocecal junction. They may be asymptomatic or cause complications such as bleeding, obstruction, or infection.

code_desc: Diverticulosis of small intestine (without mention of hemorrhage)
summary: Diverticulosis of the small intestine refers to the formation of multiple diverticula, which are small, abnormal pouches, in the walls of the small bowel. This condition is less common than diverticulosis of the colon. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulosis and enteric diverticulosis. The exact cause is not fully understood, but factors such as increased intraluminal pressure, weakness in the bowel wall, and chronic constipation are implicated. It typically affects the ileum and is more prevalent in older adults. Complications may include obstruction, perforation, or inflammation, though hemorrhage is not a primary feature in this condition.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of small intestine (without mention of hemorrhage)
summary: Diverticulitis of the small intestine refers to inflammation of diverticula, which are small pouches that protrude from the intestinal wall. This condition is less common than diverticulitis of the colon. It typically occurs in the ileum and is often associated with chronic inflammation or structural weakness of the intestinal wall. Common synonyms include ileal diverticulitis and small bowel diverticulitis. Causative agents may include bacterial overgrowth, ischemia, or chronic inflammation. The primary affected body part is the ileum, with symptoms such as abdominal pain, fever, and obstruction.

code_desc: Diverticulosis of small intestine with hemorrhage
summary: Diverticulosis of the small intestine with hemorrhage refers to the presence of diverticula in the small bowel accompanied by bleeding. It is less common than colonic diverticulosis. Synonyms include small intestinal diverticular disease and enteric diverticulosis. The condition is often associated with increased intraluminal pressure, possibly due to chronic constipation or elevated visceral pressure. Common causative factors include aging, dietary fiber deficiency, and genetic predisposition. Hemorrhage typically occurs from ruptured diverticula, leading to gastrointestinal bleeding. The ileum is most commonly affected, though the jejunum and duodenum may also be involved.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of small intestine with hemorrhage
summary: Diverticulitis of the small intestine with hemorrhage refers to inflammation of diverticula in the small bowel, often leading to bleeding. It is less common than colonic diverticulitis. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulitis and enteric diverticulitis. The condition is typically caused by increased intraluminal pressure, leading to diverticula formation and subsequent inflammation. Hemorrhage results from vascular injury within the diverticula. It commonly affects the ileum and is more prevalent in older adults. Complications may include perforation, abscess, or obstruction.

Diverticula of the colon are small, abnormal pouches that protrude from the colon wall, most commonly in the sigmoid colon. They result from increased intraluminal pressure and weakened colonic wall, often due to chronic constipation or a low-fiber diet. Common synonyms include diverticulosis and colonic diverticula. The condition is more prevalent in older adults and is associated with dietary factors, aging, and genetic predisposition. Diverticula may become inflamed or infected, leading to diverticulitis. The sigmoid colon is the most frequently affected segment.

code_desc: Diverticulosis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)
summary: Diverticulosis of the colon is a condition characterized by the formation of small, bulging sacs or pouches (diverticula) in the walls of the colon. It typically occurs in the sigmoid colon and is more common with age. The exact cause is multifactorial, involving increased intraluminal pressure and weakened colonic walls. Common synonyms include diverticular disease and colonic diverticulosis. Risk factors include a low-fiber diet, obesity, and aging. The condition is often asymptomatic but may progress to complications such as diverticulitis if the diverticula become inflamed or infected.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of colon (without mention of hemorrhage)
summary: Diverticulitis of the colon is an inflammatory condition characterized by the infection and swelling of diverticula, which are small pouches that protrude from the colon wall. Common synonyms include diverticular inflammation and acute diverticulitis. The primary causative agent is typically *Escherichia coli*, though other bacteria may also be involved. The condition most commonly affects the sigmoid colon, though other segments of the colon can be involved. It is more prevalent in older adults and is associated with factors such as low fiber diet, constipation, and increased intra-abdominal pressure. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and changes in bowel habits.

Diverticulosis of the colon with hemorrhage refers to the presence of colonic diverticula complicated by bleeding. It is characterized by small outpouchings of the colonic wall, most commonly in the sigmoid colon. Hemorrhage occurs due to rupture or erosion of diverticula, leading to acute blood loss. Common synonyms include diverticular bleeding and colonic diverticulosis with hemorrhage. Known causative factors include increased intraluminal pressure, aging, and a low-fiber diet. The condition typically affects the left side of the colon, particularly the sigmoid and descending colon.

Diverticulitis of the colon with hemorrhage refers to inflammation of colonic diverticula, often leading to bleeding. It typically affects the sigmoid colon. Common synonyms include diverticulitis with gastrointestinal bleeding and diverticular hemorrhage. The condition is primarily caused by increased intraluminal pressure, leading to diverticula formation and subsequent inflammation. Hemorrhage results from rupture or erosion of diverticula into blood vessels. Risk factors include aging, low-fiber diets, and obesity. Complications may include perforation, abscess, and peritonitis.

code_desc: Functional digestive disorders not elsewhere classified
summary: Functional digestive disorders not elsewhere classified (FDNOC) are a group of gastrointestinal conditions characterized by persistent or recurring digestive symptoms without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common synonyms include functional gastrointestinal disorders and unclassified digestive disorders. These conditions are thought to involve altered gut-brain interactions and motility. Known causative agents are often multifactorial, including stress, dietary factors, and genetic predisposition. Commonly affected body parts include the stomach, small intestine, and colon, with symptoms such as bloating, abdominal pain, and altered bowel habits.

Constipation is a common gastrointestinal condition characterized by infrequent or difficult bowel movements, often with hard, dry stools. It may result from slowed intestinal motility, dietary factors, dehydration, medications, or underlying medical conditions. Common synonyms include bowel dysfunction and obstipation. Causative agents include poor fiber intake, lack of physical activity, certain medications like opioids, and hormonal imbalances. It typically affects the large intestine, leading to discomfort and potential complications if chronic.

Constipation, unspecified, refers to infrequent or difficult passage of stool, often accompanied by hard, dry stools. Common synonyms include bowel dysfunction and slow transit constipation. It may result from dietary factors, medications, hormonal imbalances, or neurological conditions. Common causative agents include opioids, anticholinergics, and dehydration. Typically affects the large intestine, with symptoms primarily involving the gastrointestinal tract. It can lead to complications such as fecal impaction or rectal prolapse if left untreated.

Slow transit constipation is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by delayed colonic transit and difficulty passing stools. It is often associated with reduced bowel movement frequency and hard, lumpy stools. Common synonyms include colonic slow transit time and delayed gastric emptying. Known causative agents include hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, and certain medications. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the colon, leading to impaired bowel motility. It is more prevalent in older adults and can significantly impact quality of life.

Outlet dysfunction constipation, also known as pelvic floor dyssynergia or outlet obstruction constipation, is a functional bowel disorder characterized by impaired rectal evacuation due to abnormal coordination of pelvic floor muscles. Common synonyms include dyssynergia and outlet obstruction. It is often caused by pelvic floor muscle spasm, neurological disorders, or pelvic surgery. The condition primarily affects the rectum and pelvic floor muscles, leading to difficulty in passing stool despite normal bowel motility. It is more common in women and can be associated with conditions such as multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury.

Other constipation refers to chronic or infrequent bowel movements characterized by hard, dry stools and difficulty passing feces. Common synonyms include functional constipation and idiopathic constipation. It may result from altered bowel habits, dietary insufficiency, or slow colonic transit. Causative agents include medications, hypothyroidism, diabetes, and neurological disorders. Typically affects the large intestine, with symptoms such as abdominal discomfort, bloating, and fecal incontinence. It is more prevalent in elderly individuals and those with sedentary lifestyles.

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), also known as spastic colon or mucous colitis, is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic or recurrent abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. Common symptoms include diarrhea, constipation, or alternating episodes of both. The exact cause is unknown, but factors such as gut microbiota imbalance, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial stress are implicated. It primarily affects the large intestine, with symptoms often worsening after meals or during periods of stress. No structural or biochemical abnormalities are present, and the condition is more prevalent in women than in men.

Postgastric surgery syndromes refer to a group of conditions arising after surgical interventions involving the stomach, such as gastrectomy or gastric bypass. Common synonyms include dumping syndrome and postprandial syndromes. These syndromes are caused by altered gastric emptying, hormonal imbalances, or anatomical changes. Common causative agents include surgical procedures like vagotomy, pyloroplasty, or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the stomach, small intestine, and pancreas, with symptoms such as nausea, diarrhea, and hypoglycemia.

Vomiting following gastrointestinal surgery is a common postoperative complication characterized by the forceful expulsion of gastric contents. It may occur due to anesthetic agents, surgical manipulation, or delayed gastric emptying. Common synonyms include postoperative emesis and surgical vomiting. Causative agents include opioid use, anesthesia, and surgical trauma. Typically affecting the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract, this condition can also involve the esophagus and duodenum. It is often transient but may require intervention if persistent or severe.

Other postoperative functional disorders refer to transient or persistent impairments in organ function following surgery, not attributable to structural damage. Common synonyms include postoperative dysfunction and postoperative syndrome. These disorders may arise from factors such as surgical trauma, inflammation, ischemia, or anesthesia. Causative agents include surgical techniques, prolonged operative time, and systemic inflammation. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, respiratory system, and urinary system. Symptoms may manifest as nausea, ileus, urinary retention, or respiratory distress. Management focuses on supportive care and addressing underlying causes.

Functional diarrhea is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder characterized by frequent, loose, and watery stools without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea-predominant (IBS-D) and chronic non-specific diarrhea. It typically affects the large intestine, leading to altered bowel habits and abdominal discomfort. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving gut-brain axis dysfunction, altered gut motility, and visceral hypersensitivity. It predominantly affects adults, especially women, and is associated with stress, diet, and psychological factors. No structural abnormalities are present on diagnostic imaging.

Anal spasm is a sudden, involuntary contraction of the anal sphincter muscles, causing pain and difficulty with bowel movements. Common synonyms include anal fissure spasm and anal outlet spasm. It is often caused by trauma, constipation, infection, or neurological conditions. The condition primarily affects the anal canal and surrounding perianal tissues. It may be associated with conditions such as hemorrhoids, rectal prolapse, or inflammatory bowel disease. Symptoms include pain, tightness, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation. Diagnosis is typically clinical, based on patient history and physical examination. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and addressing underlying causes.

Megacolon, other than Hirschsprung's, refers to an abnormal dilation of the colon due to impaired motility. Common synonyms include toxic megacolon and spastic megacolon. It is often caused by infections, such as those caused by *Clostridium difficile*, or inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis. Other causes include medications, electrolyte imbalances, and neurologic disorders. The condition typically affects the entire colon or specific segments, leading to symptoms such as abdominal distension, pain, constipation, and fecal incontinence. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications like perforation.

code_desc: Other specified functional disorders of intestine
summary: Other specified functional disorders of the intestine refer to gastrointestinal conditions where symptoms such as pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits occur without identifiable structural or biochemical abnormalities. Common synonyms include irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional bowel disorders. While no specific causative agents are consistently identified, factors like gut motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial stress are implicated. These disorders typically affect the large intestine, with symptoms often involving altered bowel frequency, consistency, and abdominal discomfort.

Neurogenic bowel is a condition characterized by impaired bowel function due to neurological damage, leading to altered sensation, coordination, and control of defecation. Common synonyms include neurogenic bowel dysfunction and spinal cord injury-related bowel dysfunction. It is most commonly caused by spinal cord injuries, stroke, or neurodegenerative diseases. The condition primarily affects the rectum, anal sphincter, and pelvic nerves, resulting in symptoms such as constipation, fecal incontinence, or both. Management often involves bowel training, dietary modifications, and medical interventions to restore regular bowel function.

Other functional disorders of the intestine refer to gastrointestinal conditions characterized by altered bowel function without identifiable structural or biochemical abnormalities. Common synonyms include irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional bowel disorders. These conditions are often linked to altered gut-brain interaction, stress, and dietary factors. Causative agents are not well defined but may involve gut motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial factors. Typically affecting the large intestine, symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, altered bowel habits, and diarrhea or constipation. The disorder primarily impacts the colon and is more common in adults, especially women.

Unspecified functional disorder of the intestine refers to gastrointestinal symptoms without a clear organic cause, often involving altered bowel habits, bloating, or abdominal discomfort. Common synonyms include irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional bowel disorder. Causative agents are typically multifactorial, involving gut-brain axis dysfunction, stress, dietary factors, and altered gut microbiota. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, with symptoms such as diarrhea, constipation, or alternating patterns. It commonly impacts the colon and is more prevalent in adults, particularly women.

An anal fissure is a small tear in the anal canal, commonly causing pain and bleeding during bowel movements. A fistula is an abnormal connection between two epithelial-lined surfaces, often resulting from an abscess. Common synonyms include anal fissure and anal fistula. Causative agents include constipation, diarrhea, childbirth, and infection. Typically affecting the anal region, these conditions are more common in adults, particularly those with chronic bowel issues. Fissures often occur in the posterior midline, while fistulas may involve the rectum and perianal skin.

An anal fissure is a small tear in the anal canal, typically located in the posterior midline. It presents with severe pain during defecation and may be associated with bright red blood. Common synonyms include anal ulcer and anal crack. Causative agents include constipation, hard stools, childbirth, and inflammatory bowel disease. The condition primarily affects the anal canal, with the posterior midline being the most common site. It is more prevalent in adults, particularly those with chronic constipation or diarrhea.

Anal fistula is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by an abnormal tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin. It typically results from infection, most commonly due to anal abscesses. Common synonyms include anal fistula, perianal fistula, and fistula-in-ano. The condition primarily affects the perianal region, with the tract often extending from the anal canal through the sphincter muscles to the skin surface. It is most commonly seen in men and can lead to symptoms such as pain, drainage, and recurrent infections.

code_desc: Abscess of anal and rectal regions
summary: An abscess of the anal and rectal regions is a localized collection of pus resulting from an infection in the perianal or rectal tissues. Common synonyms include perianal abscess and rectal abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infections, most commonly *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Bacteroides* species. The condition primarily affects the perianal glands, anal canal, or rectum, often presenting with pain, swelling, and fever. It is more common in males and individuals with compromised immune systems or underlying conditions such as Crohn’s disease.

Peritonitis and retroperitoneal infections are inflammatory conditions affecting the peritoneum and retroperitoneal tissues, respectively. Peritonitis often results from perforation of intra-abdominal organs, leading to contamination of the peritoneal cavity. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Streptococcus*, and *Clostridium* species. Retroperitoneal infections may arise from spread of infection from adjacent structures or hematogenous dissemination. Both conditions commonly involve the abdomen, with peritonitis typically affecting the abdominal cavity and retroperitoneal infections involving the retroperitoneal space, kidneys, and surrounding structures. Synonyms include abdominal infection and retroperitoneal abscess.

code_desc: Peritonitis in infectious diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Peritonitis in infectious diseases classified elsewhere refers to inflammation of the peritoneum caused by infection, typically secondary to another underlying condition. Common synonyms include secondary peritonitis and infectious peritonitis. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*, as well as fungal or parasitic organisms. It commonly affects the abdominal cavity, with involvement of the peritoneal lining and surrounding organs. The condition is frequently associated with perforated viscus, abscesses, or systemic infections. Clinical features include abdominal pain, tenderness, fever, and signs of systemic inflammation.

Pneumococcal peritonitis is a rare but severe infection of the peritoneum caused by *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or following trauma, surgery, or dissemination from other infection sites. Common synonyms include pyogenic peritonitis due to pneumococcus. The infection leads to inflammation, purulent exudate, and potential sepsis. The peritoneum is the primary affected site, with possible involvement of adjacent organs. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent complications such as abscess formation or systemic infection.

Other suppurative peritonitis refers to a secondary infection of the peritoneum resulting from the spread of infection from adjacent organs. It is typically a complication of conditions such as appendicitis, diverticulitis, or perforated viscus. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Bacteroides*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The infection leads to the formation of abscesses within the peritoneal cavity. It commonly affects the abdomen, particularly involving the pelvic or retroperitoneal regions. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and signs of sepsis. Early diagnosis and surgical intervention are critical for favorable outcomes.

Acute generalized peritonitis is an acute inflammation of the peritoneum, typically resulting from perforation of intra-abdominal organs. It is characterized by severe abdominal pain, guarding, rebound tenderness, and systemic signs of infection. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Bacteroides* species. Often associated with perforated peptic ulcers, appendicitis, or diverticulitis, it affects the entire peritoneal cavity. Synonyms include diffuse peritonitis and acute peritoneal infection.
