The condition primarily involves the abdominal cavity and can lead to septic shock if untreated.

Peritoneal abscess is a localized collection of pus within the peritoneal cavity, often resulting from secondary infection following abdominal surgery, perforation of viscus, or pelvic inflammatory disease. Common synonyms include intra-abdominal abscess and pelvic abscess. Causative agents frequently include *Escherichia coli*, *Bacteroides* species, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition typically affects the pelvis, abdomen, or retroperitoneum, with symptoms such as fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness. It may present as a complication of appendicitis, diverticulitis, or gynecological infections. Early diagnosis and drainage are essential to prevent systemic spread and sepsis.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of the peritoneum in the absence of intra-abdominal sources of infection. It commonly occurs in patients with cirrhosis and ascites. The causative agents are typically gram-negative bacteria, most frequently *Escherichia coli*, followed by *Klebsiella* and *Enterococcus*. SBP presents with abdominal pain, fever, and altered mental status. It affects the peritoneal cavity and can lead to systemic complications if untreated. Synonyms include pyogenic peritonitis and ascitic infection. The primary affected body part is the abdomen, with involvement of the peritoneum and ascitic fluid.

Other suppurative peritonitis refers to a secondary infection of the peritoneum, typically resulting from the spread of infection from adjacent organs. It is characterized by the presence of pus within the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include secondary pyoperitoneum and secondary purulent peritonitis. Causative agents often include bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Streptococcus species, and Staphylococcus aureus. The condition commonly affects the abdomen, with involvement of the peritoneal lining and adjacent structures like the intestines, liver, or spleen. It is often associated with underlying conditions such as perforated viscus, abscesses, or trauma.

Retroperitoneal infections are infections occurring in the retroperitoneal space, the area behind the peritoneum. Common synonyms include retroperitoneal abscesses and retroperitoneal sepsis. These infections are often caused by bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. They typically affect the pancreas, kidneys, and adrenal glands, and may result from trauma, surgery, or spread from adjacent infections. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and tenderness. Diagnosis is often confirmed with imaging studies like CT scans. Treatment involves antibiotics and drainage if abscesses are present.

Psoas muscle abscess is a deep-seated infection involving the psoas major muscle, typically resulting from hematogenous spread of bacteria. Common causative agents include Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Bacteroides species. It often presents with low back pain, fever, and limited hip flexion. Synonyms include iliopsoas abscess and lumbar psoas abscess. The condition predominantly affects the lumbar region, with the psoas muscle being the primary site of infection. It may occur secondary to pyogenic arthritis, trauma, or intravenous drug use. Early diagnosis and prompt antibiotic therapy are crucial to prevent complications such as sepsis or nerve damage.

Other retroperitoneal abscess refers to a collection of pus in the retroperitoneal space, distinct from specific types like perinephric or retrocecal abscesses. It often results from contiguous spread of infection from adjacent organs or hematogenous seeding. Common causative agents include gram-negative bacilli, such as Escherichia coli, and anaerobic organisms. It may also be associated with trauma, surgery, or inflammatory conditions. Typically affecting the posterior abdominal wall, it can involve the pancreas, duodenum, or colon. Symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, and systemic toxicity. Diagnosis is confirmed by imaging, and treatment involves drainage and antimicrobial therapy.

Other retroperitoneal infections refer to inflammatory processes occurring in the retroperitoneal space outside the typical urinary tract or abdominal organs. Common synonyms include retroperitoneal abscess and retroperitoneal cellulitis. These infections are often caused by bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus. They typically affect the retroperitoneal fat, lymph nodes, and adjacent structures like the pancreas or adrenal glands. Often associated with trauma, surgery, or spread from adjacent infections, these conditions can present with back pain, fever, and systemic signs of infection. Early diagnosis and appropriate antimicrobial therapy are crucial to prevent complications.

Other specified peritonitis refers to inflammation of the peritoneum caused by factors not fitting into more specific categories such as spontaneous, secondary, or bacterial peritonitis. It may arise from trauma, surgery, or unknown causes. Common synonyms include idiopathic or unspecified peritonitis. Causative agents are often non-infectious, though infections may occur. Typically affects the abdominal cavity, with involvement of the peritoneal lining and adjacent organs. It is less common and often diagnosed when other causes are excluded.

Choleperitonitis is an inflammation of the peritoneum caused by bile leakage into the abdominal cavity, often resulting from perforation of the gallbladder or bile ducts. Common synonyms include biliary peritonitis and cholecystic peritonitis. The condition is typically caused by bacterial infection secondary to gallstones or trauma. It most commonly affects the upper abdomen, with symptoms including severe pain, fever, and abdominal distension. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications such as sepsis.

Sclerosing mesenteritis is a rare, chronic inflammatory condition characterized by fibrous thickening and scarring of the mesentery, typically involving the small intestine. Common synonyms include mesenteric panniculitis and nodular sclerosing mesenteritis. The etiology is often idiopathic, though some cases may follow surgery, infection, or autoimmune disorders. It predominantly affects the mesentery, with involvement of the fat and surrounding tissues. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, weight loss, and bowel obstruction. The condition is usually benign but can lead to complications if left untreated.

Other specified peritonitis refers to inflammation of the peritoneum caused by factors not fitting into more specific classifications such as spontaneous, secondary, or infectious peritonitis. It may result from trauma, surgery, or idiopathic causes. Common synonyms include non-infectious or secondary peritonitis. Causative agents may include foreign bodies, toxins, or systemic diseases. Typically affects the abdominal cavity, with involvement of the peritoneal lining and adjacent organs. Clinical presentation includes abdominal pain, tenderness, and signs of systemic inflammation. Diagnosis often requires imaging and laboratory evaluation.

Unspecified peritonitis refers to inflammation of the peritoneum without a clearly identified cause or specific type. It may present with abdominal pain, tenderness, and guarding. Common synonyms include generalized peritonitis and acute peritonitis. Causative agents can include bacteria such as *Escherichia coli*, *Streptococcus*, and *Staphylococcus*, as well as non-infectious factors like trauma or chemical irritation. The condition typically affects the abdominal cavity, involving the peritoneal lining and underlying organs. Diagnosis often requires imaging and laboratory tests to determine the underlying cause.

Other disorders of peritoneum encompass a group of conditions characterized by inflammation, thickening, or abnormal accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity. Common synonyms include peritonitis and ascites. These disorders may result from infections, malignancies, or systemic diseases. Causative agents include bacteria, tuberculosis, and cancer cells. Typically affected body parts include the abdominal cavity, with involvement of the visceral and parietal peritoneum. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, and fever. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and laboratory analysis of peritoneal fluid. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve antibiotics, drainage, or surgical intervention.

Peritoneal adhesions following surgery or infection refer to abnormal fibrous bands forming between visceral and parietal peritoneum, often leading to bowel obstruction or chronic pain. Common synonyms include intra-abdominal adhesions or postoperative adhesions. Causative agents include surgical trauma, infection (e.g., appendicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease), and inflammation. Typically affecting the abdomen, they most commonly involve the small intestine, cecum, and pelvic organs. Adhesions are a frequent complication of abdominal surgeries and inflammatory processes.

Other specified disorders of peritoneum refer to conditions affecting the peritoneum that do not fit into more specific categories such as peritonitis or ascites. Common synonyms include peritoneal inflammation or adhesions. These disorders may result from infections, trauma, or surgical procedures. Causative agents can include bacteria, fungi, or chemical irritants. Typically affected areas include the abdominal cavity, with involvement of the visceral and parietal layers of the peritoneum. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, and altered bowel function. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and imaging studies.

Hemoperitoneum (nontraumatic) refers to the accumulation of blood in the peritoneal cavity without external injury. Common synonyms include intraperitoneal hemorrhage and peritoneal hemorrhage. It is often caused by ruptured vascular malformations, such as arteriovenous malformations or aneurysms, or by coagulopathy. The condition typically affects the abdomen, with blood accumulating in the peritoneal space. It may present with hemodynamic instability, abdominal pain, and signs of internal bleeding. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent severe complications or mortality.

Peritoneal effusion (chronic) refers to the persistent accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, often resulting from inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic processes. Common synonyms include chronic ascites and chronic peritoneal fluid accumulation. Causative agents may include liver disease, tuberculosis, malignancies, or connective tissue disorders. The abdomen is typically affected, with fluid collection in the peritoneal space. Symptoms may include abdominal distension, discomfort, and early satiety. Diagnosis is confirmed by imaging or paracentesis. Management depends on underlying etiology and may involve diuretics, drainage, or treatment of the primary condition.

Other specified disorders of peritoneum refer to conditions affecting the peritoneum that do not fit into more specific categories such as peritonitis or ascites. Common synonyms include peritoneal inflammation or peritoneal disease. These disorders may result from infections, malignancies, or autoimmune processes. Causative agents can include bacteria, viruses, or neoplastic cells. Typically affected body parts include the abdominal cavity, omentum, and mesentery. Symptoms often involve abdominal pain, distension, and altered bowel function. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and imaging studies. Treatment depends on the underlying cause.

Unspecified disorder of peritoneum refers to a broad category of peritoneal conditions that do not fit specific diagnostic criteria. It may encompass inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic processes when the exact cause or type is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include peritonitis of unspecified origin or nonspecific peritoneal disease. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, or autoimmune factors. Typically affects the peritoneal cavity, with potential involvement of the abdominal organs. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is often made by exclusion of other specific conditions.

"Other disorders of intestine" refers to a broad category of gastrointestinal conditions not classified as inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, or infectious enteritis. Common synonyms include functional bowel disorders and non-specific intestinal syndromes. Causative agents may include dietary factors, stress, and altered gut microbiota. These conditions typically affect the small and large intestine, presenting with symptoms such as abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and bloating. They are often diagnosed through exclusion of other specific diseases and may require dietary modifications or pharmacological management.

An anal and rectal polyp refers to a benign growth arising from the mucosal lining of the anal canal or rectum. Common synonyms include rectal polyp, anal polyp, and rectal tumor. These lesions are typically caused by chronic inflammation, genetic factors, or long-standing constipation. They are most commonly found in the rectum and anal canal, with the rectum being the most frequently affected site. While most are non-cancerous, some may have malignant potential, necessitating histopathological evaluation.

Rectal prolapse is a condition in which the rectum protrudes through the anal canal, often appearing as a red, swollen mass. It commonly occurs in young children and elderly individuals, though can affect adults. Common synonyms include rectal eversion and rectal inversion. Causative factors include chronic straining, constipation, childbirth, and weakened pelvic floor muscles. The primary affected body part is the rectum, with involvement of the anal canal. It may be associated with other conditions such as hemorrhoids or fecal incontinence. Diagnosis is typically clinical, and treatment may involve medical or surgical intervention depending on severity.

Stenosis of the rectum and anus refers to the narrowing of the rectal and anal passages, leading to difficulty in passing stool and potential fecal impaction. Common synonyms include anal stricture and rectal stenosis. Causative agents may include chronic inflammatory conditions such as Crohn's disease, radiation therapy, tuberculosis, or prior surgical interventions. The condition typically affects the distal rectum and anal canal, causing symptoms like constipation, pain, and rectal bleeding. It can result from scarring, inflammation, or congenital abnormalities. Diagnosis often involves endoscopic evaluation and imaging studies.

Hemorrhage of the rectum and anus refers to bleeding originating from the anal or rectal regions. Common synonyms include anal bleeding, rectal bleeding, and hemorrhoidal bleeding. It is often caused by conditions such as hemorrhoids, anal fissures, diverticular disease, or colorectal cancer. Other causative agents may include inflammatory bowel disease, trauma, or vascular malformations. The rectum and anus are the primary affected areas, with blood typically presenting as bright red or dark stools, depending on the location and severity of the bleed.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of rectum and anus
summary: "Other specified disorders of rectum and anus" refers to conditions affecting the rectum and anus that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include anal fissure, rectal prolapse, and hemorrhoids. These disorders may result from trauma, chronic straining, infection, or inflammatory conditions. Causative agents can include bacteria, parasites, or mechanical stress. Typically affected areas include the anal canal, rectum, and surrounding perianal skin. Symptoms often involve pain, bleeding, or difficulty in bowel movements. These conditions are commonly encountered in clinical practice and may require medical or surgical intervention.

Ulcer of the anus and rectum refers to the formation of open sores in the anal or rectal mucosa, often accompanied by pain, bleeding, and discharge. Common synonyms include anal ulcer and rectal ulcer. Causative agents may include infections such as *Shigella*, *Salmonella*, *Chlamydia trachomatis*, and *Helicobacter pylori*, as well as inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease. The condition typically affects the anal canal and rectum, with potential extension into the sigmoid colon. It is more prevalent in individuals with immunocompromised states or those with a history of gastrointestinal disorders.

Anal or rectal pain refers to discomfort or pain localized to the anal canal or rectum. Common synonyms include perianal pain, analgia, and rectalgia. It may present as sharp, burning, or throbbing sensations. Common causes include hemorrhoids, anal fissures, infections (e.g., herpes, syphilis), rectal prolapse, and inflammatory bowel disease. Pain is typically felt around the anus or deep within the rectum. It may be associated with bowel movements, itching, or discharge. The condition predominantly affects the anal canal and rectal mucosa, with potential involvement of surrounding perianal tissues.

Anal sphincter tear (healed) (old) refers to a prior injury to the anal sphincter muscle that has resolved without ongoing symptoms. Common synonyms include healed anal sphincter laceration or old anal fissure. This condition is typically caused by childbirth, straining during defecation, or trauma. It most commonly affects the anal canal and surrounding perianal tissues. While the tear may have healed spontaneously or with treatment, it can sometimes lead to long-term complications such as incontinence or chronic pain. The condition is often diagnosed through physical examination or patient history.

Dysplasia of the anus refers to abnormal cellular changes in the anal epithelium, often characterized by atypical cell morphology and disrupted tissue architecture. Common synonyms include anal intraepithelial neoplasm and anal dysplasia. It is primarily associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly high-risk strains such as HPV 16 and 18. The condition typically affects the anorectal region, including the anal canal and perianal skin. It is more prevalent in individuals with immunocompromised states, such as those with HIV or who have undergone immunosuppressive therapy. Early detection and management are crucial to prevent progression to invasive anal cancer.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of rectum and anus
summary: "Other specified disorders of rectum and anus" refers to conditions not classified under more specific diagnoses, often involving inflammation, structural abnormalities, or functional issues. Common synonyms include unspecified rectal or anal disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., parasites, bacteria), trauma, or idiopathic factors. These conditions typically affect the rectum, anus, and surrounding perianal tissues, presenting with symptoms like pain, bleeding, or discharge. They may be associated with underlying systemic diseases or complications from prior surgeries. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic or histopathological evaluation.

An intestinal abscess is a localized collection of pus within the intestinal wall or surrounding tissues, typically resulting from infection. Common synonyms include enteric abscess and intra-abdominal abscess. It is most commonly caused by bacterial pathogens such as Escherichia coli, Bacteroides species, and Streptococcus. The condition often affects the terminal ileum, cecum, or pericolic regions, and may develop secondary to perforation, diverticulitis, or inflammatory bowel disease. Clinical presentation includes abdominal pain, fever, and systemic signs of infection.

Colostomy and enterostomy complications refer to adverse outcomes following surgical creation of an artificial opening for fecal diversion. Common synonyms include stoma complications and ostomy issues. These may arise from infection, ischemia, or mechanical problems. Causative agents include bacteria like *Escherichia coli* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Typically affected areas include the stoma site, peristomal skin, and adjacent abdominal tissues. Complications such as stenosis, prolapse, and parastomal hernia are frequently observed. Proper stoma care and monitoring are essential to prevent and manage these issues.

Colostomy and enterostomy complication, unspecified refers to adverse events occurring at the site of a surgically created colostomy or enterostomy, without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include stoma complications, ostomy issues, or surgical site complications. Causative agents may include infection, ischemia, mechanical obstruction, or adhesions. Typically affecting the abdominal wall and gastrointestinal tract, these complications can lead to symptoms such as pain, leakage, or infection. They often require medical or surgical intervention for resolution.

Infection of a colostomy or enterostomy refers to a bacterial or fungal infection affecting the surgically created stoma and surrounding tissues. Common synonyms include stoma infection or stomal infection. Causative agents often include *Escherichia coli*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Candida* species. The condition typically affects the stoma site, peristomal skin, and adjacent abdominal tissues. Symptoms may include redness, swelling, discharge, odor, and pain. Prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics or antifungals is essential to prevent complications such as abscess formation or stoma failure.

code_desc: Mechanical complication of colostomy and enterostomy
summary: Mechanical complication of colostomy and enterostomy refers to physical issues arising from the surgical creation or management of a colostomy or enterostomy. Common synonyms include anastomotic stricture, stomal stenosis, and intestinal obstruction. Causative agents often involve adhesions, ischemia, or improper stoma formation. Typically affecting the bowel, these complications may involve the rectum, sigmoid colon, or small intestine. Symptoms include pain, obstruction, and altered stoma function. Prompt evaluation and intervention are essential to prevent severe morbidity.

Other colostomy and enterostomy complications refer to secondary issues arising from the presence of a stoma, such as infection, obstruction, or skin irritation. Common synonyms include stoma complications and ostomy-related problems. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, foreign bodies, or mechanical trauma. These complications typically affect the peristomal skin, stoma itself, and adjacent gastrointestinal tract. They can result from improper stoma care, infection, or structural abnormalities. Prompt management is essential to prevent severe morbidity and ensure proper stoma function.

Complications of intestinal pouch refer to adverse outcomes following ileoanal reservoir surgery, a procedure used to treat ulcerative colitis or familial adenomatous polyposis. Common synonyms include pouchitis and pouch dysfunction. Causative agents often include bacterial overgrowth, such as *Escherichia coli*, and inflammatory processes. Typically affected body parts include the rectal pouch, anal canal, and surrounding tissues. Symptoms may involve inflammation, infection, strictures, or fistulas, leading to chronic discomfort and altered bowel function.

Pouchitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the ileal pouch, typically following ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) for ulcerative colitis. It presents with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fecal urgency. Common synonyms include pouch inflammation or pouch infection. The condition is often caused by bacterial overgrowth, particularly *Clostridium difficile* and *Bacteroides* species. It primarily affects the ileal pouch and anal canal, with potential involvement of the rectum. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and endoscopic findings, with treatment involving antibiotics and management of underlying conditions.

Other complications of intestinal pouch refer to secondary issues arising from surgically created pouches, such as in ulcerative colitis. Common synonyms include pouchitis and pouch-related complications. Causative agents may include bacteria like *Clostridium difficile*, *Bacteroides*, and *Escherichia coli*. These complications typically affect the pouch itself, often leading to inflammation, infection, or structural changes. The small intestine and rectal area are commonly involved, with symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent long-term damage.

"Other specified disorders of intestine" refers to gastrointestinal conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as inflammatory bowel disease or irritable bowel syndrome. Common synonyms include unspecified intestinal disorders or miscellaneous intestinal diseases. Causative agents may include infections, dietary factors, or autoimmune responses. These disorders typically affect the small and large intestine, causing symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. They are often diagnosed when symptoms do not fit established diagnostic criteria.

code_desc: Fistula of intestine, excluding rectum and anus
summary: Fistula of intestine, excluding rectum and anus, refers to an abnormal connection between two parts of the gastrointestinal tract or between the intestine and another organ. Common synonyms include enteric fistula or intestinal fistula. Causative agents often include inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, trauma, or surgery. Typically affecting the small intestine, this condition may involve the stomach, colon, or other adjacent structures. Symptoms include drainage, infection, and malnutrition. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via imaging or endoscopy. Treatment often requires surgical intervention.

Ulceration of the intestine refers to the erosion of the intestinal lining, resulting in open sores or ulcers. Common synonyms include intestinal ulcer and enteric ulcer. It is often caused by infections such as *Helicobacter pylori* or *Salmonella*, inflammatory conditions like Crohn's disease, or ischemia. The small intestine and colon are most commonly affected. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, bleeding, and malabsorption. Complications can lead to perforation or strictures. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may include antibiotics, anti-inflammatory drugs, or surgery.

Perforation of the intestine is a serious condition characterized by a hole or tear in the wall of the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly occurring in the small or large intestine. This can lead to leakage of intestinal contents into the abdominal cavity, causing peritonitis and sepsis. Common causes include trauma, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and complications from surgery or foreign bodies. It is often seen in the ileum, cecum, or colon. Synonyms include intestinal rupture, bowel perforation, and gastrointestinal perforation. Prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention are critical to prevent life-threatening complications.

code_desc: Angiodysplasia of intestine (without mention of hemorrhage)
summary: Angiodysplasia of the intestine refers to abnormal vascular malformations in the gastrointestinal tract, commonly affecting the colon and terminal ileum. These lesions consist of dilated, fragile blood vessels that can predispose to bleeding. Common synonyms include vascular ectasia and telangiectasia. The exact cause is often unknown, though age-related degeneration and chronic inflammation are implicated. It is more prevalent in the elderly and may be associated with conditions like collagen vascular disease. The lesions are typically found in the distal small bowel and large intestine.

Angiodysplasia of the intestine with hemorrhage refers to abnormal vascular malformations in the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly in the colon or small intestine, leading to recurrent, often painless gastrointestinal bleeding. It is also known as vascular ectasia or telangiectasia. The exact cause is unknown, but factors such as aging, chronic inflammation, and vascular abnormalities are implicated. It predominantly affects the elderly and is associated with conditions like diverticulosis and chronic kidney disease. The primary clinical feature is hematochezia or melena, with potential for significant blood loss and anemia.

Dieulafoy lesion is a rare, acquired, arterial bleeding disorder characterized by a submucosal arterial aneurysm protruding through a normal-appearing mucosa. It is a cause of acute gastrointestinal hemorrhage, most commonly affecting the stomach, though the small intestine may also be involved. Synonyms include arterial erosion, traumatic ulcer, and vascular anomaly. The exact cause is unknown, but factors such as chronic inflammation, mechanical trauma, and vascular abnormalities may contribute. It is more prevalent in the elderly and individuals with a history of peptic ulcer disease or anticoagulant use.

Vomiting of fecal matter, also known as fecal vomiting or coprophagia vomiting, is a rare and distressing condition characterized by the expulsion of feces through the mouth. It typically results from severe gastrointestinal dysfunction, such as intestinal obstruction, volvulus, or severe infections. Common causative agents include parasites, bacterial toxins, or physical blockages. The condition primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, with symptoms often involving the stomach and intestines. It is more commonly observed in neonates and young children but can occur in adults with underlying disease. Prompt medical evaluation is essential to identify the underlying cause and initiate appropriate treatment.

"Other specified disorders of intestine" refers to intestinal conditions that do not meet the criteria for more specific diagnoses but are clinically significant. Common synonyms include unspecified intestinal disorders or unspecified gastrointestinal disorders. Causative agents may include infections, inflammatory processes, or structural abnormalities. These disorders typically affect the small and large intestines, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. They are often diagnosed when symptoms are nonspecific or when the exact cause remains undetermined.

Unspecified disorder of the intestine refers to a broad category of gastrointestinal conditions that do not fit into more specific classifications. It may encompass a range of functional or structural abnormalities. Common synonyms include undiagnosed intestinal disorder or unspecified intestinal disease. Causative agents can vary widely, including infections, inflammatory processes, or congenital anomalies. Typically, the small intestine and large intestine are affected, though involvement can be systemic. This diagnosis is often used when clinical presentation is non-specific or diagnostic tests are inconclusive.

code_desc: Acute and subacute necrosis of liver
summary: Acute and subacute necrosis of the liver refers to rapid or moderately rapid death of liver cells, leading to impaired function. Common synonyms include acute hepatitis and subacute hepatic necrosis. Causative agents include viral infections (e.g., hepatitis B and C), drug toxicity, alcohol abuse, and autoimmune disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms often include jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. The condition can progress to cirrhosis or liver failure if untreated.

Chronic liver disease and cirrhosis refer to progressive, long-term damage to the liver leading to fibrosis and nodular regeneration of liver tissue. Common synonyms include advanced liver disease and end-stage liver disease. Causative agents include viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune conditions. The liver is the primary affected organ, with complications often involving the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and cardiovascular system. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and ascites.

Alcoholic fatty liver, also known as alcoholic steatosis, is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fat in liver cells due to chronic alcohol consumption. It is the earliest stage of alcohol-related liver disease. The primary causative agent is excessive alcohol intake, which disrupts lipid metabolism and leads to fat deposition. This condition typically affects the liver, with fat accumulation primarily in the hepatocytes. While it is generally reversible with abstinence from alcohol, it can progress to more severe forms such as alcoholic hepatitis or cirrhosis if alcohol use continues. Common synonyms include alcoholic steatosis and fatty liver from alcohol.

Acute alcoholic hepatitis is a severe liver inflammation caused by excessive alcohol consumption, typically occurring in individuals with a history of heavy drinking. It is characterized by jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and systemic symptoms such as fever and abdominal pain. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver injury and acute alcoholic liver failure. The primary causative agent is alcohol, though the exact mechanism involves oxidative stress and immune-mediated damage. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Complications may include liver failure and increased mortality if not managed promptly.

Alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver is a chronic liver disease caused by long-term heavy alcohol consumption, leading to progressive scarring and loss of liver function. It results from prolonged ethanol toxicity, which causes inflammation, fibrosis, and eventual replacement of healthy liver tissue with scar tissue. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver cirrhosis and alcohol-induced cirrhosis. The primary causative agent is chronic alcohol abuse. The condition predominantly affects the liver, leading to complications such as portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy.

Alcoholic liver damage, unspecified, refers to liver injury caused by chronic alcohol consumption without a specific subtype identified. Common synonyms include alcoholic hepatitis and alcoholic cirrhosis. The primary causative agent is excessive alcohol intake over time. This condition typically affects the liver, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potential cirrhosis. It may also involve the pancreas and gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms include jaundice, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes. Early diagnosis and cessation of alcohol use are critical to prevent progression.

Chronic hepatitis is a long-term inflammation of the liver, often leading to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or liver failure. Common synonyms include persistent hepatitis or ongoing liver inflammation. It is primarily caused by viral infections such as hepatitis B and C, but can also result from alcohol abuse, autoimmune disorders, or metabolic diseases. The liver is the main affected organ, though systemic complications may arise. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal discomfort. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent progression.

Chronic hepatitis, unspecified, refers to long-term inflammation of the liver of unknown specific cause. It may result from viral infections, autoimmune disorders, or prolonged exposure to toxins. Common synonyms include chronic liver inflammation and undetermined chronic hepatitis. Known causative agents include hepatitis B and C viruses, alcohol, medications, and autoimmune conditions. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential systemic involvement in severe cases. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and hepatic dysfunction. Diagnosis often involves blood tests and imaging.

Chronic persistent hepatitis refers to a long-term inflammatory condition of the liver characterized by ongoing immune-mediated or viral injury. Common synonyms include chronic active hepatitis and persistent hepatitis. It is most commonly caused by hepatitis B or C viruses, though autoimmune, metabolic, or drug-induced factors may also play a role. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic involvement in severe cases. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes, though many patients are asymptomatic. Prolonged inflammation can lead to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma.

Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic inflammatory liver disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of liver cells. It occurs when the body's immune system mistakenly attacks liver tissue, leading to progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis if untreated. Common synonyms include autoimmune liver disease and autoimmune liver injury. The exact causative agents are unknown, but genetic predisposition and environmental triggers are implicated. The liver is the primary affected organ, with involvement of hepatocytes. It often presents with fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. The condition is more common in women and typically affects individuals in their 20s to 40s.

Other chronic hepatitis refers to persistent liver inflammation not caused by hepatitis B or C viruses. It encompasses various conditions such as autoimmune hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Common synonyms include chronic liver inflammation and persistent hepatitis. Causative agents may include autoimmune factors, long-term alcohol use, metabolic disorders, or medications. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential progression to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or liver failure if untreated.

code_desc: Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
summary: Cirrhosis of the liver is a chronic condition characterized by the replacement of healthy liver tissue with scar tissue, leading to impaired liver function. Common synonyms include hepatic cirrhosis and chronic liver disease. It results from prolonged damage to liver cells, often due to viral hepatitis (B or C), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or autoimmune disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with complications such as portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy commonly occurring. The condition progresses slowly and can lead to liver failure if left untreated.

Biliary cirrhosis is a chronic liver disease characterized by progressive destruction of liver tissue due to long-standing biliary tract damage. It results from prolonged obstruction or inflammation of bile ducts, leading to fibrosis and eventual cirrhosis. Common synonyms include primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) and secondary biliary cirrhosis. The primary causative agent in PBC is an autoimmune process, while secondary forms result from obstructive causes such as gallstones or strictures. The liver is the main affected organ, with potential complications including portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy.

Other chronic nonalcoholic liver disease refers to a group of liver disorders not caused by alcohol or viral hepatitis. Common synonyms include nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Causative agents often involve metabolic factors such as obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes. The primary affected body part is the liver, which may progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or liver failure. It is typically associated with systemic metabolic syndrome and can lead to complications such as portal hypertension and hepatocellular carcinoma.

code_desc: Unspecified chronic liver disease without mention of alcohol
summary: Unspecified chronic liver disease without mention of alcohol refers to long-term liver damage of unknown specific cause, excluding alcohol-related etiologies. Common synonyms include chronic liver disease, unspecified. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis, autoimmune disorders, metabolic conditions, or environmental toxins. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic complications such as ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and portal hypertension. Diagnosis is often made when specific liver disease classifications are not applicable or documented. It is a broad category used when the exact pathophysiology remains undetermined.

code_desc: Liver abscess and sequelae of chronic liver disease
summary: Liver abscess is a localized collection of pus within the liver, often resulting from bacterial infection, though amoebic or fungal causes may also occur. It may develop as a complication of chronic liver disease, such as cirrhosis, leading to sequelae like portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, *Staphylococcus*, and *Entamoeba histolytica*. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential spread to adjacent structures or systemic involvement. Chronic liver disease sequelae affect the entire liver and may involve the gastrointestinal tract, cardiovascular system, and central nervous system.

An abscess of the liver is a localized collection of pus within the hepatic parenchyma, typically resulting from bacterial infection. Common synonyms include hepatic abscess and pyogenic liver abscess. The most common causative agents are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species, and Bacteroides, often originating from contiguous spread from the biliary tract, hematogenous dissemination, or trauma. The condition most frequently affects the right lobe of the liver, though it can occur in any lobule. Symptoms include fever, right upper quadrant pain, and systemic signs of infection. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by imaging studies such as ultrasound or CT scan.

Portal pyemia is a rare, life-threatening infection characterized by the spread of pyogenic bacteria from a distant source to the liver via the portal venous system. Common synonyms include hepatic pyemia and portal septicemia. It is most frequently caused by gram-negative bacilli such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella species, though other organisms like Staphylococcus aureus may also be involved. The condition typically affects the liver, leading to abscess formation, and is often associated with underlying conditions like diabetes, alcoholism, or immunosuppression. The infection may present with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and systemic signs of sepsis. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical for favorable outcomes.

Hepatic encephalopathy is a neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by liver dysfunction, leading to impaired detoxification of ammonia and other toxins. It results in altered mental status, ranging from subtle cognitive changes to coma. Common synonyms include hepatic coma and portosystemic encephalopathy. Causative agents include cirrhosis, hepatitis, and portal hypertension. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, with liver being the main organ involved. It is often associated with gastrointestinal bleeding, infections, or electrolyte imbalances.

Portal hypertension is elevated pressure in the portal venous system, primarily due to obstruction of blood flow from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver. Common synonyms include portal venous hypertension and portal system hypertension. It is most commonly caused by cirrhosis, but can also result from thrombosis, schistosomiasis, or congenital anomalies. The condition typically affects the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract, leading to complications such as esophageal varices, ascites, and splenomegaly. The increased pressure can cause collateral circulation and portal-systemic shunting.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional renal failure occurring in advanced liver disease, particularly cirrhosis. It is characterized by progressive renal dysfunction without intrinsic kidney disease. Common synonyms include hepatorenal failure and cirrhosis-associated renal failure. Causative agents are primarily liver-related, such as viral hepatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, and Budd-Chiari syndrome. The condition predominantly affects the liver and kidneys, with systemic vasodilation and altered hemodynamics playing key roles in pathogenesis. It is a life-threatening complication with high mortality.

code_desc: Other sequelae of chronic liver disease
summary: Other sequelae of chronic liver disease refer to complications arising from long-term liver damage, such as cirrhosis. Common synonyms include liver failure complications and advanced liver disease manifestations. Causative agents include hepatitis viruses, alcohol, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. These sequelae typically affect the liver, circulatory system, and gastrointestinal tract, leading to portal hypertension, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. They may also impact coagulation, immune function, and metabolic processes.

Other disorders of liver encompass a range of conditions affecting liver function and structure, not classified as specific liver diseases. Common synonyms include hepatic dysfunction and generalized liver disease. Causative agents may include toxins, infections, autoimmune factors, and metabolic disorders. These conditions typically affect the liver, sometimes involving the biliary system and gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms may include jaundice, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. Diagnosis often involves blood tests, imaging, and sometimes liver biopsy. Treatment varies depending on the underlying cause and severity.

Chronic passive congestion of the liver, also known as congestive hepatopathy or hepatic venous congestion, results from prolonged impairment of hepatic venous outflow, leading to increased sinusoidal pressure and tissue damage. Common causes include right-sided heart failure, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and portal hypertension. The condition primarily affects the liver, causing enlargement, fibrosis, and impaired function. It may also lead to ascites and systemic symptoms such as fatigue and jaundice. The right lobe is typically more affected due to its anatomical vulnerability to venous backpressure.

code_desc: Hepatitis in viral diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Hepatitis in viral diseases classified elsewhere refers to liver inflammation caused by viruses not specifically categorized under major hepatitis classifications like hepatitis A, B, or C. Common synonyms include viral hepatitis of unspecified type. Causative agents may include adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and others. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic involvement can occur. Symptoms typically include jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis often requires serological testing and imaging. This condition is frequently encountered in immunocompromised individuals or those with concurrent infections.

code_desc: Hepatitis in other infectious diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Hepatitis in other infectious diseases classified elsewhere refers to liver inflammation occurring as a complication of infectious diseases not otherwise specified. It may result from systemic infections affecting the liver secondarily. Common synonyms include hepatitis associated with other infections. Causative agents vary but may include viruses, bacteria, or parasites. Typically, the liver is affected, with possible involvement of other organs. This condition is often managed by addressing the underlying infection.

Hepatitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the liver of unknown etiology. It may present with symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Common synonyms include viral hepatitis and acute hepatitis. Causative agents can include viruses like hepatitis A, B, or C, as well as alcohol, drugs, or autoimmune factors. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Diagnosis often requires blood tests and imaging. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and severity of the condition.

Hepatic infarction is a rare condition characterized by the death of liver tissue due to arterial occlusion, leading to localized necrosis. It is often caused by emboli from cardiac sources, such as atrial fibrillation, or thrombosis within the hepatic artery. Common synonyms include hepatic arterial thrombosis and hepatic infarct. The condition primarily affects the liver, with infarcts typically occurring in the right lobe. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, and elevated liver enzymes. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications.

Hepatopulmonary syndrome is a condition characterized by abnormal gas exchange due to intrapulmonary shunting caused by portopulmonary vasodilation. It typically occurs in patients with advanced liver disease, particularly cirrhosis. Common synonyms include portopulmonary hypertension and hepatic pulmonary syndrome. Causative agents are primarily liver diseases leading to portal hypertension, such as alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis B/C, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis. The syndrome predominantly affects the lungs and liver, with clinical manifestations including hypoxemia and cyanosis.

Other specified disorders of liver refer to liver conditions that do not meet the full criteria for specific liver diseases but involve abnormal liver function or structure. Common synonyms include unspecified liver dysfunction or non-classifiable liver disorders. Causative agents may include toxins, medications, infections, or metabolic factors. These disorders typically affect the liver parenchyma, leading to impaired function, jaundice, and systemic symptoms. They are often diagnosed when other liver diseases are excluded.

Unspecified disorder of liver refers to a broad category of liver conditions that do not fit specific diagnostic criteria. It may encompass various liver pathologies such as hepatitis, cirrhosis, or metabolic disorders when the exact cause is unknown or not specified. Common synonyms include undiagnosed liver disease or non-specific liver dysfunction. Causative agents may include viral infections, alcohol abuse, toxins, or autoimmune factors. Typically affects the liver, with potential involvement of the biliary system and systemic complications. Diagnosis often requires further testing to identify underlying causes.

Cholelithiasis refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder. Common synonyms include choleliths or gallstone disease. It is primarily caused by supersaturation of bile with cholesterol, bilirubin, or calcium salts, leading to crystal formation and stone development. The gallbladder is the most commonly affected organ, though stones may also occur in the bile ducts. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, female sex, and a family history. Symptoms may include biliary colic, jaundice, or cholecystitis, depending on stone migration and obstruction.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis is an inflammatory condition of the gallbladder caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis with cholecystitis and acute calculous cholecystitis. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or pigment stones. It typically affects the gallbladder, often leading to pain in the right upper quadrant, fever, and leukocytosis. Complications may include perforation, gangrene, or sepsis if untreated.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis, without mention of obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis refers to inflammation of the gallbladder due to the presence of gallstones, typically cholesterol or bilirubin stones. It is characterized by pain in the right upper quadrant, fever, and leukocytosis. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with acute cholecystitis and calculous cholecystitis. The primary causative agents are cholesterol and bilirubin stones. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder, with potential involvement of surrounding structures if complications arise. It is more common in females, particularly those over 40 years of age.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis, with obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis and obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) in the gallbladder leading to inflammation and blockage of the cystic duct. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with acute cholecystitis and biliary obstruction. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or bilirubin stones. This condition typically affects the gallbladder and can lead to complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis. It is most commonly seen in adults, particularly those with a history of obesity, rapid weight loss, or a family history of gallstones.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) accompanied by inflammation of the gallbladder (cholecystitis). Common synonyms include gallstone disease with gallbladder inflammation or calculous cholecystitis. The condition is primarily caused by cholesterol or bilirubin stones, leading to obstruction of bile flow. It typically affects the gallbladder, with complications such as infection, perforation, or abscess formation. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, and a family history of gallstones. The most commonly affected body part is the gallbladder, with potential spread to adjacent structures like the liver or bile ducts.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis, without mention of obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder accompanied by inflammation, without evidence of bile duct obstruction. This condition typically affects the gallbladder, with inflammation involving the gallbladder wall. It is more common in females, particularly those over 40 years of age, and is associated with factors such as obesity, rapid weight loss, and a family history of gallstones.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis, with obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis, with obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones (calculi) in the gallbladder causing inflammation and blockage of the bile ducts. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis with cholecystitis and biliary obstruction. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or bilirubin stones. This condition typically affects the gallbladder and bile ducts, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and jaundice. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and can progress to complications like cholangitis or pancreatitis if left untreated.

The condition typically affects the gallbladder, with stones sometimes migrating into the common bile duct. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, and a family history of gallstones. Causative agents involve imbalances in bile composition, leading to precipitation and aggregation of bile components. The gallbladder is the most commonly affected body part.

The gallbladder is the primarily affected body part, with potential extension to the bile ducts. This condition may lead to biliary colic or, if untreated, progression to cholecystitis or cholangitis.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with acute cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of bile duct with acute cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the bile ducts accompanied by acute inflammation of the gallbladder. It primarily affects the gallbladder and bile ducts, often resulting in severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, and a history of gallstones. Complications may include cholangitis, pancreatitis, or sepsis if left untreated.

Other disorders of gallbladder encompass a range of conditions affecting gallbladder function and structure beyond gallstones and cholecystitis. Common synonyms include biliary dyskinesia and gallbladder dysfunction. These disorders may result from neurohormonal imbalances, motility issues, or inflammation. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving dietary habits, obesity, and genetic predisposition. Typically affected body parts include the gallbladder and associated bile ducts. Symptoms often include epigastric pain, bloating, and postprandial discomfort. Diagnosis may involve imaging and functional tests.

Acute cholecystitis is an acute inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct, leading to bacterial infection. Common synonyms include acute gallbladder inflammation. The primary causative agent is *Escherichia coli*, though other bacteria such as *Klebsiella* and *Bacteroides* may also be involved. The condition typically affects the gallbladder, with associated symptoms including right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea. It often occurs in individuals with a history of gallstones and may lead to complications such as gangrene or perforation if untreated.

Other cholecystitis refers to inflammation of the gallbladder not classified as acute or chronic calculous cholecystitis. It encompasses a range of non-calculous inflammatory conditions. Common synonyms include non-calculous cholecystitis and aseptic cholecystitis. Causative agents may include infections such as *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, or *Staphylococcus*, as well as ischemia, trauma, or prolonged fasting. The gallbladder is the primarily affected organ, with symptoms typically including right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea. It is less common than calculous forms but can occur in patients with gallbladder dysfunction or systemic illness.

Cholecystitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the gallbladder without a specific etiology. It is commonly caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct, leading to bile stasis and infection. Other causes may include bacterial invasion, ischemia, or trauma. The condition typically affects the gallbladder, with symptoms such as right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea. Synonyms include acute cholecystitis and chronic cholecystitis, though the latter is less commonly used. The primary affected body part is the gallbladder, with potential involvement of surrounding structures in severe cases.

Chronic cholecystitis is a long-term inflammation of the gallbladder, typically resulting from recurrent episodes of acute cholecystitis. It is most commonly caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct, leading to persistent irritation and fibrosis. Synonyms include chronic gallbladder disease or chronic calculous cholecystitis. The gallbladder is the primary affected organ, with symptoms such as right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and indigestion. Complications may include gallbladder wall thickening, stone formation, or perforation. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, and a history of gallstones.

Acute and chronic cholecystitis are inflammatory conditions of the gallbladder, primarily caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct, leading to bacterial infection. Acute cholecystitis presents with sudden onset of right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis, while chronic cholecystitis involves long-standing inflammation, often with gallstones and fibrosis. Common synonyms include gallbladder inflammation and biliary infection. Causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Bacteroides*. The gallbladder is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the bile ducts.

Obstruction of the gallbladder refers to the blockage of the cystic duct or bile duct, preventing the normal flow of bile. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis and biliary obstruction. The most frequent causative agent is gallstones, which can block the ducts. This condition typically affects the gallbladder and surrounding biliary system, leading to symptoms such as pain, inflammation, and potential complications like cholecystitis or pancreatitis. It is most commonly seen in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen.

Hydrops of the gallbladder, also known as gallbladder hydrops or acalculous gallbladder disease, is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fluid within the gallbladder wall, leading to distension. It is often associated with chronic cholecystitis or biliary tract obstruction. Common causative agents include infection, inflammation, or obstruction of the cystic duct. The gallbladder is typically affected, with the wall becoming thickened and edematous. This condition may present with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and sometimes fever. It is more commonly seen in elderly patients or those with underlying biliary disease.

Perforation of the gallbladder is a serious complication of cholecystitis, often resulting from prolonged inflammation and pressure. It occurs when the gallbladder wall ruptures, leading to leakage of bile into the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include gallbladder rupture and empyema of the gallbladder. Causative agents include gallstones, infection, and trauma. The condition typically affects the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, with potential spread to the peritoneum, causing sepsis if untreated. Prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention are critical to prevent mortality.

Fistula of gallbladder, also known as cholecystoenteric fistula, is an abnormal connection between the gallbladder and another hollow organ, most commonly the small intestine. It typically results from chronic cholecystitis or gallstone disease leading to erosion of the gallbladder wall. Common causative agents include bacterial infections, particularly those associated with ascending cholangitis. The condition predominantly affects the duodenum and jejunum, and may present with symptoms such as biliary leakage, recurrent cholangitis, or malabsorption. Diagnosis is often confirmed through imaging studies and endoscopic evaluation.

Cholesterolosis of the gallbladder is a benign condition characterized by the accumulation of cholesterol in the gallbladder wall, leading to the formation of yellowish cholesterol deposits. It is often associated with chronic gallbladder disease and is not typically linked to cholesterol gallstones. Common synonyms include cholesterol granuloma and cholesterol polyps. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder, with the mucosa and muscular layers being the most commonly involved areas. It is more prevalent in females and is often found in conjunction with gallstones. The exact causative agents are not well defined, but prolonged bile stasis and chronic inflammation are considered contributing factors.

Other specified disorders of gallbladder refer to gallbladder conditions that do not meet the criteria for specific gallbladder diseases such as cholecystitis or gallstones. Common synonyms include unspecified gallbladder dysfunction or nonspecific gallbladder disease. These disorders may arise from chronic inflammation, functional impairment, or idiopathic causes. They typically affect the gallbladder itself, with symptoms such as pain, distension, or altered bile flow. Causative agents may include prolonged biliary stasis, dietary factors, or systemic conditions affecting bile metabolism. The gallbladder is the primary affected body part.

Unspecified disorder of gallbladder refers to gallbladder dysfunction or pathology not clearly categorized under specific diagnoses such as cholecystitis or gallstones. Common synonyms include nonspecific gallbladder disease or functional gallbladder disorder. Causative agents may include infections, inflammation, or functional abnormalities. This condition typically affects the gallbladder, sometimes involving the biliary tract. It is often diagnosed when symptoms persist without a clear identifiable cause, leading to chronic discomfort and altered gallbladder function.

Other disorders of biliary tract encompass a group of conditions affecting the gallbladder and bile ducts, excluding gallstones and strictures. Common synonyms include biliary dyskinesia and biliary tract dysfunction. These disorders may result from inflammation, motility issues, or functional abnormalities. Causative agents can include infections, autoimmune processes, or metabolic factors. Typically affecting the gallbladder, bile ducts, and liver, these conditions often present with symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and jaundice. Diagnosis may involve imaging and biochemical tests. Treatment varies from lifestyle changes to pharmacologic or surgical intervention.

Postcholecystectomy syndrome refers to a collection of symptoms occurring after gallbladder removal, typically including abdominal pain, bloating, and digestive discomfort. Common synonyms include post-cholecystectomy syndrome and post-gallbladder removal syndrome. Causative agents may include bile duct stones, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, or gastrointestinal motility disorders. The condition primarily affects the biliary and gastrointestinal tracts, particularly the liver, bile ducts, and intestines. It is most commonly seen in individuals who had a history of gallstones or cholecystitis.

Cholangitis is an inflammatory condition of the bile ducts, typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, or *Enterococcus*. It often results from obstruction, such as gallstones or strictures, leading to ascending infection. The condition primarily affects the bile ducts, including the common hepatic duct and common bile duct. Symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. It is also known as ascending cholangitis or obstructive cholangitis. Prompt treatment with antibiotics and drainage is essential to prevent complications like sepsis or liver damage.

Obstruction of the bile duct refers to the blockage of any segment of the biliary tract, preventing the normal flow of bile from the liver to the small intestine. Common synonyms include biliary obstruction and choledocholithiasis. Causative agents include gallstones, tumors, strictures, or inflammation. This condition typically affects the common bile duct, hepatic ducts, or intrahepatic bile ducts. Symptoms may include jaundice, pruritus, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes. If left untreated, it can lead to cholangitis, liver damage, or pancreatitis.

Perforation of the bile duct is a serious complication characterized by a rupture in the bile duct wall, leading to leakage of bile into the peritoneal cavity. Common synonyms include bile duct rupture or cholangial perforation. It is often caused by trauma, instrumentation during procedures like endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), or severe biliary tract infections such as cholangitis. The condition typically affects the common bile duct and may occur in the context of stones, tumors, or inflammatory conditions. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, sepsis, and signs of peritonitis. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent life-threatening complications.

Fistula of the bile duct, also known as biliary fistula, is an abnormal passage connecting the bile duct to another organ or structure. It commonly results from inflammation, infection, or trauma, with cholangitis and postoperative complications being frequent causes. The condition typically affects the liver, gallbladder, and adjacent structures such as the duodenum or stomach. Symptoms may include bile leakage, infection, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies like ultrasound or CT scan, and treatment may involve surgical repair or drainage.

Spasm of the sphincter of Oddi is a condition characterized by abnormal contraction of the muscle at the distal end of the common bile duct, leading to obstruction and pain. Common synonyms include biliary spasm and sphincter of Oddi dysfunction. It is often caused by gallstones, cholecystitis, or biliary tract infections. The condition primarily affects the bile ducts and gallbladder, causing right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and sometimes jaundice. It may occur in patients with a history of biliary disease or after biliary procedures. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging and manometry.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of biliary tract
summary: "Other specified disorders of biliary tract" refers to biliary conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as gallstones or cholangitis. Common synonyms include unspecified biliary disease or miscellaneous biliary disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., *Escherichia coli*, *Clostridium perfringens*), metabolic factors, or structural abnormalities. These disorders typically affect the gallbladder, bile ducts, and liver, causing symptoms like pain, jaundice, and inflammation. They are often diagnosed when specific etiologies are unclear or when symptoms do not fit established classifications.

Unspecified disorder of the biliary tract refers to a broad category of conditions affecting the gallbladder and bile ducts when the specific diagnosis is not determined. Common synonyms include biliary tract dysfunction or non-specific biliary disease. Causative agents may include gallstones, infections, or inflammatory processes. Typically, the gallbladder, common bile duct, and liver are affected. Symptoms often involve pain, jaundice, and digestive issues. Diagnosis is usually made after ruling out more specific conditions. This term is used when clinical findings are inconclusive or when the exact cause remains undetermined.

Diseases of the pancreas encompass a range of conditions affecting this gland's exocrine and endocrine functions. Common synonyms include pancreatic disorders, pancreatitis, and pancreatic insufficiency. Causative agents vary, including alcohol, gallstones, infections (e.g., mumps, tuberculosis), autoimmune factors, and genetic mutations. These conditions primarily affect the pancreas, with potential complications involving the digestive tract, liver, and endocrine system. Acute and chronic pancreatitis are the most common forms, often leading to inflammation, enzyme dysfunction, and diabetes mellitus.

Acute pancreatitis is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas, often characterized by severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Common synonyms include acute pancreatic inflammation or acute pancreatopathy. Causative agents include gallstones, alcohol use, hypertriglyceridemia, and medications. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of surrounding structures such as the bile duct, stomach, and intestines. Complications may include fluid accumulation, pseudocysts, and systemic inflammation. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment.

Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disorder of the pancreas leading to irreversible structural damage and impaired function. Common synonyms include chronic pancreatopathy and fibrocalculous pancreatitis. It is often caused by long-term alcohol abuse, gallstones, genetic mutations (e.g., CFTR, SPINK1), or autoimmune factors. The condition primarily affects the exocrine and endocrine pancreas, resulting in malabsorption, diabetes mellitus, and pain. Complications may include pancreatic duct obstruction, pseudocysts, and chronic pain. It predominantly involves the pancreas, with potential extension to adjacent organs.

Cyst and pseudocyst of the pancreas refer to fluid-filled lesions in the pancreas, with pseudocysts being more common. Cysts are typically benign, while pseudocysts often result from pancreatitis. Common synonyms include pancreatic pseudocyst and pancreatic cyst. Causative agents include chronic pancreatitis, trauma, or post-operative complications. These lesions are typically found in the head or body of the pancreas. They may present with abdominal pain, jaundice, or obstruction. Diagnosis is often made via imaging studies such as CT or MRI. Management may involve drainage or surgical intervention depending on size and symptoms.

"Other specified diseases of pancreas" refers to pancreatic conditions not classified under more specific categories such as pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer. Common synonyms include unspecified pancreatic disorders or miscellaneous pancreatic diseases. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viral, fungal), autoimmune processes, or metabolic factors. These conditions typically affect the exocrine or endocrine pancreas, leading to dysfunction, inflammation, or structural abnormalities. They are often diagnosed when the etiology or clinical presentation does not fit established classifications.

Unspecified disease of pancreas refers to pancreatic conditions that do not meet the criteria for specific diagnosed disorders. It may encompass a range of inflammatory, degenerative, or neoplastic processes. Common synonyms include undifferentiated pancreatic disease or unspecified pancreatic disorder. Causative agents are often unknown but may include infections, autoimmune factors, or metabolic disturbances. Typically affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of adjacent structures such as the bile ducts or duodenum. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is usually made when specific etiologies are excluded.

Gastrointestinal hemorrhage refers to bleeding within the digestive tract, which can be acute or chronic. Common synonyms include upper gastrointestinal bleeding and lower gastrointestinal bleeding. It is caused by a variety of factors such as peptic ulcers, esophageal varices, diverticulosis, and malignancies. The condition typically affects the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine. Symptoms may include hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and imaging studies. Prompt evaluation is crucial to determine the source and severity of bleeding.

Hematemesis is the vomiting of blood, typically from the upper gastrointestinal tract. It may appear as bright red blood or as coffee-ground material. Common causes include peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, esophageal varices, and Mallory-Weiss tears. Other synonyms include hematemesis and hematochezia, though the latter refers to rectal bleeding. The condition primarily affects the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt evaluation to identify the source and manage complications such as hypovolemic shock.

Blood in stool, also known as hematochezia or melena, refers to the presence of blood in feces. Hematochezia indicates bright red blood, often from the lower gastrointestinal tract, while melena suggests darker, digested blood from higher in the tract. Common causes include hemorrhoids, anal fissures, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and colorectal cancer. The rectum, colon, and anus are typically affected. It may also result from gastrointestinal ulcers or vascular abnormalities. Prompt evaluation is essential to determine the source and underlying condition.

Hemorrhage of the gastrointestinal tract, unspecified, refers to acute or chronic bleeding from any part of the digestive system without specific localization. Common synonyms include gastrointestinal bleeding or GI hemorrhage. Causative agents may include peptic ulcers, esophageal varices, gastritis, diverticulosis, or malignancies. Typically affects the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, or large intestine. Symptoms often include hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia. Diagnosis usually involves endoscopy, imaging, or laboratory tests to determine source and severity.

Intestinal malabsorption is a condition characterized by impaired absorption of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to deficiencies and gastrointestinal symptoms. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and defective nutrient absorption. It can result from various causes such as celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, tropical sprue, and pancreatic insufficiency. The small intestine, particularly the proximal sections, is typically affected. Symptoms include diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. Diagnosis often involves stool tests, imaging, and biopsy. Treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause and nutritional support.

Celiac disease is a chronic autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals. It causes inflammation and damage to the small intestine's lining, impairing nutrient absorption. Common synonyms include celiac sprue and gluten-sensitive enteropathy. The primary causative agent is gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. The small intestine is predominantly affected, particularly the villi, leading to malabsorption and various systemic complications.

Tropical sprue is a malabsorption disorder primarily affecting the small intestine, particularly the jejunum. It is characterized by chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. Common synonyms include tropical enteropathy and tropical malabsorption. The exact cause is not fully understood, but it is associated with bacterial overgrowth, particularly *Bacteroides* species, and environmental factors. It is endemic in tropical regions and typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, leading to impaired absorption of nutrients such as folate, vitamin B12, and fat-soluble vitamins.

Blind loop syndrome is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by the presence of a dilated, nonfunctioning segment of intestine, often due to surgical resection or adhesions. This leads to impaired motility, bacterial overgrowth, and malabsorption. Common synonyms include postgastrectomy syndrome and intestinal stasis. Causative agents include prior abdominal surgery, particularly gastric resection, and chronic constipation. It typically affects the small intestine, especially the jejunum and ileum, and can cause symptoms such as diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies.

Other and unspecified postsurgical nonabsorption refers to the failure of surgical materials or substances to be absorbed by the body following surgery. This condition may occur with implants, sutures, or other foreign bodies. Common synonyms include postsurgical foreign body nonabsorption and implant nonabsorption. Causative agents may include non-absorbable sutures, synthetic implants, or foreign bodies. It typically affects sites such as the abdominal cavity, skin, or orthopedic regions. Symptoms may include inflammation, infection, or granuloma formation. The condition is often managed with surgical removal or anti-inflammatory treatment.

Pancreatic steatorrhea is a condition characterized by the presence of excess fat in feces due to impaired pancreatic enzyme secretion, typically resulting from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Common synonyms include fat malabsorption and steatorrhea. It is most commonly caused by chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or pancreatic cancer. The primary affected body parts are the pancreas and the gastrointestinal tract, with symptoms including bulky, foul-smelling stools, weight loss, and abdominal discomfort.
