Typically, the aorta is affected, with involvement of the ascending aorta and aortic valve, leading to complications such as regurgitation and aneurysm formation.

Other cardiovascular syphilis refers to syphilitic involvement of the heart and great vessels beyond the classic aortic aneurysm and aortitis. It encompasses conditions such as syphilitic myocarditis, pericarditis, and coronary artery aneurysms. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically affects the aorta, mitral valve, and coronary arteries. Synonyms include syphilitic heart disease and cardiovascular syphilis. The condition is rare and often presents with nonspecific symptoms, making early diagnosis challenging. It is associated with late-stage syphilis and can lead to severe cardiovascular complications if untreated.

Cardiovascular and cerebrovascular syphilis refers to late-stage complications of syphilis affecting the heart and blood vessels. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically presents 10–30 years after initial infection. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and cardiovascular syphilis. The condition primarily involves aortic aneurysms, aortitis, and arterial occlusions, leading to hypertension and peripheral artery disease. It may also cause gummas and meningovascular syphilis, affecting the central nervous system. Diagnosis often requires serological testing and imaging. Early treatment with penicillin is critical to prevent irreversible damage.

Symptomatic neurosyphilis unspecified refers to central nervous system involvement in syphilis without a specific clinical classification. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis, unspecified type, or late-stage neurosyphilis. The condition typically affects the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as headache, cognitive decline, motor dysfunction, and sensory disturbances. It may present as meningitis, myelopathy, or parenchymal disease, often in individuals with a history of untreated or inadequately treated syphilis.

Tabes dorsalis is a late-stage complication of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It results from neurosyphilis affecting the spinal cord, leading to degeneration of the posterior columns and dorsal roots. Common synonyms include syphilitic myelopathy and tabes. Clinical features include sensory ataxia, loss of reflexes, bladder dysfunction, and pain. The condition primarily affects the spinal cord, particularly the thoracic and lumbar regions, and may involve the peripheral nerves and cranial nerves. It typically occurs in untreated syphilis cases years after the initial infection.

Other cerebrospinal syphilis refers to late-stage neurosyphilis characterized by inflammation of the central nervous system. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and typically presents with symptoms such as meningitis, myelitis, or parenchymal brain lesions. Common synonyms include tabes dorsalis and general paresis. The condition primarily affects the spinal cord, brain, and meninges, leading to neurological deficits such as motor weakness, sensory loss, and cognitive decline. It is a rare but serious complication of untreated syphilis, often occurring years after the initial infection. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent irreversible damage.

Late syphilitic meningitis is a rare, chronic central nervous system complication of untreated syphilis, occurring years after primary infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it results from immune-mediated inflammation of the meninges. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis meningitis or tertiary syphilitic meningitis. The condition typically affects the brain and spinal cord, leading to symptoms such as headache, seizures, and cognitive decline. It is more common in individuals with a history of syphilis who have not received adequate treatment. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical to prevent severe neurological damage.

Late syphilitic encephalitis is a neurological complication of untreated syphilis, occurring years after primary infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it results from systemic dissemination of the spirochete to the central nervous system. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and late-stage neurosyphilis. The condition typically affects the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to inflammation and demyelination. Symptoms may include headache, seizures, cognitive decline, and motor dysfunction. It is a rare but severe manifestation of late-stage syphilis, often seen in individuals with a history of untreated infection.

Late syphilitic neuropathy is a neurological complication of untreated or inadequately treated syphilis, occurring years after the initial infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it results from tertiary syphilis and involves progressive damage to the central and peripheral nervous systems. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and tertiary syphilitic neuropathy. The condition typically affects the spinal cord, brain, and cranial nerves, leading to symptoms such as sensory loss, motor deficits, and cognitive decline. It is a serious manifestation requiring prompt diagnosis and antimicrobial therapy.

Charcôt's arthropathy, also known as tabetic arthropathy, is a neurogenic joint degeneration associated with syphilis. It results from progressive destruction of joints and bones due to loss of proprioception and reduced protective reflexes. Commonly affects the feet and hands, leading to joint dislocations, deformities, and bone fragmentation. Causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. Synonyms include neuroarthropathy and tabes dorsalis arthropathy. Typically occurs in late-stage syphilis, often in the lower extremities. Characterized by painless, progressive joint damage with minimal inflammation.

General paresis, also known as general paresis of the insane or neurosyphilis, is a late-stage complication of untreated syphilis. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it affects the central nervous system, leading to progressive motor and cognitive deficits. Common symptoms include personality changes, dementia, motor weakness, and psychiatric disturbances. The condition primarily impacts the brain and spinal cord, often resulting in severe disability. It typically occurs years after the initial syphilis infection and is associated with neurologic and psychiatric manifestations. Early treatment with penicillin can prevent progression, but damage may be irreversible once established.

Other symptomatic neurosyphilis refers to neurological complications arising from syphilis in individuals who are not in the tertiary stage of the disease. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and typically affects the central nervous system. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and symptomatic neurosyphilis. The condition may present with meningitis, myelopathy, or cranial neuropathies. It often occurs in the late latent or early tertiary stages and can lead to severe neurological deficits if untreated. Symptoms may include headache, motor dysfunction, and sensory loss. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent irreversible damage.

Symptomatic neurosyphilis is a late-stage complication of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum* infection of the central nervous system. It occurs in approximately 10-15% of untreated syphilis cases. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and tertiary syphilis affecting the nervous system. The condition typically presents with meningovascular, tabes dorsalis, or general paresis manifestations. Commonly affected areas include the brain, spinal cord, meninges, and peripheral nerves, leading to symptoms such as headache, dementia, motor deficits, and sensory loss. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent irreversible neurological damage.

Asymptomatic neurosyphilis is a stage of syphilis where the infection affects the central nervous system without producing noticeable symptoms. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. Common synonyms include latent neurosyphilis or asymptomatic cerebral syphilis. The condition typically involves the brain and spinal cord, leading to potential long-term neurological complications if left untreated. It often occurs in the late stages of syphilis and may be detected through cerebrospinal fluid analysis or imaging studies. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent progression.

Neurosyphilis unspecified refers to syphilis affecting the central nervous system without a specified clinical variant. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. Common synonyms include "general paresis" and "tabes dorsalis," though these terms are now less commonly used. The condition typically involves the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to neurological symptoms such as cognitive decline, motor dysfunction, and sensory disturbances. It often occurs in late-stage syphilis and may present with a variety of neurological manifestations. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent irreversible damage.

Late syphilitic oculopathy refers to ocular manifestations occurring in the tertiary stage of syphilis, typically 2–3 years after untreated infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it results from systemic inflammation and immune-mediated damage. Common synonyms include late-stage syphilitic eye disease and tertiary syphilis oculopathy. Affected areas include the optic nerve, retina, choroid, and meninges. Symptoms may present as optic neuropathy, uveitis, retinal granulomas, or chorioretinal scarring. Diagnosis relies on clinical findings, serological tests, and sometimes histopathology. Treatment involves long-term penicillin therapy.

Syphilis of the lung and bronchus is a rare manifestation of tertiary syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically affects individuals with a history of untreated syphilis. The infection leads to granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma and bronchial walls. Common synonyms include pulmonary syphilis and bronchial syphilis. The condition primarily involves the lungs and bronchi, occasionally extending to the pleura. Clinical presentation may include chronic cough, hemoptysis, and progressive dyspnea. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing and histopathological examination.

code_desc: Symptomatic late syphilis of other respiratory organs
summary: Symptomatic late syphilis of other respiratory organs refers to the manifestation of tertiary syphilis affecting the respiratory system, typically years after initial infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it may present as granulomatous inflammation or ulceration in the larynx, trachea, or bronchi. Common synonyms include respiratory syphilis or syphilitic tracheobronchitis. This condition is rare and often associated with late-stage disease, characterized by progressive tissue destruction and potential airway obstruction. It is more prevalent in individuals with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis.

code_desc: Syphilis of liver and other viscera
summary: Syphilis of liver and other viscera refers to involvement of internal organs by the treponemal spirochete *Treponema pallidum* in the tertiary stage of syphilis. It is a rare manifestation characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the liver, spleen, and other viscera. Synonyms include visceral syphilis and hepatosplenic syphilis. code_desc: Sexually transmitted chlamydial infection of other sites
summary: Sexually transmitted chlamydial infection of other sites refers to infection caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting areas other than the genital tract, such as the eyes, lungs, or throat. Common synonyms include ocular chlamydial infection and respiratory chlamydiosis. The bacterium is transmitted through sexual contact or from mother to infant. It commonly affects the conjunctiva, causing trachoma, and the respiratory tract in newborns, leading to pneumonia. Symptoms may include conjunctivitis, cough, and respiratory distress. Diagnosis involves nucleic acid amplification tests, and treatment typically involves antibiotics like azithromycin or doxycycline.

Chancroid is a bacterial infection characterized by painful genital ulcers, primarily affecting the genital area. Caused by *Haemophilus ducreyi*, it is commonly referred to as soft chancre or granuloma inguinale. The infection typically presents with one or more tender, suppurative ulcers with a granular base, often accompanied by inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is more prevalent in regions with limited access to healthcare and is often associated with other sexually transmitted infections. The condition is transmitted through direct sexual contact and is more common in men than women.

Granuloma inguinale, also known as donovanosis, is a chronic bacterial infection characterized by painless, ulcerative lesions primarily affecting the genital area. Caused by *Klebsiella granulomatis* (formerly *Calymmatobacterium granulomatis*), it leads to granulomatous inflammation and tissue destruction. Commonly seen in tropical regions, the infection typically involves the perineum, penis, and vulva, with lesions progressing to nodular, beefy-red ulcers. Systemic spread is rare, but complications such as lymphadenopathy and scarring may occur if untreated.

Urogenital trichomoniasis unspecified refers to an infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis* affecting the urogenital tract. It is characterized by inflammation and discharge in the genital area. Common synonyms include trichomonal infection and trichomoniasis. The causative agent is the protozoan *Trichomonas vaginalis*. The condition typically affects the vagina, urethra, and sometimes the penis in men. It is more commonly diagnosed in women but can occur in men as well. Symptoms may include itching, burning, and abnormal discharge. Transmission occurs through sexual contact.

Trichomonal vulvovaginitis is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the lower genital tract, including the vagina and vulva in females, and the urethra in males. The infection is characterized by inflammation, itching, burning, and a frothy, malodorous vaginal discharge. Common synonyms include trichomoniasis and vaginitis caused by *T. vaginalis*. It is transmitted through sexual contact and is more prevalent in women, though men can also be asymptomatic carriers. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via microscopy or nucleic acid amplification tests.

Trichomonal prostatitis is a type of prostatitis caused by infection with *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It is less common than bacterial prostatitis but can occur in men who engage in unprotected sexual activity. The infection leads to inflammation of the prostate gland, often accompanied by symptoms such as pelvic pain, dysuria, and urethral discharge. Common synonyms include trichomonal infection of the prostate or trichomoniasis of the prostate. The causative agent is *Trichomonas vaginalis*, a protozoan parasite. The condition primarily affects the prostate gland and may involve the urethra and seminal vesicles.

Trichomonal cystitis and urethritis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the lower genital tract, involving the urethra and bladder. Common synonyms include trichomoniasis. The infection leads to inflammation, characterized by symptoms such as dysuria, urinary frequency, and genital discharge. It is more commonly seen in females, though males can also be affected. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves metronidazole or tinidazole.

Other urogenital trichomoniasis refers to a parasitic infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis*, primarily affecting the urogenital tract. It is commonly known as trichomoniasis or "trich." The infection typically involves the vagina, urethra, and sometimes the bladder in females, and the urethra in males. It is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) characterized by symptoms such as itching, burning, and abnormal discharge. The causative agent, *Trichomonas vaginalis*, is a flagellated protozoan parasite. Transmission occurs through sexual contact, and it is more prevalent in women than men. Diagnosis is often confirmed through microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs).

Urogenital trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the lower genital tract, including the vagina, urethra, and sometimes the prostate in men. Common synonyms include trichomoniasis vaginalis and trichomonad infection. The infection is characterized by inflammation, discharge, and itching. It is more commonly diagnosed in women but can also occur in men. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves metronidazole or tinidazole.

Trichomoniasis of other sites refers to infection caused by *Trichomonas vaginalis* outside the genital tract. Common synonyms include extragenital trichomoniasis. The parasite primarily affects mucosal surfaces, commonly involving the urinary tract, such as the urethra and bladder, and less frequently the rectum. It may also occur in the throat following oral sexual contact. Symptoms include itching, burning, and discharge. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through microscopic examination or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves metronidazole or tinidazole, with sexual partners also requiring treatment to prevent reinfection.

Trichomoniasis unspecified refers to an infection caused by the protozoan parasite *Trichomonas vaginalis*, primarily affecting the genitourinary tract. It commonly presents as a sexually transmitted infection, predominantly in women, though men can also be affected. Symptoms may include itching, burning, and discharge. The condition is often asymptomatic, leading to delayed diagnosis. Common synonyms include trichomonal infection or trichomonad infection. The causative agent is *Trichomonas vaginalis*, and the most frequently affected areas are the vagina, urethra, and urinary tract.

code_desc: Herpesviral infection of urogenital system unspecified
summary: Herpesviral infection of the urogenital system unspecified refers to an infection caused by herpesviruses affecting the genital or urinary tract without specific identification of the viral type. Common synonyms include genital herpes and urinary tract herpes. The causative agents are typically herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and type 2 (HSV-2), though other herpesviruses may occasionally be involved. The infection primarily affects the mucous membranes of the genital area, urethra, and surrounding skin, leading to symptoms such as vesicles, ulcers, and itching.

Herpesviral infection of the penis, commonly known as genital herpes, is a sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 can also be involved. It presents with painful vesicular lesions, often accompanied by itching, burning, and flu-like symptoms. The infection typically affects the penis, scrotum, and surrounding genital areas. Recurrent outbreaks are common, with lesions healing within 2–4 weeks. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact during active lesions or asymptomatic shedding. Complications may include increased risk of HIV transmission and psychological distress.

code_desc: Herpesviral infection of other male genital organs
summary: Herpesviral infection of other male genital organs refers to infection of genital tissues outside the penis, such as the scrotum, groin, or perineum, caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1 or HSV-2. It presents with painful vesicles, ulcers, and erythema. Common synonyms include genital herpes or herpes genitalis. The infection is transmitted through direct contact and can lead to recurrent outbreaks. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and is often associated with sexual activity. Diagnosis is typically clinical, supported by viral culture or PCR. Treatment involves antiviral therapy to reduce symptoms and transmission risk.

Herpesviral cervicitis is an inflammatory condition of the cervix caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-2. It is characterized by painful ulcers, swelling, and exudate. Less frequently, HSV-1 may also be involved. The infection typically affects the lower genital tract, including the cervix, vagina, and vulva. It is often associated with sexual transmission and may present with systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Common synonyms include genital herpes and HSV cervicitis. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with multiple sexual partners.

Herpesviral vulvovaginitis is a genital infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-2, though HSV-1 can also be a cause. It presents with painful vesicular or ulcerative lesions on the vulva and vagina, often accompanied by systemic symptoms like fever and malaise. The condition is highly contagious and recurrent episodes are common due to latent viral reactivation. It primarily affects the vulva, vagina, and surrounding perineal areas. Synonyms include genital herpes and recurrent genital herpes. Complications may include neonatal herpes if transmitted during childbirth.

code_desc: Herpesviral infection of other urogenital tract
summary: Herpesviral infection of the other urogenital tract refers to infection caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1 or HSV-2, affecting areas beyond the genitalia, such as the urethra, bladder, or surrounding tissues. Common synonyms include genital herpes and urinary tract herpes. The infection is characterized by painful ulcers, vesicles, and inflammation. HSV-2 is more commonly associated with urogenital infections, while HSV-1 may also cause lesions in these regions. It is transmitted through direct contact and can lead to recurrent outbreaks. Complications may include urinary retention or secondary bacterial infections.

code_desc: Herpesviral infection of genitalia and urogenital tract
summary: Herpesviral infection of the genitalia and urogenital tract is caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 can also be responsible. It presents as painful vesicular lesions on the genitalia, perianal area, and sometimes the urethra. Common synonyms include genital herpes and recurrent herpes. The infection is characterized by recurrent episodes of ulcerative lesions, with potential complications such as lymphadenopathy, neonatal transmission, and increased risk of HIV acquisition. It is transmitted through direct contact during sexual activity.

code_desc: Herpesviral infection of perianal skin and rectum
summary: Herpesviral infection of the perianal skin and rectum is caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) or type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 is increasingly implicated. It presents as painful, clustered vesicles or ulcers in the anal and perianal regions. Common synonyms include anal herpes and perianal herpes. The infection typically affects the rectal mucosa, perianal skin, and occasionally the genital area. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with sexual risk factors. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected secretions. Complications may include secondary bacterial infections and scarring.

Anogenital herpesviral infection unspecified refers to a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection affecting the anogenital region without specifying the exact type or strain. Common synonyms include genital herpes or anogenital herpes. The primary causative agents are herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and type 2 (HSV-2). This condition typically affects the vulva, penis, perineum, anus, and surrounding areas. It presents with painful vesicles, ulcers, and sometimes systemic symptoms. Transmission occurs through direct contact, and it can recur due to viral latency.

Anogenital (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign, virus-induced growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. They typically appear as small, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like lesions in the anogenital region, including the vulva, vagina, penis, anus, and perianal area. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. The condition is highly contagious and may resolve spontaneously, but treatment is often recommended to prevent spread and complications.

code_desc: Other specified predominantly sexually transmitted diseases
summary: "Other specified predominantly sexually transmitted diseases" refers to infections primarily transmitted through sexual contact that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified or other specified STIs. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, or parasites such as *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, *Chlamydia trachomatis*, or herpes simplex virus. These infections typically affect the genital tract, urinary tract, and mucous membranes, with potential systemic complications if left untreated.

Unspecified sexually transmitted disease (USTD) refers to a sexually transmitted infection (STI) where the specific causative agent is not identified or reported. Common synonyms include undiagnosed or unspecified STI. Causative agents may include a variety of pathogens such as chlamydia, gonorrhea, herpes, or HIV, among others. Typically, USTD affects the genital tract, including the vagina, penis, anus, and mouth. It may also involve the urinary tract and lymph nodes. Symptoms can vary but often include abnormal discharge, itching, pain, or sores. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and screening tests.

Nonvenereal syphilis refers to syphilis acquired through non-sexual means, such as congenital transmission from an infected mother to her fetus. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* subspecies *pallidum*, the same bacterium responsible for venereal syphilis. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis and fetal syphilis. The infection typically affects the skin, bones, and central nervous system, leading to a range of manifestations including rash, bone deformities, and neurologic complications. It can result in severe developmental abnormalities and long-term health issues if untreated.

Initial lesions of yaws are the first clinical manifestations of a chronic bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. These lesions typically appear as painless, firm, and slightly indurated papules or nodules, often on the limbs, especially the lower extremities. Common synonyms include "papular syphilis" and "yaws sores." The infection is endemic in tropical regions and primarily affects children. The lesions may ulcerate and progress to destructive lesions if untreated. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact.

code_desc: Multiple papillomata and wet crab yaws
summary: Multiple papillomata and wet crab yaws is a rare, chronic dermatosis characterized by the presence of multiple papillomatous lesions and ulcers, typically found in tropical regions. It is also known as tropical acantholytic dermatosis or yaws. The condition is caused by the bacterium *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. It primarily affects the skin, especially the lower extremities, and is more common in children. The lesions are often accompanied by itching and may progress to scarring. The disease is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact.

code_desc: Other early skin lesions of yaws
summary: "Other early skin lesions of yaws" refers to the initial skin manifestations of yaws, a tropical infectious disease caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. Common synonyms include "early syphilitic-like lesions" and "macular or papular eruptions." These lesions typically appear on the head, neck, and extremities, presenting as painless, non-itchy macules or papules. They may progress to larger, raised plaques with a rough surface. The condition is endemic in tropical regions and is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent progression to more severe stages.

Hyperkeratosis of yaws is a chronic skin lesion associated with the infectious disease yaws, caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. It manifests as thickened, hyperkeratotic plaques, typically on the lower extremities, especially the shins. Common synonyms include yaws plaque and hyperkeratotic yaws. The condition is prevalent in tropical regions and is characterized by a slow progression, often with a central ulcer and surrounding keratinized tissue. It is distinct from other treponemal infections like syphilis and pinta.

Gummata and ulcers of yaws are chronic skin lesions caused by *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. Characterized by painless, firm nodules (gummata) and ulcerative lesions, they typically appear on the lower extremities, face, and genitalia. Common synonyms include yaws sores and tropical chancre. The disease is endemic in tropical regions and progresses through stages, including an initial inflammatory phase followed by the formation of gummata. Without treatment, it can lead to severe deformities. The condition is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact.

Gangosa, also known as granuloma inguinale, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Klebsiella granulomatis*. It presents as a painless, ulcerative lesion in the genital area, typically affecting the penis, vulva, or perianal region. The infection is characterized by indurated, beefy-red granulomatous lesions that may ulcerate and erode. It is more common in tropical regions and is often associated with poor hygiene or immunocompromised states. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical appearance and confirmed by histopathology or PCR. Treatment typically involves antibiotics such as doxycycline or azithromycin.

code_desc: Bone and joint lesions of yaws
summary: Bone and joint lesions of yaws are a manifestation of the tropical infectious disease yaws, caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. Characterized by destructive bone and joint involvement, these lesions typically present as punched-out lytic lesions in the long bones, pelvis, and skull. Synonyms include syphilis-like bone lesions and tropical syphilis. The disease primarily affects children in endemic regions, with lesions often accompanied by swelling, pain, and deformity. The condition is transmitted through direct skin contact and is part of the group of treponemal infections known as the "great syphilis" group.

Other manifestations of yaws refer to the late-stage complications of the treponemal infection caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. These include destructive lesions on the bones, skin, and mucous membranes, often leading to deformities. Common synonyms include "late yaws" or "syphilis-like lesions." The disease primarily affects the skin, bones, and joints, with characteristic features such as gnarled fingers, saddle nose, and ulcerative lesions. It is endemic in tropical regions and typically occurs in children. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum pertenue*, a spirochete related to the syphilis pathogen.

Latent yaws is a chronic, asymptomatic stage of yaws, a bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum pertenue*. It typically follows the initial acute infection and may persist for years without symptoms. Common synonyms include "inactive yaws" or "quiescent yaws." The disease primarily affects the skin, bones, and joints, leading to destructive lesions and deformities. It is most commonly seen in children in tropical regions. Transmission occurs through direct contact with lesions, and the condition is preventable with penicillin treatment.

Yaws unspecified is a chronic bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. It primarily affects the skin, bones, and joints, often leading to ulcerative lesions and destructive deformities. Common synonyms include "endemic syphilis" and "Finnish yaws." The disease is endemic in tropical regions, particularly among children. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact. Without treatment, it can result in severe disfigurement and disability. The condition is treatable with antibiotics such as penicillin.

Primary lesions of pinta are the initial cutaneous manifestations of the disease, typically appearing as asymptomatic, hypopigmented or erythematous macules or patches. These lesions often have a slight scaling and may develop a verrucous texture over time. Common synonyms include "pinta macules" or "pinta patches." The causative agent is *Treponema carateum*, a spirochete related to *Treponema pallidum*. The disease primarily affects the skin, especially in tropical regions, with lesions commonly found on the extremities, face, and trunk.

Intermediate lesions of pinta are a stage of the chronic skin infection caused by *Treponema carateum*. These lesions appear as reddish, slightly raised patches with a rough, scaly surface, typically on the extremities. They may progress to more severe forms if untreated. Common synonyms include "mucosal pinta" or "mucous membrane pinta." The disease primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, particularly in tropical regions. It is transmitted through direct contact with infected lesions. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are essential to prevent progression.

Late lesions of pinta, a chronic dermatosis, occur years after the initial infection. Caused by *Treponema carateum*, this condition primarily affects the skin, particularly the extremities, face, and mucous membranes. Characterized by hypopigmented, atrophic, and sclerotic patches, these lesions may develop into verrucous or ulcerative forms. Synonyms include "pinta chronic" and "pinta tardiva." The disease is endemic to certain regions of Central and South America. Without treatment, lesions may progress and lead to significant cosmetic and functional impairment.

Mixed lesions of pinta refer to a variant of the chronic skin infection caused by *Treponema carateum*. This condition presents with a combination of papulosquamous and verrucous lesions, often resembling syphilis. Common synonyms include "pinta with mixed lesions" and "variegated pinta." The disease typically affects the skin of the face, hands, and extremities. It is endemic to certain regions of Central and South America. The lesions may progress to depigmentation and scarring if left untreated. Diagnosis is often based on clinical appearance and serological testing.

Pinta unspecified is a chronic dermatosis caused by the spirochete *Treponema carateum*, primarily affecting tropical regions. It is characterized by asymptomatic, slowly progressing skin lesions that may evolve into depigmented patches. Common synonyms include "pinta" and "carate." The disease typically involves the skin, particularly the extremities, face, and hands. It is transmitted through direct contact with infected skin lesions. While rare, it may lead to secondary bacterial infections. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and serological tests. Treatment with antibiotics such as penicillin is effective if initiated early.

Louse-borne relapsing fever is a bacterial infection caused by *Borrelia recurrentis*, transmitted through the bite of an infected body louse. It is characterized by recurring fever, headache, muscle pain, and rash. The infection typically affects the bloodstream and lymphatic system. Common synonyms include epidemic typhus fever and louse fever. It primarily affects individuals in impoverished conditions with poor hygiene, leading to widespread louse infestation. The disease can progress to severe complications such as meningitis or circulatory collapse if untreated.

Tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF) is a spirochetal infection caused by *Borrelia* species, primarily *B. recurrentis*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected soft ticks, often in endemic regions. The disease is characterized by recurring fever episodes, typically every 2–6 days, accompanied by headache, myalgia, and arthralgia. The liver and spleen are commonly enlarged, and patients may experience lymphadenopathy. Without treatment, TBRF can lead to severe complications, including hemolytic anemia and meningitis. It is also known as relapsing fever or recurrent fever.

Relapsing fever unspecified is a recurrent, spirochetal infection characterized by intermittent fever, headache, and muscle pain. It is caused by Borrelia species, typically transmitted by lice or ticks. The disease presents with periods of fever followed by remission, often with relapses. Common synonyms include relapsing fever, spirochetal fever, and recurrent fever. It primarily affects the systemic circulation and can involve the central nervous system. The condition is more common in endemic regions and may lead to complications such as anemia, thrombocytopenia, and meningitis.

Necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis, also known as Vincent's angina or trench mouth, is a severe, painful infection of the oral mucosa characterized by necrosis and ulceration. It is primarily caused by a synergistic interaction between *Fusobacterium nucleatum* and *Treponema pallidum* subspecies *pallidum*. The condition commonly affects the gingival and buccal mucosa, often presenting with pseudomembranes, halitosis, and lymphadenopathy. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor oral hygiene.

"Other Vincent's infections" refers to infections caused by *Mycoplasma hominis* and *Ureaplasma urealyticum*, primarily affecting the genital tract. These organisms are common in genital secretions and can cause conditions such as urethritis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. They are also associated with complications in pregnancy, including preterm labor and chorioamnionitis. These infections are often asymptomatic but can lead to significant morbidity if left untreated. They are typically diagnosed through nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) and treated with antibiotics effective against atypical pathogens.

Lyme disease unspecified refers to a systemic infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, the primary spirochete transmitted through tick bites. It may present with a variety of symptoms, including erythema migrans, fatigue, joint pain, and neurological manifestations. Common synonyms include Lyme borreliosis and tick-borne spirochetosis. The disease can affect the skin, joints, nervous system, and heart. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent complications. The unspecified classification is used when the specific stage or manifestation is not clearly documented.

Meningitis due to Lyme disease is a rare but serious complication of Lyme borreliosis, caused by *Borrelia burgdorferi* and other *Borrelia* species. It typically presents with meningeal inflammation, often following untreated or inadequately treated early-stage Lyme disease. Common synonyms include meningitis associated with Borrelia infection or neuroborreliosis. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, with involvement of the meninges, cerebrospinal fluid, and sometimes the brain or spinal cord. Symptoms may include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical to prevent long-term neurological sequelae.

code_desc: Other neurologic disorders in Lyme disease
summary: Other neurologic disorders in Lyme disease refer to central or peripheral nervous system manifestations caused by *Borrelia burgdorferi* infection. Common synonyms include neuroborreliosis and Lyme neuroborreliosis. These disorders may present with meningitis, encephalitis, cranial neuropathies, and radiculopathy. The infection typically affects the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Symptoms may include headache, cognitive impairment, neuropathic pain, and motor deficits. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent long-term neurological complications.

Arthritis due to Lyme disease is a late-stage manifestation of Lyme borreliosis, caused by *Borrelia burgdorferi* and other *Borrelia* species. It typically presents as migratory, non-erosive joint inflammation, most commonly affecting the knees, wrists, and ankles. Synonyms include Lyme arthritis and borrelial arthritis. The condition often follows untreated early-stage Lyme disease and may involve synovitis and joint effusion. It is more prevalent in adults and can be recurrent if not adequately treated with antibiotics.

code_desc: Other conditions associated with Lyme disease
summary: Other conditions associated with Lyme disease include post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, which may involve persistent fatigue, joint pain, and neurological symptoms. Synonyms include chronic Lyme disease or persistent Lyme illness. The causative agent is Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted via Ixodes ticks. Commonly affected body parts include joints, heart, nervous system, and skin. These conditions may occur after inadequate or delayed treatment, leading to prolonged symptoms. Other associated conditions may involve autoimmune-like manifestations and systemic inflammation.

Lyme disease is a bacterial infection caused by *Borrelia burgdorferi* and other *Borrelia* species, transmitted through the bite of infected black-legged ticks. It is also known as Lyme borreliosis. Common symptoms include erythema migrans, fatigue, fever, and joint pain. The disease can affect the skin, joints, nervous system, and heart. Early treatment with antibiotics is effective, but untreated cases may lead to chronic complications. It is prevalent in regions with high tick populations, such as the northeastern and northcentral United States.

Other specified spirochetal infections refer to spirochete-related illnesses not classified under more specific categories like syphilis or Lyme disease. Common synonyms include spirochetal infections, other spirochetal diseases. Causative agents may include Borrelia, Treponema, or Leptospira species. These infections typically affect the skin, joints, nervous system, and cardiovascular system. Symptoms vary but often include rash, arthritis, neurological deficits, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through serological testing and clinical evaluation. Treatment involves antibiotics, with penicillin being a common choice.

Spirochetal infection unspecified refers to a bacterial infection caused by spirochetes, a type of helical-shaped bacteria. Common synonyms include syphilis, Lyme disease, and relapsing fever, though these are often specified. Causative agents may include *Treponema pallidum*, *Borrelia burgdorferi*, and *Borrelia recurrentis*. These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, joints, nervous system, and cardiovascular system. Symptoms vary widely depending on the stage and location of the infection. Diagnosis often requires serological or molecular testing when the specific spirochete is not identified.

Chlamydia psittaci infection is a zoonotic respiratory illness caused by the bacterium Chlamydia psittaci, commonly found in birds. It is also known as psittacosis or parrot fever. The infection typically affects the lungs, causing pneumonia, and may spread to other organs. Symptoms include fever, cough, headache, and muscle pain. Transmission occurs through inhalation of contaminated aerosols from infected birds. It can also cause systemic illness, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis is confirmed by serology or PCR, and treatment involves antibiotics such as tetracyclines.

The initial stage of trachoma is characterized by follicular conjunctivitis, marked by small, discrete, yellowish follicles on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. It is caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* serovars A, B, or C. Common synonyms include follicular conjunctivitis and early trachoma. The condition primarily affects the eyes, particularly the conjunctiva, and is prevalent in areas with poor hygiene and limited access to clean water. It often occurs in children and can lead to scarring and blindness if untreated. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected ocular secretions or contaminated fomites.

The active stage of trachoma is an infectious eye condition caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* serovars A, B, or C. It is characterized by follicular conjunctivitis, limbal inflammation, and scarring of the eyelids. Common synonyms include acute trachoma and follicular conjunctivitis. The infection primarily affects the conjunctiva and limbus, leading to complications such as trichiasis and corneal opacity if untreated. It is endemic in areas with poor hygiene and limited access to clean water. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected ocular secretions or fomites.

Trachoma unspecified is a chronic infectious eye disease caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*, primarily affecting the conjunctiva and cornea. It leads to scarring and can result in eyelash inversion, causing further corneal damage and potential blindness. Common synonyms include trachoma, blinding trachoma, and granulomatous conjunctivitis. The condition is more prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and limited access to healthcare, typically affecting children and young adults. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected ocular secretions or via flies. Early treatment with antibiotics can prevent progression and blindness.

Chlamydial conjunctivitis is an infectious inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It is a common cause of neonatal and adult conjunctivitis, often presenting with redness, swelling, and purulent discharge. Common synonyms include trachoma and inclusion conjunctivitis. The infection primarily affects the eyes, particularly in neonates exposed to infected genital secretions during birth. It may also involve the respiratory tract in adults. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected secretions. Complications can include corneal scarring and blindness if untreated.

Chlamydial peritonitis is an inflammatory condition of the peritoneum caused by *Chlamydophila psittaci* or *Chlamydophila felis*. It commonly affects domestic animals, particularly birds and cats, leading to symptoms such as fever, abdominal pain, and ascites. Synonyms include avian chlamydiosis and feline chlamydiosis. The infection can spread systemically, affecting multiple organs. Diagnosis often involves serology or PCR testing. Treatment typically includes antibiotics like doxycycline. The condition is zoonotic, posing a risk to human handlers.

Other chlamydial diseases refer to infections caused by *Chlamydia* species affecting various body systems beyond the genital tract. Common synonyms include atypical pneumonia and psittacosis. The primary causative agents are *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*, *Chlamydophila psittaci*, and *Chlamydia trachomatis*. These infections typically affect the respiratory tract, causing pneumonia, and may involve the eyes, gastrointestinal tract, and central nervous system. They are often transmitted via respiratory droplets or contact with infected animals. Symptoms vary but may include fever, cough, conjunctivitis, and systemic inflammation.

Other chlamydial diseases refer to infections caused by species of *Chlamydia* other than *C. trachomatis* and *C. pneumoniae*. Common synonyms include atypical pneumonia and chlamydial pneumonias. The primary causative agents are *C. pneumoniae*, *C. psittaci*, and *C. abortus*. These infections typically affect the respiratory tract, causing pneumonia, but can also involve the genital tract, eyes, and gastrointestinal system. Symptoms vary but often include fever, cough, and respiratory distress. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through serology or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment typically involves tetracyclines or macrolides.

Chlamydial infection unspecified refers to a group of infections caused by *Chlamydia* species, most commonly *C. trachomatis* and *C. pneumoniae*. It encompasses a range of clinical presentations, including conjunctivitis, pneumonia, and genital infections. Common synonyms include chlamydial disease, chlamydial infection, and chlamydial illness. The infection primarily affects the eyes, respiratory tract, and genital tract, with varying severity and symptoms. Diagnosis often requires laboratory testing due to non-specific clinical manifestations. It is a reportable disease and can lead to complications if untreated.

code_desc: Epidemic louse-borne typhus fever due to Rickettsia prowazekii
summary: Epidemic louse-borne typhus fever, caused by *Rickettsia prowazekii*, is a severe acute febrile illness transmitted via the body louse. It presents with high fever, headache, rash, and systemic toxicity. Common synonyms include epidemic typhus and louse fever. The infection primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and vascular system, with systemic involvement leading to complications such as pneumonia and multi-organ failure. It is most common in populations with poor hygiene and overcrowding, often following louse infestations.

Recrudescent typhus, also known as Brill's disease, is a rare, benign form of typhus characterized by a relapse of fever and rash following apparent recovery. It typically occurs in individuals with a history of prior typhus infection. The causative agent is *Rickettsia prowlettii*, transmitted via the human body louse. The disease primarily affects the skin, causing a macular or papular rash, and may involve the liver, leading to transient elevations in liver enzymes. Symptoms are generally milder than those of epidemic typhus, with a favorable prognosis.

code_desc: Typhus fever due to Rickettsia typhi
summary: Typhus fever due to *Rickettsia typhi*, also known as murine typhus, is an acute infectious disease caused by the bacterium *Rickettsia typhi*. It is transmitted to humans via the feces of infected fleas, typically from rats. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to fever, headache, rash, and systemic inflammation. Commonly affected body parts include the skin, liver, and spleen. Symptoms typically develop 6–14 days after exposure and may include malaise, cough, and conjunctival injection. Complications can involve pneumonia, hepatitis, and renal failure. The condition is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

code_desc: Typhus fever due to Rickettsia tsutsugamushi
summary: Typhus fever due to *Rickettsia tsutsugamushi*, also known as scrub typhus, is an acute febrile illness transmitted by mite vectors. The causative agent is *Rickettsia tsutsugamushi*, a gram-negative intracellular bacterium. It primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and visceral organs. Common symptoms include fever, headache, rash, and eschars. The disease is endemic in Asia, the Pacific Islands, and parts of Africa. Complications may involve the lungs, liver, and central nervous system. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and serological testing. Early treatment with doxycycline is effective.

Typhus fever unspecified refers to a systemic infection characterized by high fever, headache, and rash, typically caused by Rickettsia species. Common synonyms include epidemic typhus and scrub typhus, though the latter is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The disease primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and systemic organs. It is transmitted via lice or mites and is more common in areas with poor sanitation. Clinically, it presents with fever, malaise, and a maculopapular rash, often accompanied by systemic inflammation. Prompt treatment with antibiotics is essential to prevent complications.

code_desc: Spotted fever due to Rickettsia rickettsii
summary: Spotted fever due to *Rickettsia rickettsii*, also known as Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), is a tick-borne rickettsial infection. It is caused by *Rickettsia rickettsii* and transmitted primarily through the bite of infected ticks, particularly *Dermacentor variabilis* and *Dermacentor andersoni*. The disease presents with fever, headache, and a characteristic rash beginning on the wrists and ankles, spreading centripetally. Commonly affected body parts include the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs. Complications may involve the cardiovascular and neurological systems if untreated. Early antibiotic therapy is critical to prevent severe morbidity and mortality.

code_desc: Spotted fever due to Rickettsia conorii
summary: Spotted fever due to *Rickettsia conorii* is a tick-borne rickettsial infection characterized by fever, headache, and a distinctive maculopapular rash, often with central darkening. Common synonyms include Mediterranean spotted fever and Boutonneuse fever. The causative agent is *Rickettsia conorii*, transmitted primarily by *Rhipicephalus sanguineus* ticks. The disease typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and systemic organs. Lesions are most prominent on the trunk and extremities, with a characteristic "eschar" at the site of the tick bite. Systemic involvement may lead to complications such as hepatitis, pneumonia, and meningitis.

code_desc: Spotted fever due to Rickettsia siberica
summary: Spotted fever due to *Rickettsia siberica* is a tick-borne rickettsial infection characterized by fever, headache, and a maculopapular rash, often with a central eschar. Common synonyms include Siberian tick typhus and tick-borne spotted fever. The causative agent is *Rickettsia siberica*, transmitted primarily by *Dermacentor* ticks. The infection typically affects the skin, lymph nodes, and systemic organs. It is endemic in parts of Asia and Eastern Europe. Clinical severity varies, with potential for complications such as pneumonia and meningitis if untreated.

code_desc: Spotted fever due to Rickettsia australis
summary: Spotted fever due to *Rickettsia australis* is a tick-borne rickettsial infection primarily affecting the skin and mucous membranes. Commonly known as Queensland tick typhus or Australian spotted fever, it is caused by *Rickettsia australis* and transmitted through the bite of *Ixodes holocyclus* ticks. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, myalgia, and a characteristic maculopapular rash, often starting at the site of the tick bite and spreading centrifugally. Lesions are commonly found on the trunk, extremities, and mucous membranes. The infection primarily affects the skin and underlying tissues, with systemic involvement in more severe cases.

Ehrlichiosis unspecified refers to a group of tick-borne bacterial infections caused by species of the genus *Ehrlichia*, most commonly *Ehrlichia chaffeensis* and *Ehrlichia ewingii*. It primarily affects white blood cells, leading to fever, headache, and leukopenia. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected ticks, particularly the lone star tick and American dog tick. Common synonyms include human monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME) and human granulocytic ehrlichiosis (HGE), though these terms are now considered outdated. The disease typically involves the bloodstream and can affect the liver, spleen, and central nervous system if left untreated.

Ehrlichiosis chafeensis, also known as human monocytic ehrlichiosis, is a tick-borne infectious disease caused by the bacterium Ehrlichia chaffeensis. It primarily affects monocytes and is transmitted through the bite of infected ticks, most commonly the lone star tick. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, muscle pain, and leukopenia. It mainly affects the bloodstream and immune system, with systemic involvement. Common synonyms include human monocytic ehrlichiosis and monocytic ehrlichiosis. The condition is more prevalent in the southeastern United States.

Other ehrlichiosis refers to infections caused by species of the genus *Ehrlichia* that are not *Ehrlichia chaffeensis* or *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*. Common synonyms include human monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME) and granulocytic anaplasmosis. The causative agents include *Ehrlichia ewingii*, *Ehrlichia muris eauclairensis*, and *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*. These pathogens primarily affect white blood cells, particularly monocytes and neutrophils. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, myalgia, and leukopenia. It is transmitted via tick bites and commonly affects the bloodstream and immune system.

Ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne bacterial infection caused by species of the genus *Ehrlichia*, most commonly *Ehrlichia chaffeensis* and *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*. It primarily affects white blood cells, leading to fever, headache, and malaise. Common synonyms include human monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME) and anaplasmosis. The disease typically targets the monocytic lineage of white blood cells, causing systemic inflammation and potential complications such as respiratory distress or renal failure. It is prevalent in the Americas and transmitted primarily by *Amblyomma* and *Ixodes* ticks.

Other spotted fevers, also known as rickettsioses, are a group of tick-borne infectious diseases caused by bacteria of the genus Rickettsia. Common synonyms include spotted fever group rickettsioses. The causative agents include Rickettsia rickettsii (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), Rickettsia conorii (Mediterranean spotted fever), and Rickettsia typhi (typhus). These infections typically affect the skin, causing characteristic rashes, and can involve the bloodstream, leading to systemic symptoms. Commonly affected body parts include the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs such as the liver and lungs.

Spotted fever unspecified refers to a group of rickettsial infections characterized by fever, rash, and systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include spotted fever group rickettsiosis. Causative agents include Rickettsia rickettsii, R. conorii, and R. africae. The rash typically appears as maculopapular lesions, often on the trunk and extremities. The disease primarily affects the skin, vascular system, and can involve multiple organs. It is transmitted via tick bites, with symptoms usually developing 1–2 weeks post-exposure. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are essential to prevent complications.

Q fever is an acute or chronic zoonotic infection caused by *Coxiella burnetii*, a gram-negative bacterium. Common synonyms include query fever and acute Q fever. The disease is transmitted primarily through inhalation of contaminated aerosols, often from infected animals. Clinical manifestations include fever, headache, malaise, and pneumonia. In chronic cases, endocarditis is a common complication. The infection primarily affects the respiratory system and can involve the cardiovascular system. It is more prevalent in males and those with underlying heart conditions. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing.

Trench fever is a bacterial infection caused by *Bartonella quintana*, primarily affecting soldiers in crowded, unsanitary conditions during wars. It is also known as quintan fever or Maltese fever. The disease is characterized by intermittent high fever, severe headaches, and muscle pain. It typically affects the cardiovascular system, leading to complications such as endocarditis. The infection is transmitted through body lice, which serve as vectors. Commonly affected body parts include the joints, skin, and heart. Symptoms often resolve spontaneously but can be recurrent.

Rickettsialpox, caused by *Rickettsia akari*, is a tick-borne rickettsial infection transmitted through the bites of mites, particularly *Lepidoglyphus destructor*. It presents with a characteristic eschars at the site of inoculation, followed by a maculopapular rash. Common synonyms include "mitepox" and "tropical rash." The infection primarily affects the skin, but systemic involvement can occur. Fever, headache, and myalgia are typical systemic symptoms. The disease is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with close contact with mites. Diagnosis is often clinical, supported by serology or PCR. Treatment typically involves doxycycline.

Rickettsiosis due to *Ehrlichia sennetsu* is a systemic infection caused by the intracellular bacterium *Ehrlichia sennetsu*, transmitted primarily through the bite of infected chiggers. It is also known as scrub typhus or endemic typhus. The disease typically affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to fever, headache, and rash. Commonly involved organs include the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. The infection can progress to severe complications such as hepatitis, hemolytic anemia, and multi-organ failure if untreated. Diagnosis is often confirmed through serological tests and PCR. Early antibiotic treatment with doxycycline is effective.

Anaplasmosis, caused by *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*, is a tick-borne bacterial infection that primarily affects white blood cells, particularly neutrophils. Commonly known as human granulocytic anaplasmosis (HGA), it is transmitted through the bite of infected ticks, most commonly *Ixodes scapularis*. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, muscle pain, and fatigue. It can affect multiple organ systems, with the liver, spleen, and lungs being commonly involved. Severe cases may lead to respiratory distress, renal failure, and multi-organ dysfunction. Early diagnosis and treatment with doxycycline are critical to prevent complications.

Other specified rickettsioses refer to rickettsial infections not classified under more specific categories such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever or typhus. These infections are caused by various Rickettsia species, including Rickettsia conorii, Rickettsia africae, and Rickettsia typhi. Common synonyms include sporadic typhus and Mediterranean spotted fever. The disease typically affects the skin, lymph nodes, and vascular system, presenting with fever, rash, and systemic symptoms. Transmission occurs via tick or mite bites, and affected individuals often reside in endemic regions.

Other specified rickettsioses refer to rickettsial infections caused by organisms not classified under the more common categories such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever or typhus. These infections are typically caused by species like Rickettsia conorii, Rickettsia australis, and Rickettsia honei. Common synonyms include Mediterranean spotted fever and Queensland tick typhus. The disease primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and vascular system, often presenting with fever, rash, and systemic symptoms. It is transmitted through tick bites and is endemic in certain geographic regions.

Rickettsiosis unspecified refers to infections caused by rickettsial organisms when the specific agent or clinical variant cannot be identified. Common synonyms include spotted fever and typhus group infections. Causative agents may include Rickettsia species such as R. conorii, R. prowasekii, and R. typhi. These infections typically affect the skin, vascular system, and internal organs. Symptoms often include fever, rash, headache, and systemic inflammation. Transmission occurs via arthropod vectors like ticks and fleas. The condition can lead to severe complications if untreated.

Acute paralytic poliomyelitis vaccine-associated is a rare complication of oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) infection, characterized by inflammation of the anterior horn cells in the spinal cord, leading to flaccid paralysis. It is caused by the replication of the attenuated poliovirus in the vaccine, which can, in rare cases, revert to a neurovirulent form. Common synonyms include vaccine-induced poliomyelitis and vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis. The condition typically affects the limbs, with asymmetric weakness and paralysis, and may involve bulbar dysfunction in severe cases.

code_desc: Acute paralytic poliomyelitis wild virus imported
summary: Acute paralytic poliomyelitis caused by wild poliovirus is a severe viral infection affecting the central nervous system. It leads to asymmetric flaccid paralysis, often involving the limbs, and can result in permanent disability. Common synonyms include poliomyelitis and infantile paralysis. The causative agent is the poliovirus, which enters through the oral route and replicates in the intestinal tract before invading the central nervous system. The disease primarily affects children under five, though outbreaks can occur in unvaccinated populations. It is a notifiable disease due to its potential for rapid spread and serious complications.

code_desc: Acute paralytic poliomyelitis wild virus indigenous
summary: Acute paralytic poliomyelitis caused by wild poliovirus is a viral infection that leads to inflammation of the spinal cord, resulting in muscle weakness and paralysis. Common synonyms include poliomyelitis and infantile paralysis. The causative agent is the poliovirus, which belongs to the Picornaviridae family. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord. It typically presents with fever, headache, and meningismus, followed by asymmetric flaccid paralysis, often involving the lower extremities. The condition is most common in children under five years of age.

Acute paralytic poliomyelitis unspecified refers to a severe form of poliomyelitis characterized by sudden onset of muscle weakness and paralysis, typically affecting the spinal cord. Caused by the poliovirus, it leads to inflammation of motor neurons, resulting in flaccid paralysis. Common synonyms include poliomyelitis and infantile paralysis. The condition primarily affects the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, with involvement of the bulbar region potentially causing respiratory complications. It is a notifiable disease and is preventable through vaccination.

Other acute paralytic poliomyelitis is a severe form of poliomyelitis characterized by sudden onset of muscle weakness and paralysis, typically affecting the limbs. Caused by the poliovirus, it leads to inflammation of the anterior horn cells in the spinal cord. Common synonyms include acute flaccid paralysis and spinal poliomyelitis. The condition primarily affects the motor neurons, resulting in asymmetric weakness and potential long-term disability. It is most commonly seen in children but can occur in unvaccinated individuals of any age. Complications may include respiratory failure and post-polio syndrome.

code_desc: Acute paralytic poliomyelitis other and unspecified
summary: Acute paralytic poliomyelitis, also known as poliomyelitis or infantile paralysis, is a viral infection caused by the poliovirus. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the spinal cord and brainstem. The virus enters through the oral route and replicates in the throat and intestines before spreading to the central nervous system. Common symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, and muscle weakness, which may progress to paralysis, typically affecting the lower limbs. The condition can result in permanent disability or death if the respiratory muscles are involved. Vaccination remains the most effective prevention strategy.

Acute nonparalytic poliomyelitis is a viral infection caused by poliovirus, leading to inflammation of the central nervous system without paralysis. It typically affects the spinal cord and brainstem, causing symptoms such as fever, headache, vomiting, and meningismus. Common synonyms include abortive poliomyelitis and nonparalytic polio. The infection is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and primarily affects children. Most patients recover fully without long-term complications, though some may develop post-polio syndrome later in life.

Acute poliomyelitis unspecified refers to a severe viral infection caused by the poliovirus, leading to inflammation of the central nervous system. It results in muscle weakness and paralysis, primarily affecting the spinal cord and brainstem. Common synonyms include poliomyelitis and infantile paralysis. The virus spreads through contaminated food and water, and the disease predominantly affects children. Though rare in many countries due to vaccination, it remains a public health concern in under-immunized regions. The condition can lead to long-term disability or death if complications arise.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease unspecified is a rare, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by severe cognitive decline, myoclonus, and psychiatric symptoms. It belongs to the group of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies caused by misfolded prion proteins. Common synonyms include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) and human spongiform encephalopathy. The causative agent is the prion protein (PrP^Sc), which leads to spongiform changes in the brain. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the cerebral cortex, cerebellum, and brainstem, resulting in widespread neuronal loss and dysfunction.

Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD) is a rare, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by prions. It is the human form of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), commonly known as "mad cow disease." vCJD primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to severe neurological symptoms such as psychiatric disturbances, ataxia, and dementia. The disease is characterized by the accumulation of abnormal prion proteins in the brain, causing spongiform changes. It typically affects younger individuals and is associated with consumption of contaminated beef products. Synonyms include human spongiform encephalopathy and variant CJD.

Other Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) refers to a rare, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by prion-induced spongiform encephalopathy. It is distinct from sporadic and genetic forms of CJD. Common synonyms include variant CJD (vCJD) and new variant CJD. The causative agent is a misfolded prion protein (PrPSc), which leads to neuronal loss and brain parenchymal degeneration. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the cerebral cortex, cerebellum, and brainstem. Symptoms include rapid cognitive decline, psychiatric changes, myoclonus, and motor dysfunction. It is typically associated with exposure to contaminated beef products, often linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a rare, rapidly progressive, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterized by prion-induced spongiform encephalopathy. It is also known as subacute sclerosing encephalitis or Creutzfeldt disease. The causative agent is a misfolded protein called a prion, which leads to neuronal death and brain tissue degeneration. CJD primarily affects the central nervous system, causing symptoms such as cognitive decline, motor dysfunction, and psychiatric disturbances. It typically presents in middle-aged to elderly individuals and progresses to severe dementia and death within months. Variant CJD (vCJD) is linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) exposure.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, progressive neurological disorder caused by persistent measles virus infection. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to chronic inflammation and degeneration of brain tissue. Common synonyms include progressive encephalopathy and subacute spongiform encephalopathy. The condition typically manifests years after initial measles infection, predominantly in children and young adults. Clinical features include cognitive decline, seizures, and motor dysfunction. SSPE is characterized by a slow, irreversible progression resulting in severe disability and often death.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare, often fatal demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Caused by the reactivation of the JC virus in immunocompromised individuals, it leads to progressive destruction of white matter in the brain. Common synonyms include PML and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The disease typically affects the cerebral white matter, with lesions appearing in multiple regions. It is most commonly seen in patients with HIV/AIDS, lymphoma, or those on immunosuppressive therapy. Clinical features include cognitive decline, motor dysfunction, and visual disturbances. Early diagnosis and immune reconstitution are critical for improving outcomes.

Kuru is a rare, degenerative neurological disorder caused by prions, specifically the abnormal form of the prion protein (PrP^Sc). It is characterized by progressive ataxia, dementia, and motor dysfunction. Common synonyms include "laughing sickness" and "kuru disease." The condition primarily affects the cerebellum and brainstem, leading to loss of coordination and cognitive decline. It is transmitted through the consumption of infected human tissue, most commonly through ritualistic cannibalism in the Fore people of Papua New Guinea. The disease is now largely eradicated due to the cessation of the practice.

Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker syndrome (GSS) is a rare, autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive ataxia, dysarthria, and dementia. It is caused by mutations in the PRNP gene, leading to abnormal prion protein accumulation. Common synonyms include familial Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and hereditary cerebellar ataxia. The condition primarily affects the cerebellum, brainstem, and cerebral cortex, resulting in motor and cognitive decline. GSS typically presents in middle age and progresses rapidly, with a poor prognosis.

Fatal familial insomnia (FFI) is a rare, inherited prion disease characterized by progressive insomnia, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms. It is caused by a mutation in the PRNP gene, leading to misfolded prion proteins that damage the thalamus and other brain regions. Common synonyms include genetic fatal insomnia and familial fatal insomnia. The disease typically affects the central nervous system, particularly the thalamus, hypothalamus, and brainstem, resulting in severe neurological deterioration and ultimately death within 6 to 36 months.

code_desc: Other atypical virus infections of central nervous system
summary: Other atypical virus infections of the central nervous system refer to viral infections that do not fit the typical patterns of well-characterized CNS infections. These infections often present with non-specific or atypical clinical features. Common synonyms include rare or emerging viral encephalitis. Causative agents may include enteroviruses, herpesviruses, and other less commonly recognized viruses. These infections typically affect the brain and spinal cord, leading to symptoms such as fever, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. Diagnosis often requires molecular testing and clinical evaluation.

code_desc: Other atypical virus infections of central nervous system
summary: Other atypical virus infections of the central nervous system refer to viral infections that do not fit the typical patterns of well-defined CNS infections. These infections often present with non-specific or atypical clinical features. Common synonyms include rare or unusual viral encephalitis or myelitis. Causative agents may include emerging or re-emerging viruses such as Nipah, West Nile, or certain herpesviruses. These infections typically affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, altered mental status, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis often requires advanced molecular techniques due to the varied and non-specific presentations.

code_desc: Atypical virus infection of central nervous system unspecified
summary: Atypical virus infection of the central nervous system (CNS) refers to a clinically and pathologically distinct viral infection of the CNS that does not fit established diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include encephalitis of unspecified origin or viral meningitis with atypical features. Causative agents may include herpesviruses, enteroviruses, or other emerging pathogens. Typically affects the brain, meninges, and spinal cord, presenting with fever, altered mental status, seizures, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis often requires lumbar puncture and imaging. Treatment is supportive, with antiviral therapy if a specific pathogen is identified.

Sylvatic rabies, also known as wild animal rabies or丛林狂犬病, is a zoonotic viral disease caused by rabies virus variants primarily transmitted through the bite of infected wildlife, such as raccoons, skunks, bats, and foxes. The virus targets the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and progressive neurological dysfunction. Clinical signs include aggression, confusion, paralysis, and hydrophobia. The disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. It predominantly affects the brain and spinal cord, with initial infection at the site of the bite. Vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis are critical for prevention.

Urban rabies is a form of rabies transmitted primarily through the bite of infected domestic animals, most commonly dogs. It is characterized by neurological symptoms such as aggression, confusion, and paralysis. Common synonyms include canine rabies and rabies in domestic animals. The causative agent is the rabies virus, a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Rhabdoviridae family. The disease typically affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and ultimately death if untreated. It is most commonly seen in regions with poor animal vaccination programs and limited access to post-exposure prophylaxis.

Rabies unspecified refers to a clinical diagnosis of rabies when the specific variant or source of the virus is not identified. It is caused by the rabies virus, primarily transmitted through the bite of an infected animal. Common synonyms include rabies, hydrophobia, and mad dog disease. The virus affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and progressive neurological dysfunction. Clinical features include fever, agitation, hallucinations, and paralysis. The disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, though post-exposure prophylaxis can prevent infection if administered promptly. The brain and spinal cord are typically affected.

Japanese encephalitis is a viral central nervous system infection caused by the Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), a flavivirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. It primarily affects the brain, leading to inflammation and potentially severe neurological complications. Common synonyms include encephalitis Japonica and Japanese brain fever. The disease is endemic in Asia, with children and the elderly being most susceptible. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe encephalitis, often resulting in long-term disability or death. The virus replicates in the central nervous system, particularly the brain, causing inflammation and tissue damage.

Western equine encephalitis is a viral infection caused by the Western equine encephalitis virus, a member of the Togaviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, primarily affecting the central nervous system.
