The disease typically presents with fever, headache, and neurological symptoms such as seizures and altered mental status. Common synonyms include equine encephalitis virus and WEEV. The brain and spinal cord are the primary affected body parts, with potential complications including encephalitis and meningitis. It is more prevalent in North America and poses a risk to humans and horses.

Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) is a rare but severe viral infection caused by the eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV), a member of the Togaviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, primarily affecting the central nervous system. Common synonyms include EEE and eastern equine encephalomyelitis. The virus typically targets the brain and spinal cord, leading to inflammation, encephalitis, and potentially fatal outcomes. It is most commonly seen in young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. The disease is endemic in the eastern United States and parts of Canada.

St Louis encephalitis is a viral infection caused by the St Louis encephalitis virus, transmitted primarily through the Culex mosquito. It belongs to the Flaviviridae family and is endemic in the Americas. The disease typically affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain (encephalitis). Common synonyms include St Louis encephalitis virus infection and Culex-associated encephalitis. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological complications. The virus is most commonly found in elderly individuals, with higher mortality rates in this group. The primary affected body parts include the brain and spinal cord.

Australian encephalitis, also known as Murray Valley encephalitis, is a viral infection caused by flaviviruses, primarily the Murray Valley encephalitis virus. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, particularly Culex annulirostris. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain (encephalitis). Common symptoms include fever, headache, confusion, seizures, and in severe cases, coma or death. It is endemic to Australia and Papua New Guinea, with outbreaks often occurring during wet seasons. The condition predominantly affects the brain and spinal cord.

California encephalitis is a viral infection caused by the California encephalitis virus, a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, primarily in the western United States. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain (encephalitis). Common synonyms include Western equine encephalitis and St. Louis encephalitis, though these refer to related but distinct viruses. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological complications. The infection typically affects the brain and spinal cord, with potential involvement of the meninges.

Rocio virus disease is a rare, often fatal viral infection caused by the Rocio virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis and meningitis. The disease is characterized by acute onset of fever, headache, confusion, and neurological deficits. Common synonyms include Rocio encephalitis and Rocio meningencephalitis. The virus is transmitted through contact with infected rodents, particularly in rural areas of South America. The brain and spinal cord are the most commonly affected body parts, with severe cases resulting in coma or death.

Other mosquito-borne viral encephalitis refers to inflammation of the brain caused by viruses transmitted through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis and mosquito-borne encephalopathy. Causative agents vary by region and include viruses such as West Nile virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and Dengue virus. The condition typically affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, and neurological deficits. It primarily targets the brain and spinal cord, with severity ranging from mild to life-threatening.

Mosquito-borne viral encephalitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the brain caused by a virus transmitted through mosquito bites, where the specific virus is not identified. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis, mosquito-transmitted encephalitis, and arboviral encephalitis. Causative agents may include flaviviruses, alphaviruses, or other arboviruses. The central nervous system, particularly the brain, is typically affected, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and seizures. It is commonly seen in regions with high mosquito activity and can range from mild to severe illness.

code_desc: Far Eastern tick-borne encephalitis [Russian spring-summer encephalitis]
summary: Far Eastern tick-borne encephalitis (FETBE), also known as Russian spring-summer encephalitis, is a viral infection transmitted primarily by ticks. Caused by the Flavivirus genus, specifically the Far Eastern encephalitis virus, it affects the central nervous system. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, and meningeal signs, progressing to encephalitis in severe cases. Commonly affected body parts include the brain and meninges. It is endemic in eastern Europe and Asia, with outbreaks occurring during the spring and summer months.

Central European tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is a viral infectious disease transmitted primarily through the bite of infected ticks. Caused by the TBE virus, a flavivirus, it is endemic in parts of Europe and Asia. The infection typically affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, and neurological manifestations. Common synonyms include tick-borne encephalitis and TBE. The virus primarily targets the brain and spinal cord, with potential complications including meningitis, encephalitis, and meningomyelitis.

Powassan virus disease is a rare but potentially severe tick-borne illness caused by the Powassan virus, a flavivirus. It is transmitted through the bite of infected Ixodes ticks or, less commonly, through infected animal reservoirs. Symptoms include fever, headache, confusion, and neurological complications such as encephalitis or meningitis. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain and spinal cord. Common synonyms include Powassan encephalitis and tick-borne encephalitis (though the latter refers to a broader group of viruses). The condition can progress rapidly and may result in long-term neurological damage or death.

Other tick-borne viral encephalitis refers to a group of viral infections transmitted primarily by ticks, causing inflammation of the brain. Common synonyms include tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) and tick-borne viral encephalitis. The causative agents vary by region and include viruses such as tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV), Powassan virus, and others. The infection typically affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, and in severe cases, meningitis or encephalitis. The disease predominantly impacts the brain and spinal cord, with potential long-term neurological complications.

Other tick-borne viral encephalitis refers to a group of viral infections transmitted primarily through tick bites that affect the central nervous system. Common synonyms include tick-borne encephalitis and tick virus encephalitis. The causative agents vary by region and include viruses such as tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV), Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus, and Kyasanur forest disease virus. These infections typically affect the brain and spinal cord, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, and in severe cases, seizures or coma. The disease is more prevalent in forested areas of Europe, Asia, and parts of Africa.

Tick-borne viral encephalitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the brain caused by a virus transmitted through tick bites, though the specific virus is not identified. Common synonyms include tick-borne encephalitis and viral encephalitis, though the latter is broader. The causative agents are typically flaviviruses, such as Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus (TBEV). The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, and in severe cases, seizures or coma. It is most commonly seen in endemic regions of Europe and Asia.

Enteroviral encephalitis is a central nervous system infection caused by enteroviruses, most commonly echoviruses and coxsackieviruses. It presents with fever, headache, altered mental status, and neurological deficits. The infection primarily affects the brain, leading to inflammation of the brain tissue. It may also involve the spinal cord. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis and acute viral meningitis. The condition predominantly affects children and immunocompromised individuals, with symptoms ranging from mild to severe, potentially resulting in long-term neurological complications.

Adenoviral encephalitis is a rare central nervous system infection caused by adenoviruses, particularly serotypes 1, 2, 3, and 5. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or organ transplant recipients. The infection leads to inflammation of the brain, causing symptoms like fever, seizures, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis and adenovirus-induced encephalitis. The primary affected body parts are the brain and meninges, with potential involvement of the spinal cord in severe cases.

Arthropod-borne viral encephalitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the brain caused by viruses transmitted through arthropod vectors, such as mosquitoes or ticks, when the specific virus cannot be identified. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis, mosquito-borne encephalitis, and arboviral encephalitis. Causative agents may include flaviviruses, alphaviruses, or bunyaviruses. The central nervous system, particularly the brain, is typically affected, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and neurological deficits.

Other specified viral encephalitis refers to inflammation of the brain caused by viruses not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include viral meningitis or encephalitis with unspecified agents. Causative agents may include herpes simplex virus, enteroviruses, and arboviruses. The condition typically affects the brain, particularly the cerebral cortex and subcortical structures. It may present with fever, headache, confusion, and seizures. Diagnosis often requires lumbar puncture and viral testing. Treatment is supportive, with antiviral therapy used when a specific virus is identified.

Unspecified viral encephalitis refers to inflammation of the brain caused by a virus, where the specific causative agent is not identified. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis, unspecified. Causative agents may include herpes simplex virus, enteroviruses, arboviruses, and others. The condition typically affects the brain, particularly the cerebral cortex and subcortical structures. Symptoms may include fever, headache, confusion, seizures, and altered consciousness. It is a serious neurological disorder requiring prompt medical evaluation and treatment.

Enteroviral meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by enteroviruses, most commonly coxsackieviruses and echoviruses. It is a type of viral meningitis, often presenting with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. The infection typically affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and meninges. Common synonyms include viral meningitis and aseptic meningitis. It is more prevalent in children but can occur in adults. The disease is usually self-limiting, with symptoms resolving within days to weeks without specific antiviral treatment. Complications are rare but may include seizures or neurological deficits in severe cases.

Adenoviral meningitis is an inflammatory condition of the meninges caused by adenoviruses. It typically presents with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Common synonyms include viral meningitis due to adenovirus. The causative agents are adenoviruses, particularly serotypes 3, 7, and 14. It predominantly affects the central nervous system, including the brain and meninges. While most commonly seen in children, it can occur in immunocompetent adults. The illness is usually self-limiting, though complications such as encephalitis may occur. Diagnosis is confirmed through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of cerebrospinal fluid.

Lymphocytic choriomeningitis is a viral infection primarily affecting the central nervous system. Caused by the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), it is transmitted through contact with infected rodents. The disease typically presents with fever, meningitis, and meningoencephalitis. Common synonyms include acute meningitis and lymphocytic meningitis. The infection mainly affects the brain and meninges, with occasional involvement of the spinal cord. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to severe neurological complications.

Other viral meningitis refers to inflammation of the meninges caused by various viruses other than the most common ones like enteroviruses. Common synonyms include aseptic meningitis. Causative agents include herpesviruses, arboviruses, and others. It typically affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms include fever, headache, and neck stiffness. The condition is usually self-limiting, with no specific antiviral treatment required. It is more common in immunocompetent individuals and can occur following viral infections elsewhere in the body.

Viral meningitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the meninges caused by a virus, with the specific agent not identified. Common synonyms include aseptic meningitis. It is typically caused by enteroviruses, such as coxsackievirus and echovirus, though other viruses like herpes simplex virus or mumps virus may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. It is generally less severe than bacterial meningitis and has a favorable prognosis.

Enteroviral exanthematous fever, also known as Boston exanthem or epidemic exanthem, is a self-limiting viral illness caused by enteroviruses, most commonly coxsackievirus A16. It presents with fever, malaise, and a maculopapular rash, typically appearing on the trunk and spreading to the limbs. Oral ulcers and lymphadenopathy may also occur. The rash usually resolves within a week without scarring. It is more common in children and spreads through fecal-oral route. Complications are rare but may include meningitis or myocarditis.

Epidemic vertigo refers to a sudden, widespread occurrence of vertigo symptoms within a community, often linked to viral infections. Common synonyms include vestibular neuritis outbreak and epidemic vestibular syndrome. It is typically caused by viral agents such as herpes simplex virus, influenza, and Epstein-Barr virus. The condition primarily affects the inner ear and vestibular system, leading to dizziness, imbalance, and nausea. It commonly impacts adults, with a higher prevalence in the elderly. The disease spreads through respiratory or contact routes, and treatment focuses on symptom management and supportive care.

code_desc: Other specified viral infections of central nervous system
summary: "Other specified viral infections of central nervous system" refers to viral infections of the brain and spinal cord not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified viral encephalitis or meningitis. Causative agents may include herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, and others depending on the specific case. These infections typically affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and neurological deficits. The condition is often diagnosed when the causative agent is unknown or not classified under more specific viral CNS infections.

code_desc: Unspecified viral infection of central nervous system
summary: Unspecified viral infection of the central nervous system refers to a broad category of viral infections affecting the brain and spinal cord when the specific virus is not identified. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis or meningitis of undetermined etiology. Causative agents may include herpesviruses, enteroviruses, or other unidentified viruses. Typically, the infection affects the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with limited laboratory confirmation.

Chikungunya virus disease is a mosquito-borne viral infection caused by the Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), a member of the Togaviridae family. Common synonyms include chikungunya fever and chikungunya illness. The virus is primarily transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. The disease typically affects the musculoskeletal system, causing severe joint pain, fever, rash, and fatigue. It may also involve the eyes, leading to conjunctivitis. The infection is usually self-limiting but can result in chronic arthralgia in some cases. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

O'nyong-nyong fever is an acute, self-limiting viral illness endemic to western Africa. Caused primarily by the O'nyong-nyong virus, a member of the Togaviridae family, it is transmitted by *Aedes* mosquitoes. Common synonyms include African equatorial fever and banana fever. The disease typically affects the musculoskeletal system, causing severe joint pain, fever, headache, and rash. It primarily involves the joints and skin, with systemic symptoms resolving within days. The illness is more common in children and young adults, with no significant long-term complications.

Venezuelan equine fever (VEF) is an acute, febrile, viral disease primarily affecting horses, though it can also infect humans. Caused by the Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV), a member of the Togaviridae family, it is transmitted by mosquitoes. The disease is characterized by high fever, muscle pain, and neurological symptoms. In horses, it can lead to severe neurological signs and high mortality. Common synonyms include Venezuelan equine encephalitis. The central nervous system is typically affected, with involvement of the brain and spinal cord.

West Nile virus infection unspecified refers to a clinical syndrome caused by the West Nile virus, a flavivirus transmitted primarily through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include West Nile fever and West Nile encephalitis. The virus can affect the central nervous system, leading to neurological complications. Typically affected body parts include the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological manifestations. The infection is more common in older adults and immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing or PCR. No specific antiviral treatment is available; supportive care is the mainstay of management.

code_desc: West Nile virus infection with encephalitis
summary: West Nile virus infection with encephalitis is a severe neurological complication caused by the West Nile virus, a flavivirus transmitted primarily through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include West Nile encephalitis and neuroinvasive West Nile disease. The virus typically affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain (encephalitis) and spinal cord (myelitis). Symptoms may include fever, headache, confusion, seizures, and in severe cases, coma or death. The disease primarily affects the brain and spinal cord, with the elderly and immunocompromised at highest risk.

code_desc: West Nile virus infection with other neurologic manifestation
summary: West Nile virus infection with other neurologic manifestations refers to central nervous system involvement beyond encephalitis or meningitis, such as acute flaccid myelitis or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Caused by West Nile virus, a flavivirus transmitted primarily by mosquitoes, it can lead to severe neurological complications. Common synonyms include West Nile neuroinvasive disease. Typically affecting the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, the condition presents with fever, headache, and neurological deficits. It predominantly impacts older adults and immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: West Nile virus infection with other complications
summary: West Nile virus infection with other complications is a systemic illness caused by the West Nile virus, a flavivirus transmitted primarily through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include West Nile fever and West Nile encephalitis. The virus can lead to severe neurological complications such as encephalitis or meningitis. Typically affecting the central nervous system, it may also involve the liver, spleen, and skin. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to life-threatening conditions. Complications may include paralysis, cognitive impairment, and vision loss. The infection is more severe in the elderly and immunocompromised individuals.

West Nile virus infection is a flavivirus transmitted primarily through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include West Nile fever and West Nile encephalitis. The virus can cause a range of symptoms from asymptomatic infection to severe neurological illness. The causative agent is the West Nile virus, a member of the Flaviviridae family. Typically affected body parts include the central nervous system, leading to encephalitis or meningitis, and the liver, which may show signs of involvement in more severe cases. Most infections are mild, with flu-like symptoms, but neurological complications can be life-threatening.

Rift Valley fever is an acute viral disease caused by the Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV), a member of the Phlebovirus genus. It primarily affects humans and animals, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. The virus is transmitted through mosquito bites or contact with infected animal tissues. Common synonyms include African hemorrhagic fever and Rift Valley hemorrhagic fever. The disease typically affects the liver, causing hepatitis, and can lead to severe systemic illness, including hemorrhagic symptoms, retinal lesions, and encephalitis. It is more common in rural areas during periods of heavy rainfall.

Zika virus disease is a flavivirus infection primarily transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Common synonyms include Zika fever and Zika virus infection. The causative agent is the Zika virus, which belongs to the Flaviviridae family. Typically affecting the skin, joints, and central nervous system, the disease presents with fever, rash, conjunctivitis, and joint pain. In severe cases, it can lead to neurological complications such as Guillain-Barré syndrome. Congenital Zika syndrome may occur in fetuses exposed in utero, causing microcephaly and other birth defects.

"Other specified mosquito-borne viral fevers" refers to viral infections transmitted by mosquitoes that do not fit the criteria for more specific diagnoses such as dengue, chikungunya, or Zika. Common synonyms include unspecified mosquito-borne viral fever. Causative agents may include various flaviviruses, alphaviruses, and other arboviruses. These infections typically affect the fever, musculoskeletal system, and occasionally the neurological system. Symptoms often include fever, rash, joint pain, and headache. The illness is usually self-limiting but can lead to complications in vulnerable populations.

Mosquito-borne viral fever unspecified refers to a fever of unknown origin transmitted by mosquitoes, typically presenting with systemic symptoms such as chills, headache, myalgia, and rash. Common synonyms include undifferentiated mosquito fever and unspecified arboviral fever. Causative agents may include viruses like dengue, chikungunya, Zika, or West Nile virus, though the specific pathogen is not identified. The condition primarily affects the systemic circulation and may involve the skin, joints, and central nervous system. It is commonly seen in tropical and subtropical regions.

Oropouche virus disease is a viral illness caused by the Oropouche virus, a member of the family Togaviridae. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected mosquitoes, particularly those of the Haemagogus genus. The disease is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, and rash, with symptoms typically resolving within a week. Common synonyms include Oropouche fever and Oropouche illness. The virus primarily affects the vascular system and skin, with rash being a prominent feature. It is endemic to parts of South America, particularly Brazil and French Guiana.

Sandfly fever, also known as phlebotomus fever or visceral leishmaniasis, is a vector-borne illness caused by *Leishmania* parasites transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. The disease primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. It is more commonly associated with visceral leishmaniasis, which predominantly affects the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. The causative agents include *Leishmania donovani*, *L. infantum*, and *L. chagasi*. The condition is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in parts of Africa, Asia, and the Americas.

Colorado tick fever is a viral illness transmitted by the bite of infected Dermacentor ticks. Caused by the Colorado tick fever virus, a member of the Bunyaviridae family, it primarily affects the blood and lymphatic systems. Common synonyms include Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tick fever. The disease typically presents with fever, headache, muscle pain, and a characteristic rash. It mainly affects the skin, blood, and lymph nodes, with systemic involvement. The illness is endemic to the Rocky Mountain region of the United States.

Other specified arthropod-borne viral fevers refer to viral infections transmitted by arthropods, such as mosquitoes or ticks, that do not fit the criteria for more specific fevers like dengue or chikungunya. Common synonyms include arboviral fevers. Causative agents vary by region and include viruses like West Nile, Rift Valley fever, and Japanese encephalitis. These infections typically affect the fever system, with symptoms ranging from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological complications. The primary affected body parts include the skin, nervous system, and liver, depending on the virus.

Unspecified arthropod-borne viral fever is a general term for febrile illnesses transmitted by arthropods, such as mosquitoes or ticks, caused by various viruses. Common synonyms include arboviral fever or viral hemorrhagic fever. Causative agents may include viruses like dengue, chikungunya, or West Nile virus. The condition typically affects the systemic circulation, liver, and may involve the central nervous system. Symptoms include fever, headache, myalgia, and rash. It primarily affects regions with high arthropod activity, such as tropical and subtropical areas.

Sylvatic yellow fever is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, transmitted primarily through the bite of infected *Aedes* and *Haemagogus* mosquitoes. It is endemic in tropical regions of South America and Africa. The disease typically affects the liver, causing jaundice, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure. Common synonyms include jungle yellow fever and sylvatic yellow fever. Symptoms range from mild fever to severe hemorrhagic manifestations. The virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family and is closely related to dengue and Zika viruses.

Urban yellow fever is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. It is characterized by fever, headache, muscle pain, and nausea, progressing to severe hemorrhagic symptoms in some cases. Common synonyms include yellow fever and African yellow fever. The disease typically affects the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, leading to jaundice and organ failure. It is endemic in tropical regions of Africa and South America. Vaccination is the most effective preventive measure.

Yellow fever unspecified is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, a flavivirus transmitted primarily by Aedes mosquitoes. It affects the liver, leading to jaundice, liver failure, and systemic hemorrhage. Common synonyms include yellow fever, yellow fever virus infection, and viral hepatitis, type C. The disease typically involves the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, with symptoms ranging from mild fever to severe systemic illness. It is endemic in tropical regions of Africa and South America.

Junin hemorrhagic fever is a viral illness caused by the Junin virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It primarily affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhagic symptoms. Common synonyms include Argentine hemorrhagic fever and South American hemorrhagic fever. The disease typically affects the blood vessels, causing bleeding from multiple sites, and may involve the liver and kidneys. It is endemic to Argentina and is transmitted via inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, particularly *Calomys musculinus*. The illness ranges from mild to severe, with a case fatality rate of up to 5% in untreated cases.

Machupo hemorrhagic fever is a viral illness caused by the Machupo virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It is also known as Bolivian hemorrhagic fever. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhagic manifestations, fever, and systemic inflammation. Commonly affected body parts include the liver, spleen, and mucous membranes. The infection is typically transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, particularly Calomys callosus. Clinical symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe hemorrhagic syndrome. The condition is endemic in parts of South America.

Lassa fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic illness caused by the Lassa virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It is endemic in West Africa and primarily transmitted to humans through contact with rodent excreta, particularly the multimammate rat. The virus affects multiple organ systems, with common involvement of the liver, kidneys, and blood vessels. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, and hemorrhage. In severe cases, it can lead to multi-organ failure and death. Known synonyms include Lassa hemorrhagic fever and Lassa virus disease.

Other arenaviral hemorrhagic fevers are severe viral infections characterized by systemic vasculopathy, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure. Common synonyms include Lassa fever and Machupo fever. Causative agents include Lassa virus, Machupo virus, Guanarito virus, and Sabia virus. These viruses primarily affect the vascular system, leading to hemorrhage, and commonly involve the liver, kidneys, and respiratory system. The disease progresses rapidly, often resulting in shock and death if untreated. Transmission occurs via rodent vectors, with human-to-human spread possible in certain cases.

Arenaviral hemorrhagic fever unspecified refers to a severe viral illness caused by arenaviruses, typically presenting with fever, hemorrhage, and multi-system involvement. Common synonyms include viral hemorrhagic fever, though specific etiologies are often not identified. Causative agents may include Lassa fever virus, Junín virus, or Machupo virus, depending on geographic region. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy, organ failure, and potentially fatal outcomes. Commonly affected body parts include the liver, kidneys, and mucous membranes, with hemorrhagic manifestations observed in various tissues.

Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the CCHF virus, a member of the *Orthonairovirus* genus. It is transmitted primarily through tick bites and can also spread via infected animal blood or bodily fluids. Common synonyms include Crimean hemorrhagic fever and Congo hemorrhagic fever. The virus affects multiple organ systems, with common involvement of the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system. Symptoms include fever, bleeding, and multi-organ failure. It is prevalent in Africa, the Middle East, and parts of Asia.

Omsk hemorrhagic fever is an acute viral illness caused by the Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected rodents, particularly the yellow-necked mouse. The disease is characterized by fever, hemorrhagic manifestations, and systemic inflammation. Common synonyms include Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus infection and Omsk virus disease. The virus primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy and organ dysfunction, particularly in the liver and kidneys. It is endemic in parts of Russia and adjacent regions.

Kyasanur Forest disease (KFD), also known as monkey fever or forest yellow fever, is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Kyasanur Forest disease virus (KFDV), a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected ticks, primarily *Haemaphysalis spinigera*. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ involvement. Commonly affected body parts include the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. The infection is endemic to the Western Ghats of India and poses a significant public health risk in forested areas.

Marburg virus disease is a severe, often fatal viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Marburg virus, a member of the Filoviridae family. It is also known as Marburg hemorrhagic fever or Marburg virus hemorrhagic fever. The virus primarily affects the liver and vascular system, leading to coagulopathy, multi-organ failure, and severe hemorrhaging. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces. Common symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, and rapid progression to shock and organ failure. The disease is endemic in parts of Africa and has a high case fatality rate.

Ebola virus disease (EVD), also known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever, is a severe, often fatal illness caused by the Ebola virus, primarily from the Zaire species. The virus targets the vascular system and immune system, leading to systemic inflammation, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure. Commonly affected organs include the liver, kidneys, and lungs. Symptoms progress from fever and malaise to hemorrhagic manifestations, shock, and multi-organ dysfunction. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces.

Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), also known as epidemic hemorrhagic fever or nephropathia epidemica, is a viral illness caused by hantaviruses. It primarily affects the kidneys and vascular system, leading to acute renal failure, hypovolemic shock, and hemorrhagic manifestations. The disease is transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Commonly affected organs include the kidneys, liver, and lungs, with symptoms ranging from fever and headache to severe bleeding and renal dysfunction.

Other specified viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of severe viral infections characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ dysfunction. These fevers are not classified under specific well-known hemorrhagic fever viruses like Ebola or Dengue. Common synonyms include unspecified viral hemorrhagic fever. Causative agents vary and may include viruses such as Lassa, Crimean-Congo, or others not classified under major categories. The disease typically affects the vascular system, liver, and kidneys, leading to systemic inflammation and coagulopathy. Clinically, it presents with high fever, rash, bleeding manifestations, and potential organ failure.

Unspecified viral haemorrhagic fever is a severe systemic infection characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ dysfunction, with no specific virus identified. Common synonyms include undifferentiated viral haemorrhagic fever. Causative agents may include arenaviruses, filoviruses, or other unidentified pathogens. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy and organ failure. It typically involves the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, with symptoms ranging from mild fever to life-threatening shock. Diagnosis is often made by exclusion after ruling out known haemorrhagic fever viruses.

Eczema herpeticum is a severe viral infection that occurs in individuals with preexisting eczema or atopic dermatitis. It is caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1, though HSV-2 may also be involved. The infection typically presents as painful, clustered vesicles and ulcers on previously affected skin areas. Commonly affected sites include the face, scalp, and extremities. Synonyms include herpes gestationis and herpetic dermatitis. The condition can lead to systemic complications if not treated promptly with antiviral therapy.

Herpesviral vesicular dermatitis is a skin condition characterized by the presence of small, fluid-filled blisters (vesicles) caused by herpesviruses. Common synonyms include herpes zoster dermatitis and shingles. The most frequent causative agent is Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), though other herpesviruses like Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) may also be implicated. The condition typically affects the trunk, face, and limbs, with a unilateral distribution in the case of herpes zoster. Lesions often progress through stages of vesicles, crusts, and healing. It is often accompanied by pain, itching, or burning sensations.

Herpesviral gingivostomatitis and pharyngotonsillitis is an acute, often severe infection characterized by ulcerative lesions in the oral cavity and pharynx. Commonly caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), it may also involve other herpesviruses. The condition typically affects children and immunocompromised individuals. Clinical features include painful gingival inflammation, vesicular ulcers, and pharyngeal involvement. Synonyms include herpetic stomatitis and pharyngitis. The primary affected areas are the gums, tongue, buccal mucosa, and tonsils.

Herpesviral meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by herpesviruses. Common synonyms include viral meningitis and herpes simplex meningitis. The most frequent causative agents are herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and, less commonly, varicella-zoster virus (VZV) and herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2). It typically affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to severe complications if untreated.

Herpesviral encephalitis is a severe central nervous system infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). It is characterized by inflammation of the brain, often leading to fever, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. Less commonly, HSV-2, varicella-zoster virus, or other herpesviruses may be involved. The temporal lobe is frequently affected, though the infection can spread to other brain regions. Prompt antiviral therapy is critical to prevent mortality and long-term neurological complications. Synonyms include acute herpes encephalitis and HSV encephalitis.

Herpesviral ocular disease unspecified refers to ocular infections caused by herpesviruses without specific identification of the viral type. Common synonyms include herpes keratitis and herpes ophthalmic infection. The primary causative agents are herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). This condition typically affects the cornea, conjunctiva, and uvea, leading to symptoms such as pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision. It may present as dendritic keratitis or uveitis, often requiring antiviral therapy for effective management.

Herpesviral iridocyclitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the anterior uveal tract, characterized by conjunctival injection, ciliary injection, and keratic precipitates. It is primarily caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV), though other herpesviruses may occasionally be involved. Common synonyms include herpes simplex keratouveitis and herpes zoster iridocyclitis. The condition typically affects the cornea, iris, and ciliary body, often leading to complications such as glaucoma and corneal scarring if untreated. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and can present with recurrent episodes.

Herpesviral keratitis is an infectious inflammation of the cornea caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), most commonly HSV-1. It presents as a painful red eye with photophobia, tearing, and decreased vision. The infection can lead to ulceration, scarring, and potential corneal perforation. It typically affects the cornea, but may involve the conjunctiva and anterior uvea. Other causative agents include varicella-zoster virus (VZV) and, less commonly, herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Synonyms include herpetic keratitis and HSV keratitis. It predominantly affects the eye, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or those with prior herpes infections.

Herpesviral conjunctivitis is an infectious inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) or varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It presents with redness, swelling, and a copious watery discharge, often accompanied by eyelid swelling and subepithelial infiltrates. Common synonyms include HSV conjunctivitis and herpes keratoconjunctivitis. The condition primarily affects the conjunctiva and cornea, with potential involvement of the eyelids and episclera. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to complications such as corneal scarring if untreated.

Other herpesviral disease of the eye refers to infections caused by herpesviruses affecting the ocular structures. Common synonyms include herpes keratitis and herpetic eye disease. The primary causative agents are herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). These infections typically affect the cornea, conjunctiva, and sometimes the uvea. HSV is more commonly associated with corneal ulceration, while VZV often leads to episcleritis or dendritic keratitis. The condition may present with symptoms such as redness, pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. Prompt diagnosis and antiviral treatment are essential to prevent complications like scarring and vision loss.

Herpesviral ocular disease refers to a group of infections caused by herpesviruses affecting the eye. Common synonyms include herpes keratitis and ocular herpes. The primary causative agents are herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). HSV typically causes corneal infection, while VZV is associated with herpes zoster ophthalmicus. These infections often affect the cornea, conjunctiva, and sometimes the uvea. Symptoms include pain, redness, photophobia, and decreased vision. Prompt treatment with antiviral therapy is essential to prevent complications such as scarring and corneal ulcers.

Disseminated herpesviral disease refers to widespread infection caused by herpesviruses, typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include systemic herpesvirus infection or generalized herpesviral disease. Causative agents include herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The infection commonly affects multiple organs, including the lungs, liver, central nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract, leading to severe complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, and hepatitis.

Herpesviral hepatitis is a rare but severe liver inflammation caused by herpesviruses, most commonly cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus (HSV). It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or organ transplant recipients. The condition typically presents with jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatomegaly. It may also involve systemic symptoms like fever and fatigue. While less common, varicella-zoster virus and Epstein-Barr virus can occasionally cause hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic involvement may occur. Synonyms include CMV hepatitis and herpes simplex hepatitis.

Herpes simplex myelitis is a rare but severe inflammatory condition of the spinal cord caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), typically HSV-1 or HSV-2. It presents with acute neurological symptoms such as weakness, sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction. The infection leads to demyelination and neuronal damage, often resulting in long-term disability. Common synonyms include HSV myelitis or viral myelitis. The condition primarily affects the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord, though other regions may be involved. Prompt antiviral therapy is critical to prevent progression and reduce morbidity.

Other herpesviral infection refers to infections caused by herpesviruses other than herpes simplex virus (HSV) or varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Common synonyms include herpesvirus infection or herpes-related disease. Causative agents include cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), among others. These infections typically affect the mucocutaneous surfaces, lymphatic system, and visceral organs. Symptoms vary but often include fever, lymphadenopathy, and characteristic skin or mucosal lesions. Complications can range from mild to severe, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Other forms of herpesviral infections refer to infections caused by herpesviruses other than herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Common synonyms include herpesvirus infections, non-HSV/VZV herpes infections, and other herpes-related diseases. Causative agents include cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), and others. These infections typically affect various body systems, including the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system, and skin. They can manifest as mononucleosis, retinitis, encephalitis, and congenital infections, depending on the specific virus and host immune status.

Herpesviral infection unspecified refers to a clinical diagnosis made when the specific herpesvirus type cannot be identified. It encompasses infections caused by herpesviruses such as herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), among others. Common synonyms include herpes infection, viral herpes, or unspecified herpes. These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, and sometimes the central nervous system. Symptoms may include vesicular eruptions, fever, and systemic manifestations, depending on the affected site and immune status of the patient.

Varicella meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), typically occurring in children following varicella infection. It is a rare but serious complication. Common synonyms include herpes zoster meningitis and VZV meningitis. The virus spreads via respiratory droplets or direct contact with lesions. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. It predominantly affects the central nervous system, particularly the cerebrospinal fluid. Complications may involve encephalitis or prolonged neurological deficits. Early diagnosis and antiviral therapy are crucial for optimal outcomes.

Varicella encephalitis and encephalomyelitis refer to central nervous system complications following varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection. These conditions involve inflammation of the brain (encephalitis) and spinal cord (myelitis). Common synonyms include post-varicella encephalopathy and VZV-induced CNS inflammation. Causative agents are primarily the varicella-zoster virus. These disorders typically affect the brain and spinal cord, leading to neurological symptoms such as fever, seizures, altered mental status, and motor deficits. They are more common in immunocompromised individuals and can result in severe morbidity.

Varicella myelitis is a rare but serious complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection, characterized by inflammation of the spinal cord. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or during the acute varicella phase. The condition presents with neurological symptoms such as paralysis, sensory loss, and bladder dysfunction. Common synonyms include post-varicella myelitis and acute transverse myelitis associated with varicella. The causative agent is the varicella-zoster virus, and the spinal cord is the primarily affected body part, often involving the thoracic or cervical regions.

Varicella encephalitis, myelitis, and encephalomyelitis refer to central nervous system complications of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection. These conditions involve inflammation of the brain (encephalitis), spinal cord (myelitis), or both (encephalomyelitis). Common synonyms include postherpetic encephalitis and VZV-induced CNS inflammation. The causative agent is the varicella-zoster virus. Typically affected body parts include the brain, spinal cord, and cranial nerves. Symptoms may include fever, seizures, altered mental status, and motor deficits. These complications are more common in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to severe neurological sequelae.

Varicella pneumonia is a severe respiratory complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection, occurring primarily in immunocompromised individuals or young children. It presents with fever, cough, and progressive respiratory distress. Common synonyms include herpes zoster pneumonia and varicella-associated pneumonia. The causative agent is VZV, which typically affects the lungs, leading to interstitial and alveolar inflammation. It can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome and has a high mortality rate if untreated. The condition predominantly involves the lower respiratory tract.

Varicella keratitis is a corneal infection occurring in patients with active varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection. It typically presents as a dendritic ulcer on the cornea, often associated with herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Common synonyms include herpes zoster keratitis and VZV corneal infection. The causative agent is the varicella-zoster virus. It predominantly affects the cornea, with involvement of the limbus and conjunctiva. The condition is more common in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to significant visual morbidity if untreated.

Other varicella complications refer to secondary infections or systemic manifestations occurring after varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection. Common synonyms include post-varicella complications and varicella sequelae. Causative agents are primarily VZV, though bacterial superinfections may occur. Typically affected body parts include the skin, respiratory tract, and central nervous system. Complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, and secondary bacterial infections are common, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. These conditions can lead to significant morbidity and mortality if not promptly managed.

Varicella with other complications refers to a severe form of chickenpox caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV), leading to additional health issues beyond the typical rash. Common synonyms include herpes zoster and shingles, though these terms often refer to the reactivated form. Complications may involve pneumonia, encephalitis, or secondary bacterial infections. The rash typically affects the skin and mucous membranes, but systemic involvement can occur. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals, neonates, and adults. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent severe outcomes.

Varicella, also known as chickenpox, is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It presents as a pruritic rash with characteristic vesicular lesions that progress through stages of macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts. The rash typically involves the face, scalp, trunk, and extremities, often with a centrifugal distribution. Fever and malaise may accompany the eruption. The disease is generally self-limiting in healthy individuals but can lead to complications in immunocompromised patients. Common synonyms include varicella zoster and chickenpox.

Zoster encephalitis, also known as herpes zoster encephalitis or varicella-zoster virus (VZV) encephalitis, is a rare but severe central nervous system infection caused by reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. It typically affects individuals with compromised immune systems. The infection leads to inflammation of the brain, often involving the temporal and frontal lobes. Clinical features include fever, headache, seizures, and altered mental status. The condition can result in significant neurological deficits if not promptly treated with antiviral therapy.

Zoster meningitis is a rare, acute inflammation of the meninges caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with prior herpes zoster infection. Common synonyms include herpes zoster meningitis or post-herpetic meningitis. The condition presents with fever, headache, and meningeal signs. Neurological complications may arise, including cranial neuropathies and encephalitis. The virus spreads from the dorsal root ganglia to the central nervous system, affecting the meninges and sometimes the brain parenchyma. Prompt antiviral therapy with acyclovir is essential to reduce morbidity.

Postherpetic geniculate ganglionitis is a rare complication of herpes zoster infection involving the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve. It occurs when the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) persists in the ganglion after the initial infection, leading to inflammation and nerve damage. Common synonyms include Ramsay Hunt syndrome type II and postherpetic neuralgia of the facial nerve. The condition typically affects the facial nerve, causing facial weakness, hearing loss, and vertigo. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and often follows a history of herpes zoster ophthalmicus or auricularis.

Postherpetic trigeminal neuralgia is a chronic neuropathic pain condition that occurs following a herpes zoster (shingles) infection involving the trigeminal nerve. It is characterized by severe, lancinating facial pain typically affecting the second and third divisions of the trigeminal nerve. Common synonyms include postherpetic neuralgia of the trigeminal nerve and shingles-related trigeminal neuropathy. The causative agent is the varicella-zoster virus. Pain is usually localized to the cheek, upper lip, and forehead, and may persist for months or years after the rash has resolved.

Postherpetic polyneuropathy is a chronic neuropathy that occurs following herpes zoster infection, primarily affecting sensory nerves. It is characterized by persistent pain, paresthesias, and sensory loss in areas previously affected by shingles. Common synonyms include postherpetic neuropathy and herpes zoster neuropathy. The varicella-zoster virus is the causative agent. Typically, the condition affects the trunk, face, and extremities, with sensory involvement being most common. It may also involve motor and autonomic fibers in severe cases. The condition is more prevalent in older adults and those with compromised immune systems.

Postherpetic myelitis is a rare complication of herpes zoster infection characterized by inflammation of the spinal cord following varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with severe initial herpes zoster. Symptoms include spinal cord dysfunction, motor weakness, sensory loss, and autonomic disturbances. Common synonyms include postherpetic myelitis and herpes zoster myelitis. The condition primarily affects the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord regions. Causative agents are primarily VZV, though rare cases may involve other pathogens.

Other postherpetic nervous system involvement refers to neurological complications occurring after herpes zoster infection, beyond typical postherpetic neuralgia. It encompasses various conditions such as postherpetic neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction, and sensory abnormalities. Common causative agents include varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Typically affected areas include the trunk, face, and extremities. Symptoms may involve persistent pain, hypoesthesia, hyperesthesia, or motor deficits. This condition can occur in immunocompromised individuals and may require multidisciplinary management.

code_desc: Zoster with other nervous system involvement
summary: Zoster with other nervous system involvement refers to herpes zoster (shingles) complicated by neurological complications beyond the dermatomal distribution. Common synonyms include postherpetic neuralgia and herpes zoster encephalitis. The causative agent is varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Typically affected body parts include the face, trunk, and extremities, with potential involvement of cranial nerves, spinal cord, and brain. Complications may involve meningitis, encephalitis, motor deficits, and sensory loss. This condition is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with advanced age.

Zoster ocular disease unspecified refers to ocular complications arising from varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation, typically affecting the trigeminal nerve. Common synonyms include herpes zoster ophthalmicus and ophthalmic zoster. The virus can cause inflammation of the cornea, conjunctiva, and uvea, potentially leading to keratitis, uveitis, or neuralgia. It most commonly affects the eye and surrounding structures, including the eyelids and cornea. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with a history of chickenpox. Early diagnosis and antiviral therapy are crucial to prevent severe visual impairment.

Zoster conjunctivitis, also known as herpes zoster ophthalmicus, is a viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus. It typically affects the trigeminal nerve distribution, leading to a dermatomal rash on the forehead, eyelids, and around the nose. Conjunctival involvement may occur, presenting with redness, swelling, and discharge. The condition is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with a history of chickenpox. Complications such as keratitis or glaucoma may arise if the infection spreads to the eye. Early antiviral therapy is crucial to prevent severe ocular damage.

Zoster iridocyclitis is an inflammatory condition of the anterior uvea, typically associated with herpes zoster virus infection. It commonly presents with pain, redness, and photophobia. The condition often follows varicella-zoster virus reactivation, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include herpes zoster uveitis and acute herpes simplex iridocyclitis. It primarily affects the iris and ciliary body, potentially leading to complications such as glaucoma and cataracts. The cornea may also be involved, resulting in epithelial defects. Early treatment with antiviral and anti-inflammatory agents is crucial to prevent vision loss.

Zoster keratitis is a corneal inflammation caused by reactivation of herpes zoster virus (VZV), typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals or those with prior varicella infection. It often presents with severe pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. Common synonyms include herpes zoster ophthalmicus keratitis and Ramsay-Hunt syndrome keratitis. The condition primarily affects the cornea, conjunctiva, and eyelids, and may lead to scarring and vision loss if untreated. Varicella-zoster virus is the sole known causative agent.

Zoster scleritis is a severe, necrotizing inflammation of the sclera associated with herpes zoster virus infection. It typically occurs in patients with active herpes zoster ophthalmicus or disseminated varicella-zoster virus. Common synonyms include herpes zoster scleritis and zoster-associated scleritis. The condition primarily affects the sclera and can extend to the cornea and uveal tract. It is characterized by pain, redness, and potential perforation of the globe. Causative agents are predominantly varicella-zoster virus, though other herpesviruses may rarely be involved. The disease is more common in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to significant visual loss if untreated.

Other herpes zoster eye disease refers to ocular complications arising from varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation. Common synonyms include herpes zoster ophthalmicus and ophthalmic zoster. The virus typically affects the trigeminal nerve, leading to dermatomal rash and ocular involvement. Commonly affected areas include the cornea, conjunctiva, eyelids, and uvea. Complications such as keratitis, uveitis, and optic neuropathy may occur. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and the elderly. Early diagnosis and antiviral therapy are crucial to prevent severe visual loss.

Zoster ocular disease refers to ocular complications caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV) reactivation. Common synonyms include herpes zoster ophthalmicus and Ramsay Hunt syndrome when involving the facial nerve. The virus typically affects the trigeminal nerve, leading to rash and pain around the nose and forehead. Ocular manifestations may include conjunctivitis, uveitis, keratitis, and corneal ulceration. It can also cause optic neuropathy and retinal involvement. Prompt treatment with antiviral therapy is essential to prevent severe vision loss. The condition predominantly affects adults, especially those with compromised immune systems.

Disseminated zoster is a severe complication of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection characterized by widespread involvement of multiple dermatomes. Common synonyms include generalized zoster and disseminated herpes zoster. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals and can involve the central nervous system, lungs, liver, and other visceral organs. Clinical features include painful, vesicular rash, neurological deficits, and systemic symptoms. The causative agent is varicella-zoster virus, and affected body parts may include skin, brain, spinal cord, and internal organs.

Zoster with other complications refers to shingles caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV), leading to dermatomal rash and neurological symptoms. Common synonyms include herpes zoster complicating other conditions or herpes zoster with neurological involvement. The virus typically affects the trigeminal, thoracic, or lumbar dermatomes. Complications may include postherpetic neuralgia, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, or disseminated zoster. Immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk for severe or widespread disease. The condition is characterized by pain, vesicular rash, and potential systemic involvement. Early antiviral therapy is crucial to reduce complications.

Zoster without complications, also known as simple herpes zoster, is a reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) leading to a unilateral dermatomal rash with vesicles. Common synonyms include shingles, herpes zoster, and zoster. The virus remains dormant in sensory ganglia after primary varicella infection. Typically affects the thoracic or trigeminal dermatomes, with the thoracic region being the most common. Lesions progress through macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts. Systemic symptoms like fever and malaise may occur but are usually mild. No neurological or systemic complications are present.

Smallpox is a severe, contagious viral infection caused by the variola virus. It is characterized by a high fever, malaise, and a distinctive rash that progresses to fluid-filled blisters and scabs. Common synonyms include variola and smallpox disease. The infection primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, with lesions appearing on the face, arms, and legs. It is transmitted via respiratory droplets and has a high mortality rate. Historically, it was a major public health concern, but global eradication was achieved in 1980 through widespread vaccination.

Monkeypox is a viral zoonotic disease caused by the monkeypox virus, a member of the Orthopoxvirus genus. It is characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, and a distinctive rash that progresses through various stages. Common synonyms include variola minor and pox virus infection. The disease primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the eyes. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected animals or humans, or via respiratory droplets. While historically more common in Central and West Africa, outbreaks have occurred globally, particularly among immunocompromised individuals.

Measles complicated by encephalitis refers to a severe neurological complication occurring in a small percentage of measles cases, typically 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000 infections. It is caused by the measles virus, which leads to inflammation of the brain. Common synonyms include measles encephalitis or viral encephalitis following measles. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain, and can result in symptoms such as fever, seizures, altered mental status, and long-term neurological deficits. It is more common in young children and immunocompromised individuals.

Measles complicated by meningitis refers to the development of meningitis following a measles infection. It is a severe complication characterized by inflammation of the meninges, often leading to fever, headache, and altered mental status. The causative agent is the measles virus, which may directly invade the central nervous system or trigger an immune-mediated response. Common synonyms include measles encephalitis or viral meningitis secondary to measles. Typically affected body parts include the brain and meninges, with potential involvement of the spinal cord in severe cases. Complications can include seizures, hearing loss, and long-term neurological deficits.

Measles complicated by pneumonia is a severe respiratory complication of measles, occurring in approximately 1 in 5 cases. It typically develops 4–7 days after the rash appears. The causative agent is the measles virus, though secondary bacterial infections such as *Streptococcus pneumoniae* or *Haemophilus influenzae* may contribute. Common synonyms include measles pneumonia or viral pneumonia secondary to measles. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, with symptoms including cough, fever, and respiratory distress. Complications may lead to hypoxia, respiratory failure, or death if not promptly treated.

Measles complicated by otitis media refers to an ear infection that develops secondary to measles virus infection. It typically occurs in children and is characterized by inflammation of the middle ear, often leading to fluid accumulation and potential hearing loss. Common synonyms include measles-associated otitis media or post-measles otitis. The causative agent is the measles virus, which weakens the immune system, predisposing to secondary bacterial infections such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae. The primary affected body parts are the middle ear, with possible extension to the mastoid process. Complications may include hearing impairment and meningitis.

Measles with intestinal complications is a severe form of measles characterized by gastrointestinal involvement. Caused by the measles virus, it typically presents with fever, rash, and cough, but may progress to diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Complications such as malabsorption, enteritis, and even intussusception can occur. Common synonyms include measles enteritis and measles with gastrointestinal involvement. The primary affected body parts are the skin, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal system. It predominantly affects children with weakened immune systems.

Measles keratitis and keratoconjunctivitis is an ocular complication of measles infection, characterized by inflammation of the cornea and conjunctiva. It typically occurs in the convalescent phase of measles and is associated with viral shedding. Common synonyms include measles keratoconjunctivitis and acute measles conjunctivitis. The causative agent is the measles virus. It primarily affects the conjunctiva and cornea, leading to symptoms such as redness, photophobia, and decreased vision. The condition is more common in children and can result in corneal scarring if untreated.

Other measles complications refer to secondary infections and systemic manifestations occurring after the initial measles illness. Common synonyms include post-measles complications and measles sequelae. The primary causative agent is the measles virus, though secondary bacterial infections may contribute. Typically affected body parts include the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system. Complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, and otitis media are frequently observed. These can lead to severe morbidity and mortality, particularly in malnourished or immunocompromised individuals.

Measles with other complications is a severe form of measles characterized by the development of additional clinical manifestations beyond the typical rash and fever. Common synonyms include complicated measles or measles with secondary infections. Caused by the measles virus (rubeola virus), it typically affects the respiratory system, skin, and may lead to complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, and secondary bacterial infections. The disease primarily impacts children but can occur in immunocompromised individuals. Complications can be life-threatening and require prompt medical intervention.

Measles without complication is an acute viral illness caused by the measles virus (Morbillivirus). It typically presents with a high fever, cough, runny nose, and conjunctivitis, followed by a characteristic red, blotchy rash that begins on the face and spreads downward. Common synonyms include rubeola and morbilli. The rash usually resolves within a week. The disease primarily affects the skin, respiratory tract, and mucous membranes. Complications are rare in healthy individuals but can occur in immunocompromised patients.

Rubella with neurological complication unspecified refers to a viral infection caused by the rubella virus, typically presenting with fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. While primarily a systemic illness, it may lead to neurological complications such as encephalitis or meningitis, though the specific nature is not specified. Common synonyms include German measles and three-day measles. The virus is transmitted via respiratory droplets. Typically, the infection affects the skin, lymph nodes, and central nervous system, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or during congenital rubella syndrome.

Rubella encephalitis is a rare central nervous system complication of rubella infection, occurring primarily in immunocompromised individuals. It is caused by the rubella virus, a member of the Togaviridae family. The condition is characterized by inflammation of the brain, leading to symptoms such as seizures, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. It typically affects the cerebrum and cerebellum. Synonyms include congenital rubella syndrome when occurring in fetuses, though encephalitis specifically refers to the inflammatory process in the brain. The condition is more commonly associated with congenital infections but can also occur in postnatal cases.

Rubella meningitis is a rare complication of rubella infection, characterized by inflammation of the meninges. It typically occurs in the acute phase of the illness and is more common in adults. The causative agent is the rubella virus, a member of the Togaviridae family. Common synonyms include rubella encephalitis and viral meningitis due to rubella. The central nervous system, particularly the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, are primarily affected. Symptoms may include fever, headache, and neck stiffness. While generally mild, it can occasionally lead to more severe neurological complications.

Other neurological complications of rubella refer to rare but serious central nervous system disorders associated with rubella virus infection. Common synonyms include encephalitis and meningitis. The causative agent is the rubella virus. These complications typically affect the brain and spinal cord, leading to symptoms such as seizures, altered mental status, and motor deficits. They are more commonly observed in neonates and immunocompromised individuals. The condition is preventable through vaccination.

Rubella with neurological complications is a rare but serious manifestation of rubella infection, typically occurring in adults or immunocompromised individuals. Caused by the rubella virus, it can lead to encephalitis, meningitis, or peripheral neuropathy. Common synonyms include congenital rubella syndrome (though this refers to fetal infection) and postnatal rubella encephalopathy. The central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord, is typically affected, along with peripheral nerves. Symptoms may include seizures, altered mental status, and motor deficits. Early diagnosis and supportive care are critical for management.

Rubella pneumonia is a rare pulmonary complication of rubella infection, typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals. It is caused by the rubella virus, though secondary bacterial infections may also contribute. The condition presents with interstitial pneumonia, characterized by non-productive cough, fever, and hypoxia. Common synonyms include viral pneumonia associated with rubella. It primarily affects the lungs, with inflammation of the alveolar and interstitial tissues. While uncommon, it can lead to respiratory failure if not managed appropriately. The disease is more frequently observed in patients with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy.

Rubella arthritis is a transient inflammatory joint condition that occurs following rubella infection, typically in adult women. It is also known as German measles arthritis or three-day measles arthritis. Caused by the rubella virus, it primarily affects small joints of the hands and feet, presenting as non-erosive arthritis with swelling and pain. The condition is usually self-limiting and resolves within weeks. It is more common in women and often occurs after the acute phase of the illness. No specific treatment is required, as symptoms typically subside spontaneously.

Other rubella complications refer to secondary health issues arising from rubella infection, primarily affecting the fetus or newborn. Common synonyms include congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) and congenital rubella. The causative agent is the rubella virus. Typically affected body parts include the heart, eyes, ears, and central nervous system. Infection during pregnancy can lead to severe developmental abnormalities. Other complications may involve hearing loss, cataracts, and intellectual disabilities. These complications are most severe when infection occurs during the first trimester. Vaccination remains the most effective prevention strategy.

Rubella with other complications is a viral infection caused primarily by the rubella virus, also known as German measles. It typically presents with a mild fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. Complications may include encephalitis, thrombocytopenia, and, most notably, congenital rubella syndrome in fetuses exposed in utero. The rash usually begins on the face and spreads downward. Common synonyms include German measles and three-day measles. The infection primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and may involve the central nervous system and other organs in severe cases.

Rubella without complication is a viral illness caused by the rubella virus, also known as German measles. It typically presents with mild symptoms including fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include German measles and three-day measles. The rash begins on the face and spreads downward, affecting the trunk and extremities. The infection is most commonly seen in children and is generally self-limiting. Although rare, the virus can cause congenital rubella syndrome if contracted during pregnancy. The primary affected body parts include the skin, lymph nodes, and mucous membranes.

Plantar wart is a viral infection caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 1, 2, and 4. It typically appears on the soles of the feet, especially between the toes, and presents as a hard, rough lesion with a central black dot resembling a seed. Common synonyms include verruca plantaris and plantar verruca. The condition is highly contagious and spreads through direct skin contact or via contaminated surfaces. It often causes pain due to pressure from walking. Treatment options include topical agents, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

Other viral warts, also known as common warts or verrucae vulgaris, are benign skin growths caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 2 and 4. They typically appear on the hands, fingers, and knees, and may also occur on the face, soles of the feet, or genital areas. These warts are contagious and spread through direct contact. Clinically, they present as rough, hyperkeratotic lesions with a central umbilication. While generally asymptomatic, they can cause discomfort or cosmetic concern. Treatment options include topical agents, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

Viral wart unspecified refers to a benign skin lesion caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), typically presenting as a rough, hyperkeratotic growth. Common synonyms include common wart, verruca vulgaris, and plantar wart. The condition is caused by various HPV types, most commonly 2, 3, 4, and 1. It predominantly affects the hands, feet, and face, with plantar warts occurring on the soles. Transmission occurs via direct contact, and lesions may resolve spontaneously or require treatment.

code_desc: Cowpox and vaccinia not from vaccine
summary: Cowpox and vaccinia not from vaccine are zoonotic viral infections caused by members of the Orthopoxvirus genus. Cowpox is primarily caused by *Cowpox virus*, while vaccinia is caused by *Vaccinia virus*. These infections are typically acquired through contact with infected animals, such as rodents or cats. Common synonyms include cowpox disease and vaccinia infection. Lesions usually appear on the hands, face, and arms, and may spread to other body parts. The clinical presentation includes vesicular or pustular eruptions, often with a central umbilication. Systemic symptoms like fever and lymphadenopathy may also occur.

Orf virus disease is a contagious, self-limiting viral infection caused by the parapoxvirus, specifically Orf virus. Commonly known as contagious ecthyma, it primarily affects sheep and goats but can be transmitted to humans through direct contact with infected animals.
