In humans, the disease typically presents as a painful, ulcerative lesion on the hands, fingers, or face. The infection is characterized by a vesiculopustular rash that progresses to a crusted lesion. It is more common in farmers, shepherds, and veterinarians. The condition is generally mild and resolves without specific treatment.

Pseudocowpox, also known as milker's node, is a benign viral infection characterized by the development of painless, firm nodules, typically on the hands or forearms. It is caused by the cowpox virus, a member of the Orthopoxvirus genus. The condition is commonly acquired through contact with infected animals, particularly cattle. Clinically, the lesions may progress to vesicles or pustules before resolving spontaneously. It is often seen in individuals with occupational exposure to livestock, such as farmers or veterinarians. The infection is self-limiting and generally does not require specific treatment.

Paravaccinia unspecified is a rare, self-limiting viral infection characterized by cutaneous eruptions, typically following smallpox vaccination. It is caused by members of the Orthopoxvirus genus, most commonly the cowpox virus. Common synonyms include vaccinia-like disease and paravaccinia. The condition primarily affects the skin, with lesions often appearing at the site of vaccination or on the hands, face, and arms. It is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. The infection is usually mild and resolves spontaneously without specific treatment.

Other orthopoxvirus infections refer to diseases caused by orthopoxviruses other than variola (smallpox) and monkeypox. Common synonyms include camelpox, cowpox, and vaccinia. These infections are typically caused by viruses such as cowpox virus, ectromelia virus, and monkeypox virus. The primary affected body parts include the skin, where characteristic vesicular or pustular lesions develop, often on the hands, face, and limbs. Systemic symptoms like fever and malaise may also occur. These infections are generally self-limiting but can lead to complications in immunocompromised individuals. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected animals or humans.

Other orthopoxvirus infections refer to diseases caused by orthopoxviruses other than variola (smallpox) and monkeypox. Common synonyms include camelpox, cowpox, and vaccinia. These infections are typically caused by viruses such as cowpox virus, monkeypox virus, and variola virus. The primary affected body parts include the skin, with characteristic vesicular or pustular lesions. Systemic involvement may occur, particularly with monkeypox. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected animals or humans, or through aerosolized particles. Clinical manifestations vary but often include fever, malaise, and a rash. Vaccination with vaccinia vaccine can provide cross-protection.

Molluscum contagiosum is a viral infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a member of the Poxviridae family. It presents as small, raised, pearly papules with a central dimple, commonly found on the trunk, face, arms, and genital areas. The condition is highly contagious, spreading through direct skin-to-skin contact or fomite transmission. It is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include molluscum, mollusca, and pox. The infection is generally self-limiting, resolving spontaneously within several months to a couple of years.

Exanthema subitum, also known as sixth disease or roseola infantum, is a viral illness primarily affecting young children. Caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) and occasionally HHV-7, it presents with a high fever followed by a rash. The rash typically appears after the fever subsides, consisting of pink or red maculopapular lesions on the trunk and extremities. Lymphadenopathy and mild pharyngitis may also occur. The condition is self-limiting and generally benign, with no specific treatment required.

code_desc: Exanthema subitum [sixth disease] due to human herpesvirus 6
summary: Exanthema subitum, also known as sixth disease, is a viral illness caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6). It primarily affects young children, typically between 6 months and 2 years of age. The illness is characterized by a sudden onset of high fever, followed by a distinctive rash that appears after the fever subsides. The rash consists of erythematous maculopapular lesions on the face, trunk, and extremities. Other symptoms may include cough, runny nose, and mild conjunctivitis. The condition is self-limiting and usually resolves within 5–7 days without specific treatment.

code_desc: Exanthema subitum [sixth disease] due to human herpesvirus 7
summary: Exanthema subitum, also known as sixth disease, is a self-limiting viral illness caused primarily by human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7), though human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) may also be involved. It predominantly affects young children, typically between 6 months and 2 years of age. The illness is characterized by a sudden onset of high fever followed by a maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads to the trunk and limbs. Other symptoms may include cough, runny nose, and irritability. The rash usually resolves within a few days without specific treatment.

Exanthema subitum, also known as sixth disease or roseola infantum, is a viral illness primarily affecting young children. Caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) and occasionally HHV-7, it presents with a high fever lasting 3–5 days, followed by a rash that appears after the fever subsides. The rash consists of pink or red maculopapular lesions, typically on the trunk and spreading to the limbs. The condition is generally mild and self-limiting, with no specific treatment required. It is most common in children between 6 months and 2 years of age.

Erythema infectiosum, also known as fifth disease, is a viral illness caused by human parvovirus B19. It primarily affects children and is characterized by a distinctive bright red rash on the cheeks, often described as a "slapped cheek" appearance, followed by a lacy rash on the trunk and limbs. The infection is contagious and spreads via respiratory droplets. Common synonyms include five-day fever and erythema infectiosum. The rash typically resolves within a week but may persist or recur with fever or sun exposure. The disease is generally mild and self-limiting, though it can pose risks for individuals with hemolytic anemia.

Enteroviral vesicular stomatitis with exanthem is a viral infection characterized by vesicular lesions in the oral cavity and a generalized exanthem. Common synonyms include herpangina and hand, foot, and mouth disease. Caused by enteroviruses, particularly coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71, it primarily affects children. The condition typically involves fever, oral vesicles, and a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. Lesions are often painful and may ulcerate. The illness is self-limiting, with resolution within 7–10 days. Complications are rare but can include dehydration and, in severe cases, neurological involvement.

Enteroviral vesicular pharyngitis is a viral infection characterized by the presence of small, fluid-filled blisters (vesicles) in the pharynx. Common synonyms include herpangina and viral pharyngitis. It is primarily caused by enteroviruses, most commonly coxsackievirus A16 and A5. The condition typically affects the oropharynx, including the tonsils, soft palate, and uvula. It is more prevalent in children and often presents with fever, sore throat, and difficulty swallowing. The vesicles rupture to form ulcers, leading to discomfort. The illness is generally self-limiting, resolving within 7–10 days without specific treatment.

Parapoxvirus infection unspecified refers to a group of viral infections caused by parapoxviruses, which are related to the smallpox virus. Common synonyms include pseudofurunculosis and scabby mouth. The causative agents include orf virus, bovine papular stomatitis virus, and parapoxvirus. These infections typically affect the skin and mucous membranes, often presenting as painful, crusted lesions. Commonly affected areas include the face, lips, hands, and genital regions. The infection is usually transmitted through direct contact with infected animals or contaminated objects. It is more prevalent in individuals with close contact with livestock.

Bovine stomatitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the oral cavity of cattle, characterized by ulcerative lesions on the tongue, gums, and hard palate. Common synonyms include oral ulceration and mouth rot. The condition is often caused by infectious agents such as *Actinobacillus lignieresii* and *Pasteurella multocida*, though mechanical trauma or nutritional deficiencies may also contribute. Affected animals exhibit signs of pain, salivation, and reduced feed intake. The disease primarily targets the mucous membranes of the mouth, leading to discomfort and potential systemic complications if left untreated.

Sealpox is a rare, non-contagious skin condition characterized by the development of firm, red, raised lesions that typically appear on the trunk and extremities. It is most commonly observed in marine mammals, particularly seals, though it can occasionally affect humans through direct contact with infected animals. The exact causative agent remains unidentified, though some cases have been linked to viral or bacterial infections. Synonyms include seal pox and seal disease. The condition is often self-limiting, with lesions resolving over several weeks without scarring.

Other parapoxvirus infections are a group of viral diseases caused by parapoxviruses, including orf, pseudocowpox, and bovine papular stomatitis virus. These infections typically present as localized cutaneous lesions, often resembling cowpox. Common synonyms include orf and pseudocowpox. The viruses primarily affect the skin and mucous membranes, with lesions commonly found on the face, lips, and hands. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected animals or contaminated objects. The disease is more prevalent in agricultural settings and among immunocompromised individuals. Clinical manifestations range from mild papules to more severe ulcerative lesions.

Parapoxvirus infections are a group of viral diseases caused by parapoxviruses, including orf, pseudocowpox, and bovine papular stomatitis virus. These infections typically present as cutaneous lesions, often resembling cowpox but with a more localized and less systemic course. Common synonyms include orf, contagious pustular dermatitis, and pseudocowpox. The lesions usually appear on the face, lips, or hands, and are more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with close contact with infected animals. The infection is generally self-limiting but can cause significant discomfort and scarring.

Yatapoxvirus infection unspecified refers to a rare viral infection caused by members of the Yatapoxvirus genus, which includes the variola virus (smallpox). Though primarily associated with smallpox, the term encompasses unspecified yatapoxvirus infections. Common synonyms include smallpox and variola infection. The virus primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, causing characteristic rash and systemic symptoms. It is a highly contagious disease with a high mortality rate, though vaccination has significantly reduced its incidence. The infection typically manifests as a febrile illness with a progressive rash.

Tanapox virus disease is a rare, self-limiting viral infection caused by the Tanapox virus, a member of the Poxviridae family. It is characterized by a mild fever and a maculopapular rash, typically appearing on the face, trunk, and extremities. The disease is generally non-severe and resolves spontaneously within weeks. Common synonyms include Tanapox fever and African pox. The virus is transmitted through arthropod vectors, though human-to-human spread is uncommon. It primarily affects humans and non-human primates, with no known significant mortality.

Yaba pox virus disease is a rare, self-limiting viral infection caused by members of the Poxviridae family, specifically the Yaba pox virus. It is also known as yaba disease or yaba pox. The infection typically affects the skin, causing characteristic lesions such as papules, vesicles, and ulcers, often on the face, hands, and feet. Systemic symptoms like fever and lymphadenopathy may also occur. The disease is more commonly reported in tropical regions and is associated with occupational exposure, such as handling infected animals or contaminated materials. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected lesions or bodily fluids.

Other yatapoxvirus infections are rare viral diseases caused by members of the Yatapoxvirus genus, which includes the variola virus (smallpox). These infections are characterized by fever, malaise, and a vesiculopustular rash. Common synonyms include variola infections and smallpox. The rash typically begins on the face and spreads to the limbs and trunk. While variola is the most well-known, other yatapoxviruses may cause similar symptoms. These infections primarily affect the skin and mucous membranes, with systemic involvement in severe cases. The disease is highly contagious and has a high mortality rate without vaccination.

Yatapoxvirus infections are rare viral diseases caused by members of the Yatapox genus, which includes the variola virus (smallpox). These infections are characterized by fever, malaise, and a distinctive rash that progresses through macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts. The rash typically affects the face, arms, and legs. Common synonyms include smallpox and variola infection. The disease is highly contagious and can lead to severe complications, including scarring and mortality. Historically, smallpox was a major public health concern before its eradication in 1980.

code_desc: Other specified viral infections characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions
summary: "Other specified viral infections characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions" refers to viral infections that produce distinct cutaneous or mucosal manifestations but do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include viral exanthems or mucocutaneous viral infections. Causative agents may include herpesviruses, papillomaviruses, or other viruses. These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, and sometimes the oral cavity. Lesions may present as rashes, ulcers, or papules, often accompanied by systemic symptoms. The condition is diagnosed based on clinical presentation and exclusion of other known viral syndromes.

code_desc: Unspecified viral infection characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions
summary: Unspecified viral infection characterized by skin and mucous membrane lesions refers to a viral illness presenting with eruptions on the skin and mucous membranes without a specific etiological agent identified. Common synonyms include viral exanthem or unspecified viral mucocutaneous infection. Causative agents may include herpesviruses, papillomaviruses, or other viruses, though not definitively identified. Typically affects the skin, oral mucosa, genital mucosa, and sometimes the conjunctiva. Symptoms may include rash, ulcers, and systemic signs like fever. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation when specific testing is inconclusive.

Hepatitis A with hepatic coma is a severe complication of acute hepatitis A, characterized by fulminant liver failure leading to hepatic encephalopathy. Caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), it typically affects the liver, leading to impaired detoxification and ammonia accumulation. Common synonyms include acute hepatitis A with encephalopathy and fulminant hepatitis A. The condition primarily impacts the liver and central nervous system, resulting in altered mental status, confusion, and potentially coma. It is more common in individuals with pre-existing liver disease or those with compromised immune systems.

Hepatitis A is an acute viral infection of the liver caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV). It typically presents with flu-like symptoms, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Common synonyms include infectious hepatitis and serum hepatitis. The infection is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated food or water. The liver is the primary affected organ, with inflammation and potential transient liver dysfunction. Hepatic coma is absent, distinguishing it from more severe forms of hepatitis. Most patients recover fully without long-term liver damage.

code_desc: Acute hepatitis B with delta-agent with hepatic coma
summary: Acute hepatitis B with delta-agent and hepatic coma is a severe form of liver inflammation caused by co-infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and the hepatitis delta virus (HDV). The delta agent enhances viral replication and disease severity. This condition leads to rapid liver dysfunction, potentially progressing to hepatic coma, a life-threatening state of altered mental status due to hepatic encephalopathy. Common synonyms include fulminant hepatitis B with HDV and acute severe hepatitis B. The liver is the primary affected organ, with systemic complications possible.

code_desc: Acute hepatitis B with delta-agent without hepatic coma
summary: Acute hepatitis B with delta-agent without hepatic coma is a viral liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV) combined with the hepatitis delta virus (HDV). It leads to inflammation of the liver, characterized by elevated liver enzymes and jaundice. Common synonyms include acute HBV/HDV coinfection. The condition primarily affects the liver, causing transient dysfunction without progressing to hepatic coma. Transmission occurs through blood or bodily fluids. Most patients recover fully with supportive care, though some may develop chronic infection.

code_desc: Acute hepatitis B without delta-agent with hepatic coma
summary: Acute hepatitis B without delta-agent with hepatic coma is a severe form of liver inflammation caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), occurring in the absence of coinfection with the hepatitis delta virus. It leads to rapid liver dysfunction, resulting in hepatic coma, a life-threatening condition characterized by altered mental status and impaired consciousness. Common synonyms include fulminant hepatitis B and acute liver failure due to HBV. The primary affected body part is the liver, with systemic complications affecting multiple organs. Causative agents are primarily HBV, though rare cases may involve other agents.

code_desc: Acute hepatitis B without delta-agent and without hepatic coma
summary: Acute hepatitis B without delta-agent and without hepatic coma refers to a short-term liver inflammation caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), without co-infection with the hepatitis delta virus and without progression to hepatic coma. Common synonyms include acute HBV infection. The causative agent is the hepatitis B virus. Typically, the liver is the affected body part, with symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. The condition is self-limiting in most cases but can lead to chronic infection if not resolved.

code_desc: Acute delta-(super) infection of hepatitis B carrier
summary: Acute delta-(super) infection of hepatitis B carrier refers to a severe form of hepatitis B occurring in individuals already infected with hepatitis B virus (HBV) who subsequently acquire the hepatitis delta virus (HDV). This co-infection leads to more aggressive liver disease. Common synonyms include acute hepatitis B delta infection or superinfection. HDV is the causative agent, and the infection primarily affects the liver, causing inflammation and potentially leading to fulminant hepatitis. It is more common in regions with high HBV prevalence.

code_desc: Acute hepatitis C without hepatic coma
summary: Acute hepatitis C without hepatic coma is a short-term liver inflammation caused by hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, typically occurring within the first six months of infection. It is characterized by elevated liver enzymes, fatigue, nausea, and jaundice. Common synonyms include acute HCV infection and early-phase hepatitis C. The causative agent is the hepatitis C virus, primarily transmitted through blood-to-blood contact. The liver is the primary affected organ, with minimal or no evidence of hepatic encephalopathy. Most patients do not develop hepatic coma, though some may progress to chronic hepatitis.

code_desc: Acute hepatitis C with hepatic coma
summary: Acute hepatitis C with hepatic coma is a severe form of liver failure resulting from rapid progression of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. It is characterized by fulminant hepatic necrosis, leading to impaired liver function and hepatic encephalopathy. Common synonyms include acute liver failure due to HCV and fulminant hepatitis C. The causative agent is the hepatitis C virus, primarily transmitted through blood exposure. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with systemic complications affecting the central nervous system and other organs due to toxin accumulation and metabolic disturbances.

Acute hepatitis C is a short-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV). It typically presents with flu-like symptoms, fatigue, and jaundice. Common synonyms include acute HCV infection or acute viral hepatitis C. The virus primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and potential liver damage. Transmission occurs mainly through blood-to-blood contact. Most individuals clear the virus spontaneously, but some progress to chronic infection. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term complications.

Acute hepatitis E is a viral infection caused primarily by the hepatitis E virus (HEV), with genotype 1 being the most common in endemic regions. It typically presents with flu-like symptoms, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. The infection mainly affects the liver, leading to inflammation and impaired function. It is transmitted through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated water. Common synonyms include hepatitis E infection and HEV hepatitis. While generally self-limiting, it can be severe in immunocompromised individuals and during pregnancy. The disease primarily targets the liver, with rare extrahepatic manifestations.

Other specified acute viral hepatitis refers to hepatitis caused by viruses not classified under hepatitis A, B, or C. Common synonyms include acute hepatitis of unspecified etiology or acute non-A to non-C hepatitis. Causative agents may include hepatitis D, E, G, or other rare viruses. It typically affects the liver, leading to inflammation and impaired function. Symptoms include jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing and exclusion of known hepatitis viruses. The condition can range from mild to severe, requiring supportive care and monitoring.

Acute viral hepatitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the liver caused by a virus, where the specific type is not identified. Common synonyms include acute hepatitis of unspecified etiology. Causative agents may include hepatitis A, B, C, D, or E viruses, though the exact agent is not determined. The condition typically affects the liver, leading to symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and elevated liver enzymes. It can occur in individuals of any age and is often transmitted through contaminated food, water, or blood. Prompt diagnosis and management are essential to prevent complications.

code_desc: Chronic viral hepatitis B with delta-agent
summary: Chronic viral hepatitis B with delta-agent is a severe form of hepatitis B infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV) combined with the hepatitis delta virus (HDV). This co-infection leads to more aggressive liver disease, including progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Common synonyms include delta hepatitis and HBV/HDV co-infection. The primary affected body part is the liver, with systemic manifestations possible in advanced stages. Transmission occurs through blood and bodily fluids.

code_desc: Chronic viral hepatitis B without delta-agent
summary: Chronic viral hepatitis B without delta-agent is a long-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV). It occurs when the immune system fails to clear the virus, leading to persistent inflammation and potential liver damage. Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis B infection. The primary causative agent is the hepatitis B virus, which targets the liver, leading to conditions such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma if left untreated. The disease primarily affects the liver, with possible systemic manifestations. Transmission occurs through blood and bodily fluids.

Chronic viral hepatitis C is a long-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV). Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis C and HCV infection. The virus primarily targets the liver, leading to inflammation and potential fibrosis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma. Transmission occurs mainly through blood-to-blood contact. Most individuals clear the virus spontaneously, but approximately 20% develop chronic infection. Risk factors include intravenous drug use, blood transfusions before 1992, and needlestick injuries. Early diagnosis and antiviral therapy can lead to sustained virologic response and prevent disease progression.

Other chronic viral hepatitis refers to persistent liver inflammation caused by viruses other than hepatitis B or C. Common synonyms include non-B non-C hepatitis and hepatitis of unknown etiology. Causative agents may include hepatitis D, E, G, or other less common viruses. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and potential cirrhosis. It is often diagnosed when standard hepatitis tests are negative, and may present with symptoms such as fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis typically involves serological testing and liver biopsy.

Chronic viral hepatitis unspecified refers to long-term liver inflammation caused by a virus, where the specific type (e.g., hepatitis B or C) is not identified. Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis of unspecified origin. Causative agents may include hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), or other less common viruses. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, or liver failure if left untreated. It is often asymptomatic in early stages but can present with fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal discomfort. Diagnosis typically involves serological testing and liver function analysis.

code_desc: Unspecified viral hepatitis with hepatic coma
summary: Unspecified viral hepatitis with hepatic coma refers to severe liver dysfunction caused by a viral infection, leading to hepatic encephalopathy. It is a life-threatening condition characterized by impaired liver function, coagulopathy, and altered mental status. Common synonyms include acute liver failure due to viral etiology. Causative agents may include hepatitis A, B, C, D, or E viruses. The liver is the primary affected organ, with systemic complications affecting the brain, coagulation system, and other organs. Diagnosis is often made when specific viral markers are undetermined or unavailable.

code_desc: Unspecified viral hepatitis B without hepatic coma
summary: Unspecified viral hepatitis B without hepatic coma refers to a clinical diagnosis of hepatitis B infection where the specific strain or variant is not identified, and there is no evidence of hepatic encephalopathy. It is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which primarily affects the liver. Common synonyms include hepatitis B, viral hepatitis B, and HBV infection. The condition typically involves inflammation of the liver, leading to symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. Transmission occurs through blood or bodily fluids, and affected individuals may progress to chronic infection if not managed.

code_desc: Unspecified viral hepatitis B with hepatic coma
summary: Unspecified viral hepatitis B with hepatic coma refers to a severe acute or fulminant hepatitis B infection leading to hepatic failure and coma. It is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which targets the liver, causing inflammation and impaired function. Common synonyms include acute hepatitis B with hepatic encephalopathy and fulminant hepatitis B. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to systemic complications such as coagulopathy, cerebral edema, and multi-organ failure. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to improve outcomes.

Unspecified viral hepatitis B refers to hepatitis caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV) without specific identification of the viral genotype or subtype. It is characterized by inflammation of the liver, leading to impaired liver function. Common synonyms include hepatitis B, HBV infection, and viral hepatitis B. The causative agent is the hepatitis B virus, which primarily affects the liver. Symptoms may include jaundice, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Transmission occurs through blood and bodily fluids.

code_desc: Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma
summary: Unspecified viral hepatitis C without hepatic coma refers to a clinical condition where hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is present, but the specific serotype or subtype is not identified. It is characterized by liver inflammation without evidence of hepatic encephalopathy. Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis C and HCV infection. The causative agent is the hepatitis C virus, primarily transmitted through blood-to-blood contact. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential progression to cirrhosis or liver failure if left untreated.

code_desc: Unspecified viral hepatitis C with hepatic coma
summary: Unspecified viral hepatitis C with hepatic coma refers to advanced liver failure caused by hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, leading to hepatic encephalopathy. It is a severe complication characterized by altered mental status, confusion, and potentially coma due to toxin accumulation from impaired liver function. Common synonyms include hepatitis C-induced hepatic coma and fulminant hepatitis C. The causative agent is the hepatitis C virus. Typically affects the liver, with systemic effects on the central nervous system.

Unspecified viral hepatitis C refers to a form of hepatitis caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV) when the specific genotype or subtype is not identified. It is characterized by inflammation of the liver leading to impaired function. Common synonyms include hepatitis C, unspecified genotype. The causative agent is the hepatitis C virus, primarily affecting the liver. Transmission occurs mainly through blood-to-blood contact. Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, fibrosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma if left untreated. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis typically involves serological testing and molecular methods.

code_desc: Unspecified viral hepatitis without hepatic coma
summary: Unspecified viral hepatitis without hepatic coma refers to liver inflammation caused by a virus, where the specific type is not identified, and there is no evidence of hepatic encephalopathy. Common synonyms include acute viral hepatitis, unspecified hepatitis, or undetermined viral hepatitis. Causative agents may include hepatitis A, B, C, D, or E viruses. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. It typically involves the hepatocytes and can progress to more severe liver disease if left untreated.

code_desc: Human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] disease resulting in infectious and parasitic diseases
summary: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease weakens the immune system, increasing susceptibility to opportunistic infections and parasitic diseases. Common synonyms include acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and HIV-related immunosuppression. Causative agents include various bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites such as *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Pneumocystis jirovecii*, *Toxoplasma gondii*, and *Cryptosporidium*. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, central nervous system, gastrointestinal tract, and skin. The condition progresses through stages of immunosuppression, leading to severe complications without treatment.

Cytomegaloviral pneumonitis is a pulmonary infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients. The infection leads to interstitial pneumonia characterized by inflammation and multinucleated giant cells in lung tissue. Common synonyms include CMV pneumonia or CMV-induced interstitial pneumonitis. The primary affected body part is the lung, with symptoms including fever, cough, and dyspnea. Complications may arise from progressive respiratory failure.

Cytomegaloviral hepatitis is a viral infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and potential liver dysfunction. Common synonyms include CMV hepatitis or congenital CMV infection when acquired in utero. The condition typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients, and can also affect newborns. Symptoms may include fever, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. While often asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals, it can lead to severe complications in vulnerable populations.

Cytomegaloviral pancreatitis is a rare inflammatory condition of the pancreas caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV). It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients. The infection leads to pancreatic inflammation, often presenting with abdominal pain, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Common synonyms include CMV-induced pancreatitis and viral pancreatitis. While the pancreas is the primary affected organ, CMV can also involve the liver, gallbladder, and biliary system. Diagnosis is confirmed through serology, PCR, or histopathology. Treatment involves antiviral therapy, such as ganciclovir or valganciclovir.

Other cytomegaloviral diseases refer to a spectrum of infections caused by human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. Common synonyms include congenital cytomegalovirus infection and acquired cytomegalovirus disease. The virus primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients, and can involve multiple organ systems. Commonly affected body parts include the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, liver, and central nervous system. Symptoms may range from asymptomatic to severe, including pneumonia, hepatitis, and encephalitis. The disease is often diagnosed through polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing or viral culture.

Cytomegaloviral disease unspecified refers to a clinical syndrome caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection when the specific manifestation or affected organ system is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include CMV infection or CMV disease. The causative agent is human cytomegalovirus, a member of the herpesvirus family. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, or neonates, and can involve multiple organ systems including the lungs, liver, and central nervous system. Symptoms vary but may include fever, fatigue, and organ dysfunction.

Mumps orchitis is an inflammatory condition of the testicle caused by the mumps virus, typically occurring in post-pubertal males following a mumps infection. It is a complication of mumps, occurring in approximately 20-30% of cases. Common synonyms include epididymo-orchitis due to mumps. The virus spreads via the bloodstream to the testes, leading to swelling, pain, and potential infertility. The primary affected body parts are the testes and epididymis. It is more common in adolescents and young adults, and may result in atrophy of the affected testicle.

Mumps meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by the mumps virus, typically occurring in adolescents and young adults. It is a complication of mumps infection, which primarily affects the parotid glands. Common synonyms include epidemic parotitis meningitis and viral meningitis due to mumps. The virus, Morbillivirus, spreads via respiratory droplets. Symptoms include fever, headache, and neck stiffness. The central nervous system, particularly the meninges, is typically affected. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine provides effective prevention. Complications are rare but may include encephalitis or hearing loss.

Mumps encephalitis is a rare but serious central nervous system complication of mumps virus infection. It occurs when the virus spreads from the lymph nodes to the brain, causing inflammation. Common synonyms include mumps meningitis and mumps encephalomyelitis. The causative agent is the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus. Typically, it affects the cerebral cortex, cerebellum, and brainstem, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and seizures. It predominantly occurs in children and adolescents, often following a subclinical or mild mumps infection.

Mumps pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas occurring as a complication of mumps virus infection. It typically presents with acute pancreatitis symptoms following parotitis. The mumps virus is the known causative agent, though the exact mechanism of pancreatic involvement remains unclear. Common synonyms include mumps-associated pancreatitis or viral pancreatitis. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the liver and biliary system. It is more common in adults than children and often occurs after the resolution of parotid swelling. Clinical features include abdominal pain, nausea, and elevated pancreatic enzymes.

Mumps hepatitis is a rare complication of mumps virus infection, characterized by transient elevation of liver enzymes. It typically occurs in adolescents and young adults. The condition is caused by the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus, and is often asymptomatic or mild. Common synonyms include mumps-associated hepatitis or viral hepatitis following mumps. The liver is the primarily affected organ, though the virus may also involve the pancreas and central nervous system. It usually resolves spontaneously without specific treatment.

Mumps myocarditis is an inflammatory condition of the heart muscle caused by the mumps virus, typically occurring after a primary mumps infection. It is a rare but serious complication, often presenting with symptoms such as chest pain, arrhythmias, and heart failure. Common synonyms include mumps-induced myocarditis or viral myocarditis due to mumps. The virus primarily affects the myocardium, and the condition is more commonly seen in adolescents and young adults. While most cases resolve spontaneously, severe cases may require medical intervention. The causative agent is the mumps virus, and the heart is the typically affected body part.

Mumps nephritis is a rare complication of mumps infection characterized by inflammation of the kidneys. It occurs due to immune-mediated damage following mumps virus infection, typically occurring 1-3 weeks after the initial illness. Common synonyms include post-mumps glomerulonephritis and mumps-associated nephritis. The causative agent is the mumps virus, and the condition primarily affects the renal parenchyma, particularly the glomeruli. It is more common in children and adolescents. Clinical features may include hematuria, proteinuria, and elevated serum creatinine. Prompt diagnosis and management are essential to prevent progression to renal failure.

Mumps polyneuropathy is a rare complication of mumps virus infection, characterized by acute inflammatory polyneuropathy. It typically occurs 3–14 days after the onset of mumps symptoms. Common synonyms include mumps-induced neuropathy and post-mumps polyneuropathy. The causative agent is the mumps virus, though the exact pathogenic mechanism remains unclear. The condition primarily affects the peripheral nerves, particularly the cranial and spinal nerves, leading to symptoms such as facial weakness, cranial nerve palsies, and motor deficits. It is more commonly seen in adults than children.

Mumps arthritis is a rare complication of mumps virus infection, characterized by joint inflammation typically occurring 1–2 weeks after the initial illness. It is more common in adults than children. The condition is often associated with the paramyxovirus, specifically the mumps virus. Common synonyms include post-mumps arthritis and mumps-induced arthritis. It predominantly affects large joints such as the knees, wrists, and ankles, presenting with pain, swelling, and limited mobility. The arthritis is usually self-limiting and resolves without long-term joint damage.

Other mumps complications refer to secondary conditions that arise following mumps infection, typically occurring in post-pubertal males. Common synonyms include orchitis and oophoritis. The primary causative agent is the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus. Orchitis, the inflammation of the testes, is the most common complication, often leading to potential infertility. Oophoritis, inflammation of the ovaries, may occur in females. Other complications include meningitis, encephalitis, and pancreatitis, affecting the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract respectively. These complications are more frequent in older children and adults.

Mumps with other complications is a viral infection caused primarily by the mumps virus, although other agents may contribute. It typically affects the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands, leading to swelling and pain. Common complications include meningitis, encephalitis, orchitis, oophoritis, and pancreatitis. Synonyms include epidemic parotitis and parotitis with complications. The infection predominantly affects children and adolescents, with males more likely to develop orchitis. Complications can lead to long-term issues such as infertility or hearing loss.

Mumps without complication is a viral infection caused by the mumps virus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. It primarily affects the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands, leading to swelling and tenderness. Common synonyms include epidemic parotitis and parotitis. The illness typically presents with fever, headache, and muscle aches, followed by glandular swelling. It is highly contagious and spreads via respiratory droplets. Most cases resolve spontaneously without long-term complications, though rare complications such as orchitis or meningitis may occur. The condition is more common in children but can affect adults. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine provides effective prevention.

Gammaherpesviral mononucleosis, also known as infectious mononucleosis or "mono," is a viral infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) or, less commonly, cytomegalovirus (CMV). It typically affects adolescents and young adults. The illness is characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and elevated atypical lymphocytes. It primarily involves the lymphatic system and may affect the liver and spleen. Complications such as splenomegaly or hepatitis are possible but not always present. The condition is usually self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment.

Gammaherpesviral mononucleosis with polyneuropathy is a rare condition characterized by systemic mononucleosis-like symptoms caused by gamma-herpesviruses, such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) or Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). It often presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, and fatigue, accompanied by peripheral neuropathy, including sensory and motor deficits. Common synonyms include EBV-induced mononucleosis with neuropathy or KSHV-associated neurological syndrome. The condition primarily affects the nervous system, particularly peripheral nerves, and may involve the central nervous system in severe cases. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals.

Gammaherpesviral mononucleosis with meningitis is a systemic infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), though other gammaherpesviruses may contribute. It presents with symptoms of infectious mononucleosis, including fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, along with meningeal inflammation. The condition typically affects the lymphatic system and central nervous system. Common synonyms include EBV-related mononucleosis and infectious mononucleosis with meningitis. It predominantly involves the lymph nodes, spleen, and meninges.

Gammaherpesviral mononucleosis, also known as infectious mononucleosis or "mono," is a systemic infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) or, less commonly, cytomegalovirus (CMV). It is characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and atypical lymphocytosis. The condition typically affects the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen, with possible complications such as splenomegaly, hepatitis, and airway obstruction. It predominantly occurs in adolescents and young adults. Other complications may include thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and neurological manifestations.

Gammaherpesviral mononucleosis, also known as infectious mononucleosis or "mono," is an acute infectious illness primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). It is characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. The infection predominantly affects the lymphatic system, with lymph node enlargement and increased atypical lymphocytes in the blood. It commonly occurs in adolescents and young adults. Other causative agents include cytomegalovirus (CMV), though EBV is the most common. The condition typically involves the pharynx, lymph nodes, and spleen, with potential complications such as splenic rupture.

Cytomegaloviral mononucleosis, also known as mononucleosis or infectious mononucleosis, is a viral infection caused primarily by cytomegalovirus (CMV). It typically affects adolescents and young adults. The condition is characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. It is commonly referred to as "mono" and is often associated with fatigue and malaise. CMV is a member of the herpesvirus family and is transmitted through bodily fluids. The infection usually involves the lymphatic system and may affect the liver and spleen, though complications are rare in immunocompetent individuals.

Cytomegaloviral mononucleosis with polyneuropathy is a rare complication of cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals. It presents with symptoms of infectious mononucleosis, including fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly, along with peripheral neuropathy characterized by sensory and motor deficits. Common synonyms include CMV-related polyneuropathy and CMV-induced mononucleosis with neuropathy. The causative agent is human cytomegalovirus, and the condition primarily affects the nervous system, particularly peripheral nerves, and may involve the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes.

Cytomegaloviral mononucleosis with meningitis is a rare complication of cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals. It presents with symptoms of mononucleosis, including fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly, along with signs of meningitis such as headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. CMV is the causative agent, and the infection primarily affects the central nervous system. Synonyms include CMV encephalitis or CMV meningitis. The condition predominantly involves the brain and meninges, and may lead to severe neurological complications.

Cytomegaloviral mononucleosis with other complications is a systemic infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It typically presents with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Common synonyms include CMV mononucleosis or infectious mononucleosis. The virus primarily affects the lymphatic system and can involve the liver, spleen, and respiratory tract. Complications may include hepatitis, splenomegaly, and opportunistic infections, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Cytomegaloviral mononucleosis, also known as mononucleosis or infectious mononucleosis, is an acute viral infection primarily caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV). It typically affects adolescents and young adults. The infection is characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. CMV is a member of the herpesvirus family and is transmitted through saliva, blood, or other bodily fluids. While most cases are asymptomatic or mild, severe complications can occur, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. The condition primarily involves the lymphatic system and liver, with systemic symptoms common.

Other infectious mononucleosis, also known as mononucleosis or glandular fever, is an acute viral infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). It is characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. Common synonyms include "mono" and "kissing disease." The infection predominantly affects the lymphatic system and is most common in adolescents and young adults. It typically involves the pharynx, lymph nodes, and spleen, with rare complications in immunocompromised individuals. The condition is usually self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment.

Other infectious mononucleosis with polyneuropathy refers to a rare complication of infectious mononucleosis, primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). It is characterized by neurological symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy, often involving sensory and motor nerves. The condition may present with weakness, sensory loss, and reflex changes, typically affecting the lower extremities. Less commonly, it may involve cranial nerves or the central nervous system. Other causative agents, such as cytomegalovirus or HIV, may contribute in immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include mononucleosis-associated polyneuropathy and EBV-related neuropathy.

Other infectious mononucleosis with meningitis refers to a systemic infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), occasionally by cytomegalovirus (CMV) or other agents. It presents with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, often accompanied by meningitis characterized by headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. The central nervous system is typically affected, along with the lymphatic system and liver. Synonyms include EBV-related meningitis and atypical mononucleosis with central nervous system involvement. Complications may include splenic rupture and encephalitis.

code_desc: Other infectious mononucleosis with other complication
summary: Other infectious mononucleosis with other complication refers to a systemic viral infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), occasionally by cytomegalovirus (CMV). It is characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and atypical lymphocytosis. Common synonyms include infectious mononucleosis, mono, and glandular fever. The disease typically affects the lymphatic system, pharynx, and spleen. Complications may involve the liver, spleen, or central nervous system, leading to conditions such as splenomegaly, hepatitis, or encephalitis. It predominantly affects adolescents and young adults.

Other infectious mononucleosis, also known as mononucleosis or glandular fever, is a viral illness primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). It is characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Less commonly, cytomegalovirus (CMV) or other herpesviruses may be involved. The disease typically affects adolescents and young adults, with symptoms lasting several weeks. It primarily involves the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen, and may cause fatigue and malaise. Complications such as splenic rupture or airway obstruction are rare but possible.

Infectious mononucleosis unspecified without complication is a systemic viral infection characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Common synonyms include "mono" and "glandular fever." It is primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), though other agents like cytomegalovirus (CMV) may contribute. The infection predominantly affects the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen, with involvement of the pharynx and tonsils. It typically occurs in adolescents and young adults, with a self-limiting course. Complications are rare when unspecified.

Infectious mononucleosis unspecified with polyneuropathy is a systemic infection characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly, often caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) or, less commonly, cytomegalovirus (CMV). The polyneuropathy component involves peripheral nerve damage, leading to sensory and motor deficits. Common synonyms include mononucleosis syndrome and EBV-related polyneuropathy. It typically affects the lymphatic system, liver, spleen, and peripheral nerves, with symptoms often emerging 4–6 weeks post-exposure. Complications may include encephalitis or meningitis.

Infectious mononucleosis unspecified with meningitis is a systemic infection characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly, complicated by meningitis. Common synonyms include mononucleosis syndrome and EBV-related meningitis. Caused primarily by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), it may also involve cytomegalovirus or other agents. The infection typically affects the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen, with meningitis involving the central nervous system. It predominantly occurs in adolescents and young adults.

code_desc: Infectious mononucleosis unspecified with other complication
summary: Infectious mononucleosis unspecified with other complication refers to a systemic illness primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), though other agents like cytomegalovirus may contribute. It is characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. The unspecified nature indicates the presence of additional complications not otherwise specified, such as airway obstruction, splenic rupture, or neurological involvement. Common synonyms include mononucleosis syndrome and infectious mononucleosis with complications. Typically affects lymphatic system, liver, spleen, and respiratory tract.

Infectious mononucleosis unspecified is a systemic illness characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. It is commonly caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), though other agents like cytomegalovirus may contribute. The condition primarily affects adolescents and young adults. Common synonyms include "mono" and "glandular fever." Lymph nodes, liver, and spleen are typically involved, with potential complications such as splenic rupture. The diagnosis is often confirmed through blood tests showing atypical lymphocytosis and serological markers.

Keratoconjunctivitis due to adenovirus is an infectious inflammation of the cornea and conjunctiva caused by adenoviruses. Common synonyms include epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis. The condition is characterized by redness, photophobia, tearing, and a gritty sensation in the affected eye. It commonly affects the conjunctiva and cornea, with possible involvement of the eyelids and limbus. Adenovirus types 3, 4, 5, and 8 are frequent causative agents. The infection is highly contagious and often spreads through direct contact or fomites. It typically presents as a self-limiting illness, though symptoms may persist for several weeks.

Conjunctivitis due to adenovirus, also known as viral conjunctivitis or pink eye, is an inflammatory condition of the conjunctiva caused by adenoviruses. It is highly contagious and typically presents with redness, itching, and watery discharge. Common symptoms include photophobia and a gritty sensation. The infection primarily affects the eyes, often involving both conjunctival surfaces. It can occur unilaterally or bilaterally and is frequently associated with upper respiratory tract infections. Adenoviruses are the most common causative agents, with types 3, 4, and 7 being particularly prevalent.

Viral pharyngoconjunctivitis, also known as "pink eye" or "red eye," is an acute infectious condition characterized by inflammation of the pharynx and conjunctiva. It is commonly caused by adenoviruses, particularly serotypes 3, 4, and 7. Other causative agents include enteroviruses and, less frequently, herpes simplex virus. The condition typically affects the conjunctiva, pharynx, and sometimes the eyelids. Symptoms include redness, swelling, and discharge from the eyes, along with sore throat and fever. It is highly contagious and often occurs in outbreaks in schools and daycare centers.

Acute epidemic hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (enteroviral) is a highly contagious viral conjunctival infection characterized by sudden onset of redness, swelling, and subconjunctival hemorrhage. Common synonyms include epidemic conjunctivitis and viral hemorrhagic conjunctivitis. Caused primarily by enteroviruses, particularly coxsackievirus A24 variant and enterovirus 70, it predominantly affects the conjunctiva and eyelids. Symptoms include photophobia, tearing, and a gritty sensation. It is common in tropical and subtropical regions, often spreading through contaminated water or close contact. The condition is usually self-limiting, resolving within 7–14 days without specific treatment.

Other viral conjunctivitis refers to inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by viruses other than adenovirus. Common synonyms include acute viral conjunctivitis and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. Causative agents may include enteroviruses, herpes simplex virus, and varicella-zoster virus. The condition typically affects the eyes, causing redness, itching, and watery discharge. It is highly contagious and often involves both eyes. Symptoms may be accompanied by eyelid swelling and subconjunctival hemorrhage. The infection usually resolves spontaneously within 7–14 days without specific treatment.

Viral conjunctivitis unspecified is an inflammatory condition of the conjunctiva caused by a virus, typically presenting with redness, tearing, and a gritty sensation in the eye. Common synonyms include epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and viral pink eye. The most frequent causative agents are adenoviruses, though other viruses such as enteroviruses and herpes simplex virus may also be involved. The infection primarily affects the conjunctiva and sometimes the cornea, with symptoms usually resolving spontaneously within 7–14 days. It is highly contagious and commonly affects both eyes.

Epidemic myalgia, also known as epidemic muscle pain or epidemic myalgic syndrome, is a viral illness characterized by severe muscle pain and weakness. It is primarily caused by the Coxsackie B virus, though other enteroviruses may also be implicated. The condition typically affects the lower extremities, with symptoms including fever, fatigue, and myalgia. It is more common in children and often follows a seasonal pattern. The illness is self-limiting, with recovery usually occurring within a few weeks. Complications are rare but may include meningitis or myocarditis.

Ross River disease, also known as Ross River fever or epidemic polyarthritis, is a viral illness caused by the Ross River virus, transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. It primarily affects the joints, causing painful inflammation, swelling, and stiffness, most commonly in the wrists, knees, and ankles. Symptoms include fever, rash, and fatigue. The disease is endemic in Australia, Papua New Guinea, and parts of the Pacific Islands. It is a self-limiting condition, though joint pain may persist for weeks or months. No specific antiviral treatment is available, and management focuses on symptom relief.

Viral carditis unspecified refers to inflammation of the heart muscle or cardiac tissues caused by a viral infection, without specific identification of the virus. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis and viral pericarditis. Causative agents often include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. The condition typically affects the myocardium, endocardium, and pericardium, leading to symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It is more common in young adults and children. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and supportive laboratory findings.

Viral endocarditis is a rare condition characterized by inflammation of the inner lining of the heart chambers and valves, typically caused by viral infections. It is less common than bacterial endocarditis and often occurs in immunocompromised individuals. Common causative agents include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. The condition may affect the mitral and tricuspid valves, leading to valvular damage, vegetations, and potential complications such as heart failure or embolism. Synonyms include viral myocarditis and viral valvulitis.

Viral myocarditis is an inflammatory condition of the myocardium caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include viral cardiomyopathy and viral myocardial inflammation. It is typically caused by enteroviruses, such as coxsackievirus B, adenoviruses, and influenza viruses. The condition primarily affects the heart muscle, leading to symptoms like chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It can occur in individuals of all ages but is more common in children and young adults. The infection may progress to heart failure or arrhythmias if not managed appropriately. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications.

Viral pericarditis is an inflammation of the pericardium caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include acute pericarditis and viral myocarditis. It is typically characterized by chest pain, fever, and pericardial effusion. The most common causative agents include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. It predominantly affects the pericardium, with possible involvement of the myocardium. The condition is more common in younger individuals and often follows a viral upper respiratory infection. It is generally self-limiting but may require supportive care and anti-inflammatory treatment.

Viral cardiomyopathy is an inflammatory disease of the heart muscle caused by viral infections. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis and viral-induced cardiomyopathy. It is typically caused by viruses such as coxsackievirus B, adenovirus, influenza, and echovirus. The condition primarily affects the myocardium, leading to impaired cardiac function. It can present with symptoms like dyspnea, fatigue, and arrhythmias. The left ventricle is most commonly involved, and in severe cases, it may progress to heart failure or dilated cardiomyopathy. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term cardiac damage.

Viral carditis refers to inflammation of the heart caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis and viral pericarditis. It is most frequently caused by coxsackievirus B, adenovirus, echovirus, and influenza virus. The condition typically affects the myocardium, endocardium, and pericardium. Symptoms may include chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It can lead to heart failure or conduction abnormalities. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation, ECG findings, and elevated cardiac enzymes. Treatment is primarily supportive, with antiviral therapy reserved for specific cases.

Retrovirus infections not elsewhere classified refer to infections caused by retroviruses that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified retroviral infections. Causative agents may include human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV), simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV), and others. These infections typically affect the immune system, particularly CD4+ T cells, and can lead to conditions like immunodeficiency or malignancies. They may also impact the central nervous system and hematopoietic tissues. Clinical manifestations vary widely depending on the specific virus and host factors.

Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS), also known as hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), is a severe viral illness caused by hantaviruses, primarily from the genus *Hantavirus*. It primarily affects the cardiovascular and respiratory systems, leading to pulmonary edema and hypotension. The disease is typically transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Commonly affected body parts include the lungs and heart. Symptoms progress rapidly, often starting with flu-like symptoms and progressing to respiratory failure. The condition is more prevalent in rural areas with high rodent populations.

"Other specified viral diseases" refers to viral infections that do not fit into more specific categories and are defined by particular clinical or epidemiological features. Common synonyms include "unspecified viral infections" or "miscellaneous viral diseases." Causative agents vary widely and may include viruses such as hepatitis B, herpes simplex, or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). These conditions typically affect multiple body systems, with common involvement of the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and neurological systems. Clinical presentation varies depending on the virus and host factors.

Adenovirus infection unspecified refers to a clinical condition caused by adenoviruses, a group of double-stranded DNA viruses. Common synonyms include acute respiratory infection, viral conjunctivitis, or pharyngitis, depending on the affected site. The causative agents are adenoviruses, which are categorized into different serotypes. This infection typically affects the respiratory tract, eyes, gastrointestinal tract, and sometimes the urinary system. Symptoms vary but often include fever, cough, sore throat, conjunctivitis, and diarrhea. It is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces.

Enterovirus infection unspecified refers to a clinical diagnosis made when the specific enterovirus type cannot be identified. Common synonyms include non-polio enterovirus infection and unspecified enterovirus disease. Causative agents include various enteroviruses such as coxsackieviruses, echoviruses, and polioviruses. Typically affecting the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system, this condition can present with a wide range of symptoms including fever, rash, meningitis, and myositis. It is commonly seen in children but can occur in adults as well.

Coronavirus infection unspecified refers to a respiratory illness caused by any coronavirus not specifically identified. Common synonyms include unspecified coronavirus disease and unspecified viral respiratory infection. The causative agents are various coronaviruses, such as SARS-CoV-2, HKU1, NL63, OC43, and 229E. The infection primarily affects the respiratory tract, causing symptoms like cough, fever, and shortness of breath. It may also involve the gastrointestinal system and, in severe cases, lead to pneumonia or multi-organ involvement.

Parvovirus infection unspecified refers to a viral illness caused by parvoviruses, most commonly parvovirus B19. It is characterized by fever, rash, and systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include erythema infectiosum and fifth disease. The virus primarily affects red blood cell production, leading to anemia in immunocompromised individuals. It typically targets the bone marrow and skin, with the rash appearing on the face and limbs. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or blood. While most cases are mild, complications can occur in those with weakened immune systems or chronic hemolytic disorders.

Papovavirus infection unspecified refers to infections caused by members of the Papovaviridae family, which includes viruses such as human papillomavirus (HPV) and polyomavirus. Common synonyms include HPV infection or polyomavirus infection, depending on the specific virus. These viruses typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, and epithelial tissues. They can cause conditions ranging from benign warts to more severe diseases like cervical cancer. The infection is generally transmitted through direct contact and can manifest in various clinical forms depending on the viral type and host immune status.

code_desc: Other viral infections of unspecified site
summary: "Other viral infections of unspecified site" refers to viral infections where the specific site or organ system is not identified. Common synonyms include unspecified viral infections or viral infections of unknown localization. Causative agents may include herpesviruses, enteroviruses, or adenoviruses. These infections can affect multiple body systems, including the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and neurological systems. Symptoms vary widely depending on the affected area and may include fever, fatigue, rash, or organ dysfunction. Diagnosis often relies on clinical presentation and laboratory tests when specific pathogens are not identified.

Viral infection unspecified refers to a clinical diagnosis made when the specific virus causing the infection is not identified. Common synonyms include undetermined viral infection or viral illness of unspecified etiology. Causative agents may include a wide range of viruses such as influenza, rhinovirus, or enterovirus, though the exact pathogen is not determined. This condition typically affects the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal system, or skin, depending on the underlying virus. Symptoms vary but often include fever, fatigue, and systemic malaise. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and laboratory findings when available.

Tinea barbae and tinea capitis are fungal infections caused by dermatophytes, primarily *Trichophyton* and *Microsporum* species. Tinea barbae affects the beard area, while tinea capitis involves the scalp. Common synonyms include ringworm of the beard and ringworm of the scalp, respectively. Both conditions present as scaly, erythematous, circular lesions with central clearing. Tinea barbae often involves the facial hair, whereas tinea capitis typically affects children and can lead to alopecia. Diagnosis is confirmed through microscopic examination or fungal culture.

Tinea unguium, also known as onychomycosis, is a fungal infection of the nails caused primarily by dermatophytes, with *Trichophyton rubrum* being the most common agent. It may also be caused by yeasts like *Candida* species or molds. The infection typically affects the toenails, though fingernails can be involved. Clinical features include nail discoloration, thickening, brittleness, and debris accumulation under the nail. The infection often progresses slowly and may lead to nail separation from the nail bed. It is more prevalent in older adults and those with diabetes or circulatory disorders.

Tinea manuum is a fungal infection of the hands, commonly caused by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton rubrum* and *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*. It presents as scaly, itchy, and sometimes erythematous patches on the palms and fingers. The infection may spread to the nails, causing onychomycosis. Common synonyms include ringworm of the hand and tinea palmaris. It is more prevalent in individuals with frequent hand washing, moisture, or exposure to contaminated surfaces. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through potassium hydroxide examination or fungal culture. Treatment involves topical or oral antifungal agents.

Tinea pedis, commonly known as athlete's foot, is a fungal infection of the foot caused primarily by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton rubrum*, *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*, and *Candida albicans*. It typically affects the interdigital spaces, soles, and sides of the feet, leading to symptoms like itching, burning, scaling, and fissuring. The infection is contagious and often spreads in moist environments. It is more prevalent in individuals with poor foot hygiene or those who wear occlusive footwear. Treatment usually involves topical antifungal agents, with oral therapy reserved for severe cases.

Tinea corporis, also known as ringworm of the body, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Epidermophyton*. It presents as circular, erythematous, scaly patches with a raised, defined border, often accompanied by itching. The infection typically affects the trunk, arms, and legs. Common synonyms include tineas corporis and ringworm. It is contagious and spreads through direct contact with infected skin or contaminated objects. Diagnosis is usually clinical, though KOH preparation may confirm the presence of hyphae or spores. Treatment involves topical antifungals, with oral agents reserved for severe or widespread cases.

Tinea imbricata is a chronic fungal infection of the skin characterized by overlapping, annular, hypopigmented plaques with a collarette of scale. Common synonyms include "tinea imbricata" and "tinea of the tropics." It is caused primarily by *Trichophyton concentricum*, though other *Trichophyton* species may also be involved. The infection typically affects the trunk, neck, and extremities, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. It is more common in children and individuals with poor hygiene. The condition is often asymptomatic but may cause mild pruritus. Transmission occurs via direct contact or contaminated objects.

Tinea cruris, commonly known as jock itch, is a fungal infection of the groin area caused primarily by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton rubrum* and *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*. It presents as a red, itchy, circular rash with a raised border, often extending to the inner thighs and perineum. The infection thrives in warm, moist environments and is more common in males. It is contagious through direct contact or shared items. Symptoms include burning, scaling, and occasional blistering. Diagnosis is typically clinical, though fungal cultures or microscopy may confirm the presence of hyphae or spores. Treatment involves antifungal topical agents, and prevention focuses on keeping the area dry and clean.

Other dermatophytoses refer to fungal infections caused by dermatophytes affecting areas other than the scalp, nails, or groin. Common synonyms include tinea corporis and ringworm. The causative agents include Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton species. These infections typically affect the trunk, arms, legs, and face. Clinically, they present as circular, erythematous, scaly plaques with a clear center, often accompanied by pruritus. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical appearance and confirmed by potassium hydroxide preparation or culture. Treatment involves topical or systemic antifungals depending on the severity and extent of the infection.

Dermatophytosis unspecified refers to a fungal infection of the skin caused by dermatophytes, a group of fungi that infect keratinized tissues. Common synonyms include tinea or ringworm. The causative agents vary by region but commonly include *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Epidermophyton* species. This condition typically affects the scalp, feet, groin, and nails, though the exact location may be unspecified in some cases. It presents as circular, erythematous, scaly patches with possible hair loss or nail dystrophy. Diagnosis is often confirmed through clinical examination and fungal culture.

Pityriasis versicolor, also known as tinea versicolor, is a common fungal infection caused by Malassezia species, particularly *Malassezia furfur* and *Malassezia sympodialis*. It presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the skin, often with a fine scaling. The rash typically appears on the trunk, neck, and upper arms, and is more prevalent in warm, humid climates. It is not contagious but may recur due to the persistence of the yeast on the skin. The condition is more common in adolescents and young adults.

Tinea nigra is a chronic fungal infection characterized by well-demarcated, hyperpigmented, brown to black patches on the palms and soles. It is caused by the dermatophyte *Hortaea werneckii* (formerly *Exophiala werneckii*), though *Tuberostroma quercinum* may also be involved. Common synonyms include chromoblastomycosis and black ringworm. The condition is typically asymptomatic, with lesions often mistaken for melanoma. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions and affects individuals with prolonged moisture exposure, such as farmers or swimmers.

White piedra is a chronic fungal infection of the hair shafts, characterized by the presence of hard, white, calcified nodules. Common synonyms include "piedra alba" and "white stone disease." The causative agents are primarily *Trichosporon ovoforme* and *Trichosporon beigelii*, though other species may occasionally be involved. The infection typically affects the scalp, eyebrows, and beards, with a predilection for coarse hair. It is more common in tropical regions and often presents as asymptomatic or mildly pruritic lesions. Diagnosis is usually made by visual inspection or microscopic examination of the affected hair.

Black piedra is a chronic fungal infection of the hair shafts, characterized by the formation of hard, black, keratinous nodules. Commonly known as *piedra nigra*, it is caused by the dermatophyte *Trichophyton violaceum*. The infection primarily affects the scalp, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. It is more common in children and young adults, and may lead to hair breakage and cosmetic concerns. The condition is usually asymptomatic but can cause itching or discomfort. Diagnosis is typically made by visual inspection or microscopic examination of affected hair.

Other specified superficial mycoses refer to fungal infections affecting the skin, hair, or nails, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include tinea and dermatophytosis. Causative agents are dermatophytes such as Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton. These infections typically affect the scalp, feet, groin, and nails. Symptoms include itching, scaling, and ring-shaped rashes. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and microscopic examination. Treatment usually involves topical antifungals, with oral therapy for severe cases.

Superficial mycosis unspecified refers to fungal infections affecting the outer layers of the skin, hair, or nails, with the specific type not identified. Common synonyms include tinea and dermatophytosis. Causative agents are typically dermatophytes, such as *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Epidermophyton*. These infections commonly affect the feet (tinea pedis), groin (tinea cruris), scalp (tinea capitis), and body (tinea corporis). Symptoms include itching, redness, and scaling. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and fungal microscopy. Treatment usually involves topical or oral antifungal agents.

Candidal stomatitis is a fungal infection of the oral cavity caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It presents as white, curd-like plaques on mucosal surfaces, often with erythematous base.
