Common synonyms include oral thrush and candidiasis. The condition typically affects the tongue, cheeks, and palate, and is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals, infants, and those using antibiotics or corticosteroids. It may also occur in patients with poorly fitting dentures. Symptoms include burning, soreness, and difficulty swallowing. Diagnosis is usually clinical, though culture or microscopy may confirm the presence of *Candida* species.

Pulmonary candidiasis is a fungal infection of the lungs caused by *Candida* species, most commonly *Candida albicans*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, cancer, or on immunosuppressive therapy. The infection may present as chronic pneumonia with symptoms like cough, fever, and hemoptysis. It can also occur as an opportunistic infection in hospitalized patients with prolonged antibiotic use. Common synonyms include invasive pulmonary candidiasis. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, though dissemination to other organs may occur.

Candidiasis of skin and nail is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida albicans*, though other *Candida* species may also be involved. It typically affects moist areas of the skin, such as the groin, under the breasts, and between fingers, as well as nails, leading to symptoms like redness, itching, scaling, and thickening. Common synonyms include cutaneous candidiasis and tinea cruris. The infection is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor hygiene. Nail involvement, known as onychomycosis, results in discolored, brittle nails. Treatment usually involves topical or systemic antifungal agents.

Candidiasis of the vulva and vagina, also known as vaginal yeast infection or moniliasis, is a common fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It affects the vulva, vagina, and sometimes the perianal area. Symptoms include itching, burning, redness, and a thick, white, curd-like discharge. The infection is more prevalent in women with diabetes, during pregnancy, or after antibiotic use. It is not typically transmitted sexually but can occur due to hormonal changes or a weakened immune system.

Candidal cystitis and urethritis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida albicans*, though other *Candida* species may be involved. It occurs when *Candida* overgrows in the urinary tract, often in immunocompromised individuals or those with urinary catheters. Symptoms include dysuria, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. The infection typically affects the bladder (cystitis) and urethra (urethritis). Common synonyms include fungal urethritis and candidal urinary tract infection. It is more prevalent in women but can occur in men. Diagnosis is confirmed through urine culture or microscopy. Treatment involves antifungal agents such as fluconazole or nystatin.

Candidal balanitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the glans penis, typically caused by *Candida* species, most commonly *Candida albicans*. It presents with redness, itching, and a white, cheesy discharge. Common synonyms include fungal balanitis or yeast infection of the glans. The condition is more prevalent in uncircumcised males, particularly those with poor hygiene, diabetes, or immunosuppression. It may also occur in infants due to transmission from the mother during birth. Treatment usually involves antifungal agents such as topical clotrimazole or nystatin.

Other urogenital candidiasis refers to fungal infections caused by *Candida* species affecting the urogenital tract outside the vulva and vagina. Common synonyms include vulvovaginal candidiasis and genital candidiasis. The primary causative agent is *Candida albicans*, though other species like *C. glabrata* and *C. tropicalis* may also be involved. Typically, the infection affects the penis, urethra, and perineal area in males, and the vulva, vagina, and perineum in females. It is characterized by symptoms such as itching, burning, and discharge.

Candidiasis of other urogenital sites refers to fungal infections caused by *Candida* species, primarily *Candida albicans*, affecting areas outside the vulva, vagina, and penis. Common synonyms include intertrigo and mucocutaneous candidiasis. These infections typically occur in warm, moist skin folds such as the groin, axillae, and under the breasts. They may also involve the perianal region and oral mucosa. Symptoms include erythema, scaling, and satellite lesions. Risk factors include diabetes, immunosuppression, and antibiotic use. Treatment usually involves topical antifungal agents.

Candidal meningitis is a rare fungal infection of the meninges caused primarily by *Candida* species, most commonly *Candida albicans*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, neonates, or patients on broad-spectrum antibiotics. The infection may result from hematogenous spread or direct extension from adjacent infections. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. It can also affect the brain parenchyma, leading to encephalitis. Synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis, though this is more commonly associated with *Cryptococcus neoformans*. The central nervous system, particularly the meninges and brain, are the primary affected areas.

Candidal endocarditis is a rare but serious infection of the inner lining of the heart, typically affecting the heart valves. It is caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans, though other species like Candida glabrata and Candida krusei may also be involved. This condition often occurs in patients with pre-existing valvular heart disease, prosthetic valves, or those with weakened immune systems. It is also referred to as fungal endocarditis or mycotic endocarditis. Symptoms include fever, heart murmurs, and systemic signs of infection. Prompt diagnosis and antifungal therapy are essential to prevent complications such as embolism or valve destruction.

Candidal sepsis is a systemic fungal infection caused by species of *Candida*, most commonly *Candida albicans*. It occurs when opportunistic Candida organisms enter the bloodstream, often in immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include fever, chills, and signs of systemic inflammation. It can affect multiple organs, including the liver, spleen, and kidneys. Common synonyms include systemic candidiasis or fungemia. The condition is associated with catheters, surgical sites, and prolonged antibiotic use. Early diagnosis and antifungal therapy are critical to prevent mortality.

Candidal esophagitis is a fungal infection of the esophagus caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It is characterized by inflammation, erythema, and sometimes ulceration of the esophageal mucosa. Common symptoms include dysphagia, odynophagia, and retrosternal pain. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, diabetes, or on immunosuppressive therapy. Other *Candida* species, like *C. glabrata* or *C. tropicalis*, may also be involved. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus and is often associated with oral thrush. Clinically, it may present with white plaques or a "linitis plastica" appearance.

Candidal enteritis is a fungal infection of the gastrointestinal tract caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It typically affects individuals with compromised immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The condition is characterized by inflammation of the small intestine, leading to symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. Other *Candida* species, including *C. glabrata* and *C. tropicalis*, may also be involved. Synonyms include candidiasis of the intestine and fungal enteritis. The small intestine is the most commonly affected site, though involvement of the colon can occur in severe cases.

Candidal cheilitis is a fungal infection of the lips caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It presents as red, scaly, and sometimes fissured borders of the lips, often accompanied by dryness and cracking. Common synonyms include angular cheilitis and perleche. The condition is more prevalent in individuals with poor oral hygiene, diabetes, or those using topical corticosteroids. It typically affects the vermillion border of the lips and can spread to the corners of the mouth. Risk factors include moisture, trauma, and immunocompromise. Treatment involves antifungal agents and addressing underlying conditions.

Candidal otitis externa is a fungal infection of the external ear canal caused primarily by *Candida albicans*. It often occurs in individuals with compromised immune systems, diabetes, or those using corticosteroid ear drops. The condition presents with itching, erythema, and serous or purulent discharge. Common synonyms include fungal otitis externa or candidal swimmer's ear. It typically affects the ear canal and may extend to the tympanic membrane if left untreated.

Other sites of candidiasis refer to infections caused by *Candida* species in locations outside the typical mucocutaneous areas. Common synonyms include opportunistic fungal infections or mucosal candidiasis. The primary causative agent is *Candida albicans*, though other species like *C. glabrata* and *C. auris* may also be involved. These infections commonly affect the gastrointestinal tract, urinary tract, and bloodstream, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. They may present as oral thrush, esophageal candidiasis, or systemic candidemia, often requiring antifungal therapy.

Candidiasis of other sites refers to infections caused by *Candida* species in areas not typically associated with mucocutaneous or genital candidiasis. Common synonyms include opportunistic fungal infections or invasive candidiasis. The primary causative agent is *Candida albicans*, though other species like *C. glabrata* and *C. tropicalis* may also be involved. These infections commonly affect the bloodstream, central nervous system, and internal organs such as the liver, spleen, and kidneys, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. They often occur in hospitalized patients or those with underlying conditions like diabetes or HIV.

Candidiasis unspecified refers to an infection caused by Candida species, typically affecting mucocutaneous surfaces. It is a fungal infection that may present as thrush or vaginal yeast infections when localized, or as systemic candidiasis in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include moniliasis and yeast infection. The primary causative agent is Candida albicans, though other species like Candida glabrata and Candida parapsilosis may also be involved. The infection commonly affects the oral cavity, vagina, skin folds, and gastrointestinal tract, with systemic spread possible in severe cases.

Acute pulmonary coccidioidomycosis, also known as valley fever, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs following inhalation of arthroconidia. Symptoms include fever, cough, chest pain, and fatigue. The infection typically involves the pulmonary parenchyma and may spread to other organs in immunocompromised individuals. It is endemic in arid regions of the southwestern United States and parts of Central and South America.

Chronic pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, often following inhalation of arthroconidia in endemic areas. The disease may present as a subacute or chronic process with symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. It can progress to form cavitary lesions or nodules. Common synonyms include San Joaquin Valley fever and Valley fever. The infection typically involves the respiratory tract but may disseminate to other organs in immunocompromised individuals.

Pulmonary coccidioidomycosis unspecified refers to a fungal infection of the lungs caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. Commonly known as Valley fever, it is characterized by inflammation and granuloma formation in the respiratory tract. Symptoms include cough, fever, chest pain, and fatigue. The infection typically affects the lungs but can disseminate to other organs. It is endemic in arid regions of the southwestern United States, Central, and South America. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing and imaging. The unspecified classification indicates that the infection is localized to the lungs without further specification of severity or dissemination.

Cutaneous coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It typically presents as a localized skin lesion following inhalation of arthroconidia, often in endemic regions. Common synonyms include San Joaquin Valley fever and desert rheumatism. The infection primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the lungs. Lesions may appear as papules, nodules, or ulcers, often with a central ulcer and surrounding erythema. Systemic dissemination can occur in immunocompromised individuals, leading to more severe manifestations.

Coccidioidomycosis meningitis is a severe fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It occurs when the infection spreads from the lungs to the central nervous system. Common synonyms include San Joaquin fever and valley fever meningitis. The disease typically affects the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid, leading to symptoms such as headache, fever, and altered mental status. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those living in endemic regions like the southwestern United States. Complications may include brain abscesses or meningitis.

Disseminated coccidioidomycosis is a severe fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It occurs when the initial pulmonary infection spreads to other organs. Common synonyms include blastomycosis and valley fever. The infection typically affects the skin, bones, central nervous system, and viscera. Symptoms include fever, cough, and skin lesions. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those living in arid regions. The disease can be life-threatening if not treated promptly with antifungal therapy.

Prostatic coccidioidomycosis is a rare fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*, typically affecting individuals with compromised immune systems. It presents as a localized infection of the prostate gland, often following hematogenous dissemination from a primary pulmonary or cutaneous infection. Symptoms may include pelvic pain, urinary retention, and systemic signs of infection. The condition is uncommon and often misdiagnosed due to its rarity and nonspecific clinical presentation. Synonyms include coccidioidal prostatitis and disseminated coccidioidomycosis involving the prostate.

Other forms of coccidioidomycosis refer to disseminated or extrapulmonary manifestations of the infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. These forms occur when the fungus spreads beyond the lungs to other organs, commonly affecting the skin, bones, joints, central nervous system, and mucous membranes. Common synonyms include disseminated coccidioidomycosis and coccidioidal meningitis. Symptoms vary depending on the affected site but often include skin lesions, arthralgia, meningitis, and granulomas. The disease is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those living in endemic regions.

Other forms of coccidioidomycosis refer to disseminated or extrapulmonary manifestations of the fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. These forms occur when the infection spreads beyond the lungs to other organs, commonly affecting the skin, bones, joints, central nervous system, and lymph nodes. Synonyms include coccidioidal osteomyelitis, meningitis, and cutaneous coccidioidomycosis. Symptoms vary depending on the affected site but often include fever, pain, and swelling. Diagnosis typically involves imaging, culture, and serology.

Coccidioidomycosis unspecified refers to infection caused by *Coccidioides* species, primarily *C. immitis* and *C. posadasii*. It is a fungal infection acquired through inhalation of spores from contaminated soil. The disease typically presents as a pulmonary infection, though it can disseminate to other organs. Common synonyms include Valley fever and San Joaquin fever. Clinically, it may manifest as acute or chronic pneumonia, with symptoms such as fever, cough, and fatigue. Dissemination can affect the skin, bones, and central nervous system, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Acute pulmonary histoplasmosis capsulati, also known as acute pulmonary histoplasmosis, is a fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, and chest pain. The infection occurs after inhalation of spores from contaminated soil, commonly in endemic areas. While typically self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, it can progress to disseminated disease in immunocompromised patients. The condition is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and may mimic tuberculosis or other pneumonia. Common synonyms include acute histoplasmosis and pulmonary histoplasmosis.

Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis capsulati, also known as chronic cavitary histoplasmosis, is a progressive fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to the formation of chronic, non-healing cavities. The infection typically occurs in individuals with pre-existing lung disease or immunocompromise. Common symptoms include chronic cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. The condition is more prevalent in endemic areas and can progress to disseminated histoplasmosis if left untreated.

Pulmonary histoplasmosis capsulati unspecified refers to a form of histoplasmosis affecting the lungs, characterized by the presence of encapsulated yeast forms of *Histoplasma capsulatum*. Common synonyms include chronic cavitary histoplasmosis and pulmonary histoplasmosis. The infection is caused by inhalation of spores from the fungus *Histoplasma capsulatum*, which is endemic in certain regions. Typically, the lungs are the primary site of involvement, with possible dissemination to other organs in immunocompromised individuals. The condition is more common in males and those with prolonged exposure to contaminated environments.

Disseminated histoplasmosis capsulati, also known as chronic cavitary histoplasmosis, is a severe fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection spreads beyond the lungs to involve multiple organs, including the lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Clinical features include fever, weight loss, and persistent cough. The disease is characterized by the formation of granulomas and caseous necrosis in affected tissues. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging, biopsy, and fungal culture. Treatment typically involves antifungal therapy with amphotericin B or itraconazole.

Histoplasmosis capsulati unspecified refers to a fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*, primarily affecting the lungs. It is a dimorphic fungus that exists as a mold in the environment and as a yeast within host cells. The infection typically presents as a chronic pulmonary disease, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include pulmonary histoplasmosis and chronic cavitary histoplasmosis. The lungs are the most commonly affected organ, though dissemination can occur in severe cases.

Histoplasmosis duboisii is a severe, disseminated fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma duboisii*, a thermally dimorphic fungus. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. The infection typically begins in the lungs and spreads systemically, involving multiple organs such as the skin, bones, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include disseminated histoplasmosis and African histoplasmosis. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa and is characterized by chronic granulomatous lesions and opportunistic dissemination.

Histoplasmosis unspecified refers to infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*, a dimorphic fungal pathogen. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation. The infection may disseminate to other organs, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include pulmonary histoplasmosis and endemic mycosis. Symptoms range from asymptomatic to fever, cough, and chest pain. Diagnosis is confirmed through serology, culture, or biopsy. The disease is endemic in regions with high bird or bat activity, such as the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys in the United States.

Acute pulmonary blastomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis*, primarily affecting the lungs. It presents with symptoms such as fever, cough, chest pain, and dyspnea. Common synonyms include acute pulmonary blastomycosis and pulmonary blastomycosis. The infection typically begins in the lungs and can disseminate to other organs, particularly the skin, bones, and genitourinary tract. It is more prevalent in regions with moist, humid climates. Diagnosis often involves imaging, serology, and biopsy. Treatment usually requires antifungal therapy, such as itraconazole or amphotericin B.

Chronic pulmonary blastomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis*, a dimorphic fungus. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to chronic inflammation and granuloma formation. Common synonyms include chronic pulmonary blastomycosis and pulmonary blastomycosis. The infection typically presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, and weight loss. It is more common in individuals living in endemic areas, particularly the Mississippi and Ohio river valleys. The disease can progress to disseminate beyond the lungs, affecting other organs. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging, serology, and fungal cultures. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy with itraconazole or amphotericin B.

Pulmonary blastomycosis unspecified refers to an infection of the lungs caused by the fungus *Blastomyces dermatitidis*. It is a systemic fungal infection that primarily affects the respiratory system, though it can disseminate to other organs. Common synonyms include pulmonary blastomycosis and blastomycosis. The infection typically presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. It is more common in individuals exposed to moist soil or decaying organic matter. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging, serology, and fungal culture. The disease can progress to severe pneumonia or extrapulmonary involvement if untreated.

Cutaneous blastomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis* and related species. It typically presents as a single, painless, ulcerative lesion with a central crater and rolled border, often on the face, neck, or extremities. Common synonyms include cutaneous blastomycosis and sporotrichoid blastomycosis. The infection may disseminate systemically if untreated. Diagnosis is confirmed by histopathology and fungal culture. It is more prevalent in endemic regions with moist soil and decaying organic matter.

Disseminated blastomycosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis*. It typically begins as a pulmonary infection and can disseminate to multiple organs, including the skin, bones, lymph nodes, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include disseminated blastomycosis and systemic blastomycosis. The infection is more prevalent in endemic areas with moist soil and decaying organic matter. Clinical manifestations vary but often include fever, weight loss, and characteristic cutaneous lesions. Diagnosis is confirmed through culture, histopathology, or serology.

Blastomycotic meningoencephalitis is a fungal infection of the central nervous system caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis*. It presents with fever, headache, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. The infection typically spreads hematogenously from the lungs to the brain and meninges. Common synonyms include pulmonary blastomycosis with CNS involvement and disseminated blastomycosis. The disease primarily affects the lungs and central nervous system, with the latter being more severe and often leading to complications such as hydrocephalus or brain abscesses.

Other forms of blastomycosis refer to extrapulmonary manifestations of the fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis* or *Blastomyces gilchristii*. These forms typically affect the skin, bones, lymph nodes, and genitourinary tract. Common synonyms include disseminated blastomycosis and extrapulmonary blastomycosis. The infection often presents as chronic granulomatous lesions, with cutaneous involvement being the most common extrapulmonary site. It predominantly occurs in individuals with compromised immune systems or in endemic regions.

Other forms of blastomycosis refer to extrapulmonary manifestations of the fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis* or *Blastomyces gilchristii*. These forms typically affect the skin, bones, genitourinary tract, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include disseminated blastomycosis and extrapulmonary blastomycosis. The infection often presents with chronic granulomatous lesions, ulcerations, or nodules, and may mimic other granulomatous diseases. Diagnosis involves clinical presentation, imaging, and fungal culture or PCR. Treatment usually requires antifungal therapy, such as itraconazole or amphotericin B.

Blastomycosis unspecified is a fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis* or *Blastomyces gilchristii*. It primarily affects the lungs but can disseminate to other organs. Common synonyms include North American blastomycosis and Gilchrist's disease. The infection typically presents with flu-like symptoms, cough, and chest pain, progressing to chronic lung disease. Dissemination may involve the skin, bones, and genitourinary tract. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging, culture, or serology. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy, with varying duration based on disease severity and immune status.

Pulmonary paracoccidioidomycosis is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* and *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis. Common synonyms include South American blastomycosis and mucocutaneous paracoccidioidomycosis. The infection often spreads to the skin, mucous membranes, and lymph nodes. Clinically, it presents with cough, fever, weight loss, and chest pain. Diagnosis is confirmed by fungal culture or serology. It is endemic in Latin America and more common in males, particularly smokers.

Disseminated paracoccidioidomycosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* or *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects individuals in endemic regions of Latin America. The infection typically begins as a pulmonary lesion but can disseminate to multiple organs, including the skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes, and visceral organs. Common synonyms include South American blastomycosis and paracoccidioidomycosis. Clinically, it presents with chronic symptoms such as cough, weight loss, and cutaneous lesions. The disease is more prevalent in males and those with compromised immune systems.

Other forms of paracoccidioidomycosis refer to non-lung presentations of the fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* or *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. These forms typically affect the mucocutaneous tissues, including the oral cavity, skin, and genital areas. They may also involve the lymph nodes, bones, and viscera. Common synonyms include mucocutaneous paracoccidioidomycosis and disseminated paracoccidioidomycosis. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions and often presents with chronic, progressive lesions.

Paracoccidioidomycosis unspecified is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* or *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects the lungs and mucous membranes, often spreading to the skin, lymph nodes, and internal organs. Common synonyms include South American blastomycosis and undulant fever. The disease is endemic in Latin America and typically presents with respiratory symptoms, skin lesions, and systemic involvement. It is more common in males and those with compromised immune systems. Diagnosis is confirmed by fungal culture, histopathology, or serology. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy with drugs like itraconazole or amphotericin B.

Pulmonary sporotrichosis is a rare fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii*, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. It presents as a chronic, progressive pneumonia with nodular or cavitary lesions in the lungs. The infection may spread from the skin or lymph nodes to the lungs via hematogenous dissemination. Common synonyms include pulmonary sporotrichosis and sporotrichoid pneumonia. The disease typically involves the lungs, but can also affect the skin, lymph nodes, and other organs. Diagnosis is confirmed through fungal culture or histopathology. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy such as itraconazole or amphotericin B.

Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis is a chronic subcutaneous fungal infection caused primarily by *Sporothrix schenckii*. It typically presents as a painless, slowly progressing nodule at the site of inoculation, followed by lymphangitic spread along the lymphatic channels. Common synonyms include sporotrichoid infection and lymphocutaneous mycosis. The infection commonly affects the arms, hands, and legs, often following trauma or insect bites. Clinically, it is characterized by indurated, erythematous nodules and may mimic other granulomatous or pyogenic infections. Early diagnosis and antifungal therapy are essential to prevent dissemination.

Disseminated sporotrichosis is a severe fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* and other *Sporothrix* species. It occurs when the infection spreads beyond the initial site, often from a localized cutaneous lesion. Common synonyms include systemic sporotrichosis and disseminated sporotrichoidal infection. Typically affecting immunocompromised individuals, it can involve the lungs, bones, central nervous system, and viscera. Clinical manifestations include nodules, abscesses, and systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss. Diagnosis is confirmed through culture or PCR, and treatment involves antifungal agents such as amphotericin B or itraconazole.

Cerebral sporotrichosis is a rare fungal infection of the central nervous system caused by *Sporothrix schenckii*. It typically presents as a chronic, progressive illness with symptoms such as headache, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. The infection often spreads from a cutaneous lesion via the lymphatic system to the brain. Common synonyms include central nervous system sporotrichosis and neurosporotrichosis. The disease predominantly affects the brain and spinal cord, with rare involvement of other neural structures. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with occupational exposure to soil or plants.

Sporotrichosis arthritis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species. It typically presents as a subcutaneous infection that may progress to involve joints, leading to painful, asymmetric arthritis. Common synonyms include rhinosporidiosis and lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. The infection often begins at sites of trauma or puncture wounds, commonly affecting the hands, feet, and upper limbs. It may spread via lymphatics to regional lymph nodes and subsequently to joints, causing swelling, pain, and limited mobility. Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical presentation, culture, or molecular testing.

Sporotrichosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Sporothrix schenckii* and other related species. "Other forms of sporotrichosis" refer to atypical presentations or variants beyond the classic lymphocutaneous form. These may include osteoarticular, pulmonary, cutaneous, or disseminated infections. Common synonyms include rhinosporidiosis and chromoblastomycosis, though these are distinct entities. The infection typically affects the skin, lymph nodes, bones, or lungs, with varying clinical manifestations depending on the route of exposure and immune status.

Other forms of sporotrichosis refer to non-cutaneous manifestations of infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* species complex. These include disseminated, osteoarticular, and central nervous system forms. Common synonyms include sporotrichoid infection and disseminated sporotrichosis. The causative agents are primarily *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species such as *S. brasiliensis* and *S. globosa*. These forms typically affect the bones, joints, and occasionally the lungs or brain, often in immunocompromised individuals. Clinical presentation varies but may include fever, localized swelling, and systemic symptoms.

Sporotrichosis unspecified is a subcategory of sporotrichosis, a fungal infection caused primarily by *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species. It refers to cases where the clinical presentation does not fit the classic nodular or lymphocutaneous forms. Common synonyms include disseminated sporotrichosis and generalized sporotrichosis. The infection typically affects the skin, lymph nodes, and may disseminate to internal organs such as the lungs, bones, or central nervous system. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with occupational exposure to soil or plants.

Cutaneous chromomycosis is a chronic fungal infection characterized by the formation of pigmented, hyperkeratotic lesions on the skin. Common synonyms include chromoblastomycosis and chromomycosis. It is caused by dematiaceous fungi such as *Fonsecaea*, *Cladophialophora*, and *Lophophora*. The infection typically affects the lower extremities, especially in individuals with compromised immune systems or those living in tropical regions. Lesions are often asymptomatic but may become ulcerated or secondarily infected. Diagnosis is confirmed through histopathology and fungal culture.

Pheomycotic brain abscess is a rare, chronic suppurative infection of the central nervous system characterized by the presence of sulfur granules composed of *Corynebacterium species*. Common synonyms include granulomatous brain abscess and sulfur granule abscess. The condition is typically caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* or *Corynebacterium minutissimum*. It predominantly affects the central nervous system, with abscesses most commonly located in the brain, particularly the frontal and temporal lobes. The infection often arises from contiguous spread from adjacent infected structures or hematogenous dissemination. Clinical presentation includes fever, headache, and neurological deficits.

Subcutaneous pheomycotic abscess and cyst is a chronic, granulomatous infection caused by dematiaceous fungi, commonly *Cladophora* and *Exophiala* species. It presents as slow-growing, firm, erythematous nodules or cysts, often with a central umbilication. The condition is typically found on the scalp, face, and neck, and may mimic pyogenic abscesses. Clinically, it is also known as chromoblastomycosis or phaeohyphomycosis. Diagnosis requires fungal culture and histopathology, and treatment involves antifungal therapy and surgical drainage.

Chromomycosis refers to a group of fungal infections caused by dematiaceous fungi, characterized by chronic, granulomatous skin lesions. Other forms of chromomycosis include infections caused by species such as *Cladophialophora bantiana*, *Fonsecaea pedrosoi*, and *Lophophora sp.* These infections typically affect the skin, especially in tropical and subtropical regions. Common synonyms include chromoblastomycosis and phaeohyphomycosis. Lesions are often found on the lower extremities, face, and hands, and may present as nodules or plaques with central ulceration. The infections are usually acquired through traumatic implantation of fungal elements.

Chromomycosis unspecified is a chronic fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, typically caused by dematiaceous fungi such as *Fonsecaea pedrosoi*, *Cladophialophora bainieri*, and *Ajellomyces spp*. It presents as slow-growing, brownish or blackish nodules or plaques, often on the lower extremities. Common synonyms include chromoblastomycosis and chromomycosis. The infection is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions and may spread through traumatic inoculation of the fungus. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with poor hygiene.

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is a severe fungal infection caused primarily by *Aspergillus fumigatus*, though other *Aspergillus* species may also be involved. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with hematologic malignancies or on immunosuppressive therapy. The infection typically begins in the lungs, leading to necrotizing pneumonia, fungal balls (aspergillomas), and dissemination to other organs. Common synonyms include aspergillosis and invasive aspergillosis. The condition is characterized by fever, cough, hemoptysis, and progressive respiratory decline.

Other pulmonary aspergillosis refers to non-invasive or subclinical forms of aspergillosis affecting the lungs. It encompasses conditions such as aspergilloma, where fungal hyphae grow within pre-existing lung cavities, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, characterized by an allergic reaction to *Aspergillus* antigens. Common causative agents include *Aspergillus fumigatus*, *A. niger*, and *A. flavus*. Typically affecting the lungs, this condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying lung disease. Symptoms may include cough, hemoptysis, and wheezing.

Tonsillar aspergillosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Aspergillus* species, most commonly *Aspergillus fumigatus*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, neutropenia, or prolonged corticosteroid use. The infection manifests as a granulomatous or necrotizing lesion within the tonsillar tissues, often presenting with symptoms like sore throat, fever, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Synonyms include aspergilloma of the tonsils or fungal tonsillitis. The condition predominantly involves the oropharyngeal region, particularly the palatine tonsils.

Disseminated aspergillosis is a severe fungal infection caused by *Aspergillus* species, most commonly *A. fumigatus*. It occurs in immunocompromised individuals and spreads beyond the lungs to involve multiple organs, including the brain, skin, and kidneys. Synonyms include invasive aspergillosis and systemic aspergillosis. The infection progresses rapidly and is often fatal without prompt antifungal therapy. Clinically, it presents with fever, respiratory symptoms, and signs of organ involvement. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical for improving outcomes.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity reaction to *Aspergillus* species, most commonly *A. fumigatus*. It primarily affects individuals with preexisting lung conditions such as cystic fibrosis or asthma. The disease is characterized by airway inflammation, mucus plugging, and immunological responses leading to bronchiectasis. Symptoms include cough, wheezing, and fever. ABPA is also known as allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis or aspergillosis. The condition predominantly involves the respiratory tract, particularly the bronchi and lungs.

Other forms of aspergillosis refer to non-invasive and less common manifestations of Aspergillus infection beyond the typical allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and invasive aspergillosis. Common synonyms include chronic necrotizing pulmonary aspergillosis and aspergilloma. These conditions are primarily caused by *Aspergillus fumigatus*, though other species may also be involved. They typically affect the lungs, causing chronic inflammation, cavities, and fungal masses, often in individuals with pre-existing lung disease or immunocompromised states.

Other forms of aspergillosis encompass non-invasive and invasive fungal infections caused primarily by *Aspergillus* species, most commonly *A. fumigatus*. These include chronic necrotizing pulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Synonyms include fungal ball, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), and chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis. The infections typically affect the lungs, causing cavities, inflammation, and allergic reactions. Systemic involvement may occur in immunocompromised individuals, leading to invasive aspergillosis. Symptoms vary from cough and hemoptysis to fever and respiratory failure. Diagnosis relies on imaging, culture, and serological tests.

Aspergillosis unspecified refers to invasive or chronic fungal infections caused by Aspergillus species, typically Aspergillus fumigatus, when the specific type is not identified. It commonly affects the lungs, leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and hemoptysis. The infection may disseminate to other organs, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include aspergillosis, invasive aspergillosis, and chronic pulmonary aspergillosis. It is characterized by granulomatous or necrotizing pulmonary lesions and can progress to severe respiratory failure if untreated.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection begins in the lungs, leading to symptoms like cough, fever, and chest pain. It may disseminate to other organs, particularly the central nervous system. Common synonyms include cryptococcal pneumonia and pulmonary cryptococcal infection. The lungs are the primary site of involvement, with potential spread to the brain, skin, and other tissues.

Cerebral cryptococcosis is a fungal infection of the central nervous system caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and less commonly by *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection leads to meningitis, characterized by inflammation of the meninges, and may result in parenchymal involvement, including brain abscesses or granulomas. Common synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and central nervous system cryptococcosis. The condition predominantly involves the brain and meninges, often presenting with headache, fever, and neurological deficits.

Cutaneous cryptococcosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically presents as a single or multiple cutaneous nodules or plaques, often on the face, neck, or extremities. The infection may result from direct inoculation or hematogenous dissemination. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. Synonyms include cryptococcal cutaneous infection or cryptococcal dermatitis. The condition may be asymptomatic or associated with systemic disease.

Osseous cryptococcosis is a rare fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and less commonly by *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects individuals with compromised immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection manifests as osteomyelitis, often involving the spine, skull, and long bones. Common synonyms include cryptococcal osteomyelitis and fungal osteomyelitis. Clinical features include bone pain, swelling, and sometimes neurological deficits if the spinal column is involved. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging and fungal cultures or PCR. Treatment involves antifungal therapy, often with amphotericin B and flucytosine, followed by maintenance therapy.

Disseminated cryptococcosis is a severe fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* var. *grubii* and *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection spreads from the lungs to the central nervous system, leading to meningitis, and may involve other organs. Common synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and disseminated cryptococcal infection. Clinical features include fever, headache, altered mental status, and cranial nerve deficits. The disease is characterized by the formation of granulomas and encapsulated yeast cells in affected tissues.

Other forms of cryptococcosis refer to infections caused by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and *Cryptococcus gattii* that affect sites other than the lungs or central nervous system. These include skin, bone, and disseminated infections. Common synonyms include cryptococcal osteomyelitis, cryptococcal arthritis, and cryptococcal meningitis (though the latter is more common in other forms). These infections typically occur in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS, and may present with localized or systemic symptoms depending on the affected organ.

Cryptococcosis unspecified refers to an infection caused by Cryptococcus species, primarily *Cryptococcus neoformans* and *Cryptococcus gattii*, without specific localization. It typically affects the central nervous system, lungs, or disseminated sites. Common synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and cryptococcal infection. The disease is more common in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. Symptoms vary depending on the affected organ but may include fever, headache, cough, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis involves isolation of the fungus from clinical specimens or serological testing. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy with amphotericin B and fluconazole.

Pulmonary mucormycosis is a severe fungal infection caused by filamentous fungi of the order Mucorales. Common synonyms include zygomycosis and rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis when involving the sinuses and brain. The primary causative agents are *Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, *Lichtheimia*, and *Saprobic* species. It typically affects the lungs, but can spread to the sinuses, brain, and eyes, especially in immunocompromised individuals. The infection is characterized by rapid tissue necrosis and vascular invasion, often leading to significant morbidity and mortality if not promptly treated with antifungal therapy and surgical debridement.

Rhinocerebral mucormycosis is a severe, invasive fungal infection caused by filamentous fungi of the order Mucorales. Common synonyms include zygomycosis and phycomycosis. The primary causative agents are Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia species. This infection typically affects the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and can disseminate to the orbit and brain. It is most commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with diabetes mellitus or neutropenia. The infection progresses rapidly and is associated with high morbidity and mortality if not treated promptly with antifungal therapy and surgical debridement.

Gastrointestinal mucormycosis is a rare, invasive fungal infection caused by filamentous fungi of the order Mucorales. Common causative agents include *Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, and *Absidia* species. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with diabetes mellitus or neutropenia. The infection primarily involves the stomach and intestines, leading to mucosal ulceration, necrosis, and perforation. It may spread to adjacent organs, causing severe complications. Synonyms include zygomycosis and phycomycosis. Early diagnosis and aggressive antifungal therapy are critical for improved outcomes.

Cutaneous mucormycosis is a rare but severe fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales, most commonly Rhizopus, Rhizomucor, and Lichtheimia species. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with diabetes mellitus. The infection presents as a rapidly progressing, painful ulcerative lesion with black eschars, often on the face, legs, or hands. It may arise from trauma or contamination with soil or organic matter. Common synonyms include phycomycosis and zygomycosis. Early diagnosis and aggressive antifungal therapy are critical to prevent systemic spread and mortality.

Disseminated mucormycosis is a severe, invasive fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales, most commonly *Rhizopus*, *Aspergillus*, and *Mucor* species. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with diabetes or on immunosuppressive therapy. The infection spreads hematogenously, involving multiple organs, including the lungs, brain, skin, and gastrointestinal tract. It presents with rapidly progressing necrotic lesions, often with black eschars, and can lead to systemic complications and high mortality if not promptly treated with antifungal therapy and surgical debridement. Synonyms include zygomycosis and phycomycosis.

Mucormycosis unspecified refers to an invasive fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales. Common synonyms include zygomycosis and phycomycosis. The primary causative agents are Rhizopus, Mucor, and Rhizomucor species. This condition typically affects the sinuses, lungs, skin, and brain, often in immunocompromised individuals. It is characterized by rapid tissue necrosis, fever, and systemic dissemination. Diagnosis is confirmed through histopathology and culture. Treatment involves antifungal therapy and surgical debridement. Early recognition is critical to improve outcomes.

Other zygomycoses refer to infections caused by fungi in the order Mucorales, excluding the more commonly recognized rhinocerebral and pulmonary forms. These infections are rare and typically occur in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include mucormycosis and zygomycosis. Causative agents include species of *Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, *Absidia*, and *Rhizomucor*. These infections primarily affect the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and occasionally the lungs or gastrointestinal tract. Clinical manifestations include necrotic lesions, fever, and systemic spread if left untreated. Early diagnosis and aggressive antifungal therapy are critical for improved outcomes.

Zygomycosis unspecified refers to infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales, typically affecting immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include mucormycosis and zygomycosis. The causative agents include species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Rhizomucor. This condition primarily affects the sinuses, lungs, skin, and brain, often leading to rapid tissue necrosis. It is characterized by angioinvasion and can progress to systemic infection. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through histopathology and culture. Treatment involves antifungal therapy and surgical debridement.

Eumycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection characterized by the formation of subcutaneous nodules and sinus tracts with granular material. It is caused by dimorphic fungi, primarily *Madurella mycetomatis*, though other species like *Madurella grisea* and *Pseudallescheria boydii* may also be involved. Common synonyms include mycetoma and chromoblastomycosis. The infection typically affects the feet and lower limbs, often following trauma, and may spread to deeper tissues. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Actinomycetoma is a chronic, suppurative infection characterized by granulomatous inflammation and formation of sulfur granules. Common synonyms include madura foot and mycetoma. It is caused by aerobic actinomycetes such as *Nocardia* and *Actinomyces*, though some cases may involve fungi. The infection typically affects the subcutaneous tissues of the lower extremities, especially in tropical and subtropical regions. It presents with painless, slowly enlarging nodules, sinus tracts, and discharge. Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and microbiological examination of exudates. Treatment involves long-term antibiotic therapy and, in some cases, surgical debridement.

Mycetoma unspecified is a chronic granulomatous infection characterized by the formation of subcutaneous nodules and sinus tracts with purulent discharge. It is caused by filamentous fungi or actinomycetes. Common synonyms include madura foot and chromoblastomycosis. The condition typically affects the feet, legs, and hands, with a predilection for tropical and subtropical regions. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and microbiological examination of exudates. Treatment involves antifungal or antibiotic therapy, depending on the causative agent.

Lobomycosis, also known as granuloma inguinale or donovanosis, is a chronic granulomatous infection primarily affecting the genital and perianal regions. Caused by *Calcutta nodule bacillus* (*Klebsiella granulomatis*), it presents as painless, beefy-red ulcers with a granulomatous base. The infection is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact and is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. It predominantly affects males and can lead to significant tissue destruction if left untreated. The condition is characterized by progressive ulceration and may involve the thighs, perineum, and anal area.

Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous infection primarily affecting the nasal passages and adjacent structures. Caused by *Rhinosporidium seeberi*, a protozoan organism, it presents as painless, polypoid nodules with a characteristic central ulcerated lesion. Common synonyms include rhinosporidial sinusitis and rhinosporidiosis. The infection typically involves the nasal mucosa, nasopharynx, and occasionally the conjunctiva or larynx. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often associated with exposure to contaminated water. Diagnosis is based on clinical features and histopathological examination. Treatment usually involves surgical excision, with limited response to antifungal or antibiotic therapy.

Allescheriasis is a rare parasitic infection caused by *Allescheria* species, formerly classified under *Thalassarhodophyta*. It primarily affects the respiratory tract, particularly the lungs, and is more common in immunocompromised individuals. The infection is often acquired through inhalation of contaminated water or soil. Common synonyms include thalassarhodophyta infection or marine algae infection. Symptoms may include cough, fever, and respiratory distress. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through microscopic examination of sputum or biopsy samples. Treatment involves antifungal therapy, though outcomes can be variable.

Geotrichosis is a fungal infection caused by species of *Geotrichum*, most commonly *Geotrichum candidum*. It is a rare opportunistic infection that primarily affects immunocompromised individuals. The infection typically involves the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the lungs. It may present as a chronic, granulomatous lesion or as a superficial infection. Synonyms include geotrichomycosis and candidosis. The condition is often seen in patients with prolonged antibiotic use, diabetes, or other immunosuppressive states. Diagnosis is confirmed through fungal culture and histopathological examination. Treatment usually involves antifungal agents such as amphotericin B or fluconazole.

Penicillosis is a fungal infection caused by species of the genus Penicillium, commonly affecting immunocompromised individuals. It primarily involves the skin, nails, and mucous membranes, often presenting as chronic granulomatous lesions. Common synonyms include penicillium infection or mycotic granuloma. The causative agents include *Penicillium marneffei*, *P. rubrum*, and *P. notatum*. The infection is more prevalent in tropical regions and can disseminate systemically if left untreated. Clinically, it manifests as nodules, ulcers, or hyperpigmentation, often accompanied by systemic symptoms in severe cases.

Other specified mycoses refer to fungal infections that do not fit the criteria for more specific categories such as dermatophytosis, candidiasis, or systemic mycoses. These infections are often caused by less common fungi and may affect various body sites. Common synonyms include superficial mycoses or localized fungal infections. Causative agents may include species like *Trichophyton*, *Candida*, or *Aspergillus*, depending on the site. Typically affected areas include the skin, nails, and mucous membranes, though systemic involvement can occur in immunocompromised individuals.

Unspecified mycosis refers to fungal infections where the specific type or site is not clearly identified. It may involve any part of the body but commonly affects the skin, nails, or mucous membranes. Common synonyms include superficial mycosis or dermatomycosis. Causative agents are typically dermatophytes, yeast, or molds, though the exact organism is often undetermined. This diagnosis is used when clinical presentation and laboratory findings are insufficient to specify a more precise fungal infection.

code_desc: Plasmodium falciparum malaria with cerebral complications
summary: Plasmodium falciparum malaria with cerebral complications is a severe form of malaria caused by the protozoan parasite *Plasmodium falciparum*. It leads to cerebral malaria, characterized by neurological symptoms due to parasite-induced endothelial damage and sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in the brain microvasculature. Common synonyms include cerebral malaria and severe falciparum malaria. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, causing altered mental status, seizures, and coma. Other affected systems include the liver, kidneys, and cardiovascular system. Prompt treatment with antimalarial drugs is critical to prevent mortality.

code_desc: Other severe and complicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria
summary: Other severe and complicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria refers to life-threatening complications arising from P. falciparum infection, beyond typical severe malaria. Common synonyms include cerebral malaria, severe malarial anemia, and multi-organ failure. The causative agent is Plasmodium falciparum, the most virulent species. It primarily affects the brain, kidneys, liver, and circulatory system, leading to symptoms like seizures, renal failure, jaundice, and hypoglycemia. It predominantly occurs in children and immunocompromised individuals, with high mortality if untreated.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria unspecified refers to a severe, life-threatening malaria infection caused by the Plasmodium falciparum parasite. It is characterized by high parasitemia, fever, chills, and systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include falciparum malaria and malignant malaria. The parasite primarily affects red blood cells, leading to complications such as cerebral malaria, anemia, and organ failure. It predominantly affects individuals in tropical and subtropical regions with limited access to preventive measures or treatment. The disease can progress rapidly and requires prompt antimalarial therapy to prevent mortality.

code_desc: Plasmodium vivax malaria with rupture of spleen
summary: Plasmodium vivax malaria with rupture of spleen is a severe complication of vivax malaria, characterized by splenic rupture due to intense parasitic infection and immune response. Caused by *Plasmodium vivax*, this condition primarily affects the spleen, leading to life-threatening hemorrhage. Common synonyms include splenic rupture in vivax malaria or acute splenic rupture associated with *P. vivax*. Typically affects the spleen, and may involve the abdominal cavity. It is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: Plasmodium vivax malaria with other complications
summary: Plasmodium vivax malaria with other complications is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium vivax*, a protozoan transmitted via infected Anopheles mosquitoes. It primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and malaise. Complications may include hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, and, in severe cases, jaundice or hepatic dysfunction. Common synonyms include tertian malaria or benign tertian fever. The infection is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, with a higher incidence in areas with limited healthcare access.

Plasmodium vivax malaria without complication is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium vivax*, a protozoan transmitted via infected Anopheles mosquitoes. It primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to intermittent fever, chills, headache, and malaise. Common synonyms include tertian malaria or benign tertian fever. The parasite forms hypnozoites in the liver, causing relapses. While generally less severe than *P. falciparum* malaria, it can still cause significant morbidity. The infection typically affects the reticuloendothelial system and erythrocytes, with no major organ complications in uncomplicated cases.

Plasmodium malariae malaria with nephropathy is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium malariae*, a less common malaria parasite. It primarily affects the kidneys, leading to nephrotic syndrome characterized by proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema. The infection typically presents with mild fever and intermittent chills. While the liver and spleen may be mildly enlarged, the kidneys are the main affected organ. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Synonyms include falciparum-like malaria and benign tertian malaria. The condition is often asymptomatic or presents with non-specific symptoms.

code_desc: Plasmodium malariae malaria with other complications
summary: Plasmodium malariae malaria with other complications is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium malariae*, characterized by intermittent fever, chills, and sweating. It is less common than other malaria species and often presents with mild symptoms. Complications may include splenomegaly, anemia, and renal impairment. The parasite primarily affects the liver and red blood cells. Synonyms include quartan malaria, due to its four-day fever cycle. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, affecting mainly children and immunocompromised individuals.

Plasmodium malariae malaria without complication is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium malariae*, a less common species of malaria parasite. It typically presents with mild, intermittent fever, chills, and headache. The infection primarily affects the red blood cells and is characterized by a cyclical fever pattern every 72 hours. It is often asymptomatic or underdiagnosed due to its mild symptoms. Common synonyms include tertian malaria. The disease predominantly affects the reticuloendothelial system and is more commonly seen in individuals with weakened immune systems or those living in endemic areas.

Plasmodium ovale malaria is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium ovale*, a less common species of malaria parasite. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected *Anopheles* mosquito. The infection typically affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and malaise. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Common synonyms include *P. ovale* malaria or tertian malaria. Unlike *P. falciparum*, it has a longer incubation period and may relapse due to hypnozoites in the liver. The disease is generally less severe than falciparum malaria but can cause prolonged symptoms.

Malaria due to simian plasmodia is a parasitic infection caused by species of *Plasmodium* originally found in primates. Common synonyms include simian malaria and primate malaria. The causative agents include *Plasmodium knowlesi*, *P. cynomolgus*, and *P. fieldi*. This condition primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and anemia. It is typically transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes and is more common in tropical regions. While rare in humans, it can cause severe illness and is often diagnosed in travelers or individuals exposed to endemic areas.

"Other malaria not elsewhere classified" refers to malaria cases caused by Plasmodium species not specifically identified or classified under other specified categories. Common synonyms include unspecified malaria or malaria due to unknown species. Causative agents may include Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae, though the exact species is not determined. The disease typically affects the red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and systemic symptoms. It primarily impacts the liver and bloodstream, with potential complications affecting multiple organs if untreated.

Unspecified malaria refers to a clinical diagnosis of malaria where the specific Plasmodium species cannot be identified. Common synonyms include *malaria, unspecified* or *malaria, not otherwise specified*. Causative agents typically include *Plasmodium falciparum*, *P. vivax*, *P. ovale*, and *P. malariae*, though the exact species may not be determined. The disease primarily affects the red blood cells, leading to systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, and anemia. It predominantly affects the liver and bloodstream, with potential complications involving the brain, lungs, and kidneys.

Visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar, is a severe parasitic infection caused by *Leishmania donovani* complex species, including *L. infantum* and *L. donovani*. It primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to enlargement of the spleen and liver. Common symptoms include fever, weight loss, anemia, and splenomegaly. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. If left untreated, it can be fatal. It predominantly affects visceral organs, particularly the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a parasitic skin infection caused by Leishmania species transmitted through the bite of infected sand flies. Common synonyms include diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis and localized cutaneous leishmaniasis. The disease typically affects the skin, causing ulcers, nodules, or lesions, most commonly on the face, ears, and extremities. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. The causative agents include *Leishmania tropica*, *Leishmania major*, *Leishmania aethiopica*, and *Leishmania mexicana*. The infection is characterized by progressive skin lesions that may resolve spontaneously or require treatment with antimonials, amphotericin B, or miltefosine.

Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is a chronic parasitic infection caused by species of *Leishmania*, primarily *L. braziliensis*. It presents with skin ulcers and mucosal damage, often affecting the nose, mouth, and throat. Common synonyms include diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis and mucosal leishmaniasis. The disease is transmitted via sandfly bites and is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. Clinical features include non-healing sores, nodules, and progressive destruction of mucous membranes. Diagnosis involves microscopy, serology, or PCR, and treatment typically includes antimonials or amphotericin B.

Leishmaniasis unspecified refers to cases of leishmaniasis where the specific type or subtype cannot be determined. It is caused by various species of *Leishmania* parasites transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. Common synonyms include visceral leishmaniasis and cutaneous leishmaniasis when the subtype is not clearly identified. The disease typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, or internal organs, leading to ulcers, swelling, and systemic symptoms. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Gambiense trypanosomiasis, also known as human African trypanosomiasis or sleeping sickness, is a parasitic disease caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense*. The infection is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The parasite invades the bloodstream and lymphatic system, leading to systemic symptoms. Early stages present with fever, headache, and joint pain, while later stages affect the central nervous system, causing neurological symptoms such as confusion and sleep disturbances. The disease primarily affects sub-Saharan Africa, with the central nervous system being the main target organ.

Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis, also known as East African sleeping sickness, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense*. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The disease primarily affects sub-Saharan Africa, with a higher incidence in rural areas. The parasite invades the bloodstream and central nervous system, leading to severe neurological symptoms. Common symptoms include fever, headache, joint pain, and progressive sleep disturbances. If untreated, it can result in coma and death. The infection predominantly affects the blood, lymphatic system, and brain.

African trypanosomiasis unspecified refers to infection caused by *Trypanosoma brucei* species, transmitted via tsetse fly bites. It affects the bloodstream and central nervous system, leading to fever, headache, and eventually neurological symptoms. Common synonyms include sleeping sickness and trypanosomiasis. The disease primarily impacts sub-Saharan Africa, targeting the blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Without treatment, it progresses to severe neurological complications and is fatal.

code_desc: Acute Chagas' disease with heart involvement
summary: Acute Chagas disease with heart involvement is a severe form of Chagas disease caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It typically presents within the first few weeks to months after infection, often following vector transmission or transfusion. The parasite invades cardiac myocytes, leading to myocarditis, arrhythmias, and conduction abnormalities. Common synonyms include acute Chagas myocarditis or acute cardiac Chagas disease. The heart is the primary affected organ, though the gastrointestinal tract may also be involved. Clinical features include fever, fatigue, and chest pain, with potential progression to heart failure or sudden cardiac death.

code_desc: Acute Chagas' disease without heart involvement
summary: Acute Chagas disease without heart involvement is a parasitic infection caused primarily by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It typically presents with non-specific symptoms such as fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include acute Chagas' disease and acute American trypanosomiasis. The infection primarily affects the bloodstream and lymphatic system, with occasional involvement of the liver and spleen. It is transmitted mainly through the feces of infected triatomine bugs, though other routes like blood transfusion or congenital transmission can occur. The disease is more severe in immunocompromised individuals but often resolves spontaneously in otherwise healthy hosts.

Chagas disease, or American trypanosomiasis, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. In its chronic phase, it commonly affects the heart, leading to cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, and potentially heart failure. The disease is transmitted primarily through the feces of triatomine bugs, but also via blood transfusion, congenital transmission, and contaminated food. Synonyms include American trypanosomiasis and Chagas' disease. The myocardium is typically affected, along with the nervous system and digestive tract in some cases.

code_desc: Chagas' disease with digestive system involvement unspecified
summary: Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It primarily affects the heart and digestive system, though the exact involvement can vary. The disease is transmitted through the feces of infected triatomine bugs, blood transfusions, or congenitally. Common synonyms include Chagas' disease and American trypanosomiasis. The parasite primarily targets the heart muscle, leading to cardiomyopathy, and may also affect the esophagus and colon, causing megaesophagus or megacolon. The digestive system involvement is often unspecified in clinical descriptions.

Megaesophagus in Chagas disease is a chronic dilation of the esophagus resulting from neuronal damage caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi* infection. Common synonyms include esophageal dilation and acquired megaesophagus. The primary causative agent is the protozoan parasite *T. cruzi*, transmitted via vector bites or congenital routes. The condition predominantly affects the distal esophagus, leading to impaired peristalsis and difficulty in swallowing. It is a hallmark feature of the chronic phase of Chagas disease, often associated with cardiac and gastrointestinal complications. The affected body parts include the esophagus, stomach, and potentially the intestines in severe cases.

Megacolon in Chagas disease is a chronic complication of Trypanosoma cruzi infection, characterized by severe dilation of the colon. It results from progressive ganglionopathy and loss of neuromuscular coordination in the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include chronic megacolon and acquired megacolon. The causative agent is Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted via vector-borne or congenital routes. The condition primarily affects the colon, leading to impaired bowel function, constipation, and potential bowel perforation. It typically develops years after initial infection and is more common in adults.

code_desc: Other digestive system involvement in Chagas' disease
summary: Other digestive system involvement in Chagas disease refers to the gastrointestinal complications arising from *Trypanosoma cruzi* infection. Common synonyms include megacolon and megaesophagus. The parasite causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis, leading to dilation of the esophagus and colon. Typically affected body parts include the esophagus, stomach, and colon. Symptoms may include dysphagia, regurgitation, and constipation. The condition is more prevalent in chronic stages and can result in severe functional impairment. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent irreversible damage.

code_desc: Chagas' disease (chronic) with digestive system involvement
summary: Chagas disease, in its chronic phase, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It primarily affects the digestive system, leading to megacolon and/or megaesophagus due to progressive ganglionopathy. Common synonyms include American trypanosomiasis and Chagas' disease. The infection is transmitted through triatomine bugs, blood transfusion, or congenital routes. Chronic involvement typically results in dilation and dysfunction of the esophagus and colon, causing severe complications such as malnutrition and aspiration pneumonia. The heart is also commonly affected in later stages, but the focus here is on gastrointestinal manifestations.

code_desc: Chagas' disease with nervous system involvement unspecified
summary: Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It primarily affects the heart and digestive system but can involve the nervous system. The disease progresses through acute and chronic phases. Nervous system involvement, when present, may manifest as neurological deficits, seizures, or encephalopathy. Common synonyms include Chagas' disease and American trypanosomiasis. The parasite is transmitted through triatomine insect bites, blood transfusions, or congenital transmission. Typically affected body parts include the heart, esophagus, and colon, with potential neurological complications in advanced stages.

Meningitis in Chagas disease is a rare complication of Trypanosoma cruzi infection, occurring in the chronic phase. It is characterized by inflammation of the meninges, often presenting with fever, headache, and altered mental status. Synonyms include neurocysticercosis-like meningitis or Chagas meningitis. The causative agent is Trypanosoma cruzi, though the pathogenesis involves immune-mediated mechanisms rather than direct parasitic invasion. The central nervous system, particularly the brain and meninges, is typically affected. It is more common in endemic regions and may be associated with other neurological manifestations of Chagas disease.

Meningoencephalitis in Chagas disease is a severe neurological complication of Trypanosoma cruzi infection. It involves inflammation of the brain and meninges, typically occurring in late-stage disease. Synonyms include central nervous system involvement in Chagas. The causative agent is Trypanosoma cruzi. Commonly affected areas include the cerebral cortex, cerebellum, and meninges. Symptoms may include seizures, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. It is more prevalent in adults and can lead to significant morbidity and mortality.

code_desc: Other nervous system involvement in Chagas' disease
summary: Other nervous system involvement in Chagas disease refers to neurological complications arising from Trypanosoma cruzi infection. Common synonyms include neurocysticercosis and Chagas' encephalopathy. The causative agent is Trypanosoma cruzi. Typically affected body parts include the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves. Symptoms may present as seizures, motor deficits, sensory loss, or autonomic dysfunction. The condition can lead to chronic neurological disability and is more prevalent in late-stage disease. It is a significant cause of morbidity in endemic regions.

code_desc: Chagas' disease (chronic) with nervous system involvement
summary: Chagas disease, or American trypanosomiasis, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. In its chronic phase, the disease may involve the nervous system, leading to neurological complications such as encephalitis, myelitis, or peripheral neuropathy. Common synonyms include Chagas' disease and American trypanosomiasis. The infection primarily affects the heart, digestive system, and nervous system. Neurological involvement can result in cognitive deficits, seizures, and motor dysfunction. Transmission occurs mainly through triatomine insect vectors, blood transfusion, or congenital routes.

code_desc: Chagas' disease (chronic) with other organ involvement
summary: Chagas disease, in its chronic phase, is a systemic parasitic infection caused primarily by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It can lead to severe complications involving multiple organs, most notably the heart, esophagus, and colon. Common synonyms include American trypanosomiasis and South American trypanosomiasis. Chronic involvement often results in cardiomyopathy, megacolon, and megaesophagus. The disease is transmitted through vector bites, blood transfusions, or congenital transmission. Long-term infection may cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and gastrointestinal dysfunction.

Toxoplasma oculopathy unspecified refers to ocular involvement caused by *Toxoplasma gondii* without specific localization. It commonly presents with chorioretinitis, uveitis, or retinal lesions. Synonyms include toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis and ocular toxoplasmosis. The causative agent is *Toxoplasma gondii*, a protozoan parasite. Typically affects the retina, choroid, and vitreous.
