Often occurs in immunocompromised individuals or congenitally. May lead to vision loss if untreated. Clinical features include blurred vision, floaters, and photophobia. Diagnosis is confirmed via serology and imaging. Treatment involves antiparasitic therapy.

Toxoplasma chorioretinitis is an inflammatory eye condition caused by the protozoan *Toxoplasma gondii*. It primarily affects the retina and choroid, leading to focal necrotizing lesions. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis and ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals or congenitally. Clinical features include decreased vision, floaters, and scotomata. It is a leading cause of infectious blindness in developed countries. Diagnosis is confirmed through serology and imaging. Treatment involves antiparasitic medications such as pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine.

Other toxoplasma oculopathy refers to ocular manifestations caused by *Toxoplasma gondii* infection, excluding the classic chorioretinitis. It encompasses a range of ocular complications such as uveitis, retinal vasculitis, and optic neuritis. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic uveitis and retinochoroiditis. The causative agent is *Toxoplasma gondii*, a protozoan parasite. This condition typically affects the uvea, retina, and optic nerve, often occurring in immunocompromised individuals or following reactivation of latent infection. Clinical presentation may include pain, vision loss, and inflammatory eye findings.

Toxoplasma oculopathy is a form of ocular toxoplasmosis caused by the protozoan *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically presents as a focal chorioretinitis with a characteristic "scraped" appearance, often involving the posterior pole. The condition is most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or on immunosuppressive therapy. It may also occur in congenitally infected infants. Common synonyms include ocular toxoplasmosis and chorioretinitis due to *T. gondii*. The primary affected body parts are the retina and choroid, with potential involvement of the vitreous and optic nerve in severe cases.

Toxoplasma hepatitis is a rare form of liver inflammation caused by the protozoan parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection can lead to fever, hepatomegaly, and elevated liver enzymes. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic hepatitis and toxoplasma-associated liver disease. While the liver is the primary affected organ, the parasite can disseminate to other organs, including the brain, eyes, and lymph nodes. Diagnosis often involves serological testing and imaging, with treatment typically requiring antiparasitic medications.

Toxoplasma meningoencephalitis is a central nervous system infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection leads to inflammation of the meninges and brain tissue, resulting in symptoms like fever, headache, seizures, and altered mental status. Common synonyms include cerebral toxoplasmosis and lymphocytic meningoencephalitis. The causative agent is the protozoan *Toxoplasma gondii*, which typically infects the brain and meninges, often forming characteristic multinucleated giant cells.

Pulmonary toxoplasmosis is a rare extraintestinal manifestation of toxoplasmosis, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. It is caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*, a protozoan parasite. The infection typically presents as interstitial pneumonia, characterized by non-productive cough, fever, and dyspnea. Common synonyms include atypical pneumonia or opportunistic infection. The lungs are the primary affected organ, though systemic involvement may occur. Diagnosis often relies on imaging and serological testing, with treatment involving antiparasitic medications such as pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine.

Toxoplasma myocarditis is a rare inflammatory condition of the heart muscle caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection can lead to myocardial inflammation, arrhythmias, and heart failure. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic myocarditis or congenital toxoplasmosis with cardiac involvement. The primary causative agent is *Toxoplasma gondii*, and the myocardium is the most commonly affected body part. It may also involve the central nervous system, particularly in congenital cases.

Toxoplasma myositis is a rare inflammatory muscle condition caused by the protozoan *Toxoplasma gondii*. It primarily affects skeletal muscles, often presenting with muscle pain, weakness, and swelling. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic myositis and toxoplasma-induced myositis. The infection typically occurs through ingestion of oocysts from contaminated food or water. While most infections are asymptomatic or mild, immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or on immunosuppressive therapy, are at higher risk for severe disease. The condition can also involve other organs, leading to systemic toxoplasmosis.

Toxoplasma tubulo-interstitial nephropathy is a renal complication caused by *Toxoplasma gondii* infection. It primarily affects the renal tubules and interstitium, leading to inflammation and potential renal dysfunction. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic interstitial nephritis and toxoplasma-associated renal disease. The infection typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients. Clinical features may include fever, malaise, and renal impairment. The condition can progress to acute renal failure if left untreated. Early diagnosis and antiparasitic therapy are essential for recovery.

Toxoplasmosis with other organ involvement is a systemic infection caused primarily by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, leading to dissemination beyond the central nervous system. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic encephalitis with multi-organ involvement. The infection can involve the brain, eyes, liver, and lymph nodes. Clinical manifestations include fever, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. Complications may arise from organ-specific involvement, such as retinochoroiditis or hepatic dysfunction. Diagnosis is confirmed through serology, imaging, and sometimes biopsy. Treatment involves antiparasitic medications like pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine.

Toxoplasmosis with other organ involvement is a systemic infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*, a protozoan parasite. Common synonyms include congenital toxoplasmosis and extraintestinal toxoplasmosis. The infection typically affects the brain, eyes, and lymph nodes, but can involve other organs such as the liver, lungs, and heart. It is transmitted through ingestion of oocysts, undercooked meat, or congenital transmission. Immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, are at higher risk for disseminated disease. Clinical manifestations vary from asymptomatic to severe neurological complications.

Toxoplasmosis unspecified refers to an infection caused by the protozoan *Toxoplasma gondii*, typically acquired through ingestion of oocysts or tissue cysts. It may present as acute or latent infection, often asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals. Common synonyms include toxoplasmosis, congenital toxoplasmosis, and ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection primarily affects the eyes, brain, and other organs, especially in immunocompromised patients. It can lead to severe complications such as chorioretinitis, encephalitis, and systemic dissemination.

Babesiosis unspecified is a parasitic infection caused by species of the genus *Babesia*, most commonly *Babesia microti* in the United States. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected ticks, though transfusion-transmission can also occur. The infection affects red blood cells, leading to hemolytic anemia, fever, chills, and fatigue. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. Less commonly, it can involve the liver and spleen, causing hepatosplenomegaly. Synonyms include babesial infection and tick-borne babesiosis.

Babesiosis due to *Babesia microti* is a tick-borne protozoal infection transmitted primarily by *Ixodes* ticks. It causes intraerythrocytic parasitemia, leading to hemolytic anemia, fever, chills, and fatigue. Common synonyms include babesial infection or babesiosis. The causative agent is *Babesia microti*, though other species like *B. duncani* may also be involved. The infection typically affects red blood cells, with systemic symptoms more common in immunocompromised individuals. Complications may include renal failure and multiorgan dysfunction.

Babesiosis due to *Babesia duncani* is a tick-borne hemolytic disease caused by the intraerythrocytic parasite *Babesia duncani*. Common synonyms include western Nebraska babesiosis and Pacific coast babesiosis. The infection primarily affects erythrocytes, leading to hemolysis and anemia. It is typically acquired through the bite of infected *Ixodes* ticks, particularly in western North America. Symptoms may include fever, chills, fatigue, and jaundice. The disease can be severe in immunocompromised individuals, with potential complications such as renal failure and multiorgan involvement.

Babesiosis due to *Babesia divergens* is a tick-borne hemolytic disease caused by the intraerythrocytic protozoan parasite *Babesia divergens*. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, leading to severe hemolytic anemia, fever, and multiorgan involvement. Common synonyms include babesial infection and babesiosis. The parasite infects red blood cells, causing intravascular hemolysis. Typical affected body parts include the liver, spleen, and kidneys, with potential complications such as renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Other babesiosis refers to infection caused by species of *Babesia* other than *Babesia microti*, the most common cause in the United States. It is transmitted primarily through tick bites, particularly from *Ixodes* species. Common synonyms include non-*Babesia microti* babesiosis and babesiosis caused by other *Babesia* species. The infection primarily affects red blood cells, leading to hemolysis. Symptoms include fever, anemia, and fatigue. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals and can involve the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

Babesiosis is a tick-borne protozoal infection caused by species of *Babesia*, most commonly *B. microti* in the United States. It primarily affects red blood cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. The infection is often asymptomatic or presents with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, and fatigue. In immunocompromised individuals, it can progress to severe illness. Common synonyms include babesial infection or babesiosis. The disease is typically transmitted through the bite of infected Ixodes ticks and can also be spread through blood transfusions. The liver and spleen are commonly involved in more severe cases.

Acanthamebiasis unspecified is a parasitic infection caused by *Acanthamoeba* species, though the specific strain is not identified. It primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, often following trauma or contact with contaminated water. Common synonyms include granulomatous amebic encephalitis and Acanthamoeba infection. The disease is characterized by chronic, granulomatous inflammation, leading to ulcers, nodules, or abscesses. While typically localized, severe cases may involve the central nervous system. Diagnosis is often challenging without specific laboratory tests.

Meningoencephalitis due to *Acanthamoeba culbertsoni* is a severe central nervous system infection caused by free-living amoebae. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals and is characterized by inflammation of the brain and meninges. Common synonyms include granulomatous amoebic encephalitis and amoebic meningoencephalitis. The infection often presents with fever, headache, seizures, and altered mental status. It primarily affects the brain and meninges, with possible involvement of the spinal cord. Diagnosis is challenging and requires specialized laboratory techniques. Early treatment with antiamoebic agents is critical for improving outcomes.

Conjunctivitis due to *Acanthamoeba* is a rare but severe form of infectious conjunctivitis caused by free-living amoebae, primarily *Acanthamoeba polyphaga* and *Acanthamoeba castellani*. It typically affects contact lens wearers who use contaminated water or improper storage solutions. The infection presents with redness, irritation, and a gritty sensation, often leading to corneal ulcers if untreated. Common synonyms include amebic conjunctivitis and amoebic keratoconjunctivitis. The condition primarily affects the conjunctiva and cornea, with potential for serious ocular complications.

Keratoconjunctivitis due to *Acanthamoeba* is a severe, potentially sight-threatening infection affecting the cornea and conjunctiva. Common synonyms include amoebic keratitis and Acanthamoeba keratitis. The causative agent is *Acanthamoeba*, a free-living amoeba found in water and soil. It typically affects the cornea and conjunctiva, often in individuals who use contaminated contact lenses. The infection is characterized by severe pain, redness, photophobia, and corneal ulcers. Diagnosis is challenging and requires specialized laboratory testing. Treatment involves prolonged use of antiamoebic agents, often with poor outcomes if not promptly addressed.

Other acanthamebic disease refers to infections caused by species of *Acanthamoeba* that do not fit the classical description of primary amebic meningoencephalitis. Common synonyms include granulomatous amebic encephalitis and acanthamoebiasis. The causative agents are various *Acanthamoeba* species, such as *A. castellani* and *A. polyphaga*. These infections primarily affect the central nervous system, leading to chronic, progressive neurological symptoms. They may also involve the eyes, causing keratitis, and occasionally other tissues. The disease is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals.

Acanthamebiasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Acanthamoeba* species, primarily *Acanthamoeba castellanii* and *Acanthamoeba polyphaga*. It typically affects the skin, eyes, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include granulomatous amebic encephalitis and amoebic keratitis. The infection often enters through contaminated water or soil, leading to localized granulomas or systemic dissemination. Cutaneous lesions are common, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Ocular involvement can cause severe corneal ulcers, while CNS involvement may result in fever, seizures, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopy, culture, or PCR. Treatment involves antiamoebic medications such as chlorhexidine, idoxuridine, and miltefosine.

Naegleriasis is a rare but severe central nervous system infection caused by *Naegleria fowleri*, a free-living amoeba. Commonly known as "primary amoebic meningoencephalitis," the infection typically occurs after water contaminated with the amoeba enters the nasal passages. The organism invades the brain, leading to rapid progression of symptoms including fever, headache, nausea, and neurological deficits. The infection is almost always fatal if not diagnosed early. The meninges and brain are the primary affected areas, with the disease often resulting in death within days to weeks.

"Other specified protozoal diseases" refers to protozoal infections not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous protozoal infections. Causative agents may include *Giardia lamblia*, *Cryptosporidium parvum*, and *Toxoplasma gondii*. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and central nervous system. Symptoms vary but often include diarrhea, malabsorption, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through stool analysis or serological testing. Treatment depends on the specific organism and may involve antiparasitic medications.

Unspecified protozoal disease refers to a group of infections caused by protozoa when the specific organism is not identified. Common synonyms include undifferentiated protozoal infection or unspecified protozoan disease. Causative agents may include various protozoan parasites such as *Plasmodium*, *Leishmania*, *Trypanosoma*, or *Toxoplasma*, depending on the clinical context. These infections typically affect the bloodstream, liver, lymphatic system, or central nervous system. Symptoms vary but often include fever, malaise, and organ dysfunction. Diagnosis is challenging without specific identification of the protozoan species.

code_desc: Schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma haematobium [urinary schistosomiasis]
summary: Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma haematobium*, also known as urinary schistosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by the trematode *S. haematobium*. The parasite's cercariae penetrate the skin upon contact with contaminated freshwater, leading to migration and maturation in the venous plexus of the bladder. Adult worms produce eggs that are excreted in urine, causing inflammation and fibrosis of the urinary tract. Commonly affected areas include the bladder, ureters, and urethra. Complications may involve hematuria, bladder cancer, and urogenital pathology.

code_desc: Schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni [intestinal schistosomiasis]
summary: Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma mansoni* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the trematode *Schistosoma mansoni*, which primarily affects the intestinal tract. The parasite's eggs migrate through the intestinal wall, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potential complications such as colonic strictures or hematochezia. Common synonyms include intestinal schistosomiasis and Mansoni schistosomiasis. The infection is endemic in parts of Africa, the Middle East, and South America, with the liver and intestines being the most commonly affected organs.

Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma japonicum* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the trematode *S. japonicum*, transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater. The larvae penetrate the skin and migrate to the portal venous system, primarily affecting the liver and intestines. Common synonyms include Japanese schistosomiasis and oriental schistosomiasis. The disease is endemic in parts of Asia, particularly China, and can lead to granulomatous inflammation, fibrosis, and organ damage. Chronic infection may result in portal hypertension, hepatosplenomegaly, and gastrointestinal symptoms.

Cercarial dermatitis, also known as swimmer's itch, is an allergic skin reaction caused by the penetration of cercariae, the larval stage of certain trematode flukes, into the skin. The most common causative agents are species of *Schistosoma* and *Fasciola*. The condition typically affects areas of the skin exposed to infested freshwater, such as the legs, arms, and torso. Symptoms include an itchy, red rash with small blisters, usually appearing within hours to days after exposure. The reaction is self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment.

Other schistosomiasis refers to infections caused by schistosome species other than *Schistosoma hematobium*, *S. mansoni*, and *S. japonicum*. Common synonyms include visceral schistosomiasis and hepatosplenic schistosomiasis. The causative agents include *S. intercalatum*, *S. mekongi*, *S. guineensis*, and *S. mattheei*. These species primarily affect the liver and spleen, leading to granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis. The disease is endemic in parts of Africa, the Middle East, and South America. Clinical manifestations include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and portal hypertension. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by detecting parasite eggs in stool or urine.

Schistosomiasis unspecified refers to infection caused by Schistosoma species when the specific type is not identified. Common synonyms include bilharzia and snail fever. The causative agents are various Schistosoma trematodes, such as *S. mansoni*, *S. haematobium*, and *S. japonicum*. The disease primarily affects the intestines, bladder, and liver, leading to chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Symptoms include abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, hematuria, and portal hypertension. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater.

Opisthorchiasis is a parasitic infection caused by liver flukes of the genus *Opisthorchis*, most commonly *Opisthorchis viverrini* and *Opisthorchis felineus*. It results from ingestion of undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae. The flukes primarily infect the bile ducts and gallbladder, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potentially cholangiocarcinoma. Symptoms include abdominal pain, jaundice, and liver dysfunction. The disease is endemic in parts of Asia and Eastern Europe. Synonyms include clonorchiasis and opisthorchosis.

Clonorchiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the liver fluke *Clonorchis sinensis*, commonly known as the Chinese liver fluke. It is transmitted through the consumption of undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae. The parasites primarily infect the biliary system, leading to inflammation and fibrosis of the liver. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and cholangitis. Chronic infection can result in cholangiocarcinoma. The condition is endemic in parts of Asia, particularly in Korea, China, and Vietnam. Synonyms include opisthorchiasis and clonorchiasis.

Dicroceliasis is a parasitic infection caused by liver flukes of the genus *Dicrocoelium*, most commonly *Dicrocoelium dendriticum*. It primarily affects the bile ducts and liver, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. Common synonyms include hepatic fluke infection and ruminal fluke disease. The parasite is acquired through ingestion of contaminated vegetation, often by grazing animals. Humans may become accidental hosts, typically presenting with symptoms such as abdominal pain, jaundice, and fatigue. The condition is more prevalent in rural areas with poor sanitation and in regions where livestock farming is common.

Fascioliasis is a parasitic infection caused by the liver flukes *Fasciola hepatica* and *Fasciola gigantica*. Common synonyms include liver fluke disease and sheep liver fluke infection. The parasites primarily affect the liver, causing inflammation and fibrosis. Infection occurs through ingestion of metacercariae found in contaminated water or vegetation. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and hepatomegaly. Severe cases may lead to liver failure. The condition is prevalent in agricultural regions where livestock and humans share the same environment.

Paragonimiasis is a parasitic infection caused by lung flukes of the genus *Paragonimus*, most commonly *Paragonimus westermani*. It is acquired through ingestion of undercooked crustaceans. The parasites migrate to the lungs, causing pneumonia-like symptoms, and may spread to other organs such as the brain, liver, and abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include lung fluke disease and pulmonary paragonimiasis. Clinical manifestations include cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, and sometimes neurological symptoms if the parasites reach the central nervous system. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool examination or serology.

Fasciolopsiasis is a helminthic infection caused by the intestinal fluke *Fasciolopsis buski*. Common synonyms include giant intestinal fluke disease. The parasite primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the cecum and colon. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, transmitted through ingestion of contaminated water or food. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by stool examination for ova. The infection is more common in children and individuals with poor sanitation. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs such as praziquantel.

"Other specified fluke infections" refers to parasitic infections caused by trematodes not classified under more specific categories such as schistosomiasis or fascioliasis. Common synonyms include miscellaneous fluke infections. Causative agents may include species like *Echinostoma* or *Metagonimus*, though exact identification varies. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, liver, or bile ducts, often leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and liver dysfunction. Transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated food or water.

Fluke infection unspecified refers to parasitic infections caused by trematodes (flukes) when the specific species is not identified. Common synonyms include liver fluke infection or schistosomiasis, though these terms may refer to specific types. Causative agents include species such as * Fasciola hepatica*, * Schistosoma* spp., and * Clonorchis sinensis*. These parasites typically affect the liver, bile ducts, intestines, or bladder, depending on the species. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and gastrointestinal disturbances. Diagnosis often requires stool or blood tests, and treatment involves antiparasitic medications.

Echinococcus granulosus infection of the liver, also known as hepatic hydatid disease, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*. The infection leads to the formation of cysts within the liver, which can grow slowly over years. Common synonyms include hepatic hydatid cyst and alveolar echinococcosis, though the latter typically affects the liver and other organs. The liver is the most commonly affected site, followed by the lungs. Cysts may cause symptoms such as pain, swelling, and complications like rupture or secondary infection. Diagnosis is often confirmed via imaging and serology.

Echinococcus granulosus infection of the lung, also known as pulmonary hydatid disease, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*. The infection typically results from ingestion of eggs shed in the feces of infected dogs. The larvae form cysts in the lungs, which may grow slowly over years. Common symptoms include cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Other affected organs include the liver, brain, and bones. Diagnosis is often via imaging and serology, with treatment involving surgery and/or antiparasitic drugs.

Echinococcus granulosus infection of bone, also known as cystic echinococcosis or hydatid disease, is caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. This condition typically affects the bones of the spine, pelvis, and long bones, though it most commonly involves the liver and lungs. The infection manifests as a unilocular cyst containing daughter cysts, leading to localized pain, swelling, and potential pathological fractures. Diagnosis is often achieved through imaging and serological tests, with treatment involving surgical removal and antiparasitic therapy.

Echinococcus granulosus infection of the thyroid gland is a rare parasitic condition caused by the larval stage of the hydatid tapeworm. Also known as hydatid disease or cystic echinococcosis, it results from ingestion of eggs from infected animals. The parasite forms a unilocular cyst within the thyroid, often asymptomatic but potentially leading to mass effect or complications. Commonly affected organs include the liver and lungs, though thyroid involvement is uncommon. Diagnosis typically involves imaging and serology, with treatment involving surgical excision or antiparasitic drugs.

Echinococcus granulosus infection, also known as hydatid disease, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The infection typically involves multiple sites, most commonly the liver and lungs, but can affect other organs such as the brain, spleen, and kidneys. The parasite forms cysts that grow slowly, leading to tissue damage and potential complications if left untreated. Synonyms include hydatidosis and echinococcosis. Diagnosis is often achieved through imaging and serology, with treatment involving antiparasitic drugs or surgical intervention.

Echinococcus granulosus infection, also known as hydatid disease, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The infection typically affects the liver and lungs but can involve other organs such as the brain, heart, and bones. It results from ingestion of eggs shed in the feces of infected dogs. The larvae form cysts that grow slowly, leading to tissue damage and potential complications. Diagnosis is often confirmed by imaging and serological tests. Treatment involves surgical removal and anthelmintic therapy.

code_desc: Echinococcus granulosus infection other and multiple sites
summary: Echinococcus granulosus infection, also known as hydatid disease, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. The infection typically affects the liver and lungs but can involve multiple sites including the brain, spleen, and kidneys. It is characterized by the formation of hydatid cysts, which are fluid-filled structures that may cause local symptoms or complications if they rupture. The disease is transmitted through ingestion of eggs shed in the feces of infected dogs. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and alveolar echinococcosis, though the latter refers to a related but distinct species, Echinococcus multilocularis.

Echinococcus granulosus infection unspecified refers to a parasitic disease caused by the tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*. It typically manifests as hydatid cysts in various organs, most commonly the liver and lungs. The infection is transmitted through ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and cystic echinococcosis. The parasite's larval stage forms fluid-filled cysts, leading to progressive tissue damage and potential complications if left untreated. Diagnosis often involves imaging and serological tests.

Echinococcus multilocularis infection of the liver, also known as alveolar echinococcosis, is a chronic parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus multilocularis*. It primarily affects the liver, leading to the formation of multicystic, invasive lesions that mimic malignancy. The infection is commonly found in endemic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs from contaminated soil or food. Clinical manifestations include abdominal pain, weight loss, and hepatomegaly. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by imaging and serology, with treatment involving antiparasitic drugs and surgical intervention.

Echinococcus multilocularis infection, also known as alveolar echinococcosis, is a parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus multilocularis*. This infection typically affects the liver but can disseminate to multiple sites including the lungs, brain, and other organs. It is characterized by the formation of cysts that grow slowly and may mimic malignancies. Common synonyms include alveolar echinococcosis and multilocular echinococcosis. The disease is endemic in certain regions of Europe, Asia, and North America, primarily affecting foxes and dogs, with humans as accidental hosts.

Echinococcus multilocularis infection, also known as alveolar echinococcosis, is a chronic parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis. It primarily affects the liver but can involve other organs such as the lungs, brain, and kidneys. The infection is characterized by the formation of multifocal, infiltrative lesions that mimic malignancy. Common synonyms include alveolar echinococcosis and multilocular echinococcosis. The disease is endemic in certain regions of Europe, Asia, and North America, often transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food or water.

code_desc: Echinococcus multilocularis infection other and multiple sites
summary: Echinococcus multilocularis infection, also known as alveolar echinococcosis, is a chronic parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis. This infection typically affects the liver but can spread to other organs such as the lungs, brain, and kidneys. It is characterized by the formation of multicystic, infiltrative lesions that mimic malignancies. Common synonyms include alveolar echinococcosis and hepatic alveolar echinococcosis. The disease is endemic in certain regions of Europe, Asia, and North America, primarily affecting individuals exposed to infected foxes or dogs.

Echinococcus multilocularis infection unspecified refers to a parasitic disease caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus multilocularis*. Commonly known as alveolar echinococcosis, this condition primarily affects the liver but can involve other organs. The infection is typically acquired through ingestion of contaminated food or water, often linked to contact with infected animals such as foxes or dogs. Clinical manifestations include slow-growing cysts, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging and serological tests. The infection is endemic in certain regions of Europe, Asia, and North America.

Echinococcosis unspecified of liver is a parasitic infection caused by *Echinococcus* species, most commonly *E. granulosus* and *E. multilocularis*. It results from ingestion of eggs from infected animals, leading to formation of hydatid cysts in the liver. The disease is characterized by slow-growing cysts that may cause pain, mass effect, or complications like rupture. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and cystic echinococcosis. While the liver is the primary site, other organs such as the lungs, brain, and kidneys may also be involved.

Echinococcosis unspecified refers to infections caused by the larval stage of *Echinococcus* species, typically *E. granulosus* or *E. multilocularis*, when the specific type is not identified. It is a parasitic disease characterized by the formation of hydatid cysts in various organs, most commonly the liver and lungs. The infection is transmitted through ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments or direct contact with infected animals. Symptoms depend on cyst location and size, often presenting as asymptomatic or with nonspecific signs. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by imaging and serological tests.

Other echinococcosis refers to infections caused by species of the genus *Echinococcus* other than *E. granulosus* and *E. multilocularis*. Common synonyms include alveolar echinococcosis and cystic echinococcosis, depending on the species involved. The primary causative agents are *E. granulosus*, *E. multilocularis*, *E. oligarthrus*, and *E. vogeli*. These infections typically affect the liver and lungs, with *E. multilocularis* often causing more aggressive alveolar disease. The condition is zoonotic, with definitive hosts including dogs and intermediate hosts such as humans and livestock.

Echinococcosis other and unspecified refers to infections caused by tapeworms of the genus *Echinococcus*, primarily *E. granulosus* and *E. multilocularis*. These parasites cause cystic lesions in various organs, most commonly the liver and lungs. The disease is also known as hydatid disease or echinococcal cyst disease. It is typically acquired through ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments or direct contact with infected animals. The infection can lead to chronic, slowly progressing disease with potential for severe complications if left untreated.

Taenia solium taeniasis is a helminthic infection caused by the tapeworm *Taenia solium*, acquired through ingestion of undercooked pork containing *T. solium* cysticerci. The adult worm resides in the small intestine, where it attaches to the intestinal wall. Common synonyms include pork tapeworm infection and cysticercosis. The primary affected body parts are the gastrointestinal tract and, in the case of cysticercosis, various tissues including the brain, eyes, and muscles. The disease can present with abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and in severe cases, neurological complications.

Taenia saginata taeniasis is a parasitic infection caused by the beef tapeworm *Taenia saginata*. It occurs through ingestion of undercooked beef containing viable cysticerci. The adult worm attaches to the intestinal wall and can grow up to 2–7 meters in length. Common synonyms include beef tapeworm infection and T. saginata infestation. The primary affected body part is the small intestine. Symptoms are usually mild, including abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and occasional passage of proglottids. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via stool examination for eggs or segments. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs such as praziquantel.

Taeniasis unspecified refers to infection caused by the tapeworm *Taenia* species, typically acquired through ingestion of undercooked meat containing cysticerci. Common synonyms include pork tapeworm infection and beef tapeworm infection, though the exact species may not be identified. The causative agents include *Taenia solium* (pork tapeworm) and *Taenia saginata* (beef tapeworm). The primary affected body part is the small intestine, where the adult tapeworm attaches and resides. Symptoms may include abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and passage of proglottids.

Cysticercosis of the central nervous system (CNS) is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*. It results from ingestion of eggs from contaminated food or water, leading to cyst formation in the CNS. Common synonyms include neurocysticercosis and cerebral cysticercosis. The infection typically affects the brain and spinal cord, causing seizures, headaches, and neurological deficits. It is a significant cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions. The disease can present as parenchymal, ventricular, or meningeal forms, depending on the location of the cysts.

Cysticercosis of the eye is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*, resulting from ingestion of tapeworm eggs. The larvae form cysts in ocular tissues, leading to inflammation and potential vision loss. Common synonyms include ocular cysticercosis and ocular hydatidosis. It typically affects the retina, vitreous, and uvea. Symptoms may include pain, visual disturbances, and ocular swelling. Diagnosis is often via imaging, and treatment may involve antiparasitic drugs or surgical intervention.

Myositis in cysticercosis refers to inflammation of muscle tissue caused by the parasitic infection *Taenia solium*. The larvae (cysticerci) can invade skeletal muscles, leading to localized inflammation, pain, and sometimes necrosis. Common synonyms include cysticercal myositis or muscular cysticercosis. The condition is caused by ingestion of *T. solium* eggs, leading to larval migration. Typically affected areas include the neck, trunk, and limbs. It is more common in endemic regions and may present with muscle swelling, tenderness, and systemic symptoms. Diagnosis often involves imaging and serological tests.

Cysticercosis of other sites refers to the presence of *Taenia solium* cysticerci in organs other than the central nervous system. Common synonyms include extraneural cysticercosis. The causative agent is the larval stage of the pork tapeworm *Taenia solium*. This condition typically affects tissues such as the eyes, liver, lungs, and subcutaneous tissues. Clinical manifestations depend on the location and number of cysts, often presenting with localized pain, swelling, or inflammation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies and serological tests. Treatment may involve antiparasitic drugs and surgical intervention if necessary.

Cysticercosis of other sites refers to the presence of *Taenia solium* cysticerci in tissues outside the central nervous system, such as the eyes, heart, liver, and muscles. Caused by ingestion of *T. solium* eggs, the larvae develop into cysts, leading to inflammation and potential organ dysfunction. Common synonyms include extraneural cysticercosis and visceral cysticercosis. The condition is more prevalent in endemic regions and can result in severe complications depending on the affected organ. Diagnosis often involves imaging and serological tests, with treatment focusing on antiparasitic therapy and management of symptoms.

Cysticercosis unspecified refers to infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Taenia solium*. The parasite forms cysts in various tissues, most commonly in the central nervous system, muscles, and eyes. Common synonyms include neurocysticercosis when affecting the brain. The condition results from ingestion of eggs from contaminated food or water. Clinical manifestations depend on the location and number of cysts, ranging from asymptomatic to severe neurological symptoms. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging and serological tests. Treatment involves antiparasitic drugs and management of complications.

Diphyllobothriasis is a parasitic infection caused by the tapeworm *Diphyllobothrium latum*, commonly known as the broad tapeworm. It is acquired through ingestion of undercooked freshwater fish containing the larval stage. The adult worm resides in the small intestine, where it attaches to the intestinal wall. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and nutrient deficiencies due to the worm's ability to absorb vitamins. The infection is more prevalent in regions with high fish consumption and poor food safety practices.

Sparganosis is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Spirometra erinacei*. Common synonyms include cysticercosis and larval cyticercosis. The infection typically affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and occasionally the eyes, lungs, and brain. It is acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or undercooked meat. Clinical presentation varies, with migratory subcutaneous nodules and localized inflammation being common. Diagnosis is often based on clinical findings and imaging, with serologic tests providing additional support. Treatment usually involves antiparasitic medications such as praziquantel.

Hymenolepiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the tapeworm *Hymenolepis nana* or *Hymenolepis diminuta*. It primarily affects the small intestine and is commonly seen in children in crowded living conditions. The infection is characterized by the presence of adult worms in the intestinal lumen. *Hymenolepis nana* is the most common causative agent, often referred to as the dwarf tapeworm. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Transmission occurs through ingestion of contaminated food or water, or via the fecal-oral route.

Dipylidiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the tapeworm *Dipylidium caninum*, commonly found in dogs and cats. It is transmitted to humans via ingestion of infected fleas or intermediate hosts. The adult worms reside in the small intestine, where they attach to the intestinal wall. Common synonyms include canine tapeworm infection and flea tapeworm disease. Symptoms may include abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and anal itching. Children are most commonly affected, often through contact with infected pets. The infection is typically diagnosed via stool examination for proglottids or eggs. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs such as praziquantel.

"Other specified cestode infections" refers to parasitic infections caused by tapeworms that do not fall under the more commonly recognized categories such as cysticercosis or echinococcosis. Common synonyms include unspecified cestode infections. Causative agents may include species like Hymenolepis nana, Diphyllobothrium latum, or Taenia solium, depending on the region. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, but can also involve the liver, lungs, or brain, depending on the parasite species and host immune response.

Cestode infection unspecified refers to infestation by tapeworms caused by species within the class Cestoda. Common synonyms include tapeworm infection or cestodiasis. Causative agents may include *Taenia* spp., *Diphyllobothrium* spp., or *Echinococcus* spp., depending on the species. The infection typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, with larvae sometimes migrating to other organs such as the liver, lungs, or brain. Symptoms vary based on the species and life stage, ranging from abdominal discomfort to severe complications like cyst formation. Diagnosis often requires imaging or stool analysis.

Dracunculiasis, also known as Guinea worm disease, is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode Dracunculus medinensis. The disease is transmitted through contaminated water containing copepods that harbor the larvae. Upon ingestion, the larvae develop into adult worms, with the female migrating through subcutaneous tissues to the lower extremities, where she emerges through the skin, causing painful ulcers. The infection is primarily found in impoverished communities with limited access to clean water. The condition predominantly affects the lower limbs, leading to severe disability and secondary infections if left untreated.

Onchocerciasis with eye involvement unspecified refers to a parasitic infection caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*, transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. The disease leads to microfilariae migration in tissues, causing inflammation and damage. Eye involvement, though unspecified, may result in visual impairment, conjunctival inflammation, or scarring. Common synonyms include river blindness and loiasis (though loiasis is caused by *Loa loa*). The infection primarily affects the skin and eyes, with systemic involvement possible in severe cases.

Onchocerciasis with endophthalmitis is a severe ocular complication of onchocerciasis, caused by the filarial nematode *Onchocerca volvulus*. The microfilariae migrate to the eye, leading to inflammation and granulomatous reaction, which can result in endophthalmitis. Common synonyms include river blindness with ocular involvement and ocular onchocerciasis. The condition primarily affects the cornea, iris, and retina, potentially causing blindness. It is endemic in tropical regions where blackflies are prevalent.

Onchocerciasis with glaucoma is a condition resulting from the ocular complications of onchocerciasis, a parasitic infection caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*. The disease leads to inflammation and scarring of the eye, potentially causing glaucoma due to obstructed aqueous outflow. Common synonyms include river blindness with secondary glaucoma and onchocercal glaucoma. Typically affecting the eyes, it may also involve the skin and lymphatic system. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. Prolonged ocular involvement can result in irreversible vision loss.

Onchocerciasis with other eye involvement is a parasitic infection caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*, transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. The disease leads to ocular complications such as uveitis, retinal lesions, and visual impairment. Common synonyms include river blindness and loa-loa disease, though loa-loa is caused by a different parasite. The infection primarily affects the skin and eyes, with severe ocular involvement leading to blindness. It is endemic in tropical regions of Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East.

Onchocerciasis with eye disease, also known as river blindness, is a parasitic infection caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. The adult worms produce microfilariae, which migrate to the skin and eyes, causing inflammation and severe ocular complications. Common symptoms include conjunctival inflammation, uveitis, and progressive visual loss. The eyes are the primary affected organ, with potential for irreversible blindness. The condition is endemic in tropical regions, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.

Onchocerciasis without eye disease refers to infection by *Onchocerca volvulus* that primarily affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues, rather than the eyes. Common synonyms include loiasis or African river blindness when ocular involvement is absent. The parasite is transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. Clinical features include pruritic skin lesions, nodules, and hyperpigmentation. Lymphatic involvement may occur, leading to lymphadenopathy. The condition is endemic in tropical regions of Africa, and without ocular manifestations, diagnosis relies on clinical symptoms and serological testing.

Filariasis due to *Wuchereria bancrofti* is a tropical parasitic infection caused by filarial worms transmitted via mosquito vectors. The adult worms reside in lymphatic vessels, leading to chronic inflammation and lymphatic damage. Common synonyms include bancroftian filariasis and lymphatic filariasis. The disease primarily affects the lymphatic system, causing lymphedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, with *Wuchereria bancrofti* being the most common causative agent, followed by *Brugia malayi* and *Brugia timori*.

Filariasis due to *Brugia malayi* is a parasitic infection caused by the filarial worm *Brugia malayi*, transmitted via the bite of infected mosquitoes. Common synonyms include tropical pulmonary eosinophilia and lymphatic filariasis. The infection primarily affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and hydrocele. It may also involve the lungs, causing eosinophilic inflammation. The disease is endemic in Southeast Asia and is characterized by chronic inflammation and tissue damage. Diagnosis is typically based on microfilariae detection in blood or serological tests. Treatment involves antifilarial drugs such as diethylcarbamazine.

Filariasis due to *Brugia timori* is a parasitic infection caused by the filarial worm *Brugia timori*, transmitted via the bite of infected mosquitoes. Commonly known as Timor filariasis, it primarily affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and elephantiasis. The disease is endemic to Southeast Asia, particularly Indonesia. Clinical manifestations include swelling of the lower extremities, hydrocele, and lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is often confirmed through microfilariae detection in blood or serological tests. Treatment typically involves antifilarial drugs such as diethylcarbamazine or ivermectin.

Loiasis, also known as African eye worm infection, is a parasitic disease caused by the filarial nematode *Loa loa*. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected cyclops, which are found in freshwater. The adult worms migrate through subcutaneous tissues, often causing visible movement under the skin, particularly around the eyes. Common symptoms include skin rash, swelling, and ocular involvement. The disease is endemic in Central and West Africa. While generally non-fatal, severe cases may lead to complications such as meningitis or blindness.

Mansonelliasis is a neglected tropical disease caused by filarial nematodes of the genus Mansonella. Common synonyms include loa-loa filariasis and subcutaneous filariasis. The primary causative agents are Mansonella perstans and Mansonella ozzardi. The infection typically affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and lymphatic system, leading to symptoms such as skin nodules, itching, and sometimes lymphadenopathy. Transmission occurs through blood-feeding flies, primarily Simulium species. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, with M. perstans being the most widely distributed species.

Other filariases refer to parasitic infections caused by nematodes of the family Filariodidae, excluding the more commonly known lymphatic filariases. These infections are typically transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Common synonyms include tropical pulmonary eosinophilia and other filarial infections. The causative agents include *Brugia malayi*, *Wuchereria bancrofti*, and *Mansonella perstans*. These parasites primarily affect the lymphatic system, lungs, and skin, leading to conditions such as lymphadenopathy, pulmonary symptoms, and dermatitis. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Filariasis unspecified refers to infections caused by filarial nematodes when the specific species is not identified. Common synonyms include lymphatic filariasis and elephantiasis. The causative agents typically include Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori, which are transmitted via mosquito vectors. The disease primarily affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and hydrocele. It may also involve the genital and subcutaneous tissues, causing swelling and fibrosis. The condition is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often associated with poor sanitation and limited access to healthcare.

Trichinellosis is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genus *Trichinella*, most commonly *Trichinella spiralis*. It is acquired by consuming undercooked meat containing encysted larvae. The infection primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract and skeletal muscles, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and muscle inflammation. Synonyms include trichiniasis and trichinelliasis. The larvae migrate through the bloodstream, causing systemic involvement, particularly in the muscles, and may lead to severe complications in immunocompromised individuals.

Ancylostomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the hookworms *Ancylostoma duodenale* and *Necator americanus*. It primarily affects the small intestine, where adult worms attach to the intestinal mucosa, causing blood loss and anemia. The larvae penetrate the skin, typically through contaminated soil, leading to a condition known as cutaneous larva migrans. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fatigue. The infection is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas with poor sanitation. It is also referred to as hookworm disease or soil-transmitted helminthiasis.

Necatoriasis is a parasitic infection caused by the hookworm *Necator americanus*, a common soil-transmitted helminth. Infection occurs through skin penetration of infective larvae, typically from contaminated soil. The larvae migrate through the bloodstream to the lungs, then to the intestines, where they mature into adult worms and attach to the intestinal wall. Common symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and anemia due to blood loss. The condition is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas with poor sanitation. Synonyms include hookworm infection and cutaneous larva migrans, though the latter refers to a different species. The primary affected body parts are the skin, lungs, and small intestine.

Other hookworm diseases refer to infections caused by nematode parasites of the genus Ancylostoma and Necator americanus. These parasites primarily affect the small intestine, causing anemia, malnutrition, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Common synonyms include hookworm infection and soil-transmitted helminthiasis. The larvae penetrate the skin, typically through contaminated soil, leading to cutaneous larva migrans. The adult worms attach to the intestinal mucosa, leading to blood loss and iron deficiency anemia. Children and immunocompromised individuals are most commonly affected.

Hookworm disease unspecified refers to infection caused by hookworms, typically *Ancylostoma duodenale* or *Necator americanus*, leading to intestinal infestation. Common synonyms include ancylostomiasis and necatoriasis. The worms attach to the intestinal mucosa, causing blood loss, anemia, and gastrointestinal symptoms. The primary affected body parts are the small intestine and, in severe cases, the lungs during larval migration. Clinical manifestations include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fatigue. The condition is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions with poor sanitation.

Ascariasis with intestinal complications is a parasitic infection caused by *Ascaris lumbricoides*, a nematode worm. Common synonyms include intestinal roundworm infection or large intestinal roundworm disease. The larvae migrate through the lungs before maturing in the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, and intestinal obstruction. Complications may include bowel perforation, malnutrition, and secondary infections. The primary affected body parts are the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the small intestine, and the lungs during the migratory phase. It is most prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and hygiene.

Ascariasis pneumonia is a complication of intestinal ascariasis caused by *Ascaris lumbricoides*. It occurs when larvae migrate through the lungs, leading to inflammation and symptoms such as cough, fever, and hemoptysis. Common synonyms include pulmonary ascariasis or larva migrans syndrome. The condition primarily affects the lungs, though larvae may also reach the liver or other organs. It is more common in children in endemic areas with poor sanitation. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with treatment involving anthelmintic drugs.

Ascariasis with other complications is a parasitic infection caused primarily by *Ascaris lumbricoides*. The larvae migrate through the lungs, causing pulmonary symptoms, before maturing into adult worms in the small intestine. Complications may include intestinal obstruction, appendicitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis. Other synonyms include intestinal ascariasis or large intestinal roundworm infection. The condition predominantly affects the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and occasionally the biliary or pancreatic ducts. It is most common in children in endemic regions with poor sanitation.

Ascariasis with other complications is a parasitic infection caused primarily by *Ascaris lumbricoides*. It occurs when larvae migrate through the lungs and then mature into adult worms in the small intestine. Complications may include intestinal obstruction, appendicitis, cholangitis, or pneumonia due to larval migration. Common synonyms include intestinal roundworm infection and ascariasis with visceral larva migrans. The infection predominantly affects the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and occasionally the biliary system. It is most common in children in endemic areas with poor sanitation.

Ascariasis unspecified refers to infection caused by the parasitic roundworm *Ascaris lumbricoides*. Common synonyms include intestinal roundworm infection and giant roundworm disease. The larvae migrate through the lungs before maturing in the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, coughing, and malnutrition. The primary affected body parts are the gastrointestinal tract and lungs. Transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated soil or food. While most infections are asymptomatic, severe cases may result in intestinal obstruction or visceral larva migrans.

Intestinal strongyloidiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Strongyloides stercoralis*. It primarily affects the small intestine, where the larvae migrate and cause inflammation. The infection can be asymptomatic or present with gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. In immunocompromised individuals, it may lead to disseminated strongyloidiasis, a severe and potentially life-threatening condition. Common synonyms include strongyloidiasis and filariasis. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Cutaneous strongyloidiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the larvae of *Strongyloides stercoralis*, which penetrate the skin, typically through contact with contaminated soil. The condition is also known as cutaneous larva migrans or creeping eruption. It presents as a pruritic, serpiginous rash on the skin, most commonly affecting the feet, hands, and buttocks. The larvae migrate through the epidermis, causing inflammation and characteristic linear tracks. While the infection is usually self-limiting, systemic involvement can occur in immunocompromised individuals.

Disseminated strongyloidiasis is a severe, systemic manifestation of strongyloidiasis caused by *Strongyloides stercoralis*. It occurs in immunocompromised individuals, leading to widespread migration of larvae beyond the intestinal tract. Common synonyms include hyperinfection syndrome and disseminated strongyloidiasis. The infection affects multiple organs, including the lungs, liver, brain, and skin, causing symptoms such as cough, fever, abdominal pain, and neurological deficits. Without prompt treatment, it can be life-threatening.

Strongyloidiasis unspecified refers to infection caused by the nematode *Strongyloides stercoralis*, a soil-transmitted helminth. The infection is characterized by larval migration through the lungs and subsequent development in the small intestine. Common synonyms include filariasis and threadworm infection. The parasite primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and skin. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and skin rashes. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool examination or serological tests. Treatment typically involves anthelmintic drugs such as ivermectin.

Trichuriasis is a parasitic infection caused by the whipworm *Trichuris trichiura*, primarily affecting the large intestine. It is also known as whipworm infection or threadworm disease. The adult worms attach to the intestinal mucosa, causing inflammation and ulceration, particularly in the cecum and ascending colon. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, rectal prolapse, and anemia. Common in areas with poor sanitation, it is transmitted through ingestion of infective eggs in contaminated soil. Children and immunocompromised individuals are most susceptible.

Enterobiasis, also known as pinworm infection, is a common intestinal parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Enterobius vermicularis*. The infection primarily affects the large intestine and rectum, with female worms migrating to the perianal area to lay eggs, causing intense pruritus. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs, often through contaminated hands, surfaces, or fomites. It is most common in children and spreads easily in crowded environments. Symptoms include anal itching, restlessness, and sleep disturbances. Complications are rare but may include secondary bacterial infections or spread to other areas like the vagina or lungs.

Anisakiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the ingestion of larvae of nematodes from the genus *Anisakis*. Common synonyms include *Anisakidosis* and *Anisakiasis*. The primary causative agents are *Anisakis simplex* and *Pseudoterranova decipiens*. The larvae typically attach to the gastric mucosa, causing acute inflammation, ulceration, and severe epigastric pain. Symptoms may include vomiting, nausea, and abdominal pain. The condition predominantly affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the stomach, and is commonly associated with consumption of raw or undercooked marine fish or cephalopods.

Intestinal capillariasis is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genus *Capillaria*, primarily *Capillaria philippinensis*. It affects the small intestine, leading to inflammation, ulceration, and malabsorption. Common synonyms include capillariidosis and intestinal capillariidiasis. The infection is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often associated with contaminated food or water. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through stool examination for eggs or adult worms. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs such as albendazole or ivermectin.

Trichostrongyliasis is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genus *Trichostrongylus*, commonly affecting the gastrointestinal tract. It is prevalent in animals, particularly ruminants, but can also occur in humans through contaminated food or water. Common synonyms include gastrointestinal strongyloidiasis and trichostrongyloidiasis. The primary causative agents are *Trichostrongylus* species, such as *T. axei* and *T. colubriformis*. The infection typically affects the small intestine, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss.

Intestinal angiostrongyliasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Angiostrongylus costaraviensis* or *Angiostrongylus cantonensis*. It primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the small intestine, and may involve the lungs during migration. Common synonyms include eosinophilic enteritis and eosinophilic granuloma of the intestine. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and eosinophilia. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often linked to consumption of contaminated food or water.

Mixed intestinal helminthiases refer to concurrent infections of the intestines caused by multiple species of parasitic worms. Common synonyms include polyparasitism or mixed helminth infection. Causative agents may include *Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Trichuris trichiura*, * hookworms* (e.g., *Ancylostoma duodenale*, *Necator americanus*), and *Strongyloides stercoralis*. These infections primarily affect the small and large intestines, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, malnutrition, and anemia. They are prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and are often acquired through contaminated food or water.

"Other specified intestinal helminthiases" refers to parasitic infections caused by helminths not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified intestinal worm infestations. Causative agents may include hookworms, whipworms, and tapeworms, depending on regional prevalence. These infections primarily affect the small and large intestines, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. They are commonly seen in areas with poor sanitation and are often transmitted through contaminated soil or food. Diagnosis typically involves stool examination for ova and parasites. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs tailored to the specific helminth involved.

Intestinal helminthiasis unspecified refers to infection of the intestines by parasitic worms when the specific type is not identified. Common synonyms include intestinal worm infestation or helminthic infection. Causative agents may include roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, or flukes, though the exact species is unspecified. The condition typically affects the small and large intestines, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and malnutrition. It is commonly seen in areas with poor sanitation and hygiene.

Intestinal parasitism unspecified refers to the presence of parasitic organisms in the gastrointestinal tract without a specific identification of the parasite. Common synonyms include intestinal infestation or helminthic infection. Causative agents may include protozoa such as Giardia lamblia or Entamoeba histolytica, and helminths like Ascaris lumbricoides or Trichuris trichiura. The small intestine is typically affected, though involvement of the large intestine or other gastrointestinal regions may occur. Symptoms often include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through stool examination.

Visceral larva migrans is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of certain nematodes, most commonly *Toxocara canis* and *Toxocara cati*. It occurs when humans ingest eggs from contaminated soil, leading to larval migration through various organs. Common synonyms include visceral larva infection and toxocariasis. The larvae typically affect the liver, lungs, and eyes, causing inflammation and tissue damage. Symptoms may include fever, cough, abdominal pain, and in severe cases, visceral involvement leading to organ dysfunction. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and serological testing.

Gnathostomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Gnathostoma spinigerum* and other related species. It is acquired through ingestion of raw or undercooked meat containing the larvae. The larvae migrate through tissues, causing cutaneous and visceral lesions. Common synonyms include visceral larva migrans and cutaneous larva migrans. The infection typically affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and can involve the lungs, liver, and brain. Symptoms include itching, swelling, and migratory skin lesions. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and serology. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs such as albendazole or ivermectin.

Angiostrongyliasis due to *Parastrongylus cantonensis*, also known as rat lungworm disease, is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Parastrongylus cantonensis*. The larvae migrate through the bloodstream, primarily affecting the central nervous system, leading to eosinophilic meningitis. Common symptoms include headache, neck stiffness, fever, and neurological deficits. The infection is acquired through ingestion of contaminated food or water, often via intermediate hosts like snails or slugs. It predominantly affects the brain and spinal cord, with rare extraneural involvement.

Syngamiasis is a rare condition characterized by the fusion of adjacent epithelial cells, typically in the oral cavity. It is most commonly observed in the hard palate and is often associated with chronic irritation or trauma. The condition is also known as palatal syngamiasis or epithelial syngamiasis. It is caused by persistent mechanical pressure, such as from ill-fitting dentures, leading to abnormal cell adhesion. The causative agents are not infectious but rather related to physical factors. Clinically, it presents as a white, firm lesion with fused epithelial cells, and is generally benign.

Internal hirudiniasis is a rare parasitic infection caused by the leech *Hirudo medicinalis*. It occurs when leeches penetrate the skin and establish residence in body cavities, most commonly the abdominal or thoracic regions. The condition is characterized by localized inflammation, pain, and sometimes systemic symptoms due to leech secretions. Synonyms include leech infestation or leechworm disease. While uncommon, it is more frequently reported in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor hygiene. The primary causative agent is the medicinal leech, though other leech species may occasionally be involved.

Other specified helminthiases refer to parasitic worm infections caused by organisms not classified under more specific categories such as ascariasis or schistosomiasis. Common synonyms include unspecified helminthic infections. Causative agents may include various nematodes, trematodes, or cestodes, depending on the region and transmission route. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, liver, or skin, depending on the parasite. They are often diagnosed when the specific helminth cannot be definitively identified or when the infection does not meet criteria for more precisely defined helminthiases.

Helminthiasis unspecified refers to infestation by parasitic worms without specific identification of the causative agent. Common synonyms include intestinal worm infection or helminthic infection. Causative agents may include nematodes, cestodes, or trematodes such as Ascaris lumbricoides, Taenia species, or Schistosoma. Typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, liver, lungs, or other organs depending on the parasite. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and stool examination. Treatment depends on the identified helminth.

code_desc: Pediculosis due to Pediculus humanus capitis
summary: Pediculosis due to *Pediculus humanus capitis*, commonly known as head lice infestation, is a contagious ectoparasitic infection caused by the human head louse. The causative agent, *Pediculus humanus capitis*, attaches to the scalp and feeds on blood, leading to intense pruritus and irritation. It primarily affects the scalp, particularly behind the ears and along the neck. Common synonyms include "lice infestation" or "head lice." Transmission occurs through direct head-to-head contact or sharing of personal items. The condition is prevalent among school-aged children and is often diagnosed by the presence of nits or live lice on the hair shafts.

code_desc: Pediculosis due to Pediculus humanus corporis
summary: Pediculosis due to *Pediculus humanus corporis* is a parasitic infestation caused by the body louse, which feeds on human blood. Common synonyms include body louse infestation or linen louse disease. The louse attaches to clothing and transfers to the skin for feeding. It primarily affects the trunk, neck, and scalp, especially in individuals with poor hygiene or overcrowded living conditions. Symptoms include intense pruritus, erythematous papules, and possible secondary bacterial infections. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infested clothing or bedding.

Pediculosis unspecified refers to infestation by lice without specifying the type or location. It encompasses head, body, or pubic lice infestations. Common synonyms include lice infestation or pediculosis. The causative agents are Pediculus humanus capitis (head lice), Pediculus humanus corporis (body lice), and Phthirus pubis (pubic lice). Typically affects the scalp, body, or pubic areas. Symptoms include itching, irritation, and visible nits or lice. Transmission occurs through direct contact or shared personal items. Treatment involves topical insecticides and thorough cleaning of affected areas.

Phthiriasis is a parasitic infestation caused by lice, most commonly *Pediculus humanus capitis* (head lice) or *Pediculus humanus corporis* (body lice). It is characterized by intense pruritus and the presence of nits or live lice on the scalp, eyebrows, or body hair. Common synonyms include pediculosis. The condition primarily affects the scalp, neck, and axillae, and is prevalent in children and individuals living in crowded conditions. Transmission occurs through direct contact or shared personal items. Treatment typically involves topical insecticides and thorough hygiene measures.

Mixed pediculosis and phthiriasis refers to concurrent infestations by head lice (*Pediculus humanus capitis*) and pubic lice (*Phthirus pubis*). Commonly known as head and body lice infestation, it affects the scalp and pubic areas. These ectoparasites feed on human blood, causing intense itching and skin irritation. Transmission occurs through direct contact or shared personal items. While pediculosis primarily affects the scalp, phthiriasis typically involves the pubic region. Both conditions are more prevalent in crowded living conditions and among children or sexually active individuals. Treatment involves topical insecticides and thorough hygiene measures.

Scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by the mite *Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*. It presents as intense pruritus, especially at night, with characteristic burrows, papules, and vesicles. Common synonyms include scabetic dermatitis and itch. The mites burrow into the epidermis, triggering an allergic reaction. Typical affected areas include the webs of fingers, wrists, elbows, axillae, genitalia, and buttocks. Transmission occurs via close skin-to-skin contact. Diagnosis is often clinical, though skin scraping may confirm the presence of mites or eggs. Treatment involves topical acaricides such as permethrin.

Cutaneous myiasis is an infestation of the skin by fly larvae, typically introduced through wounds or natural openings. Common synonyms include myiasis and fly larvae infestation. It is caused by various fly species, most commonly from the families Calliphoridae, Sarcophagidae, and Oestridae. The larvae feed on tissue, leading to localized inflammation, ulceration, and sometimes necrosis. Commonly affected areas include the ears, nose, eyes, and wounds. The condition is more prevalent in tropical regions and among individuals with compromised immunity or poor hygiene. Early diagnosis and removal of larvae are essential to prevent complications.

Wound myiasis is an infestation of living tissue by fly larvae, commonly occurring in open wounds or necrotic areas. It is also known as myiasis or wound myiasis. The condition is typically caused by species of flies such as *Dermatobia hominis*, *Lucilia species*, and *Chrysomya species*. It most commonly affects the skin, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Infestation leads to localized inflammation, pain, and tissue damage. It is often seen in individuals with poor hygiene, immunocompromised states, or those with chronic wounds. Early diagnosis and removal of larvae are essential to prevent complications.

Ocular myiasis is an infestation of the eye by fly larvae, typically caused by species such as *Dermatobia hominis*, *Chrysops* spp., or *Cochliomyia hominivorax*. It presents as a painful, red, and swollen eye with visible larvae in the conjunctival or corneal tissues. Common synonyms include ocular myiasis, eye myiasis, and larval infestation of the eye. The condition primarily affects the conjunctiva, cornea, and orbit, often leading to vision loss if untreated. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions where fly populations are abundant.

Nasopharyngeal myiasis is an infestation of the nasal and pharyngeal cavities by fly larvae. Common synonyms include nasal myiasis and pharyngeal myiasis. The condition is typically caused by larvae of flies such as *Cochliomyia hominivorax* (screw worm) and *Dermatobia hominis*. It most commonly affects the nasal passages, nasopharynx, and occasionally the larynx. Symptoms include nasal discharge, foul odor, pain, and difficulty breathing. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often associated with poor hygiene or trauma to the nasal mucosa.

Aural myiasis is a parasitic infestation of the ear canal caused by fly larvae. Common synonyms include ear myiasis or auricular myiasis. The primary causative agents are species of the genus *Cochliomyia*, particularly *Cochliomyia hominivorax* (screw-worm fly). This condition typically affects the external auditory canal, often in tropical and subtropical regions. Infestation can lead to severe pain, otorrhea, and potential hearing loss if left untreated. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor hygiene. Prompt diagnosis and removal of larvae are essential for effective treatment.

Genitourinary myiasis is an infestation of the genital or urinary tract by fly larvae. Common synonyms include genital myiasis and urinary myiasis. It is typically caused by species of the genus *Dermatobia* or *Chrysomya*. The condition predominantly affects the genitalia, perineum, and urinary meatus, often presenting with symptoms such as pain, swelling, and discharge.
