Common synonyms include laryngeal paresis and vocal cord paralysis. Causative agents may include neurological disorders such as stroke, Parkinson’s disease, or trauma. It typically affects the vocal cords, arytenoids, and other laryngeal muscles, resulting in hoarseness, breathiness, and difficulty swallowing. The condition may be unilateral or bilateral, depending on the underlying cause.

code_desc: Paralysis of vocal cords and larynx unilateral
summary: Unilateral paralysis of the vocal cords and larynx refers to the loss of function in one side of the laryngeal muscles, typically affecting the vocal fold. This condition may result from damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, often due to tumors, trauma, infections, or surgical complications. Common synonyms include unilateral vocal cord palsy and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. The primary affected body parts are the vocal cords and larynx, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, breathy voice, and potential airway obstruction.

code_desc: Paralysis of vocal cords and larynx bilateral
summary: Bilateral paralysis of the vocal cords and larynx involves the loss of function in both sides of the laryngeal muscles, leading to impaired vocalization, breathing difficulties, and potential airway obstruction. Common synonyms include bilateral vocal cord palsy and laryngeal palsy. Causative agents may include neurological disorders such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, or motor neuron disease, as well as trauma, surgery, or infections. The condition primarily affects the larynx, vocal cords, and associated nerves, particularly the recurrent laryngeal nerves.

code_desc: Paralysis of vocal cords and larynx
summary: Paralysis of the vocal cords and larynx refers to the loss of voluntary control over the muscles of the larynx, leading to impaired voice production and breathing. Common synonyms include laryngeal paresis or vocal cord palsy. This condition can result from nerve damage, such as from trauma, surgery, stroke, or infections like vocal cord paralysis. It typically affects the vocal cords, arytenoid cartilages, and surrounding musculature, causing symptoms like hoarseness, breathiness, and difficulty swallowing. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is most commonly involved.

code_desc: Polyp of vocal cord and larynx
summary: Polyp of the vocal cord and larynx refers to a benign, gelatinous growth that develops on the vocal cords or other areas of the larynx. Common synonyms include vocal cord polyp, laryngeal polyp, and vocal fold polyp. These lesions are often caused by chronic vocal strain, vocal abuse, or inflammation. They typically affect the vocal cords, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, voice fatigue, and breathing difficulties. The condition is more common in individuals who use their voice extensively, such as singers or teachers. Treatment may involve voice therapy, corticosteroids, or surgical removal if symptoms persist.

Nodules of the vocal cords, also known as vocal nodules or singer's nodules, are benign growths that develop on the vocal folds due to repetitive strain from overuse or improper vocal technique. Common causative agents include vocal overuse, vocal abuse, and improper phonation. These nodules typically affect the anterior and middle regions of the vocal cords, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, breathiness, and vocal fatigue. They are most commonly found in individuals who use their voice extensively, such as teachers, singers, and public speakers.

"Other diseases of vocal cords" encompasses a range of non-specific conditions affecting the larynx, often involving inflammation, granulation, or structural changes. Common synonyms include laryngeal granuloma, laryngeal stenosis, and vocal cord edema. Causative agents may include chronic irritation from smoking, vocal overuse, infections, or foreign bodies. These conditions typically affect the vocal cords, arytenoids, and surrounding laryngeal structures, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, dysphonia, and breathing difficulties. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic evaluation and may involve biopsy for definitive assessment.

Edema of the larynx refers to swelling of the laryngeal tissues, often leading to airway obstruction. Common synonyms include laryngeal edema and laryngeal swelling. It is commonly caused by allergic reactions, infections, trauma, or inflammatory conditions. Causative agents may include allergens, anaphylactic agents, viral infections like epiglottitis, or irritants. The condition typically affects the vocal cords, epiglottis, and subglottic region, potentially compromising respiration. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt intervention to prevent respiratory failure.

Laryngeal spasm is an abrupt, involuntary contraction of the laryngeal muscles, leading to transient airway obstruction. Common synonyms include laryngospasm and spasmodic laryngitis. It is often triggered by irritation, acid reflux, or allergens. Causative agents may include gastric reflux, upper respiratory infections, or exposure to irritants. The condition typically affects the larynx and vocal cords, causing symptoms such as stridor, hoarseness, and difficulty breathing. It is more common in children and can occur during sleep or after anesthesia. The spasm is usually self-limiting but may require intervention in severe cases.

Stenosis of the larynx refers to the narrowing of the laryngeal airway, leading to obstructive breathing difficulties. Common synonyms include laryngeal stricture and laryngeal stenosis. It can result from trauma, prolonged intubation, infection, or inflammation. Causative agents may include infectious agents such as tuberculosis or fungi, as well as iatrogenic factors. The condition typically affects the supraglottic and glottic regions, potentially involving the subglottis. Symptoms include stridor, dyspnea, and voice changes. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent airway compromise.

"Other diseases of larynx" refers to a broad category of laryngeal conditions not classified as benign or malignant neoplasms. Common synonyms include laryngeal disorders and laryngeal inflammation. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viruses, bacteria), trauma, or autoimmune processes. These conditions typically affect the vocal cords, arytenoids, and subglottic region, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, dysphonia, and respiratory distress. They may result from chronic irritation, reflux, or systemic diseases affecting the laryngeal mucosa.

Retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal abscesses are collections of pus in the retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal spaces, typically affecting children. Common synonyms include retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal infections or abscesses. These conditions are often caused by bacterial pathogens such as Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae. They usually occur in the posterior pharyngeal wall and surrounding tissues, leading to symptoms like sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and respiratory distress. The retropharyngeal space is more common in children, while the parapharyngeal space can affect both adults and children.

"Other abscess of pharynx" refers to a localized collection of pus in the pharyngeal region not classified as a peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscess. Common synonyms include pharyngeal abscess or midline pharyngeal abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infections, most commonly Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and anaerobes. The condition often affects the posterior pharyngeal wall, extending from the tonsillar area to the upper mediastinum. It may result from trauma, foreign bodies, or spread from adjacent infections. Clinically, it presents with severe sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing.

"Other diseases of pharynx" encompasses a variety of non-specific inflammatory and degenerative conditions affecting the pharyngeal mucosa. Common synonyms include pharyngitis and pharyngeal inflammation. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or fungal pathogens, as well as environmental irritants. These conditions typically affect the pharyngeal walls, including the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx. Symptoms often involve sore throat, dysphagia, and hoarseness. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and endoscopic evaluation. Treatment varies depending on the underlying cause and may include antimicrobial therapy, anti-inflammatory agents, or supportive care.

code_desc: Upper respiratory tract hypersensitivity reaction site unspecified
summary: Upper respiratory tract hypersensitivity reaction site unspecified refers to an allergic response affecting the upper airway without a specific location identified. Common synonyms include allergic rhinitis, allergic upper airway disease, and non-specific rhinitis. Causative agents often include environmental allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold spores, and animal dander. Typically affected body parts include the nose, nasal passages, throat, and sometimes the ears. Symptoms may involve sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and postnasal drip. The reaction is mediated by IgE antibodies and involves mast cell degranulation.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of upper respiratory tract
summary: "Other specified diseases of upper respiratory tract" refers to conditions affecting the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pharynx, or larynx that are not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include unspecified upper respiratory tract disorders. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or fungal pathogens, as well as environmental irritants. These conditions often present with symptoms such as nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, and difficulty breathing. They can affect individuals of all ages but are more common in children and the elderly. Diagnosis typically involves clinical evaluation and imaging if necessary.

code_desc: Disease of upper respiratory tract unspecified
summary: Disease of upper respiratory tract unspecified refers to a broad category of conditions affecting the nose, pharynx, larynx, or adjacent structures when the specific diagnosis is not identified. Common synonyms include acute rhinosinusitis, pharyngitis, or laryngitis, though these may not always apply. Causative agents can include viral pathogens such as rhinovirus, influenza virus, or bacterial agents like Streptococcus pyogenes. Typically, the nasal passages, throat, and vocal cords are affected, with symptoms such as congestion, sore throat, and hoarseness. This diagnosis is often used when clinical presentation is nonspecific or diagnostic testing is inconclusive.

code_desc: Bronchitis not specified as acute or chronic
summary: Bronchitis not specified as acute or chronic refers to inflammation of the bronchial tubes without clear distinction between acute and chronic forms. Common synonyms include acute bronchitis and chronic bronchitis, though the classification is unspecified. It is often caused by viral infections, such as respiratory syncytial virus or influenza, though bacterial agents like *Streptococcus pneumoniae* may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the bronchi, leading to symptoms like cough, mucus production, and wheezing. It is commonly seen in smokers and individuals with underlying respiratory conditions.

Simple chronic bronchitis is a long-term inflammation of the bronchial tubes characterized by persistent cough and mucus production. It is commonly referred to as chronic bronchitis or chronic obstructive bronchitis. The condition is often caused by prolonged exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational dusts. It primarily affects the larger airways, leading to bronchial hyperresponsiveness and impaired mucociliary clearance. The lower respiratory tract, particularly the bronchi, is the main site of involvement. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Mucopurulent chronic bronchitis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by persistent bronchial inflammation and excessive mucus production, often with purulent secretion. It is defined by a productive cough lasting at least three months in two consecutive years. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and obstructive bronchitis. Causative agents include cigarette smoke, air pollutants, and respiratory infections. The condition primarily affects the large airways, including the trachea and bronchi, leading to bronchial wall thickening and airflow obstruction. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

code_desc: Mixed simple and mucopurulent chronic bronchitis
summary: Mixed simple and mucopurulent chronic bronchitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the bronchial airways characterized by persistent cough and production of both clear (simple) and purulent (mucopurulent) sputum. It often results from long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, or occupational dust. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis with mucopurulent secretion and persistent bronchial inflammation. Causative agents include bacterial infections, viral agents, and environmental irritants. The condition primarily affects the large airways, leading to bronchial hypersecretion and impaired mucociliary clearance. It is commonly associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Unspecified chronic bronchitis refers to persistent inflammation of the bronchial tubes without a specific identified cause. It is characterized by chronic cough and mucus production lasting at least three months in two consecutive years. Common synonyms include chronic bronchial inflammation or unspecified chronic obstructive bronchitis. Causative agents may include long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, or occupational dusts. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airflow obstruction and increased respiratory secretions.

Unilateral pulmonary emphysema, also known as MacLeod's syndrome, is a rare condition characterized by localized destruction of lung tissue on one side, leading to hyperinflation and air trapping. It typically affects the upper lobe of the lung. Common synonyms include unilateral pulmonary emphysema and congenital emphysema. The condition is often associated with congenital abnormalities such as bronchial atresia or persistent fetal ductus arteriosus. Causative agents may include vascular anomalies, chronic infection, or obstructive lesions. It predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the right upper lobe.

Panlobular emphysema, also known as centrilobular emphysema, is a form of obstructive lung disease characterized by the destruction of the alveolar walls, primarily affecting the central parts of the acini. It is most commonly associated with long-term cigarette smoking and is often seen in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The condition leads to enlarged air spaces and reduced gas exchange, primarily impacting the upper lobes of the lungs. Other causative agents include chronic exposure to air pollutants and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Centrilobular emphysema is a type of obstructive lung disease characterized by the destruction of the air spaces around the central part of the acinus, primarily affecting the distal acinar regions. It is commonly associated with long-term cigarette smoking and is a hallmark feature of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Other synonyms include centriacinar emphysema. The condition predominantly affects the upper lung zones, leading to reduced gas exchange and airflow limitation. Key causative agents include tobacco smoke, air pollutants, and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Other emphysema refers to a group of lung conditions characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to reduced gas exchange and air trapping. It is often a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Common synonyms include centrilobular emphysema and panacinar emphysema. Causative agents include long-term cigarette smoke exposure, air pollution, and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition primarily affects the alveoli in the lungs, particularly in the upper lobes, leading to progressive loss of lung elasticity and airflow obstruction.

Emphysema unspecified is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to reduced gas exchange and hyperinflation of the lungs. Common synonyms include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and pulmonary emphysema. The primary causative agent is long-term exposure to irritants, most commonly cigarette smoke. Other causes include air pollution, occupational dusts, and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli in the distal airways, leading to progressive dyspnea and impaired respiratory function.

code_desc: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with (acute) lower respiratory infection
summary: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with an acute lower respiratory infection is a progressive lung condition characterized by airflow limitation and inflammation, often exacerbated by an acute infection. Common synonyms include COPD with pneumonia or exacerbation of COPD. Causative agents include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and alveoli, leading to symptoms such as cough, sputum production, and dyspnea. It is commonly seen in smokers and individuals with a history of respiratory infections.

code_desc: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with (acute) exacerbation
summary: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation refers to a sudden worsening of symptoms in patients with existing COPD, characterized by increased breathlessness, cough, and sputum production. Common synonyms include COPD exacerbation or acute COPD flare-up. Causative agents often include respiratory infections (e.g., viral or bacterial pathogens), air pollution, or exposure to irritants. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the airways and alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory distress.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease unspecified (COPD unspecified) refers to a group of progressive lung diseases characterized by airflow limitation that is not fully reversible. It encompasses conditions such as chronic bronchitis and emphysema. Common synonyms include chronic obstructive lung disease and obstructive lung disease. Known causative agents include long-term exposure to cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational dusts. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the bronchi and alveoli. Symptoms include chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnea. The condition typically affects middle-aged and older adults.

Mild intermittent asthma uncomplicated is a respiratory condition characterized by episodic airflow obstruction with symptoms occurring less than twice a week. Common synonyms include mild intermittent asthma and mild asthma. It is typically triggered by allergens such as pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as respiratory infections or environmental irritants. The primary affected body parts are the airways of the lungs, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, which are usually reversible with bronchodilators. No significant complications or systemic involvement are present.

Mild intermittent asthma with acute exacerbation refers to episodic airway inflammation and narrowing, typically triggered by allergens, respiratory infections, or environmental irritants. Symptoms include wheezing, shortness of breath, and coughing, often worsening during exacerbations. Common synonyms include acute asthma flare-up or asthma attack. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to reversible airflow obstruction. It is commonly seen in children and adults with a history of atopic conditions. Treatment involves bronchodilators and corticosteroids to relieve symptoms and prevent complications.

code_desc: Mild intermittent asthma with status asthmaticus
summary: Mild intermittent asthma with status asthmaticus refers to episodic airway inflammation and narrowing, characterized by reversible airflow obstruction and symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. Status asthmaticus is a severe, prolonged exacerbation that does not respond adequately to standard bronchodilator therapy. Common synonyms include asthma exacerbation and acute severe asthma. Causative agents may include allergens, respiratory infections, irritants, or exercise. Typically affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to impaired gas exchange.

Mild intermittent asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by episodic airflow obstruction and airway inflammation, with symptoms occurring less than twice a week. Common synonyms include mild asthma and intermittent asthma. It is often triggered by allergens such as pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as respiratory infections, exercise, and weather changes. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi and bronchioles in the lungs. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, which typically resolve spontaneously or with minimal treatment.

Mild persistent asthma uncomplicated is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by intermittent symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, occurring more than twice a week but not daily. It is typically managed with low-dose inhaled corticosteroids. Common synonyms include mild persistent asthma and intermittent asthma. Causative agents often include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as irritants such as smoke and air pollution. The primary affected body part is the airway, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles.

Mild persistent asthma with acute exacerbation refers to recurring respiratory symptoms, including wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, that occur more than twice a week but less than once daily. It involves temporary worsening of asthma symptoms, often triggered by allergens, respiratory infections, or environmental irritants. Common synonyms include acute asthma flare-up or exacerbation. Causative agents may include allergens like pollen, dust mites, or pet dander, as well as viral infections, cold air, or exercise. The primary affected body parts are the airways of the lungs, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles.

code_desc: Mild persistent asthma with status asthmaticus
summary: Mild persistent asthma with status asthmaticus refers to chronic airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness leading to recurrent wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, with episodes of severe exacerbation unresponsive to standard bronchodilators. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and severe exacerbation of asthma. Causative agents include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as respiratory infections, pollutants, and irritants. The primary affected body parts are the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, with systemic involvement possible during severe attacks.

Mild persistent asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by intermittent symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, occurring more than twice a week but not daily. It is typically managed with low-dose inhaled corticosteroids. Common synonyms include intermittent asthma and mild asthma. Causative agents often include allergens like dust mites, pollen, and pet dander, as well as respiratory infections and environmental irritants. The primary affected body parts are the airways of the lungs, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles.

Moderate persistent asthma uncomplicated is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by recurring bronchial inflammation and airflow obstruction, with symptoms occurring more than twice a week but not daily. Common synonyms include moderate persistent asthma and persistent asthma. Causative agents include allergens such as dust mites, pollen, and pet dander, as well as irritants like tobacco smoke and air pollution. The condition primarily affects the airways of the lungs, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It is typically managed with a combination of inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-agonists.

Moderate persistent asthma with acute exacerbation is characterized by recurring wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, with symptoms occurring more than twice a week but not daily. It involves partial airway obstruction and increased airway hyperresponsiveness. Common synonyms include asthma flare-up or acute asthma attack. Causative agents often include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as respiratory infections, irritants, or stress. The primary affected body parts are the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to inflammation and narrowing.

code_desc: Moderate persistent asthma with status asthmaticus
summary: Moderate persistent asthma with status asthmaticus is a severe exacerbation of chronic asthma characterized by persistent airflow obstruction and worsening symptoms despite standard treatment. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and severe exacerbation. Causative agents often include allergens, viral infections, irritants, or medication noncompliance. It typically affects the airways, leading to bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion, and airway inflammation. The condition primarily impacts the lungs, causing respiratory distress, hypoxia, and potential respiratory failure if untreated.

Moderate persistent asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by recurring symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and coughing. It involves variable airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Common synonyms include persistent asthma and moderate asthma. Causative agents include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as irritants such as tobacco smoke and air pollutants. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airway narrowing and impaired gas exchange.

Severe persistent asthma uncomplicated is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by frequent and intense bronchoconstriction, leading to persistent airflow limitation and hyperresponsiveness. Common synonyms include severe asthma and refractory asthma. It is typically caused by a combination of genetic predisposition, environmental allergens, and irritants such as pollen, dust mites, and air pollution. The primary affected body parts are the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, resulting in symptoms like wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough. Management involves long-term controller medications and avoidance of triggers.

Severe persistent asthma with acute exacerbation is a critical worsening of chronic asthma symptoms, characterized by increased airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and mucus production. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and status asthmaticus. Causative agents often include viral infections, allergens, pollutants, or medication noncompliance. The condition primarily affects the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to respiratory distress, hypoxia, and potential respiratory failure if untreated.

code_desc: Severe persistent asthma with status asthmaticus
summary: Severe persistent asthma with status asthmaticus is a life-threatening exacerbation of chronic asthma characterized by prolonged and severe bronchospasm, airway inflammation, and mucus plugging, unresponsive to standard bronchodilator therapy. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and asthmatic status. Causative agents include allergens, viral infections, pollutants, and irritants. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory failure. It commonly involves the lungs and can extend to the cardiovascular system due to hypoxia and hypercapnia.

Severe persistent asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing, often occurring daily. It is marked by persistent airflow limitation and frequent exacerbations. Common synonyms include severe asthma and refractory asthma. Causative agents include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and animal dander, as well as irritants such as tobacco smoke and air pollutants. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airway hyperresponsiveness and remodeling. It predominantly impacts the respiratory system, particularly the lungs.

Unspecified asthma refers to asthma cases where the specific type or trigger cannot be clearly identified. It is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by variable and recurring symptoms, such as wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Common synonyms include unspecified bronchial asthma and undifferentiated asthma. Causative agents may include allergens, irritants, respiratory infections, or genetic factors. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi and bronchioles in the lungs. It typically affects the respiratory system and can impact overall quality of life.

Other asthma refers to asthma cases not classified under specific subtypes like allergic or non-allergic asthma. It encompasses a broad range of asthma presentations with varied triggers. Common synonyms include idiopathic asthma and unspecified asthma. Causative agents may include environmental irritants, occupational exposures, and respiratory infections. The condition primarily affects the airways, leading to bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and airflow obstruction. Symptoms typically involve wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, predominantly impacting the lungs and airways.

Other and unspecified asthma refers to asthma cases where the specific type or cause cannot be clearly defined. It may include atypical presentations or when underlying triggers remain undetermined. Common synonyms include unspecified asthma or undifferentiated asthma. Causative agents may involve allergens, irritants, infections, or genetic factors. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the airways, leading to inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and airflow obstruction. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, often worsening with exposure to triggers. It can occur in individuals of all ages but is more commonly diagnosed in children and young adults.

code_desc: Bronchiectasis with acute lower respiratory infection
summary: Bronchiectasis with acute lower respiratory infection is a condition characterized by abnormal dilation of the bronchi accompanied by an acute exacerbation of infection. It often presents with chronic cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis. Common synonyms include chronic bronchial infection and recurrent bronchial infection. Causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*. The infection typically affects the lungs, particularly the larger airways, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent inflammation.

Bronchiectasis with acute exacerbation refers to a sudden worsening of symptoms in patients with pre-existing bronchiectasis, characterized by increased cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis. Common synonyms include acute bronchiectatic exacerbation or acute decompensation. Causative agents often include bacterial infections such as *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*. The condition primarily affects the large airways, particularly in the lungs, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent infections. It is commonly seen in patients with underlying lung disease or immunocompromised states.

Bronchiectasis uncomplicated refers to the abnormal and permanent dilation of bronchi without evidence of acute infection or hemoptysis. It results from impaired clearance of airway secretions, leading to chronic inflammation and structural damage. Common synonyms include chronic bronchiectasis and dilated bronchi. Causative agents include recurrent infections (e.g., tuberculosis, pertussis), immunodeficiency, and congenital disorders. The condition primarily affects the middle and lower lobes of the lungs, with the left lower lobe being most commonly involved. Symptoms include chronic cough, sputum production, and recurrent respiratory infections.

Coalworker pneumoconiosis is a chronic lung disease caused by long-term inhalation of coal dust. It leads to the accumulation of coal particles in the lungs, resulting in inflammation and fibrosis. Common synonyms include coal miner's disease and black lung. The primary causative agent is coal dust, particularly from bituminous coal. The condition predominantly affects the respiratory system, particularly the lungs and bronchioles. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and reduced lung function. It is most commonly seen in individuals with prolonged occupational exposure to coal dust.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to asbestos and other mineral fibres
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to asbestos and other mineral fibres is a chronic lung disease caused by the inhalation of fibrous mineral particles, primarily asbestos. Common synonyms include asbestosis and mineral fibre pneumoconiosis. The condition leads to progressive scarring and fibrosis of lung tissue, resulting in impaired respiratory function. Causative agents include asbestos, erionite, crocidolite, and other silicate minerals. The lungs are predominantly affected, with fibrosis typically localized in the upper lung zones. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, and increased risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma.

Pneumoconiosis due to talc dust is a chronic lung disease caused by inhalation of talc particles, a mineral composed primarily of magnesium silicate. It is classified as a type of pneumoconiosis, a group of lung disorders resulting from long-term inhalation of inorganic dust. Common synonyms include talc pneumoconiosis and silicosis-like disease. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive fibrosis and impaired respiratory function. While talc is not a silicate like quartz, it can cause similar pathological changes. It is more commonly associated with occupational exposure in industries such as ceramics, cosmetics, and agriculture.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to other dust containing silica
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to other dust containing silica, also known as silicosis, is a chronic lung disease caused by inhalation of respirable crystalline silica particles. Common synonyms include silicosis and pneumoconiosis. The primary causative agent is crystalline silica, found in materials like sand, stone, and concrete. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive fibrosis, nodular scarring, and impaired respiratory function. It typically occurs in occupational settings such as mining, construction, and manufacturing. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and increased susceptibility to infections. Early diagnosis and prevention are critical to mitigate long-term complications.

Aluminosis is a pulmonary condition characterized by the accumulation of aluminum in lung tissue, leading to fibrosis and impaired function. Common synonyms include aluminum pneumoconiosis and aluminopneumonia. It is primarily caused by prolonged inhalation of aluminum dust or fumes, often encountered in industrial settings such as aluminum production or welding. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, with granular nodules and interstitial fibrosis typically observed in the upper lobes. Chronic exposure is required for clinical manifestation, and symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung capacity. Early diagnosis and exposure cessation are critical to prevent progression.

Bauxite fibrosis is a form of pulmonary fibrosis caused by inhalation of bauxite dust, a mineral rich in aluminum oxide. It leads to progressive scarring and thickening of lung tissue, resulting in impaired gas exchange and respiratory dysfunction. Common synonyms include aluminum oxide pneumoconiosis and bauxite lung. The primary causative agent is prolonged exposure to bauxite dust in occupational settings such as mining and processing. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the alveolar regions, and is associated with chronic cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung capacity.

Berylliosis is a granulomatous disease caused by inhalation of beryllium particles, leading to pulmonary and systemic manifestations. Common synonyms include chronic beryllium disease and beryllium poisoning. The causative agent is beryllium, a lightweight metal used in aerospace and electronics. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation, fibrosis, and nodular lesions. Systemic involvement may occur, affecting lymph nodes, skin, and other organs. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fatigue. Diagnosis involves serologic testing for beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test and imaging studies. Prolonged exposure increases risk, and prevention focuses on reducing occupational exposure.

Graphite fibrosis is a rare pulmonary condition characterized by the deposition of graphite particles in lung tissue, leading to fibrotic changes. It is primarily caused by occupational exposure to graphite, often in industrial settings. Common synonyms include graphite pneumoconiosis and graphite lung disease. The condition typically affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli and interstitial tissue. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung function. Long-term exposure increases the risk of progressive respiratory impairment. Diagnosis involves imaging and biopsy, with treatment focusing on managing symptoms and preventing further exposure.

Siderosis refers to the accumulation of iron in tissues, typically due to inhalation of iron particles. It is commonly known as pulmonary siderosis or iron dust disease. The condition is caused by prolonged exposure to iron dust, often in industrial settings. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis. In severe cases, iron may deposit in other organs, such as the liver and spleen. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and chest discomfort. Diagnosis is confirmed through radiographic findings and biopsy. Prevention involves reducing occupational exposure to iron dust.

Stannosis is a rare condition characterized by the accumulation of tin in body tissues, typically due to chronic exposure to tin compounds. Common synonyms include tin poisoning and tin toxicity. It is most commonly caused by inhalation of metallic tin dust, often encountered in industrial settings such as tin smelting. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to respiratory symptoms, and may also involve the liver and other organs. Clinical manifestations include cough, shortness of breath, and gastrointestinal disturbances. Early diagnosis and removal from exposure are critical to prevent long-term complications.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to other specified inorganic dusts
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to other specified inorganic dusts refers to lung disease caused by prolonged inhalation of mineral dusts not classified as coal, silica, or asbestos. Common synonyms include occupational lung disease from non-specific inorganic dusts. Causative agents include metal dusts, such as beryllium, tin, and tungsten, as well as other industrial minerals. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired respiratory function. It is commonly seen in workers exposed to these dusts in mining, manufacturing, and construction industries.

Unspecified pneumoconiosis refers to chronic lung disease caused by inhalation of mineral dust, when the specific type of dust is not identified. It is characterized by inflammation, fibrosis, and nodular changes in the lungs. Common synonyms include unspecified occupational lung disease or undiagnosed pneumoconiosis. Causative agents may include silica, coal, asbestos, or other mineral particles. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to reduced lung function and increased risk of respiratory infections. It is typically diagnosed in individuals with a history of occupational exposure to dust.

Pneumoconiosis associated with tuberculosis is a combined occupational lung disease resulting from long-term inhalation of mineral dust and Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. It commonly affects miners and industrial workers. The condition leads to progressive fibrosis and nodular scarring of the lungs, compounded by tuberculosis-related granulomas and cavities. Synonyms include mixed dust and tuberculosis disease, or tuberculosis with pneumoconiosis. The primary causative agents are inhaled mineral particles and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The lungs are typically affected, with involvement of the upper lobes in tuberculosis and diffuse parenchymal changes in pneumoconiosis.

Byssinosis, also known as Monday fever or brown lung disease, is a respiratory condition caused by inhalation of cotton, flax, or hemp dust. It primarily affects workers in textile industries. The condition is characterized by coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, often worsening after weekends off. Chronic exposure leads to airway inflammation and fibrosis. Common causative agents include cotton and flax dust. The lungs are typically affected, with symptoms often beginning in the upper airways and progressing to the lower respiratory tract.

Flax-dressers' disease, also known as byssinosis or brown lung, is a chronic respiratory condition caused by prolonged inhalation of cotton, flax, or hemp dust. It primarily affects workers in textile industries. The disease leads to inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma, resulting in symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and wheezing. Common causative agents include fibers from flax, cotton, and hemp. The condition typically affects the lower respiratory tract, including the bronchi and alveoli, and is characterized by progressive lung function decline.

Cannabinosis is a rare condition characterized by chronic cannabis use leading to a range of psychiatric and physical symptoms. Common synonyms include cannabis toxicity and cannabinoid intoxication. It is primarily caused by prolonged or heavy use of cannabis, particularly high-potency strains. The condition typically affects the central nervous system, causing mood disturbances, cognitive impairment, and psychotic features. It may also lead to cardiovascular and gastrointestinal issues. While primarily affecting the brain, the liver and respiratory system can be impacted with long-term use. The condition is more commonly observed in adolescents and young adults.

code_desc: Airway disease due to other specific organic dusts
summary: Airway disease due to other specific organic dusts refers to respiratory conditions caused by inhalation of organic dusts not classified as fungal, bacterial, or parasitic. Common synonyms include hypersensitivity pneumonitis from non-typical organic dusts. Causative agents include bird proteins, mold spores, and agricultural dusts. The condition primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, leading to inflammation, airflow obstruction, and fibrosis. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and wheezing. It is often occupational, affecting individuals exposed to contaminated environments. Early diagnosis and avoidance of the causative agent are critical for management.

Farmer's lung, also known as hypersensitivity pneumonitis or allergic alveolitis, is an interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of organic dusts, particularly mold spores from hay, straw, or grain. The condition results from an immune-mediated response to these antigens. It primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation and fibrosis of the alveoli. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever, often following repeated exposure. Common causative agents include *Aspergillus* and *Penicillium* species. The disease typically affects farmers, agricultural workers, and others exposed to moldy organic materials.

Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of moldy sugarcane dust. It is also known as farmer's lung or by the synonym sugarcane fever. The condition is primarily caused by the inhalation of spores from thermophilic actinomycetes, particularly *Actinomyces israelii* and *Nocardia* species. Symptoms include acute respiratory symptoms such as cough, fever, and dyspnea, often resembling acute bacterial pneumonia. The disease typically affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and granuloma formation. It is most common among agricultural workers handling moldy sugarcane.

Bird fancier's lung, also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis, is an interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of avian proteins. Common causative agents include feather dust, bird dander, and other allergens from birds such as pigeons, parrots, and canaries. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and fibrosis of the alveoli. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever, often following repeated exposure. It typically presents as a chronic or acute-on-chronic illness, with characteristic imaging findings of ground-glass opacities and nodular shadows. Early diagnosis and avoidance of the allergen are crucial for preventing progressive lung damage.

Suberosis is a rare, non-inflammatory, degenerative condition characterized by the thinning and atrophy of the subcutaneous fat layer. It is often associated with aging, malnutrition, or systemic diseases. Common synonyms include lipoatrophy and subcutaneous fat atrophy. Causative agents may include chronic illness, hormonal imbalances, or genetic factors. The condition typically affects the face, limbs, and upper back, leading to a gaunt appearance. It is more prevalent in elderly individuals and those with prolonged corticosteroid use. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, with imaging sometimes used to assess fat layer thickness.

Maltworker's lung, also known as byssinosis or cotton worker's lung, is a respiratory condition caused by inhalation of dust from raw cotton, flax, or hemp. It primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Symptoms include coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, often worsening after exposure. The condition is commonly seen in workers in textile mills and is associated with chronic respiratory impairment. Prolonged exposure leads to progressive lung damage, with the lower respiratory tract being most affected.

Mushroom-worker's lung, also known as mycetoma or Madura foot, is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by fungi or actinomycetes. It primarily affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues, often starting in the feet or hands. Common causative agents include *Madurella mycetomatis* and *Exophiala* species. The infection leads to the formation of granulomas and sinus tracts with purulent discharge. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, typically affecting agricultural workers exposed to soil and plant material.

"Maple-bark-stripper's lung," also known as byssinosis or brown lung disease, is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease caused by prolonged inhalation of cotton, flax, or hemp dust. It primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, leading to airway inflammation, narrowing, and reduced lung function. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and wheezing. The condition is commonly seen in workers in textile mills and flax processing plants. Prolonged exposure to these dusts results in progressive lung damage, with a characteristic brown discoloration of lung tissue due to lipid accumulation.

Air conditioner and humidifier lung, also known as humidifier lung or hypersensitivity pneumonitis, is an inflammatory lung condition caused by inhalation of microbial contaminants from improperly maintained air conditioning or humidification systems. Common causative agents include *Aspergillus*, *Actinomyces*, and *Staphylococcus* species. The condition typically affects the alveoli and interstitial tissues of the lungs, leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and dyspnea. Prolonged exposure may result in progressive pulmonary fibrosis. It primarily affects individuals with prolonged or frequent exposure to contaminated indoor air systems.

code_desc: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to other organic dusts
summary: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to other organic dusts is an inflammatory lung disease caused by inhalation of various organic allergens not classified as mold, bird, or thermophilic actinomycetes. Common synonyms include extrinsic allergic alveolitis and allergic pulmonary granulomatosis. Causative agents may include bacteria, fungi, or animal proteins from sources like agricultural dust, bedding, or environmental molds. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing interstitial inflammation and granuloma formation. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever, with progression leading to fibrosis if untreated. It typically involves the alveoli and interstitium.

code_desc: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to unspecified organic dust
summary: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to unspecified organic dust is an inflammatory lung condition triggered by inhalation of organic allergens, leading to immune-mediated lung injury. Common synonyms include extrinsic allergic alveolitis and farmer's lung. Causative agents may include molds, bacteria, and animal proteins, though the specific agent is unspecified. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing interstitial inflammation and potential fibrosis. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever, often following repeated exposure. It typically involves the alveoli and interstitium, with radiographic findings resembling acute or chronic interstitial lung disease.

code_desc: Bronchitis and pneumonitis due to chemicals gases fumes and vapors
summary: Bronchitis and pneumonitis due to chemical gases, fumes, and vapors are inflammatory lung conditions caused by inhalation of toxic substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and occupational lung disease. Causative agents include chlorine, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and organic vapors. These conditions primarily affect the bronchi and alveoli, leading to symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. Prolonged exposure can result in chronic respiratory impairment. The upper and lower respiratory tracts are typically involved, with potential for diffuse lung injury.

code_desc: Pulmonary edema due to chemicals gases fumes and vapors
summary: Pulmonary edema due to chemical gases, fumes, and vapors is a life-threatening condition caused by inhalation of toxic substances that damage lung tissue, leading to fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and toxic pulmonary edema. Causative agents include chlorine, ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and organic solvents. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, with potential systemic involvement. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, frothy sputum, and hypoxia. Rapid exposure can result in acute respiratory failure.

code_desc: Upper respiratory inflammation due to chemicals gases fumes and vapors not elsewhere classified
summary: Upper respiratory inflammation due to chemicals, gases, fumes, and vapors not elsewhere classified refers to irritation and inflammation of the upper airway caused by exposure to various airborne chemical agents. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and irritant-induced rhinitis. Causative agents may include industrial solvents, chlorine, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and volatile organic compounds. Typically affected areas include the nose, pharynx, larynx, and trachea. Symptoms often include cough, sore throat, hoarseness, and nasal congestion. This condition is commonly seen in occupational settings with poor ventilation.

code_desc: Other acute and subacute respiratory conditions due to chemicals gases fumes and vapors
summary: Other acute and subacute respiratory conditions due to chemicals, gases, fumes, and vapors refer to inhalation injuries caused by exposure to toxic substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and toxic inhalation injury. Causative agents include chlorine, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and volatile organic compounds. These conditions typically affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, bronchitis, and pulmonary edema. The severity depends on the type and duration of exposure, with potential for systemic toxicity. Prompt decontamination and supportive care are critical for management.

code_desc: Chronic respiratory conditions due to chemicals gases fumes and vapors
summary: Chronic respiratory conditions due to chemicals, gases, fumes, and vapors result from prolonged exposure to harmful substances in occupational or environmental settings. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis, occupational lung disease, and toxic inhalation syndrome. Causative agents include silica, asbestos, sulfur dioxide, and organic solvents. These conditions primarily affect the lungs, causing inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung function. Long-term exposure can lead to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), interstitial lung disease, or lung cancer.

code_desc: Other respiratory conditions due to chemicals gases fumes and vapors
summary: Other respiratory conditions due to chemicals, gases, fumes, and vapors refer to lung injuries caused by inhalation of toxic substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and toxic inhalation syndrome. Causative agents include chlorine, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and organic solvents. These conditions typically affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing irritation, inflammation, and potential damage to the alveoli. Symptoms may include cough, shortness of breath, and pulmonary edema. Prolonged exposure can lead to chronic respiratory issues. The severity depends on the type and concentration of the inhaled substance.

code_desc: Unspecified respiratory condition due to chemicals gases fumes and vapors
summary: Unspecified respiratory condition due to chemicals, gases, fumes, and vapors refers to respiratory symptoms caused by exposure to harmful airborne substances, though the specific agent is not identified. Common synonyms include chemical-induced respiratory irritation or toxic inhalation syndrome. Causative agents may include industrial solvents, pesticides, cleaning agents, and combustion byproducts. Typically affects the upper and lower respiratory tract, including the nose, throat, bronchi, and lungs, leading to symptoms like coughing, shortness of breath, and wheezing.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food and vomit
summary: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food and vomit, also known as aspiration pneumonia, occurs when gastric or oral contents are inhaled into the lungs. Common causative agents include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. This condition typically affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly the basal segments of the lungs. Risk factors include altered consciousness, swallowing disorders, and gastrointestinal reflux. Symptoms include cough, fever, and respiratory distress. It is a serious condition requiring prompt medical evaluation and treatment.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of oils and essences
summary: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of oils and essences is an inflammatory lung condition caused by the inhalation of volatile oils, essential oils, or aromatic substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis or irritant-induced lung injury. Causative agents include turpentine, mineral oil, perfumes, and volatile solvents. The condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is often seen in occupational or environmental exposures and can result in acute or chronic lung damage. Early recognition and removal from the irritant source are critical for recovery.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of other solids and liquids
summary: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of other solids and liquids refers to lung inflammation caused by the aspiration of non-respiratory substances such as oils, chemicals, or foreign bodies. Common synonyms include aspiration pneumonitis and chemical pneumonitis. Causative agents may include hydrocarbons, detergents, or gastric contents. The condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is commonly seen in patients with altered consciousness or swallowing disorders. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as pulmonary edema or fibrosis.

code_desc: Acute pulmonary manifestations due to radiation
summary: Acute pulmonary manifestations due to radiation refer to lung injury occurring shortly after radiation therapy. Common synonyms include radiation pneumonitis and radiation-induced lung injury. Causative agents are ionizing radiation, typically from therapeutic modalities like radiotherapy. The condition primarily affects the lungs, with inflammation and edema in the alveoli and interstitial tissue. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever. It commonly occurs in patients receiving thoracic or mediastinal irradiation. The severity depends on radiation dose and volume, with the upper lobes being most frequently involved. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent progression to fibrosis.

code_desc: Chronic and other pulmonary manifestations due to radiation
summary: Chronic and other pulmonary manifestations due to radiation refer to lung damage resulting from exposure to ionizing radiation, commonly seen in patients undergoing thoracic radiotherapy. Synonyms include radiation pneumonitis and radiation-induced lung disease. Causative agents are ionizing radiation, often from therapeutic treatments or nuclear accidents. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired gas exchange. Commonly affected areas include the alveoli and interstitium. Symptoms may include dyspnea, cough, and reduced oxygenation. Long-term complications can lead to pulmonary fibrosis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Acute drug-induced interstitial lung disorders are inflammatory conditions of the lung parenchyma caused by medication exposure. Common synonyms include drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis and drug-induced interstitial pneumonia. Causative agents include amiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, and nitrofurantoin. These disorders primarily affect the alveoli and interstitium, leading to symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia. They can progress rapidly, necessitating prompt discontinuation of the offending drug and supportive care. The lungs are the main affected body part, with potential for diffuse involvement.

Chronic drug-induced interstitial lung disorders are a group of lung diseases characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the interstitial tissue, primarily caused by prolonged exposure to certain medications. Common synonyms include drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis and drug-related interstitial pneumonitis. Known causative agents include amiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, and nitrofurantoin. These conditions typically affect the lungs, leading to symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and reduced exercise tolerance. The disease process can progress to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure if left untreated. Early recognition and discontinuation of the offending agent are critical for improving outcomes.

Drug-induced interstitial lung disorders unspecified refer to pulmonary infiltrates and interstitial lung disease caused by medications without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis and drug-related interstitial pneumonia. Causative agents may include chemotherapy drugs, antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and NSAIDs. Typically, the lungs are affected, with symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia. The condition is often idiopathic in nature but linked to prior drug exposure. Early recognition and discontinuation of the offending agent are critical for recovery.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to smoke inhalation
summary: Respiratory conditions due to smoke inhalation result from exposure to toxic gases and particulates from burning materials. Common synonyms include inhalation injury and smoke inhalation syndrome. Causative agents include carbon monoxide, cyanide, carbon dioxide, and irritant particles from combustion. These conditions primarily affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing inflammation, edema, and potential airway obstruction. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, hypoxia, and in severe cases, respiratory failure. The lungs and airways are typically the most affected body parts.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to other specified external agents
summary: Respiratory conditions due to other specified external agents refer to lung disorders caused by substances not classified as allergens, irritants, or chemicals. Common synonyms include inhalation injuries and toxic respiratory syndromes. Causative agents may include smoke, dust, fumes, and biological agents like spores or viruses. These conditions typically affect the airways, lungs, and respiratory membranes, leading to inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Diagnosis often involves clinical history, imaging, and pulmonary function tests.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to unspecified external agent
summary: Respiratory conditions due to unspecified external agents refer to lung disorders caused by environmental factors not specifically identified. Common synonyms include inhalation injuries and toxic respiratory syndromes. Causative agents may include chemicals, pollutants, or irritants. These conditions typically affect the airways and lungs, leading to inflammation, bronchoconstriction, or pulmonary edema. Symptoms often include coughing, dyspnea, and hypoxia. The exact mechanism and prognosis depend on the nature and duration of exposure.

Adult respiratory distress syndrome, also known as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), is a severe lung condition characterized by widespread inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common causative agents include sepsis, pneumonia, trauma, and pancreatitis. It typically affects the lungs, causing hypoxemia and respiratory failure. The syndrome is marked by non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, bilateral infiltrates on imaging, and poor oxygenation despite adequate ventilatory support. It often progresses rapidly and requires intensive care management.

Acute pulmonary edema is a sudden accumulation of fluid in the alveoli of the lungs, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include cardiogenic pulmonary edema and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) when of non-cardiogenic origin. It is typically caused by left ventricular failure, hypertension, myocardial infarction, or valvular disease. Other causes include sepsis, pneumonia, and exposure to toxins. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, with systemic involvement possible in severe cases. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, frothy sputum, and hypoxia. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent respiratory failure.

Chronic pulmonary edema is a persistent accumulation of fluid in the lung interstitium and alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange. It commonly results from long-standing heart failure, particularly left-sided, or chronic lung diseases. Synonyms include congestive pulmonary edema and interstitial pulmonary edema. Causative agents include hypertension, valvular heart disease, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, with secondary involvement of the cardiovascular system. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, and reduced exercise tolerance.

Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia is a rare interstitial lung disease characterized by persistent infiltration of eosinophils in the lungs. It presents with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. Common synonyms include eosinophilic granuloma of the lung and Löffler's syndrome. The condition is often associated with parasitic infections like *Strongyloides stercoralis* or *Schistosoma*, as well as allergic reactions or drug-induced causes. It primarily affects the alveoli and interstitial spaces of the lungs, leading to inflammation and potential fibrosis. Diagnosis typically involves imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage, and histopathological examination. Treatment depends on the underlying cause, often involving corticosteroids and antiparasitic therapy.

Acute eosinophilic pneumonia is a rare inflammatory lung disorder characterized by rapid onset of respiratory symptoms and infiltration of eosinophils in the alveoli. Common synonyms include acute eosinophilic pulmonary infiltrate and eosinophilic pneumonia. It is often idiopathic, though allergic reactions, drug hypersensitivity, and parasitic infections may be causative. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing diffuse interstitial infiltrates. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia. Diagnosis involves imaging, eosinophilia, and bronchoalveolar lavage. Treatment typically involves corticosteroids.

Eosinophilic asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by elevated eosinophils in bronchial secretions. It is a subset of asthma with persistent airway inflammation and airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include allergic asthma and eosinophilic bronchitis. Causative agents often include allergens such as pollen, dust mites, and animal dander. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles. It is associated with increased risk of severe exacerbations and may require targeted therapies like biologics.

code_desc: Other pulmonary eosinophilia not elsewhere classified
summary: Other pulmonary eosinophilia not elsewhere classified refers to a group of lung disorders characterized by elevated eosinophils in the lungs without a specific identifiable cause. Common synonyms include idiopathic pulmonary eosinophilia and eosinophilic pneumonia of unknown origin. Causative agents may include parasitic infections, allergic reactions, or unknown factors. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is typically diagnosed when other forms of eosinophilic lung disease are excluded.

Pulmonary eosinophilia not elsewhere classified refers to an increase in eosinophils in the lungs without a specific identifiable cause. It is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of lung tissue, often leading to inflammation and respiratory symptoms. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic lung disease. Known causative agents may include parasitic infections, allergic reactions, or drug-induced hypersensitivity. Typically, the lungs are affected, with possible involvement of the airways and alveoli. The condition may present with cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia.

Alveolar proteinosis is a rare pulmonary disorder characterized by the abnormal accumulation of surfactant proteins and lipids within the alveolar spaces, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include diffuse pulmonary surfactant deposition and lipoproteinosis of the lungs. The condition may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to exposure to inhaled substances such as silica or hydrocarbons. It predominantly affects the lungs, causing progressive dyspnea, hypoxemia, and a characteristic "cotton-glass" appearance on imaging. The disease can also be associated with autoimmune disorders or infections.

Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis is a rare, chronic lung disorder characterized by the accumulation of microliths, small calcium-containing deposits, within the alveoli. Common synonyms include alveolar microlithiasis and pulmonary microlithiasis. The condition is typically idiopathic, though some cases may be associated with genetic mutations or environmental exposures. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive respiratory symptoms such as dyspnea and cough. The disease is most commonly seen in adults and may be linked to familial inheritance in some instances.

Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis (IPH) is a rare disorder characterized by recurrent alveolar hemorrhage, leading to iron overload and hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the lungs. Common synonyms include acute interstitial pneumonia with hemosiderosis and hemosiderosis. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic factors and immune-mediated mechanisms are implicated. It primarily affects the lungs, with systemic involvement possible in some cases. The condition predominantly occurs in children, though it can occur in adults. Known causative agents include infections, autoimmune diseases, and certain medications, though many cases remain idiopathic.

Other alveolar and parieto-alveolar conditions refer to a group of lung disorders affecting the alveoli and adjacent parietal tissues. These conditions may include infections, inflammatory, or neoplastic processes. Common synonyms include interstitial lung disease and alveolar infiltrates. Causative agents vary but may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or autoimmune factors. Typically affecting the lungs, these conditions can involve the alveolar sacs, interstitium, and pleura. Symptoms often include dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and biopsy. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve antibiotics, antifungals, corticosteroids, or immunosuppressants.

Alveolar and parieto-alveolar conditions refer to inflammatory or infectious processes affecting the alveoli and parietal pleura of the lungs. Common synonyms include pneumonia and pleuritis. These conditions are often caused by bacterial, viral, or fungal pathogens, with *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, and *Influenza virus* being frequent agents. They typically affect the lower respiratory tract, particularly the alveoli and pleural lining, leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. Complications may include pleural effusion or respiratory failure.

Pulmonary fibrosis unspecified refers to a group of interstitial lung diseases characterized by progressive scarring and thickening of lung tissue, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and unspecified interstitial lung disease. While specific causes are often unknown, potential factors include environmental exposures, autoimmune disorders, and infections. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the interstitial spaces and alveoli. Symptoms typically include dyspnea, dry cough, and reduced exercise tolerance. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, with no specific organ preference beyond the respiratory system.

Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (IIP) refers to a group of interstitial lung diseases of unknown cause, characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma. Common synonyms include idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung disease. Known causative agents are often unidentified, though environmental exposures and genetic factors may contribute. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive dyspnea and impaired gas exchange. It typically involves the alveolar and interstitial tissues, with varying patterns of fibrosis. The disease predominantly affects middle-aged to elderly individuals, with a higher prevalence in males.

code_desc: Other interstitial pulmonary diseases with fibrosis in diseases classified elsewhere
summary: "Other interstitial pulmonary diseases with fibrosis in diseases classified elsewhere" refers to interstitial lung abnormalities characterized by fibrosis, not fitting into more specific categories. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and unspecified interstitial lung disease. Causative agents may include environmental exposures, medications, or connective tissue disorders. Typically affects the lungs, particularly the interstitial tissue, leading to impaired gas exchange and reduced lung compliance. The condition is often diagnosed when the underlying cause is unclear or classified under another disease category.

code_desc: Other interstitial pulmonary diseases with fibrosis
summary: Other interstitial pulmonary diseases with fibrosis refer to a group of diffuse lung disorders characterized by abnormal fibrosis of the lung interstitium, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and interstitial lung disease with fibrosis. Causative agents may include environmental exposures, occupational agents, autoimmune diseases, and certain medications. These conditions primarily affect the lungs, causing progressive scarring and reduced lung function, often leading to respiratory failure if left untreated.

Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia (LIP) is a rare, non-specific lung disorder characterized by the infiltration of lymphocytes into the lung interstitium. It is often associated with immunodeficiency states, such as HIV or common variable immunodeficiency. LIP may also occur in the context of autoimmune diseases or as a reactive process. Common synonyms include interstitial lymphocytic pneumonia and lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia. The primary affected body part is the lung, with involvement of the alveolar septa and interstitium. Causative agents are often unknown, but infections, immune dysregulation, and chronic inflammation are implicated. The condition can lead to progressive dyspnea and hypoxia.

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare, progressive lung disease characterized by the abnormal growth of smooth muscle-like cells in the lungs, lymphatic system, and kidneys. Common synonyms include pulmonary LAM and tuberous sclerosis complex-associated LAM. The condition is primarily caused by mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes, which are involved in regulating cell growth. It predominantly affects women of childbearing age and is often associated with tuberous sclerosis complex. LAM leads to the formation of cysts in the lungs, lymphatic dilation, and can result in respiratory failure. The kidneys may also be affected, with angiomyolipomas developing.

Adult pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH) is a rare granulomatous disorder characterized by the proliferation of Langerhans cells in the lungs. It is also known as eosinophilic granuloma or Hamman-Rich syndrome. The exact cause is unknown, though smoking is a significant risk factor. The disease primarily affects the lungs, causing nodular lesions, interstitial inflammation, and sometimes cystic changes. It may also involve other organs, such as the bones and skin, but the lungs are most commonly affected. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and chest pain. Diagnosis is typically made through imaging and biopsy.

Surfactant mutations of the lung refer to genetic alterations affecting surfactant proteins, leading to impaired lung function. Common synonyms include congenital surfactant deficiency and pulmonary surfactant dysfunction. These mutations are often caused by inherited defects in genes such as SFTPA1, SFTPB, SFTPC, and SFTPD. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing respiratory distress, especially in newborns. It leads to alveolar instability, reduced lung compliance, and increased risk of respiratory failure. Affected individuals may present with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome or chronic lung disease. The disease primarily targets the alveoli and distal airways.

code_desc: Other interstitial lung diseases of childhood
summary: Other interstitial lung diseases of childhood refer to a group of rare lung disorders characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium. Common synonyms include diffuse parenchymal lung disease and interstitial pneumonia. These conditions may result from infections, autoimmune disorders, or environmental exposures. They primarily affect the alveoli and surrounding tissues, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common causative agents include viral infections, collagen vascular diseases, and inhalation of harmful substances. The lungs are typically the main affected body part, with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia.

Other specified interstitial pulmonary diseases refer to a group of lung disorders characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the interstitial tissue, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and interstitial lung disease. Causative agents may include environmental exposures, occupational dusts, drugs, or autoimmune conditions. These diseases primarily affect the lungs, causing symptoms such as dyspnea and cough. They can involve both the alveoli and interstitium, leading to impaired gas exchange and reduced lung function.

Other specified interstitial pulmonary diseases refer to a group of lung disorders characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the interstitial tissue, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonias and interstitial lung disease. Causative agents may include environmental exposures, occupational dusts, drugs, or autoimmune conditions. These diseases primarily affect the lungs, particularly the alveolar walls and surrounding connective tissue, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory distress.

Interstitial pulmonary disease unspecified refers to a group of lung disorders characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the interstitial tissue surrounding the alveoli. Common synonyms include diffuse parenchymal lung disease and unspecified interstitial lung disease. Causative agents may include environmental exposures, autoimmune conditions, or idiopathic factors. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the alveolar walls and interstitium. Symptoms typically include progressive dyspnea and dry cough. The exact cause is often unknown in idiopathic cases.

Gangrene and necrosis of the lung refer to the death of lung tissue due to lack of blood supply or infection. Common synonyms include pulmonary infarction and necrotizing pneumonia. Causative agents include emboli, bacterial infections (e.g., Streptococcus, Staphylococcus), and systemic diseases like vasculitis.
