Causative agents often include pulpitis, trauma, or infection. It typically affects the root canal system, particularly in the apical region, and is more commonly observed in posterior teeth. The condition may lead to pulp obliteration and is often detected radiographically as dense opacities within the pulp chamber or canal.

code_desc: Acute apical periodontitis of pulpal origin
summary: Acute apical periodontitis of pulpal origin is a severe, painful inflammation of the periapical tissues caused by pulp infection. It typically arises from untreated dental caries, trauma, or pulp necrosis, leading to bacterial proliferation and abscess formation at the root apex. Common synonyms include acute periapical abscess and apical abscess. The condition primarily affects the apical region of the tooth, most commonly in the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth. *Streptococcus* species and *Prevotella* are frequent causative agents. Clinical features include severe pain, swelling, and tenderness upon percussion.

Chronic apical periodontitis is a long-standing inflammatory condition affecting the periapical tissues surrounding the root of a tooth. It typically results from persistent infection originating from a non-vital pulp, often due to dental caries, trauma, or previous dental procedures. Common synonyms include apical abscess and periapical granuloma. The primary causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and other periodontal pathogens. The condition most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, particularly molars. Clinically, it presents with mild to moderate pain, swelling, and radiolucency on imaging.

A periapical abscess with sinus is a localized infection at the root apex of a tooth, accompanied by a draining sinus tract. It results from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial invasion, leading to pus formation. Common causative agents include *Streptococcus*, *Prevotella*, and *Actinomyces* species. This condition typically affects the maxillary or mandibular posterior teeth. Synonyms include apical abscess with drainage and radicular abscess with sinus. It is often associated with untreated dental caries or trauma. The sinus tract may drain into the oral cavity or skin, causing persistent discharge and localized swelling.

A periapical abscess without sinus is a localized infection at the root tip of a tooth, characterized by pus accumulation without a visible drainage tract. Common synonyms include apical abscess and radicular abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Streptococcus* species, *Prevotella*, and *Fusobacterium*. The condition most frequently affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, often resulting from untreated dental caries, trauma, or periodontal disease. It presents with pain, swelling, and possible fever, requiring prompt endodontic or surgical intervention.

Radicular cyst, also known as a periapical cyst or granuloma, is a slow-growing, fluid-filled lesion arising from the apex of a non-vital tooth. It is most commonly caused by persistent infection or inflammation of the pulp, often due to dental caries, trauma, or endodontic failure. The cyst typically affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior regions, particularly around molars and premolars. It is lined by stratified squamous epithelium and contains a viscous fluid. Radiographically, it appears as a well-defined radiolucency adjacent to the root tip. Treatment usually involves endodontic therapy or surgical excision.

code_desc: Unspecified diseases of pulp and periapical tissues
summary: Unspecified diseases of pulp and periapical tissues refer to conditions affecting the dental pulp and surrounding periapical regions that do not fit specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include "diseases of pulp and periapical tissues, unspecified" and "undetermined pulp and periapical disease." Causative agents may include bacterial infections, trauma, or systemic factors. These conditions typically affect the teeth and adjacent supporting structures, often presenting with symptoms such as pain, swelling, and radiographic changes. The exact etiology and pathology are not clearly defined, necessitating further diagnostic evaluation.

code_desc: Other diseases of pulp and periapical tissues
summary: "Other diseases of pulp and periapical tissues" refers to non-specific inflammatory or degenerative conditions affecting the dental pulp and surrounding periapical tissues. Common synonyms include apical periodontitis and periapical abscess. These conditions are typically caused by bacterial infection, often originating from untreated dental caries or trauma. They commonly affect the roots of posterior teeth, particularly molars, and may present with pain, swelling, or radiolucency on imaging. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical symptoms and radiographic findings.

code_desc: Other and unspecified diseases of pulp and periapical tissues
summary: "Other and unspecified diseases of pulp and periapical tissues" refers to inflammatory or degenerative conditions affecting the dental pulp and surrounding periapical tissues when the specific diagnosis is not clearly defined. Common synonyms include nonspecific pulpitis and periapical inflammation. Causative agents often include bacterial infections, trauma, or unknown factors. These conditions typically affect the root canal system and periapical region of teeth, leading to symptoms such as pain, swelling, and radiolucency on imaging. They are commonly associated with untreated dental caries or trauma.

Acute gingivitis plaque induced is an inflammatory condition of the gums caused by the accumulation of bacterial plaque. It is characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding of the gingival tissues. Common synonyms include gingival inflammation and early periodontal disease. The primary causative agents are gram-negative bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, and *Fusobacterium nucleatum*. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, often involving multiple teeth. Poor oral hygiene is a major contributing factor.

Acute gingivitis non-plaque induced is a transient inflammatory condition of the gingiva not associated with dental plaque. It presents as red, swollen, and sometimes bleeding gums. Common synonyms include acute gingival inflammation and non-plaque-related gingivitis. Causative agents may include hormonal changes, medications, or systemic conditions. Typically affecting the marginal and interdental gingiva, this condition is often self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment. It is distinct from plaque-induced gingivitis, which is primarily caused by bacterial biofilm.

Acute gingivitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the gums, characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding upon brushing. Common synonyms include gingival inflammation and marginal gingivitis. It is primarily caused by bacterial plaque accumulation, leading to an immune response. The most common causative agents are *Streptococcus* species, *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, and *Fusobacterium nucleatum*. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, often involving multiple teeth. It is prevalent in adolescents and young adults, and may progress to periodontitis if untreated.

Chronic gingivitis plaque induced is a persistent inflammatory condition of the gums caused by the accumulation of dental plaque. It is characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding of the gingival tissues. Common synonyms include chronic gingivitis and plaque-induced gingivitis. The primary causative agent is bacterial plaque, particularly species such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, leading to gingival recession if left untreated. It is most commonly seen in adults but can occur in adolescents. Poor oral hygiene is a major contributing factor.

Chronic gingivitis non-plaque induced is a persistent inflammatory condition of the gingiva not caused by dental plaque. Common synonyms include chronic inflammatory gingivitis and non-plaque-associated gingivitis. It is often associated with systemic factors such as hormonal changes, malnutrition, or certain medications. Causative agents may include hormonal fluctuations, vitamin deficiencies, or allergic reactions. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, presenting with redness, swelling, and bleeding upon probing. Unlike plaque-induced gingivitis, it lacks the characteristic microbial deposits.

Chronic gingivitis is a mild, persistent inflammation of the gums characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding upon brushing. It is the earliest stage of periodontal disease. Common synonyms include gingival inflammation and marginal gingivitis. The primary causative agent is dental plaque, a biofilm composed of bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. It typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva, often involving multiple teeth. Poor oral hygiene, hormonal changes, and systemic conditions can contribute to its development.

Aggressive periodontitis unspecified refers to a rapidly progressive form of periodontal disease characterized by severe attachment loss and bone destruction in otherwise healthy individuals. Common synonyms include rapidly progressive periodontitis and juvenile periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, though other bacteria may contribute. It typically affects the interdental areas of the anterior and premolar regions, leading to early tooth loss if untreated. The condition is more prevalent in younger individuals and often presents with minimal clinical signs.

Aggressive periodontitis localized is a rapidly progressive form of periodontal disease characterized by severe attachment loss and bone destruction in otherwise healthy teeth. Common synonyms include juvenile periodontitis and early-onset periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, though other bacteria may also be involved. It typically affects adolescents and young adults, with the molars and premolars being the most commonly involved teeth. The condition presents with minimal plaque and gingival inflammation, contrasting with its severe tissue destruction.

Aggressive periodontitis generalized is a rapidly progressive form of periodontal disease characterized by severe attachment loss and bone destruction in otherwise healthy individuals. Common synonyms include rapid-onset periodontitis and juvenile periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, though other bacteria may contribute. It typically affects interdental areas and molars, with early involvement of the gingiva and supporting structures. The condition often presents in adolescents and young adults, with a familial tendency noted in some cases. Systemic factors and immune responses are believed to play a role in its pathogenesis.

Aggressive periodontitis is a rapidly progressive form of periodontal disease characterized by severe attachment loss and bone destruction in otherwise healthy individuals. Common synonyms include juvenile periodontitis and early-onset periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, though other bacteria such as *Treponema denticola* and *Tannerella forsythia* may also be involved. This condition typically affects the interdental areas and molars, often sparing the anterior teeth. It is more prevalent in younger individuals and can lead to significant tooth loss if untreated.

Chronic periodontitis unspecified is a long-standing inflammatory condition affecting the supporting structures of the teeth, leading to progressive attachment loss and bone resorption. It is characterized by the presence of deep periodontal pockets and clinical attachment loss. Common synonyms include chronic periodontal disease and chronic inflammatory periodontal disease. The primary causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, though other bacteria may contribute. The condition typically affects the gingiva, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, predominantly in the interdental areas. It is most commonly seen in adults and is associated with poor oral hygiene and systemic factors.

Chronic periodontitis localized is a slowly progressing inflammatory disease characterized by attachment loss and bone resorption around specific teeth. It typically affects a limited number of teeth, often in the posterior regions. Common synonyms include localized aggressive periodontitis and chronic adult periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, though other periodontal pathogens may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the gingival tissues, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone supporting the teeth.

Chronic periodontitis generalized is a progressive inflammatory disease affecting the supporting structures of the teeth, leading to loss of periodontal attachment and alveolar bone resorption. It typically involves multiple teeth and is characterized by plaque-induced inflammation. Common synonyms include chronic periodontal disease and adult periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, with other bacteria such as *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans* and *Tannerella forsythia* also implicated. The condition primarily affects the gingiva, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, commonly involving the posterior teeth.

Chronic periodontitis is a progressive inflammatory disease characterized by the destruction of the supporting structures of the teeth, including the gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone. It is primarily caused by bacterial plaque accumulation leading to persistent infection. Common synonyms include chronic periodontal disease and adult periodontitis. The main causative agents are gram-negative anaerobic bacteria, such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Treponema denticola*, and *Fusobacterium nucleatum*. The condition typically affects the gingival tissues and periodontal pockets around the teeth, predominantly in adults.

Periodontosis is a rare, non-inflammatory condition characterized by progressive resorption of alveolar bone, leading to tooth mobility and loss. It is distinct from periodontitis, which involves inflammation. Common synonyms include cemento-osseous dysplasia and periapical osteitis. The condition is often associated with chronic infection, particularly from *Actinomyces* species, and may involve trauma or systemic factors. It typically affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior regions, with lesions often found around the roots of affected teeth. The exact etiology remains unclear, but it is considered a multifactorial disorder.

Other periodontal diseases encompass a group of inflammatory conditions affecting the supporting structures of the teeth, primarily caused by bacterial plaque. Common synonyms include periodontitis and periodontal disease. The primary causative agents are gram-negative anaerobic bacteria, such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. These diseases typically affect the gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, leading to progressive destruction and potential tooth loss if untreated. They are more prevalent in adults and often associated with poor oral hygiene and systemic factors.

Periodontal disease unspecified refers to a general category of inflammatory conditions affecting the supporting structures of the teeth, including gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone. Common synonyms include unspecified periodontitis and generalized periodontitis. Causative agents are primarily bacterial, with *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, and *Treponema denticola* being frequently implicated. The condition typically affects the gums and surrounding tissues, leading to inflammation, bleeding, and potential tooth loss if untreated. It often involves multiple teeth and is associated with poor oral hygiene.

Gingival recession localized refers to the apical displacement of the gingival margin, exposing root surfaces in a specific area of the dentition. Common synonyms include localized gingival recession and localized root exposure. It is often caused by periodontal disease, aggressive tooth brushing, trauma, or anatomical factors. The condition typically affects the maxillary anterior teeth and molars, though it can occur in any dental region. It may lead to increased susceptibility to dental caries and root sensitivity. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent progression and maintain periodontal health.

Gingival recession generalized refers to the apical migration of the gingival margin, exposing root surfaces across multiple teeth. It is commonly associated with periodontal disease, aggressive brushing, or genetic factors. Synonyms include generalized gingival recession and root exposure. Causative agents include periodontitis, trauma, and hormonal changes. Typically affects the maxillary and mandibular anterior and posterior regions, with a predilection for the interproximal areas. It may lead to increased susceptibility to caries and sensitivity.

Gingival recession refers to the apical displacement of the gingival margin, exposing the root surface. It is a common periodontal condition often associated with periodontal disease, aggressive brushing, or systemic factors. Synonyms include gingival margin recession and root exposure. Causative agents may include bacterial plaque, bruxism, hormonal changes, or genetic predisposition. Typically affecting the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth, it can lead to increased susceptibility to caries and root surface pathology. The condition is often asymptomatic but may cause aesthetic concerns or functional issues.

Gingival enlargement refers to the abnormal increase in the size of the gingiva, often resulting in a swollen, red, and sometimes bleeding gums. Common synonyms include gingival hyperplasia and gingival hypertrophy. It is commonly caused by local irritants such as plaque and calculus, or systemic factors like medications (e.g., phenytoin, cyclosporine), hormonal changes, or systemic diseases. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental papillae, with the maxillary anterior teeth being most commonly involved. It may lead to periodontal complications if left untreated.

code_desc: Gingival and edentulous alveolar ridge lesions associated with trauma
summary: Gingival and edentulous alveolar ridge lesions associated with trauma refer to inflammatory or ulcerative conditions resulting from mechanical irritation or injury to the gums and bone supporting teeth. Common synonyms include traumatic ulcers and traumatic gingivitis. Causative agents include ill-fitting dentures, sharp occlusal surfaces, or foreign bodies. These lesions typically affect the marginal gingiva and the alveolar ridge, especially in edentulous areas. Clinical features include redness, swelling, pain, and sometimes ulceration. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and patient history. Treatment involves removing the irritant and local care.

Horizontal alveolar bone loss refers to the uniform resorption of the alveolar bone along the tooth root's long axis, typically resulting in a reduction of bone height. It is a common finding in periodontal disease and is often associated with chronic inflammation. Common synonyms include apical bone loss and vertical bone loss. Causative agents include periodontitis, trauma, and systemic conditions such as diabetes. This condition primarily affects the alveolar ridge, particularly around the molars and premolars. It may lead to tooth mobility and eventual tooth loss if left untreated.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of gingiva and edentulous alveolar ridge
summary: "Other specified disorders of gingiva and edentulous alveolar ridge" refers to non-specific, clinically defined conditions affecting the gingiva and bone in the absence of teeth. Common synonyms include generalized gingival hyperplasia and fibrous hyperplasia. Causative agents may include medications (e.g., anticonvulsants, immunosuppressants), hormonal changes, or systemic diseases. These conditions typically affect the gingival tissues and alveolar ridges, leading to overgrowth, inflammation, or fibrous changes. They are often diagnosed when specific etiologies are not identified. The condition is more prevalent in adults and may impact oral hygiene and prosthetic denture fit.

code_desc: Disorder of gingiva and edentulous alveolar ridge unspecified
summary: Disorder of gingiva and edentulous alveolar ridge unspecified refers to non-specific inflammation or changes affecting the gums and bone supporting teeth in areas lacking teeth. Common synonyms include generalized gingival inflammation and alveolar ridge changes. Causative agents may include poor oral hygiene, systemic conditions, or trauma. Typically affects the gingival tissues and alveolar ridges, often seen in edentulous patients. This diagnosis is used when specific etiology or condition is not identified.

code_desc: Exfoliation of teeth due to systemic causes
summary: Exfoliation of teeth due to systemic causes refers to the premature loss of primary or permanent teeth caused by underlying medical conditions. Common synonyms include systemic tooth loss and generalized dental exfoliation. Causative agents may include metabolic disorders such as hypophosphatemia, endocrine conditions like hypoparathyroidism, and certain infections. Typically, this condition affects the primary dentition more commonly, with the maxillary central incisors being the most frequently involved. It is often associated with generalized skeletal abnormalities and other systemic manifestations.

code_desc: Complete loss of teeth unspecified cause
summary: Complete loss of teeth, unspecified cause, refers to the total absence of all permanent teeth without a specific etiology identified. Common synonyms include total edentulism and complete tooth loss. Causative agents may include trauma, severe periodontal disease, congenital absence, or systemic conditions such as osteogenesis imperfecta. This condition typically affects the maxilla and mandible, impacting chewing, speech, and facial structure. It may result from progressive tooth loss due to decay, infection, or developmental anomalies. Diagnosis often requires dental imaging and thorough clinical evaluation to determine underlying factors.

code_desc: Complete loss of teeth due to trauma
summary: Complete loss of teeth due to trauma refers to the total absence of all permanent teeth resulting from physical injury. Common synonyms include total tooth avulsion and ankylosis. Causative agents typically involve high-impact events such as motor vehicle accidents, sports injuries, or physical assaults. The condition most commonly affects the maxilla and mandible, with the anterior teeth being the most frequently impacted. It may lead to significant functional and aesthetic complications if not managed promptly.

code_desc: Complete loss of teeth due to periodontal diseases
summary: Complete loss of teeth due to periodontal diseases refers to the total absence of all permanent teeth resulting from severe periodontal infection and tissue destruction. Common synonyms include advanced periodontal disease and tooth loss from periodontitis. The primary causative agents are *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, and other periodontal pathogens. This condition typically affects the maxillary and mandibular arches, leading to significant functional and aesthetic impairment. It is often associated with progressive alveolar bone resorption and gingival recession.

code_desc: Complete loss of teeth due to caries
summary: Complete loss of teeth due to caries refers to the total absence of all permanent teeth resulting from severe dental decay. Common synonyms include total tooth loss and edentulism. The primary causative agent is Streptococcus mutans, which produces acid that demineralizes tooth structure. This condition typically affects the maxilla and mandible, leading to significant functional and aesthetic impairment. It often occurs in individuals with poor oral hygiene, limited access to dental care, or untreated dental caries.

code_desc: Complete loss of teeth due to other specified cause
summary: Complete loss of teeth due to other specified cause refers to the total absence of all permanent teeth resulting from factors not classified under common dental conditions like periodontitis or trauma. Common synonyms include total edentulism and complete tooth loss. Causative agents may include severe trauma, congenital absence, or systemic diseases such as osteoradionecrosis. This condition typically affects the maxilla and mandible, leading to significant functional and aesthetic impairments. It is often managed through prosthetic rehabilitation.

Complete loss of teeth, also known as edentulism, refers to the absence of all permanent teeth in the upper and lower jaws. This condition can result from trauma, periodontal disease, caries, or congenital absence. Common synonyms include total edentulism and complete tooth loss. It most commonly affects the maxilla and mandible, leading to functional and aesthetic challenges. Complications may include difficulty in chewing, speech impairment, and facial structure changes. Treatment often involves dentures or dental implants to restore function and appearance.

code_desc: Unspecified atrophy of edentulous alveolar ridge
summary: Unspecified atrophy of the edentulous alveolar ridge refers to the generalized shrinkage of the bone in the jaw following tooth loss, without a specific identifiable cause. Common synonyms include alveolar ridge atrophy and post-extraction bone resorption. This condition is primarily caused by the loss of mechanical stimulation from missing teeth, leading to resorption of the alveolar bone. It typically affects the maxilla and mandible, particularly in areas where teeth were previously present. The atrophy can result in reduced bone volume, complicating dental implant placement and affecting facial aesthetics.

Minimal atrophy of the mandible refers to a slight reduction in the size or density of the lower jawbone, often observed in advanced stages of periodontal disease or long-term tooth loss. Synonyms include mild mandibular resorption and slight mandibular bone loss. Common causative agents include periodontitis, trauma, osteoporosis, and prolonged absence of teeth. This condition typically affects the posterior regions of the mandible, leading to reduced vertical dimension and potential functional or aesthetic concerns. It is often asymptomatic but may contribute to difficulties in denture fitting or speech.

Moderate atrophy of the mandible refers to a progressive reduction in the size and density of the lower jawbone, leading to a visible and measurable decrease in its volume. Common synonyms include mandibular resorption and alveolar atrophy. This condition is often associated with long-term tooth loss, periodontal disease, or osteoporosis. It may also result from trauma, radiation therapy, or systemic conditions affecting bone metabolism. The most commonly affected areas include the alveolar ridge and the body of the mandible, leading to facial contour changes and potential functional and aesthetic complications.

Severe atrophy of the mandible refers to significant loss of bone mass in the lower jaw, leading to a markedly reduced contour and structural weakness. Common synonyms include advanced mandibular resorption and severe mandibular osteopenia. This condition is often associated with long-term tooth loss, periodontal disease, or systemic conditions such as osteoporosis. It may also result from trauma, radiation therapy, or chronic infection. The mandible is typically affected, with the posterior regions showing the most pronounced changes. Clinically, it can lead to functional and aesthetic complications, including difficulty in denture retention and altered facial structure.

Minimal atrophy of the maxilla refers to a slight reduction in the volume of the upper jawbone, typically observed in the posterior regions. Common synonyms include mild maxillary resorption and minor alveolar atrophy. This condition is often associated with long-term tooth loss, periodontal disease, or aging. It may also result from trauma or surgical interventions. The maxillary sinus and alveolar ridge are typically affected, leading to changes in facial structure and potential challenges in dental implant placement. The condition is generally asymptomatic but can impact oral function and aesthetics.

Moderate atrophy of the maxilla refers to a progressive reduction in the volume and density of the upper jawbone, leading to a loss of alveolar bone supporting the teeth. Common synonyms include maxillary resorption and alveolar atrophy. This condition is often caused by tooth loss, periodontal disease, or long-term lack of stimulation from chewing. It typically affects the anterior and posterior regions of the maxilla, resulting in facial contour changes, difficulty in denture retention, and potential complications in implant placement.

Severe atrophy of the maxilla refers to significant loss of bone volume in the upper jaw, leading to a collapsed facial structure. Common synonyms include maxillary resorption and maxillary hypoplasia. Causative agents may include long-term tooth loss, periodontal disease, osteoporosis, or prolonged use of dentures without proper support. This condition typically affects the alveolar bone, sinus floor, and surrounding soft tissues, resulting in facial deformity, impaired dental function, and aesthetic concerns. It is often seen in elderly patients or those with chronic oral health issues.

Atrophy of the edentulous alveolar ridge refers to the progressive resorption and reduction of the bone and soft tissue in the jaw following tooth loss. Common synonyms include alveolar ridge resorption and post-extraction bone loss. This condition is primarily caused by the absence of functional stimulation from teeth, leading to osteoclastic activity. It typically affects the maxilla and mandible, with the posterior regions often showing more pronounced atrophy. Other contributing factors may include poor oral hygiene, systemic conditions, and lack of prosthetic support. The resulting changes can complicate dental implant placement and affect facial aesthetics and mastication.

A retained dental root refers to a tooth root that remains in the jaw after the crown has been lost or extracted. Common synonyms include persistent root, residual root, or non-extracavated root. This condition is often caused by incomplete extraction, trauma, or pathological processes such as periodontal disease or infection. It typically affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior regions, particularly molars. Retained roots can lead to complications like infection, cyst formation, or impaction of adjacent teeth. Diagnosis is usually made through clinical examination and radiographic imaging.

code_desc: Partial loss of teeth unspecified cause
summary: Partial loss of teeth unspecified cause refers to the absence of some teeth without a specified etiology. Common synonyms include dental attrition, tooth loss of unknown origin, and non-specific tooth loss. Causative agents may include trauma, periodontal disease, caries, or systemic conditions, though the exact cause is not identified. This condition typically affects the maxilla and mandible, with the anterior and posterior regions commonly involved. It may lead to functional and aesthetic concerns, impacting chewing and speech. Diagnosis often requires clinical examination and imaging to assess the extent of tooth loss and underlying pathology.

code_desc: Partial loss of teeth due to trauma
summary: Partial loss of teeth due to trauma refers to the fracture or avulsion of one or more teeth resulting from physical injury. Common synonyms include dental trauma, traumatic tooth loss, and tooth fracture. Causative agents typically involve accidents, sports injuries, or assaults. This condition most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth, particularly incisors and canines. It may lead to aesthetic, functional, and psychological concerns if not promptly treated.

code_desc: Partial loss of teeth due to periodontal diseases
summary: Partial loss of teeth due to periodontal diseases refers to the irreversible destruction of periodontal tissues leading to tooth mobility and eventual tooth loss. Common synonyms include periodontal tooth loss and gingival recession-associated tooth loss. Causative agents include *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, and *Treponema denticola*. This condition typically affects the maxillary and mandibular anterior and posterior regions, with a higher prevalence in adults. It is associated with chronic inflammation, bone resorption, and gingival recession.

code_desc: Partial loss of teeth due to caries
summary: Partial loss of teeth due to caries refers to the irreversible destruction of one or more teeth caused by dental caries, commonly known as tooth decay. This condition results from the action of cariogenic bacteria, primarily *Streptococcus mutans*, which produce acid that demineralizes tooth structure. It typically affects the anterior and posterior teeth, especially in areas difficult to clean, such as between teeth or in the pits and fissures of molars. Synonyms include dental caries, tooth decay, and cavities. The condition often leads to pulp involvement, infection, and eventual tooth loss if untreated.

code_desc: Partial loss of teeth due to other specified cause
summary: Partial loss of teeth due to other specified cause refers to the absence of one or more teeth resulting from reasons not classified under common dental conditions such as decay, trauma, or periodontal disease. Common synonyms include dental attrition, non-traumatic tooth loss, or unspecified tooth loss. Causative agents may include systemic diseases, developmental anomalies, or iatrogenic factors. This condition typically affects the maxillary and mandibular arches, with the anterior and posterior regions being commonly involved. It may impact chewing, speech, and overall oral function.

Partial loss of teeth refers to the absence of one or more teeth in the dental arch, leading to functional and aesthetic concerns. Common synonyms include dental attrition, tooth loss, and edentulism. This condition may result from trauma, periodontal disease,龋齿 (dental caries), or congenital absence. It typically affects the maxilla and mandible, with anterior teeth being more commonly impacted. The loss can compromise chewing efficiency, speech, and facial structure, often necessitating restorative dental interventions.

Unsatisfactory restoration of a tooth refers to a dental restoration that fails to meet functional, aesthetic, or structural requirements. Common synonyms include failed dental restoration or inadequate dental repair. This condition may result from improper technique, material failure, or poor oral hygiene. Causative agents include bacterial infection, mechanical trauma, or inadequate bonding. Typically affects posterior and anterior teeth, with the maxillary and mandibular arches being most commonly involved. It often leads to pain, sensitivity, or further dental complications.

Open restoration margins of a tooth refer to gaps or spaces that form between a dental restoration and the surrounding tooth structure, allowing bacterial ingress. This condition can lead to secondary caries, gingival inflammation, and potential failure of the restoration. Common synonyms include marginal leakage or open margins. Causative factors may include improper cementation, occlusal trauma, or poor marginal adaptation. It typically affects posterior teeth, particularly molars, where restorations are more prone to stress and microleakage. Early detection and intervention are crucial to prevent complications.

code_desc: Unrepairable overhanging of dental restorative materials
summary: Unrepairable overhanging of dental restorative materials refers to a condition where excess restorative material extends beyond the anatomical contours of the tooth, creating a marginal discrepancy that cannot be adequately corrected. Common synonyms include marginal overhang and excessive restoration. This condition is often caused by improper placement or curing of composite resins, amalgam, or ceramic materials. It typically affects posterior and anterior teeth, particularly in areas with complex anatomy or where marginal adaptation is challenging. If left untreated, it can lead to secondary caries, gingival inflammation, and periodontal issues.

Fractured dental restorative material refers to the breakage or cracking of dental fillings, crowns, or other restorative substances used in tooth restoration. Common synonyms include fractured restoration or broken dental filling. This condition is often caused by physical trauma, bruxism, or material fatigue. It typically affects posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to high occlusal forces. The affected body parts include the dental restoration and surrounding tooth structure. Early detection and repair are essential to prevent further damage and maintain oral function.

code_desc: Contour of existing restoration of tooth biologically incompatible with oral health
summary: A contour of existing restoration that is biologically incompatible with oral health refers to a dental restoration whose shape or margin does not harmonize with the natural anatomy of the tooth, leading to plaque accumulation, gingival inflammation, or periodontal disease. Common synonyms include malcontoured restoration or faulty restoration. Causative agents often involve improper restoration design, inadequate marginal adaptation, or poor occlusal relationships. This condition typically affects the gingival margins and periodontal tissues around the restored tooth.

code_desc: Allergy to existing dental restorative material
summary: Allergy to existing dental restorative material refers to an immune-mediated reaction to materials used in dental restorations. Common synonyms include allergic reaction to dental fillings or dental material hypersensitivity. Causative agents often include metals like nickel, mercury, and palladium, as well as resins and latex. Symptoms may manifest as oral mucosal irritation, swelling, or systemic reactions. Typically affected body parts include the oral cavity, lips, and surrounding tissues. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation and allergy testing. Management may involve removal of the allergen and replacement with alternative materials.

code_desc: Poor aesthetic of existing restoration of tooth
summary: Poor aesthetic of existing restoration of tooth refers to the unsightly appearance of dental restorations such as fillings, crowns, or veneers that do not blend naturally with the surrounding tooth structure. Common synonyms include dental disfigurement, restorative mismatch, or aesthetic compromise. Causative factors may include improper color matching, poor technique, or degradation of materials. This condition typically affects the anterior teeth, which are more visible during smiling and speaking. It can lead to patient dissatisfaction and may necessitate replacement or modification of the restoration.

"Other unsatisfactory restoration of tooth" refers to a dental condition where a previously placed restoration, such as a filling or crown, fails to meet functional or aesthetic standards. Common synonyms include failed restoration, inadequate restoration, or defective restoration. Causative factors may include poor technique, material failure, secondary caries, or occlusal trauma. This condition typically affects posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their complex anatomy and high functional demands. It can lead to pain, sensitivity, or further tooth damage if not addressed promptly.

Unsatisfactory restoration of a tooth refers to a dental restoration that fails to meet functional, aesthetic, or structural requirements. Common synonyms include failed restoration, inadequate restoration, or compromised restoration. This condition may result from poor technique, material failure, secondary caries, or occlusal trauma. Causative agents include inadequate bonding, poor margin adaptation, or recurrent caries. It typically affects posterior teeth due to high occlusal forces, but can occur in any tooth. Symptoms may include pain, sensitivity, fracture, or periapical pathology. Early diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent further complications.

Primary occlusal trauma refers to damage to the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone caused by excessive occlusal forces. It typically results from abnormal tooth contact during occlusion, often due to malocclusion, bruxism, or faulty restorations. Common synonyms include occlusal overload and traumatic occlusion. The condition primarily affects the periodontium surrounding the teeth, particularly those with excessive occlusal forces. It is most commonly seen in posterior teeth and can lead to gingival recession, periodontal pocket formation, and tooth mobility if left untreated.

Secondary occlusal trauma refers to damage to the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone caused by excessive occlusal forces resulting from malocclusion or parafunctional habits. Common synonyms include occlusal overload and traumatic occlusion. Causative agents often include bruxism, malocclusion, missing teeth, or improper dental restorations. Typically, the condition affects the teeth and supporting structures, particularly in the posterior regions of the mouth. It can lead to periodontal inflammation, gingival recession, and tooth mobility if left untreated.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of teeth and supporting structures
summary: "Other specified disorders of teeth and supporting structures" refers to dental and periodontal conditions not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified dental anomalies or generalized periodontal disease. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, trauma, systemic diseases, or genetic factors. These disorders typically affect the teeth, gums, alveolar bone, and surrounding soft tissues. They may present with symptoms such as tooth mobility, gingival recession, or loss of dental structure. Diagnosis often requires clinical and radiographic evaluation to determine the extent and underlying cause.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of teeth and supporting structures
summary: "Other specified disorders of teeth and supporting structures" refers to dental and periodontal conditions not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified dental anomalies or generalized periodontal disease. Causative agents may include trauma, infection (e.g., *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*), systemic diseases (e.g., diabetes), or genetic factors. These disorders typically affect the teeth, gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, leading to symptoms such as tooth mobility, gingival recession, and loss of attachment. They may present with variable severity and are often diagnosed clinically when specific etiologies are unclear.

code_desc: Disorder of teeth and supporting structures unspecified
summary: "Disorder of teeth and supporting structures unspecified" refers to a broad category of dental conditions affecting teeth, gums, or surrounding bone without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include generalized dental disease or unspecified dental disorder. Causative agents may include trauma, infection, genetic factors, or systemic conditions. Typically affects the teeth, periodontal tissues, and alveolar bone. This diagnosis is used when the exact nature of the disorder is not clearly defined or documented.

Developmental odontogenic cysts are benign, fluid-filled lesions arising from odontogenic tissues during tooth development. Common synonyms include odontogenic keratocyst and developmental cyst of the jaw. These cysts are typically caused by developmental disturbances in tooth formation, though specific causative agents are not well defined. They most commonly occur in the maxilla and mandible, particularly in the posterior regions. They may contain keratinized material and have a tendency for recurrence following surgical removal. These cysts are often asymptomatic and are frequently discovered incidentally on radiographic imaging.

Developmental (nonodontogenic) cysts of the oral region are congenital lesions arising from embryonic remnants of the oral epithelium, not related to tooth development. Common synonyms include thyroglossal duct cysts, branchial cleft cysts, and cystic hygromas. These cysts are typically caused by developmental anomalies during embryogenesis. They most commonly occur in the midline of the neck (thyroglossal duct cysts) or along the sides of the neck (branchial cleft cysts). Cystic hygromas are often found in the posterior cervical region. These lesions are usually asymptomatic but may present with swelling, infection, or obstruction.

code_desc: Other cysts of oral region not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other cysts of the oral region not elsewhere classified" refers to cystic lesions in the mouth that do not fit into more specific categories such as dentigerous or epidermoid cysts. Common synonyms include retained epithelial cysts and developmental cysts. These cysts are typically caused by developmental anomalies, trauma, or obstruction of epithelial remnants. They most commonly occur in the mandible or maxilla, often near unerupted teeth. The condition may present as a slow-growing, painless swelling, and diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and histopathological examination.

Cyst of oral region unspecified refers to a fluid-filled sac occurring in the oral cavity without specific localization. Common synonyms include ranula, mucocele, or epulis. It is typically caused by blocked salivary glands or trauma leading to retention. These cysts most commonly affect the lower lip, floor of the mouth, or buccal mucosa. They are usually benign, slow-growing, and may present as a painless swelling. Diagnosis is often made clinically, with imaging or biopsy if needed. Treatment typically involves surgical excision to prevent recurrence.

Atrophy of the salivary gland refers to the degeneration and shrinkage of salivary gland tissue, leading to reduced saliva production. Common synonyms include salivary gland hypoplasia and sialoadenosis. This condition may result from chronic inflammation, autoimmune disorders, infections, or prolonged use of medications such as anticholinergics. It commonly affects the parotid and submandibular glands, which are the major salivary glands. Symptoms may include dry mouth, altered taste, and difficulty in chewing. The condition is more prevalent in older adults and individuals with systemic diseases like Sjögren's syndrome.

Hypertrophy of the salivary gland refers to the abnormal enlargement of salivary glands, most commonly the parotid or submandibular glands. It may result from chronic irritation, infection, or obstruction of salivary flow. Common synonyms include salivary gland hyperplasia or sialadenosis. Causative agents may include recurrent sialadenitis, autoimmune conditions, or metabolic disorders. The condition typically affects the parotid glands, often presenting as a painless, firm swelling, and is more prevalent in middle-aged women.

Sialoadenitis unspecified refers to inflammation of a salivary gland without a specific etiology identified. Common synonyms include nonspecific sialadenitis and acute sialadenitis when no clear cause is determined. It is often caused by bacterial or viral infections, though the exact pathogen may not be identified. The parotid and submandibular glands are most commonly affected. Symptoms include swelling, pain, and tenderness in the affected area. It typically occurs in individuals with reduced salivary flow, such as those with dehydration or decreased oral intake.

Acute sialoadenitis is an inflammatory condition of the salivary glands, most commonly affecting the parotid and submandibular glands. It is often caused by bacterial infections, particularly *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Streptococcus* species, though viral agents may also play a role. The condition presents with sudden onset of pain, swelling, and tenderness in the affected gland, often accompanied by fever. Obstruction of salivary ducts, such as from sialolithiasis, is a common predisposing factor. It typically occurs in the head and neck region, with the parotid gland being the most frequently involved.

Acute recurrent sialoadenitis is a condition characterized by repeated episodes of inflammation of the salivary glands, most commonly the parotid and submandibular glands. It often presents with swelling, pain, and tenderness in the affected area, particularly during meals. Common synonyms include recurrent salivary gland inflammation and sialadenitis. The condition is frequently associated with bacterial infections, such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, and can be linked to obstruction of salivary ducts due to stones or mucus plugs. It typically affects the major salivary glands in the head and neck region.

Chronic sialoadenitis is a long-standing inflammatory condition of the salivary glands, often leading to fibrosis and ductal changes. Common synonyms include chronic salivary gland inflammation and sialadenosis. It is typically caused by recurrent infections, autoimmune processes, or obstruction of salivary ducts. The parotid gland is most commonly affected, followed by the submandibular gland. Risk factors include dehydration, poor oral hygiene, and systemic diseases such as Sjögren's syndrome. Symptoms may include persistent swelling, pain, and reduced salivary flow. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical findings and imaging studies. Treatment focuses on managing underlying causes and relieving symptoms.

Sialoadenitis is an inflammation of the salivary glands, commonly affecting the parotid and submandibular glands. It may present as swelling, pain, and tenderness in the affected area. Common synonyms include salivary gland inflammation and sialadenopathy. Causative agents include bacterial infections such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, viral agents like mumps, and obstructive causes such as sialolithiasis. It often occurs in individuals with reduced saliva flow, such as those with dehydration or autoimmune conditions. The condition can be acute or chronic, with varying degrees of severity.

An abscess of the salivary gland is a localized collection of pus resulting from a bacterial infection within a salivary gland. Common synonyms include sialadenitis with suppuration and salivary gland abscess. The most common causative agents are *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Streptococcus species*. This condition typically affects the submandibular and parotid glands, often secondary to obstruction of the salivary ducts, leading to stasis and subsequent infection. It presents with pain, swelling, redness, and fever, and may require drainage and antibiotic therapy.

Fistula of the salivary gland is an abnormal passage connecting the gland to the skin or another structure, often resulting from infection, stone obstruction, or trauma. Common synonyms include salivary gland fistula and sialocele. The most common causative agents are bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Streptococcus* species. This condition typically affects the parotid and submandibular glands, with the submandibular gland being more frequently involved. It presents as a chronic, draining lesion, often accompanied by swelling and pain in the affected area.

Sialolithiasis is the formation of salivary gland stones, most commonly in the submandibular gland. It results from calcification of salivary secretions, often due to dehydration, infection, or anatomical factors. Common synonyms include sialolith, salivary calculus, or sialostasis. The condition typically affects the submandibular and parotid glands, with the submandibular gland being the most frequently involved. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and ductal obstruction, often exacerbated during meals. Treatment may involve hydration, sialagogues, lithotripsy, or surgical removal.

A mucocele of the salivary gland is a benign, cystic lesion resulting from the obstruction or rupture of a salivary gland duct, leading to the accumulation of mucin. Common synonyms include ranula and sialolithiasis. It is typically caused by trauma, sialoliths, or ductal obstruction. The most commonly affected areas are the floor of the mouth, lower lip, and buccal mucosa. Clinically, it presents as a soft, fluctuant swelling, often with a bluish hue. The condition is more prevalent in children and young adults, with a female predominance. Treatment usually involves surgical excision to prevent recurrence.

Disturbances of salivary secretion refer to abnormalities in the production, composition, or flow of saliva. Common synonyms include xerostomia (dry mouth) and hypersalivation. These conditions may result from various causes such as medications (e.g., anticholinergics, antidepressants), autoimmune disorders (e.g., Sjögren’s syndrome), radiation therapy, or infections. They typically affect the salivary glands, particularly the parotid and submandibular glands, leading to symptoms like dryness, difficulty swallowing, or excessive salivation. The oral cavity and throat are commonly impacted, affecting overall oral health and comfort.

"Other diseases of salivary glands" encompass a variety of non-specific inflammatory and structural conditions affecting the salivary glands, including sialadenitis, sialolithiasis, and autoimmune disorders. Common synonyms include salivary gland inflammation and salivary gland dysfunction. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, viral agents, or autoimmune mechanisms. These conditions typically affect the parotid and submandibular glands, often presenting with swelling, pain, and reduced saliva production. They are more common in older adults and individuals with compromised immune function.

Disease of salivary gland unspecified refers to any pathological condition affecting the salivary glands when the specific type or cause is not identified. Common synonyms include nonspecific salivary gland disease or undiagnosed salivary gland disorder. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune processes, or obstructive factors, though they are often not definitively determined. This condition typically affects the major salivary glands, particularly the parotid and submandibular glands, and may present with symptoms such as swelling, pain, and altered saliva production.

Recurrent oral aphthae, also known as canker sores or aphthous ulcers, are recurrent, painful, shallow ulcers that develop in the oral mucosa. The exact cause is multifactorial, involving genetic, immune, and environmental factors. Common triggers include stress, trauma, nutritional deficiencies, and food sensitivities. The lesions typically affect non-keratinized mucosa, such as the cheeks, lips, tongue, and floor of the mouth. They are not contagious and usually resolve spontaneously within 7–14 days. No single causative agent is identified, but immune dysregulation and epithelial injury are thought to play key roles.

Other forms of stomatitis refer to inflammatory conditions affecting the oral mucosa, distinct from aphthous or herpes-related ulcers. Common synonyms include oral mucositis and erythematous stomatitis. Causative agents may include irritants, allergens, infections (e.g., candida, herpes simplex virus), medications, or systemic diseases. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and gums, presenting as redness, pain, and sometimes ulceration. It is often a secondary manifestation of underlying health issues or treatment-related side effects.

Cellulitis and abscess of the mouth refer to bacterial infections of the oral soft tissues, often involving the lips, cheeks, tongue, and floor of the mouth. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus pyogenes*, and *Porphyromonas gingivalis*. Synonyms include oral cellulitis, pericoronitis, and odontogenic infection. Symptoms include redness, swelling, pain, and pus formation. Abscesses may develop as localized collections of pus. These infections can spread rapidly and may require antibiotics or surgical drainage. Risk factors include dental disease, trauma, and immunocompromise.

Oral mucositis (ulcerative) unspecified refers to inflammation and ulceration of the oral mucosa without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include oral ulceration, stomatitis, and aphthous ulcers. It is often associated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, infections, or autoimmune disorders. Causative agents may include herpes simplex virus, Candida, or mechanical trauma. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and soft palate, causing pain, erythema, and erosive lesions. It can significantly impact oral function and nutrition.

code_desc: Oral mucositis (ulcerative) due to antineoplastic therapy
summary: Oral mucositis (ulcerative) due to antineoplastic therapy is an inflammatory condition characterized by painful ulcers and erosions in the oral mucosa, commonly induced by chemotherapy or radiation. Synonyms include chemotherapy-induced oral ulcers and mucositis. Causative agents include alkylating agents, antimetabolites, and radiation. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and palate, leading to significant discomfort, difficulty in eating, and increased risk of infection. It is a common and debilitating side effect in cancer patients undergoing antineoplastic treatment.

code_desc: Oral mucositis (ulcerative) due to other drugs
summary: Oral mucositis (ulcerative) due to other drugs refers to painful ulcerative lesions in the oral mucosa caused by medications not classified as chemotherapy or radiation. Common synonyms include drug-induced oral ulceration and medication-associated stomatitis. Causative agents may include anticonvulsants, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and certain antibiotics. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and soft palate, leading to discomfort, difficulty in eating, and increased risk of infection. It is often dose-related and may resolve upon discontinuation of the causative agent.

Oral mucositis (ulcerative) due to radiation is an inflammatory and ulcerative condition affecting the oral mucosa, commonly occurring in patients undergoing head and neck radiation therapy. It is characterized by painful erosions, ulcers, and mucosal swelling. Common synonyms include radiation-induced oral ulceration and mucositis. The primary causative agent is ionizing radiation, which damages rapidly dividing epithelial cells. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, palate, and gingiva, leading to significant discomfort and potential complications in nutrition and speech.

Other oral mucositis (ulcerative) refers to inflammatory ulcerative lesions of the oral mucosa, often resulting from mucosal damage. Common synonyms include oral ulcers, aphthous ulcers, and recurrent aphthous stomatitis. Causative agents may include viral infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus), immune-mediated factors, nutritional deficiencies, or mechanical trauma. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and gingiva. It presents as painful, shallow ulcers with erythematous borders, often recurring in a cyclical pattern. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, though biopsy may be required in atypical cases.

Oral mucositis (ulcerative) is an inflammatory condition characterized by painful ulcers and erosions in the oral mucosa. Common synonyms include oral ulcerative mucositis and stomatitis. It is often caused by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus), or autoimmune disorders. The condition primarily affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and gingiva. Symptoms include burning, pain, and difficulty in eating or speaking. It is a common complication in cancer patients undergoing treatment and can significantly impact quality of life.

Diseases of the lips encompass a range of conditions affecting the vermilion border and surrounding skin. Common synonyms include cheilitis and lip disorders. These conditions may result from infections, such as herpes simplex virus (HSV-1), or irritants, allergens, or nutritional deficiencies. They often affect the vermillion border, labial mucosa, and perioral skin. Symptoms include redness, cracking, scaling, and pain. Chronic conditions like actinic cheilitis, caused by UV exposure, may lead to premalignant changes. Diagnosis is typically clinical, with treatment varying based on underlying cause.

Cheek and lip biting is a repetitive self-injurious behavior characterized by the habitual biting of the lips or cheeks, often leading to tissue damage and ulceration. Common synonyms include lip biting and cheek biting. It is commonly associated with stress, anxiety, or obsessive-compulsive tendencies. Known causative agents may include psychological factors, neurological conditions, or developmental disorders. Typically affected body parts include the lower lip, upper lip, and inner cheeks, with the lower lip being most frequently involved. The condition may persist into adulthood if not addressed.

code_desc: Leukoplakia of oral mucosa including tongue
summary: Leukoplakia of the oral mucosa, including the tongue, is a chronic, precancerous condition characterized by white, adherent patches on the mucous membranes. Common synonyms include oral leukoplakia and oral white patch. It is primarily caused by chronic irritation from tobacco use, alcohol consumption, or ill-fitting dental prostheses. The condition typically affects the buccal mucosa, tongue, and floor of the mouth. Clinically, it presents as non-removable, white plaques that cannot be attributed to any other diagnosable process. Early diagnosis and removal of irritants are essential to reduce the risk of malignant transformation.

Minimal keratinized residual ridge mucosa refers to a thin layer of keratinized mucosa remaining over the alveolar ridge after tooth loss. This condition is commonly seen in edentulous patients. Synonyms include atrophic mucosa and residual ridge atrophy. It is often caused by long-term tooth absence, leading to bone resorption and reduced soft tissue thickness. The most commonly affected areas are the maxillary and mandibular ridges. The mucosa appears pale, smooth, and lacks the normal texture of healthy keratinized tissue. It is associated with increased susceptibility to trauma and infection.

Excessive keratinized residual ridge mucosa refers to an abnormal thickening and keratinization of the mucosa over the residual ridge following tooth loss. This condition is often associated with chronic irritation and pressure from ill-fitting dentures. Common synonyms include hyperkeratotic residual ridge and keratinized mucosa of the edentulous ridge. Causative agents include poorly adapted dentures, trauma, and chronic inflammation. It typically affects the maxillary and mandibular ridges, particularly in areas of denture-bearing surfaces. The mucosa appears thickened, dry, and sometimes fissured, leading to discomfort and potential complications with denture retention.

Leukokeratosis nicotina palati, also known as nicotinic leukokeratosis or smoker's palate, is a chronic, asymptomatic condition characterized by white, keratinized patches on the hard palate. It is primarily caused by chronic tobacco use, particularly pipe or cigar smoking. The condition results from repeated irritation and chronic inflammation of the palatal mucosa. It typically affects the midline of the hard palate and is more common in older adults. The lesions are non-cancerous but may mimic oral cancer, necessitating proper diagnosis. Other synonyms include palatal leukokeratosis and nicotinic keratosis.

code_desc: Other disturbances of oral epithelium including tongue
summary: Other disturbances of oral epithelium including tongue refer to non-specific inflammatory or degenerative changes affecting the oral mucosa, particularly the tongue. Common synonyms include oral mucositis and epithelial dysplasia. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., herpes simplex virus), irritants, autoimmune disorders, or chronic inflammation. These conditions typically affect the tongue, buccal mucosa, and gingiva, presenting as erythema, ulceration, or leukoplakia. They are often associated with systemic diseases or prolonged exposure to irritants. Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation and biopsy when necessary.

code_desc: Leukoplakia and other disturbances of oral epithelium including tongue
summary: Leukoplakia is a chronic, precancerous condition characterized by white, adherent patches on the oral mucosa, commonly affecting the tongue, gums, and cheeks. It results from chronic irritation or inflammation, often due to tobacco use, alcohol consumption, or ill-fitting dentures. Other epithelial disturbances may include erythroplakia, lichen planus, and candidiasis. These conditions may present as white, red, or mixed lesions and are associated with risk factors such as smoking, poor oral hygiene, and immunosuppression. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent malignant transformation.

Hairy leukoplakia is a white, corrugated lesion on the tongue and oral mucosa, characterized by hyperkeratosis and papillary projections. It is commonly associated with immunosuppression, particularly in HIV-infected individuals. The condition is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and is often referred to as hairy tongue or pseudoleukoplakia. It typically affects the lateral borders of the tongue, and may also involve the buccal mucosa. The lesions are non-removable and not caused by irritants or candida. It is a marker of immune compromise and may precede the diagnosis of HIV.

code_desc: Granuloma and granuloma-like lesions of oral mucosa
summary: Granuloma and granuloma-like lesions of the oral mucosa refer to inflammatory nodular lesions characterized by a granulomatous reaction, often in response to foreign bodies, infections, or immune-mediated processes. Common synonyms include foreign body granuloma, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis. Causative agents may include bacteria (e.g., *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*), fungi, or chronic irritation. These lesions typically affect the hard palate, gingiva, and buccal mucosa. They present as firm, painless nodules and may mimic neoplastic processes, necessitating histopathological evaluation for accurate diagnosis.

Oral submucous fibrosis is a chronic, progressive, inflammatory condition characterized by fibrosis of the oral mucosa, leading to stiffness and restricted mouth opening. Common synonyms include oral fibromatosis and leukoplakia-like changes. It is primarily caused by chronic tobacco use, including smokeless and smokeless forms, and areca nut chewing. The condition predominantly affects the buccal mucosa, palate, and gingiva. It is more common in males and is associated with an increased risk of oral cancer. Clinical features include white patches, burning sensation, and trismus. Early diagnosis and cessation of risk factors are crucial for management.

Irritative hyperplasia of the oral mucosa is a reactive proliferative lesion characterized by thickening and overgrowth of the mucosal epithelium in response to chronic irritation. Common synonyms include oral fibrous hyperplasia and fibrous hyperplasia of the mouth. It is typically caused by chronic mechanical irritation from ill-fitting dentures, sharp teeth, or chronic trauma. The condition most commonly affects the buccal mucosa, palate, and gingiva. Clinically, it presents as a firm, non-ulcerative lesion with a fibrous texture. It is benign and often resolves with removal of the irritant.

Unspecified lesions of oral mucosa refer to abnormal changes in the oral mucosal tissues that do not meet the criteria for specific diagnoses. Common synonyms include indeterminate oral mucosal lesions or non-specific oral mucosal changes. Causative agents may include trauma, infections (e.g., viral, bacterial, fungal), autoimmune conditions, or neoplastic processes. These lesions typically affect the buccal mucosa, tongue, floor of the mouth, and gingiva. Clinical presentation varies, often presenting as ulcers, erosions, or plaques. Diagnosis requires further evaluation to determine the underlying cause.

"Other lesions of oral mucosa" refers to a broad category of non-specific, non-malignant oral conditions not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include mucosal inflammation, reactive changes, and non-specific ulcers. These lesions may result from trauma, infection, or irritants. Causative agents include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and physical or chemical irritants. Typically affecting the buccal mucosa, tongue, palate, and gingiva, these lesions present as erythema, ulcers, or plaques, often resolving with removal of the causative factor.

code_desc: Other and unspecified lesions of oral mucosa
summary: "Other and unspecified lesions of oral mucosa" refers to non-specific, clinically defined abnormalities of the oral mucosa not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include "unspecified oral mucosal lesions" or "miscellaneous oral mucosal conditions." Causative agents may include trauma, infections (e.g., viral, fungal), autoimmune disorders, or chronic irritation. These lesions typically affect the buccal mucosa, tongue, palate, and gingiva. They are often diagnosed when no specific etiology can be identified, requiring further investigation for accurate management.

Glossitis is an inflammation of the tongue, characterized by swelling, redness, and loss of papillae. It may present with pain, burning, or altered taste. Common synonyms include atrophic glossitis and geographic tongue. Causative agents include infections (e.g., candida, herpes simplex), nutritional deficiencies (e.g., B12, iron), allergic reactions, and irritants. The condition typically affects the dorsal surface of the tongue, with involvement of the fungiform and foliate papillae. It is more prevalent in individuals with poor oral hygiene or systemic diseases.

Geographic tongue, also known as benign migratory glossitis, is a chronic, non-scarring condition characterized by irregular, map-like patches on the tongue's surface. These patches, which may shift over time, result from the atrophy of filiform papillae, exposing underlying mucosa. The exact cause is unknown, though factors like stress, irritants, and nutritional deficiencies may contribute. It typically affects the dorsal surface of the tongue, with no known pathogenic agents. The condition is generally asymptomatic but may cause mild burning or sensitivity. Common synonyms include benign migratory glossitis and erythema migrans.

Median rhomboid glossitis is a chronic, non-ulcerative, atrophic lesion located in the midline of the dorsal surface of the tongue. It is characterized by a rhomboid-shaped, smooth, red patch with a defined border. Common synonyms include median rhomboid glossitis and median lingual patch. The exact cause is unknown, but it is often associated with fungal infections, particularly *Candida albicans*, and may be linked to local irritants or nutritional deficiencies. It predominantly affects the midline of the tongue, most commonly in adults, especially those with altered oral hygiene or immunocompromised states.

Hypertrophy of tongue papillae refers to the abnormal enlargement of the papillae on the surface of the tongue. Common synonyms include lingual papillitis and papillary hyperplasia. This condition is often caused by chronic irritation, such as from ill-fitting dentures, smoking, or spicy foods. It may also be associated with infections like candidiasis or viral infections. The dorsal and ventral surfaces of the tongue are typically affected, leading to a coarse, bumpy appearance. It is more common in individuals with poor oral hygiene or systemic conditions such as diabetes.

Atrophy of tongue papillae refers to the wasting or shrinkage of the lingual papillae, leading to a smooth, glossy appearance of the tongue. Common synonyms include glossitis and atrophic glossitis. This condition is often caused by nutritional deficiencies, particularly vitamin B12 or iron deficiency, as well as infections like syphilis or fungal infections. It may also result from chronic irritation or autoimmune disorders. The dorsal surface of the tongue is typically affected, with the filiform papillae being most commonly involved. Symptoms may include burning sensation, altered taste, and difficulty in swallowing.

Plicated tongue, also known as lingual frenulum plicature or folded tongue, is a congenital condition characterized by an abnormally tight lingual frenulum that causes the tongue to appear folded or notched. It may result from genetic factors or developmental anomalies. The condition typically affects the underside of the tongue, limiting its mobility. Common synonyms include frenulum plicature and lingual plication. While no specific causative agent is consistently identified, it is often associated with familial patterns. The primary affected body part is the tongue, with potential impacts on speech, swallowing, and oral hygiene.

Glossodynia is a chronic condition characterized by persistent burning or painful sensations on the tongue without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include burning mouth syndrome and oral dysesthesia. The exact etiology is often unclear, though factors such as nutritional deficiencies, hormonal changes, oral infections, and psychosomatic elements may contribute. The condition primarily affects the mucosal surfaces of the tongue, and may also involve the lips and palate. It is more commonly seen in postmenopausal women and can significantly impact quality of life.

"Other diseases of tongue" encompasses a variety of non-specific or less commonly classified tongue disorders. Common synonyms include mucosal disorders, inflammatory conditions, and idiopathic tongue lesions. These conditions may arise from infections, autoimmune processes, or environmental factors. Causative agents can include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or irritants. Typically, the dorsal surface, lateral borders, and underside of the tongue are affected. Symptoms often involve pain, swelling, ulceration, or altered taste. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and exclusion of more specific conditions.

"Disease of tongue unspecified" refers to a broad category of tongue disorders where the specific diagnosis is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include "undifferentiated tongue disorder" or "nonspecific tongue pathology." Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viral, bacterial, fungal), trauma, nutritional deficiencies, or systemic conditions. The tongue is the primary affected body part, with symptoms such as pain, swelling, discoloration, or altered taste. Diagnosis often requires further evaluation to determine the exact underlying cause.

Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the esophagus, leading to structural changes and dysfunction. Common synonyms include eosinophilic esophagitis and eosinophilic oesophagitis. It is often associated with allergic triggers such as food allergens, environmental allergens, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. The condition primarily affects the esophagus, with symptoms including dysphagia, food impaction, and reflux. It is more common in males and typically diagnosed in childhood or adolescence.

Other esophagitis without bleeding refers to inflammation of the esophagus not caused by known specific agents such as GERD or infections, and without associated gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include idiopathic or non-specific esophagitis. Causative agents may include irritants, medications, or unknown factors. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, causing symptoms like dysphagia, chest pain, and heartburn. It is often diagnosed through endoscopy and biopsy when no clear etiology is identified.

Other esophagitis with bleeding refers to inflammation of the esophagus not caused by the more common types such as reflux or infectious agents, leading to gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include non-specific or idiopathic esophagitis. Causative agents may include medications like NSAIDs, corrosive substances, or systemic diseases such as vasculitis. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, with symptoms including dysphagia, pain, and hematemesis. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy to identify underlying causes.

Other esophagitis refers to inflammation of the esophagus caused by factors other than the common types such as gastroesophageal reflux disease or infections. It may result from chemical irritation, medications, or autoimmune conditions. Common synonyms include non-ulcerative esophagitis and eosinophilic esophagitis. Causative agents include NSAIDs, alcohol, and allergens. The condition typically affects the lower esophagus, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. It is often diagnosed through endoscopy and biopsy.

Esophagitis unspecified without bleeding refers to inflammation of the esophageal mucosa of unknown etiology, without associated gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include non-specific esophagitis or idiopathic esophagitis. Causative agents may include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), infections, medications, or autoimmune factors. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, with symptoms such as dysphagia, heartburn, and chest pain. Diagnosis is often made through endoscopy and biopsy when no specific cause is identified.

Esophagitis unspecified with bleeding refers to inflammation of the esophagus of unknown origin accompanied by gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include erosive esophagitis with hemorrhage or non-specific esophagitis with bleeding. Causative agents may include NSAIDs, alcohol, acid reflux, infections, or systemic diseases. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, leading to mucosal damage and potential ulceration. Symptoms often include dysphagia, chest pain, and hematemesis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy.

Esophagitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the esophagus without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include non-specific esophagitis and idiopathic esophagitis. It may result from various irritants such as gastric reflux, medications, or infections, though the exact cause is often unclear. The condition typically affects the lower esophageal region, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, heartburn, and chest pain. It is commonly associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) but can occur independently.
