Diagnosis is usually based on endoscopic findings and clinical presentation when no specific etiology is identified.

code_desc: Gastro-esophageal reflux disease with esophagitis without bleeding
summary: Gastro-esophageal reflux disease (GERD) with esophagitis without bleeding is a chronic condition characterized by the backward flow of stomach contents into the esophagus, causing inflammation and irritation. Common synonyms include reflux esophagitis and acid reflux disease. The primary causative agent is the relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, often exacerbated by factors such as obesity, hiatal hernia, or dietary habits. The condition typically affects the esophagus, with potential involvement of the pharynx and larynx. Symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia. Complications may involve strictures or Barrett's esophagus, though bleeding is absent in this presentation.

code_desc: Gastro-esophageal reflux disease with esophagitis with bleeding
summary: Gastro-esophageal reflux disease (GERD) with esophagitis and bleeding is a chronic condition characterized by the backward flow of stomach contents into the esophagus, causing inflammation and erosion. Common synonyms include reflux esophagitis and acid-induced esophagitis. The primary causative agent is gastric acid, though bile and pepsin may also contribute. It typically affects the lower esophagus, with potential extension to the upper portion. Complications such as bleeding can occur due to mucosal damage, leading to hematemesis or melena. Risk factors include obesity, hiatal hernia, and dietary habits.

Gastro-esophageal reflux disease with esophagitis is a chronic condition characterized by the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, causing inflammation and damage to the esophageal lining. Common synonyms include reflux esophagitis and acid reflux disease. The primary causative agent is the backward flow of stomach acid, often exacerbated by factors such as obesity, hiatal hernia, or delayed gastric emptying. The condition predominantly affects the esophagus, with potential complications including stricture, Barrett's esophagus, and aspiration pneumonia.

Gastro-esophageal reflux disease without esophagitis refers to the chronic reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus without evidence of esophageal inflammation or mucosal damage. Common synonyms include non-erosive reflux disease and silent reflux. Causative factors include transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation, hiatal hernia, and increased abdominal pressure. Common symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, and chest discomfort. Typically affected body parts include the esophagus and stomach. Risk factors include obesity, smoking, and dietary habits. This condition is often managed with lifestyle modifications and pharmacologic agents.

Achalasia of the cardia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing, coupled with impaired peristalsis in the esophageal body. This results in progressive dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain. Common synonyms include cardia achalasia and esophageal achalasia. The exact cause is often idiopathic, though some cases may be associated with autoimmune mechanisms or viral infections. The condition primarily affects the esophagus, particularly the distal segment and the lower esophageal sphincter.

Ulcer of esophagus without bleeding refers to a localized erosion or ulceration of the esophageal mucosa that does not involve active hemorrhage. Common synonyms include esophageal ulcer and non-bleeding esophageal ulcer. Causative agents often include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or infection with *Helicobacter pylori*. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, particularly in individuals with chronic acid exposure. It may present with dysphagia, chest pain, or odynophagia, but lacks overt signs of bleeding.

Ulcer of esophagus with bleeding refers to the presence of an open sore in the esophageal lining accompanied by gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Common synonyms include esophageal ulcer with hematemesis or erosive esophagitis with bleeding. Causative agents often include gastric acid reflux, NSAID use, infections such as *Helicobacter pylori*, and systemic diseases like vasculitis. The condition primarily affects the lower esophagus, with potential extension into the gastric cardia. Symptoms include chest pain, dysphagia, and hematemesis. Complications may involve severe anemia or perforation.

An ulcer of the esophagus is a localized erosion of the esophageal mucosa, often resulting from chronic acid exposure. Common synonyms include esophageal ulcer and reflux esophagitis. The primary causative agent is gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), though infections such as *Helicobacter pylori* or medications like NSAIDs may contribute. The condition typically affects the distal esophagus, with symptoms including dysphagia, chest pain, and bleeding. Complications may include strictures or Barrett's esophagus. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy.

Esophageal obstruction is a condition characterized by the blockage of the esophagus, hindering the passage of food or liquid. Common synonyms include esophageal dysphagia and esophageal stenosis. Causative agents may include tumors, strictures, foreign bodies, or inflammatory conditions such as eosinophilic esophagitis. The primary affected body part is the esophagus, with symptoms often involving difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, and chest pain. It can occur at any level of the esophagus but is most commonly seen in the distal or mid-esophageal regions. Prompt evaluation is essential to determine the underlying cause and initiate appropriate treatment.

Perforation of the esophagus is a serious condition characterized by a full-thickness tear in the esophageal wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the mediastinum or pleural space. Common synonyms include esophageal rupture and esophageal perforation. Causative agents include iatrogenic injury during endoscopy, trauma, ingestion of caustic substances, and spontaneous rupture in conditions like Boerhaave syndrome. The condition most commonly affects the distal esophagus, often in the mid to lower regions. It can result in severe complications such as mediastinitis, sepsis, and pleural effusion if not promptly treated.

Dyskinesia of the esophagus refers to abnormal motility disorders affecting the muscular function of the esophagus, leading to impaired swallowing and reflux. Common synonyms include esophageal dysmotility and achalasia. It may result from neurological conditions, such as Parkinson's disease, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents include neuromuscular diseases, prolonged acid reflux, and idiopathic factors. The primary affected body parts are the esophageal muscles, particularly the lower esophageal sphincter, which fails to relax properly during swallowing. Symptoms include difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, and chest pain.

Diverticulum of esophagus acquired, also known as esophageal diverticulum or Zenker's diverticulum, refers to a protrusion of the esophageal wall containing mucosa and submucosa. It typically arises from weakness in the muscular layer, often at the level of the upper esophageal sphincter. Common causative factors include increased intraluminal pressure from chronic straining, such as from vomiting or coughing. The condition most frequently affects the distal esophagus, particularly in older adults, and may lead to symptoms like dysphagia, regurgitation, and aspiration.

Gastro-esophageal laceration-hemorrhage syndrome refers to traumatic injuries to the lower esophagus and upper stomach, often resulting in significant bleeding. Common synonyms include Boerhaave syndrome and Mallory-Weiss tear syndrome. It is typically caused by forceful vomiting, retching, or physical trauma. The condition predominantly affects the esophagus and stomach, with hemorrhage being a primary complication. Diagnosis is often confirmed via endoscopy, and treatment involves hemostasis, fluid resuscitation, and sometimes surgical intervention.

Barrett's esophagus without dysplasia is a condition characterized by the replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus with metaplastic columnar epithelium, typically due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease. Common synonyms include reflux esophagitis with metaplasia or esophageal metaplasia. The primary causative agent is prolonged exposure to gastric acid and bile reflux. It predominantly affects the distal esophagus, with a higher prevalence in males over 50 years of age. While it does not involve dysplasia, it remains a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Barrett's esophagus with dysplasia is a precancerous condition characterized by the replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus with metaplastic columnar epithelium, accompanied by varying degrees of dysplasia. It commonly arises from chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), where persistent acid exposure leads to epithelial changes. The primary affected body part is the distal esophagus. Synonyms include metaplastic esophagitis with dysplasia and columnar-lined esophagus with dysplasia. Risk factors include long-term GERD, obesity, and smoking. Early detection through endoscopy and biopsy is critical for monitoring and managing this condition.

Barrett's esophagus is a chronic condition characterized by the replacement of the normal squamous epithelium of the lower esophagus with metaplastic columnar epithelium, typically due to prolonged gastroesophageal reflux disease. Common synonyms include reflux esophagitis with metaplasia and metaplastic esophagitis. The primary causative agent is chronic acid reflux, often associated with a hiatal hernia. It predominantly affects the distal esophagus, with potential extension into the gastric cardia. This condition is a significant risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Esophageal polyp is a benign, pedunculated growth arising from the esophageal mucosa, most commonly in the mid-esophagus. It is typically composed of hyperplastic or inflammatory tissue, though rare cases may involve neoplastic elements. Common synonyms include esophageal hamartoma and esophageal papilloma. Causative agents are often unknown, but chronic irritation, reflux, or inflammatory conditions may contribute. The condition predominantly affects the distal esophagus and is more common in adults, particularly males. Symptoms may include dysphagia, odynophagia, or hematemesis, though many patients are asymptomatic.

Esophagogastric junction polyp is a benign lesion arising at the gastroesophageal junction, typically composed of mucosal or submucosal tissue. Common synonyms include gastric cardia polyp and fundic gland polyp. It is often associated with chronic gastritis, Helicobacter pylori infection, or long-term use of proton pump inhibitors. These polyps most commonly affect the distal esophagus and proximal stomach. They are usually asymptomatic but may cause dysphagia or bleeding. Diagnosis is typically made via endoscopy, and management depends on size, symptoms, and risk of malignancy.

"Other specified disease of esophagus" refers to esophageal conditions that do not fit into more specific categories such as reflux esophagitis or cancer. Common synonyms include unspecified esophageal disease or miscellaneous esophageal disorders. Causative agents may include chronic irritation, infections, or systemic diseases. This condition typically affects the esophageal mucosa and may involve complications like stricture or ulceration. It is often diagnosed when symptoms or findings do not align with established classifications.

"Other specified diseases of esophagus" refers to esophageal conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as strictures, motility disorders, or cancer. Common synonyms include unspecified esophageal disease or miscellaneous esophageal disorders. Causative agents may include chronic irritation, infections (e.g., Candida, herpes), or inflammatory processes. These conditions typically affect the esophageal mucosa, muscular layers, or sphincters, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, pain, or reflux. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy.

Disease of esophagus unspecified refers to a broad category of esophageal disorders where the specific diagnosis is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include esophageal disease, esophageal disorder, or unspecified esophageal condition. Causative agents may include infections, reflux, motility disorders, or inflammatory conditions. Typically affects the esophageal mucosa, muscular layers, or sphincters. It may present with dysphagia, pain, or bleeding. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment depends on underlying cause and severity.

code_desc: Disorders of oesophagus in diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Disorders of oesophagus in diseases classified elsewhere refer to oesophageal complications arising from systemic conditions not primarily classified as oesophageal diseases. Common synonyms include secondary oesophageal disorders or oesophageal manifestations of systemic illness. Causative agents may include autoimmune diseases, infections, or metabolic disorders. Typically affected body parts include the oesophagus, with possible involvement of the stomach or gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms often include dysphagia, reflux, and stricture formation. These conditions are often managed through treatment of the underlying systemic disease.

Acute gastric ulcer with hemorrhage is a sudden, severe condition characterized by the presence of an ulcer in the stomach lining accompanied by bleeding. Common synonyms include acute gastric ulceration with hematemesis or melena. It is often caused by Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or alcohol use. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum or body, and can lead to significant blood loss, hypovolemic shock, and anemia if left untreated. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications.

Acute gastric ulcer with perforation is a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease, characterized by a sudden rupture of the gastric wall, leading to peritonitis. Common synonyms include gastric perforation and acute gastric rupture. Causative agents include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol consumption. The condition primarily affects the stomach, most commonly the antrum or body. It presents with severe epigastric pain, guarding, and rebound tenderness, often requiring urgent surgical intervention.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Acute gastric ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation is a severe gastrointestinal emergency characterized by simultaneous bleeding and rupture of a gastric ulcer. Common synonyms include acute ulcerative perforation with hemorrhage and gastric ulcer complications. Causative agents include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, alcohol consumption, and stress. Typically affects the gastric antrum or body. Presents with severe epigastric pain, hematemesis, hypovolemic shock, and peritonitis. Requires immediate surgical intervention and medical management to stabilize the patient.

code_desc: Acute gastric ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Acute gastric ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation refers to a sudden development of an ulcer in the stomach lining, characterized by inflammation and erosion without bleeding or rupture. Common synonyms include acute gastritis with ulceration or erosive gastritis. Causative agents often include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), Helicobacter pylori infection, alcohol, and stress. The condition typically affects the antrum or body of the stomach, presenting with epigastric pain, nausea, and possible vomiting. It is a common gastrointestinal disorder requiring prompt evaluation and management to prevent complications.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with hemorrhage refers to a long-standing ulcer in the stomach lining that has ruptured, leading to bleeding. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer with bleeding or chronic gastric ulcer complicated by hemorrhage. Causative agents often include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol consumption. The primary affected body part is the stomach, particularly the antrum or body. Symptoms may include hematemesis, melena, and abdominal pain. Complications can lead to anemia or shock if bleeding is severe.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with perforation refers to a complication of a long-standing gastric ulcer that has eroded through the stomach wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include perforated gastric ulcer or gastric ulcer perforation. Causative agents typically include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive acid secretion. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum or body, and can lead to severe peritonitis if not promptly treated.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastric ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation refers to a severe complication of gastric ulcers characterized by persistent ulceration leading to gastrointestinal bleeding and a full-thickness tear in the stomach wall. Common synonyms include complicated gastric ulcer and perforated gastric ulcer with hemorrhage. Causative agents often include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive alcohol use. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum and body, and can lead to life-threatening peritonitis if perforation occurs.

code_desc: Chronic gastric ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Chronic gastric ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation refers to a persistent erosion in the gastric mucosa that has not progressed to bleeding or wall rupture. Common synonyms include chronic peptic ulcer and gastric ulcer disease. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) is also a significant factor. This condition typically affects the antrum or body of the stomach, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, dyspepsia, and potential complications if left untreated.

code_desc: Gastric ulcer unspecified as acute or chronic without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Gastric ulcer unspecified as acute or chronic without hemorrhage or perforation refers to an ulceration in the stomach lining that has not been classified as acute or chronic and does not involve bleeding or perforation. Common synonyms include peptic ulcer disease (PUD) of the stomach. The primary causative agents are Helicobacter pylori infection and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). This condition typically affects the antrum or body of the stomach, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, dyspepsia, and possible weight loss.

Acute duodenal ulcer with hemorrhage is a sudden onset condition characterized by erosion of the duodenal mucosa, leading to bleeding. Common synonyms include acute gastric ulcer and duodenal ulcer hemorrhage. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and stress are also significant contributors. This condition primarily affects the first part of the duodenum. Symptoms include epigastric pain, hematemesis, and melena. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt endoscopic intervention to control bleeding and prevent complications.

Acute duodenal ulcer with perforation is a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease, characterized by a full-thickness break in the duodenal wall, leading to peritonitis. Common synonyms include duodenal perforation and gastric ulcer perforation. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and stress are also implicated. This condition predominantly affects the second and third portions of the duodenum. Symptoms include severe epigastric pain, guarding, and systemic signs of infection. Prompt surgical intervention is often required to prevent morbidity and mortality.

code_desc: Acute duodenal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Acute duodenal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation is a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease, typically affecting the second or third portion of the duodenum. It involves simultaneous bleeding from the ulcer and a full-thickness tear in the duodenal wall, leading to peritonitis. Common causative agents include *Helicobacter pylori* infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Symptoms include severe epigastric pain, hematemesis, and signs of peritoneal irritation. The condition requires urgent endoscopic and surgical intervention. Synonyms include duodenal ulcer perforation with bleeding and acute duodenal ulcer complication.

code_desc: Acute duodenal ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Acute duodenal ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation refers to a sudden development of an ulcer in the duodenum, typically in the first part, without complications such as bleeding or perforation. Common synonyms include acute gastric ulcer and acute duodenal erosion. The primary causative agents are Helicobacter pylori infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). This condition predominantly affects the duodenum, with the first portion being the most commonly involved site. It is often associated with dyspepsia, epigastric pain, and may present with nausea or vomiting.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified duodenal ulcer with hemorrhage
summary: Chronic or unspecified duodenal ulcer with hemorrhage refers to a long-standing or unspecified ulcer in the duodenum that has caused bleeding. Common synonyms include duodenal ulcer with bleeding or chronic duodenal ulcer hemorrhage. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and stress can also contribute. The condition primarily affects the duodenum, particularly the second part, and may lead to complications such as anemia due to chronic blood loss.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified duodenal ulcer with perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified duodenal ulcer with perforation refers to a complication of a long-standing duodenal ulcer that has eroded through the duodenal wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include perforated duodenal ulcer and duodenal ulcer perforation. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and stress can also contribute. The condition typically affects the second or third portion of the duodenum, leading to severe abdominal pain, peritonitis, and systemic symptoms. Prompt surgical intervention is often required.

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified duodenal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified duodenal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation refers to a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease affecting the duodenum. Common synonyms include complicated duodenal ulcer and duodenal ulcer with perforation and bleeding. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though NSAID use and acid hypersecretion also contribute. This condition typically affects the second and third parts of the duodenum. Hemorrhage results from erosion into blood vessels, while perforation leads to peritonitis. Clinical presentation includes abdominal pain, hematemesis, melena, and signs of peritonitis.

code_desc: Chronic duodenal ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation

code_desc: Duodenal ulcer unspecified as acute or chronic without hemorrhage or perforation

code_desc: Acute peptic ulcer site unspecified with hemorrhage

code_desc: Acute peptic ulcer site unspecified with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Acute peptic ulcer site unspecified with both hemorrhage and perforation refers to a severe gastrointestinal condition involving the stomach or duodenum, characterized by sudden onset of ulceration complicated by bleeding and a hole in the wall. Common synonyms include acute ulcerative hemorrhage with perforation. Causative agents often include Helicobacter pylori infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). This condition typically affects the upper gastrointestinal tract, leading to symptoms such as severe abdominal pain, hematemesis, and peritonitis. Prompt medical intervention is critical to prevent life-threatening complications.

code_desc: Acute peptic ulcer site unspecified without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Acute peptic ulcer site unspecified without hemorrhage or perforation refers to a sudden inflammation of the stomach or duodenum lining, typically caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use. code_desc: Chronic or unspecified peptic ulcer site unspecified with perforation

code_desc: Chronic or unspecified peptic ulcer site unspecified with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified peptic ulcer site unspecified with both hemorrhage and perforation refers to a long-standing ulcer in the gastrointestinal tract, typically in the stomach or duodenum, complicated by both bleeding and a perforation. code_desc: Chronic peptic ulcer site unspecified without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Chronic peptic ulcer site unspecified without hemorrhage or perforation refers to a long-standing ulcer in the gastrointestinal tract, typically in the stomach or duodenum, lacking active bleeding or penetration. code_desc: Peptic ulcer site unspecified unspecified as acute or chronic without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Peptic ulcer site unspecified, acute or chronic, without hemorrhage or perforation, refers to an ulcer in the gastrointestinal tract, typically in the stomach or duodenum, caused by factors such as *Helicobacter pylori* infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). code_desc: Acute gastrojejunal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Acute gastrojejunal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation is a severe gastrointestinal emergency involving simultaneous bleeding and rupture of an ulcer in the stomach or duodenum. code_desc: Acute gastrojejunal ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Acute gastrojejunal ulcer refers to an ulceration involving the stomach and duodenum without associated bleeding or perforation. Common synonyms include acute gastric and duodenal ulcer. code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastrojejunal ulcer with hemorrhage
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastrojejunal ulcer with hemorrhage refers to a long-standing ulcer involving the stomach or duodenum, often associated with bleeding. code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastrojejunal ulcer with perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastrojejunal ulcer with perforation refers to a complication of peptic ulcer disease where a long-standing ulcer in the stomach or duodenum erodes through the wall, leading to perforation. code_desc: Chronic or unspecified gastrojejunal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation
summary: Chronic or unspecified gastrojejunal ulcer with both hemorrhage and perforation refers to a severe complication of peptic ulcer disease involving the stomach and duodenum. code_desc: Chronic gastrojejunal ulcer without hemorrhage or perforation

code_desc: Gastrojejunal ulcer unspecified as acute or chronic without hemorrhage or perforation
summary: Gastrojejunal ulcer unspecified as acute or chronic without hemorrhage or perforation refers to an ulcer located at the junction between the stomach and the jejunum, without specified duration or complications. Acute gastritis without bleeding is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining characterized by epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Common synonyms include acute gastric inflammation and acute non-bleeding gastritis. It is typically caused by infection with *Helicobacter pylori*, NSAID use, alcohol consumption, or stress. The primary affected body part is the stomach mucosa, with involvement of the gastric antrum and body. Symptoms usually resolve within days to weeks with appropriate management. Complications are rare in the absence of bleeding.

Acute gastritis with bleeding is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining characterized by sudden onset and gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include erosive gastritis and acute gastric ulceration. It is often caused by Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), alcohol, or stress. The primary affected body part is the stomach, particularly the antrum and body. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis. Complications may involve significant blood loss and anemia. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy.

Acute gastritis is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining, typically characterized by sudden onset and irritation of the gastric mucosa. Common synonyms include acute gastric inflammation and acute stomach lining inflammation. It is often caused by factors such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), alcohol, Helicobacter pylori infection, or stress. The primary affected body part is the stomach, with symptoms including epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite. The condition can lead to erosion or ulceration if left untreated.

Alcoholic gastritis without bleeding is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining caused primarily by chronic alcohol consumption. Prolonged ethanol exposure irritates and erodes the gastric mucosa, leading to inflammation. Common synonyms include alcohol-induced gastritis or ethanol gastritis. The primary causative agent is alcohol, though other factors like NSAID use may contribute. The condition typically affects the gastric mucosa, particularly the antrum and body of the stomach. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and dyspepsia, though bleeding is absent in this specific presentation.

Alcoholic gastritis with bleeding is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining caused by chronic alcohol consumption, leading to erosion and potential ulceration. Prolonged alcohol use irritates the gastric mucosa, impairing its protective mechanisms and increasing susceptibility to acid damage. This can result in gastrointestinal bleeding, often presenting as hematemesis or melena. Common synonyms include alcoholic gastritis with hemorrhage or alcohol-induced gastric ulceration. The primary causative agent is ethanol, with contributing factors such as malnutrition and concurrent use of NSAIDs. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum and body, and may involve the duodenum in severe cases.

Alcoholic gastritis is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining caused by chronic alcohol consumption. Prolonged ethanol intake irritates and erodes the gastric mucosa, leading to inflammation and potential ulceration. Common synonyms include alcohol-induced gastritis or ethanol gastritis. The primary causative agent is ethanol, which disrupts the mucosal barrier and impairs protective mechanisms. The condition predominantly affects the stomach lining, particularly the antrum and corpus. It is often associated with other gastrointestinal issues such as peptic ulcer disease and malabsorption.

Chronic superficial gastritis without bleeding is a long-standing inflammation of the gastric mucosa, primarily affecting the surface layers. It is characterized by the absence of visible bleeding in endoscopic findings. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis and non-erosive gastritis. The condition is often caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection, chronic use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or excessive alcohol consumption. It typically affects the antrum and body of the stomach, with possible involvement of the duodenum. Symptoms may include epigastric discomfort, bloating, and nausea, though many patients are asymptomatic.

Chronic superficial gastritis with bleeding is a long-standing inflammation of the gastric mucosa, primarily affecting the surface layer, often accompanied by minor bleeding. It is typically caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection, NSAID use, alcohol consumption, or autoimmune factors. The stomach is the primarily affected body part, with the antrum being a common site. Symptoms may include dyspepsia, epigastric pain, and occult blood in stool. The condition can progress to more severe forms if left untreated.

Chronic superficial gastritis is a long-standing inflammation of the gastric mucosa, primarily affecting the surface layer. It is commonly caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection, chronic use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or excessive alcohol consumption. The condition typically involves the antrum of the stomach and may present with symptoms such as dyspepsia, nausea, and epigastric pain. Synonyms include chronic gastritis and superficial gastritis. It is often asymptomatic but can progress to more severe forms if left untreated.

Chronic atrophic gastritis without bleeding is a long-term inflammatory condition characterized by the gradual loss of gastric glandular cells in the stomach lining, leading to atrophy. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis with atrophy and autoimmune gastritis. It is primarily caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection or autoimmune mechanisms. The condition predominantly affects the corpus and fundus of the stomach, leading to reduced acid production and potential vitamin B12 deficiency. It is often asymptomatic but may present with dyspepsia or anemia.

Chronic atrophic gastritis with bleeding is a long-standing inflammation of the stomach lining leading to atrophy of the gastric glands and reduced acid production. It is often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection or autoimmune mechanisms. The condition may cause chronic bleeding due to vascular malformations or erosion. Common synonyms include autoimmune gastritis and H. pylori-induced gastritis. The stomach, particularly the antrum and corpus, is typically affected. Complications may include vitamin B12 deficiency and an increased risk of gastric cancer.

Chronic atrophic gastritis is a long-term inflammatory condition characterized by the gradual loss of gastric glandular cells in the stomach lining, leading to atrophy and reduced acid production. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis with atrophy and intestinal metaplasia. It is primarily caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection, autoimmune mechanisms, and prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The condition predominantly affects the gastric body and fundus, and may progress to intestinal metaplasia or dysplasia, increasing the risk of gastric cancer.

Unspecified chronic gastritis without bleeding refers to long-standing inflammation of the gastric mucosa without evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding. Unspecified chronic gastritis with bleeding refers to long-standing inflammation of the stomach lining, characterized by the presence of bleeding. Other gastritis without bleeding refers to inflammation of the stomach lining not associated with gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include non-erosive gastritis and chronic gastritis. Other gastritis with bleeding refers to inflammation of the stomach lining not classified as erosive or Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis, accompanied by gastrointestinal bleeding. Other gastritis refers to chronic inflammation of the stomach lining not classified as specific types such as erosive or autoimmune gastritis. Gastritis unspecified without bleeding refers to inflammation of the stomach lining without evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis and non-erosive gastritis. Gastritis unspecified with bleeding refers to inflammation of the stomach lining without a specific etiology, accompanied by gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include erosive gastritis and acute gastritis with hemorrhage. The condition typically affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and melena. Gastritis unspecified refers to inflammation of the stomach lining without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis and non-specific gastritis. It is often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), alcohol consumption, or stress. The condition typically affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Duodenitis without bleeding refers to inflammation of the duodenum without associated gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include non-bleeding duodenitis and superficial duodenitis. Duodenitis with bleeding refers to inflammation of the duodenum accompanied by gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include duodenal ulcer with hemorrhage or erosive duodenitis. The condition is often caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), alcohol, or stress. Duodenitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. Common synonyms include duodenal inflammation and duodenal gastritis. Gastroduodenitis unspecified without bleeding refers to inflammation of the stomach and duodenum without evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding. Gastroduodenitis unspecified with bleeding refers to inflammation of the stomach and duodenum without a specific etiology, accompanied by gastrointestinal bleeding. Gastroduodenitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the stomach and duodenum without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis and duodenitis. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is often made through endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment focuses on symptom management and addressing underlying causes.

Functional dyspepsia is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder characterized by persistent or recurrent upper abdominal symptoms, including epigastric pain, bloating, early satiety, and nausea, without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include non-ulcer dyspepsia and indigestion. While no specific causative agent is known, it is associated with impaired gastric motility, visceral hypersensitivity, and possibly Helicobacter pylori infection. The condition primarily affects the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract, often leading to significant morbidity and reduced quality of life.

Acute dilatation of the stomach, also known as gastric distension or gastric distention, refers to a rapid and excessive expansion of the stomach cavity. This condition is often caused by obstruction of gastric emptying, such as from peptic ulcer disease, gastric tumors, or postoperative adhesions. It may also result from ingestion of air or gas. Commonly affected areas include the gastric lumen and surrounding tissues. Symptoms typically include epigastric pain, distension, nausea, and vomiting. Prompt evaluation is necessary to identify underlying causes and prevent complications such as gastric perforation or volvulus.

Adult hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a rare condition characterized by thickening of the pyloric muscle, leading to gastric outlet obstruction. It typically affects the distal stomach and proximal duodenum. Common synonyms include pyloric stenosis and gastric outlet obstruction. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy and imaging. Treatment involves endoscopic dilation or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Hourglass stricture and stenosis of stomach
summary: Hourglass stricture and stenosis of the stomach refer to a severe narrowing of the stomach, typically at the pyloric region, creating a constricting, hourglass-like appearance. This condition is often caused by chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, or malignancy. It may also result from post-surgical scarring or inflammatory processes. Common synonyms include pyloric stenosis and gastric outlet obstruction. The primary affected area is the pylorus, with secondary involvement of the duodenum. Symptoms include epigastric pain, vomiting, and weight loss. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy and imaging studies.

Pylorospasm not elsewhere classified refers to abnormal, involuntary contractions of the pyloric sphincter, leading to obstruction of gastric emptying. Common synonyms include pyloric spasm and gastric outlet obstruction. The condition may result from neuromuscular dysfunction, motility disorders, or secondary to peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, or post-surgical changes. It typically affects the pylorus, the lower part of the stomach, and may cause symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. Diagnosis is often made through endoscopy and manometry, and treatment may involve antispasmodics, prokinetics, or surgical intervention in severe cases.

Gastric diverticulum refers to a small outpouching of the gastric wall, typically occurring in the distal stomach. It is often acquired, associated with chronic vomiting or increased intraluminal pressure. Common synonyms include gastric diverticula and Zenker's diverticulum, though the latter typically affects the esophagus. Causative factors include long-term vomiting, hiatal hernia, or chronic gastritis. These diverticula most commonly occur in the gastric antrum and may lead to symptoms such as epigastric pain, bleeding, or obstruction. They are generally benign but may require surgical intervention if symptomatic.

Obstruction of the duodenum refers to a blockage in the first segment of the small intestine, impeding the passage of digestive contents from the stomach. Common synonyms include duodenal stenosis and duodenal obstruction. Causes include peptic ulcer disease, tumors, strictures, and post-surgical adhesions. It typically affects the duodenum, particularly the second part, and may lead to symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Complications can include bowel ischemia and perforation if left untreated. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies and endoscopy.

Fistula of the stomach and duodenum is an abnormal passage connecting the stomach or duodenum to another visceral structure, such as the intestine, pancreas, or bile duct. Common synonyms include gastric-enteric fistula and duodenal-enteric fistula. Causative agents often include peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, trauma, or post-surgical complications. This condition typically affects the gastric and duodenal walls, leading to symptoms like leakage of gastric contents, infection, and malnutrition. It is more common in the duodenum, particularly at the bulb, and may present with abdominal pain, weight loss, and signs of peritonitis.

Polyps of the stomach and duodenum are abnormal growths that arise from the mucosal lining, typically benign. Common synonyms include gastric polyps and duodenal polyps. They are often classified as hyperplastic, adenomatous, or fundic gland polyps. Hyperplastic polyps are frequently associated with chronic gastritis and Helicobacter pylori infection. Adenomatous polyps carry a risk of malignant transformation. These lesions most commonly affect the stomach body and the duodenal bulb. While many are asymptomatic, they may cause bleeding or obstruction. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy and histopathological examination.

Angiodysplasia of the stomach and duodenum refers to abnormal vascular malformations in the gastrointestinal tract, typically involving dilated, fragile blood vessels. Common synonyms include vascular malformations, telangiectases, and angiectatic lesions. The condition is often associated with chronic blood loss, leading to iron deficiency anemia. While the exact cause is unknown, it is linked to factors such as aging, chronic hypertension, and certain medications like NSAIDs. It most commonly affects the distal stomach and duodenum, with lesions appearing as small, red, vascular protrusions.

code_desc: Dieulafoy lesion (hemorrhagic) of stomach and duodenum
summary: Dieulafoy lesion is a rare, acute, life-threatening condition characterized by a submucosal arterial channel that protrudes through the gastric or duodenal mucosa, leading to sudden, severe bleeding. Common synonyms include arteriovenous malformation and vascular ectasia. The exact cause is unknown, though it may involve congenital vascular anomalies or mucosal trauma. It typically affects the stomach, particularly the greater curvature, and the duodenum, especially the second and third parts. The condition is more common in older adults and those with a history of NSAID use or peptic ulcer disease.

Achlorhydria is a condition characterized by the absence or significant reduction of hydrochloric acid in gastric juice. It results from impaired function of the parietal cells in the stomach. Common synonyms include hypochlorhydria and achlorhydria. Causes include chronic atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, long-term use of proton pump inhibitors, and surgical removal of the stomach. The primary affected body part is the stomach, with potential complications such as malabsorption, nutrient deficiencies, and increased risk of gastrointestinal infections.

Gastroparesis is a condition characterized by delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction. It results in impaired stomach motility, leading to symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, bloating, and early satiety. Common synonyms include delayed gastric emptying and diabetic gastroparesis. Known causes include diabetes mellitus, postviral syndromes, neurological disorders like Parkinson’s disease, and certain medications. It primarily affects the stomach, with secondary impacts on the gastrointestinal tract. The condition is more common in older adults and can significantly affect quality of life.

code_desc: Other diseases of stomach and duodenum
summary: "Other diseases of stomach and duodenum" refers to conditions affecting the stomach and duodenum not classified as ulcers, cancers, or infections. Common synonyms include gastritis, duodenitis, and functional disorders. Causative agents may include NSAIDs, alcohol, stress, or autoimmune factors. These conditions typically affect the stomach, small intestine, and colon, presenting with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and vomiting. Indeterminate colitis refers to chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by symptoms and endoscopic findings that do not clearly distinguish between ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Common synonyms include unclassified colitis or indeterminate inflammatory bowel disease. The exact causative agents are unknown, though genetic and immune factors are implicated. It typically affects the colon and rectum, with variable involvement of the terminal ileum. Diagnosis relies on clinical, endoscopic, histological, and imaging features due to the overlapping presentation with other inflammatory bowel diseases.

Eosinophilic gastritis or gastroenteritis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteropathy and eosinophilic enteritis. The condition is often associated with allergic reactions, parasitic infections, or hypersensitivity to food antigens. It primarily affects the stomach and small intestine, though the duodenum and colon may also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and malabsorption. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopic biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration. Treatment may include corticosteroids, dietary modifications, and elimination of allergens.

Eosinophilic colitis is an inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of eosinophils into the colon mucosa. It may present with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and eosinophilic colonic inflammation. The condition can be idiopathic or secondary to allergic reactions, parasitic infections, or drug-induced causes. It primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the rectum and sigmoid colon. In some cases, it may be associated with systemic eosinophilia or other allergic disorders.

Microscopic colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease characterized by chronic, non-bloody diarrhea. It is diagnosed via histopathology showing crypt architecture abnormalities without gross inflammation. Common synonyms include collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis. The condition is primarily caused by an immune-mediated response, though specific pathogens like *Clostridioides difficile* or viral agents may contribute. It predominantly affects the large intestine, particularly the colon, and is more common in middle-aged to elderly individuals.

code_desc: Other specified noninfective gastroenteritis and colitis
summary: Other specified noninfective gastroenteritis and colitis refers to gastrointestinal inflammation not caused by infectious agents, with a specific etiology not otherwise specified. Common synonyms include unspecified noninfectious colitis and noninfectious gastroenteritis. Causative agents may include medications, food intolerances, autoimmune conditions, or radiation. Typically affects the small intestine and colon, presenting with symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and inflammation. It is often diagnosed when no specific cause is identified despite thorough evaluation.

code_desc: Other specified noninfective gastroenteritis and colitis
summary: Other specified noninfective gastroenteritis and colitis refers to inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract not caused by infectious agents. It encompasses a range of disorders with overlapping symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and inflammation. Common synonyms include noninfectious colitis and inflammatory bowel disease variants. Causative agents may include medications, autoimmune responses, or dietary factors. Typically affects the colon and small intestine, with inflammation leading to mucosal damage. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic evaluation and biopsy.

Noninfective gastroenteritis and colitis unspecified refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract without an infectious cause. It encompasses a range of conditions affecting the stomach and colon. Common synonyms include acute noninfectious colitis and gastroenteritis. Causative agents may include medications, food intolerances, autoimmune disorders, or ischemia. Typically, the stomach, small intestine, and colon are affected. Symptoms often include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and cramping. The condition is diagnosed when infectious causes are ruled out through appropriate testing.

Acute reversible ischemia of the small intestine is a sudden reduction in blood flow to the small bowel, leading to tissue hypoxia and potential necrosis. Common synonyms include mesenteric ischemia and acute intestinal infarction. Causative agents include emboli, thrombosis, hypotension, or vasospasm. The condition primarily affects the jejunum and ileum. It is often associated with underlying cardiovascular disease or hypercoagulable states. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent irreversible damage and complications such as perforation or sepsis.

Acute infarction of the small intestine, also known as acute mesenteric infarction or intestinal ischemia, occurs when there is a sudden reduction or cessation of blood flow to a segment of the small intestine, leading to tissue death. Common causes include embolism, thrombosis, or vasospasm, often originating from the heart or atherosclerotic vessels. The ileum is most commonly affected, though any part of the small intestine may be involved. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent complications such as perforation and sepsis.

Acute (reversible) ischemia of the large intestine refers to a sudden reduction in blood flow to a segment of the colon, leading to tissue hypoxia without permanent damage. Common synonyms include acute colonic ischemia and acute mesenteric ischemia. Causative agents often include emboli, thrombosis, or hypoperfusion due to cardiovascular disease. The sigmoid colon and rectum are most commonly affected. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, and altered bowel habits. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent progression to necrosis.

Acute infarction of the large intestine, also known as acute colonic infarction or ischemic colitis, is a severe condition characterized by sudden loss of blood flow to a segment of the colon, leading to tissue necrosis. It is commonly caused by embolism, thrombosis, or hypoperfusion. The sigmoid colon and rectum are most frequently affected. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, distension, and bloody diarrhea. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as perforation and sepsis.

code_desc: Acute (reversible) ischemia of intestine part unspecified
summary: Acute (reversible) ischemia of the intestine refers to a sudden reduction in blood flow to a portion of the intestine, leading to temporary oxygen deprivation. Common synonyms include acute mesenteric ischemia and acute intestinal ischemia. Causative agents often include emboli, thrombosis, or hypotension. This condition typically affects the small intestine, though the large intestine may also be involved. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent irreversible damage and complications such as necrosis.

code_desc: Acute infarction of intestine part unspecified
summary: Acute infarction of the intestine, unspecified, refers to a sudden loss of blood flow to a portion of the intestine, leading to tissue death. Common synonyms include acute intestinal infarction and bowel infarction. Causative agents often involve embolism, thrombosis, or reduced perfusion. Typically affects the small or large intestine, with the terminal ileum and sigmoid colon being most commonly involved. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, distension, and bowel dysfunction. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as perforation and sepsis.

Acute vascular disorders of the intestine refer to sudden disruptions in blood flow to the gastrointestinal tract, leading to ischemia and potential necrosis. Common synonyms include acute mesenteric ischemia and acute intestinal infarction. Causative agents often involve embolism, thrombosis, or hypoperfusion, frequently originating from cardiac sources or atherosclerosis. These conditions predominantly affect the small intestine, though the colon may also be involved. Clinical presentation typically includes severe abdominal pain, distension, and bowel dysfunction. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent irreversible damage and mortality.

Chronic vascular disorders of the intestine refer to long-term conditions affecting the blood vessels within the gastrointestinal tract, leading to impaired blood flow and tissue damage. Common synonyms include chronic mesenteric ischemia and ischemic bowel disease. These disorders are often caused by atherosclerosis, thrombosis, or embolism, which reduce blood supply to the intestines. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the colon may also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal pain, weight loss, and postprandial discomfort. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications such as bowel necrosis.

Angiodysplasia of the colon without hemorrhage refers to abnormal vascular malformations in the colonic submucosa that do not currently cause bleeding. Common synonyms include colonic vascular ectasia and angiectasia. The exact cause is often unknown, though age-related degenerative changes, chronic inflammation, and vascular malformations are implicated. It typically affects the distal colon, particularly the rectum and sigmoid colon. While asymptomatic, it may predispose to gastrointestinal bleeding if the vessels rupture. No specific causative agent is identified, but risk factors include advanced age and conditions like chronic heart failure or coagulopathy.

Angiodysplasia of the colon with hemorrhage refers to abnormal vascular malformations in the colonic mucosa that predispose to recurrent, often painless gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include colonic angiodysplasia and acquired diverticular angiodysplasia. The condition is associated with aging, chronic hypertension, and possibly genetic factors. It typically affects the distal colon, especially the splenic flexure. Hemorrhage is usually intermittent and may lead to anemia. No specific causative agent is identified, but risk factors include long-standing constipation and use of anticoagulants.

Angiodysplasia of the colon is a condition characterized by abnormal development of blood vessels in the colonic mucosa, leading to recurrent episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include colonic angiodysplasia and acquired submucosal telangiectasia. The exact cause is often unknown, though factors such as chronic hypertension, atherosclerosis, and age-related vascular changes are implicated. It predominantly affects the distal colon, particularly the splenic flexure, and is more common in older adults. The primary clinical manifestation is painless hematochezia, which can lead to iron deficiency anemia.

Necrotizing enterocolitis unspecified is a severe intestinal disorder characterized by inflammation and necrosis of the bowel, primarily affecting premature infants. It typically involves the small intestine, though the large intestine may also be affected. Common synonyms include necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and necrotizing enterocolitis of unspecified site. Known causative agents include bacterial overgrowth, hypoxia, and necrotizing infections. The condition is associated with prematurity, feeding intolerance, and sepsis. It can lead to perforation, peritonitis, and multiorgan failure if not promptly treated.

Stage 1 necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is an acute intestinal inflammation primarily affecting preterm infants, characterized by bowel necrosis and systemic inflammation. Common synonyms include necrotizing enterocolitis stage I and early NEC. Causative agents include bacterial overgrowth, hypoxia, and prematurity. It typically involves the distal small intestine, with symptoms such as abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, and bloody stools. Early diagnosis is critical to prevent progression to more severe stages.

Stage 2 necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a severe intestinal disorder characterized by inflammation and tissue death, primarily affecting the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include necrotizing enterocolitis stage II and intermediate NEC. It is often caused by bacterial overgrowth, prematurity, and intestinal ischemia. The condition typically affects the distal small intestine and colon, with potential complications such as perforation and sepsis. Clinical features include abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, and bloody stools. It is most commonly seen in preterm infants, though can occur in full-term neonates under certain conditions.

Stage 3 necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a severe intestinal infection primarily affecting premature infants, characterized by extensive necrosis of the bowel wall, perforation, and systemic inflammation. Common synonyms include severe NEC and fulminant NEC. Causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Clostridium* species. The condition typically affects the distal small intestine and large bowel, leading to complications such as sepsis, peritonitis, and multiorgan failure. It is a life-threatening condition requiring urgent surgical intervention.

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a severe intestinal disorder primarily affecting premature infants. It involves inflammation and necrosis of the bowel, often leading to perforation. Common synonyms include necrotizing enterocolitis of the newborn and neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis. Causative agents include bacterial overgrowth, hypoxia, and formula feeding. The condition typically affects the distal small intestine, with involvement of the colon in some cases. Risk factors include prematurity, infection, and poor placental perfusion. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent mortality and long-term complications.

Other vascular disorders of the intestine refer to conditions affecting the blood vessels supplying the gastrointestinal tract, leading to ischemia or infarction. Common synonyms include intestinal ischemia and mesenteric vascular disease. Causative agents may include emboli, thrombosis, or vasculitis. These disorders typically affect the small intestine, with the terminal ileum being most commonly involved. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and bowel necrosis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies and angiography. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as perforation and sepsis.

Vascular disorder of intestine unspecified refers to abnormal blood flow in the intestinal vessels without a specific diagnosis. It encompasses conditions like mesenteric ischemia or thrombosis. Common synonyms include mesenteric vascular disease and intestinal circulatory disorder. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, embolism, or vasculitis. Typically affects the small intestine, sometimes the large intestine. Symptoms include abdominal pain, bleeding, and bowel infarction. Diagnosis often requires imaging and angiography. Treatment depends on underlying cause and may involve surgery or anticoagulation.

Paralytic ileus is a condition characterized by the temporary absence of peristalsis in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to bowel obstruction without mechanical blockage. Common synonyms include adynamic ileus and intestinal atony. It is often caused by surgical interventions, electrolyte imbalances, infections, or systemic illnesses such as diabetes or sepsis. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the large intestine may also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, and absence of bowel sounds. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical findings and imaging studies. Treatment focuses on correcting underlying causes and supportive care.

Intussusception is a condition in which a segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment, leading to obstruction and potential ischemia. Common synonyms include ileocolic intussusception and intestinal invagination. It is most commonly caused by viral infections, lymphoid hyperplasia, or benign tumors. The ileum and cecum are the most frequently affected areas. It predominantly affects infants and young children, typically under 2 years of age. Symptoms include intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and the passage of currant jelly stool. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as bowel necrosis.

Volvulus is a condition characterized by the twisting of a loop of intestine upon itself, leading to obstruction and potential ischemia. Common synonyms include intestinal volvulus and bowel volvulus. It is often caused by congenital malformations such as malrotation, or acquired factors like adhesions or tumors. The most commonly affected areas are the cecum, sigmoid colon, and small intestine. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and bowel obstruction. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as necrosis and perforation.

Gallstone ileus is a rare complication of cholelithiasis characterized by the passage of a gallstone into the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly causing an intestinal obstruction. It typically occurs in elderly patients with a history of biliary disease. The stone often lodges in the terminal ileum, leading to partial or complete bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include "gallstone obstruction" or "cholelithiasis with intestinal obstruction." Known causative agents include cholesterol and pigment stones. The condition primarily affects the small intestine, particularly the terminal ileum, and may also involve the colon. Complications include bowel ischemia and perforation if not promptly treated.

Fecal impaction is a severe constipation condition characterized by the accumulation of hardened stool in the rectum or colon, leading to bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include rectal impaction and chronic constipation with fecal mass. It is often caused by prolonged use of laxatives, neurological disorders, or reduced physical activity. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the rectum, and can lead to complications such as bowel incontinence, fecal incontinence, or intestinal perforation if left untreated.

"Other impaction of intestine" refers to the mechanical obstruction of the gastrointestinal tract not caused by tumors, strictures, or adhesions. Common synonyms include intestinal obstruction due to foreign bodies or masses. Causative agents may include ingested foreign objects, fecal impaction, or intussusception. This condition typically affects the small or large intestine, often presenting with symptoms such as abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. It is more common in children and elderly patients with altered bowel function. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications like bowel ischemia or perforation.

"Other impaction of intestine" refers to the mechanical obstruction of the gastrointestinal tract due to the accumulation of non-organic material, such as stool, foreign bodies, or masses. Common synonyms include intestinal obstruction from non-organic causes or fecal impaction. Causative agents may include dietary factors, neuromuscular disorders, or structural abnormalities. It typically affects the colon, particularly in the sigmoid or rectal regions, and can lead to symptoms like abdominal pain, distension, constipation, and vomiting. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies and clinical evaluation.

code_desc: Intestinal adhesions [bands] unspecified as to partial versus complete obstruction
summary: Intestinal adhesions [bands] unspecified as to partial versus complete obstruction refer to abnormal fibrous bands that form between intra-abdominal structures, potentially causing bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include adhesions, intra-abdominal adhesions, and post-surgical adhesions. Causative agents often include prior abdominal surgery, infection, inflammation, or trauma. These adhesions typically affect the small intestine and colon, with the small bowel being most commonly involved. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, distension, and bowel obstruction, though severity varies depending on adhesion extent and location.

Intestinal adhesions, also known as adhesion bands, are fibrous bands of tissue that form between abdominal organs and the peritoneum, often leading to partial intestinal obstruction. Common synonyms include intra-abdominal adhesions and post-surgical adhesions. Causative agents include prior abdominal surgery, infection, inflammation, or trauma. These adhesions most commonly affect the small intestine, particularly the ileum, and may involve the colon. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and alternating constipation and diarrhea. Diagnosis is typically made through imaging or laparoscopy.

Intestinal adhesions with complete obstruction refer to the formation of fibrous bands between abdominal organs or tissues, leading to a total blockage of the intestinal lumen. Common synonyms include adhesions with bowel obstruction and intestinal strictures. Causative agents often include prior abdominal surgery, infection, inflammation, or trauma. This condition typically affects the small intestine, particularly the ileum, and can also involve the colon. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and distension. It is a serious complication requiring prompt medical evaluation and intervention.

Intestinal adhesions [bands] with obstruction (postinfection) refer to the formation of fibrous bands between abdominal organs, often following infection, leading to bowel obstruction. Common synonyms include postinfectious adhesions and secondary intestinal obstruction. Causative agents may include bacterial or viral infections, such as typhoid fever or appendicitis. Typically affecting the small intestine, these adhesions can cause partial or complete blockage, resulting in symptoms like abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting. The condition is more common in women and can lead to complications such as bowel ischemia or perforation if left untreated.

Unspecified intestinal obstruction refers to a blockage in the gastrointestinal tract where the specific cause or location is not identified. Common synonyms include nonspecific intestinal obstruction or undetermined intestinal obstruction. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, hernias, or inflammatory conditions. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the large intestine may also be involved. Symptoms typically include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Diagnosis often requires imaging studies such as X-ray or CT scan to determine the extent and cause of the obstruction.

Other intestinal obstruction refers to a blockage in the gastrointestinal tract not caused by a specific identifiable lesion such as a tumor, volvulus, or hernia. It is often idiopathic or secondary to generalized conditions. Common synonyms include non-specific intestinal obstruction and generalized bowel obstruction. Causative agents may include electrolyte imbalances, neurogenic disorders, or systemic diseases. It typically affects the small intestine and can lead to symptoms like abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. The condition may be associated with motility disorders or inflammatory processes. Diagnosis often involves imaging and clinical evaluation.

Other and unspecified intestinal obstruction refers to a blockage in the intestines caused by an unspecified or unknown etiology. Common synonyms include mechanical bowel obstruction and ileus. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, hernias, or foreign bodies. It typically affects the small intestine, though the large intestine can also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Diagnosis is often made through imaging studies such as X-rays or CT scans. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve bowel rest, fluids, and surgical intervention if necessary.

Ileus unspecified refers to a generalized lack of peristalsis in the intestines, leading to bowel obstruction without a specific identifiable cause. Common synonyms include paralytic ileus and adynamic ileus. It is often caused by postoperative factors, electrolyte imbalances, medications such as opioids, or systemic illnesses like sepsis. The small intestine is typically affected, though the large intestine may also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, and absence of bowel sounds. Diagnosis is usually made clinically, and management focuses on correcting underlying causes and supportive care.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of small intestine with perforation and abscess without bleeding
summary: Diverticulitis of the small intestine with perforation and abscess without bleeding is an inflammatory condition characterized by the rupture of diverticula in the small bowel, leading to peritonitis and localized abscess formation. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulitis and perforated diverticulitis. Causative agents are primarily *Escherichia coli* and other gram-negative bacteria. The condition typically affects the ileum, with complications such as perforation and abscess formation occurring in the peritoneal cavity. It is less common than colonic diverticulitis but can present with severe abdominal pain, fever, and systemic inflammation.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of small intestine with perforation and abscess with bleeding
summary: Diverticulitis of the small intestine with perforation and abscess with bleeding is a severe complication of diverticular disease, characterized by inflammation, rupture, and infection of diverticula in the small bowel. This condition often leads to peritonitis, abscess formation, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulitis with perforation and abscess. Causative agents typically include *Escherichia coli* and other gram-negative bacteria. The ileum is most commonly affected, though any segment of the small intestine may be involved. Complications such as sepsis and intestinal obstruction may occur.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of small intestine with perforation and abscess
summary: Diverticulitis of the small intestine with perforation and abscess refers to the inflammation and infection of diverticula in the small bowel, leading to perforation and formation of an abscess. It is less common than colonic diverticulitis. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulitis and enteric perforation with abscess. Causative agents often include *Escherichia coli* and other gram-negative bacteria. The condition typically affects the ileum and is associated with complications such as peritonitis and sepsis. It is more prevalent in older adults and those with underlying bowel disease.

code_desc: Diverticulosis of small intestine without perforation or abscess without bleeding
summary: Diverticulosis of the small intestine refers to the formation of diverticula, which are small, abnormal pouches in the intestinal wall, typically arising from weak points in the muscular layer. This condition is less common than diverticulosis of the colon and often asymptomatic. It is more frequently observed in the ileum. Common synonyms include intestinal diverticulosis and small bowel diverticulosis. The exact cause is not fully understood, but factors such as increased intraluminal pressure and weak areas in the bowel wall are implicated. It may be associated with conditions like Crohn’s disease or chronic constipation. The small intestine, particularly the ileum, is the most commonly affected site. Complications such as perforation or bleeding are rare in this form.

code_desc: Diverticulosis of small intestine without perforation or abscess with bleeding
summary: Diverticulosis of the small intestine without perforation or abscess with bleeding refers to the presence of diverticula in the small bowel, typically in the ileum, without complications such as perforation or abscess formation. It is often associated with chronic constipation and increased intraluminal pressure. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulosis and ileal diverticulosis. Known causative factors include chronic straining during defecation and a low-fiber diet. Bleeding is a common presenting symptom, though often occult. The condition predominantly affects the ileum and is more common in older adults.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of small intestine without perforation or abscess without bleeding
summary: Diverticulitis of the small intestine without perforation or abscess refers to inflammation of diverticula in the small bowel, typically occurring in the distal ileum. It is less common than colonic diverticulitis and often presents with abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulitis and ileal diverticulitis. The condition is associated with factors like chronic constipation, low fiber diet, and aging. Causative agents are primarily related to increased intraluminal pressure, though specific pathogens are rarely identified. It typically affects the terminal ileum and is more prevalent in older adults.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of small intestine without perforation or abscess with bleeding
summary: Diverticulitis of the small intestine without perforation or abscess with bleeding refers to inflammation of diverticula in the small bowel, typically involving the ileum, without complications such as perforation or abscess formation. It may present with abdominal pain, bleeding, and systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include small bowel diverticulitis and ileal diverticulitis. The condition is often associated with increased intraluminal pressure, though causative agents are not well-defined. It is more common in older adults and may be linked to dietary factors and chronic constipation.

code_desc: Diverticular disease of small intestine without perforation or abscess
summary: Diverticular disease of the small intestine, also known as small bowel diverticulosis, refers to the formation of diverticula in the walls of the small intestine. Unlike the more common colonic diverticulosis, this condition is less frequent and typically occurs in the duodenum or jejunum. It is often asymptomatic but can cause complications such as obstruction or bleeding. Known causative factors include increased intraluminal pressure, weakened intestinal walls, and chronic constipation. While no specific pathogen is implicated, it is associated with age-related degeneration of the muscularis propria. The condition is rarely complicated by perforation or abscess, distinguishing it from more severe forms of diverticular disease.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of large intestine with perforation and abscess without bleeding
summary: Diverticulitis of the large intestine with perforation and abscess without bleeding refers to an acute inflammation of colonic diverticula leading to bowel wall perforation and localized abscess formation. Common synonyms include perforated diverticulitis and complicated diverticulitis. The condition is primarily caused by increased intraluminal pressure leading to weakened colonic wall rupture. It most commonly affects the sigmoid colon. Known causative agents include *Escherichia coli* and other gram-negative bacteria. Complications may involve peritonitis or sepsis if not promptly treated.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of large intestine with perforation and abscess with bleeding
summary: Diverticulitis of the large intestine with perforation and abscess with bleeding is a severe complication of diverticulitis, characterized by perforation of diverticula leading to peritonitis, abscess formation, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include perforated diverticulitis and complicated diverticulitis. Causative agents are typically *Escherichia coli* and other gastrointestinal pathogens. The condition most commonly affects the sigmoid colon, with potential spread to adjacent structures. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, fever, and hematochezia. Complications may involve sepsis and bowel obstruction.

code_desc: Diverticulitis of large intestine with perforation and abscess
