code_desc: Toxic liver disease with chronic persistent hepatitis
summary: Toxic liver disease with chronic persistent hepatitis is a condition characterized by prolonged liver inflammation due to exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis and toxic chronic hepatitis. Causative agents often include medications such as acetaminophen, alcohol, and certain herbal supplements. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Long-term exposure can lead to fibrosis, though cirrhosis is less common compared to other forms of chronic liver disease.

code_desc: Toxic liver disease with chronic lobular hepatitis
summary: Toxic liver disease with chronic lobular hepatitis is a condition characterized by persistent inflammation of the liver lobules, often resulting from prolonged exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury and chronic toxic hepatitis. Causative agents include medications such as acetaminophen, alcohol, and certain herbal supplements. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic effects in severe cases. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Chronic progression can lead to fibrosis or cirrhosis if left untreated.

code_desc: Toxic liver disease with chronic active hepatitis without ascites
summary: Toxic liver disease with chronic active hepatitis without ascites refers to a progressive liver inflammation caused by exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis and chemical hepatitis. Causative agents often include medications such as acetaminophen, alcohol, and certain herbs. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to necrosis and fibrosis. It may present with symptoms like jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. Ascites is typically absent, distinguishing it from more advanced cirrhotic stages. The disease can progress to cirrhosis if left untreated.

code_desc: Toxic liver disease with chronic active hepatitis with ascites
summary: Toxic liver disease with chronic active hepatitis and ascites refers to progressive liver inflammation caused by prolonged exposure to hepatotoxic substances, leading to fibrosis and impaired function. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury and chronic hepatitis with ascites. Causative agents include alcohol, certain medications, and toxins. The condition primarily affects the liver, with ascites indicating fluid accumulation in the abdominal cavity due to portal hypertension. It may also involve the biliary system and lead to systemic complications.

code_desc: Toxic liver disease with chronic active hepatitis
summary: Toxic liver disease with chronic active hepatitis is a condition characterized by prolonged inflammation and damage to the liver, often resulting from exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis and toxic hepatitis. Causative agents may include medications (e.g., acetaminophen, anticonvulsants), alcohol, and certain chemicals. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic involvement. Clinical features include jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatic necrosis. Chronic progression can lead to fibrosis and cirrhosis if left untreated.

code_desc: Toxic liver disease with hepatitis not elsewhere classified
summary: Toxic liver disease with hepatitis not elsewhere classified refers to liver inflammation caused by exposure to toxic substances, excluding other specific hepatitis types. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis and chemical hepatitis. Causative agents often include medications (e.g., acetaminophen, anticonvulsants), industrial chemicals, and herbal supplements. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to hepatocellular injury, elevated liver enzymes, and potentially fulminant hepatic failure. It may also involve the biliary system and, in severe cases, systemic effects. Early diagnosis and removal of the toxin are critical for recovery.

code_desc: Toxic liver disease with fibrosis and cirrhosis of liver
summary: Toxic liver disease with fibrosis and cirrhosis refers to progressive liver damage caused by exposure to hepatotoxic substances, leading to fibrous scarring and eventual cirrhosis. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury and toxic hepatitis. Causative agents include alcohol, certain medications (e.g., acetaminophen, antitubercular drugs), industrial chemicals, and herbal supplements. The liver is the primary affected organ, with systemic complications such as portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy often developing as the disease progresses.

code_desc: Toxic liver disease with other disorders of liver
summary: Toxic liver disease with other disorders of liver refers to liver injury caused by exposure to toxic substances, often in conjunction with other liver abnormalities. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury and hepatotoxicity. Causative agents may include medications, alcohol, industrial chemicals, and herbal supplements. The liver is the primary affected organ, but systemic effects can occur. Symptoms may include jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatic failure. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, laboratory tests, and exclusion of other liver diseases. Management focuses on removing the toxin and supporting liver function.

Toxic liver disease unspecified refers to liver injury caused by exposure to exogenous substances, where the specific toxin is not identified. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury and chemical liver damage. Causative agents may include medications, herbal supplements, industrial chemicals, and environmental toxins. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms often include jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatic dysfunction. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation and exclusion of other liver diseases.

code_desc: Acute and subacute hepatic failure without coma
summary: Acute and subacute hepatic failure without coma refers to rapid or subacute loss of liver function, characterized by elevated serum enzymes and bilirubin, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy, though without coma. Common synonyms include acute-on-chronic liver failure and subacute liver failure. Causative agents include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B, C), drug toxicity (e.g., acetaminophen, NSAIDs), autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic involvement. It is distinct from fulminant hepatic failure due to the absence of coma.

code_desc: Acute and subacute hepatic failure with coma
summary: Acute and subacute hepatic failure with coma is a severe, life-threatening condition characterized by rapid loss of liver function leading to hepatic encephalopathy and altered mental status. Common synonyms include fulminant hepatic failure and acute-on-chronic liver failure. Causative agents include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B, C), drug toxicity (e.g., paracetamol overdose), autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with systemic complications affecting the brain, circulatory system, and kidneys. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to improve outcomes.

Acute and subacute hepatic failure refers to rapid loss of liver function, occurring over days to weeks. It is characterized by jaundice, coagulopathy, and hepatic encephalopathy. Common synonyms include acute liver failure and subacute liver failure. Causative agents include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B, C), drug toxicity (e.g., acetaminophen overdose), autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic disorders. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential systemic complications affecting the brain, kidneys, and circulatory system.

Chronic hepatic failure without coma refers to progressive and irreversible loss of liver function over months to years, without the development of hepatic encephalopathy. Common synonyms include end-stage liver disease and decompensated cirrhosis. Causative agents often include chronic viral hepatitis (B, C), alcoholic liver disease, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential complications involving the gastrointestinal tract, coagulation system, and renal function.

Chronic hepatic failure with coma refers to advanced liver dysfunction leading to encephalopathy and loss of consciousness. It results from prolonged liver damage, often due to cirrhosis, hepatitis, or drug toxicity. Common synonyms include hepatic encephalopathy and terminal liver failure. The condition primarily affects the liver, but systemic complications involve the brain, kidneys, and circulatory system. Symptoms include confusion, altered mental status, and metabolic disturbances. It is a life-threatening complication requiring immediate medical intervention.

Chronic hepatic failure refers to progressive and irreversible loss of liver function over time, leading to systemic complications. Common synonyms include chronic liver failure and end-stage liver disease. It is often caused by long-term alcohol abuse, viral hepatitis (especially B and C), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, but dysfunction can lead to ascites, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and hepatic encephalopathy. Other systems may be impacted due to systemic effects of liver failure.

Hepatic failure unspecified without coma refers to severe liver dysfunction without evidence of hepatic encephalopathy. It involves impaired liver function leading to systemic effects such as coagulopathy, ascites, and jaundice. Common synonyms include acute liver failure and decompensated cirrhosis. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis, drug toxicity, alcoholic liver disease, and metabolic disorders. The liver is primarily affected, with potential involvement of the biliary system and systemic organs due to toxin accumulation and metabolic derangements.

Hepatic failure unspecified with coma refers to a severe impairment of liver function leading to altered mental status and unconsciousness, without a specific etiology identified. Common synonyms include acute liver failure with encephalopathy and hepatic coma. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis, drug overdose, alcohol abuse, or metabolic disorders. The condition primarily affects the liver, but systemic complications such as cerebral edema and coagulopathy can occur. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention.

Hepatic failure unspecified refers to acute or chronic loss of liver function without a specific identifiable cause. It may present with jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and fluid retention. Common synonyms include acute liver failure and decompensated cirrhosis. Causative agents can include viral hepatitis, drug toxicity, alcohol abuse, or metabolic disorders. Typically affects the liver, but may involve the kidneys, brain, and circulatory system due to systemic complications. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other specific liver diseases.

code_desc: Chronic persistent hepatitis not elsewhere classified
summary: Chronic persistent hepatitis not elsewhere classified refers to a long-standing inflammatory liver condition with persistent elevation of liver enzymes, not attributable to specific viral hepatitis or other defined etiologies. Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis of unspecified origin. Causative agents may include autoimmune factors, metabolic disorders, or environmental toxins. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and hepatic dysfunction. Diagnosis typically involves elevated ALT/AST levels and exclusion of other causes.

code_desc: Chronic lobular hepatitis not elsewhere classified
summary: Chronic lobular hepatitis not elsewhere classified refers to persistent inflammation of the liver parenchyma, primarily affecting the lobular architecture, with no specific etiology identified. Common synonyms include chronic non-alcoholic hepatitis and chronic cryptogenic hepatitis. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis C), autoimmune conditions, metabolic disorders, or prolonged exposure to toxins. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential systemic manifestations. Diagnosis is typically made when other causes of chronic hepatitis are excluded.

code_desc: Chronic active hepatitis not elsewhere classified
summary: Chronic active hepatitis not elsewhere classified refers to persistent inflammation of the liver with active parenchymal damage, not attributable to specific viral hepatitis types. Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis with active inflammation. Causative agents may include autoimmune factors, drugs, toxins, or unknown origins. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential systemic involvement. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and hepatic dysfunction. Diagnosis typically involves liver biopsy and exclusion of other hepatitis types. It is associated with progressive fibrosis and risk of cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.

code_desc: Other chronic hepatitis not elsewhere classified
summary: Other chronic hepatitis not elsewhere classified refers to persistent liver inflammation of unknown or unspecified etiology. Common synonyms include undetermined chronic hepatitis and unspecified chronic hepatitis. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis not classified elsewhere, autoimmune factors, or metabolic disorders. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and potential cirrhosis. It is typically diagnosed when specific causes such as hepatitis B or C, alcohol use, or autoimmune hepatitis are excluded. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes.

Chronic hepatitis unspecified refers to long-term inflammation of the liver of unknown etiology. Common synonyms include chronic liver inflammation, unspecified. Known causative agents may include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B or C), autoimmune disorders, metabolic diseases, or prolonged alcohol use. Typically affects the liver, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis often requires exclusion of other specific causes. It is a broad category used when the exact cause cannot be determined.

Hepatic fibrosis unspecified refers to the abnormal accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins in the liver, leading to scar formation without a specific etiology. Common synonyms include non-specific liver fibrosis or unspecified liver scarring. Causative agents may include chronic viral hepatitis, alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune conditions. The liver is the primary affected organ, with fibrosis progressing to cirrhosis if left untreated. Clinically, it may present with elevated liver enzymes, portal hypertension, or systemic symptoms. Diagnosis typically involves imaging or biopsy.

Hepatic fibrosis early fibrosis refers to the initial stage of liver scarring caused by chronic injury. It is characterized by the accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins, primarily collagen, in response to persistent inflammation or damage. Common synonyms include compensated cirrhosis and early-stage liver fibrosis. Causative agents include viral hepatitis (B and C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with fibrosis typically beginning in the periphery and progressing toward the central vein. Early detection is crucial to prevent progression to cirrhosis.

Hepatic fibrosis advanced fibrosis refers to the late stage of liver scarring, characterized by extensive deposition of extracellular matrix leading to architectural distortion. Common synonyms include cirrhosis and severe fibrosis. Causative agents include chronic viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic complications such as portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent progression to liver failure.

Hepatic fibrosis is a progressive scarring of liver tissue resulting from chronic injury, leading to impaired liver function. Common synonyms include cirrhosis and hepatic sclerosis. It is typically caused by long-term exposure to hepatitis B or C, alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic complications may arise. Early stages may be asymptomatic, but advanced fibrosis can lead to portal hypertension, ascites, and liver failure. Diagnosis often involves imaging, blood tests, and biopsy.

Hepatic sclerosis, also known as cirrhosis, is a late-stage liver disease characterized by replacement of healthy liver tissue with fibrous scar tissue, leading to impaired liver function. Common causes include chronic alcohol abuse, viral hepatitis (B and C), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune disorders. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to complications such as portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. It typically involves the hepatic parenchyma and can progress to liver failure if left untreated.

Hepatic fibrosis with hepatic sclerosis refers to advanced scarring of liver tissue due to chronic injury, leading to loss of functional liver cells and replacement by fibrous tissue. Common synonyms include cirrhosis and late-stage fibrosis. Causative agents include chronic viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential complications affecting the cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and renal systems. This condition significantly impairs liver function and can lead to liver failure.

Primary biliary cirrhosis, also known as primary biliary cholangitis, is a chronic, progressive liver disease characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts. This leads to cholestasis, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis. The exact cause is unknown, though autoimmune mechanisms are implicated. It predominantly affects middle-aged women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 9:1. The liver is the primary affected organ, with bile duct damage leading to impaired bile flow and subsequent hepatic dysfunction. Complications include portal hypertension, malabsorption, and increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

Secondary biliary cirrhosis is a progressive liver disease resulting from prolonged bile duct obstruction, leading to liver damage and fibrosis. Common synonyms include biliary cirrhosis and cholestatic cirrhosis. It is most commonly caused by chronic biliary obstruction, such as from gallstones, strictures, or parasitic infections. The condition primarily affects the liver, with fibrosis and nodular regeneration of hepatic tissue. It may also lead to complications like portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. The gallbladder and bile ducts are typically involved in the pathogenesis. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent irreversible liver damage.

Biliary cirrhosis unspecified refers to advanced liver scarring resulting from prolonged bile duct damage, leading to impaired bile flow. It is a form of chronic liver disease characterized by progressive fibrosis and nodular regeneration. Common synonyms include primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) and biliary cirrhosis. Causative agents are often autoimmune, infectious, or metabolic, though the exact cause may be unknown. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential involvement of the gallbladder and bile ducts. Symptoms may include jaundice, pruritus, and fatigue.

Unspecified cirrhosis of the liver refers to end-stage liver disease characterized by diffuse fibrosis and nodular regeneration of liver tissue, with the underlying cause not clearly identified. Common synonyms include cryptogenic cirrhosis. Known causative agents may include chronic hepatitis, alcohol abuse, metabolic disorders, or prolonged liver injury. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic complications affecting other organs. This diagnosis is typically made when no specific etiology can be definitively established despite thorough evaluation.

Other cirrhosis of liver refers to liver scarring resulting from causes not classified under specific types such as alcoholic or viral cirrhosis. It encompasses a variety of etiologies including metabolic disorders, autoimmune conditions, and prolonged exposure to toxins. Common synonyms include unspecified cirrhosis and non-alcoholic/non-viral cirrhosis. Causative agents may include genetic disorders like hemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, or prolonged drug use. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic complications affecting other organs due to liver dysfunction.

code_desc: Other and unspecified cirrhosis of liver
summary: Other and unspecified cirrhosis of liver refers to advanced scarring of the liver tissue resulting from unknown or unspecified causes. It is a late-stage liver disease characterized by nodular regeneration of liver tissue and impaired function. Common synonyms include unspecified cirrhosis and undetermined cirrhosis. Causative agents may include chronic alcohol abuse, viral hepatitis, metabolic disorders, or prolonged exposure to toxins. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic complications affecting other organs. This condition is typically diagnosed when the specific etiology cannot be definitively identified.

An abscess of the liver is a localized collection of pus within the liver parenchyma, typically resulting from bacterial infection. Common synonyms include hepatic abscess and pyogenic liver abscess. The most common causative agents are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella species, and Bacteroides, often originating from contiguous infections such as cholangitis or portal vein thrombosis. Other causes include hematogenous spread from distant infections. The liver is the primary affected organ, though abscesses may occasionally involve adjacent structures like the diaphragm or peritoneum. Clinical presentation often includes fever, right upper quadrant pain, and systemic signs of infection.

Phlebitis of the portal vein refers to inflammation of the portal vein, often leading to thrombosis. It is commonly associated with infections, malignancies, or hypercoagulable states. Synonyms include portal vein thrombophlebitis and portal vein inflammation. Causative agents may include bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Staphylococcus, as well as conditions like cirrhosis or pancreatic cancer. The condition primarily affects the portal venous system, potentially leading to complications such as portal hypertension and liver dysfunction.

Nonspecific reactive hepatitis is an inflammatory liver condition of unknown etiology, often presenting with mild elevations in liver enzymes. Common synonyms include viral hepatitis of undetermined origin and subclinical hepatitis. While no specific pathogen is identified, it may follow viral infections, medications, or toxins. The liver is the primary affected organ, with inflammation typically limited to the parenchyma. Symptoms are usually nonspecific, including fatigue, malaise, and mild jaundice. It is generally self-limiting and does not progress to chronic disease.

Granulomatous hepatitis not elsewhere classified is a rare inflammatory liver condition characterized by the formation of granulomas, which are small collections of immune cells. It is not classified under other specific hepatitis types. Common synonyms include granulomatous liver disease and idiopathic granulomatous hepatitis. Causative agents may include infections such as tuberculosis, fungal infections, or mycobacteria, as well as autoimmune disorders or drug reactions. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic involvement can occur. Diagnosis often requires histopathological examination and exclusion of other causes.

Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic inflammatory liver disease caused by immune-mediated attack on liver cells. It is characterized by elevated liver enzymes, hypergammaglobulinemia, and interface hepatitis on biopsy. Common synonyms include autoimmune liver disease and type 1 autoimmune hepatitis. The condition is associated with genetic predisposition and environmental triggers, though specific causative agents are not well defined. It predominantly affects women and typically involves the liver, with potential progression to cirrhosis if untreated.

Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a chronic liver disease characterized by hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and hepatocellular injury in the absence of significant alcohol consumption. Common synonyms include nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) with advanced features. The condition is associated with metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, and obesity. Causative agents include excess caloric intake, sedentary lifestyle, and genetic predisposition. Typically, the liver is affected, with potential progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.

Other specified inflammatory liver diseases refer to liver inflammation not classified under more specific categories such as hepatitis or autoimmune liver disease. Common synonyms include unspecified or undiagnosed inflammatory liver conditions. Causative agents may include drugs, toxins, infections, or metabolic disorders. These conditions typically affect the liver, with possible involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms often include elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is usually made by exclusion of other known liver diseases.

Other specified inflammatory liver diseases refer to chronic liver inflammation not classified under more specific conditions like hepatitis or autoimmune liver disease. Common synonyms include unspecified chronic hepatitis and non-A to non-E hepatitis. Causative agents may include viral infections, toxins, drugs, or metabolic disorders. These conditions primarily affect the liver, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potential cirrhosis. They are often diagnosed when specific etiologies are excluded. The disease can also involve the biliary system and may present with symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes.

Inflammatory liver disease unspecified refers to liver inflammation of unknown origin or unspecified etiology. It may present with symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. Common synonyms include non-specific hepatitis and undifferentiated hepatitis. Causative agents are often not identified, though viral hepatitis, autoimmune disorders, and drug-induced liver injury may be potential contributors. The liver is the primary affected organ, with possible involvement of the biliary system. Diagnosis typically involves elevated liver enzymes and imaging studies. Treatment is directed at managing symptoms and addressing underlying causes when identified.

code_desc: Fatty (change of) liver not elsewhere classified
summary: Fatty liver not elsewhere classified refers to the accumulation of fat in liver cells in the absence of a specific diagnosis such as alcoholic liver disease or viral hepatitis. Common synonyms include non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) when alcohol use is not a factor. Causative agents may include obesity, insulin resistance, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and excessive alcohol consumption. The liver is the primary affected organ, with fat deposition leading to inflammation and potential progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis. It is typically asymptomatic but can present with elevated liver enzymes.

Chronic passive congestion of the liver, also known as congestive hepatopathy or hepatic venous congestion, results from prolonged obstruction of hepatic blood flow, typically due to right-sided heart failure or superior vena cava syndrome. This leads to accumulation of blood in the liver sinusoids, causing enlargement and fibrosis. Commonly affected areas include the hepatic parenchyma, with possible involvement of the spleen and gastrointestinal tract. Synonyms include congestive liver disease and portal hypertension-related hepatic congestion. The condition is often associated with cardiovascular disorders and can progress to cirrhosis if untreated.

Central hemorrhagic necrosis of the liver is a severe form of hepatic necrosis characterized by coagulative necrosis with hemorrhage, primarily affecting the central regions of the liver. It is often associated with ischemia, drug toxicity, or sepsis. Common synonyms include central necrosis and coagulative necrosis. Causative agents include ethanol, drugs like acetaminophen, and infectious agents such as hepatitis viruses. The condition typically affects the liver parenchyma, leading to impaired function and potential liver failure.

Infarction of the liver, also known as hepatic infarction or liver necrosis due to vascular occlusion, occurs when there is a sudden blockage of blood flow to a portion of the liver, leading to tissue death. Common causes include embolism, thrombosis, or severe hypotension. This condition typically affects the parenchyma of the liver, most commonly the right lobe due to its vascular anatomy. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, and elevated liver enzymes. It is a rare but serious complication, often associated with conditions like atrial fibrillation or coagulopathy.

Peliosis hepatis is a rare condition characterized by the presence of multiple blood-filled cystic spaces within the liver parenchyma. Common synonyms include hepatic peliosis and cavernous hemangioma-like lesion. It is primarily caused by chronic hepatitis C virus infection, but other agents such as HIV, immunosuppressive drugs, and certain toxins may also contribute. The liver is the most commonly affected organ, though involvement of other organs is rare. Clinically, it may present with abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and in severe cases, liver failure. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging and histopathological examination.

Hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD), also known as sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), is a condition characterized by obstruction of the hepatic sinusoids, leading to increased portal pressure and liver dysfunction. It commonly occurs following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, chemotherapy, or exposure to toxins. Causative agents include chemotherapeutic agents like busulfan and cyclophosphamide, as well as viral infections and certain medications. The primary affected body part is the liver, with associated symptoms such as hepatomegaly, ascites, and jaundice.

Portal hypertension is a condition characterized by elevated pressure in the portal venous system, primarily due to obstructed blood flow through the liver. Common synonyms include portal venous hypertension and increased portal pressure. It is most commonly caused by cirrhosis, but can also result from thrombosis, schistosomiasis, or congenital anomalies. The condition typically affects the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract, leading to complications such as esophageal varices, ascites, and splenomegaly.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional renal failure occurring in advanced liver disease, particularly cirrhosis. It is characterized by progressive renal dysfunction without underlying kidney disease. Common synonyms include hepatorenal failure and cirrhotic renal failure. Causative agents include portal hypertension, systemic vasodilation, and reduced effective arterial blood volume. The condition primarily affects the liver and kidneys, with systemic manifestations involving the circulatory system. It is a life-threatening complication associated with ascites and hepatic encephalopathy.

Hepatopulmonary syndrome is a condition characterized by abnormal pulmonary vasodilation secondary to liver disease, leading to intrapulmonary shunting and hypoxemia. Common synonyms include hepatic pulmonary syndrome and portopulmonary hypertension. It is typically caused by cirrhosis, often due to chronic hepatitis, alcohol abuse, or non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. The primary affected body parts are the liver and lungs, with clinical manifestations including dyspnea, cyanosis, and reduced oxygen saturation. The syndrome is associated with portal hypertension and impaired hepatic clearance of vasoactive substances.

"Other specified diseases of liver" refers to liver conditions not classified under more specific categories such as hepatitis or cirrhosis. Common synonyms include unspecified liver disease and other liver disorders. Causative agents may include toxins, infections, or metabolic disorders. These conditions typically affect the liver parenchyma, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, or functional impairment. They may present with symptoms such as jaundice, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis often requires imaging, blood tests, and clinical evaluation.

"Other specified diseases of liver" refers to liver conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as hepatitis or cirrhosis. Common synonyms include unspecified liver disease or undifferentiated liver disorder. Causative agents may include toxins, infections, or metabolic disorders. These conditions typically affect the liver parenchyma, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, or dysfunction. They may present with symptoms like jaundice, ascites, or hepatic encephalopathy. Diagnosis often requires imaging, biopsy, or laboratory tests to identify underlying causes.

Liver disease unspecified refers to a broad category of liver disorders where the specific diagnosis cannot be determined. It may encompass various conditions such as hepatitis, cirrhosis, or fatty liver disease. Common synonyms include undiagnosed liver disease or unspecified hepatic disorder. Causative agents may include viral infections, alcohol abuse, metabolic disorders, or autoimmune conditions. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic effects on metabolism, coagulation, and detoxification processes. This diagnosis is often used when clinical findings are non-specific or when further testing is pending.

code_desc: Liver disorders in diseases classified elsewhere
summary: "Liver disorders in diseases classified elsewhere" refers to hepatic complications arising from systemic conditions not primarily classified as liver diseases. Common synonyms include secondary liver involvement or hepatic manifestations of systemic illness. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., HIV, hepatitis B/C), autoimmune diseases, metabolic disorders, or malignancies. Typically affected body parts include the liver, but may also involve the biliary system and gastrointestinal tract. These disorders often present with elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, or hepatic dysfunction, necessitating a comprehensive evaluation of the underlying condition.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis without obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis without obstruction refers to inflammation of the gallbladder caused by the presence of gallstones, though bile flow is not physically blocked. Common synonyms include acute cholecystitis with gallstones and non-obstructive cholecystitis. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or pigment stones. This condition typically affects the gallbladder, often in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. It is more common in females, particularly those over 40 years of age, and may present with epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis with obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis and obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) in the gallbladder causing inflammation and blockage of the cystic duct. This leads to infection and impaired bile flow. Common synonyms include acute cholecystitis with stone disease. Causative agents are primarily cholesterol and pigment stones. The condition typically affects the gallbladder and may involve the bile ducts. It is more common in females, particularly those over 40 years of age, and is associated with obesity, rapid weight loss, and a history of previous gallstones.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) in the gallbladder, leading to inflammation. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with acute inflammation. The condition is primarily caused by cholesterol or bilirubin stones. It typically affects the gallbladder, often resulting in pain in the upper right abdomen, fever, and nausea. Complications may involve the bile ducts or surrounding tissues. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, and a family history of gallstones.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with chronic cholecystitis without obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with chronic cholecystitis without obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder accompanied by long-standing inflammation of the gallbladder wall, without bile duct blockage. Common synonyms include gallstone disease and chronic cholecystitis. Causative agents are primarily cholesterol and bilirubin stones. The condition typically affects the gallbladder, with potential complications such as gallbladder wall thickening and fibrosis. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and often asymptomatic until complications arise.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with chronic cholecystitis with obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with chronic cholecystitis and obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) in the gallbladder, leading to chronic inflammation (cholecystitis) and blockage of the cystic duct. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with chronic inflammation and biliary obstruction. Causative agents include cholesterol, bilirubin, and calcium salts. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder and may extend to the bile ducts, causing complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and often presents with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and fever.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute and chronic cholecystitis without obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute and chronic cholecystitis without obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder accompanied by inflammation, both acute and chronic, without bile duct blockage. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with cholecystitis. Causative agents are primarily cholesterol and bilirubin stones. The gallbladder is the primarily affected organ, with inflammation often extending to surrounding tissues. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, and nausea, though obstruction is absent in this specific presentation.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with acute and chronic cholecystitis with obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with acute and chronic cholecystitis with obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) leading to inflammation of the gallbladder. Acute cholecystitis is characterized by sudden onset, fever, right upper quadrant pain, and possible obstruction of the cystic duct. Chronic cholecystitis results from prolonged inflammation, often with fibrosis and reduced gallbladder function. Common causative agents include cholesterol and bilirubin stones. Typically affects the gallbladder, with potential extension to surrounding structures like the liver or bile ducts. Synonyms include gallstone disease with cholecystitis and biliary obstruction.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis without obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis without obstruction refers to inflammation of the gallbladder associated with the presence of gallstones, but without bile duct blockage. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with cholecystitis and calculous cholecystitis. Causative agents are primarily cholesterol and bilirubin stones. The condition typically affects the gallbladder, with inflammation potentially spreading to adjacent structures. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and often presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis with obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis and obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) in the gallbladder accompanied by inflammation (cholecystitis) and blockage of bile flow, typically due to stone impaction in the cystic duct. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with cholecystitis and biliary obstruction. Causative agents include cholesterol, bilirubin, and pigment stones. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder and may involve the bile ducts, leading to complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and often presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder with other cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones (cholelithiasis) in the gallbladder accompanied by inflammation (cholecystitis). Common synonyms include gallstone disease with gallbladder inflammation. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or bilirubin stones. This condition typically affects the gallbladder, often leading to complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and may present with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis without obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis without obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder without accompanying inflammation or bile duct blockage. Common synonyms include gallstone disease, cholesterolosis, or biliary sludge. Causative agents typically involve cholesterol supersaturation, leading to stone formation. This condition predominantly affects the gallbladder, with stones often composed of cholesterol. It may be asymptomatic or present with intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort. No acute inflammation or obstructive symptoms are present.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis with obstruction
summary: Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis with obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder that cause blockage of the cystic duct or common bile duct, leading to biliary obstruction, but without accompanying gallbladder inflammation. Common synonyms include gallstone disease with obstruction and biliary obstruction without cholecystitis. Causative agents include cholesterol, bilirubin, and calcium salts. The condition typically affects the gallbladder and bile ducts, often leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and jaundice.

Calculus of gallbladder without cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder without accompanying inflammation. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis and gallstone disease. The primary causative agents are cholesterol, bilirubin, and calcium salts. This condition typically affects the gallbladder, with stones forming in the gallbladder lumen. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and may be asymptomatic or present with intermittent biliary colic. Complications such as choledocholithiasis or pancreatitis can occur if stones migrate.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with cholangitis unspecified without obstruction
summary: Calculus of bile duct with cholangitis unspecified without obstruction refers to the presence of a bile duct stone accompanied by inflammation of the bile ducts, without evidence of physical blockage. Common synonyms include bile duct stone with cholangitis and choledocholithiasis with cholangitis. Causative agents often include bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus. The condition typically affects the bile ducts, particularly the common bile duct, and may involve the liver and gallbladder. It is associated with symptoms like abdominal pain, fever, and jaundice.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with cholangitis unspecified with obstruction
summary: Calculus of bile duct with cholangitis unspecified and obstruction refers to the presence of a bile duct stone causing inflammation of the bile ducts and blockage of bile flow. Common synonyms include choledocholithiasis with cholangitis. Causative agents are primarily gallstones, often originating from the gallbladder. The condition typically affects the bile ducts, including the common hepatic and common bile duct. It can lead to complications such as sepsis, liver dysfunction, and pancreatitis if left untreated.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with acute cholangitis without obstruction
summary: Calculus of bile duct with acute cholangitis without obstruction refers to an inflammatory condition of the bile ducts caused by the presence of bile stones, despite the absence of physical blockage. Common synonyms include acute cholangitis without biliary obstruction and calculous cholangitis. The condition is typically caused by bacterial infection, often involving *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Enterococcus* species. It primarily affects the bile ducts, particularly the common hepatic and common bile duct, leading to symptoms such as fever, abdominal pain, and jaundice.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with acute cholangitis with obstruction
summary: Calculus of bile duct with acute cholangitis and obstruction refers to the presence of a gallstone in the bile duct causing inflammation and blockage of the biliary system. Common synonyms include choledocholithiasis with cholangitis. The condition is typically caused by gallstones (cholelithiasis) that migrate from the gallbladder into the common bile duct. It most commonly affects the common bile duct and can lead to complications such as ascending cholangitis, liver dysfunction, and sepsis. The obstruction leads to bile stasis, bacterial overgrowth, and subsequent inflammation. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent severe morbidity.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with chronic cholangitis without obstruction
summary: Calculus of bile duct with chronic cholangitis without obstruction refers to the presence of gallstones in the bile ducts accompanied by long-standing inflammation of the bile ducts, without evidence of bile flow blockage. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis with chronic cholangitis and biliary calculus disease. Causative agents include bacteria such as *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Pseudomonas*, often associated with ascending cholangitis. The condition primarily affects the bile ducts, including the common hepatic and common bile duct, and may involve the gallbladder. It is more common in individuals with prior biliary tract infections or structural abnormalities.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with chronic cholangitis with obstruction
summary: Calculus of bile duct with chronic cholangitis and obstruction is a condition characterized by the presence of bile stones in the bile ducts, leading to persistent inflammation and blockage of bile flow. Common synonyms include choledocholithiasis with cholangitis. Causative agents include gallstones formed from cholesterol or bilirubin. The condition typically affects the bile ducts, including the common hepatic and common bile duct, and may lead to complications such as cholangiocarcinoma or liver damage. It is more prevalent in individuals with prior biliary tract disease or gallstone history.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with acute and chronic cholangitis without obstruction

It is associated with high morbidity and mortality due to systemic inflammatory response syndrome and multi-organ failure.

Idiopathic acute pancreatitis is an inflammation of the pancreas of unknown cause, characterized by sudden onset of severe abdominal pain, often radiating to the back. Common synonyms include acute pancreatitis of unknown etiology. While no specific causative agent is identified, possible contributors may include gallstones, alcohol use, or hypertriglyceridemia. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of surrounding structures such as the bile duct and stomach. It typically presents with elevated pancreatic enzymes and systemic inflammatory response.

code_desc: Biliary acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection
summary: Biliary acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas triggered by gallstones or biliary sludge obstructing the pancreatic duct. Common synonyms include gallstone pancreatitis and obstructive pancreatitis. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or pigment stones in the bile duct. The condition typically affects the head of the pancreas and may present with epigastric pain radiating to the back. It is often associated with cholecystitis and may lead to systemic inflammation without progression to necrosis or infection. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated serum amylase and lipase levels, and imaging such as ultrasound or CT.

code_desc: Biliary acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis
summary: Biliary acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas triggered by bile duct obstruction, most commonly due to gallstones. It leads to pancreatic necrosis without evidence of infection. Common synonyms include acute calculous pancreatitis and biliary pancreatitis. The primary affected areas are the pancreas and surrounding abdominal structures. Causative agents include gallstones, biliary sludge, and sometimes biliary tract abnormalities. Symptoms typically include severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Complications may involve fluid collections or pseudocysts.

code_desc: Biliary acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis
summary: Biliary acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis is a severe form of pancreatitis caused by gallstones obstructing the pancreatic duct, leading to inflammation and necrosis of pancreatic tissue. Infected necrosis occurs when the necrotic tissue becomes colonized by bacteria, often from the gut. Common synonyms include acute calculous pancreatitis with sepsis. Causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Enterococcus* species. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, with potential spread to adjacent organs such as the peritoneum and bile ducts. It is associated with high morbidity and mortality.

Biliary acute pancreatitis is an inflammation of the pancreas caused by obstruction of the common bile duct, most commonly due to gallstones. It presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Common synonyms include acute calculous pancreatitis. Causative agents primarily involve gallstones, though cholangitis or biliary stricture may also contribute. The condition predominantly affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of the liver and gastrointestinal tract. It is more prevalent in middle-aged individuals, particularly women. Complications may include pseudocysts, infection, or systemic inflammatory response syndrome.

code_desc: Alcohol induced acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection
summary: Alcohol induced acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by excessive alcohol consumption. It typically presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Common synonyms include alcoholic pancreatitis and ethanol-induced pancreatitis. The primary causative agent is alcohol, though other factors may contribute. The pancreas is the main affected organ, with inflammation occurring in the acinar and ductal cells. This condition usually resolves without complications, but prompt management is essential to prevent progression.

code_desc: Alcohol induced acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis
summary: Alcohol induced acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis is a severe inflammatory condition of the pancreas caused primarily by excessive alcohol consumption. It is characterized by necrosis of pancreatic tissue without evidence of infection. Common synonyms include alcoholic pancreatitis and ethanol-induced pancreatitis. Causative agents are primarily ethanol, though other factors may contribute. The pancreas is the main affected organ, with potential involvement of surrounding tissues such as the stomach and duodenum. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, nausea, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. Complications may include pseudocysts and systemic inflammation.

code_desc: Alcohol induced acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis
summary: Alcohol induced acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis is a severe form of pancreatitis caused by alcohol consumption, leading to pancreatic inflammation and necrosis complicated by infection. Common synonyms include alcoholic pancreatitis with sepsis and necrotizing pancreatitis. Causative agents primarily involve ethanol, though other toxins may contribute. The pancreas is the main affected organ, with potential spread to adjacent tissues and the bloodstream. It is characterized by severe abdominal pain, fever, and systemic inflammation, often requiring intensive care and surgical intervention.

Alcohol induced acute pancreatitis is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by excessive alcohol consumption. It is characterized by severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. Common synonyms include alcoholic pancreatitis or ethanol-induced pancreatitis. The primary causative agent is alcohol, though it may also occur in conjunction with gallstones. The pancreas is the main affected organ, with potential involvement of the surrounding abdominal structures. It typically presents as a self-limiting condition but can lead to complications such as pseudocysts or necrosis.

code_desc: Drug induced acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection
summary: Drug induced acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by medication, typically presenting with epigastric pain radiating to the back. Common synonyms include drug-related acute pancreatitis and medication-induced pancreatitis. Causative agents often include antibiotics (e.g., azathioprine, valproic acid), antineoplastics, and corticosteroids. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with no evidence of tissue death or microbial involvement. It is a reversible condition, often resolving with drug discontinuation and supportive care.

code_desc: Drug induced acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis
summary: Drug induced acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis is a severe inflammatory condition of the pancreas caused by medications, leading to pancreatic tissue death without infection. Common synonyms include drug-induced necrotizing pancreatitis. Causative agents include antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin, clarithromycin), antifungals (e.g., amphotericin B), and others like valproic acid and corticosteroids. The pancreas is typically affected, with necrosis often involving the head and body. Symptoms include severe epigastric pain, nausea, and elevated amylase/lipase levels. Complications may include pseudocysts and systemic inflammatory response syndrome.

code_desc: Drug induced acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis
summary: Drug induced acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis is a severe form of pancreatitis caused by medications that trigger pancreatic inflammation and subsequent necrosis, which becomes infected. Common synonyms include drug-induced necrotizing pancreatitis. Causative agents include antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin, clarithromycin), antifungals (e.g., amphotericin B), and chemotherapy drugs (e.g., 5-fluorouracil). The pancreas is typically affected, with necrosis extending to surrounding tissues, leading to systemic complications.

Drug induced acute pancreatitis is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by medications. Common synonyms include medication-induced or pharmacologic pancreatitis. Causative agents include thiazide diuretics, azathioprine, valproic acid, and corticosteroids. It typically affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of surrounding structures. Symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. The condition can range from mild to severe, with complications such as pseudocysts or systemic inflammation. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and laboratory findings. Prompt discontinuation of the offending drug is critical for recovery.

code_desc: Other acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection
summary: Other acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection refers to a sudden inflammation of the pancreas that does not involve tissue death or bacterial infection. Common synonyms include mild acute pancreatitis and non-severe acute pancreatitis. Causative agents often include gallstones, alcohol use, hypertriglyceridemia, and medications. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with inflammation typically confined to the gland. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. This condition is generally less severe than acute pancreatitis with necrosis or infection and often resolves with supportive care.

code_desc: Other acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis
summary: Other acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis refers to a severe form of acute pancreatitis characterized by pancreatic necrosis without evidence of infection. Common synonyms include necrotizing pancreatitis and severe acute pancreatitis. Causative agents often include gallstones, alcohol use, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypercalcemia. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of surrounding tissues such as the peripancreatic fat and retroperitoneum. It is associated with systemic inflammation and may lead to complications like pseudocysts, organ failure, and fluid collections.

code_desc: Other acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis
summary: Other acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis is a severe form of pancreatitis characterized by the presence of infected pancreatic necrosis. It typically follows an initial episode of acute pancreatitis, leading to tissue death and subsequent bacterial infection. Common causative agents include gallstones and alcohol use. The infection can spread to surrounding tissues, affecting the abdominal cavity and potentially leading to systemic complications. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, but adjacent structures such as the peritoneum and retroperitoneum may also be involved. Synonyms include infected necrotizing pancreatitis and necrotizing pancreatitis with infection.

Other acute pancreatitis refers to inflammation of the pancreas not classified as gallstone or alcohol-related. It encompasses various etiologies such as hypertriglyceridemia, medications, infections, or trauma. Common synonyms include idiopathic or miscellaneous acute pancreatitis. Causative agents may include certain drugs like azathioprine or valproic acid, as well as systemic diseases. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the surrounding abdominal structures. Symptoms typically include severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis involves imaging and laboratory tests to identify underlying causes.

code_desc: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection unspecified
summary: Acute pancreatitis without necrosis or infection unspecified refers to sudden inflammation of the pancreas without evidence of tissue death or infection. Common synonyms include acute interstitial pancreatitis and mild acute pancreatitis. Causative agents often include gallstones, alcohol use, hypertriglyceridemia, and medications. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of surrounding structures such as the abdomen. Symptoms typically include severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. It is usually diagnosed through clinical presentation and imaging studies.

code_desc: Acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis unspecified
summary: Acute pancreatitis with uninfected necrosis unspecified refers to sudden inflammation of the pancreas characterized by necrotic tissue damage without evidence of infection. Common synonyms include acute necrotizing pancreatitis. Causative agents often include gallstones, alcohol use, hypertriglyceridemia, and medications. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of surrounding abdominal organs. Symptoms typically include severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. Complications may involve fluid collections, pseudocysts, or systemic inflammatory response syndrome.

code_desc: Acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis unspecified
summary: Acute pancreatitis with infected necrosis unspecified refers to a severe form of acute pancreatitis where necrotic tissue in the pancreas becomes infected, though the specific organism is not identified. Common synonyms include infected pancreatic necrosis and necrotizing pancreatitis. Causative agents often include gallstones, alcohol abuse, hypertriglyceridemia, and trauma. The condition primarily affects the pancreas but can involve adjacent structures such as the peritoneum, retroperitoneum, and sometimes the liver or spleen. It is associated with systemic inflammation and may lead to multi-organ failure if not managed promptly.

Acute pancreatitis unspecified refers to sudden inflammation of the pancreas without a clearly identified cause. Common synonyms include acute pancreatitis, unspecified etiology. Causative agents may include gallstones, alcohol use, hyperlipidemia, medications, or infections. The condition typically affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of surrounding tissues such as the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms often include severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt evaluation and management to prevent complications.

Alcohol-induced chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disorder of the pancreas caused by long-term alcohol consumption. It leads to irreversible structural damage, including fibrosis and calcification. Common synonyms include alcoholic pancreatitis and chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis. The primary causative agent is ethanol, though genetic and environmental factors may contribute. The pancreas is the main affected organ, with potential complications involving the gastrointestinal tract, bile ducts, and surrounding tissues. Symptoms include abdominal pain, malabsorption, and diabetes mellitus.

Other chronic pancreatitis refers to long-term inflammation of the pancreas not caused by gallstones or alcohol. It may result from genetic factors, autoimmune processes, or recurrent acute episodes. Common synonyms include idiopathic and non-alcoholic chronic pancreatitis. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, leading to fibrosis, enzyme deficiency, and potential diabetes. It can also cause pain, malabsorption, and pancreatic duct abnormalities. Causative agents may include hereditary disorders like cystic fibrosis or mutations in the PRSS1 or SPINK1 genes. The disease typically involves the exocrine and endocrine pancreas, with complications such as steatorrhea and pancreatic insufficiency.

A pancreatic cyst is a fluid-filled sac that develops within the pancreas. Common synonyms include pancreatic pseudocyst and serous cystadenoma. These cysts are typically caused by pancreatitis, trauma, or congenital factors. They most commonly occur in the body or tail of the pancreas. Pseudocysts are non-neoplastic and often result from acute or chronic pancreatitis, while cystadenomas are neoplastic and may be benign or malignant. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, or digestive issues, depending on the cyst's size and location.

Pseudocyst of the pancreas is a fluid-filled cavity that forms in the pancreas following acute or chronic pancreatitis. It lacks a distinct epithelial lining and is surrounded by fibrous tissue. Common synonyms include pancreatic pseudocyst and exocrine pancreatic pseudocyst. Causative agents include alcohol abuse, gallstone disease, trauma, and hyperlipidemia. Typically affecting the head or body of the pancreas, pseudocysts may cause abdominal pain, nausea, and obstruction. They can resolve spontaneously or require drainage or surgical intervention.

Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) is a disorder characterized by inadequate secretion of digestive enzymes from the pancreas, leading to malabsorption of nutrients. Common synonyms include pancreatic insufficiency and maldigestion syndrome. It is most commonly caused by chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or pancreatic surgery. The condition primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in symptoms such as steatorrhea, weight loss, and abdominal pain. Malabsorption can also impact the liver and intestines, leading to systemic complications. Diagnosis typically involves fecal elastase testing.

"Other specified diseases of pancreas" refers to pancreatic conditions that do not fit into more specific categories such as pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer. Common synonyms include unspecified pancreatic disorders. Causative agents may include autoimmune factors, infections like mumps or tuberculosis, or metabolic disorders. These conditions typically affect the exocrine or endocrine pancreas, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, malabsorption, or endocrine dysfunction. Diagnosis often requires imaging and laboratory tests.

"Other specified diseases of pancreas" refers to pancreatic conditions not classified under more specific categories such as pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer. Common synonyms include unspecified pancreatic disease or other pancreatic disorders. Causative agents may include autoimmune processes, infections, or metabolic factors. These conditions typically affect the exocrine or endocrine function of the pancreas, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, malabsorption, or diabetes. They may involve the pancreas itself or its ductal system, with variable involvement of surrounding structures.

Disease of pancreas unspecified refers to pancreatic conditions where the specific diagnosis remains undetermined despite clinical evaluation. Common synonyms include unspecified pancreatic disorder or undiagnosed pancreatic disease. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune factors, or metabolic disturbances, though exact causes are often unclear. This condition typically affects the pancreas, potentially leading to complications such as inflammation, dysfunction, or hormonal imbalances. It may present with symptoms like abdominal pain, jaundice, or digestive issues, but diagnosis is challenging without further testing.

code_desc: Disorders of gallbladder biliary tract and pancreas in diseases classified elsewhere
summary: Disorders of gallbladder, biliary tract, and pancreas in diseases classified elsewhere refer to conditions affecting these organs that are categorized under other primary diagnoses. Common synonyms include biliary and pancreatic complications. Causative agents may include gallstones, infections, or systemic diseases. Typically affected body parts include the gallbladder, bile ducts, and pancreas. These disorders often present with symptoms like abdominal pain, jaundice, and digestive issues. They are frequently associated with underlying conditions such as diabetes or autoimmune diseases.

Celiac disease is a chronic autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals. It primarily affects the small intestine, causing inflammation and damage to the intestinal villi, which impairs nutrient absorption. Common synonyms include celiac sprue and nontropical sprue. The causative agent is gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. Symptoms may include gastrointestinal issues, malnutrition, and extraintestinal manifestations. The disease predominantly affects the gastrointestinal tract but can also involve the liver, pancreas, and nervous system. Diagnosis typically involves serological testing and biopsy.

Tropical sprue is a malabsorption disorder primarily affecting the small intestine, particularly the jejunum. It is characterized by chronic inflammation and villous atrophy, leading to impaired nutrient absorption. Common synonyms include tropical enteropathy and tropical malabsorption. The exact cause is not fully understood, but it is associated with bacterial overgrowth, particularly *Campylobacter jejuni*, and environmental factors. It predominantly affects individuals in tropical regions, with symptoms such as diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia. The condition is often responsive to antibiotics and vitamin supplementation.

code_desc: Blind loop syndrome not elsewhere classified
summary: Blind loop syndrome not elsewhere classified refers to the abnormal retention of intestinal contents in a dilated, non-functioning segment of the gastrointestinal tract, leading to bacterial overgrowth. Common synonyms include small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and intestinal stasis. Causative agents are often related to structural abnormalities such as strictures, adhesions, or surgical alterations. The condition primarily affects the small intestine, particularly the jejunum and ileum, and can result in malabsorption, diarrhea, and nutritional deficiencies.

Pancreatic steatorrhea is a condition characterized by the presence of excess fat in feces due to impaired pancreatic enzyme secretion, leading to malabsorption. Common synonyms include fatty stools and steatorrhea. It is most commonly caused by chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or pancreatic duct obstruction. The primary affected body parts are the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the small intestine, where fat digestion and absorption occur. Symptoms include oily, foul-smelling stools, weight loss, and abdominal discomfort. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool analysis and imaging studies.

Non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS) is a condition characterized by gastrointestinal and extraintestinal symptoms following gluten ingestion, in the absence of celiac disease or wheat allergy. Common symptoms include bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fatigue, and headache. Synonyms include gluten intolerance and non-celiac gluten sensitivity. The causative agent is gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. While the exact mechanism is unclear, it is believed to involve immune and gut-related factors. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, with possible involvement of the nervous system and muscles. Diagnosis is based on symptom improvement after gluten withdrawal.

code_desc: Malabsorption due to intolerance not elsewhere classified
summary: Malabsorption due to intolerance not elsewhere classified refers to impaired nutrient absorption caused by non-specific intolerance mechanisms, not attributable to a specific known disorder. Common synonyms include non-specific malabsorption and undiagnosed malabsorption. Causative agents may include dietary sensitivities, enzyme deficiencies, or unknown factors. Typically affects the small intestine, leading to symptoms like diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. It is often diagnosed after ruling out other specific malabsorption syndromes.

Other malabsorption due to intolerance refers to impaired nutrient absorption caused by non-pathological, often dietary-related factors. Common synonyms include dietary intolerance and non-enzymatic malabsorption. Causative agents may include certain foods, additives, or substances like lactose, fructose, or artificial sweeteners. This condition typically affects the small intestine, particularly the proximal portion, where most nutrient absorption occurs. Symptoms often include diarrhea, bloating, and abdominal discomfort following ingestion of specific foods. It is generally not associated with structural or enzymatic defects.

Whipple's disease is a rare systemic bacterial infection caused by *Tropheryma whipplei*. It primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, leading to chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and malabsorption. The disease can also involve the joints, eyes, and central nervous system, causing arthritis, uveitis, and encephalopathy. Synonyms include intestinal lymphogranuloma and Whipple's enteropathy. The infection is characterized by chronic inflammation and fibrosis, often progressing to multisystem involvement if untreated. Diagnosis typically involves biopsy and PCR detection of *T. whipplei* DNA.

Other intestinal malabsorption refers to impaired absorption of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract due to various underlying conditions. Common synonyms include generalized malabsorption and non-specific malabsorption. Causative agents may include celiac disease, tropical sprue, infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and chronic inflammatory bowel disease. The small intestine is typically affected, particularly the jejunum and ileum. Symptoms often include diarrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, dietary assessment, and laboratory tests to identify the underlying cause.

Other intestinal malabsorption refers to impaired absorption of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract not attributable to specific known disorders such as celiac disease or lactose intolerance. Common synonyms include generalized malabsorption and nonspecific intestinal malabsorption. Causative agents may include chronic pancreatitis, short bowel syndrome, or infections. This condition typically affects the small intestine, particularly the proximal segments, leading to deficiencies in fat, proteins, carbohydrates, and vitamins. Symptoms often include diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies.

Intestinal malabsorption unspecified refers to impaired absorption of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and generalized malabsorption. Causative agents may include celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, pancreatic insufficiency, or infections. The primary affected body parts are the small intestine, particularly the jejunum and ileum. Symptoms often include diarrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins. Diagnosis typically involves clinical evaluation, dietary assessment, and laboratory tests. Treatment focuses on addressing underlying causes and nutritional support.

Vomiting following gastrointestinal surgery is a common postoperative complication, often resulting from anesthesia, surgical manipulation, or delayed gastric emptying. Synonyms include postoperative emesis and surgical vomiting. Common causative agents include anesthetic agents, opioids, and surgical trauma. It typically affects the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms may include nausea, retching, and forceful expulsion of gastric contents. The condition is more prevalent after procedures such as gastrectomy, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and bowel resection. Management involves supportive care, antiemetics, and addressing underlying causes.

Postgastric surgery syndromes refer to a group of gastrointestinal disorders that occur following gastric surgery, such as gastric bypass or vagotomy. Common synonyms include dumping syndrome and postprandial syndromes. These conditions are caused by altered gastrointestinal motility, hormonal imbalances, or anatomical changes. Symptoms often involve nausea, diarrhea, hypoglycemia, and abdominal pain. They typically affect the stomach, small intestine, and pancreas. Causative agents include surgical procedures, rapid gastric emptying, and altered hormone secretion.

Postsurgical malabsorption not elsewhere classified refers to impaired nutrient absorption occurring after gastrointestinal surgery, typically due to altered anatomy or function. Common synonyms include postoperative malabsorption syndrome and post-bariatric malabsorption. Causative agents may include surgical procedures such as gastric bypass, biliopancreatic diversion, or small bowel resection. The condition primarily affects the jejunum and ileum, leading to deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins, proteins, and minerals. Symptoms include diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. It is often managed with dietary modifications and supplementation.

code_desc: Postprocedural intestinal obstruction unspecified as to partial versus complete
summary: Postprocedural intestinal obstruction, unspecified as to partial versus complete, refers to a blockage of the intestines occurring after a medical procedure, without clarification on the extent of the obstruction. Common synonyms include postoperative bowel obstruction and postinterventional intestinal blockage. Causative agents may include adhesions, inflammation, or mechanical compression from the procedure. Typically affecting the small or large intestine, this condition can result from surgical interventions, endoscopic procedures, or trauma. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, and altered bowel habits. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical findings and imaging studies.

Postprocedural partial intestinal obstruction refers to a partial blockage of the intestine occurring after a surgical or diagnostic procedure. It is commonly caused by adhesions, edema, or kinking of the bowel. Synonyms include postoperative bowel obstruction and adhesion-related ileus. The small intestine is most frequently affected, though the colon may also be involved. Symptoms typically include abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, and decreased bowel sounds. Diagnosis is often made clinically, supported by imaging studies such as abdominal X-rays or CT scans. Management may involve conservative measures, nasogastric decompression, and, in severe cases, surgical intervention.

Postprocedural complete intestinal obstruction is a severe complication following abdominal procedures, characterized by a total blockage of the intestine, preventing the passage of contents. Common synonyms include postoperative bowel obstruction and postoperative ileus. It is often caused by adhesions, bowel wall edema, or mechanical obstruction from foreign bodies or surgical clips. The small intestine is most frequently affected, though the large intestine may also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal distension, pain, vomiting, and absence of bowel sounds.
