Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as bowel necrosis.

Postprocedural intestinal obstruction refers to a blockage of the intestines occurring after a surgical or diagnostic procedure. It is commonly caused by adhesions, inflammation, or mechanical compression from surgical instruments or sutures. Synonyms include postoperative bowel obstruction and adhesion-related intestinal blockage. The small intestine is most frequently affected, though the large intestine may also be involved. It typically presents with abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and absence of bowel sounds. Diagnosis is often made through imaging studies such as abdominal X-rays or CT scans. Treatment may involve conservative management or surgical intervention depending on severity.

Postcholecystectomy syndrome refers to persistent or new symptoms following cholecystectomy, often including abdominal pain, bloating, and dyspepsia. Common synonyms include post-cholecystectomy syndrome and post-gallbladder removal syndrome. Causative agents may include bile duct stones, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, chronic pancreatitis, or irritable bowel syndrome. The condition typically affects the biliary tract, gallbladder bed, and gastrointestinal system, with symptoms often localized to the right upper quadrant. It may also involve the pancreas and duodenum. Diagnosis requires thorough evaluation to identify underlying pathologies.

code_desc: Intraoperative hemorrhage and hematoma of a digestive system organ or structure complicating a digestive system procedure
summary: Intraoperative hemorrhage and hematoma of a digestive system organ or structure complicating a digestive system procedure refers to bleeding or blood accumulation occurring during or after a surgical procedure involving the digestive tract. Common synonyms include surgical bleeding, postoperative hematoma, or procedural hemorrhage. Causative agents may include coagulopathy, vascular injury, or surgical trauma. Typically affected areas include the stomach, intestines, liver, or pancreas. This condition can lead to complications such as hypovolemic shock or organ dysfunction if not promptly managed.

code_desc: Intraoperative hemorrhage and hematoma of a digestive system organ or structure complicating other procedure
summary: Intraoperative hemorrhage and hematoma of a digestive system organ or structure complicating another procedure refers to uncontrolled bleeding or blood collection within the digestive tract during or after a surgical procedure, leading to hematoma formation. Common synonyms include surgical bleeding, postoperative hematoma, or iatrogenic hemorrhage. Causative agents may include coagulopathy, anticoagulant use, or surgical trauma. Typically affected areas include the stomach, intestines, liver, and spleen. This complication can result from procedures such as cholecystectomy, gastrectomy, or bowel resection.

code_desc: Intraoperative hemorrhage and hematoma of a digestive system organ or structure complicating a procedure
summary: Intraoperative hemorrhage and hematoma of a digestive system organ or structure complicating a procedure refers to uncontrolled bleeding or blood collection within the digestive tract during or after surgical intervention. Common synonyms include surgical bleeding, postoperative hematoma, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Causative agents may include coagulopathy, vascular anomalies, trauma, or iatrogenic injury. Typically affected areas include the liver, spleen, stomach, intestines, and rectum. This complication can lead to hemodynamic instability and requires immediate management.

code_desc: Accidental puncture and laceration of a digestive system organ or structure during a digestive system procedure
summary: Accidental puncture and laceration of a digestive system organ or structure during a digestive system procedure refers to unintended injury to the gastrointestinal tract or adjacent structures during endoscopic, surgical, or diagnostic interventions. Common synonyms include iatrogenic perforation or traumatic injury during gastrointestinal procedures. Causative agents often involve endoscopes, surgical instruments, or excessive manipulation. Typically affected areas include the stomach, duodenum, colon, and rectum. Such injuries can lead to peritonitis, hemorrhage, or sepsis if not promptly managed.

code_desc: Accidental puncture and laceration of a digestive system organ or structure during other procedure
summary: Accidental puncture and laceration of a digestive system organ or structure during another procedure refers to unintended injury to the gastrointestinal tract or adjacent structures during unrelated medical interventions. Common synonyms include iatrogenic injury or procedural trauma. Causative agents often involve surgical instruments, endoscopes, or diagnostic devices. Typically affected areas include the stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. This condition can lead to bleeding, infection, or perforation, requiring immediate intervention. It is a recognized complication in procedures such as laparoscopy, endoscopy, or abdominal surgery.

code_desc: Accidental puncture and laceration of a digestive system organ or structure during a procedure
summary: Accidental puncture and laceration of a digestive system organ or structure during a procedure refers to unintended injury to the gastrointestinal tract or adjacent structures during medical interventions. Common synonyms include iatrogenic perforation or traumatic injury. Causative agents often involve surgical instruments, endoscopic devices, or blunt force. Typically affected areas include the stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. This complication can occur during procedures such as endoscopy, laparotomy, or abdominal surgery. Prompt identification and management are critical to prevent infection, hemorrhage, and other severe sequelae.

code_desc: Other intraoperative complications of digestive system
summary: Other intraoperative complications of the digestive system refer to unexpected adverse events occurring during surgical procedures involving the gastrointestinal tract. These may include bleeding, infection, injury to adjacent structures, or organ perforation. Common synonyms include surgical site complications, intraoperative hemorrhage, or bowel injury. Causative agents may involve surgical technique, underlying pathology, or equipment. Typically affected areas include the stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. These complications can lead to prolonged hospitalization and increased morbidity if not promptly managed.

Postprocedural hepatic failure refers to acute liver dysfunction occurring after a medical or surgical procedure. Common synonyms include postoperative liver failure and iatrogenic hepatic failure. It is often caused by medications, anesthetic agents, or surgical trauma. Known causative agents include contrast media, certain antibiotics, and anesthetics. Typically, the liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic complications may arise. This condition is characterized by elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, and coagulopathy, and can lead to fulminant hepatic failure in severe cases.

Postprocedural hepatorenal syndrome is a rare, potentially reversible form of acute kidney injury occurring following liver procedures, particularly in patients with underlying liver disease. It is characterized by progressive renal dysfunction in the absence of significant intrinsic renal disease. Common synonyms include postprocedural acute kidney injury and postoperative hepatorenal failure. Causative agents may include contrast media, anesthetic agents, and hemodynamic instability. Typically affects the kidneys and is associated with hepatic dysfunction, often seen in patients with cirrhosis or after liver transplantation.

code_desc: Postprocedural hemorrhage of a digestive system organ or structure following a procedure
summary: Postprocedural hemorrhage refers to bleeding that occurs after a procedure involving the digestive system. Common synonyms include procedural bleeding or iatrogenic hemorrhage. It is often caused by trauma during endoscopic, surgical, or interventional procedures. Commonly affected areas include the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the stomach, duodenum, and colon. Causative agents may include endoscopes, biopsy instruments, or surgical instruments. Risk factors include coagulopathy, anticoagulant use, and vascular abnormalities. Clinical presentation may include hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia, necessitating prompt evaluation and management.

Complications of intestinal pouch refer to adverse outcomes following surgical creation of an artificial pouch, commonly used in conditions like ulcerative colitis or familial adenomatous polyposis. Common synonyms include pouchitis and pouch-related complications. Causative agents include bacterial overgrowth, infections, and immune-mediated inflammation. Typically affected body parts include the pouch itself, surrounding tissues, and adjacent organs such as the bladder. Symptoms may involve diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fecal incontinence. Complications may include strictures, fistulas, and pouch failure.

Retained cholelithiasis following cholecystectomy refers to the presence of gallstones in the biliary tract despite prior gallbladder removal. This condition may occur due to incomplete stone removal during surgery or migration of stones into the common bile duct. Common synonyms include postcholecystectomy syndrome and residual gallstones. Causative agents include cholesterol and pigment stones. Typically affected body parts include the common bile duct, cystic duct, and sometimes the liver. Symptoms may mimic biliary colic or cholangitis.

code_desc: Postprocedural hematoma and seroma of a digestive system organ or structure following a procedure
summary: Postprocedural hematoma and seroma following a digestive system procedure refer to collections of blood (hematoma) or serous fluid (seroma) that develop after surgical or interventional procedures involving the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include postoperative bleeding or fluid accumulation. Causative agents may include surgical trauma, coagulopathy, or vascular injury. Typically affected areas include the stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. These complications can occur after procedures such as endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), laparoscopic surgery, or biopsy. Early recognition and management are essential to prevent complications like infection or organ dysfunction.

code_desc: Other postprocedural complications and disorders of digestive system
summary: Other postprocedural complications and disorders of the digestive system refer to adverse effects occurring after medical procedures involving the digestive tract. Common synonyms include postoperative gastrointestinal complications and procedural digestive disorders. Causative agents may include surgical trauma, infections, anesthetic agents, or adverse reactions to medications. These conditions typically affect the stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. Symptoms may involve pain, bleeding, obstruction, or inflammation. They can arise from procedures such as endoscopy, surgery, or diagnostic imaging. Prompt diagnosis and management are essential to prevent severe outcomes.

code_desc: Other intraoperative and postprocedural complications and disorders of digestive system
summary: Other intraoperative and postprocedural complications and disorders of the digestive system refer to adverse events occurring during or after surgical procedures involving the digestive tract. Common synonyms include postoperative gastrointestinal complications and surgical digestive tract disorders. Causative agents may include anesthesia, surgical trauma, infection, or underlying disease. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. These complications can manifest as bleeding, leakage, infection, or obstruction, often requiring further intervention.

Hematemesis is the vomiting of blood, typically originating from the upper gastrointestinal tract. It is a sign of bleeding in the esophagus, stomach, or duodenum. Common synonyms include hematemesis and melena, though melena refers to black, tarry stools. Causative agents include peptic ulcers, esophageal varices, gastritis, and Mallory-Weiss tears. Alcohol, NSAIDs, and coagulopathy can contribute to its development. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt evaluation to identify the source and manage bleeding.

Melena is a clinical sign characterized by the passage of dark, sticky, tarry stools due to the presence of digested blood. It typically indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding, as the blood is broken down by stomach acid. Common synonyms include black tarry stools or melena. Causative agents include peptic ulcers, gastritis, esophageal varices, and malignancies. The condition primarily affects the upper gastrointestinal tract, including the stomach and duodenum. It is distinct from hematochezia, which involves fresh blood from lower gastrointestinal sources. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent complications such as hypovolemic shock.

Gastrointestinal hemorrhage unspecified refers to bleeding from the digestive tract without a specific source identified. Common synonyms include upper or lower gastrointestinal bleeding, though the exact origin remains undetermined. Causative agents may include peptic ulcers, esophageal varices, gastritis, or vascular malformations. The condition can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, from the esophagus to the rectum, with symptoms such as hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopy or imaging to locate the source of bleeding.

Gastrointestinal mucositis (ulcerative) is an inflammatory condition characterized by ulceration and erosion of the mucosal lining of the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include ulcerative colitis and inflammatory bowel disease. It is primarily caused by chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or infectious agents such as *Clostridioides difficile*. The condition typically affects the colon and rectum, though it may involve other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding. It is a common side effect of cancer treatments and requires management to prevent complications.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of the digestive system
summary: "Other specified diseases of the digestive system" refers to conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as inflammatory bowel disease or infectious gastroenteritis. Common synonyms include unspecified digestive disorders. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune factors, or unknown etiologies. These conditions typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and liver. Symptoms may involve pain, inflammation, or functional disturbances, with diagnosis often requiring endoscopic or imaging evaluation.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of the digestive system
summary: "Other specified diseases of the digestive system" refers to digestive disorders not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified digestive diseases or miscellaneous digestive disorders. These conditions may arise from infections, inflammation, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents can include bacteria, viruses, or parasites. Typically affected body parts include the esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. Symptoms vary but often involve pain, altered bowel habits, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and diagnostic imaging or endoscopy.

Disease of the digestive system unspecified refers to a broad category of conditions affecting the gastrointestinal tract when the specific diagnosis is not determined. Common synonyms include undiagnosed gastrointestinal disorder or unspecified digestive illness. Causative agents may include infections, inflammatory processes, or structural abnormalities, though exact causes are often unknown. This term typically encompasses conditions affecting the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas, and gallbladder. It is often used when symptoms are non-specific or diagnostic tests fail to identify a precise etiology.

Colostomy complication unspecified refers to adverse events occurring after colostomy creation or maintenance, with the specific nature of the complication not clearly defined. Common synonyms include colostomy-related complications or unspecified colostomy issues. Causative agents may include infection, ischemia, mechanical obstruction, or fistula formation. Typically affected body parts include the stoma site, abdominal cavity, and surrounding tissues. This diagnosis is often used when the exact complication cannot be precisely categorized.

Colostomy hemorrhage refers to bleeding from a colostomy site, often resulting from trauma, infection, or vascular complications. Common synonyms include stoma bleeding or colostomy bleed. Causative agents may include ischemia, surgical complications, or coagulopathy. It typically affects the abdominal region, with bleeding originating from the stoma or surrounding tissue. Patients may present with bright red blood on the stoma appliance or perineal area. Management involves assessing the cause, stabilizing the patient, and addressing the underlying issue. Prompt evaluation is essential to prevent complications such as anemia or infection.

Colostomy infection is an inflammatory condition affecting the stoma or surrounding peristomal skin, often resulting from bacterial contamination. Common synonyms include peristomal infection and stoma infection. Causative agents typically include *Escherichia coli*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The infection primarily affects the stoma site and adjacent perineal or abdominal skin. Symptoms may include redness, swelling, pain, and purulent discharge. It can lead to complications such as granulation tissue formation or fistula development if left untreated. Proper hygiene and timely medical intervention are essential for management.

Colostomy malfunction refers to the failure of a surgically created colostomy to function properly, leading to complications such as obstruction, leakage, or infection. Common synonyms include colostomy failure or colostomy dysfunction. Causative agents may include adhesions, strictures, or infection. Typically affected body parts include the colon and the stoma site. This condition can result from improper surgical technique, postoperative complications, or patient-related factors such as poor hygiene or adherence to care protocols. Prompt evaluation and intervention are essential to prevent further complications.

Other complications of colostomy encompass a range of issues arising from the surgical creation of a stoma. Common synonyms include stoma-related complications and post-colostomy problems. Causative agents may include infection, ischemia, or mechanical trauma. Typically affected body parts include the stoma site, surrounding skin, and adjacent organs. Conditions such as stoma retraction, parastomal hernia, and infection are frequently observed. These complications can lead to pain, leakage, and impaired function, necessitating medical intervention. Proper stoma care and follow-up are essential for prevention and management.

Colostomy complications refer to adverse outcomes following colostomy creation or maintenance. Common issues include infection, leakage, and obstruction. Synonyms may include stoma complications or diverting colostomy problems. Causative agents often involve bacterial pathogens such as *Escherichia coli* or *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Typically affected areas include the stoma site, surrounding skin, and bowel segments. Complications may also involve electrolyte imbalances or hernias. Proper stoma care and monitoring are essential to prevent and manage these issues.

Enterostomy complication unspecified refers to any adverse event occurring at the site of an enterostomy that cannot be specifically classified. Common synonyms include enterostomy-related complications or enterostomy issues. Causative agents may include infection, mechanical obstruction, ischemia, or adhesion formation. Typically affected body parts include the abdomen, particularly around the stoma site. Symptoms may involve pain, leakage, bleeding, or infection. This diagnosis is often used when the specific complication is not clearly identified.

Enterostomy hemorrhage refers to bleeding from a surgically created enterostomy site, commonly following procedures such as ileostomy or colostomy. It may result from trauma, infection, ischemia, or erosion into blood vessels. Common synonyms include enteric fistula hemorrhage or stoma bleeding. Causative agents may include mechanical injury, inflammatory bowel disease, or neoplastic growths. The condition typically affects the small or large intestine, with bleeding often presenting as bright red blood per rectum or on stoma output. Prompt evaluation is essential to identify the source and manage complications.

Enterostomy infection is an inflammatory condition affecting the stoma or surrounding peristomal skin, typically occurring after ostomy surgery. It is characterized by redness, swelling, pain, and purulent discharge. Common synonyms include stoma infection and peristomal infection. Causative agents often include *Escherichia coli*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The infection primarily affects the stoma site and adjacent peristomal skin. It may result from poor peristomal hygiene, appliance leakage, or contamination. Prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics and wound care is essential to prevent complications.

Enterostomy malfunction refers to the failure of an enterostomy to function properly, leading to complications such as leakage, blockage, or infection. Common synonyms include enterostomy failure or stoma dysfunction. Causative agents may include infection, adhesions, ischemia, or improper stoma care. Typically affecting the small or large intestine, this condition can occur following surgical creation of a stoma for conditions like colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, or diverticular disease. Symptoms often include pain, discharge, and difficulty in managing the stoma. Prompt evaluation and management are essential to prevent further complications.

Other complications of enterostomy refer to secondary issues arising from the presence of an artificial stoma, commonly affecting the peristomal skin and surrounding area. Synonyms include stoma-related complications and enterostomy-related problems. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, such as *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Escherichia coli*, as well as mechanical irritation from stoma appliances. Typically affected body parts include the peristomal skin, abdominal wall, and adjacent tissues. Complications may manifest as infection, dermatitis, leakage, or obstruction. Early recognition and proper stoma care are essential for management.

Enterostomy complications refer to adverse events following the creation of an artificial opening between the gastrointestinal tract and the body surface. Common synonyms include stoma complications and enterostomy-related issues. These complications may arise from infection, obstruction, ischemia, or mechanical trauma. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Escherichia coli* and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Typically affected areas include the stoma site, surrounding skin, and underlying tissues. Symptoms may present as pain, discharge, bleeding, or infection. Proper stoma care and monitoring are essential to prevent and manage these complications.

Gastrostomy complication unspecified refers to adverse events occurring at the gastrostomy site without a specific diagnosis identified. Common synonyms include gastrostomy site complication or unspecified gastrostomy-related issue. Causative agents may include infection, leakage, obstruction, or mechanical failure. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, surrounding abdominal tissues, and the gastrostomy tube insertion site. Symptoms may present as pain, swelling, discharge, or gastrointestinal bleeding. Management depends on the underlying cause and may involve antibiotics, tube replacement, or surgical intervention.

Gastrostomy hemorrhage refers to bleeding originating from a gastrostomy site, typically following placement of a gastric tube. Common synonyms include gastric tube bleeding or gastrostomy tract hemorrhage. Causative agents may include trauma during insertion, infection, ulceration, or coagulopathy. It commonly affects the gastric mucosa, peristomal area, or surrounding tissues. Symptoms may present as hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia. Management involves identifying the source, controlling bleeding, and addressing underlying causes. Complications can include anemia or hemodynamic instability if not promptly managed.

Gastrostomy infection refers to an infection that occurs at the site of a gastrostomy tube, a surgically created opening in the stomach for enteral feeding. Common synonyms include gastrostomy site infection or perigastrostomy infection. It is typically caused by bacterial pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Escherichia coli*. The infection primarily affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues around the gastrostomy site, occasionally extending into the gastric wall. Symptoms may include redness, swelling, drainage, and fever. Prompt treatment with antibiotics and proper wound care is essential to prevent complications.

Gastrostomy malfunction refers to the failure of a gastrostomy tube to function properly, leading to complications such as leakage, blockage, or infection. Common synonyms include gastrostomy tube dysfunction or gastric tube failure. Causative agents may include improper placement, tube blockage by food or secretions, infection, or structural changes in the gastrointestinal tract. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, surrounding abdominal tissues, and the site of tube insertion. This condition can result in malnutrition, aspiration, or peritonitis if not promptly addressed.

Other complications of gastrostomy encompass a range of issues arising from the presence of a gastrostomy tube. Common synonyms include gastrostomy-related complications and post-gastrostomy problems. Causative agents may include infection, mechanical irritation, or improper tube placement. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the stomach and surrounding areas, as well as the skin at the insertion site. Complications may manifest as leakage, infection, granulation tissue, or obstruction. These issues can lead to local or systemic symptoms requiring medical intervention.

Gastrostomy complications refer to adverse outcomes following the placement of a gastrostomy tube for enteral nutrition. Common synonyms include gastric tube complications and enteral access issues. Causative agents may include infection, mechanical trauma, or improper tube placement. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, peritoneum, and surrounding tissues. Complications such as infection, leakage, obstruction, and tube displacement are frequently observed. Proper technique and post-insertion care are essential to minimize risks.

Esophagostomy complications unspecified refer to adverse outcomes following esophagostomy placement, a surgical procedure creating an opening into the esophagus. Common synonyms include esophageal stoma complications or post-esophagostomy issues. Causative agents may include infection, mechanical trauma, or foreign body reaction. Typically affecting the esophagus and surrounding tissues, these complications can lead to inflammation, stricture, or fistula formation. They may occur in patients with chronic swallowing disorders or those requiring enteral nutrition support.

Esophagostomy hemorrhage refers to bleeding originating from the surgical site of an esophagostomy, a procedure creating an opening in the esophagus for feeding. Common synonyms include esophageal stoma bleeding or post-esophagostomy hemorrhage. Causative agents may include infection, trauma, or vascular injury during or after the procedure. Typically affecting the esophageal stoma site, this condition can lead to significant blood loss and requires prompt evaluation and management. It is commonly seen in veterinary medicine, particularly in dogs and cats with chronic gastrointestinal disorders.

Esophagostomy infection is an infection that occurs at the site of an esophagostomy, a surgical opening created in the esophagus for enteral feeding. It is commonly caused by bacterial pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, and *Escherichia coli*. The infection may lead to localized inflammation, purulent discharge, and potential systemic spread. It typically affects the esophageal wall and surrounding tissues. Synonyms include esophagostomy site infection or esophagostomy tract infection. This condition is often seen in patients with prolonged esophagostomy use, particularly in veterinary medicine and critical care settings.

Esophagostomy malfunction refers to the failure of an esophagostomy tube to function properly, often due to blockage, leakage, or infection. Common synonyms include esophagostomy tube failure or esophagostomy complications. Causative agents may include bacterial infections such as *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* or *Staphylococcus aureus*, as well as mechanical issues from tube displacement or clogging. This condition typically affects the esophagus and surrounding tissues, leading to complications such as aspiration, dehydration, or local inflammation. It is commonly seen in veterinary patients, particularly in cats and dogs, following esophagostomy placement for nutritional support.

Other complications of esophagostomy include stricture formation, leakage, infection, and fistula development. Common synonyms are esophageal complications or post-esophagostomy issues. Causative agents may involve bacterial infections such as *Escherichia coli* or *Staphylococcus aureus*. These complications typically affect the esophagus, surrounding tissues, and adjacent organs like the trachea or lungs. They often occur due to improper placement, trauma, or infection at the surgical site. Prompt diagnosis and management are essential to prevent severe morbidity.

Esophagostomy complications refer to adverse outcomes following the surgical creation of an esophageal opening for feeding or drainage. Common synonyms include esophageal stoma complications and post-esophagostomy issues. Causative agents may include infection by bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, as well as mechanical trauma from the stoma device. Typically affected body parts include the esophagus, surrounding tissues, and adjacent structures like the trachea. Complications may present as infection, stricture, leakage, or fistula formation. Prompt management is essential to prevent severe morbidity.

code_desc: Infection due to gastric band procedure
summary: Infection due to gastric band procedure, also known as plication or band-related infection, is a rare but serious complication following adjustable gastric banding. It typically occurs at the site of the band or surrounding tissues. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *Escherichia coli*. The infection may affect the abdominal wall, subcutaneous tissue, or the band itself, leading to erythema, swelling, pain, and purulent discharge. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics and possible surgical intervention are essential to prevent severe complications.

code_desc: Other complications of gastric band procedure
summary: Other complications of gastric band procedure encompass issues arising beyond the initial placement, including band erosion, pouch dilation, and slippage. Common synonyms include gastric band malfunction and post-operative band-related complications. Causative agents may include improper band positioning, patient non-compliance, or infection. These complications typically affect the stomach, esophagus, and surrounding abdominal structures. Symptoms often include pain, nausea, vomiting, and difficulty swallowing. Management may involve medical intervention or surgical revision.

Complications of gastric band procedure may include band erosion, slippage, or migration, often leading to obstruction or ulceration. Common synonyms are gastric band complications or adjustable gastric band issues. Causative agents may involve improper placement, overinflation, or infection. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, esophagus, and adjacent tissues. Other complications may involve port malfunction, infection, or nutritional deficiencies. These issues can result in pain, vomiting, or malabsorption, requiring intervention such as band adjustment or removal.

code_desc: Infection due to other bariatric procedure
summary: Infection due to other bariatric procedure refers to postoperative infections following bariatric surgeries such as gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy. Common synonyms include post-bariatric surgical infection or complications from weight loss surgery. Causative agents often include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*. Typically affected body parts include the surgical site, abdominal cavity, and sometimes the lungs or urinary tract. Symptoms may present as fever, wound drainage, or localized pain. Prompt antibiotic therapy and surgical intervention are often required for optimal management.

code_desc: Other complications of other bariatric procedure
summary: "Other complications of other bariatric procedures" refers to secondary issues arising from procedures like gastric banding, sleeve gastrectomy, or biliopancreatic diversion. Common synonyms include post-bariatric complications or secondary bariatric morbidity. Causative agents may include infections, nutritional deficiencies, or mechanical issues. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and metabolic systems. Symptoms may involve malabsorption, vitamin deficiencies, and gastrointestinal obstruction. These complications often require medical or surgical intervention.

Complications of other bariatric procedures encompass a range of issues arising from surgeries like gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy, or adjustable gastric banding. Common synonyms include post-bariatric complications or bariatric surgery sequelae. Causative agents may include infection, leakage, blood clots, or nutritional deficiencies. Typically affected body parts include the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and surgical sites. Symptoms may involve pain, nausea, malnutrition, or metabolic disturbances. These complications can occur immediately post-surgery or develop over time, necessitating ongoing monitoring and management.

Cholera is an acute diarrheal illness caused by *Vibrio cholerae*, primarily transmitted through contaminated water or food. It is characterized by profuse, watery diarrhea and vomiting, leading to rapid fluid loss and dehydration. Common synonyms include cholera morbus and rice-water stool. The small intestine is the primary site of infection. Without prompt rehydration, it can progress to severe hypovolemic shock and death. The disease is endemic in areas with poor sanitation and is a public health concern in developing regions.

Typhoid and paratyphoid fevers are systemic bacterial infections caused by *Salmonella typhi* and *Salmonella paratyphi*, respectively. These illnesses, often referred to as enteric fever or typhoid fever, primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract and bloodstream. Common symptoms include prolonged fever, headache, malaise, and abdominal pain. Complications may involve the spleen, liver, and intestinal walls. The infections are transmitted through contaminated food or water, commonly affecting individuals in areas with poor sanitation.

Other salmonella infections refer to systemic illnesses caused by *Salmonella* species other than *S. typhi* and *S. paratyphi*, which cause typhoid and paratyphoid fevers. Common synonyms include nontyphoidal salmonellosis. The primary causative agents are *S. enterica* subspecies *enterica* and *S. enterica* subspecies *dublin*. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, causing symptoms like diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain. In severe cases, the bacteria can invade the bloodstream, leading to sepsis or localized infections such as osteomyelitis or meningitis.

Shigellosis is an acute bacterial infection caused by *Shigella* species, including *S. dysenteriae*, *S. flexneri*, *S. boydii*, and *S. sonnei*. It primarily affects the intestines, leading to inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa. Common symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea (often bloody), and tenesmus. The infection is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, commonly through contaminated food or water. It predominantly affects children in developing countries but can occur in any population. Complications such as dehydration and reactive arthritis may arise. Synonyms include bacillary dysentery and shigella infection.

Other bacterial intestinal infections refer to a group of illnesses caused by various bacteria that invade the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include bacterial gastroenteritis and enteric infections. Causative agents may include *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Campylobacter*, and *E. coli* strains. These infections typically affect the small and large intestines, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. They are often acquired through contaminated food or water and can range from mild to severe, sometimes requiring antibiotic treatment.

code_desc: other bacterial food-borne intoxications, not elsewhere classified
summary: Other bacterial food-borne intoxications, not elsewhere classified, refer to illnesses caused by ingestion of toxins produced by bacteria in contaminated food, excluding those classified under specific categories like botulism or staphylococcal poisoning. Common synonyms include food poisoning from bacterial toxins. Causative agents may include *Bacillus cereus*, *Clostridium perfringens*, and *Clostridium botulinum* (though botulism is typically classified separately). These toxins primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract, causing symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. The illness is usually self-limiting and resolves without specific treatment.

Amoebiasis is an intestinal infection caused by the protozoan *Entamoeba histolytica*. It leads to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. In severe cases, the parasite can invade the liver, causing abscesses. Common synonyms include amoebic dysentery and intestinal amoebiasis. The disease primarily affects the large intestine but can spread to other organs. Transmission occurs through ingestion of contaminated food or water. It is more prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and is a significant cause of morbidity in tropical regions.

Other protozoal intestinal diseases refer to infections caused by various protozoan parasites affecting the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include protozoal gastroenteritis and intestinal protozoa infections. Causative agents include Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium parvum, Cyclospora cayetanensis, and Entamoeba histolytica. These pathogens primarily affect the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. They are often acquired through contaminated water or food and are more prevalent in travelers and immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: viral and other specified intestinal infections
summary: Viral and other specified intestinal infections are gastrointestinal disorders characterized by inflammation of the intestines, primarily caused by viruses such as rotavirus, norovirus, and adenovirus. Bacterial agents like Salmonella and E. coli may also be responsible. These infections typically affect the small intestine and may involve the large intestine. Common symptoms include diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fever. They are often transmitted through contaminated food or water. The condition is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include gastroenteritis, infectious diarrhea, and enteric infections.

"Other specified intestinal infections" refers to intestinal infections not classified under more specific categories, often involving inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include unspecified or unspecified intestinal infections. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, or parasites such as *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Giardia*, or *Cryptosporidium*. These infections typically affect the small and large intestines, causing symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and nausea. They are often acquired through contaminated food or water and can lead to dehydration if severe.

code_desc: other gastroenteritis and colitis of infectious origin
summary: Other gastroenteritis and colitis of infectious origin refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract caused by infectious agents, excluding those classified under specific known pathogens. Common synonyms include infectious colitis and enterocolitis. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Clostridioides difficile*, *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, and *Campylobacter*, as well as parasites like *Entamoeba histolytica* and viruses such as norovirus. The condition typically affects the colon and small intestine, leading to symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. It is often acquired through contaminated food or water.

code_desc: gastroenteritis and colitis of unspecified origin
summary: Gastroenteritis and colitis of unspecified origin refer to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily affecting the stomach and colon, with an unknown cause. Common synonyms include acute gastroenteritis and inflammatory bowel disease of unspecified type. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or parasitic pathogens, though the exact cause is not identified in this classification. Symptoms typically involve diarrhea, abdominal pain, and sometimes fever. The condition predominantly affects the intestines but can involve the stomach as well. It is commonly seen in individuals with weakened immune systems or those exposed to contaminated food or water.

code_desc: respiratory tuberculosis, bacteriologically and histologically confirmed
summary: Respiratory tuberculosis, bacteriologically and histologically confirmed, is a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation, caseous necrosis, and cavitation. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and TB. The infection spreads via airborne droplets. Histological findings include caseating granulomas, while bacteriologic confirmation involves acid-fast bacilli on smear or culture. Typical affected areas include the upper lobes of the lungs, with potential dissemination to other organs.

code_desc: tuberculosis of lung, confirmed by culture only
summary: Tuberculosis of the lung, confirmed by culture only, is a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and cavitation. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and TB. The disease is spread via airborne droplets. Diagnosis is confirmed by isolation of the organism from clinical specimens. It may present with persistent cough, fever, weight loss, and hemoptysis. While culture is definitive, it may take weeks for results. Other mycobacteria, such as *M. bovis*, can also cause similar presentations.

Tuberculosis of the lung, confirmed histologically, is an infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis in lung tissue. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and pulmonary TB. The disease typically affects the upper lobes of the lungs, leading to cavities, fibrosis, and potential dissemination to other organs. Histological confirmation reveals caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells and acid-fast bacilli. It is a major global health concern, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: tuberculosis of lung, confirmed by unspecified means
summary: Tuberculosis of the lung, confirmed by unspecified means, is an infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It affects the pulmonary system, leading to granulomatous inflammation and potential cavitation. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and TB. The disease spreads via airborne droplets. Clinical features include chronic cough, fever, weight loss, and hemoptysis. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through sputum smear, culture, or nucleic acid amplification tests, though the exact method may be unspecified. The lungs are the most commonly affected body parts, though extrapulmonary involvement can occur.

code_desc: respiratory tuberculosis, not confirmed bacteriologically or histologically
summary: Respiratory tuberculosis, not confirmed bacteriologically or histologically, refers to a clinical diagnosis of tuberculosis affecting the respiratory system in the absence of definitive bacterial or histological evidence. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and suspected tuberculosis. The primary causative agent is *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. This condition typically affects the lungs, particularly the upper lobes, and may present with symptoms such as chronic cough, fever, and weight loss. Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation, imaging, and response to anti-tuberculosis therapy.

code_desc: tuberculosis of lung, bacteriologically and histologically negative
summary: Tuberculosis of the lung, bacteriologically and histologically negative, refers to a clinical diagnosis of tuberculosis based on imaging and clinical findings, despite the absence of acid-fast bacilli in sputum or histological confirmation. It is often considered a diagnosis of exclusion. Common synonyms include clinical tuberculosis or suspected tuberculosis. The causative agent is *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. Typically affects the upper lobes of the lungs, and may present with chronic cough, weight loss, and fever. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with a history of TB exposure.

code_desc: tuberculosis of lung, bacteriological and histological examination not done
summary: Tuberculosis of the lung, bacteriological and histological examination not done, refers to a clinical diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis made without definitive laboratory confirmation. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis, TB, or consumption. The causative agent is *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the upper lobes of the lungs, presenting with chronic cough, fever, weight loss, and hemoptysis. The condition is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis. Without laboratory confirmation, the diagnosis relies on clinical and radiological findings.

code_desc: tuberculosis of lung, without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Tuberculosis of the lung is a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the upper lobes of the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and cavitation. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and consumption. The condition is characterized by persistent cough, weight loss, and hemoptysis. It spreads via airborne droplets and may progress to fibrosis or disseminated disease if untreated. While bacteriological or histological confirmation is not mentioned, clinical features and radiographic findings are often used for diagnosis.

code_desc: tuberculosis of intrathoracic lymph nodes, without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Tuberculosis of intrathoracic lymph nodes refers to the involvement of lymph nodes within the thoracic cavity by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Common synonyms include tuberculous lymphadenopathy and lymph node tuberculosis. The disease typically affects the mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, often presenting with non-caseating granulomas. It is a form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis and may occur in conjunction with pulmonary tuberculosis. Clinical features include lymph node enlargement, constitutional symptoms, and sometimes respiratory symptoms. Diagnosis is based on clinical and radiological findings when bacteriological or histological confirmation is not available.

code_desc: tuberculosis of larynx, trachea and bronchus, without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Tuberculosis of the larynx, trachea, and bronchus is a form of pulmonary tuberculosis that affects the upper airway. Caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, it may present with symptoms such as hoarseness, stridor, and cough. Common synonyms include laryngeal tuberculosis and bronchial tuberculosis. The disease typically involves the larynx, trachea, and major bronchi, leading to narrowing and potential airway obstruction. It is more common in individuals with compromised immune systems or those co-infected with HIV. Diagnosis is often based on clinical features and imaging rather than bacteriological or histological confirmation.

code_desc: tuberculous pleurisy, without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Tuberculous pleurisy is an inflammatory condition of the pleura caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It often presents with chest pain, fever, and pleural effusion. Common synonyms include tuberculous effusion and tuberculous pleural disease. The infection typically affects the lungs and pleura, with the pleura being the primary site of involvement. It is more common in individuals with a history of tuberculosis or immunocompromise. The disease may progress to fibrosis or calcification of the pleura if left untreated. Clinical features may overlap with other pleural diseases, necessitating further diagnostic evaluation.

code_desc: primary respiratory tuberculosis without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Primary respiratory tuberculosis is an initial infection of the lungs caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It typically affects the upper lobes and may present with symptoms such as cough, fever, and weight loss. Common synonyms include acute miliary tuberculosis and primary complex. The disease results from the body's immune response to the tubercle bacillus, leading to granuloma formation and potential cavitation. It is most commonly seen in individuals with compromised immunity or recent exposure to the pathogen. The condition may progress to active disease if the immune system fails to contain the infection.

code_desc: other respiratory tuberculosis, without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Other respiratory tuberculosis refers to tuberculosis affecting the respiratory system without definitive bacteriological or histological confirmation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Common synonyms include atypical tuberculosis or undiagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. The causative agent is typically Mycobacterium tuberculosis, though other mycobacteria may occasionally be involved. The condition primarily affects the lungs, including the bronchi and alveoli, and may present with symptoms such as chronic cough, fever, and weight loss. It is often diagnosed clinically based on epidemiological and clinical criteria when laboratory confirmation is unavailable.

code_desc: respiratory tuberculosis unspecified, without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Respiratory tuberculosis unspecified, without bacteriological or histological confirmation, refers to a clinical diagnosis of tuberculosis affecting the respiratory system based on clinical symptoms and epidemiological factors rather than definitive laboratory evidence. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis or TB without confirmation. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Typically affects the lungs, particularly the upper lobes, and may involve bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli. Symptoms include chronic cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. It is prevalent in populations with compromised immunity or poor healthcare access.

Tuberculosis of the nervous system, also known as neuro-tuberculosis, is a chronic infection caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It commonly affects the meninges, brain, spinal cord, and cranial nerves. The condition may present as tuberculous meningitis, tuberculoma, or granulomatous lesions. Symptoms include fever, headache, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and often results from hematogenous spread. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, imaging, and microbiological testing. Treatment requires long-term antitubercular therapy.

Tuberculosis of other organs refers to extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It commonly affects lymph nodes, bones, joints, kidneys, and the central nervous system. Synonyms include miliary tuberculosis and disseminated tuberculosis. The disease spreads via hematogenous routes, leading to granulomatous inflammation and tissue destruction. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis often involves imaging, biopsy, and acid-fast bacilli staining. Treatment follows standard anti-tubercular therapy, with adjustments based on affected organ and drug susceptibility.

Miliary tuberculosis is a severe form of pulmonary tuberculosis characterized by the dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis through the bloodstream, leading to the formation of small, millet-seed-like nodules in various organs. Common synonyms include hematogenous tuberculosis and miliary TB. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It typically affects the lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow, but can involve multiple systemic sites. The condition often presents with fever, weight loss, and respiratory symptoms, and is more common in immunocompromised individuals.

Plague is an acute infectious disease caused by *Yersinia pestis*, primarily transmitted through the bite of infected fleas. It is also known as the Black Death. The disease typically affects the lymph nodes, causing bubonic plague, characterized by swollen and painful lymph glands. Pneumonic plague, a more severe form, affects the lungs and can lead to rapid respiratory failure. Septicemic plague involves the bloodstream. Common synonyms include Black Death, Pest, and the Plague. It is most commonly found in rodents and their fleas, with outbreaks historically linked to poor sanitation and close contact with infected animals.

Tularaemia, also known as rabbit fever or plague of the rabbits, is a bacterial infection caused by *Francisella tularensis*. It primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and lungs. Transmission occurs through insect vectors, direct contact with infected animals, or inhalation of aerosolized bacteria. Common symptoms include ulcerative lesions, swollen lymph nodes, fever, and respiratory distress. The disease can present in various forms, including glandular, ulceroglandular, and pneumonic. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are crucial to prevent complications.

Anthrax is a severe, often fatal bacterial infection caused by *Bacillus anthracis*. It primarily affects animals but can be transmitted to humans through contact with infected animal products. Common synonyms include woolsorter's disease and malignant pustule. The infection typically manifests as cutaneous, inhalational, or gastrointestinal anthrax, with the skin, lungs, and digestive tract being the most commonly affected body parts. Symptoms range from localized skin lesions to systemic illness with high mortality if untreated.

Brucellosis is a zoonotic infectious disease caused by bacteria of the genus *Brucella*, including *B. melitensis*, *B. abortus*, *B. suis*, and *B. canis*. Common synonyms include undulant fever and Malta fever. The infection typically affects the reticuloendothelial system, with common involvement of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It may also lead to chronic arthritis, endocarditis, and neurological complications. Transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated animal products or direct contact with infected animals. Clinical features include fever, sweating, malaise, and weight loss. Diagnosis is confirmed through blood culture or serological tests.

Glanders and melioidosis are acute, often fatal bacterial infections. Glanders is caused by *Burkholderia mallei*, while melioidosis is caused by *Burkholderia pseudomallei*. Both are endemic in tropical regions. Glanders primarily affects horses, but can infect humans through direct contact with infected animals. Melioidosis, often called "climatic fever," typically affects the lungs and can disseminate systemically. Common synonyms include "malleosis" for glanders and "whipworm fever" for melioidosis. Both diseases present with fever, abscesses, and respiratory symptoms.

Melioidosis, unspecified, is a bacterial infection caused primarily by *Burkholderia pseudomallei*. It is also known as Whitmore's disease. The infection can present with a wide range of clinical manifestations, including acute septicemia, pulmonary involvement, or localized abscesses. Common synonyms include tropical granuloma and gumbo disease. The disease typically affects the lungs, skin, and soft tissues, but can disseminate to multiple organs. It is endemic in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, often occurring in individuals with underlying health conditions or immunocompromise.

Rat-bite fever is a bacterial infection transmitted through bites or scratches from infected rodents, most commonly rats. It is also known as streptobacillary or spirillary fever. The causative agents include *Streptobacillus moniliformis* and *Spirillum minus*. The infection typically affects the skin, joints, and cardiovascular system, causing symptoms such as fever, rash, arthritis, and endocarditis. It is more prevalent in individuals with frequent rodent exposure, such as laboratory workers or those in endemic areas. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are essential to prevent complications.

Erysipeloid is a bacterial skin infection characterized by a raised, reddish, often itchy rash with well-defined borders. Common synonyms include erysipelas and erysipelatous infection. It is primarily caused by *Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae*, a gram-positive bacillus. The infection typically affects the extremities, particularly the hands and arms, in individuals exposed to contaminated animal products. It may occur following cuts or abrasions and can present with systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. The condition is more common in fishermen, butchers, and others with occupational exposure to infected animals.

Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection caused by *Leptospira* species, commonly transmitted through contact with contaminated water or soil. It affects multiple organ systems, with the kidneys and liver being most commonly involved. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe manifestations such as jaundice, renal failure, and hemorrhage. Known synonyms include Weil's disease and swamp fever. The infection is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often affecting individuals exposed to contaminated environments. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent complications.

code_desc: other zoonotic bacterial diseases, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other zoonotic bacterial diseases, not elsewhere classified" refers to bacterial infections transmitted from animals to humans that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified zoonotic bacterial infections. Causative agents may include *Brucella*, *Coxiella burnetii*, and *Rickettsia* species. These diseases typically affect the skin, respiratory system, and systemic organs. Symptoms vary but often include fever, fatigue, and localized infection. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and laboratory testing. Treatment involves antibiotics tailored to the specific pathogen.

Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*. It primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes of the upper respiratory tract. The disease is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and nerve damage, leading to sensory loss and deformities. Common synonyms include leprosy and Hansen's disease. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets, though the exact mode is not fully understood. The disease progresses slowly and is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Early diagnosis and treatment with multidrug therapy can prevent complications.

Infection due to other mycobacteria refers to diseases caused by mycobacterial species other than *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and *Mycobacterium leprae*. Common synonyms include non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infections. Causative agents include *Mycobacterium avium complex*, *Mycobacterium kansasii*, and *Mycobacterium abscessus*. These infections typically affect the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, and soft tissues. They are often opportunistic, occurring in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying lung disease. Symptoms vary depending on the affected site but may include chronic cough, weight loss, and skin lesions. Diagnosis involves culture and nucleic acid amplification testing.

Listeriosis is a severe bacterial infection caused primarily by *Listeria monocytogenes*. It is a foodborne illness that can affect immunocompromised individuals, pregnant women, and the elderly. Common synonyms include listerial infection or listeriosis. The bacteria invade the bloodstream and can lead to meningitis, sepsis, and miscarriage. Typically affected body parts include the central nervous system, liver, spleen, and placenta. Symptoms range from fever and muscle aches to severe neurological complications. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are critical for improving outcomes.

Diphtheria is an acute bacterial infection caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*, occasionally *C. ulcerans* or *C. pseudotuberculosis*. It primarily affects the respiratory tract, leading to a pseudomembrane formation in the throat. Common synonyms include croup and false croup. The disease can cause severe systemic toxicity due to diphtheria toxin, potentially leading to myocarditis, neuropathy, and respiratory failure. It is highly contagious and typically occurs in unvaccinated individuals. The pharynx, larynx, and nasal passages are most commonly affected.

Whooping cough, also known as pertussis, is a highly contagious respiratory infection caused by *Bordetella pertussis*. It is characterized by severe coughing fits followed by a high-pitched "whoop" sound during inhalation. The disease primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, including the trachea and bronchi. Common synonyms include the 100-day cough and the plague of the infants. Symptoms typically begin with mild cold-like symptoms before progressing to persistent coughing. It is most severe in infants and young children, though adults can also be affected. Vaccination with DTaP or Tdap is the primary prevention method.

Scarlet fever is an acute bacterial infection caused primarily by *Streptococcus pyogenes*, also known as group A streptococcus. It is characterized by a sore throat, fever, and a distinctive diffuse, sandpaper-like rash that typically begins on the neck and spreads to the trunk and extremities. The rash fades in areas where pressure is applied, leaving a pale ring. Common synonyms include scarlatina and erythrophlegmon. The condition primarily affects the pharynx, skin, and lymph nodes, with complications such as rheumatic fever or post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis possible if untreated.

Meningococcal infection is a severe bacterial illness caused by *Neisseria meningitidis*, commonly known as meningococcus. It can lead to meningitis, an inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord, or sepsis, a life-threatening blood infection. Other synonyms include meningococcal meningitis and meningococcemia. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, but can also involve the bloodstream and other organs. It is more common in children, adolescents, and young adults, often presenting with fever, headache, stiff neck, and rash. Prompt treatment with antibiotics is critical to prevent complications and mortality.

Streptococcal sepsis is a severe systemic infection caused by Streptococcus species, most commonly Group A Streptococcus (GAS). It results from the body's overwhelming response to bacterial toxins and infection, leading to systemic inflammation and potential multi-organ failure. Common synonyms include streptococcal septicemia and GAS sepsis. The infection typically affects the bloodstream, lungs, and soft tissues, often originating from local infections such as pharyngitis, skin infections, or pneumonia. Prompt antibiotic treatment is critical to prevent progression to septic shock.

code_desc: sepsis due to streptococcus, group d and enterococcus
summary: Sepsis due to *Streptococcus* group D and *Enterococcus* refers to a systemic inflammatory response syndrome caused by these gram-positive bacteria. Common synonyms include bacterial sepsis and septicemia. Causative agents include *Enterococcus faecalis*, *E. faecium*, and *Streptococcus bovis*. These organisms typically affect the bloodstream, leading to multi-organ dysfunction. They are often associated with infections such as urinary tract infections, endocarditis, and intra-abdominal infections. Prompt antimicrobial therapy is essential to prevent progression to septic shock.

Sepsis is a life-threatening systemic response to infection, characterized by organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response. It can occur in the absence of a clearly identified infectious source, referred to as 'other sepsis.' Common synonyms include septicemia and systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Causative agents are diverse, including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, abdomen, urinary tract, and skin. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria such as fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and altered mental status, along with laboratory findings like elevated white blood cell count and organ dysfunction. Prompt treatment with antibiotics and supportive care is critical.

code_desc: sepsis due to other gram-negative organisms
summary: Sepsis due to other gram-negative organisms refers to a life-threatening systemic infection caused by gram-negative bacteria not classified as *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, or *Pseudomonas*. Common synonyms include gram-negative sepsis or septicemia from non-enteric gram-negative rods. Causative agents may include *Enterobacter*, *Serratia*, *Proteus*, and *Acinetobacter*. This condition typically affects the bloodstream, lungs, urinary tract, and abdomen, often following trauma, surgery, or underlying infections. It is characterized by fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and organ dysfunction. Prompt antibiotic therapy and supportive care are critical for management.

Actinomycosis is a chronic, suppurative bacterial infection caused by *Actinomyces* species, most commonly *A. israelii*. It is characterized by the formation of abscesses and granulomas, often with sulfur granules. The infection typically affects the cervicofacial region, but can also involve the thoracic and abdominal regions. Common synonyms include "lumpy jaw" and "actinomycotic infection." The disease is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with poor oral hygiene. Clinically, it presents with localized pain, swelling, and drainage, often requiring prolonged antibiotic therapy.

Nocardiosis is a chronic, granulomatous infection caused by aerobic actinomycetes, most commonly *Nocardia asteroides*. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV or on immunosuppressive therapy. The infection typically involves the lungs, presenting with symptoms like cough, fever, and weight loss. It can disseminate to the brain, skin, and other organs. Synonyms include nocardial infection or actinomycotic infection. Diagnosis is confirmed by acid-fast staining and culture. Treatment involves long-term antibiotic therapy, often with sulfonamides or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Bartonellosis is a bacterial infection caused by species of the genus Bartonella, most commonly Bartonella henselae and Bartonella quintana. It is also known as cat-scratch disease or trench fever. The infection typically affects the lymph nodes, causing swollen, painful lymphadenopathy, often following a scratch or bite from an infected animal, particularly cats. Other systemic manifestations may include fever, fatigue, and skin lesions. Bartonella species are transmitted through arthropod vectors or direct contact with infected animals. The disease can present acutely or chronically, with varying severity depending on the host's immune status.

code_desc: other bacterial diseases, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other bacterial diseases, not elsewhere classified" refers to bacterial infections that do not fit into more specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous bacterial infections or unspecified bacterial diseases. Causative agents may include a wide range of bacteria such as *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas*. These infections can affect various body systems, including the respiratory, urinary, skin, and gastrointestinal tracts. Clinical presentation varies depending on the site of infection and the specific pathogen involved.

Bacterial infection of unspecified site refers to a systemic infection where the specific location of the infection is not identified. Common synonyms include sepsis, bloodstream infection, or generalized bacterial infection. Causative agents may include common bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Streptococcus species. This condition typically affects multiple body systems and can involve the lungs, urinary tract, skin, or bloodstream. It is often associated with fever, chills, and systemic inflammation, requiring prompt antibiotic therapy and source control.

Staphylococcal infection, unspecified site, refers to an infection caused by *Staphylococcus* species without a specified location. Common synonyms include staph infection or staphylococcal disease. The primary causative agents are *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Staphylococcus epidermidis*. This infection can affect various body parts, including skin, soft tissues, bones, joints, and bloodstream. It often presents as abscesses, cellulitis, or systemic infections. Symptoms vary depending on the site but may include redness, swelling, pain, and fever. Prompt diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic therapy are essential for effective management.

Congenital syphilis is a bacterial infection transmitted from an infected mother to her fetus through the placenta. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it can lead to severe multisystem involvement. Common synonyms include neonatal syphilis and congenital treponemal infection. Typically affecting the skin, bones, liver, and central nervous system, it may present with characteristic rashes, hepatosplenomegaly, and skeletal abnormalities. Without treatment, it can result in serious complications including deafness, blindness, and intellectual disability. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical for improving outcomes.

Early syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically presents 10 to 90 days after exposure with a painless ulcerative lesion, known as a chancre, at the site of inoculation. Common synonyms include primary syphilis. The infection may also involve regional lymphadenopathy. If untreated, it can progress to secondary syphilis. Commonly affected body parts include the genitalia, anus, rectum, and mouth. The disease is highly contagious during this stage.

Late syphilis is a chronic, systemic infection caused by *Treponema pallidum* that develops years after an untreated primary or secondary syphilis infection. It typically affects multiple organ systems, including the skin, bones, central nervous system, and cardiovascular system. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and cardiovascular syphilis. Characteristic manifestations include gummas, aseptic meningitis, tabes dorsalis, and aortic aneurysms. The condition is often asymptomatic in its early stages but can lead to severe complications if left untreated.

Other and unspecified syphilis refers to syphilis cases where the clinical stage or specific manifestation is not clearly documented. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, a spirochete. Common synonyms include unspecified syphilis or syphilis, unspecified. This condition may affect multiple body systems, including the skin, mucous membranes, cardiovascular system, and central nervous system. It often presents with nonspecific symptoms such as rash, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis typically relies on serological tests due to the lack of definitive clinical features. Treatment involves penicillin-based antibiotics, with alternative options for penicillin-allergic patients.

Gonococcal infection, caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection affecting mucosal surfaces. Common synonyms include gonorrhea and clap. It typically involves the genitourinary tract, with symptoms such as urethritis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. In men, it may present as urethral discharge and dysuria; in women, it often causes cervicitis or pelvic pain. Complications include infertility and disseminated infection. The infection is spread through sexual contact and can affect the throat, eyes, and rectum. Prompt antibiotic treatment is essential to prevent complications.

"Other sexually transmitted chlamydial diseases" refers to infections caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting sites other than the genital tract. Common synonyms include non-genital chlamydial infections. The primary causative agent is *C. trachomatis*, which can cause conjunctivitis, pneumonia, and systemic infections. These infections typically affect the eyes, respiratory tract, and occasionally the urogenital tract in immunocompromised individuals. The disease is transmitted through sexual contact or from mother to child. Clinical manifestations vary by affected site, ranging from conjunctival inflammation to bronchopulmonary symptoms.

Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the urogenital tract, with common symptoms including frothy, malodorous vaginal discharge, itching, and irritation. In men, it may cause urethral discharge and discomfort. The infection is more prevalent in women, though men can also be asymptomatic carriers. Synonyms include trichomonal vaginitis or trichomoniasis genitalis. Transmission occurs through sexual contact, and treatment typically involves antiprotozoal medications such as metronidazole or tinidazole.

Anogenital herpesviral infection, commonly known as genital herpes, is a chronic, recurrent viral infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 can also be a cause. It affects the anogenital region, including the vulva, penis, anus, and perianal area. Characterized by painful vesicles, ulcers, and itching, the infection is transmitted through sexual contact. It is a lifelong condition with periodic outbreaks, often triggered by stress, immunosuppression, or hormonal changes. Complications may include transmission to neonates and increased risk of HIV acquisition.

code_desc: other predominantly sexually transmitted diseases, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other predominantly sexually transmitted diseases, not elsewhere classified" refers to sexually transmitted infections (STIs) that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified STIs or STIs with unknown etiology. Causative agents may include various bacteria, viruses, or parasites, though specific agents are often unidentified. These conditions typically affect the genital, anal, or urinary tract, and may present with symptoms such as ulcers, rashes, or discharge. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and exclusion of other known STIs.

Anogenital (venereal) warts, unspecified site, are benign, contagious growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 and 11. They appear as small, flesh-colored or grayish papules, often in clusters, and are typically found in the genital or anal areas. Common synonyms include genital warts, condyloma acuminata, and venereal warts. The condition is transmitted through sexual contact and is more prevalent in individuals with compromised immune systems or those who are not vaccinated against HPV.

Perianal (venereal) warts, also known as anogenital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 and 11. They typically appear in the anogenital region, including the perianal area, anus, and surrounding skin. These warts are contagious and spread through direct skin-to-skin contact. They present as small, flesh-colored or grayish papules that may cluster and have a rough surface. While generally not life-threatening, they can cause discomfort, bleeding, and psychological distress. Treatment options include topical medications, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

Cervical (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts, are benign growths caused by certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. These warts typically appear on the genitalia, including the vulva, penis, anus, and perineum. They present as small, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like lesions and may be asymptomatic or cause itching or discomfort. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity. While not life-threatening, they can lead to complications such as cervical dysplasia if left untreated. Vaccination against HPV is recommended for prevention.

Urethral (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign growths caused by certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 and 11. These warts typically appear on the genitalia, including the urethral meatus, penis, vulva, and perianal region. They present as small, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like lesions that may be asymptomatic or cause itching, bleeding, or discomfort. Transmission occurs through sexual contact.
