The condition is highly contagious and can be diagnosed visually or via histopathology. Treatment options include topical agents, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

Vaginal (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign growths caused by certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. These warts typically appear on the vulva, vagina, cervix, or perianal region. They present as small, flesh-colored or reddish bumps that may cluster and cause itching or discomfort. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. While not cancerous, HPV infection is a risk factor for cervical cancer. Treatment options include topical agents, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

Vulval (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts, are benign growths caused by certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. They typically appear on the vulva, perineum, and surrounding areas. These warts are contagious and spread through direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity. Clinically, they present as small, flesh-colored or pink papules, sometimes with a rough surface. They may be solitary or clustered and can cause mild itching or discomfort. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical appearance, though biopsy may be performed for confirmation.

Penile (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign growths caused by certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 and 11. These lesions typically appear as small, flesh-colored or reddish bumps on the penis, scrotum, groin, or surrounding areas. They are highly contagious and spread through direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity. While generally not life-threatening, they can cause discomfort, itching, and may increase the risk of other HPV-related conditions. Treatment options include topical medications, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

Scrotal (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. These warts typically appear on the penis, scrotum, groin, or perineum. They present as small, flesh-colored, cauliflower-like lesions that may be asymptomatic or cause itching or discomfort. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. While not life-threatening, they can be contagious and may require medical intervention for removal. Vaccination against HPV can help prevent infection.

Anogenital (venereal) warts, also known as genital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. These warts typically appear on the genitalia, perianal area, and sometimes the mouth or throat. They present as small, flesh-colored or pink, cauliflower-like lesions that may be asymptomatic or cause itching, bleeding, or discomfort. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. The condition is common and often diagnosed through visual examination, with treatment options including topical agents, cryotherapy, or surgical removal.

Yaws is a chronic bacterial infection caused by *Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue*. It primarily affects children in tropical regions and is characterized by painless skin lesions, often on the face, hands, and feet. Common synonyms include "lues morbus" and "frictional syphilis." The disease progresses through stages, including papular, verrucous, and destructive phases, leading to disfiguring nodules and bone lesions. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact. Without treatment, yaws can cause severe disability, but it is curable with penicillin.

Pinta, also known as carate, is a chronic bacterial skin infection caused by *Treponema carateum*. It primarily affects the skin, especially in tropical regions. The disease typically begins with a small, painless lesion that may progress to a diffuse, reddish rash. Commonly affected areas include the face, scalp, and extremities. The infection is transmitted through direct contact with infected skin. It is more prevalent in rural, impoverished communities with limited access to healthcare. The condition is often mistaken for leprosy due to similar clinical features. Treatment with antibiotics such as penicillin is effective in most cases.

Relapsing fevers are infectious diseases characterized by recurrent episodes of fever, often accompanied by headache, muscle pain, and malaise. They are caused by spirochetes of the genus * Borrelia *, primarily transmitted through lice or ticks. Common synonyms include recurrent fever and periodic fever. The disease typically affects the systemic circulation, with involvement of the liver, spleen, and central nervous system. Symptoms may relapse after apparent recovery, leading to a cyclical pattern. Complications can include anemia, thrombocytopenia, and meningitis. The condition is more prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and limited access to healthcare.

Other spirochaetal infections are bacterial infections caused by spirochetes other than *Treponema pallidum*, the agent of syphilis. Common synonyms include relapsing fever and yaws. Causative agents include *Borrelia* species, *Treponema carateum*, and *Spirochaeta* species. These infections typically affect the skin, joints, and central nervous system. They are often transmitted through arthropod vectors or direct contact. Symptoms may include fever, rash, joint pain, and neurological complications. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by serology or dark-field microscopy. Treatment involves antibiotics such as tetracyclines or penicillin.

Trachoma is a chronic bacterial infection of the conjunctiva caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It leads to progressive scarring of the eyelids, resulting in inturned eyelashes (trichiasis) that rub the cornea, causing pain, photophobia, and eventual blindness. Common synonyms include granuloma inguinale and lymphogranuloma venereum, though these refer to different clinical presentations. The infection primarily affects the eyes, particularly the conjunctiva and cornea, and is most prevalent in impoverished communities with poor sanitation and close personal contact.

"Other diseases caused by chlamydiae" refers to infections resulting from various species of *Chlamydia*, including *C. trachomatis*, *C. pneumoniae*, and *C. psittaci*. These pathogens can cause a range of conditions such as trachoma, pneumonia, and psittacosis. Common synonyms include chlamydial infections or chlamydiosis. *C. trachomatis* primarily affects the eyes and genital tract, while *C. pneumoniae* is associated with respiratory tract infections. *C. psittaci* causes psittacosis, typically affecting the lungs. These infections are often transmitted through respiratory droplets, sexual contact, or contaminated materials.

Typhus fever is an acute infectious disease caused by Rickettsia bacteria, primarily Rickettsia prowlettii. It is transmitted through the feces of infected body lice, often in unsanitary conditions. Common synonyms include epidemic typhus and louse fever. The disease typically affects the systemic circulation, leading to high fever, headache, rash, and systemic toxicity. It primarily targets the skin, lymph nodes, and vascular system, with severe cases potentially affecting the central nervous system. Complications may include pneumonia, renal failure, and circulatory collapse. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are crucial for recovery.

Spotted fever, a group of tick-borne rickettsioses, is caused by bacteria of the genus Rickettsia, including R. rickettsii, R. conorii, and R. africae. Common synonyms include Rocky Mountain spotted fever and African tick-bite fever. The infection typically presents with fever, headache, and a characteristic rash, often beginning at the site of the tick bite and spreading centripetally. Commonly affected body parts include the arms, legs, and trunk. Severe cases may involve complications such as meningitis, pneumonia, and multi-organ failure. Early antibiotic treatment is crucial to prevent progression.

Other rickettsioses refer to infections caused by rickettsial organisms other than the primary species like Rickettsia prowazekii and Rickettsia typhi. Common synonyms include spotted fever group rickettsioses. Causative agents include Rickettsia conorii, Rickettsia africae, and Rickettsia rickettsii. These infections are typically transmitted via tick bites. Clinically, they present with fever, headache, rash, and eschar. The rash often begins at the site of the bite and spreads centripetally. Commonly affected body parts include the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the liver and lungs.

Acute poliomyelitis is a viral infection caused by the poliovirus, leading to inflammation of the central nervous system. It primarily affects the spinal cord and brain, resulting in muscle weakness and paralysis, often asymmetric. Common synonyms include poliomyelitis and infantile paralysis. The virus spreads through fecal-oral transmission. Most infections are asymptomatic, but some progress to paralytic disease. Complications may include respiratory failure and post-polio syndrome. Vaccination has significantly reduced its incidence globally.

code_desc: atypical virus infections of central nervous system
summary: Atypical virus infections of the central nervous system (CNS) refer to viral illnesses that present with non-specific or unusual clinical features, often lacking typical signs of classic CNS infections. Common synonyms include viral encephalitis and meningitis with atypical presentations. Causative agents may include herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, enteroviruses, and others. These infections typically affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as fever, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. Diagnosis often requires lumbar puncture and polymerase chain reaction testing.

Rabies is a viral encephalitis caused by the rabies virus, a member of the Rhabdoviridae family. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected animal, most commonly dogs, bats, raccoons, and skunks. The virus affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the brain. Symptoms progress from fever and anxiety to confusion, hallucinations, and ultimately paralysis and death. Common synonyms include hydrophobia and furious rabies. The disease primarily targets the central nervous system and is almost always fatal once clinical signs appear. Vaccination is the most effective preventive measure.

Mosquito-borne viral encephalitis is an inflammation of the brain caused by viral infections transmitted through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include viral meningitis and acute encephalitis. Key causative agents include Japanese encephalitis virus, West Nile virus, dengue virus, and Zika virus. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and meninges. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe neurological complications such as seizures, coma, and death. It is more common in tropical and subtropical regions, with outbreaks often linked to seasonal mosquito activity.

Tick-borne viral encephalitis (TBE) is a viral infection affecting the central nervous system, primarily transmitted through tick bites. Common synonyms include summer meningoencephalitis and tick encephalitis. Caused by flaviviruses such as TBE virus, it typically affects the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe encephalitis. The disease is endemic in Europe and Asia, with higher incidence in forested areas. Complications may include neurological deficits, seizures, and long-term disability. Early diagnosis and supportive care are critical for managing outcomes.

code_desc: other viral encephalitis, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other viral encephalitis, not elsewhere classified" refers to inflammation of the brain caused by viruses that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified viral encephalitis. Causative agents may include enteroviruses, arboviruses, or other rare viral pathogens. The condition typically affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain. Symptoms may include fever, headache, confusion, seizures, and altered mental status. It is often diagnosed when the causative virus cannot be definitively identified through standard testing.

Viral meningitis is an inflammation of the meninges caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include aseptic meningitis. It is typically caused by enteroviruses, such as coxsackievirus and echovirus, though other viruses like herpes simplex virus, mumps, and West Nile virus can also be responsible. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. It is generally less severe than bacterial meningitis and often resolves without specific antiviral treatment.

code_desc: other viral infections of central nervous system, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other viral infections of the central nervous system, not elsewhere classified" refers to viral infections affecting the brain and spinal cord caused by agents not specifically categorized under other CNS infections. Common synonyms include unspecified viral encephalitis or meningitis. Causative agents may include enteroviruses, herpesviruses, and other less commonly identified viruses. These infections typically affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis often requires lumbar puncture and viral testing.

Dengue fever, also known as classical dengue or breakbone fever, is a viral infection caused by any of the four dengue virus serotypes (DENV 1-4). Transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, it primarily affects the vascular system and immune response. Common symptoms include high fever, severe headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and rash. The infection typically involves the skin, liver, and circulatory system, with potential complications such as plasma leakage, hemorrhage, and shock. It predominantly affects tropical and subtropical regions, with children and travelers being at higher risk.

Dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) is a severe, life-threatening complication of dengue infection. It is caused by any of the four dengue virus serotypes transmitted by *Aedes* mosquitoes. DHF is characterized by plasma leakage, leading to fluid accumulation, hypovolemic shock, and multi-organ involvement. Common synonyms include dengue shock syndrome and severe dengue. The condition primarily affects the circulatory system, liver, and hematologic system, with symptoms such as fever, bleeding, thrombocytopenia, and hypotension. It predominantly occurs in children and individuals with prior dengue exposure.

Other mosquito-borne viral fevers refer to a group of illnesses caused by various viruses transmitted through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include viral hemorrhagic fevers and arboviral infections. Causative agents include dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever viruses. These infections primarily affect the fever, musculoskeletal system, and sometimes the neurological system. Symptoms typically include high fever, rash, joint pain, and headache. The illness can range from mild to severe, with potential complications such as hemorrhage, encephalitis, or organ failure. The affected body parts often include the skin, joints, and central nervous system.

code_desc: other arthropod-borne viral fevers, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other arthropod-borne viral fevers, not elsewhere classified" refers to febrile illnesses caused by viruses transmitted by arthropods, such as mosquitoes or ticks, but not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include undifferentiated arthropod-borne viral fever. Causative agents may include viruses like Chikungunya, Dengue, and Yellow fever, though specific identification may not be possible. These fevers typically affect the systemic circulation, causing fever, rash, joint pain, and sometimes neurological involvement. The illness is often self-limiting but can lead to complications in vulnerable populations.

Yellow fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, a flavivirus transmitted primarily by *Aedes* and *Sthinophorus* mosquitoes. It is endemic in parts of Africa and South America. The disease typically affects the liver, causing jaundice (hence the name), and may involve the kidneys, cardiovascular system, and gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include yellow fever, jaundice fever, and African fever. Symptoms include fever, chills, headache, muscle pain, and in severe cases, bleeding and organ failure. Vaccination is the most effective preventive measure.

Arenaviral haemorrhagic fever is a severe viral illness characterized by fever, systemic vasculopathy, and coagulopathy leading to hemorrhage. Common synonyms include viral hemorrhagic fever and arenavirus infection. Caused by arenaviruses such as Lassa, Junín, Machupo, and Guanarito, it primarily affects the vascular system and organs like the liver, spleen, and kidneys. Symptoms include high fever, malaise, and progressive bleeding from mucous membranes and skin. The disease can progress rapidly, leading to multi-organ failure and high mortality if untreated. Transmission occurs via rodent contact or vector-borne routes.

Dengue is a viral infection transmitted by *Aedes* mosquitoes, caused by one of four serotypes of the dengue virus (DENV 1-4). It is also known as breakbone fever due to severe musculoskeletal pain. Common symptoms include high fever, headache, rash, and joint pain. In severe cases, it can progress to dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome, affecting the circulatory system and leading to plasma leakage, fluid accumulation, and organ impairment. The disease primarily affects the skin, liver, and blood vessels, with systemic involvement in severe cases. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Dengue without warning signs refers to a mild form of dengue fever characterized by the absence of severe symptoms such as plasma leakage or organ involvement. It is commonly caused by the Dengue virus (DENV), with serotypes 1-4 being responsible. Synonyms include classic dengue or uncomplicated dengue. Typically affecting the systemic circulation and liver, this form presents with fever, headache, myalgia, and rash. It primarily impacts the blood vessels and liver, with minimal risk of progression to severe dengue.

Dengue with warning signs is a severe form of dengue fever characterized by clinical indicators that predict progression to dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Common synonyms include severe dengue and dengue shock. Caused by the dengue virus (DENV), typically transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, it affects the circulatory system, liver, and hematopoietic system. Warning signs include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, clinical fluid retention, and mucosal bleeding. It predominantly affects individuals in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly children and those with prior dengue infections.

Severe dengue, also known as dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome, is a life-threatening complication of dengue infection caused by any of the four dengue virus serotypes. It typically affects children and young adults, with symptoms including high fever, plasma leakage, fluid accumulation, and hemorrhagic manifestations. The disease primarily impacts the circulatory system, leading to hypovolemic shock, and may involve the liver, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract. Early recognition and supportive care are critical to prevent mortality.

Dengue, unspecified, is a viral infection caused by any of the four dengue virus serotypes (DENV 1-4). It is transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. Common synonyms include dengue fever and dengue virus infection. The disease typically affects the vascular system, leading to fever, rash, and thrombocytopenia. In severe cases, it can progress to dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome, affecting the circulatory system and organs. The primary affected body parts include the skin, liver, and blood vessels. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

code_desc: other viral haemorrhagic fevers, not elsewhere classified
summary: Other viral haemorrhagic fevers (OVHF) refer to severe viral infections characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ dysfunction. Common synonyms include unclassified viral haemorrhagic fevers. Causative agents may include viruses such as Lassa, Rift Valley fever, and others not classified under specific categories like Ebola or Marburg. These infections primarily affect the vascular system, liver, and kidneys, leading to coagulopathy and organ failure. Symptoms range from mild flu-like illness to severe shock and death. Transmission occurs through vectors, direct contact, or aerosols, depending on the virus.

Herpesviral infections, particularly those caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV), are highly contagious viral infections characterized by recurrent outbreaks of blisters or sores. Common synonyms include cold sores and fever blisters. HSV-1 and HSV-2 are the primary causative agents, with HSV-1 typically affecting the oral region and HSV-2 the genital area. These infections are spread through direct contact and can cause painful lesions on the lips, mouth, genitals, and surrounding areas. The virus remains latent in nerve cells and can reactivate under certain conditions, leading to recurrent episodes.

Varicella, commonly known as chickenpox, is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus (VZV). It primarily affects children but can occur in adults. The disease is characterized by a pruritic rash that progresses through stages of macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts. Commonly affected areas include the face, scalp, and trunk, with lesions also appearing on the oral mucosa and extremities. Complications may include secondary bacterial infections, pneumonia, or encephalitis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. The infection is typically self-limiting, with a recovery period of 1–2 weeks. Vaccination provides effective prevention.

Herpes zoster, or shingles, is a viral infection caused by the reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in previously infected individuals. It presents as a painful, unilateral rash with grouped vesicles along sensory dermatomes. Common synonyms include shingles and zona. The condition typically affects the trunk, face, and scalp, with the thoracic dermatomes being the most frequently involved. Neuropraxia and postherpetic neuralgia may occur. Complications can include ocular involvement, encephalitis, and bacterial superinfection. The rash evolves from macules to vesicles, crusting within 7–10 days.

Measles is an acute viral infection caused by the measles virus (Morbillivirus), characterized by a high fever, cough, runny nose, and conjunctivitis, followed by a maculopapular rash. Common synonyms include rubeola. The disease primarily affects the respiratory tract and skin, with systemic involvement. It is highly contagious, spreading via respiratory droplets. Complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis, and blindness can occur, particularly in young children and immunocompromised individuals. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine is the most effective prevention strategy.

Rubella, also known as German measles or rubeola, is a viral infection caused by the rubella virus. It typically presents with a mild fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy. The rash begins on the face and spreads to the trunk and extremities. Common synonyms include German measles and three-day measles. The virus is transmitted via respiratory droplets. It primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and mucous membranes. Congenital rubella syndrome can occur if a pregnant woman is infected, affecting multiple organs in the fetus. The disease is generally self-limiting in healthy individuals.

Viral warts are benign skin growths caused by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV). Common synonyms include寻常疣, plantar warts, and flat warts. They typically affect the hands, feet, and face, with plantar warts occurring on the soles of the feet. Transmission occurs through direct skin contact or indirect exposure to contaminated surfaces. The lesions are characterized by rough, hyperkeratotic papules, often with a central punctum. While generally asymptomatic, they may cause discomfort, especially in plantar locations. Treatment options include topical agents, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

code_desc: other viral infections characterised by skin and mucous membrane lesions, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other viral infections characterised by skin and mucous membrane lesions, not elsewhere classified" refers to viral infections causing skin and mucous membrane lesions without a more specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include unspecified viral exanthems or viral mucocutaneous syndromes. Causative agents may include herpesviruses, papillomaviruses, or other less commonly identified viruses. These infections typically affect the skin, oral mucosa, and genital areas, presenting with eruptions, ulcers, or vesicles. They are often diagnosed clinically when no specific viral agent is identified.

Acute hepatitis A is a viral infection of the liver caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV). It is typically transmitted through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated food or water. Common synonyms include infectious hepatitis and serum hepatitis. The infection primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation, elevated liver enzymes, and jaundice. Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and dark urine. Most patients recover fully without long-term liver damage. The disease is usually self-limiting, with no specific antiviral treatment required. Vaccination provides effective prevention.

Acute hepatitis B is a viral infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), leading to inflammation of the liver. Common synonyms include acute HBV infection or hepatitis B. The virus is transmitted through contact with infectious body fluids. Symptoms may include jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and abdominal pain. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic symptoms can occur. Most adults recover fully, but some may progress to chronic infection. Risk factors include unprotected sexual contact, needle sharing, and perinatal transmission. Vaccination is the most effective prevention method.

Other acute viral hepatitis refers to inflammation of the liver caused by viruses other than hepatitis A, B, or C. Common synonyms include acute non-A non-B hepatitis and acute viral hepatitis not otherwise specified. Causative agents may include hepatitis D, E, G, and other less common viruses. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and elevated liver enzymes. It is typically transmitted through blood, bodily fluids, or contaminated food and water. Diagnosis often involves serological testing and liver function analysis.

Chronic viral hepatitis is a long-term inflammatory liver disease caused by persistent infection with hepatitis viruses. Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis or persistent viral hepatitis. The primary causative agents are hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV), though hepatitis D virus (HDV) can also contribute. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. It may present with fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes, though many patients are asymptomatic. Diagnosis involves serological testing and liver function assessment.

Unspecified viral hepatitis refers to liver inflammation of viral origin when the specific virus cannot be identified. Common synonyms include undetermined or unknown etiology hepatitis. Causative agents may include hepatitis A, B, C, D, or E viruses, though the exact pathogen is not confirmed. The condition typically affects the liver, leading to symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. It may present acutely or chronically, with varying degrees of severity. Diagnosis often involves serological testing and liver function analysis. The prognosis depends on the underlying cause and patient's overall health.

code_desc: human immunodeficiency virus [hiv] disease resulting in malignant neoplasms
summary: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease leads to progressive immune system deterioration, increasing susceptibility to opportunistic infections and certain malignancies. Common synonyms include acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and HIV-related malignancies. The causative agent is the human immunodeficiency virus, primarily HIV-1 and less commonly HIV-2. Malignant neoplasms such as Kaposi's sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and cervical cancer frequently occur, predominantly affecting the skin, lymphatic system, and genital tract. These cancers are more prevalent in individuals with advanced immunosuppression.

code_desc: human immunodeficiency virus [hiv] disease resulting in other specified diseases
summary: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease resulting in other specified diseases refers to advanced HIV infection where the immune system is severely compromised, leading to opportunistic infections and malignancies not classified under AIDS-defining illnesses. Common synonyms include AIDS-related complications and HIV-associated opportunistic infections. The causative agent is the human immunodeficiency virus, primarily affecting CD4+ T lymphocytes. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system, and skin, with conditions such as pneumocystis pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma, and cryptococcal meningitis commonly observed.

code_desc: human immunodeficiency virus [hiv] disease resulting in other conditions
summary: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease resulting in other conditions refers to the progression of HIV infection to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), leading to opportunistic infections and malignancies. Common synonyms include AIDS-related complications and HIV-associated comorbidities. The causative agent is the human immunodeficiency virus, primarily transmitted through unprotected sexual contact, blood transfusions, or mother-to-child transmission. The immune system, particularly CD4+ T cells, is predominantly affected, leading to systemic complications involving the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system, and other organs.

Acute HIV infection syndrome refers to the early phase of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, occurring within 2-4 weeks after exposure. It is characterized by flu-like symptoms such as fever, fatigue, rash, and lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include acute retroviral syndrome and primary HIV infection. The causative agent is HIV-1 or, less commonly, HIV-2. This syndrome typically affects the immune system, particularly CD4+ T cells, and may involve the lymphatic system, skin, and mucosal surfaces. It is a critical stage for diagnosis and initiation of antiretroviral therapy.

code_desc: hiv disease resulting in other specified conditions
summary: HIV disease resulting in other specified conditions refers to complications or secondary infections that arise due to the immunosuppressive effects of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Common synonyms include opportunistic infections and AIDS-related complications. The causative agent is the human immunodeficiency virus, primarily HIV-1 and less commonly HIV-2. These conditions typically affect the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and central nervous systems, as well as the skin and mucous membranes. The immune system's compromised state leads to increased susceptibility to various infections and malignancies.

Unspecified human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) disease refers to HIV infection without a specified stage or clinical manifestation. It is caused by human immunodeficiency virus types 1 and 2 (HIV-1 and HIV-2). Common synonyms include HIV infection, HIV-positive status, or undifferentiated HIV disease. The virus primarily targets the immune system, particularly CD4+ T cells, leading to progressive immunodeficiency. Initially, it may present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and lymphadenopathy. Without treatment, it can progress to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), affecting multiple organ systems.

Cytomegaloviral disease is a viral infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It is a common opportunistic infection in immunocompromised individuals. The virus can cause a wide range of clinical manifestations, including retinitis, pneumonia, hepatitis, and encephalitis. Common synonyms include CMV infection or cytomegalovirus retinitis. The disease typically affects the retina, lungs, liver, and central nervous system, and can lead to severe complications if left untreated.

Mumps is a viral infection caused by the mumps virus, a member of the paramyxovirus family. It primarily affects the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands, leading to swelling and tenderness. Common synonyms include epidemic parotitis and parotiditis. The disease is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets. Symptoms include fever, headache, and muscle aches, with swelling of the parotid glands typically appearing 16–18 days after exposure. Complications may involve the central nervous system, pancreas, or testes. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine is effective in preventing the disease.

Infectious mononucleosis, also known as glandular fever or mono, is a viral infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). It commonly affects adolescents and young adults. The condition is characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Fatigue may persist for weeks. Other symptoms include pharyngitis, malaise, and occasionally rash. It is transmitted through saliva, hence the nickname "kissing disease." The infection typically involves the lymphatic system and may affect the liver and spleen. Most cases resolve spontaneously without specific treatment.

Viral conjunctivitis is an inflammatory condition of the conjunctiva caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include pink eye and contagious conjunctivitis. It is typically caused by adenoviruses, though enteroviruses and herpes simplex virus can also be responsible. The infection primarily affects the eyes, leading to redness, swelling, and a gritty sensation. It is highly contagious and often accompanies upper respiratory infections. The condition usually affects both eyes and resolves spontaneously within 7–14 days without specific treatment.

code_desc: other viral diseases, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other viral diseases, not elsewhere classified" refers to viral infections that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous viral infections or unspecified viral diseases. Causative agents may include viruses such as enteroviruses, parvoviruses, or others not classified elsewhere. These infections can affect various body systems, including the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and neurological systems. Clinical presentations vary widely depending on the virus and host factors, often presenting with fever, fatigue, and systemic symptoms. Diagnosis typically relies on clinical evaluation and laboratory testing.

Viral infection of unspecified site refers to a systemic viral illness where the specific location of infection is not identified. Common synonyms include undifferentiated viral infection or viral syndrome. Causative agents may include influenza viruses, enteroviruses, parvovirus B19, or herpesviruses. Typically, the infection affects multiple body systems, with symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and malaise. It often involves the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or neurological systems. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and laboratory findings when specific testing is not available.

Dermatophytosis, also known as ringworm or tinea, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes, which are fungi that thrive on keratin. Common causative agents include *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Epidermophyton* species. The infection typically affects the skin, hair, and nails, with common presentations on the scalp (tinea capitis), body (tinea corporis), feet (tinea pedis), and groin (tinea cruris). It is contagious and often spreads through direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects. Symptoms include itching, redness, and circular, scaly patches. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by fungal microscopy or culture.

Other superficial mycoses refer to fungal infections affecting the skin, hair, and nails. Common synonyms include tinea and dermatophytosis. These infections are caused by dermatophytes, such as *Trichophyton*, *Candida*, and *Microsporum* species. They typically affect areas like the scalp, feet, groin, and nails. Symptoms include itching, scaling, and ring-shaped rashes. Diagnosis is often clinical, supported by microscopic examination or culture. Treatment involves topical or oral antifungals, depending on the severity and location of the infection.

Candidiasis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Candida* species, most commonly *Candida albicans*. It results from an overgrowth of these yeast organisms, often in immunocompromised individuals or those with disrupted mucosal barriers. Common synonyms include moniliasis and thrush. The infection typically affects mucous membranes, such as the mouth, vagina, and gastrointestinal tract, but can also occur on the skin, particularly in warm, moist areas. Symptoms include redness, itching, and white discharge. Systemic candidiasis can affect organs like the heart, kidneys, and brain, leading to severe complications.

Candidiasis of other sites refers to fungal infections caused by *Candida* species in areas not typically associated with common candidiasis, such as the nails, skin, or mucous membranes. Common synonyms include cutaneous candidiasis and superficial candidiasis. The primary causative agent is *Candida albicans*, though other species like *C. glabrata* and *C. parapsilosis* may also be involved. These infections commonly affect the skin folds, nail beds, and mucous membranes, often in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor hygiene. Symptoms include redness, itching, and scaling, with nail involvement presenting as thickening and discoloration.

Coccidioidomycosis, also known as Valley fever, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, where the fungus forms spherules that rupture, releasing endospores. The infection often presents as a subacute or chronic respiratory illness, with symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. In immunocompromised individuals, it can disseminate to other organs, including the skin, bones, and central nervous system. The disease is endemic in arid regions of the southwestern United States, Central America, and parts of Mexico.

Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*, commonly found in soil enriched with bird or bat droppings. It primarily affects the lungs, where the fungus is inhaled as spores. In immunocompetent individuals, it often presents as a mild, self-limiting illness with flu-like symptoms. In immunocompromised patients, such as those with HIV/AIDS, it can progress to disseminated disease involving multiple organs. Synonyms include pulmonary histoplasmosis and Ohio valley fever. The infection typically involves the respiratory tract, but may spread to the lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and central nervous system in severe cases.

Blastomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Blastomyces dermatitidis* and related species. It primarily affects the lungs but can disseminate to other organs. Common synonyms include North American blastomycosis and Gilchrist's disease. The infection typically presents with flu-like symptoms, followed by chronic pulmonary disease. Dissemination may involve skin, bones, and genitourinary tract. Diagnosis is confirmed by culture, serology, or histopathology. Treatment involves antifungal agents like itraconazole or amphotericin B. It is endemic in certain regions of North America and Africa.

Paracoccidioidomycosis, also known as South American blastomycosis or Venezuelan fever, is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* and *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects the lungs and mucous membranes of the oral and nasal cavities, often spreading to the skin, lymph nodes, and visceral organs. The infection is endemic in Latin America and typically presents with respiratory symptoms, cutaneous lesions, and systemic involvement. It is more common in males and those with compromised immune systems. Diagnosis is based on clinical features, imaging, and mycological examination.

Sporotrichosis is a subcutaneous fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species. It typically presents as a chronic, progressive lesion following traumatic inoculation, often from thorn pricks or plant contact. Common synonyms include "rose gardener's disease" and "groin sporotrichosis." The infection primarily affects the skin, lymph nodes, and occasionally the lungs or disseminates systemically. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with occupational exposure to soil or plants.

Chromomycosis and phaeomycotic abscess are chronic fungal infections caused by pigmented dematiaceous fungi. Common synonyms include chromoblastomycosis and phaeohyphomycosis. The causative agents include species of *Madurella* (e.g., *M. mycetomatis*), *Cladophialophora*, and *Fonsecaea*. These infections typically affect the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and sometimes bones, often following trauma or insect bites. Chromomycosis presents with verrucous lesions, while phaeomycotic abscesses are characterized by suppurative nodules. Both conditions are more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Aspergillosis is a fungal infection caused by species of the genus *Aspergillus*, most commonly *A. fumigatus*. It primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. The infection can manifest as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, invasive aspergillosis, or chronic pulmonary aspergillosis. Symptoms include cough, fever, and hemoptysis. Invasive disease may spread to other organs, such as the brain or heart. Synonyms include aspergilloma and mycotic ball. The condition is more prevalent in patients with cystic fibrosis, tuberculosis, or those on immunosuppressive therapy.

Cryptococcosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection typically involves the lungs and central nervous system, leading to pneumonia and meningitis. It may also disseminate to other organs. Synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and pulmonary cryptococcosis. The disease is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and can be life-threatening if untreated.

Zygomycosis is a severe, often life-threatening fungal infection caused by fungi in the order Mucorales. Common synonyms include mucormycosis. The infection is characterized by rapid tissue invasion and thrombosis of small vessels. Causative agents include *Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, *Absidia*, and *Rhizomucor* species. It typically affects the sinuses, lungs, brain, and skin, often in immunocompromised individuals or those with diabetes. The infection progresses rapidly and requires prompt antifungal therapy and surgical debridement for optimal outcomes.

Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection characterized by the formation of subcutaneous nodules and sinus tracts with discharge of grains. Common synonyms include madura foot and chromoblastomycosis. It is caused by filamentous fungi (eumycetoma) or actinomycetes (actinomycetoma). Common fungal agents include *Madurella mycetomatis*, while bacterial causes include *Nocardia* species. The infection typically affects the feet, legs, and hands, often entering through minor trauma. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

"Other mycoses, not elsewhere classified" refers to fungal infections that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous mycoses or unspecified fungal infections. Causative agents may include dermatophytes, yeast, and molds. These infections typically affect the skin, nails, and mucous membranes. They may present as superficial or systemic infections, often with symptoms such as itching, scaling, or discoloration. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and laboratory tests. Treatment varies depending on the organism and infection site, often involving antifungal medications.

Opportunistic mycoses are fungal infections that occur in immunocompromised individuals, exploiting weakened host defenses. Common synonyms include opportunistic fungal infections or secondary mycoses. These infections are caused by fungi such as *Candida*, *Aspergillus*, *Cryptococcus*, and *Pneumocystis*. Typically affecting the lungs, skin, mucous membranes, and systemic organs, they often manifest as pneumonia, oral thrush, or disseminated disease. These pathogens are usually non-pathogenic in healthy hosts but can cause severe illness in those with compromised immunity, such as patients with HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, or those on prolonged antibiotic therapy.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria is a severe, life-threatening parasitic infection caused by the protozoan Plasmodium falciparum. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito. The parasite invades red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, anemia, and potentially cerebral malaria. Common synonyms include falciparum malaria and malignant malaria. It primarily affects the red blood cells and can involve the liver, spleen, and brain. Complications may include organ failure and death if untreated.

Plasmodium vivax malaria is a parasitic infection caused by the Plasmodium vivax parasite, transmitted through the bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito. It is characterized by intermittent fever, chills, headache, and malaise. Common synonyms include tertian malaria, due to its typical 48-hour fever cycle. The parasite primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to splenomegaly and anemia. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Unlike P. falciparum, P. vivax can remain dormant in the liver, causing relapses.

*Plasmodium malariae* malaria is a protozoal infection caused by the parasite *Plasmodium malariae*, one of the less common human malaria parasites. It typically presents with mild, intermittent fever and is often asymptomatic or underdiagnosed. The infection primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to periodic chills, fever, and sweating. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Common synonyms include tertian malaria, though this term is more commonly associated with *P. vivax*. The disease is generally less severe than other malaria types but can cause chronic infection if left untreated.

"Other parasitologically confirmed malaria" refers to malaria cases caused by Plasmodium species other than *P. falciparum*, *P. vivax*, *P. ovale*, or *P. malariae*. Common synonyms include "non-falciparum malaria" or "other Plasmodium species malaria." Causative agents include *P. knowlesi*, *P. malariae*, and *P. ovale*. The disease primarily affects the erythrocytes, leading to fever, chills, and anemia. It is typically endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. While less severe than falciparum malaria, it can still cause complications such as splenomegaly and hemolytic anemia.

Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease caused by protozoan organisms of the genus *Leishmania*, transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. Common synonyms include visceral leishmaniasis, kala-azar, and cutaneous leishmaniasis. The disease primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs, particularly the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Clinical manifestations vary from localized skin ulcers to systemic illness characterized by fever, weight loss, and organ enlargement. The causative agents include species such as *L. donovani*, *L. infantum*, and *L. tropica*.

African trypanosomiasis, also known as sleeping sickness, is a parasitic disease caused by *Trypanosoma brucei* species. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The infection primarily affects the bloodstream and central nervous system, leading to progressive neurological symptoms. Two subspecies, *T. b. gambiense* and *T. b. rhodesiense*, cause distinct forms of the disease, with the former being more prevalent and chronic. Common symptoms include fever, headache, and sleep disturbances, ultimately leading to coma and death if untreated.

Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It is primarily transmitted through the feces of infected triatomine bugs, though other routes include blood transfusion and congenital transmission. The disease typically affects the heart, gastrointestinal tract, and nervous system. Chronic infection can lead to cardiomyopathy, megacolon, and megaesophagus. Symptoms may include fever, swelling at the site of infection, and later, severe cardiac or digestive complications. It is endemic in Latin America but is increasingly recognized globally.

Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*, a protozoan parasite. Common synonyms include congenital toxoplasmosis and ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection typically affects the eyes, brain, and other organs, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or fetuses. It is transmitted through ingestion of oocysts from contaminated food or water, or via congenital transmission. Symptoms may include fever, lymphadenopathy, and ocular inflammation. In severe cases, it can lead to vision loss or neurological complications. The infection is often asymptomatic in healthy individuals but can be life-threatening in those with weakened immune systems.

Pneumocystosis, also known as Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection primarily involves the lungs, leading to interstitial pneumonia characterized by non-productive cough, fever, and dyspnea. Rarely, extrapulmonary involvement may occur, though this is less common. The condition is a significant opportunistic infection with a high mortality rate if untreated.

code_desc: other protozoal diseases, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other protozoal diseases, not elsewhere classified" refers to parasitic infections caused by protozoa that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous protozoal infections. Causative agents may include organisms like *Leishmania*, *Trypanosoma*, and *Toxoplasma*, among others. These infections typically affect the skin, mucous membranes, central nervous system, and viscera. They are often transmitted via vectors such as mosquitoes, sandflies, or contaminated food and water. Clinically, symptoms vary widely depending on the organism and affected organ systems.

Schistosomiasis, also known as bilharziasis, is a parasitic disease caused by trematode flatworms of the genus *Schistosoma*. The most common species are *S. mansoni*, *S. haematobium*, and *S. japonicum*. Infection occurs through contact with freshwater contaminated with cercariae, which penetrate the skin. The parasites mature in the bloodstream, primarily affecting the intestines and bladder. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, blood in urine, and liver enlargement. Chronic infection can lead to fibrosis and organ damage.

Other fluke infections refer to parasitic diseases caused by trematodes that infect various organs beyond the liver and intestines. Common synonyms include digenean infections or fluke infestations. Causative agents include *Fasciola hepatica* and *Fasciola gigantica* (liver flukes), *Clonorchis sinensis* (liver fluke), and *Schistosoma* species (blood flukes). These infections typically affect the liver, bile ducts, intestines, and vascular system. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and gastrointestinal distress. Diagnosis often involves stool examination, serology, or imaging. Treatment usually involves antiparasitic medications such as praziquantel.

Echinococcosis is a chronic parasitic infection caused by larval stages of the tapeworm *Echinococcus*. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and cystic echinococcosis. The primary causative agents are *Echinococcus granulosus* and *Echinococcus multilocularis*. The infection typically affects the liver and lungs, forming hydatid cysts. It is prevalent in endemic areas where dogs serve as definitive hosts. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs from contaminated environments. The disease can lead to cyst growth, organ dysfunction, and potentially life-threatening complications if left untreated.

Taeniasis is a parasitic infection caused by tapeworms of the genus *Taenia*, most commonly *Taenia solium* (pork tapeworm) and *Taenia saginata* (beef tapeworm). It occurs through ingestion of undercooked meat containing larval cysts. The adult worms reside in the small intestine, where they attach to the intestinal wall. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss. In severe cases, cysticercosis can develop when larvae migrate to other tissues, particularly the brain, eyes, and muscles. Synonyms include cysticercosis (for larval stage) and taeniases.

Cysticercosis is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*, the pork tapeworm. The larvae form cysts in various tissues, most commonly in the central nervous system, leading to neurocysticercosis. Other affected areas include the muscles, eyes, and liver. Synonyms include neurocysticercosis when involving the brain and spinal cord. The infection results from ingestion of tapeworm eggs, often through contaminated food or water. Symptoms depend on the location of the cysts and may include seizures, headaches, or visual disturbances. Diagnosis typically involves imaging and serological tests. Treatment varies based on the affected organ and may include antiparasitic drugs and surgical intervention.

Diphyllobothriasis and sparganosis are helminthic infections caused by tapeworms. Diphyllobothriasis is caused by *Diphyllobothrium latum*, while sparganosis is caused by the larvae of *Spirometra erinacei* or *Spirometra mansonoides*. Diphyllobothriasis primarily affects the small intestine, whereas sparganosis involves migration of larvae to subcutaneous tissues, eyes, lungs, and brain. Common synonyms include broad tapeworm infection and sparganous infection. Both conditions are acquired through ingestion of contaminated food or water or via intermediate hosts.

Other cestode infections refer to parasitic infections caused by tapeworms other than the most commonly recognized species like *Taenia solium* or *Diphyllobothrium latum*. Common synonyms include tapeworm infections or cestodiasis. Causative agents include *Echinococcus granulosus*, *Echinococcus multilocularis*, *Hymenolepis nana*, and *Spirometra erinacei*. These infections typically affect the intestines but can also involve the liver, lungs, brain, and other organs, depending on the species. Symptoms vary but often include abdominal pain, weight loss, and cyst formation in extraintestinal sites. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging or serology.

Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. Adult worms reside in subcutaneous tissues, producing microfilariae that migrate to the skin and eyes, leading to severe itching, skin lesions, and potentially blindness. It primarily affects the skin, eyes, and lymphatic system. The condition is endemic in tropical regions of Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East.

Filariasis is a parasitic disease caused by filarial worms transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Common synonyms include lymphatic filariasis and elephantiasis. The causative agents include *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*, and *Brugia timori*. The infection primarily affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and elephantiasis of the limbs, genitals, and breasts. It can also cause hydrocele and other complications. The disease is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, with significant socioeconomic impact due to disability and stigma.

Hookworm disease is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genus *Ancylostoma* and *Necator*. Common synonyms includeancylostomiasis and necatoriasis. The larvae penetrate the skin, typically through contaminated soil, and migrate to the lungs before reaching the intestines, where they mature into adult worms. The primary affected body parts are the skin at the site of entry, lungs, and small intestine. Symptoms include cutaneous reactions, coughing, and gastrointestinal issues such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and iron deficiency anemia. The disease is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions with poor sanitation.

Ascariasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Ascaris lumbricoides*, a nematode roundworm. Common synonyms include intestinal roundworm infection and human ascariasis. The larvae migrate through the lungs before maturing into adult worms in the small intestine. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, coughing, and malnutrition. The infection primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, with adult worms residing in the duodenum and jejunum. It is prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and is a significant cause of morbidity in children.

Strongyloidiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Strongyloides stercoralis*. It primarily affects the intestines, with larvae migrating through the bloodstream to the lungs and then returning to the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include filariasis and threadworm infection. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Chronic infection can lead to intestinal symptoms, malabsorption, and in severe cases, disseminated strongyloidiasis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool examination or serology.

code_desc: other intestinal helminthiases, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other intestinal helminthiases, not elsewhere classified" refers to parasitic infections caused by helminths that affect the intestines but are not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include miscellaneous intestinal worm infections. Causative agents may include species such as *Hymenolepis nana*, *Dientamoeba fragilis*, and *Enterobius vermicularis*. These infections typically affect the small intestine and sometimes the large intestine, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. They are commonly found in areas with poor sanitation and hygiene.

Unspecified intestinal parasitism refers to the presence of parasitic infection in the gastrointestinal tract without identification of the specific parasite. Common synonyms include non-specific intestinal protozoa or unidentified intestinal helminth infection. Causative agents may include protozoa such as Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, or Cryptosporidium, and helminths like Ascaris lumbricoides or hookworms. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though involvement of the colon may occur. Symptoms typically include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. Diagnosis often requires stool examination.

Other helminthiases refer to parasitic infections caused by various types of helminths, excluding the major categories such as nematodes, cestodes, and trematodes. Common synonyms include intestinal worm infections and helminthic infestations. Causative agents vary widely and include species such as *Strongyloides stercoralis*, *Trichuris trichiura*, and *Ascaris lumbricoides*. These infections primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract but can also involve the lungs, skin, and other organs. They are commonly found in tropical and subtropical regions, affecting both children and immunocompromised individuals.

Pediculosis and phthiriasis are parasitic infestations caused by lice. Pediculosis is commonly caused by *Pediculus humanus capitis* (head lice), *Pediculus humanus corporis* (body lice), and *Pediculus humanus pubis* (pubic lice). Phthiriasis refers to infestation by *Pediculus* species, particularly head lice. These conditions typically affect the scalp, body, and pubic area, causing intense itching and irritation. Common synonyms include head lice, body lice, and pubic lice. Transmission occurs through direct contact or shared personal items.

Myiasis is an infestation of living tissue by fly larvae. Common synonyms include fly蛆 disease and myiasis. It is caused by various dipteran flies, with *Dermatobia hominis*, *Lucilia* species, and *Wohlfahrtia magnifica* being notable causative agents. The condition typically affects the skin, wounds, and mucous membranes, often in tropical and subtropical regions. Larvae feed on tissue, causing inflammation, ulceration, and sometimes systemic complications. It is more common in areas with poor hygiene and in immunocompromised individuals.

"Other infestations" refers to parasitic infections caused by organisms not classified under the main categories of ectoparasites or endoparasites. Common synonyms include miscellaneous parasitic infestations. Causative agents may include protozoa, helminths, or arthropods. These infestations typically affect the skin, gastrointestinal tract, respiratory system, or blood. Examples include giardiasis, toxoplasmosis, and leishmaniasis. Symptoms vary but often include itching, inflammation, and systemic illness. Diagnosis usually involves clinical evaluation and laboratory testing. Treatment depends on the specific parasite involved.

Sequelae of tuberculosis refer to long-term complications or residual damage following active tuberculosis infection. Common synonyms include post-tuberculosis complications or tuberculosis-related sequelae. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These sequelae typically affect the lungs, leading to fibrosis, cavities, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. They may also involve other organs such as the pleura, lymph nodes, or central nervous system. Symptoms may include persistent cough, hemoptysis, and respiratory insufficiency. Diagnosis often requires imaging and clinical evaluation. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing further complications.

code_desc: sequelae of other and unspecified infectious and parasitic diseases
summary: Sequelae of other and unspecified infectious and parasitic diseases refer to long-term complications or residual effects following an infectious or parasitic illness. Common synonyms include late effects, post-infectious complications, or residual conditions. Causative agents vary widely and may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites such as *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Plasmodium* species, or *Toxoplasma gondii*. These sequelae can affect multiple body systems, including the nervous system, respiratory tract, liver, and joints, leading to symptoms like chronic pain, neurological deficits, or organ dysfunction. The condition is often diagnosed when specific etiologies are unknown or unspecified.

code_desc: streptococcus and staphylococcus as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: Streptococcus and staphylococcus species can cause infections not classified under specific chapters, such as cellulitis, abscesses, or sepsis. Common synonyms include bacterial skin infections or soft tissue infections. Causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Streptococcus pyogenes*. These pathogens typically affect the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and sometimes deeper structures like muscles or joints. They may also lead to systemic complications. Clinically, presentations vary from localized erythema and swelling to more severe systemic illness.

code_desc: streptococcus, group c, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: Streptococcus group C, classified under other chapters, refers to infections caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci not typically categorized under other common streptococcal groups. Common synonyms include beta-hemolytic streptococcus group C and S. pyogenes-like organisms. Causative agents include Streptococcus equi subsp. zooepidemicus and Streptococcus dysgalactiae subsp. dysgalactiae. These organisms commonly affect the respiratory tract, skin, and soft tissues, occasionally leading to systemic infections such as sepsis or arthritis. They are less frequently associated with pharyngitis or scarlet fever compared to group A streptococci.

code_desc: streptococcus, group g, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: Streptococcus group G, classified under other chapters, refers to infections caused by Group G Streptococcus (GGS) species, including *Streptococcus dysgalactiae subsp. dysgalactiae* and *S. dysgalactiae subsp. equisimilis*. These bacteria can cause a range of infections, primarily affecting the skin, soft tissues, and occasionally the respiratory tract. Common synonyms include GGS and *S. dysgalactiae*. They are often implicated in conditions such as cellulitis, abscesses, and pharyngitis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying health conditions.

code_desc: streptococcus, other specified group, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: Streptococcus, other specified group, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters refers to infections caused by streptococcal species not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include Group B Streptococcus (GBS) and Streptococcus agalactiae. These organisms can cause a range of infections, including sepsis, meningitis, and pneumonia, typically affecting the bloodstream, central nervous system, and respiratory tract. They are particularly significant in neonatal and immunocompromised populations.

code_desc: other bacterial agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: "Other bacterial agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters" refers to bacterial infections that do not fit into specific disease categories in standard classifications. Common synonyms include miscellaneous bacterial infections or unspecified bacterial diseases. Causative agents may include *Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia*, and *Rickettsia*. These infections typically affect the respiratory, urinary, and cardiovascular systems, as well as the skin and mucous membranes. They often present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, cough, or rash, and may require specialized diagnostic methods for accurate identification.

code_desc: haemophilus influenzae [h influenzae] type b, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: *Haemophilus influenzae* type b (Hib) is a gram-negative coccobacillus that can cause a range of invasive infections, particularly in young children. Though Hib is classified under other chapters, it is a known cause of meningitis, epiglottitis, septic arthritis, and pneumonia. Common synonyms include Hib disease or Hib infection. The bacterium requires specific growth factors and is often found in the upper respiratory tract. It primarily affects the respiratory system, central nervous system, and joints, with highest incidence in unvaccinated children under five years old.

code_desc: haemophilus influenzae [h influenzae] other specified type, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: *Haemophilus influenzae* (H. influenzae) other specified type, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters, refers to infections caused by non-type b serovars of H. influenzae. Common synonyms include non-type b H. influenzae. These strains can cause a range of infections, including meningitis, epiglottitis, and respiratory tract infections. Typically affecting the respiratory system, central nervous system, and occasionally the joints or bloodstream, these infections are more common in young children and immunocompromised individuals. The causative agent is *Haemophilus influenzae* serotype other than b.

code_desc: haemophilus influenzae [h influenzae] type not specified, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: *Haemophilus influenzae* type not specified, as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters refers to infections caused by non-typeable *H. influenzae* that are not classified under specific diseases in other chapters. Common synonyms include non-typeable *H. influenzae* (NTHi). This organism is a common cause of respiratory tract infections, particularly in children. It can affect the respiratory system, leading to conditions such as otitis media, bronchitis, and sinusitis. It may also cause invasive infections like meningitis and septic arthritis, though these are typically classified elsewhere. The bacteria are gram-negative and require specific growth factors.

code_desc: other and unspecified bacterial agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: "Other and unspecified bacterial agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters" refers to bacterial infections where the specific organism is not identified or is classified under a different chapter. Common synonyms include "unspecified bacterial infection" or "other bacterial disease." Causative agents may include a wide range of bacteria such as *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*, or *E. coli*. These infections can affect various body systems, including the respiratory, urinary, and gastrointestinal tracts, as well as the skin and soft tissues. The condition is often diagnosed when the causative agent is not isolated or is not covered under more specific classifications.

code_desc: viral agents as the cause of diseases classified to other chapters
summary: Viral agents can cause diseases that are classified under other chapters in medical classifications due to their diverse manifestations. Common synonyms include viral infections or viral diseases. Known causative agents include herpesviruses, flaviviruses, and adenoviruses. These viruses typically affect the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and nervous systems. Conditions such as viral hepatitis, herpes zoster, and dengue fever fall into this category. Symptoms vary widely depending on the affected organ system and the specific virus involved.

"Other and unspecified infectious diseases" refers to infections not classified under more specific categories, often due to unknown or unspecified causative agents. Common synonyms include "undetermined infectious diseases" or "miscellaneous infections." Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites, though specific pathogens are not identified. These infections can affect any body system, but are commonly seen in the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. They are typically diagnosed through clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and exclusion of other known infections.

Acute sinusitis is an inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting less than four weeks, often following a viral upper respiratory infection. Common synonyms include acute rhinosinusitis. It is typically caused by viral agents, though bacterial pathogens like *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis* may contribute. The condition primarily affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses, leading to symptoms such as nasal congestion, facial pain, and purulent nasal discharge.

Acute pharyngitis is an inflammation of the pharynx, commonly presenting with sore throat, fever, and lymphadenopathy. It is often caused by viral agents such as adenovirus, rhinovirus, and influenza virus, though bacterial causes like Group A Streptococcus may also occur. Common synonyms include sore throat and pharyngitis. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, with symptoms typically involving the posterior throat. It is more prevalent in children and young adults, often following upper respiratory infections.

Acute tonsillitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the tonsils, typically presenting with sore throat, fever, and swollen, red tonsils often with white or yellow exudates. Common synonyms include acute pharyngitis and tonsillar inflammation. The most common causative agents are Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, viral pathogens such as adenovirus and Epstein-Barr virus, and occasionally other bacteria like Haemophilus influenzae. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal tonsils, with involvement of the surrounding lymphoid tissues. It is more prevalent in children but can occur in adults.

Acute laryngitis and tracheitis refer to inflammation of the larynx and trachea, commonly caused by viral infections such as influenza or rhinovirus. Bacterial agents like Streptococcus pyogenes may also contribute. Symptoms include hoarseness, cough, and stridor. The condition typically affects the upper airway, with the larynx and trachea being the primary sites of involvement. It is more common in children and individuals with compromised immune systems. Synonyms include acute laryngotracheitis and viral croup. The illness is usually self-limiting but may require supportive care or antibiotics if bacterial in origin.

Acute obstructive laryngitis, also known as croup or laryngotracheobronchitis, and epiglottitis are distinct but related upper airway conditions. Croup typically presents with a barking cough, stridor, and respiratory distress due to inflammation and swelling of the larynx and trachea, commonly caused by viral agents such as parainfluenza virus. Epiglottitis involves acute inflammation of the epiglottis, often caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b, leading to severe airway obstruction. Both conditions primarily affect the larynx, trachea, and epiglottis, with croup more common in young children and epiglottitis more severe and potentially life-threatening.

code_desc: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple and unspecified sites
summary: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple and unspecified sites refer to inflammatory conditions affecting various upper respiratory tract areas without specific localization. Common synonyms include common cold, viral coryza, and rhinopharyngitis. These infections are typically caused by viruses such as rhinovirus, coronavirus, and adenovirus. They commonly affect the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and sometimes the sinuses and ears. Symptoms include nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, and fever. The condition is usually self-limiting and more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: Other acute upper respiratory infections of multiple sites
summary: Other acute upper respiratory infections of multiple sites refer to infections involving more than one area of the upper respiratory tract, such as the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and bronchi. Common synonyms include acute rhinosinusitis, pharyngitis, and bronchitis. Causative agents often include viruses like rhinovirus, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus, though bacterial causes may also occur. Typically affecting the nose, throat, and lungs, this condition presents with symptoms such as cough, sore throat, nasal congestion, and fever. It is commonly seen in children and immunocompromised individuals.

code_desc: Influenza due to identified zoonotic or pandemic influenza virus
summary: Influenza due to identified zoonotic or pandemic influenza virus refers to infection caused by influenza viruses that originated in animals and have the potential to cause widespread outbreaks. Common synonyms include avian influenza, swine influenza, and pandemic influenza. Causative agents include Influenza A viruses, such as H1N1, H5N1, H7N9, and others. These viruses typically affect the respiratory tract, causing symptoms like fever, cough, sore throat, and muscle aches. Severe cases may lead to pneumonia, respiratory failure, and systemic complications. The condition is characterized by rapid transmission and potential for global spread, especially with pandemic strains.

code_desc: Influenza due to other identified influenza virus
summary: Influenza due to other identified influenza virus refers to a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses not classified as A(H1N1), A(H3N2), or B. Common synonyms include seasonal influenza and other influenza types. Causative agents include influenza C and D viruses. The infection primarily affects the upper and lower respiratory tract, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, and fatigue. It is typically mild but can cause complications like pneumonia, especially in vulnerable populations. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets.

Influenza, virus not identified refers to a clinical diagnosis of influenza when the specific viral strain cannot be determined through laboratory testing. Common synonyms include untyped influenza or influenza of unknown origin. It is typically caused by influenza viruses, most commonly Influenza A or B, though other agents may be involved. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, causing fever, cough, sore throat, and body aches. It may also lead to complications such as pneumonia, particularly in high-risk populations. Diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms and epidemiological context when laboratory confirmation is unavailable.

Viral pneumonia, not elsewhere classified, is an inflammatory lung condition caused by viral infection, typically affecting the alveoli. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonia and viral respiratory infection with pneumonia. Causative agents include influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus, and parainfluenza viruses. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the alveoli and interstitial tissue. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is more common in young children, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with viral detection methods used for confirmation.

Bacterial pneumonia, not elsewhere classified, is an acute infection of the lungs caused by bacteria that do not fit specific categories such as community-acquired or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Common causative agents include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*.
