The infection is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and is more prevalent in areas with poor sanitation.

Acute amoebiasis is an intestinal infection caused primarily by *Entamoeba histolytica*, though *E. dispar* and *E. murlini* may also be involved. It is characterized by inflammation, ulceration, and bloody diarrhea. Common synonyms include amoebic colitis and intestinal amoebiasis. The disease typically affects the large intestine, with possible extraintestinal spread to the liver, forming abscesses. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and malaise. Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated water or food.

Amoeboma of the intestine is a granulomatous lesion caused by *Entamoeba histolytica*. It mimics a neoplasm and is most commonly found in the ileum. The condition results from chronic infection and immune response to the parasite. Synonyms include intestinal amoebic granuloma or pseudotumor. It is more prevalent in individuals with a history of amoebic dysentery. The lesion typically presents as a solitary, well-circumscribed mass, often associated with intermittent abdominal pain and weight loss. Diagnosis requires histopathological examination and identification of the parasite.

code_desc: intestinal infections due to entamoeba, unspecified
summary: Intestinal infections due to *Entamoeba* are parasitic infections caused by species of the protozoan genus *Entamoeba*, most commonly *E. histolytica*. These infections primarily affect the large intestine, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Less commonly, the parasite can invade other organs, causing extraintestinal complications. Synonyms include amebic dysentery and amebiasis. The infection is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated food or water.

Extraintestinal infections due to *Entamoeba* are rare but serious conditions caused by *Entamoeba histolytica*, the primary pathogen, though *Entamoeba coli* and *Entamoeba nana* may occasionally contribute. These infections primarily affect the liver, leading to amebic abscesses, and can also involve the lungs, brain, and other organs. Common synonyms include amebiasis outside the intestine or extraintestinal amebiasis. Clinically, patients may present with fever, abdominal pain, and localized symptoms depending on the affected organ. Diagnosis often requires imaging and laboratory confirmation.

Amoebic liver abscess is a parasitic infection caused primarily by *Entamoeba histolytica*, leading to a localized collection of pus in the liver. It often results from hematogenous spread of the parasite from an intestinal infection. Common synonyms include liver abscess due to *E. histolytica* and extraintestinal amebiasis. The condition typically affects the right lobe of the liver, presenting with symptoms such as right upper quadrant pain, fever, and weight loss. It is more common in individuals with a history of amoebic colitis or travel to endemic areas.

Amoebic lung abscess is a rare, severe infection caused by *Entamoeba histolytica*, primarily affecting immunocompetent individuals. It results from hematogenous spread of the parasite from the gastrointestinal tract to the lungs. Common synonyms include pulmonary amoebiasis and extraintestinal amoebiasis. The condition typically presents with fever, cough, hemoptysis, and chest pain. Radiologically, it may mimic bacterial pneumonia or tuberculosis. Complications include pleural effusion and dissemination to other organs. Early diagnosis and treatment with antiamoebic drugs like metronidazole are crucial for favorable outcomes.

Cutaneous amoebiasis is a rare infection caused by *Entamoeba histolytica* or *Entamoeba dispar*, typically acquired through traumatic inoculation of contaminated soil. It presents as a painless, erythematous nodule that may ulcerate and form a chronic lesion, often on the lower extremities. Synonyms include amoebic cutaneous infection or cutaneous amebiasis. The disease is more common in tropical regions and affects individuals with compromised skin integrity. Diagnosis is confirmed by identifying trophozoites or cysts in tissue samples. Treatment involves antiamoebic drugs such as metronidazole.

Amoebiasis of other specified sites refers to infection caused by *Entamoeba histolytica* or other amoebae affecting organs or tissues not typically associated with intestinal amoebiasis. Common synonyms include extraintestinal amoebiasis. The causative agent is primarily *E. histolytica*, though other species like *Entamoeba dispar* may be involved. Typically affected sites include the liver, lungs, brain, and skin. It often presents with localized abscesses or inflammation, and may occur in immunocompromised individuals or following hematogenous spread from the intestine.

Amoebiasis, unspecified, is an intestinal infection caused by the protozoan *Entamoeba histolytica*. It may also involve extraintestinal sites such as the liver, lungs, or brain. Common synonyms include amebiasis and intestinal amoebiasis. The disease is characterized by symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. In severe cases, it can lead to amoebic liver abscesses. Transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated food or water. The infection is more prevalent in areas with poor sanitation. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through stool examination or serological tests. Treatment involves antiparasitic medications such as metronidazole.

"Other specified protozoal intestinal infections" refers to parasitic infections caused by protozoa that do not fit into more specific categories such as giardiasis or cryptosporidiosis. Common synonyms include unspecified protozoal enteritis. Causative agents may include species like Cyclospora cayetanensis, Dientamoeba fragilis, or others not typically classified under major protozoal infections. These infections primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract, causing symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. They are commonly acquired through contaminated food or water and are more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals.

Protozoal intestinal infections, unspecified, refer to parasitic diseases caused by protozoa that affect the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include amoebiasis and giardiasis, though these terms may specify particular agents. Causative agents vary but often include Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, and Cryptosporidium species. These infections primarily affect the small intestine and may involve the colon. Symptoms typically include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. Transmission occurs through contaminated food or water, and the infections are more common in areas with poor sanitation.

code_desc: gastroenteritis or colitis without specification of infectious agent
summary: Gastroenteritis or colitis without specification of infectious agent refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily affecting the colon and small intestine. Common synonyms include acute gastroenteritis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in chronic cases. Causative agents may include viruses, bacteria, parasites, or autoimmune factors. Symptoms typically involve diarrhea, abdominal pain, cramping, and sometimes fever. The condition can affect the stomach, small intestine, and colon, with variable severity and duration depending on the underlying cause.

code_desc: gastroenteritis or colitis without specification of origin
summary: Gastroenteritis or colitis without specification of origin refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily affecting the colon and small intestine. Common synonyms include infectious colitis, acute gastroenteritis, and enteritis. Causative agents may include viruses (e.g., norovirus, rotavirus), bacteria (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella), parasites, or non-infectious factors like medications or autoimmune conditions. Symptoms typically include diarrhea, abdominal pain, cramping, and sometimes fever. The condition predominantly affects the mucosal lining of the intestines, leading to fluid loss and electrolyte imbalance.

code_desc: infectious gastroenteritis or colitis without specification of infectious agent
summary: Infectious gastroenteritis or colitis without specification of infectious agent refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract caused by pathogens, typically affecting the stomach, small intestine, and/or colon. Common synonyms include acute gastroenteritis and infectious colitis. Causative agents may include bacteria (e.g., *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Campylobacter*), viruses (e.g., norovirus, rotavirus), and parasites (e.g., *Giardia*, *Entamoeba*). Symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The condition primarily affects the digestive system, with variable severity and duration depending on the causative agent.

Congenital syphilis is a bacterial infection transmitted from an infected mother to her fetus through the placenta. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it can lead to severe multisystem involvement. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis and neonatal syphilis. The infection typically affects the skin, bones, eyes, ears, and central nervous system. Clinical manifestations may include rash, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal abnormalities, and neurosyphilis. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent long-term complications.

Early congenital syphilis, symptomatic, refers to the manifestation of syphilis in a newborn within the first two years of life, typically presenting with systemic symptoms. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it results from maternal transmission during pregnancy. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis and neonatal syphilis. Affected body parts include the skin, bones, liver, and central nervous system. Symptoms may involve rash, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and skeletal abnormalities. It is a serious condition requiring prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent long-term complications.

Early congenital syphilis, latent refers to a non-active stage of syphilis in a newborn that may progress to active disease. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and typically occurs when a mother transmits the infection during pregnancy. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis, latent congenital syphilis, and asymptomatic congenital syphilis. The infection may affect multiple systems, including the skin, bones, teeth, and central nervous system, though symptoms may not be apparent initially. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term complications.

Late congenital syphilitic oculopathy is a chronic ocular manifestation of congenital syphilis, typically presenting in childhood or adolescence. It results from untreated or inadequately treated syphilis during pregnancy, caused by *Treponema pallidum*. The condition primarily affects the eye, leading to uveitis, choroiditis, and optic neuropathy. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis ophthalmopathy and late-onset congenital syphilis eye disease. Other affected systems may include the central nervous system and skin, but the ocular involvement is a hallmark of the disease.

Late congenital neurosyphilis is a severe manifestation of syphilis that develops in infants or children exposed to Treponema pallidum in utero. It typically presents after the first year of life and is characterized by neurological symptoms such as seizures, developmental delay, and cranial nerve abnormalities. Common synonyms include congenital neurosyphilis and late neurosyphilis. The causative agent is Treponema pallidum, and the condition primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord. It may also involve the bones and skin. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent long-term complications.

Other late congenital syphilis, symptomatic refers to manifestations of syphilis that occur after the first year of life and are not classified as early or late congenital syphilis. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and typically presents with a variety of symptoms including skin lesions, bone abnormalities, and neurological involvement. Common synonyms include late congenital syphilis and symptomatic congenital syphilis. The condition may affect the skin, bones, teeth, and central nervous system. It is a serious, progressive disease requiring prompt treatment with penicillin.

Late congenital syphilis, latent refers to a non-active stage of syphilis that develops years after initial infection, typically in individuals who were infected during pregnancy. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, the spirochete responsible for syphilis. This condition may progress to active disease if left untreated. Common synonyms include latent congenital syphilis or asymptomatic congenital syphilis. It primarily affects the bones, teeth, and central nervous system, and may lead to complications such as Hutchinson's teeth, saddle nose, and neurosyphilis. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term sequelae.

Congenital syphilis, unspecified, refers to syphilis transmitted from an infected mother to her fetus during pregnancy. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it can lead to a range of systemic manifestations. Common synonyms include congenital syphilis and neonatal syphilis. The condition typically affects multiple organ systems, including the skin, bones, teeth, central nervous system, and eyes. Infants may present with rash, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, or neurologic symptoms. Without treatment, it can result in severe complications, including deafness, visual impairment, and developmental delays.

Early syphilis is a systemic infection caused by *Treponema pallidum*, a spirochete. It typically presents 10 to 90 days after exposure with a painless ulcerative lesion, known as a chancre, at the site of inoculation. Common synonyms include primary and secondary syphilis. The infection may also involve lymphadenopathy and, in the secondary stage, mucocutaneous lesions, rash, and systemic symptoms. It primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and lymph nodes, with potential systemic spread if untreated. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are critical to prevent progression to late-stage syphilis.

Primary genital syphilis is an early stage of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically presents as a painless, firm ulcer (chancre) at the site of infection, most commonly on the penis, vagina, anus, or mouth. The lesion is usually solitary, indurated, and has a clean base. It may be accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy. Synonyms include primary syphilic chancre or genital chancre. The infection is transmitted through direct contact with a syphilitic sore during sexual activity. If untreated, it can progress to secondary and tertiary stages.

Primary anal syphilis is the initial stage of syphilis infection affecting the anal region. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it typically presents as a painless ulcerative lesion known as a chancre, often accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include anal chancre or primary syphilis of the anus. The condition primarily affects the anal canal and perianal area, though it may spread to adjacent tissues. It is transmitted through direct contact with a syphilitic sore during sexual activity. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are crucial to prevent progression to later stages of the disease.

Primary syphilis of other sites refers to the initial stage of syphilis affecting areas outside the classic genital or oral regions. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it presents as a painless ulcer or chancre at the site of inoculation. Common synonyms include extragenital syphilis and non-primary syphilis. While the genitalia and mouth are most commonly affected, other sites such as the hands, feet, or mucous membranes may be involved. The lesion is typically solitary, firm, and indurated, often accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent progression to secondary or tertiary syphilis.

code_desc: secondary syphilis of skin or mucous membranes
summary: Secondary syphilis of the skin or mucous membranes is a systemic infection stage of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically occurs weeks to months after the primary infection and is characterized by a widespread rash, often with mucous membrane lesions. Common synonyms include generalized syphilis and eruptive syphilis. The rash may appear on the palms, soles, trunk, and mucous membranes, and may include flat or raised lesions, often accompanied by fever, lymphadenopathy, and constitutional symptoms. The condition is highly contagious and can progress to latent or tertiary syphilis if untreated.

Secondary syphilis of other sites refers to the dissemination of *Treponema pallidum* beyond the primary and secondary mucocutaneous lesions, affecting various non-genital areas. Common synonyms include generalized secondary syphilis and extragenital secondary syphilis. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum* subspecies *pallidum*. Typically affected sites include the skin, mucous membranes, nails, and occasionally the oral cavity, conjunctiva, and respiratory tract. Characteristic findings include rash, mucosal lesions, and systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological testing and clinical evaluation.

Latent early syphilis refers to the asymptomatic phase of syphilis occurring within the first two years after infection. It is characterized by the absence of clinical symptoms but the presence of detectable treponemal antibodies. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. This stage may progress to late syphilis if untreated. Common synonyms include early latent syphilis or incipient syphilis. It typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and systemic organs, though no specific lesions are present during this phase. Diagnosis relies on serological testing.

Other specified early syphilis refers to syphilis manifestations that do not meet the criteria for primary, secondary, or latent syphilis but occur within the first year of infection. It may include asymptomatic infections or atypical presentations. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. Common synonyms include early-stage syphilis or unspecified early syphilis. Typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and systemic organs. It may present with non-specific symptoms and requires serological testing for diagnosis.

Early syphilis, unspecified, refers to the initial stages of syphilis, typically within the first two years of infection. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum*, a spirochete transmitted primarily through sexual contact. Common synonyms include primary and secondary syphilis. The infection often presents with a painless chancre at the site of entry, followed by a widespread rash, mucous membrane lesions, and systemic symptoms. It commonly affects the skin, mucous membranes, and lymph nodes. If untreated, it may progress to late-stage syphilis, leading to severe complications.

Late syphilis is a chronic, systemic infection caused by *Treponema pallidum* that develops years after an untreated primary or secondary syphilis infection. It primarily affects the skin, bones, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and tertiary syphilis. Characteristic manifestations include gummatous lesions, cardiovascular syphilis, and neurologic complications such as tabes dorsalis and general paresis. The disease progresses slowly and can lead to severe tissue destruction and organ dysfunction if left untreated.

Neurosyphilis is a late-stage complication of syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum* infection of the central nervous system. It typically occurs in individuals with untreated syphilis and may manifest as asymptomatic neurosyphilis, meningovascular syphilis, or tabes dorsalis. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis, syphilitic meningitis, and tabes dorsalis. The condition primarily affects the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to neurological deficits such as dementia, motor dysfunction, and sensory loss. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent irreversible damage.

Asymptomatic neurosyphilis is a stage of syphilis where the infection affects the central nervous system without causing noticeable symptoms. It typically occurs in the late stages of untreated syphilis. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. Common synonyms include latent neurosyphilis or asymptomatic cerebral syphilis. It commonly involves the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to potential long-term neurological complications. Diagnosis often requires lumbar puncture and serological testing.

Symptomatic late neurosyphilis is a severe manifestation of syphilis occurring years after primary infection, characterized by central nervous system involvement. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it presents with neurological symptoms such as meningitis, myelopathy, or tabes dorsalis. Common synonyms include neurosyphilis and late neurosyphilis. Typically affects the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, leading to cognitive decline, motor deficits, and sensory loss. It is associated with late-stage syphilis and requires prompt treatment with penicillin to prevent irreversible damage.

Neurosyphilis, unspecified, refers to central nervous system involvement in syphilis without a specified subtype. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it results from untreated or inadequately treated syphilis. Common synonyms include general paresis and tabes dorsalis. The condition typically affects the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to neurological symptoms such as cognitive decline, motor dysfunction, and sensory disturbances. It is a late-stage complication of syphilis and can present with varied clinical manifestations. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are critical to prevent irreversible damage.

Cardiovascular late syphilis is a manifestation of tertiary syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically presents years after the initial infection and affects the aorta, leading to aortic aneurysm and aortitis. Common synonyms include aortitis and aortic aneurysm of syphilis. The condition may also involve other cardiovascular structures, such as the coronary arteries and valves, though less commonly. It is characterized by progressive inflammation and weakening of the aortic wall, resulting in complications like rupture or embolism. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent severe morbidity and mortality.

code_desc: symptomatic late syphilis of other sites
summary: Symptomatic late syphilis of other sites refers to manifestations of tertiary syphilis affecting organs or tissues outside the classic sites such as the skin, bones, and cardiovascular system. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and typically presents years after the initial infection. Common synonyms include late-stage syphilis or tertiary syphilis. Affected areas may include the nervous system (neurosyphilis), liver, eyes, and joints. Symptoms vary widely and may include neurological deficits, vision loss, or systemic inflammation. Diagnosis often requires serological testing and clinical evaluation.

Ocular late syphilis is a manifestation of tertiary syphilis affecting the eye, typically occurring years after the initial infection. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and is characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the uvea, leading to uveitis, choroiditis, and retinal lesions. Common synonyms include syphilitic uveitis and ocular tertiary syphilis. The condition primarily affects the uvea, choroid, and retina, potentially resulting in vision loss if untreated. It is often associated with systemic syphilis and may present with symptoms such as blurred vision, photophobia, and floaters. Early diagnosis and treatment with penicillin are crucial to prevent irreversible damage.

code_desc: late syphilis involving the musculoskeletal system
summary: Late syphilis involving the musculoskeletal system is a manifestation of tertiary syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum*. It typically presents years after the initial infection and may involve bone and joint tissues. Common synonyms include syphilitic osteochondritis and syphilitic arthropathy. The condition often affects the long bones, vertebrae, and joints, leading to destructive lesions, periostitis, and joint inflammation. It may also cause pseudogout-like symptoms due to calcium deposits in affected areas. Diagnosis is confirmed through serologic tests and imaging, with treatment requiring prolonged antibiotic therapy.

code_desc: late syphilis of skin or mucous membranes
summary: Late syphilis of skin or mucous membranes refers to the tertiary stage of syphilis, characterized by the development of gummas, which are soft, painless, non-ulcerative granulomas. Common synonyms include syphilitic gumma and syphilitic granuloma. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. This condition typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, bones, and internal organs. Lesions often appear on the face, ears, and extremities. It results from reactivation of the infection years after the initial syphilis infection, often in individuals who were untreated or inadequately treated.

code_desc: symptomatic late syphilis of other specified sites
summary: Symptomatic late syphilis of other specified sites refers to manifestations of tertiary syphilis affecting body regions not typically included in major classifications. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it may present as skin lesions, nodules, or ulcerations. Common synonyms include late-stage syphilis and tertiary syphilis. Affected sites may include the skin, mucous membranes, bones, or internal organs. Symptoms often develop years after initial infection and may involve systemic complications. Diagnosis relies on clinical findings and serological tests. Treatment typically involves penicillin therapy.

code_desc: symptomatic late syphilis of unspecified site
summary: Symptomatic late syphilis of unspecified site refers to clinical manifestations occurring 1 year or more after primary or secondary syphilis infection, without a known specific anatomical location. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it may present with diverse symptoms such as skin rashes, neurological involvement, or organ damage. Common synonyms include late-stage syphilis or tertiary syphilis. Typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, cardiovascular system, and central nervous system. Without treatment, it can lead to severe complications and disability.

Other specified late syphilis refers to syphilis manifestations occurring more than 2 years after initial infection but not fitting the criteria for tertiary syphilis. It is caused by *Treponema pallidum* and may present with diverse symptoms. Common synonyms include late-stage syphilis or asymptomatic syphilis. Typically affected areas include the skin, mucous membranes, bones, and central nervous system. It may manifest as gummas, neurosyphilis, or cardiovascular syphilis. Diagnosis involves serological testing and clinical evaluation. Treatment with penicillin remains the gold standard.

Late syphilis, unspecified, refers to the tertiary stage of syphilis that occurs years after the initial infection. Caused by *Treponema pallidum*, it is characterized by systemic complications affecting multiple organs. Common synonyms include tertiary syphilis and late-stage syphilis. Typical manifestations include gummas, cardiovascular syphilis, neurosyphilis, and skin lesions. The condition may involve the skin, bones, cardiovascular system, and central nervous system. It is often asymptomatic initially but can lead to severe, irreversible damage if left untreated. Diagnosis is confirmed through serological tests and clinical evaluation.

code_desc: latent syphilis, unspecified as early or late
summary: Latent syphilis, unspecified as early or late, refers to a clinically asymptomatic stage of syphilis following the initial infection. It is characterized by the presence of antibodies without active lesions. The causative agent is *Treponema pallidum*. Common synonyms include "asymptomatic syphilis" and "inactive syphilis." This stage typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and central nervous system. It may progress to late-stage syphilis if left untreated. Diagnosis is primarily serological.

Syphilis, unspecified, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium *Treponema pallidum*. It progresses through distinct stages, though the unspecified form may refer to early or late manifestations without specific stage designation. Common synonyms include syphilis, venereal syphilis, and hard chancre. The infection typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and can involve systemic complications such as neurosyphilis and cardiovascular syphilis if left untreated. It is transmitted through direct contact with syphilitic sores.

Gonococcal genitourinary infection is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. Common synonyms include gonorrhea and clap. It primarily affects the genitourinary tract, including the urethra, cervix, endocervix, rectum, and throat. Symptoms may include dysuria, urethral discharge, and pelvic pain. Complications can involve disseminated gonococcal infection, arthritis, and infertility. Transmission occurs through unprotected sexual contact. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by nucleic acid amplification tests or culture. Treatment involves antibiotic therapy, with increasing concern for antimicrobial resistance.

code_desc: gonococcal infection of lower genitourinary tract without periurethral or accessory gland abscess
summary: Gonococcal infection of the lower genitourinary tract refers to a sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It commonly affects the urethra, cervix, and sometimes the bladder. Synonyms include gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis. The infection typically presents with symptoms such as dysuria, urethral discharge, and cervical inflammation. It is more prevalent in sexually active individuals and can lead to complications if untreated. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through nucleic acid amplification tests or culture. Treatment involves antibiotics effective against *N. gonorrhoeae*.

Gonorrhoea of the penis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It primarily affects the urethra, leading to inflammation, pain, and a purulent discharge. Common synonyms include gonococcal urethritis. The infection is typically transmitted through unprotected vaginal, anal, or oral sex. Symptoms may include burning during urination, swelling, and redness of the penile shaft. If left untreated, it can lead to complications such as epididymitis or infertility. The condition is commonly seen in men who have sex with men, but can affect anyone engaging in high-risk sexual behavior.

code_desc: other specified gonococcal infection of lower genitourinary tract without periurethral or accessory gland abscess
summary: Other specified gonococcal infection of the lower genitourinary tract refers to a gonococcal infection affecting the urethra, cervix, or vagina, without involvement of the periurethral glands or accessory glands. Common synonyms include gonococcal urethritis or cervicitis. The causative agent is *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. This condition typically affects the mucous membranes of the genital and urinary tracts, primarily in sexually active individuals. Symptoms may include dysuria, discharge, and itching. It is a sexually transmitted infection that requires prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics.

code_desc: gonococcal infection of lower genitourinary tract without periurethral or accessory gland abscess, unspecified
summary: Gonococcal infection of the lower genitourinary tract without periurethral or accessory gland abscess refers to a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It typically affects the urethra, cervix, and sometimes the Bartholin's glands. Common synonyms include gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis. The infection is characterized by inflammation and discharge, often presenting with dysuria and abnormal secretions. It primarily affects the genital and urinary tracts in both men and women, with a higher prevalence in women. Early diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antibiotics are essential to prevent complications.

code_desc: gonococcal infection of lower genitourinary tract with periurethral or accessory gland abscess
summary: Gonococcal infection of the lower genitourinary tract with periurethral or accessory gland abscess is a severe complication of untreated gonorrhea, primarily affecting the urethra, prostate, and seminal vesicles. Caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, it presents with pain, swelling, and purulent discharge. Common synonyms include gonococcal urethritis with abscess formation and gonococcal prostatitis. The infection often involves the periurethral glands and accessory sex organs, leading to abscess formation and potential systemic spread. Prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics is essential to prevent complications.

code_desc: gonococcal infection of other specified genitourinary organ
summary: Gonococcal infection of other specified genitourinary organs refers to Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection affecting genital or urinary tract sites not typically classified as primary, secondary, or disseminated gonococcal infection. Common synonyms include gonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, or epididymitis. The causative agent is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus. Typically affected sites include the urethra, cervix, epididymis, and Bartholin glands. It often presents with symptoms such as dysuria, discharge, and pelvic pain. Complications may include infertility or systemic spread.

Gonococcal genitourinary infection, unspecified, refers to a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It affects the genitourinary tract, including the urethra, cervix, vagina, and rectum. Common synonyms include gonorrhea and Neisseria infection. Symptoms may include discharge, pain during urination, and swelling. The infection can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease if untreated. It is primarily transmitted through sexual contact. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are essential to prevent long-term health issues.

Gonococcal pelviperitonitis is a severe pelvic inflammatory disease caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It typically affects women and results from ascending infection from the lower genital tract. Common synonyms include gonococcal pelvic infection and gonococcal salpingitis. The condition can lead to inflammation of the fallopian tubes, ovaries, and peritoneum, often presenting with abdominal pain, fever, and malaise. Complications may include infertility and ectopic pregnancy if untreated. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are crucial to prevent long-term sequelae.

Gonococcal infection of other sites refers to disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection beyond the urogenital tract. Common synonyms include disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) and gonococcal arthritis. The bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the causative agent. This condition typically affects joints, skin, and mucous membranes. It presents with migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, and characteristic skin lesions such as erythema nodosum or pustules. Systemic symptoms like fever and malaise are common. It occurs more frequently in women and individuals with HIV. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications.

Gonococcal infection of the musculoskeletal system, also known as gonococcal arthritis or disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), is a complication of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. It typically affects young adults and presents with migratory joint pain, swelling, and skin lesions. Commonly involved joints include the knees, wrists, and ankles. The infection can also lead to tenosynovitis and dermatitis. Synonyms include gonococcal arthritis and DGI. The causative agent is Neisseria gonorrhoeae, which spreads hematogenously from the genitourinary tract to joints and skin.

Gonococcal infection of the rectum is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It typically affects men who have sex with men and is often asymptomatic or presents with rectal discharge, pain, or bleeding. Common synonyms include rectal gonorrhea or rectal discharge due to *N. gonorrhoeae*. The infection primarily involves the rectal mucosa and may spread to adjacent structures. It is often part of a disseminated gonococcal infection, affecting other sites such as the joints or skin. Diagnosis is confirmed through nucleic acid amplification tests or culture.

Gonococcal infection of the anus, also known as anorectal gonorrhea, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It typically affects the anorectal region, periurethral glands, and sometimes the urethra in men. Common symptoms include rectal pain, discharge, and bleeding. It may present with or without systemic symptoms. Diagnosis is confirmed through nucleic acid amplification tests or culture. Complications may include proctitis, epididymitis, or disseminated gonococcal infection. It is more commonly seen in men who have sex with men but can occur in any population engaging in receptive anal intercourse.

Gonococcal pharyngitis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It presents with sore throat, redness, and sometimes exudate in the pharynx. Common synonyms include pharyngeal gonorrhea or gonococcal angina. The infection primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, occasionally involving the larynx. It is more common in men who have sex with men but can occur in women and other groups. Symptoms may be mild or absent, leading to underdiagnosis. Diagnosis is confirmed via nucleic acid amplification tests or culture. Treatment involves appropriate antibiotic therapy to prevent complications.

Gonococcal infection of the eye, also known as ophthalmia neonatorum or gonococcal conjunctivitis, is a severe bacterial infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It primarily affects newborns, often acquired during passage through an infected birth canal. The infection leads to conjunctival inflammation, chemosis, and potentially corneal ulceration. In adults, it may occur following sexual contact. Prompt treatment with appropriate antibiotics is critical to prevent permanent vision loss. Common synonyms include gonococcal conjunctivitis and neonatal ophthalmia.

code_desc: gonococcal infection of other specified sites
summary: Gonococcal infection of other specified sites refers to Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection affecting areas not typically classified under genital, rectal, or pharyngeal sites. Common synonyms include disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) when systemic. The causative agent is Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Typically affected body parts include joints, skin, and occasionally the heart or eyes. Symptoms may include arthritis, dermatitis, and tenosynovitis. This condition often presents with migratory joint pain and skin lesions, and is more common in women. It can lead to complications such as endocarditis or septic arthritis if untreated.

Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is a systemic complication of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, characterized by extragenital dissemination of the organism. Common synonyms include gonococcal arthritis and disseminated gonococcal disease. The causative agent is Neisseria gonorrhoeae. DGI typically affects joints, skin, and mucous membranes, presenting with migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, and dermatitis. It often occurs in individuals with compromised immune systems or those who engage in high-risk sexual behaviors. The infection can lead to severe complications if not promptly treated with appropriate antibiotics.

Gonococcal infection, unspecified, refers to a systemic infection caused by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. It encompasses various clinical presentations, including disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), which commonly affects joints, skin, and mucous membranes. Synonyms include disseminated gonococcal infection and gonococcal arthritis. The infection typically involves the genitourinary tract, but can spread to joints, skin, and other organs. Symptoms may include fever, joint pain, rash, and systemic inflammation. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with appropriate antibiotics are essential to prevent complications.

Chlamydial lymphogranuloma, also known as donovanosis or granuloma inguinale, is a chronic bacterial infection caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* serovars L1-L3. It primarily affects the genital and anal regions, causing painless ulcers and granulomatous lesions. The infection is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. It may progress to extensive tissue destruction if untreated. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and biopsy. Treatment typically involves antibiotics such as doxycycline or erythromycin. Complications may include lymphadenopathy and systemic spread.

Non-ulcerative sexually transmitted chlamydial infection is a common bacterial infection caused primarily by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It typically affects the genital tract, including the cervix, urethra, and rectum, and may also involve the eyes and throat. Common synonyms include chlamydial genital infection and non-gonococcal urethritis. The infection often presents without symptoms but can lead to serious complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility if untreated. Transmission occurs through sexual contact, and diagnosis is usually confirmed via nucleic acid amplification tests.

code_desc: chlamydial infection of lower genitourinary tract
summary: Chlamydial infection of the lower genitourinary tract is a sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. Common synonyms include chlamydia and genital chlamydial infection. The infection typically affects the cervix, urethra, and sometimes the fallopian tubes in females, and the urethra in males. It often presents with asymptomatic or mild symptoms such as abnormal discharge, burning during urination, or pelvic pain. If untreated, it can lead to serious complications like pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility. Transmission occurs through sexual contact, and diagnosis is usually confirmed by nucleic acid amplification tests.

code_desc: chlamydial infection of internal reproductive organs
summary: Chlamydial infection of internal reproductive organs refers to a sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by *Chlamydia trachomatis*. It commonly affects the cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries in women, leading to conditions such as pelvic inflammatory disease. In men, it often involves the epididymis and urethra. Synonyms include chlamydial cervicitis, chlamydial salpingitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) of chlamydial origin. The infection is often asymptomatic but can cause infertility and ectopic pregnancy if untreated.

code_desc: non-ulcerative sexually transmitted chlamydial infection of other specified site
summary: Non-ulcerative sexually transmitted chlamydial infection of other specified site refers to a chlamydial infection affecting sites not typically associated with genital ulceration. It is caused primarily by *Chlamydia trachomatis*, though other species may occasionally be involved. Common synonyms include non-ulcerative chlamydial infection and chlamydial infection of unspecified site. This condition often affects the cervix, urethra, rectum, and eyes, though it may occur in other genital or perigenital areas. Symptoms may include discharge, irritation, or asymptomatic carriage, making it a significant public health concern due to its potential for complications and transmission.

code_desc: non-ulcerative sexually transmitted chlamydial infection of unspecified site
summary: Non-ulcerative sexually transmitted chlamydial infection of unspecified site refers to a genital infection caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* without the presence of ulcers. Common synonyms include chlamydial infection, non-ulcerative chlamydial infection, and unspecified chlamydial infection. The infection typically affects the cervix, urethra, rectum, or eyes. It is often asymptomatic but can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease or infertility if untreated. Transmission occurs through sexual contact.

code_desc: other specified sexually transmissible infections due to chlamydia
summary: "Other specified sexually transmissible infections due to chlamydia" refers to chlamydial infections that do not meet the criteria for specific STIs like chlamydia trachomatis infection. Common synonyms include chlamydial genital infection. The causative agent is Chlamydia trachomatis. These infections typically affect the genital tract, including the cervix, urethra, and rectum. They may also involve the eyes (conjunctivitis) or lungs (pneumonia in newborns). Symptoms may include discharge, itching, or pain, though many infections are asymptomatic. Transmission occurs through sexual contact.

code_desc: sexually transmissible infections due to chlamydia, unspecified
summary: Sexually transmissible infections due to chlamydia, unspecified, refer to infections caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis* affecting the genital tract. Common synonyms include chlamydial infection and non-gonococcal urethritis. The infection primarily affects the cervix, urethra, and rectum in both men and women. It can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility if untreated. Symptoms may include abnormal discharge, pain, and bleeding. Transmission occurs through sexual contact. Early diagnosis and antibiotic treatment are essential to prevent long-term health issues.

Chancroid is a bacterial infection characterized by painful genital ulcers, typically affecting the penis, scrotum, or perineum. Caused by *Haemophilus ducreyi*, it is transmitted through sexual contact. Common synonyms include soft chancre and granuloma inguinale. The infection often presents with a tender, undermined ulcer with a purulent base, sometimes accompanied by inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is more prevalent in areas with limited access to healthcare and is frequently associated with HIV. Diagnosis is usually clinical, though culture of *H. ducreyi* may confirm the condition. Treatment with antibiotics such as azithromycin or ceftriaxone is effective.

Granuloma inguinale, also known as donovanosis, is a chronic bacterial infection caused by *Klebsiella granulomatis*. It primarily affects the genital area, particularly the perineum, groin, and anal regions. The infection leads to painless, progressive ulceration with granulomatous inflammation and indurated nodules. It is more common in tropical and subtropical regions. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and histopathological findings of Donovan bodies. Treatment typically involves antibiotics such as doxycycline or azithromycin.

Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the protozoan *Trichomonas vaginalis*. It primarily affects the genitourinary tract, with the most common sites being the vagina, urethra, and prostate in men. The infection is characterized by inflammation, discharge, and itching. Common synonyms include trichomonal infection or trichomonadiasis. It is more prevalent in women, though men can also be asymptomatic carriers. Transmission occurs through sexual contact, and diagnosis is typically confirmed by microscopic examination of secretions or nucleic acid amplification tests.

Sexually transmissible infestations are parasitic infections spread primarily through sexual contact. Common synonyms include sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). These infestations are caused by various pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. Common causative agents include *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, *Chlamydia trachomatis*, *Treponema pallidum*, and *Herpes simplex virus*. Typically affected body parts include the genitalia, rectum, mouth, and eyes. Symptoms may vary but often include ulcers, rashes, discharge, and itching. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications and transmission.

Anogenital herpes simplex infection is a viral infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 can also be responsible. It affects the genital and anal regions, causing painful vesicular lesions that may rupture to form ulcers. Common synonyms include genital herpes and anogenital herpes. The infection is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity. Lesions typically appear on the vulva, penis, perineum, and anal area. Symptoms may include itching, burning, and flu-like symptoms. Recurrent outbreaks are common, and the infection is chronic, with latent viral activity in sensory neurons.

code_desc: herpes simplex infection of genitalia or urogenital tract
summary: Herpes simplex infection of the genitalia or urogenital tract is a viral infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 can also be a cause. It presents as painful, recurrent ulcers or vesicles on the genital or anal areas, often accompanied by systemic symptoms like fever and lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include genital herpes and urogenital herpes. The infection is transmitted through direct contact and can lead to complications such as neonatal herpes or increased risk of HIV transmission.

code_desc: herpes simplex infection of perianal skin or rectum
summary: Herpes simplex infection of the perianal skin or rectum is a viral infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and, less commonly, type 2 (HSV-2). It presents as painful, clustered vesicles or ulcers in the anal or perianal region. Common synonyms include anal herpes and perianal herpes. The infection typically affects the perianal skin, rectal mucosa, and sometimes the genital area. Transmission occurs through direct contact with lesions or bodily fluids. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with a history of genital herpes.

code_desc: anogenital herpes simplex infection without further specification
summary: Anogenital herpes simplex infection is a viral sexually transmitted infection caused primarily by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), though HSV-1 can also be implicated. It presents with painful vesicles, ulcers, or erosions in the genital or anal regions. Common synonyms include genital herpes and anogenital herpes. The infection typically affects the vulva, penis, perineum, and anal area, with symptoms often recurring due to latent viral reactivation. Transmission occurs through direct contact with active lesions or asymptomatic shedding.

Anogenital warts, also known as genital warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign skin growths caused by certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 and 11. These warts typically appear in the anogenital region, including the vulva, penis, perineum, anus, and surrounding areas. They present as small, flesh-colored or grayish papules that may be solitary or clustered. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity. While generally not life-threatening, they can cause discomfort, psychological distress, and may increase the risk of certain cancers if caused by high-risk HPV types.

Anal warts, also known as condyloma acuminata or genital warts, are benign growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. They typically appear as small, flesh-colored or reddish bumps in the anal region, often accompanied by itching or discomfort. The condition is highly contagious and spreads through direct skin-to-skin contact. While primarily affecting the anal area, warts may also occur on the genitalia, perineum, or around the urethral opening. Diagnosis is usually clinical, and treatment options include topical medications, cryotherapy, or surgical removal.

Genital warts, also known as venereal warts or condyloma acuminata, are benign, contagious growths caused by certain strains of the human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly types 6 and 11. They typically appear as small, flesh-colored or pink, cauliflower-like lesions on the genitalia, perineum, and anal area. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity. The condition is highly prevalent and often asymptomatic, though some individuals may experience itching or bleeding. HPV infection is a major cause of cervical cancer and other anogenital malignancies.

Extragenital condylomata acuminata refers to genital warts that occur outside the genital area, commonly affecting the perineum, anal region, and sometimes the thighs or mouth. Also known as anogenital warts or venereal warts, this condition is primarily caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly types 6 and 11. These warts are contagious and spread through direct skin-to-skin contact. They present as flesh-colored, cauliflower-like growths and may cause itching or discomfort. Diagnosis is usually clinical, and treatment options include topical agents, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

Anogenital warts, unspecified, are benign growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, most commonly types 6 and 11. They appear as small, flesh-colored or grayish papules in the anogenital region, often with a rough surface. Common synonyms include genital warts and condyloma acuminata. The condition typically affects the vulva, vagina, penis, anus, and perineum. Transmission occurs via sexual contact. While generally not life-threatening, they can cause discomfort, bleeding, and may increase the risk of certain cancers. Treatment options include topical medications, cryotherapy, and surgical removal.

code_desc: other specified predominantly sexually transmitted infections
summary: "Other specified predominantly sexually transmitted infections" refers to infections primarily transmitted through sexual contact that do not meet the criteria for specific STIs like HIV, syphilis, or gonorrhea. Common synonyms include unspecified STIs or other STIs. Causative agents may include various bacteria, viruses, or parasites, such as *Mycoplasma genitalium* or *Trichomonas vaginalis*. These infections typically affect the genital tract, including the urethra, vagina, cervix, and anus, and may present with symptoms like discharge, itching, or pain. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and laboratory testing.

Predominantly sexually transmitted infections, unspecified, refers to a group of infections primarily transmitted through sexual contact, with the specific pathogen not identified. Common synonyms include unspecified sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) or undetermined sexually transmitted infections. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, or parasites such as *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*, *Chlamydia trachomatis*, *Human papillomavirus (HPV)*, or *Herpes simplex virus (HSV)*. These infections typically affect the genital tract, urinary tract, and mucous membranes, with potential systemic complications if left untreated.

Tuberculosis of the respiratory system, commonly known as pulmonary tuberculosis, is an infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and cavitation. Symptoms include chronic cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. The disease can spread through airborne droplets. Other synonyms include consumption and phthisis. While the lungs are most commonly affected, the infection may disseminate to other organs, such as the lymph nodes, brain, or kidneys. Early diagnosis and treatment with anti-tuberculosis drugs are essential to prevent complications and transmission.

Respiratory tuberculosis, confirmed, is a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and cavitation. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and TB of the lungs. The infection may spread to other organs via hematogenous dissemination. Symptoms include persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, and fever. Diagnosis is confirmed through microbiological tests, imaging, and clinical evaluation. It is a major global health concern, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.

Respiratory tuberculosis, not confirmed, refers to a clinical suspicion of tuberculosis affecting the respiratory system without definitive diagnostic confirmation. Common synonyms include suspected pulmonary tuberculosis or possible tuberculosis. The causative agent is typically Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs, particularly the upper lobes, and may involve bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli. Symptoms include chronic cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation, imaging, and nucleic acid amplification tests, though culture remains the gold standard. Confirmation requires positive microbiological or histopathological evidence.

code_desc: respiratory tuberculosis, without mention of bacteriological or histological confirmation
summary: Respiratory tuberculosis is a chronic infectious disease primarily affecting the lungs, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is characterized by progressive parenchymal destruction, cavitation, and fibrosis. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and tuberculosis of the lungs. The infection typically spreads via airborne droplets, leading to granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis. It commonly involves the upper lobes of the lungs and may disseminate to other organs. Symptoms include persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, and fever. The disease progresses slowly and can remain latent for years before becoming active.

Tuberculosis of the nervous system, also known as neuro-tuberculosis, is a rare but serious extrapulmonary form of tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It commonly affects the meninges, brain, spinal cord, and cranial nerves. Symptoms include headache, fever, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. The condition often presents as tuberculous meningitis or tuberculoma. Other synonyms include tuberculous encephalomyelitis and tuberculous myelitis. Diagnosis typically involves imaging, lumbar puncture, and microbiological testing. Treatment requires long-term antitubercular therapy.

Tuberculous meningitis is a severe form of meningitis caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It results from the dissemination of tubercle bacilli from a primary focus, often the lungs, to the central nervous system. Common synonyms include tuberculous meningitis and tubercular meningitis. The infection typically affects the meninges, spinal cord, and cranial nerves, leading to inflammation and potential complications such as hydrocephalus and cranial nerve palsies. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with a history of tuberculosis.

Tuberculous meningoencephalitis is a severe central nervous system infection caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It involves inflammation of the meninges and brain parenchyma, often complicating pulmonary tuberculosis. Common synonyms include tuberculous meningitis and tubercular encephalitis. The condition typically affects the brain and spinal cord, with symptoms such as fever, headache, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and can lead to significant morbidity if untreated.

Meningeal tuberculoma is a granulomatous lesion formed by tuberculous infection within the meninges. It results from the dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often following hematogenous spread from a primary focus. Common synonyms include tuberculous meningoma and tuberculous granuloma. The condition typically affects the cerebral and spinal meninges, with involvement of the cranial nerves and brain parenchyma. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and may present with symptoms such as headache, fever, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging and microbiological studies.

Tuberculous granuloma of the brain, also known as tuberculous meningitis or tubercular encephalitis, is a chronic inflammatory lesion caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically presents as a granulomatous reaction with caseous necrosis, often involving the meninges, basal ganglia, and ventricles. Common synonyms include tuberculous brain abscess and tuberculous neurogranuloma. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, with the brain and spinal cord being the most commonly involved sites. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and may progress to tuberculous meningitis if left untreated.

code_desc: tuberculosis of other specified part of nervous system
summary: Tuberculosis of other specified parts of the nervous system refers to extrapulmonary tuberculosis affecting neural structures not classified under more specific categories, such as the meninges, brain, or spinal cord. Common synonyms include tuberculous meningitis or tuberculous myelitis, though these are more specific. The causative agent is *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the meninges, brain, spinal cord, or cranial nerves, leading to inflammation, mass lesions, or granuloma formation. Clinical presentation varies but often includes neurological deficits, fever, and headache. Diagnosis involves imaging, CSF analysis, and microbiological testing.

code_desc: tuberculosis of the nervous system, unspecified
summary: Tuberculosis of the nervous system, unspecified, refers to tuberculosis affecting any part of the central or peripheral nervous system without specific localization. Common synonyms include tuberculous meningitis, tuberculous encephalitis, and tuberculous myelitis. The primary causative agent is *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. This condition typically involves the meninges, brain, spinal cord, or cranial nerves. It often presents with symptoms such as fever, headache, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical evaluation, imaging, and microbiological testing. Treatment involves long-term anti-tuberculosis therapy.

code_desc: tuberculosis of other systems and organs
summary: Tuberculosis of other systems and organs refers to extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* complex. It affects various body parts beyond the lungs, including lymph nodes, bones, joints, brain, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include disseminated tuberculosis and miliary tuberculosis. The disease often presents with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and fatigue. Diagnosis typically involves imaging, biopsy, and acid-fast bacilli staining. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS.

Tuberculosis of the heart, also known as cardiac tuberculosis or tuberculous pericarditis, is a rare extrapulmonary form of tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the pericardium, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. In some cases, the myocardium or endocardium may be involved. The condition is more common in individuals with weakened immune systems or those co-infected with HIV. Symptoms may include chest pain, fever, and pericardial effusion. Diagnosis often requires imaging and biopsy, with treatment involving long-term antitubercular therapy.

Tuberculosis of the eye, also known as ocular tuberculosis or tuberculous uveitis, is a rare but serious infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It typically affects the uvea, leading to anterior or posterior uveitis, and may involve the retina, choroid, or optic nerve. Common synonyms include tuberculous ocular infection and tubercular uveitis. The disease often presents with symptoms such as eye pain, redness, blurred vision, and photophobia. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with a history of systemic tuberculosis. Complications can include cataracts, glaucoma, and permanent vision loss if untreated.

Tuberculosis of the ear, also known as otitic tuberculosis or tuberculous otitis, is a rare form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the middle ear and mastoid process, leading to chronic suppurative otitis media. The disease may spread to adjacent structures such as the temporal bone, brain, or cranial nerves. Common symptoms include ear discharge, hearing loss, and facial weakness. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with a history of tuberculosis. Early diagnosis and treatment with antitubercular therapy are essential to prevent severe complications.

Tuberculosis of endocrine glands, also known as tuberculous adenitis or scrofula, is a rare form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the lymph nodes near the thyroid and parotid glands, though other endocrine glands may be involved. The infection presents as painless, slowly progressive swelling, often with caseous necrosis. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with a history of tuberculosis. Diagnosis involves imaging, biopsy, and microbiological testing. Treatment follows standard anti-tuberculosis therapy.

Tuberculosis of the musculoskeletal system, also known as osteoarticular tuberculosis or Pott's disease, is a chronic infectious condition caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the spine, especially the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, but can also involve joints and bones. The disease leads to progressive destruction of bone and cartilage, often accompanied by cold abscesses and fibrosis. Common synonyms include tuberculous arthritis and spinal tuberculosis. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis.

Tuberculosis of bones or joints, also known as osteoarticular tuberculosis, is a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the spine (Pott's disease), hips, knees, and shoulders. The infection leads to progressive destruction of bone and joint tissues, often accompanied by cold abscesses and fibrosis. Common synonyms include tuberculous arthritis and spinal tuberculosis. The disease is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. Diagnosis involves imaging, microbiological tests, and clinical evaluation. Treatment includes long-term antitubercular therapy.

Tuberculous myositis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation of tuberculosis, characterized by inflammation and destruction of skeletal muscle tissue due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. It often presents with muscle pain, swelling, and weakness. Common synonyms include tuberculous muscle infection or tuberculosis of the muscle. The condition typically affects the lower extremities, particularly the thighs and calves, but can occur in other muscle groups. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and may be associated with systemic tuberculosis. Diagnosis is confirmed through microbiological testing, imaging, and histopathological examination.

code_desc: tuberculosis of other specified part of the musculoskeletal system
summary: Tuberculosis of other specified parts of the musculoskeletal system refers to tuberculosis affecting bones or joints not classified under more specific categories. It is caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and less commonly by other mycobacteria. The condition typically involves the spine (Pott's disease), hips, knees, and other joints. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and limited mobility. It may present as a chronic, progressive infection with potential for destruction of bone and joint structures. Diagnosis often requires imaging and microbiological testing.

code_desc: tuberculosis of the musculoskeletal system, unspecified
summary: Tuberculosis of the musculoskeletal system, unspecified, refers to infection of bones or joints by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Common synonyms include skeletal tuberculosis and osteoarticular tuberculosis. The causative agent is typically Mycobacterium tuberculosis, though other mycobacteria may occasionally be involved. This condition primarily affects the spine (pott's disease), long bones, and joints. It presents with chronic pain, swelling, and potential deformity. Diagnosis often involves imaging and microbiological testing. Treatment includes prolonged antibiotic therapy.

Tuberculosis of the genitourinary system, also known as genitourinary tuberculosis, is a chronic infection caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and reproductive organs. Common synonyms include renal tuberculosis and urogenital tuberculosis. The disease often results from hematogenous spread from a primary tuberculosis focus, leading to granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis. Symptoms may include flank pain, hematuria, and urinary frequency. It is more common in males and can lead to infertility or renal failure if untreated.

Tuberculous peripheral lymphadenopathy refers to the formation of enlarged, often painless lymph nodes caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is a manifestation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Common synonyms include tuberculous lymphadenitis and scrofula. The condition typically affects cervical lymph nodes but can involve axillary, inguinal, and other peripheral lymph node groups. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with prolonged exposure to tuberculosis. The lymph nodes are usually firm, non-tender, and may coalesce, sometimes leading to fistulous tracts. Diagnosis is confirmed through microbiological testing, imaging, and histopathological examination.

Tuberculosis of the digestive system, also known as gastrointestinal tuberculosis, is a chronic infectious disease caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. It typically affects the intestines, particularly the ileum, and may involve the stomach, liver, or other abdominal organs. Common synonyms include intestinal tuberculosis and abdominal tuberculosis. The disease often presents with symptoms such as abdominal pain, weight loss, and malabsorption. It is more prevalent in individuals with compromised immune systems or a history of pulmonary tuberculosis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy, biopsy, and microbiological testing.

Cutaneous tuberculosis is a rare form of tuberculosis caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* or other *Mycobacterium* species. It presents as chronic, indolent skin lesions, often resembling lupus vulgaris. Common synonyms include lupus tuberculosis and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. The disease typically affects sun-exposed areas such as the face, ears, and extremities. Lesions may appear as papules, nodules, or ulcers with a granulomatous appearance. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying tuberculosis. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation, histopathology, and microbiological testing.

code_desc: tuberculosis of other specified organ or site
summary: Tuberculosis of other specified organ or site refers to tuberculosis affecting body parts not covered by more specific classifications, such as the brain, bones, or joints. It is caused primarily by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and less commonly by other *Mycobacterium* species. Common synonyms include extrapulmonary tuberculosis. The condition typically affects the lymphatic system, bones, joints, and occasionally the genitourinary or gastrointestinal tracts. Clinical presentation varies depending on the affected organ, often presenting with localized inflammation, mass formation, or systemic symptoms. Diagnosis involves imaging, biopsy, and microbiological testing.

Common synonyms include hematogenous dissemination of tuberculosis and miliary TB. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The disease often presents with systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and night sweats.

code_desc: acute miliary tuberculosis of a single specified site
summary: Acute miliary tuberculosis of a single specified site refers to a rare form of tuberculosis characterized by the rapid dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to a specific organ or tissue, resulting in the formation of small, millet seed-like granulomas. Common synonyms include miliary tuberculosis with localized involvement. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This condition typically affects the lungs, but can also involve the liver, spleen, brain, or other organs, depending on the site of infection. It is often associated with immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying conditions that impair immune response.

code_desc: acute miliary tuberculosis of multiple sites
summary: Acute miliary tuberculosis of multiple sites is a severe form of tuberculosis characterized by widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis through the bloodstream, leading to the formation of small, millet-seed-like nodules in various organs. Common synonyms include miliary TB and hematogenous dissemination of TB. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This condition typically affects the lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, and brain, with systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and night sweats. It is most commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals or those with untreated pulmonary tuberculosis.

Acute miliary tuberculosis is a severe form of tuberculosis characterized by widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis through the bloodstream, leading to the formation of small, millet-seed-like nodules (miliary lesions) primarily in the lungs. It is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and can affect other organs such as the liver, spleen, and brain. Common synonyms include miliary TB and disseminated tuberculosis. The condition typically presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and respiratory symptoms, and is more common in immunocompromised individuals.

Other specified miliary tuberculosis refers to a form of tuberculosis characterized by widespread dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis through the bloodstream, leading to the formation of small,粟粒-like nodules primarily in the lungs. It is classified under the broader category of miliary tuberculosis when the clinical presentation does not fit the more specific subtypes. Common synonyms include disseminated tuberculosis and hematogenous tuberculosis. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and the lungs are typically affected, though other organs such as the liver, spleen, and brain may also be involved.

Miliary tuberculosis is a severe form of tuberculosis characterized by the dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis throughout the body via the bloodstream, leading to the formation of small,粟粒-like granulomas primarily in the lungs. Common synonyms include hematogenous tuberculosis and miliary TB. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It typically affects the lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow, but can involve multiple organs. The condition is often associated with immunocompromised individuals and may present with systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, and night sweats.

Latent tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic, asymptomatic infection caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* in which the bacteria remain dormant within macrophages. It is not contagious and does not produce active disease. Common synonyms include inactive TB or tuberculous infection. The bacteria typically reside in the lungs but can affect other organs. It is often identified through tuberculin skin tests or interferon-gamma release assays. Latent TB is a precursor to active TB and requires treatment to prevent progression.

"Other specified tuberculosis" refers to tuberculosis cases that do not meet the criteria for pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis but are clinically or radiologically significant. It is a category used when the site or nature of the infection is not clearly defined. Common synonyms include unspecified tuberculosis or undetermined tuberculosis. The causative agent is typically Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It may affect various body parts, including lymph nodes, bones, or the central nervous system, but the exact location is not clearly specified in the clinical presentation.

Tuberculosis, unspecified, refers to an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, primarily affecting the lungs. It is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis. Common synonyms include pulmonary tuberculosis and consumption. The disease typically involves the respiratory system but can disseminate to other organs. Symptoms include persistent cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. Diagnosis is confirmed through sputum smear, culture, or nucleic acid amplification tests. Treatment involves multidrug therapy with antibiotics such as isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol.

Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*. It primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes of the upper respiratory tract. The infection leads to granulomatous inflammation and nerve damage, resulting in sensory loss, muscle weakness, and characteristic skin lesions. Common synonyms include Hansen's disease and leprosy. The disease is transmitted via prolonged close contact with infected individuals, though its exact mode of transmission remains incompletely understood. Early diagnosis and multidrug therapy can prevent severe complications and disability.

Paucibacillary leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*, characterized by minimal bacillary load. It primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. Common synonyms include tuberculoid leprosy and paucibacillary type. The condition presents with hypopigmented, anesthetic skin patches and nerve thickening, often leading to sensory loss. It is less contagious than multibacillary leprosy and typically occurs in individuals with strong immune responses. Early diagnosis and treatment with multidrug therapy are essential to prevent disability.

Multibacillary leprosy is a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*, also known as Hansen's disease. It is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and nerve damage, leading to loss of sensation and deformities. Common synonyms include lepromatous leprosy and Hansen's disease. The infection primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucosal surfaces of the upper respiratory tract. It is more severe than paucibacillary leprosy and requires multidrug therapy to prevent complications and transmission.

Leprosy reactions are immune-mediated inflammatory responses in patients with leprosy, often triggered by Mycobacterium leprae. They manifest as erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) or reversal reactions.
