They are often associated with systemic infections, trauma, or immunocompromised states.

"Other specified intracranial abscess" refers to a localized collection of pus within the cranial cavity that does not meet the criteria for specific types such as brain abscess or subdural abscess. Common synonyms include unspecified intracranial abscess or non-classifiable intracranial abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infections, often secondary to trauma, surgery, or hematogenous spread. Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and anaerobes. The condition most commonly affects the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, or brainstem, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, and neurological deficits.

Intracranial abscess, unspecified, refers to a localized collection of pus within the cranial cavity, typically resulting from bacterial infection. Common synonyms include cerebral abscess and brain abscess. Causative agents often include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *E. coli*, though other pathogens may be involved. The condition most commonly affects the cerebral hemispheres, though it can occur in other intracranial regions. It is often associated with complications from sinusitis, otitis media, or trauma. Symptoms may include fever, headache, seizures, and neurological deficits. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent severe neurological complications.

Intraspinal epidural abscess is a rare but serious infection characterized by the accumulation of pus within the epidural space, potentially extending into the spinal canal. Common synonyms include spinal epidural abscess and intramedullary abscess. It is typically caused by bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and anaerobes. The condition most commonly affects the thoracic and lumbar spine, though cervical involvement is also possible. It often presents with back pain, fever, and neurological deficits, requiring prompt antibiotic therapy and surgical drainage to prevent severe complications.

Spinal cord abscess is a rare but severe infection characterized by localized collection of pus within the spinal cord parenchyma. Common synonyms include spinal epidural abscess and intramedullary abscess. It is typically caused by bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and less commonly, gram-negative organisms. The condition most frequently affects the thoracic and cervical spinal regions. Symptoms include back pain, neurological deficits, and fever. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics and surgical drainage are essential to prevent permanent neurological damage.

code_desc: other specified site of infectious abscess of the central nervous system
summary: "Other specified site of infectious abscess of the central nervous system" refers to a localized collection of pus within the central nervous system (CNS) at a site not classified as brain, spinal cord, or meninges. Common synonyms include CNS abscess with unspecified location. Causative agents often include bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and anaerobes. It may also result from fungal or parasitic infections. Typically affects the brain parenchyma, but can occur in other CNS regions. Symptoms include fever, headache, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis is confirmed via imaging and microbiological studies.

code_desc: infectious abscess of the central nervous system, site unspecified
summary: Infectious abscess of the central nervous system, site unspecified, refers to a localized collection of pus within the brain or spinal cord caused by microbial infection. Common synonyms include cerebral abscess and spinal abscess. Causative agents often include bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and anaerobes, as well as fungi in immunocompromised patients. The condition typically affects the brain, particularly the frontal, temporal, or parietal lobes, and may also involve the spinal cord. Symptoms include fever, headache, neurological deficits, and altered mental status.

code_desc: infectious granulomas of the central nervous system
summary: Infectious granulomas of the central nervous system (CNS) are focal inflammatory lesions formed in response to persistent microbial infection. Common synonyms include tuberculomas and granulomatous CNS infections. They are typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but other pathogens such as fungi, parasites, and atypical mycobacteria can also induce similar lesions. These granulomas most commonly affect the brain, particularly the basal ganglia and white matter, and less frequently the spinal cord. Clinical presentation varies but often includes focal neurological deficits, seizures, or increased intracranial pressure. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and biopsy.

Parasitic intracerebral granuloma is a focal inflammatory lesion in the brain caused by parasitic infection. Common synonyms include cerebral granuloma and neurocysticercosis. The most frequent causative agent is *Taenia solium*, leading to cysticercosis. Other parasites such as *Toxocara canis* and *Echinococcus granulosus* may also cause similar lesions. These granulomas typically affect the cerebral parenchyma, particularly the cortex and white matter. Symptoms vary depending on location and size, often including seizures, headaches, and focal neurological deficits. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by imaging and serological tests.

Intracranial granuloma is a localized inflammatory lesion characterized by the formation of granulomatous tissue within the central nervous system. It typically results from an immune response to foreign bodies, infections, or autoimmune conditions. Common synonyms include granuloma of the central nervous system and CNS granuloma. Known causative agents include tuberculosis, fungal infections, syphilis, and non-tuberculous mycobacteria. It may also occur in association with sarcoidosis or as a complication of trauma or surgery. The condition most commonly affects the brain, particularly the meninges, and less frequently the spinal cord.

Fungal intracranial granuloma is a chronic inflammatory lesion formed in response to fungal infection within the central nervous system. Common synonyms include fungal brain granuloma and mycotic granuloma. It is typically caused by organisms such as *Coccidioides immitis*, *Histoplasma capsulatum*, *Blastomyces dermatitidis*, and *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis*. These infections often affect the brain and meninges, leading to symptoms such as headache, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those residing in endemic regions.

"Other specified intracranial granuloma" refers to granulomatous inflammation of the central nervous system not attributable to a more specific cause, such as tuberculosis or sarcoidosis. It is a broad category encompassing various granulomatous conditions with unknown or unspecified etiology. Common synonyms include idiopathic intracranial granuloma or non-specific granuloma. Causative agents are often unknown, though some cases may be linked to infectious or autoimmune processes. Typically affects the brain and meninges, with symptoms including headache, seizures, and focal neurological deficits.

Intracranial granuloma, unspecified, refers to a granulomatous lesion within the skull or central nervous system of unknown specific origin. It is characterized by the presence of granulomas, which are inflammatory aggregates of immune cells, typically forming in response to infection, foreign bodies, or autoimmune processes. Common synonyms include intracranial granulomatous disease and non-specific intracranial granuloma. Causative agents may include fungal infections, tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, or foreign body reactions. The condition typically affects the brain and meninges, though it may involve other cranial structures. Diagnosis often requires imaging and biopsy.

Intraspinal intramedullary granuloma is a rare, benign lesion within the spinal cord, characterized by granulomatous inflammation. It is often associated with infectious agents such as tuberculosis or fungal organisms. Common synonyms include spinal granuloma and intramedullary granuloma. The condition typically affects the thoracic and cervical spinal regions. It may present with neurological deficits such as weakness, sensory loss, or spasticity. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via MRI and biopsy. Treatment involves addressing the underlying cause, often with antitubercular or antifungal therapy.

Intraspinal subdural granuloma is a rare, chronic inflammatory lesion forming within the subdural space of the spinal canal. It typically presents as a well-circumscribed mass causing spinal cord compression. Common synonyms include spinal subdural granuloma and intradural extramedullary granuloma. Causative agents often include tuberculosis, fungal infections, and foreign bodies. It most commonly affects the thoracic and lumbar regions, though cervical involvement is also possible. The condition is often associated with a history of infection or prior spinal surgery. Clinical features include back pain, neurological deficits, and radiculopathy. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via MRI and histopathological examination.

Intraspinal extradural granuloma is a rare, chronic inflammatory lesion located within the extradural space of the spinal canal. It is characterized by the presence of granulomatous inflammation, often associated with foreign body reaction or infection. Common synonyms include spinal granuloma and intraspinal foreign body reaction. Causative agents may include tuberculosis, fungal infections, or non-infectious agents such as silicone or other foreign materials. The condition typically affects the thoracic and lumbar spine, causing spinal cord compression and neurological deficits. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and biopsy.

Intraspinal epidural granuloma is a rare, benign inflammatory lesion that forms within the epidural space of the spine. It is characterized by granulomatous inflammation, often in response to foreign bodies or infectious agents. Common synonyms include epidural granuloma and intraspinal foreign body reaction. Causative agents may include silicone, cement, or other implanted materials. Typically affecting the thoracic and lumbar regions, this condition can cause spinal cord compression, leading to neurological deficits. Diagnosis is usually made via imaging and histopathological examination.

code_desc: other specified site of infectious granulomas of the central nervous system
summary: "Other specified site of infectious granulomas of the central nervous system" refers to granulomatous inflammation in the CNS caused by infectious agents, occurring at sites not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include granulomatous encephalitis or myelitis. Causative agents may include fungi, parasites, or atypical mycobacteria. Typically affects the brain or spinal cord, often presenting with neurological symptoms such as fever, seizures, or focal deficits. Diagnosis requires imaging and microbiological testing.

code_desc: infectious granulomas of the central nervous system, site unspecified
summary: Infectious granulomas of the central nervous system, site unspecified, refer to granulomatous inflammation in the CNS caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include tuberculomas and fungal granulomas. Causative agents may include Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungi such as Cryptococcus neoformans, and other pathogens. These lesions typically affect the brain and spinal cord, often presenting with neurological symptoms. Diagnosis usually requires imaging and biopsy. The condition is associated with immune compromise or chronic infection. Treatment depends on the underlying pathogen and may involve antimicrobial therapy.

code_desc: infectious cysts of the central nervous system
summary: Infectious cysts of the central nervous system (CNS) are fluid-filled lesions caused by infectious agents, often resulting from bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infections. Common synonyms include pyogenic abscesses and granulomatous cysts. Causative agents vary by region and include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Nocardia*, *Cryptococcus*, and parasites like *Toxoplasma gondii* or *Echinococcus*. These cysts typically affect the brain and spinal cord, often presenting with symptoms such as headache, fever, neurological deficits, and increased intracranial pressure. They may develop from contiguous spread, hematogenous dissemination, or direct inoculation. Diagnosis involves imaging and microbiological analysis.

An epidural infectious cyst is a rare, localized collection of fluid and inflammatory cells within the epidural space, typically resulting from a bacterial infection. Common synonyms include epidural abscess and spinal epidural infection. Causative agents often include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and less commonly, gram-negative bacilli. The condition most frequently affects the lumbar region, though it can occur along the spinal column. It is often associated with contiguous spread from adjacent infections or hematogenous dissemination. Clinical presentation may include back pain, fever, and neurological deficits. Early diagnosis and antibiotic therapy are critical to prevent spinal cord damage.

A subdural infectious cyst is a rare, localized collection of fluid within the subdural space, typically resulting from an infectious process. It may arise from bacterial or fungal infections, often following trauma, surgery, or meningitis. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *Candida*. The condition predominantly affects the cerebral hemispheres, with symptoms such as headache, fever, and neurological deficits. It is sometimes referred to as a subdural empyema or subdural abscess. The cyst can lead to increased intracranial pressure and requires prompt antibiotic therapy and drainage.

code_desc: other specified infectious cysts of the central nervous system
summary: "Other specified infectious cysts of the central nervous system" refers to cystic lesions in the brain or spinal cord caused by infectious agents, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include pyogenic cysts or abscess-like cysts. Causative agents may include bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, or fungi like Cryptococcus. These cysts typically affect the brain, particularly the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum, or brainstem, and may present with neurological symptoms such as headache, fever, and focal deficits.

code_desc: infectious cysts of the central nervous system, unspecified
summary: Infectious cysts of the central nervous system, unspecified, refer to fluid-filled sacs within the brain or spinal cord caused by infectious agents. These cysts may result from bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infections. Common synonyms include pyogenic cysts or abscesses. Causative agents vary but may include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*, or *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, as well as fungi like *Cryptococcus* or parasites like *Toxoplasma*. The condition typically affects the brain, particularly the cerebrum, cerebellum, or brainstem, and may also involve the spinal cord.

code_desc: other specified non-viral and unspecified infections of the central nervous system
summary: "Other specified non-viral and unspecified infections of the central nervous system" refers to infections of the brain or spinal cord not caused by viruses and not specifically classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include unspecified CNS infections. Causative agents may include bacteria, fungi, or parasites. Typically affected areas include the brain, meninges, and spinal cord. These infections may present with fever, headache, altered mental status, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis often requires lumbar puncture and imaging. Treatment depends on the identified pathogen.

code_desc: non-viral and unspecified infections of the central nervous system, unspecified
summary: Non-viral and unspecified infections of the central nervous system refer to infectious processes affecting the brain, spinal cord, or meninges caused by agents other than viruses. Common synonyms include "unspecified central nervous system infections" or "infections of the central nervous system, not otherwise specified." Causative agents may include bacteria, fungi, parasites, or other microorganisms. These infections typically affect the brain, spinal cord, and meninges, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, altered mental status, and neurological deficits. Diagnosis often requires lumbar puncture and microbiological testing.

Dengue without warning signs refers to a mild form of dengue fever characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, and rash, without the severe systemic manifestations seen in dengue hemorrhagic fever. It is caused by any of the four dengue virus serotypes transmitted primarily by *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus* mosquitoes. Common synonyms include classic dengue or uncomplicated dengue. Typically affecting the systemic circulation and skin, this form generally does not require hospitalization and has a favorable prognosis.

Dengue with warning signs is a severe form of dengue fever characterized by clinical indicators that predict progression to dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. Common synonyms include severe dengue and dengue shock. Caused by the dengue virus (DENV), transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, it typically affects the circulatory system, liver, and platelet count. Symptoms include persistent abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding manifestations, and altered mental status. It predominantly affects children and young adults, with a higher risk in areas with high dengue endemicity. Early recognition and prompt management are critical to prevent complications.

Severe dengue, also known as dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome, is a life-threatening complication of dengue virus infection. Caused by any of the four serotypes of the dengue virus, it typically affects individuals who have had a prior dengue infection. The disease primarily impacts the circulatory system, leading to plasma leakage, fluid accumulation, and hypovolemic shock. Commonly affected body parts include the skin, where petechiae and ecchymoses may appear, and the gastrointestinal tract, which may experience bleeding. Other manifestations involve respiratory distress and organ dysfunction. Early recognition and supportive care are critical for improving outcomes.

Dengue fever, unspecified, is a viral infection caused by any of the four dengue virus serotypes. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito. Common synonyms include dengue virus infection and dengue illness. The disease typically affects the vascular system, causing fever, headache, muscle pain, and rash. It may progress to severe dengue, involving plasma leakage, fluid accumulation, and organ impairment. The liver and hematologic system are commonly affected. It primarily occurs in tropical and subtropical regions.

Chikungunya virus disease is an acute febrile illness caused by the chikungunya virus, an alphavirus transmitted primarily by *Aedes* mosquitoes. Common synonyms include chikungunya fever and chikungunya infection. The disease typically presents with sudden onset of high fever, severe joint pain, and rash. Affected body parts include joints, particularly the hands, feet, wrists, and knees, often leading to arthralgia and arthritis. Additional symptoms may include headache, muscle pain, and fatigue. The illness is generally self-limiting but can persist for weeks or months, with potential for chronic joint pain.

Colorado tick fever is a viral illness transmitted by the bite of infected ticks, primarily the American dog tick (*Dermacentor variabilis*). It is also known as mountain fever or tick fever. The virus, *Coltivirus*, causes acute symptoms including fever, headache, myalgia, and fatigue. The illness typically affects the systemic and musculoskeletal systems. It is endemic to the Rocky Mountain region of the United States. Most cases are mild and self-limiting, though complications can occur in immunocompromised individuals.

O'nyong-nyong fever is an acute, self-limiting viral illness characterized by sudden onset of high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, and rash. Common synonyms include Kikongo fever and African trypanosomiasis. Caused by the virus *Culicoides sonorensis*, it is transmitted through the bite of infected sand flies. The disease primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and central nervous system. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly among rural populations. Symptoms typically resolve within a week without specific treatment.

Oropouche virus disease is a viral illness caused by the Oropouche virus, a member of the Togaviridae family. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected mosquitoes, particularly species of the Haemagogus genus. The disease is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, and rash, often with lymphadenopathy. Common synonyms include Oropouche fever and Oropouche virus infection. The virus primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and lymphatic system, with systemic involvement in more severe cases. It is endemic in parts of South America, particularly Brazil and the Caribbean.

Rift Valley fever (RVF) is an acute viral illness caused by the Rift Valley fever virus, a member of the Phlebovirus genus. Common synonyms include RVF and Rift Valley fever virus. The disease primarily affects humans and animals, with mosquitoes serving as the main vector. It typically manifests as a flu-like illness, but can progress to severe complications such as ocular disease, encephalitis, or hemorrhagic fever. The liver is commonly affected, leading to hepatitis. Outbreaks often occur in sub-Saharan Africa, with sporadic cases reported in other regions.

Sandfly fever, also known as phlebotomine fever or visceral leishmaniasis, is a vector-borne illness caused by *Leishmania* parasites. Transmission occurs through the bite of infected sandflies. The disease primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, leading to fever, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. The causative agents include *Leishmania donovani*, *L. infantum*, and *L. tropica*. While visceral leishmaniasis is a severe form, sandfly fever often refers to the cutaneous form, characterized by skin lesions at the site of the bite.

West Nile virus infection is a flavivirus transmitted primarily through mosquito bites. Common synonyms include West Nile fever and West Nile encephalitis. The virus can cause a range of symptoms from asymptomatic infection to severe neurological disease. The most common causative agent is West Nile virus (WNV), with serotype 1 being the predominant strain. Typically, the infection affects the central nervous system, leading to meningitis, encephalitis, or acute flaccid paralysis. It can also involve the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. The disease is more severe in the elderly and immunocompromised individuals.

Yellow fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the yellow fever virus, a member of the Flaviviridae family. Transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, it is endemic in parts of Africa and South America. The disease typically affects the liver, leading to jaundice, hence its name. Common synonyms include African yellow fever and gold fever. Symptoms include fever, chills, headache, and muscle pain, progressing to severe hepatitis, renal failure, and bleeding in advanced stages. The liver and spleen are most commonly affected, with potential involvement of the kidneys and gastrointestinal tract.

Zika virus disease is a flavivirus infection primarily transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. It can also spread through sexual contact and from mother to fetus. Common synonyms include Zika fever and Zika syndrome. The virus typically affects the skin, joints, and central nervous system. Symptoms often include fever, rash, conjunctivitis, and joint pain. In severe cases, it can lead to Guillain-Barré syndrome. Neurological complications, such as microcephaly in newborns, are significant concerns, particularly in pregnant women. The disease is generally mild but can have serious consequences in specific populations.

Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) is a severe viral illness caused by the CCHF virus, a member of the Bunyaviridae family. It is transmitted primarily through tick bites or contact with infected animal blood. Common synonyms include Crimean hemorrhagic fever and Congo hemorrhagic fever. The virus affects multiple organ systems, with common involvement of the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system. Symptoms include fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. It is endemic in Africa, the Middle East, and parts of Asia.

Omsk hemorrhagic fever is an acute viral illness caused by the Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It is endemic in parts of Russia and is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected rodents, particularly the yellow-necked mouse. The disease presents with fever, headache, muscle pain, and hemorrhagic manifestations, often affecting the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs. Complications may include renal failure and coagulopathy. Common synonyms include Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus infection and Omsk virus disease.

Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD), also known as monkey fever or chikungunya-like fever, is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Kyasanur Forest Disease virus (KFDV), a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected ticks, primarily *Haemaphysalis spinigera*. The disease primarily affects the lymph nodes, spleen, and liver, leading to fever, headache, muscle pain, and in severe cases, hemorrhage and multi-organ failure. It is endemic to the Western Ghats of India.

Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever is a viral illness caused by the Alkhurma hemorrhagic fever virus (AHFV), a member of the Flaviviridae family. It is transmitted primarily through the bite of infected ticks, particularly *Hyalomma* species. The disease presents with fever, headache, muscle pain, and gastrointestinal symptoms, often progressing to hemorrhagic manifestations. Common synonyms include tick-borne hemorrhagic fever and Alkhurma virus infection. The virus primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy and multi-organ involvement, particularly the liver and kidneys. It is endemic in the Middle East and parts of Africa.

Ross River disease is a viral illness caused by the Ross River virus, transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. It primarily affects the joints and muscles, leading to arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue. Common synonyms include acute sero-negative arthritis and epidemic polyarthritis. The disease is endemic in Australia, Papua New Guinea, and parts of the Pacific Islands. Symptoms typically develop 2–4 weeks post-infection and can last for several weeks to months. The condition is not contagious and usually resolves spontaneously, though some individuals may experience prolonged or recurrent symptoms.

Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), also known as SFTS or tick-borne hemorrhagic fever, is a viral illness caused by the SFTS virus, a member of the Phlebovirus genus. It is transmitted primarily through tick bites, particularly from *Hemiphlebotomus* species. The disease presents with high fever, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and multi-organ dysfunction. Commonly affected systems include the hematopoietic, hepatic, and renal systems. Severe cases may lead to coagulopathy, shock, and multi-organ failure.

"Other specified arthropod-borne viral fevers" refers to viral infections transmitted by arthropods, such as mosquitoes or ticks, that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include "arboviral fevers" or "vector-borne viral fevers." Causative agents may include viruses like dengue, chikungunya, or rift valley fever. These infections typically affect the fever, musculoskeletal system, and may involve the liver or central nervous system. Symptoms include fever, rash, joint pain, and in severe cases, hemorrhage or encephalitis. The condition is often diagnosed based on clinical presentation and travel history.

Arthropod-borne viral fever, virus unspecified, refers to febrile illnesses transmitted by vectors such as mosquitoes or ticks, caused by various arboviruses. Common synonyms include viral hemorrhagic fever and tropical fever. Causative agents may include dengue, chikungunya, Zika, or yellow fever viruses. Typically affecting the systemic circulation, these fevers often present with high fever, headache, myalgia, and rash. The illness may involve the liver, spleen, and hematologic system, with severity varying by virus and host factors.

Filovirus disease is a severe viral infection caused by filoviruses, including Ebola and Marburg viruses. It is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. Common synonyms include Ebola virus disease and Marburg virus disease. The viruses are transmitted through direct contact with bodily fluids. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy and widespread organ dysfunction. It is often fatal without prompt supportive care. The main affected body parts include the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system.

Ebola disease, also known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever, is a severe and often fatal viral illness caused by the Ebola virus. The virus belongs to the Filoviridae family and includes several species, with Ebola virus species Zaire, Sudan, and Bundibugyo being the most clinically significant. The disease primarily affects the vascular system and immune system, leading to widespread hemorrhage, organ failure, and shock. Commonly affected body parts include the liver, kidneys, and blood vessels. Symptoms range from fever and fatigue to severe bleeding and multi-organ dysfunction. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces.

Bundibugyo virus disease is a rare, severe viral illness caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a member of the Filoviridae family. It is also known as Bundibugyo hemorrhagic fever. The virus primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. Common symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, and bleeding from mucous membranes. The disease typically affects the liver, kidneys, and blood clotting system. Outbreaks have been reported in Uganda, with a high case fatality rate. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals.

Ebola virus disease (EVD), also known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever, is a severe, often fatal illness caused by the Ebola virus, primarily from the Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, and Reston species. The virus targets the vascular system and immune system, leading to systemic inflammation, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure. Commonly affected body systems include the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system. Symptoms range from fever and fatigue to hemorrhaging and shock. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces.

Sudan virus disease is a severe hemorrhagic fever caused by the Sudan virus, a member of the Filoviridae family. It is also known as Sudan hemorrhagic fever or Sudan virus infection. The virus primarily affects the vascular system, leading to coagulopathy, organ failure, and high mortality. Common symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, and bleeding manifestations. The disease typically affects the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system. Transmission occurs through contact with infected bodily fluids. There is no specific antiviral treatment, and supportive care is the mainstay of management.

Atypical Ebola disease refers to a less severe form of Ebola virus infection, characterized by milder symptoms compared to classic Ebola hemorrhagic fever. It is caused by the Ebola virus, primarily species Zaire ebolavirus. Common synonyms include mild Ebola and non-hemorrhagic Ebola. The disease typically affects the vascular system and can involve the liver, kidneys, and immune system. Patients may present with fever, fatigue, and gastrointestinal symptoms without significant hemorrhage. It is less commonly associated with multi-organ failure and high mortality rates seen in the classic form.

"Other specified Ebola disease" is a category used when the clinical presentation of Ebola virus disease (EVD) does not meet the criteria for the more specific types, such as Ebola virus hemorrhagic fever. It may include atypical or mild cases. The causative agent is the Ebola virus, primarily from the Filoviridae family. Common synonyms include atypical Ebola disease or unspecified Ebola disease. The virus typically affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhage, and can involve multiple organ systems, particularly the liver, kidneys, and immune system.

Ebola disease, virus unspecified, is a severe viral hemorrhagic fever caused by members of the Ebolavirus genus. It is characterized by fever, severe headache, muscle pain, weakness, and gastrointestinal symptoms, often progressing to internal and external bleeding. The causative agents include Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, and Tai Forest ebolaviruses. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, leading to multi-organ failure. Common synonyms include Ebola hemorrhagic fever and Ebola virus disease. The infection is highly contagious and typically affects the liver, kidneys, and coagulation system.

Marburg disease is a severe, often fatal viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Marburg marburgvirus, a member of the Filoviridae family. It is also known as Marburg hemorrhagic fever or Marburg virus disease. The virus primarily affects the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, leading to systemic inflammation, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure. Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, and hemorrhagic manifestations. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces. The disease has a high case fatality rate, typically ranging from 24% to 88%.

Marburg virus disease is a severe hemorrhagic fever caused by the Marburg marburgvirus, a member of the Filoviridae family. It is also known as Marburg hemorrhagic fever or Marburg virus hemorrhagic fever. The virus primarily affects the liver and vascular system, leading to systemic inflammation, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure. Common symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle pain, and bleeding from multiple sites. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or animals. The disease has a high mortality rate, often exceeding 50%, and is endemic in parts of sub-Saharan Africa.

Atypical Marburg disease is a rare, severe viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Marburg virus, a member of the Filoviridae family. It presents with non-specific symptoms such as fever, headache, and malaise, often progressing to severe systemic involvement. Unlike typical Marburg disease, it lacks the characteristic hemorrhagic manifestations. Common synonyms include atypical Marburg hemorrhagic fever. The virus primarily affects the liver, kidneys, and immune system, leading to multi-organ dysfunction. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals.

"Other specified Marburg disease" refers to a rare, severe viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Marburg virus, a member of the Filoviridae family. It is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. The disease primarily affects the liver, kidneys, and vascular system, leading to coagulopathy and shock. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces. Common synonyms include Marburg virus disease. The condition is typically seen in individuals exposed to infected bats or healthcare workers in outbreak settings.

Marburg disease is a severe viral hemorrhagic fever caused by members of the Filoviridae family, including the Marburg virus and Ebola virus. It is characterized by high fever, hemorrhage, multi-organ failure, and a high case fatality rate. The disease primarily affects the vascular system, liver, and coagulation system. Common synonyms include Marburg hemorrhagic fever and filovirus hemorrhagic fever. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or animals. The virus is endemic in parts of Africa, with outbreaks often linked to fruit bats as natural reservoirs.

Other specified filovirus disease refers to infections caused by filoviruses that do not meet the criteria for Ebola virus disease or Marburg virus disease. Common synonyms include unspecified filovirus infection. Causative agents include Lloviu virus, Cuevavirus, and Reston virus. These viruses primarily affect the vascular system and cause hemorrhagic fever. Symptoms include fever, hemorrhage, organ failure, and coagulopathy. The disease typically involves the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system. Transmission occurs through direct contact with bodily fluids. The condition is rare and often associated with outbreaks in specific regions.

Filovirus disease, virus unspecified, refers to severe hemorrhagic fever caused by filoviruses such as Ebola or Marburg viruses. It is characterized by high fever, hemorrhage, multi-organ failure, and a high mortality rate. Common synonyms include Ebola hemorrhagic fever and Marburg virus disease. The viruses replicate in macrophages and lymph nodes, leading to systemic inflammation and coagulopathy. Typically affected body parts include the liver, spleen, and vascular system. The disease progresses rapidly and requires immediate supportive care.

Arenavirus disease is a group of viral infections caused by arenaviruses, which are RNA viruses. Common synonyms include Lassa fever, hemorrhagic fever, and South American hemorrhagic fever. The causative agents include Lassa virus, Junín virus, Machupo virus, and Guanarito virus. These viruses primarily affect the vascular system and can cause fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. They typically target the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes, leading to systemic inflammation and coagulopathy. Transmission occurs through rodent bites or contact with infected bodily fluids. The disease is more prevalent in tropical regions of Africa and South America.

Argentine haemorrhagic fever, also known as Argentine hemorrhagic fever or Junin fever, is a viral illness caused by the Junin virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It primarily affects the vascular system, leading to fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. The disease is endemic in Argentina, affecting agricultural workers exposed to infected rodents, particularly the grass mouse. Common symptoms include high fever, headache, muscle pain, and gastrointestinal disturbances. Severe cases may involve bleeding from mucous membranes and internal organs. The spleen, liver, and kidneys are typically affected, with potential for shock and death if untreated.

Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, also known as Machupo virus disease, is a viral illness caused by the Machupo virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It primarily affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhagic manifestations. The disease typically involves fever, headache, muscle pain, and progressive bleeding from mucous membranes and skin. The kidneys are commonly affected, resulting in renal failure. It is endemic to Bolivia and occurs in rural areas with high rodent exposure. The case fatality rate varies but can be significant without prompt treatment.

Lassa fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic illness caused by the Lassa virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It is primarily transmitted to humans through contact with infected Mastomys rats. Common synonyms include Lassa hemorrhagic fever and Lassa virus disease. The virus primarily affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhage, organ failure, and multi-organ dysfunction. Symptoms include fever, headache, weakness, and vomiting, often progressing to shock and death. The disease predominantly affects the liver, kidneys, and circulatory system, with severe cases involving hemorrhagic manifestations.

Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever (VHF), also known as Machupo virus disease, is a viral illness caused by the Machupo virus, a member of the Arenaviridae family. It primarily affects the vascular system, leading to hemorrhagic manifestations, fever, and systemic symptoms. The disease typically involves the liver, spleen, and blood vessels, causing coagulopathy and organ dysfunction. Common symptoms include high fever, headache, muscle pain, and bleeding from mucous membranes. It is endemic to northern South America, particularly Venezuela, and is transmitted through infected rodents, mainly Calomys callosus.

"Other specified arenavirus disease" refers to arenavirus infections not classified under more specific categories like Lassa fever or hemorrhagic fever. Common synonyms include unspecified arenavirus infection. Causative agents include various arenaviruses such as Lujo, Machupo, and Sabia viruses. These infections typically affect the vascular system, leading to hemorrhage, and may involve the liver, kidneys, and central nervous system. Symptoms include fever, fatigue, and in severe cases, multi-organ failure. Transmission occurs via rodent contact, primarily in endemic regions of Africa and South America.

Arenavirus disease, unspecified, refers to clinical illness caused by any arenavirus, a family of RNA viruses. Common synonyms include hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and lymphocytic choriomeningitis. Causative agents include Lassa fever virus, Junín virus, Machupo virus, and others. The disease typically affects the vascular system, kidneys, and central nervous system. Symptoms range from fever and fatigue to severe hemorrhage and organ failure. It is primarily transmitted through rodent vectors, with human-to-human spread occurring in some cases. The condition can be life-threatening without prompt treatment.

Hantavirus disease is a severe, often fatal illness caused by hantaviruses, primarily transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Common synonyms include hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), depending on the region and virus type. The most common causative agents include *Sin Nombre virus* and *Hantaan virus*. The disease typically affects the lungs and kidneys, leading to pulmonary edema and acute renal failure. Symptoms include fever, muscle pain, and respiratory distress. Early diagnosis and supportive care are critical for improving outcomes.

Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), also known as epidemic kidney disease or Korean haemorrhagic fever, is a viral illness caused by hantaviruses. It primarily affects the kidneys and vascular system, leading to acute renal failure, haemorrhagic manifestations, and systemic inflammation. The disease is transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents. Commonly affected organs include the kidneys, liver, and lungs, with symptoms ranging from fever and haemorrhage to severe hypotension and multi-organ failure.

Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is a severe, often fatal respiratory illness caused by hantaviruses, primarily transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta. Common synonyms include hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in some regions, though HPS refers specifically to the pulmonary form. The virus primarily affects the lungs, causing non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Symptoms include fever, muscle pain, and rapid respiratory failure. It primarily affects the respiratory system and kidneys, with high mortality rates if untreated.

Atypical hantavirus disease refers to a clinical syndrome caused by hantaviruses, distinct from classic hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. It is characterized by non-specific symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and muscle aches, often without prominent hemorrhagic features. Common synonyms include atypical hantavirus infection or non-renal hantavirus disease. The causative agents include various hantaviruses, such as Seoul, Puumala, and Dobrava. Typically, the disease affects the vascular system and may involve the lungs, leading to pulmonary symptoms in some cases.

Other specified hantavirus disease refers to hantavirus infections not classified under the more specific categories such as hantavirus pulmonary syndrome or hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. It encompasses cases where the clinical presentation or causative agent does not fit established subtypes. Common synonyms include unspecified hantavirus infection. Causative agents include various hantaviruses, such as those from the genus *Hantavirus*. The disease primarily affects the respiratory and renal systems, often leading to pulmonary edema and acute kidney injury. It is transmitted through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta.

Hantavirus disease, unspecified, refers to clinical manifestations caused by hantaviruses, a group of RNA viruses transmitted primarily through rodent excreta. Common synonyms include hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), though the unspecified category may encompass a broader range of presentations. The virus primarily affects the vascular system, leading to symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and in severe cases, pulmonary edema or renal failure. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, kidneys, and blood vessels. The causative agents are various hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre virus and Hantaan virus, depending on the geographic region.

Henipavirus encephalitis is a severe neurological infection caused by henipaviruses, including Hendra virus and Nipah virus. It is characterized by acute inflammation of the brain, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, seizures, and coma. Common synonyms include Hendra virus encephalitis and Nipah virus encephalitis. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, with the brain being the most commonly involved organ. Transmission occurs through contact with infected animals or bodily fluids, often leading to high mortality rates.

Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) is a viral respiratory illness caused by the MERS coronavirus (MERS-CoV). It is also known as camel coronavirus or human coronavirus EMC. The virus primarily affects the respiratory system, causing severe acute respiratory infection. Symptoms include fever, cough, and shortness of breath, which can progress to pneumonia and respiratory failure. MERS is zoonotic, with camels serving as a reservoir, and transmission occurs through close contact with infected dromedaries or between humans. The disease has a high mortality rate, typically affecting the lungs and sometimes leading to multi-organ failure.

Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) is an acute respiratory illness characterized by fever, cough, and shortness of breath. It is caused by the SARS coronavirus (SARS-CoV), a member of the Coronaviridae family. The disease primarily affects the lungs, leading to pneumonia and respiratory failure. Common synonyms include atypical pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) in severe cases. SARS spreads through respiratory droplets and close contact. It predominantly impacts the lower respiratory tract, with systemic involvement in severe cases.

"Other specified zoonotic viral diseases" refers to viral infections transmitted from animals to humans that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include "zoonotic viral infections" or "animal-to-human viral diseases." Causative agents vary widely, including rabies virus, hantavirus, and others. These diseases typically affect the nervous system, respiratory tract, or skin, depending on the pathogen. Symptoms range from fever and fatigue to severe neurological complications. Transmission occurs through bites, contact with bodily fluids, or inhalation of aerosolized particles.

Zoonotic viral disease, virus unspecified, refers to illnesses transmitted from animals to humans caused by a variety of viruses. Common synonyms include zoonosis or animal-borne viral infection. Causative agents may include rabies, hantavirus, or Ebola virus, among others. These diseases typically affect the respiratory, neurological, or gastrointestinal systems. Symptoms vary widely depending on the specific virus but often include fever, fatigue, and systemic inflammation. Transmission occurs through direct contact, vector bites, or consumption of contaminated animal products. The condition is a public health concern due to its potential for rapid spread and severe outcomes.

Mumps is a viral infection caused by the mumps virus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. It primarily affects the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands, leading to swelling and tenderness. Common synonyms include epidemic parotitis and parotitis. The infection is transmitted via respiratory droplets and is more common in children. Symptoms include fever, headache, and muscle aches, with swelling of the parotid glands on one or both sides. Complications may involve the testes, ovaries, pancreas, and central nervous system. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine provides effective prevention.

Mumps without complication is a viral infection caused primarily by the mumps virus, although rare cases may involve other paramyxoviruses. It typically presents with fever, headache, and swelling of the parotid glands, leading to characteristic puffy cheeks. Common synonyms include epidemic parotitis and parotid gland inflammation. The infection predominantly affects the salivary glands, particularly the parotid glands, and is more common in children. Complications are uncommon in otherwise healthy individuals, though they can occur in immunocompromised patients. The disease is generally self-limiting and resolves within 7–10 days.

Orchitis due to mumps virus is an inflammation of the testicle caused by the mumps virus, typically occurring in post-pubertal males following a mumps infection. It is a common complication of mumps, affecting approximately 20-30% of cases. The virus spreads through respiratory droplets and causes swelling, pain, and tenderness in the affected testicle. Common synonyms include mumps orchitis and viral orchitis. The primary causative agent is the mumps virus, and the testes are the typically affected body parts. Complications may include infertility due to testicular atrophy.

Meningitis due to mumps virus is an inflammatory condition affecting the meninges, typically occurring as a complication of mumps infection. It is caused by the mumps virus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. Common synonyms include aseptic meningitis and viral meningitis. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord. Symptoms include fever, headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. It is more common in children and adolescents, and often follows the initial viremic phase of mumps. The condition is generally self-limiting but can lead to complications such as encephalitis or hearing loss. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine provides effective prevention.

Encephalitis due to mumps virus is a rare but serious central nervous system infection caused by the mumps virus. It typically occurs in children and young adults, often following a primary mumps infection. The virus leads to inflammation of the brain, causing symptoms such as fever, headache, confusion, and seizures. Common synonyms include mumps encephalitis or viral encephalitis associated with mumps. The condition primarily affects the brain, particularly the cerebrum and meninges, and can result in long-term neurological complications.

Pancreatitis due to mumps virus is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas caused by mumps viral infection. It is a rare but recognized complication, typically occurring in children and young adults. The virus directly infects pancreatic acinar cells, leading to inflammation and potential necrosis. Common synonyms include mumps-associated pancreatitis and viral pancreatitis. The primary causative agent is the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus. The pancreas is the main affected organ, with systemic symptoms such as fever, abdominal pain, and elevated serum amylase and lipase levels.

"Other specified mumps" refers to mumps cases that do not meet the standard clinical criteria but are still classified as mumps due to laboratory confirmation. It is caused by the mumps virus, a member of the Paramyxoviridae family. Common synonyms include atypical mumps or unspecified mumps. The condition typically affects the parotid glands, causing swelling and pain, but may also involve other salivary glands or organs. It predominantly affects children and adolescents, with symptoms including fever, headache, and malaise. Complications such as orchitis, oophoritis, or meningitis may occur.

Infectious mononucleosis, commonly known as "mono" or glandular fever, is a viral infection primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). It is characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. The infection typically affects the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen. Other symptoms may include fatigue, malaise, and rash. It is most common in adolescents and young adults. Less frequently, it can be caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV). The disease is usually self-limiting, with recovery over several weeks.

Mononucleosis due to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), commonly known as infectious mononucleosis or "mono," is a viral infection primarily affecting adolescents and young adults. Caused by the Epstein-Barr virus, it is transmitted through saliva, hence the nickname "the kissing disease." The infection typically presents with fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and fatigue. It commonly affects the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen, leading to hepatosplenomegaly. Other symptoms may include pharyngitis, rash, and malaise. The condition is usually self-limiting, though complications such as splenic rupture or airway obstruction can occur.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) mononucleosis is a viral infection caused by human herpesvirus 5. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, though it can occur in healthy persons. Common synonyms include CMV infection or congenital CMV. The virus replicates in mononuclear cells, leading to lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and fever. Symptoms may include fatigue, malaise, and respiratory or gastrointestinal involvement. CMV is transmitted via bodily fluids and can cause severe complications in neonates, such as hearing loss and retinitis.

"Other specified infectious mononucleosis" refers to a clinical diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis that does not meet the full criteria for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) or cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections. It is typically characterized by fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, and atypical lymphocytosis. Common synonyms include atypical mononucleosis or undifferentiated infectious mononucleosis. The condition primarily affects the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen. It is most commonly seen in adolescents and young adults. While EBV is the most common causative agent, other pathogens such as adenovirus or toxoplasma may be implicated in some cases.

Infectious mononucleosis, unspecified, is a viral infection characterized by fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Commonly known as "mono" or "kissing disease," it is primarily caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), though other agents like cytomegalovirus may contribute. The infection typically affects the lymphatic system, liver, and spleen. It is most common in adolescents and young adults. Symptoms are usually self-limiting, though fatigue may persist. Complications such as splenic rupture or airway obstruction can occur. The condition is transmitted via saliva, hence its colloquial name.

Cytomegaloviral disease is a viral infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It is a common opportunistic infection in immunocompromised individuals. The virus can cause a wide range of clinical manifestations, including retinitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, and encephalitis. Common synonyms include cytomegalovirus infection or congenital CMV. The disease typically affects the retina, lungs, liver, and central nervous system, with severe complications in neonates and transplant recipients.

Cytomegaloviral hepatitis is a viral infection caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV), a member of the herpesvirus family. It primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and potential liver dysfunction. Common synonyms include CMV hepatitis or congenital CMV infection when acquired in utero. The condition typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients, as well as newborns. Symptoms may include fever, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. While often asymptomatic in immunocompetent individuals, it can lead to severe complications in vulnerable populations.

Cytomegaloviral pancreatitis is a rare inflammatory condition of the pancreas caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV). It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or organ transplant recipients. The infection leads to pancreatitis through direct viral invasion and subsequent inflammation. Common synonyms include CMV pancreatitis or CMV-induced pancreatitis. The virus primarily affects the pancreas, but may also involve the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract. Clinical presentation may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. Diagnosis is confirmed through serology, PCR, or histopathology. Treatment involves antiviral therapy with ganciclovir or valganciclovir.

"Other specified cytomegaloviral disease" refers to CMV infections that do not meet the criteria for specific categories like congenital, acquired, or symptomatic CMV. It encompasses rare or atypical presentations. Causative agent is human cytomegalovirus (HCMV). Common synonyms include unspecified CMV disease. Typically affects immunocompromised individuals, with involvement of lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and central nervous system. May present with fever, organ dysfunction, or systemic symptoms. Diagnosis involves viral culture, PCR, or serology. Treatment depends on clinical context and patient immune status.

Cytomegaloviral disease, unspecified, refers to a clinical syndrome caused by cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, typically affecting immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include CMV infection or congenital CMV. The virus, a member of the herpesvirus family, can lead to systemic involvement, most commonly affecting the lungs, liver, and central nervous system. Symptoms may include fever, pneumonia, hepatitis, and neurological complications. The disease can be congenital, acquired, or reactivated, with severity varying based on immune status.

Epidemic myalgia, also known as epidemic muscle pain or myalgic encephalomyelitis, is a viral illness characterized by severe muscle pain, fatigue, and systemic symptoms. Common causative agents include hantaviruses, particularly the Sin Nombre virus. The condition primarily affects the skeletal muscles, with pain often localized in the lower limbs. It may also involve the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms. The disease typically presents with abrupt onset and can progress to severe weakness and prolonged recovery. It is more common in endemic areas and often occurs in outbreaks.

Viral conjunctivitis is an inflammatory condition of the conjunctiva caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include pink eye and red eye. It is typically caused by adenoviruses, though enteroviruses and herpes simplex virus can also be responsible. The infection primarily affects the eyes, leading to redness, swelling, and a gritty sensation. It is highly contagious and often accompanies symptoms such as watery discharge and photophobia. The condition usually affects both eyes and is more common in children and young adults. It generally resolves spontaneously within 7–14 days without specific treatment.

Conjunctivitis due to adenovirus, also known as viral conjunctivitis or pink eye, is an infectious inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by adenoviruses. It typically presents with redness, itching, and a watery discharge. Common synonyms include epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and pharyngoconjunctival fever. The condition primarily affects the eyes, often involving both eyes, and may be accompanied by symptoms such as photophobia and swollen lymph nodes. Adenoviruses are the main causative agents, with types 3, 4, and 7 being most frequently implicated. The infection is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact or respiratory droplets.

Acute epidemic haemorrhagic conjunctivitis is a highly contagious viral infection characterized by sudden onset of red, irritated eyes with subconjunctival haemorrhage. Common synonyms include epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and haemorrhagic conjunctivitis. The primary causative agent is adenovirus, particularly types 8, 19, 37, and 5. It predominantly affects the conjunctiva, with involvement of the cornea in some cases. Symptoms include photophobia, tearing, and a gritty sensation. The infection is often spread through direct contact with infected secretions or contaminated surfaces.

Other specified viral conjunctivitis refers to conjunctival inflammation caused by viruses not classified under the more specific categories such as adenovirus or enterovirus. Common synonyms include acute viral conjunctivitis and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. The condition is typically caused by adenoviruses, but other agents like herpes simplex virus or enteroviruses may also be implicated. It primarily affects the conjunctiva, often involving the eyelids and cornea. Symptoms include redness, itching, and watery discharge, with a tendency for contagious spread. The infection is usually self-limiting but may require supportive care.

Viral conjunctivitis, unspecified, is an infectious inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by a virus. Common synonyms include epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and viral pink eye. It is typically caused by adenoviruses, enteroviruses, or herpesviruses. The condition primarily affects the conjunctiva and may involve the cornea. Symptoms include redness, watery discharge, itching, and photophobia. It is highly contagious and often occurs in outbreaks. The infection is usually self-limiting, resolving within 7–14 days without specific treatment.

Viral carditis refers to inflammation of the heart caused by viral infection. It commonly affects the myocardium, endocardium, and pericardium. Common causative agents include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and echovirus. Synonyms include viral myocarditis, viral endocarditis, and viral pericarditis. The condition typically presents with symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It is more prevalent in children and young adults. Complications may include heart failure and conduction abnormalities. Early diagnosis and supportive care are essential for management.

code_desc: dilated cardiomyopathy secondary to viral myocarditis
summary: Dilated cardiomyopathy secondary to viral myocarditis is a condition characterized by left ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction resulting from viral infection of the myocardium. Common synonyms include viral-induced cardiomyopathy and post-viral dilated cardiomyopathy. Known causative agents include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, influenza virus, and parvovirus B19. The primary affected body part is the heart, particularly the left ventricle, leading to heart failure and arrhythmias. It typically affects adults and children, with a predilection for males.

Acute viral carditis is an inflammatory condition of the heart muscle, valves, or pericardium caused by viral infections. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis, viral pericarditis, and acute viral endocarditis. It is most frequently caused by coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. The condition primarily affects the myocardium, pericardium, and endocardium, leading to symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It can progress to heart failure or conduction abnormalities if left untreated. The disease is more common in children and young adults, often following a viral upper respiratory infection.

Chronic viral carditis refers to long-term inflammation of the heart muscle or heart valves caused by viral infections. It is a rare but serious complication of viral myocarditis. Common synonyms include chronic viral myocarditis and viral cardiomyopathy. Known causative agents include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and echovirus. The condition typically affects the myocardium, endocardium, and pericardium, leading to symptoms such as dyspnea, fatigue, and arrhythmias. It may progress to heart failure or conduction abnormalities if left untreated.

Aseptic myocarditis of newborn, also known as viral myocarditis or perinatal myocarditis, is an inflammatory condition of the myocardium in newborns, typically caused by viral infections. Common causative agents include coxsackievirus B, adenovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus. The condition primarily affects the heart muscle, leading to impaired cardiac function. It is often associated with perinatal infections or neonatal sepsis. Symptoms may include tachycardia, poor feeding, and respiratory distress. The inflammation is non-bacterial in nature, hence the term "aseptic." It can lead to heart failure if not managed appropriately.

Coxsackie carditis is a viral myocarditis caused by coxsackievirus, particularly serotypes A and B. It is characterized by inflammation of the heart muscle, leading to symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis and coxsackievirus-induced myocarditis. The condition primarily affects the myocardium, and may involve the pericardium and endocardium. It is more common in children and young adults, often following a viral upper respiratory infection. Complications may include arrhythmias and heart failure.

Other specified viral carditis refers to inflammation of the heart caused by viruses not classified under more specific categories such as myocarditis or pericarditis. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis and viral pericarditis. Causative agents often include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and echovirus. The condition typically affects the myocardium, endocardium, and pericardium, leading to symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It is more common in children and young adults, often following viral infections.

Viral carditis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the heart muscle or heart tissues caused by a viral infection, without specific identification of the affected cardiac structure. Common synonyms include viral myocarditis and viral pericarditis. Causative agents often include coxsackievirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. The condition typically affects the myocardium, endocardium, or pericardium, leading to symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and arrhythmias. It is more common in children and young adults.

code_desc: viral haemorrhagic fever, not elsewhere classified
summary: Viral haemorrhagic fever, not elsewhere classified, is a severe systemic infection characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and multi-organ failure. It is caused by various arenaviruses, filoviruses, and other agents. Common synonyms include hemorrhagic fever and viral hemorrhagic fever. The disease typically affects the vascular system, liver, and kidneys, leading to coagulopathy and shock. Symptoms progress rapidly, often resulting in high mortality. Affected body parts include skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs. The condition is primarily transmitted through vectors or direct contact with infected bodily fluids.

Adenovirus infection of unspecified site refers to an illness caused by adenoviruses, which are double-stranded DNA viruses. Common synonyms include adenoviral infection or acute respiratory disease syndrome. The causative agents are adenoviruses, with serotypes 3, 7, 14, 21, and 22 most commonly associated with respiratory illness. Typically affecting the respiratory tract, conjunctiva, gastrointestinal tract, and urinary tract, this infection can present with symptoms such as fever, cough, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, and diarrhea. It is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces.

Enterovirus infection of unspecified site refers to a viral illness caused by enteroviruses, a group of RNA viruses including polioviruses, coxsackieviruses, and echoviruses. Common synonyms include non-polio enterovirus infection and enteroviral syndrome. The infection typically affects the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal system, and central nervous system. Symptoms may include fever, rash, meningitis, or encephalitis. While the exact site of infection is unspecified, it often involves multiple systems. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and laboratory testing.

Coronavirus infection, unspecified site, refers to a respiratory illness caused by various coronaviruses, most commonly SARS-CoV-2. It presents with symptoms such as fever, cough, shortness of breath, and fatigue. The infection primarily affects the respiratory tract, including the lungs and airways. Common synonyms include viral respiratory infection and COVID-19 (when caused by SARS-CoV-2). Other causative agents include SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, though these are less common. The condition can range from mild to severe, with potential complications like pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome.

Parvovirus infection of unspecified site refers to infection caused by parvoviruses, most commonly parvovirus B19, which affects various tissues. It is characterized by fever, rash, and systemic symptoms. Common synonyms include erythema infectiosum and fifth disease. The virus primarily targets erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, leading to transient aplastic crisis in individuals with underlying hemolytic anemia. Other sites may involve the skin, joints, and central nervous system. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or blood. The infection is typically self-limiting but can be severe in immunocompromised patients.

code_desc: other viral infections of unspecified site
summary: "Other viral infections of unspecified site" refers to viral infections where the specific location of infection is not identified. Common synonyms include unspecified viral infections or viral infections of unknown site. Causative agents may include herpesviruses, enteroviruses, or respiratory viruses. These infections can affect various body systems, including the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and nervous systems. Symptoms vary depending on the affected area but often include fever, fatigue, and localized inflammation. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation and laboratory testing when available.

code_desc: unspecified viral infection of unspecified site
summary: Unspecified viral infection of unspecified site refers to a viral illness where the specific virus and affected organ system are not identified. Common synonyms include undifferentiated viral infection or viral syndrome. Causative agents may include influenza, enteroviruses, adenoviruses, or herpesviruses. Typically affects multiple body systems, including respiratory, gastrointestinal, and neurological. Symptoms vary but often include fever, fatigue, and malaise. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and exclusion of other causes. Treatment is supportive, focusing on symptom relief.

"Other specified viral diseases" refers to viral infections that do not meet the criteria for more specific viral disorders but are clinically significant. Common synonyms include unspecified viral infections or viral illnesses of unspecified etiology. These conditions may be caused by various viruses such as enteroviruses, herpesviruses, or flaviviruses. They commonly affect the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and central nervous systems. Symptoms vary widely depending on the virus and host factors, often presenting with fever, fatigue, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis typically relies on clinical presentation and laboratory testing.

Unspecified viral disease refers to a broad category of illnesses caused by viruses that have not been identified or are not classified under specific known viral infections. Common synonyms include undifferentiated viral infection or viral syndrome. Causative agents may include a variety of viruses such as influenza, adenovirus, or enterovirus, though the exact pathogen is often undetermined. These conditions typically affect the respiratory, gastrointestinal, or systemic systems, presenting with symptoms like fever, fatigue, and malaise. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation rather than specific pathogen identification.

code_desc: influenza due to identified seasonal influenza virus
summary: Influenza due to identified seasonal influenza virus is a respiratory infection caused by influenza A or B viruses. Common synonyms include seasonal flu or epidemic influenza. The virus primarily affects the upper and lower respiratory tract, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, and body aches. It is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets. Complications may include pneumonia, particularly in high-risk groups like the elderly, young children, and those with chronic illnesses. Vaccination is a key preventive measure.

code_desc: influenza due to identified zoonotic or pandemic influenza virus
summary: Influenza due to identified zoonotic or pandemic influenza virus refers to acute respiratory infections caused by influenza viruses that originated in animals or have pandemic potential. Common synonyms include avian influenza, swine flu, and pandemic flu. Causative agents include Influenza A viruses, such as H1N1, H5N1, H7N9, and H9N2, as well as rare subtypes. The infection primarily affects the respiratory tract, causing symptoms like fever, cough, sore throat, and muscle aches. In severe cases, it may lead to pneumonia, respiratory failure, and systemic complications. Transmission occurs through respiratory droplets or contact with infected secretions.

Influenza, virus not identified refers to a respiratory infection caused by an influenza virus that cannot be specifically identified to subtype. Common synonyms include undifferentiated influenza or untyped influenza. While the exact virus is not determined, it is typically caused by influenza A or B viruses. The infection primarily affects the respiratory tract, including the nose, throat, and lungs. Symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, and muscle aches. It can lead to complications such as pneumonia, especially in high-risk populations. The condition is contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets.

Acute viral hepatitis is an inflammatory liver condition caused by viral infection, typically presenting with jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and elevated liver enzymes. Common synonyms include hepatitis A, B, or C depending on the causative agent. The primary causative agents are hepatitis A virus (HAV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV), though other viruses like Epstein-Barr or cytomegalovirus can also cause it. The liver is the main affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system and systemic symptoms. It is typically self-limiting but can progress to fulminant hepatic failure in severe cases.

Acute hepatitis A is a viral infection of the liver caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV). It is typically transmitted via the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated food or water. Common synonyms include infectious hepatitis and epidemic hepatitis. The infection primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and impaired function. Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Most individuals recover fully without long-term liver damage. The condition is more common in children and individuals with poor sanitation. Vaccination provides effective prevention.

Acute hepatitis B is a short-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV). It typically presents with symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and abdominal pain. Common synonyms include hepatitis B infection and acute HBV infection. The virus primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and impaired function. Transmission occurs through contact with infectious bodily fluids. Most adults recover fully, but some may develop chronic infection. Risk factors include unprotected sex, needle sharing, and perinatal transmission. The condition can progress to fulminant hepatitis in severe cases.

Acute hepatitis C is a short-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV). It typically presents with flu-like symptoms, fatigue, and jaundice. The virus primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and potential liver damage. Common synonyms include acute HCV infection or acute viral hepatitis C. Transmission occurs mainly through blood-to-blood contact. Most individuals clear the virus spontaneously, but some progress to chronic infection. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent long-term complications.

Acute hepatitis D is a viral infection caused by the hepatitis D virus (HDV), which requires co-infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) to replicate. It leads to inflammation of the liver, often resulting in more severe disease than hepatitis B alone. Common synonyms include delta hepatitis and hepatitis B-D co-infection. The primary affected body part is the liver, with symptoms such as jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. Transmission occurs through blood-to-blood contact. Complications may include fulminant hepatitis and increased risk of cirrhosis.

Acute hepatitis E is a viral infection caused primarily by the Hepatitis E virus (HEV), with genotypes 1 and 2 being the most common in humans. It is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, often through contaminated water. The disease typically affects the liver, causing inflammation and elevated liver enzymes. Common symptoms include jaundice, fatigue, nausea, and abdominal pain. It is more severe in pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include hepatitis E infection or HEV infection. The condition predominantly impacts the hepatic system.

Other specified acute viral hepatitis refers to hepatitis caused by viruses not classified under hepatitis A, B, or C. Common synonyms include acute hepatitis of unspecified etiology. Causative agents may include hepatitis D, E, G, or other less common viruses. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and impaired function.
