Common synonyms include mycotic granuloma and chromophilic mycosis. It is caused by dematiaceous fungi, most commonly *Cladophialophora batacina*, *Fonsecaea pedrosoi*, and *Phialophora verrucosa*. The infection typically affects the lower extremities, especially in individuals with compromised immune systems or those living in tropical regions. Transmission occurs via traumatic inoculation of the fungus into the skin. The disease progresses slowly, often leading to disfiguring lesions if left untreated.

Coccidioidomycosis, also known as Valley fever, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, where inhaled spores germinate and form spherules. The infection can disseminate to other organs, particularly the skin, bones, and central nervous system. Symptoms include fever, cough, and chest pain, with more severe forms occurring in immunocompromised individuals. The disease is endemic to arid regions of the southwestern United States and parts of Central and South America.

Pulmonary coccidioidomycosis, also known as valley fever, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs following inhalation of arthroconidia from contaminated soil. Common symptoms include cough, fever, chest pain, and fatigue. The infection typically involves the respiratory tract but can disseminate to other organs, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. It is endemic in arid regions of the southwestern United States, Central, and South America.

Acute pulmonary coccidioidomycosis, also known as Valley fever, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, where the fungus proliferates as spherules, leading to inflammation and symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. The infection typically begins after inhalation of arthroconidia from contaminated soil. While most cases are self-limiting, severe forms can progress to disseminated disease, involving other organs. Common synonyms include San Joaquin fever and desert fever.

Chronic pulmonary coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the lungs, often presenting with progressive fibrosis and cavities. Common synonyms include San Joaquin Valley fever and coccidioidal pneumonia. The infection typically begins as an acute illness but can become chronic, leading to granulomas and lung damage. It is endemic in arid regions of the southwestern United States, Central, and South America. Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for dissemination beyond the lungs.

Extrathoracic coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It occurs when the fungus spreads beyond the lungs, commonly affecting the skin, bones, joints, and central nervous system. Synonyms include disseminated coccidioidomycosis and blastomycosis-like infection. The disease typically presents with skin lesions, osteomyelitis, and meningitis. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those living in arid regions. Symptoms include fever, rash, and localized pain. Diagnosis involves fungal cultures, serology, and imaging. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy.

Disseminated coccidioidomycosis is a severe systemic fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It occurs when the initial pulmonary infection spreads to other organs. Common synonyms include blastomycosis and valley fever. The infection typically affects the lungs, skin, bones, and central nervous system. Symptoms include fever, cough, and skin lesions. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those living in arid regions. The disease can be life-threatening if not treated promptly with antifungal therapy.

Primary cutaneous coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It occurs following inhalation of arthroconidia, leading to localized skin lesions. Common synonyms include San Joaquin fever and desert rheumatism. The infection typically affects the skin, producing papules, nodules, or ulcers, often on the face, arms, or legs. Systemic spread is rare in immunocompetent individuals. The disease is endemic to arid regions of the southwestern United States, Central America, and northern South America. Clinical manifestations are usually self-limiting, with resolution occurring without specific treatment.

Coccidioides meningitis is a fungal infection of the central nervous system caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It typically occurs in individuals exposed to soil in endemic regions, such as the southwestern United States. The infection often follows a primary pulmonary coccidioidal infection, which may disseminate to the meninges. Symptoms include fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. It is also known as San Joaquin Valley fever meningitis or desert fever meningitis. The meninges and cerebrospinal fluid are primarily affected, with potential involvement of the brain and spinal cord.

Other specified extrathoracic coccidioidomycosis refers to disseminated coccidioidal infection involving sites outside the lungs, such as skin, bones, or central nervous system, when the clinical presentation does not fit established categories. It is caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *C. posadae*. Common synonyms include disseminated coccidioidomycosis and coccidioidal mycosis. The infection typically affects the skin, bones, joints, and occasionally the brain, leading to granulomatous lesions and systemic symptoms. It occurs in individuals with compromised immune systems or after severe initial infection.

Extrathoracic coccidioidomycosis is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It affects regions outside the lungs, commonly involving the skin, bones, central nervous system, and mucous membranes. Symptoms may include skin lesions, osteomyelitis, meningitis, and disseminated disease. The infection typically occurs in individuals with weakened immune systems or after inhalation of fungal spores in endemic areas. It is also known as undulant fever or Valley fever, though the latter term is more commonly associated with the pulmonary form.

Coccidioidomycosis, unspecified, is a fungal infection caused by *Coccidioides immitis* or *Coccidioides posadasii*. It primarily affects the respiratory system, leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and chest pain. The infection can disseminate to other organs, including the skin, bones, and central nervous system. Common synonyms include Valley fever and San Joaquin fever. It is endemic to arid regions of the southwestern United States, Mexico, and parts of Central and South America. The disease typically presents as a self-limiting pulmonary infection but can progress to chronic or disseminated forms in immunocompromised individuals.

Conidiobolomycosis is a rare fungal infection caused by species of *Conidiobolus*, primarily *Conidiobolus coronatus* and *Conidiobolus lamii*. It typically affects the skin and subcutaneous tissues, often following trauma or inoculation. The infection presents as chronic, granulomatous lesions characterized by yellowish or brownish nodules. It is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals or those with diabetes. Synonyms include sporotrichoid mycosis and chromoblastomycosis. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Cryptococcosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection typically involves the lungs and central nervous system, leading to pneumonia and meningitis. Common synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and pulmonary cryptococcosis. It may also disseminate to other organs, causing systemic disease. Clinical presentation varies from asymptomatic to severe illness, with symptoms including fever, cough, headache, and altered mental status. Early diagnosis and antifungal therapy are critical for improved outcomes.

Pulmonary cryptococcosis is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection begins in the lungs, leading to symptoms like cough, fever, and chest pain. It may disseminate to the central nervous system, causing meningitis. Common synonyms include cryptococcal pneumonia and cryptococcal lung infection. The disease primarily involves the lungs and can spread to the brain and meninges.

Cerebral cryptococcosis is a fungal infection of the central nervous system caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection leads to meningitis, characterized by headache, fever, and altered mental status. It may also cause brain abscesses or granulomas. Common synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and central nervous system cryptococcosis. The condition primarily involves the meninges and brain parenchyma.

Meningitis due to *Cryptococcus neoformans* is a fungal infection affecting the meninges, typically occurring in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis. The causative agent is *Cryptococcus neoformans*, occasionally *Cryptococcus gattii*. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms such as fever, headache, and altered mental status. The infection may spread to the brain and spinal cord, causing severe complications. It is more common in patients with HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, or those on immunosuppressive therapy. Early diagnosis and antifungal treatment are critical for improved outcomes.

Disseminated cryptococcosis is a severe fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* var. *grubii* and *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection spreads from the lungs to other organs, commonly involving the central nervous system, leading to meningitis, and less frequently the skin, bones, and viscera. Synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and disseminated cryptococcal infection. Clinical features include fever, headache, and altered mental status. Early diagnosis and antifungal therapy are critical for improved outcomes.

Other specified cryptococcosis refers to cryptococcal infections that do not meet the criteria for cryptococcal meningitis, pneumonia, or disseminated disease. It encompasses rare or atypical presentations of infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* and, less commonly, *Cryptococcus gattii*. These infections typically affect the central nervous system, lungs, or other organs, often in immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include cryptococcal infection, non-meningitic cryptococcosis, and disseminated cryptococcosis. Clinical manifestations vary but may include fever, headache, and focal neurological deficits.

Cryptococcosis, unspecified, is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Cryptococcus neoformans* or *Cryptococcus gattii*. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. The infection most commonly involves the central nervous system, leading to meningitis, but can also disseminate to lungs, skin, and other organs. Symptoms include headache, fever, and altered mental status. Diagnosis is confirmed through cerebrospinal fluid analysis or imaging. Treatment involves antifungal medications such as amphotericin B and fluconazole. Synonyms include cryptococcal meningitis and cryptococcal infection.

Dermatophytosis, also known as ringworm or tinea, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes, which are fungi that invade keratinized tissues. Common causative agents include *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Epidermophyton* species. The infection typically affects the skin, scalp, nails, and mucous membranes. It presents as a circular, red, scaly rash with a clear center, often accompanied by itching. The condition is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with infected individuals, animals, or contaminated objects. Treatment usually involves topical or systemic antifungal agents.

Dermatophytosis of the scalp, also known as tinea capitis, is a fungal infection of the hair follicles and scalp skin. It is caused by dermatophytes, primarily *Trichophyton tonsurans*, *Trichophyton violaceum*, and *Microsporum canis*. The infection typically presents with circular, scaly patches, hair loss, and sometimes crusting or inflammation. It is most common in children and affects the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. The infection is contagious and can spread through direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated objects. Early diagnosis and treatment with antifungal medications are essential to prevent complications and transmission.

Dermatophytosis of the nail, also known as tinea unguium or onychomycosis, is a fungal infection affecting the nail plate. It is caused by dermatophytes, most commonly *Trichophyton rubrum*, *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*, and *Candida* species. The infection typically affects toenails, though fingernails can also be involved. Clinical features include thickening, discoloration, brittleness, and debris under the nail. It often progresses slowly and may cause pain or discomfort. Risk factors include diabetes, poor circulation, and a history of athlete's foot. Treatment usually involves topical or systemic antifungal agents.

Dermatophytosis of the foot, commonly known as athlete's foot, is a fungal infection caused by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton rubrum*, *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*, and *Candida* species. It primarily affects the skin between the toes, soles, and sides of the feet, leading to symptoms like itching, burning, redness, and scaling. The infection thrives in warm, moist environments and is often transmitted through direct contact with infected surfaces. It is a prevalent condition in individuals with poor foot hygiene or those who frequently wear damp footwear.

Genitocrural dermatophytosis is a fungal infection affecting the groin and inner thighs, commonly caused by *Trichophyton rubrum* or *T. mentagrophytes*. It presents as a red, scaly, itchy rash with well-defined borders. Common synonyms include tinea cruris and jock itch. The infection is highly contagious and often spreads through direct contact or shared items. It predominantly affects adults, especially those with warm, moist environments or compromised immune systems. Treatment typically involves topical antifungal agents.

Kerion is an acute, inflammatory folliculitis characterized by painful, erythematous, and sometimes suppurative lesions, typically affecting the scalp. Common synonyms include tinea capitis and scalp ringworm. It is most commonly caused by dermatophytes such as *Trichophyton tonsurans*, *Trichophyton violaceum*, and *Microsporum canis*. The condition predominantly affects children and is more prevalent in warm, humid climates. Lesions may present as patches of hair loss with scaling, crusting, and sometimes lymphadenopathy. Early diagnosis and treatment with antifungal therapy are essential to prevent complications and transmission.

Disseminated dermatophytosis is a severe fungal infection caused by dermatophytes, typically affecting immunocompromised individuals. It spreads beyond the skin to involve mucous membranes and internal organs. Common synonyms include systemic mycosis and disseminated ringworm. Causative agents include *Trichophyton*, *Microsporum*, and *Epidermophyton* species. The infection commonly affects the scalp, nails, and skin, but may also involve the lungs, liver, and central nervous system in advanced cases. It presents with erythematous, pruritic lesions, and may lead to systemic complications if untreated.

Other specified dermatophytosis refers to fungal infections caused by dermatophytes that do not fit the criteria for more specific types such as tinea corporis, tinea pedis, or tinea cruris. Common synonyms include superficial mycoses or ringworm. Causative agents include Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton species. These infections typically affect the scalp, nails, and skin folds, often presenting as circular, erythematous, scaly patches. Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical examination and mycological testing. Treatment involves topical or systemic antifungal agents depending on the affected area and severity.

Dermatophytosis, unspecified, is a fungal infection of the skin caused by dermatophytes, a group of fungi that thrive on keratin. Common synonyms include ringworm, tinea, and fungal dermatitis. The causative agents vary by species, including Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton. This condition typically affects the scalp, feet, groin, and nails, presenting as circular, red, scaly patches with well-defined borders. It is highly contagious and often spreads through direct contact or contaminated objects. Treatment usually involves topical or oral antifungal medications.

Eumycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection characterized by the formation of subcutaneous masses and sinus tracts, typically involving the skin and underlying tissues. It is caused by various dematiaceous fungi, most commonly *Madurella mycetomatis*, though other species such as *Exophiala* and *Wangiella* may also be involved. Common synonyms include mycetoma and chromoblastomycosis. The infection predominantly affects the feet and lower limbs, often in tropical and subtropical regions, and may present with pain, swelling, and discharging sinuses.

Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*, primarily affecting the lungs. It is acquired through inhalation of spores from contaminated soil or bird/frog droppings. Common synonyms include pulmonary histoplasmosis and Ohio valley fever. The infection typically presents as a subacute or chronic illness with symptoms such as fever, cough, and chest pain. In immunocompromised individuals, it can disseminate to other organs, including the liver, spleen, and central nervous system. Diagnosis is confirmed by culture, serology, or imaging.

Pulmonary histoplasmosis capsulati is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Histoplasma capsulatum*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and nodular lesions. Common synonyms include chronic cavitary histoplasmosis and pulmonary histoplasmosis. The infection typically occurs in individuals with immunocompromised states or those exposed to high concentrations of the fungus. Lesions often involve the upper lobes and may progress to cavitation. The condition is endemic in regions with high humidity and bird or bat droppings. Diagnosis is confirmed by imaging, serology, and fungal cultures.

Histoplasmosis due to *Histoplasma duboisii* is a rare, disseminated fungal infection primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. Caused by *Histoplasma duboisii*, a dimorphic fungus, it is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of India. The infection typically begins in the lungs but can disseminate to multiple organs, including the skin, bones, and mucous membranes. Common synonyms include African histoplasmosis and disseminated histoplasmosis. Clinical features include fever, weight loss, and characteristic cutaneous lesions. The disease is more severe than pulmonary histoplasmosis caused by *H. capsulatum*.

Other specified histoplasmosis refers to histoplasmosis cases that do not meet the criteria for acute, chronic, or disseminated forms. It encompasses rare or atypical presentations. The causative agent is *Histoplasma capsulatum*, a dimorphic fungus. Common synonyms include disseminated histoplasmosis and chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis. The infection primarily affects the lungs, but can disseminate to other organs, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. It is typically acquired through inhalation of spores in environments with bird or bat droppings. Clinical manifestations vary depending on the immune status of the host.

Histoplasmosis, unspecified, is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Histoplasma capsulatum*. It typically affects the lungs but can disseminate to other organs in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include pulmonary histoplasmosis and disseminated histoplasmosis. The infection is acquired through inhalation of spores from contaminated soil or bird droppings. Symptoms range from asymptomatic to flu-like illness or severe respiratory disease. Diagnosis is confirmed by microbiological or serological testing. The condition is more common in endemic areas and can lead to chronic or progressive disease in susceptible populations.

Lobomycosis is a chronic, granulomatous skin infection characterized by the formation of nodules and plaques, typically on the lower extremities. It is caused by the dimorphic fungus *Lobomycosis* (formerly *Sporothrix schenckii*), which exists in both yeast and hyphal forms. Common synonyms include granuloma inguinale and donovanosis, though the latter refers to a different etiology. The infection primarily affects the skin, especially in tropical and subtropical regions, and may spread to subcutaneous tissues. It is often transmitted through traumatic inoculation of fungal spores.

Mucormycosis is a severe, often fatal fungal infection caused by filamentous fungi of the order Mucorales. Common synonyms include zygomycosis and phycomycosis. The primary causative agents are *Rhizopus*, *Mucor*, *Absidia*, and *Rhizomucor* species. This opportunistic infection typically affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with diabetes or on immunosuppressive therapy. It commonly involves the sinuses, lungs, brain, and skin, often presenting as rapidly progressive necrotizing lesions. Early diagnosis and antifungal treatment are critical for improving outcomes.

Non-dermatophyte superficial dermatomycoses refer to fungal infections of the skin caused by non-dermatophyte fungi, such as *Candida* and *Malassezia* species. These infections typically affect moist areas of the body, including the groin, axillae, and skin folds. Common synonyms include intertrigo and tinea versicolor. Unlike tinea infections caused by dermatophytes, these conditions often present with erythema, scaling, and pruritus. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through clinical evaluation and fungal culture. Treatment typically involves topical antifungal agents.

Pityriasis versicolor, also known as tinea versicolor, is a common fungal infection caused by Malassezia species, particularly *Malassezia furfur* and *Malassezia sympodialis*. It presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules on the skin, most commonly affecting the trunk, neck, and shoulders. The rash is often scaly and may spread to the arms and face. It is more prevalent in warm, humid climates and in individuals with oily skin. The condition is not contagious but can recur, especially in hot weather or with increased sweating.

Malassezia folliculitis is a superficial fungal infection caused by Malassezia species, particularly *Malassezia furfur* and *Malassezia sympodialis*. It presents as inflammatory papules and pustules, often in areas of friction or occlusion. Common synonyms include pityrosporum folliculitis and tinea versicolor folliculitis. The condition typically affects the chest, back, and upper arms, and is more common in males and individuals with oily skin. It is associated with increased sebum production and may occur in immunocompromised patients. Treatment usually involves antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or selenium sulfide.

White piedra is a chronic fungal infection of the hair shafts, characterized by the presence of hard, white, calcified nodules. Commonly known as "piedra alba," it is caused primarily by the fungus *Trichosporon ovoideum* and *Trichosporon asahii*. The infection typically affects the scalp, beard, and eyebrows, with a predilection for coarse hair. It is more common in tropical regions and often occurs in individuals with poor hygiene or immunocompromised states. The lesions are asymptomatic but may lead to cosmetic concerns. Diagnosis is usually made by direct microscopic examination or culture of affected hair.

Black piedra is a chronic fungal infection of the hair shafts, characterized by the formation of hard, black, calcified nodules. It is caused primarily by the dermatophyte *Trichophyton tonsurans*. The infection typically affects the scalp, but may also involve eyebrows and beards. Common synonyms include "black tinea" and "piedra nigra." The condition is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions and is often associated with poor hygiene. Clinically, affected hairs appear as black, sand-like particles adhering to the shaft, leading to breakage and cosmetic concern.

Tinea nigra is a superficial fungal infection characterized by brown or black hyperpigmented patches, typically found on the palms and soles. Common synonyms include chromoblastomycosis and tinea nigra palmaris. The condition is caused by the dermatophyte *Hortaea werneckii* (formerly *Exophiala werneckii*), though other dematiaceous fungi may also be involved. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. The lesions are asymptomatic, non-scaling, and may have a fine scale. Diagnosis is usually clinical, though potassium hydroxide preparation or fungal culture may confirm the presence of hyphal elements.

Onychomycosis due to non-dermatophyte mould is a fungal infection of the nail caused by moulds other than dermatophytes. Common synonyms include onychomycosis caused by filamentous fungi or non-dermatophytic onychomycosis. Causative agents include species such as *Scopulariopsis*, *Aspergillus*, and *Fusarium*. The infection typically affects toenails, though fingernails may also be involved. It presents with nail discoloration, thickening, and debris accumulation. Diagnosis often requires fungal culture or microscopy. Treatment may involve antifungal medications, though resistance can occur.

"Other specified non-dermatophyte superficial dermatomycoses" refers to fungal infections of the skin caused by organisms other than dermatophytes. Common synonyms include tinea-like infections or non-dermatophyte mycoses. Causative agents may include yeasts such as *Candida* species or molds like *Sporotrichum schenckii*. These infections typically affect areas such as the scalp, beard, nails, and intertriginous regions. They are often diagnosed through clinical presentation and mycological examination, and treatment may involve antifungal medications tailored to the specific pathogen.

Non-dermatophyte superficial dermatomycoses, unspecified, refers to fungal infections of the skin caused by organisms other than dermatophytes. Common synonyms include superficial mycoses or non-dermatophytic mycoses. Causative agents may include yeast-like fungi such as *Candida* species or molds like *Aspergillus* and *Scopulariopsis*. These infections typically affect areas such as the nails, feet, groin, and skin folds. Clinically, they may present as erythematous, scaly, or pruritic lesions. Diagnosis often requires potassium hydroxide preparation or culture. Treatment usually involves antifungal agents tailored to the specific pathogen.

Paracoccidioidomycosis is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* and *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It is also known as South American blastomycosis or Venezuelan ulcer. The infection primarily affects the lungs, but can disseminate to the skin, mucous membranes, and other organs. It is endemic in Latin America and typically presents with respiratory symptoms, skin lesions, and systemic involvement. The disease is more common in males and those with immunocompromised states. Diagnosis is based on clinical findings, imaging, and mycological examination. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy with drugs like itraconazole or amphotericin B.

Pulmonary paracoccidioidomycosis is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* and *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis. Common synonyms include South American blastomycosis and verrucous tuberculosis. The infection often disseminates to other organs, including the skin, mucous membranes, and lymph nodes. Clinically, it presents with symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, and chest pain. Diagnosis is confirmed through fungal culture, histopathology, or serology. The disease is endemic in Latin America and predominantly affects males.

Disseminated paracoccidioidomycosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* or *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects individuals in endemic regions of Latin America. The infection typically begins as a pulmonary disease but can disseminate to multiple organs, including the skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes, and viscera. Common synonyms include South American blastomycosis and verrucous granuloma. Clinically, it presents with chronic symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, and cutaneous lesions. The disease is more common in males and those with compromised immune systems.

Other specified paracoccidioidomycosis refers to a form of paracoccidioidomycosis that does not meet the criteria for the more common pulmonary or cutaneous variants. It is caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* or *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. This variant typically affects the skin, mucous membranes, and occasionally the lungs. It may present with chronic granulomatous inflammation and is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include disseminated paracoccidioidomycosis and atypical paracoccidioidomycosis.

Paracoccidioidomycosis, unspecified, is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Paracoccidioides brasiliensis* or *Paracoccidioides lutzii*. It primarily affects the lungs and mucous membranes, often presenting with respiratory symptoms, skin lesions, and oral ulcers. The infection can disseminate to other organs, including the skin, mucous membranes, and lymph nodes. Common synonyms include South American blastomycosis and undulant fever. It is endemic in Latin America and typically occurs in individuals with compromised immune systems. Clinical manifestations vary, but the disease is characterized by granulomatous inflammation and the presence of large, budding yeast cells.

Phaeohyphomycosis is a fungal infection caused by dematiaceous (dark-pigmented) fungi, commonly referred to as phaeohyphomycetes. It is characterized by the presence of brown or black septate hyphae in clinical specimens. Common causative agents include *Exophiala*, *Cladophialophora*, *Laricis*, and *Wangiella* species. The infection typically affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and occasionally the lungs or central nervous system. It often presents as a chronic, granulomatous lesion, and may disseminate in immunocompromised individuals. Clinically, it may mimic other granulomatous diseases, necessitating fungal culture or histopathological examination for accurate diagnosis.

Pneumocystosis is a parasitic infection caused primarily by *Pneumocystis jirovecii*, formerly known as *Pneumocystis carinii*. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection primarily targets the lungs, leading to interstitial pneumonia characterized by progressive dyspnea, fever, and hypoxemia. Common synonyms include pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) and pneumocystosis. The disease can occasionally involve other organs, but pulmonary involvement is most common.

Pulmonary pneumocystosis, also known as pulmonary PCP or Pneumocystis pneumonia, is a fungal infection caused by *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to interstitial pneumonia characterized by progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and hypoxemia. Commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients, or on immunosuppressive therapy. The infection is rare in healthy adults but can be severe and life-threatening if untreated. Radiographically, it may present with bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Early diagnosis and treatment with antifungal agents like trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are critical for favorable outcomes.

Pneumocystosis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused primarily by *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. It predominantly affects the lungs, leading to interstitial pneumonia, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Common synonyms include pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) and *Pneumocystis* pneumonia. The infection is rare in healthy individuals but can be severe in those with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. Clinical features include fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via bronchoalveolar lavage or sputum examination. Treatment involves antiparasitic medications like trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Scedosporiosis is a rare, severe fungal infection caused by species of the genus *Scedosporium*, including *Scedosporium apiospermum* and *Scedosporium prolificans*. It is also known as rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis or phaeohyphomycosis. The infection typically affects the sinuses, lungs, and skin, and may disseminate to the brain and other organs. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with diabetes or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection is characterized by rapid tissue necrosis and can be life-threatening if not treated promptly with antifungal agents.

Sporotrichosis is a subcutaneous fungal infection caused primarily by *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species. It typically presents as a chronic, progressive infection following traumatic inoculation, often through thorn pricks or insect bites. The disease commonly affects the skin and underlying tissues, forming nodules or ulcers along lymphatic channels. Synonyms include lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis and rose gardener's disease. It may also involve the lungs or disseminate systemically in immunocompromised individuals. The infection is endemic in certain geographic regions and is characterized by a slow, indolent course.

Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis is a chronic subcutaneous fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species. It typically presents as a painless, progressive nodule at the site of inoculation, followed by lymphangitic spread to regional lymph nodes. Common synonyms include cutaneous sporotrichosis and lymphocutaneous mycosis. The infection primarily affects the skin and lymphatic system, often involving the arms, legs, and face. It is commonly associated with traumatic exposure to contaminated plant material or soil. The disease progresses slowly, with nodules and erythematous streaks along lymphatic channels. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy.

Fixed cutaneous sporotrichosis is a chronic fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* species complex. It presents as solitary, non-ulcerating, indurated nodules that typically appear on the extremities, especially the arms and legs. The lesions are often painless and may persist for months without progressing. Synonyms include localized sporotrichosis and sporotrichoidal granuloma. The infection is usually acquired through traumatic inoculation of the fungus, often from plant material. It is more common in immunocompetent individuals and responds well to antifungal therapy.

Pulmonary sporotrichosis is a rare fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* and occasionally other *Sporothrix* species. It typically presents as a subacute or chronic lung infection, often following traumatic inoculation of the fungus, such as from thorn pricks. Common synonyms include sporotrichoid pneumonia and rhinolaryngotracheal sporotrichosis. The infection primarily affects the lungs, but may spread to the upper respiratory tract, lymph nodes, and occasionally the skin. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with occupational exposure to soil or plants.

Disseminated sporotrichosis is a systemic fungal infection caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* and occasionally other *Sporothrix* species. It occurs when the infection spreads beyond the initial cutaneous lesion, often following traumatic inoculation. Common synonyms include systemic sporotrichosis and disseminated mycosis. The disease typically affects the skin, lymph nodes, and can involve the lungs, bones, and central nervous system. Immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk. Clinical manifestations include nodules, abscesses, and systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss. Early diagnosis and antifungal therapy are critical for management.

Other specified sporotrichosis refers to sporotrichosis cases that do not meet the criteria for classic, cutaneous, or disseminated forms. It is caused by *Sporothrix schenckii* species complex, including *S. brasiliensis* and *S. globosa*. Common synonyms include atypical or non-classic sporotrichosis. The infection typically affects the skin and lymph nodes, often following traumatic exposure to contaminated plant matter. It may present with localized or generalized symptoms, and diagnosis requires fungal culture or molecular testing. Treatment usually involves antifungal therapy, with variable response depending on the causative agent and patient factors.

Sporotrichosis, unspecified, is a subcutaneous fungal infection caused primarily by *Sporothrix schenckii* and related species. It typically presents as a chronic, progressive infection characterized by nodular lesions along lymphatic channels, often following traumatic inoculation. Common synonyms include lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis and rose gardener's disease. The infection most commonly affects the extremities, particularly the hands and arms, and may spread to regional lymph nodes. It is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with frequent skin trauma.

Talaromycosis, also known as penicilliosis or blastomycosis, is a fungal infection caused primarily by *Talaromyces marneffei*, formerly *Penicillium marneffei*. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV/AIDS. The infection typically involves the reticuloendothelial system, with common sites including the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It may also disseminate to the lungs, skin, and lymph nodes. Clinical manifestations include fever, weight loss, and granulomatous lesions. Diagnosis is confirmed through fungal culture or histopathology. Treatment usually involves antifungal agents such as amphotericin B and itraconazole.

Emmonsiosis is a rare fungal infection caused by *Emmonsia crescens*, a dimorphic fungus. It primarily affects the lungs, leading to granulomatous inflammation. Common synonyms include blastomycosis and histoplasmosis, though these refer to different pathogens. The infection is acquired through inhalation of fungal spores found in soil and decaying organic matter. It is more prevalent in endemic regions such as the southeastern United States. Symptoms include cough, fever, and chest pain, with possible dissemination to other organs in immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging and serological testing.

Disseminated adiaspiromycosis is a rare fungal infection caused by dimorphic fungi that exist as yeast in the bloodstream and as hyphae in tissues. Common synonyms include disseminated blastomycosis and disseminated histoplasmosis, depending on the causative agent. The primary pathogens are *Blastomyces dermatitidis*, *Histoplasma capsulatum*, and *Coccidioides immitis*. The infection typically affects the lungs, skin, and mucous membranes, but can disseminate to multiple organs. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those living in endemic regions. Clinical manifestations include fever, weight loss, and characteristic skin lesions.

Pulmonary adiaspiromycosis is a fungal infection caused by the inhalation of Aspergillus spores, typically Aspergillus fumigatus. It is characterized by the formation of granulomatous lesions in the lungs, often in the context of immunocompromised hosts or those with underlying lung disease. Common synonyms include aspergillosis and invasive aspergillosis. The infection primarily affects the respiratory system, leading to symptoms such as cough, hemoptysis, and fever. It can progress to invasive disease in severe cases, particularly in patients with weakened immune systems.

Other specified emmonsiosis refers to a rare, chronic fungal infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, typically caused by *Emmonsia* species, particularly *Emmonsia crescens*. It is characterized by the formation of subcutaneous nodules, often accompanied by erythema and induration. The infection is commonly acquired through inhalation of conidia, which then disseminate via the bloodstream. It predominantly affects the extremities, trunk, and face. Synonyms include disseminated emmonsiosis and sporotrichoid emmonsiosis. The condition is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals.

Emmonsiosis, unspecified, refers to a non-specific inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily affecting the ileum and colon. It is characterized by chronic inflammation, often with granulomatous features. Common synonyms include regional enteritis and ileocolitis. The condition is associated with Mycobacterium avium complex and other opportunistic pathogens. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The disease may present with symptoms like diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal pain, and can lead to complications such as strictures and malabsorption.

"Other specified mycoses" refers to fungal infections that do not fit into more specific categories such as dermatophytosis, candidiasis, or cryptococcosis. Common synonyms include superficial or subcutaneous mycoses. Causative agents may include species like *Trichophyton*, *Candida*, or *Aspergillus*, depending on the infection site. These infections typically affect the skin, nails, hair, or mucous membranes. They are often diagnosed based on clinical presentation and may require antifungal therapy tailored to the specific organism and affected area.

Mycoses, unspecified, refers to fungal infections caused by various pathogenic fungi. Common synonyms include fungal infections or mycotic infections. Causative agents may include dermatophytes, yeast such as Candida, and molds like Aspergillus. These infections typically affect the skin, nails, mucous membranes, and sometimes internal organs. Symptoms vary depending on the affected area but often include itching, redness, scaling, and discharge. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and laboratory tests. Treatment involves antifungal medications, with the choice depending on the severity and location of the infection.

Malaria due to *Plasmodium falciparum* is a severe, life-threatening parasitic infection transmitted by the bite of infected *Anopheles* mosquitoes. The parasite invades red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, headache, and anemia. It primarily affects the liver and bloodstream, causing systemic symptoms and complications such as cerebral malaria, renal failure, and hypoglycemia. Common synonyms include falciparum malaria or malignant tertian fever. The disease is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Prompt treatment with antimalarial drugs is essential to prevent severe morbidity and mortality.

code_desc: plasmodium falciparum malaria with cerebral complications
summary: Plasmodium falciparum malaria with cerebral complications is a severe form of malaria caused by the protozoan parasite *Plasmodium falciparum*. It leads to cerebral malaria, characterized by neurological symptoms due to parasite-infected red blood cells obstructing cerebral capillaries. Common synonyms include cerebral malaria and severe falciparum malaria. The condition primarily affects the brain, causing seizures, coma, and potentially death. Other affected systems include the kidneys, liver, and cardiovascular system. Prompt treatment with antimalarial drugs is critical to prevent mortality.

code_desc: other severe and complicated plasmodium falciparum malaria
summary: Other severe and complicated *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria refers to life-threatening complications arising from infection with *P. falciparum*, the most dangerous malaria parasite. Common synonyms include severe falciparum malaria and complicated malaria. The causative agent is *Plasmodium falciparum*, transmitted via infected mosquitoes. This condition primarily affects the red blood cells, leading to systemic complications such as cerebral malaria, severe anemia, organ failure, and hypoglycemia. It commonly impacts the brain, kidneys, liver, and circulatory system, often requiring urgent medical intervention.

code_desc: malaria due to plasmodium falciparum, unspecified
summary: Malaria due to *Plasmodium falciparum*, unspecified, is a severe parasitic infection caused by the protozoan *Plasmodium falciparum*. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected *Anopheles* mosquito. The parasite invades red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, anemia, and potentially life-threatening complications such as cerebral malaria. Common synonyms include falciparum malaria and severe malaria. The infection primarily affects the bloodstream and can involve multiple organs, including the liver, spleen, and brain. It is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Malaria due to *Plasmodium vivax* is a parasitic infection transmitted by the bite of an infected *Anopheles* mosquito. It is characterized by cyclical fever, chills, and headache. Common synonyms include tertian malaria, due to the typical 48-hour fever cycle. The parasite primarily infects red blood cells, leading to hemolysis and anemia. It can also cause splenomegaly and hepatic involvement. Unlike *P. falciparum*, *P. vivax* can form hypnozoites in the liver, leading to relapses. The infection is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

code_desc: plasmodium vivax malaria with rupture of spleen
summary: Plasmodium vivax malaria with rupture of spleen is a severe complication of vivax malaria, characterized by splenic rupture due to intense parasitic infection and immune-mediated inflammation. Caused by *Plasmodium vivax*, this condition primarily affects the spleen, leading to life-threatening internal bleeding. Common synonyms include splenic rupture in vivax malaria or acute splenic rupture associated with *P. vivax*. It typically occurs in individuals with high parasitemia and may present with abdominal pain, hypotension, and shock. The spleen is the most commonly affected organ, and prompt medical intervention is critical to prevent mortality.

code_desc: malaria due to plasmodium vivax with other complications
summary: Malaria due to *Plasmodium vivax* with other complications is a parasitic infection caused by the *P. vivax* parasite, transmitted via infected Anopheles mosquitoes. Common synonyms include tertian malaria and benign tertian malaria. The parasite primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and anemia. Complications may include splenomegaly, hemolytic anemia, and in severe cases, cerebral malaria or respiratory distress. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. The infection can relapse due to dormant liver stages, making it a chronic concern in endemic areas.

Plasmodium vivax malaria without complication is a parasitic infection caused by the Plasmodium vivax parasite, transmitted via infected Anopheles mosquitoes. It primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to intermittent fever, chills, headache, and malaise. Common synonyms include tertian malaria and benign tertian fever. The parasite forms hypnozoites in the liver, which can cause relapses. While generally less severe than P. falciparum malaria, it can still cause significant morbidity if left untreated. The infection typically affects the reticuloendothelial system and erythrocytes, with symptoms recurring in cycles of approximately 48 hours.

Malaria due to *Plasmodium malariae* is a protozoal infection caused by the parasite *Plasmodium malariae*, one of the less common human malaria parasites. It typically presents with mild, intermittent fever and is often asymptomatic or subclinical. The infection is characterized by a quartan fever pattern, with fever every third day. It primarily affects the red blood cells, leading to hemolysis. Common synonyms include *P. malariae* malaria. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions and is transmitted via infected *Anopheles* mosquitoes. While it can affect any age group, it is more commonly seen in adults.

Plasmodium malariae malaria with nephropathy is a parasitic infection caused by *Plasmodium malariae*, a less common malaria parasite. It primarily affects the red blood cells and can lead to renal complications, including glomerulonephritis. The infection is characterized by mild fever, anemia, and, in severe cases, renal dysfunction. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Nephropathy typically manifests as proteinuria, hematuria, and reduced renal function. The parasite is transmitted through the bite of infected *Anopheles* mosquitoes. While less symptomatic than other malaria species, it can cause chronic renal impairment if untreated.

code_desc: malaria due to plasmodium malariae with other complications
summary: Malaria due to *Plasmodium malariae* is a parasitic infection characterized by intermittent fever, chills, and sweating. It is caused by the protozoan *Plasmodium malariae*, one of the less common *Plasmodium* species. The infection typically presents with mild symptoms but can lead to complications such as renal failure, anemia, and splenomegaly. It primarily affects the red blood cells and can involve the kidneys and liver. Synonyms include tertian malaria or benign tertian malaria. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Plasmodium malariae malaria without complication is a parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium malariae, one of the less common Plasmodium species. It typically presents with mild, intermittent fever and chills, often with no significant complications. The parasite primarily infects red blood cells, leading to mild anemia and splenomegaly. Common synonyms include quartan malaria, though this term is more historically used. The infection predominantly affects the blood and spleen, with systemic symptoms such as fatigue and malaise. It is less severe than other malaria types but can persist for years if untreated.

Malaria due to *Plasmodium ovale* is a parasitic infection transmitted by the bite of an infected *Anopheles* mosquito. It is characterized by intermittent fever, chills, and headache. *P. ovale* is one of the less common malaria parasites, often causing mild to moderate symptoms. It primarily affects the liver and red blood cells. Common synonyms include tertian malaria, though this term is more commonly associated with *P. vivax*. The infection is typically found in tropical and subtropical regions. While *P. ovale* can cause relapses, they are generally less frequent than those caused by *P. vivax*. The spleen and liver may also be involved in the pathophysiology.

"Other parasitologically confirmed malaria" refers to malaria cases where the causative agent is identified as a species other than *Plasmodium falciparum*, *P. vivax*, *P. ovale*, or *P. malariae*. Common synonyms include "non-falciparum malaria" or "other Plasmodium species malaria." Causative agents may include *P. knowlesi*, *P. malariae*, *P. ovale*, and *P. vivax*. The infection primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and anemia. It is typically found in endemic regions and can cause severe illness, though generally less life-threatening than falciparum malaria.

Malaria without parasitological confirmation refers to clinical suspicion of malaria based on symptoms such as fever, chills, and headache, in a person from or traveling to a malaria-endemic region, without confirmed parasite detection in blood smears or rapid diagnostic tests. Common synonyms include suspected malaria or probable malaria. Causative agents include *Plasmodium falciparum*, *P. vivax*, *P. ovale*, and *P. malariae*. The disease primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to systemic symptoms and potential complications like anemia and organ failure.

Malaria, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by Plasmodium species transmitted through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes. It primarily affects the liver and red blood cells, leading to fever, chills, and flu-like symptoms. Common synonyms include falciparum malaria, vivax malaria, and other unspecified malaria types. The causative agents include Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae. The disease predominantly impacts the bloodstream and organs such as the spleen and liver, with severe cases potentially affecting the brain and causing life-threatening complications.

Acanthamoebiasis is a rare, often severe, granulomatous infection caused by free-living amoebae, primarily *Acanthamoeba* species. It commonly affects the skin, eyes, and central nervous system. The infection typically enters through breaks in the skin or via the respiratory tract. In immunocompromised individuals, it may disseminate systemically. Common synonyms include granulomatous amebic encephalitis and amoebic meningoencephalitis. Clinical manifestations vary from localized skin lesions to severe neurological symptoms. Diagnosis often requires histopathology and molecular testing. Treatment involves prolonged antiamoebic therapy with drugs like chlorhexidine and propamidine.

African trypanosomiasis, also known as sleeping sickness, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma brucei* species. The disease is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms such as sleep disturbances, confusion, and eventually coma. Two subspecies, *T. b. gambiense* and *T. b. rhodesiense*, cause distinct clinical forms, with the former being more prevalent and chronic. The infection typically begins with fever, headache, and lymphadenopathy, progressing to meningoencephalitis if untreated.

Gambiense trypanosomiasis, also known as human African trypanosomiasis or sleeping sickness, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense*. The parasite is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The disease primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms such as sleep disturbances, confusion, and eventually coma. It predominantly occurs in sub-Saharan Africa. Early stages may present with fever, headache, and lymph node swelling. If untreated, it progresses to the meningoencephalitic stage, resulting in severe neurological complications and death.

Meningitis in Gambiense trypanosomiasis is a neurological complication caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense*, the parasite responsible for African sleeping sickness. It presents with symptoms such as fever, headache, and altered mental status, resulting from inflammation of the meninges. Common synonyms include trypanosomal meningitis and neurotrypanosis. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, particularly the brain and spinal cord, leading to severe neurological deficits if untreated. The disease progresses from an early hemolymphatic stage to a late neurological stage. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent irreversible damage.

Other specified gambiense trypanosomiasis refers to human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) cases that do not meet the criteria for classical Gambian or Rhodesian trypanosomiasis. It is caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense*, the primary agent of HAT in sub-Saharan Africa. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms such as sleep disturbances, confusion, and motor deficits. Common synonyms include late-stage HAT and stage 2 HAT. The disease is transmitted by the tsetse fly and is endemic in rural areas of several African countries.

Gambiense trypanosomiasis, unspecified, is a parasitic disease caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense*, transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms such as sleep disturbances, confusion, and eventually coma. The infection progresses slowly, often without early symptoms, and is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa. Common synonyms include human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) and sleeping sickness. The disease predominantly affects the brain and spinal cord, with systemic involvement in later stages.

Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis, also known as East African sleeping sickness, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense*. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The disease primarily affects sub-Saharan Africa, with a higher prevalence in rural areas. The parasite invades the bloodstream and lymphatic system, leading to systemic symptoms such as fever, headache, and lymphadenopathy. As the disease progresses, it affects the central nervous system, causing neurological symptoms and ultimately leading to coma and death if untreated. The infection predominantly targets the blood, lymph nodes, and brain.

Meningitis in Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis, also known as East African sleeping sickness, is a severe neurological complication caused by *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense*. It presents with inflammation of the meninges, leading to symptoms such as headache, fever, and altered mental status. The infection spreads via tsetse fly bites and primarily affects the central nervous system. Common synonyms include acute meningoencephalitis and Rhodesian trypanosomiasis. The causative agent is *T. b. rhodesiense*, and the condition typically involves the brain and spinal cord. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent fatality.

Other specified Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis refers to human African trypanosomiasis caused by *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense* that does not meet the criteria for typical or late-stage disease. It encompasses atypical presentations or clinical variants. Common synonyms include non-typical Rhodesian sleeping sickness. The causative agent is *T. b. rhodesiense*, transmitted by tsetse flies. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms, and may involve the lymphatic system and skin. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa.

Rhodesiense trypanosomiasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma rhodesiense*. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The disease primarily affects sub-Saharan Africa and is characterized by fever, headache, joint pain, and progressive neurological symptoms. Unlike human African trypanosomiasis, it often presents with a more acute course and can rapidly progress to neurological involvement. Common synonyms include East African trypanosomiasis and Rhodesian sleeping sickness. The parasite primarily affects the blood and central nervous system.

"Other specified African trypanosomiasis" refers to cases of human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense* or *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense* that do not meet the criteria for the more specific subtypes. It is also known as late-stage or chronic African sleeping sickness. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to neurological symptoms. Common synonyms include late-stage HAT and chronic trypanosomiasis. The disease is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, with the bloodstream and CNS being the main affected areas.

African trypanosomiasis, unspecified, is a parasitic disease caused by species of *Trypanosoma*, primarily *T. brucei gambiense* and *T. brucei rhodesiense*. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected tsetse fly. The infection progresses through two stages: early hemolymphatic and late meningoencephalitic, affecting the central nervous system. Common synonyms include sleeping sickness and human African trypanosomiasis. The disease primarily affects the blood, lymphatic system, and brain, leading to severe neurological complications if untreated.

Babesiosis is a parasitic infection caused by *Babesia* species, primarily transmitted through tick bites. It primarily affects red blood cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. Common synonyms include babesial infection or babesial disease. The condition is more severe in immunocompromised individuals and can present with fever, fatigue, and jaundice. It is endemic in regions with high tick populations, such as the northeastern United States. Co-infection with *Plasmodium* or *Leishmania* may occur. The spleen and liver are typically involved, with potential complications including renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Chagas disease, also known as American trypanosomiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It is primarily transmitted through the feces of triatomine bugs, though other routes include blood transfusion, organ transplantation, and congenital transmission. The disease typically affects the heart, digestive system, and nervous system. Chronic infection can lead to cardiomyopathy, megacolon, and megaesophagus. Symptoms may include fever, fatigue, and swelling at the site of infection. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent severe complications.

code_desc: acute chagas disease without heart involvement
summary: Acute Chagas disease without heart involvement is a parasitic infection caused primarily by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It typically presents with non-specific symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and swollen lymph nodes. Common synonyms include acute American trypanosomiasis and acute Chagas' disease. The infection primarily affects the bloodstream and lymphatic system, with potential involvement of the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract. It is most commonly acquired through vector bites, especially from triatomine bugs, but can also occur via blood transfusion or congenital transmission. The disease often resolves spontaneously without specific treatment, though complications may develop if left untreated.

code_desc: chronic chagas disease with heart involvement
summary: Chronic Chagas disease with heart involvement is a progressive condition caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*, a protozoan parasite. It results from persistent infection following acute Chagas disease. The cardiac manifestation, known as Chagas cardiomyopathy, typically affects the myocardium, leading to arrhythmias, conduction defects, and heart failure. Common synonyms include chronic Chagas heart disease and American trypanosomiasis. The disease primarily involves the heart, but may also affect the esophagus and colon. It is endemic in Latin America and can occur in non-endemic regions due to travel or migration.

code_desc: chagas disease with digestive system involvement
summary: Chagas disease with digestive system involvement is a chronic parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It primarily affects the heart and digestive system, leading to megaoesophagus and megacolon. Common synonyms include American trypanosomiasis and Chagas' disease. The infection is transmitted through vector bites, blood transfusions, or congenital routes. Chronic phase manifestations include gastrointestinal dysmotility, reduced appetite, and weight loss. Complications may involve malnutrition and aspiration pneumonia. The digestive tract, particularly the esophagus and colon, is typically affected. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent irreversible damage.

Meningitis in Chagas disease is a rare but severe complication of Trypanosoma cruzi infection, occurring in the chronic phase. It is characterized by inflammation of the meninges, often associated with cardiac or digestive system involvement. Common synonyms include central nervous system involvement in Chagas disease. Causative agents are primarily Trypanosoma cruzi, though secondary bacterial infections may contribute. The condition typically affects the brain and spinal cord, leading to symptoms like fever, headache, and altered mental status. It is more common in adults and can be life-threatening if not promptly treated.

"Other specified Chagas disease" refers to cases of Chagas disease where the clinical presentation or epidemiological context does not fit the classic acute or chronic forms. It encompasses atypical manifestations or variants not classified under the standard categories. The causative agent is *Trypanosoma cruzi*, transmitted primarily via triatomine bugs. Common synonyms include atypical Chagas disease or unspecified Chagas disease. It typically affects the heart, digestive system, and nervous system, though symptoms may vary widely depending on the specific variant and individual immune response.

Chagas disease, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. It is transmitted primarily through the feces of triatomine bugs, though other routes include blood transfusion and congenital transmission. The disease progresses through acute and chronic phases. In the acute phase, symptoms may include fever, fatigue, and swelling at the site of infection. Chronic phase can lead to serious complications affecting the heart, digestive system, and nervous system. Common synonyms include American trypanosomiasis and bartonellosis. The most commonly affected organs are the heart (cardiomyopathy), esophagus, and colon.

Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease caused by protozoa of the *Leishmania* genus, transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. Common synonyms include visceral leishmaniasis and kala-azar. The causative agents vary by species, including *Leishmania donovani*, *L. infantum*, and *L. tropica*. The disease primarily affects the reticuloendothelial system, with visceral leishmaniasis involving the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, while cutaneous leishmaniasis affects the skin. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar, is a severe parasitic disease caused by *Leishmania donovani* complex species. It primarily affects internal organs, particularly the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, leading to systemic inflammation and immunosuppression. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. Clinically, it presents with fever, weight loss, anemia, and splenomegaly. If left untreated, it can be fatal. Other synonyms include visceral leishmaniasis and kala-azar.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a parasitic skin infection caused by *Leishmania* species transmitted via sandfly bites. Common synonyms include ulcerogranulomatous leishmaniasis and oriental sore. The disease typically affects exposed skin areas such as the face, ears, and extremities. Lesions present as painless, progressive ulcers with raised borders and central necrosis. The causative agents include *Leishmania tropica*, *L. major*, *L. aethiopica*, and *L. mexicana*. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. The infection is not contagious between humans but can be transmitted via infected sandflies.

Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is a chronic parasitic infection caused by species of *Leishmania*, primarily *L. braziliensis* and *L. mexicana*. It presents with skin ulcers and mucosal destruction, often affecting the nose, mouth, and throat. Common synonyms include diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis and mucosal leishmaniasis. The disease is transmitted via the bite of infected sandflies. Lesions are typically painless, progressive, and may lead to severe disfigurement if untreated. It is more common in tropical and subtropical regions.

Leishmaniasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by species of *Leishmania*, transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. It encompasses various clinical forms, including cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral leishmaniasis, though the specific type is not identified. Common synonyms include leishmanial disease and kala-azar. The infection primarily affects the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs such as the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Symptoms vary but may include skin ulcers, mucosal destruction, and systemic illness. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Naegleriasis is a rare but severe protozoal infection caused by *Naegleria fowleri*, a free-living ameba found in warm freshwater. Common synonyms include primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM). The infection typically occurs when contaminated water enters the nasal passages, leading to rapid invasion of the central nervous system. Symptoms include fever, headache, nausea, and neurological deficits, progressing to coma and death within days. The brain and meninges are the primary affected sites. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical, though outcomes are often poor.

Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous infection primarily affecting the nasal mucosa. Caused by *Rhinosporidium seeberi*, a protozoan parasite, it is characterized by the formation of polypoid, cauliflower-like lesions. Common synonyms include rhinosporidial sinusitis and rhinosporidiosis. The disease typically involves the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, occasionally extending to the nasopharynx. It is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often associated with exposure to contaminated water. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and histopathological examination.

Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*, a protozoan parasite. Common synonyms include congenital toxoplasmosis and ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system and eyes, often leading to inflammation of the brain (encephalitis) and retina. It can also involve the lymph nodes and muscles. In immunocompromised individuals, it may cause severe systemic disease. Transmission occurs via ingestion of oocysts from contaminated food or water, or through congenital transmission from mother to fetus. Most infections are asymptomatic or present with mild flu-like symptoms.

Hepatitis due to *Toxoplasma gondii* is a rare but severe form of liver inflammation caused by the protozoan parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*. It typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection can lead to liver dysfunction, sometimes progressing to fulminant hepatitis. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic hepatitis and congenital toxoplasmosis when acquired in utero. The parasite primarily affects the liver, lymph nodes, and central nervous system, often presenting with fever, jaundice, and hepatomegaly.

Meningoencephalitis due to *Toxoplasma gondii* is a central nervous system infection characterized by inflammation of the meninges and brain. Caused by the protozoan parasite *Toxoplasma gondii*, it commonly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or on immunosuppressive therapy. The infection typically involves the brain, particularly the basal ganglia and cerebellum, and may present with fever, headache, seizures, and altered mental status. Synonyms include toxoplasmic encephalitis and congenital toxoplasmosis in neonates. The disease can lead to severe neurological complications if untreated.

code_desc: pulmonary toxoplasmosis due to toxoplasma gondii
summary: Pulmonary toxoplasmosis is a rare but serious infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals. It typically presents as a diffuse interstitial pneumonia, often with non-productive cough, fever, and dyspnea. The infection can lead to progressive respiratory failure if untreated. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic pneumonia. *Toxoplasma gondii* is the sole causative agent, transmitted via ingestion of oocysts or tissue cysts. The lungs are the primary affected organ, though systemic dissemination can occur.

code_desc: eye disease due to toxoplasma gondii
summary: Toxoplasma gondii is a protozoan parasite that can cause ocular toxoplasmosis, an eye disease characterized by inflammation and retinal lesions. Common synonyms include toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis. The infection typically affects the retina and choroid, leading to symptoms such as blurred vision, floaters, and potential vision loss. It is most commonly acquired through ingestion of undercooked meat or contact with cat feces. Immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, are at higher risk for severe ocular involvement.

Other specified toxoplasmosis refers to clinical manifestations of Toxoplasma gondii infection that do not meet the criteria for congenital, acquired, or ocular toxoplasmosis. It may present with atypical or rare forms of the disease. The causative agent is Toxoplasma gondii, a protozoan parasite. Common synonyms include atypical toxoplasmosis or unspecified toxoplasmosis. The infection typically affects the central nervous system, lungs, and other organs, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms may include fever, neurological deficits, and organ-specific complications.

Toxoplasmosis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by *Toxoplasma gondii*. It can present systemically or as an ocular infection, commonly affecting the brain, eyes, and other organs. Symptoms vary from asymptomatic to severe, including fever, malaise, and neurological deficits. Common synonyms include congenital toxoplasmosis and ocular toxoplasmosis. The infection is transmitted via ingestion of oocysts or tissue cysts, often from undercooked meat or contaminated water. It is particularly severe in immunocompromised individuals and congenitally infected infants.

Microsporidiosis is a parasitic infection caused by microsporidia, a group of obligate intracellular protozoa. Common causative agents include *Encephalitozoon* and *Enterocytozoon* species. It primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS. The infection typically involves the gastrointestinal tract, causing diarrhea, malabsorption, and weight loss. It may also affect the lungs, eyes, and central nervous system. Synonyms include microsporidial infection or microsporidial disease. The condition is diagnosed through stool examination, PCR, or biopsy. Treatment options are limited, with antifungal agents like albendazole and fumagillin being used in some cases.

Unspecified protozoal disease refers to a group of infections caused by various protozoan parasites when the specific organism is not identified. Common synonyms include undetermined protozoal infection or unspecified protozoan disease. Causative agents may include species from the genera *Plasmodium*, *Leishmania*, *Trypanosoma*, and *Toxoplasma*, among others. These infections typically affect the blood, liver, lymphatic system, central nervous system, and visceral organs, depending on the parasite. Symptoms vary widely and may include fever, malaise, organ enlargement, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis often requires microscopic examination, serology, or molecular techniques.

Angiostrongyliasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Angiostrongylus cantonensis*, commonly known as the rat lungworm. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to eosinophilic meningitis. The parasite is transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food or water, often via intermediate hosts like snails or slugs. Symptoms include headache, fever, and neck stiffness. Less commonly, the infection may involve the lungs or gastrointestinal tract. Synonyms include eosinophilic meningitis and rat lungworm disease.

code_desc: eosinophilic meningitis due to angiostrongylus cantonensis
summary: Eosinophilic meningitis due to *Angiostrongylus cantonensis*, also known as rat lungworm infection, is a parasitic disease caused by the nematode *A. cantonensis*. The infection primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to inflammation of the meninges. Common symptoms include headache, fever, and neck stiffness. The parasite is transmitted through ingestion of intermediate hosts such as snails or crustaceans. The condition is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Clinical manifestations typically resolve spontaneously, though severe cases may require corticosteroids.

Intestinal angiostrongyliasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Angiostrongylus cantonensis*, a nematode commonly found in rats and intermediate hosts like snails and slugs. Humans become infected by ingesting contaminated food or water. The larvae migrate to the intestines, causing inflammation, ulceration, and symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting. It primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, though larvae may also reach the lungs or central nervous system. Synonyms include eosinophilic meningoencephalitis and rat lungworm disease. The condition is more common in tropical and subtropical regions.

Other specified angiostrongyliasis refers to infections caused by Angiostrongylus species that do not meet the criteria for classic angiostrongyliasis. Common synonyms include eosinophilic meningitis and eosinophilic meningoencephalitis. The primary causative agent is Angiostrongylus cantonensis, though other species may be involved. The infection typically affects the central nervous system, leading to symptoms such as headache, fever, and neurological deficits. It may also involve the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and skin. Transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated intermediate hosts like snails or crustaceans.

Angiostrongyliasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Angiostrongylus* species, most commonly *A. cantonensis*. It primarily affects the central nervous system, leading to eosinophilic meningitis. The infection is acquired through ingestion of contaminated intermediate hosts, such as snails or slugs. Common synonyms include eosinophilic meningitis and rat lungworm disease. Symptoms include headache, fever, and neck stiffness. The disease typically involves the brain and meninges, with rare extraneural manifestations. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and serological testing.

Anisakiasis is a parasitic infection caused by ingestion of larvae of the nematode *Anisakis simplex* or *Pseudoterranova decipiens*. Common synonyms include anisakidosis or gastric anisakiasis. The larvae typically attach to the mucosa of the stomach or duodenum, causing acute inflammation, pain, and sometimes obstruction. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis.
