Diagnosis is often confirmed by endoscopy and identification of the parasite. It is commonly associated with consumption of raw or undercooked fish.

Ascariasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Ascaris lumbricoides*, a nematode worm. It is transmitted through ingestion of contaminated soil or food. The larvae migrate through the lungs, causing transient respiratory symptoms, before maturing into adult worms in the small intestine. Common synonyms include intestinal roundworm infection and human ascariasis. The primary affected body parts are the lungs and small intestine, with potential complications such as intestinal obstruction, malnutrition, and secondary infections.

Capillariasis is a parasitic infection caused by species of the genus *Capillaria*, primarily affecting the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include intestinal capillariasis and capillaridiasis. The most prevalent causative agents are *Capillaria philippinensis* and *Capillaria hepatica*. The disease typically affects the small intestine, liver, and lungs, with symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, often transmitted through ingestion of contaminated food or water.

Capillariasis of the intestine, also known as intestinal capillariasis or capillaridiasis, is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Capillaria philippinensis*. The parasite primarily affects the small intestine, leading to inflammation and ulceration of the mucosa. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. The condition is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in Southeast Asia. Diagnosis is often achieved through stool examination for eggs. While rare in developed countries, it remains a significant health issue in areas with poor sanitation and close contact with contaminated water or food.

Other specified capillariasis refers to infections caused by species of the genus Capillaria that do not fit the criteria for more specific diagnoses such as Capillaria philippinensis or Capillaria hepatica. Common synonyms include capillariidosis. The causative agents are various Capillaria species, with C. philippinensis being the most prevalent. These infections typically affect the lungs, liver, or gastrointestinal tract, depending on the species. Symptoms may include cough, abdominal pain, and gastrointestinal distress. Diagnosis is often achieved through stool or tissue examination for characteristic eggs.

Capillariasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by species of the genus *Capillaria*. Common synonyms include capillaridosis and intestinal capillariasis. The primary causative agents are *Capillaria philippinensis*, *Capillaria hepatica*, and *Capillaria aerophila*. This condition typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, liver, and lungs, with symptoms including abdominal pain, diarrhea, and respiratory issues. It is commonly associated with ingestion of contaminated food or water, often in tropical and subtropical regions. The disease may present with chronic inflammation and granulomatous lesions in affected organs.

Dracunculiasis, also known as Guinea worm disease, is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Dracunculus medinensis*. The disease is transmitted when individuals drink water contaminated with copepods harboring the larvae. The adult female worm migrates through subcutaneous tissues, causing painful, serous, and often ulcerative lesions, typically on the lower limbs. The infection is characterized by a slow, progressive course, with the worm emerging through the skin after a 10–14 month incubation period. It is primarily found in rural, water-scarce regions of Africa and parts of the Middle East.

Enterobiasis, also known as pinworm infection, is a common intestinal parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Enterobius vermicularis*. The infection primarily affects the anal and perianal regions, with female worms laying eggs around the anus, causing intense itching. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs, often through contaminated hands, surfaces, or fomites. The condition is most commonly seen in children and in settings with close personal contact. Symptoms include perianal pruritus, especially at night, and occasionally abdominal discomfort. Complications are rare but may include secondary bacterial infections or spread to other areas such as the vagina or urethra.

Filariasis is a parasitic disease caused by filarial worms transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Common synonyms include lymphatic filariasis and elephantiasis. The primary causative agents are *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*, and *Brugia timori*. The disease typically affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and hydrocele. In advanced stages, it can cause severe swelling of the limbs and genitalia, resulting in disfigurement and disability. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Loiasis, also known as African eye worm infection, is a parasitic disease caused by the filarial nematode *Loa loa*. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected cyclops, which are found in freshwater. The adult worms migrate through subcutaneous tissues, often causing visible movement of the worm under the skin, particularly around the eyes. Common symptoms include skin nodules, eyelid swelling, and occasional itching. The disease is endemic in tropical regions of Africa and is typically asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic in most cases.

Mansonelliasis is a neglected tropical disease caused by filarial nematodes of the genus Mansonella. Common synonyms include loa loa filariasis and subcutaneous filariasis. The primary causative agents are Mansonella perstans and Mansonella ozzardi. The infection typically affects the subcutaneous tissues, lymphatic system, and occasionally the eyes. Symptoms include skin nodules, lymphadenopathy, and ocular lesions. Transmission occurs via blood-feeding insects, and the disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions. Diagnosis is often based on microfilariae detection in blood or tissue samples.

Filariasis due to *Brugia* species is a parasitic infection caused by filarial nematodes, primarily *Brugia malayi* and *Brugia timori*. Common synonyms include lymphatic filariasis and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. The parasites are transmitted via vector mosquitoes, leading to chronic inflammation and damage primarily in the lymphatic system, causing lymphedema and hydrocele. In some cases, the infection may affect the lungs, resulting in eosinophilic pulmonary infiltrates. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, with a predilection for the lower extremities and genitalia.

Lymphatic filariasis is a parasitic disease caused by infection with filarial worms, primarily *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*, and *Brugia timori*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The disease affects the lymphatic system, leading to chronic swelling and fibrosis of the limbs, genitalia, and other affected areas. Common synonyms include elephantiasis and filariasis. Chronic complications include lymphedema and hydrocele. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas with poor sanitation and limited access to healthcare.

Subcutaneous dirofilariasis is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genus *Dirofilaria*, most commonly *Dirofilaria immitis* and *Dirofilaria repens*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The infection primarily affects subcutaneous tissues, often presenting as a mobile, painless nodule, typically on the limbs, trunk, or head. Synonyms include cutaneous dirofilariasis and filariasis. The condition is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with biopsy confirming the presence of adult worms.

Other specified filariasis refers to filarial infections caused by nematode parasites not classified under the major categories of lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, or bancroftian filariasis. Common synonyms include non-bancroftian filariasis and other filarial infections. Causative agents may include Brugia malayi, Wuchereria bancrofti, or Loa loa, depending on regional prevalence. The disease typically affects the lymphatic system, skin, and subcutaneous tissues, leading to swelling, inflammation, and sometimes chronic disability. Transmission occurs via infected vector mosquitoes, and clinical manifestations vary based on the specific parasite and immune response.

Filariasis, unspecified, is a parasitic disease caused by filarial worms transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Common synonyms include lymphatic filariasis and elephantiasis. The causative agents include Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori. The disease primarily affects the lymphatic system, leading to lymphedema and hydrocele. It may also involve the skin, eyes, and reproductive organs. Symptoms include swelling, inflammation, and in severe cases, chronic disability. The infection is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions.

Gnathostomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode * Gnathostoma spinigerum*, commonly acquired through ingestion of undercooked infected intermediate hosts such as fish or crustaceans. The larvae migrate through tissues, causing cutaneous and visceral lesions. Common synonyms include visceral larva migrans and gnathostome infection. The condition typically affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and internal organs such as the lungs, liver, and brain. Symptoms include itching, swelling, and sometimes severe allergic reactions. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and serological testing.

Hookworm disease is a parasitic infection caused by nematodes of the genera *Ancylostoma* and *Necator*. Common synonyms include ancylostomiasis and necatoriasis. The parasites enter through the skin, typically via contaminated soil, and migrate to the lungs before reaching the small intestine where they attach to the intestinal wall. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and iron-deficiency anemia. The infection primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract and lungs, with skin involvement during the migratory phase. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, particularly in areas with poor sanitation.

Ancylostomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by hookworms of the genus *Ancylostoma*, primarily *Ancylostoma duodenale* and *Ancylostoma ceylanicum*. It is transmitted through skin penetration by infective larvae, leading to larva migrans syndrome. The worms primarily reside in the small intestine, where they feed on blood, causing anemia, protein loss, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Common synonyms include hookworm infection and cutaneous larva migrans. The condition predominantly affects the skin and gastrointestinal tract, with systemic involvement in severe cases.

Necatoriasis is a parasitic infection caused by the hookworm *Necator americanus*, a common soil-transmitted helminth. Infection occurs through penetration of the skin by infective larvae, typically from contaminated soil. The larvae migrate through the bloodstream to the lungs, then to the intestines where they mature into adult worms. Common synonyms include cutaneous larva migrans and ground itch. The condition primarily affects the skin, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract, with symptoms including itching, cough, and abdominal pain. It is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions with poor sanitation.

Cutaneous larva migrans (CLM), also known as creeping eruption, is a parasitic skin infection caused by the larvae of hookworms, most commonly *Ancylostoma braziliense* and *Ancylostoma caninum*. The larvae penetrate the skin, leading to an itchy, serpiginous rash that migrates over days. The condition typically affects the feet, hands, and other exposed areas in warm, moist environments. It is common in tropical and subtropical regions where contact with contaminated soil is frequent. Diagnosis is often clinical, based on the characteristic rash and travel history.

Oesophagostomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Oesophagostomum* species, commonly known as large stomach worms. It primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the small intestine and caecum, in animals such as horses, donkeys, and rodents. The infection is characterized by intestinal inflammation, malabsorption, and weight loss. In humans, it is a rare zoonotic disease, often acquired through ingestion of infective larvae from contaminated soil. Synonyms include large stomach worm infection and intestinal oesophagostomiasis.

Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is a parasitic infection caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. The adult worms reside in subcutaneous tissues, producing microfilariae that migrate to the skin and eyes, leading to severe itching, skin lesions, and potentially blindness. It primarily affects the skin, eyes, and lymphatic system. The condition is endemic in tropical regions, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.

Onchocerciasis of the eye, also known as river blindness, is a chronic infectious disease caused by the parasitic nematode *Onchocerca volvulus*. The infection leads to ocular lesions, inflammation, and eventual visual impairment due to microfilariae-induced damage to the cornea and uvea. Common synonyms include loiasis and onchocercal keratitis. The disease primarily affects the skin and eyes, with severe ocular involvement leading to blindness if left untreated. Transmission occurs through the bite of infected blackflies.

Onchocerciasis of the skin, also known as river blindness, is a chronic parasitic infection caused by *Onchocerca volvulus*. The disease results from microfilariae released by adult worms in subcutaneous tissues, leading to inflammatory dermatitis, nodules, and severe skin lesions. Common synonyms include loiasis and river blindness. The infection primarily affects the skin, eyes, and peripheral nerves, causing itching, rashes, and potential blindness. Transmission occurs through the bite of infected blackflies.

"Other specified onchocerciasis" refers to cases of onchocerciasis where the clinical presentation or epidemiological context does not fully meet the criteria for classic onchocerciasis but is still attributable to *Onchocerca volvulus*. It may involve atypical symptoms or geographic variations. Common synonyms include atypical onchocerciasis or unspecified onchocerciasis. The causative agent is *Onchocerca volvulus*, transmitted by blackflies. Typically affects skin, eyes, and subcutaneous tissues, causing rash, itching, and potential blindness.

Onchocerciasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by the filarial worm *Onchocerca volvulus*. It is transmitted through the bite of infected blackflies. The disease leads to skin inflammation, intense itching, and the formation of subcutaneous nodules. In advanced stages, it can cause blindness due to microfilariae-induced ocular damage. Common synonyms include river blindness and loa-loa disease, though the latter is caused by a different organism. The infection primarily affects the skin and eyes, with systemic involvement possible in severe cases.

Strongyloidiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Strongyloides stercoralis*. It primarily affects the intestines, with larvae migrating through the lungs and skin during the early stages. Common synonyms include filariasis and threadworm infection. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Chronic infection can lead to complications such as disseminated strongyloidiasis, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and skin eruptions. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool examination or serological tests. Treatment typically involves antihelmintic drugs like ivermectin.

Syngamosis is a rare condition characterized by the fusion of adjacent joints, typically in the fingers or toes, leading to decreased mobility and deformity. It is often associated with congenital disorders or genetic syndromes. Common synonyms include syndactyly and arthrogryposis. Causative agents may include genetic mutations, maternal infections, or exposure to teratogens. The condition primarily affects the hand and foot joints, with the interphalangeal joints being most commonly involved. It can also occur in other joints, particularly in cases of systemic disease. Early diagnosis and multidisciplinary management are essential for optimal outcomes.

Toxocariasis is a parasitic infection caused by the larvae of *Toxocara canis* and *Toxocara cati*, commonly found in dogs and cats. It results from accidental ingestion of eggs from contaminated soil. The larvae migrate through various organs, primarily the liver, lungs, and eyes, causing inflammation and tissue damage. Common synonyms include visceral larva migrans and ocular larva migrans. Symptoms vary depending on the affected organs, ranging from fever and cough to vision loss. The condition is more prevalent in children who play in soil contaminated with feces from infected animals.

Trichinosis is a parasitic infection caused by the roundworm *Trichinella spiralis* and other *Trichinella* species. It results from consuming undercooked meat containing larval encysted worms. The infection primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract and skeletal muscles, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and muscle inflammation. Common synonyms include trichiniasis and trichinelliasis. The larvae migrate through the bloodstream, leading to systemic involvement, particularly in the muscles, and can cause fever, swelling, and eosinophilia.

Trichostrongyliasis is a helminthic infection caused by nematodes of the family Trichostrongylidae. Common synonyms include gastrointestinal strongyloidiasis and small intestinal nematodiasis. The primary causative agents are species such as *Strongyloides stercoralis*, *Trichuris trichiura*, and *Hookworm* species. These parasites primarily affect the small intestine and large intestine, with *Strongyloides* occasionally migrating to the lungs and other tissues. The infection is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, often transmitted through contaminated soil. Clinical manifestations include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption, with severe cases potentially leading to intestinal obstruction or disseminated infection.

Trichuriasis is a helminthic infection caused by *Trichuris trichiura*, a whipworm. It primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the cecum and colon. Common synonyms include whipworm infection or intestinal trichuriasis. Transmission occurs via ingestion of infective eggs in contaminated soil. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rectal prolapse, especially in children. Chronic infection may lead to anemia and growth retardation. The condition is prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and is more common in tropical and subtropical regions.

Uncinariosis is a parasitic infection caused by the nematode *Uncinaria stenocephala*, primarily affecting dogs and cats. It is also known as hookworm disease. The larvae penetrate the skin, typically through the feet, leading to localized inflammation and itching. In severe cases, systemic symptoms such as anemia and weight loss may occur. The infection is most commonly found in the skin, particularly around the paws, and can occasionally involve the lungs during larval migration. Transmission occurs through contact with contaminated soil or feces.

code_desc: other specified diseases due to nematodes
summary: "Other specified diseases due to nematodes" refers to parasitic infections caused by nematodes not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include filariasis and other nematode-related infections. Causative agents may include *Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*, and *Onchocerca volvulus*. These infections typically affect the lymphatic system, skin, and eyes. Symptoms may include lymphedema, elephantiasis, and ocular lesions. Transmission occurs via vector-borne routes, such as mosquitoes or blackflies. The condition is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions.

Diseases due to nematodes, unspecified, refer to infections caused by roundworms without specific identification of the parasite species. Common synonyms include helminthic infections or nematode infestations. Causative agents may include species like *Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Trichuris trichiura*, or *Enterobius vermicularis*. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, though some nematodes may involve the lungs, liver, or other organs. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malnutrition. Transmission occurs via ingestion of eggs or larvae in contaminated soil or food.

Cysticercosis is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*, the pork tapeworm. It occurs when humans ingest eggs from contaminated food or water. The larvae form cysts in various tissues, most commonly in the central nervous system, leading to neurocysticercosis, which can cause seizures and other neurological symptoms. Other affected areas include the muscles, eyes, and liver. Synonyms include neurocysticercosis and pork tapeworm infection. The condition is prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and limited access to clean water.

Cysticercosis of the central nervous system (CNS) is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*. It results from ingestion of tapeworm eggs, leading to formation of cysts in the brain and spinal cord. Common synonyms include neurocysticercosis and cerebral cysticercosis. The disease typically affects the cerebral parenchyma, meninges, and spinal cord. Symptoms vary from seizures and headaches to increased intracranial pressure. Diagnosis is often via imaging and serological tests. Treatment involves antiparasitic drugs and management of complications.

Cysticercosis of the eye is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*, resulting from ingestion of tapeworm eggs. The larvae form cysts in ocular tissues, leading to inflammation and potential vision loss. Common synonyms include ocular cysticercosis and intraocular cysticercoid. Typically affecting the retina, vitreous, and choroid, it may also involve the orbit. Clinical manifestations include pain, visual disturbances, and cyst formation. Diagnosis is often via imaging and serology, with treatment focusing on antiparasitic therapy and management of complications.

Other specified cysticercosis refers to infections caused by the larval stage of *Taenia solium*, when the cysts are located in sites not typically classified under neurocysticercosis or visceral cysticercosis. Common synonyms include extraneural cysticercosis and non-neurological cysticercosis. The condition primarily affects tissues such as subcutaneous areas, muscles, and occasionally the liver or lungs. Clinical manifestations depend on the location and number of cysts, often presenting as painless nodules or mass lesions. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging and serological tests. Treatment may involve antiparasitic medications and surgical intervention if necessary.

Cysticercosis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by the larvae of *Taenia solium*, the pork tapeworm. The disease results from ingestion of eggs, leading to formation of cysts in various tissues. Common synonyms include neurocysticercosis when affecting the central nervous system. Typically, cysts develop in the brain, muscles, and subcutaneous tissues. Symptoms depend on the location and number of cysts, ranging from asymptomatic to seizures, edema, or organ dysfunction. Diagnosis often involves imaging and serological tests. Treatment varies based on affected organs and may include antiparasitic drugs and surgical intervention.

Diphyllobothriasis is a helminthic infection caused by the tapeworm *Diphyllobothrium latum*, also known as the broad tapeworm. It is acquired through ingestion of undercooked freshwater fish containing plerocercoids. The adult worms reside in the small intestine, where they attach to the intestinal wall. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and nutrient deficiencies due to parasitic consumption. Common synonyms include broad tapeworm infection and fish tapeworm disease. The primary affected body part is the small intestine.

Dipylidiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the tapeworm *Dipylidium caninum*, commonly found in dogs and cats. It is transmitted to humans via ingestion of infected fleas or intermediate hosts. The infection primarily affects the small intestine, where the tapeworm attaches to the intestinal wall. Common synonyms include canine tapeworm infection and flea tapeworm disease. Symptoms may include abdominal discomfort, weight loss, and the passage of proglottids. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through stool examination. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs such as praziquantel.

Echinococcosis is a chronic parasitic infection caused by larval stages of the tapeworm *Echinococcus*. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and cystic echinococcosis. The most common causative agents are *Echinococcus granulosus* and *Echinococcus multilocularis*. The infection typically affects the liver and lungs, forming fluid-filled cysts. It is more prevalent in endemic regions with close contact between humans and infected animals. Diagnosis is often confirmed through imaging and serology, and treatment may involve surgery, medication, or both.

Echinococcus infection of the liver, also known as hydatid disease, is caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus* or *Echinococcus multilocularis*. The infection leads to the formation of cysts in the liver, which can grow slowly over years. Common synonyms include hepatic hydatidosis and alveolar echinococcosis. The liver is the most frequently affected organ, though cysts may also develop in the lungs, brain, and other abdominal organs. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and occasionally jaundice. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging and serological tests. Treatment involves surgical removal, medication, or a combination of both.

Echinococcus infection of the lung, also known as pulmonary hydatid disease, is caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm *Echinococcus granulosus*. This condition results from ingestion of eggs, typically from contaminated food or water, leading to systemic dissemination via the bloodstream. The lungs are the most commonly affected organ, followed by the liver. Lesions appear as cysts that may grow slowly over years, potentially causing symptoms such as cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Complications include cyst rupture, secondary infection, and allergic reactions. Diagnosis is often confirmed by imaging and serological tests.

Echinococcus infection of bone, also known as echinococcal osteomyelitis, is a rare parasitic infection caused by species of the genus *Echinococcus*, most commonly *E. granulosus* and *E. multilocularis*. The infection results from the migration of hydatid cysts to the skeletal system, typically affecting the vertebrae, long bones, and pelvis. Clinically, it presents with chronic inflammation, pain, and sometimes mass formation. Diagnosis often involves imaging and serological tests, with treatment requiring surgical intervention and antiparasitic therapy.

code_desc: echinococcus infection of central nervous system
summary: Echinococcus infection of the central nervous system, also known as neurocysticercosis, is caused by the larval stage of *Echinococcus granulosus* or *Echinococcus multilocularis*. It primarily affects the brain and spinal cord, leading to cyst formation. Common synonyms include cerebral echinococcosis and neurocysticercosis. The infection is acquired through ingestion of eggs from contaminated food or water. Symptoms vary depending on cyst location and size, often including seizures, headaches, and increased intracranial pressure. Diagnosis typically involves imaging and serological tests. Treatment may involve antiparasitic drugs and surgical intervention.

Other specified echinococcosis refers to echinococcal infections caused by species of *Echinococcus* not classified under cystic echinococcosis or alveolar echinococcosis. Common synonyms include miscellaneous echinococcosis or unspecified echinococcosis. The causative agents include *Echinococcus multilocularis*, *E. granulosus*, and *E. oligarthrus*. These infections typically affect the liver, lungs, and rarely the brain or other organs. Clinical presentation varies depending on the species and location of the lesion, often presenting as slow-growing cysts or infiltrative masses. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by imaging and serologic testing.

Echinococcosis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of tapeworms of the genus *Echinococcus*. Common synonyms include hydatid disease and cystic echinococcosis. The primary causative agents are *Echinococcus granulosus* and *Echinococcus multilocularis*. The infection typically affects the liver and lungs, forming fluid-filled cysts. It is more prevalent in endemic regions and often results from ingestion of eggs from infected animals. Clinical presentation varies depending on the affected organ and cyst size. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by imaging and serology.

Hymenolepiasis is a helminthic infection caused by the dwarf tapeworm *Hymenolepis nana* or *Hymenolepis diminuta*. It primarily affects the small intestine, with *H. nana* being the most common agent in humans. The infection is characterized by the presence of adult worms in the intestinal lumen. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. It is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. Synonyms include dwarf tapeworm infection and cyclophylaxia. Transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated food or water, or through intermediate hosts like beetles.

Sparganosis is a parasitic infection caused by the larval stage of *Spirometra* species, commonly acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or undercooked meat. Synonyms include larval sparganosis and visceral sparganosis. The larvae typically migrate to subcutaneous tissues, eyes, and lungs, causing localized inflammation and cyst formation. Clinical manifestations depend on the affected organ, with ocular involvement being a common presentation. Diagnosis is often based on clinical findings and imaging, with treatment involving surgical removal or antiparasitic drugs.

Taeniasis is a parasitic infection caused by tapeworms of the genus *Taenia*, most commonly *Taenia solium* (pork tapeworm) and *Taenia saginata* (beef tapeworm). It occurs through ingestion of undercooked meat containing larval cysts. The adult worms reside in the small intestine, where they attach to the intestinal wall. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss. In severe cases, cysticercosis can develop when larvae migrate to other tissues, affecting the brain, muscles, and eyes. Synonyms include taeniarhynchosis and cysticercosis (when larvae are involved).

Taeniasis due to *Taenia solium* is a parasitic infection caused by the ingestion of *T. solium* eggs or undercooked pork containing cysticerci. The adult tapeworm resides in the small intestine, where it attaches to the intestinal wall. Common synonyms include pork tapeworm infection and cysticercosis. The primary affected body parts are the small intestine, with potential migration of larvae to tissues such as the brain, eyes, and muscles, leading to cysticercosis. Symptoms vary from asymptomatic to abdominal pain, weight loss, and neurological complications.

Taeniasis due to *Taenia saginata*, also known as beef tapeworm infection, is a parasitic intestinal infection caused by the adult form of *Taenia saginata*. The parasite attaches to the intestinal wall and absorbs nutrients, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss. Infection occurs through ingestion of undercooked beef containing viable eggs or larvae. The adult worm resides in the small intestine, and segments may be passed in feces. Common synonyms include beef tapeworm disease and taeniasis saginata. The primary affected body part is the small intestine.

Other specified taeniasis refers to infections caused by tapeworms other than the most commonly recognized species like *Taenia solium* or *Taenia saginata*. Common synonyms include unspecified taeniasis or taeniasis due to other *Taenia* species. The causative agents may include *Taenia asiatica*, *Taenia hydatigena*, or *Taenia ovis*. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, with adult worms residing in the small intestine. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, weight loss, and occasional passage of proglottids. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through stool examination for eggs or segments. Treatment typically involves antiparasitic medications such as praziquantel.

Taeniasis, unspecified, is a parasitic infection caused by tapeworms of the genus *Taenia*. Common synonyms include beef tapeworm infection and pork tapeworm infection, though the exact species may not be specified. The causative agents typically include *Taenia saginata* (beef tapeworm) and *Taenia solium* (pork tapeworm). The infection primarily affects the small intestine, with adult worms attaching to the intestinal wall. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through stool examination for tapeworm segments or eggs. Treatment involves anthelmintic medications such as praziquantel or albendazole.

code_desc: other specified diseases due to cestodes
summary: "Other specified diseases due to cestodes" refers to parasitic infections caused by tapeworms that do not fit the criteria for more specific classifications. Common synonyms include cestode infestation or tapeworm disease. Causative agents include *Echinococcus*, *Diphyllobothrium*, and *Hymenolepis* species. These infections typically affect the intestines but can also involve the liver, lungs, and brain, leading to complications such as cyst formation or tissue damage. Clinical presentation varies depending on the species and location of infection.

Diseases due to cestodes, unspecified, refer to infections caused by tapeworms, which are flat, segmented parasitic worms. Common synonyms include cestodiasis and tapeworm infection. These infections are caused by various species of cestodes, such as *Taenia solium*, *Taenia saginata*, *Echinococcus granulosus*, and *Diphyllobothrium latum*. The parasites typically affect the intestinal tract, but can also migrate to other organs, leading to complications such as cyst formation in the liver or brain. Symptoms vary depending on the species and location of infection, ranging from abdominal pain and weight loss to more severe neurological manifestations.

Clonorchiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the liver fluke *Clonorchis sinensis*, commonly acquired through consumption of undercooked freshwater fish. The parasite primarily affects the biliary system, leading to inflammation and fibrosis of the liver. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, and cholangitis. Chronic infection can result in cholangiocarcinoma. Synonyms include opisthorchiasis and Chinese liver fluke disease. The condition is endemic in parts of Asia, particularly Korea, China, and Vietnam.

Dicrocoeliasis is a parasitic liver fluke infection caused by *Dicrocoelium dendriticum*. Common synonyms include hepatic fluke disease and groaneck fluke infection. The fluke primarily affects the bile ducts and liver, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. It is commonly found in ruminants but can also infect humans through ingestion of infected ants. Clinical signs include abdominal pain, jaundice, and malabsorption. The disease is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through stool examination for eggs. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs such as triclabendazole.

Fascioliasis is a parasitic infection caused by liver flukes of the genus *Fasciola*, most commonly *Fasciola hepatica* and *Fasciola gigantica*. It primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. The infection occurs through ingestion of metacercariae found in contaminated water or vegetation. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and hepatomegaly. In chronic cases, it may result in portal hypertension and liver failure. Synonyms include liver fluke infection and fasciolosis. The disease is endemic in agricultural regions with poor sanitation.

Fasciolopsiasis is a parasitic infection caused by the fluke *Fasciolopsis buski*, commonly found in humans and animals. It is also known as buffalo liver fluke disease. The parasite primarily affects the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Transmission occurs through ingestion of contaminated water or food containing cercariae. The condition is more prevalent in regions with poor sanitation and is often associated with consumption of raw or undercooked aquatic plants. While less common than other liver fluke infections, fasciolopsiasis can cause significant morbidity in endemic areas.

Opisthorchiasis is a parasitic infection caused by liver flukes of the genus *Opisthorchis*, most commonly *Opisthorchis viverrini* and *Opisthorchis felineus*. It is acquired through consumption of undercooked freshwater fish. The flukes primarily infect the bile ducts and liver, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potentially cholangiocarcinoma. Symptoms include abdominal pain, jaundice, and liver enlargement. Synonyms include clonorchiasis and liver fluke infection. The condition is endemic in parts of Asia and Eastern Europe.

Paragonimiasis is a parasitic infection caused by lung flukes of the genus *Paragonimus*, most commonly *Paragonimus westermani*. It results from ingestion of undercooked crustaceans contaminated with metacercariae. The parasites migrate to the lungs, causing pneumonia-like symptoms, but can also affect the brain, liver, and abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include lung fluke disease and paragonimiasis. Clinically, it presents with cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, and sometimes neurological symptoms if the parasites reach the central nervous system. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool examination or imaging.

Schistosomiasis is a parasitic infection caused by trematodes of the genus *Schistosoma*. Common synonyms include bilharzia and snail fever. The disease results from penetration of cercariae into the skin, leading to infection with adult worms in the mesenteric or portal venous systems. Common species include *Schistosoma haematobium*, *S. mansoni*, and *S. japonicum*. The infection typically affects the intestines, bladder, and liver, causing inflammation, fibrosis, and organ damage. Chronic infection can lead to complications such as portal hypertension and bladder cancer.

Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma haematobium* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the trematode *S. haematobium*, transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater. The cercariae penetrate the skin and develop into adult worms in the venous plexus of the bladder. Common synonyms include urogenital schistosomiasis and bilharzia. The infection primarily affects the urinary tract, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and hematuria. Complications may include bladder cancer and infertility. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and parts of the Caribbean.

Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma mansoni* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the trematode *Schistosoma mansoni*. The cercariae penetrate the skin upon contact with contaminated water, leading to migration of larvae to the portal venous system. Adult worms reside in the mesenteric veins, causing granulomatous inflammation and fibrosis. Common synonyms include bilharzia and snail fever. The disease primarily affects the intestines and liver, with potential complications such as portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and intestinal obstruction. Chronic infection may result in significant morbidity and increased risk of bladder cancer.

Schistosomiasis due to *Schistosoma japonicum* is a chronic parasitic infection caused by the trematode *S. japonicum*, transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater. The larvae penetrate the skin and mature into adult worms in the mesenteric veins, primarily affecting the liver and intestines. Common synonyms include oriental schistosomiasis and Chinese schistosomiasis. Clinical manifestations include abdominal pain, diarrhea, liver enlargement, and portal hypertension. Chronic infection may lead to fibrosis and organ damage. The disease is endemic in parts of Asia, particularly China, and is a significant public health concern in affected regions.

Other schistosomiases refer to infections caused by species of *Schistosoma* other than *S. haematobium*, *S. japonicum*, *S. mansoni*, and *S. mekongi*. Common synonyms include non-urogenital schistosomiasis and schistosomiasis due to other species. Causative agents include *S. intercalatum*, *S. guineensis*, *S. mattheei*, and *S. spinale*. These infections primarily affect the intestinal tract, liver, and occasionally the lungs. Clinical manifestations include abdominal pain, diarrhea, liver enlargement, and portal hypertension. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through stool or urine examination for parasite eggs.

Cercarial dermatitis, also known as swimmer's itch, is a skin condition caused by the penetration of cercariae, the larval stage of certain trematode flukes. These parasites are released into freshwater by infected snails and can penetrate human skin during swimming or wading. The condition typically affects the legs, arms, and torso, presenting as an itchy, red, papular rash. Common causative agents include species of *Schistosoma* and *Trichobilharzia*. The reaction is an allergic response to the larvae, which are usually not capable of completing their life cycle in humans.

Schistosomal pneumonitis is an inflammatory lung condition caused by the migration of *Schistosoma mansoni* or *Schistosoma japonicum* cercariae through the pulmonary parenchyma. The larvae trigger an immune response leading to granulomatous inflammation and interstitial lung disease. Common synonyms include pulmonary schistosomiasis and schistosomal lung disease. It typically affects the lungs, with possible involvement of the pleura and hilar lymph nodes. Symptoms include cough, fever, and dyspnea, often occurring during the early stages of infection. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, serology, and imaging findings.

code_desc: schistosomiasis due to unspecified or unknown schistosoma species
summary: Schistosomiasis due to unspecified or unknown Schistosoma species is a parasitic infection caused by trematodes of the genus Schistosoma, though the exact species may not be identified. Common synonyms include bilharzia and snail fever. The causative agents include Schistosoma mansoni, S. haematobium, S. japonicum, and others. The infection primarily affects the intestinal and urinary systems, leading to inflammation and fibrosis. It is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, often transmitted through contact with contaminated freshwater. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, blood in urine, and long-term complications such as organ damage.

code_desc: other specified diseases due to trematodes
summary: "Other specified diseases due to trematodes" refers to parasitic infections caused by flukes that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include trematodiasis and fluke infections. Causative agents include species such as *Schistosoma*, *Clonorchis*, and *Fasciola*. These infections typically affect the liver, intestines, bladder, and lungs, depending on the parasite species. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and organ damage. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool or blood tests, and treatment involves antiparasitic medications.

Diseases due to trematodes, unspecified, refer to infections caused by fluke parasites belonging to the class Trematoda. Common synonyms include trematodic infections or fluke infestations. Causative agents may include species such as *Schistosoma*, *Clonorchis*, and *Fasciola*. These parasites typically affect the liver, intestines, lungs, or vascular system, depending on the species. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through stool or blood tests, and treatment involves antiparasitic medications.

code_desc: other and unspecified infestation by parasitic worms
summary: "Other and unspecified infestation by parasitic worms" refers to infections caused by parasitic nematodes or cestodes not specifically identified. Common synonyms include unspecified helminth infection. Causative agents may include hookworms, whipworms, or tapeworms. Typically affects the intestines, lungs, or skin. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and anemia. Diagnosis often relies on stool examination or imaging. Treatment involves anthelmintic drugs. This category encompasses infections where the specific parasite is not documented.

Mixed intestinal helminthiases refer to concurrent infections of the intestines caused by multiple species of parasitic worms. Common synonyms include polymicrobial intestinal helminthiasis or mixed worm infestation. Causative agents may include *Ascaris lumbricoides*, *Trichuris trichiura*, *Hookworms* (e.g., *Ancylostoma duodenale*, *Necator americanus*), and *Strongyloides stercoralis*. These infections primarily affect the small and large intestines, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, malnutrition, and anemia. They are prevalent in areas with poor sanitation and are often transmitted through contaminated soil or food.

code_desc: intestinal parasitic infestation not otherwise specified
summary: Intestinal parasitic infestation not otherwise specified refers to the presence of parasitic organisms in the gastrointestinal tract without a specific identification of the parasite. Common synonyms include intestinal helminthiasis or unspecified intestinal parasitism. Causative agents may include protozoa such as Giardia lamblia or Entamoeba histolytica, and helminths like Ascaris lumbricoides or Trichuris trichiura. The small intestine is typically affected, though other parts of the gastrointestinal tract may also be involved. Symptoms often include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption.

Intestinal helminthiasis, unspecified, refers to infection of the gastrointestinal tract by parasitic worms. Common synonyms include intestinal worm infestation or helminthic infection. Causative agents may include roundworms, hookworms, whipworms, and tapeworms. The condition typically affects the small and large intestines, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and malnutrition. It is commonly seen in areas with poor sanitation and hygiene. Diagnosis is often confirmed through stool examination for ova or larvae. Treatment involves anthelmintic medications.

code_desc: other specified other and unspecified infestation by parasitic worms
summary: "Other specified or unspecified infestation by parasitic worms refers to infestations caused by nematodes, cestodes, or trematodes not classified under more specific categories. Diagnosis often involves stool examination or imaging."

code_desc: other and unspecified infestation by parasitic worms, unspecified
summary: "Other and unspecified infestation by parasitic worms, unspecified" refers to infections caused by unspecified parasitic worms that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include "unspecified helminthiasis" or "other worm infestation." Causative agents may include various nematodes, cestodes, or trematodes, such as hookworms, tapeworms, or flukes. Typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, liver, or skin, depending on the parasite. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, weight loss, and allergic reactions. Diagnosis often requires stool exams or imaging. Treatment depends on the specific worm identified.

Diphyllobothriasis and sparganosis are helminthic infections caused by tapeworms. Diphyllobothriasis is caused by *Diphyllobothrium latum*, while sparganosis is due to *Spirometra erinacei* or *S. mansoni*. Both infections involve larval migration. Diphyllobothriasis primarily affects the small intestine, with adult worms attaching to the intestinal wall. Sparganosis involves migrating larvae that can localize in various tissues, including the eye, skin, and subcutaneous tissues. Common synonyms include broad tapeworm infection and sparganum infection. Both conditions are acquired through ingestion of contaminated food or water.

Helminthiases, unspecified, refer to infections caused by parasitic worms (helminths) when the specific type is not identified. Common synonyms include helminthic infections or worm infestations. Causative agents may include nematodes, cestodes, or trematodes such as Ascaris lumbricoides, Taenia species, or Schistosoma. These infections typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, liver, lungs, and blood vessels, depending on the parasite. Symptoms vary but often include abdominal pain, weight loss, and malnutrition. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and stool examination. Treatment involves anthelmintic medications.

Pediculosis is a parasitic infestation caused by lice, most commonly *Pediculus humanus capitis* (head lice), *Pediculus humanus corporis* (body lice), and *Pediculus humanus pubis* (pubic lice). It is characterized by intense pruritus due to an allergic reaction to louse secretions. Common synonyms include head lice, body lice, and crabs. The condition primarily affects the scalp, body, and pubic area, with head lice being the most prevalent in children. Transmission occurs through direct contact or shared personal items. Complications may include secondary bacterial infections from scratching.

Pediculosis capitis, commonly known as head lice infestation, is a contagious ectoparasitic infection caused by *Pediculus humanus capitis*. It affects the scalp and is most prevalent in children. The condition is characterized by the presence of live lice, nits (eggs), and sometimes lice feces, leading to pruritus and discomfort. Transmission occurs through direct head-to-head contact or via shared personal items. It is a common public health issue in schools and households, particularly among preschool and elementary school-aged children.

Pediculosis corporis is a skin infestation caused by the human body louse, *Pediculus humanus corporis*. It is characterized by intense pruritus and the presence of nits or lice on the body. Common synonyms include body lice infestation or louse disease. The condition primarily affects the torso, especially in areas with coarse hair such as the back, neck, and shoulders. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infested clothing or bedding. It is more prevalent in crowded, unsanitary conditions and is often associated with poverty or homelessness.

code_desc: pediculosis of unspecified site or type
summary: Pediculosis of unspecified site or type refers to infestation by head, body, or pubic lice, when the specific location is not specified. Common synonyms include lice infestation or pediculosis capitis/body/pubic. The causative agents are Pediculus humanus capitis (head lice), Pediculus humanus corporis (body lice), and Phthirus pubis (pubic lice). It typically affects the scalp, body, or pubic area, causing pruritus and visible nits or live lice. Transmission occurs through direct contact or shared personal items.

Myiasis is an infestation of living tissue by fly larvae. Common synonyms include myiatic infection or fly larvae infestation. It is caused by various species of flies, most commonly from the families Calliphoridae, Sarcophagidae, and Fanniidae. The causative agents include species such as *Lucilia serriata*, *Chrysomya megacephala*, and *Fannia canicularis*. Myiasis typically affects the skin, particularly in wounds, nasal passages, ears, and eyes, and can also occur in the gastrointestinal tract. The condition is more prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions and is often associated with poor hygiene or open wounds.

Ocular myiasis is an infestation of the eye by fly larvae, typically caused by species such as *Dermatobia hominis*, *Chrysops* spp., or *Oestrus ovis*. It presents as a painful, red, swollen eye with visible larvae in the conjunctival or corneal tissues. Common synonyms include ocular myiasis, fly larvae infestation, or ophthalmic myiasis. The condition predominantly affects the conjunctiva, cornea, and orbital tissues, often leading to severe inflammation, ulceration, and potential vision loss if untreated. It is more common in tropical regions and among individuals with compromised immune systems or poor hygiene.

Nasopharyngeal myiasis is an infestation of the nasal and pharyngeal passages by fly larvae. Common synonyms include nasal myiasis and pharyngeal myiasis. The condition is typically caused by larvae of flies such as *Cochliomyia hominivorax* (screw-worm) and *Lucilia species*. It predominantly affects the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, and occasionally the larynx. Symptoms include nasal discharge, epistaxis, and a foreign body sensation. It is more common in tropical and subtropical regions and often occurs in individuals with compromised nasal defenses or those living in unsanitary conditions.

Laryngeal myiasis is a parasitic infection involving the larynx, characterized by the presence of fly larvae (maggots) in the airway. Common synonyms include larval infestation of the larynx or myiasis of the larynx. It is typically caused by species of flies such as *Dermatobia hominis* or *Chrysomya spp.*, though other species may also be involved. The condition predominantly affects the larynx and upper respiratory tract, often leading to symptoms like stridor, cough, and respiratory distress. It is more commonly seen in tropical regions and may occur in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor hygiene. Prompt diagnosis and removal of the larvae are essential to prevent airway obstruction and complications.

Cutaneous myiasis is an infestation of the skin by fly larvae. Common synonyms include furuncular myiasis and myiasis. It is typically caused by species of flies such as *Dermatobia hominis*, *Chrysomya megacephala*, and *Lucilia sericata*. The condition most commonly affects exposed areas of the body, including the face, neck, and extremities. Infestation occurs when female flies lay eggs on open wounds or mucous membranes, leading to larval penetration and development within the tissue. Clinical presentation includes erythematous nodules with a central punctum, often accompanied by pain and purulent discharge. Treatment involves manual removal of larvae and appropriate antimicrobial therapy.

Other specified myiasis refers to infestations caused by fly larvae that do not fit the criteria for more specific types of myiasis. Common synonyms include secondary or accidental myiasis. Causative agents may include species such as *Dermatobia hominis*, *Lucilia sericata*, and *Chrysomya megacephala*. This condition typically affects the skin, particularly in warm, moist areas such as the ears, nose, and genital regions. It often occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor hygiene. The larvae feed on tissue and can cause significant local inflammation and discomfort.

Myiasis, unspecified, refers to infestation of living tissue by fly larvae. It is a general term encompassing various types of myiasis caused by different fly species. Common synonyms include fly larvae infestation and myiasis. Causative agents may include species from the families Calliphoridae, Sarcophagidae, and Oestridae. Typically affected body parts include the skin, ears, nasal passages, and gastrointestinal tract, depending on the species involved. The condition can range from mild to severe, often requiring medical intervention for removal of larvae and treatment of secondary infections.

External hirudiniasis is a condition caused by the bite of leeches, typically *Hirudo medicinalis*, leading to localized inflammation, pain, and potential hemorrhage. Common synonyms include leech bite reaction or leech infestation. The condition primarily affects exposed skin areas such as the legs, arms, and face. Symptoms include erythema, swelling, and sometimes systemic reactions like anaphylaxis. It is often encountered in individuals who come into contact with leeches in aquatic environments or during medical procedures involving leech therapy.

Tinea pedis, commonly known as athlete's foot, is a fungal infection of the feet caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum, Trichophyton mentagrophytes, and Epidermophyton floccosum. It typically affects the interdigital spaces, soles, and heels, presenting with symptoms like itching, burning, scaling, and maceration. The infection is often transmitted in moist environments like public showers or locker rooms. It is more prevalent in males and individuals with compromised immune systems or poor foot hygiene.

Scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by the mite *Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*. It presents as intense pruritus, especially at night, with characteristic burrows and rash. Common synonyms include scabies mite infestation or sarcoptic dermatitis. The mites burrow into the epidermis, triggering an allergic reaction. Typically affected areas include the webs of fingers, wrists, elbows, axillae, genitalia, and buttocks. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact. The condition is more severe in immunocompromised individuals and young children. Treatment involves topical acaricides such as permethrin.

Classical scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by the mite *Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*. It is characterized by intense pruritus and a papular rash, typically appearing in skin folds such as the webs of the fingers, wrists, elbows, knees, and genital area. Common synonyms include scabies, itch, and sarcoptic mange. The condition is transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact and is more prevalent in crowded living conditions. Secondary bacterial infections may occur due to scratching. Diagnosis is often clinical, though skin scraping may confirm the presence of mites.

Crusted scabies, also known as Norwegian scabies, is a severe form of scabies characterized by hyperkeratotic, crusted lesions containing numerous mites, eggs, and fecal matter. It is caused by *Sarcoptes scabiei* var. *canis* in immunocompromised individuals. The condition presents with intense pruritus and widespread scaling, often involving the hands, feet, and scalp. Common synonyms include Norwegian scabies and scabetic crusting. It is more prevalent in those with HIV, leprosy, or other immunosuppressive conditions. The lesions are typically thick, adherent, and may merge, leading to significant skin involvement.

"Other and unspecified scabies" refers to scabies cases where the specific type, such as classic scabies or crusted scabies, cannot be definitively identified. It is caused by the mite *Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis*. Common synonyms include unspecified scabies or scabies, unspecified. The condition typically affects the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, and genital areas. It presents with intense pruritus and a characteristic rash, often with burrows. Diagnosis may be challenging without direct mite detection. Treatment usually involves topical acaricides.

Tungiasis is a skin infestation caused by the burrowing sand flea *Tunga penetrans*. Commonly known as "penny mouse" or "tungia," the flea attaches to the skin, typically on the feet, and burrows into the epidermis, leading to painful, inflamed nodules. The condition is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, especially in areas with poor sanitation. Affected individuals often experience intense itching, ulceration, and secondary bacterial infections. Diagnosis is usually clinical, and treatment involves removing the flea and managing inflammation.

Cimicosis is an infestation caused by the bed bug *Cimex lectularius*, leading to intense pruritic skin lesions and allergic reactions. Common synonyms include bed bug infestation or bed bug bite reaction. The condition is primarily caused by the saliva of bed bugs during feeding. It typically affects the exposed skin areas such as the face, neck, arms, and hands. Symptoms include erythematous papules, vesicles, and secondary infections from scratching. Cimicosis is commonly found in areas with poor hygiene or overcrowding, and diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and history of exposure.

Infestation by mites refers to the presence of mites on or within the human body, causing irritation and allergic reactions. Common synonyms include scabies and demodicosis. The primary causative agent is *Sarcoptes scabiei*, responsible for scabies, while *Demodex folliculorum* and *Demodex brevis* are associated with demodicosis. These mites typically affect the skin, particularly in interdigital spaces, wrists, and genital areas in scabies, and facial skin in demodicosis. Symptoms include intense itching, rash, and skin lesions.

Infestation by *Demodex* refers to a condition caused by the parasitic mites *Demodex folliculorum* and *Demodex brevis*, which reside in hair follicles and sebaceous glands. Commonly known as demodicosis or rosacea demodex, it typically affects the face, particularly the nose, cheeks, and forehead. While often asymptomatic, it may lead to erythema, papules, and comedones. In immunocompromised individuals, it can progress to more severe forms with generalized skin involvement. The mites are cosmopolitan, and infestation is more prevalent in adults, especially those with oily skin or chronic inflammatory conditions.

code_desc: infestation of the skin by other specified parasitic mites
summary: Infestation of the skin by other specified parasitic mites refers to a group of dermatological conditions caused by mites not classified under scabies, demodicosis, or acariasis. Common synonyms include "other mite infestations" or "non-specific mite dermatitis." Causative agents may include *Sarcoptes scabiei* (varieties other than *varientis*), *Demodex folliculorum*, and *Cheyletiella* species. These infestations typically affect the skin of the trunk, limbs, and scalp, presenting with pruritus, erythema, and papules. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and skin scraping.

Infestation by other specified ectoparasite refers to the presence of external parasites not classified under more specific categories such as lice, mites, or ticks. Common synonyms include generalized ectoparasitism or unspecified ectoparasitic infestation. Causative agents may include fleas, flies, or other non-traditional ectoparasites. This condition typically affects the skin, hair, and mucous membranes, causing itching, irritation, and secondary infections. It is commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals or those in poor hygiene conditions. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation and identification of the parasite. Treatment involves targeted antiparasitic therapy and environmental control.

code_desc: infestation by unknown or unspecified ectoparasite
summary: Infestation by an unknown or unspecified ectoparasite refers to a condition where an individual is harboring an external parasite, but the specific type is not identified. Common synonyms include ectoparasitic infestation or unspecified parasitic infestation. Causative agents may include lice, mites, ticks, or fleas, though the exact species is not determined. This condition typically affects the skin, scalp, hair, or ears, causing symptoms such as itching, irritation, and skin lesions. Diagnosis often relies on clinical presentation and response to treatment.

"Other specified parasitic diseases" refers to parasitic infections that do not meet the criteria for more specific parasitic disorders but are nonetheless clinically significant. These may include conditions like cutaneous larva migrans or leishmaniasis. Common causative agents include nematodes, protozoa, and ectoparasites. Typically affecting the skin, gastrointestinal tract, or bloodstream, these diseases are often acquired through vector bites, contaminated food, or environmental exposure. Symptoms vary but may include rash, itching, fever, or organ dysfunction. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, travel history, and laboratory tests. Treatment is often targeted at the specific parasite involved.

Unspecified parasitic diseases refer to parasitic infections where the specific causative agent or affected organ system is not clearly identified. Common synonyms include undetermined parasitic infections or unspecified protozoal or helminthic diseases. Causative agents may include protozoa, helminths, or ectoparasites, though exact species are often unknown. These conditions typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, liver, blood, or skin, but the precise site and pathogen remain unspecified. They are often diagnosed based on clinical symptoms and limited diagnostic findings.

Sepsis without septic shock is a life-threatening systemic infection characterized by the body's dysregulated response to pathogens, leading to organ dysfunction without hypotension or hypoperfusion. Common synonyms include systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) with infection. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, though viruses and fungi can also be involved. Typically affects the lungs, bloodstream, and other organs, with manifestations such as fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and altered mental status. Early recognition and treatment are critical to prevent progression to septic shock.

Sepsis with septic shock is a life-threatening condition resulting from a dysregulated immune response to infection, leading to systemic inflammation, hemodynamic instability, and organ dysfunction. Common synonyms include septic shock and severe sepsis. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, though viruses and fungi can also be responsible. The condition typically affects the circulatory system, lungs, kidneys, and liver, with widespread tissue hypoperfusion and multi-organ failure. Early recognition and aggressive management are critical to improving outcomes.

code_desc: mycetoma of unknown or unspecified type
summary: Mycetoma of unknown or unspecified type is a chronic, granulomatous infection characterized by the formation of subcutaneous nodules and sinus tracts with purulent discharge. It is typically caused by filamentous fungi or actinomycetes, though the exact agent may not be identified. Common synonyms include madura foot and chromoblastomycosis. The infection most commonly affects the feet, legs, and hands, often in tropical or subtropical regions. It presents with progressive swelling, pain, and disfigurement, and may lead to severe disability if left untreated. Diagnosis is based on clinical features and microbiological examination of discharge.

Pythiosis is a chronic, granulomatous fungal infection caused primarily by *Pythium insulare* and *Pythium debaryanum*. It commonly affects the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and mucous membranes, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. The infection often presents as painless, slowly expanding nodules or ulcers, which may lead to tissue necrosis. Synonyms include phytophthora disease and pythiaceous mycosis. It is more prevalent in individuals with compromised immune systems or those exposed to contaminated water or soil. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent severe complications.

Protothecosis is a rare, opportunistic fungal infection caused by species of *Prototheca*, which are non-photosynthetic algae. Common synonyms include algal infection or protothecal infection. The primary causative agents are *Prototheca zopfii* and *Prototheca wickerhamii*. Typically affecting immunocompromised individuals, the infection most commonly involves the skin, eyes, and occasionally the central nervous system or internal organs. It presents as chronic, granulomatous inflammation with possible abscess formation. Diagnosis is often confirmed through histopathology and culture. Treatment may involve antifungal agents, though response can be variable.

code_desc: other specified disorders of infectious origin not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other specified disorders of infectious origin not elsewhere classified" refers to infectious conditions that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified infectious diseases. Causative agents vary widely, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. These disorders typically affect multiple body systems, with common involvement of the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and skin systems. Symptoms depend on the pathogen and site of infection, often including fever, inflammation, and systemic manifestations. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and laboratory findings when specific etiologies are not identified.

Sequelae of tuberculosis refer to long-term complications or residual damage following active tuberculosis infection. Common synonyms include post-tuberculosis complications or tuberculosis-related sequelae. The causative agent is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These sequelae typically affect the lungs, leading to fibrosis, cavities, or bronchiectasis. They may also involve the pleura, causing pleural thickening or effusion. In some cases, extrapulmonary tuberculosis can result in damage to other organs such as the kidneys, spine, or brain. Symptoms may include chronic cough, dyspnea, and fatigue. Early diagnosis and treatment can reduce the risk of developing these long-term complications.

Sequelae of trachoma refer to long-term complications arising from repeated *Chlamydia trachomatis* infections, primarily affecting the conjunctiva and cornea. Common synonyms include trachomatous scarring and trachomatous trichiasis. The condition leads to irreversible conjunctival scarring, eyelash inversion, and corneal opacity, ultimately causing chronic eye irritation, pain, and potentially blindness. It predominantly affects the ocular surface, with the lower eyelid and cornea being the most commonly involved structures. The disease is prevalent in areas with poor hygiene and limited access to healthcare.

Sequelae of leproy refer to long-term complications arising from untreated or inadequately treated leprosy, caused primarily by *Mycobacterium leprae*. Common synonyms include leprosy complications or post-leprosy disabilities. The disease primarily affects the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucosa of the upper respiratory tract. Untreated cases may lead to nerve damage, resulting in loss of sensation, muscle weakness, and deformities. Skin lesions may progress to ulcers and nodules. Late complications include claw hand, foot drop, and facial disfigurement. These sequelae can significantly impact physical function and quality of life. Early diagnosis and multidrug therapy are crucial to prevent progression.

Sequelae of poliomyelitis refer to long-term complications resulting from poliovirus infection, which primarily affects the central nervous system. Common synonyms include post-polio syndrome and residual paralysis. The causative agent is the poliovirus, which leads to neuronal damage, particularly in the spinal cord. Typically affected body parts include the lower limbs, resulting in muscle atrophy, weakness, and deformities. Other sequelae may involve joint contractures, respiratory insufficiency, and fatigue. These manifestations often develop years after the initial infection, as surviving motor neurons degenerate over time.

Sequelae of viral encephalitis refer to long-term neurological complications following an infection of the brain by a virus. Common synonyms include post-encephalitic syndrome or chronic encephalitis. Causative agents include herpes simplex virus, enteroviruses, and West Nile virus. These sequelae typically affect the central nervous system, leading to cognitive deficits, motor impairments, seizures, and psychiatric symptoms. The condition may result in permanent disability and requires multidisciplinary management.

Sequelae of diphtheria refer to long-term complications arising after recovery from diphtheria infection. Caused primarily by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*, the disease can lead to severe systemic effects. Common sequelae include myocarditis, peripheral neuropathy, and laryngeal stenosis. These complications result from toxin-mediated damage to tissues. Myocarditis may cause heart failure, while neuropathy often involves cranial nerves. Laryngeal involvement can lead to airway obstruction. The condition predominantly affects the respiratory tract, cardiovascular system, and nervous system. Prompt treatment with antitoxin and antibiotics is crucial to minimize long-term damage.

code_desc: sequelae of other specified infectious diseases
summary: Sequelae of other specified infectious diseases refer to long-term complications or residual effects following an infection caused by specific pathogens. Common synonyms include late effects or post-infectious complications. Causative agents vary widely, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites. These sequelae often affect multiple body systems, with common involvement of the respiratory, neurological, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal systems. Symptoms may include chronic pain, organ dysfunction, or neurological deficits, depending on the original infection and its impact on host tissues.

Infection, unspecified, refers to a microbial invasion of body tissues causing localized or systemic inflammation. It may present with fever, pain, swelling, and malaise. Common synonyms include "infection, unspecified site" or "infection, unspecified type." Causative agents can include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites. Typically affected body parts vary depending on the source, but common sites include the respiratory tract, urinary tract, skin, and bloodstream. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and laboratory testing. Treatment depends on the identified pathogen and severity of the infection.

Acute nasopharyngitis, commonly known as a common cold, is an inflammatory condition affecting the nasal passages and pharynx. It is typically caused by viral infections, most commonly rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, and adenoviruses. The condition presents with symptoms such as nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, and cough. It primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, including the nose, nasopharynx, and throat. It is highly contagious and usually self-limiting, resolving within 7–10 days without specific treatment. Bacterial causes are rare unless complications arise.

Acute sinusitis is an inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting less than four weeks, typically following a viral upper respiratory infection. Common synonyms include acute rhinosinusitis. It is often caused by viral agents, though bacterial pathogens like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis* may contribute. The condition primarily affects the maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses, leading to symptoms such as nasal congestion, facial pain, and purulent nasal discharge. It is more common in adults and can sometimes be associated with allergies or nasal structural abnormalities.

Acute pharyngitis is an inflammation of the pharynx, commonly presenting with sore throat, pain, and difficulty swallowing. It is often caused by viral infections, though bacterial pathogens such as *Streptococcus pyogenes* can also be responsible. Common synonyms include acute sore throat and pharyngitis. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, with symptoms often extending to the tonsils and larynx. It is more prevalent in children and young adults, typically resolving within a week without specific treatment in viral cases.

Acute bacterial pharyngitis is an inflammation of the pharynx caused by bacterial infection, commonly presenting with sore throat, fever, and swollen lymph nodes. Common synonyms include strep throat and bacterial pharyngitis. The most frequent causative agent is *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Group A streptococcus). Other bacteria, such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Moraxella catarrhalis*, may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, tonsils, and surrounding lymphoid tissues, often leading to exudate and potential complications if untreated.

Acute viral pharyngitis is an inflammatory condition of the pharynx caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include viral sore throat and acute pharyngitis. It is typically characterized by soreness, redness, and swelling of the pharyngeal mucosa. Common causative agents include rhinovirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. The condition primarily affects the pharynx, with possible involvement of the tonsils and larynx. It is more common in children and often presents with systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. The illness is usually self-limiting and resolves within a week without specific treatment.

Pharyngitis due to adenovirus is an inflammatory condition of the pharynx caused by adenoviral infection. Common synonyms include viral pharyngitis and acute pharyngitis. Adenovirus is the primary causative agent, though other viruses may contribute. The infection typically affects the pharyngeal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as sore throat, fever, and lymphadenopathy. It is more common in children but can occur in adults. The illness is usually self-limiting, with resolution within 7–14 days. Complications are rare but may include bronchiolitis or pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals.

Other specified acute viral pharyngitis refers to inflammation of the pharynx caused by viruses not classified under more specific diagnoses such as streptococcal pharyngitis. Common synonyms include viral sore throat or viral pharyngitis. Causative agents include rhinovirus, adenovirus, influenza virus, and coronavirus. The condition typically affects the pharyngeal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as sore throat, redness, and sometimes exudate. It is commonly seen in children and adolescents, often following upper respiratory tract infections.

Acute viral pharyngitis, unspecified, is an inflammation of the pharynx caused by a viral infection. Common synonyms include viral sore throat and acute pharyngitis. It is typically caused by rhinoviruses, adenoviruses, and influenza viruses. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as sore throat, fever, and swollen lymph nodes. It is a common upper respiratory infection, often self-limiting, and more prevalent in children. The exact causative agent is usually not identified in clinical practice.
