Other specified acute pharyngitis refers to inflammation of the pharynx not classified as viral, bacterial, or due to a known specific agent. It encompasses cases where the cause is unclear or not otherwise specified. Common synonyms include nonspecific acute pharyngitis. Causative agents may include environmental irritants, allergens, or viral agents not typically associated with pharyngitis. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, causing symptoms such as sore throat, irritation, and difficulty swallowing. It is commonly seen in individuals exposed to irritants or those with underlying respiratory conditions.

Acute pharyngitis, unspecified, refers to sudden inflammation of the pharynx without a specified cause. Common synonyms include acute sore throat and pharyngitis. It is typically caused by viral agents such as rhinovirus, adenovirus, or influenza virus, though bacterial causes like Group A Streptococcus may also occur. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as pain, dryness, and difficulty swallowing. It commonly involves the posterior pharyngeal wall and may extend to the tonsillar regions. The illness is usually self-limiting, resolving within a few days.

Acute tonsillitis is an inflammation of the tonsils, typically caused by viral or bacterial infection. Common synonyms include acute sore throat and tonsillar infection. The most frequent causative agents are Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, adenovirus, and rhinovirus. It primarily affects the palatine tonsils, leading to symptoms such as sore throat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, and white or yellow exudates on the tonsils. The condition is common in children but can occur in adults. Complications may include peritonsillar abscess or rheumatic fever if streptococcal.

Streptococcal tonsillitis is an acute bacterial infection of the pharynx, primarily caused by Group A Streptococcus (GAS). It presents with sore throat, fever, and visible exudate on the tonsils. Common synonyms include strep throat and acute pharyngitis. The infection typically affects the tonsils, pharyngeal walls, and adjacent lymphoid tissues. It is more common in children but can occur in adults. Complications may include peritonsillar abscess or rheumatic fever if untreated. Diagnosis is often confirmed via rapid antigen detection or throat culture. Treatment involves antibiotic therapy to prevent complications.

Other specified acute tonsillitis refers to inflammation of the tonsils caused by non-specific agents, typically viral or bacterial in origin, when the exact pathogen cannot be definitively identified. Common synonyms include acute tonsillitis of unspecified cause. It often presents with sore throat, fever, and swollen tonsils. Known causative agents include Streptococcus pyogenes, adenovirus, and rhinovirus. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal tonsils, with possible involvement of the surrounding lymphoid tissues. It is most common in children and adolescents.

Acute tonsillitis, unspecified, is a sudden inflammation of the tonsils, typically causing pain, swelling, and redness. It is commonly caused by viral agents such as adenovirus or Epstein-Barr virus, though bacterial causes like group A Streptococcus may also occur. Symptoms include sore throat, fever, and difficulty swallowing. The condition primarily affects the palatine tonsils, located at the back of the throat. Common synonyms include acute sore throat and tonsillar inflammation. It predominantly affects children and young adults.

Acute laryngopharyngitis is an inflammation of the larynx and pharynx, often presenting with sore throat, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Common synonyms include acute pharyngolaryngitis and acute laryngitis with pharyngeal involvement. It is typically caused by viral agents such as rhinovirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. Bacterial causes, like Streptococcus pyogenes, may also contribute. The condition primarily affects the pharyngeal and laryngeal mucosa, with symptoms often resolving within 7–10 days without specific treatment.

Acute laryngitis or tracheitis refers to inflammation of the larynx or trachea, typically caused by viral infections such as influenza or rhinovirus. Common synonyms include acute upper airway infection or croup. It presents with symptoms like hoarseness, cough, and stridor. The condition primarily affects the laryngeal mucosa and tracheal lining. Bacterial causes, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, may occur secondary to viral infections. It is more common in children but can affect individuals of all ages. Risk factors include viral exposure, upper respiratory tract infections, and irritants.

Acute laryngitis is an inflammation of the larynx, typically caused by viral infections, though bacterial or fungal causes may occur. It presents with symptoms such as hoarseness, sore throat, and a dry cough. Common synonyms include laryngeal inflammation or acute pharyngolaryngitis. The condition primarily affects the vocal cords and surrounding mucosal tissues of the larynx. It is more common in adults and children, often following upper respiratory tract infections. Risk factors include vocal strain, smoking, and exposure to irritants. Most cases resolve spontaneously within 1–2 weeks without specific treatment.

Acute tracheitis is an inflammatory condition of the trachea, typically presenting with a sudden onset of cough, stridor, and respiratory distress. It is commonly caused by viral infections, though bacterial agents such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Haemophilus influenzae* may also be involved. The condition often follows upper respiratory tract infections and is more prevalent in children. Symptoms may include fever, hoarseness, and chest discomfort. The trachea is the primary affected site, with inflammation leading to narrowing of the airway. Synonyms include acute tracheobronchitis and laryngotracheitis.

Acute laryngotracheitis is an acute inflammation of the larynx and trachea, commonly presenting with a barking cough, stridor, and hoarseness. It predominantly affects children, particularly those under five years old. Common synonyms include croup and acute laryngotracheobronchitis. The primary causative agent is the parainfluenza virus, though respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza viruses may also be responsible. The condition typically involves the larynx, trachea, and upper airway, leading to airway narrowing and respiratory distress.

Acute obstructive laryngitis or epiglottitis is a sudden inflammation of the larynx or epiglottis, leading to airway obstruction. Common synonyms include acute laryngotracheobronchitis and epiglottic swelling. It is often caused by viral infections, particularly parainfluenza virus, or bacterial agents like Haemophilus influenzae. The condition primarily affects the larynx, epiglottis, and surrounding airway structures. It is most common in children but can occur in adults. Symptoms include stridor, dyspnea, fever, and a high-pitched cough. Rapid onset and potential for airway compromise require prompt medical evaluation.

Acute obstructive laryngitis is an inflammation of the larynx causing airway narrowing, often leading to stridor and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include acute laryngotracheitis and croup. It is typically caused by viral infections, most commonly parainfluenza viruses, but may also result from bacterial infections, allergens, or irritants. The condition primarily affects the larynx and upper trachea, with symptoms often worsening at night. It is most common in young children due to their smaller airways and anatomical predisposition. Prompt recognition is essential to prevent complications such as airway obstruction.

Acute epiglottitis is a severe, potentially life-threatening inflammation of the epiglottis, typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Haemophilus influenzae* type b. It leads to rapid swelling and obstruction of the upper airway, causing difficulty breathing, stridor, and drooling. Common synonyms include acute laryngitis, epiglottic swelling, and laryngotracheitis. The condition primarily affects the epiglottis and surrounding structures of the larynx, predominantly in children, though it can occur in adults. Prompt diagnosis and management are critical to prevent airway compromise.

code_desc: Acute obstructive laryngitis or epiglottitis, unspecified
summary: Acute obstructive laryngitis or epiglottitis refers to sudden inflammation and swelling of the larynx or epiglottis, leading to airway obstruction. Common synonyms include acute laryngeal obstruction and epiglottic inflammation. Causative agents often include viral infections such as parainfluenza, influenza, and adenovirus, though bacterial causes like Haemophilus influenzae may also occur. The condition primarily affects the larynx, epiglottis, and surrounding airway structures, commonly seen in children. It presents with severe sore throat, stridor, and difficulty breathing, requiring prompt medical evaluation and management.

code_desc: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple and unspecified sites
summary: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple and unspecified sites refer to infections involving multiple areas of the upper respiratory tract without specific localization. Common synonyms include viral pharyngitis and rhinopharyngitis. These infections are typically caused by viruses such as rhinovirus, adenovirus, and influenza virus. They commonly affect the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and sometimes the ears. Symptoms include sore throat, runny nose, cough, and fever. They are generally self-limiting and more prevalent in children. Bacterial causes are less common but may occur in secondary infections.

code_desc: Acute upper respiratory infection, site unspecified
summary: Acute upper respiratory infection, site unspecified, refers to a short-term infection affecting the upper respiratory tract without a specific site identified. Common synonyms include common cold, viral coryza, or acute rhinosinusitis. It is typically caused by viruses such as rhinovirus, coronavirus, and influenza virus. The infection commonly affects the nose, throat, and sometimes the sinuses. Symptoms include nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, and fever. It is generally self-limiting and more prevalent in children, though adults can also be affected. Bacterial causes are less common but may occur in complications such as sinusitis or otitis media.

code_desc: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple sites
summary: Acute upper respiratory infections of multiple sites refer to viral infections affecting multiple areas of the upper respiratory tract. Common synonyms include common cold, rhinopharyngitis, and upper respiratory tract infection. Causative agents are primarily rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, and influenza viruses. Typically affected body parts include the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and sometimes the ears. Symptoms often involve rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, and fever. The condition is self-limiting and commonly occurs during seasonal changes.

Vasomotor or allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages characterized by symptoms such as sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, and itching. It can be triggered by allergens like pollen, dust mites, or pet dander, or by non-allergic factors such as temperature changes, odors, or irritants. Common synonyms include allergic rhinitis, hay fever, and non-allergic rhinitis. The primary affected body parts are the nasal mucosa and paranasal sinuses. It is a common condition that can significantly impact quality of life.

Allergic rhinitis is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by an immune response to allergens. Common synonyms include hay fever and allergic rhinitis. It is caused by allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold spores, and pet dander. The condition typically affects the nose, leading to symptoms like sneezing, nasal congestion, runny nose, and itching. It may also involve the eyes, throat, and ears, causing allergic conjunctivitis and postnasal drip. The disease is often seasonal or perennial, depending on the allergen. It is a common condition, affecting millions worldwide, and is often managed with antihistamines, nasal corticosteroids, and allergen avoidance.

Allergic rhinitis due to pollen, commonly known as hay fever, is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by an immune response to airborne pollen. It typically presents with symptoms such as sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and itching. Common causative agents include grass, tree, and weed pollens. The condition primarily affects the upper respiratory tract, particularly the nose, and may also involve the eyes, leading to allergic conjunctivitis. It is a prevalent allergic disorder, often with a seasonal pattern, and can significantly impact quality of life.

code_desc: Allergic rhinitis due to other seasonal allergens
summary: Allergic rhinitis due to other seasonal allergens refers to inflammation of the nasal passages triggered by airborne allergens that are not pollen or dust mites. Common synonyms include non-pollen seasonal allergic rhinitis and seasonal allergic rhinitis (non-pollen type). Causative agents may include mold spores, animal dander, or other environmental irritants. The condition typically affects the nasal cavity, leading to symptoms such as sneezing, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea. It often occurs seasonally, with symptoms peaking during specific times of the year when allergen exposure is high.

code_desc: Allergic rhinitis due to house dust mite
summary: Allergic rhinitis due to house dust mite is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by allergens from house dust mites. Common synonyms include allergic rhinitis and hay fever. The primary causative agents are the proteins from the fecal matter of *Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus* and *Dermatophagoides farinae*. This condition typically affects the nasal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as sneezing, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea. It may also involve the eyes, causing conjunctival irritation. The disease is chronic and often begins in childhood, with symptoms exacerbated by environmental factors like humidity and temperature changes.

Other allergic rhinitis refers to an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by an immune response to allergens. Common synonyms include allergic rhinitis not otherwise specified (AR-NOS) and non-IgE-mediated rhinitis. Causative agents often include environmental allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold spores, and pet dander. The primary affected body parts are the nasal mucosa, leading to symptoms like sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and itching. It may also affect the eyes, causing allergic conjunctivitis. The condition is typically seasonal or perennial, depending on the allergen exposure.

Allergic rhinitis, unspecified, is an inflammatory condition of the nasal passages triggered by an immune response to allergens. Common synonyms include hay fever and allergic rhinitis. It is typically caused by inhalation of allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold spores, or animal dander. The condition primarily affects the nasal mucosa, leading to symptoms like sneezing, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and itching. It may also involve the eyes, causing conjunctival irritation. The disease is chronic and often begins in childhood, with symptoms fluctuating based on allergen exposure.

Non-allergic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nasal passages not mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies. It commonly presents with symptoms such as nasal congestion, runny nose, and postnasal drip. Common synonyms include vasomotor rhinitis and non-allergic nasal inflammation. Causative agents may include environmental irritants like smoke, perfumes, temperature changes, and humidity. It typically affects the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, with symptoms often triggered by non-allergic stimuli. The condition is more prevalent in adults and can be persistent or intermittent in nature.

Non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophils (NARE) is a chronic inflammation of the nasal passages characterized by eosinophilic infiltration without evidence of allergic triggers. Common synonyms include eosinophilic rhinitis and non-allergic eosinophilic rhinitis. It is often associated with nasal polyps and may be linked to environmental exposures such as irritants, infections, or occupational agents. Symptoms include nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and postnasal drip. The condition primarily affects the nasal mucosa and may involve the paranasal sinuses. It is more common in adults and can coexist with asthma or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.

Other specified non-allergic rhinitis refers to rhinitis symptoms not caused by allergies, with no specific underlying condition identified. Common synonyms include idiopathic rhinitis and nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia syndrome. Causative agents may include environmental irritants, hormonal changes, medications, or viral infections. Symptoms typically affect the nasal passages, causing congestion, runniness, and postnasal drip. It often occurs without nasal polyps or significant eosinophilia. The condition is chronic and may require management with nasal sprays or lifestyle modifications.

Non-allergic rhinitis, unspecified, is a chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa not mediated by immunoglobulin E. It presents with symptoms such as nasal congestion, runny nose, and postnasal drip. Common synonyms include vasomotor rhinitis and non-allergic rhinitis without nasal polyps. Causative agents may include environmental irritants like smoke, pollution, temperature changes, and strong odors. It commonly affects the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, with symptoms often triggered by non-specific stimuli. The condition is more prevalent in adults and can be challenging to manage due to its variable presentation and lack of specific allergens.

Mixed rhinitis refers to the presence of both allergic and non-allergic rhinitis symptoms. It is characterized by nasal congestion, runny nose, and sneezing, often with variable severity. Common synonyms include combined or dual rhinitis. Causative agents may include allergens such as pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as irritants like smoke, perfumes, and changes in temperature. The condition primarily affects the nasal passages, with symptoms often extending to the sinuses and throat. It is more prevalent in adults and can be challenging to manage due to overlapping symptoms with other nasal conditions.

Vasomotor rhinitis is a non-allergic, inflammatory condition characterized by episodic nasal congestion, runny nose, and postnasal drip, often triggered by environmental stimuli. Common synonyms include non-allergic rhinitis and hyperreactive rhinitis. It is caused by autonomic nervous system dysfunction, though specific causative agents are not well defined. The condition primarily affects the nasal passages, with symptoms often worsening in response to temperature changes, humidity, or irritants. It typically occurs in adults and is not associated with eosinophils or IgE-mediated immune responses.

Chronic rhinitis, nasopharyngitis, or pharyngitis refers to persistent inflammation of the nasal passages, nasopharynx, or pharynx. Common synonyms include chronic nasal congestion, postnasal drip, and sore throat. Causative agents may include viral infections, allergens, irritants, or bacterial pathogens. These conditions typically affect the upper respiratory tract, including the nose, nasopharynx, and throat. Symptoms often include nasal obstruction, runny nose, postnasal drainage, and sore throat. Chronic cases may result from ongoing exposure to irritants or unresolved acute infections.

Chronic rhinitis is a persistent inflammation of the nasal mucosa lasting more than 12 weeks. It is characterized by symptoms such as nasal congestion, runny nose, postnasal drip, and reduced sense of smell. Common synonyms include chronic rhinosinusitis and perennial rhinitis. Causative agents may include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and pet dander, as well as irritants, infections, or anatomical abnormalities. The condition primarily affects the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses, often leading to discomfort and impaired quality of life.

Chronic nasopharyngitis is a persistent inflammation of the nasopharynx, often characterized by symptoms such as nasal congestion, postnasal drip, and a sore throat. Common synonyms include chronic pharyngitis and persistent nasopharyngeal inflammation. It is typically caused by recurrent viral infections, allergens, or environmental irritants. Bacterial agents like *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae* may also contribute. The condition primarily affects the nasopharynx, but may extend to the nasal passages and oropharynx, leading to secondary complications such as sinusitis or otitis media.

Chronic pharyngitis is a persistent inflammation of the pharynx, often lasting more than three months. Common synonyms include chronic sore throat and laryngopharyngeal reflux. It is commonly caused by recurrent infections, postnasal drip, allergens, or irritants. Known causative agents include bacteria such as *Streptococcus* species, viruses, and environmental irritants like cigarette smoke. The condition typically affects the pharyngeal mucosa, with symptoms including sore throat, dryness, and a sensation of a foreign body. It may also involve the larynx and tonsils. Long-term exposure to irritants or underlying conditions like GERD can contribute to its development.

Chronic rhinosinusitis is a persistent inflammatory disorder of the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses lasting more than 12 weeks. Common synonyms include chronic sinusitis and rhinosinusitis. It is often caused by bacterial, viral, or fungal infections, though allergens and immune responses also play a role. The condition primarily affects the nasal cavity and maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses. Symptoms include nasal congestion, facial pain, and impaired sense of smell. It may lead to complications such as nasal polyps or orbital involvement if left untreated.

Samter syndrome, also known as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), is a triad of asthma, nasal polyps, and aspirin sensitivity. It is characterized by chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and a heightened reaction to aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The condition is often associated with a genetic predisposition and involves an abnormal inflammatory response, particularly involving leukotrienes. Commonly affected body parts include the nasal passages, paranasal sinuses, and lungs. Causative agents include aspirin and other NSAIDs, though the exact mechanism remains complex and multifactorial.

Other specified chronic rhinosinusitis refers to chronic inflammation of the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses that does not meet the criteria for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps or chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps. It is often used when the underlying cause is unclear or when symptoms are atypical. Common synonyms include unspecified chronic rhinosinusitis. Known causative agents may include allergens, irritants, or infections. Typically affects the nasal cavity and maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.

Chronic rhinosinusitis, unspecified, is a long-term inflammation of the nasal passages and paranasal sinuses lasting more than 12 weeks. It is characterized by symptoms such as nasal obstruction, facial pain, and nasal discharge. Common synonyms include chronic sinusitis and chronic rhinitis. Causative agents may include bacterial, viral, or fungal infections, along with allergens and environmental irritants. The condition primarily affects the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, with potential involvement of the throat and ears. It is often associated with structural abnormalities or immune responses.

Silent sinus syndrome is a rare condition characterized by progressive atrophy of the maxillary sinus and subsequent retraction of the orbital floor, leading to enophthalmos and diplopia. It is often asymptomatic, hence the term "silent." Common synonyms include pneumatization defect of the maxillary sinus and inverted papillae of the maxillary sinus. The condition is typically caused by chronic sinusitis or mucoceles, leading to volume loss in the sinus. It predominantly affects the maxillary sinus and can involve the orbit, causing visual and ocular motility disturbances.

code_desc: Cyst or mucocele of nose or nasal sinus
summary: A cyst or mucocele of the nose or nasal sinus is a fluid-filled lesion resulting from the obstruction of a mucous gland duct, leading to mucous retention. Common synonyms include nasal mucocele and mucous retention cyst. It is typically caused by trauma, infection, or anatomical obstruction. The condition most commonly affects the maxillary sinus, ethmoid sinus, or nasal cavity. It presents as a painless, slowly enlarging swelling, potentially causing nasal obstruction or facial deformity if left untreated.

A deviated nasal septum is a condition characterized by the displacement of the nasal septum, the structure dividing the nasal cavity into two halves, to one side. This deviation can lead to obstructed breathing, nasal congestion, and recurrent sinus infections. Common synonyms include septal deviation and septal shift. Causative agents often include congenital factors, trauma, or developmental abnormalities. The condition primarily affects the nasal passages, potentially impacting airflow and contributing to chronic rhinosinusitis or sleep apnea. It is most commonly observed in the nasal cavity and may involve the turbinates and sinuses.

Hypertrophy of nasal turbinates refers to the abnormal enlargement of the inferior, middle, or superior nasal turbinates, leading to nasal obstruction. Common synonyms include nasal turbinate hypertrophy and nasal congestion due to turbinate enlargement. This condition is often caused by chronic inflammation, allergies, infections, or anatomical abnormalities. It primarily affects the nasal cavity, particularly the turbinates, and may result in symptoms such as nasal congestion, postnasal drip, and reduced sense of smell. The inferior turbinate is most commonly involved.

code_desc: Chronic diseases of tonsils or adenoids
summary: Chronic diseases of tonsils or adenoids refer to long-standing inflammation or enlargement of the palatine tonsils or pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids). Common synonyms include chronic tonsillitis and chronic adenoid hypertrophy. These conditions are often caused by recurrent bacterial or viral infections, such as Streptococcus pyogenes. They predominantly affect the throat, nasal passages, and ears, leading to symptoms like sore throat, snoring, and hearing loss. Chronic cases may require medical or surgical intervention to alleviate symptoms and prevent complications.

Hypertrophy of tonsils refers to the abnormal enlargement of the palatine tonsils, often leading to obstructive symptoms. Common synonyms include tonsillar hypertrophy and enlarged tonsils. This condition is typically caused by chronic inflammation, recurrent infections, or allergic reactions. The tonsils, located in the oropharynx, are the most commonly affected structures. It may also involve the adenoids in children. Symptoms include difficulty breathing, snoring, and swallowing. It is more prevalent in children but can occur in adults. Treatment may involve medical management or surgical removal.

Hypertrophy of adenoids refers to the abnormal enlargement of the lymphoid tissue located in the nasopharynx. Common synonyms include adenoid hypertrophy and nasopharyngeal lymphoid hyperplasia. This condition is often caused by chronic inflammation, recurrent infections, or allergic reactions. It typically affects children and can lead to nasal obstruction, breathing difficulties, and sleep disturbances. The enlarged adenoids may also contribute to ear infections and speech changes. The primary affected body parts include the nasopharynx, Eustachian tubes, and upper airway.

code_desc: Hypertrophy of tonsils with hypertrophy of adenoids
summary: Hypertrophy of tonsils with hypertrophy of adenoids refers to the abnormal enlargement of both the palatine tonsils and the adenoids, commonly seen in children. This condition may result from chronic inflammation, recurrent infections, or allergic reactions. Common synonyms include enlarged tonsils and adenoids or tonsillar and adenoidal hypertrophy. The primary affected areas are the oropharynx, where the tonsils are located, and the nasal cavity, where the adenoids reside. Causative agents often include bacteria such as Streptococcus pyogenes, viruses, and allergens.

code_desc: Other specified chronic diseases of tonsils or adenoids
summary: "Other specified chronic diseases of tonsils or adenoids" refers to long-standing inflammatory or structural conditions of the tonsils or adenoids not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include chronic tonsillitis or adenoid hypertrophy. Causative agents may include recurrent bacterial or viral infections, allergies, or immune responses. These conditions typically affect the pharyngeal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and adenoids, leading to symptoms such as obstructive sleep apnea, recurrent sore throats, or breathing difficulties. They are more common in children but can occur in adults.

code_desc: Chronic diseases of tonsils or adenoids, unspecified
summary: Chronic diseases of tonsils or adenoids, unspecified, refer to long-standing inflammation or dysfunction of the tonsils or adenoids without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include chronic tonsillitis or chronic adenoiditis. These conditions are often caused by recurrent bacterial or viral infections, though no single pathogen is consistently identified. They typically affect the pharyngeal tonsils, palatine tonsils, and adenoids, leading to symptoms such as sore throat, breathing difficulties, and sleep disturbances. The condition is more prevalent in children but can occur in adults.

Chronic laryngitis or laryngotracheitis refers to prolonged inflammation of the larynx and/or trachea, often resulting from recurrent or persistent irritation. Common synonyms include chronic pharyngolaryngitis and chronic laryngotracheal inflammation. Causative agents may include viral infections, prolonged vocal strain, environmental irritants, acid reflux, or chronic smoking. The condition primarily affects the larynx, trachea, and surrounding structures, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, chronic cough, and throat discomfort. It is more common in individuals with occupational voice use or underlying respiratory conditions.

code_desc: Diseases of vocal cords or larynx, not elsewhere classified
summary: Diseases of vocal cords or larynx, not elsewhere classified, refer to conditions affecting the laryngeal structures not specifically categorized elsewhere. Common synonyms include laryngitis, vocal cord disorders, and laryngeal pathology. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viruses, bacteria), trauma, irritants, or chronic overuse. Typically affecting the vocal cords, arytenoids, and epiglottis, these conditions may present with hoarseness, dysphonia, or respiratory symptoms. They can be acute or chronic, often requiring evaluation by an otolaryngologist.

code_desc: Paralysis of vocal cords or larynx
summary: Paralysis of the vocal cords or larynx refers to the loss of motor function in the muscles controlling the larynx, leading to impaired vocalization and breathing. Common synonyms include laryngeal palsy and vocal cord palsy. This condition can result from neurological disorders such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, or trauma. It may also arise from infections, tumors, or surgical complications. The primary affected areas are the vocal cords, arytenoids, and surrounding laryngeal structures. Symptoms include hoarseness, stridor, and difficulty swallowing. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve speech therapy, medication, or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Polyp of vocal cord or larynx
summary: A polyp of the vocal cord or larynx is a benign, soft tissue growth that develops on the vocal folds or other structures within the larynx. Common synonyms include vocal cord polyp, laryngeal polyp, or vocal fold polyp. It is often caused by vocal abuse, chronic irritation, or inflammation. The condition typically affects the vocal cords, leading to symptoms such as hoarseness, voice fatigue, and breathiness. While most polyps are non-cancerous, they may require removal if they interfere with normal voice function or cause discomfort.

Nodules of the vocal cords are benign growths that develop on the vocal folds, typically due to vocal overuse or strain. Common synonyms include vocal nodules, singer's nodules, and vocal cord nodules. They are often caused by repetitive vocal abuse, such as in professional voice users. These lesions usually affect the anterior and middle portions of the vocal cords, leading to symptoms like hoarseness, breathiness, and vocal fatigue. They are most commonly found in adults, particularly those with occupations requiring frequent voice use.

Oedema of the larynx, also known as laryngeal edema or laryngeal swelling, is a condition characterized by swelling of the laryngeal tissues, leading to airway obstruction. It can result from allergic reactions, infections, trauma, or anaphylaxis. Common causative agents include allergens, irritants, and certain medications. The condition typically affects the vocal cords, epiglottis, and surrounding mucosal tissues. Symptoms include hoarseness, stridor, and difficulty breathing. It is a medical emergency when severe, requiring prompt intervention to prevent airway compromise.

Laryngeal spasm is an abrupt, involuntary contraction of the laryngeal muscles, leading to transient airway obstruction. Common synonyms include laryngospasm and spasmodic laryngitis. It is often triggered by irritation, allergens, or acid reflux, and may occur during intubation or in response to foreign bodies. The condition typically affects the vocal cords and surrounding structures of the larynx. Symptoms include stridor, coughing, and difficulty breathing, often resolving spontaneously. It is more common in children and can be associated with conditions like asthma or gastroesophageal reflux disease.

Stenosis of the larynx refers to the narrowing of the laryngeal airway, leading to breathing difficulties. Common synonyms include laryngeal stricture and laryngeal stenosis. It can result from trauma, prolonged intubation, infection, or inflammation. Causative agents include scar tissue, granulomatous diseases, and neoplasms. The condition typically affects the glottis, subglottis, or supraglottis, often causing hoarseness, stridor, and respiratory distress. It is more common in adults but can occur in children following infections or injury. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent airway compromise.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of vocal cords or larynx, not elsewhere classified
summary: "Other specified diseases of vocal cords or larynx, not elsewhere classified" refers to laryngeal conditions that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified laryngeal disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., viruses, bacteria), trauma, or environmental irritants. Typically affects the vocal cords, glottis, and surrounding laryngeal structures. Symptoms may involve hoarseness, dysphonia, or breathing difficulties. This category encompasses a range of conditions with variable etiologies and presentations.

code_desc: Diseases of vocal cords or larynx, not elsewhere classified, unspecified
summary: Diseases of vocal cords or larynx, not elsewhere classified, unspecified, refer to inflammatory or structural conditions affecting the larynx without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include laryngitis, laryngeal inflammation, or unspecified laryngeal disorders. Causative agents may include viral infections (e.g., Epstein-Barr virus), bacterial infections, irritants, or chronic overuse. Typically affects the vocal cords, arytenoids, and surrounding mucosal tissues, leading to symptoms like hoarseness, sore throat, and difficulty speaking. Often diagnosed when specific etiologies are not identified.

Nasal polyps are non-cancerous, inflammatory growths that develop in the nasal passages or paranasal sinuses. They are typically soft, edematous, and pedunculated, often leading to nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and loss of smell. Common synonyms include nasal polyps, ethmoidal polyps, and sinus polyps. The exact cause is multifactorial, but chronic inflammation, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and genetic factors are implicated. They most commonly affect the nasal cavity and ethmoid sinuses, with a predilection for the maxillary and frontal sinuses in some cases.

Polypoid sinus degeneration refers to the chronic inflammation and structural changes in the paranasal sinuses leading to the formation of polyps. Common synonyms include nasal polyps and chronic sinusitis with polypoid changes. It is often associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma, and chronic infections. The condition primarily affects the maxillary, ethmoid, and frontal sinuses. It is characterized by mucosal thickening, edema, and secretion accumulation, resulting in nasal obstruction, postnasal drip, and reduced sense of smell. The exact causative agents are multifactorial, involving immune responses and environmental factors.

Other specified nasal polyp refers to non-allergic, non-inflammatory polyps that occur in the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses, not fitting the criteria for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis or chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Common synonyms include non-allergic nasal polyps and idiopathic nasal polyps. Causative agents are often unclear, though chronic inflammation, environmental irritants, and genetic factors may contribute. These polyps typically affect the nasal passages and maxillary sinuses, causing symptoms such as nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and facial pressure.

Nasal polyp, unspecified, refers to the presence of non-cancerous, inflammatory growths in the nasal passages or paranasal sinuses. Common synonyms include ethmoidal polyps and sinus polyps. The condition is often associated with chronic inflammation, allergies, and conditions like asthma or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Causative agents include allergic rhinitis, infections, and immune responses. It typically affects the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, leading to symptoms such as nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, and hyposmia. The exact etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic and environmental factors.

An abscess of the upper respiratory tract is a localized collection of pus resulting from infection in the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, or pharynx. Common synonyms include nasal abscess, sinus abscess, and pharyngeal abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial pathogens such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *Anaerobes*. The condition most commonly affects the maxillary, frontal, or ethmoid sinuses, as well as the nasal septum and tonsillar regions. Symptoms include pain, swelling, fever, and difficulty breathing or swallowing. Prompt antibiotic therapy and drainage are essential for resolution.

Retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal abscess refers to a collection of pus in the retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal spaces, typically affecting children. Common synonyms include retropharyngeal infection or parapharyngeal cellulitis. Causative agents often include Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and anaerobes. These abscesses primarily affect the pharyngeal region, potentially extending into the neck. They are often associated with upper respiratory infections and can cause airway obstruction, dysphagia, and stridor. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications.

Peritonsillar abscess, also known as quinsy, is a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and the surrounding tissues. It typically arises from complications of acute tonsillitis, often due to Streptococcus pyogenes. The abscess most commonly affects the peritonsillar region, causing severe sore throat, trismus, and unilateral tonsillar swelling. Patients may present with fever, difficulty swallowing, and muffled voice. It predominantly occurs in adolescents and young adults. Other causative agents include Streptococcus viridans and anaerobic bacteria. The condition may spread to adjacent structures, leading to airway compromise if untreated.

code_desc: Other specified abscess of upper respiratory tract
summary: "Other specified abscess of upper respiratory tract" refers to localized collections of pus in the upper airway not classified elsewhere, such as peritonsillar or retropharyngeal abscesses. Common synonyms include peritonsillar abscess and retropharyngeal abscess. Causative agents often include Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and anaerobes. These abscesses typically affect the tonsillar region, pharynx, or surrounding soft tissues. They are often associated with infection following trauma, surgery, or upper respiratory tract infections. Clinical presentation includes fever, sore throat, dysphagia, and trismus. Prompt drainage and antibiotic therapy are essential for management.

code_desc: Abscess of upper respiratory tract, unspecified
summary: Abscess of the upper respiratory tract, unspecified, refers to a localized collection of pus in the upper airway structures, typically involving the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, or pharynx. Common synonyms include nasal abscess, sinus abscess, and pharyngeal abscess. It is most commonly caused by bacterial infections, with *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* being frequent pathogens. The condition often results from trauma, foreign bodies, or spread from adjacent infections. Symptoms include localized pain, swelling, fever, and difficulty breathing or swallowing. Prompt antibiotic therapy and drainage are usually required for resolution.

code_desc: Other specified upper respiratory tract disorders
summary: "Other specified upper respiratory tract disorders" refers to conditions affecting the nose, nasal sinuses, pharynx, or larynx that do not fit specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include rhinopharyngitis or acute upper respiratory infection. Causative agents may include viral pathogens like rhinovirus, bacteria such as Streptococcus, or environmental irritants. These disorders typically present with symptoms like nasal congestion, sore throat, and cough, primarily affecting the upper respiratory tract.

Upper respiratory tract disorders, unspecified refer to conditions affecting the nose, pharynx, larynx, or adjacent structures without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include acute rhinitis, pharyngitis, and laryngitis. Causative agents may include viral infections (e.g., rhinovirus, influenza), bacterial pathogens (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes), allergens, or irritants. These disorders typically present with symptoms such as nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, and hoarseness. They are common in both adults and children, often linked to environmental exposures or immune responses.

Bronchitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the bronchial tubes, leading to coughing, often with mucus, and sometimes wheezing. It can be acute or chronic. Common synonyms include bronchial inflammation and bronchial infection. The condition is typically caused by viral infections, though bacterial agents like *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* can also be responsible. Chronic bronchitis is often associated with smoking and long-term exposure to irritants. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi, with symptoms originating from the respiratory tract.

Acute noninfectious bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchial tubes not caused by infection. Common synonyms include acute bronchial inflammation and noninfectious bronchial irritation. It is often triggered by irritants such as smoke, dust, or chemical fumes. The condition typically affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like cough, mucus production, and wheezing. It is commonly seen in smokers and individuals exposed to environmental pollutants. Unlike infectious bronchitis, it does not involve bacterial or viral pathogens. The prognosis is generally favorable with removal of the irritant and supportive care.

Chronic bronchitis is a long-term inflammatory condition characterized by persistent cough and mucus production lasting at least three months per year for two consecutive years. It primarily affects the bronchial tubes, leading to airway obstruction and impaired lung function. Common synonyms include chronic obstructive bronchitis and chronic productive cough. Causative agents include cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational irritants. The condition predominantly impacts the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, and is a key component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Simple chronic bronchitis is a long-term inflammatory condition characterized by persistent cough and mucus production. It primarily affects the large airways, leading to bronchial hyperresponsiveness and airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and chronic cough with mucus. Causative agents include cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational irritants. The condition typically involves the trachea and bronchi, with symptoms worsening over time. It is often associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Mucopurulent chronic bronchitis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by persistent bronchial inflammation and increased mucus production, often with purulent (pus-like) secretions. It is commonly associated with long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke or air pollution. The primary affected areas are the large airways, including the bronchi. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and chronic obstructive bronchitis. Causative agents include respiratory pathogens like *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Moraxella catarrhalis*, as well as environmental irritants. The condition leads to airflow obstruction and increased risk of respiratory infections.

code_desc: Mixed simple and mucopurulent chronic bronchitis
summary: Mixed simple and mucopurulent chronic bronchitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the bronchial airways characterized by persistent cough and production of both clear (simple) and purulent (mucopurulent) sputum. It often results from long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, or occupational dusts. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis with mixed secretions. Causative agents include bacterial pathogens like *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae*, as well as viral infections. The condition primarily affects the large airways, including the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to mucosal inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance.

Protracted bacterial bronchitis is a chronic bronchial infection characterized by persistent cough lasting more than four weeks, often accompanied by mucus production. Common synonyms include bacterial bronchitis and chronic bronchitis. It is typically caused by *Bordetella pertussis*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*. The condition primarily affects the large airways, including the trachea and bronchi, and is most commonly seen in children, though it can occur in adults. Clinical features include cough with or without fever, and it may mimic asthma or other chronic respiratory conditions.

Other specified chronic bronchitis refers to chronic inflammation of the bronchial airways not classified under other specific types of chronic bronchitis. It is characterized by persistent cough and mucus production for at least three months in two consecutive years. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis not otherwise specified. Causative agents often include long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational dusts. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airflow obstruction and increased respiratory symptoms.

Chronic bronchitis, unspecified, is a long-term inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes characterized by persistent cough and mucus production. It is often associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Common synonyms include chronic bronchial inflammation and chronic productive cough. Causative agents include cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational irritants. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to airway narrowing and impaired airflow. It is more prevalent in smokers and individuals exposed to respiratory irritants over prolonged periods.

Other specified bronchitis refers to bronchial inflammation not classified under acute or chronic bronchitis. It encompasses various subtypes with distinct clinical features. Common synonyms include unspecified bronchitis or unspecified bronchial inflammation. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or fungal pathogens, though often unspecified. The condition primarily affects the bronchi, leading to symptoms such as cough, mucus production, and wheezing. It may occur in individuals with underlying respiratory conditions or as a secondary complication. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation and exclusion of other bronchial disorders.

Bronchitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the bronchial tubes, leading to coughing, mucus production, and possible breathlessness. It may be acute or chronic. Common synonyms include acute bronchitis and chronic bronchitis. Causative agents often include viral infections, such as influenza or respiratory syncytial virus, and bacterial pathogens like Streptococcus pneumoniae. Environmental irritants, such as cigarette smoke or air pollution, can also contribute. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi, with symptoms often involving the respiratory system.

Emphysema is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to reduced gas exchange and air trapping. Common synonyms include pulmonary emphysema and bullae formation. The primary causative agent is long-term exposure to irritants, most commonly cigarette smoke. Other causes include air pollution, occupational dusts, and genetic factors such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli in the upper lobes, resulting in progressive dyspnea and reduced lung function.

MacLeod syndrome is a rare inherited disorder characterized by congenital hypogonadism and absence of the testes or ovaries. It is caused by mutations in the SOX9 gene, leading to defective development of the gonads and genitalia. Common synonyms include persistent Müllerian duct syndrome and Swyer syndrome. The condition primarily affects the reproductive system, resulting in ambiguous genitalia and infertility. It may also be associated with other abnormalities, such as kidney malformations. The syndrome is typically diagnosed in childhood or adolescence due to delayed puberty or infertility.

Panlobular emphysema, also known as centrilobular emphysema, is a type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls in the central regions of the acinus. It is most commonly associated with long-term cigarette smoking and is often seen in individuals with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The condition primarily affects the upper lobes of the lungs, leading to air trapping, reduced gas exchange, and progressive dyspnea. Clinically, it presents with chronic cough, sputum production, and exertional breathlessness. Radiographically, it appears as centrilobular nodules and bullae.

Centrilobular emphysema is a type of obstructive lung disease characterized by the destruction of the central portions of the acini, primarily affecting the respiratory bronchioles and alveoli. It is commonly associated with long-term cigarette smoking and is a hallmark of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Other synonyms include centriacinar emphysema. The condition typically involves the upper lung zones and leads to air trapping, reduced gas exchange, and progressive dyspnea. Pathologically, it results from protease-antiprotease imbalance and chronic inflammation.

Other specified emphysema refers to a form of pulmonary emphysema that does not meet the criteria for centrilobular, panacinar, or mixed emphysema. It is characterized by abnormal and permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, leading to reduced gas exchange. Common synonyms include non-specific emphysema. Causative agents often include long-term cigarette smoking, chronic bronchitis, and exposure to environmental pollutants. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the alveoli and airways. This condition is typically associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Emphysema, unspecified, is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to reduced gas exchange and airflow limitation. Common synonyms include pulmonary emphysema and chronic obstructive emphysema. It is primarily caused by long-term exposure to irritants, most commonly cigarette smoke, though occupational exposures and genetic factors like alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency may also contribute. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli in the upper lobes, resulting in hyperinflation and impaired respiratory function.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a progressive lung condition characterized by persistent airflow limitation and associated with an enhanced chronic inflammatory response to noxious particles or gases. Common synonyms include emphysema and chronic bronchitis. The primary causative agent is long-term exposure to irritants, most commonly cigarette smoke. The disease typically affects the airways and alveoli in the lungs, leading to symptoms such as chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnea. It is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide.

code_desc: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation, unspecified
summary: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation, unspecified, refers to a sudden worsening of symptoms in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), characterized by increased breathlessness, cough, and sputum production. Common synonyms include COPD exacerbation and acute COPD flare-up. Causative agents often include respiratory infections, air pollutants, and smoking. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the airways and alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory distress.

code_desc: Certain specified chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
summary: Certain specified chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) refers to a group of progressive lung disorders characterized by airflow limitation and associated with an abnormal inflammatory response of the lungs to noxious particles or gases. Common synonyms include emphysema and chronic bronchitis. The primary causative agents are long-term exposure to tobacco smoke, air pollution, and occupational dusts. The condition primarily affects the airways and alveoli in the lungs, leading to chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnea. It predominantly impacts the respiratory system, particularly the bronchioles and alveolar sacs.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, unspecified (COPD) is a progressive lung condition characterized by persistent airflow limitation, leading to difficulty in breathing. Common synonyms include chronic bronchitis and emphysema. It is primarily caused by long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, and occupational dusts. The disease mainly affects the airways and alveoli in the lungs, causing inflammation, mucus production, and destruction of lung tissue. Symptoms include chronic cough, sputum production, and dyspnea, with exacerbations often triggered by infections or environmental factors.

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by variable and recurring symptoms, including wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It involves airway hyperresponsiveness and reversible airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include reactive airway disease and bronchial asthma. Causative agents include allergens like pollen, dust mites, and animal dander, as well as irritants such as smoke and pollution. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi and bronchioles in the lungs.

Allergic asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways triggered by allergens, leading to bronchoconstriction, airway hyperresponsiveness, and airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include allergic bronchial asthma and atopic asthma. Causative agents often include airborne allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold spores, and animal dander. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, causing symptoms like wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It is commonly associated with other atopic conditions such as allergic rhinitis and eczema.

Allergic asthma with exacerbation is a worsening of asthma symptoms triggered by allergens, leading to increased airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction. Common synonyms include allergic asthma flare-up or allergic bronchial asthma exacerbation. Causative agents often include pollen, dust mites, mold, pet dander, and cockroach allergens. The primary affected body parts are the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles. Symptoms include cough, wheezing, dyspnea, and chest tightness. It commonly affects the respiratory system, with potential systemic involvement in severe cases.

Allergic asthma with status asthmaticus is a severe exacerbation of asthma triggered by allergens, leading to persistent airflow obstruction and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include severe asthma exacerbation and acute severe asthma. Causative agents often include allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold, and animal dander. The condition primarily affects the airways, causing bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and mucus hypersecretion. It can lead to hypoxia and respiratory failure if not promptly treated. The lungs and airways are the main affected body parts.

Allergic asthma, uncomplicated, is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways triggered by allergens, leading to bronchoconstriction, airway hyperresponsiveness, and reversible airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include allergic bronchial asthma and atopic asthma. Causative agents often include house dust mites, pollen, animal dander, mold spores, and cockroach allergens. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, causing symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It typically presents in childhood or early adulthood and is associated with other atopic conditions like allergic rhinitis and eczema.

Non-allergic asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness without a clear allergic component. It is often triggered by environmental factors such as cold air, exercise, respiratory infections, or irritants like smoke and chemical fumes. Common synonyms include exercise-induced bronchoconstriction and non-allergic bronchial hyperreactivity. The condition primarily affects the bronchial airways, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It is more prevalent in adults and can occur in individuals without a history of allergies or atopy.

Non-allergic asthma with exacerbation refers to a worsening of asthma symptoms not triggered by allergens. It involves airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction, leading to increased breathlessness, coughing, and wheezing. Common synonyms include non-allergic bronchial hyperresponsiveness and asthma exacerbation without allergic triggers. Causative agents may include viral infections, air pollution, exercise, cold air, and stress. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and alveoli, causing impaired gas exchange and airflow obstruction.

Non-allergic asthma with status asthmaticus is a severe, persistent asthma exacerbation not triggered by allergens. It involves prolonged bronchial inflammation and airway obstruction, leading to respiratory distress. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and refractory asthma. Causative agents may include respiratory infections, environmental irritants, exercise, or stress. The condition primarily affects the airways, including the bronchi and bronchioles, causing widespread bronchoconstriction and mucus hypersecretion. It can lead to hypoxia and respiratory failure if not promptly treated.

Non-allergic asthma, uncomplicated, is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness not mediated by IgE antibodies. Common synonyms include intrinsic asthma and non-atopic asthma. It is often triggered by factors such as viral infections, exercise, cold air, pollutants, or stress. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. Unlike allergic asthma, it lacks a clear association with allergens and is typically managed with bronchodilators and anti-inflammatory medications.

code_desc: Other specified forms of asthma or bronchospasm
summary: "Other specified forms of asthma or bronchospasm" refers to bronchial narrowing not classified under specific asthma types, often due to unclear etiology or atypical presentation. Common synonyms include unspecified asthma or bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Causative agents may include allergens, irritants, infections, or drug reactions. Typically affects the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms like wheezing, dyspnea, and cough. It is commonly seen in individuals with a history of respiratory conditions or exposure to triggers. Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation and response to bronchodilators.

Aspirin-induced asthma (AIA), also known as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), is a pharmacogenetic condition characterized by bronchoconstriction and asthma symptoms triggered by aspirin or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Common synonyms include aspirin-sensitive asthma and NSAID-exacerbated asthma. The condition typically affects the respiratory system, causing nasal polyps, rhinorrhea, and bronchospasm. It is associated with a genetic predisposition and is more prevalent in adults. The primary causative agent is aspirin, though other NSAIDs may also provoke symptoms.

Exercise-induced bronchospasm, also known as exercise-induced asthma or exercise-induced airway obstruction, is a reversible narrowing of the airways triggered by physical exertion. Common causative agents include cold air, allergens, and respiratory infections. It typically affects the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. The condition is often seen in athletes and individuals with underlying asthma. It is more prevalent in cold, dry environments and can be managed with pre-exercise bronchodilators.

Cough variant asthma (CVA) is a form of asthma characterized primarily by a chronic, dry cough without accompanying wheezing or shortness of breath. It is often misdiagnosed as post-infectious cough or upper airway cough syndrome. Common synonyms include cough asthma and atypical asthma. The condition is caused by airway hyperresponsiveness, often triggered by allergens, respiratory infections, or environmental irritants. It predominantly affects the respiratory tract, particularly the trachea and bronchi, and is more common in children and young adults. Diagnosis typically involves bronchoprovocation testing and response to bronchodilators.

Unspecified asthma is a broad term used when asthma is diagnosed but the specific type or trigger is not clearly identified. It encompasses various forms of asthma without a defined etiology. Common synonyms include idiopathic asthma and unspecified bronchial asthma. Causative agents may include environmental allergens, irritants, genetic factors, or unknown triggers. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchial tubes, leading to inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and airflow obstruction. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness, often worsening with exposure to triggers.

Unspecified asthma with exacerbation refers to a sudden worsening of asthma symptoms without a specific trigger identified. Common synonyms include acute asthma exacerbation or asthma flare-up. Causative agents may include allergens, respiratory infections, environmental irritants, or medication non-compliance. The condition primarily affects the airways, leading to bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and increased mucus production. It commonly involves the lungs and can impact breathing, causing dyspnea, wheezing, and hypoxia. It is typically managed with bronchodilators and corticosteroids to alleviate symptoms and prevent complications.

Unspecified asthma with status asthmaticus refers to a severe exacerbation of asthma where the underlying trigger is not clearly identified. It involves persistent and severe bronchoconstriction, airway inflammation, and increased mucus production, leading to significant airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include acute severe asthma and asthma exacerbation. Known causative agents may include allergens, respiratory infections, irritants, or medication non-compliance. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, and can lead to respiratory failure if not promptly treated.

Unspecified asthma, uncomplicated, refers to asthma without a specified type or trigger, characterized by recurrent episodes of airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Common synonyms include unspecified asthma or asthma, unspecified. Causative agents may include allergens, irritants, infections, or genetic factors. Typically affects the airways, particularly the bronchi and bronchioles, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough. It commonly occurs in the lungs and can impact respiratory function.

Bronchiectasis is a chronic lung condition characterized by irreversible dilation of the bronchi, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent infections. Common synonyms include dilated bronchi and bronchial dilatation. It is often caused by recurrent infections, such as those due to *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, or underlying conditions like cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The primary affected areas are the large airways, particularly the bronchi in the lungs, with symptoms including chronic cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis. Complications may involve pneumonia, respiratory failure, and progressive lung damage.

Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to defective chloride ion transport. This results in thick, sticky mucus production that primarily affects the lungs and pancreas. Common synonyms include mucoviscidosis and CF. The condition is autosomal recessive, with both parents typically being carriers. Affected individuals experience chronic respiratory infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and digestive issues. Other organs such as the liver, sinuses, and intestines may also be involved. It is the most common life-threatening genetic disease in Caucasians.

Classical cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to defective chloride ion transport. This results in thick, sticky mucus production, primarily affecting the lungs and pancreas. Common synonyms include cystic fibrosis and mucoviscidosis. The condition predominantly impacts the respiratory and digestive systems, causing chronic lung infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and malabsorption. It may also affect the liver, sinuses, and sweat glands. The disease is characterized by progressive pulmonary damage and gastrointestinal complications, often leading to reduced life expectancy if untreated.

Atypical cystic fibrosis, also known as congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD) or non-symptomatic cystic fibrosis, is a variant of cystic fibrosis characterized by the absence of symptoms typically associated with the disease. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, most commonly the ΔF508 mutation. This condition primarily affects males, leading to infertility due to the absence of vas deferens. While lung function is usually normal, some individuals may develop pancreatic insufficiency or other CF-related complications. It is often diagnosed through genetic testing or infertility evaluations.

Subclinical cystic fibrosis refers to a mild or atypical form of the disease where symptoms are minimal or absent, often leading to delayed diagnosis. It is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, most commonly the ΔF508 mutation. While typically affecting the lungs and pancreas, it may present with subtle signs such as slight nasal polyps, meconium ileus, or pancreatic insufficiency. Common synonyms include non-classic cystic fibrosis and mild cystic fibrosis. The condition primarily impacts the respiratory and digestive systems, though it may also involve the liver and sweat glands.

Cystic fibrosis, unspecified, is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to defective chloride ion transport. This results in thick, sticky mucus accumulation in the lungs, pancreas, and other organs. Common synonyms include cystic fibrosis, CF, and congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (in males). The condition primarily affects the respiratory and digestive systems, causing chronic lung infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and malabsorption. It is an autosomal recessive disorder, typically diagnosed in infancy or early childhood.

Chronic bronchiolitis is a long-term inflammation of the small airways, primarily the bronchioles, leading to airflow obstruction and impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include chronic bronchiolar disease and obstructive bronchiolitis. It is often caused by viral infections, particularly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and can be associated with environmental irritants, allergens, or genetic factors. The condition predominantly affects the lower respiratory tract, including the bronchioles and alveoli, and is commonly seen in infants, young children, and immunocompromised individuals. Chronic symptoms may include persistent cough, wheezing, and dyspnea.

Chronic obliterative bronchiolitis is a progressive, irreversible inflammatory condition characterized by the obliteration of small airways due to fibrosis and granulation tissue. It is often associated with exposure to inhaled toxins, such as silica, coal dust, or other occupational irritants. Common synonyms include chronic bronchiolitis obliterans and byssinosis. The condition primarily affects the terminal bronchioles and alveoli, leading to airflow obstruction and respiratory failure. It is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and is more prevalent in individuals with a history of occupational lung exposure.

Diffuse panbronchiolitis is a rare, chronic inflammatory lung disease primarily affecting the respiratory bronchioles. It is characterized by diffuse inflammation and fibrosis of the small airways, leading to progressive airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include chronic bronchiolitis and panbronchiolitis. The exact cause is unknown, though some cases may be associated with bacterial infections, particularly *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition predominantly affects the lower respiratory tract, including bronchioles and alveoli, and is more common in individuals with underlying immunodeficiency or chronic sinusitis.

Other specified chronic bronchiolitis refers to chronic inflammation of the bronchioles that does not fit the criteria for other specific types of bronchiolitis. It may present with persistent cough, wheezing, and airflow obstruction. Common synonyms include chronic nonspecific bronchiolitis. Causative agents are often unidentified, though exposure to environmental irritants, allergens, or recurrent infections may contribute. The condition primarily affects the small airways, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory distress. It is commonly seen in individuals with a history of respiratory illnesses or chronic lung disease.

Chronic bronchiolitis, unspecified, is a long-term inflammation of the bronchioles, the smallest airways in the lungs. It leads to narrowing and obstruction, causing symptoms such as chronic cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath. Common synonyms include chronic bronchiolar disease and persistent bronchiolitis. Causative agents may include viral infections, environmental irritants, and long-term exposure to pollutants. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the distal airways, and is often associated with underlying respiratory conditions like asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

Tracheobronchitis is an inflammation of the trachea and bronchi, often presenting with cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include acute bronchitis and upper airway infection. It is typically caused by viral agents such as rhinovirus, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus. Bacterial causes like Streptococcus pneumoniae or Mycoplasma pneumoniae may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the respiratory tract, involving the trachea, bronchi, and sometimes the bronchioles. It is more common in children and individuals with compromised immune systems. Symptoms usually resolve within a few weeks without specific treatment.

Tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica is a rare, benign, chronic condition characterized by the proliferation of cartilage and bone within the trachea and bronchi, leading to a cobblestone appearance. Common synonyms include tracheobronchial osteochondromatosis and tracheobronchial osteochondroplasia. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic factors and chronic inflammation may play a role. It typically affects the trachea and mainstem bronchi, most commonly in middle-aged to elderly individuals. The condition is usually asymptomatic but can cause cough, stridor, or hemoptysis in severe cases.

Tracheobronchomegaly refers to the abnormal dilation of the trachea and main bronchi, often resulting from chronic inflammation, infection, or structural abnormalities. Common synonyms include bronchomegaly and tracheal dilation. It is frequently associated with conditions such as tuberculosis, bronchial asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The condition predominantly affects the trachea and major bronchi, leading to airway narrowing and respiratory symptoms. It may also be linked to congenital anomalies or neoplastic processes. Diagnosis typically involves imaging studies like chest X-ray or CT scan.

Other specified tracheobronchitis refers to inflammation of the trachea and bronchi that does not meet the criteria for acute or chronic bronchitis. It is often a nonspecific diagnosis used when the cause or duration of symptoms is unclear. Common synonyms include unspecified tracheobronchitis or unspecified bronchitis. Causative agents may include viral infections, such as respiratory syncytial virus or influenza, or environmental irritants. The condition typically affects the upper airway, including the trachea and bronchi, and may present with cough, wheezing, and dyspnea.

Tracheobronchitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the trachea and bronchi without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include acute tracheobronchitis and viral tracheobronchitis. It is typically caused by viral infections, though bacterial agents may also contribute. The condition primarily affects the respiratory tract, involving the trachea and bronchi. Symptoms include cough, sore throat, and difficulty breathing. It is commonly seen in children and individuals with compromised immune systems. The inflammation is usually self-limiting and responds to supportive care.

code_desc: Other specified lower respiratory tract disease
summary: "Other specified lower respiratory tract disease" refers to respiratory conditions affecting the trachea, bronchi, and lungs that do not fit specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include unspecified or unspecified lower respiratory infection. Causative agents may include viruses, bacteria, and fungi. Typically affects the bronchi and alveoli, often presenting with symptoms like cough, sputum production, and shortness of breath. It is a broad category used when the exact cause or specific disease is not clearly identified.

Lower respiratory tract disease, unspecified refers to inflammation or infection affecting the trachea, bronchi, or lungs without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include acute bronchitis, pneumonia, or bronchiolitis. Causative agents may include viruses (e.g., influenza, RSV), bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae), or fungi. Typically affects the bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli, leading to symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and sputum production. It is commonly seen in individuals with compromised immune systems or those exposed to environmental irritants.

Pneumonia is an inflammatory condition of the lungs, primarily affecting the alveoli, which become filled with fluid or pus. It is commonly caused by bacterial, viral, or fungal infections, with *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Influenza virus*, and *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* being frequent agents. Symptoms include fever, cough, shortness of breath, and chest pain. Pneumonia can affect one or both lungs and is often classified as community-acquired, hospital-acquired, or aspiration pneumonia. Synonyms include pulmonary infection, lung infection, and pneumonia.

Bacterial pneumonia is an acute infection of the lungs caused by bacterial invasion of the alveoli, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation. Common synonyms include pneumococcal pneumonia and lobar pneumonia. The most frequent causative agents are *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. It typically affects the lower lobes of the lungs, though it can involve any lung region. Symptoms include fever, cough, pleuritic chest pain, and purulent sputum.
