It is more common in individuals with compromised immunity or underlying respiratory conditions.

Pneumonia due to *Chlamydophila pneumoniae* is a respiratory infection characterized by inflammation of the lung parenchyma. It is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, particularly in adults. The infection is typically mild to moderate in severity, often presenting with cough, fever, and dyspnea. *Chlamydophila pneumoniae* is an intracellular bacterium that primarily affects the lower respiratory tract. It is also known as *Chlamydia psittaci* or *Chlamydophila psittaci* in some contexts. The condition is more prevalent in individuals with compromised immune systems or those exposed to environmental risk factors.

Pneumonia due to *Escherichia coli* is a bacterial infection of the lungs caused by *E. coli*, a gram-negative bacillus. It commonly occurs in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying conditions such as aspiration or hospital-acquired infections. The infection typically affects the alveoli, leading to inflammation, consolidation, and impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include *E. coli pneumonia* or *gram-negative pneumonia*. Other causative agents may include *Klebsiella* or *Pseudomonas*, but *E. coli* is a notable pathogen, particularly in neonates or patients with gastrointestinal dysfunction.

Pneumonia due to *Haemophilus influenzae* is a lower respiratory tract infection caused by the bacterium *Haemophilus influenzae*, a gram-negative coccobacillus. It commonly affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. This condition is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. *H. influenzae* is a known causative agent of both community-acquired and hospital-acquired pneumonia. Synonyms include bacterial pneumonia and respiratory tract infection. The infection typically affects the lungs, with possible spread to adjacent structures in severe cases.

Pneumonia due to *Klebsiella pneumoniae* is a bacterial lung infection characterized by lobar consolidation and suppurative inflammation. It commonly affects the lower lobes of the lungs. *K. pneumoniae* is a gram-negative bacillus, often associated with hospital-acquired infections. It may cause severe symptoms including fever, cough, purulent sputum, and pleural effusion. The infection is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with underlying conditions such as diabetes. Complications may include sepsis and abscess formation. Synonyms include Klebsiella pneumonia and hospital-acquired pneumonia.

Pneumonia due to *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is a respiratory infection caused by the atypical bacterium *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*. It commonly presents with mild, persistent cough and fever, often affecting children and young adults. The infection primarily involves the lower respiratory tract, causing interstitial pneumonia. It is sometimes referred to as "walking pneumonia" due to its typically mild course. Other synonyms include atypical pneumonia or mycoplasmal pneumonia. The disease is spread through respiratory droplets and is more prevalent in crowded environments. Complications are rare but may include bronchitis or pleural effusion.

Pneumonia due to *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* is a severe bacterial lung infection characterized by inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include hospital-acquired pneumonia and ventilator-associated pneumonia. This opportunistic pathogen thrives in moist environments and is frequently associated with immunocompromised patients or those with underlying lung disease. It commonly affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly in individuals with cystic fibrosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or those in intensive care. The infection often presents with symptoms such as fever, cough, purulent sputum, and hypoxia.

Pneumonia due to *Staphylococcus* is an infection of the lungs caused by *Staphylococcus aureus*, a common bacterial pathogen. It often occurs in immunocompromised individuals or following trauma, surgery, or aspiration. The infection leads to inflammation of the alveoli, resulting in symptoms such as fever, cough, and purulent sputum. It may present as community-acquired or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Common synonyms include staphylococcal pneumonia or *S. aureus* pneumonia. The primary affected body part is the lung parenchyma, with potential spread to pleura or bloodstream in severe cases.

Pneumonia due to *Streptococcus pneumoniae* is a bacterial infection affecting the lungs, characterized by inflammation of the alveoli. Common synonyms include pneumococcal pneumonia. The causative agent is *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, a gram-positive coccus. It typically affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly the alveoli and bronchioles. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain. It is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, especially in children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. Complications may include pleural effusion, sepsis, and respiratory failure.

Pneumonia due to beta-haemolytic streptococcus is a bacterial lung infection primarily caused by *Streptococcus pyogenes* (Group A Streptococcus). It is also known as streptococcal pneumonia. The infection typically affects the alveoli, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation. Common synonyms include streptococcal pneumonia and GABHS pneumonia. It is more prevalent in children and immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include fever, cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Complications may involve pleural effusion or sepsis. The condition is treated with antibiotics such as penicillin.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other specified bacteria
summary: Pneumonia due to other specified bacteria refers to lung infection caused by bacterial pathogens not classified under common categories like streptococci, staphylococci, or mycoplasma. Common synonyms include bacterial pneumonia with unspecified organisms. Causative agents may include Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. This condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation, fluid accumulation, and impaired gas exchange. It is commonly seen in individuals with weakened immune systems or underlying respiratory conditions.

Bacterial pneumonia, unspecified, is an acute infection of the lungs caused by bacteria, leading to inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include lobar pneumonia and pneumococcal pneumonia. Causative agents often include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli and bronchioles, and may spread to adjacent tissues. Symptoms typically include fever, cough, chest pain, and difficulty breathing. It is more common in individuals with weakened immune systems or underlying respiratory conditions.

Viral pneumonia is an inflammatory lung condition caused by viral infection, leading to fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonia and viral lung infection. It is typically caused by respiratory viruses such as influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus, and coronavirus. The infection primarily affects the alveoli and interstitial tissue of the lungs, causing symptoms like fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is more common in children, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. Complications may include respiratory failure and secondary bacterial infections.

Pneumonia due to adenovirus is an infectious lung infection caused by adenoviruses, which are common respiratory pathogens. It typically presents with fever, cough, and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include viral pneumonia and adenoviral pneumonia. Adenovirus types 3, 7, and 14 are frequently implicated. The infection primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. It is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals. Complications may include bronchiolitis and respiratory failure. Diagnosis is often confirmed through viral culture or molecular testing. Treatment is supportive, as antiviral therapy is limited.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to Respiratory syncytial virus
summary: Pneumonia due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a lower respiratory tract infection caused by the RSV, a common paramyxovirus. It primarily affects the bronchioles and alveoli, leading to inflammation, mucus production, and airway obstruction. Common synonyms include RSV pneumonia and viral bronchiolitis. The infection typically presents with cough, fever, and dyspnea, with more severe symptoms in infants, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. Complications may include bronchopneumonia and respiratory failure. The virus spreads via respiratory droplets and is a major cause of hospitalization in young children and adults with underlying lung disease.

Pneumonia due to parainfluenza virus is a lower respiratory tract infection caused by parainfluenza viruses, particularly types 1, 2, 3, and 4. Common synonyms include viral croup and acute laryngotracheobronchitis. It primarily affects the trachea, bronchi, and alveoli, often leading to symptoms such as cough, fever, and difficulty breathing. The infection is more common in children but can occur in adults, especially those with compromised immune systems. It is transmitted via respiratory droplets and typically presents with a sudden onset of respiratory symptoms. Complications may include bronchopneumonia and respiratory failure in severe cases.

Pneumonia due to Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is a respiratory infection caused by the hMPV, a member of the paramyxovirus family. It primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, leading to inflammation of the alveoli. Common synonyms include hMPV pneumonia and metapneumovirus pneumonia. The virus is a common cause of viral pneumonia, particularly in young children, elderly individuals, and immunocompromised patients. Symptoms include cough, fever, and respiratory distress. Complications may involve bronchiolitis and worsening of chronic lung disease. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets.

code_desc: Pneumonia due to other specified virus
summary: Pneumonia due to other specified virus is an inflammatory lung infection caused by viral agents not classified under influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, or adenovirus. Common synonyms include viral pneumonia with unspecified agent. Causative agents may include parainfluenza, enteroviruses, and others. The infection primarily affects the alveoli, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, and dyspnea. It commonly occurs in immunocompromised individuals or during viral outbreaks. Diagnosis often relies on clinical presentation and imaging, with treatment focusing on supportive care.

Viral pneumonia, unspecified, is an inflammatory lung condition caused by a variety of viruses. It affects the alveoli, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonia and viral respiratory infection. Causative agents may include influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus, and coronavirus. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, with potential involvement of the respiratory tract. It is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, as specific viral identification may not always be possible.

Fungal pneumonia is an infection of the lungs caused by various fungal pathogens. It typically affects immunocompromised individuals or those exposed to environmental fungi. Common causative agents include *Histoplasma capsulatum*, *Coccidioides immitis*, *Aspergillus* species, and *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. Synonyms include pulmonary mycosis or opportunistic fungal infection. The condition primarily involves the alveoli and interstitial tissues of the lungs, leading to inflammation, consolidation, and potential respiratory failure if untreated.

Pneumonia due to *Pneumocystis* is a fungal infection primarily affecting the lungs. Commonly known as pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), it is caused by *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. This condition predominantly occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. The infection leads to interstitial pneumonia characterized by diffuse inflammation and alveolar filling. Symptoms include fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is a significant opportunistic infection, often requiring prophylaxis in high-risk populations. The lungs are the primary affected body part.

Other specified fungal pneumonia refers to fungal infections of the lungs caused by organisms not classified under more specific categories such as histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis. Common synonyms include non-specific fungal pneumonia. Causative agents may include Aspergillus, Penicillium, or other molds. This condition typically affects the alveoli and bronchioles, leading to inflammation and impaired gas exchange. It is often seen in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying lung disease. Clinical presentation may include fever, cough, and dyspnea, with radiographic findings of infiltrates or nodules. Diagnosis is confirmed through imaging, microbiological cultures, and serological tests.

Fungal pneumonia, unspecified, refers to an infection of the lungs caused by various fungal pathogens, typically affecting individuals with compromised immune systems. Common causative agents include *Histoplasma capsulatum*, *Coccidioides immitis*, *Aspergillus* species, and *Pneumocystis jirovecii*. The infection may present with symptoms such as fever, cough, and respiratory distress. It primarily affects the lungs, though it can spread to other organs in severe cases. Synonyms include pulmonary mycosis and opportunistic fungal infection. The condition is often diagnosed through imaging, sputum analysis, and serological tests.

Other specified pneumonia refers to pneumonia cases that do not meet the criteria for specific types such as bacterial, viral, or fungal pneumonia but are clinically significant. Common synonyms include unspecified pneumonia or non-classifiable pneumonia. Causative agents may include atypical pathogens like Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, or Legionella, or mixed infections. The condition typically affects the lungs, particularly the alveoli, leading to inflammation and impaired gas exchange. It is often diagnosed when the causative agent is unknown or does not fit established categories.

Pneumonia, organism unspecified, refers to an inflammatory lung condition characterized by infection of the alveoli, typically caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, or fungi. Common synonyms include acute respiratory infection and pulmonary infection. While the specific causative agent is not identified, common pathogens include *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, influenza virus, and respiratory syncytial virus. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to symptoms such as fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. It can occur in both adults and children, with higher prevalence in immunocompromised individuals.

Acute bronchiolitis is an acute inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles), primarily affecting infants and young children. It is commonly caused by viral infections, most notably respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), though other agents like parainfluenza and human metapneumovirus may also be involved. The condition presents with symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. It typically affects the lower respiratory tract, leading to bronchial narrowing and increased mucus production. While usually self-limiting, severe cases may require hospitalization due to respiratory failure. Synonyms include viral bronchiolitis and acute viral bronchiolitis.

code_desc: Acute bronchiolitis due to respiratory syncytial virus
summary: Acute bronchiolitis due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a viral lower respiratory tract infection characterized by inflammation and narrowing of the small airways. Common synonyms include RSV bronchiolitis and viral bronchiolitis. Caused primarily by RSV, it typically affects infants and young children, with symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. The infection primarily targets the bronchioles, leading to mucus plugging and airflow obstruction. Complications may include pneumonia or respiratory failure in high-risk populations.

Other specified acute bronchiolitis refers to a clinical diagnosis of bronchiolitis that does not meet the criteria for viral bronchiolitis but is otherwise acute in onset. It may involve inflammation of the small airways, leading to symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. Common synonyms include unspecified acute bronchiolitis. Causative agents are typically viral, though bacterial or environmental factors may be implicated. The condition primarily affects the bronchioles in the lower respiratory tract, commonly seen in young children but can occur in adults with underlying lung disease.

Acute bronchiolitis, unspecified, is an acute inflammation of the bronchioles, typically presenting with cough, wheezing, and respiratory distress. It is most common in young children, particularly infants. Common synonyms include viral bronchiolitis and acute viral bronchiolitis. The primary causative agent is the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), though other viruses like influenza and parainfluenza may also be responsible. The condition primarily affects the small airways in the lungs, leading to bronchoconstriction and mucus plugging. It is a self-limiting illness, often requiring supportive care.

Acute bronchitis is an inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes, typically characterized by a productive cough lasting less than three weeks. Common synonyms include acute tracheobronchitis. It is most commonly caused by viral infections, though bacterial and fungal agents can also be responsible. The condition primarily affects the large airways, including the trachea and bronchi. Symptoms often include cough, sputum production, and chest discomfort. It is more prevalent in adults and can follow upper respiratory tract infections. Complications are rare but may include pneumonia in vulnerable populations.

Acute bronchitis due to *Streptococcus* is an inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes, typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Streptococcus pneumoniae* or *Streptococcus pyogenes*. It presents with cough, often productive of mucus, chest discomfort, and fever. Common synonyms include bacterial bronchitis or streptococcal bronchitis. The primary affected body parts are the bronchi and bronchioles, with potential involvement of the lungs. It is more prevalent in adults and can progress to pneumonia if untreated.

Acute bronchitis due to Rhinovirus is an inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes, typically following a viral upper respiratory infection. It is characterized by cough, often with mucus, and may include fever and chest discomfort. Rhinovirus is a common causative agent, though other viruses like RSV or influenza may also contribute. The condition primarily affects the large airways, with inflammation and increased secretions. It is more prevalent in adults and can occur as a complication of viral rhinitis. Synonyms include viral bronchitis or acute viral bronchial infection.

code_desc: Acute bronchitis due to Respiratory syncytial virus
summary: Acute bronchitis due to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is an inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes, primarily affecting the lower respiratory tract. It is caused by the RSV, a common viral pathogen. Symptoms include cough, fever, and wheezing, often following an upper respiratory infection. Common synonyms include viral bronchitis or RSV-induced bronchitis. The condition predominantly affects the bronchi and bronchioles, with potential involvement of the alveoli in severe cases. It is more prevalent in young children and elderly individuals.

code_desc: Acute bronchitis due to Parainfluenza virus
summary: Acute bronchitis due to parainfluenza virus is an inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes, typically presenting with cough, fever, and respiratory symptoms. Caused by parainfluenza viruses, particularly types 1, 2, and 3, it is a common viral infection affecting the lower respiratory tract. Synonyms include viral bronchitis or acute viral bronchitis. The infection primarily affects the bronchi and may involve the trachea. It is more common in children but can occur in adults, especially those with compromised immune systems. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets.

code_desc: Acute bronchitis due to Haemophilus influenzae
summary: Acute bronchitis due to *Haemophilus influenzae* is an inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes characterized by cough, often with mucus production, and chest discomfort. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, with *H. influenzae* being a common causative agent. Other pathogens may include *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Moraxella catarrhalis*. The infection primarily affects the large airways, leading to bronchial inflammation and hypersecretion. It is more common in adults and can occur following viral upper respiratory infections. Symptoms usually resolve within a few weeks with appropriate antibiotic therapy. Synonyms include bacterial bronchitis or acute bacterial tracheobronchitis.

Acute bronchitis due to Coxsackievirus is an inflammatory condition of the bronchial tubes, primarily affecting the large airways. It is caused by Coxsackievirus, a member of the enterovirus family. Common synonyms include viral bronchitis or acute viral bronchitis. The infection typically presents with cough, fever, and respiratory symptoms. While Coxsackievirus is a known causative agent, it is less commonly associated with bronchitis compared to respiratory syncytial virus or influenza. The condition predominantly affects the trachea and bronchi, with symptoms usually resolving within a few weeks.

Other specified acute bronchitis refers to acute bronchial inflammation not attributable to a specific infectious agent, such as viruses or bacteria. It is often a non-specific response to irritants or environmental factors. Common synonyms include acute non-infectious bronchitis or irritant-induced bronchitis. Causative agents may include tobacco smoke, air pollutants, allergens, or occupational exposures. The condition primarily affects the bronchial tubes, leading to symptoms such as cough, mucus production, and chest discomfort. It typically involves the large airways and is distinct from infectious bronchitis caused by pathogens like respiratory syncytial virus or Mycoplasma.

Acute bronchitis, unspecified, is an acute inflammation of the bronchial tubes, typically characterized by cough, sputum production, and sometimes fever. It is commonly caused by viral infections, though bacterial or environmental factors may contribute. Common synonyms include acute tracheobronchitis and acute bronchial inflammation. The condition primarily affects the bronchi and may involve the trachea. It is more prevalent in adults and often follows upper respiratory infections. Symptoms usually resolve within a few weeks without specific treatment.

An abscess of the lung or mediastinum is a localized collection of pus resulting from infection, typically caused by bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, or *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. It often arises from hematogenous spread, direct extension from adjacent infections, or aspiration. Common synonyms include pulmonary abscess and mediastinal abscess. The condition primarily affects the lungs, but may also involve the mediastinum, leading to symptoms like fever, cough, and chest pain. Complications may include pleural effusion or spread to surrounding structures.

Gangrene or necrosis of the lung refers to the death of lung tissue due to lack of blood supply or infection. Common synonyms include pulmonary infarction and necrotizing pneumonia. It is often caused by embolism, infection, or trauma. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, or *Clostridium* species. The condition typically affects the pulmonary parenchyma, particularly in the peripheral regions, and can lead to complications like abscess formation or respiratory failure.

Abscess of the lung with pneumonia is a severe pulmonary infection characterized by localized collection of pus within lung tissue, often secondary to bacterial pneumonia. It typically results from anaerobic and aerobic bacteria, including *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Escherichia coli*. The condition commonly affects the upper lobes of the lungs and is associated with symptoms such as fever, cough, chest pain, and purulent sputum. It may develop from unresolved pneumonia or hematogenous spread. Complications include pleural effusion and sepsis. Synonyms include lung abscess and pyogenic pneumonia.

Abscess of the lung without pneumonia is a localized collection of pus within the lung parenchyma, typically resulting from bacterial infection. Common synonyms include pulmonary abscess and lung abscess. The most frequent causative agents are anaerobic bacteria, such as *Bacteroides* and *Fusobacterium*, often in combination with aerobic organisms like *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. This condition predominantly affects the upper lobes of the lungs, especially in individuals with underlying conditions such as bronchiectasis or immunosuppression. It may present with fever, cough, and hemoptysis, and is often diagnosed via imaging and microbiological analysis.

An abscess of the mediastinum is a localized collection of pus within the mediastinal compartment, typically resulting from infection. Common synonyms include mediastinal empyema or mediastinal abscess. It is often caused by bacterial pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species, and gram-negative rods. The condition may arise from contiguous spread of infection from the lungs, heart, or esophagus, or from hematogenous dissemination. It commonly affects the posterior mediastinum and can involve the pleura, pericardium, or great vessels. Symptoms include fever, chest pain, and respiratory distress. Early diagnosis and drainage are essential to prevent complications.

code_desc: Other specified abscess of lung or mediastinum
summary: "Other specified abscess of lung or mediastinum" refers to localized collections of pus in the lung or mediastinal tissues, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include lung abscess and mediastinal abscess. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Escherichia coli*. Typically affects the lungs, particularly the upper lobes, and may extend into the mediastinum. It is often associated with underlying conditions like aspiration, immunosuppression, or trauma.

code_desc: Abscess of lung or mediastinum, unspecified
summary: Abscess of the lung or mediastinum, unspecified, refers to a localized collection of pus in the lung tissue or mediastinal space, typically caused by bacterial infection. Common synonyms include pulmonary abscess and mediastinal abscess. Causative agents often include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Escherichia coli*. The condition primarily affects the lungs, but can also involve the mediastinum. It is often associated with underlying conditions such as aspiration, immunosuppression, or chronic lung disease. Symptoms may include fever, cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging and microbiological analysis.

Pyothorax, also known as empyema or purulent pleuritis, is a severe infection of the pleural cavity characterized by the accumulation of pus. It typically results from bacterial invasion following pneumonia, trauma, or surgical procedures. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, and *Haemophilus influenzae*. The condition primarily affects the lungs and pleura, leading to symptoms such as fever, chest pain, and respiratory distress. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics and drainage are essential to prevent complications.

Respiratory infections, not elsewhere classified, refer to infections of the respiratory tract that do not fit specific categories such as upper or lower respiratory tract infections. Common synonyms include unspecified respiratory infections. Causative agents may include bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae, viruses such as influenza, and fungi. These infections typically affect the nose, throat, bronchi, and lungs, causing symptoms like cough, fever, and difficulty breathing. They are often diagnosed when the exact type or location of the infection is unclear.

"Other specified lung infections" refers to lung infections not classified under more specific categories such as tuberculosis, pneumonia, or fungal infections. Common synonyms include unspecified or unspecified pulmonary infections. Causative agents may vary but often include bacteria, viruses, or fungi. These infections typically affect the lungs, particularly the bronchi and alveoli, and may present with symptoms like cough, fever, and dyspnea. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and imaging, with treatment guided by identified pathogens.

Lung infections, unspecified, refer to inflammatory processes in the respiratory tract caused by various pathogens. Common synonyms include pneumonia, bronchopneumonia, and pulmonary infection. Causative agents may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites. Typically affecting the lungs, these infections can involve the alveoli, bronchioles, and bronchi. Symptoms often include cough, fever, dyspnea, and chest pain. The condition may be acute or chronic, with severity varying based on the causative agent and host factors. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through clinical evaluation, imaging, and laboratory tests.

Pneumoconiosis is a chronic lung disease caused by the inhalation and retention of inorganic dust particles, leading to progressive fibrosis and impaired respiratory function. Common synonyms include dust lung and occupational lung disease. The condition is primarily caused by exposure to silica, coal, and asbestos. It typically affects the lungs, causing nodular scarring and reduced lung elasticity. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and increased risk of respiratory infections and lung cancer. The disease is most commonly seen in miners, construction workers, and those in industries involving dust exposure.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to dust containing silica
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to dust containing silica, also known as silicosis, is a lung disease caused by inhalation of respirable silica particles. Common synonyms include silicosis and pneumoconiosis. The causative agent is crystalline silica, found in materials like sand, stone, and concrete. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive fibrosis and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and chest pain. It is typically seen in occupational settings such as mining, construction, and quarrying. Long-term exposure increases the risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer.

Pneumoconiosis due to talc dust is a chronic lung disease caused by the inhalation of talc particles, a mineral composed primarily of magnesium silicate. Common synonyms include talc pneumoconiosis and silicosis-like disease. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to the formation of nodular fibrosis in the upper lung zones. While talc itself is not classified as a silica-containing dust, it can cause similar pathological changes. Occupational exposure in industries such as ceramics, cosmetics, and mining increases risk. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and progressive respiratory impairment. The disease is generally non-malignant but can lead to complications such as tuberculosis.

code_desc: Other specified pneumoconiosis due to dust containing silica
summary: Other specified pneumoconiosis due to dust containing silica refers to chronic lung disease caused by inhalation of silica-containing dust, excluding silicosis and other specified types. Common synonyms include silicosis and silicotic lung disease. The primary causative agent is crystalline silica, found in materials like quartz, sand, and granite. Prolonged exposure leads to inflammation, fibrosis, and nodular scarring in the lungs, primarily affecting the upper lobes. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and increased risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer. It is commonly seen in miners, construction workers, and those involved in stone cutting.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to dust containing silica, unspecified
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to dust containing silica, unspecified, is a chronic lung disease caused by inhalation of silica-containing dust. It leads to progressive scarring and fibrosis of lung tissue. Common synonyms include silicosis and silicotic lung disease. The primary causative agent is crystalline silica, found in materials like sand, stone, and concrete. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, and increased risk of tuberculosis. It is commonly seen in miners, construction workers, and those exposed to silica dust in industrial settings.

Coal worker pneumoconiosis, also known as coal dust lung or black lung disease, is a chronic lung disease caused by long-term inhalation of coal mine dust. The condition leads to the accumulation of coal particles in the lungs, resulting in inflammation and fibrosis. The primary causative agent is coal dust, particularly silica and other mineral particles found in coal mines. It predominantly affects the respiratory system, with the lungs and bronchioles being the main sites of involvement. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and progressive respiratory impairment. The disease is most commonly seen in miners and those exposed to coal dust over prolonged periods.

code_desc: Pneumoconiosis due to mineral fibres including asbestos
summary: Pneumoconiosis due to mineral fibres, including asbestos, is a chronic lung disease caused by inhalation of fibrous mineral dust. Common synonyms include asbestosis and fibrosing pleural disease. The primary causative agent is asbestos, though other mineral fibres like crocidolite and amosite may also contribute. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, leading to progressive fibrosis, scarring, and impaired respiratory function. It may also involve the pleura, causing pleural plaques or effusions. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, and chest pain, with potential complications such as lung cancer or mesothelioma. Prolonged occupational exposure is a key risk factor.

Pneumoconiosis associated with tuberculosis is a combined occupational lung disease resulting from long-term inhalation of mineral dust and subsequent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Common synonyms include tuberculosis-related pneumoconiosis and mixed pulmonary disease. Causative agents include silica, coal, and asbestos dust, along with M. tuberculosis. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to fibrosis, nodules, and cavities. It is commonly seen in miners and industrial workers. Symptoms include chronic cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. Diagnosis involves imaging and microbiological testing.

Aluminosis of the lung is a diffuse interstitial lung disease characterized by the accumulation of aluminum in the pulmonary parenchyma, leading to fibrosis and impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include aluminum pneumoconiosis and aluminopneumonia. It is primarily caused by prolonged inhalation of aluminum dust or fumes, commonly encountered in industrial settings such as aluminum production and welding. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, particularly the alveolar regions and interstitium, and may lead to progressive respiratory impairment. It is more prevalent in occupational populations with inadequate protective measures.

Bauxite fibrosis of the lung is a rare occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of bauxite dust, primarily affecting individuals exposed to aluminum ore processing. It is characterized by interstitial lung fibrosis, leading to progressive dyspnea and reduced lung function. Common synonyms include aluminum dust pneumoconiosis and bauxite pneumoconiosis. The condition predominantly affects the lungs, with fibrotic changes primarily in the upper lobes. Causative agents include aluminum oxide and other mineral particles present in bauxite. Prolonged exposure in mining and refining industries increases the risk of developing this condition.

Berylliosis is a granulomatous lung disease caused by inhalation of beryllium compounds. It is also known as chronic beryllium disease or beryllium poisoning. The condition results from an immune response to beryllium exposure, leading to the formation of non-caseating granulomas. Common causative agents include beryllium metal, oxide, and salts. The lungs are primarily affected, with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fatigue. Long-term exposure increases the risk of progression to pulmonary fibrosis and may lead to systemic involvement. Diagnosis often involves serological testing for beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test and chest imaging.

Graphite fibrosis of the lung is a rare occupational lung disease caused by prolonged inhalation of graphite particles. It leads to progressive fibrosis and inflammation of the lung parenchyma. Common synonyms include graphite pneumoconiosis and chronic graphite lung disease. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, particularly the alveoli and interstitial tissue. Causative agents are primarily crystalline graphite particles, often encountered in industries such as battery manufacturing, foundry work, and carbon production. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung function. The disease is typically bilateral and involves the lower lung zones. Early diagnosis and exposure cessation are critical to prevent progression.

Siderosis refers to the accumulation of iron in body tissues, typically due to inhalation of iron particles. It is commonly known as pneumoconiosis or sideroconiosis when affecting the lungs. The condition is primarily caused by occupational exposure to iron dust, such as in welding or metalworking. Chronic inhalation leads to pulmonary fibrosis and impaired lung function. While siderosis primarily affects the respiratory system, systemic involvement is rare. It is often asymptomatic but can progress to cough, dyspnea, and reduced exercise tolerance. No known infectious agents are involved, and treatment is mainly supportive.

Stannosis is a rare condition characterized by the accumulation of tin in body tissues, typically due to chronic exposure to tin compounds. Common synonyms include tin poisoning and tin toxicity. It is most commonly caused by inhalation of tin dust, particularly in industrial settings. The condition primarily affects the respiratory system, leading to pulmonary fibrosis and respiratory distress. Systemic involvement may occur, affecting the liver and kidneys. Symptoms include cough, shortness of breath, and fatigue. Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical evaluation and analysis of tissue samples for tin content. Prevention involves minimizing occupational exposure to tin compounds.

Other specified pneumoconiosis refers to chronic lung diseases caused by inhalation of mineral dusts not classified under specific pneumoconioses like asbestosis or silicosis. Common synonyms include unspecified pneumoconiosis or other occupational lung diseases. Causative agents include coal, metal, or other mineral dusts. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired gas exchange. It is typically associated with occupational exposure and may present with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung function. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, imaging, and exclusion of other lung diseases.

Pneumoconiosis, unspecified, is a chronic lung disease caused by the inhalation and retention of mineral dust particles in the lungs. It leads to progressive fibrosis and inflammation of lung tissue. Common synonyms include "dust lung disease" and "occupational lung disease." Causative agents typically include silica, coal, and asbestos. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and reduced pulmonary function. It is commonly seen in individuals with occupational exposure to dust. The disease can lead to complications like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and increased risk of lung cancer.

code_desc: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to organic dust
summary: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to organic dust is an inflammatory lung disease triggered by inhalation of allergens such as mold spores, bird droppings, or other organic particles. It is also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis or farmer's lung. The immune system reacts to these antigens, causing inflammation and fibrosis in the lungs. Common causative agents include *Aspergillus*, *Penicillium*, and *Sporothrix* species. Typically affects the alveoli and interstitium of the lungs, leading to symptoms like cough, dyspnea, and fever. Chronic exposure can result in progressive pulmonary fibrosis.

Farmer lung, also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis, is an interstitial lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of organic dusts. Common causative agents include mold spores, bird proteins, and agricultural antigens. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation and fibrosis. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever. It typically affects farmers, livestock workers, and others exposed to contaminated environments. Chronic exposure can lead to progressive respiratory impairment. Diagnosis involves clinical history, imaging, and lung function tests.

Bagassosis is a type of hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of fungal spores from moldy sugarcane dust. Common synonyms include farmer’s lung and byssinosis. The primary causative agent is *Aspergillus* species, though other fungi may also be involved. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and progressive respiratory symptoms. It typically occurs in agricultural workers exposed to contaminated environments. Chronic exposure can result in irreversible lung damage and impaired pulmonary function. Early diagnosis and avoidance of exposure are critical for preventing long-term complications.

Bird fancier lung, also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis, is an interstitial lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of avian proteins. Common causative agents include antigens from feathers, dust, and dander of birds such as pigeons, parrots, and canaries. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and fibrosis of the alveoli. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever, often following exposure to contaminated environments. It typically affects individuals with prolonged occupational or recreational exposure to birds.

Suberosis is a rare, chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the progressive destruction of subcutaneous tissue, leading to skin atrophy and ulceration. It primarily affects the lower extremities, particularly the legs. Common synonyms include subcutaneous lipodystrophy and subcutaneous atrophy. The condition is often associated with autoimmune disorders, infections, or long-term corticosteroid use. Causative agents may include Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungal infections, or systemic lupus erythematosus. The affected areas typically show thinning of the skin, loss of subcutaneous fat, and secondary complications such as infection or lymphedema.

Malt worker lung, also known as byssinosis or cotton worker's lung, is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease caused by prolonged inhalation of organic dust from raw cotton, flax, or hemp. It primarily affects the upper airways and is characterized by cough, shortness of breath, and wheezing. The condition is associated with exposure to endotoxins and fungal spores present in the fibers. While byssinosis is the most common synonym, other terms include cotton dust disease or textile worker's lung. The lungs are the main affected organ, with inflammation and fibrosis occurring in the airways and alveoli.

Mushroom worker lung, also known as byssinosis or brown lung disease, is a chronic obstructive lung condition caused by prolonged inhalation of fungal spores and organic dust from mushroom cultivation. Common causative agents include *Penicillium* and *Aspergillus* species. The condition primarily affects the lower respiratory tract, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and airflow limitation. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and wheezing. It predominantly impacts workers in mushroom farms and processing facilities, with the lungs being the main affected organ.

Maple bark stripper lung is a rare, non-allergic interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of maple sap or resin. It primarily affects individuals working in the maple syrup industry, particularly those involved in stripping bark. The condition is characterized by progressive dyspnea and bilateral ground-glass opacities on imaging. Common synonyms include maple sap lung and maple bark lung. The causative agent is primarily the sap and resins from maple trees, with *Acer saccharum* being the most common source. The lungs are typically affected, with minimal involvement of other organs.

Air conditioner or humidifier lung, also known as humidifier fever or mold-associated lung disease, is an acute respiratory condition caused by inhalation of microbial contaminants from improperly maintained air conditioning or humidification systems. Common causative agents include bacteria, fungi, and endotoxins. Symptoms typically involve fever, chills, cough, and dyspnea. The condition primarily affects the respiratory tract, with inflammation and irritation of the airways. It is most commonly seen in individuals exposed to contaminated systems in healthcare or residential settings.

code_desc: Other specified hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to organic dust
summary: Other specified hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to organic dust is an inflammatory lung condition triggered by inhalation of specific organic dusts, not classified under other hypersensitivity pneumonitis types. Common synonyms include extrinsic allergic alveolitis. Causative agents include mold spores, bird proteins, and fungal agents. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing interstitial inflammation and potential fibrosis. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever. It typically involves the alveoli and interstitial tissue, with severity varying based on exposure duration and immune response.

code_desc: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to organic dust, unspecified
summary: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis due to organic dust, unspecified is an inflammatory lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of organic dust antigens. It results from an immune-mediated response to inhaled allergens, leading to interstitial pneumonia. Common causative agents include mold spores, bird proteins, and bacterial components. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. It may progress to chronic fibrosis if left untreated. Synonyms include extrinsic allergic alveolitis and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (in some cases).

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to solids or liquids
summary: Pneumonitis due to solids or liquids, also known as aspiration pneumonia, occurs when foreign material enters the lungs, causing inflammation. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and aspiration pneumonia. Causative agents include gastric contents, food, or other substances inhaled into the respiratory tract. This condition typically affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly the alveoli and bronchioles. It is more common in individuals with impaired swallowing, sedation, or neurological conditions. Symptoms include cough, fever, and respiratory distress. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as lung abscess or respiratory failure.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomit
summary: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomit, also known as aspiration pneumonia, occurs when foreign material enters the lungs, causing inflammation. Common synonyms include吸入性肺炎 (inhalation pneumonia) and aspiration pneumonitis. Causative agents include food particles, gastric contents, and oral secretions. Typically affecting the lower respiratory tract, it often involves the right lower lobe. Risk factors include altered consciousness, swallowing disorders, and gastrointestinal reflux. Symptoms may include cough, fever, and respiratory distress. It is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to oils or essences
summary: Pneumonitis due to oils or essences is an inflammatory lung condition caused by inhalation of volatile oils or aromatic essences. Common synonyms include essential oil pneumonitis and aromatic pneumonitis. Causative agents include eucalyptus, pine, and turpentine oils. Typically affecting the alveoli and bronchioles, this condition presents with cough, dyspnea, and fever. It is often seen in occupational or environmental exposures. Diagnosis is based on clinical history and imaging, with resolution usually occurring after removal from the irritant.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to aspiration of blood
summary: Pneumonitis due to aspiration of blood, also known as hemoptysis-induced pneumonia or pulmonary aspiration of blood, occurs when blood is inhaled into the lungs, leading to inflammation and injury. Common causative agents include trauma, coagulopathy, or vascular abnormalities. The condition typically affects the lower respiratory tract, particularly the alveoli and bronchioles. Symptoms include cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It is often associated with conditions such as pulmonary embolism, trauma, or coagulation disorders. Prompt diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications like respiratory failure.

Lipoid pneumonitis is a rare, non-infectious lung inflammation characterized by the presence of lipid-laden macrophages in alveolar spaces. It is often associated with inhalation of hydrocarbons or lipid-containing substances. Common synonyms include lipid pneumonia and hydrocarbon aspiration pneumonia. Causative agents include petroleum products, mineral oils, and certain industrial oils. The condition typically affects the lungs, with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. It may present as acute or chronic, and imaging often shows diffuse ground-glass opacities. Diagnosis is confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage and histopathological examination.

code_desc: Other specified pneumonitis due to solids or liquids
summary: "Other specified pneumonitis due to solids or liquids" refers to lung inflammation caused by inhalation of foreign substances such as solids or liquids, not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include aspiration pneumonitis or chemical pneumonitis. Causative agents include gastric contents, hydrocarbons, or industrial chemicals. Typically affects the lungs, with symptoms like cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. It often occurs in patients with impaired consciousness or swallowing disorders. Diagnosis is based on clinical history and imaging, with treatment focusing on supportive care and removal of the irritant.

code_desc: Pneumonitis due to solids or liquids, unspecified
summary: Pneumonitis due to solids or liquids, unspecified refers to inflammation of lung tissue caused by aspiration of foreign materials such as food, liquids, or other substances. This condition typically results from inhalation of non-respiratory particles into the airways and lungs. Common synonyms include aspiration pneumonia or foreign body pneumonia. Causative agents are primarily solid or liquid substances inhaled accidentally. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the lower respiratory tract. It is more common in individuals with impaired consciousness, swallowing disorders, or those under anesthesia.

Mendelson syndrome is an acute chemical pneumonia caused by aspiration of gastric contents into the lungs, typically occurring during general anesthesia or in cases of vomiting. Common synonyms include anesthetic aspiration pneumonia and acid aspiration syndrome. The condition is primarily caused by gastric acid, though other gastric contents may contribute. It most commonly affects the lungs, leading to inflammation, edema, and potential respiratory failure. The upper airway and bronchi are typically involved, with symptoms including cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Prompt recognition and treatment are essential to prevent severe complications.

Other specified pneumonitis refers to inflammatory lung injury not classified under more specific categories, often due to known or suspected exposures. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonitis or non-specific pneumonitis. Causative agents may include environmental toxins, drugs, or infections, though the exact cause is often unclear. The condition primarily affects the lung parenchyma, particularly the interstitial tissue, leading to inflammation and potential fibrosis. It can present with symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia. Diagnosis typically involves imaging and biopsy, with treatment directed at identifying and removing the inciting agent.

Pneumonitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of lung tissue without a specific identified cause. It may present as non-specific interstitial pneumonia or acute respiratory distress. Common synonyms include interstitial pneumonitis and diffuse alveolar damage. Causative agents may include viral, bacterial, or environmental exposures, though often unspecified. Typically affects the alveoli and interstitial spaces of the lungs, leading to symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia. It is often diagnosed through imaging and clinical presentation when a specific etiology cannot be determined.

code_desc: Airway disease due to specific organic dust
summary: Airway disease due to specific organic dust refers to respiratory conditions caused by inhalation of organic dusts containing allergens or irritants. Common synonyms include hypersensitivity pneumonitis and extrinsic allergic alveolitis. Causative agents often include mold spores, bird proteins, and agricultural dusts. The condition typically affects the lungs, causing inflammation and symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. It primarily impacts the lower respiratory tract, with potential progression to interstitial lung disease if exposure persists.

code_desc: Byssinosis due to exposure to cotton
summary: Byssinosis, also known as cotton worker's disease or brown lung, is a respiratory condition caused by inhalation of cotton, hemp, or flax dust. It primarily affects workers in textile industries. The condition is characterized by cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath, often worsening after the first week of work. Chronic exposure leads to airway inflammation, fibrosis, and reduced lung function. The causative agents include cotton dust and its associated endotoxins. Typically, the lower respiratory tract is affected, with involvement of the bronchioles and alveoli. Symptoms may include chest tightness and increased sputum production.

code_desc: Byssinosis due to exposure to flax
summary: Byssinosis, also known as brown lung disease, is a chronic obstructive pulmonary condition caused by inhalation of cotton, flax, or hemp dust. It primarily affects workers in textile industries, particularly those handling flax. The condition leads to airway inflammation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and progressive airflow limitation. Symptoms include cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath, often worsening after exposure. The lungs are typically affected, with histopathological changes resembling chronic bronchitis and fibrosis. Prolonged exposure increases the risk of respiratory failure and exacerbates existing lung diseases.

code_desc: Byssinosis due to exposure to cannabis
summary: Byssinosis due to exposure to cannabis is a respiratory condition caused by inhalation of cannabis smoke, leading to airway inflammation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. It is also known as "hashish asthma" or "cannabis-induced bronchitis." The primary causative agent is the inhalation of cannabis smoke, which contains irritants and toxic compounds. Symptoms include cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. The condition typically affects the upper and lower respiratory tract, with involvement of the bronchi and alveoli. Prolonged exposure may result in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease-like symptoms.

code_desc: Other specified airway disease due to specific organic dust
summary: "Other specified airway disease due to specific organic dust" refers to respiratory conditions caused by inhalation of specific organic dusts not classified under other categories. Common synonyms include hypersensitivity pneumonitis or extrinsic allergic alveolitis. Causative agents include molds, bird droppings, and agricultural dusts. The condition primarily affects the lungs, causing inflammation and airflow obstruction. Symptoms include cough, dyspnea, and fever. It typically affects the lower respiratory tract, with possible involvement of the bronchi and alveoli. Diagnosis involves exposure history, imaging, and pulmonary function tests.

code_desc: Airway disease due to specific organic dust, unspecified
summary: Airway disease due to specific organic dust, unspecified refers to respiratory conditions caused by inhalation of organic dust particles, such as mold, bacteria, or animal allergens. Common synonyms include hypersensitivity pneumonitis and allergic alveolitis. Causative agents may include bird droppings, agricultural dust, or fungal spores. The condition typically affects the lungs, causing inflammation and symptoms like cough, dyspnea, and fever. It primarily impacts the lower respiratory tract, leading to interstitial lung involvement in chronic cases. Diagnosis often requires exposure history and imaging studies.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to inhalation of chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours
summary: Respiratory conditions due to inhalation of chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours encompass a range of lung and airway disorders caused by exposure to toxic substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis, toxic inhalation injury, and occupational lung disease. Causative agents include industrial solvents, gases like chlorine or ammonia, and combustion products. These exposures typically affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, leading to inflammation, irritation, and potential damage to the alveoli and bronchioles. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and respiratory distress, with severity depending on the substance and duration of exposure.

code_desc: Bronchitis or pneumonitis due to chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours
summary: Bronchitis or pneumonitis due to chemicals, gases, fumes, or vapours refers to inflammation of the bronchi or lung parenchyma caused by inhalation of noxious substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonia or toxic bronchitis. Causative agents include industrial chemicals, smoke, aerosols, and irritant gases such as chlorine, ammonia, and sulfur dioxide. Typically affects the respiratory tract, with symptoms including cough, dyspnea, and chest discomfort. The condition can lead to acute or chronic respiratory impairment, particularly in occupational or environmental exposure settings.

code_desc: Pulmonary oedema due to chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours
summary: Pulmonary oedema due to chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours is an acute lung injury caused by inhalation of toxic substances. It leads to fluid accumulation in the alveoli, impairing gas exchange. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and toxic pulmonary oedema. Causative agents include chlorine, ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and organic solvents. Typically affects the lungs, with symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and hypoxia. Severe cases may progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome. The condition primarily impacts the respiratory system, with potential systemic involvement in severe exposures.

code_desc: Upper respiratory inflammation due to chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours, not elsewhere classified
summary: Upper respiratory inflammation due to chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours, not elsewhere classified refers to irritation and inflammation of the upper airway caused by exposure to harmful airborne substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis or inhalation injury. Causative agents may include industrial chemicals, solvents, aerosols, and irritant gases such as chlorine or ammonia. Typically affected areas include the nose, pharynx, larynx, and trachea. Symptoms often involve cough, sore throat, hoarseness, and difficulty breathing. The condition is often acute but can lead to chronic respiratory issues with prolonged exposure.

code_desc: Other specified respiratory conditions due to inhalation of chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours
summary: Other specified respiratory conditions due to inhalation of chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours refer to acute or chronic respiratory illnesses caused by exposure to harmful airborne substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis, toxic inhalation injury, and occupational lung disease. Causative agents may include industrial solvents, pesticides, chlorine, ammonia, and welding fumes. These conditions typically affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, and inflammation. The lungs are most commonly involved, with potential for systemic effects depending on the toxin.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to inhalation of chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours, unspecified
summary: Respiratory conditions due to inhalation of chemicals, gases, fumes or vapours, unspecified refer to acute or chronic lung injuries caused by exposure to toxic substances. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis, toxic inhalation injury, and gas-induced lung damage. Causative agents may include industrial chemicals, solvents, gases like chlorine or ammonia, and combustion byproducts. These conditions typically affect the upper and lower respiratory tract, leading to inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms may include cough, shortness of breath, and respiratory distress. The severity depends on the substance, exposure duration, and individual susceptibility.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to other external agents
summary: Respiratory conditions due to other external agents refer to lung disorders caused by environmental factors not classified as infections, allergens, or occupational exposures. Common synonyms include inhalation injuries and chemical pneumonitis. Causative agents may include smoke, toxic gases, vapors, and particulate matter. These conditions typically affect the airways and alveoli, leading to inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms often include cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. The upper and lower respiratory tracts are commonly involved, with severity varying based on exposure type and duration.

code_desc: Acute pulmonary manifestations due to radiation
summary: Acute pulmonary manifestations due to radiation refer to lung injury occurring shortly after exposure to ionizing radiation. Common synonyms include radiation pneumonitis and radiation-induced lung injury. Causative agents are ionizing radiation, often from radiotherapy or nuclear accidents. Typically affected body parts include the lungs, with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. The condition results from inflammation and edema due to radiation-induced damage to alveolar structures and vascular endothelium. It commonly occurs in patients receiving thoracic radiation therapy.

code_desc: Chronic or other pulmonary manifestations due to radiation
summary: Chronic or other pulmonary manifestations due to radiation refer to long-term lung damage caused by ionizing radiation therapy. Common synonyms include radiation pneumonitis and radiation-induced lung disease. Causative agents are ionizing radiation, typically from cancer treatments. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, and decreased oxygen saturation. It commonly occurs in patients treated for thoracic malignancies. The alveoli and interstitium are most frequently involved, resulting in reduced lung function and potential respiratory failure.

Acute drug-induced interstitial lung disorders are a group of pulmonary conditions characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium, often leading to progressive respiratory failure. Common synonyms include drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis and drug-induced interstitial pneumonia. Causative agents include medications such as amiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, and nitrofurantoin. These disorders typically affect the lungs, causing symptoms like dyspnea, cough, and hypoxemia. Early recognition and discontinuation of the offending agent are critical for improved outcomes.

Chronic drug-induced interstitial lung disorders are a group of lung diseases characterized by progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium, resulting from long-term exposure to certain medications. Common synonyms include drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis and drug-related interstitial pneumonitis. Causative agents include amiodarone, bleomycin, methotrexate, and nitrofurantoin. These conditions primarily affect the lungs, leading to symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and reduced exercise tolerance. Early diagnosis and discontinuation of the offending agent are critical to prevent irreversible lung damage.

Aspergillus-induced allergic or hypersensitivity conditions refer to immune-mediated reactions triggered by exposure to Aspergillus species, primarily *A. fumigatus*. Common synonyms include allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) and aspergillus hypersensitivity syndrome. These conditions typically affect the respiratory tract, causing symptoms such as cough, wheezing, and fever. They are more common in individuals with underlying asthma or cystic fibrosis. The immune response involves IgE-mediated inflammation and eosinophilic infiltration, leading to airway damage and fibrosis. Systemic manifestations may occur in immunocompromised patients.

code_desc: Other specified respiratory conditions due to other external agents
summary: "Other specified respiratory conditions due to other external agents" refers to respiratory disorders caused by external factors not classified elsewhere, such as chemical irritants, environmental pollutants, or occupational exposures. Common synonyms include chemical pneumonitis and inhalation injury. Causative agents may include industrial chemicals, smoke, or toxic gases. These conditions typically affect the airways and lung parenchyma, leading to inflammation, edema, and impaired gas exchange. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and respiratory distress. The condition is often diagnosed based on exposure history and clinical presentation.

code_desc: Respiratory conditions due to other external agents, unspecified
summary: Respiratory conditions due to other external agents, unspecified refer to lung disorders caused by environmental factors not classified elsewhere, such as irritants, chemicals, or particulate matter. Common synonyms include inhalation injuries and chemical pneumonitis. Causative agents may include smoke, dust, fumes, or toxic gases. These conditions typically affect the airways and alveoli, leading to inflammation, bronchospasm, or pulmonary edema. Symptoms often include cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. The unspecified nature indicates lack of precise identification of the causative agent or mechanism.

code_desc: Other specified lung diseases due to external agents
summary: "Other specified lung diseases due to external agents" refers to lung conditions caused by environmental or occupational exposures not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include inhalation injury or occupational lung disease. Causative agents may include chemicals, dust, fumes, or irritants. These conditions typically affect the respiratory tract, particularly the airways and alveoli. Symptoms may include cough, dyspnea, and inflammation. Affected body parts primarily include the lungs, with potential involvement of the upper airway. The severity varies based on exposure duration and type.

code_desc: Lung diseases due to external agents, unspecified
summary: Lung diseases due to external agents, unspecified refer to respiratory conditions caused by environmental factors such as chemicals, pollutants, or irritants, where the specific agent is not identified. Common synonyms include occupational lung disease and environmental lung injury. Causative agents may include dust, fumes, gases, and allergens. These conditions typically affect the airways, alveoli, and interstitial lung tissue, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, or impaired gas exchange. Symptoms often include cough, dyspnea, and reduced lung function. The condition is often associated with occupational exposure or environmental pollution.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a severe lung condition characterized by widespread inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli, leading to impaired gas exchange and hypoxemia. Common synonyms include adult respiratory distress syndrome and acute lung injury. It is typically caused by direct lung injury (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration) or indirect factors (e.g., sepsis, trauma). The primary affected body parts are the lungs, with systemic involvement possible. ARDS predominantly affects the alveolar-capillary membrane, resulting in respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation.

Pulmonary oedema is the accumulation of fluid in the alveoli and interstitial spaces of the lungs, leading to impaired gas exchange. Common synonyms include pulmonary congestion and cardiac pulmonary oedema. It is typically caused by left ventricular failure, hypertension, or valvular disease, though other causes include pneumonia, sepsis, and high-altitude exposure. The condition primarily affects the lungs, but can also involve the heart and systemic circulation. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, and frothy sputum. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent respiratory failure.

Pulmonary eosinophilia is a clinical syndrome characterized by increased eosinophils in the lungs, often associated with inflammation and tissue damage. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic lung disease. It is caused by various agents such as parasitic infections, allergic reactions, drug hypersensitivity, and autoimmune disorders. The condition typically affects the lungs, leading to symptoms like cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. In some cases, it may involve the skin, gastrointestinal tract, or other organs, depending on the underlying cause.

Asthmatic pulmonary eosinophilia is a condition characterized by the presence of elevated eosinophils in the lungs, often associated with asthma. It is also known as eosinophilic asthma or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Common causative agents include allergens, parasitic infections, and fungal organisms such as *Aspergillus fumigatus*. The primary affected body parts are the airways and lungs, with symptoms including wheezing, cough, and dyspnea. This condition can lead to airway inflammation and remodeling, complicating asthma management.

Idiopathic eosinophilic pneumonitis is a rare lung disorder characterized by infiltration of eosinophils in the pulmonary parenchyma without a known cause. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and Löffler's syndrome. The condition may be associated with parasitic infections, allergic reactions, or drug hypersensitivity. It typically affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and fever. The disease can be acute or chronic, with variable radiographic findings. Eosinophilic infiltration is often found in alveoli and interstitium, leading to inflammation and potential fibrosis. Diagnosis involves imaging, blood tests, and bronchoalveolar lavage.

Idiopathic acute eosinophilic pneumonitis is a rare, inflammatory lung disorder characterized by acute onset of respiratory symptoms and increased eosinophils in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Common synonyms include acute eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic alveolitis. The condition is often associated with allergens, medications, or infections, though causative agents are frequently unidentified. It primarily affects the lungs, causing interstitial inflammation and alveolar filling with eosinophils. Clinically, it presents with fever, cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia, typically resolving with corticosteroid therapy.

Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonitis is a rare lung disorder characterized by persistent eosinophilic infiltration of the lungs without an identifiable cause. Common synonyms include chronic eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), though the latter is distinct. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to inflammation and impaired gas exchange. Causative agents are unknown, hence the term "idiopathic." It typically presents with cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia, with imaging showing diffuse interstitial lung changes. Treatment often involves corticosteroids.

Other specified idiopathic eosinophilic pneumonitis refers to a group of interstitial lung diseases characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the lungs without a known specific cause. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. While the exact cause is unknown, some cases may be associated with environmental exposures or allergic reactions. The primary affected body part is the lung, with inflammation and infiltration of eosinophils in the alveoli and interstitium. Symptoms include dyspnea, cough, and fever. The condition is typically diagnosed through imaging, biopsy, and exclusion of other causes.

Idiopathic eosinophilic pneumonitis, unspecified, is a rare lung disorder characterized by infiltration of eosinophils in the pulmonary parenchyma without a known cause. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic lung disease. The condition may be associated with parasitic infections, allergic reactions, or unknown factors. It typically affects the lungs, causing symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia. The exact etiology remains unclear in many cases, leading to the "idiopathic" designation. The disease can present acutely or chronically, with variable radiographic and histopathological findings.

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) is a parasitic lung disease characterized by eosinophilia, cough, and respiratory symptoms. Common synonyms include tropical eosinophilia and hypereosinophilic syndrome when systemic involvement occurs. Caused primarily by *Strongyloides stercoralis* and, less commonly, *Wuchereria bancrofti*, it affects the lungs and sometimes the skin and gastrointestinal tract. The infection leads to airway inflammation and granuloma formation, often presenting with fever and wheezing. Diagnosis involves eosinophil count and serological testing. Treatment typically includes antiparasitic drugs like ivermectin.

Other specified pulmonary eosinophilia refers to a group of pulmonary conditions characterized by eosinophilia without a clear alternative diagnosis. It may present with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and chest discomfort. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic alveolitis. Causative agents are often unknown, though some cases may be associated with allergens, infections, or drug reactions. The lungs are primarily affected, with infiltration of eosinophils in the alveoli or interstitium. It is typically diagnosed when other forms of eosinophilic disorders are excluded.

Pulmonary eosinophilia, unspecified, is a condition characterized by an increased number of eosinophils in the lungs, often associated with inflammation. It may present with symptoms such as cough, dyspnea, and chest discomfort. Common synonyms include eosinophilic pneumonia and eosinophilic lung disease. Causative agents may include parasitic infections, allergic reactions, or drug-induced hypersensitivity. Typically, the lungs are affected, but systemic involvement can occur. The exact cause is often unknown in unspecified cases.

Idiopathic interstitial pneumonitis refers to a group of chronic lung diseases characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the interstitial tissue in the lungs, with no known specific cause. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and interstitial lung disease. While the exact cause is unknown, environmental exposures, genetic factors, and autoimmune conditions may contribute. The primary affected body parts are the lungs, particularly the alveolar walls and surrounding interstitium. It predominantly affects the lower lung zones and can lead to progressive dyspnea and reduced lung function.

Acute interstitial pneumonitis, also known as acute non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema or diffuse alveolar damage, is an inflammatory lung condition characterized by infiltration of inflammatory cells and edema in the alveolar interstitium. It typically affects the lungs, leading to impaired gas exchange and hypoxemia. Common causative agents include infections, drug reactions, inhalational injuries, and autoimmune diseases. The condition primarily involves the alveoli and interstitial tissue of the lungs, often presenting with symptoms such as dyspnea, cough, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on imaging.

code_desc: Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema syndrome
summary: Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema syndrome is a rare lung disorder characterized by coexisting interstitial pulmonary fibrosis and airspace destruction, leading to progressive respiratory impairment. Common synonyms include UIP-emphysema overlap syndrome and combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema. Causative agents may include environmental exposures, autoimmune diseases, or idiopathic factors. The condition primarily affects the lungs, particularly the distal airways and alveolar regions, resulting in impaired gas exchange and reduced lung compliance. It is typically seen in middle-aged to older adults.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonitis (COP), also known as usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), is a chronic interstitial lung disease of unknown cause. It is characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the lung parenchyma, with organizing pneumonia as a key histopathological feature. Common synonyms include idiopathic interstitial pneumonia and UIP. The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to progressive dyspnea and impaired gas exchange.
