Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and exclusion of other known conditions.

code_desc: Genetic or developmental disorders involving lips or oral mucosa
summary: Genetic or developmental disorders involving lips or oral mucosa encompass congenital anomalies affecting the structure and function of the lips, palate, and oral mucosa. Common conditions include cleft lip and palate, which result from failure of facial processes to fuse properly during embryonic development. Other disorders may involve abnormal mucosal pigmentation or texture. Causative agents include genetic mutations, environmental factors, and teratogens. These conditions typically affect the upper lip, palate, and surrounding oral mucosa, leading to functional and aesthetic concerns. Synonyms include orofacial clefts, lip defects, and oral mucosal abnormalities.

Xerostomia, also known as dry mouth, is a condition characterized by reduced saliva production leading to oral dryness. Common causes include medications such as anticholinergics, antidepressants, and antihistamines, as well as conditions like Sjögren’s syndrome, diabetes, and radiation therapy. It commonly affects the mouth, lips, and throat, causing discomfort, difficulty in swallowing, and increased risk of dental caries. Symptoms may also include altered taste and speech difficulties. The salivary glands, particularly the parotid and submandibular glands, are typically involved in the pathophysiology of this condition.

Oral submucous fibrosis is a chronic, progressive, inflammatory condition characterized by fibrous thickening of the oral mucosa, leading to restricted mouth opening and tissue stiffness. Common synonyms include oral fibromatosis and leukoplakia-like changes. The primary causative agent is areca nut chewing, often combined with tobacco use. It predominantly affects the buccal mucosa, palate, and gingiva. The condition is more prevalent in males and is associated with an increased risk of oral cancer. Early diagnosis and cessation of risk factors are critical for management.

Contact gingivostomatitis is an inflammatory condition of the oral mucosa and gingiva, typically caused by direct physical or chemical irritation. Common synonyms include traumatic stomatitis and irritant stomatitis. It is often due to ill-fitting dentures, sharp teeth, or ingestion of irritants. The condition primarily affects the gingiva and adjacent mucosal surfaces, presenting with redness, swelling, and ulceration. It is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals. Healing occurs with removal of the irritant, though secondary infections may occur.

Allergic contact gingivostomatitis is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction characterized by inflammation of the oral mucosa, particularly the gingiva and buccal mucosa. It typically presents with erythema, swelling, and sometimes ulceration. Common causative agents include dental materials, topical anesthetics, and certain foods. Synonyms include allergic stomatitis and contact stomatitis. The condition is often seen in individuals with a history of atopy or previous allergic reactions. It is more prevalent in children and adolescents. The oral cavity is the primary affected area, with involvement of the lips, tongue, and palate.

Irritant contact gingivostomatitis is an inflammatory condition of the oral mucosa caused by direct contact with irritants such as chemicals, allergens, or physical trauma. Common synonyms include acute chemical stomatitis and irritant stomatitis. It typically affects the gingiva and mucous membranes of the mouth, including the lips, tongue, and palate. Causative agents may include topical medications, dental materials, or spicy foods. Symptoms include erythema, edema, and ulceration. The condition is often self-limiting but may require symptomatic treatment to manage discomfort.

Diseases of the tongue encompass a variety of conditions affecting the muscular and mucosal structures of the oral cavity. Common synonyms include oral mucosal disorders and lingual pathologies. These conditions may arise from infections, autoimmune processes, nutritional deficiencies, or trauma. Causative agents include bacteria, viruses (e.g., herpes simplex), fungi, and parasites. Commonly affected areas include the dorsal surface, underside, and lateral borders of the tongue. Symptoms often involve pain, swelling, ulcers, or color changes. Conditions such as geographic tongue, oral thrush, and glossitis are frequently observed.

Glossitis is an inflammatory condition of the tongue characterized by swelling, redness, and loss of papillae. It may present with pain, burning, or altered taste. Common synonyms include atrophic glossitis and geographic tongue. Causative agents include infections (e.g., fungal, bacterial, viral), nutritional deficiencies (e.g., iron, B12, folate), allergic reactions, and irritants. It typically affects the dorsal and lateral surfaces of the tongue, with the circumvallate papillae often involved. The condition can be localized or diffuse, depending on the underlying cause.

Geographic tongue, also known as benign migratory stomatitis or erythema migrans, is a chronic, benign condition characterized by irregular, red, smooth patches on the dorsal surface of the tongue, surrounded by a white or yellowish border. The affected areas may change location over time, giving the appearance of a map. The exact cause is unknown, though it may be associated with stress, irritants, or allergic reactions. It commonly affects adults and is more prevalent in females. No specific treatment is required, as the condition is usually asymptomatic or causes mild discomfort.

Atrophy of tongue papillae refers to the wasting or shrinkage of the lingual papillae, leading to a smooth, glossy appearance of the tongue. Common synonyms include fungiform papilla atrophy and lingual papilla hypoplasia. This condition is often associated with nutritional deficiencies, particularly iron deficiency anemia, and can also result from chronic inflammation, infections, or systemic diseases. It typically affects the dorsal surface of the tongue, with the filiform papillae being most commonly involved. The condition may also be seen in patients with gastrointestinal disorders or those on long-term medication use.

Median rhomboid glossitis is a chronic, non-epithelialized lesion located in the midline of the dorsal tongue. It appears as a smooth, red, oval or rhomboid-shaped area, often with a fissured or rugated surface. Common synonyms include median rhomboid glossitis and median rhomboid geographic tongue. The exact cause is unknown, but it is associated with fungal infections, particularly *Candida albicans*, and may be linked to local trauma, nutritional deficiencies, or immune suppression. It typically affects the midline of the tongue, most commonly in adults, and is more prevalent in males.

Hypertrophy of tongue papillae refers to the abnormal enlargement of the lingual papillae, the small bumps on the tongue's surface. Common synonyms include lingual papillitis and enlarged tongue papillae. This condition is often caused by chronic irritation, smoking, or geographic tongue. It typically affects the dorsal surface of the tongue, particularly the fungiform and filiform papillae. The affected areas may appear red, inflamed, or have a cobblestone appearance. It is more common in individuals with oral mucosal disorders or those who consume spicy or acidic foods regularly.

Macroglossia is a condition characterized by an enlarged tongue, often exceeding the normal size relative to the oral cavity. It can be congenital or acquired, resulting from various causes such as genetic disorders, hormonal imbalances, or tumors. Common synonyms include giant tongue and enlarged tongue. Causative agents may include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Down syndrome, or hemifacial microsomia. The tongue is the primary affected body part, and the condition can lead to speech, swallowing, and breathing difficulties. It may also cause dental and airway complications. Early diagnosis and intervention are essential to manage functional and aesthetic concerns.

"Other specified diseases of tongue" refers to tongue disorders not classified under more specific categories, such as infections, tumors, or developmental anomalies. Common synonyms include unspecified tongue disorders or miscellaneous tongue conditions. Causative agents may include trauma, irritants, autoimmune factors, or systemic diseases. Typically, the tongue is affected, with symptoms like pain, swelling, or altered sensation. These conditions are often diagnosed when specific etiologies are not identified or are too rare to classify separately.

Diseases of tongue, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the tongue without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include glossitis, geographic tongue, and lingual disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., candida, herpes simplex virus), nutritional deficiencies, allergic reactions, or trauma. Typically affected body parts include the tongue's surface, mucosa, and submucosal layers. Symptoms may involve pain, swelling, discoloration, or altered taste. These conditions often require further diagnostic evaluation to determine the exact cause and appropriate treatment.

Diseases of salivary glands encompass a range of conditions affecting the major and minor salivary glands, leading to symptoms such as swelling, pain, and secretion abnormalities. Common synonyms include sialadenitis and sialolithiasis. Causative agents include bacterial infections (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus), viral agents, and obstructive factors like salivary stones. These conditions typically affect the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands, with the parotid gland being the most commonly involved. Inflammation, blockage, and tumor formation are common pathologies.

Atrophy of salivary gland refers to the shrinkage and loss of function in salivary glands, leading to reduced saliva production. Common synonyms include sialoadenosis and glandular atrophy. It is often associated with aging, autoimmune conditions such as Sjögren’s syndrome, radiation therapy, and chronic infections. The parotid and submandibular glands are most commonly affected. Symptoms may include dry mouth, difficulty in chewing, and increased susceptibility to dental caries. The condition can be primary or secondary to systemic diseases. Diagnosis typically involves clinical evaluation and imaging studies. Treatment focuses on managing underlying causes and alleviating symptoms.

Hypertrophy of the salivary gland refers to the abnormal enlargement of one or more salivary glands, most commonly the parotid or submandibular glands. It may result from chronic inflammation, infection, or obstruction of the gland ducts. Common synonyms include salivary gland hyperplasia or enlargement. Causative agents include viral infections such as mumps, bacterial infections, or chronic sialadenitis. The condition typically affects the parotid glands, though the submandibular and sublingual glands may also be involved. It is often asymptomatic but can cause swelling, discomfort, or difficulty in swallowing.

Sialoadenitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the salivary glands, most commonly the parotid and submandibular glands. It can be acute or chronic, often presenting with swelling, pain, and tenderness. Common synonyms include salivary gland inflammation and sialadenopathy. Causative agents include bacterial infections such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, viral infections like mumps, and obstructive causes such as sialolithiasis. It typically affects the parotid and submandibular glands, with symptoms often exacerbated by dry mouth or dehydration.

An abscess of the salivary gland is a localized collection of pus resulting from a bacterial infection within the glandular tissue. Common synonyms include sialadenitis with secondary suppuration and salivary gland abscess. The condition is typically caused by bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and *E. coli*. It most commonly affects the submandibular and parotid glands, often due to obstruction of the salivary ducts, leading to stasis and subsequent infection. Clinically, it presents with pain, swelling, erythema, and tenderness in the affected area.

Sialolithiasis is the formation of salivary gland stones, most commonly in the submandibular gland. It results from calcification of salivary ducts, often due to dehydration, infection, or ductal obstruction. Common synonyms include sialolith, salivary calculus, and sialolith formation. The condition typically affects the submandibular and parotid glands, with stones often lodged in the submandibular duct. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and decreased salivation during meals. It is more prevalent in males and can lead to complications such as infection or abscess if untreated.

A mucocele of the salivary gland is a benign, cystic lesion resulting from the obstruction of a salivary gland duct, leading to retention of mucus. Common synonyms include ranula and sialolithiasis. It is typically caused by trauma, ductal obstruction, or sialoliths. The most commonly affected sites are the floor of the mouth, lower lip, and buccal mucosa. Clinically, it presents as a painless, bluish, fluctuant swelling. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical examination and imaging. Treatment options include surgical excision or marsupialization.

Disturbances of salivary secretion refer to abnormalities in the production, composition, or flow of saliva. Common synonyms include xerostomia (dry mouth) and sialadenitis (inflammation of salivary glands). These conditions may result from dehydration, medications (e.g., anticholinergics), autoimmune disorders, infections, or radiation therapy. They predominantly affect the major salivary glands—parotid, submandibular, and sublingual—as well as the minor glands in the oral mucosa. Symptoms include dryness, difficulty swallowing, and increased susceptibility to dental caries.

Sialophagia is a condition characterized by the sensation of a lump or glob in the throat, often due to the presence of mucus or saliva. It is commonly associated with postnasal drip, chronic pharyngitis, or gastroesophageal reflux disease. Synonyms include globus pharyngis and pharyngeal globus. Common causative agents include allergies, sinus infections, and acid reflux. The condition typically affects the pharynx and may involve the larynx. It is generally not associated with dysphagia but can cause discomfort and anxiety. Diagnosis is usually clinical, with exclusion of organic pathology.

Sialoschesis is a rare, chronic condition characterized by the formation of sialoliths (salivary stones) within the salivary glands, most commonly the submandibular gland. It is also known as sialolithiasis or salivary calculi. The condition results from the deposition of calcium salts in the salivary ducts, leading to obstruction and subsequent gland dysfunction. Common causative agents include calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate. It typically affects the submandibular, sublingual, and parotid glands, with the submandibular gland being the most frequently involved. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and decreased salivation during meals.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of salivary glands
summary: "Other specified diseases of salivary glands" refers to salivary gland disorders not classified under more specific categories, such as sialadenitis or sialolithiasis. Common synonyms include idiopathic sialadenopathy and non-specific salivary gland inflammation. Causative agents may include viral infections (e.g., mumps), bacterial infections, autoimmune conditions, or exposure to toxins. These conditions typically affect the major salivary glands, particularly the parotid and submandibular glands, leading to symptoms such as swelling, pain, and reduced saliva production. The exact cause is often unclear in many cases.

Diseases of salivary glands, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the major and minor salivary glands without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include sialadenitis and sialolithiasis. Causative agents may include bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, viruses, or obstruction from stones. These conditions typically affect the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands, leading to symptoms like swelling, pain, and reduced saliva flow. They are often associated with infection, inflammation, or blockage of salivary ducts.

code_desc: Cysts of oral or facial-neck region
summary: Cysts of the oral or facial-neck region are closed sac-like structures filled with fluid or semi-solid material, commonly arising from odontogenic tissues or epithelial remnants. Common synonyms include odontogenic keratocysts, follicular cysts, and dentigerous cysts. These cysts are typically caused by developmental abnormalities, retention of epithelial cells, or inflammatory processes. They most frequently occur in the maxilla and mandible, particularly around unerupted teeth, and may also develop in the neck region. While benign, they can cause expansion of bone and compress adjacent structures if left untreated.

Developmental odontogenic cysts are benign, fluid-filled lesions originating from odontogenic tissues during tooth development. Common synonyms include radicular cyst, periapical cyst, and follicular cyst. These cysts are typically caused by inflammatory processes, such as pulpal necrosis, leading to granuloma formation and subsequent cyst development. They most commonly occur in the maxilla and mandible, particularly in the posterior regions, and are associated with non-vital teeth. Radiographically, they appear as unilocular or multilocular radiolucencies surrounding the roots of affected teeth.

code_desc: Developmental nonodontogenic cysts of oral region
summary: Developmental nonodontogenic cysts of the oral region are congenital lesions arising from embryonic remnants of the oral epithelium, not associated with tooth development. Common synonyms include nasolabial cyst and thyroglossal duct cyst. These cysts are typically caused by developmental anomalies during embryogenesis. They most commonly occur in the midline of the neck (thyroglossal duct cysts) or the maxillofacial region (nasolabial cysts). They are generally asymptomatic but may cause swelling or cosmetic concerns. Diagnosis is often made via imaging and clinical examination. Surgical excision is the primary treatment.

code_desc: Other specified cysts of oral or facial-neck region
summary: "Other specified cysts of oral or facial-neck region" refers to non-specific, uncommon cystic lesions in the oral cavity, face, or neck that do not fit into more defined categories such as epidermoid or dentigerous cysts. These cysts may arise from developmental, inflammatory, or traumatic causes. Common synonyms include miscellaneous cysts or unspecified cysts. Causative agents may include retained epithelial cells, infection, or trauma. Typically, these cysts affect the jaw, palate, gingiva, or submandibular regions. They are often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally during routine examinations.

code_desc: Cysts of oral or facial-neck region, unspecified
summary: Cysts of the oral or facial-neck region, unspecified, refer to fluid-filled sacs that develop in the oral cavity, face, or neck. Common synonyms include odontogenic cysts, developmental cysts, and retained epithelial cysts. These cysts are often caused by developmental abnormalities, trauma, or obstruction of epithelial remnants. Common causative agents include inflammatory processes, odontogenic infections, or congenital factors. Typically affected areas include the jaw, palate, tongue, and neck. They may present as painless swellings and are often diagnosed through imaging and clinical examination.

Diseases of the jaws encompass a range of conditions affecting the maxilla and mandible, including infections, tumors, and developmental abnormalities. Common synonyms include odontogenic diseases and maxillofacial disorders. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus* and *Streptococcus*, as well as viral agents like herpes simplex. These conditions typically affect the teeth, gums, and surrounding bone structures, often leading to pain, swelling, and functional impairment. They may also involve the temporomandibular joint and adjacent soft tissues.

Inflammatory conditions of the jaws encompass a group of disorders characterized by redness, swelling, pain, and sometimes pus in the jaw area. Common synonyms include periapical abscess, periodontal abscess, and osteomyelitis. These conditions are typically caused by bacterial infections, often originating from dental caries, periodontal disease, or trauma. They commonly affect the maxilla and mandible, with involvement of the surrounding soft tissues and bone. In severe cases, the infection can spread to adjacent structures, leading to systemic complications if left untreated.

Alveolitis of the jaw, also known as dry socket or alveolar osteitis, is an inflammatory condition characterized by pain and necrosis of the socket following tooth extraction. It typically occurs 2–4 days post-extraction and is most common after the removal of lower molars. The condition is caused by the dislodgement of the blood clot in the extraction site, leading to exposure of the underlying bone and nerves. Common causative factors include improper post-operative care, smoking, and infection. It primarily affects the alveolar bone and surrounding soft tissues in the oral cavity.

Exostosis of the jaw, also known as osteochondroma or jaw bone tumor, is a benign bony growth that arises from the surface of a bone. It is commonly caused by genetic factors, such as mutations in the EXT1 or EXT2 genes, or may result from trauma. This condition typically affects the mandible and maxilla, often presenting as a slow-growing, painless swelling. It is more prevalent in adolescents and young adults. Synonyms include osteochondroma and jaw osteoma. The lesion is usually sessile or pedunculated and may be associated with other skeletal abnormalities in some cases.

Stafne mandibular bone cavity is a benign, asymptomatic developmental anomaly characterized by a well-defined, unilocular radiolucency in the mandible, most commonly located in the posterior region. It is also known as Stafne bone cavity or Stafne defect. The exact etiology is unclear, but it is thought to result from an odontogenic cyst or a developmental anomaly involving the mandibular canal. It typically affects the posterior mandible and is often discovered incidentally on panoramic radiographs. No specific treatment is required as it is generally asymptomatic and does not progress.

"Other specified diseases of jaws" refers to jaw conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as osteomyelitis or tumors. Common synonyms include unspecified jaw disorders or miscellaneous jaw diseases. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, or systemic conditions. These disorders typically affect the mandible and maxilla, causing pain, swelling, or functional impairment. They may arise from inflammatory processes, developmental anomalies, or complications from dental procedures. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and imaging. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and may involve antibiotics, surgery, or supportive care.

Diseases of jaws, unspecified refer to conditions affecting the maxilla and mandible without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include undiagnosed jaw disorders or unspecified jaw pathology. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, developmental anomalies, or systemic diseases. Typically, these conditions affect the bones, teeth, and surrounding soft tissues of the oral cavity. Symptoms may include pain, swelling, deformity, or functional impairment. Diagnosis often requires imaging and clinical evaluation due to the lack of specific identification. Treatment varies depending on underlying causes and may involve surgery, medication, or supportive care.

code_desc: Disorders of tooth development or eruption
summary: Disorders of tooth development or eruption encompass abnormalities in the formation, eruption timing, or structure of teeth. Common synonyms include dental dysplasia, hypodontia, and delayed eruption. These conditions may result from genetic factors, such as mutations in genes like MSX1 or PAX9, or environmental influences like radiation, infection, or nutritional deficiencies. Typically affecting the maxilla and mandible, they can involve enamel hypoplasia, supernumerary teeth, or impacted teeth. Clinical manifestations vary from missing teeth to malpositioned or malformed dental structures, impacting both function and aesthetics.

Fluoride-related opacities or lesions refer to white or cloudy opacities in the enamel of teeth caused by excessive fluoride exposure during tooth development. Common synonyms include dental fluorosis and mottled enamel. The primary causative agent is fluoride, often from drinking water, dental products, or industrial exposure. These lesions typically affect the permanent teeth, especially the incisors and first molars, and may range from mild discoloration to severe pitting and structural damage. The condition is most commonly seen in children exposed to high fluoride levels during critical developmental periods.

Nonfluoride enamel opacities are white or brown discolorations of dental enamel caused by developmental disturbances during tooth formation. Common synonyms include enamel hypoplasia and mottled enamel. These opacities result from factors such as nutritional deficiencies, systemic illnesses, or exposure to certain chemicals. Lead, mercury, and other toxicants may contribute. They typically affect the anterior teeth, especially incisors, and are often bilateral. The condition is distinct from fluorosis and is associated with enamel hypomineralization.

Disturbances in tooth formation, also known as dental dysplasia or amelogenesis imperfecta, refer to abnormalities in the development of tooth structure. These conditions affect enamel and dentin formation, leading to weakened, discolored, or malformed teeth. Common causative agents include genetic mutations, systemic diseases, and environmental factors during tooth development. Typically, the condition affects primary and permanent teeth, with enamel hypoplasia and hypomineralization being common features. It may be localized or generalized, impacting both anterior and posterior teeth.

Root anomaly refers to an abnormal development or presence of a tooth root, often leading to structural or functional complications. Common synonyms include root fusion, root resorption, and root malformation. It may result from genetic factors, trauma, or infection. Causative agents include trauma, inflammatory processes, and certain systemic conditions. Typically affecting permanent teeth, it is most commonly observed in the maxillary and mandibular anterior regions. This condition can impact tooth stability, periodontal health, and orthodontic treatment planning.

Cementum dysplasia is a rare developmental disorder characterized by abnormal formation of cementum, the calcified tissue covering the roots of teeth. It is also known as cementum hyperplasia or cementoma. The condition is typically caused by genetic mutations, particularly in the WNT10A gene. It most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular incisors and can lead to localized swelling, radiolucency, and altered tooth structure. The disorder is usually benign and may present in childhood or adolescence. It is often associated with other developmental anomalies, such as hypodontia or malocclusion.

Disturbances in tooth eruption refer to abnormalities in the timing, sequence, or pattern of tooth emergence through the gums. Common synonyms include delayed eruption, premature eruption, and ectopic eruption. These disturbances may result from genetic factors, local infection, trauma, or systemic conditions such as hypocalcemia or hypothyroidism. They most commonly affect the primary and permanent dentition, with the maxillary and mandibular incisors and molars being the most frequently involved. Such anomalies can lead to malocclusion, crowding, or impacted teeth, requiring orthodontic or surgical intervention.

Teething syndrome refers to a collection of symptoms experienced by infants and young children during the eruption of their primary teeth. Common symptoms include irritability, excessive drooling, gum swelling, and mild fever. Synonyms include teething pain, eruptional gingivitis, and dental eruption syndrome. The condition is caused by the mechanical pressure of emerging teeth on the gums, though no specific infectious agent is known. Typically affected body parts include the gums, mouth, and surrounding areas, with symptoms often localized to the gingival tissues. It is most common in children between 6 and 24 months of age.

Ankylosis of teeth is a condition characterized by the fusion of a tooth root to the surrounding alveolar bone, resulting in loss of normal physiological mobility. Common synonyms include dental ankylosis and cementoblastoma. It is often caused by trauma, infection, or inflammatory processes that stimulate excessive bone formation. The condition typically affects the anterior maxillary teeth, particularly the incisors, and can lead to malocclusion and impaired dental development. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent complications in tooth eruption and alignment.

code_desc: Other specified disturbances in tooth eruption
summary: "Other specified disturbances in tooth eruption" refers to abnormal tooth eruption patterns not classified under specific developmental disorders. Common synonyms include delayed eruption, premature eruption, or irregular eruption. Causative agents may include genetic factors, systemic diseases (e.g., hypothyroidism, rickets), local infections, or trauma. These disturbances typically affect the primary or permanent teeth, with the lower anterior teeth being most commonly involved. The condition may lead to malocclusion or functional impairments if left untreated.

Disturbances in tooth eruption, unspecified, refer to abnormal timing or sequence of tooth emergence without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include delayed eruption, premature eruption, or failed eruption. Causative agents may include genetic factors, nutritional deficiencies, systemic diseases, or local infection. Typically affects primary and permanent teeth, with maxillary and mandibular incisors and molars being most commonly involved. The condition may lead to malocclusion or spacing issues if left unaddressed.

Embedded teeth, also known as impacted teeth or retained teeth, occur when a tooth fails to erupt into its proper position within the mouth. Commonly affecting the maxillary and mandibular third molars, this condition is often due to lack of space, soft tissue obstruction, or bone resistance. Causative factors include genetic predisposition, overcrowding, and developmental anomalies. Synonyms include impacted teeth and retained teeth. Clinically, they may lead to infection, cyst formation, or damage to adjacent structures. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent complications.

Impacted teeth refer to teeth that fail to erupt into their proper position within the dental arch, often due to lack of space, obstruction by other teeth or bone, or developmental anomalies. Common synonyms include unerupted teeth and malpositioned teeth. Causative factors may include overcrowding, presence of a bony barrier, or abnormal tooth development. This condition most frequently affects third molars (wisdom teeth) and maxillary canines. It can lead to complications such as infection, cyst formation, and damage to adjacent teeth. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial for effective management.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of tooth development or eruption
summary: "Other specified disorders of tooth development or eruption" refers to conditions affecting tooth formation or eruption that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include delayed eruption, hypodontia, and hyperdontia. These disorders may result from genetic factors, systemic diseases, or environmental influences. Typically, they affect the maxillary and mandibular dental arches, impacting both primary and permanent teeth. Causative agents may include syndromes like cleidocranial dysplasia, environmental toxins, or nutritional deficiencies. The condition can lead to malocclusion, spacing issues, or functional impairments.

code_desc: Disorders of tooth development or eruption, unspecified
summary: Disorders of tooth development or eruption, unspecified, refer to abnormalities in the formation or emergence of teeth without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include hypodontia, hyperdontia, and delayed eruption. Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental influences, systemic diseases, or infections. These conditions typically affect the primary and permanent dentition, involving the maxilla and mandible. Symptoms may include missing, extra, or improperly positioned teeth, leading to functional and aesthetic concerns. The exact cause is often unknown, necessitating further diagnostic evaluation.

code_desc: Diseases of hard tissues of teeth
summary: Diseases of hard tissues of teeth encompass conditions affecting enamel, dentin, and cementum. Common synonyms include dental caries, pulpitis, and periodontal disease. Causative agents vary, with bacteria such as *Streptococcus mutans* playing a key role in caries. These conditions primarily affect the teeth, particularly the enamel and dentin, and can lead to cavities, tooth decay, and structural damage. Periodontal diseases involve the supporting structures, including gums and alveolar bone. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent irreversible damage and maintain oral health.

Dental caries, also known as tooth decay or cavities, is a chronic bacterial infection caused by acid-producing microorganisms such as *Streptococcus mutans* and *Lactobacillus*. These bacteria metabolize dietary sugars to produce acids that demineralize tooth enamel and dentin. The condition typically affects the crown of the tooth, particularly in pits, fissures, and around the cervical region. It is a prevalent oral health issue worldwide, often leading to cavities, pulpitis, and potential tooth loss if untreated. Risk factors include poor oral hygiene, frequent sugar intake, and reduced salivary flow.

code_desc: Certain specified diseases of hard tissues of teeth
summary: " Certain specified diseases of hard tissues of teeth" refers to pathological conditions affecting enamel, dentin, and cementum. Common synonyms include dental caries, dental decay, and tooth decay. Causative agents often involve Streptococcus mutans and other cariogenic bacteria, along with dietary factors and poor oral hygiene. These conditions primarily affect the teeth, particularly the enamel and dentin, leading to cavities and structural damage. They are most commonly seen in the primary and permanent dentition, especially in areas difficult to clean. Early detection and preventive care are essential to minimize progression and complications.

Excessive attrition of teeth refers to the overwear of tooth structure due to abnormal contact between opposing teeth, often leading to loss of enamel and dentin. Common synonyms include bruxism, tooth wear, and attrition. Primary causative agents include bruxism, malocclusion, and parafunctional habits such as clenching. It typically affects the occlusal surfaces of the anterior and posterior teeth, with the incisors and canines often showing the most significant wear. The condition may also lead to gingival recession and altered occlusion if left untreated.

Abrasion of teeth refers to the gradual wearing away of dental enamel due to mechanical friction, commonly from toothbrushing or dental appliances. It typically affects the occlusal and cervical regions of the teeth. Common synonyms include tooth wear and attrition. Causative agents include abrasive toothpaste, improper brushing techniques, bruxism, and ill-fitting dentures. The condition primarily impacts the anterior and posterior teeth, leading to sensitivity, irregular surfaces, and potential enamel loss. It is more prevalent in adults and often associated with parafunctional habits.

Erosion of teeth refers to the loss of tooth structure due to chemical dissolution, typically from acidic substances. Common synonyms include dental erosion and tooth surface loss. It is primarily caused by exposure to acids from dietary sources, such as citrus fruits, carbonated beverages, and vinegar, as well as gastric reflux or vomiting. The condition most commonly affects the enamel of the anterior teeth, including incisors and canines, and may progress to dentin exposure. It is often asymptomatic in early stages but can lead to sensitivity, discoloration, and structural damage if left untreated.

Abfraction is a non-carious cervical lesion characterized by V-shaped notches at the cervical region of teeth. It results from mechanical stress caused by bruxism, parafunctional habits, or excessive occlusal forces. Common synonyms include cervical wear and occlusal stress-induced tooth wear. The condition typically affects the incisal edges of anterior teeth and the cervical areas of posterior teeth. It is often associated with toothbrush abrasion and improper oral hygiene practices. The primary causative agents are occlusal trauma and abrasive behaviors.

Pathological resorption of teeth refers to the abnormal breakdown and loss of tooth structure due to excessive resorption by odontoclasts. Common synonyms include dental resorption and internal resorption. It is often caused by trauma, infection, or inflammatory processes, with *Actinomyces* and *Streptococcus* species being frequent causative agents. The condition typically affects the root dentin and can involve the pulp, leading to tooth weakening and potential loss. It commonly occurs in molars and premolars, especially in the maxilla. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent irreversible damage.

code_desc: Posteruptive colour changes of dental hard tissues
summary: Posteruptive color changes of dental hard tissues refer to alterations in the color of enamel and dentin that occur after tooth eruption. These changes are often due to secondary enamel formation or hypoplasia, leading to white, yellow, or brown discolorations. Common synonyms include enamel hypoplasia, enamel fluorosis, and post-eruptive dental discoloration. Causative agents may include trauma, infection, systemic diseases, or environmental factors like fluoride exposure. The condition typically affects the anterior teeth, particularly incisors and canines, and may involve both enamel and dentin layers.

Chronic dental injuries refer to long-standing damage to teeth and surrounding structures, often resulting from repeated trauma, bruxism, or decay. Common synonyms include dental trauma and persistent tooth damage. Causative agents may include physical trauma, occlusal forces, erosion from acidic diet, and poor oral hygiene. These injuries typically affect the enamel, dentin, pulp, and supporting structures of the teeth, with the anterior and posterior teeth being most commonly involved. Symptoms may include sensitivity, discoloration, and structural compromise. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent further complications.

Nontraumatic fracture of tooth refers to a break in a tooth not caused by external force. Common synonyms include dental fracture and tooth fracture. It is often caused by bruxism, dental caries, or excessive occlusal forces. Typically affecting the anterior or posterior teeth, this condition may involve enamel, dentin, or pulp. It is more common in adults and can lead to pain, sensitivity, or infection if left untreated. Early diagnosis and appropriate management are essential to prevent complications and restore function.

Deposits on teeth, also known as dental plaque or calculus, are accumulations of bacterial biofilm and mineralized deposits on tooth surfaces. Common synonyms include dental plaque, tartar, and calculus. These deposits are primarily caused by poor oral hygiene, leading to the buildup of bacteria and their byproducts. The most common causative agents include Streptococcus mutans and other oral bacteria. Deposits typically affect the gingival margins and interdental spaces, leading to gingivitis and periodontal disease if left untreated.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of hard tissues of teeth
summary: "Other specified diseases of hard tissues of teeth" refers to dental conditions affecting enamel, dentin, or cementum that do not fit specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include unspecified dental hard tissue disorders. Causative agents may include trauma, caries, bruxism, or developmental anomalies. These conditions typically affect the enamel, dentin, or cementum of primary or permanent teeth, often leading to structural damage, discoloration, or loss. They may occur in isolation or as part of broader systemic conditions. Diagnosis relies on clinical and radiographic evaluation.

code_desc: Diseases of hard tissues of teeth, unspecified
summary: Diseases of hard tissues of teeth, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting enamel, dentin, or cementum without specific identification. Common synonyms include dental caries, dental decay, and tooth demineralization. Causative agents often involve bacteria such as *Streptococcus mutans*, acid exposure, poor oral hygiene, and dietary factors. These conditions primarily affect the tooth structure, leading to cavities, erosion, or structural damage. They commonly occur in the enamel and dentin layers, impacting both primary and permanent teeth, especially in areas difficult to clean.

code_desc: Diseases of pulp or periapical tissues
summary: Diseases of pulp or periapical tissues refer to conditions affecting the dental pulp and surrounding periapical regions. Common synonyms include pulpitis and periapical abscess. These conditions are typically caused by bacterial infections, often originating from untreated dental caries or trauma. The most commonly affected areas are the teeth, particularly the root apices. Pulp diseases may present with pain, sensitivity, or swelling, while periapical diseases often result in abscess formation. Diagnosis usually involves clinical examination and radiographic imaging. Treatment may include root canal therapy or extraction, depending on the severity and extent of the infection.

Pulpitis is an inflammation of the dental pulp, typically caused by bacterial infection or physical trauma. It results in pain, often described as sharp or throbbing, and may be sensitive to temperature changes. Common synonyms include pulp infection or pulp inflammation. Causative agents include *Streptococcus* species, *Actinomyces*, and *Porphyromonas*. The condition primarily affects the pulp of the tooth, most commonly in the posterior teeth due to their complex anatomy and higher susceptibility to caries and trauma.

Necrosis of pulp is the death of the soft tissue within a tooth's pulp due to loss of blood supply. Common synonyms include pulp gangrene and pulpal necrosis. It is most commonly caused by bacterial infection, trauma, or irreversible pulpitis. The condition typically affects the dental pulp of anterior and posterior teeth, leading to symptoms such as pain, swelling, and discoloration. If left untreated, it can progress to abscess formation and systemic complications. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent further damage and preserve the tooth.

A pulp abscess is a localized infection within the dental pulp, typically resulting from bacterial invasion due to caries, trauma, or periodontal disease. It is characterized by pus accumulation within the pulp chamber and may lead to periapical inflammation. Common synonyms include periapical abscess and pulpal abscess. The most common causative agent is *Streptococcus species*, though other bacteria such as *Actinomyces* and *Prevotella* may also be involved. This condition primarily affects the teeth, particularly the maxillary and mandibular molars, and can cause severe pain, swelling, and drainage.

Phoenix abscess is a rare, recurrent, and often chronic suppurative infection typically occurring in the oral cavity, particularly around the mandibular molar region. It is characterized by the formation of a persistent, fluctuant swelling that may drain spontaneously. Common synonyms include recurrent odontogenic abscess and chronic periapical abscess. The condition is most commonly caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Porphyromonas gingivalis*. It predominantly affects the maxillofacial region, especially in adults with compromised immune function or poor dental hygiene.

Pulp degeneration refers to the progressive loss of vitality and function in the dental pulp, often resulting in irreversible damage. Common synonyms include pulp necrosis and pulp gangrene. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, trauma, or prolonged exposure to irritants. The condition primarily affects the pulp of the tooth, leading to inflammation, necrosis, and potential abscess formation. It most commonly occurs in the posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their complex anatomy and susceptibility to caries. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent further complications and preserve dental health.

code_desc: Abnormal hard tissue formation in pulp
summary: Abnormal hard tissue formation in the pulp, also known as pulpal calcification or dentinogenesis imperfecta, refers to the excessive deposition of mineralized tissue within the dental pulp. This condition can result from various factors, including trauma, infection, or genetic disorders. Common causative agents include pulp necrosis, chronic inflammation, and hereditary conditions such as dentinogenesis imperfecta type I. It typically affects the pulp chamber and root canals, leading to radiopaque areas on imaging. The condition is most commonly observed in the anterior teeth and may contribute to pulp obliteration and root canal obliteration.

A periapical abscess is a localized infection at the root tip of a tooth, typically resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial invasion. Common synonyms include apical abscess and periapical granuloma. The causative agents are primarily anaerobic bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, and *Prevotella species*. This condition most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, particularly molars, due to their complex root structures and proximity to the maxillary sinus. Clinical features include pain, swelling, and possible drainage.

Periapical abscess with facial involvement is a localized infection originating from the apex of a tooth root, extending into the surrounding facial tissues. It typically results from untreated dental caries or pulp necrosis, leading to bacterial invasion and pus formation. Common causative agents include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus species*, and *Actinomyces*. This condition commonly affects the maxillary or mandibular posterior regions, causing swelling, pain, and potential cellulitis. Synonyms include apical periodontal abscess with facial spread and dental abscess with extraosseous extension.

A periapical abscess with sinus is a localized infection at the root tip of a tooth, extending to form a draining sinus tract. Common synonyms include apical abscess with sinus and granuloma with sinus. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Streptococcus* species, *Actinomyces*, and *Prevotella*. The condition primarily affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, often resulting from untreated dental caries or pulp necrosis. The sinus tract allows pus to drain, providing temporary relief but not resolving the underlying infection.

A periapical abscess without sinus is a localized infection at the root tip of a tooth, characterized by pus accumulation without an associated draining tract. Common synonyms include apical abscess and radicular abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Streptococcus* species, *Actinomyces*, and *Prevotella*. The condition primarily affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, often resulting from untreated dental caries, trauma, or failed endodontic treatment. Clinically, it presents with pain, swelling, and tenderness in the affected area.

"Other specified periapical abscess" refers to a localized infection at the root apex of a tooth, typically resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial invasion. Common synonyms include periapical granuloma or abscess. Causative agents are often anaerobic bacteria such as *Propionibacterium*, *Fusobacterium*, and *Prevotella*. This condition most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, particularly molars. It presents with pain, swelling, and possible drainage. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical findings and radiographic evidence of periapical lesions. Treatment involves root canal therapy or surgical drainage.

A periapical abscess, unspecified, is a localized infection at the root tip of a tooth, typically resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial invasion. Common synonyms include apical abscess and periapical granuloma. The causative agents are often anaerobic bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, and *Treponema denticola*. This condition primarily affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, with the apical region of the root being the most commonly involved site. It presents with pain, swelling, and possible drainage.

Periapical periodontitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the periapical tissues surrounding the root of a tooth, typically resulting from pulp infection or necrosis. Common synonyms include periapical abscess and apical periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Streptococcus species*, often associated with dental caries or trauma. It commonly affects the apical region of molars and premolars, leading to pain, swelling, and potential formation of a periapical lesion. The condition may progress to a chronic state if left untreated, necessitating endodontic intervention.

code_desc: Acute apical periodontitis of pulpal origin
summary: Acute apical periodontitis of pulpal origin is an inflammatory condition affecting the periapical tissues, typically resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial infection. It is characterized by severe, localized pain, often radiating to the jaw, and may present with swelling or tenderness. Common synonyms include acute apical abscess and periapical abscess. The primary causative agents are anaerobic and facultative bacteria, such as *Streptococcus*, *Prevotella*, and *Fusobacterium*. This condition most commonly affects the roots of posterior teeth, particularly molars.

Chronic apical periodontitis is a long-standing inflammatory condition affecting the tissues surrounding the root apex of a tooth, typically resulting from persistent infection originating from a non-vital pulp. Common synonyms include apical periodontal abscess and periapical granuloma. The primary causative agent is *Enterococcus faecalis*, though other bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Prevotella* species may also be involved. This condition most commonly affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth, particularly those with previous dental trauma, caries, or incomplete root canal treatment. Clinically, it presents with localized swelling, tenderness, and radiolucency on imaging.

Other specified periapical periodontitis refers to inflammation of the periapical tissues caused by infection, typically resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial invasion. Common synonyms include apical periodontitis and periapical abscess. The condition is most commonly caused by *Streptococcus* species, *Actinomyces*, and *Prevotella*. It typically affects the apical region of the tooth, most frequently in the maxillary and mandibular posterior teeth. Clinical features include pain, swelling, and radiolucency on imaging. Treatment involves endodontic therapy or extraction.

Periapical periodontitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the periapical tissues surrounding the root of a tooth, typically resulting from pulp necrosis and subsequent bacterial infection. Common synonyms include apical periodontitis and periapical abscess. The condition is most commonly caused by dental caries, trauma, or untreated pulpitis, leading to microbial invasion of the root canal. It typically affects the apical region of the tooth, with the maxillary molars and mandibular premolars being the most frequently involved. Clinical signs include pain, swelling, and radiolucency on imaging.

A radicular cyst, also known as a periapical cyst or granuloma, is a benign, fluid-filled lesion that develops at the root tip of a non-vital tooth. It arises from the degeneration of the dental pulp and is typically associated with chronic apical periodontitis. The most common causative agent is a necrotic pulp, often resulting from untreated dental caries or trauma. The cyst is most frequently found in the maxillary and mandibular posterior regions, particularly around molars. It may cause bone resorption and, if left untreated, can lead to tooth loosening or pathologic fracture.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of pulp or periapical tissues
summary: "Other specified diseases of pulp or periapical tissues" refers to inflammatory or degenerative conditions of the dental pulp or surrounding periapical tissues that do not fit into more specific classifications. Common synonyms include pulpitis and periapical abscess. Causative agents often include bacterial infections, such as *Streptococcus* species, and trauma. These conditions typically affect the tooth root and surrounding bone, often resulting from untreated caries, dental trauma, or failed endodontic treatment. Symptoms may include pain, swelling, and mobility of the affected tooth.

code_desc: Diseases of pulp or periapical tissues, unspecified
summary: Diseases of pulp or periapical tissues, unspecified, refer to inflammatory or infectious conditions affecting the dental pulp or surrounding periapical tissues without specific identification of the underlying cause. Common synonyms include pulpitis and periapical abscess. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Streptococcus* species, *Porphyromonas*, and *Fusobacterium*. These conditions typically affect the teeth and their supporting structures, particularly in the maxillary and mandibular regions. Symptoms may include pain, swelling, and sensitivity. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical examination and radiographic findings.

code_desc: Certain specified disorders of teeth or supporting structures
summary: " Certain specified disorders of teeth or supporting structures" refers to a group of conditions affecting the teeth, gums, bones, or periodontal ligaments. Common synonyms include dental caries, periodontal disease, and dental trauma. Causative agents may include bacteria (e.g., *Streptococcus mutans*), trauma, genetic factors, or systemic diseases. These disorders typically affect the oral cavity, including the enamel, dentin, pulp, gingiva, and alveolar bone. They can lead to tooth decay, gum inflammation, bone loss, or tooth loss if left untreated.

code_desc: Exfoliation of teeth due to systemic causes
summary: Exfoliation of teeth due to systemic causes refers to the premature loss of primary or permanent teeth caused by underlying systemic diseases. Common synonyms include pathological tooth loss and systemic tooth exfoliation. Causative agents may include rickets, hypoparathyroidism, syphilis, and certain metabolic disorders. This condition typically affects the primary dentition in children, though permanent teeth may also be involved. The process is often associated with generalized developmental abnormalities and may be accompanied by other systemic symptoms.

code_desc: Loss of teeth due to accident, extraction or local periodontal disease
summary: Loss of teeth due to accident, extraction, or local periodontal disease refers to the absence of one or more teeth resulting from trauma, intentional removal, or progressive gum disease. Common synonyms include dental loss, tooth loss, and edentulism. Causative agents include trauma, periodontitis, and surgical extraction. Typically affected body parts are the maxilla and mandible, with the anterior and posterior regions commonly impacted. This condition can lead to functional and aesthetic complications if not managed appropriately.

Atrophy of the edentulous alveolar ridge refers to the progressive resorption and reduction of bone volume in the jaw following tooth loss. This condition is commonly observed in individuals who have lost all their teeth, leading to a diminished ridge height and width. Common synonyms include alveolar ridge atrophy and post-extraction bone resorption. The primary causative agent is the absence of functional stimulation from teeth, which triggers osteoclastic activity. The maxilla and mandible are typically affected, with the posterior regions often showing more pronounced changes. This condition can compromise the stability and success of dental implants and prosthetics.

A retained dental root refers to a tooth root that remains in the jaw after the clinical crown has been lost, often due to trauma, disease, or incomplete extraction. Common synonyms include impacted root or residual root. Causative agents may include periodontal disease, trauma, or failed extraction. This condition typically affects the maxillary and mandibular posterior regions, particularly molars. It can lead to infection, cyst formation, or impaction of adjacent teeth. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to prevent complications.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of teeth and supporting structures
summary: "Other specified disorders of teeth and supporting structures" refers to dental and periodontal conditions not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified dental anomalies and generalized periodontal disease. Causative agents may include trauma, infection, systemic diseases, or genetic factors. These disorders typically affect the teeth, gums, alveolar bone, and surrounding soft tissues. They may present with symptoms such as pain, swelling, mobility, or tooth loss. Diagnosis often requires clinical and radiographic evaluation to determine the extent and underlying cause of the condition.

code_desc: Unspecified disorders of teeth and supporting structures
summary: Unspecified disorders of teeth and supporting structures refer to dental conditions that do not fit specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include generalized dental anomalies or undiagnosed dental pathologies. Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental influences, infections, or trauma. These disorders typically affect the teeth, gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone. Symptoms may involve tooth loss, malocclusion, or structural abnormalities. Diagnosis is often made when specific conditions cannot be definitively identified. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may include restorative, orthodontic, or surgical interventions.

Gingival diseases refer to inflammatory conditions affecting the gums, primarily caused by bacterial plaque accumulation. Common synonyms include gingivitis and periodontal disease. The main causative agents are bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. These conditions typically affect the marginal and interdental gingiva, leading to redness, swelling, bleeding, and potential recession. Poor oral hygiene is a major risk factor, and if untreated, can progress to periodontitis, involving destruction of supporting structures.

Allergic gingivitis is an inflammatory condition of the gums caused by an allergic reaction, often triggered by irritants such as dental materials, foods, or oral hygiene products. It presents with red, swollen, and sometimes bleeding gums. Common synonyms include allergic stomatitis or contact gingivitis. Causative agents may include metals, acrylics, or certain toothpaste ingredients. The condition typically affects the marginal gingiva, and symptoms often resolve upon removal of the allergen. It is more common in individuals with a predisposition to allergies or sensitivities.

Catarrhal gingivitis is an inflammatory condition characterized by red, swollen, and often bleeding gums. It is primarily caused by the accumulation of bacterial plaque along the gumline. Common synonyms include marginal gingivitis and hyperplastic gingivitis. The main causative agents are gram-negative anaerobic bacteria, particularly *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental papillae, leading to gingival inflammation without significant loss of attachment. It is commonly associated with poor oral hygiene and can progress to more severe periodontal disease if left untreated.

Eruptive gingivitis is an acute, self-limiting inflammation of the gingiva associated with the eruption of teeth, commonly seen in children and adolescents. It presents as diffuse redness, swelling, and sometimes bleeding of the gums, particularly around erupting primary or permanent teeth. Common synonyms include gingival eruption eruption and eruption-associated gingivitis. The condition is typically caused by the mechanical irritation of erupting teeth and the presence of plaque biofilm. It predominantly affects the gingiva surrounding the upper and lower anterior teeth.

Atrophic senile gingivitis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by recession of the gingival margin and loss of interdental papilla, leading to a retraction of the gingiva. It commonly affects the posterior regions of the upper and lower jaws. Synonyms include desquamative gingivitis and atrophic glossitis. The condition is primarily associated with aging, poor oral hygiene, and systemic factors such as malnutrition or vitamin deficiencies. It is not caused by a specific pathogen but is linked to chronic irritation and reduced salivary flow. The affected areas typically include the marginal and interdental gingiva.

Acute multiple gingival abscesses refer to the sudden onset of multiple pus-filled lesions in the interdental papillae, commonly associated with rapid plaque accumulation and poor oral hygiene. Synonyms include acute interdental abscesses and multiple gingival脓肿. The condition is typically caused by *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans* and *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, among other periodontal pathogens. It predominantly affects the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth, especially in individuals with compromised immune systems or those with preexisting periodontal disease. Clinically, it presents with erythematous, painful swellings, spontaneous drainage, and halitosis.

code_desc: Developmental or acquired deformities or conditions of gingiva
summary: Developmental or acquired deformities or conditions of gingiva refer to abnormalities in the structure or appearance of the gingival tissues. Common synonyms include gingival deformities, gingival anomalies, and periodontal deformities. These conditions may result from genetic factors, trauma, infections, or systemic diseases. Causative agents include trauma, periodontitis, hormonal changes, and systemic conditions such as diabetes. Typically affected areas include the marginal gingiva, interdental papilla, and attached gingiva. These deformities can manifest as gingival recession, hyperplasia, or altered contour, impacting both function and aesthetics.

Pericoronitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the soft tissues surrounding a partially erupted tooth, most commonly the third molar. It occurs when bacteria accumulate in the operculum, the flap of gum tissue covering the emerging tooth. Common synonyms include follicular inflammation and operculitis. The primary causative agents are oral bacteria such as *Streptococcus* and *Porphyromonas* species. This condition typically affects the mandibular third molars, often in adolescents and young adults. Symptoms include pain, swelling, and halitosis.

Other specified gingival diseases refer to gingival conditions that do not meet the criteria for specific classifications such as periodontitis or gingivitis. Common synonyms include localized aggressive periodontitis and generalized aggressive periodontitis. These conditions are often caused by bacterial plaque, with *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans* being a known causative agent. They typically affect the interdental papilla and marginal gingiva, presenting with rapid attachment loss and gingival recession. The exact etiology may involve genetic, immunologic, or environmental factors.

Gingival diseases, unspecified, refer to inflammatory conditions affecting the gums without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include gingivitis and periodontitis. These conditions are primarily caused by bacterial plaque accumulation, leading to inflammation, redness, swelling, and bleeding of the gingival tissues. Other causative agents may include hormonal changes, systemic diseases, or poor oral hygiene. The gums, particularly the marginal and interdental areas, are typically affected. The condition can progress to more severe forms if left untreated, potentially leading to periodontal destruction.

Periodontal disease is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the supporting structures of the teeth, primarily caused by bacterial plaque accumulation. Common synonyms include periodontitis and gum disease. The main causative agents are gram-negative anaerobic bacteria, such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. It typically affects the gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, leading to gingival inflammation, recession, and potential tooth loss if left untreated. The disease progresses through stages from gingivitis to advanced periodontitis.

Acute periodontitis is a sudden, severe inflammation of the supporting structures of the teeth, primarily affecting the gums and periodontal ligament. It is often triggered by bacterial infection, most commonly by *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans* and *Porphyromonas gingivalis*. The condition typically presents with pain, swelling, and bleeding of the gums, and may lead to tooth mobility. It commonly affects the interdental papillae and is often associated with periodontal pockets. Synonyms include acute gingivitis and acute suppurative periodontitis.

Aggressive periodontitis is a rapidly progressive form of periodontal disease characterized by severe attachment loss and bone destruction in otherwise healthy individuals. Common synonyms include juvenile periodontitis and early-onset periodontitis. The primary causative agent is *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, though other bacteria such as *Treponema denticola* and *Tannerella forsythia* may also be involved. The condition typically affects the interdental areas of the anterior and molar teeth, leading to periodontal pockets and tooth mobility. It often occurs in young adults and is associated with a familial predisposition.

Periodontosis is a rare, non-inflammatory condition characterized by progressive resorption of alveolar bone and loss of periodontal ligament, leading to tooth mobility and potential tooth loss. It is distinct from periodontitis, which involves inflammation. Common synonyms include cemento-osseous dysplasia and fibrous dysplasia of the jaw. The condition is often idiopathic, though some cases may be associated with genetic factors or hormonal influences. It primarily affects the maxilla and mandible, with lesions typically localized to the posterior regions. Radiographically, it presents as radiolucent areas with a geographic pattern.

Necrotising periodontal diseases are severe, rapidly progressive infections characterized by necrosis of gingival and periodontal tissues. Common synonyms include necrotizing gingivitis and necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis. The primary causative agents are *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, *Treponema denticola*, and *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, often in conjunction with *Spirochaeta* species. These infections typically affect the interdental papillae, gingiva, and periodontal ligament, leading to ulceration, foul odor, and tooth mobility. They are commonly associated with poor oral hygiene, immunocompromise, and malnutrition.

Necrotising ulcerative periodontitis (NUP), also known as trench mouth or Vincent's angina, is a severe, acute infection of the gums and supporting tissues. It is characterized by necrosis, ulceration, and a foul odor. Common causative agents include *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, *Treponema denticola*, and *Spirochaeta* species. The condition primarily affects the interdental papillae and gingival margins, often in immunocompromised individuals. It is associated with pain, halitosis, and tissue destruction.

Noma, also known as "hansen's disease" or "rodent ulcer," is a rapidly progressive, necrotizing infection of the face, primarily affecting children in malnourished populations. Caused by *Candida albicans* and *Streptococcus species*, it leads to severe destruction of the mucous membranes and underlying tissues. The condition typically affects the lower face, including the lips, cheeks, and palate, resulting in extensive tissue loss and facial disfigurement. Without treatment, noma can lead to life-threatening complications and long-term disability.

Other specified necrotising periodontal diseases refer to necrotizing conditions of the periodontium that do not meet the full criteria for necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis. Common synonyms include necrotizing gingivitis and necrotizing periodontal disease. Causative agents often include *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, *Treponema denticola*, and *Prevotella intermedia*. These conditions typically affect the gingiva and periodontal tissues, presenting with necrosis, ulceration, and a foul odor. They are more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals or those with poor oral hygiene.

Necrotising periodontal diseases, unspecified, are severe, rapidly progressing infections characterized by necrosis of gingival and periodontal tissues. Common synonyms include necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis and necrotizing periodontitis. The condition is primarily caused by *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, *Treponema species*, and *Actinobacillus actinomycetemcomitans*. It typically affects the interdental papillae and periodontal ligament, leading to pain, halitosis, and tissue destruction. The disease is more prevalent in immunocompromised individuals and those with poor oral hygiene.

Abscess of periodontium is a localized suppurative infection involving the periodontal tissues, typically resulting from untreated dental caries or periodontal disease. It presents as a painful, fluctuant swelling with possible drainage. Common synonyms include periapical abscess and periodontal abscess. The causative agents are often anaerobic bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Fusobacterium nucleatum*, and *Prevotella intermedia*. The infection most commonly affects the apical region of molars and premolars, though it can occur in any tooth.

Linear gingival erythema is a non-specific, inflammatory condition characterized by red, flat, linear lesions on the gingiva. It is often associated with chronic malnutrition, particularly niacin deficiency. Common synonyms include angular cheilitis and desquamative gingivitis. The condition typically affects the marginal and interdental gingiva. It is most commonly observed in malnourished individuals, especially those with alcoholism or eating disorders. The lesions may extend beyond the gingiva to involve the buccal mucosa. The exact causative agents are not fully understood, but nutritional deficiencies and systemic conditions are implicated.

Other specified periodontal disease refers to periodontal conditions that do not fit the criteria for more specific classifications but are recognized as distinct entities. It may involve localized or generalized inflammation of the gingiva and supporting structures. Common synonyms include unspecified periodontal disease or other periodontal conditions. Causative agents often include bacteria such as *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans* and *Porphyromonas gingivalis*. The disease typically affects the gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone, leading to gingival recession and potential tooth loss if untreated.

Periodontal disease, unspecified, refers to inflammatory conditions affecting the supporting structures of the teeth, including gums, periodontal ligament, and alveolar bone. Common synonyms include gingivitis and periodontitis, though the latter is more severe. Causative agents are primarily bacterial, with *Porphyromonas gingivalis*, *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, and *Treponema denticola* being frequently implicated. The disease typically affects the gums and surrounding tissues, leading to inflammation, bleeding, and potential tooth loss if untreated. It commonly occurs in the interdental papillae and marginal gingiva.

code_desc: Certain specified disorders of gingiva or edentulous alveolar ridge
summary: Certain specified disorders of gingiva or edentulous alveolar ridge refer to abnormal conditions affecting the gums or bone structure in the mouth where teeth are absent. Common synonyms include gingival diseases and alveolar ridge abnormalities. These conditions may result from infections, trauma, or systemic factors. Causative agents include bacteria, hormonal changes, and poor oral hygiene. Typically affected areas include the gingival margins, interdental papilla, and alveolar bone. Conditions such as gingivitis, periodontitis, and alveolar ridge resorption are included in this category.

Gingival recession refers to the apical displacement of the gingival margin, exposing the root surface. Common synonyms include gingival retraction and root exposure. It is often associated with periodontal disease, aggressive brushing, and trauma. Causative agents include plaque biofilm, systemic conditions like diabetes, and genetic factors. Typically affecting the maxillary and mandibular anterior teeth, it may also occur in posterior regions. The condition is a key indicator of gingival health and periodontal status.

Gingival enlargement refers to the abnormal growth of gum tissue, leading to increased volume and potential recession of the gingival margin. Common synonyms include gingival hyperplasia and hypertrophy. It is often associated with local irritants such as plaque and calculus, or systemic conditions like diabetes, leukemia, and phenytoin use. Hormonal changes, medications, and genetic factors may also contribute. The condition typically affects the interdental papilla and marginal gingiva, with possible involvement of the attached gingiva. It can lead to periodontal complications if left untreated.

code_desc: Gingival or edentulous alveolar ridge lesions associated with trauma
summary: Gingival or edentulous alveolar ridge lesions associated with trauma refer to inflammatory or ulcerative conditions arising from mechanical irritation or injury to the gums or bone supporting teeth. Common synonyms include traumatic ulcers, traumatic mucositis, and traumatic gingivitis. Causative agents are primarily mechanical, such as ill-fitting dentures, sharp occlusal contacts, or dental appliances. These lesions typically affect the gingiva and alveolar ridge, often in the maxillary and mandibular regions. Clinical features include erythema, swelling, ulceration, and pain, often resolving with removal of the irritant.

Hypoplasminogenaemia is a condition characterized by decreased levels of plasma proteins, particularly albumin and globulins, leading to impaired oncotic pressure and fluid retention. It may result from malnutrition, liver dysfunction, or chronic inflammation. Common synonyms include hypoalbuminaemia and hypoproteinemia. Causative agents include protein malnutrition, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, and chronic infections. Typically affects the circulatory system, causing edema, and may impact the liver and kidneys.

Cotton-roll gingivitis is an inflammatory condition of the gingiva characterized by redness, swelling, and bleeding upon probing, often associated with plaque accumulation. It is commonly referred to as marginal gingivitis or hyperplastic gingivitis. The primary causative agent is dental plaque, a biofilm composed of bacteria such as *Porphyromonas gingivalis* and *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*. This condition typically affects the marginal and interdental papillae, with the lower anterior teeth being most commonly involved. It is a precursor to periodontitis if left untreated.

Gingival ulceration refers to the presence of painful, shallow ulcers on the gums, often resulting from trauma, infection, or inflammatory conditions. Common synonyms include gingival erosion and ulcerative gingivitis. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans*, viral infections like herpes simplex, or physical injury. Typically affecting the marginal and interdental papillae, this condition is frequently observed in the anterior region of the mouth. It is often associated with periodontal disease or systemic conditions like Behçet’s disease. Clinical presentation includes redness, swelling, and a punched-out appearance of the ulcerated areas.

code_desc: Other specified disorders of gingival or edentulous alveolar ridge
summary: "Other specified disorders of gingival or edentulous alveolar ridge" refers to non-specific, localized changes in the gingiva or alveolar ridge not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include localized gingival hyperplasia and alveolar ridge irregularities. Causative agents may include trauma, poor oral hygiene, hormonal changes, or systemic conditions. These disorders typically affect the marginal gingiva and alveolar bone, often presenting as swelling, recession, or irregular contours. They are usually diagnosed clinically and managed with improved oral hygiene, local treatments, or surgical intervention as needed.

Dentofacial anomalies refer to developmental abnormalities affecting the teeth and facial structures. Common synonyms include craniofacial dysplasias and skeletal discrepancies. These conditions may result from genetic factors, environmental influences, or a combination of both. They often involve malocclusion, skeletal discrepancies, and irregular tooth eruption. Typically affected areas include the maxilla, mandible, and associated dentition. Causative agents may include syndromes such as Down syndrome, cleidocranial dysplasia, and environmental factors like teratogens or nutritional deficiencies. Early diagnosis and multidisciplinary management are essential for optimal outcomes.

Major anomalies of jaw size refer to developmental abnormalities affecting the size and structure of the maxilla or mandible.
