Common synonyms include macrognathia (enlarged jaw) and micrognathia (reduced jaw). These anomalies may result from genetic factors, syndromes such as Down syndrome or Treacher Collins syndrome, or environmental influences during fetal development. They typically affect the facial skeleton, leading to malocclusion, airway obstruction, and functional or aesthetic concerns. The condition may involve either the upper or lower jaw, or both, and often requires multidisciplinary management.

Micrognathia is a congenital condition characterized by an abnormally small lower jaw, leading to facial disproportion. It may be present at birth and can result from genetic syndromes, developmental anomalies, or environmental factors. Common synonyms include retrognathia and mandibular hypoplasia. Causative agents include genetic disorders such as Treacher Collins syndrome, Pierre Robin sequence, and Down syndrome, as well as maternal exposure to teratogens. The condition primarily affects the mandible and can impact breathing, feeding, and dental development. It may also be associated with other craniofacial abnormalities.

code_desc: Other specified major anomalies of jaw size
summary: "Other specified major anomalies of jaw size" refers to abnormalities in the size or structure of the maxilla or mandible that do not fit specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include mandibular hypoplasia or hyperplasia, and maxillary hypoplasia. Causative agents may include genetic disorders, syndromes such as Treacher Collins or Pierre-Robin, environmental factors, or congenital malformations. These anomalies typically affect the facial skeleton, leading to discrepancies in dental alignment, speech, and mastication. They may also impact airway function and require multidisciplinary management.

code_desc: Major anomalies of jaw size, unspecified
summary: Major anomalies of jaw size, unspecified refer to developmental abnormalities affecting the size of the maxilla or mandible without specific identification of the anomaly. Common synonyms include macrognathia, micrognathia, and dysgnathia. These conditions may result from genetic disorders, syndromes, or environmental factors. Typically, the mandible and maxilla are affected, leading to facial asymmetry, malocclusion, and functional or aesthetic concerns. Causes may include congenital syndromes such as Treacher Collins or Pierre-Robinson syndrome, or syndromes like Down syndrome.

Anomalies of jaw-cranial base relationship refer to malformations involving the spatial relationship between the mandible and the cranial base, leading to malocclusion and facial dysmorphia. Common synonyms include skeletal Class III malocclusion and retrognathia. These anomalies are often caused by genetic factors, syndromes such as Down syndrome, or environmental influences like trauma or infections. Typically affecting the maxilla, mandible, and cranial base, they may result in altered facial proportions, breathing difficulties, and dental misalignment. Early diagnosis and multidisciplinary management are crucial for optimal functional and aesthetic outcomes.

Anomalies of dental arch relationship refer to malocclusions resulting from discrepancies between the maxillary and mandibular dental arches. Common synonyms include malocclusion, dental malalignment, and occlusal anomalies. These conditions may arise from genetic factors, environmental influences, or a combination of both. Causative agents include genetic predisposition, thumb-sucking, oral habits, and premature loss of teeth. Typically affected body parts include the maxilla, mandible, and teeth, leading to issues such as overbite, underbite, and spacing or crowding.

Anomalies of tooth position refer to malocclusions or irregularities in the alignment and positioning of teeth within the dental arch. Common synonyms include malocclusion, dental malalignment, and dental irregularity. These conditions may result from genetic factors, environmental influences, or a combination of both. Causative agents include genetic predisposition, oral habits, trauma, and skeletal discrepancies. Typically affected body parts include the maxilla and mandible, with the anterior and posterior teeth most commonly involved. Such anomalies can affect function, aesthetics, and oral health.

Food impaction is the mechanical obstruction of the gastrointestinal tract by a foreign body, most commonly food. It often occurs in the esophagus due to dysphagia or structural abnormalities. Common synonyms include foreign body obstruction and esophageal impaction. Causative agents include nondigestible items like bones, seeds, and small objects. It typically affects the esophagus but can occur in the stomach or intestines. Symptoms include dysphagia, pain, and regurgitation. Prompt diagnosis and removal are essential to prevent complications such as aspiration or perforation.

Malocclusion refers to the improper alignment of the teeth when the jaws close, leading to functional and aesthetic issues. Common synonyms include dental malalignment and malocclusion. It is often caused by genetic factors, prolonged thumb-sucking, tongue thrusting, or premature loss of primary teeth. Typically affecting the maxilla and mandible, malocclusion can involve overbite, underbite, crossbite, or open bite. It may impact speech, chewing, and oral health, necessitating orthodontic intervention.

Class II division 2 malocclusion is a type of skeletal malocclusion characterized by a retruded mandible relative to the maxilla, resulting in a Class II molar relationship with the upper anterior teeth protruding. Common synonyms include retrognathic mandible and molar relationship. Causative factors may include genetic influences, prolonged thumb sucking, or environmental factors affecting jaw development. This condition typically affects the maxilla and mandible, leading to aesthetic and functional concerns such as speech difficulties and chewing problems.

Angle Class I malocclusion is a dental condition characterized by a normal occlusal relationship with the first molars in a mesiobuccal position, but with other malocclusions such as crowding or spacing. Common synonyms include mild malocclusion or normal occlusion with minor discrepancies. Causative factors may include genetic influences, environmental factors like thumb-sucking, or early loss of primary teeth. This condition typically affects the maxillary and mandibular arches, leading to issues with tooth alignment and bite function. It is the most common type of malocclusion, often requiring orthodontic intervention for optimal dental alignment and aesthetics.

Other specified malocclusion refers to malocclusion that does not meet the criteria for Class I, II, or III malocclusion but involves abnormal alignment of teeth and jaws. Common synonyms include irregular occlusion and dental misalignment. Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental influences, or habits such as thumb sucking. Typically affects the maxilla, mandible, and dental arches, leading to functional and aesthetic concerns. It is often diagnosed when specific patterns of tooth positioning or jaw discrepancies are present but do not fit standard classifications. Treatment may involve orthodontic intervention.

Malocclusion, unspecified, refers to an improper alignment of the teeth when the jaws close, without a specific classification. It may involve overbite, underbite, or crossbite. Common synonyms include dental malocclusion and malalignment. Causative factors may include genetic predisposition, jaw growth discrepancies, oral habits, or trauma. Typically affects the maxilla and mandible, with implications for occlusion, chewing, and speech. It can contribute to periodontal issues and temporomandibular joint dysfunction. Diagnosis is often based on clinical examination and dental imaging.

Dentofacial functional abnormalities refer to malfunctions in the coordination of the teeth, jaws, and facial muscles during mastication, swallowing, and speech. These conditions often result from discrepancies between the dental and skeletal structures, leading to improper occlusion and functional inefficiencies. Common synonyms include malocclusion, functional jaw deviation, and temporomandibular dysfunction. Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental influences, trauma, or systemic diseases. Typically affecting the maxilla, mandible, temporomandibular joint, and surrounding musculature, these abnormalities can impact oral health, speech, and overall quality of life.

Dentofacial parafunctional disorders refer to abnormal, non-functional oral habits that affect the teeth, jaws, and facial structures. Common synonyms include bruxism, parafunctional activity, and oral parafunctions. These disorders are often caused by stress, malocclusion, sleep disorders, or psychological factors. Typically affecting the teeth, temporomandibular joint (TMJ), and surrounding musculature, they may lead to wear, pain, and functional impairment. The condition is prevalent in both children and adults, with significant impacts on oral health and quality of life.

Temporomandibular joint disorders (TMJ disorders) refer to conditions affecting the temporomandibular joint and surrounding muscles, leading to pain, limited movement, and clicking or popping sounds. Common synonyms include TMJ syndrome and myofascial pain. Causative factors include bruxism, arthritis, trauma, and stress. These disorders typically affect the temporomandibular joint, jaw muscles, and adjacent structures such as the ear and temporality. Symptoms often include jaw pain, difficulty chewing, and headaches.

Other specified dentofacial anomalies refer to malformations of the dental and facial structures that do not fit specific diagnostic categories. These may include abnormalities in tooth number, shape, or position, as well as skeletal discrepancies. Common synonyms include dental malformations and facial dysmorphisms. Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental exposures, or syndromic conditions. These anomalies typically affect the maxilla, mandible, teeth, and surrounding soft tissues, often leading to functional and aesthetic concerns.

Dentofacial anomalies, unspecified, refer to abnormalities involving the development or structure of the teeth and facial bones without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include congenital facial malformations and developmental dental anomalies. Causative agents may include genetic factors, syndromes, environmental exposures, or teratogens. These anomalies typically affect the maxilla, mandible, dental arches, and associated soft tissues, leading to malocclusion, facial asymmetry, and functional or aesthetic concerns. The condition is often diagnosed clinically due to the absence of a more precise classification.

Sensory disturbances affecting the orofacial complex refer to altered sensations such as numbness, tingling, or pain in the mouth, face, and adjacent structures. Common synonyms include orofacial sensory loss and trigeminal neuropathy. Causative agents may include trauma, infections, diabetes, multiple sclerosis, or tumors. Typically affected areas include the lips, tongue, gums, and facial skin. These disturbances often involve the trigeminal nerve, which innervates the face and oral cavity. Symptoms may be unilateral or bilateral, depending on the underlying cause. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications and improve quality of life.

Burning mouth syndrome (BMS) is a chronic condition characterized by a burning sensation in the mouth without an identifiable cause. Common synonyms include oral burning syndrome and glossopyrosis. It primarily affects the tongue, lips, and palate. Known causative agents include hormonal changes, nutritional deficiencies, oral infections, and psychological factors such as anxiety or depression. The syndrome is more common in postmenopausal women. Symptoms may persist for months and can significantly impact quality of life. Diagnosis is often based on clinical evaluation and exclusion of other conditions.

code_desc: Other specified sensory disturbances affecting orofacial complex
summary: "Other specified sensory disturbances affecting orofacial complex" refers to abnormal sensory function in the mouth and face not attributable to a specific neurological or systemic disorder. Common synonyms include orofacial sensory dysfunction and atypical sensory disturbances of the orofacial region. Causative agents may include trauma, infections, autoimmune conditions, or neurodegenerative diseases. Typically affects the lips, tongue, gums, and facial skin, often presenting with altered sensation such as hypoesthesia or dysesthesia. The condition may impact speech, swallowing, and oral motor function.

code_desc: Sensory disturbances affecting orofacial complex, unspecified
summary: Sensory disturbances affecting orofacial complex, unspecified, refer to abnormal sensations such as numbness, tingling, or pain in the mouth, face, or adjacent areas without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include orofacial sensory abnormalities or unclassified sensory disorders of the face and mouth. Causative agents may include trauma, infections, neurological conditions, or systemic diseases. Typically affected areas include the lips, tongue, gums, cheeks, and jaw. The condition may be associated with conditions like trigeminal neuralgia, multiple sclerosis, or diabetes. Diagnosis often requires a thorough neurological and dental evaluation.

code_desc: Other specified diseases or disorders of orofacial complex
summary: "Other specified diseases or disorders of the orofacial complex" refers to conditions affecting the mouth, face, and adjacent structures that do not fit into more specific diagnostic categories. Common synonyms include unspecified orofacial disorders. These conditions may arise from genetic, infectious, autoimmune, or environmental factors. Typically affecting the teeth, gums, mucous membranes, and facial bones, they can present with symptoms such as pain, swelling, deformity, or functional impairment. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and imaging. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and affected structures.

code_desc: Diseases or disorders of orofacial complex, unspecified
summary: Diseases or disorders of the orofacial complex, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the mouth, face, and adjacent structures without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include unspecified orofacial disorders or unspecified oral and facial conditions. Causative agents may include infections, trauma, autoimmune factors, or developmental anomalies. Typically affected areas include the teeth, gums, lips, tongue, palate, and facial bones. This category encompasses a wide range of conditions that impact oral and facial function and appearance, often requiring further diagnostic evaluation to determine the exact cause.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of the oesophagus
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the oesophagus refer to structural changes in the oesophagus resulting from disease or injury. Common synonyms include oesophageal strictures, diverticula, and motility disorders. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, reflux, infections, or neoplasms. These alterations typically affect the mid- to lower oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, odynophagia, and aspiration. Conditions like achalasia, caustic injury, and Barrett’s oesophagus are frequent causes. The alterations can impair normal peristalsis and cause narrowing or dilation of the oesophageal lumen.

Oesophageal obstruction refers to the blockage of the oesophagus, preventing the passage of food or liquid. Common synonyms include dysphagia and oesophageal stricture. Causative agents may include foreign bodies, tumours, strictures from inflammation or caustic ingestion, and motility disorders such as achalasia. The condition typically affects the mid to distal oesophagus, leading to symptoms like difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, and chest pain. It can result from both benign and malignant processes, often requiring endoscopic or surgical intervention for relief.

Acquired esophageal diverticulum refers to a protrusion of the esophageal wall containing mucosa and submucosa into the surrounding muscle layer. Common synonyms include esophageal diverticulum and traction diverticulum. It is typically caused by increased intraluminal pressure and weak points in the esophageal wall, often associated with conditions like achalasia or chronic cough. The most commonly affected areas are the mid-esophagus and the distal esophagus. This condition may lead to symptoms such as dysphagia and regurgitation.

Oesophageal web is a thin, circumferential membrane that partially obstructs the oesophagus, most commonly at the lower end. It is often associated with nutritional deficiencies, particularly iron and vitamin B12 deficiency, and may occur in conditions like Plummer-Vinson syndrome. Other causes include chronic inflammation, infections, or malignancy. The condition typically affects the mid to lower oesophagus and can lead to dysphagia, especially for solid foods. Synonyms include oesophageal membrane or oesophageal stricture. It is more prevalent in females and the elderly.

Perforation of the oesophagus is a life-threatening condition characterized by a full-thickness tear in the oesophageal wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the mediastinum and pleural spaces. Common synonyms include oesophageal rupture and esophageal perforation. Causative agents include trauma, iatrogenic injury during endoscopy or surgery, and spontaneous rupture, often due to conditions like corrosive ingestion or connective tissue disorders. The oesophagus is typically affected, with the mid- to distal segments being most commonly involved. Complications include mediastinitis, sepsis, and pleural effusion. Early diagnosis and management are critical to improve outcomes.

Spontaneous rupture of the oesophagus, also known as Boerhaave syndrome, is a rare but life-threatening condition characterized by a tear in the distal oesophagus following forceful vomiting. Common synonyms include traumatic oesophageal rupture and iatrogenic oesophageal rupture. It is typically caused by excessive intra-abdominal pressure from vomiting, often in the context of alcohol intoxication or gastric distension. The condition predominantly affects the distal oesophagus and can lead to mediastinitis, pleural effusion, and sepsis if not promptly treated.

"Other specified perforation of oesophagus" refers to a tear in the esophageal wall not caused by common causes like trauma, foreign bodies, or peptic ulceration. It is a rare, often iatrogenic condition, typically occurring during medical procedures such as endoscopy or surgery. Common synonyms include esophageal rupture not otherwise specified. Causative agents may include instrumentation, accidental injury, or spontaneous rupture in immunocompromised patients. The condition primarily affects the mid to distal esophagus, leading to mediastinitis and potentially life-threatening complications if untreated.

Perforation of the oesophagus, unspecified, refers to a sudden rupture in the oesophageal wall, leading to leakage of gastric contents into the mediastinum or pleural spaces. Common synonyms include oesophageal rupture and Boerhaave syndrome. Causative agents often include forceful vomiting, trauma, or iatrogenic injury. The condition typically affects the mid to distal oesophagus. Symptoms include chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and sepsis. Prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention are critical to prevent complications such as mediastinitis and respiratory failure.

code_desc: Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the oesophagus
summary: "Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the oesophagus" refers to structural changes in the oesophagus not classified under other specific disorders. Common synonyms include oesophageal strictures, webs, or diverticula of unspecified origin. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, infections, trauma, or iatrogenic procedures. These alterations typically affect the mid to distal oesophagus, leading to dysphagia and potential complications such as obstruction or aspiration. The condition is often diagnosed endoscopically and managed with dilation, surgery, or medical therapy.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of the oesophagus, unspecified
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the oesophagus, unspecified, refer to structural changes in the oesophagus resulting from external factors rather than congenital causes. Common synonyms include acquired oesophageal strictures or deformities. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, caustic ingestion, radiation therapy, or surgical interventions. These alterations typically affect the mid or distal oesophagus, leading to dysphagia and potential complications such as aspiration. The condition is often diagnosed through endoscopy or imaging studies.

Motility disorders of the oesophagus refer to impaired coordination of muscle contractions in the oesophagus, leading to difficulty in swallowing. Common synonyms include dysphagia and achalasia. These disorders can result from neuromuscular dysfunction, such as damage to the myenteric plexus, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents may include chronic reflux, infections, or autoimmune conditions. Typically affected body parts include the oesophagus, with symptoms often involving the upper gastrointestinal tract. Conditions like achalasia, diffuse spasm, and scleroderma-associated oesophageal dysfunction are frequently associated.

Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing, combined with impaired peristalsis in the esophageal body. This results in dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain. Common synonyms include cardia spasm and esophageal achalasia. The exact cause is often unknown, though some cases are associated with autoimmune mechanisms or neuronal damage. It primarily affects the esophagus, particularly the lower third and the gastroesophageal junction.

code_desc: Motility disorder of cervical or upper oesophagus
summary: Motility disorder of the cervical or upper oesophagus refers to impaired coordinated muscle function in the upper gastrointestinal tract, affecting the passage of food from the pharynx to the stomach. Common synonyms include dysphagia, achalasia, and diffuse esophageal spasm. Causative agents may include neurological conditions such as stroke or Parkinson’s disease, as well as structural abnormalities. The condition primarily affects the pharynx, upper oesophagus, and occasionally the lower oesophagus. Symptoms include difficulty swallowing, regurgitation, and chest pain. Diagnosis often involves manometry and endoscopy.

Disorder of oesophageal peristalsis refers to impaired coordinated muscle contractions in the oesophagus, leading to difficulty in swallowing (dysphagia). Common synonyms include oesophageal dysmotility and achalasia. Causative agents may include neurological conditions such as stroke or Parkinson's disease, or structural abnormalities. The primary affected body part is the oesophagus, with symptoms often involving both solids and liquids. This condition can result in regurgitation, chest pain, and aspiration. It is more common in the elderly and may require endoscopic or pharmacological management.

Hypertensive peristalsis refers to increased intensity and frequency of gastrointestinal peristaltic movements, often associated with elevated intraluminal pressure. It is commonly observed in conditions such as intestinal obstruction, severe constipation, or postoperative states. Synonyms include hyperperistalsis and increased bowel motility. Causative agents may include mechanical obstruction, electrolyte imbalances, or medications like anticholinergics. The condition primarily affects the small and large intestines, leading to symptoms such as cramping, bloating, and altered bowel habits.

Hypotensive peristalsis refers to weakened or reduced peristaltic activity in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to delayed gastric emptying and impaired bowel motility. Common synonyms include gastroparesis and delayed gastric emptying. It is often caused by diabetes mellitus, neurological disorders, medications like opioids, and post-surgical complications. The condition primarily affects the stomach and intestines, resulting in symptoms such as bloating, nausea, vomiting, and constipation. It is more commonly observed in the upper gastrointestinal tract but can extend to the small intestine.

Spastic peristalsis is a condition characterized by hyperactive, uncoordinated contractions of the gastrointestinal smooth muscle, leading to abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits. It is often associated with functional gastrointestinal disorders. Common synonyms include irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and spastic colon. Causative agents may include stress, infections, dietary factors, and neurologic disorders. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the colon, and is more common in young adults. It is typically diagnosed through clinical evaluation and exclusion of other organic diseases.

code_desc: Other specified disorder of oesophageal peristalsis
summary: Other specified disorder of oesophageal peristalsis refers to impaired coordination of esophageal muscle contractions that do not meet criteria for other specific esophageal motility disorders. Common synonyms include ineffective esophageal motility and non-specific esophageal dysmotility. Causative agents may include chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, neurological conditions, or idiopathic factors. The primary affected body part is the esophagus, with symptoms such as dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain. Diagnosis typically involves manometry and imaging studies. Treatment focuses on managing underlying conditions and alleviating symptoms.

Disorder of oesophageal peristalsis, unspecified, refers to impaired coordinated muscle contractions in the oesophagus, leading to difficulty in swallowing (dysphagia). Common synonyms include esophageal dysmotility and ineffective esophageal peristalsis. Causative agents may include neurological conditions, such as stroke or Parkinson’s disease, or structural abnormalities. The primary affected body part is the oesophagus, with symptoms often involving both solids and liquids. This condition may also be associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease. Diagnosis typically involves manometry or barium studies.

code_desc: Disorder of lower oesophageal sphincter function
summary: Disorder of lower oesophageal sphincter function refers to impaired function of the lower oesophageal sphincter, leading to abnormal reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus. Common synonyms include gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and achalasia. Causative agents may include hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, and certain medications. The primary affected body parts are the oesophagus and stomach. Symptoms often include heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia. This condition can result in complications such as oesophagitis, stricture, or Barrett's oesophagus.

code_desc: Other specified motility disorders of oesophagus
summary: Other specified motility disorders of oesophagus refer to abnormal movement of the oesophagus that do not fit the criteria for more specific conditions like achalasia or diffuse esophageal spasm. Common synonyms include ineffective esophageal motility and non-specific esophageal dysmotility. These disorders may result from neurological dysfunction, myopathy, or unknown causes. They typically affect the body’s ability to propel food from the pharynx to the stomach, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain. The primary affected body part is the oesophagus, with possible involvement of the upper gastrointestinal tract.

Motility disorders of oesophagus, unspecified, refer to impaired movement of the oesophagus that affects the passage of food to the stomach. Common synonyms include oesophageal dysmotility and achalasia. Causes may include neurological damage, inflammation, or structural abnormalities. These disorders typically affect the oesophageal body and lower oesophageal sphincter. Symptoms often include dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain. The exact cause is often unknown, but conditions like scleroderma or Chagas disease may contribute. Diagnosis usually involves manometry and endoscopy. Treatment options vary depending on the underlying cause and severity.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition characterized by the backward flow of stomach contents into the oesophagus, causing irritation and inflammation. Common synonyms include reflux disease and acid reflux. It is primarily caused by a weakened lower oesophageal sphincter, allowing gastric acid and bile to reflux. Common causative factors include obesity, hiatal hernia, and dietary habits. The condition typically affects the oesophagus, with potential complications such as oesophagitis, stricture, or Barrett's oesophagus. Symptoms often include heartburn and regurgitation.

Non-erosive gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (NERD) is a chronic condition characterized by the reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus without visible mucosal damage. Common synonyms include non-erosive reflux disease and silent reflux. It is primarily caused by transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation, often associated with obesity, hiatal hernia, or dietary factors. The oesophagus is typically affected, with symptoms such as heartburn and regurgitation. Unlike erosive disease, it lacks visible mucosal breaks on endoscopy. NERD is more common in adults and may be linked to increased oesophageal sensitivity.

Erosive gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition characterized by the reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus, leading to mucosal injury. Common synonyms include reflux oesophagitis and oesophagitis due to acid reflux. The primary causative agent is gastric acid, though bile and pepsin may also contribute. It typically affects the oesophagus, with potential extension to the larynx and lungs. Risk factors include obesity, hiatal hernia, and delayed gastric emptying. Symptoms often include heartburn and regurgitation, and complications may involve strictures or Barrett's oesophagus.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD), unspecified, is a chronic condition characterized by the backward flow of stomach contents into the oesophagus, causing irritation and inflammation. Common synonyms include reflux disease and acid reflux. It is primarily caused by transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation, though factors like obesity, hiatal hernia, and dietary habits may contribute. The oesophagus is typically affected, with potential complications such as oesophagitis, stricture, or Barrett's oesophagus. Symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation, often worsening after meals or when lying down.

code_desc: Columnar metaplastic epithelium of the oesophagus
summary: Columnar metaplastic epithelium of the oesophagus, also known as Barrett's oesophagus, is a condition where the normal squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus is replaced by columnar epithelium. This change is commonly associated with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Prolonged exposure to gastric acid and bile is believed to cause the metaplasia. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus and is a known precursor to oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Synonyms include Barrett's oesophagus and columnar metaplasia.

Barrett epithelium is a metaplastic change in the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly occurring in the distal esophagus. It results from chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease, where the normal stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium resembling that of the small intestine. This condition is a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Synonyms include Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia of the esophagus. It is primarily associated with long-standing acid reflux and is typically found in the lower esophagus.

Dysplasia of Barrett epithelium refers to the abnormal proliferation of columnar epithelial cells in the distal esophagus, typically resulting from chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease. This condition is a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Common synonyms include Barrett's esophagus with dysplasia. The primary causative agent is prolonged exposure to gastric acid and bile reflux. It predominantly affects the lower esophagus, with dysplasia progressing through low-grade to high-grade stages. Early detection through endoscopy and biopsy is critical for management.

Barrett ulcer refers to the presence of an ulcer in the distal esophagus, typically associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). It occurs when the normal squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by metaplastic columnar epithelium, a condition known as Barrett's esophagus. The ulcers are often erosive and may be complicated by bleeding or stricture. Common causative agents include chronic acid reflux, Helicobacter pylori infection, and long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The primary affected body part is the lower esophagus. Synonyms include reflux ulcer and erosive esophagitis with Barrett's metaplasia.

code_desc: Other specified columnar metaplastic epithelium of the oesophagus
summary: "Other specified columnar metaplastic epithelium of the oesophagus" refers to the presence of columnar epithelium in the oesophagus, not classified as Barrett's oesophagus. It is often associated with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and may involve the lower oesophagus. Common synonyms include columnar metaplasia not otherwise specified. Causative agents include long-term acid reflux and mechanical irritation. This condition typically affects the distal oesophagus and is considered a precursor to Barrett's oesophagus.

code_desc: Columnar metaplastic epithelium of the oesophagus, unspecified
summary: Columnar metaplastic epithelium of the oesophagus, unspecified, refers to the abnormal replacement of the normal squamous epithelium in the lower oesophagus with columnar epithelium, often resembling that of the gastric mucosa. This condition is commonly associated with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Synonyms include Barrett's esophagus, though the term may be used more broadly. It typically affects the distal oesophagus and is linked to long-term exposure to gastric acid and bile reflux. The primary causative agent is persistent acid reflux, which leads to epithelial changes as a reparative response.

Oesophagitis refers to inflammation of the oesophagus, typically caused by acid reflux, infections, or irritants. Common synonyms include gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and eosinophilic oesophagitis. The primary causative agents are gastric acid, *Helicobacter pylori*, and certain medications. It commonly affects the lower oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as heartburn, dysphagia, and odynophagia. Chronic cases may result in complications like strictures or Barrett's oesophagus. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment focuses on acid suppression, lifestyle modifications, and addressing underlying causes.

Infectious oesophagitis is an inflammation of the oesophagus caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include oesophageal infection or fungal/ bacterial/ viral oesophagitis. It is typically caused by *Candida albicans*, *Helicobacter pylori*, *Herpes simplex virus*, *Varicella-zoster virus*, or *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. The oesophagus is the primary affected body part, with symptoms such as dysphagia, odynophagia, and stricture formation. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and culture. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying oesophageal disorders.

Oesophageal phlegmon is a rare, severe infection characterized by diffuse inflammation and pus formation in the oesophageal wall. It often presents with pain, dysphagia, and fever. Common synonyms include oesophageal abscess and phlegmonous oesophagitis. The condition is typically caused by bacterial infections, most commonly *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus* species, and anaerobes. It may result from penetrating trauma, foreign bodies, or extension from adjacent infections. The oesophagus is the primary affected site, with potential involvement of surrounding structures such as the mediastinum. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications like perforation or sepsis.

Other specified infectious oesophagitis refers to inflammatory conditions of the oesophagus caused by pathogens not classified under more specific categories such as candida or herpes simplex virus. Common synonyms include non-CDI oesophagitis and unspecified infectious oesophagitis. Causative agents may include bacteria like *Clostridium difficile* (though typically associated with colitis), *Mycobacterium* species, or other atypical organisms. It typically affects the oesophageal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, odynophagia, and potential ulceration. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic evaluation and microbiological testing.

Infectious oesophagitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the oesophagus caused by an infectious agent, with the specific pathogen not identified. Common synonyms include oesophageal infection or infectious oesophagitis. Causative agents may include fungi such as *Candida*, bacteria like *Helicobacter pylori* or *Mycoplasma*, and viruses such as herpes simplex virus. The condition typically affects the oesophageal mucosa, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, odynophagia, and possible ulceration. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals.

Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophagus, leading to structural changes and dysfunction. Common synonyms include eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) and eosinophilic gastritis when involving the stomach. It is primarily caused by allergic reactions to food allergens or environmental triggers. The oesophagus is most commonly affected, though involvement of the stomach and intestines may occur. Symptoms include dysphagia, food impaction, and reflux-like symptoms. Diagnosis involves endoscopic evaluation and histological confirmation of eosinophilia.

Oesophagitis due to external causes refers to inflammation of the oesophagus resulting from physical, chemical, or thermal injury. Common synonyms include chemical oesophagitis and caustic oesophagitis. Causative agents often include strong acids, alkalis, and other corrosive substances. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as pain, dysphagia, and stricture formation. It is commonly seen in children and adults who ingest harmful substances accidentally or intentionally. Prompt medical evaluation is essential to prevent complications like strictures or perforation.

Chemical oesophagitis is an inflammatory condition of the oesophagus caused by exposure to caustic substances. Common synonyms include corrosive oesophagitis and chemical injury of the oesophagus. It is typically caused by ingestion of strong acids, alkalis, or other irritants. The condition predominantly affects the distal oesophagus, leading to mucosal damage, ulceration, and potential stricture formation. Symptoms include dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis is often based on clinical history and endoscopic evaluation. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as strictures or perforation.

Drug-induced oesophagitis is an inflammation of the oesophagus caused by the ingestion of medications that are not adequately dissolved or retained in the oesophagus. Common synonyms include medication-induced oesophagitis and pill-induced oesophagitis. It is typically caused by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), bisphosphonates, and certain antibiotics. The condition primarily affects the lower oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. It is often associated with improper medication administration, such as swallowing pills with insufficient water or lying down immediately after ingestion.

Radiation oesophagitis is an inflammatory condition of the oesophagus caused by exposure to ionizing radiation, commonly occurring in patients undergoing radiotherapy for thoracic malignancies. It presents with dysphagia, odynophagia, and possible stricture formation. Common synonyms include radiation-induced oesophagitis and radiotherapy-related oesophagitis. The primary causative agent is ionizing radiation, particularly in the treatment of lung, breast, or mediastinal cancers. The oesophagus is the predominantly affected body part, with the mid to lower regions most commonly involved.

code_desc: Oesophagitis due to external causes, unspecified
summary: Oesophagitis due to external causes, unspecified refers to inflammation of the oesophagus caused by external factors other than infections or reflux. Common synonyms include chemical oesophagitis and caustic oesophagitis. Causative agents may include corrosive substances, foreign bodies, or physical trauma. Typically, the condition affects the distal oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as pain, dysphagia, and stricture formation. It is often associated with accidental ingestion of harmful substances or prolonged exposure to irritants. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and endoscopic findings. Treatment focuses on removing the causative agent and managing complications.

Other specified oesophagitis refers to inflammation of the oesophagus caused by factors not fitting the criteria for common types such as gastro-oesophageal reflux disease or eosinophilic oesophagitis. Common synonyms include unspecified oesophagitis or non-classifiable oesophagitis. Causative agents may include medications, infections, or irritants. It typically affects the distal oesophagus and may present with symptoms like dysphagia and odynophagia. Diagnosis is often made after excluding more specific conditions.

Oesophagitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the oesophagus of unknown cause. Common synonyms include gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) when related to acid reflux. Causative agents may include gastric acid, infections (e.g., *Candida*, *Herpes simplex*, *H. pylori*), medications (e.g., NSAIDs), or caustic substances. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, heartburn, and odynophagia. It may present with complications like stricture or Barrett's oesophagus if left untreated. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and biopsy.

Oesophageal ulcer is a localized erosion of the oesophageal mucosa, often resulting from acid reflux or infection. Common synonyms include gastro-oesophageal ulcer and reflux ulcer. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though non-ulcer dyspepsia may also be a factor. In some cases, caustic agents or medications like NSAIDs can contribute. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus, with symptoms such as dysphagia, chest pain, and haematemesis. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy.

Oesophageal erosion refers to the superficial loss of the oesophageal mucosa, often resulting from chemical or mechanical injury. Common synonyms include oesophageal ulcer and mucosal damage. It is frequently caused by gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), caustic ingestion, or prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus, with symptoms such as dysphagia, odynophagia, and heartburn. Diagnosis is usually made via endoscopy, and treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause and managing symptoms.

Infectious oesophageal ulcer is a condition characterized by the presence of ulcers in the oesophagus caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include infectious esophagitis and ulcerative esophagitis. The most frequent causative agents are *Candida albicans*, *Herpes simplex virus*, *Varicella-zoster virus*, and *Helicobacter pylori*. It typically affects the distal oesophagus and is more common in immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis is often confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy.

Bacterial oesophageal ulcer is a localized inflammatory lesion of the oesophageal mucosa caused by bacterial infection. Common causative agents include *Helicobacter pylori*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. It may also occur secondary to other conditions such as reflux disease or immunosuppression. Synonyms include infectious oesophageal ulcer and bacterial gastritis of the oesophagus. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus, often associated with symptoms like dysphagia, odynophagia, and haematemesis. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopy and microbiological testing.

Fungal oesophageal ulcer is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by erosion and ulceration of the oesophageal mucosa due to fungal infection. Common synonyms include oesophageal candidiasis and fungal oesophagitis. The most frequent causative agent is *Candida albicans*, though other species like *Aspergillus* and *Cryptococcus* may also be involved. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS, diabetes, or on immunosuppressive therapy. The condition primarily involves the oesophagus, causing symptoms like dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy and histopathological examination.

Parasitic oesophageal ulcer is a rare condition characterized by ulceration of the oesophageal mucosa caused by parasitic infection. Common synonyms include oesophageal ulceration due to parasites or parasitic oesophagitis. The most common causative agent is *Fasciola hepatica*, though *Schistosoma* species and *Strongyloides stercoralis* may also be implicated. Typically affecting the distal oesophagus, this condition presents with dysphagia, odynophagia, and weight loss. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and serological testing. Treatment focuses on antiparasitic therapy and management of complications.

Viral oesophageal ulcer is a rare condition characterized by inflammation and ulceration of the oesophageal mucosa caused by viral infection. Common synonyms include viral oesophagitis with ulceration. The most frequently implicated virus is herpes simplex virus (HSV), though coxsackievirus and cytomegalovirus may also be involved. It typically affects the distal oesophagus and is more common in immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms include dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis is often made via endoscopy and viral testing. Treatment involves antiviral therapy and supportive care.

"Other specified infectious oesophageal ulcer" refers to an ulcerative lesion of the oesophagus caused by an infectious agent not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include infectious oesophageal ulcer, unspecified. Causative agents may include *Candida* species, *Herpes simplex virus*, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, or *H. pylori*. Typically affects the distal oesophagus, presenting with dysphagia, odynophagia, and potential bleeding. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and microbiological testing.

Infectious oesophageal ulcer, unspecified, refers to an ulcerative lesion of the oesophagus caused by an infectious agent. Common synonyms include infectious esophagitis and ulcerative esophagitis. Causative agents may include *Candida albicans*, *Herpes simplex virus*, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, and *Helicobacter pylori*. The oesophagus is typically affected, with symptoms such as dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and microbiological testing. Treatment depends on the identified pathogen and may include antifungals, antivirals, or antibiotics.

code_desc: Oesophageal ulcer due to allergic or immunologic disorder
summary: Oesophageal ulcer due to allergic or immunologic disorder refers to ulceration of the oesophageal mucosa caused by hypersensitivity or autoimmune mechanisms. Common synonyms include eosinophilic oesophagitis and allergic oesophagitis. Causative agents often involve food allergens, environmental allergens, or immune-mediated responses. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, food impaction, and chest pain. It is more prevalent in children and young adults, with a male predominance. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy, showing eosinophilic infiltration.

code_desc: Oesophageal ulcer due to external causes
summary: Oesophageal ulcer due to external causes refers to damage to the oesophageal mucosa resulting from external agents rather than endogenous factors like acid reflux. Common synonyms include chemical oesophagitis and caustic injury. Causative agents often include strong acids, alkalis, or corrosive substances ingested accidentally or intentionally. The oesophagus is typically affected, with lesions most commonly seen in the mid to lower regions. Symptoms may include pain, dysphagia, and stricture formation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy.

Chemical oesophageal ulcer is a severe inflammatory condition of the oesophageal mucosa caused by caustic ingestion. Common synonyms include caustic oesophagitis and corrosive oesophagitis. Causative agents typically include strong acids (e.g., hydrochloric acid) or alkalis (e.g., lye). The condition primarily affects the oesophagus, with potential extension to the pharynx and stomach. Symptoms include pain, dysphagia, and stricture formation. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt decontamination and supportive care.

Drug-induced oesophageal ulcer is a mucosal injury of the oesophagus caused by prolonged contact of corrosive substances with the oesophageal lining. Common synonyms include medication-induced oesophagitis and drug-related oesophageal erosion. Causative agents often include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), bisphosphonates, and iron supplements. These medications may remain in the oesophagus due to improper administration, such as swallowing with insufficient water. The condition primarily affects the distal oesophagus and can lead to symptoms like dysphagia, odynophagia, and haematemesis. Early diagnosis and appropriate management are crucial to prevent complications.

Radiation oesophageal ulcer is a severe mucosal injury of the oesophagus caused by ionizing radiation, typically occurring during radiotherapy for thoracic or cervical malignancies. It presents with dysphagia, odynophagia, and bleeding. Common synonyms include radiation-induced oesophageal ulcer and radiotherapy-associated oesophagitis. Causative agents are ionizing radiation, often in conjunction with chemotherapy. The condition primarily affects the mid to lower oesophagus, leading to necrosis and stricture formation. Complications may include perforation and fistula formation.

code_desc: Oesophageal ulcer due to other specified external causes
summary: Oesophageal ulcer due to other specified external causes refers to ulcers in the oesophagus resulting from identifiable external factors not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include acquired oesophageal ulcer and secondary oesophageal ulcer. Causative agents may include corrosive substances, foreign bodies, or trauma from medical procedures. Typically affecting the distal oesophagus, this condition presents with dysphagia, pain, and potential bleeding. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy, and management focuses on removing the causative agent and treating complications.

code_desc: Oesophageal ulcer due to external causes, unspecified
summary: Oesophageal ulcer due to external causes, unspecified, refers to an ulceration of the oesophageal mucosa caused by external factors other than known pathogens or conditions. Common synonyms include traumatic oesophageal ulcer or iatrogenic oesophageal ulcer. Causative agents may include foreign bodies, corrosive substances, or medical instruments. Typically, the mid to lower oesophagus is affected. This condition is often associated with ingestion of caustic materials, prolonged intubation, or esophageal instrumentation. Symptoms may include dysphagia, odynophagia, and hematemesis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by endoscopy.

"Other specified oesophageal ulcer" refers to an ulcer in the oesophagus that does not meet the criteria for specific types such as reflux or infectious ulcers. It may result from various causes, including trauma, medications like NSAIDs, or systemic diseases. Common synonyms include unspecified oesophageal ulcer or non-specific oesophageal ulcer. The oesophageal mucosa is typically affected, often in the mid to distal regions. Diagnosis is usually made through endoscopy and biopsy, with treatment directed at underlying causes.

Oesophageal ulcer, unspecified, refers to an ulceration in the lining of the oesophagus without a specific cause or location identified. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer of the oesophagus and reflux ulcer. It is often associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or infection with *Helicobacter pylori*. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as dysphagia, chest pain, and haematemesis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy.

Vascular disorders of the oesophagus encompass conditions involving abnormal blood vessel structures within the oesophagus, leading to potential bleeding or structural compromise. Common synonyms include oesophageal varices and arteriovenous malformations. These disorders are often caused by portal hypertension, liver cirrhosis, or congenital anomalies. They predominantly affect the lower oesophagus and may present with haematemesis or melena. Risk factors include chronic alcohol use and liver disease. Early diagnosis and management are critical to prevent life-threatening haemorrhage.

Oesophageal varices are dilated, twisted veins in the lower oesophagus, typically resulting from portal hypertension. Common synonyms include oesophageal varices and gastric varices. The primary cause is liver cirrhosis, often due to chronic hepatitis or alcohol-related liver disease. Other causes include schistosomiasis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and congenital hepatic fibrosis. These varices are most commonly found in the lower oesophagus and can rupture, leading to life-threatening haemorrhage. They are associated with portal hypertension, which increases venous pressure in the oesophagus.

Oesophageal varices with bleeding refer to the rupture and hemorrhage of dilated veins in the lower oesophagus, commonly caused by portal hypertension. This condition is often associated with liver cirrhosis, alcoholic liver disease, or schistosomiasis. The varices result from increased pressure in the portal venous system, leading to collateral circulation. Bleeding can be life-threatening, presenting as hematemesis or melena. The primary affected area is the oesophagus, with potential involvement of the gastric cardia. Synonyms include oesophageal variceal hemorrhage and portal hypertensive bleeding.

Oesophageal varices without bleeding refer to dilated submucosal veins in the lower oesophagus, typically resulting from portal hypertension. Common synonyms include oesophageal varices and varices of the oesophagus. The primary causative agent is liver cirrhosis, often due to chronic hepatitis or alcohol abuse. Other causes include Budd-Chiari syndrome and congenital portosystemic shunts. These varices predominantly affect the distal oesophagus and are associated with an increased risk of variceal bleeding. They are commonly found in patients with advanced liver disease.

Oesophageal varices, unspecified, refer to the abnormal dilation of veins in the lower oesophagus, typically resulting from portal hypertension. Common synonyms include oesophageal varices and varices of the oesophagus. The primary cause is liver disease, particularly cirrhosis, which increases pressure in the portal venous system. Other causes may include thrombosis of the portal vein or schistosomiasis. These varices are most commonly found in the distal oesophagus and can rupture, leading to life-threatening haemorrhage. The condition predominantly affects individuals with chronic liver disease.

code_desc: Angiodysplasia or arteriovenous malformation of oesophagus
summary: Angiodysplasia or arteriovenous malformation of the oesophagus refers to abnormal vascular formations in the oesophageal wall, characterized by dilated or malformed blood vessels. Common synonyms include oesophageal angiodysplasia and AVM. It is often associated with chronic oesophageal irritation, long-term anticoagulant use, or conditions like haemorrhoids. The condition typically affects the distal oesophagus and is more prevalent in older adults. It can lead to recurrent haematemesis due to vessel rupture. Causative factors include vascular developmental anomalies, trauma, or systemic disorders such as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.

Intramural haemorrhage of the oesophagus refers to bleeding within the wall of the oesophagus, often resulting from trauma, esophageal varices, or vascular malformations. Common synonyms include oesophageal haemorrhage and submucosal haemorrhage. Causative agents may include peptic ulceration, Mallory-Weiss tears, or coagulopathy. The condition typically affects the mid to lower oesophagus and can present with hematemesis or melena. It is a serious complication requiring prompt evaluation and management to prevent airway obstruction or hypovolemic shock.

Gastro-oesophageal laceration-haemorrhage syndrome refers to traumatic injuries to the lower oesophagus and upper stomach, often resulting in haemorrhage. Common synonyms include Boerhaave syndrome and traumatic oesophageal rupture. Causative agents typically involve forceful vomiting, coughing, or physical trauma. The condition predominantly affects the oesophagus and gastric fundus. Symptoms include chest pain, haematemesis, and subcutaneous emphysema. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as mediastinitis and sepsis.

code_desc: Other specified vascular disorders of the oesophagus
summary: "Other specified vascular disorders of the oesophagus" refers to rare conditions involving abnormal blood vessel formations in the oesophagus not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include esophageal vascular malformations and vascular anomalies of the oesophagus. These disorders may result from congenital developmental issues, trauma, or acquired conditions. Causative agents may include vascular malformations, varices, or arteriovenous malformations. Typically, the condition affects the mid to lower oesophagus, leading to symptoms such as bleeding, dysphagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and imaging studies.

code_desc: Vascular disorders of the oesophagus, unspecified
summary: Vascular disorders of the oesophagus, unspecified, refer to abnormal blood vessel conditions affecting the oesophagus without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include oesophageal vascular anomalies and unspecified oesophageal vasculopathy. Causative agents may include trauma, hypertension, or congenital abnormalities. These disorders typically affect the lower oesophagus and may present with symptoms such as haematemesis or dysphagia. They can lead to complications like bleeding or stricture formation. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and imaging studies. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and severity.

"Other specified diseases of oesophagus" refers to oesophageal conditions not classified under more specific categories such as reflux disease or cancer. Common synonyms include miscellaneous oesophageal disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., fungi, viruses), trauma, or idiopathic factors. These conditions typically affect the oesophageal mucosa, submucosa, or muscular layers, leading to symptoms like dysphagia, pain, or bleeding. They are often diagnosed through endoscopy and biopsy, and management varies based on underlying cause.

Diseases of oesophagus, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the oesophagus without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include oesophageal disorders or oesophagitis. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., *Candida*, *Herpes simplex*), reflux, or inflammatory processes. Typically, the condition affects the mucosa, submucosa, and muscular layers of the oesophagus. Symptoms often include dysphagia, odynophagia, and chest pain. Diagnosis may involve endoscopy, biopsy, or imaging. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and may include antacids, antibiotics, or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of the stomach
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the stomach refer to structural changes in the stomach that develop over time, often due to disease or injury. Common synonyms include gastric deformities and acquired gastric anomalies. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, or surgical interventions. These alterations typically affect the gastric wall, mucosa, and lumen, leading to changes in shape, size, or motility. Conditions such as gastric volvulus, atony, or scarring can result in functional and structural impairments. The fundus, body, and antrum are commonly involved areas.

Gastric outlet obstruction is a condition characterized by the blockage of the passage of food from the stomach into the duodenum. Common synonyms include pyloric stenosis and peptic ulcer obstruction. It is typically caused by peptic ulcer disease, gastric cancer, or benign strictures. The primary affected area is the pylorus, though obstruction may extend into the proximal duodenum. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies and endoscopy, with treatment focusing on relieving the obstruction and addressing the underlying cause.

Gastric fistula, acquired, is an abnormal passage connecting the stomach to another organ or body cavity, typically resulting from trauma, surgery, infection, or malignancy. Common synonyms include gastric-enteric fistula and gastric-pancreatic fistula. Causative agents often include peptic ulcer disease, gastric cancer, postoperative complications, or inflammatory conditions like Crohn's disease. The condition most commonly affects the duodenum, jejunum, or transverse colon, leading to symptoms such as malnutrition, electrolyte imbalances, and recurrent infections. It requires prompt diagnosis and management to prevent complications.

Gastric volvulus is a condition characterized by the abnormal rotation of the stomach around its longitudinal or transverse axis, leading to obstruction and potential ischemia. Common synonyms include gastric torsion and gastric inversion. It is often caused by an enlarged diaphragmatic hernia, congenital malformations, or postoperative complications. The condition primarily affects the stomach, with the fundus and body being the most commonly involved segments. Symptoms include epigastric pain, vomiting, and distension. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications such as necrosis and perforation.

Gastric diverticulum refers to a small, abnormal pouch-like protrusion of the stomach wall, typically arising from the muscularis propria. It is most commonly found in the distal stomach, particularly in the greater curvature. Common synonyms include gastric diverticula and epiploic diverticula. The condition is often idiopathic, though increased intraluminal pressure may contribute. It may be associated with conditions such as achalasia or chronic vomiting. While generally asymptomatic, complications like bleeding or perforation can occur. The most frequently affected area is the gastric fundus or body.

code_desc: Hourglass stricture and stenosis of stomach
summary: Hourglass stricture and stenosis of the stomach refer to a severe, circumferential narrowing of the gastric lumen, typically occurring in the distal portion, resembling an hourglass shape. This condition is often caused by chronic inflammation, peptic ulcer disease, or malignancy. Common synonyms include gastric stenosis and pyloric stenosis. It primarily affects the antrum or pylorus, leading to obstructive symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. The narrowing can result from fibrosis, scarring, or tumor infiltration, and may necessitate endoscopic dilation or surgical intervention.

Gastroptosis is a condition characterized by the abnormal downward displacement of the stomach from its normal anatomical position. It is also known as gastric ptosis or stomach prolapse. Common synonyms include gastric ptosis and stomach prolapse. The condition is often associated with weakened abdominal muscles, obesity, or prior abdominal surgeries. It typically affects the stomach, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, bloating, and early satiety. The lower esophageal sphincter may also be involved, contributing to reflux symptoms. While not a common disorder, gastroptosis can significantly impact quality of life and may require supportive care or surgical intervention in severe cases.

code_desc: Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the stomach
summary: "Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the stomach" refers to structural changes in the stomach not classified elsewhere, such as scarring, adhesions, or deformities. Common synonyms include gastric scarring or post-inflammatory gastric changes. Causative agents may include chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, surgery, or infections like *Helicobacter pylori*. Typically affects the gastric wall, antrum, or body, leading to altered motility or obstruction. Often diagnosed incidentally or through endoscopy.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of the stomach, unspecified
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the stomach, unspecified, refer to structural changes in the stomach not caused by congenital factors. Common synonyms include gastric structural abnormalities and acquired gastric deformities. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, or surgical interventions. These alterations typically affect the stomach wall, fundus, body, or antrum, leading to changes in shape, size, or motility. The condition may present with symptoms such as dyspepsia, nausea, or altered gastric emptying. Diagnosis often involves imaging or endoscopic evaluation.

Gastroduodenal motor or secretory disorders refer to abnormalities in the function of the stomach and duodenum, affecting motility or secretion. Common synonyms include gastroparesis, dyspepsia, and duodenal dysmotility. These conditions may result from neurological damage, hormonal imbalances, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents include diabetes mellitus, vagus nerve damage, infections, and medications. Typically affecting the stomach and duodenum, symptoms often include nausea, vomiting, bloating, and epigastric pain. Diagnosis involves endoscopy, manometry, and gastric emptying studies. Treatment focuses on symptom management and addressing underlying causes.

Abnormal gastric motility refers to impaired movement of the stomach muscles, leading to delayed or accelerated emptying of gastric contents. Common synonyms include dysgastric motility and gastroparesis. It is often caused by diabetes mellitus, post-viral infections, neurological disorders, or medications like opioids. The primary affected body part is the stomach, with symptoms such as bloating, nausea, and early satiety. This condition can also impact the small intestine and contribute to malnutrition if left untreated.

Gastroparesis is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction. Common synonyms include delayed gastric emptying and diabetic gastroparesis. It is often caused by diabetes mellitus, post-vagotomy, or neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. The primary affected body part is the stomach, where motility is impaired. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, early satiety, and abdominal distension. Diagnosis typically involves gastric emptying studies. Management focuses on dietary modifications, prokinetic agents, and addressing underlying causes.

Other specified abnormal gastric motility refers to impaired stomach emptying not attributable to a specific known disorder. It may present with symptoms like nausea, vomiting, and early satiety. Common synonyms include dysmotility and delayed gastric emptying. Causative factors may include diabetes mellitus, neurological conditions, or medications. The primary affected body part is the stomach, with potential involvement of the upper gastrointestinal tract. Diagnosis often involves gastric emptying studies. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and addressing underlying causes.

Abnormal gastric motility, unspecified, refers to impaired or excessive movement of the stomach contents, leading to symptoms such as dyspepsia, nausea, and vomiting. Common synonyms include dysmotility and gastroparesis. Causative agents may include diabetes mellitus, neurological disorders, medications like opioids, and post-surgical complications. The primary affected body part is the stomach, with potential involvement of the upper gastrointestinal tract. This condition can result from dysfunction of the enteric nervous system or impaired coordination of gastric muscles. Diagnosis often involves gastric emptying studies or manometry.

Acute dilatation of the stomach, also known as gastric distension or gastric pneumatosis, refers to a sudden and severe expansion of the stomach due to gas accumulation. Common synonyms include gastric distension and gastric pneumatosis. It is often caused by obstruction of gastric outflow, such as from peptic ulcer perforation, gastric volvulus, or foreign body ingestion. The condition primarily affects the stomach, but may involve adjacent structures like the esophagus or intestines. Symptoms include epigastric pain, distension, vomiting, and in severe cases, respiratory compromise due to diaphragmatic elevation. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as perforation or shock.

Acid hypersecretion refers to an excessive production of gastric acid by the stomach lining, leading to increased acidity in the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include hyperchlorhydria and gastric hypersecretion. It is often caused by conditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, chronic gastritis, or use of certain medications like NSAIDs. The primary affected area is the stomach, but symptoms may extend to the esophagus, causing heartburn and peptic ulcers. This condition can also contribute to complications like gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and duodenal ulcers.

Achlorhydria is a condition characterized by the absence or severe reduction of gastric acid secretion. It results from dysfunction of the parietal cells in the stomach. Common synonyms include hypochlorhydria and achlorhydria. Known causes include chronic atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, long-term use of proton pump inhibitors, and certain autoimmune disorders. The primary affected body part is the stomach, where reduced acid impairs digestion and increases susceptibility to infections. It may also contribute to vitamin B12 deficiency and malabsorption.

code_desc: Other specified gastroduodenal motor or secretory disorders
summary: Other specified gastroduodenal motor or secretory disorders refer to functional gastrointestinal disorders with abnormal motility or secretion not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include functional dyspepsia and gastroparesis. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving psychosocial factors, autonomic dysfunction, or medications. These conditions primarily affect the stomach and duodenum, leading to symptoms like epigastric pain, bloating, nausea, and early satiety. Diagnosis is typically based on exclusion of organic disease and symptom patterns. Treatment focuses on symptom management and lifestyle modifications.

code_desc: Gastroduodenal motor or secretory disorders, unspecified
summary: Gastroduodenal motor or secretory disorders, unspecified, refer to impaired function of the stomach or duodenum involving either motility or secretion. Common synonyms include dysmotility, gastroparesis, or exocrine insufficiency. Causative agents may include diabetes mellitus, infections, medications, or neurological conditions. These disorders typically affect the stomach and duodenum, leading to symptoms such as delayed gastric emptying, nausea, vomiting, and malabsorption. The exact etiology is often unspecified, necessitating further diagnostic evaluation.

Gastritis is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining, characterized by erosion or ulceration of the gastric mucosa. Common synonyms include gastric inflammation and acute/chronic gastritis. It is often caused by Helicobacter pylori infection, prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), excessive alcohol consumption, or stress. The primary affected body part is the stomach, particularly the antrum and body. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy.

Autoimmune gastritis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the immune system attacking the parietal cells in the gastric mucosa, leading to reduced acid production and vitamin B12 deficiency. Common synonyms include atrophic gastritis and autoimmune atrophic gastritis. The primary causative agent is the autoimmune response against intrinsic factor and parietal cells. It typically affects the stomach, particularly the corpus region, and is associated with pernicious anemia. The condition is more prevalent in middle-aged individuals and is linked to genetic predisposition and environmental factors.

Helicobacter pylori induced gastritis is a chronic inflammation of the stomach lining caused by infection with *Helicobacter pylori*, a spiral-shaped bacterium. Common synonyms include *H. pylori* gastritis or bacterial gastritis. The infection typically affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and is associated with increased risk of gastric cancer. Transmission occurs via oral-oral or fecal-oral routes, and diagnosis is often confirmed through endoscopy, urea breath tests, or stool antigen testing. Treatment involves eradication therapy with antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors.

Eosinophilic gastritis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of eosinophils into the gastric mucosa. It is often associated with allergic reactions or parasitic infections. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and allergic gastritis. Known causative agents include food allergens, medications, and parasites such as *Strongyloides stercoralis*. The stomach is typically affected, though other gastrointestinal tract regions may also be involved. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopy and histopathological examination.

Lymphocytic gastritis is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by infiltration of lymphocytes in the gastric mucosa. It is often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, though other causes may include autoimmune mechanisms or dietary factors. Common synonyms include chronic lymphocytic gastritis and lymphocytic infiltration of the stomach. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum, and may present with symptoms such as dyspepsia, nausea, and weight loss. It is more commonly seen in adults and can be linked to conditions like celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease.

Allergic gastritis is a rare condition characterized by inflammation of the stomach lining due to an allergic reaction. It typically presents with symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Common causative agents include food allergens like milk, eggs, and shellfish. Synonyms include hypersensitivity gastritis and allergic gastroenteritis. The condition primarily affects the stomach, though it may involve the gastrointestinal tract. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic evaluation and biopsy. Management involves identifying and avoiding allergens, along with symptomatic treatment.

code_desc: Allergic gastritis due to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity
summary: Allergic gastritis due to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining triggered by an immune response involving IgE antibodies. It occurs when the stomach mucosa reacts to allergens such as food proteins, medications, or environmental agents. Common symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Synonyms include IgE-mediated gastritis or food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome. Causative agents often include cow's milk, eggs, seafood, and certain medications. The primary affected body part is the stomach, though systemic manifestations may occur in severe cases.

code_desc: Allergic gastritis due to non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity
summary: Allergic gastritis due to non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining triggered by immune responses not involving IgE antibodies. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome and non-IgE-mediated food allergy. Causative agents often include cow's milk, soy, eggs, and gluten. The condition typically affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. It is more commonly seen in infants and young children but can occur in adults. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, elimination diets, and response to dietary modifications.

Other specified allergic gastritis refers to an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining caused by allergic reactions to specific dietary or environmental allergens. It is a subset of allergic gastritis not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include allergic gastritis, food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome, and allergic gastroenteritis. Causative agents often include cow's milk, soy, eggs, and other food proteins. The stomach is the primary affected body part, with symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis typically involves elimination diets and allergy testing.

Allergic gastritis, unspecified, is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining triggered by an allergic reaction. It is characterized by symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.
