Common causative agents include food allergens like milk, eggs, or seafood. The stomach is the primary affected body part. Synonyms include allergic gastroenteritis and hypersensitivity gastritis. The condition may occur in individuals with a history of food allergies or other allergic disorders. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment focuses on allergen avoidance and anti-inflammatory therapy.

Gastritis due to duodenogastric reflux is an inflammation of the gastric mucosa caused by the backward flow of duodenal contents into the stomach. Common synonyms include reflux gastritis and duodenogastric reflux disease. The condition is often associated with peptic ulcer disease and may be exacerbated by factors such as delayed gastric emptying or structural abnormalities. Causative agents include gastric acid, bile salts, and pancreatic enzymes. The primary affected body part is the stomach, particularly the antrum, with potential involvement of the duodenum. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Menetrier disease is a rare, chronic condition characterized by hypertrophy of the gastric mucosa, leading to excessive secretion of gastric acid and mucus. It primarily affects the greater curvature of the stomach. Common synonyms include hypertrophic gastritis and Menetrier syndrome. The exact cause is unknown, though some cases may be associated with chronic gastritis or Helicobacter pylori infection. The condition can lead to protein-losing gastropathy and an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma. It predominantly affects middle-aged adults, with no significant gender predilection.

code_desc: Gastritis of unknown aetiology with specific endoscopic or pathological features
summary: Gastritis of unknown aetiology with specific endoscopic or pathological features refers to chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa without a clearly identified cause, characterized by distinct endoscopic changes such as erythema, edema, or atrophy, and/or histopathological findings like chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis of unknown origin. While Helicobacter pylori infection is a known cause, this classification is used when no specific aetiology is identified. It typically affects the stomach lining, particularly the antrum and corpus.

code_desc: Acute superficial gastritis of unknown aetiology
summary: Acute superficial gastritis of unknown aetiology refers to inflammation of the gastric mucosa without a clearly identified cause. Common synonyms include acute gastritis or non-specific gastritis. While Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID use are common causes, this condition is diagnosed when no specific aetiology is found. It typically affects the stomach lining, particularly the antrum and body. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. The condition is often self-limiting but may require symptomatic treatment and monitoring for underlying causes.

code_desc: Chronic superficial gastritis of unknown aetiology
summary: Chronic superficial gastritis of unknown aetiology is a long-standing inflammation of the gastric mucosa, primarily affecting the surface layer. Common synonyms include chronic atrophic gastritis and non-specific gastritis. While the exact cause is often unclear, it may be associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, although this is not always present. Other potential factors include dietary habits, medications, and autoimmune processes. The stomach is the primary affected body part, with involvement of the antrum and body. Symptoms may include dyspepsia, nausea, and abdominal discomfort.

code_desc: Acute haemorrhagic gastritis of unknown aetiology
summary: Acute haemorrhagic gastritis of unknown aetiology is a sudden inflammation and bleeding of the stomach lining with no identifiable cause. Common synonyms include acute gastritis with haemorrhage and haemorrhagic gastritis. While specific causative agents are often unclear, potential contributors may include NSAID use, alcohol, infections, or systemic diseases. The condition primarily affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, vomiting blood, and melena. It is typically diagnosed endoscopically and managed with supportive care, acid suppression, and treatment of underlying conditions if identified.

code_desc: Chronic atrophic gastritis of unknown aetiology
summary: Chronic atrophic gastritis of unknown aetiology is a long-standing inflammatory condition characterized by progressive atrophy of the gastric mucosa, leading to reduced acid and intrinsic factor production. Common synonyms include chronic atrophic gastritis and autoimmune gastritis. While Helicobacter pylori infection is a known cause, this variant lacks a clear etiology. It primarily affects the body and fundus of the stomach, often associated with vitamin B12 deficiency and an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

Metaplastic gastritis of unknown aetiology is a rare, chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the abnormal transformation of gastric epithelium into other cell types, such as intestinal or pyloric metaplasia. Despite its name, the exact cause remains unclear. It is often associated with long-standing gastritis, Helicobacter pylori infection, or chronic irritation. Common synonyms include intestinal metaplasia and pyloric metaplasia. The stomach, particularly the antrum, is typically affected. While not a precancerous condition, it may increase the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

Granulomatous gastritis of unknown aetiology is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the presence of granulomas in the gastric mucosa, with no identifiable cause. Common synonyms include idiopathic granulomatous gastritis and chronic granulomatous gastritis. While specific causative agents are often unknown, some cases may be associated with infections such as tuberculosis or fungal infections, or autoimmune processes. The stomach is the primary affected site, though involvement of adjacent organs may occur. Clinically, it may present with dyspepsia, weight loss, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Diagnosis typically requires endoscopic biopsy and histopathological evaluation.

Hypertrophic gastritis of unknown aetiology is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by thickening of the gastric mucosa, primarily affecting the antrum. It is often asymptomatic but may present with epigastric discomfort or dyspepsia. Common synonyms include chronic atrophic gastritis and hypertrophic gastropathy. While the exact cause is unknown, it may be associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, although this is not always the case. The condition predominantly involves the stomach, particularly the antral region, and may lead to complications such as peptic ulceration or gastric outlet obstruction.

code_desc: Other specified gastritis of unknown aetiology with specific endoscopic or pathological features
summary: Other specified gastritis of unknown aetiology with specific endoscopic or pathological features refers to chronic gastritis characterized by distinct histological or endoscopic findings, such as atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, or dysplasia, without a known specific cause. Common synonyms include chronic atrophic gastritis or non-specific gastritis. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori, although the exact cause remains unclear in some cases. This condition typically affects the gastric mucosa, particularly the antrum and body, and is associated with long-standing inflammation. It may progress to more severe conditions like gastric cancer.

Gastritis due to external causes refers to inflammation of the stomach lining resulting from external factors rather than chronic or autoimmune origins. Common synonyms include acute gastritis from irritants. Causative agents often include NSAIDs, alcohol, Helicobacter pylori infection, and corrosive substances. The condition typically affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. It may also involve the duodenum in cases of reflux or ulceration. Diagnosis is usually based on endoscopic findings and histopathological analysis. Treatment focuses on eliminating the causative agent and managing symptoms.

Alcoholic gastritis is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining caused by chronic alcohol consumption. Prolonged alcohol intake irritates and erodes the gastric mucosa, leading to inflammation and potential ulceration. Common synonyms include ethanol-induced gastritis or alcoholic gastric inflammation. The primary causative agent is ethanol, which disrupts the mucosal barrier and increases gastric acid secretion. The condition typically affects the stomach lining, particularly the antrum and body. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Complications can include bleeding or perforation if left untreated.

Radiation gastritis is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining caused by exposure to ionizing radiation, commonly occurring in patients undergoing abdominal or thoracic radiation therapy. It is characterized by mucosal damage, ulceration, and symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Common synonyms include radiation-induced gastritis and radiation-related gastric mucositis. Causative agents are ionizing radiation therapies targeting the abdomen or chest. The primary affected body part is the stomach, though adjacent organs may also be involved.

Chemical gastritis is an inflammatory condition of the stomach lining caused by exposure to corrosive substances. Common synonyms include corrosive gastritis or chemical injury of the gastric mucosa. It is typically induced by ingestion of strong acids or alkalis, such as hydrochloric acid, sodium hydroxide, or cleaning agents. The condition primarily affects the gastric mucosa, leading to erosion, ulceration, and potential perforation. Symptoms include severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and hematemesis. Prompt medical intervention is crucial to prevent complications and manage tissue damage.

Drug-induced gastritis is an inflammation of the stomach lining caused by the use of certain medications. Common synonyms include drug-related gastritis or medication-induced gastritis. It is typically caused by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, and antibiotics such as clarithromycin. The condition primarily affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms like epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Prolonged use increases the risk of complications such as ulcers and bleeding.

code_desc: Gastritis due to external causes, unspecified
summary: Gastritis due to external causes, unspecified refers to inflammation of the stomach lining caused by external factors not specifically identified. Common synonyms include acute gastritis of unknown origin or irritant-induced gastritis. Causative agents may include NSAIDs, alcohol, stress, or ingestion of corrosive substances. The condition typically affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is often diagnosed when no specific etiology is identified through further investigation.

Gastric phlegmon is a rare, diffuse purulent inflammation of the gastric wall, typically secondary to perforation or obstruction. It is characterized by the accumulation of pus within the gastric wall and adjacent tissues. Common synonyms include gastric abscess and gastric cellulitis. Causative agents often include *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Clostridium* species. The condition primarily affects the stomach, with potential spread to adjacent organs such as the pancreas, liver, or peritoneum. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying gastrointestinal disorders.

Other specified gastritis refers to chronic inflammation of the stomach lining that does not meet the criteria for specific types such as erosive or autoimmune gastritis. It is often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or excessive alcohol consumption. Common synonyms include unspecified gastritis or non-erosive gastritis. The condition primarily affects the gastric mucosa, leading to symptoms like dyspepsia, epigastric pain, and nausea. It may also contribute to peptic ulcer disease if left untreated.

Gastritis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the stomach lining without a specific etiology identified. Common synonyms include chronic gastritis and acute gastritis, though the latter is more often specified. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAIDs, alcohol, stress, or autoimmune factors. The primary affected body part is the gastric mucosa. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and dyspepsia. Diagnosis is typically made through endoscopy and biopsy if necessary. Treatment depends on underlying causes and may involve antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors, or lifestyle modifications.

Vascular disorders of the stomach refer to abnormalities affecting the blood vessels supplying the gastric mucosa, leading to ischemia, hemorrhage, or infarction. Common synonyms include gastric ischemia and angioenteropathy. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, vasculitis, hypotension, or emboli. These conditions typically affect the gastric wall, particularly the antrum and fundus, and can result in ulceration, bleeding, or perforation. They are often associated with systemic vascular diseases or complications from medical treatments like anticoagulation. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent severe complications.

Gastric varices are abnormal dilations of the gastric veins, most commonly occurring in the fundus or body of the stomach. They are typically a complication of portal hypertension, often secondary to liver cirrhosis. Other causes include schistosomiasis, chronic alcoholism, and congenital abnormalities. These varices are prone to rupture, leading to life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding. They may also be associated with esophageal varices. Synonyms include portal hypertensive gastric varices and non-esophageal varices. The primary affected area is the stomach, particularly the fundus and lesser curvature.

Angiodysplasia of the stomach is a rare vascular abnormality characterized by malformations of blood vessels in the gastric mucosa, leading to recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include gastric angiodysplasia and vascular ectasia. The exact cause is often unknown, though it may be associated with conditions like hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. It typically affects the distal stomach, particularly the antrum, and is more common in older adults. The lesions appear as small, red, velvety mucosal elevations and can cause chronic blood loss, leading to anemia.

Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) of the stomach is an abnormal tangle of arteries and veins that bypass normal capillary beds, leading to increased blood flow and risk of bleeding. Common synonyms include gastric AVM and hemangioma. The exact cause is often unknown, though some cases may be associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. It typically affects the gastric mucosa, especially the antrum. Symptoms may include hematemesis or melena, and diagnosis is often made via endoscopy. Complications include acute bleeding and iron deficiency anemia.

Portal hypertensive gastropathy is a diffuse, non-atrophic gastritis characterized by eosinophilic infiltration of the gastric mucosa, typically occurring in patients with portal hypertension. Common synonyms include portal hypertensive gastritis and portal hypertension-related gastropathy. It is most commonly caused by liver cirrhosis, often due to chronic hepatitis, alcohol abuse, or schistosomiasis. The condition primarily affects the gastric mucosa, particularly the fundus and body, and may lead to symptoms such as epigastric pain and gastrointestinal bleeding. It is a histological finding rather than a distinct clinical entity.

Diffuse vascular ectasia of the stomach is a rare condition characterized by widespread dilation and abnormal proliferation of blood vessels in the gastric mucosa. Common synonyms include gastric angiectasia and diffuse gastric telangiectasia. It is often associated with chronic conditions such as hemolytic uremic syndrome, collagen vascular diseases, and long-term use of anticoagulants. The primary affected body part is the stomach, with mucosal bleeding being a common presenting feature. The condition may also involve the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the esophagus and duodenum.

code_desc: Other specified vascular disorders of the stomach
summary: "Other specified vascular disorders of the stomach" refers to rare conditions involving abnormal blood vessel structures in the stomach not classified elsewhere. These disorders typically affect the stomach wall, leading to symptoms such as bleeding, pain, or ulceration. They are often diagnosed via endoscopy or imaging studies. While rare, they can be associated with systemic conditions or syndromes. Treatment depends on the specific lesion and may involve endoscopic or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Vascular disorders of the stomach, unspecified
summary: Vascular disorders of the stomach, unspecified, refer to abnormal blood vessel conditions affecting the gastric wall without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include gastric vascular anomalies and unspecified gastric vasculopathy. Causative agents may include hypertension, atherosclerosis, or genetic factors. These disorders typically affect the stomach wall, potentially leading to bleeding, ischemia, or ulceration. They may occur in conjunction with systemic conditions or as isolated findings. Clinical presentation varies but often includes gastrointestinal bleeding or abdominal pain. Diagnosis is usually made through endoscopy or imaging.

A gastric polyp is a benign growth arising from the gastric mucosa, commonly found in the stomach. It may be hyperplastic, adenomatous, or fundic gland polyps. Common synonyms include gastric hyperplastic polyp and fundic gland polyp. Causative factors include chronic gastritis, Helicobacter pylori infection, and long-term use of proton pump inhibitors. These lesions typically affect the greater curvature of the stomach, with fundic and antral regions being most commonly involved. While generally benign, adenomatous polyps carry a low risk of malignant transformation.

Hyperplastic polyp of the stomach is a benign lesion characterized by excessive growth of the mucosal lining, often associated with chronic gastritis. Common synonyms include fundic gland polyp and hyperplastic gastritis. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, which induces chronic inflammation. These polyps typically occur in the gastric fundus and body. They are more common in older adults and may be asymptomatic. While generally non-cancerous, they carry a low risk of malignant transformation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy and histopathological examination.

Fundic gland polyp of the stomach is a benign mucosal proliferation arising from the fundic glands, typically located in the gastric fundus. Common synonyms include gastric fundic gland polyp and hyperplastic polyp. The exact cause is unknown, though chronic gastritis, Helicobacter pylori infection, and long-term use of proton pump inhibitors may contribute. These polyps are most commonly found in the gastric body and fundus. They are usually asymptomatic but may cause bleeding or obstruction if large. They are more prevalent in older adults and are rarely malignant.

Hamartomatous polyp of the stomach is a benign neoplasm composed of a mixture of normal gastric tissues in a disorganized arrangement. It is also known as a gastric hamartoma or gastric lipoma. The condition is typically sporadic but may be associated with genetic syndromes such as Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. These polyps most commonly occur in the greater curvature of the stomach and are usually asymptomatic, though they may cause bleeding or obstruction. They are not premalignant but may be found incidentally during endoscopic examination.

"Other specified gastric polyp" refers to benign gastric growths not classified as hyperplastic, fundic, or lymphoid polyps. Common synonyms include unspecified gastric polyps or miscellaneous gastric polyps. Causative agents may include chronic gastritis, Helicobacter pylori infection, or long-term use of proton pump inhibitors. These polyps typically affect the gastric mucosa, most commonly the antrum. They are generally asymptomatic but may cause bleeding or obstruction if large. Diagnosis is usually made via endoscopy with histopathological confirmation.

Gastric polyp, unspecified, refers to a benign growth arising from the gastric mucosa without specific subtype identification. Common synonyms include gastric neoplasm, unspecified and gastric tumor, unspecified. While the exact cause is often unknown, factors such as chronic gastritis, Helicobacter pylori infection, and long-term use of NSAIDs may contribute. These lesions typically occur in the stomach, most commonly in the antrum. They are generally asymptomatic but may cause bleeding or obstruction if large. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy and biopsy.

"Other specified diseases of stomach" refers to gastric conditions not classified under more specific categories such as gastritis or ulcers. Common synonyms include unspecified gastric disorders or miscellaneous stomach diseases. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., *Helicobacter pylori*), autoimmune factors, or idiopathic causes. These conditions typically affect the stomach lining, leading to symptoms like pain, inflammation, or bleeding. They may involve the gastric mucosa, antrum, or body, and are often diagnosed when specific etiologies are excluded.

Diseases of the stomach, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the stomach without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include gastric disorders or general gastropathies. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., *Helicobacter pylori*), NSAIDs, alcohol, or autoimmune factors. These conditions typically affect the stomach lining, leading to symptoms like pain, nausea, and bleeding. They may involve the mucosa, muscularis, or other layers of the gastric wall. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy or imaging. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and may include medications, lifestyle changes, or surgery.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of the duodenum
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the duodenum refer to structural changes in the first part of the small intestine that develop over time, often due to chronic inflammation, ulcers, or external compression. Common synonyms include duodenal deformity and duodenal stricture. Causative agents may include peptic ulcer disease, Crohn's disease, or post-surgical scarring. These alterations typically affect the duodenum, particularly the second and third segments, leading to symptoms such as obstruction, pain, and malabsorption.

Obstruction of the duodenum refers to a blockage in the first segment of the small intestine, hindering the passage of chyme from the stomach. Common synonyms include duodenal stenosis and duodenal occlusion. Causes include peptic ulcer disease, tumors, strictures from inflammation, or congenital anomalies. It typically affects the duodenum, particularly the second part, and may lead to symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Complications can include intestinal obstruction, malnutrition, and perforation if left untreated. Diagnosis often involves imaging and endoscopic evaluation.

Diverticulum of the duodenum is a rare congenital or acquired outpouching of the duodenal wall, most commonly occurring in the second or third portion. It may present with symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, or intestinal obstruction. Common synonyms include duodenal diverticulum and Meckel's diverticulum, though the latter typically refers to a congenital remnant of the vitelline duct. Causative factors include increased intraluminal pressure, genetic predisposition, and chronic inflammation. The condition predominantly affects the distal duodenum and may be associated with complications like perforation, bleeding, or obstruction.

Fistula of the duodenum is an abnormal passage connecting the duodenum to another organ or structure, most commonly the jejunum, bile duct, or pancreas. It often results from chronic inflammation, infection, or ulceration. Common synonyms include duodenal-enteric fistula and duodenal-pancreatic fistula. Causative agents include peptic ulcer disease, Crohn’s disease, and post-surgical complications. The condition typically affects the second and third parts of the duodenum, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, malabsorption, and recurrent infections.

Deformity of the duodenum, acquired, refers to structural abnormalities in the duodenum resulting from external factors rather than congenital causes. Common synonyms include duodenal stricture, duodenal obstruction, or acquired duodenal malformation. Causative agents may include peptic ulcer disease, inflammation, trauma, or neoplasms. The condition typically affects the second and third parts of the duodenum, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and malabsorption. It may result from chronic inflammation, scarring, or compression from adjacent structures. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies and endoscopy.

code_desc: Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the duodenum
summary: "Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the duodenum" refers to structural changes in the duodenum not classified under other specific disorders. Common synonyms include duodenal deformities or acquired duodenal anomalies. Causative agents may include trauma, surgery, chronic inflammation, or peptic ulcer disease. These alterations typically affect the second to third portions of the duodenum, leading to symptoms such as obstruction, malabsorption, or pain. The condition is often diagnosed through imaging or endoscopic evaluation.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of the duodenum, unspecified
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the duodenum, unspecified, refer to structural changes in the duodenum resulting from external factors rather than congenital causes. These alterations typically affect the second and third portions of the duodenum, leading to symptoms such as obstruction, malabsorption, or altered gastric emptying. The condition is often diagnosed through imaging or endoscopic evaluation.

Duodenitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. Common synonyms include duodenal inflammation and duodenal gastritis. It is often caused by Helicobacter pylori infection, prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or excessive alcohol consumption. The primary affected area is the duodenal mucosa, particularly the bulb and proximal regions. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Chronic duodenitis can lead to complications such as ulcers or strictures if left untreated.

Helicobacter pylori associated duodenitis is an inflammatory condition of the duodenum caused by infection with *Helicobacter pylori*. This gram-negative bacterium adheres to the gastric and duodenal mucosa, leading to chronic inflammation. Common synonyms include *H. pylori* gastritis or duodenal gastritis. The infection typically affects the antrum of the stomach and the proximal duodenum. It is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease and is associated with symptoms such as dyspepsia, abdominal pain, and nausea. Complications may include gastritis, ulcers, and increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

Eosinophilic duodenitis is an inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of eosinophils into the duodenal mucosa. It is often associated with parasitic infections, particularly *Strongyloides stercoralis*, but can also result from allergic reactions or immune-mediated processes. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and eosinophilic enteropathy. The duodenum is the primary affected site, though other gastrointestinal regions may be involved. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopic biopsy and histopathological examination.

Lymphocytic duodenitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the duodenum characterized by infiltration of lymphocytes into the mucosal layer. It is often associated with celiac disease and may present with symptoms such as abdominal pain and malabsorption. Common synonyms include lymphocytic gastritis and lymphocytic enteritis. The primary causative agent is gluten in genetically susceptible individuals. The condition typically affects the duodenum, though it may involve other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopic biopsy.

Allergic duodenitis is an inflammatory condition of the duodenum caused by hypersensitivity reactions to ingested substances. It is characterized by mucosal irritation, edema, and sometimes erosions. Common synonyms include hypersensitivity duodenitis and allergic gastrointestinal inflammation. Causative agents often include food allergens such as dairy, eggs, or gluten, as well as medications like NSAIDs. The primary affected body part is the duodenum, with symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopy and biopsy.

code_desc: Duodenitis of unknown aetiology with specific endoscopic or pathologic features
summary: Duodenitis of unknown aetiology with specific endoscopic or pathologic features refers to inflammation of the duodenum without a clearly identified cause, characterized by distinct endoscopic findings such as erythema, erosions, or ulcers, and/or histopathologic changes. code_desc: Acute haemorrhagic duodenitis of unknown aetiology

Granulomatous duodenitis of unknown aetiology is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the presence of granulomas in the duodenum, with no identifiable cause. The condition is often associated with systemic symptoms such as weight loss and abdominal pain.

Duodenitis due to external causes refers to inflammation of the duodenum resulting from external factors such as trauma, foreign bodies, or medical procedures. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy. Management focuses on removing the causative agent and providing supportive care.

Alcoholic duodenitis is an inflammatory condition of the duodenum caused by chronic alcohol consumption. Prolonged alcohol intake leads to mucosal damage, reduced blood flow, and impaired mucosal defense mechanisms. Common synonyms include alcohol-induced duodenitis and alcoholic gastritis. The primary causative agent is ethanol, which directly irritates the gastrointestinal tract. The condition typically affects the first part of the duodenum, often accompanied by symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is frequently associated with other alcohol-related gastrointestinal disorders.

Drug-induced duodenitis is an inflammation of the duodenum caused by medications. Common synonyms include drug-related duodenal inflammation or medication-induced duodenitis. It is typically caused by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, and proton pump inhibitors. The condition primarily affects the duodenum, with possible extension to the stomach. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is often based on endoscopic findings and clinical history. Management involves discontinuation of the causative agent and supportive care.

Chemical duodenitis refers to inflammation of the duodenum caused by exposure to noxious substances. Common synonyms include irritant duodenitis or chemical gastritis. It is typically induced by ingestion of corrosive agents such as strong acids or alkalis, or by prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The condition primarily affects the duodenum, with potential extension to the stomach and proximal small intestine. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is often made through endoscopy and biopsy, with treatment focusing on neutralizing the irritant and managing complications.

Radiation duodenitis is an inflammatory condition of the duodenum caused by exposure to ionizing radiation, typically as a complication of abdominal or pelvic radiotherapy. It results from direct damage to the gastrointestinal mucosa. Common synonyms include radiation-induced duodenal injury and radiation enteropathy. The primary causative agent is ionizing radiation, often from therapeutic treatments for malignancies such as lymphoma or gynecologic cancers. Infectious duodenitis refers to inflammation of the duodenum caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include bacterial duodenitis and infectious duodenum inflammation. Duodenal phlegmon is a rare, diffuse, purulent inflammation of the duodenum, typically resulting from bacterial infection. Common synonyms include duodenal abscess and duodenal cellulitis. Other specified infectious duodenitis refers to inflammation of the duodenum caused by pathogens not classified under more specific categories. Infectious duodenitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the duodenum caused by an infectious agent. Common synonyms include duodenal infection or duodenal inflammation. Treatment involves antimicrobial therapy and management of underlying conditions.

Other specified duodenitis refers to inflammation of the duodenum that does not meet the criteria for specific types such as erosive or reflux. It may present with symptoms like abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Common synonyms include unspecified duodenitis or non-erosive duodenitis. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, or bile reflux. The primary affected body part is the duodenum, particularly the first portion. Diagnosis often relies on endoscopic findings and clinical presentation. Treatment focuses on addressing underlying causes and managing symptoms.

Duodenitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the duodenum without a specified cause or type. Common synonyms include chronic duodenitis and nonspecific duodenitis. It is often associated with Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, or gastritis. The primary affected body part is the duodenum, particularly the first part. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. The condition may be linked to peptic ulcer disease and can lead to complications such as bleeding or stricture if left untreated. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy.

Vascular disorders of the duodenum refer to abnormalities affecting blood flow to or within the duodenum, leading to ischemia, infarction, or hemorrhage. Common synonyms include duodenal ischemia and vascular malformations of the duodenum. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, vasculitis, thrombosis, or trauma. These conditions typically affect the duodenum, particularly the second and third segments, and can result in symptoms such as abdominal pain, bleeding, and malabsorption. They are often associated with systemic vascular diseases or iatrogenic causes. Early diagnosis is crucial to prevent complications like perforation or stricture.

Duodenal varices are dilated veins in the duodenum, most commonly resulting from portal hypertension, often due to liver cirrhosis. These varices are a complication of portal venous system obstruction and can lead to life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Synonyms include gastric varices and portal hypertensive duodenal varices. They typically affect the second and third portions of the duodenum. Other causes may include congenital abnormalities, thrombosis, or schistosomiasis. Clinical presentation includes hematemesis and melena, necessitating endoscopic evaluation and management.

Angiodysplasia of the duodenum is a rare vascular abnormality characterized by malformations of blood vessels in the duodenal mucosa, leading to recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include duodenal telangiectasia and vascular ectasia. The exact cause is often unknown, though it may be associated with conditions such as chronic inflammation, atherosclerosis, or genetic disorders. It typically affects the second and third portions of the duodenum. The condition is more prevalent in the elderly and may present with hematemesis or melena. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy.

Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) of the duodenum is an abnormal tangle of arteries and veins within the duodenal wall, leading to increased blood flow and potential hemorrhage. Common synonyms include duodenal AVM and hemangiomatous malformation. The condition is typically idiopathic, though rare cases may have genetic associations. It most commonly affects the second and third portions of the duodenum. Symptoms include gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal pain, and anemia. Diagnosis is often made via endoscopy or imaging studies. Treatment may involve endoscopic therapy, embolization, or surgical resection.

code_desc: Other specified vascular disorders of the duodenum
summary: "Other specified vascular disorders of the duodenum" refers to abnormal blood vessel conditions in the duodenum that do not fit into more specific categories. Common synonyms include duodenal vascular malformations or vascular anomalies of the duodenum. These disorders may result from congenital abnormalities, trauma, or inflammatory processes. Causative agents can include genetic factors, vascular dysplasia, or acquired conditions like vasculitis. Typically affecting the duodenum, these disorders may present with gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal pain, or obstruction. They are often diagnosed via endoscopy or imaging studies.

code_desc: Vascular disorders of the duodenum, unspecified
summary: Vascular disorders of the duodenum, unspecified, refer to abnormal blood vessel conditions affecting the duodenum without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include duodenal vascular anomalies and unspecified duodenal vascular disease. These disorders may result from congenital abnormalities, trauma, or acquired factors such as hypertension or atherosclerosis. They typically affect the duodenum, potentially leading to complications like bleeding, ischemia, or obstruction. The exact causative agents are often unspecified, but vascular malformations, aneurysms, or thrombosis may be implicated.

A duodenal polyp is a benign growth arising from the mucosal lining of the duodenum, most commonly in the second part. Common synonyms include duodenal tumor or duodenal neoplasm. These polyps are often hyperplastic or adenomatous, with adenomas being precancerous. They may be associated with chronic inflammation, Helicobacter pylori infection, or genetic syndromes like familial adenomatous polyposis. Typically affecting adults, they may cause symptoms such as abdominal pain, bleeding, or obstruction. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy and biopsy.

Hyperplastic duodenal polyp is a benign lesion arising from the duodenum, typically associated with chronic inflammation or Helicobacter pylori infection. It is characterized by hyperplasia of the mucosal glands and is often found in the second or third portion of the duodenum. Common synonyms include duodenal glandular hyperplasia and inflammatory polyp. While no specific causative agent is consistently identified, H. pylori is a known contributing factor. These polyps are typically solitary and may cause symptoms such as abdominal pain or bleeding. They are most commonly seen in adults, particularly those with a history of peptic ulcer disease.

Other specified duodenal polyp refers to a benign growth in the duodenum that does not fit the criteria for more specific types such as adenomas or lipomas. It is a broad category encompassing various histological types. Common synonyms include unspecified duodenal polyp and non-classifiable duodenal polyp. Causative agents are often unknown, though chronic inflammation or genetic factors may contribute. These polyps typically affect the second to third portions of the duodenum and are usually discovered incidentally during endoscopic procedures.

Duodenal polyp, unspecified, refers to a benign growth arising in the duodenum without specific subtype identification. Common synonyms include duodenal neoplasm, unspecified and duodenal tumor, unspecified. Causative agents are often unknown, though chronic inflammation, genetic syndromes, and long-term use of proton pump inhibitors may contribute. The condition typically affects the second to fourth segments of the duodenum. It is more common in adults and may present with symptoms such as abdominal pain, bleeding, or obstruction. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy and biopsy.

"Other specified diseases of duodenum" refers to duodenal conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as strictures, ulcers, or tumors. Common synonyms include unspecified duodenal disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., *Helicobacter pylori*), autoimmune factors, or idiopathic causes. Typically affects the duodenum, particularly the second and third parts. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and may involve medications, dietary changes, or surgery.

Diseases of the duodenum, unspecified, refer to inflammatory, ulcerative, or neoplastic conditions affecting the duodenum without specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include duodenal disorders or duodenal pathology. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAID use, or autoimmune factors. Typically, the first part of the small intestine is affected, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, nausea, and malabsorption. These conditions may present as ulcers, strictures, or tumors, often requiring endoscopic or histopathological evaluation for confirmation.

Gastric ulcer is a chronic condition characterized by the erosion of the stomach lining, leading to the formation of a crater-like lesion. Common synonyms include peptic ulcer disease (PUD) when referring to both gastric and duodenal ulcers. The primary causative agents are Helicobacter pylori infection and the prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It typically affects the antrum and body of the stomach, though it may occur anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms often include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Complications such as bleeding or perforation may arise if left untreated.

Gastric erosion refers to the superficial loss of the gastric mucosal lining, often without full-thickness involvement. It is a form of mucosal injury commonly seen in the stomach. Synonyms include superficial gastritis and acute gastric mucosal damage. Causative agents include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), alcohol, stress, and Helicobacter pylori infection. The condition typically affects the gastric antrum and body. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is often associated with conditions like peptic ulcer disease or critical illness. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy.

Helicobacter pylori associated gastric ulcer is a chronic condition characterized by the formation of ulcers in the stomach lining due to infection with *Helicobacter pylori*. This bacterium, a common gastric pathogen, causes inflammation and erosion of the mucosa, leading to ulceration. Common synonyms include *H. pylori* gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. The primary affected area is the gastric antrum, though ulcers may occur anywhere in the stomach. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and bloating. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopy and histopathological examination. Treatment involves eradication of the bacterium with antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors.

code_desc: Helicobacter pylori associated and drug-induced gastric ulcer
summary: Helicobacter pylori associated and drug-induced gastric ulcer refers to ulcers in the stomach lining caused by either infection with *Helicobacter pylori* or prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Common synonyms include *H. pylori*-related gastric ulcer and NSAID-induced gastric ulcer. The primary causative agent is *H. pylori*, a bacterium that colonizes the stomach. Drug-induced ulcers are typically caused by NSAIDs or corticosteroids. These ulcers most commonly affect the antrum and body of the stomach, leading to symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and bleeding.

Stress ulcer of the stomach, also known as stress-induced gastritis or stress-related mucosal damage, is an acute lesion of the gastric mucosa caused by severe physiological stress. Common causative agents include critical illness, major surgery, trauma, or burns. These ulcers typically occur in the gastric antrum and body, leading to bleeding or perforation. The condition is associated with impaired mucosal defense mechanisms and increased gastric acid secretion. It is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients. Synonyms include stress gastritis and stress ulceration.

Eosinophilic gastric ulcer is a rare inflammatory condition characterized by the presence of eosinophils in gastric ulcers, typically located in the antrum. It is often associated with systemic eosinophilic disorders or allergic reactions. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastritis and allergic gastric ulcer. Causative agents may include parasites such as *Strongyloides stercoralis*, food allergens, or medications. The stomach is the primary affected site, though involvement of the esophagus or duodenum may occur. Clinical features include abdominal pain, nausea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis requires endoscopic biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration. Treatment involves addressing underlying causes and managing symptoms.

Lymphocytic gastric ulcer is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of lymphocytes into the gastric mucosa, leading to ulceration. It is also known as lymphocytic gastritis. The exact cause is unclear, but it is associated with Helicobacter pylori infection in some cases. The condition primarily affects the stomach, particularly the antrum, and may present with symptoms such as dyspepsia. It is often linked to autoimmune processes and can coexist with other gastrointestinal disorders. The histopathological hallmark is a dense lymphocytic infiltration of the gastric mucosa without significant neutrophilic infiltration.

code_desc: Gastric ulcer due to external causes
summary: Gastric ulcer due to external causes refers to a break in the stomach lining resulting from external factors rather than peptic disease. Common synonyms include stress ulcer and traumatic gastritis. Causative agents often include severe trauma, burns, major surgery, or critical illness. These ulcers typically affect the stomach wall, particularly the antrum or body. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, bleeding, and perforation. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy, and management focuses on addressing the underlying cause and preventing complications.

Alcohol-induced gastric ulcer is a type of peptic ulcer caused by chronic or excessive alcohol consumption, which irritates and erodes the gastric mucosa. Common synonyms include alcohol-related gastric ulcer and ethanol-induced gastritis. The primary causative agent is ethanol, which disrupts the mucosal barrier and impairs protective mechanisms. This condition typically affects the stomach lining, particularly the antrum and body. It is often associated with other factors like NSAID use or H. pylori infection. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy.

Chemical gastric ulcer is a type of peptic ulcer caused by exposure to corrosive substances, such as strong acids or alkalis, which damage the gastric mucosa. Common synonyms include caustic gastritis or chemical injury of the stomach. Causative agents often include industrial chemicals, cleaning agents, or ingested substances like hydrochloric acid or lye. The condition typically affects the stomach lining, particularly the antrum and body, leading to inflammation, necrosis, and potential perforation if left untreated. It is often associated with accidental or intentional ingestion.

Drug-induced gastric ulcer is a condition characterized by the development of an ulcer in the stomach lining due to the prolonged or excessive use of certain medications. Common synonyms include medication-induced gastric ulcer and drug-related peptic ulcer. Causative agents often include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, and anticoagulants. The stomach is typically affected, with lesions occurring in the antrum or body. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and bleeding. Diagnosis is usually based on endoscopic findings and patient medication history.

Radiation gastric ulcer is a type of peptic ulcer that develops in the stomach following exposure to ionizing radiation, commonly during cancer radiotherapy. It results from radiation-induced damage to the gastric mucosa, leading to erosion and ulceration. Common synonyms include radiation-induced gastric ulcer and radiogenic gastric ulcer. The primary causative agent is ionizing radiation, particularly in the abdominal region. This condition typically affects the gastric antrum and body, and is often associated with other gastrointestinal complications such as strictures or perforation.

code_desc: Other specified gastric ulcer due to external causes
summary: "Other specified gastric ulcer due to external causes" refers to a gastric ulcer resulting from identifiable external factors not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include traumatic gastric ulcer or iatrogenic gastric ulcer. Causative agents may include physical trauma, foreign bodies, or medical procedures such as endoscopy. The stomach is the typically affected body part. This condition is characterized by mucosal damage in the gastric lining, often presenting with epigastric pain, bleeding, or perforation. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopic evaluation and histopathological analysis.

code_desc: Gastric ulcer due to external causes, unspecified
summary: Gastric ulcer due to external causes, unspecified refers to an ulceration of the stomach lining caused by an external factor, such as trauma, foreign bodies, or surgical injury, rather than by common pathogens like *Helicobacter pylori* or NSAIDs. This condition typically affects the stomach wall, particularly the antrum or body. Common synonyms include traumatic gastric ulcer or injury-related gastric ulcer. Causative agents are often non-specific, involving physical trauma or iatrogenic factors. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, bleeding, and perforation if left untreated.

Infectious secondary gastric ulcer is a type of gastric ulcer caused by infection, most commonly *Helicobacter pylori*, which leads to chronic gastritis and erosion of the gastric mucosa. Other causative agents may include certain viruses or bacteria. This condition typically affects the stomach, particularly the antrum, and can lead to complications such as bleeding or perforation. It is often associated with other gastrointestinal infections and may present with symptoms like epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Synonyms include *H. pylori-associated gastric ulcer* and *infectious gastritis with ulceration*.

Other specified gastric ulcer refers to a gastric ulcer that does not meet the criteria for a more specific subtype, such as benign or malignant. It is typically characterized by an erosion or defect in the gastric mucosa, often associated with chronic inflammation. Common synonyms include non-specific gastric ulcer or unspecified gastric ulcer. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and stress. The stomach is the primary affected body part, with lesions most commonly found in the antrum or body. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Gastric ulcer, unspecified, refers to a break in the stomach lining causing pain and potential bleeding. Common synonyms include peptic ulcer disease (PUD) when unspecified. Primary causative agents are Helicobacter pylori infection and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The stomach is the typically affected body part, though duodenal involvement may occur. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Complications such as perforation or hemorrhage may arise if untreated. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and testing for H. pylori. Treatment focuses on eradicating infection, reducing acid secretion, and protecting the gastric mucosa.

Peptic ulcer, site unspecified, refers to an ulceration in the lining of the gastrointestinal tract, typically occurring in the stomach or duodenum. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer and duodenal ulcer when the site is known. The primary causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori* infection, though nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are also a significant risk factor. The condition is characterized by chronic inflammation, erosion, and potential complications such as bleeding or perforation. It predominantly affects the stomach and duodenum, with symptoms including epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Anastomotic ulcer is a localized erosion that develops at the site of a surgical anastomosis, typically following gastrointestinal surgery. It is often associated with poor healing, ischemia, or infection. Common synonyms include postoperative ulcer and surgical ulcer. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori, NSAIDs, or bacterial infections. The condition most commonly affects the stomach, duodenum, or intestines, particularly after procedures such as gastric resection or colorectal surgery. Symptoms include pain, bleeding, and obstruction, requiring endoscopic or surgical intervention.

Anastomotic erosion refers to the breakdown of tissue at a surgical anastomosis, leading to leakage or fistula formation. It commonly occurs after gastrointestinal surgeries, such as esophagectomy or colorectal resection. Common synonyms include anastomotic leak and anastomotic fistula. Causative factors include infection, ischemia, technical errors, and poor tissue healing. The condition typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the stomach, intestines, and esophagus. It is a serious complication associated with high morbidity and mortality if not promptly managed.

Helicobacter pylori associated anastomotic ulcer is a type of peptic ulcer that develops at the site of a previous gastric or esophageal anastomosis, often following surgery. It is primarily caused by infection with *Helicobacter pylori*, a gram-negative bacterium. This condition is characterized by chronic inflammation and erosion of the mucosal lining at the anastomotic site. Common synonyms include post-surgical anastomotic ulcer and H. pylori-related anastomotic ulcer. The stomach and esophagus are the most commonly affected areas, with symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

Drug-induced anastomotic ulcer is a gastrointestinal condition characterized by the formation of an ulcer at the site of a surgically created anastomosis, often following procedures such as gastric bypass or resection. It is commonly associated with the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroids. Other causative agents may include anticoagulants and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). The stomach and small intestine are typically affected. Synonyms include postoperative anastomotic ulcer and NSAID-induced anastomotic ulcer. This condition can lead to complications such as bleeding or perforation.

Peptic anastomotic ulcer is a type of peptic ulcer that develops at the site of a surgical anastomosis, typically following gastric or esophageal surgery. It results from disrupted mucosal defense mechanisms and exposure to gastric acid and pepsin. Common synonyms include postoperative ulcer and surgical ulcer. Helicobacter pylori infection and prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are major causative agents. This condition most commonly affects the stomach or esophagus, particularly at the site of surgical reconstruction. It can lead to complications such as bleeding, perforation, and stricture.

Other specified anastomotic ulcer refers to a peptic ulcer that occurs at a surgical anastomosis, typically following gastrointestinal surgery. It is not classified under the more specific categories of gastric or duodenal ulcers. Common synonyms include postoperative anastomotic ulcer or surgical anastomotic ulcer. Causative agents may include Helicobacter pylori infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or acid hypersecretion. These ulcers most commonly affect the stomach or duodenum at sites of surgical reconstruction, such as after gastric bypass or resection.

Anastomotic ulcer, unspecified, refers to an ulcer that develops at the site of a surgical anastomosis, typically following gastrointestinal surgery. It is characterized by erosion of the mucosal layer, often leading to bleeding or perforation. Common synonyms include postoperative ulcer and surgical anastomotic ulcer. Causative agents include gastric acid, Helicobacter pylori, and mechanical stress. It most commonly affects the stomach, duodenum, or colon, depending on the surgical site. Risk factors include poor surgical technique, ischemia, and infection. Diagnosis is usually confirmed endoscopically.

Duodenal ulcer is a chronic condition characterized by the erosion of the duodenal mucosa, typically occurring in the first part of the duodenum. It is most commonly caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use. Other contributing factors include acid hypersecretion and genetic predisposition. Common synonyms include gastric ulcer and peptic ulcer. The primary affected area is the duodenum, with symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Complications may include bleeding, perforation, or obstruction.

Duodenal erosion refers to the superficial loss of the duodenal mucosa, often without full-thickness involvement. It is a common finding in patients with peptic disease. Common synonyms include duodenal ulcer and duodenal gastritis. Causative agents include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and excessive acid secretion. The primary affected area is the second portion of the duodenum. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via endoscopy.

Helicobacter pylori-associated duodenal ulcer is a chronic gastrointestinal condition characterized by the formation of ulcers in the duodenum, primarily due to infection with *Helicobacter pylori*. This bacterium colonizes the stomach and duodenum, leading to inflammation and erosion of the mucosal lining. Common synonyms include *H. pylori*-induced duodenal ulcer or pylori-related duodenal ulcer. The infection typically affects the stomach and duodenum, with ulcers most commonly occurring in the first part of the duodenum. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and bleeding. Diagnosis is often confirmed through endoscopy and microbiological testing.

code_desc: Helicobacter-pylori associated and drug-induced duodenal ulcer
summary: Helicobacter pylori-associated and drug-induced duodenal ulcer is a condition characterized by the development of ulcers in the duodenum, often due to infection with *Helicobacter pylori* or prolonged use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Common synonyms include *H. pylori* gastritis and NSAID-induced ulcer. The primary causative agent is *H. pylori*, a spiral-shaped bacterium that colonizes the stomach and duodenum. Drug-induced ulcers are typically caused by NSAIDs or corticosteroids. The condition predominantly affects the duodenum, with secondary involvement of the stomach. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and bleeding.

Stress ulcer of the duodenum refers to the development of mucosal breaks in the duodenum, often associated with severe systemic illness or critical illness. Common synonyms include stress gastritis and critical illness-related mucosal damage. Causative agents include sepsis, trauma, burns, and major surgery. These ulcers typically affect the proximal duodenum and are linked to impaired mucosal defense mechanisms. They may present with bleeding or perforation, requiring endoscopic evaluation and management.

Eosinophilic duodenal ulcer is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by the presence of eosinophils in the duodenal mucosa, leading to ulcer formation. It is often associated with parasitic infections, particularly *Strongyloides stercoralis*, or allergic reactions. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastritis and eosinophilic gastroenteritis. The duodenum is the primary affected site, though involvement may extend to the stomach and small intestine. Symptoms include abdominal pain, malabsorption, and weight loss. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopy and histopathological examination. Treatment focuses on eliminating the causative agent and managing inflammation.

code_desc: Duodenal ulcer due to external causes
summary: Duodenal ulcer due to external causes refers to an ulcer in the duodenum resulting from external factors rather than peptic mechanisms. Common synonyms include traumatic duodenal ulcer and iatrogenic duodenal ulcer. Causative agents may include foreign bodies, instrumentation, or surgical procedures. The primary affected body part is the duodenum, particularly the second portion. This condition is often associated with mechanical injury, chemical irritation, or iatrogenic trauma. Clinical presentation may include epigastric pain, nausea, and hematemesis. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via endoscopy. Treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause and managing complications.

Drug-induced duodenal ulcer is a condition characterized by the formation of ulcers in the duodenum caused by medications that impair gastric mucosal defense. Common causative agents include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroids. It is also known as NSAID-induced ulcer or corticosteroid-induced ulcer. The duodenum is typically affected, with symptoms such as epigastric pain, nausea, and bleeding. Prolonged use of these drugs disrupts the mucosal barrier, leading to erosion and ulceration.

Radiation duodenal ulcer is a rare complication arising from prolonged exposure to ionizing radiation, typically during radiotherapy for abdominal or pelvic malignancies. It results from damage to the duodenal mucosa due to radiation-induced ischemia and inflammation. Common synonyms include radiation-induced duodenal ulcer and radiogenic duodenal ulcer. The primary causative agent is ionizing radiation, often from external beam therapy. The duodenum, particularly the second and third segments, is most commonly affected. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and gastrointestinal bleeding. Diagnosis is often made through endoscopy and imaging studies.

Chemical duodenal ulcer is a type of peptic ulcer caused by corrosive agents rather than acid or pepsin. Common synonyms include corrosive ulcer and chemical gastritis. It results from ingestion of strong acids, alkalis, or other caustic substances. The duodenum is typically affected, with damage extending through the mucosal layers. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is often confirmed by endoscopy. Treatment involves neutralizing the chemical, managing complications, and preventing further injury. Long-term damage can lead to stricture or perforation.

code_desc: Duodenal ulcer due to other specified external causes
summary: Duodenal ulcer due to other specified external causes refers to a peptic ulcer located in the duodenum resulting from external factors not classified elsewhere, such as trauma, radiation, or foreign bodies. Common synonyms include traumatic duodenal ulcer and injury-induced duodenal ulcer. Causative agents may include physical trauma, iatrogenic injury, or exposure to corrosive substances. The primary affected body part is the duodenum, particularly the second or third portion. Symptoms often include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via endoscopy. Treatment involves addressing the underlying cause and managing symptoms with medications such as proton pump inhibitors.

code_desc: Duodenal ulcer due to external causes, unspecified
summary: Duodenal ulcer due to external causes, unspecified refers to an ulcer in the duodenum caused by an external factor, such as trauma, foreign bodies, or iatrogenic injury, rather than by Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs. Common synonyms include traumatic duodenal ulcer or iatrogenic duodenal ulcer. The primary causative agents are physical trauma, surgical procedures, or ingestion of corrosive substances. The condition typically affects the first part of the duodenum, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, bleeding, and obstruction. Diagnosis is often confirmed through endoscopy.

Infectious duodenal ulcer is a localized erosion in the duodenum caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Helicobacter pylori*. It may also result from nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use or other pathogens. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and bleeding. The duodenum is the primary affected site, with involvement of the first portion being most common. Synonyms include *H. pylori*-induced duodenal ulcer and gastric ulcer if the lesion extends into the stomach. Complications such as perforation or obstruction may occur.

Bacterial duodenal ulcer is a chronic condition characterized by the formation of ulcers in the duodenum, primarily caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection. It is a type of peptic ulcer disease, often associated with the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The infection leads to inflammation and erosion of the duodenal lining, resulting in pain, bleeding, and potential perforation. Common synonyms include *H. pylori-induced duodenal ulcer* and *peptic ulcer disease of the duodenum*. The primary affected area is the duodenum, particularly the first part, with secondary involvement of the stomach in some cases.

Viral duodenal ulcer is a rare condition characterized by the formation of ulcers in the duodenum caused by viral infections. Although traditionally associated with Helicobacter pylori and NSAID use, certain viruses such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) or herpes simplex virus (HSV) may contribute in immunocompromised individuals. The condition typically affects the duodenum, with symptoms including abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is less common than bacterial ulcers and often presents with atypical features. Diagnosis requires endoscopic evaluation and virological testing. Treatment involves antiviral therapy and management of underlying immune compromise.

Fungal duodenal ulcer is a rare condition characterized by the presence of fungal infection in the duodenum, leading to ulceration. It is uncommon compared to bacterial peptic ulcers and typically occurs in immunocompromised individuals. Common causative agents include *Candida* species, *Aspergillus*, and *Mucorales*. Synonyms include fungal duodenal infection or mycotic duodenal ulcer. The duodenum is the primary affected site, with symptoms resembling those of peptic ulcer disease, such as epigastric pain and bleeding. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic examination and histopathological analysis.

Parasitic duodenal ulcer is a rare condition characterized by ulceration of the duodenum caused by parasitic infection. Common synonyms include duodenal ulcer due to parasites or helminthic duodenal ulcer. The most frequently implicated causative agents are *Fasciola hepatica* and *Clonorchis sinensis*, though other parasites such as *Schistosoma* species may also be involved. These parasites typically affect the duodenum and upper gastrointestinal tract, leading to inflammation, erosion, and ulcer formation. Clinical presentation often includes abdominal pain, nausea, and weight loss. Diagnosis usually requires endoscopic evaluation and parasitological testing.

Infectious duodenal ulcer, unspecified, refers to an ulcer in the duodenum caused by an infectious agent. Common synonyms include duodenal ulcer with infectious etiology. The most frequent causative agent is *Helicobacter pylori*, though other pathogens such as *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, or *Campylobacter* may also be implicated. The primary affected body part is the duodenum, particularly the second part. Symptoms often include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopy and microbiological testing. Treatment focuses on eradicating the infectious agent and managing symptoms.

Other specified duodenal ulcer refers to a peptic ulcer located in the duodenum that does not meet the criteria for a more specific subtype, such as gastric or duodenal ulcer with complications. It is typically caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use. Common synonyms include unspecified duodenal ulcer or other duodenal ulcer. The primary affected area is the duodenum, particularly the first part. Symptoms may include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is confirmed via endoscopy.

Duodenal ulcer, unspecified, refers to an open sore in the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. It is typically caused by *Helicobacter pylori* infection or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use. Common synonyms include duodenal ulcer disease and gastric ulcer, though the latter may refer to gastric lesions. Symptoms often include epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. The duodenum is the primary affected area, with the second part being most commonly involved. Complications such as bleeding or perforation may occur if left untreated.

code_desc: Diseases of the stomach or the duodenum, unspecified
summary: Diseases of the stomach or the duodenum, unspecified refer to conditions affecting the upper gastrointestinal tract without specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, and duodenitis. Causative agents may include *Helicobacter pylori* infection, NSAID use, alcohol, and stress. These conditions typically affect the mucosal lining of the stomach and duodenum, leading to inflammation, erosion, or ulceration. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment varies depending on the underlying cause.

code_desc: Nonstructural developmental anomalies of small intestine
summary: Nonstructural developmental anomalies of the small intestine refer to congenital abnormalities in the structure or development of the small intestine without involvement of the muscular or neural layers. These anomalies may include malrotation, atresia, or intestinal duplication. Common synonyms include malformations of the small intestine and congenital intestinal defects. Causative agents may include genetic factors, maternal infections, or environmental exposures. These conditions typically affect the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, often leading to obstruction, bleeding, or malabsorption. Early diagnosis and surgical intervention are critical for optimal outcomes.

Syndromic diarrhoea is a rare genetic disorder characterized by chronic, watery diarrhea, facial dysmorphism, and other systemic features. It is typically caused by mutations in the TRPV6 gene, which encodes a calcium channel involved in intestinal absorption. Common synonyms include autosomal recessive diarrheal disorder and Malabsorption Syndrome with Diarrhea. The condition primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, leading to malabsorption and dehydration. It also involves craniofacial abnormalities, such as a broad nasal bridge and micrognathia, and may affect the skin and nails. Early diagnosis and supportive care are essential for managing symptoms and preventing complications.

Congenital intestinal transport defect refers to an inherited disorder affecting the absorption of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract. It is characterized by impaired transport of substances such as glucose, amino acids, and electrolytes across the intestinal epithelium. Common synonyms include congenital malabsorption syndrome and congenital intestinal dysabsorption. Causative agents often involve mutations in genes encoding transport proteins, such as SLC52A3 for riboflavin transporter. The small intestine is typically affected, leading to malnutrition, dehydration, and growth failure if untreated.

Congenital intestinal motility disorders are rare conditions characterized by impaired peristalsis in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to chronic constipation or intestinal obstruction. Common synonyms include congenital megacolon and Hirschsprung's disease. These disorders are often caused by aganglionosis, a deficiency of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, typically affecting the distal colon. Other causative agents may include genetic mutations, infections, or environmental factors. The primary affected body parts are the large intestine, with symptoms such as abdominal distension, vomiting, and failure to pass meconium. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications.

code_desc: Other specified nonstructural developmental anomalies of small intestine
summary: Other specified nonstructural developmental anomalies of small intestine refer to congenital abnormalities of the small intestine that do not involve structural malformations. These may include functional or developmental issues such as aganglionosis or impaired motility. Common synonyms include intestinal dysmotility or congenital intestinal hypotonia. Causative agents may include genetic mutations, maternal infections, or environmental factors. These anomalies typically affect the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, leading to symptoms like feeding intolerance, vomiting, and malabsorption.

code_desc: Nonstructural developmental anomalies of small intestine, unspecified
summary: Nonstructural developmental anomalies of small intestine, unspecified refer to congenital abnormalities of the small intestine that do not involve structural defects such as malrotation or atresia. These anomalies may include functional or morphological irregularities. Common synonyms include unspecified small intestinal developmental anomalies. Causative agents may include genetic factors, environmental exposures, or teratogens. Typically, the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum are affected. These conditions are often diagnosed prenatally or in early infancy and may present with gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting, feeding difficulties, or malabsorption.

Obstruction of the small intestine refers to a blockage that prevents the passage of intestinal contents, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, and distension. Common synonyms include intestinal obstruction and small bowel obstruction. Causative agents may include adhesions, hernias, tumors, foreign bodies, or inflammatory conditions. The jejunum and ileum are typically affected, with the ileum being most commonly involved. This condition can be partial or complete and may require surgical intervention if complications such as bowel ischemia or perforation occur.

Intussusception of the small intestine is a condition where a segment of the intestine telescopes into an adjacent segment, causing obstruction and potentially compromising blood supply. Common synonyms include ileoileal intussusception and intestinal invagination. It is often caused by lymphoid hyperplasia, Meckel's diverticulum, or tumors. The ileum is most frequently involved, though other parts of the small intestine may also be affected. Symptoms typically include abdominal pain, vomiting, and a palpable mass. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications such as bowel necrosis.

Volvulus of the small intestine is a medical emergency characterized by the twisting of a segment of the bowel upon itself, leading to intestinal obstruction and compromised blood supply. Common synonyms include intestinal volvulus and mesenteric torsion. It is often caused by anatomical abnormalities such as malrotation, which predisposes to twisting. The ileum is most commonly affected, though any segment of the small intestine may be involved. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and bowel obstruction. Prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention are critical to prevent bowel necrosis and perforation.

code_desc: Intestinal adhesions or bands of small intestine with obstruction
summary: Intestinal adhesions refer to abnormal bands of fibrous tissue that form between loops of the intestine or between the intestine and abdominal wall, potentially causing obstruction. Common synonyms include intestinal bands or adhesions. Causative agents often include prior abdominal surgery, infection, inflammation, or trauma. These adhesions most commonly affect the small intestine, particularly the ileum, and can lead to partial or complete bowel obstruction, resulting in symptoms such as abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation.

code_desc: Obstructive ileus of small intestine due to impaction
summary: Obstructive ileus of the small intestine due to impaction is a mechanical bowel obstruction caused by a physical blockage in the small intestine, preventing the passage of intestinal contents. Common synonyms include small bowel obstruction and intestinal impaction. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, foreign bodies, or fecal matter. The condition typically affects the jejunum or ileum, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. It requires prompt evaluation to prevent complications like bowel ischemia or perforation.

Gallstone ileus of the small intestine occurs when a gallstone obstructs the intestinal lumen, most commonly at the terminal ileum. It results from a perforation of the gallbladder, allowing the stone to pass into the biliary tree and subsequently into the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include "gallstone ileus" and "choledocholithiasis with intestinal obstruction." The primary causative agent is a gallstone, often associated with chronic cholecystitis. The condition typically affects the terminal ileum and is more common in elderly patients with a history of gallstones and biliary tract disease.

Enterolith of the small intestine is a rare condition characterized by the formation of a calcified mass within the intestinal lumen. Common synonyms include intestinal calculus and enteric stone. It is typically caused by chronic inflammation, bacterial overgrowth, and mineral deposition.
