The condition most commonly affects the ileum, though other segments of the small intestine may be involved. Clinical presentation often includes abdominal pain, obstruction, and secondary complications such as perforation or peritonitis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via imaging studies or endoscopy. Treatment typically involves surgical removal of the enterolith.

code_desc: Other specified obstructive ileus of small intestine due to impaction
summary: Other specified obstructive ileus of the small intestine due to impaction refers to a partial or complete blockage of the small bowel caused by a physical obstruction, typically from a foreign body, bezoar, or tumor. This condition leads to impaired intestinal motility and may result in symptoms such as abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Common synonyms include mechanical ileus and bowel obstruction. It most commonly affects the jejunum and ileum, with causative agents often involving ingested objects, dietary fiber accumulation, or neoplastic growths.

code_desc: Obstructive ileus of small intestine due to impaction, unspecified
summary: Obstructive ileus of the small intestine due to impaction, unspecified, refers to a mechanical blockage in the small bowel causing intestinal contents to back up. Common synonyms include small bowel obstruction and intestinal impaction. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, foreign bodies, or fecal matter. This condition typically affects the jejunum and ileum, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt evaluation and intervention to prevent complications like bowel ischemia or perforation.

code_desc: Other specified obstruction of small intestine
summary: "Other specified obstruction of small intestine" refers to mechanical blockage of the small bowel not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include ileus or intestinal obstruction. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, foreign bodies, or hernias. The ileum is most commonly affected, though any segment of the small intestine may be involved. Symptoms typically include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and absence of bowel movements. Diagnosis is often confirmed via imaging studies such as abdominal X-rays or CT scans. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications like bowel ischemia or perforation.

Obstruction of the small intestine, unspecified, refers to a blockage in any segment of the small bowel, preventing the passage of intestinal contents. Common synonyms include small bowel obstruction and intestinal obstruction. Causative agents may include adhesions, hernias, tumors, or foreign bodies. This condition typically affects the jejunum or ileum, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and constipation. It can result from inflammatory processes, post-surgical complications, or mechanical blockages. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications like bowel ischemia or perforation.

code_desc: Other acquired anatomical alterations of small intestine
summary: Other acquired anatomical alterations of small intestine refer to structural changes in the small intestine resulting from non-congenital causes. Common synonyms include acquired intestinal strictures and malformations. These alterations may arise from inflammatory processes, such as Crohn's disease, or from complications of surgery, infection, or radiation. Causative agents include pathogens like *Clostridioides difficile*, autoimmune conditions, and previous abdominal surgeries. The jejunum and ileum are typically affected, leading to symptoms such as obstruction, malabsorption, and chronic pain.

Fistula of the small intestine is an abnormal passage connecting the intestine to another organ or body surface. Common synonyms include enterocutaneous or enteroenteric fistula. It is often caused by infection, inflammation, or trauma, with Crohn’s disease being a major causative agent. Other causes include diverticulitis, surgery, or malignancy. The condition typically affects the ileum and may lead to complications such as infection, malnutrition, and fluid loss. It is more common in the ileocecal region and can result in chronic drainage and significant morbidity if untreated.

Pneumatosis intestinalis of the small intestine is a condition characterized by the presence of gas-filled cysts within the wall of the small bowel. Common synonyms include intestinal pneumatosis and colonic pneumatosis when involving the colon. It is often associated with underlying conditions such as bowel ischemia, inflammatory bowel disease, or mechanical obstruction. Causative agents may include infection, trauma, or iatrogenic causes. The small intestine, particularly the duodenum and jejunum, is typically affected, though it can occur in other gastrointestinal segments. The condition is often asymptomatic but may present with abdominal pain, distension, or bleeding.

code_desc: Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of small intestine
summary: "Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of small intestine" refers to structural changes in the small intestine not classified under other specific categories. Common synonyms include acquired intestinal deformities or structural abnormalities. Causative agents may include trauma, surgery, inflammatory conditions, or congenital anomalies that develop postnatally. These alterations typically affect the duodenum, jejunum, or ileum, leading to symptoms such as obstruction, malabsorption, or bleeding. The condition is often diagnosed through imaging or endoscopic evaluation.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of small intestine, unspecified
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of small intestine, unspecified refer to structural changes in the small intestine resulting from external factors rather than congenital causes. Common synonyms include acquired structural abnormalities and acquired intestinal deformities. These alterations may arise from inflammatory processes, trauma, surgical interventions, or malformations. Causative agents can include infections, chronic inflammation, or previous surgeries. The primary affected body parts are the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, with symptoms often involving malabsorption, obstruction, or altered motility.

Motility disorders of the small intestine refer to impaired movement of the bowel, leading to altered digestion and absorption. Common synonyms include intestinal dysmotility and small bowel dyskinesia. These disorders can result from neuromuscular dysfunction, hormonal imbalances, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents may include diabetes mellitus, scleroderma, infections, or medications like opioids. The primary affected body parts are the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Symptoms often include diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. Diagnosis typically involves imaging, manometry, and clinical evaluation.

Paralytic ileus is a condition characterized by the absence of peristalsis in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to bowel obstruction without mechanical blockage. Common synonyms include adhesive ileus and functional bowel obstruction. It is often caused by postoperative inflammation, electrolyte imbalances, infections, or medications such as opioids. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the large intestine may also be involved. Symptoms include abdominal distension, pain, nausea, and vomiting. It typically occurs after abdominal surgery or in critically ill patients. Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and imaging studies. Treatment involves bowel rest, intravenous fluids, and addressing underlying causes.

code_desc: Other specified motility disorders of small intestine
summary: Other specified motility disorders of small intestine refer to functional impairments of gastrointestinal motility that do not meet the criteria for more specific conditions like gastroparesis or intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Common synonyms include functional intestinal dysmotility and unspecified intestinal motility disorders. These conditions may result from neurological dysfunction, medications, or systemic illnesses. They typically affect the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as abdominal distension, pain, and altered bowel habits. Causes may include diabetes, autonomic neuropathy, or inflammatory bowel disease.

code_desc: Motility disorders of small intestine, unspecified
summary: Motility disorders of small intestine, unspecified, refer to impaired movement of the small bowel leading to altered digestion and absorption. Common synonyms include small intestinal dysmotility and post-infectious intestinal pseudo-obstruction. Causes may include neurological damage, diabetes mellitus, inflammatory bowel disease, or medications. These disorders primarily affect the small intestine, causing symptoms like abdominal pain, bloating, and malabsorption. The condition is often diagnosed when other specific motility disorders are excluded.

code_desc: Noninfectious enteritis or ulcer of small intestine
summary: Noninfectious enteritis or ulcer of the small intestine refers to inflammatory or ulcerative lesions in the small bowel not caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include nonspecific enteritis and small bowel ulceration. Causative agents may include medications (e.g., NSAIDs), autoimmune conditions (e.g., Crohn’s disease), ischemia, or radiation. The jejunum and ileum are typically affected. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment depends on underlying cause and may involve anti-inflammatory drugs, immunosuppressants, or dietary modifications.

Primary ulcer of the small intestine, also known as Crohn's disease ulceration or non-tuberculous intestinal ulcer, is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by transmural ulcers in the small bowel. It is most commonly associated with Crohn's disease, though it can occur independently. Causative agents include genetic predisposition, immune dysregulation, and environmental factors. The ileum is most frequently affected, with ulcers often presenting as linear or circumferential lesions. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Complications may involve strictures, fistulas, and malabsorption.

code_desc: Primary nonspecific ulceration of small intestine
summary: Primary nonspecific ulceration of the small intestine refers to chronic, non-specific inflammation and ulceration of the small bowel mucosa without a known specific etiology. Common synonyms include chronic nonspecific small intestinal ulceration and lymphocytic colitis-like enteropathy. The condition is often associated with autoimmune mechanisms and may involve the ileum and jejunum. Causative agents are not well defined, but immune-mediated processes, infections, and dietary factors may contribute. It is typically characterized by diffuse, shallow ulcers and is more common in middle-aged individuals.

code_desc: Chronic non-specific multiple ulcers of small intestine
summary: Chronic non-specific multiple ulcers of the small intestine refers to recurrent, non-infectious ulcers in the small bowel without a specific etiology. Common synonyms include chronic nonspecific ulcerative enteritis and chronic enteropathy. Causative agents are often unknown, though factors like ischemia, autoimmune processes, or chronic inflammation may contribute. The condition typically affects the duodenum and jejunum, with symptoms including abdominal pain, malabsorption, and weight loss. It is distinct from Crohn's disease and is often diagnosed through endoscopy and histopathology.

Cryptogenic multifocal ulcerous stenosing enteritis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by segmental, transmural inflammation and stricturing of the small intestine. Common synonyms include Crohn's disease and regional enteritis. The etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic, immune, and environmental factors, though no single causative agent is definitively identified. The condition primarily affects the terminal ileum but can involve any segment of the gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and intestinal obstruction. Complications may include fistulas, abscesses, and malabsorption.

code_desc: Other specified primary ulcer of small intestine
summary: "Other specified primary ulcer of small intestine" refers to ulcers in the small intestine that do not fit the criteria for more specific conditions like Crohn's disease or tuberculosis. Common synonyms include unspecified primary small intestinal ulcer. Causative agents may include NSAIDs, infections (e.g., *Helicobacter pylori*), or ischemia. Typically affects the duodenum and jejunum. Clinical presentation includes abdominal pain, bleeding, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is often made via endoscopy and biopsy. Management depends on underlying cause and may involve anti-inflammatory agents, antibiotics, or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Primary ulcer of small intestine, unspecified
summary: Primary ulcer of the small intestine, unspecified, refers to an ulcerative lesion in the small intestine without a known secondary cause such as infection or malignancy. Common synonyms include small intestinal ulcer and unspecified small bowel ulcer. Causative agents may include NSAIDs, Helicobacter pylori (though more commonly associated with gastric ulcers), ischemia, or idiopathic factors. The duodenum and jejunum are typically affected. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, bleeding, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is often confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic enteritis of small intestine
summary: Drug-induced or toxic enteritis of the small intestine is an inflammatory condition of the small bowel caused by exposure to certain medications or toxins. Common synonyms include drug-induced small bowel injury and toxic enteropathy. Causative agents include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), antibiotics like amoxicillin-clavulanate, and chemotherapy agents. The condition primarily affects the mucosal lining of the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. It is often reversible upon discontinuation of the offending agent.

code_desc: Allergic or dietetic enteritis of small intestine
summary: Allergic or dietetic enteritis of the small intestine is an inflammatory condition of the small intestine caused by hypersensitivity or intolerance to specific dietary components. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enteropathy and eosinophilic gastroenteritis. Causative agents often include cow's milk protein, gluten, or other dietary allergens. The condition primarily affects the mucosal lining of the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. It is more commonly seen in infants and young children but can occur in adults. Diagnosis typically involves endoscopy, biopsy, and dietary evaluation.

code_desc: IgE mediated allergic enteritis of small intestine
summary: IgE mediated allergic enteritis of the small intestine is a hypersensitivity disorder characterized by inflammation of the small bowel due to immune response against dietary antigens. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enteropathy and allergic gastroenteritis. Causative agents often include cow's milk, soy, wheat, and eggs. The condition primarily affects the mucosa of the small intestine, leading to malabsorption, diarrhea, and growth failure. It is most commonly seen in infants and young children.

Eosinophilic enteritis is an inflammatory condition characterized by the infiltration of eosinophils into the gastrointestinal tract. It is often associated with allergic reactions or parasitic infections. Common synonyms include eosinophilic gastroenteritis and eosinophilic colitis. Causative agents may include parasites such as *Strongyloides stercoralis*, helminths, or allergic responses to food. The condition typically affects the small intestine and colon, though involvement of the stomach and esophagus can occur. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Diagnosis is confirmed through endoscopic biopsy showing eosinophilic infiltration.

Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) is a delayed, non-IgE-mediated food allergy characterized by gastrointestinal symptoms. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enterocolitis and food protein-induced proctocolitis. Causative agents often include cow's milk, soy, rice, oats, and shellfish. The condition typically affects the small intestine and colon, leading to symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, and dehydration. It predominantly occurs in infancy and early childhood.

code_desc: Other specified allergic or dietetic enteritis of small intestine
summary: Other specified allergic or dietetic enteritis of small intestine refers to inflammatory conditions of the small intestine caused by allergic reactions or dietary intolerances not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include food allergy-induced enteritis and non-IgE-mediated enteropathy. Causative agents may include cow's milk, soy, eggs, or gluten, though diagnosis often requires exclusion of other known causes. The small intestine, particularly the duodenum and jejunum, is typically affected, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, malabsorption, and abdominal pain.

code_desc: Allergic or dietetic enteritis of small intestine, unspecified
summary: Allergic or dietetic enteritis of the small intestine refers to inflammation of the small intestine caused by an allergic reaction or dietary intolerance. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enteropathy and allergic gastroenteritis. Causative agents often include cow's milk protein, gluten, or other dietary allergens. The condition typically affects the duodenum and jejunum, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. It is most commonly seen in infants and young children but can occur in adults with underlying sensitivities. Diagnosis is often based on clinical presentation and response to dietary modifications.

code_desc: Enteritis or ulcer of small intestine due to other external causes
summary: Enteritis or ulcer of the small intestine due to other external causes refers to inflammation or ulceration of the small intestine resulting from factors other than infectious agents. Common synonyms include non-infectious enteritis and secondary small intestinal ulceration. Causative agents may include medications like NSAIDs, radiation therapy, or autoimmune conditions. The ileum is typically affected, with symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and biopsy, and management focuses on addressing the underlying cause and supportive care.

code_desc: Enteritis or ulcer of small intestine due to foreign body
summary: Enteritis or ulcer of the small intestine due to foreign body is an inflammatory or ulcerative condition caused by the ingestion of a foreign object that irritates or perforates the intestinal wall. Common synonyms include foreign body-induced enteritis and intestinal ulceration from ingestion. Causative agents are typically non-digestible objects such as batteries, coins, or sharp items. The condition primarily affects the small intestine, particularly the duodenum and jejunum. Symptoms include abdominal pain, vomiting, and bleeding. Diagnosis is often confirmed via imaging or endoscopy. Prompt removal of the foreign body is essential to prevent complications such as perforation or infection.

code_desc: Enteritis or ulcer of small intestine due to radiation
summary: Enteritis or ulcer of the small intestine due to radiation is a gastrointestinal condition caused by exposure to ionizing radiation, typically during cancer treatment. It results in inflammation and ulceration of the intestinal mucosa, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and malabsorption. Common synonyms include radiation enteritis and radiation-induced small bowel ulceration. The primary causative agent is ionizing radiation, often from external beam therapy. The small intestine, particularly the jejunum and ileum, is most commonly affected. This condition can develop weeks to months after radiation therapy.

code_desc: Enteritis or ulcer of small intestine due to trauma
summary: Enteritis or ulcer of the small intestine due to trauma refers to inflammation or ulceration of the small bowel resulting from physical injury. Common synonyms include traumatic enteritis and traumatic intestinal ulceration. Causative agents may include foreign bodies, surgical procedures, or blunt force trauma. The condition typically affects the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, bleeding, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy or imaging. Treatment involves addressing the underlying trauma and managing complications such as infection or perforation.

code_desc: Enteritis or ulcer of small intestine due to other external causes, unspecified
summary: Enteritis or ulcer of the small intestine due to other external causes, unspecified refers to inflammation or ulceration of the small intestine caused by external factors not specifically identified. Common synonyms include acute enteritis and small intestinal ulceration. Causative agents may include toxins, foreign bodies, or physical trauma. The condition typically affects the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is usually made through endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment focuses on removing the causative agent and managing symptoms.

code_desc: Other specified noninfectious enteritis or ulcer of small intestine
summary: Other specified noninfectious enteritis or ulcer of small intestine refers to inflammation or ulceration of the small intestine not caused by infectious agents, with a specific diagnosis not otherwise classified. Common synonyms include unspecified noninfectious enteritis or ulcer of the small intestine. Causative agents may include medications, autoimmune conditions, or ischemia. Typically affects the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is often made through endoscopy and biopsy.

code_desc: Noninfectious enteritis or ulcer of small intestine, unspecified
summary: Noninfectious enteritis or ulcer of small intestine, unspecified refers to inflammation or ulceration of the small intestine not caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include nonspecific enteritis and small bowel ulceration. Causative agents may include medications, autoimmune conditions, ischemia, or idiopathic factors. The condition typically affects the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy. Treatment depends on underlying cause and may involve dietary changes, anti-inflammatory drugs, or immunosuppression.

Coeliac disease is a chronic autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten ingestion in genetically susceptible individuals. It causes inflammation and damage to the small intestine's lining, impairing nutrient absorption. Common synonyms include celiac sprue and gluten-sensitive enteropathy. The primary causative agent is gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. The small intestine is the main affected body part, particularly the duodenum. Symptoms may include gastrointestinal distress, malnutrition, and systemic complications. Diagnosis typically involves serological testing and intestinal biopsy. Strict gluten-free diet is the mainstay of management.

Intestinal malabsorption or protein-losing enteropathy refers to impaired absorption of nutrients or proteins due to damage or dysfunction of the intestinal mucosa. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and enteropathy. Causative agents include infections (e.g., parasitic, bacterial), inflammatory conditions (e.g., Crohn's disease), celiac disease, and neoplasms. The primary affected body parts are the small intestine, particularly the jejunum and ileum, leading to systemic complications such as hypoalbuminemia and edema.

Intestinal malabsorption is a condition characterized by the impaired absorption of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to deficiency of essential nutrients. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and nutrient malabsorption. It can result from various causes such as celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, tropical sprue, and pancreatic insufficiency. The small intestine is typically affected, particularly the jejunum and ileum. Symptoms include diarrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins and proteins. Diagnosis often involves clinical evaluation, dietary history, and tests such as fecal fat analysis or intestinal biopsy.

Bacterial overgrowth syndrome (BOS) refers to an abnormal increase in the number of bacteria in a normally sterile environment, often in the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and intestinal dysbiosis. It is frequently caused by conditions that disrupt normal gut motility, such as diabetes mellitus, scleroderma, or prior abdominal surgery. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Bacteroides*, and *Clostridium* species. The small intestine is most commonly affected, leading to symptoms like bloating, diarrhea, and malabsorption.

Tropical sprue is a malabsorption syndrome primarily affecting the small intestine, particularly the jejunum. It is characterized by chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and deficiencies in vitamins and minerals. Common synonyms include tropical enteropathy and tropical malabsorption. The exact cause is often unknown, but it is associated with bacterial overgrowth, particularly *Campylobacter* and *Salmonella*, and may involve environmental factors. It is endemic in tropical regions and typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, leading to systemic symptoms due to nutrient deficiencies.

code_desc: Malabsorption or intolerance of specific nutrients
summary: Malabsorption or intolerance of specific nutrients refers to the impaired digestion or absorption of certain nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and nutrient intolerance. Causative agents may include celiac disease, lactose intolerance, pancreatic insufficiency, and infections such as giardiasis. The small intestine is typically affected, particularly the duodenum and jejunum, leading to deficiencies in fat, carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, or minerals. Symptoms may include diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies.

Short bowel syndrome (SBS) is a condition characterized by the malabsorption of nutrients due to extensive loss of small intestine. Common synonyms include short gut syndrome and post-operative short bowel syndrome. It is typically caused by surgical resection of a significant portion of the small bowel, often following trauma, necrotizing enterocolitis, or congenital malformations. The primary affected body parts are the jejunum and ileum, with complications including dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and nutritional deficiencies. Management involves enteral or parenteral nutrition, and in severe cases, intestinal transplantation may be required.

Intestinal failure is a condition characterized by the inability of the gastrointestinal tract to absorb sufficient nutrients, fluids, and electrolytes to maintain metabolic needs. Common synonyms include short bowel syndrome and prolonged intestinal failure. It is often caused by extensive small bowel resection, necrotizing enterocolitis, or chronic inflammation. The small intestine is typically affected, with the jejunum and ileum being the most commonly involved segments. Patients may require parenteral nutrition for survival. Complications include infections, metabolic imbalances, and liver dysfunction.

Other specified intestinal malabsorption refers to impaired absorption of nutrients in the small intestine due to unspecified or non-classifiable causes. Common synonyms include unspecified malabsorption syndrome and non-classifiable malabsorption. Causative agents may include chronic pancreatitis, celiac disease, or tropical sprue, though the exact cause is often unknown. The primary affected body part is the small intestine, particularly the jejunum and ileum. Symptoms typically include diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. This condition is diagnosed when other specific malabsorption disorders are excluded.

Intestinal malabsorption, unspecified, refers to impaired absorption of nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to deficiencies. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and defective nutrient uptake. Causative agents may include infections, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or surgical alterations. The small intestine is typically affected, with symptoms such as diarrhea, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. The condition may present with steatorrhea and electrolyte imbalances. Diagnosis often involves clinical evaluation and tests like stool analysis or imaging. Treatment focuses on addressing underlying causes and nutritional support.

Protein-losing enteropathy is a condition characterized by excessive loss of plasma proteins through the gastrointestinal tract, leading to hypoalbuminemia. Common synonyms include enteric protein loss and intestinal protein malabsorption. It is often caused by inflammatory bowel disease, lymphangiectasia, or infections such as parasitic infestations. The primary affected body parts are the small intestine, particularly the jejunum and ileum, where increased vascular permeability or lymphatic leakage occurs. This condition is commonly seen in dogs and cats, with clinical signs including edema, ascites, and weight loss.

code_desc: Other specified intestinal malabsorption or protein-losing enteropathy
summary: Other specified intestinal malabsorption or protein-losing enteropathy refers to a group of disorders characterized by impaired nutrient absorption or excessive protein loss through the gastrointestinal tract. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and protein-losing enteropathy. Causative agents may include infections, inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, and neoplasms. These conditions primarily affect the small intestine, leading to symptoms such as weight loss, diarrhea, and edema. The exact cause is often multifactorial, involving structural, functional, or inflammatory abnormalities in the intestinal mucosa.

code_desc: Intestinal malabsorption or protein-losing enteropathy, unspecified
summary: Intestinal malabsorption or protein-losing enteropathy refers to impaired absorption of nutrients or proteins through the gastrointestinal tract, leading to systemic deficiencies. Common synonyms include malabsorption syndrome and protein-losing enteropathy. Causes include celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, infections, and lymphatic disorders. The small intestine is typically affected, with symptoms such as diarrhea, weight loss, and edema. It may also result in hypoalbuminemia and increased risk of infections. The condition can be idiopathic or secondary to other gastrointestinal pathologies.

code_desc: Certain vascular disorders of small intestine
summary: Certain vascular disorders of the small intestine refer to conditions affecting blood flow to the small intestine, leading to ischemia or infarction. Common synonyms include intestinal ischemia and mesenteric vascular disease. Causative agents may include thrombosis, embolism, vasculitis, or hypoperfusion. These disorders typically affect the jejunum and ileum, with symptoms such as abdominal pain, bleeding, and bowel infarction. They can result from atherosclerosis, cardiac arrhythmias, or inflammatory conditions. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent severe complications like perforation or necrosis.

Angiodysplasia of the small intestine is a condition characterized by abnormal vascular malformations in the gastrointestinal tract, leading to recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include vascular malformations, telangiectases, and arteriovenous malformations. The exact cause is often unknown, though factors like chronic venous hypertension and aging may contribute. It typically affects the distal ileum and is more common in older adults. The lesions are fragile and prone to rupture, resulting in chronic blood loss and iron deficiency anemia.

Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) of the small intestine is an abnormal connection between arteries and veins, leading to increased blood flow and potential hemorrhage. Common synonyms include vascular malformation and hemangioma. Causative agents are often unknown, though some cases may be associated with hereditary conditions like hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. The small intestine, particularly the duodenum and jejunum, is typically affected. Symptoms may include gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging or endoscopy.

Vasculitis of mesenteric arteries is an inflammatory condition characterized by inflammation and necrosis of the arterial walls in the mesentery, leading to reduced blood flow and potential bowel ischemia. Common synonyms include mesenteric artery vasculitis and granulomatous mesenteric angiitis. Causative agents may include infectious organisms such as Bartonella, Mycobacterium, and Treponema, as well as autoimmune conditions like polyarteritis nodosa. The small and medium mesenteric arteries are typically affected, often presenting with abdominal pain, bowel infarction, and systemic symptoms.

Varices of the small intestine are abnormal dilations of veins, typically occurring in the distal ileum. They are most commonly associated with portal hypertension, often due to liver cirrhosis, leading to collateral circulation. Other causes include chronic intestinal inflammation, neoplasms, or congenital anomalies. These varices are prone to rupture, causing life-threatening hemorrhage. They are less frequently encountered than esophageal or gastric varices and may present with gastrointestinal bleeding, abdominal pain, or mass effect. Diagnosis is often made via endoscopy or imaging studies. Synonyms include intestinal varices or mesenteric varices.

code_desc: Certain vascular disorders of small intestine, unspecified
summary: Certain vascular disorders of small intestine, unspecified refer to conditions affecting the blood vessels of the small intestine without a specific diagnosis. These disorders may involve abnormal blood flow, vessel wall changes, or thrombosis. Common synonyms include small intestinal vasculopathy and unspecified intestinal ischemia. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, vasculitis, or hypercoagulable states. Typically, the duodenum and jejunum are affected, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, bleeding, and malabsorption. The condition is often diagnosed through endoscopy and angiography.

Polyps of the small intestine are abnormal growths that protrude from the mucosal surface of the intestinal lining. Common synonyms include intestinal hamartomas and juvenile polyps. These lesions are typically benign but can occasionally be malignant. Known causative agents include genetic syndromes such as familial adenomatous polyposis and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, as well as inflammatory conditions. They most commonly affect the ileum, though they may occur throughout the small intestine. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, bleeding, and intussusception. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through endoscopy and biopsy.

Hamartoma of the small intestine is a benign tumor composed of abnormal proliferation of pancreatic and intestinal tissue. It is also known as intestinal hamartoma or gastrointestinal hamartoma. The condition is often associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, a genetic disorder characterized by hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract. These lesions typically occur in the jejunum and ileum, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, bleeding, and intestinal obstruction. They are not caused by infectious agents but are linked to mutations in the STK11 gene. Hamartomas are generally asymptomatic but can lead to complications if they grow large or obstruct the bowel.

Hyperplastic polyp of the small intestine is a benign lesion characterized by abnormal proliferation of mucosal glands. Common synonyms include hyperplastic polyps and hamartomatous polyps. These polyps are typically associated with chronic inflammation, particularly in the setting of celiac disease, and are caused by persistent exposure to inflammatory mediators. They most commonly occur in the ileum and are often found in patients with familial adenomatous polyposis or other hereditary syndromes. While generally asymptomatic, they may cause bleeding or obstruction.

code_desc: Inflammatory fibroid polyp of small intestine
summary: Inflammatory fibroid polyp of the small intestine is a benign lesion characterized by fibrous tissue with inflammatory changes, often associated with chronic irritation or inflammation. Common synonyms include inflammatory fibrous polyp and fibrous hamartoma. It is typically caused by long-standing inflammatory conditions such as Crohn's disease or infections. The polyp most commonly affects the ileum, though it can occur in other parts of the small intestine. Clinically, it presents with symptoms like abdominal pain, bleeding, and obstruction. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy and histopathological examination.

Lymphoid hyperplasia of the small intestine is a condition characterized by the proliferation of lymphoid tissue within the intestinal wall, commonly observed in the duodenum and jejunum. It is often associated with chronic inflammation, infections, or immune responses. Common synonyms include lymphoid hyperplasia of the gastrointestinal tract and reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. Causative agents may include parasitic infections, such as *Strongyloides stercoralis*, or autoimmune conditions. The primary affected areas are the small intestine, particularly the proximal segments. This condition is typically benign but can mimic malignancy on histopathological examination.

code_desc: Other specified polyps of small intestine
summary: "Other specified polyps of small intestine" refers to benign growths in the small intestine that do not fit into more specific categories such as adenomatous or hyperplastic polyps. Common synonyms include unspecified small intestinal polyps. These polyps may arise from mucosal hyperplasia or inflammatory processes. Known causes include chronic inflammation, genetic syndromes, and idiopathic factors. They typically affect the duodenum and jejunum, and are often asymptomatic, discovered incidentally during endoscopy.

Polyps of the small intestine, unspecified, refer to abnormal growths arising from the mucosal lining of the small intestine, typically benign. These lesions are often asymptomatic but may cause bleeding, obstruction, or intussusception. Common synonyms include small intestinal hamartomas and juvenile polyps. Causative agents are largely unknown, though genetic syndromes like Peutz-Jeghers or familial adenomatous polyposis may contribute. They most commonly affect the duodenum and jejunum, with a predilection for the proximal small bowel. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via endoscopy and biopsy.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of small intestine
summary: "Other specified diseases of small intestine" refers to conditions affecting the small intestine that do not fit into more specific classifications. Common synonyms include unspecified small intestinal diseases. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune processes, or idiopathic factors. These conditions typically affect the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, leading to symptoms such as malabsorption, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy.

Diseases of small intestine, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the small intestine without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include nonspecific small intestinal disease and undiagnosed small bowel pathology. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune disorders, or inflammatory processes. Typically, the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum are affected. Symptoms often involve malabsorption, diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis may require endoscopy, imaging, or biopsy. Management depends on underlying cause and may involve dietary changes, medications, or surgery.

Appendicitis is an inflammation of the appendix, a small tube attached to the large intestine. It typically presents with abdominal pain starting around the navel and migrating to the lower right quadrant, accompanied by fever, nausea, and loss of appetite. Common synonyms include acute appendicitis and appendicular inflammation. The condition is most commonly caused by obstruction of the appendix, often due to fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign bodies. It primarily affects the appendix and surrounding tissues in the right lower abdomen. If untreated, it can lead to perforation and peritonitis.

Acute appendicitis is an inflammation of the appendix, typically caused by obstruction leading to bacterial infection. Common synonyms include acute appendicitis and appendicitis. The condition is most commonly caused by fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign bodies. It primarily affects the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, with the appendix being the main affected organ. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and vomiting. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation and imaging. Prompt surgical removal (appendectomy) is the standard treatment to prevent perforation and complications.

Acute appendicitis with generalized peritonitis is a severe complication of appendicitis where the inflamed appendix ruptures, leading to widespread infection of the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include perforated appendicitis and secondary peritonitis. The causative agent is typically *Escherichia coli* or other gastrointestinal pathogens. The condition primarily affects the abdomen, with inflammation spreading to the peritoneum. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and guarding. It is most common in young adults and requires urgent surgical intervention to prevent sepsis and mortality.

Acute appendicitis with localised peritonitis is an inflammation of the appendix accompanied by localized peritoneal irritation. It typically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and fever. Common synonyms include acute appendicitis with peritonitis. The primary causative agent is usually *Escherichia coli*, though other bacteria may be involved. The condition primarily affects the appendix and surrounding peritoneum, often leading to complications such as abscess formation if untreated. It predominantly occurs in young adults.

code_desc: Acute appendicitis without localised or generalised peritonitis
summary: Acute appendicitis without localised or generalised peritonitis refers to inflammation of the appendix without evidence of perforation or spread of infection to the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include simple appendicitis or uncomplicated appendicitis. The condition is typically caused by obstruction of the appendix, often due to fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign bodies. It predominantly affects the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. Symptoms include epigastric or periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, nausea, anorexia, and fever. Diagnosis is primarily clinical with supportive imaging.

Chronic appendicitis is a prolonged inflammatory condition of the appendix, often presenting with intermittent right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Unlike acute appendicitis, it lacks a clear onset and may be mistaken for other gastrointestinal disorders. Common synonyms include persistent or recurrent appendicitis. The condition is typically caused by partial obstruction of the appendix, often due to fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign bodies. It primarily affects the appendix and surrounding tissues, with potential involvement of the cecum and terminal ileum. Diagnosis can be challenging due to nonspecific symptoms and variable imaging findings.

Other specified appendicitis refers to appendicitis that does not meet the criteria for acute or chronic appendicitis but is still clinically significant. It may present with atypical symptoms or imaging findings. Common synonyms include atypical appendicitis or non-specific appendicitis. Causative agents are typically bacterial, with *Escherichia coli* and *Bacteroides* species being common. The condition primarily affects the appendix, with inflammation extending to surrounding structures if untreated. It most commonly occurs in adolescents and young adults.

Appendicitis, unspecified refers to inflammation of the appendix without specific localization or etiology. It is typically caused by obstruction of the appendix lumen, often due to fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign bodies. Common synonyms include acute appendicitis and simple appendicitis. The condition primarily affects the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, involving the cecum and surrounding structures. Complications such as perforation or abscess formation may occur if untreated. It is most common in individuals aged 10 to 30 years.

Certain specified diseases of the appendix refer to conditions primarily affecting the vermiform appendix, most commonly appendicitis. This acute inflammation is typically caused by obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, often due to fecaliths, lymphoid hyperplasia, or foreign bodies. Other less common causes include tumors or infections. The condition predominantly affects the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. Synonyms include acute appendicitis and appendicular inflammation. Complications such as perforation, abscess formation, or peritonitis may occur if untreated.

Megaloappendix is a rare condition characterized by an enlarged, often inflamed appendix, typically due to chronic infection or obstruction. It is also known as appendicitis with megacolon or giant appendicitis. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Salmonella*, and *Shigella* species. The condition primarily affects the appendix, but may involve adjacent structures such as the cecum and terminal ileum. It is more commonly seen in children and immunocompromised individuals. Diagnosis often requires imaging and histopathological evaluation to differentiate from other inflammatory conditions.

Hyperplasia of the appendix refers to abnormal growth and enlargement of the appendix, often leading to increased size and potential dysfunction. It is a rare condition, sometimes associated with chronic inflammation or infection. Common synonyms include appendiceal hypertrophy and appendicular hyperplasia. While the exact cause is not well understood, it may be linked to inflammatory processes or genetic factors. The appendix is the primary affected organ, and the condition may present with symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits. It is typically diagnosed through imaging studies or histopathological examination.

Appendicular concretions refer to solid masses formed within the appendages of the body, most commonly in the urinary system. These concretions, also known as calculi or stones, are typically composed of minerals such as calcium oxalate or urate. They most frequently occur in the kidneys and bladder, but can also form in the gallbladder, pancreas, and other organs. Common causative agents include dehydration, dietary factors, metabolic disorders, and urinary stasis. These concretions can cause obstruction, infection, and pain, necessitating medical intervention for removal or dissolution.

Diverticulum of appendix, acquired, refers to the formation of small pouches or sacculations in the wall of the appendix, typically due to increased intraluminal pressure. It is a rare condition, often associated with chronic appendicitis or inflammatory bowel disease. Common synonyms include appendiceal diverticula and acquired appendiceal diverticulum. The primary causative agent is chronic inflammation leading to weakening of the appendix wall. It most commonly affects the distal portion of the appendix and is usually asymptomatic, though it may complicate with infection or perforation.

Fistula of the appendix, also known as appendiceal fistula or appendicofestinal fistula, is an abnormal passage connecting the appendix to another organ, most commonly the cecum or colon. It typically results from chronic appendicitis leading to necrosis and subsequent tract formation. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Bacteroides*, and *Klebsiella* species. This condition predominantly affects the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, often presenting with recurrent abdominal pain and bowel dysfunction. It is more frequently observed in individuals with a history of appendicitis or inflammatory bowel disease.

Intussusception of the appendix is a rare condition where a segment of the appendix telescopes into itself, leading to obstruction and potential ischemia. It is a variant of intestinal intussusception, typically affecting children. Common synonyms include appendiceal intussusception and self-intussusception. The exact cause is often idiopathic, though it may be associated with lymphoid hyperplasia or previous appendicitis. The appendix is the most commonly involved segment, and the condition can lead to perforation if not promptly treated.

Mucocele of the appendix is a rare, benign cystic lesion formed due to obstruction of the appendiceal lumen, leading to distention and accumulation of mucus. It is also known as appendiceal mucocele or mucinous cystadenoma. The condition is typically caused by obstruction from fecaliths, tumors, or inflammatory processes. It most commonly affects the appendix, though it may involve other gastrointestinal structures. Clinically, it may present with abdominal pain, distension, or no symptoms. Diagnosis is usually made via imaging studies such as CT or ultrasound. Surgical excision is the primary treatment.

"Other specified diseases of appendix" refers to appendiceal conditions not classified under more specific categories such as appendicitis or appendicular abscess. Common synonyms include appendiceal disorders of unspecified type. Causative agents may include bacterial infections like *Escherichia coli* or *Salmonella*, though etiology is often unclear. The appendix is the primary affected body part, with symptoms typically involving abdominal pain, inflammation, and possible perforation. This category encompasses rare or unspecified appendiceal pathologies.

Diseases of the appendix, unspecified, refer to inflammatory or infectious conditions affecting the appendix without specific identification of the underlying pathology. Common synonyms include appendicitis and appendicular disease. Causative agents often involve bacterial infections such as *Escherichia coli*, *Streptococcus*, and *Salmonella*. The appendix is the primary affected body part, typically located in the lower right quadrant of the abdomen. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, and nausea. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through clinical evaluation and imaging. Treatment typically involves surgical removal of the appendix (appendectomy).

Obstruction of the large intestine, also known as bowel obstruction or colonic obstruction, is a blockage that prevents the passage of fecal matter through the colon. Common causes include adhesions, tumors, diverticulitis, and hernias. It typically affects the sigmoid colon or rectum. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. If left untreated, it can lead to bowel ischemia and perforation. Diagnosis is often made through imaging studies such as abdominal X-rays or CT scans. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications.

Intussusception of the large intestine is a condition where a segment of the bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, causing obstruction. Common synonyms include ileo-colic intussusception and intestinal invagination. It is most commonly seen in infants and young children, though it can occur in adults. Causative factors include lymphoid hyperplasia, tumors, or Meckel's diverticulum. The condition typically affects the cecum and ascending colon, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, and bloody stools. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications like bowel necrosis.

Volvulus of the large intestine is a condition in which a loop of the bowel twists upon itself, leading to intestinal obstruction and potential ischemia. Common synonyms include intestinal volvulus and sigmoid volvulus. It is most frequently caused by adhesions, congenital malformations, or anatomical abnormalities. The sigmoid colon is the most commonly affected segment, followed by the cecum. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent bowel necrosis and perforation.

code_desc: Adhesions of large intestine with obstruction
summary: Adhesions of the large intestine with obstruction refer to the formation of fibrous bands between abdominal organs, leading to bowel blockage. Common synonyms include intestinal adhesion syndrome and bowel obstruction due to adhesions. Causative agents often include prior abdominal surgeries, infections, or inflammatory conditions like diverticulitis. The large intestine, particularly the cecum, ascending colon, and sigmoid colon, is typically affected. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and constipation. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies such as CT scan or barium enema. Treatment may involve conservative management or surgical intervention depending on severity.

Impaction of the large intestine refers to the mechanical obstruction of the colon, typically due to the accumulation of hardened stool. Common synonyms include fecal impaction and colonic obstruction. Causative agents include chronic constipation, dehydration, medications, and neurologic disorders. The condition predominantly affects the sigmoid colon and rectum. It is more common in elderly individuals, infants, and those with mobility or neurological impairments. Symptoms include abdominal distension, pain, nausea, and fecal incontinence. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as bowel perforation or sepsis.

Stenosis of the rectum refers to the narrowing of the rectal lumen, leading to difficulty in passing stool. Common synonyms include rectal stricture and rectal outlet obstruction. It is often caused by chronic inflammation, such as from ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, or by radiation therapy. Less commonly, it may result from trauma, tumors, or congenital abnormalities. The condition primarily affects the rectum, with symptoms including constipation, tenesmus, and fecal impaction. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through endoscopic and imaging studies. Treatment may involve dilation, surgery, or management of underlying conditions.

code_desc: Other specified obstruction of large intestine
summary: "Other specified obstruction of large intestine" refers to mechanical blockage of the large bowel not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include large bowel obstruction with unspecified cause. Causative agents may include adhesions, tumors, strictures, or fecal impaction. The condition typically affects the colon, particularly the transverse or sigmoid segments. Symptoms include abdominal pain, distension, constipation, and vomiting. It is often diagnosed via imaging and may require surgical intervention if complications arise.

Obstruction of the large intestine, unspecified, refers to a blockage in any portion of the colon or rectum that prevents the normal passage of fecal matter. Common synonyms include colonic obstruction and megacolon. Causative agents may include tumors, strictures, adhesions, diverticular disease, or fecal impaction. The condition typically affects the colon, with the sigmoid and rectal regions being most commonly involved. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, distension, constipation, and vomiting. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies such as X-ray or CT scan. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications like bowel perforation or sepsis.

code_desc: Other acquired anatomical alterations of large intestine
summary: "Other acquired anatomical alterations of large intestine" refers to structural changes in the colon not classified as tumors, inflammatory bowel disease, or congenital anomalies. Common synonyms include acquired colonic deformities or structural abnormalities. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, strictures, adhesions, or prior surgeries. These alterations typically affect the colon, particularly the sigmoid and rectal regions, leading to symptoms like obstruction, altered bowel habits, or pain. They are often diagnosed through imaging or endoscopic evaluation.

Fistula of the large intestine, also known as enterocutaneous or enterovesical fistula, is an abnormal connection between the colon and another body structure, such as the skin or bladder. Common causes include inflammatory bowel disease, infection, trauma, or surgery. It typically affects the sigmoid colon or rectum. Symptoms may include drainage, infection, and altered bowel habits. Diagnosis is often confirmed with imaging studies or endoscopy. Treatment involves addressing the underlying cause and may require surgical intervention.

Pneumatosis intestinalis of the large intestine refers to the presence of gas within the bowel wall, typically appearing as cystic or saccular structures. Common synonyms include intestinal pneumatosis and colonic pneumatosis. It is often associated with conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sepsis, and inflammatory bowel disease. Causative agents may include gas-forming bacteria, mechanical obstruction, or impaired venous return. The large intestine, particularly the sigmoid and rectum, is most commonly affected. It is often asymptomatic but can present with abdominal pain, distension, or bowel obstruction in severe cases.

Rectal prolapse is a condition in which the rectum protrudes through the anus, often appearing as a red, swollen mass. It commonly occurs in elderly individuals and those with chronic constipation or diarrhea. Synonyms include rectal eversion and rectal protrusion. Causative factors include chronic straining, pelvic floor weakness, and neurogenic disorders. The condition primarily affects the rectum and anus, with complications such as bleeding, infection, and obstruction. It is more prevalent in females and may be associated with other pelvic organ prolapses.

code_desc: Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of large intestine
summary: "Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of large intestine" refers to structural changes in the large intestine not classified under other specific conditions. Common synonyms include acquired colonic deformities or structural abnormalities. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, strictures, or surgical interventions. These alterations typically affect the colon, rectum, and associated mesenteric structures. Symptoms may include altered bowel habits, pain, or obstruction. Diagnosis often involves imaging or endoscopic evaluation. The condition is usually secondary to underlying disease processes or prior surgical procedures.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of large intestine, unspecified
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the large intestine, unspecified, refer to structural changes in the colon or rectum resulting from disease or injury. Common synonyms include colonic deformities or structural abnormalities of the large bowel. Causative agents may include inflammatory conditions like Crohn's disease, infections, trauma, or neoplasms. These alterations typically affect the colon, rectum, and associated mesenteric structures, leading to complications such as obstruction, perforation, or altered bowel function. The condition is often diagnosed through imaging or endoscopic evaluation.

Motility disorders of the large intestine refer to impaired movement of the colon, leading to altered bowel habits. Common synonyms include chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction and slow transit constipation. These conditions may result from neuromuscular dysfunction, autonomic neuropathy, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents include diabetes mellitus, scleroderma, and certain medications. Typically affecting the colon and rectum, symptoms include constipation, abdominal distension, and fecal incontinence. Diagnosis often involves imaging and manometry. Treatment focuses on dietary management, medications, and in severe cases, surgical intervention.

Pseudo-obstruction of the colon, also known as colonic pseudo-obstruction or Ogilvie syndrome, is a condition characterized by the dilation of the colon without an obstructing physical mass. It is often associated with underlying systemic illness, electrolyte imbalances, or medications. Common causative agents include sepsis, electrolyte disturbances, and certain drugs like opioids or anticholinergics. The condition typically affects the transverse and sigmoid colon, leading to symptoms such as abdominal distension, pain, and constipation. It can progress to bowel ischemia if left untreated.

Slow transit constipation is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by delayed colonic transit, leading to infrequent, hard, and painful bowel movements. Common synonyms include colonic inertia and delayed gastric emptying. It is often caused by altered colonic motility, neurological dysfunction, or hormonal imbalances. The primary affected body part is the colon, with symptoms including abdominal distension, bloating, and fecal impaction. It may occur in isolation or as part of a broader syndrome such as Hirschsprung’s disease or systemic conditions like hypothyroidism. Diagnosis typically involves colonic transit studies and anorectal manometry.

Megacolon is an abnormal dilation of the colon, characterized by impaired peristalsis and accumulation of fecal matter. It can be congenital or acquired. Common synonyms include hypertrophic or toxic megacolon. Causative agents include Hirschsprung’s disease, chronic constipation, infections, and neuromuscular disorders. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the descending and sigmoid colon. Symptoms include abdominal distension, pain, and constipation. Severe cases may lead to bowel obstruction or perforation. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via imaging studies such as barium enema or CT scan. Treatment involves medical management and, in some cases, surgical intervention.

Toxic megacolon is a severe complication characterized by dilatation of the colon accompanied by systemic toxicity. It typically affects the large intestine, particularly the sigmoid colon. Common causes include inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, as well as infections like Clostridium difficile, and less commonly, ischemia or medications like anticholinergics. Synonyms include acute colonic pseudo-obstruction and toxic dilatation of the colon. Symptoms include abdominal distension, pain, fever, and systemic signs of sepsis. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent perforation and mortality.

Other specified megacolon refers to a rare, acquired form of megacolon not classified as Hirschsprung's disease or toxic megacolon. It is characterized by chronic dilation of the colon due to impaired peristalsis. Common synonyms include idiopathic megacolon and chronic megacolon. Causative agents may include neurodegenerative disorders, medications, or chronic constipation. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the sigmoid and rectosigmoid regions. Symptoms include abdominal distension, constipation, and fecal incontinence. Diagnosis is typically made via imaging and exclusion of other causes. Treatment focuses on bowel management and addressing underlying conditions.

Megacolon, unspecified, refers to an abnormal dilation of the colon characterized by impaired peristalsis and fecal retention. It may result from congenital or acquired causes, including Hirschsprung's disease, chronic constipation, or neuromuscular disorders. Common synonyms include dilated colon and mega colon. The primary affected body part is the colon, with possible involvement of the rectum. Causative agents vary but may include genetic factors, neurologic conditions, or structural abnormalities. The condition often presents with symptoms such as abdominal distension, constipation, and fecal incontinence.

Acquired hypoganglionosis of the large intestine is a rare condition characterized by the loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus of the colon, leading to impaired neuromuscular function and bowel motility disorders. Common synonyms include aganglionosis and neuronal degeneration of the colon. It is often associated with chronic inflammatory conditions, infections, or neurodegenerative diseases. The primary affected body part is the large intestine, particularly the colon. Causative agents may include chronic infections like typhoid fever, autoimmune disorders, or prolonged use of neurotoxic medications. The condition typically presents with chronic constipation, bowel obstruction, and altered bowel habits.

code_desc: Other specified motility disorders of large intestine
summary: Other specified motility disorders of the large intestine refer to functional impairments of bowel movement that do not fit the criteria for more specific conditions like irritable bowel syndrome or chronic idiopathic constipation. Common synonyms include functional dysmotility and slow transit constipation. These disorders are often idiopathic but may be associated with neurological conditions, medications, or hormonal imbalances. They primarily affect the colon, leading to symptoms such as constipation, abdominal distension, and altered bowel habits. The exact pathophysiology is not fully understood, but impaired neuromuscular coordination is a common feature.

code_desc: Motility disorders of large intestine, unspecified
summary: Motility disorders of the large intestine, unspecified, refer to impaired movement of the colon leading to altered bowel function. Common synonyms include chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction and dysmotility. These conditions may result from neurological, muscular, or structural abnormalities. Causative agents include diabetes mellitus, Parkinson’s disease, and certain medications. The primary affected body part is the large intestine, with symptoms such as constipation, diarrhea, or alternating bowel habits. Diagnosis often involves imaging and motility studies. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and addressing underlying causes.

Certain noninfectious colitis or proctitis refers to inflammatory conditions of the colon or rectum not caused by infectious agents. Common synonyms include ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, and ischemic colitis. Causative agents may include immune-mediated processes, ischemia, or medications. Typically affecting the large intestine, these conditions often involve the rectum and may extend proximally. Symptoms include diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and abdominal pain. Diagnosis involves endoscopy and histopathological evaluation. Management varies from anti-inflammatory drugs to immunosuppression, depending on the underlying cause.

Primary ulcer of the colon, also known as acute colitis or ulcerative colitis, is an inflammatory condition characterized by diffuse ulceration of the colonic mucosa. It is typically associated with infectious agents such as *Shigella*, *Salmonella*, *Campylobacter*, and *Entamoeba histolytica*. The disease primarily affects the large intestine, with inflammation and ulceration most commonly seen in the rectum and sigmoid colon. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding. It is distinct from secondary ulcers caused by other conditions like ischemia or cancer.

Microscopic colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease characterized by chronic, watery diarrhea without visible mucosal inflammation on endoscopy. It encompasses two subtypes: collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis. Common synonyms include collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis. The condition is associated with autoimmune mechanisms and may be linked to medications like NSAIDs or antibiotics. It primarily affects the colon, with inflammation evident only under high-power microscopy. The small intestine is rarely involved.

Collagenous colitis is a chronic, inflammatory condition of the large intestine characterized by a thickened subepithelial collagen layer in the colon. It is a form of microscopic colitis, often presenting with chronic, non-bloody diarrhea. Common synonyms include collagenous colitis and collagenous colitis. The exact cause is unknown, though it may be associated with medications like nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and autoimmune factors. The primary affected body part is the colon, particularly the ascending colon. It predominantly affects middle-aged to elderly individuals, with a female predominance.

Lymphocytic colitis is a type of microscopic colitis characterized by chronic, non-bloody diarrhea. It is marked by an increased number of lymphocytes in the colon's mucosa. Common synonyms include collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis. The exact cause is unknown, though infections, medications, and autoimmune factors may contribute. It primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the colon. The condition is more common in middle-aged and elderly individuals, with a slight female predominance. Symptoms include frequent, watery stools and abdominal discomfort. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through colonoscopy and histopathological examination.

Other specified microscopic colitis refers to inflammatory conditions of the colon that do not meet the full criteria for collagenous colitis or lymphocytic colitis. It is characterized by chronic, non-specific inflammation with minimal histological changes. Common synonyms include unspecified microscopic colitis. Causative agents are largely unknown, though infections, medications, and autoimmune factors may contribute. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the colon, and is more common in older adults. Symptoms include chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss.

Microscopic colitis, unspecified, is a chronic inflammatory condition of the colon characterized by normal histology on gross examination but subepithelial inflammation visible only under high magnification. Common synonyms include collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis. The exact causative agents are unknown, though infections, medications, and autoimmune factors may contribute. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, causing chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. It predominantly occurs in middle-aged to older adults.

Allergic or dietetic colitis refers to inflammation of the colon caused by an allergic reaction or adverse dietary intake. It is often seen in infants and young children. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome and allergic colitis. Causative agents typically include cow's milk protein, soy, and other dietary allergens. The condition primarily affects the colon, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, blood in stool, and abdominal distension. It is usually diagnosed through clinical evaluation and dietary exclusion.

code_desc: Food protein-induced proctitis or colitis of infants
summary: Food protein-induced proctitis or colitis of infants is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by inflammation of the rectum or colon due to adverse reactions to dietary proteins. Common synonyms include food protein-induced proctocolitis and allergic proctocolitis. The condition is typically caused by cow's milk protein, though soy protein may also be implicated. It primarily affects the distal gastrointestinal tract, with symptoms such as rectal bleeding, diarrhea, and mucus in stool. The condition is most commonly seen in formula-fed infants and often resolves with dietary modification.

code_desc: Other specified allergic or dietetic colitis
summary: Other specified allergic or dietetic colitis refers to inflammation of the colon caused by dietary or allergic factors not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome and allergic colitis. Causative agents often include cow's milk protein, soy, or other dietary allergens. The condition typically affects the large intestine, with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and blood in stool. It is most commonly seen in infants and young children, often resolving with dietary modifications or elimination of the allergen.

Allergic or dietetic colitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the colon caused by an allergic reaction or dietary intolerance. Common synonyms include food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome and allergic colitis. Causative agents often include cow's milk protein, soy, and other food allergens. The condition typically affects the large intestine, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and blood in stool. It is most commonly seen in infants and young children, though it can occur in older individuals with known allergies or dietary sensitivities.

Diversion colitis is an inflammatory condition of the colon that occurs secondary to colonic diversion, such as after ileostomy or colostomy. It is characterized by mucosal inflammation, ulceration, and sometimes stricturing of the diverted segment. Common synonyms include anastomotic colitis and postoperative colitis. The primary causative agent is often *Clostridioides difficile*, though other pathogens may contribute. The condition typically affects the distal colon or rectum, and may involve the anastomotic site if present. It is more common in patients with prior abdominal surgery or inflammatory bowel disease.

code_desc: Colitis or proctitis due to external causes
summary: Colitis or proctitis due to external causes refers to inflammation of the colon or rectum resulting from external factors such as trauma, radiation, chemical exposure, or infections from pathogens like *Shigella*, *Salmonella*, or *Clostridioides difficile*. Common synonyms include radiation proctitis, chemical colitis, and traumatic colitis. The condition typically affects the rectum and sigmoid colon, with symptoms such as rectal bleeding, pain, and altered bowel habits. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy and stool studies to identify the underlying cause.

Chemical colitis or proctitis is an inflammatory condition of the colon or rectum caused by exposure to irritant or toxic substances. Common synonyms include toxic colitis and chemical proctitis. Causative agents often include antidiarrheal agents like bismuth subsalicylate, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and certain enemas. The condition typically affects the rectum and distal colon, presenting with symptoms such as rectal pain, urgency, and bloody diarrhea. It is often associated with medication use or rectal administration of irritants. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and exclusion of other causes.

Radiation-induced colitis is a gastrointestinal condition caused by damage to the colon from ionizing radiation, typically during pelvic or abdominal radiation therapy. It results in inflammation, ulceration, and fibrosis of the colonic mucosa. Common synonyms include radiation colitis or radiogenic colitis. Causative agents are primarily ionizing radiation, often used in cancer treatment. The condition primarily affects the colon, with symptoms such as diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and abdominal pain. It can occur acutely during or shortly after treatment or develop as a late effect months to years later.

Radiation proctitis is an inflammatory condition of the rectum caused by exposure to ionizing radiation, commonly following pelvic radiation therapy for cancers such as prostate or gynecologic malignancies. It presents with symptoms like rectal bleeding, diarrhea, and pain. Common synonyms include radiation-induced proctitis and radiogenic proctitis. The primary causative agent is ionizing radiation, which damages the rectal mucosa. The condition typically affects the rectum and may involve the anal canal. It is classified as acute or chronic based on the timing of onset relative to radiation therapy.

Drug-induced colitis is an inflammatory condition of the colon caused by medication exposure. Common synonyms include drug-related colitis and medication-induced colitis. It is often associated with antibiotics such as cephalosporins and amoxicillin-clavulanate, as well as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and anticonvulsants. The colon is typically affected, with symptoms including diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. The condition can range from mild to severe, sometimes leading to pseudomembranous colitis due to *Clostridioides difficile* overgrowth. Early recognition and discontinuation of the causative agent are critical for management.

code_desc: Other specified colitis or proctitis due to external causes
summary: "Other specified colitis or proctitis due to external causes" refers to inflammation of the colon or rectum caused by external factors such as trauma, radiation, or foreign bodies. Common synonyms include radiation proctitis or traumatic colitis. Causative agents may include physical injury, radiation exposure, or chemical irritants. The condition typically affects the rectum and sigmoid colon, with symptoms such as rectal pain, bleeding, and discharge. It is often diagnosed in patients undergoing radiation therapy or those with a history of rectal trauma.

code_desc: Colitis or proctitis due to external causes, unspecified
summary: Colitis or proctitis due to external causes, unspecified refers to inflammation of the colon or rectum caused by external factors, such as trauma, radiation, or foreign bodies, without a known specific etiology. Common synonyms include radiation proctitis, traumatic colitis, and foreign body-induced colitis. Causative agents may include physical injury, radiation therapy, or chemical exposure. The condition typically affects the rectum and distal colon, leading to symptoms like rectal pain, bleeding, and altered bowel habits. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic evaluation and imaging to identify the underlying cause.

code_desc: Other specified noninfectious colitis or proctitis
summary: Other specified noninfectious colitis or proctitis refers to inflammatory conditions of the colon or rectum that do not fit into more specific classifications and are not caused by infectious agents.
