Common synonyms include idiopathic colitis or proctitis. Causative agents may include medications, autoimmune disorders, or radiation. Typically affects the colon and rectum, with symptoms such as diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and abdominal pain. It is often diagnosed when no specific cause is identified.

Noninfectious colitis or proctitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the colon or rectum without an infectious cause. Common synonyms include idiopathic colitis, non-specific colitis, and non-infectious rectal inflammation. Causative agents may include medications, autoimmune disorders, radiation, ischemia, or inflammatory bowel disease. Typically affects the large intestine, particularly the rectum and sigmoid colon. Symptoms include diarrhea, rectal pain, and bleeding. Diagnosis is made after excluding infectious etiologies through appropriate testing.

code_desc: Certain vascular disorders of large intestine
summary: Certain vascular disorders of the large intestine refer to conditions affecting blood flow to the colon and rectum. Common synonyms include ischemic colitis and mesenteric vascular disease. These disorders are often caused by reduced blood flow due to thrombosis, embolism, or vasculitis. They typically affect the sigmoid colon and rectum, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and rectal bleeding. Risk factors include atherosclerosis, hypertension, and cardiac conditions. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications like bowel necrosis.

Angiodysplasia of the colon is a condition characterized by abnormal, fragile blood vessels in the colonic mucosa, leading to recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding. Common synonyms include colonic angiodysplasia and vascular ectasia. The exact cause is often unknown, though age-related degeneration of blood vessels is implicated. It typically affects the distal colon and rectum, with a predilection for older adults. The condition is associated with conditions like chronic heart failure and collagen vascular diseases. Clinically, it presents with intermittent hematochezia and iron deficiency anemia. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by endoscopy.

Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) of the large intestine is an abnormal tangle of arteries and veins that bypass capillaries, leading to increased vascular pressure and risk of bleeding. Common synonyms include hemangioma and vascular malformation. The condition is often idiopathic, though some cases may be associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. It typically affects the rectum and sigmoid colon, causing symptoms such as rectal bleeding and anemia. AVMs in the large intestine are less common than those in the gastrointestinal tract but can be life-threatening due to potential massive hemorrhage.

Vasculitis of the large intestine refers to inflammation of blood vessels within the colon, leading to vessel wall damage and potential ischemia. Common synonyms include granulomatous vasculitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune disorders, or medications. It typically affects the colon, with involvement of medium to large vessels. Symptoms include abdominal pain, bleeding, and bowel ischemia. The condition can be associated with systemic vasculitis or occur as an isolated lesion. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy and biopsy.

Varices of the large intestine are abnormal, enlarged veins that develop in the walls of the colon or rectum, most commonly as a complication of portal hypertension. They are often associated with liver cirrhosis and portal vein obstruction. Common synonyms include colonic varices and rectal varices. These varices are typically found in the lower gastrointestinal tract, particularly in the rectum and sigmoid colon. They can rupture, leading to life-threatening hemorrhage. Causative factors include chronic liver disease, alcohol abuse, and conditions causing portal hypertension. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications.

Acute haemorrhagic rectal ulcer is a sudden onset condition characterized by bleeding and ulceration of the rectal mucosa. Common synonyms include acute rectal ulcer and rectal haemorrhage. It is often caused by infections such as *Shigella*, *Salmonella*, or *Campylobacter*, or by inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis. The rectum is the primary affected area, with symptoms including rectal bleeding, pain, and tenesmus. The condition may also be associated with systemic symptoms such as fever and malaise. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications.

code_desc: Other specified vascular disorders of large intestine
summary: "Other specified vascular disorders of large intestine" refers to rare conditions involving abnormal blood vessel formation or function in the large intestine, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include angiodysplasia and vascular malformations. Causative agents may include genetic factors, chronic inflammation, or vascular abnormalities. These disorders typically affect the colon and rectum, leading to symptoms such as bleeding, anemia, and abdominal pain. They are often diagnosed via endoscopy or imaging.

code_desc: Vascular disorders of large intestine, unspecified
summary: Vascular disorders of the large intestine, unspecified, refer to conditions involving abnormal blood vessel function or structure in the colon or rectum, leading to ischemia, hemorrhage, or other vascular complications. Common synonyms include colonic ischemia, angiodysplasia, and vascular malformations. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, hypertension, anticoagulant use, or inflammatory bowel disease. These disorders typically affect the colon and rectum, with symptoms such as rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, and altered bowel habits. Diagnosis often requires endoscopic or imaging evaluation.

A polyp of the large intestine is a benign growth arising from the mucosal lining of the colon or rectum. Common synonyms include colonic polyp and rectal polyp. These lesions are typically adenomatous, though hyperplastic or inflammatory types may also occur. They are most frequently found in the sigmoid colon and rectum. Risk factors include age, family history, and inflammatory bowel disease. While generally asymptomatic, they may cause bleeding, changes in bowel habits, or obstruction. Histopathological evaluation is essential to rule out malignancy.

Hyperplastic polyp of the large intestine is a benign lesion characterized by abnormal proliferation of epithelial cells, typically arising from the mucosa. Common synonyms include hyperplastic polypoid lesion and serrated polyp. It is often associated with chronic inflammation, particularly in the setting of inflammatory bowel disease. The primary causative agents include long-standing irritation, infection, and genetic predisposition. These polyps most commonly affect the rectum and sigmoid colon, and are more prevalent in older adults. They are generally asymptomatic but may cause bleeding or obstruction if large.

Inflammatory polyp of the large intestine is a benign lesion characterized by hyperplastic proliferation of mucosal tissue in response to chronic inflammation. Common synonyms include hyperplastic polyp and pseudopolyp. It is typically associated with conditions such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. The primary causative agents are inflammatory processes leading to mucosal damage and repair. These polyps most commonly affect the rectum and sigmoid colon, often presenting as solitary or multiple lesions. They are usually asymptomatic but may cause bleeding or altered bowel habits. Histologically, they show prominent inflammatory infiltrate and mucosal hyperplasia.

code_desc: Benign lymphoid polyp of large intestine
summary: Benign lymphoid polyp of the large intestine, also known as hyperplastic polyp or inflammatory polyp, is a non-neoplastic lesion characterized by hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue in the colonic submucosa. It is commonly associated with chronic inflammation, such as in inflammatory bowel disease. These polyps are typically found in the rectum and sigmoid colon. They are not premalignant and are often asymptomatic, discovered incidentally during colonoscopy. No specific causative agents are identified, but recurrent inflammation is a contributing factor.

Hamartomatous polyp of the large intestine is a benign neoplasm characterized by disorganized growth of normal tissue types. Common synonyms include juvenile polyp and hamartoma. It is typically caused by mutations in genes such as APC or PTCH1, often associated with syndromes like Peutz-Jeghers or juvenile polyposis. These polyps most commonly occur in the colon and rectum, and may present with symptoms like bleeding, obstruction, or intussusception. They are more prevalent in children and young adults, though they can occur at any age.

code_desc: Inflammatory fibroid polyp of large intestine
summary: Inflammatory fibroid polyp of the large intestine is a benign lesion characterized by fibrous tissue proliferation with inflammatory changes. It commonly occurs in the rectum and sigmoid colon. Synonyms include inflammatory fibrous polyp and inflammatory fibromatosis. The exact cause is unknown, though chronic inflammation and irritation may contribute. It is typically associated with long-standing colitis or inflammatory bowel disease. The polyp is firm, well-circumscribed, and may cause symptoms such as rectal bleeding or altered bowel habits. Histologically, it shows fibrous stroma with inflammatory infiltrate and possible epithelial proliferation.

code_desc: Other specified polyp of large intestine
summary: "Other specified polyp of large intestine" refers to benign growths in the colon or rectum that do not fit the criteria for adenomas, hyperplastic polyps, or serrated polyps. Common synonyms include unspecified colonic polyps or non-classifiable polyps. Causative factors are largely unknown, though genetic predisposition and chronic inflammation may play roles. These polyps typically affect the colon, particularly the rectum and sigmoid colon, and are often detected incidentally during colonoscopy. They carry a low risk of malignant transformation but may require surveillance.

Polyp of large intestine, unspecified refers to a benign growth arising from the mucosal lining of the colon or rectum, typically characterized by a broad base. Common synonyms include colorectal polyp or colonic polyp. The exact cause is often unknown, though genetic factors, chronic inflammation, and lifestyle factors such as diet and obesity may contribute. These lesions are most commonly found in the sigmoid colon and rectum. While generally asymptomatic, they carry a risk of malignant transformation and are often detected incidentally during colonoscopy.

code_desc: Certain infections of the large intestine
summary: Certain infections of the large intestine, also known as enterocolitis or bacillary dysentery, are caused by pathogens such as *Shigella*, *Salmonella*, *Campylobacter*, and *Entamoeba histolytica*. These infections primarily affect the colon and rectum, leading to symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, and tenesmus. They are often transmitted through contaminated food or water. Risk factors include poor hygiene and immunocompromised states. Complications may include dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and in severe cases, systemic infection. Prompt treatment with appropriate antimicrobial therapy is essential to prevent progression and reduce morbidity.

Colonic abscess is a localized collection of pus within the colon, often resulting from infection secondary to diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, or trauma. Common synonyms include pericolonic abscess and pelvic abscess. Causative agents typically include gram-negative bacilli, such as Escherichia coli, and anaerobic organisms. The condition most commonly affects the sigmoid colon, but can occur in any segment of the large intestine. It may present with fever, abdominal pain, and altered bowel habits, and is often associated with systemic signs of infection. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications such as perforation or sepsis.

A rectal abscess is a localized collection of pus within the rectum or perirectal tissues, typically caused by bacterial infection. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Bacteroides* species. It often results from obstruction of anal glands or trauma. Synonyms include perianal abscess, ischiorectal abscess, and anal abscess. The condition primarily affects the rectum and surrounding perianal tissues, causing pain, swelling, and fever. It is more common in males and individuals with conditions like Crohn’s disease or diabetes.

Perirectal abscess is a localized collection of pus in the perirectal space, typically resulting from infection of anal glands or crypts. Common synonyms include anal abscess and ischiorectal abscess. The most common causative agents are *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Escherichia coli*. It predominantly affects the perianal region, with the ischiorectal fossa being a common site. The condition is more prevalent in males and often presents with pain, swelling, and tenderness. It may be associated with fever and systemic signs of infection. Prompt drainage is usually required for resolution.

An ischiorectal abscess is a deep perianal infection involving the ischiorectal fossa, typically presenting as a painful, fluctuant mass near the anal canal. Common synonyms include perirectal abscess and ischioanal abscess. It is most commonly caused by anaerobic bacteria, often in conjunction with gram-positive cocci, such as *Escherichia coli*, *Bacteroides*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition predominantly affects the perianal region, particularly around the anal sphincter, and may extend into the pelvis if untreated. It is more prevalent in males and individuals with underlying conditions like diabetes or immunosuppression.

Rectal cellulitis is a bacterial infection of the rectal mucosa and surrounding tissues, often presenting with erythema, swelling, pain, and tenderness. Common synonyms include perirectal cellulitis and rectal abscess. It is typically caused by anaerobic and aerobic bacteria such as *Escherichia coli*, *Bacteroides*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition most commonly affects the perirectal area, including the anal canal and adjacent skin. It may develop secondary to trauma, surgery, or underlying conditions like hemorrhoids or fissures. Prompt antibiotic therapy is essential to prevent progression to abscess formation.

code_desc: Other specified infections of the large intestine
summary: "Other specified infections of the large intestine" refers to infectious processes of the colon and rectum not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include colonic infection and enterocolitis. Causative agents may include bacteria such as Salmonella, Shigella, and E. coli, as well as parasites like Entamoeba histolytica. These infections typically affect the colon, rectum, and sometimes the terminal ileum, leading to symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. The condition is often diagnosed through clinical presentation and laboratory testing.

code_desc: Infections of the large intestine, unspecified
summary: Infections of the large intestine, unspecified, refer to inflammatory conditions affecting the colon and rectum caused by various pathogens. Common synonyms include colitis and enterocolitis. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Salmonella*, *Shigella*, *Campylobacter*, and *Clostridioides difficile*, as well as parasites like *Entamoeba histolytica*. These infections typically present with symptoms like diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. They can affect the entire large intestine, with varying severity and clinical manifestations depending on the causative agent and host factors.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of large intestine
summary: "Other specified diseases of large intestine" refers to conditions affecting the colon or rectum that do not fit into more specific classifications. Common synonyms include unspecified colonic disorders or other specified intestinal diseases. Causative agents vary but may include infections, inflammatory processes, or structural abnormalities. These conditions typically affect the colon, rectum, and associated tissues, often presenting with symptoms like abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and rectal bleeding. Diagnosis is usually made after excluding more specific conditions through endoscopic or histopathological evaluation.

Diseases of the large intestine, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the colon and rectum without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include colonic disorders and rectal diseases. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., bacteria, parasites), inflammatory processes, or structural abnormalities. These conditions typically affect the colon, rectum, and associated tissues. Symptoms may involve changes in bowel habits, abdominal pain, bleeding, or obstruction. Diagnosis often requires imaging or endoscopic evaluation. Treatment varies depending on the underlying cause and severity.

code_desc: Fissure or fistula of anal regions
summary: Fissure or fistula of the anal regions refers to abnormal tracts or tears in the anal canal. A fissure is a linear tear, often causing pain and bleeding during defecation, while a fistula is an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the skin. Common synonyms include anal fissure and anal fistula. Causative agents include constipation, childbirth, infections (e.g., *Clostridium difficile*), and inflammatory bowel disease. These conditions typically affect the anal canal and perianal skin, with fissures more common in the posterior midline and fistulas often associated with abscesses.

An anal fissure is a small tear in the anal canal, typically located in the posterior midline. It presents with severe anal pain, often described as a sharp, burning sensation during and after defecation. Common synonyms include anal ulcer and anal crack. The condition is most frequently caused by constipation, hard stools, or childbirth. Other causes may include diarrhea, anal intercourse, or inflammatory bowel disease. It predominantly affects the distal anal canal and is more common in young adults and women. Diagnosis is usually clinical, based on history and physical examination.

Anal fistula is a chronic abnormal tract connecting the epithelium of the anal canal to the perianal skin, often resulting from infection. Common synonyms include anal fistula, perianal fistula, and anal fistulous tract. It is most commonly caused by anal abscesses, particularly those originating from cryptoglandular infections. Other causes may include Crohn’s disease, tuberculosis, or trauma. The condition typically affects the perianal region, with the tract often extending from the anal canal to the skin surface, leading to recurrent drainage and discomfort. It is more prevalent in males and individuals with inflammatory bowel disease.

Anorectal fistula is an abnormal tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin, often resulting from infection or inflammation. Common synonyms include anal fistula and perianal fistula. It is typically caused by abscesses, particularly those originating from anal glands, though other causes such as trauma, surgery, or inflammatory bowel disease may also contribute. The condition most commonly affects the perianal region, with the anal canal being the primary site of involvement. Symptoms include pain, drainage, and recurrent infections.

code_desc: Other specified fissure or fistula of anal regions
summary: "Other specified fissure or fistula of anal regions" refers to abnormal tracts or tears in the anal canal not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include anal fistula or fissure of unspecified type. Causative agents may include infection, trauma, or inflammatory bowel disease. Typically affects the anal canal and perianal area. It is often associated with chronic inflammation or obstruction. Diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and imaging. Treatment may involve surgical intervention to drain or excise the tract. This condition is more common in adults, particularly those with underlying gastrointestinal disorders.

code_desc: Fissure or fistula of anal regions, unspecified
summary: Fissure or fistula of anal regions, unspecified refers to an abnormal opening or tract in the anal area, often resulting from chronic inflammation, infection, or trauma. Common synonyms include anal fissure, anal fistula, or anal sinus tract. Causative agents may include infectious organisms such as *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, or *Clostridium* species. This condition typically affects the perianal region, with fissures commonly located at the posterior midline and fistulas often originating from abscesses or inflammatory bowel disease.

Stenosis of the anal canal refers to the narrowing of the anal canal, leading to difficulty in passing stools and potential pain. Common synonyms include anal stricture and anal canal stenosis. It is often caused by chronic inflammation, trauma, surgery, or infection. Known causative agents include anal fissures, hemorrhoids, tuberculosis, and Crohn's disease. The condition typically affects the anal canal, with symptoms such as constipation, tenesmus, and anal pain. It may occur in both males and females, though more commonly in females due to anatomical factors. Diagnosis is usually made through physical examination and imaging studies. Treatment may involve dilation, surgery, or management of underlying conditions.

An ulcer of the anus, also known as an anal ulcer or anal fissure, is a break in the anal mucosa characterized by pain, bleeding, and sometimes drainage. Common synonyms include anal fissure and anal ulceration. It is typically caused by chronic constipation, trauma from hard stools, or infections such as syphilis, tuberculosis, or Crohn's disease. The condition primarily affects the anorectal region, often involving the anal canal. It may be associated with systemic conditions and requires careful evaluation to determine underlying causes.

Anal prolapse is the protrusion of rectal tissue through the anal canal, often accompanied by mucosa or full-thickness layers of the rectum. Common synonyms include rectal prolapse and rectal eversion. It is typically caused by chronic straining, constipation, childbirth, or weakened pelvic floor muscles. The condition primarily affects the anal canal and rectum, with the prolapsed tissue often appearing as a red, fleshy mass. It is more common in women and elderly individuals, and may lead to symptoms such as rectal bleeding, discomfort, and difficulty in bowel movements.

code_desc: Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the anal canal
summary: "Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of the anal canal" refers to structural changes in the anal canal not classified elsewhere, such as strictures, fissures, or fistulas. Common synonyms include anal stricture, anal fissure, and anal fistula. Causative agents may include chronic constipation, infection, trauma, or inflammatory bowel disease. These conditions typically affect the anal canal and surrounding perianal tissues, leading to symptoms like pain, bleeding, and difficulty in passing stool. They are more common in adults, particularly those with a history of gastrointestinal disorders or recurrent anal infections.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of the anal canal, unspecified
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the anal canal, unspecified refer to structural changes in the anal canal resulting from disease or injury, not classified under specific conditions. Common synonyms include anal canal deformities or acquired anal anomalies. Causative agents may include trauma, surgery, chronic inflammation, or congenital defects. These alterations typically affect the anal canal itself, potentially involving the surrounding perianal tissues. Symptoms may include fecal incontinence, pain, or difficulty with bowel movements. The condition is often diagnosed through physical examination or imaging studies.

Haemorrhoids, also known as piles or rectal varices, are swollen, inflamed veins in the anal canal or rectum. They result from increased venous pressure, often due to chronic constipation, straining during bowel movements, pregnancy, or prolonged sitting. Common symptoms include pain, itching, and bleeding during defecation. Internal hemorrhoids may prolapse and require manual reduction. External hemorrhoids can thrombose, leading to severe pain. The condition primarily affects the anal and rectal regions, with a higher prevalence in adults, particularly those with sedentary lifestyles or dietary habits that contribute to constipation.

First degree haemorrhoids are internal hemorrhoids that remain above the dentate line and do not prolapse. They are typically painless but may cause bleeding during bowel movements. Common synonyms include internal hemorrhoids stage I. Causative factors include chronic constipation, straining during defecation, and increased abdominal pressure. They commonly affect the rectum and are often associated with anal fissures or other anorectal conditions. Diagnosis is usually made through visual inspection or anoscopy. Management includes dietary modifications, stool softeners, and topical treatments.

Second degree haemorrhoids are internal haemorrhoids that prolapse during straining but reduce spontaneously. They are commonly associated with chronic constipation, straining during bowel movements, and increased abdominal pressure. These hemorrhoids typically affect the lower rectum and anal canal. Synonyms include second-degree rectal hemorrhoids or prolapsing hemorrhoids. They are classified based on their degree of prolapse and are often managed with lifestyle modifications, topical treatments, or minimally invasive procedures.

Third-degree haemorrhoids are severe internal haemorrhoids that prolapse outside the anal canal and cannot be manually reduced. They are characterized by significant swelling, pain, and bleeding. Common synonyms include severe internal haemorrhoids and prolapsed haemorrhoids. Causative factors include chronic constipation, straining during bowel movements, pregnancy, and portal hypertension. These conditions typically affect the anal canal and rectum, often leading to complications such as thrombosis or infection.

Fourth degree haemorrhoids are severe anal prolapses where the hemorrhoidal tissue protrudes outside the anus and cannot be manually reduced. They are classified as the most advanced stage of hemorrhoidal disease. Common synonyms include severe internal hemorrhoids and anal prolapse. Causative factors include chronic straining during defecation, constipation, pregnancy, and increased abdominal pressure. These conditions primarily affect the anal canal and rectum, often leading to significant discomfort, bleeding, and complications such as thrombosis or infection.

Haemorrhoids, unspecified, refer to the swelling and inflammation of veins in the anal canal, leading to discomfort, bleeding, and itching. Common synonyms include piles and anal varices. The condition is often caused by increased venous pressure from straining during bowel movements, chronic constipation, diarrhea, pregnancy, or obesity. It primarily affects the anal region, with internal hemorrhoids located inside the rectum and external hemorrhoids protruding outside the anus. Risk factors include age, family history, and lifestyle factors.

Perianal venous thrombosis is a condition characterized by the formation of a blood clot in the veins surrounding the anus, leading to localized pain, swelling, and tenderness. Common synonyms include thrombosed hemorrhoid and anal thrombosis. It is often caused by venous congestion, trauma, or increased intra-abdominal pressure. The condition typically affects the rectal and anal regions, with the thrombosis most commonly occurring in the superior rectal veins. It is more prevalent in individuals with chronic constipation, pregnancy, or obesity.

Residual haemorrhoidal skin tags are small, soft, flesh-colored or reddish tags that remain after treatment of hemorrhoids. They are composed of fibrous tissue and skin and often occur in the anal region. Common synonyms include anal skin tags or post-hemorrhoidal tags. These tags are typically caused by chronic hemorrhoidal disease, leading to inflammation and tissue proliferation. They are most commonly found around the anus, particularly in individuals with a history of internal hemorrhoids. While generally benign, they may cause discomfort or cosmetic concern.

code_desc: Other specified haemorrhoids or perianal venous conditions
summary: Other specified haemorrhoids or perianal venous conditions refer to hemorrhoidal or perianal venous disorders that do not meet the criteria for internal or external hemorrhoids, or thrombosed hemorrhoids. Common synonyms include anal venous malformations and perianal varicosities. These conditions are often caused by chronic straining, constipation, pregnancy, or prolonged sitting. They typically affect the anal canal and perianal region, presenting with symptoms such as pain, swelling, and bleeding. Diagnosis is usually made clinically, and treatment may involve lifestyle modifications, topical therapies, or surgical intervention.

code_desc: Haemorrhoids or perianal venous conditions, unspecified
summary: Haemorrhoids, or perianal venous conditions, refer to swollen, inflamed veins in the anal canal or surrounding area. Common synonyms include piles and anal venous malformations. They are typically caused by increased venous pressure from straining during bowel movements, chronic constipation, pregnancy, or obesity. The condition primarily affects the anorectal region, with symptoms such as rectal bleeding, itching, pain, and discomfort. While not a malignant condition, it can significantly impact quality of life.

Infections of the anal region refer to inflammatory or infectious processes affecting the perianal and anal areas. Common synonyms include perianal infections, anal abscesses, and anal fissures. These infections are often caused by bacteria such as *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Clostridium* species. They typically affect the perianal skin, anal glands, and surrounding tissues. Symptoms may include pain, swelling, redness, and drainage. Conditions like anal fistulas and hemorrhoids can also predispose individuals to these infections. Prompt treatment is essential to prevent complications such as sepsis or chronic drainage.

An abscess of the anal region is a localized collection of pus resulting from an infection in the perianal or anal glands. Common synonyms include perianal abscess and anal abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly by *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Bacteroides* species. The condition predominantly affects the perianal area, including the anal canal and surrounding tissues. It often presents with pain, swelling, redness, and fever. Complications may include fistula formation if left untreated. Prompt drainage and antibiotic therapy are essential for management.

An anal abscess is a localized collection of pus in the perianal or rectal tissues, typically resulting from an infection of an anal gland. Common synonyms include perianal abscess and ischiorectal abscess. It is most commonly caused by bacterial infections, with *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Bacteroides* species being frequent pathogens. The condition primarily affects the perianal region, but may also involve the ischiorectal fossa. It often presents with pain, swelling, and fever, and is more prevalent in individuals with conditions such as Crohn’s disease or diabetes.

Anorectal abscess is a localized collection of pus in the anorectal region, typically resulting from infection of anal glands. Common synonyms include perianal abscess and anal abscess. The condition is most commonly caused by bacterial infections, with *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Bacteroides* species being frequent pathogens. It predominantly affects the perianal and ischiorectal spaces. Symptoms include pain, swelling, fever, and tenderness. It is more common in males and individuals with underlying conditions such as diabetes or immunosuppression.

An intrasphincteric abscess is a collection of pus within the sphincter muscle of the anal canal, typically resulting from an infection originating from an anal gland. Common synonyms include perisphincteric abscess and suprasphincteric abscess, though the latter refers to a location above the sphincter. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Bacteroides* species. This condition most commonly affects the perianal region, often presenting with pain, swelling, and fever. It is a complication of anal fissures or fistulas and may require surgical drainage.

code_desc: Other specified abscess of anal region
summary: "Other specified abscess of anal region" refers to an abscess localized in the anal area that does not fit the criteria for more specific classifications such as perianal or anal fistula. Common synonyms include perianal abscess or anal abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infections, most commonly *Staphylococcus aureus*. The condition primarily affects the perianal skin and subcutaneous tissues, often resulting from blocked glands or trauma. It presents with pain, swelling, and sometimes fever, and may require drainage or surgical intervention.

Abscess of the anal region, unspecified, refers to a localized collection of pus in the perianal or anal canal tissues. Common synonyms include perianal abscess and anal abscess. It is typically caused by bacterial infections, most commonly *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, and *Bacteroides* species. The condition predominantly affects the perianal glands and surrounding tissues, often resulting from obstructed crypts or trauma. It is more common in males and individuals with compromised immune systems or underlying conditions such as Crohn’s disease. Symptoms include pain, swelling, redness, and fever. Prompt drainage and antibiotic therapy are usually required for resolution.

code_desc: Other specified infections of the anal region
summary: "Other specified infections of the anal region" refers to infections of the anal canal or perianal area not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include perianal abscess, anal fissure with infection, or anal fistula. Causative agents may include *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, or *Clostridium* species. These infections typically affect the anal canal, perianal skin, and surrounding tissues, often presenting with pain, swelling, discharge, or fever. They may result from trauma, obstruction, or underlying conditions like diabetes or immunosuppression.

code_desc: Infections of the anal region, unspecified
summary: Infections of the anal region, unspecified, refer to inflammatory or infectious processes affecting the perianal or anal area without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include perianal abscess, anal fissure, or anal itching. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, or *Clostridium* species. Typically affecting the perianal skin, anal canal, and surrounding tissues, these infections may present with pain, swelling, discharge, or erythema. They are often associated with conditions like hemorrhoids, fistulas, or sexually transmitted infections.

An anal polyp is a benign growth arising from the anal canal or rectum, typically arising from the mucosal lining. Common synonyms include anal赘生物 and rectal polyp. These lesions are often hyperplastic or inflammatory in nature, though some may be neoplastic. They are most frequently found in the distal rectum and anal canal. Known causative factors include chronic inflammation, infection, and possibly genetic predisposition. Symptoms may include rectal bleeding, mucus discharge, and discomfort. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through anoscopy or colonoscopy.

Inflammatory anal polyp is a benign, inflammatory lesion arising from the anal canal, often associated with chronic irritation or infection. It presents as a solitary, pedunculated or broad-based mass, typically located at the anal verge. Common synonyms include anal polypoid lesion and anal hypertrophy. Causative agents may include chronic anal fissures, hemorrhoids, or infections such as amoebiasis or tuberculosis. The condition predominantly affects the anal canal and perianal region, commonly seen in adults with a history of anal trauma or inflammatory bowel disease.

Lymphoid polyps are benign, reactive proliferations of lymphoid tissue, commonly found in the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. They result from chronic inflammation, often due to allergic rhinitis or recurrent infections. Synonyms include inflammatory polyps and hyperplastic lymphoid nodules. These polyps are typically non-neoplastic and may present with nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, or facial pain. They are most frequently encountered in adults, particularly those with a history of atopy or chronic sinus disease. Causative agents include allergens, viral infections, and environmental irritants.

Hypertrophied anal papillae refer to the enlargement of the normal anal papillae, small projections within the anal canal. Common synonyms include enlarged anal papillae or hypertrophic anal papillae. This condition is often associated with chronic irritation, infection, or inflammatory processes. Known causative agents include fungal infections such as Candida, as well as bacterial infections like those caused by *Escherichia coli* or *Staphylococcus aureus*. It typically affects the anal canal, particularly the transitional zone between the anal canal and the rectum. The condition is more common in individuals with a history of anal fissures, hemorrhoids, or recurrent anal infections.

Other specified anal polyp refers to a benign growth in the anal canal that does not meet the criteria for specific types such as hyperplastic or inflammatory polyps. It is a nonspecific term used when the polyp's features are atypical or insufficiently defined. Common synonyms include anal polyp, unspecified, or non-classifiable anal polyp. The exact causative agents are often unknown, though chronic inflammation, trauma, or infection may contribute. These polyps typically affect the anal canal and may be associated with conditions like hemorrhoids or inflammatory bowel disease. They are generally asymptomatic but may cause bleeding or discomfort.

Anal polyp, unspecified, refers to a benign growth arising from the anal canal mucosa, typically presenting as a solitary or multiple elevated lesion. Common synonyms include anal tumor, anal growth, or anal mass. While the exact cause is often unknown, factors such as chronic inflammation, trauma, or genetic predisposition may contribute. These polyps are most commonly found in the distal anal canal and may be associated with conditions like hemorrhoids or inflammatory bowel disease. They are generally asymptomatic but can cause bleeding, discomfort, or changes in bowel habits.

code_desc: Certain specified diseases of anal canal
summary: Certain specified diseases of the anal canal encompass a range of conditions affecting the anal region, including hemorrhoids, anal fissures, and anal fistulas. Common synonyms include anal disorders and anorectal diseases. These conditions are often caused by chronic constipation, infection, or trauma. Hemorrhoids result from venous congestion, while fissures are typically due to hard stools. Anal fistulas are often associated with abscesses or inflammatory bowel disease. The anal canal and surrounding perianal tissues are the primary affected areas.

Anal spasm is a sudden, involuntary contraction of the anal sphincter muscles, causing pain and difficulty in passing stool. Common synonyms include anal fissure spasm and rectal spasm. It is often caused by chronic constipation, straining during defecation, or previous trauma. The condition primarily affects the anal canal and surrounding perianal tissues. It may be associated with conditions such as hemorrhoids or inflammatory bowel disease. Pain is typically exacerbated by attempts to defecate, leading to a cycle of pain and constipation. Treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and addressing underlying causes.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of anal canal
summary: "Other specified diseases of anal canal" refers to anal conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as fissures or hemorrhoids. Common synonyms include unspecified anal disorders. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., HIV, fungal or parasitic organisms), trauma, or inflammatory processes. These conditions typically affect the anal canal and surrounding perianal tissues, causing symptoms like pain, itching, and bleeding. They may result from chronic irritation, poor hygiene, or underlying systemic diseases. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and may involve endoscopic or histopathological examination.

Diseases of the anal canal, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the anal canal without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include anal disorders or unspecified anal diseases. Causative agents may include infections (e.g., bacteria, parasites), trauma, or inflammatory processes. These conditions typically affect the anal canal, rectum, and surrounding perianal tissues. Symptoms often include pain, itching, bleeding, and discharge. They may be associated with underlying conditions such as hemorrhoids, fissures, or sexually transmitted infections. Diagnosis often requires clinical evaluation and may involve endoscopic or histopathological examination.

Infectious liver disease refers to conditions caused by pathogens that lead to liver inflammation and dysfunction. Common synonyms include viral hepatitis and infectious hepatitis. Causative agents include viruses such as hepatitis A, B, and C, as well as parasites like schistosoma and bacteria such as hepatitis E. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic symptoms may occur. Transmission routes vary, including ingestion, blood contact, and vector-borne mechanisms. Clinical manifestations range from mild hepatitis to fulminant liver failure.

An abscess of the liver is a localized collection of pus within the liver parenchyma, typically resulting from bacterial infection. Common synonyms include hepatic abscess and pyogenic liver abscess. The most common causative agents are *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, *Bacteroides*, and *Staphylococcus aureus*. It often arises from hematogenous spread, biliary tract infection, or trauma. The liver is the primary affected organ, though adjacent structures may also be involved. Symptoms include fever, right upper quadrant pain, and systemic signs of infection.

Other specified infectious liver disease refers to liver infections caused by pathogens not classified under more specific categories such as hepatitis A, B, or C. Common synonyms include unspecified viral hepatitis and other infectious hepatitis. Causative agents may include parasites like *Leishmania* or *Toxoplasma*, bacteria such as *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, or fungi. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system and systemic spread in severe cases. Clinical presentation often includes jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and systemic symptoms. Diagnosis typically requires serological testing and imaging.

Infectious liver disease, unspecified refers to liver inflammation or damage caused by an infectious agent, though the specific pathogen is not identified. Common synonyms include undetermined infectious hepatitis and unspecified hepatic infection. Causative agents may include viruses such as hepatitis A, B, or C, as well as bacterial, parasitic, or fungal organisms. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic involvement in severe cases. Symptoms often include jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis typically requires clinical evaluation and laboratory testing.

Acute or subacute hepatic failure refers to the rapid loss of liver function, typically within days to weeks. Common synonyms include acute liver failure and subacute liver failure. It is characterized by coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and jaundice. Causative agents include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B, C), drug toxicity (e.g., acetaminophen overdose), autoimmune hepatitis, and metabolic disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic complications affecting the brain, kidneys, and circulatory system. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to improve outcomes.

code_desc: Acute or subacute hepatic failure due to hepatitis virus
summary: Acute or subacute hepatic failure due to hepatitis virus refers to rapid loss of liver function caused by viral hepatitis. Common synonyms include acute liver failure and subacute liver failure. Causative agents include hepatitis A, B, C, D, and E viruses. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential systemic involvement. Symptoms may include jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and elevated liver enzymes. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt intervention to prevent mortality.

code_desc: Other acute or subacute hepatic failure
summary: Other acute or subacute hepatic failure refers to sudden or rapidly progressive liver dysfunction not caused by common viral hepatitis or drug-induced injury. It may present with jaundice, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy. Common synonyms include acute-on-chronic liver failure and subacute liver failure. Causative agents include toxins, metabolic disorders, autoimmune hepatitis, and ischemic injury. The liver is primarily affected, with potential systemic involvement. Diagnosis requires exclusion of known causes and assessment of liver function tests.

code_desc: Acute or subacute hepatic failure, unspecified
summary: Acute or subacute hepatic failure, unspecified, refers to a rapid decline in liver function, often within weeks, leading to coagulopathy, encephalopathy, and hepatic encephalopathy. Common synonyms include acute liver failure and subacute liver failure. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B, C), drug-induced toxicity (e.g., acetaminophen overdose), autoimmune hepatitis, or metabolic disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic complications affecting the brain, kidneys, and circulatory system.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fat in liver cells, not caused by alcohol consumption. Common synonyms include hepatic steatosis and simple fatty liver. The primary causative agents include obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. It typically affects the liver, with fat deposition in hepatocytes. In advanced stages, it may progress to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), fibrosis, or cirrhosis. The condition is prevalent in adults, particularly those with metabolic risk factors. Early diagnosis and lifestyle modifications are crucial for prevention and management.

code_desc: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease without non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
summary: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) without non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fat in the liver in the absence of significant inflammation or fibrosis. Common synonyms include simple hepatic steatosis. It is primarily caused by metabolic factors such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. The liver is the main affected organ, with fat deposition occurring in hepatocytes. This condition is typically asymptomatic but can progress to more severe liver disease if left unmanaged.

Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a chronic liver disease characterized by hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and hepatocellular injury in the absence of significant alcohol consumption. Common synonyms include non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) with histological features. Causative agents include obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. It is typically associated with visceral adiposity and systemic metabolic disturbances.

code_desc: Other specified non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
summary: Other specified non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) refers to cases of fatty liver disease not classified under more specific subtypes, such as non-alcoholic steatohepatitis or simple steatosis. It is characterized by the accumulation of fat in the liver, excluding alcohol-related causes. Common synonyms include unspecified NAFLD or non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, unspecified. Causative factors often involve metabolic syndrome, obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis if left untreated.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, unspecified (NAFLD) is a condition characterized by excessive fat accumulation in liver cells in the absence of significant alcohol consumption. Common synonyms include simple hepatic steatosis and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) when inflammation is present. Causative factors include obesity, insulin resistance, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis. It is typically asymptomatic but may lead to hepatic dysfunction and increased cardiovascular risk.

Hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis refers to advanced scarring of liver tissue due to chronic injury, leading to impaired function. Common synonyms include liver cirrhosis and fibrotic liver disease. Causative agents include chronic viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with progressive replacement of healthy tissue by fibrous scar. Complications may involve portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. Early detection and management of underlying causes are critical to prevent progression.

Hepatic fibrosis is a progressive scarring of liver tissue resulting from chronic injury, leading to impaired liver function. Common synonyms include cirrhosis and hepatic sclerosis. It is caused by prolonged exposure to toxins, viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with fibrous tissue replacing healthy parenchyma. Complications may involve portal hypertension, ascites, and liver failure. Early detection and management of underlying causes are critical to prevent progression to end-stage liver disease.

Hepatic cirrhosis is a late-stage liver disease characterized by widespread replacement of healthy liver tissue with fibrous scar tissue, leading to impaired liver function. Common synonyms include cirrhosis and hepatic fibrosis. It is typically caused by chronic alcohol abuse, viral hepatitis (especially B and C), non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with complications often involving the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and cardiovascular system. Long-term progression can result in portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy.

code_desc: Certain specified fibrosis or cirrhosis of liver
summary: Certain specified fibrosis or cirrhosis of liver refers to advanced scarring of liver tissue due to chronic injury. Common synonyms include hepatic cirrhosis and fibrosis. Causative agents include chronic viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with fibrosis progressing to nodular regeneration and impaired function. Symptoms may include jaundice, ascites, and portal hypertension. This condition is classified under ICD-10 code K74.

code_desc: Hereditary North American Indian childhood cirrhosis
summary: Hereditary North American Indian childhood cirrhosis, also known as progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis or Byler disease, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired bile flow leading to progressive liver damage. Caused by mutations in the ATP8B1 gene, it results in cholestasis, jaundice, and eventually cirrhosis. The condition primarily affects the liver, causing fibrosis and impaired bile secretion. It typically manifests in early childhood, with symptoms including pruritus, jaundice, and growth retardation. The disease is most commonly seen in individuals of North American Indian descent.

Idiopathic copper-associated cirrhosis is a rare, progressive liver disease characterized by the accumulation of copper in liver tissue, leading to fibrosis and cirrhosis. It is often associated with Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder causing copper toxicity. Common synonyms include Wilson's disease-related cirrhosis and hepatolenticular degeneration. The primary causative agent is a mutation in the ATP7B gene, which impairs copper excretion. The liver is the main affected organ, with copper deposition also occurring in the brain, kidneys, and cornea. Early diagnosis and chelation therapy are critical to prevent irreversible damage.

code_desc: Other specified hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis
summary: Other specified hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis refers to advanced scarring of the liver not classified under more specific categories. It may result from various chronic liver injuries, including alcohol abuse, viral hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or autoimmune conditions. Common synonyms include unspecified cirrhosis or fibrosis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential complications affecting the gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and cardiovascular system. This condition is characterized by impaired liver function and increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Alcoholic liver disease (ALD) is a spectrum of liver injury caused by chronic heavy alcohol consumption. Common synonyms include alcoholic hepatitis, alcoholic cirrhosis, and alcohol-induced liver damage. The primary causative agent is excessive alcohol intake, leading to oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis. Typically affecting the liver, it may progress to cirrhosis, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. The condition primarily impacts the liver but can also involve the gastrointestinal tract and pancreas. Early stages may present with fatigue and jaundice, while advanced cases can result in liver failure.

Alcoholic fatty liver, also known as alcoholic steatosis, is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fat in liver cells due to chronic alcohol consumption. It is primarily caused by excessive alcohol intake, which disrupts lipid metabolism and leads to hepatic fat deposition. The liver is the main affected organ, and the condition often precedes more severe forms of alcoholic liver disease, such as alcoholic hepatitis or cirrhosis. Common synonyms include alcoholic steatosis and fatty liver disease associated with alcohol use. Early stages may be asymptomatic, but progressive alcohol use can result in inflammation and liver dysfunction.

Alcoholic hepatitis is an acute inflammatory condition of the liver caused by excessive alcohol consumption. It results from direct toxic effects of ethanol and its metabolites, leading to necrosis and inflammation of liver cells. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver injury and acute alcoholic hepatitis. The primary causative agent is chronic alcohol abuse. The condition typically affects the liver, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms include jaundice, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes. It is more severe in individuals with a history of heavy drinking and can progress to cirrhosis if alcohol use continues.

Alcoholic hepatitis with cirrhosis is a severe liver condition caused by prolonged heavy alcohol consumption, leading to inflammation and scarring of the liver tissue. It is a form of alcoholic liver disease and represents the advanced stage of alcoholic liver injury. Common synonyms include alcoholic cirrhosis and end-stage alcoholic liver disease. The primary causative agent is chronic alcohol use. The liver is the predominantly affected organ, with systemic complications such as ascites, jaundice, and hepatic encephalopathy commonly occurring.

Other specified alcoholic hepatitis refers to liver inflammation caused by excessive alcohol consumption, not fitting the criteria for alcoholic cirrhosis or acute alcoholic hepatitis. It is characterized by elevated liver enzymes and histological changes indicative of hepatitis. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver disease and alcoholic steatohepatitis. The primary causative agent is chronic alcohol use. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Diagnosis is based on clinical evaluation, laboratory tests, and exclusion of other liver diseases.

Alcoholic hepatitis, unspecified, is an inflammatory condition of the liver caused by excessive alcohol consumption. It leads to liver cell damage, inflammation, and necrosis. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver disease and alcoholic hepatitis. The primary causative agent is chronic alcohol use, though the exact mechanism is multifactorial. The liver is the main affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms may include jaundice, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes. It is typically seen in individuals with a history of heavy alcohol use.

Alcoholic liver fibrosis is a progressive scarring of the liver caused by chronic alcohol consumption. Prolonged ethanol exposure leads to inflammation and deposition of extracellular matrix proteins, resulting in fibrous tissue formation. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver disease and alcoholic cirrhosis. The primary causative agent is excessive alcohol intake. The liver is the predominantly affected organ, with potential complications such as portal hypertension and hepatic encephalopathy. Early stages may be reversible, but advanced fibrosis often progresses to cirrhosis.

code_desc: Alcoholic cirrhosis of liver without hepatitis
summary: Alcoholic cirrhosis of the liver without hepatitis is a chronic liver disease caused by prolonged heavy alcohol consumption, leading to progressive scarring and loss of liver function. It is characterized by the replacement of healthy liver tissue with fibrous scar tissue, resulting in impaired detoxification and metabolic functions. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver cirrhosis and alcoholic liver disease. The primary causative agent is chronic alcohol abuse. The liver is the predominantly affected organ, with potential complications affecting the gastrointestinal tract, coagulation system, and other organs due to systemic effects of liver failure.

Other specified alcoholic liver disease refers to alcoholic liver injury that does not meet the full criteria for alcoholic hepatitis or cirrhosis. It encompasses a range of liver abnormalities caused by chronic alcohol consumption. Common synonyms include alcoholic liver injury and unspecified alcoholic liver disease. The primary causative agent is long-term alcohol use. This condition typically affects the liver, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potential progression to cirrhosis. It may also involve the biliary system and is associated with systemic effects such as malnutrition and immune dysfunction.

Alcoholic liver disease, unspecified, refers to liver damage caused by chronic alcohol consumption without specific classification as alcoholic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or fatty liver. Common synonyms include alcohol-induced liver injury and alcoholic liver damage. The primary causative agent is excessive alcohol intake over prolonged periods. The condition typically affects the liver, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, and potential cirrhosis. It may also involve the pancreas and gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms include jaundice, ascites, and coagulopathy. Early diagnosis and cessation of alcohol use are critical for prevention of progression.

Drug-induced or toxic liver disease refers to liver damage caused by medications, supplements, or toxins. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis and hepatotoxicity. Causative agents include acetaminophen, NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, and certain antibiotics. The liver is typically affected, with symptoms such as jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatic necrosis. The condition can range from mild injury to acute liver failure. It is often reversible if the causative agent is discontinued promptly.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with acute hepatic necrosis or acute hepatitis
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with acute hepatic necrosis or acute hepatitis refers to liver injury caused by medications, chemicals, or toxins. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and toxic hepatitis. Causative agents include acetaminophen, anticonvulsants, antibiotics, and certain herbal supplements. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation, necrosis, and impaired function. It can progress rapidly and may result in fulminant hepatic failure. The liver is the main affected organ, though systemic symptoms may occur. Early diagnosis and discontinuation of the offending agent are critical for recovery.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis refers to liver inflammation and damage caused by prolonged exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced chronic hepatitis and toxic hepatitis. Causative agents often include medications such as acetaminophen, anticonvulsants, and certain antibiotics. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and potential cirrhosis. It may also involve the biliary system. Symptoms include fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Early diagnosis and discontinuation of the offending agent are critical for recovery.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis with cirrhosis
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis refers to progressive liver damage caused by prolonged exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and toxic hepatitis. Causative agents include acetaminophen, antitubercular drugs, anabolic steroids, and certain herbal supplements. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and eventual cirrhosis. It may also involve systemic manifestations such as jaundice, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy. Early diagnosis and discontinuation of the causative agent are critical for preventing irreversible liver damage.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis without cirrhosis
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis without cirrhosis refers to liver inflammation caused by medications or toxins, leading to chronic hepatitis but not progressing to cirrhosis. Common synonyms include drug-induced chronic hepatitis and toxic liver injury. Causative agents include acetaminophen, anticonvulsants, antibiotics, and certain herbal supplements. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic effects. Diagnosis involves clinical history, liver function tests, and exclusion of other causes. Prognosis is generally favorable with discontinuation of the offending agent.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis, unspecified
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic hepatitis, unspecified refers to liver inflammation and damage caused by prolonged exposure to medications or toxins. Common synonyms include drug-induced chronic hepatitis or toxic hepatitis. Causative agents may include acetaminophen, anticonvulsants, antibiotics, and herbal supplements. The liver is the primary affected organ, often presenting with elevated liver enzymes, fatigue, and jaundice. Chronic progression can lead to fibrosis or cirrhosis if not managed. Diagnosis typically involves liver function tests and exclusion of other causes.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis is a condition characterized by impaired bile flow leading to jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. It results from exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced cholestasis and toxic cholestasis. Causative agents include medications such as statins, antifungals, anesthetics, and certain antibiotics. Typically, the liver is affected, with possible involvement of the biliary tract. Symptoms may include pruritus, dark urine, and right upper quadrant pain. The condition can progress to cholangiopathy or cirrhosis if left untreated.

code_desc: Chronic drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis
summary: Chronic drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis is a progressive liver condition characterized by impaired bile flow and accumulation of bile pigments, leading to jaundice and pruritus. Common synonyms include drug-induced cholestasis and toxic cholestasis. Causative agents include medications such as statins, antifungals, and anabolic steroids. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary tract. Symptoms often include fatigue, dark urine, and elevated liver enzymes. Long-term exposure can result in fibrosis or cirrhosis.

code_desc: Other specified drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis
summary: Other specified drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis refers to liver injury characterized by impaired bile flow, often secondary to medication or toxin exposure. Common synonyms include drug-induced cholestasis or toxic cholestasis. Causative agents may include certain antibiotics, anticonvulsants, and anabolic steroids. The condition typically affects the liver, particularly the bile ducts and parenchyma, leading to jaundice, pruritus, and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels. It is distinct from other forms of drug-induced liver injury and is often reversible upon discontinuation of the offending agent.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis, unspecified
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with cholestasis, unspecified, refers to liver injury characterized by impaired bile flow, often resulting from medication or toxin exposure. Common synonyms include drug-induced cholestasis and toxic cholestasis. Causative agents may include antibiotics, antifungals, anticonvulsants, and certain herbal supplements. The liver is typically affected, with possible involvement of the biliary tract. Symptoms may include jaundice, pruritus, and elevated liver enzymes. This condition can progress to cholangiopathy or liver failure if not addressed.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fatty liver
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fatty liver refers to liver injury caused by medications or toxins, often accompanied by hepatic steatosis. Common synonyms include drug-induced steatohepatitis and toxic fatty liver. Causative agents include acetaminophen, statins, antituberculosis drugs, and certain antibiotics. The condition typically affects the liver, with fatty infiltration and inflammation. It may progress to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, or cirrhosis if left untreated. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic effects can occur with severe toxicity.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic fatty liver disease
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with chronic fatty liver disease refers to liver damage caused by medications or toxins, leading to accumulation of fat in liver cells. Common synonyms include drug-induced steatosis and toxic steatohepatitis. Causative agents include alcohol, antituberculosis drugs, statins, and certain anabolic steroids. The liver is typically affected, with potential progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis involves clinical history, imaging, and liver function tests.

code_desc: Other specified drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fatty liver
summary: Other specified drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fatty liver refers to liver injury caused by medications or toxins, accompanied by hepatic steatosis. Common synonyms include drug-induced steatosis or toxic fatty liver. Causative agents may include antiretrovirals, anticonvulsants, statins, and certain herbal supplements. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to inflammation, fat accumulation, and potential fibrosis. It is often reversible upon discontinuation of the offending agent. The liver is the main affected body part, though systemic effects may occur in severe cases.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fatty liver, unspecified
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fatty liver, unspecified refers to liver injury caused by medications or toxins, often accompanied by fatty infiltration of the liver. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis and toxic fatty liver. Causative agents may include acetaminophen, statins, anticonvulsants, and certain herbal supplements. The liver is typically affected, with possible involvement of other organs in severe cases. Symptoms may include jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, laboratory tests, and imaging. Treatment involves discontinuation of the offending agent and supportive care.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with granulomatous hepatitis
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with granulomatous hepatitis is a form of liver injury characterized by the formation of granulomas in response to toxic agents. Common synonyms include drug-induced granulomatous hepatitis and toxic granulomatous hepatitis. Causative agents often include anticonvulsants like phenytoin, hydantoin derivatives, and certain antibiotics such as isoniazid. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic involvement may occur. This condition typically presents with elevated liver enzymes, jaundice, and sometimes fever. It is distinct from other forms of hepatitis due to the presence of granulomatous inflammation.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fibrosis or cirrhosis of liver
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with fibrosis or cirrhosis refers to liver damage caused by exposure to hepatotoxic substances, leading to progressive scarring and loss of liver function. Common synonyms include drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and toxic hepatitis. Causative agents include acetaminophen, alcohol, antitubercular drugs, and certain antibiotics. The liver is the primary affected organ, with fibrosis and cirrhosis developing over time due to persistent injury and inflammation. This condition can result in portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic encephalopathy if left untreated.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with vascular disorders of the liver
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with vascular disorders of the liver refers to liver injury caused by medications or toxins, often accompanied by vascular abnormalities such as sinusoidal obstruction syndrome. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatic injury and hepatic vasculopathy. Causative agents include acetaminophen, methotrexate, and certain antituberculosis drugs. The condition primarily affects the liver, with potential involvement of the biliary system and systemic vasculature. It can lead to portal hypertension, ascites, and hepatic failure if untreated.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with liver tumours
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease with liver tumours refers to liver damage and tumor formation caused by exposure to hepatotoxic substances. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis with neoplasia and toxic liver injury with malignancy. Causative agents include acetaminophen, certain anticonvulsants, chemotherapy drugs, and herbal supplements. The liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic effects may occur. This condition can lead to cirrhosis, fibrosis, and various types of liver tumors, including hepatocellular carcinoma. Early diagnosis and discontinuation of the causative agent are critical for management.

code_desc: Other specified drug-induced or toxic liver disease
summary: Other specified drug-induced or toxic liver disease refers to liver injury caused by medications or substances not classified under other specific categories of drug-induced liver injury. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis or toxic hepatitis. Causative agents may include acetaminophen, anticonvulsants, antibiotics, and certain herbal supplements. The liver is typically affected, with symptoms such as jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatic dysfunction. This condition is often diagnosed when the etiology is known but does not fit into more specific classifications.

code_desc: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease, unspecified
summary: Drug-induced or toxic liver disease, unspecified refers to liver injury caused by medications, supplements, or chemicals, with the specific agent not identified. Common synonyms include drug-induced hepatitis and chemical liver injury. Causative agents may include acetaminophen, NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, and certain herbal products. The liver is typically affected, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms may include jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, and hepatic dysfunction. Diagnosis often requires a thorough medication history and exclusion of other liver diseases.

Autoimmune liver disease refers to a group of conditions where the immune system mistakenly attacks liver cells, leading to inflammation and potential liver damage. Common synonyms include autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. These conditions are caused by a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental factors. They primarily affect the liver, with autoimmune hepatitis targeting hepatocytes, while primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis involve bile ducts. The diseases can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure if left untreated.

Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic inflammatory liver disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of hepatocytes. It occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks liver cells, leading to progressive liver damage. Common synonyms include autoimmune liver disease and autoimmune liver injury. The exact causative agents are unknown, but genetic predisposition and environmental triggers are implicated. The liver is the primary affected organ, and the condition can lead to cirrhosis and liver failure if untreated. It typically affects women more frequently than men.

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), formerly known as primary biliary cirrhosis, is a chronic, autoimmune liver disease characterized by the progressive destruction of small bile ducts in the liver. The immune system mistakenly attacks the bile ducts, leading to impaired bile flow, cholestasis, and eventual liver damage. Common synonyms include primary biliary cirrhosis and autoimmune cholangitis. The condition primarily affects the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to fibrosis and cirrhosis over time. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic and environmental factors are believed to play a role. It predominantly affects middle-aged women.

code_desc: Primary biliary cholangitis with overlap syndrome
summary: Primary biliary cholangitis with overlap syndrome is a chronic cholestatic liver disease characterized by progressive destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts, often accompanied by features of autoimmune hepatitis or primary sclerosing cholangitis. Common synonyms include autoimmune cholangiopathy and overlap syndrome. The condition is associated with antimitochondrial antibodies and is thought to have an autoimmune etiology, though specific causative agents remain unclear. It predominantly affects the liver, leading to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and eventually liver failure. The biliary system, particularly the intrahepatic bile ducts, is the primary site of injury.

Other specified primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) refers to cases of cholestatic liver disease that meet diagnostic criteria for PBC but lack the typical features of classic PBC, such as antimitochondrial antibodies or progressive fibrosis. It may involve varying degrees of biliary injury and fibrosis. Common synonyms include autoimmune cholangiopathy and unspecified primary biliary cholangitis. Causative agents are primarily autoimmune, though environmental factors may contribute. The condition primarily affects the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to cholestasis, liver damage, and eventual cirrhosis if untreated.

Primary biliary cholangitis, unspecified, is a chronic, progressive liver disease characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts. Common synonyms include primary biliary cirrhosis and autoimmune cholangitis. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic and environmental factors are implicated. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to cholestasis, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis. It predominantly occurs in middle-aged women and may present with fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice. Complications include portal hypertension and liver failure.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic, progressive cholestatic liver disease characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of the bile ducts, leading to strictures and eventual cirrhosis. Common synonyms include biliary cirrhosis and sclerosing cholangitis. The exact cause is unknown, though it is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis. The condition primarily affects the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, leading to impaired bile flow and increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma. It predominantly occurs in adults, with a male preponderance.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis with cirrhosis is a chronic liver disease characterized by progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the bile ducts, leading to cirrhosis. It is often associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis. The condition results in bile duct obstruction, cholangitis, and eventual liver failure. Common synonyms include biliary cirrhosis and autoimmune cholangitis. Known causative agents include autoimmune mechanisms and genetic factors, though specific pathogens are not well established.
