The liver and bile ducts are the primary affected body parts.

Other specified primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) refers to cases of primary sclerosing cholangitis that do not meet the full diagnostic criteria for classic PSC but exhibit similar histopathological or clinical features. It is often associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis. The condition involves progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the bile ducts, leading to strictures and cholangiocarcinoma risk. Common synonyms include uncertain or atypical PSC. Causative agents are largely unknown, though genetic and environmental factors are implicated. The liver and bile ducts are primarily affected, with potential complications such as cholangitis and cirrhosis.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disease of the bile ducts, leading to progressive stricturing and obstruction. Common synonyms include biliary cirrhosis and chronic sclerosing cholangitis. The exact cause is unknown, though it is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, particularly ulcerative colitis. The condition primarily affects the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, leading to cholestasis, portal hypertension, and eventual cirrhosis. It is more common in males and typically presents in middle age. Complications include cholangiocarcinoma and recurrent cholangitis.

Other specified autoimmune liver disease refers to autoimmune liver conditions that do not meet the full criteria for autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, or primary sclerosing cholangitis. It encompasses a range of rare, overlapping, or undefined autoimmune liver disorders. Common synonyms include autoimmune liver disease not otherwise specified. Known causative agents are primarily immune-mediated, though specific triggers are often unknown. The disease typically affects the liver, leading to inflammation and fibrosis, and may involve the biliary system. It predominantly affects middle-aged women.

Autoimmune liver disease, unspecified refers to a group of chronic liver disorders characterized by immune-mediated injury to liver cells, leading to inflammation and potential fibrosis. Common synonyms include autoimmune hepatitis and autoimmune liver injury. The exact causative agents are not fully understood, but genetic predisposition and environmental factors are implicated. The liver is the primary affected organ, with systemic manifestations possible in some cases. It is typically diagnosed in adults, though it can occur in children. The condition is associated with other autoimmune disorders and may progress to cirrhosis if untreated.

Certain specified inflammatory liver diseases refer to a group of conditions characterized by immune-mediated inflammation of the liver. Common synonyms include autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cholangitis. These conditions are often caused by autoimmune mechanisms, although viral infections such as hepatitis B and C can also contribute. The liver is the primary affected organ, with inflammation leading to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and potential liver failure. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal discomfort. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent progression.

Idiopathic granulomatous hepatitis is a rare, chronic inflammatory liver disease characterized by the formation of non-caseating granulomas. Common synonyms include sarcoidosis of the liver and granulomatous hepatitis of unknown origin. The exact cause is unknown, though it is often associated with sarcoidosis. The condition primarily affects the liver, with granulomas typically found in the portal tracts. It may also involve other organs, such as the lungs, lymph nodes, and skin. The disease is more common in women and typically presents with elevated liver enzymes, fatigue, and hepatomegaly. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other granulomatous diseases and confirmation by histopathology.

Hepatic berylliosis is a granulomatous disease caused by inhalation of beryllium, leading to systemic exposure and organ involvement. It primarily affects the lungs but can involve the liver, spleen, and lymph nodes. The condition is characterized by the formation of noncaseating granulomas in affected tissues. Common synonyms include beryllium disease and chronic beryllium disease. The causative agent is beryllium, a metal used in aerospace and electronics industries. The liver is typically affected in the systemic form, often presenting with elevated liver enzymes and hepatic granulomas.

Chronic hepatitis, not elsewhere classified, refers to long-term inflammation of the liver of unknown specific cause. Common synonyms include chronic hepatitis of unspecified origin. Causative agents may include viral infections like hepatitis B or C, autoimmune disorders, or prolonged alcohol use. The condition primarily affects the liver, leading to progressive fibrosis and potential cirrhosis. Symptoms may include fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal discomfort. Diagnosis often involves liver function tests and imaging. Management focuses on identifying and addressing underlying causes and monitoring disease progression.

Other specified inflammatory liver disease refers to chronic liver inflammation not classified under more specific categories like hepatitis or autoimmune liver disease. It may involve infiltration of inflammatory cells and parenchymal damage. Common synonyms include non-specific liver inflammation or unspecified chronic hepatitis. Causative agents can include medications, toxins, or unknown factors. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of biliary tract and surrounding tissues. Clinical presentation varies but often includes elevated liver enzymes, fatigue, and jaundice. Diagnosis typically requires exclusion of other known liver diseases.

Inflammatory liver disease, unspecified refers to liver inflammation of unknown origin or unspecified type. Common synonyms include non-specific hepatitis and undetermined liver inflammation. Causative agents may include viral infections, autoimmune disorders, toxins, or metabolic factors. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of the biliary system. Symptoms often include jaundice, fatigue, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis typically involves blood tests and imaging, with treatment directed at underlying causes when identified.

Vascular disorders of the liver encompass conditions affecting the blood vessels within the liver, leading to impaired blood flow and potential tissue damage. Common synonyms include hepatic vascular anomalies and portal hypertension-related disorders. Causative agents may include alcohol abuse, autoimmune diseases, infections, or congenital abnormalities. These disorders typically affect the portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic veins, with conditions such as Budd-Chiari syndrome and portal vein thrombosis being prevalent. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, ascites, and jaundice, depending on the specific vascular pathology involved.

Infarction of the liver, also known as hepatic infarction or hepatic necrosis due to arterial occlusion, is a rare condition resulting from sudden interruption of blood flow to a portion of the liver. It is typically caused by embolism or thrombosis of the hepatic artery, leading to ischemia and necrosis of liver tissue. Common synonyms include hepatic infarction and arterial liver infarction. The condition predominantly affects the right lobe of the liver, as it receives the majority of its blood supply from the right hepatic artery. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, and elevated liver enzymes. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications.

Peliosis hepatis is a rare condition characterized by the formation of multiple blood-filled cystic spaces within the liver parenchyma. Common synonyms include hepatic peliosis and cavernous hemangioma of the liver. It is primarily associated with chronic use of anabolic steroids, immunosuppressive agents, and certain infections such as HIV. The condition typically affects the liver, though extraparenchymal involvement can occur. Clinically, it may present with abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, and in severe cases, hemoperitoneum or liver failure. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by imaging studies and histopathological examination.

Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) of the liver is a rare, non-cirrhotic condition characterized by the formation of regenerative nodules in the liver parenchyma due to impaired hepatic artery flow. Common synonyms include hepatic nodular regenerative hyperplasia and non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis. Causative agents include medications (e.g., methotrexate, tamoxifen), infections (e.g., schistosomiasis), and systemic disorders (e.g., myeloproliferative diseases). It typically affects the liver, with nodules distributed throughout the parenchyma. The condition is often asymptomatic but may present with portal hypertension or splenomegaly. Diagnosis is confirmed by liver biopsy.

Portal vein thrombosis is a condition characterized by the formation of a blood clot within the portal vein, which carries blood from the gastrointestinal tract to the liver. Common synonyms include portal venous occlusion and portal thrombosis. It is often caused by conditions such as cirrhosis, liver cancer, or hypercoagulable states. Other causative agents may include infections, trauma, or post-surgical complications. The liver is typically affected, leading to portal hypertension and potential complications like ascites or variceal bleeding. The condition can also impact the spleen and gastrointestinal system.

Splenic vein thrombosis is a condition characterized by the formation of a blood clot within the splenic vein, often leading to splenomegaly and portal hypertension. Common synonyms include splenic vein occlusion and splenic vein embolism. Causative agents may include hypercoagulable states, infections, trauma, or tumors. It typically affects the splenic vein and can involve the portal venous system. The condition is associated with increased risk of splenic infarction and may present with abdominal pain, fullness, or systemic symptoms. It is more common in individuals with underlying liver disease or chronic inflammatory conditions.

Budd-Chiari syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow, leading to hepatic congestion and dysfunction. Common synonyms include hepatic venous outflow obstruction and posthepatic portal hypertension. Causative agents include thrombosis, hepatic vein compression, or congenital anomalies. The condition primarily affects the liver, causing features such as ascites, hepatomegaly, and elevated portal pressure. It may also involve the inferior vena cava and right atrium. Clinically, it presents with abdominal pain, jaundice, and signs of liver failure. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications like liver necrosis or variceal bleeding.

Hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD), also known as sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), is a condition characterized by obstruction of the hepatic sinusoids, leading to portal hypertension and liver dysfunction. It is commonly associated with chemotherapy, particularly myelosuppressive agents, and bone marrow transplantation. Other causes include toxins, infections, and metabolic disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, with symptoms such as jaundice, ascites, and hepatomegaly. VOD can progress to liver failure if not managed appropriately.

Portal hypertension is elevated pressure in the portal venous system, primarily due to obstructed blood flow through the liver. Common causes include cirrhosis, schistosomiasis, and thrombosis. It leads to collateral vessel formation, ascites, and variceal bleeding. The condition predominantly affects the liver and gastrointestinal tract. Synonyms include portal venous hypertension and portal systemic hypertension. Clinically, it is associated with splenomegaly and increased risk of gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Diagnosis often involves imaging and measurement of portal pressure. Management focuses on reducing portal pressure and preventing complications.

Idiopathic portal hypertension is a condition characterized by elevated portal venous pressure without an identifiable cause. It is also known as cryptogenic portal hypertension. Common synonyms include cryptogenic portal hypertension and idiopathic portal hypertension. The condition typically affects the liver and spleen, leading to splenomegaly and portal-systemic shunts. Known causative agents are often absent, though some cases may be associated with chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, or other unknown factors. The primary clinical manifestations include ascites, esophageal varices, and hypersplenism.

Non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis is a liver condition characterized by fibrous tissue proliferation in the portal tracts without progressing to cirrhosis. It is often associated with chronic inflammation and is a precursor to cirrhosis in some cases. Common synonyms include portal fibrosis without cirrhosis and non-cirrhotic portal tract fibrosis. Known causative agents include autoimmune hepatitis, chronic viral hepatitis, and prolonged alcohol use. The liver is the primary affected organ, with fibrosis localized to the portal regions. It may present with mild elevations in liver enzymes and is often detected incidentally on biopsy.

Partial nodular transformation of the liver, also known as regenerative nodular transformation or nodular regenerative hyperplasia, is a benign hepatic condition characterized by the formation of regenerative nodules in the liver parenchyma. It is typically associated with portal hypertension, often due to conditions such as cirrhosis or Budd-Chiari syndrome. The nodules result from an imbalance between hepatic cell proliferation and fibrosis. Common synonyms include regenerative nodular hyperplasia and nodular regenerative hyperplasia. The liver is the primarily affected organ, with no significant involvement of other body systems.

Splanchnic arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal direct connection between an artery and a vein in the abdominal organs. Common synonyms include visceral arteriovenous fistula and mesenteric arteriovenous fistula. It is often caused by trauma, iatrogenic injury, or neoplasms. The condition typically affects the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms may include abdominal bruits, varicosities, and signs of volume overload. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by imaging studies such as ultrasound or angiography. Treatment may involve embolization or surgical repair.

Secondary portal hypertension is increased pressure in the portal venous system due to obstruction distal to the splenic hilum. Common synonyms include portal hypertension of portal origin. It is most commonly caused by liver cirrhosis, but can also result from thrombosis of the portal vein, schistosomiasis, or hematologic disorders. The condition typically affects the liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract, leading to collateral circulation, ascites, and esophageal varices. Clinically, it is associated with portal vein resistance and impaired blood flow from the intestines to the liver.

Other specified portal hypertension refers to portal hypertension not attributable to cirrhosis or other specified causes. It is characterized by elevated portal venous pressure due to obstructive or non-obstructive factors. Common synonyms include non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and portal hypertension of unknown etiology. Causative agents may include schistosomiasis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, and congenital hepatic fibrosis. The condition primarily affects the liver and portal venous system, leading to complications such as esophageal varices, ascites, and splenomegaly.

Portal hypertension, unspecified, refers to elevated pressure within the portal venous system without a specific identified cause. Common synonyms include portal hypertension, unspecified etiology. It is often caused by liver cirrhosis, thrombosis, or congenital anomalies. The condition primarily affects the liver and may lead to complications such as esophageal varices, ascites, and splenomegaly. It is typically associated with portal vein obstruction or increased resistance to blood flow through the liver. The main affected body parts include the liver, gastrointestinal tract, and abdomen.

Passive congestion of the liver, also known as hepatic venous congestion or congestive hepatopathy, occurs due to impaired venous outflow from the liver, leading to engorgement of sinusoids and centrilobular necrosis. Common causes include right heart failure, hepatic vein thrombosis, or Budd-Chiari syndrome. This condition primarily affects the liver, with characteristic findings of enlarged, firm liver and elevated liver enzymes. It may also lead to ascites and peripheral edema. Synonyms include hepatic venous congestion and congestive liver disease. The main affected body parts are the liver and systemic venous system.

Hepatic artery aneurysm is a rare, localized dilation of the hepatic artery, typically occurring in the distal portion. It is often asymptomatic but can present with abdominal pain, bleeding, or rupture. Common synonyms include hepatic artery aneurysm and hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm. Causative agents include trauma, infection, and atherosclerosis. It predominantly affects the right hepatic artery and is more common in females. Complications such as hemorrhage or embolism may occur, necessitating imaging and interventional management.

Hepatic haemorrhage refers to bleeding within the liver parenchyma, often resulting from trauma, coagulopathy, or vascular abnormalities. Common synonyms include hepatic hemorrhage and liver hemorrhage. Causative agents may include blunt abdominal injury, anticoagulant therapy, cirrhosis, or ruptured hepatic hemangiomas. The liver is the primary affected organ, with bleeding potentially leading to hemoperitoneum or hypovolemic shock. Clinical presentation may include hypotension, abdominal pain, and signs of internal bleeding. Prompt diagnosis and management are critical to prevent complications and improve outcomes.

Ischaemia reperfusion injury of the liver occurs when blood flow is restored to liver tissue after a period of reduced perfusion, leading to oxidative stress and cellular damage. Common synonyms include reperfusion injury and ischemia-reperfusion injury. Causative agents include shock, trauma, surgery, and transplantation. The liver is typically affected, with injury also potentially involving other organs. This condition is associated with inflammation, necrosis, and impaired function, often complicating procedures requiring temporary circulatory compromise.

code_desc: Other specified vascular disorders of the liver
summary: "Other specified vascular disorders of the liver" refers to rare vascular abnormalities of the liver not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include hepatic vascular malformations or congenital hepatic fibrosis. These conditions may result from genetic mutations, developmental anomalies, or acquired factors. They typically affect the liver parenchyma, portal vein, or hepatic arteries, leading to complications such as portal hypertension, hemorrhage, or liver dysfunction. The exact causative agents vary, but genetic predisposition and abnormal vascular development are often implicated.

code_desc: Vascular disorders of the liver, unspecified
summary: Vascular disorders of the liver, unspecified, refer to abnormalities in the blood vessels supplying or draining the liver, leading to impaired circulation. Common synonyms include hepatic vascular anomalies and liver vasculopathy. Causative agents may include hypertension, coagulopathy, or congenital malformations. These conditions typically affect the hepatic artery, portal vein, or sinusoids. Symptoms may include portal hypertension, liver dysfunction, or bleeding. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic involvement in severe cases. Diagnosis often requires imaging and vascular studies.

Certain specified diseases of the liver encompass a range of conditions affecting liver structure and function. Common synonyms include hepatic disorders, liver disease, and hepatopathy. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B and C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, and drug-induced injury. These conditions typically affect the liver, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, cirrhosis, or failure. They may also involve the biliary system and, in some cases, the gastrointestinal tract. Symptoms often include jaundice, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent progression and complications.

Chronic liver disease refers to long-term damage or dysfunction of the liver, often leading to fibrosis, cirrhosis, or liver failure. Common synonyms include hepatic insufficiency and chronic liver dysfunction. Causative agents include viral hepatitis (B, C), alcohol abuse, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, autoimmune disorders, and metabolic conditions. The liver is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic effects on coagulation, metabolism, and immune function. Early diagnosis and management are critical to prevent progression to end-stage liver disease.

Hepatic cyst is a fluid-filled sac within the liver, typically benign. Common synonyms include hepatic cystic lesion and simple hepatic cyst. It is most commonly congenital, arising from biliary duct anomalies, though acquired forms may occur due to trauma or infection. The condition predominantly affects the liver, with cysts often located in the right lobe. Rarely, it may involve other organs, such as the pancreas or kidneys, in cases of polycystic disease. Most cysts are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging studies. Complications may include infection, rupture, or mass effect.

Polycystic liver disease (PLD) is a chronic condition characterized by the development of multiple fluid-filled cysts in the liver. It is often inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and is frequently associated with polycystic kidney disease. Common synonyms include hepatic cystic disease and hereditary polycystic liver disease. The primary affected body part is the liver, though the kidneys are also commonly involved. Causative agents include mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes. The disease typically progresses slowly, leading to liver enlargement and potential complications such as pain, infection, or rupture.

Other specified hepatic cyst refers to a non-epididymal, non-pancreatic cyst of the liver that does not meet the criteria for specific types such as simple or hydatid cyst. It may include congenital or acquired cysts of undefined origin. Common synonyms include unspecified hepatic cyst or miscellaneous hepatic cyst. Causative agents are often unknown, though some may arise from trauma, infection, or congenital factors. Typically affects the liver parenchyma, with no specific predilection for particular regions.

Hepatic cyst, unspecified, refers to a fluid-filled sac within the liver without a specific type or cause identified. Common synonyms include simple hepatic cyst and congenital hepatic cyst. It is typically a benign condition, often asymptomatic, and may be discovered incidentally on imaging. The primary affected body part is the liver, though cysts can occur in other organs. Causative agents are usually unknown, but may include congenital factors, trauma, or parasitic infections. Most cases are solitary and do not require treatment unless they cause symptoms or complications.

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional renal failure occurring in patients with advanced liver disease, particularly cirrhosis. It is characterized by progressive renal dysfunction without underlying kidney disease. Common synonyms include functional renal failure and cirrhosis-associated renal failure. Causative agents are primarily related to liver failure, such as hepatitis B or C, alcohol-related cirrhosis, and drug-induced liver injury. The condition predominantly affects the kidneys, leading to oliguria, azotemia, and fluid retention. It is a life-threatening complication with poor prognosis.

Portopulmonary hypertension (PPH) is a form of pulmonary hypertension characterized by elevated pulmonary artery pressures in patients with liver disease, particularly cirrhosis. It is a rare condition that may develop independently or as part of porto-systemic shunting. Common synonyms include cirrhotic pulmonary hypertension and portal hypertension-associated pulmonary hypertension. The primary causative agents are liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension, often due to chronic liver disease, alcohol abuse, or viral hepatitis. The condition primarily affects the pulmonary vasculature, leading to right heart strain and potentially right heart failure.

Hepatopulmonary syndrome is a condition characterized by abnormal pulmonary vasodilation secondary to liver disease, leading to intrapulmonary shunting and hypoxemia. It commonly occurs in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. Synonyms include portal-arterial shunting syndrome and hepatic pulmonary syndrome. Known causative agents include chronic liver disease, particularly cirrhosis, and portal hypertension. The primary affected body parts are the liver and lungs, with clinical manifestations primarily involving respiratory and hepatic systems.

Hepatic encephalopathy is a neurological disorder caused by liver dysfunction, leading to impaired detoxification and accumulation of toxins in the brain. Common synonyms include hepatic coma and portosystemic encephalopathy. It is typically caused by liver cirrhosis, but can also result from acute liver failure, gastrointestinal bleeding, or portal hypertension. The condition primarily affects the central nervous system, causing symptoms such as confusion, altered mental status, and in severe cases, coma. The liver and brain are the main organs involved, with the brain being the primary site of dysfunction.

Intrahepatic cholestasis, not elsewhere classified, is a liver disorder characterized by impaired bile flow within the liver, leading to cholestasis. Common synonyms include cholestatic jaundice and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. It is often caused by drugs, pregnancy, or underlying liver disease. The condition primarily affects the liver, causing jaundice, pruritus, and elevated serum bile acids. It may also involve the biliary system and gastrointestinal tract, leading to symptoms such as dark urine and pale stools. The exact cause is not always identifiable, but it is typically managed with supportive care and addressing underlying factors.

Cholestasis of parenteral nutrition is a condition characterized by impaired bile flow, leading to jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. It commonly occurs in patients receiving long-term total parenteral nutrition (TPN). Synonyms include parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis and TPN cholestasis. Causative agents include fat emulsion toxicity, nutritional deficiencies, and impaired bile salt synthesis. The liver is typically affected, with possible involvement of the biliary tract. Clinical features include pruritus, dark urine, and steatorrhea. Early recognition and adjustment of TPN regimen are critical to prevent complications.

Other specified intrahepatic cholestasis is a rare liver disorder characterized by impaired bile flow within the liver, leading to cholestasis without a specific identifiable cause. It may present with pruritus, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Common synonyms include unspecified intrahepatic cholestasis and non-specific intrahepatic cholestasis. Known causative agents may include drugs, infections, or metabolic disorders. The condition typically affects the liver, with bile accumulation leading to systemic symptoms. It is often diagnosed when other forms of cholestasis are excluded.

Intrahepatic cholestasis, unspecified, is a disorder characterized by impaired bile flow within the liver, leading to elevated serum bile acids and jaundice. Common synonyms include cholestasis, unspecified, and intrahepatic cholestasis of unknown origin. It may result from various causes such as drug toxicity, viral hepatitis, or autoimmune liver disease. Typically affecting the liver, it can also involve the gallbladder and biliary tract. The condition is more common in women, particularly during pregnancy, and may present with pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools. The exact cause is often unknown, hence the "unspecified" designation.

code_desc: Hepatic failure without mention whether acute or chronic
summary: Hepatic failure refers to the loss of liver function, which can be acute or chronic, though the term encompasses both without specifying the duration. Common synonyms include liver failure and hepatic dysfunction. Causative agents include viral hepatitis, alcohol abuse, drug toxicity, and metabolic disorders. The liver is the primary affected organ, but systemic complications may involve the brain (hepatic encephalopathy), kidneys, and circulatory system. Symptoms include jaundice, coagulopathy, and altered mental status. It is a life-threatening condition requiring prompt medical intervention.

Chronic hepatic failure refers to progressive and irreversible loss of liver function over time, leading to impaired detoxification, metabolism, and synthesis of essential proteins. Common synonyms include chronic liver failure and end-stage liver disease. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis (B, C), alcoholic liver disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and autoimmune hepatitis. The liver is the primary affected organ, with systemic complications such as ascites, encephalopathy, and coagulopathy often occurring. It typically affects adults, though onset can vary.

"Other specified diseases of liver" refers to liver conditions not classified under more specific categories such as hepatitis or cirrhosis. Common synonyms include unspecified liver disease and other liver disorders. Causative agents may include toxins, drugs, metabolic disorders, or infections. These conditions typically affect the liver parenchyma, leading to inflammation, fibrosis, or dysfunction. They may present with symptoms like jaundice, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis often requires imaging, blood tests, and clinical evaluation. The exact cause and affected areas vary depending on the underlying condition.

Diseases of liver, unspecified refer to liver conditions where the specific diagnosis is not identified. Common synonyms include undiagnosed liver disease or non-specific liver pathology. Causative agents may include viral hepatitis, alcohol abuse, drug toxicity, or metabolic disorders. Typically, the liver is the primary affected organ, though systemic manifestations may occur. Symptoms often include jaundice, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. Diagnosis usually involves imaging, blood tests, and sometimes biopsy. Treatment depends on underlying causes and may involve lifestyle changes, medications, or supportive care.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of gallbladder or bile ducts
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of the gallbladder or bile ducts refer to structural changes resulting from disease or injury. Common synonyms include gallbladder disease, biliary tract abnormalities, and cholelithiasis. Causative agents may include gallstones, chronic inflammation, infections like cholangitis, or tumors. These conditions typically affect the gallbladder, common bile duct, and surrounding hepatic structures. Symptoms often involve pain, obstruction, and altered bile flow. Complications can include cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, and biliary cirrhosis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies such as ultrasound or MRI.

code_desc: Obstruction of gallbladder or bile ducts
summary: Obstruction of the gallbladder or bile ducts refers to the blockage of bile flow from the liver to the small intestine. Common synonyms include cholangitis, choledocholithiasis, and biliary obstruction. This condition is most commonly caused by gallstones, which can lodge in the cystic or common bile duct. Other causes include tumors, strictures, or inflammation. The gallbladder and bile ducts are typically affected, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, jaundice, and fever. Complications may include cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis if the obstruction persists.

Obstruction of the cystic duct is a blockage of the duct that drains bile from the gallbladder into the common bile duct. It commonly results from gallstones, strictures, or tumors. This condition can lead to cholecystitis, cholangitis, or pancreatitis. Synonyms include cystic duct obstruction and biliary duct blockage. The gallbladder and bile ducts are typically affected. It is a component of acute cholecystitis and may occur secondary to choledocholithiasis. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are essential to prevent complications such as sepsis or liver damage.

Obstruction of the gallbladder occurs when the cystic duct or bile duct becomes blocked, preventing bile flow. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis and biliary obstruction. The most frequent cause is gallstones (cholelithiasis), which can block the ducts. Other causes include tumors, strictures, or inflammation. This condition typically affects the gallbladder and bile ducts, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and jaundice. It is more common in adults, particularly women, and can result in complications like cholecystitis or cholangitis if left untreated.

Obstruction of the bile duct refers to a blockage that prevents the normal flow of bile from the liver to the small intestine. Common synonyms include biliary obstruction and choledocholithiasis. It is often caused by gallstones, tumors, or strictures. The condition typically affects the common bile duct, gallbladder, and liver. Symptoms may include jaundice, abdominal pain, and pruritus. If left untreated, it can lead to cholangitis, liver damage, or pancreatitis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies such as ultrasound or MRI. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve surgery, endoscopic intervention, or medication.

code_desc: Other specified obstruction of gallbladder or bile ducts
summary: "Other specified obstruction of gallbladder or bile ducts" refers to partial or complete blockage of the bile flow not classified under specific categories like gallstones or tumors. Common synonyms include biliary obstruction of unspecified origin. Causative agents may include strictures, inflammation, or foreign bodies. Typically affects the gallbladder, common bile duct, and surrounding liver tissue. Symptoms include jaundice, abdominal pain, and elevated liver enzymes. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies like ultrasound or MRI. Treatment depends on underlying cause and may involve surgery or endoscopic intervention.

code_desc: Obstruction of gallbladder or bile ducts, unspecified
summary: Obstruction of gallbladder or bile ducts, unspecified, refers to a blockage in the biliary system preventing the normal flow of bile. Common synonyms include biliary obstruction and cholestasis. Causative agents may include gallstones, tumors, strictures, or inflammation. This condition typically affects the gallbladder, common bile duct, and sometimes the liver. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, jaundice, and itching. It can lead to complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis if left untreated. Diagnosis usually involves imaging studies like ultrasound or MRI. Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may involve surgery, lithotomy, or medication.

Hydrops of the gallbladder, also known as gallbladder hydrops or acalculous gallbladder disease, is a condition characterized by the accumulation of fluid within the gallbladder wall, leading to distension. It is typically caused by chronic cholecystitis, biliary obstruction, or infection. Common causative agents include bacteria such as *Escherichia coli* and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder, with associated symptoms like right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and fever. It is more common in elderly patients and those with underlying biliary tract disorders.

code_desc: Fistula of gallbladder or bile duct
summary: Fistula of the gallbladder or bile duct refers to an abnormal connection between the gallbladder or bile duct and another adjacent structure, such as the small intestine, liver, or abdominal wall. Common synonyms include biliary-enteric fistula and cholecystoenteric fistula. This condition is often caused by chronic cholecystitis, gallstones, or trauma, leading to erosion of surrounding tissues. It typically affects the biliary system and adjacent gastrointestinal tract, resulting in symptoms like bile leakage, infection, and digestive disturbances. The condition is more common in individuals with long-standing gallbladder disease.

A gallbladder polyp is a growth projecting from the gallbladder wall, typically benign. Common synonyms include gallbladder polypoid lesion and cholesterol polyp. It is often composed of cholesterol deposits, though adenomyomas or inflammatory polyps may also occur. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder, with polyps most commonly found in the fundus. While usually asymptomatic, larger polyps may cause symptoms similar to gallstones. Risk factors include obesity, hyperlipidemia, and chronic gallbladder disease. Most polyps are not cancerous, but larger or symptomatic lesions may require further evaluation.

Cholesterolosis of the gallbladder is a non-neoplastic condition characterized by the presence of cholesterol-rich macrophages (cholesterol clefts) in the gallbladder wall. It is often associated with chronic gallbladder disease and is considered a histopathological finding rather than a distinct disease. Common synonyms include xanthoma of the gallbladder and cholesterol granuloma. The condition is typically seen in the gallbladder wall, particularly in the mucosa and submucosa, and is frequently linked to long-standing gallstones or chronic cholecystitis. Causative agents are primarily related to chronic inflammation and cholesterol deposition.

code_desc: Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of gallbladder or bile ducts
summary: "Other specified acquired anatomical alterations of gallbladder or bile ducts" refers to structural changes in the gallbladder or bile ducts not classified elsewhere, such as strictures, malformations, or scars. Common synonyms include acquired biliary abnormalities or anatomical bile duct alterations. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, surgery, trauma, or infection. These conditions typically affect the gallbladder, common bile duct, and surrounding hepatic structures, leading to impaired bile flow and potential complications like cholestasis or obstruction.

code_desc: Acquired anatomical alterations of gallbladder or bile ducts, unspecified
summary: Acquired anatomical alterations of gallbladder or bile ducts, unspecified refer to structural changes in the gallbladder or bile ducts resulting from disease or injury, without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include gallbladder deformity, bile duct distortion, or biliary tract abnormalities. Causative agents may include chronic inflammation, gallstones, strictures, or surgical interventions. These alterations typically affect the gallbladder wall, bile ducts, or their junctions, leading to impaired bile flow and potential complications such as cholangitis or obstructive jaundice.

Cholelithiasis refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder. Common synonyms include choleliths or gallstone disease. It is primarily caused by supersaturation of bile with cholesterol, bilirubin, or calcium salts, leading to crystal formation and stone development. Gallstones typically affect the gallbladder but may migrate to the common bile duct, causing obstruction and complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, diabetes, and a family history of gallstones. The condition is more prevalent in females and older adults.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct with acute cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct with acute cholecystitis refers to the inflammation of the gallbladder caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis with acute cholecystitis and calculous cholecystitis. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or pigment stones. This condition typically affects the gallbladder and is commonly associated with the biliary tract. It is more prevalent in females and often presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Complications may include perforation or sepsis if left untreated.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct with other cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct with other cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder or cystic duct accompanied by inflammation of the gallbladder. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis with cholecystitis or calculous cholecystitis. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or bilirubin stones. This condition typically affects the gallbladder and may involve the cystic duct, leading to obstruction and infection. It is most commonly seen in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, and a family history of gallstones.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct with cholangitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct with cholangitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder or cystic duct accompanied by inflammation of the bile ducts, often due to obstruction. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis with cholangitis or ascending cholangitis. Causative agents are primarily cholesterol and pigment stones. This condition typically affects the gallbladder, common bile duct, and sometimes the liver. It is associated with symptoms such as abdominal pain, fever, and jaundice. Complications may include sepsis or abscess formation if untreated.

code_desc: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct without cholecystitis or cholangitis
summary: Calculus of gallbladder or cystic duct without cholecystitis or cholangitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder or cystic duct without accompanying inflammation. Common synonyms include gallstone disease, biliary lithiasis, and cholelithiasis. The primary causative agent is cholesterol, with secondary contributors such as bilirubin or calcium salts. This condition typically affects the gallbladder and cystic duct, often leading to symptoms like biliary colic. It is more common in females, particularly those over 40 years of age, and is associated with factors like obesity and rapid weight loss.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with cholangitis
summary: Calculus of bile duct with cholangitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the bile ducts accompanied by inflammation of the bile passages. This condition, also known as choledocholithiasis with cholangitis, typically results from obstruction of the common bile duct by a stone, leading to bacterial infection. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Enterococcus*. The primary affected body parts are the bile ducts, gallbladder, and liver. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes. Complications can include sepsis and liver dysfunction if left untreated.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct with cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of bile duct with cholecystitis refers to the presence of gallstones in the bile ducts accompanied by inflammation of the gallbladder. Common synonyms include choledocholithiasis with cholecystitis and ascending cholangitis. The condition is typically caused by gallstones obstructing the ducts, leading to bile stasis and bacterial infection. Common causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Enterobacter*. It primarily affects the gallbladder and bile ducts, often resulting in right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice. Complications may include cholangitis, pancreatitis, and sepsis if left untreated.

code_desc: Calculus of bile duct without cholangitis or cholecystitis
summary: Calculus of bile duct without cholangitis or cholecystitis refers to the presence of a gallstone in the bile duct without accompanying inflammation of the bile duct or gallbladder. Common synonyms include bile duct stone or choledocholithiasis. This condition is typically caused by gallstones from the gallbladder migrating into the common bile duct. It most commonly affects the common bile duct, though stones may also occur in the intrahepatic or extrahepatic ducts. Clinical presentation may be asymptomatic or include obstructive symptoms such as jaundice or abdominal pain.

Intrahepatic cholelithiasis refers to the formation of gallstones within the liver parenchyma, rather than in the gallbladder. It is a rare condition, often associated with chronic liver disease, biliary tract abnormalities, or metabolic disorders. Common synonyms include hepatic lithiasis and intrahepatic biliary calculi. Causative agents may include cholesterol, bilirubin, or calcium salts. The primary affected body part is the liver, particularly the bile ducts. Symptoms may include jaundice, abdominal pain, and cholangitis. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging studies such as ultrasound or MRI.

Other specified cholelithiasis refers to gallstone disease that does not meet the criteria for gallstone disease with complications or acute cholecystitis. It encompasses gallstones in the gallbladder or bile ducts without associated symptoms or complications. Common synonyms include asymptomatic cholelithiasis and silent gallstones. Causative agents include cholesterol, bilirubin, and pigment stones. The gallbladder and bile ducts are typically affected. This condition is often detected incidentally during imaging studies.

Cholelithiasis, unspecified, refers to the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder without specifying their composition or location. Common synonyms include gallstone disease and cholelithiasis. Causative agents include cholesterol, bilirubin, and calcium salts. It typically affects the gallbladder, with stones potentially migrating to the bile ducts, causing obstruction and complications such as cholecystitis or cholangitis. Risk factors include obesity, rapid weight loss, and a family history of gallstones. The condition is more prevalent in females and older adults.

Cholecystitis is an inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly acute, often resulting from gallstones obstructing the cystic duct. It is characterized by right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Common synonyms include acute cholecystitis and gallbladder inflammation. The primary causative agent is usually gallstones, though infection can also play a role. The condition predominantly affects the gallbladder, with potential complications such as gangrene, perforation, or empyema. It is more prevalent in females and individuals with a history of gallstones or biliary tract disease.

Acute cholecystitis is an acute inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly caused by obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone. This leads to bacterial infection, typically involving *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Enterococcus* species. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder, often resulting in right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea. It is more prevalent in females and individuals with a history of gallstones. Complications may include gangrene, perforation, or abscess formation. Synonyms include acute suppurative cholecystitis and acute calculous cholecystitis.

Acute on chronic cholecystitis refers to a sudden exacerbation of chronic gallbladder inflammation, often triggered by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct. It is characterized by severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Common synonyms include acute cholecystitis superimposed on chronic disease or recurrent acute cholecystitis. The primary causative agent is gallstones, though bacterial infection may also play a role. The gallbladder is the primarily affected organ, with potential involvement of the bile ducts. Complications may include gangrene, perforation, or sepsis.

Other specified acute cholecystitis refers to acute inflammation of the gallbladder that does not meet the criteria for typical acute calculous or acalculous cholecystitis. It may present with similar symptoms but lacks definitive evidence of gallstones or other specified etiologies. Common synonyms include unspecified acute cholecystitis. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, such as *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, or *Staphylococcus*, though the exact cause is often unclear. The gallbladder is the primarily affected organ, with potential involvement of adjacent structures like the bile ducts or liver.

Acute cholecystitis, unspecified, is an acute inflammation of the gallbladder, typically caused by gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct, leading to bacterial infection. Common synonyms include acute calculous cholecystitis. The most common causative agents are gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder, with possible involvement of adjacent structures like the liver or bile ducts. Symptoms include right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea. It is more common in females and individuals with a history of gallstones.

Chronic cholecystitis is a long-term inflammation of the gallbladder, typically resulting from recurrent episodes of acute cholecystitis. It is most commonly caused by gallstones obstructing the cystic duct, leading to persistent irritation and fibrosis. Synonyms include chronic gallbladder disease or chronic biliary inflammation. The condition predominantly affects the gallbladder, with possible involvement of adjacent structures such as the liver and bile ducts. It is more prevalent in middle-aged individuals, particularly women, and is associated with symptoms like right upper quadrant pain, dyspepsia, and sometimes jaundice.

Other specified cholecystitis refers to inflammation of the gallbladder not classified as acute or chronic calculous or acalculous cholecystitis. It encompasses rare or atypical forms with unclear etiology or presentation. Common synonyms include unspecified or undetermined cholecystitis. Causative agents may include bacterial infections, though often unspecified. The gallbladder is the primary affected organ, with inflammation potentially extending to adjacent structures. This condition is typically diagnosed when other forms of cholecystitis do not fit.

Cholecystitis, unspecified, refers to inflammation of the gallbladder of unknown etiology. Common synonyms include acute cholecystitis and chronic cholecystitis, though the unspecified designation implies insufficient information to determine the type. The primary causative agent is typically gallstones, which obstruct the cystic duct, leading to bacterial infection. Other causes may include ischemia or trauma. The condition primarily affects the gallbladder, with potential involvement of adjacent structures such as the liver and bile ducts. Symptoms include right upper quadrant pain, fever, and nausea.

Cholangitis is an inflammation of the bile ducts, typically caused by bacterial infection, most commonly *Escherichia coli*. It often results from obstruction, such as from gallstones or strictures, leading to ascending infection. Common synonyms include acute cholangitis and obstructive cholangitis. The condition primarily affects the bile ducts, including the common hepatic duct and common bile duct. Symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, jaundice, and chills. Complications may involve sepsis or liver damage if untreated. Prompt diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics and biliary drainage are essential.

Certain specified biliary diseases refer to conditions affecting the bile ducts and gallbladder, often involving obstruction, inflammation, or infection. Common synonyms include cholangitis, cholecystitis, and biliary obstruction. Causative agents may include bacteria such as *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Pseudomonas*, as well as gallstones, tumors, or parasitic infections. These conditions typically affect the gallbladder, common bile duct, and liver, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, jaundice, and fever. They are often associated with gallstone disease and can result in complications such as cholangitis or pancreatitis.

Haemorrhage of the bile duct, also known as biliary haemorrhage or cholangial bleeding, refers to the rupture or injury of a bile duct leading to blood loss into the biliary tree. Common causes include trauma, stones, tumors, or inflammation. It may occur in the context of cholangiocarcinoma, liver metastases, or iatrogenic injury during procedures like endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). The condition typically affects the intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts, leading to symptoms such as jaundice, abdominal pain, and hematemesis. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications like sepsis or liver failure.

Postcholecystectomy syndrome refers to persistent gastrointestinal symptoms following cholecystectomy, often including epigastric pain, bloating, and dyspepsia. Common synonyms include post-gallbladder removal syndrome and post-cholecystectomy discomfort. Causative agents may include bile duct stones, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, or residual gallbladder tissue. The condition typically affects the biliary tract, gallbladder bed, and upper gastrointestinal system. It may also be associated with irritable bowel syndrome or peptic ulcer disease. Diagnosis often requires imaging and endoscopic evaluation to identify underlying pathology.

Dyskinesia of the sphincter of Oddi is a condition characterized by abnormal contraction or relaxation of the sphincter muscle that controls bile and pancreatic duct outflow. Common synonyms include sphincter of Oddi dysfunction and biliary dyskinesia. It is often caused by biliary tract disease, gallstones, or inflammation. The condition primarily affects the bile and pancreatic ducts, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and jaundice. It may also contribute to secondary biliary cirrhosis if left untreated. The gallbladder and liver are typically involved, with pain often radiating to the back or right shoulder.

Adenomyomatosis of the gallbladder is a benign proliferative disorder characterized by hyperplasia of the gallbladder wall, particularly the muscularis and mucosa, leading to the formation of intramural diverticula. Common synonyms include gallbladder adenomyomatosis and gallbladder hyperplasia. The condition is typically associated with chronic cholecystitis and is caused by repeated episodes of gallbladder inflammation. It predominantly affects the gallbladder wall, especially the fundus, and is more common in middle-aged women. The exact etiology is not fully understood, but it is believed to result from chronic irritation and pressure from gallstones.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of gallbladder or biliary tract
summary: "Other specified diseases of gallbladder or biliary tract" refers to gallbladder or bile duct disorders not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include unspecified gallbladder disease or unspecified biliary tract disease. Causative agents may include infection, inflammation, or structural abnormalities. These conditions typically affect the gallbladder and bile ducts, leading to symptoms such as pain, jaundice, or digestive issues. They are often diagnosed when the exact nature of the disease is not clearly defined.

code_desc: Diseases of gallbladder or biliary tract, unspecified
summary: Diseases of gallbladder or biliary tract, unspecified, refer to conditions affecting the gallbladder or bile ducts without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, and biliary colic. Causative agents may include gallstones, bacterial infections, or inflammatory processes. Typically, the gallbladder and bile ducts are affected, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, and jaundice. These conditions often result from obstruction, infection, or chronic inflammation of the biliary system.

Cystic diseases of the pancreas refer to a group of conditions characterized by the formation of fluid-filled cysts within the pancreatic tissue. Common synonyms include pancreatic cysts and pancreatic neoplasms. These can be congenital, such as annular pancreas, or acquired, like pseudocysts. Causative agents include chronic pancreatitis, trauma, or neoplastic processes. Typically affecting the head, body, and tail of the pancreas, these conditions may lead to symptoms such as abdominal pain, jaundice, and digestive issues. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies and endoscopic evaluation.

A pancreatic cyst is a fluid-filled sac that develops within or adjacent to the pancreas. Common synonyms include pancreatic pseudocyst and serous cystadenoma. These cysts are typically caused by pancreatitis, trauma, or congenital factors. They most commonly occur in the body or tail of the pancreas. Pseudocysts are often a complication of acute pancreatitis, while serous cystadenomas are usually benign neoplasms. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, jaundice, or digestive issues, depending on the cyst's size and location. Diagnosis is usually confirmed with imaging studies such as CT or MRI.

Pseudocyst of the pancreas is a fluid-filled cystic structure that forms in the pancreas following acute or chronic pancreatitis. It lacks an epithelial lining and is composed of pancreatic tissue surrounded by fibrous tissue. Common synonyms include pancreatic pseudocyst and exocrine pancreatic pseudocyst. Causative agents include gallstone disease, alcohol abuse, and trauma. Typically, the pseudocyst develops in the pancreatic region, often near the head or body of the pancreas, and may extend into the peritoneal cavity. It can cause complications such as infection, hemorrhage, or obstruction.

code_desc: Other specified cystic diseases of the pancreas
summary: Other specified cystic diseases of the pancreas refer to cystic lesions of the pancreas that do not meet the criteria for specific established conditions such as pancreatic cystadenoma or intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm. These cysts may be congenital or acquired, with causes including genetic mutations, chronic pancreatitis, or trauma. Common synonyms include non-specific pancreatic cysts and miscellaneous pancreatic cystic lesions. They typically affect the body and tail of the pancreas, and may be associated with systemic conditions like von Hippel-Lindau disease or Caroli’s disease. Cytological and imaging features are essential for diagnosis.

code_desc: Cystic diseases of the pancreas, unspecified
summary: Cystic diseases of the pancreas, unspecified, refer to non-specific pancreatic cystic lesions that may include serous, mucinous, or pseudocystic formations. Common synonyms include pancreatic cysts and pancreatic pseudocysts. These conditions are often associated with chronic pancreatitis, trauma, or post-surgical complications. Causative agents may include long-standing inflammation, obstructive processes, or genetic factors. Typically affecting the body and tail of the pancreas, these lesions can present with abdominal pain, jaundice, or digestive symptoms. Diagnosis is usually confirmed via imaging studies such as CT or MRI.

Acute pancreatitis is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas, often characterized by severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Common synonyms include acute pancreatic inflammation and acute pancreatopathy. Causative agents include gallstones, alcohol use, hypertriglyceridemia, and certain medications. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of surrounding structures such as the bile duct, stomach, and duodenum. Complications may include fluid accumulation, necrosis, and systemic inflammatory response syndrome. It typically presents with nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes.

Acute idiopathic pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas of unknown cause. Common synonyms include acute interstitial pancreatitis and acute non-biliary pancreatitis. It typically affects the pancreas, with possible involvement of surrounding tissues. Known causative agents may include gallstones, alcohol, medications, infections, or trauma, though no single cause is identified in idiopathic cases. Symptoms include severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. The condition can lead to complications such as pseudocysts or systemic inflammation. Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and laboratory findings.

Acute alcohol-induced pancreatitis is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by excessive alcohol consumption. It is characterized by severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. Common synonyms include alcoholic pancreatitis or ethanol-induced pancreatitis. Causative agents are primarily ethanol and its metabolites. The pancreas is the primarily affected organ, with potential involvement of the surrounding abdominal structures. It is a common cause of acute pancreatitis, often occurring after binge drinking or chronic alcohol use.

Acute biliary pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas caused by obstruction of the pancreatic duct by gallstones. Common synonyms include gallstone pancreatitis and obstructive pancreatitis. The primary causative agent is cholesterol or pigment stones from the gallbladder. The condition typically affects the head of the pancreas and is associated with biliary tract abnormalities. Symptoms include severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. It is a common cause of acute pancreatitis and often requires hospitalization for management.

Acute drug-induced pancreatitis is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by medication. Common synonyms include drug-related pancreatitis or medication-induced pancreatitis. Causative agents include corticosteroids, azathioprine, valproic acid, and certain antibiotics. It typically affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of adjacent structures. Symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. The condition can range from mild to severe, with complications such as pseudocysts or systemic inflammation. Prompt discontinuation of the offending drug is critical for recovery.

Hereditary acute pancreatitis is a recurrent form of pancreatitis caused by genetic mutations, most commonly in the PRSS1 or SPINK1 genes. It is characterized by episodic inflammation of the pancreas, often presenting with severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The condition typically affects the pancreas and can lead to chronic complications over time. Common synonyms include familial acute pancreatitis and inherited acute pancreatitis. Causative agents include genetic mutations, with a strong family history often present. The primary affected body part is the pancreas, with potential involvement of the bile ducts and surrounding structures.

Acute exacerbation of chronic pancreatitis refers to a sudden worsening of symptoms in a patient with a previously diagnosed chronic pancreatitis. Common synonyms include recurrent acute pancreatitis or flare-up of chronic pancreatitis. It is often caused by gallstones, alcohol use, or hypertriglyceridemia. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, leading to inflammation, pain, and potential complications such as pseudocysts or pancreatic necrosis. It may also involve the bile ducts and surrounding abdominal organs. Clinical features include severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and elevated pancreatic enzymes. Early recognition and management are critical to prevent severe complications.

Other specified acute pancreatitis refers to acute pancreatitis with a known cause that does not fit into the more specific categories such as gallstone or alcohol-related pancreatitis. Common synonyms include idiopathic or unspecified acute pancreatitis. Causative agents may include medications, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, or trauma. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of surrounding structures such as the bile ducts and stomach. Symptoms typically include severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting.

Acute pancreatitis, unspecified, is a sudden inflammation of the pancreas characterized by severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and fever. Common synonyms include acute pancreatitis, unspecified etiology. Causative agents may include gallstones, alcohol use, hypertriglyceridemia, medications, or trauma. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential involvement of adjacent structures such as the bile ducts, stomach, and intestines. It is a medical emergency requiring prompt evaluation and management to prevent complications like necrosis or systemic inflammation.

Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disorder of the pancreas leading to irreversible structural damage and loss of function. Common synonyms include chronic pancreatopathy and fibrocalculous pancreatitis. It is primarily caused by long-term alcohol abuse, recurrent gallstones, or genetic factors such as cystic fibrosis or hereditary pancreatitis. The condition predominantly affects the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, malabsorption, diabetes, and steatorrhea. The pancreas, bile ducts, and surrounding structures are typically involved.

Calcific pancreatitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the pancreas characterized by the formation of calcium deposits within the pancreatic parenchyma. It often results from recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis, leading to fibrosis and calcification. Common synonyms include chronic pancreatitis with calcification or calcified pancreatitis. Known causative agents include gallstones, alcohol abuse, hyperlipidemia, and hyperparathyroidism. The condition typically affects the head and body of the pancreas, potentially leading to complications such as pseudocysts, duct obstruction, and diabetes mellitus.

Groove pancreatitis, also known as ductal pancreatitis or pancreatic ductal stenosis, is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by narrowing of the pancreatic duct. It is often associated with long-standing alcohol abuse, gallstones, or post-cholecystectomy changes. The condition typically affects the head of the pancreas and can lead to recurrent pancreatitis, pancreatic duct obstruction, and secondary complications such as pseudocysts. It may present with epigastric pain, jaundice, and malabsorption. Diagnosis is usually confirmed through imaging studies like MRI or ERCP.

Hereditary chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disorder of the pancreas caused by genetic mutations, most commonly in the PRSS1 or SPINK1 genes. It leads to persistent pancreatic inflammation, fibrosis, and eventual loss of exocrine and endocrine function. Common synonyms include familial chronic pancreatitis and autosomal dominant chronic pancreatitis. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, leading to exocrine insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, and an increased risk of pancreatic cancer. It typically presents in adulthood with recurrent abdominal pain, malabsorption, and steatorrhea.

Chronic alcohol-induced pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disorder of the pancreas caused by long-term alcohol consumption. It leads to irreversible damage, fibrosis, and loss of exocrine and endocrine function. Common synonyms include alcoholic pancreatitis and chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis. The primary causative agent is excessive alcohol intake. The pancreas is the main affected organ, with potential complications involving the gastrointestinal tract, bile ducts, and surrounding structures. It is characterized by recurrent abdominal pain, malabsorption, and diabetes mellitus.

Chronic idiopathic pancreatitis is a long-term inflammatory condition of the pancreas of unknown cause, leading to progressive fibrosis and loss of exocrine and endocrine function. Common synonyms include chronic recurrent pancreatitis and chronic non-alcoholic pancreatitis. While the exact etiology is unclear, it may be associated with genetic factors, autoimmune processes, or recurrent episodes of acute pancreatitis. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, often resulting in complications such as diabetes mellitus, malabsorption, and pancreatic duct strictures. It predominantly occurs in middle-aged individuals and is more common in males.

Tropical pancreatitis is a chronic, recurrent form of pancreatitis predominantly observed in tropical regions. It is characterized by persistent inflammation of the pancreas, often leading to fibrosis and exocrine insufficiency. Common synonyms include tropical calcific pancreatitis and endemic pancreatitis. The condition is associated with parasitic infections, particularly *Ascaris lumbricoides* and *Clonorchis sinensis*, as well as nutritional deficiencies and viral infections. It primarily affects the pancreas, with calcifications and fibrosis commonly seen on imaging. The disease is more prevalent in children and young adults in endemic areas.

Other specified chronic pancreatitis refers to long-standing inflammation of the pancreas that does not meet the criteria for specific types such as alcoholic or hereditary pancreatitis. It may result from various causes including autoimmune, metabolic, or obstructive factors. Common synonyms include unspecified chronic pancreatitis. The pancreas is typically affected, leading to exocrine and endocrine dysfunction. Known causative agents may include medications, infections, or idiopathic factors. Symptoms often include abdominal pain, malabsorption, and diabetes mellitus.

Chronic pancreatitis, unspecified, is a long-term inflammatory condition of the pancreas leading to irreversible structural damage and impaired function. Common synonyms include chronic pancreatitis, unspecified etiology. Known causative agents include alcohol abuse, gallstones, genetic factors, and autoimmune processes. The condition primarily affects the pancreas, with potential involvement of the gastrointestinal tract and liver. Symptoms may include persistent abdominal pain, malabsorption, and diabetes mellitus. The exact cause is often unspecified in clinical documentation.

Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is a chronic inflammatory condition of the pancreas mediated by the immune system. It is characterized by fibro-inflammatory changes and often presents with obstructive jaundice. Common synonyms include IgG4-related pancreatitis and autoimmune pancreatopathy. The condition is associated with elevated serum IgG4 levels and may involve other organs, such as the bile ducts, kidneys, and salivary glands. Causative agents are not well defined, but it is considered an autoimmune disorder. AIP typically affects the pancreas and bile ducts, and may lead to pancreatic insufficiency and diabetes mellitus.

Obstructive pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas caused by blockage of the pancreatic duct or its branches. Common synonyms include biliary pancreatitis and obstructive cholangitis. It is most commonly caused by gallstones or strictures, leading to impaired drainage and subsequent enzymatic injury. The condition typically affects the head of the pancreas and may involve the bile duct. Symptoms include epigastric pain, nausea, and jaundice. Complications may include pseudocysts, infection, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosis often involves imaging studies such as ultrasound, CT, or MRI. Treatment focuses on relieving the obstruction and managing complications.

Certain specified diseases of the pancreas encompass a range of conditions affecting the exocrine and endocrine functions of the gland. Common synonyms include pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, and diabetes mellitus. Causative agents vary, including alcohol, gallstones, infections, genetic mutations, and autoimmune factors. These diseases primarily affect the pancreas, with potential complications involving the digestive tract, liver, and endocrine system. Chronic pancreatitis leads to progressive damage, while acute cases may present with inflammation and pain. Pancreatic cancer is often associated with genetic predispositions and environmental risk factors.

Atrophy of the pancreas refers to the progressive shrinkage and loss of functional tissue in the pancreas, leading to impaired exocrine and endocrine function. Common synonyms include pancreatic hypoplasia and pancreatic degeneration. Causative agents may include chronic pancreatitis, long-term alcohol abuse, diabetes mellitus, and certain genetic disorders. The condition primarily affects the exocrine pancreas, reducing digestive enzyme production, and may also impact insulin secretion. It typically involves the entire pancreas but can be localized. Symptoms include malabsorption, weight loss, and diabetes. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to prevent complications.

Secondary pancreatic insufficiency is a condition characterized by reduced exocrine pancreatic function due to damage or disease affecting the pancreas, rather than primary pancreatic disease. Common synonyms include exocrine pancreatic insufficiency secondary to underlying conditions. Causative agents include chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, pancreatic cancer, and prolonged use of certain medications. It typically affects the gastrointestinal tract, leading to malabsorption of nutrients, steatorrhea, and weight loss. The condition may also impact the liver and biliary system in some cases.

Pancreatic steatorrhoea is a condition characterized by the presence of undigested fat in the stool, resulting from impaired exocrine pancreatic function. It commonly occurs due to chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or pancreatic duct obstruction. The primary symptom is fatty, foul-smelling, and voluminous stools. Malabsorption of nutrients, particularly fat-soluble vitamins, often accompanies this condition. The small intestine is the primary site affected, with fat malabsorption leading to steatorrhoea. Synonyms include steatorrhea and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

"Other specified diseases of pancreas" refers to pancreatic conditions not classified under more specific categories such as pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer. Common synonyms include unspecified pancreatic disease or other pancreatic disorders. Causative agents may include autoimmune factors, infections, or metabolic disorders. These conditions typically affect the pancreas, potentially leading to exocrine or endocrine dysfunction. They may present with symptoms like abdominal pain, jaundice, or malabsorption, and are often diagnosed through imaging or biopsy. The exact etiology and clinical manifestations vary depending on the underlying cause.

Diseases of the pancreas, unspecified, refer to pancreatic conditions that do not meet specific diagnostic criteria for known pancreatic disorders. Common synonyms include "pancreatic disease, unspecified" and "undetermined pancreatic pathology." Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune processes, or metabolic factors, though they are not definitively identified. These conditions typically affect the exocrine and endocrine components of the pancreas, leading to dysfunction in digestion and hormone regulation. The pancreas is the primary affected organ, with potential systemic implications.

Peritonitis is an inflammation of the peritoneum, the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity. It can be acute or chronic, often resulting from infection, trauma, or perforation of intra-abdominal organs. Common causative agents include bacteria such as *Escherichia coli*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. Synonyms include abdominal infection and peritoneal inflammation. The condition typically affects the abdominal cavity, with involvement of the peritoneal layers and adjacent organs like the intestines, liver, and spleen. Symptoms include abdominal pain, fever, and distension. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications such as sepsis.

Primary peritonitis is an infection of the peritoneal cavity without an underlying intra-abdominal source. It commonly occurs in patients with cirrhosis and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Other causative agents include *Escherichia coli*, *Klebsiella*, and *Streptococcus pneumoniae*. The condition typically affects the abdominal cavity, leading to symptoms such as abdominal pain, fever, and ascites. It is also known as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or pyoperitonitis. Complications may include sepsis and multi-organ failure if untreated.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is an infection of the peritoneal cavity in the absence of intra-abdominal sources of infection. It commonly occurs in patients with cirrhosis and ascites. The infection is typically caused by gram-negative bacteria such as *Escherichia coli* and *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, though gram-positive organisms may also be involved. SBP presents with symptoms like abdominal pain, fever, and altered mental status. The peritoneum is the primary affected site, with ascitic fluid showing neutrophilic pleocytosis. Early diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are critical to prevent complications and mortality.

Other specified primary peritonitis refers to peritoneal inflammation not classified as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or secondary to intra-abdominal sources. It is characterized by the presence of neutrophils in ascitic fluid without an identifiable intra-abdominal infection. Common synonyms include idiopathic peritonitis and non-infectious peritonitis. Causative agents may include immune-mediated processes or unknown etiologies. The condition primarily affects the peritoneum, often in patients with cirrhosis or immunocompromised states. Clinical features include abdominal pain, fever, and ascites. Diagnosis relies on ascitic fluid analysis and exclusion of other causes.

Secondary peritonitis is an acute inflammation of the peritoneum resulting from the leakage of intestinal contents or other intra-abdominal infections into the peritoneal cavity. Common synonyms include spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and secondary bacterial peritonitis. It is most commonly caused by perforation of the gastrointestinal tract, such as from peptic ulcer disease, diverticulitis, or appendicitis. Other causes include trauma, surgical complications, or infection spread from adjacent organs. The condition typically affects the abdominal cavity, with involvement of the peritoneum, intestines, and surrounding structures.
