It predominantly affects the colon, particularly the sigmoid colon, but can occur in other parts of the gastrointestinal tract. The exact causative agents are not fully understood, but factors such as age, dietary habits, and genetic predisposition play a role.

Diverticular disease of the intestine, unspecified, refers to the presence of diverticula, which are small, abnormal pouches that form in the walls of the digestive tract. Common synonyms include diverticulosis and diverticular disease. The condition is primarily caused by increased intraluminal pressure, often due to a low-fiber diet, leading to weakening of the colonic wall. It most commonly affects the sigmoid colon. While not always symptomatic, it can progress to diverticulitis, characterized by inflammation or infection of the diverticula. The disease is more prevalent in older adults.

Acute vascular disorders of the intestine refer to sudden disruptions in blood flow to the gastrointestinal tract, leading to ischemia and potential necrosis. Common synonyms include intestinal infarction and mesenteric ischemia. Causative agents may include emboli, thrombosis, or hypoperfusion. These conditions primarily affect the small intestine, with involvement of the colon less common. Risk factors include atherosclerosis, cardiac arrhythmias, and hypercoagulable states. Clinical presentation often includes abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent severe complications and mortality.

Acute mesenteric arterial infarction is a sudden occlusion of a mesenteric artery, leading to intestinal ischemia and potential necrosis. Common synonyms include acute mesenteric embolism or thrombosis. Causative agents often include emboli from cardiac sources, atherosclerosis, or vasospasm. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the colon may also be involved. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and signs of shock. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent bowel necrosis and mortality.

Acute mesenteric arterial ischaemia is a severe condition characterized by reduced blood flow to the intestines due to occlusion or spasm of the mesenteric arteries. Common synonyms include acute mesenteric infarction and acute intestinal ischaemia. Causative agents include embolism, thrombosis, and vasospasm. It typically affects the small intestine, with possible involvement of the colon. Risk factors include atherosclerosis, cardiac arrhythmias, and hypercoagulable states. Symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent bowel necrosis and mortality.

Acute mesenteric venous occlusion is a rare but serious condition characterized by sudden blockage of the veins in the mesentery, leading to impaired venous return and potential bowel infarction. Common synonyms include mesenteric venous thrombosis and acute mesenteric venous thrombosis. Causative agents often include hypercoagulable states, malignancy, infections, or trauma. The small intestine is typically affected, with involvement of the ileum being most common. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, distension, and signs of bowel ischemia. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent severe complications.

code_desc: Other specified acute vascular disorders of intestine
summary: Other specified acute vascular disorders of the intestine refer to acute conditions involving impaired blood flow to the intestinal tissues, not classified under other specific categories. Common synonyms include acute mesenteric ischemia and acute intestinal infarction. Causative agents may include emboli, thrombosis, or hypoperfusion. These disorders typically affect the small intestine, though the colon may also be involved. Symptoms often include severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potential bowel ischemia. Early diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent complications such as necrosis and perforation.

code_desc: Acute vascular disorders of intestine, unspecified
summary: Acute vascular disorders of the intestine, unspecified, refer to sudden disruptions in blood flow to the gastrointestinal tract, leading to ischemia or infarction. Common synonyms include acute mesenteric ischemia and acute intestinal ischemia. Causative agents may include embolism, thrombosis, hypotension, or vasospasm. These conditions primarily affect the small intestine, with involvement of the colon less common. Symptoms typically include severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and bowel dysfunction. Prompt diagnosis and intervention are critical to prevent necrosis and complications such as sepsis or perforation.

Chronic vascular disorders of the intestine refer to long-term conditions affecting blood vessels within the gastrointestinal tract, leading to impaired blood flow and tissue damage. Common synonyms include chronic mesenteric ischemia and chronic intestinal ischemia. These disorders are often caused by atherosclerosis, thrombosis, or embolism. They primarily affect the small intestine, with involvement of the colon less common. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, weight loss, and malabsorption. Diagnosis typically involves imaging studies and angiography. Management focuses on addressing underlying vascular disease and improving perfusion.

Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia (NOMI) is a condition characterized by reduced blood flow to the intestines due to vasospasm or embolism, not from arterial occlusion. Common synonyms include mesenteric ischaemia without occlusion and non-thrombotic mesenteric ischaemia. Causative agents include cardiac arrhythmias, hypotension, and emboli from atrial fibrillation or valvular disease. It typically affects the small intestine, with potential involvement of the colon. The condition is more common in elderly patients and can lead to bowel infarction if untreated.

Ischaemic colitis is an acute inflammation of the colon caused by reduced blood flow, typically due to occlusion of the mesenteric arteries or veins. Common synonyms include acute colonic ischemia and mesenteric infarction. Causative agents include atherosclerosis, embolism, hypotension, and thrombosis. It most commonly affects the splenic flexure and descending colon. Symptoms include abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and fever. The condition is more prevalent in the elderly and those with cardiovascular disease. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications such as perforation or necrosis.

Other specified non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia refers to reduced blood flow to the intestines due to vascular dysfunction, not caused by embolism or thrombosis. Common synonyms include mesenteric hypoperfusion and non-occlusive mesenteric disease. Causative agents may include hypotension, heart failure, or vasospasm. It typically affects the small intestine, with possible involvement of the colon. The condition is often associated with systemic illnesses and can lead to bowel ischemia, necrosis, and perforation if untreated.

Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia, unspecified, refers to reduced blood flow to the intestines due to vascular compromise without a defined embolic or thrombotic cause. Common synonyms include non-occlusive mesenteric artery disease and mesenteric ischaemia of unknown origin. It is often associated with conditions like hypotension, sepsis, or hypercoagulable states. The small intestine is typically affected, leading to bowel ischemia, necrosis, and potential perforation. The condition may present with abdominal pain, distension, and systemic signs of shock. Diagnosis is often made through imaging and clinical evaluation when other causes are excluded.

code_desc: Other specified chronic vascular disorders of intestine
summary: "Other specified chronic vascular disorders of intestine" refers to long-standing vascular abnormalities affecting the intestinal tract that do not fit specific categories like Crohn's disease or ischemic colitis. Common synonyms include chronic mesenteric ischemia and chronic intestinal vascular insufficiency. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, thrombosis, or embolism. These conditions primarily affect the small and large intestines, leading to chronic ischemia, malabsorption, and bowel dysfunction. They are often associated with systemic vascular diseases and may present with abdominal pain, weight loss, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

code_desc: Chronic vascular disorders of intestine, unspecified
summary: Chronic vascular disorders of intestine, unspecified refer to long-term abnormalities in blood vessel function within the gastrointestinal tract, leading to impaired circulation. Common synonyms include chronic mesenteric ischemia and chronic intestinal ischemia. Causative agents may include atherosclerosis, thrombosis, embolism, or vasculitis. These conditions typically affect the small and large intestines, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, weight loss, and gastrointestinal bleeding. The exact etiology is often unspecified, necessitating further diagnostic evaluation.

code_desc: Other specified ischaemic vascular disorders of intestine
summary: "Other specified ischaemic vascular disorders of intestine" refers to reduced blood flow to the intestinal tissues due to vascular abnormalities not classified elsewhere. Common synonyms include mesenteric ischaemia and intestinal hypoperfusion. Causative agents may include emboli, thrombosis, or vasculitis. Typically affects the small and large intestine, with the terminal ileum and colon being most commonly involved. Symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, and bowel dysfunction. It is often associated with underlying cardiovascular disease or coagulopathy.

code_desc: Ischaemic vascular disorders of intestine, unspecified
summary: Ischaemic vascular disorders of the intestine, unspecified, refer to reduced blood flow to the intestinal tissues, leading to inadequate oxygen and nutrient supply. Common synonyms include intestinal ischaemia and mesenteric ischaemia. Causative agents may include emboli, thrombosis, or vasospasm, often secondary to atherosclerosis or cardiac conditions. The small intestine is most commonly affected, though the large intestine can also be involved. Symptoms typically include abdominal pain, cramping, and potential bowel infarction if untreated. This condition is often associated with systemic circulatory disorders.

Non-abdominal wall hernia refers to the protrusion of intra-abdominal contents through a weakness or defect in a structure other than the abdominal wall, such as the diaphragm, pelvic floor, or inguinal canal. Common synonyms include diaphragmatic hernia, hiatal hernia, and inguinal hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, congenital defects, and muscular weakness. These hernias typically affect the diaphragm, esophagus, pelvic floor, or inguinal region, leading to symptoms such as dyspnea, reflux, or bowel obstruction depending on the location.

Diaphragmatic hernia is a condition where abdominal organs protrude through a defect in the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. Common synonyms include congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) and Morgagni hernia. It is often caused by developmental defects during fetal life or traumatic injury. The most commonly affected areas are the left hemidiaphragm, with the stomach and bowel frequently involved. In congenital cases, it is associated with pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory distress. Acquired hernias may result from trauma, surgery, or increased intra-abdominal pressure.

Pelvic hernia refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakness or defect in the pelvic floor muscles or fascia. Common synonyms include pelvic organ prolapse and hernia of the pelvic region. It is often caused by increased intra-abdominal pressure, childbirth, aging, or chronic straining. The condition typically affects the bladder, uterus, rectum, or small intestine, leading to symptoms such as pressure, discomfort, or a sensation of heaviness in the lower abdomen. It is more common in women due to pelvic floor weakness and childbirth. Treatment may involve pelvic floor therapy, pessaries, or surgical repair.

Intra-abdominal hernia refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect or weakness in the abdominal wall. Common synonyms include hernia and abdominal hernia. It is often caused by increased intra-abdominal pressure, chronic coughing, obesity, or prior surgery. The most commonly affected areas are the inguinal canal, umbilical region, and femoral canal. Hernias may contain bowel loops, fat, or omentum. Complications such as incarceration or strangulation can lead to bowel obstruction or necrosis, requiring urgent surgical intervention.

Primary intra-abdominal hernia refers to a protrusion of visceral organs through a congenital or acquired weakness in the abdominal wall, without direct communication with the abdominal cavity. Common synonyms include ventral hernia and epigastric hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, aging, and prior surgery. Typically affecting the inguinal, umbilical, or epigastric regions, these hernias may contain omentum, fat, or bowel. They are distinct from incisional hernias, which result from surgical incisions. Clinical presentation often includes a reducible mass with possible pain or discomfort.

Secondary intra-abdominal hernia refers to a protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakened or previously damaged abdominal wall, often resulting from prior surgical incisions, trauma, or chronic conditions like ascites. Common synonyms include incisional hernia and postoperative hernia. Causative factors include surgical complications, obesity, and increased intra-abdominal pressure. Typically affecting the umbilical, inguinal, or incisional regions, this condition is more prevalent in adults and may present with pain, swelling, or bowel obstruction.

"Other specified intra-abdominal hernia" refers to hernias not classified under more specific categories, such as inguinal or umbilical. It encompasses hernias occurring in less common sites, including the femoral, epigastric, or obturator regions. Common synonyms include unspecified or unspecified intra-abdominal hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure from chronic coughing, obesity, or straining. Typically affects the lower abdominal wall, groin, or pelvic regions. Often presents with a reducible swelling, and may be associated with pain or discomfort. Surgical repair is usually required for symptomatic cases.

Intra-abdominal hernia, unspecified, refers to the protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect in the abdominal wall without a specific localization. Common synonyms include undiagnosed hernia or unspecified hernia. It may result from weakness in the abdominal musculature, increased intra-abdominal pressure, or congenital defects. Commonly affected areas include the inguinal, femoral, umbilical, and epigastric regions. Causative factors may include chronic coughing, obesity, pregnancy, or prior abdominal surgery. This condition can lead to complications such as incarceration or strangulation if left untreated.

"Other specified non-abdominal wall hernia" refers to hernias occurring outside the abdominal wall, not classified under more specific categories. Common synonyms include inguinal, femoral, or umbilical hernias when applicable. Causative factors often involve weakened connective tissue, increased intra-abdominal pressure, or congenital defects. These hernias typically affect the groin, abdomen, or navel regions. They may contain bowel loops or fat and are prone to complications like strangulation. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by imaging if necessary. Treatment often involves surgical repair.

Non-abdominal wall hernia, unspecified refers to a protrusion of intra-abdominal contents through a weakness or defect in the abdominal wall, excluding inguinal, femoral, or umbilical hernias. Common synonyms include generalized abdominal wall hernia or unspecified abdominal hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure, congenital defects, or prior surgery. Typically affects the epigastric, lumbar, or flank regions. It may present as a bulge, discomfort, or pain, often worsened by straining. Diagnosis is usually clinical, with imaging used for confirmation. Treatment involves surgical repair to prevent complications like incarceration or strangulation.

Inguinal hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through a weak spot in the abdominal wall in the groin area. It commonly occurs in males and is often associated with increased intra-abdominal pressure. Common synonyms include groin hernia and indirect/ direct hernia. Causative factors include congenital defects, chronic coughing, obesity, and heavy lifting. The condition typically affects the inguinal canal, with indirect hernias more common in infants and direct hernias more prevalent in adults. It may present as a bulge that becomes more prominent when straining.

A femoral hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through the femoral canal, typically occurring in females. It is less common than inguinal hernias. Common synonyms include femoral canal hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure and weakness in the femoral canal. It most commonly affects the groin area, specifically the femoral triangle. Risk factors include pregnancy, obesity, and chronic cough. Symptoms may include a bulge, pain, or discomfort in the groin. Complications such as strangulation can occur, requiring prompt surgical intervention.

An umbilical hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through the umbilical ring, resulting in a bulge at the navel. Common synonyms include navel hernia or umbilical herniation. It occurs due to weakness in the abdominal wall, often from congenital factors or increased intra-abdominal pressure. The condition typically affects the umbilical region, and may extend into the lower abdomen. It is more common in infants, pregnant women, and individuals with obesity or ascites. In adults, it may be associated with conditions such as chronic cough or constipation. Surgical repair is often recommended to prevent complications like incarceration or strangulation.

A paraumbilical hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakness near the umbilicus. It commonly occurs in adults, particularly women, and is often associated with increased intra-abdominal pressure. Common synonyms include umbilical hernia and epigastric hernia. The defect typically involves the transverse fascia and may contain omentum or fat. Causative factors include obesity, pregnancy, and chronic coughing. The hernia is usually located around the navel and may become incarcerated or strangulated, requiring surgical intervention.

An epigastric hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect in the epigastric region, typically between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus. It often results from congenital weakness or acquired trauma. Common synonyms include midline hernia or epigastric ventral hernia. Causative factors include increased intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, chronic coughing, or heavy lifting. The hernia most commonly affects the midline abdominal wall, sometimes involving the rectus abdominis muscles. It is generally less symptomatic than inguinal hernias but may present with discomfort or a palpable bulge.

An incisional hernia occurs when abdominal contents protrude through a weakness in the abdominal wall at the site of a previous surgical incision. Common synonyms include surgical hernia or postoperative hernia. It is primarily caused by insufficient tissue repair following surgery, often exacerbated by factors such as infection, obesity, or chronic cough. The most commonly affected areas include the umbilical, lower abdominal, and groin regions. This condition may present as a bulge that becomes more prominent with straining and can lead to complications such as incarceration or strangulation if left untreated.

Parastomal hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect near a stoma, commonly occurring after ostomy surgery. It results from weakened fascial integrity and increased intra-abdominal pressure. Common synonyms include peristomal hernia and stoma hernia. Causative factors include improper stoma placement, obesity, and chronic cough. Typically affecting the perineal or umbilical regions, it may involve the small intestine, omentum, or bladder. Symptoms include bulging, pain, and potential obstruction. Management ranges from observation to surgical repair.

"Other specified hernias" refers to hernias that do not fit the criteria for inguinal, umbilical, or epigastric hernias. Common synonyms include incisional, ventral, or spigelian hernias. These hernias result from weakened abdominal walls due to factors such as prior surgery, trauma, or chronic straining. They commonly occur in the abdominal wall, particularly at sites of surgical incisions or along the rectus sheath. Causative agents include surgical procedures, obesity, and increased intra-abdominal pressure. Diagnosis is typically made through physical examination and imaging. Treatment often involves surgical repair.

Hernias, unspecified, refer to the protrusion of an organ or tissue through a weak spot or defect in the surrounding muscle or connective tissue. Common synonyms include hernia, inguinal hernia, and umbilical hernia. Causative agents often involve increased intra-abdominal pressure from chronic coughing, obesity, or heavy lifting. Typically affected areas include the groin, abdomen, and navel. This condition may present as a visible bulge, discomfort, or pain, and can vary in severity. It is more common in males and often requires surgical intervention for repair.

Crohn disease is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract, classified as an inflammatory bowel disease. It can affect any part of the digestive system, most commonly the terminal ileum and colon. The condition is characterized by transmural inflammation, leading to ulcers, strictures, and fistulas. Common synonyms include regional ileitis and granulomatous enteritis. While the exact cause is unknown, genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. It is associated with a strong familial predisposition and may involve complications such as malnutrition and increased risk of colorectal cancer.

code_desc: Crohn disease of upper gastrointestinal tract
summary: Crohn disease of the upper gastrointestinal tract is a chronic inflammatory condition that can affect the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum. It is characterized by transmural inflammation, leading to ulcers, strictures, and fibrosis. Common synonyms include Crohn's disease of the upper GI tract and Crohn's gastroduodenitis. The exact cause is unknown, but genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. It is part of the inflammatory bowel disease spectrum and often occurs alongside colonic involvement. The disease can present with symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss.

Crohn disease of the small intestine is a chronic inflammatory condition characterized by transmural inflammation that can affect any segment of the gastrointestinal tract, though the ileum is most commonly involved. It is classified as an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and is often associated with granulomas. Common synonyms include regional ileitis and terminal ileitis. The exact cause is unknown, but genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. The small intestine, particularly the ileum, is the primary site of involvement, with complications such as strictures, fistulas, and abscesses frequently occurring.

Crohn disease of the appendix refers to a segment of the appendix affected by Crohn disease, an inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural inflammation and granuloma formation. It is a rare manifestation of Crohn disease, often presenting with appendiceal perforation or abscess. Common synonyms include appendiceal Crohn disease or Crohn's appendicitis. The condition is associated with genetic predisposition, immune dysregulation, and environmental factors. It typically affects the terminal ileum and appendix, with possible involvement of other gastrointestinal segments.

Crohn disease of the large intestine, also known as regional enteritis or granulomatous colitis, is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the gastrointestinal tract. It is characterized by transmural inflammation, leading to strictures, fistulas, and ulcers. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. It commonly affects the terminal ileum and colon, with involvement of the rectum being less frequent. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. Complications may involve abscesses, malnutrition, and increased cancer risk.

Crohn disease of the anal region is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the anorectal area, characterized by transmural inflammation and granuloma formation. Common synonyms include anal Crohn disease and perianal Crohn disease. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. It typically involves the terminal ileum and colon but can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract. Perianal manifestations such as fistulas, abscesses, and fissures are common. The disease can lead to significant morbidity due to pain, drainage, and complications from strictures or malignancy.

code_desc: Crohn disease of both small and large intestine
summary: Crohn disease of both small and large intestine is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the gastrointestinal tract, characterized by transmural inflammation and granuloma formation. Common synonyms include regional enteritis and granulomatous colitis. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. It typically involves the terminal ileum and colon, with possible involvement of other segments. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. Complications may involve strictures, fistulas, and malabsorption.

Crohn disease of anastomotic sites refers to inflammatory bowel disease that occurs at surgically created intestinal connections, commonly following resection for ulcerative colitis or other inflammatory conditions. It is characterized by transmural inflammation, stricturing, and fistula formation. Common synonyms include anastomotic Crohn disease and postoperative Crohn disease. While the exact causative agents are not fully understood, genetic predisposition, immune dysregulation, and environmental factors play roles. The small intestine and ileocolic junction are most frequently affected, often leading to complications requiring further surgery.

code_desc: Crohn disease of other specified site
summary: Crohn disease of other specified site refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract occurring in locations not typically classified as ileocolic, jejunoileal, or gastroduodenal. It encompasses areas such as the upper gastrointestinal tract, perianal region, or other uncommon sites. Common synonyms include Crohn’s disease of unspecified site or Crohn’s enteritis of other sites. The exact causative agents are unknown, though genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. The disease typically affects the small intestine and colon, but can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract, leading to symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss.

Crohn disease, unspecified site, is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. It can affect any portion from the mouth to the anus, though commonly involves the terminal ileum and colon. Common synonyms include Crohn's disease and regional ileitis. The exact cause is unknown, but genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. It is associated with complications such as strictures, fistulas, and abscesses. The disease presents with symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue.

Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by diffuse, continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa. Common synonyms include ulcerative colitis and pancolitis. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic, immunological, and environmental factors are implicated. It primarily affects the large intestine, with involvement typically starting in the rectum and extending proximally. The condition is associated with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. It is distinct from Crohn’s disease, as it does not affect the small intestine and does not exhibit skip lesions.

Ulcerative pancolitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous inflammation and ulcers affecting the entire colon. It is a type of ulcerative colitis, with "pancolitis" indicating involvement of the entire large intestine. Common synonyms include pancolonic ulcerative colitis and total colitis. The exact cause is unknown, but genetic, immunological, and environmental factors are implicated. The primary affected body part is the colon, with involvement of the mucosa and submucosa, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding.

Left sided ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation limited to the left half of the colon, including the rectum. Common synonyms include left colitis and distal ulcerative colitis. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic, immunological, and environmental factors are implicated. The primary affected areas are the sigmoid colon and rectum, with possible extension to the descending colon. Symptoms typically include diarrhea, rectal bleeding, abdominal pain, and urgency. Complications may involve strictures, fistulas, and an increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Ulcerative rectosigmoiditis is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the rectum and sigmoid colon, characterized by diffuse ulceration and mucosal inflammation. It is a form of ulcerative colitis, primarily involving the distal colon. Common synonyms include left-sided colitis and ulcerative proctitis. The exact cause is unknown, but genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. It typically presents with diarrhea, rectal bleeding, and abdominal pain, predominantly affecting the rectum and sigmoid colon.

Ulcerative proctitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the rectum, characterized by ulceration and mucosal inflammation. It is a form of ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum. Common synonyms include proctitis and rectal ulceration. The primary causative agent is *Clostridioides difficile*, though other pathogens like *Shigella* or *Salmonella* may also be involved. It typically presents with symptoms such as rectal pain, bleeding, and urgency. The condition primarily affects the rectal mucosa, with involvement extending proximally in some cases. It is more common in immunocompromised individuals and those with prior antibiotic use.

Other specified ulcerative colitis refers to ulcerative colitis that does not meet the criteria for more specific subtypes, such as ulcerative colitis with primary sclerosing cholangitis or pancolitis. It is characterized by chronic inflammation and ulceration of the colon mucosa. Common synonyms include unspecified ulcerative colitis. The exact causative agents are unknown, but genetic and environmental factors are implicated. The condition typically affects the colon, with inflammation often beginning in the rectum and extending proximally. Symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding.

Ulcerative colitis, unspecified, is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by diffuse, continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colon and rectum. It is marked by symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. The exact cause is unknown, though genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. Common synonyms include ulcerative colitis, unspecified, and unspecified ulcerative colitis. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, with involvement typically starting in the rectum and extending proximally. No single causative agent is identified, but dysbiosis and immune dysregulation are thought to play key roles.

Indeterminate colitis refers to chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by inflammation of the colon without clear differentiation between ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Common synonyms include unclassified colitis and inflammatory bowel disease, unclassified. The exact causative agents are unknown, though genetic, immunological, and environmental factors are implicated. It typically affects the colon, with variable involvement of the terminal ileum. Symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. Diagnosis relies on endoscopic, histological, and imaging findings when clinical features do not fit established categories.

Other specified inflammatory bowel diseases (OSIBD) refer to chronic inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract that do not meet the full criteria for ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. Common synonyms include indeterminate colitis and unclassified inflammatory bowel disease. The exact causative agents are unknown, but genetic, immunological, and environmental factors are implicated. These conditions typically affect the colon and terminal ileum, with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. Diagnosis is based on clinical, endoscopic, and histological findings when definitive classification is not possible.

Inflammatory bowel diseases, unspecified, refer to chronic inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract characterized by recurring episodes of inflammation. Common synonyms include irritable bowel syndrome and unspecified colitis. While specific causes are not well defined, genetic, immune, and environmental factors are implicated. The primary affected areas are the colon and small intestine, though the exact location and extent can vary. Symptoms often include diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss. The condition is typically diagnosed when specific subtypes such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis cannot be definitively established.

Functional oesophageal or gastroduodenal disorders refer to gastrointestinal conditions characterized by symptoms such as dysphagia, heartburn, and epigastric pain, without identifiable structural or biochemical abnormalities. Common synonyms include functional dyspepsia and non-ulcer dyspepsia. These disorders are often linked to altered gastrointestinal motility, visceral hypersensitivity, or psychosocial factors. Causative agents are not well-defined, but may involve stress, dietary habits, and altered gut-brain interactions. The primary affected areas are the oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum.

Globus is a sensation of a lump in the throat without obstruction, often described as a foreign body feeling. It is commonly associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and can be exacerbated by anxiety or stress. Other synonyms include globus pharyngeus and epiglottic syndrome. The condition typically affects the pharynx and esophagus, with symptoms persisting despite normal endoscopic findings. Causative agents may include acid reflux, muscle spasms, or psychogenic factors. It is more prevalent in middle-aged adults and can significantly impact quality of life.

Functional swallowing disorder, also known as dysphagia of unknown organic cause, refers to difficulty swallowing without identifiable structural or neurological abnormalities. Common synonyms include oropharyngeal dysphagia and non-organic dysphagia. It is often caused by psychological factors such as anxiety or depression, or by chronic conditions like gastroesophageal reflux disease. The disorder primarily affects the oropharynx and esophagus, leading to symptoms such as choking, coughing, and food retention. Diagnosis typically involves a thorough clinical evaluation and exclusion of other organic causes.

Functional heartburn is a chronic, non-cardiac condition characterized by persistent upper abdominal burning sensations, often mistaken for cardiac issues. Common synonyms include non-cardiac chest pain and gastroesophageal reflux-like symptoms. It is typically caused by abnormal esophageal sensitivity rather than acid reflux. The primary affected area is the lower chest and upper abdomen. Unlike typical heartburn, it lacks evidence of gastroesophageal reflux disease. Risk factors include stress, anxiety, and certain dietary triggers. It is more common in women and often responds to proton pump inhibitors or antacids.

Functional dyspepsia is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder characterized by persistent or recurrent upper abdominal pain or discomfort without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include dyspepsia and non-ulcer dyspepsia. It is often associated with symptoms such as bloating, early satiety, and epigastric burning. While no specific causative agent is identified, factors like gastric motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, and Helicobacter pylori infection may contribute. The condition primarily affects the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract, with symptoms typically localized to the epigastric region.

Functional nausea or vomiting refers to persistent or recurrent nausea and vomiting without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include psychogenic vomiting and neurogenic nausea. It is often associated with gastrointestinal motility disorders or central nervous system dysfunction. Known causative agents may include stress, anxiety, depression, and certain medications. Typically, the upper gastrointestinal tract is affected, with symptoms originating from the stomach or duodenum. The condition is more common in adolescents and young adults, and may be linked to functional gastrointestinal disorders such as irritable bowel syndrome.

Functional belching disorders refer to recurrent, unexplained belching not attributable to organic disease. Common synonyms include aerophagia and excessive belching. These conditions are often linked to gastrointestinal motility issues, anxiety, or dietary habits. The primary affected area is the upper gastrointestinal tract, particularly the stomach and esophagus. Causative agents may include swallowing air, gastroesophageal reflux, or stress. Symptoms typically involve frequent belching without associated pain or structural abnormalities. Diagnosis relies on exclusion of other pathologies. Management focuses on lifestyle modifications and addressing underlying psychological factors.

Adult rumination syndrome is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by the passive regurgitation of undigested food into the mouth without chewing. It often occurs shortly after eating and is associated with a feeling of fullness and discomfort. Common synonyms include cyclic vomiting syndrome and pseudo-vomiting. The exact cause is unknown, but it may be triggered by psychological factors, stress, or gastroesophageal reflux disease. The primary affected body parts are the esophagus, stomach, and mouth. It predominantly affects adults, particularly women, and is often misdiagnosed as a psychiatric or gastrointestinal disorder.

code_desc: Other specified functional oesophageal or gastroduodenal disorders
summary: Other specified functional oesophageal or gastroduodenal disorders refer to gastrointestinal symptoms that do not meet the full criteria for established functional disorders like GERD or dyspepsia. Common synonyms include functional dyspepsia and non-cardiac chest pain. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving psychosocial factors, motility disturbances, and visceral hypersensitivity. These disorders primarily affect the oesophagus and gastroduodenal regions, causing symptoms such as dysphagia, epigastric pain, and bloating. They are typically diagnosed after excluding structural or organic causes through endoscopy and imaging.

code_desc: Functional oesophageal or gastroduodenal disorders, unspecified
summary: Functional oesophageal or gastroduodenal disorders, unspecified, refer to chronic gastrointestinal symptoms without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common symptoms include dysphagia, heartburn, and epigastric pain. Synonyms include functional dyspepsia and non-ulcer dyspepsia. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving motility abnormalities, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial factors. These disorders primarily affect the oesophagus and gastroduodenum, with no specific organ involvement. Diagnosis is typically made after ruling out organic diseases through endoscopy and imaging.

code_desc: Irritable bowel syndrome or certain specified functional bowel disorders
summary: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a functional gastrointestinal disorder, is characterized by chronic or recurrent abdominal pain and altered bowel habits, including diarrhea, constipation, or both. Common synonyms include functional bowel disorder and spastic colon. While no specific causative agent is identified, factors such as gut microbiota imbalance, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial stress may contribute. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, with symptoms often exacerbated by dietary factors and emotional stress. It predominantly impacts the colon, leading to discomfort and changes in bowel movements.

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), also known as spastic colon or mucous colitis, is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. Common symptoms include diarrhea, constipation, or alternating patterns, often associated with bloating and gas. The exact cause is unknown, though factors such as gut motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial stress are implicated. IBS primarily affects the large intestine, with no structural abnormalities present. It commonly occurs in young to middle-aged adults and is more prevalent in women.

Irritable bowel syndrome with constipation predominance (IBS-C) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic constipation, abdominal pain, and altered bowel habits. Common synonyms include constipation-predominant IBS and IBS-C. The exact cause is unknown, but factors such as gut motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, and altered gut microbiota are implicated. It primarily affects the large intestine, leading to symptoms like bloating, straining during defecation, and infrequent stools. The condition typically impacts the colon and is more common in women. No specific causative agents are identified, though dietary, psychological, and hormonal factors may contribute.

Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea predominance (IBS-D) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by recurrent abdominal pain and altered bowel habits, primarily diarrhoea. Common synonyms include diarrhoea-predominant IBS and IBS with diarrhoea. The exact cause is unknown, though factors like gut microbiota imbalance, visceral hypersensitivity, and immune system activation may contribute. It primarily affects the large intestine, leading to symptoms such as bloating, urgency, and stool frequency. The condition typically impacts the colon and is more common in women. No structural or biochemical abnormalities are present.

Irritable bowel syndrome, mixed type (IBS-M) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by alternating episodes of diarrhea and constipation. Common synonyms include spastic colon and irritable colon. The exact cause is unknown, but factors such as gut motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, and gut microbiota alterations are implicated. It typically affects the large intestine, causing symptoms like abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits. The condition is more prevalent in women and often begins in early adulthood. No structural or biochemical abnormalities are present, and management focuses on symptom relief through dietary changes, medications, and lifestyle modifications.

Irritable bowel syndrome, unsubtyped (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic or recurrent abdominal pain and altered bowel habits without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common synonyms include spastic colon and irritable colon. Causative agents are not well defined, but may involve gut-brain axis dysfunction, visceral hypersensitivity, and gut microbiota imbalance. Typically affects the large intestine, with symptoms such as diarrhea, constipation, or a mix of both. It predominantly impacts the small and large intestines, with variable involvement depending on subtype.

Irritable bowel syndrome, type unspecified (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic or recurrent abdominal pain and altered bowel habits, such as diarrhea, constipation, or a mix of both. Common synonyms include spastic colon and irritable colon. While no specific causative agent is identified, factors like gut microbiota imbalance, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial stress may contribute. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, with symptoms often involving the abdomen, rectum, and lower gastrointestinal tract. It typically occurs in adults, with a higher prevalence in women.

Functional constipation is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder characterized by difficulty in passing stools, infrequent bowel movements, and hard or lumpy stools without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common synonyms include slow transit constipation and outlet obstruction constipation. It is often associated with altered colonic motility, pelvic floor dysfunction, or dietary factors. Common causative agents may include low fiber intake, dehydration, lack of physical activity, and psychological stress. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, particularly the colon, and can lead to symptoms such as bloating, straining, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation.

Functional diarrhoea is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder characterized by frequent, loose or watery stools without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea-predominant subtype and functional diarrhoea. It is often associated with altered gut motility and visceral hypersensitivity. Known causative agents may include stress, dietary factors, infections, or medications. The primary affected body part is the large intestine, with symptoms typically involving the colon. The condition predominantly affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the colon, and is more common in young to middle-aged adults.

Functional bloating is a common gastrointestinal complaint characterized by a sensation of abdominal distension without an identifiable organic cause. It often presents with discomfort, fullness, and visible abdominal swelling. Common synonyms include aerophagia, dyspepsia, and meteorism. Causative factors may include dietary habits, stress, irritable bowel syndrome, or altered gut motility. Typically affects the abdomen, with symptoms often worsening after meals. No structural abnormalities are detected on imaging or endoscopy.

Functional abdominal pain syndrome (FAPS) is a chronic condition characterized by recurrent abdominal pain without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include functional abdominal pain and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), though IBS is distinct. The exact cause is unknown, but factors such as gastrointestinal motility disturbances, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial stress may contribute. The abdomen is the primary affected area, with pain often localized to the lower quadrants. Symptoms may be associated with bloating, altered bowel habits, and fatigue. Diagnosis is based on Rome IV criteria, emphasizing the absence of structural abnormalities.

code_desc: Other specified irritable bowel syndrome or functional bowel disorders
summary: Other specified irritable bowel syndrome or functional bowel disorders refer to gastrointestinal conditions with symptoms like abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits, but without identifiable structural or biochemical causes. Common synonyms include functional dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome not otherwise specified. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving gut-brain axis dysfunction, altered gut motility, and psychosocial factors. These disorders typically affect the small intestine and colon, with symptoms localized to the abdomen. They are more prevalent in adults, particularly females, and may be associated with stress or anxiety.

code_desc: Irritable bowel syndrome or functional bowel disorders, unspecified
summary: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), or functional bowel disorders, is a chronic gastrointestinal condition characterized by abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits without identifiable structural or biochemical abnormalities. Common synonyms include functional colopathy and spastic colon. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving gut-brain axis dysfunction, altered gut motility, and psychosocial factors. The condition primarily affects the large intestine, with symptoms such as diarrhea, constipation, or alternating patterns. It predominantly impacts the colon and is more common in women.

Functional anorectal disorders refer to a group of conditions characterized by anorectal symptoms without identifiable structural or organic causes. Common synonyms include anorectal dysfunction and functional anorectal disorders. These conditions often involve symptoms such as fecal incontinence, constipation, rectal pain, and anal discomfort. Known causative agents may include pelvic floor dyssynergia, altered bowel habits, and psychosocial factors. They typically affect the anorectal region, rectum, and pelvic floor muscles, with a higher prevalence in females and individuals with a history of pelvic surgery or childbirth.

Functional faecal incontinence refers to the involuntary loss of stool without an underlying structural or organic bowel disease. It is often caused by factors such as altered bowel habits, pelvic floor dysfunction, or impaired sphincter control. Common synonyms include fecal incontinence without anatomic abnormalities and non-organic fecal incontinence. Causative agents may include constipation, diarrhea, neurological conditions, or medications. The condition primarily affects the rectum and anal sphincter, leading to leakage of stool. It is commonly seen in elderly individuals and those with cognitive impairments.

Functional anorectal pain is a chronic condition characterized by recurrent anal or rectal pain without an identifiable organic cause. Common synonyms include anal fissure-like pain, proctalgia fugax, and levator ani syndrome. It is often associated with pelvic floor dysfunction, spasm, or nerve irritation. Known causative agents may include constipation, straining during defecation, or psychosocial factors. The condition typically affects the anal canal, rectum, and surrounding pelvic floor muscles, causing intermittent or persistent discomfort. It is more common in adults and may be linked to stress or lifestyle factors.

Functional defaecation disorders refer to a group of conditions characterized by chronic constipation or altered bowel habits without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common synonyms include functional constipation and chronic idiopathic constipation. These disorders are often associated with altered bowel motility, pelvic floor dysfunction, or visceral hypersensitivity. Known causative agents may include dietary factors, psychosocial stress, and altered gut-brain interaction. The primary affected body parts are the colon and pelvic floor muscles, with symptoms such as straining, incomplete evacuation, and infrequent bowel movements.

Other specified functional anorectal disorders refer to chronic or recurrent anorectal symptoms not attributable to a specific organic cause. Common symptoms include rectal pain, discomfort, and altered bowel habits. Synonyms include functional anorectal pain and unspecified anorectal dysfunction. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving pelvic floor dysfunction, psychosocial factors, and neurogenic influences. These disorders predominantly affect the rectum and anal canal, with symptoms often persisting despite normal anatomical and biochemical findings.

Functional anorectal disorders, unspecified refer to chronic or recurrent symptoms affecting the anorectal region without a specific identifiable structural or organic cause. Common symptoms include rectal pain, urgency, fecal incontinence, and altered bowel habits. Synonyms include functional anorectal pain and pelvic floor dysfunction. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving pelvic floor muscle dysfunction, neurogenic factors, and psychosocial elements. These disorders typically affect the rectum, anus, and surrounding pelvic structures. Diagnosis is made after excluding other organic conditions through appropriate evaluation.

code_desc: Functional digestive disorders of infants, toddlers or children
summary: Functional digestive disorders in infants, toddlers, and children refer to gastrointestinal symptoms without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits. Synonyms include functional abdominal pain syndrome and irritable bowel syndrome in children. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving gut-brain interaction, dietary factors, and psychosocial stress. These disorders primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract, with involvement of the stomach, intestines, and associated organs. They are more common in children with a family history of similar conditions or gastrointestinal sensitivity.

Infant regurgitation refers to the passive flow of stomach contents back into the esophagus, commonly observed in healthy infants. It is often referred to as spitting up or vomiting in babies. The primary cause is the immature lower esophageal sphincter, which allows gastric contents to reflux. Other factors include overfeeding, swallowing air, or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Typically affecting the esophagus and stomach, it may also involve the larynx or airway in severe cases. While usually benign, persistent or forceful regurgitation may indicate an underlying condition requiring medical evaluation.

Infantile colic is a common condition characterized by prolonged, unexplained crying in otherwise healthy infants, typically occurring in the late afternoon or evening. Common synonyms include "colic" and "infantile colic." The exact cause is unknown, though it is believed to involve gastrointestinal discomfort, immature nervous system development, or sensitivity to environmental factors. It primarily affects the abdomen, with symptoms including bloating, irritability, and leg pulling. The condition usually resolves by 3 to 4 months of age.

Infant dyschezia refers to the difficulty infants have in coordinating the muscles required for defecation, leading to prolonged straining and incomplete evacuation. Common synonyms include infantile constipation and fecal incontinence. It is often caused by delayed neuromuscular development, insufficient fiber intake, or inadequate fluid consumption. The condition primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, particularly the rectum and anal sphincter. It is most commonly observed in infants between 4 and 12 months of age. Early intervention with dietary adjustments and bowel training can improve outcomes.

code_desc: Other functional digestive disorders of infants, neonates or toddlers
summary: Other functional digestive disorders in infants, neonates, and toddlers refer to gastrointestinal symptoms without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common symptoms include vomiting, abdominal pain, and feeding difficulties. Synonyms include functional gastrointestinal disorders and non-specific digestive disturbances. Causative agents are often unknown, though stress, dietary factors, and gut-brain interactions may play a role. These conditions primarily affect the stomach, intestines, and esophagus, with symptoms typically resolving as the child matures.

code_desc: Functional digestive disorders of infants, toddlers or children, unspecified
summary: Functional digestive disorders in infants, toddlers, or children refer to gastrointestinal symptoms without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits. Synonyms include functional abdominal pain and irritable bowel syndrome in children. Causative agents are often multifactorial, involving gut-brain interaction, dietary factors, and psychosocial elements. These disorders primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract, with symptoms commonly localized to the abdomen. They are more prevalent in children with a history of stress or anxiety.

Functional gallbladder disorder refers to a group of conditions characterized by gallbladder dysfunction without evidence of structural abnormalities. Common synonyms include biliary dyskinesia and gallbladder motility disorder. The condition is often associated with impaired gallbladder emptying, leading to symptoms such as right upper quadrant pain, bloating, and nausea. Known causative agents include obesity, rapid weight loss, diabetes, and hormonal imbalances. It typically affects the gallbladder and may involve the biliary tract, with symptoms often triggered by fatty meals. Diagnosis is usually made after ruling out gallstones and other structural diseases.

Functional sphincter of Oddi disorder is a condition characterized by abnormal function of the sphincter of Oddi, leading to recurrent biliary pain without an identifiable structural cause. Common synonyms include biliary dyskinesia and functional biliary obstruction. The disorder is often associated with impaired relaxation of the sphincter, resulting in elevated bile pressure. Known causative agents may include gallstones, chronic cholecystitis, or prior biliary surgery. It typically affects the bile ducts and gallbladder, causing right upper quadrant pain, often after meals. Diagnosis is usually made after ruling out other biliary pathologies.

Other specified functional gastrointestinal disorders refer to gastrointestinal symptoms that cannot be fully explained by structural or biochemical abnormalities. Common synonyms include functional dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome. These conditions are often associated with altered gut motility, visceral hypersensitivity, and psychosocial factors. Known causative agents include stress, dietary factors, and infections. Typically affected body parts include the stomach, small intestine, and colon. Symptoms may involve bloating, pain, and altered bowel habits. Diagnosis is based on Rome criteria and exclusion of other organic diseases.

Functional gastrointestinal disorders, unspecified, refer to chronic or recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms without an identifiable structural or biochemical cause. Common symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, altered bowel habits, and early satiety. These conditions are often diagnosed by exclusion. Synonyms include functional bowel disorders and irritable bowel syndrome (when applicable). Causative agents are typically multifactorial, involving gut-brain axis dysfunction, motility abnormalities, and psychosocial factors. Commonly affected areas include the stomach, small intestine, and colon.

Vomiting following gastrointestinal surgery is a common postoperative complication characterized by forceful expulsion of stomach contents. It may occur due to anesthesia, surgical manipulation, or delayed gastric emptying. Common synonyms include postoperative emesis and surgical vomiting. Causative agents include anesthetic agents, opioid use, and postoperative ileus. Typically affecting the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract, it may also involve the intestines. The condition is often transient but can lead to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances if prolonged.

Dumping syndrome is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by rapid gastric emptying following meals, leading to symptoms such as abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and hypoglycemia. It commonly occurs after gastric surgery, particularly vagotomy or gastrectomy. Synonyms include early and late dumping syndrome. Causative agents include surgical procedures that disrupt normal gastric motility. The primary affected body parts are the stomach and small intestine, with systemic effects including the cardiovascular and endocrine systems.

code_desc: Malfunction or complication of external stoma of digestive organs
summary: Malfunction or complication of an external stoma of digestive organs refers to issues arising from a surgically created opening on the abdominal wall for waste diversion. Common synonyms include stoma dysfunction, stoma complications, or stoma-related issues. Causative agents may include infection, ischemia, mechanical obstruction, or adhesions. Typically affected body parts include the small intestine, colon, or rectum. Complications may manifest as stenosis, prolapse, parastomal hernia, or fistula formation, often leading to symptoms like pain, leakage, or obstruction.

code_desc: Colostomy or enterostomy malfunction or complication
summary: Colostomy or enterostomy malfunction or complication refers to functional or structural issues following surgical creation of a colostomy or enterostomy. Common synonyms include stoma dysfunction, stoma leakage, or stoma obstruction. Causative agents may include infection, adhesions, ischemia, or mechanical trauma. Typically affected body parts include the stoma site, surrounding skin, and adjacent bowel segments. Complications may involve infection, prolapse, stricture, or output abnormalities. Proper stoma care and timely medical intervention are essential for management.

Gastrostomy malfunction refers to the failure of a gastrostomy tube to function properly, often resulting in leakage, blockage, or infection. Common synonyms include gastrostomy tube dysfunction or gastric tube failure. Causative agents may include tube clogging from mucus or food, infection, or improper placement. Typically affected body parts include the stomach and surrounding tissues, with potential complications involving the abdominal wall or adjacent organs. It may also lead to peritonitis or fistula formation if left untreated.

Postsurgical malabsorption, not elsewhere classified, refers to impaired nutrient absorption following gastrointestinal surgery, typically due to altered anatomy or function. Common synonyms include postoperative malabsorption syndrome and post-bariatric malabsorption. Causative agents may include surgical procedures such as gastric bypass, biliopancreatic diversion, or small bowel resection. This condition primarily affects the proximal small intestine, leading to deficiencies in fat, vitamins, and minerals. Symptoms include weight loss, steatorrhea, and nutritional deficiencies. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, laboratory findings, and imaging. Management involves dietary modification, supplementation, and monitoring.

code_desc: Other specified diseases of the digestive system
summary: "Other specified diseases of the digestive system" refers to conditions not classified under more specific categories, such as inflammatory bowel disease or cancer. Common synonyms include unspecified digestive disorders. Causative agents may include infections, autoimmune factors, or unknown etiologies. These conditions typically affect the gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, and pancreas. Symptoms may involve pain, inflammation, malabsorption, or altered bowel habits. Diagnosis often requires endoscopy, imaging, or laboratory tests. Treatment varies based on underlying cause and clinical presentation.

code_desc: Diseases of the digestive system, unspecified
summary: Diseases of the digestive system, unspecified refer to conditions affecting the gastrointestinal tract without a specific diagnosis. Common synonyms include unspecified gastrointestinal disorders. Causative agents may vary and can include infections, inflammatory processes, or structural abnormalities. These conditions typically affect the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation. Diagnosis often requires further investigation such as endoscopy or imaging.
